Fascicle One Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
To begin with, the ultimate principle is concentrated and pure, transcending the realm of words and forms. The wondrous Way is profound and subtle, far beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
The *tāpa* flower radiates its colors; the sun of wisdom flows with its light. The script upon palm leaves rises like soaring patterns, scattering its brilliance amidst auspicious winds.

The spiritual source is vast and deep, where one seeks the mystery by pointing at the moon. The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is empty and void, wherein one relies upon the trap and the snare [to catch the fish and the hare].

Reaching far, the true path of Vulture Peak proclaims compassion according to the inclinations and desires of beings; the ritual statutes of the Elephant Fan accord the transmission of the Dharma to their capacities and conditions.
Beginning at the Deer Park, it opened the subtle words of the Four Noble Truths; ending at the Śāla Grove, it expounded the secret treasury of the Three *I*s.
The *Vinaya* marks the beginning of disciplined conduct, while the *Nirvāṇa* distinguishes the school of permanence and bliss. Thus, it guides the seven...

Turning the Wheel of Dharma amidst the multitude, he cut off the four torrents and proclaimed the categories of precepts. Thus, the Five Sections were established as enduring models and the Seven Groups were divided into schools.
He bestowed blessings and protection upon the four modes of birth and widely propagated his exalted legacy for ten thousand years, raising his wondrous feet toward the pure heavens.
Is it not by the power of *śīla* that one overcomes the perilous path?

Since the transformation of the body concealed the Twin Śāla trees and the light was shrouded by the thousand-fold folds [of the robe], although the spirit was concentrated within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the sublime intent remains capable of exposition.

Therefore, Mahākāśyapa secured the dark thread of the profound mystery, and Upagupta maintained its flourishing lineage. The flavor of the Way remained pure and singular, and people held no divergent views. Until...

Within the source of dreams there was turbidity; by the waters of the teachings, there was clarity. The branches divided into the seven leaves of the *saṃghāṭī*, and the flowers scattered into the sections of the five masters.
Thus, the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṃghikas first divided at the site of the council; later, after a hundred years, the five schools and eighteen sects emerged as the lineage flowed on.
From that time forth, like myriad peaks rising together, each vied to lead the way: the divergent paths of Dharmottara and Dharmatrāta.
The differing tenets of the Western Mountains and the Northern Mountains are like golden branches splitting apart or jade ridges dividing into peaks;

though their relative weight may differ, there is no separation in the protocols for upholding or transgressing the precepts. This is because their emotional perceptions are limited and their realization lacks uniformity, such that each champions its own school and labels its own teachings as supreme.

Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka* (Tánwúshèngzàng) is as lofty as the sun and moon shining brightly, while the [Sarvāstivāda]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the extant portion.)

He established the foundational tenets; like the waves of the vast ocean, they were difficult to fathom. Consequently, he was able to return to the Middle Kingdom, where the waters of the Dharma flowed eastward.

The golden countenance [of the Buddha] acted according to the opportune moment, and the transformation was proclaimed at the Jade Gate. Heresy was overturned and faith was established; the True Path became ever more renewed.

The White Horse Temple was first constructed in Luoyang, and the Red Bird (the Sun) rose anew in Jiangzuo. Dharmatrāta initiated the path, beginning the exposition of the Vinaya; thus the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*...

The original [Vinaya] had already been transmitted, yet the school of the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya) remained obscure. Then there was Buddhayaśas—whose name means "Awakened Brilliance" in the language of Qin—who finally propagated the school of the Four-Part Vinaya.
Thus, these texts flourished here in the Eastern Land. What is now called the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is the title that clarifies its essential doctrine;
it is indeed the teaching received and transmitted by our former master, Faxiang. The term "Four Parts" (*caturvarga*) is a specific designation for one of the five schools.

The Vinaya is a specific name for one of the Three Piṭakas. It is designated by its numerical category, hence it is called "Four-Part" (*Caturvarga*). It is termed "Vinaya" based on its dharma-content.

Because its phrasing has been pared down and abridged, it is called "Eliminating the Redundant" (*Śaṅfan*). Because it meticulously collects the original texts, it is named "Supplementing the Omissions" (*Bùquē*).

Because it addresses practical duties while upholding the core principles, it is referred to as "Ritual Procedures" (*Xíngshì*). Because it resolves and selects essential meanings, it is further titled "Commentary" (*Chão*). As for "Preface" (*Xù*), it means "origin" or "source," manifesting—

The "Preface" (xu) refers to the initial point from which the essential tenets (zong) are originated; thus it is called a preface. Furthermore, it is said that it sets forth the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching and the gradual commencement of its practice;
hence it is termed a "preface. Therefore, it is titled *The Preface to the Channfan Bubue Xingshi Chao of the Four-Part Vinaya*.

In explaining the text of the *Śāstra-ṭīkā*, I shall briefly open six sections: first, the causes for the arising of the teaching; second, the reasons for its compilation; third, the period of its sectarian division;
fourth, the differing eras of the translation of the Vinaya root text; fifth, the distinct interpretations of the school’s tenets along with an analysis of the title;
and sixth, the critical judgment and explanation of the text.

Regarding the causes for the initial establishment of the teachings, this section is divided into three parts: first, a general clarification of the intent behind establishing the precepts; second, a clarification of the intent behind establishing extensive rules to supplement those that were brief;

and third, a clarification of the intent behind the benefits of establishing extensive rules. Now, regarding the first section, the general clarification of the intent behind establishing the precepts:

this was when the Great Sage descended, first opening the foundation of transformation. Desiring to rescue and deliver all beings from existence so they might together ascend to the other shore, he...

Afflictions are difficult to purify, and there is no means by which the Way can be attained. Therefore, the Great Sage established the practice of the Three Learnings to gather and deliver all sentient beings.
Among these, he first instituted the training in the precepts (*śīla*). The precepts are the foundation of all virtues and the life-force of the Buddha-dharma. Thus, a sutra says:
Relying upon and depending on this precept, one attains the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
If this precept were absent, none of the various wholesome merits could arise. Therefore, those training in the Three Vehicles must necessarily follow this path; thus, the Vinaya says:
The training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) was established in order to subdue the three poisons and bring them to an end. Furthermore, the *Prātimokṣa* states:
"With pure morality and wisdom, one attains the foremost path. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also says: "The precepts were established to open the gate to Nirvāṇa.
Moreover, the Vinaya possesses four meanings not found in other sūtras: first, morality is the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues arise.

First, it is long-lasting. Second, all disciples of the Buddha rely upon the precepts for their abiding; all sentient beings exist by virtue of the precepts. Third, they are the initial gateway to Nirvana.
Fourth, they are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, capable of adorning the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the second point, clarifying the intention behind establishing extensive rules to supplement what was brief: when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, for twelve years he spoke only a single verse: "Commit no evil..."
"Act; practice all that is wholesome; purify your own minds—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. Thus, the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* states:
"For twelve years, he preached this *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* to the community of monks who were free from worldly affairs; from that time onward, it was explained in detail and with full analysis.
This is precisely its meaning. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* states: "After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he traveled together with the bhikṣus through the country of Surāṣṭra."
Gradually traveling on, he arrived at Vairaṇyā and accepted an invitation from a brahmin to observe the rains retreat for one summer, subsisting solely on horse fodder.
At that time, Śāriputra, while in a secluded place, had this thought:
"Among the teachings of the six past Buddhas, which ones endured for a long time, and which did not? He immediately questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Vipaśyin, Śikhin..."
The Dharmas of the four Buddhas—Kakutsunda, [Kanakamuni], Kāśyapa, and [Śākyamuni]—remain for a long time; the Dharmas of the other two Buddhas do not remain for long. Why is this?
It is because these two World-Honored Ones taught only the abbreviated teachings and did not teach the extensive teachings;
therefore, their Dharmas do not remain for long. As for the other four Buddhas, because they established extensive teachings for their disciples, their Dharmas remain for a long time. Śāriputra.

Because of Ānanda’s request, [the assembly] wished that, like the four Buddhas, he might establish a broad code of discipline for the benefit of the Dharma and cause it to endure for a long time. The Buddha said, "Cease for now;
I myself know the proper time. This was because my disciples had not yet attained renown, had not yet received offerings, and had not yet given rise to outflows (*āsrava*);
therefore, the precepts had not yet been established. Twelve years later, due to the initial transgression of Sudinna, [the rules were set forth].

[The preceding portion] is abbreviated; [I shall now] compose a broad exposition to supplement it. Regarding the benefits of composing this broad exposition, let us first rely upon the scriptural texts (*vinaya*).
For every single precept established by the Buddha, ten merits and benefits are said to arise.

First, "gathering the Saṃgha" means that when those of lower rank maintain the precepts, they become members of the Dharma-conforming assembly and are thus included within the community. Second, "causing the Saṃgha to rejoice" means that if those of middle rank maintain...
1. Precepts: Whatever one undertakes, it brings joy to the hearts of the multitude. 2. Third, causing the Sangha to dwell in peace and happiness:

This means that if an elder (sthavira) upholds the precepts, he adorns the assembly of monks and is able to provide shelter and benefit to his followers. 3. Fourth, causing those who have not yet had faith to believe:

This means that when the virtue of the precepts is fulfilled within, it produces goodness in others externally; it inspires faith and reverence in people, making one fit to serve as a teacher and model, upon whom others rely for their deliverance.

World-Honored One, for this reason, those who have not yet left the household life will believe in and delight in leaving it, and having followed him in his renunciation, their faith—which they already possess—will be further increased.
Having received disciples as followers, he is further able to instruct them, causing them to maintain and advance in their mental conduct.

Sixth, he causes those who are difficult to tame and harmonize to become tamed and harmonized; that is to say, among his assembly, there may be those who violate the teachings, transgress the prohibitions, or do not comply with his majestic authority.

[The term] "rites" (儀) refers to being able to thus administer punishment and subdue [the offender] so that they may reform. Regarding the seventh, "those who possess shame and remorse attain peace and happiness":

this means that if among the assembly there is a person with the aspiration for the Way who, having lost their composure, commits an offense, they constantly harbor shame and fear, reforming the past and cultivating the future, seeking to wash away their transgressions;
such a person can further rescue others and serve as a place of refuge. Eighth, "severing present existence."
9. Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*): having already eliminated arisen evils, one's body and mind are pure; thus, one should now observe the *poṣadha*, practicing without any lapses or outflows.
10. Regarding "cutting off future outflows": ensuring that unarisen evils never arise again. 11. Regarding "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time":
those who uphold the precepts maintain purity themselves and are further able to cause others to uphold the precepts, thereby benefiting and supporting the times.

The assembly has transmitted these transformations from one to another, so that they have not fallen into decline for a thousand years. The three preceding sections, though distinct, all constitute the first gate concerning the origins of the teaching's emergence.
Regarding the origins of the Second Council, the *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (付法藏傳) states:

The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You should now know that for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have diligently practiced asceticism for the sake of sentient beings, single-mindedly seeking the unsurpassed, supreme Dharma.
My former vows are now fulfilled; I am about to enter parinirvāṇa. With this profound Dharma..."
"I entrust this to you. In the future, you should respectfully follow my intention and widely proclaim and disseminate it so that it shall not be interrupted.
Kāśyapa replied, "Excellent! I accept your instruction and shall uphold the True Dharma. Thereafter, the Tathāgata frequently sat in dialogue with Kāśyapa while preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the devas and humans said, "The World-Honored One takes Kāśyapa as his teacher. Thus it was with Kāśyapa.

He then took leave of the Tathāgata and went to the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain, where he practiced walking meditation and contemplation, proclaimed the sublime Dharma, and delivered all sentient beings.
Following the five-hundred-fold council of the four divisions, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara.

His body was wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cloth and placed within a nested set of four coffins made of gold, silver, copper, and iron; these were filled with fragrant oil and surrounded by a great accumulation of incense.
They took firewood and lit it, but the gods immediately extinguished the flames.

At that time, because Anuruddha possessed the divine eye, he said to the people, "The gods extinguish the fire because they are waiting for Kāśyapa to arrive. At that moment, Kāśyapa was in the kingdom of Pāvā.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he emitted a supreme radiance and the great earth shook.
[The monk] then thought to himself, "Could it be that the Tathāgata is manifesting these signs because he intends to enter nirvāṇa?

He immediately entered samādhi and, observing with his divine eye, saw that the Tathāgata had relinquished his life-span in his entirety by the banks of the Hiranyavatī River. Having made this observation, he was filled with grief and displeasure.
"The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa; how swiftly! The eye of the world is extinguished, and unwholesomeness increases.
Then, together with his disciples, he headed toward the city of Kuśinagara. Along the way, he thought to himself, "Shall I be able to see the Buddha’s relics before they are cremated?
The devas, knowing that Kāśyapa had formed such a thought, therefore extinguished the fire. As Kāśyapa proceeded further, he encountered a Brahmā.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa saw him from afar as he walked along the road holding a *mandārava* flower in his right hand.
He asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from the city of Kuśinagara. Kāśyapa asked again, "Do you know my teacher? He replied, "I do.
He has already entered *parinirvāṇa* seven days ago; all the devas and humans have made great offerings for him, and I have come from there."
From where did this flower come? Upon hearing these words, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples were all overcome with great sorrow and distress.
Among them were bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire; hearing that the World-Honored One had already entered parinirvāṇa, they threw their bodies to the ground.
They were like trees whose roots have been severed and which fall over; the bhikṣus were likewise, wailing and sobbing, their tears falling like rain. All...
"To say that the Sugata has entered *nirvāṇa*—how can it be so soon? Some rolled about on the ground like logs.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was among the assembly, and he said to the people: "Venerable ones, stop for a moment; do not grieve so greatly.
We have attained liberation from that 'great fool' (mahallaka). While he was still in the world, he frequently instructed us..."
"We shall determine what is appropriate and what is inappropriate; we shall decide what should be done and what should not be done.
From this day forward, we shall abide by our own authority; whatever we wish to do, we shall do, and whatever we wish not to do, we shall not do. When Mahākāśyapa heard this, he was displeased.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "Arise quickly and take up your robes and bowls. Before the World-Honored One’s śarīra have been cremated, we must see them.
Let us proceed with all haste. Thereupon, Kāśyapa, together with five hundred bhikṣus, went to the city of Kuśinagara and reached the space between the twin trees.
He circumambulated the coffin three times, prostrated himself in homage, and spoke these verses (as recorded in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*).
Having transcended the home of the three realms, you have forever crossed the stream of birth and death.
Tranquil, signless, and vow-less, you are subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable. The Buddha-sun is exceedingly bright and pure; it can dispel the darkness of ignorance.
Having practiced asceticism through accumulated kalpas, you vowed to deliver all suffering beings. Why is it that on this very day...?
Having cast aside your original compassion, you lie entirely within a golden coffin, silent and unmoving.
We pray that the Honored One among gods and humans will manifest your golden body, causing all sentient beings everywhere to give rise to immeasurable vows.
At that time, from within the golden coffin and amidst the thousand layers of woolen cloth, the World-Honored One extended his golden feet, their radiance shining brilliantly like the midday sun;
yet the coffin and the cloth remained unimpaired as the feet were clearly revealed. Thereupon, Kāśyapa bared his right shoulder.
He touched his feet in prostration and spoke these verses again:
The Tathāgata’s ankles are full, And the marks of the thousand-spoked wheels appear. His fingers are slender, long, soft, and joined by webbed nets;
With great compassion he rescues sentient beings, Severing the net of all worldly doubts.
Therefore, today I prostrate at the feet of the Most Victorious One.

Having realized the Four Noble Truths and proclaimed the mass of the Buddha’s virtues, and having already offered praise and worship, it is fitting that you now withdraw your feet and enter [nirvana].
After he had spoken this verse, he addressed the bhikṣus: "It is not our duty to cremate the relics of the World-Honored One. Why is this?"

"O King and Householder, you should personally provide offerings to seek the most supreme merit. We, however, ought to compile the Eye of the Dharma so that the torch of the Dharma does not quickly perish.
For the sake of future generations, we shall act as a source of illumination and ensure the succession of the Three Jewels."
[They] ensured it would not be interrupted. The account of the Five Hundred Councils states: Before Kāśyapa had arrived, the fire would not ignite.
When Kāśyapa reached the place of the Tathāgata’s coffin, the coffin opened of its own accord, and the World-Honored One manifested his feet.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa saw that the wheels on the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet were stained and defiled, and he immediately asked Ānanda: "The World-Honored One’s countenance was upright and handsome, and his body was of golden hue."
"Who has defiled the wheel-mark on your feet? Ānanda replied, "The minds of women are soft;
when she came forward to prostrate before the Buddha, tears fell upon it, and as she grasped the World-Honored One’s foot with her hand, she defiled it. When Kāśyapa heard this, he was displeased.

At that time, Kāśyapa prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and the fourfold assembly likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Then the World-Honored One’s feet returned within the coffin, becoming hidden and invisible.
It manifested once more. Kāśyapa lamented with grief and circumambulated the coffin seven times; the fire did not burn it, but ignited spontaneously. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
When the Buddha’s relics were being carried into the city of Kuśinagara, the kings of the eight nations assembled their armies and surrounded them in an attempt to seize them.
At that time, a brahmin of the Śyāma clan said to the kings, "The Tathāgata was of great compassion; how could there be fighting or strife?"
The Buddha’s relics were divided into eight portions and given to eight kings, who then erected eight stupas. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Formerly, while I was traveling on the road, I heard Upananda say to the bhikṣus as follows: 'Venerable ones, please stop,' and so forth, as explained at length above."
"We should now debate the Dharma and Vinaya together, lest the non-Buddhists give rise to further words of derision and suspicion.
If the Sramaṇa Gautama’s system of law and discipline were like smoke [fading away], then while the World-Honored One was still alive, everyone studied the precepts together;
yet now that he has passed into extinction, there are none who study the precepts. Elders, you should now appoint those bhikṣus who are learned, wise, and are arhats."
At that time, four hundred and ninety-nine people were selected; they were all arhats, possessed of great learning and wisdom.
Next, Ānanda was selected, and he was also included in the number. Kāśyapa did not permit it, saying, "Ānanda is still on the stage of training (śaikṣa);

as he still possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, he should not be allowed in the number. The bhikṣus spoke again, saying, "Ānanda is the one who attended upon and made offerings to the Buddha."

He constantly followed the Buddha’s movements and personally received the teachings from the World-Honored One; he would surely have questioned the World-Honored One on various matters here and there, so it is fitting that he be included among our number.
Furthermore, it is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the great arhats intended to enter extinction.
Kāśyapa then went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and struck the *gandī* bell, announcing to them: "Venerable sirs, do not yet pass away."
[The defilements] are extinguished. One should repay the Buddha’s kindness. The Venerable Ones have attained liberation by relying on the Buddha’s holy teaching;
now you should compile this holy teaching to show it to future generations, so that the Dharma does not fall into ruin. This is repaying the Buddha’s kindness. I am the Elder;

for one to disobey the Elder’s command is a *dūṣaṇa* (offense) according to the Buddha’s regulation. Because the Arhats were in accord with the Buddha’s words, they did not disobey what the Elder commanded. At that time—
Thus, they were able to assemble four hundred and ninety-nine persons who were well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and possessed both types of liberation.

As for the two types of liberation, they are liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) and liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*). According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is said that there was one person short of a thousand.
Next, Ānanda was summoned, and they deliberated together: "In what place should we assemble the Dharma and Vinaya? [A place] abundant in..."
"Food and bedding are not lacking; everyone says that only in Rājagṛha are dwellings, food, and bedding so abundant.
It would be fitting for us to go there together to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya. Kāśyapa made the formal motion (jñapti), and having done so, they all departed together.
At that time, Ānanda was traveling on the road, and he thought to himself: "He is like a newborn calf who, though still nursing, is now among five hundred great oxen."
[He] proceeded. Now I am likewise; I am still but a learner (*śaikṣa*), and my task remains unfinished, yet I travel together with five hundred arhats.
At that time, there was a Bhikṣu Vātsīputra in the kingdom of Vaiśālī who possessed great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Perceiving through his insight that Ānanda still possessed desire, he caused him to give rise to a mind of weary detachment and spoke this verse:
Dwelling in tranquility beneath an empty tree, his mind was intent upon Nirvāṇa; sitting in meditation, he was not negligent—what more need be said?
When Ānanda heard this verse, he dwelt alone with diligence, his mind free from negligence, serene and undisturbed.
Ānanda, this was a marvelous phenomenon: having practiced walking meditation throughout the night, his body was utterly exhausted when dawn was about to break.
He sat down for a short while, and as he was about to lean back to lie down, before his head even reached the pillow, in that very interval his mind attained untainted liberation.
Having become an Arhat, he immediately spoke these verses:
Having heard many various teachings and constantly making offerings to the World-Honored One, he has already severed birth and death;
Gautama now wishes to lie down.
Having realized the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he went directly to Kāśyapa’s dwelling during the night. Finding Kāśyapa closing his room, Kāśyapa spoke these words:
"If you have already realized the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), please come in so that we may meet. He then entered through the door-key and saw Kāśyapa.
At that time, the arhats were traveling from Vaiśālī toward Rājagṛha. Kāśyapa asked, "Which Piṭaka shall we compile first?
They then consulted together and declared, "We shall compile the Vinaya Piṭaka first; the Vinaya Piṭaka is the life-span of the Buddha’s Dharma. Thereupon, they took it up.
Upāli, Kāśyapa made the formal motion (*jñapti*) to appoint him. During a single summer retreat, he recited the Mahāvinaya-piṭaka eighty times.
This concludes the general explanation of the second section on the origins of the Second Council.
Regarding the third section, the period of division, it is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the transmission through the five masters;
second, the clarification of the reasons for the division. Now, first, regarding the clarification of the transmission through the five masters:

when the Tathāgata’s work of transformation was nearing completion and the karmic responses of sentient beings were exhausted, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Whatever I now possess..."

The Supreme True Dharma has been entirely entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Therefore, Kāśyapa, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, shall successively proclaim the True Dharma to extensively benefit sentient beings.
King Ajātaśatru, seeing this, threw himself down from his elephant and entreated him, saying, "Venerable One, you may announce your own nirvāṇa to us.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having completed the tasks for which he was transformed, reflected again: "My years have reached their extreme..."
Māyā said: "My body is worn out by old age; this putrid and decaying frame is truly loathsome and distressing. When the time for *nirvāṇa* arrives, I shall immediately reflect upon it.
Having circumambulated and paid homage to all the stūpas containing the Tathāgata’s relics, and having completed his prostrations, he returned to Rājagṛha.
Ānanda followed him constantly, never leaving his side, fearing that if he entered *nirvāṇa*, he might not see him again. Later, Kāśyapa spoke to Ānanda:
He said, "You enter the city alone; I shall also go. Because of this, he entered the great city of Rājagṛha alone.
Upon reaching the gate of King Ajātaśatru’s palace, he addressed the gatekeeper, saying, "Please inform the king on my behalf. The gatekeeper replied, "The king is currently fast asleep;
we do not dare to wake him. He said, "If the king awakens, you may convey my message. King Ajātaśatru then dreamed of a rafter...
He broke [the staff], whereupon he was startled into realization. His disciples reported this in detail, and the King immediately went in search of the Venerable One.

However, the Venerable had already gone to Mount Kukkuṭapāda and entered parinirvāṇa. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 135, states: "Mahākāśyapa entered the city of Rājagṛha for his final almsround.
Not long after he had finished eating, he ascended Mount Kukkuṭapāda. This mountain has three peaks, shaped like a cock standing on its haunches."
He entered and sat cross-legged within it, making this solemn vow:

"May this body of mine, along with my robes and bowl, remain for a long time without decaying, even until fifty-seven *koṭis* and sixty hundred thousand years. The *Dharmakośa-saṃgraha* states: "Nine hundred and sixty million [years].
At the time when Maitreya Tathāgata appears in the world, he shall perform the Buddha-work and make this [vow].
Having made this vow, he immediately entered parinirvāṇa. At that moment, the three peaks merged into one, covering the Venerable One as he remained seated in solemn stillness (and so forth).
Furthermore, the *Dharmatrāta-dharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Kāśyapa arrived at Mount Kukkuṭapāda; having sat down in the full lotus posture..."

He made this vow, saying: "Now, let this body of mine, wearing the rag-robes given by the Buddha and carrying my own alms-bowl, remain until the time of Maitreya without decaying or perishing, so that his disciples may all behold my body.
Furthermore, I think that if King Ajātaśatru does not see me, boiling blood will surely flow from his face and his life will not be saved. If I can cause King Ajātaśatru..."
When Ānanda arrived, the mountain opened for him so that he might enter; when he departed, it closed once more.

He then passed away, at which point the great earth shook violently. Śakra and the various devas rained down flowers and burned incense as offerings to his *śarīra*, wailing in grief before restraining themselves and returning to the heavens. King Ajātaśatru was then asleep.
In the middle of the night, he dreamed that the main beam of his house broke. He immediately woke up in a state of alarm and fear. His attendants informed the king:
"Mahākāśyapa wishes to enter *nirvāṇa* and has come to bid you farewell; he found you asleep at rest and sent me to convey this message.

Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground, wailing aloud with tears streaming down his face: "How little merit I possess! That the various sages enter *nirvāṇa* and I do not behold them even once!"
Having seen this, he immediately went to the Bamboo Grove and paid homage at Ānanda’s feet. He then led Ānanda toward Mount Kukkutapāda.
Once the King had arrived there, the mountain opened of its own accord. Kāśyapa was within it, his body intact and undecomposed, with *mandārava* flowers covering him.
At that time, the King cried out in lamentation and threw himself to the ground. He piled up various kinds of fragrant wood, intending to perform the cremation. Ānanda—
It is difficult to stop his words. Kāśyapa remains in meditative absorption, awaiting Maitreya; he cannot be burned.
When Maitreya emerges, he will lead a retinue of nine hundred and sixty billion to this mountain and behold Kāśyapa. At that time, the assembly of Maitreya will all think:
"The disciples of Śākyamuni Tathāgata were so physically humble and lowly; how could their Buddha also have been like this?"
"It shall be no different from this. Thereupon, Kāśyapa leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations.
He transformed his body into a massive form that filled the entire *dharmadhātu*. At that time, Maitreya Buddha approached Kāśyapa and took the *saṃghāṭī* robe.
Then the great assembly, witnessing such supernatural power, cast off their prideful minds and attained the state of *arhat*. After the King had made his offerings, he returned to his own realm.
At that time, Mount Kukkuṭapāda closed back together as it was before. It was asked:
"Regarding the three Kāśyapas—namely, Kumāra-Kāśyapa, Mahākāśyapa, and Daśabala-Kāśyapa—which one among them did the World-Honored One entrust with the Dharma?

The answer is: According to the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Maitreya praised him, saying: "He who abides in the superior dhūta practices and possesses few desires and contentment is Kumāra-Kāśyapa. For this reason...

This refers to the one who took the precepts through a self-vow. Some call him Suvarṇa (Golden), while others call him Aniccha (Free from Desire) because he constantly practiced *dhūta* austerities; thus we know it is he.
If this is so, and he is the "Younger Kāśyapa," why do the sūtras refer to him as Mahākāśyapa?

The answer is that he is not the eldest among the three brothers; rather, he is called Mahākāśyapa because he was able to practice *dhūta*, possessed few desires, and was known for his meditative concentration, and because he constantly practiced...
It is the Great Dharma; therefore, it is called "Great. When Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the most supreme Dharma to Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable One, you should know that formerly the Bhagavat entrusted the Dharma to me.
Now I am aged and decrepit and am about to enter parinirvāṇa. This supreme eye of the world is now to be entrusted to you. You must diligently guard and protect it."
The Dharma. Ānanda received the instruction and upheld its essence for his time. King Ajātaśatru invited Ānanda, saying:

"Since the Tathāgata and Kāśyapa entered parinirvāṇa, I have committed many transgressions and have not seen them at all. If you, Venerable One, should pass into extinction, I pray that you will grant me your notice.
Ānanda replied, "Very well. Later, Ānanda went to the Bamboo Grove and heard a bhikṣu reciting the *Dharmapada*.
Verse:
If a person lives for a hundred years And never beholds the water-wading crane, It would not be as good as living for a single day And having the fortune to behold it.
Having heard this, Ānanda spoke to the bhikṣus: "This is not the word of the Buddha; it is not to be practiced. You should now listen as I recite the Buddha’s verses:
‘If one lives for a hundred years, Without understanding the law of arising and ceasing, It is not as good as living for a single day.’"
Having thus attained understanding, the bhikṣu then spoke to his teacher. The teacher said to him, "Ānanda is aged and infirm; his wisdom and compassion have declined."
"It contains many errors and contradictions; it is not to be trusted. You should now simply recite it as you did before. Later, Ānanda heard this and still recited the previous verse.
He immediately asked for its meaning, and [the Buddha] replied: "Venerable One, my teacher told me that Ānanda is old and decrepit."
"His words are mostly false and vain; he merely recites according to his former practice. Ānanda thought to himself, "He may slight my words or perhaps accept other teachings.
He immediately entered into samādhi to seek out someone of superior virtue who might be able to turn him back from his intent, but he saw no one capable of doing so. Thereupon, he spoke these words:
"The various sufferings of the world are such that it is extremely difficult to dwell here for long. Today, I ought to enter parinirvāṇa. He further thought:
"King Ajātaśatru has a prior engagement with me; I should respond to him. He then went to the royal palace and addressed the gatekeeper.

"Please inform the King on my behalf. The gatekeeper replied, "The King is currently asleep; were he to wake up, my punishment would not be small. Ānanda said, "If the King wakes, you may convey my message.
King Ajātaśatru dreamed that the shaft of his parasol snapped (symbolizing the loss of protection), whereupon he was startled awake.
The gatekeeper delivered the full message; upon hearing it, the King fainted and only regained consciousness after a long time. Then the garden deity spoke.
"O King, Ānanda has now set out for Vaiśālī. Thereupon, [the king] immediately arrayed the fourfold army and proceeded to the banks of the Ganges.
At that time, Ānanda was traveling by boat in the middle of the river, and the great earth shook in six ways.

Then, five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, having seen this omen, flew through the air to visit him; they sought refuge and requested ordination. Immediately, he transformed the Ganges so that it became gold.
On the ground, he preached the Dharma to the various rishis according to their needs. Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and they attained arhatship.

They all simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa. Ānanda ascended into the air and performed the eighteen transformations; he entered the Vāyu-vega-samādhi (the Samādhi of the Swift Wind) and divided his body into four parts.
One part went toward the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to [visit] Śakra Devendra; one part [he gave] to the Great Ocean... Sa... [The text is incomplete here].
The Naga King Kāla divided [the relics] into two portions: one was given to the son of Vaiśālī, and one was bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru.

Thus, stupas were erected at these four locations. Some say that Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa while flowing down the river for the sake of protecting the intentions of both King Ajātaśatru and the people of Vaiśālī; this is why he neither advanced nor retreated. (From the *Xinsu*).
It is said: down to the third master, Madhyāntika, and the fourth, Śāṇakavāsin, both were those who personally received and served Ānanda.
As Ānanda was about to pass away, he entrusted the Dharma-transmission to these two men.

Madhyāntika’s transformation took place in Kaśmīra, while Śāṇakavāsin flourished in the Middle Kingdom; thus, they were contemporaries who ruled over their respective domains. The fifth master was named...
Upagupta was a disciple who lived during the Buddha’s lifetime. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha named Saccaka, who possessed exceptional talent and sharp intelligence;
his skill in debate was peerless, and he harbored deep arrogance, enjoying great renown throughout the world. He wrapped his belly in copper plates and carried a flaming bowl upon his head.
It is said that his wisdom was overflowing; he wrapped himself in metal plates. Amidst the darkness of the world where nothing could be seen, he desired to illuminate the blindness with light.
Coming to the Buddha’s presence, wishing to compete in verbal eloquence, he said, "Gautama, I wish to go forth.
If my wisdom is equal to that of Śāriputra, I shall find it sweet and joyful; if it does not reach such a level, I shall return."
“Householder,” the Buddha said, “even if you were to accumulate hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies in order to hope to equal Śāriputra, such a thing would ultimately be impossible.
Having heard this, the man took his leave of the Buddha and withdrew. Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed the assembly, saying:
“One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this man will at that time attain the path of an Arhat and extensively transform sentient beings, causing them to...”

They attained liberation in numbers beyond measure. Śāṇakavāsin, observing that it was time for him to pass on his lineage, went to his father and requested that he allow [the boy] to go forth as a monk.
He said to his father, "The Buddha has prophesied that after a hundred years, this person will perform great deeds for the sake of the Buddha's work."

Benefiting sentient beings, his father immediately entrusted him to Śāṇakavāsin. Returning to the monastery, he ordained him, granted him full ordination (*upasampadā*), and completed the *karmavācanā*.
He immediately attained arhatship, possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and became skilled in eloquence.
The teachings he expounded were inexhaustible. He thought to himself, "Today I have beheld the Dharma-body, yet I have not yet seen the physical form of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs.
Having reflected thus, he felt a profound sense of longing and attachment. At that time, there was an elderly nun, one hundred and twenty years of age, who had once seen the Tathāgata.
Knowing that she had seen the Buddha, Upagupta wished to go to her location and immediately dispatched [a messenger].
The messenger informed the bhikṣuṇī, "The Venerable Guptaka wishes to come and see you.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī immediately filled a bowl with oil and placed it behind the door of her room. When Guptaka arrived at her dwelling and was about to enter the room, she said:

After spilling a few drops of oil and exchanging greetings, they took their seats. He asked, "Sister, when the World-Honored One was still in the world, what were the deportment and conduct of the bhikṣus like?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "In the past, when the Buddha was in the world..."
"The group of six bhikṣus was the most coarse and violent; though they entered this room, they never left me so much as a single drop of oil.
Yet now, Venerable Sir, your wisdom is lofty and supreme, and the people of the world call you the Buddha Without Marks. Nevertheless, you have entered my room."
"A few drops of oil were discarded. Observing this, it is certain that the people during the Buddha's lifetime were truly marvelous.

When Kūṭadanta heard these words, he deeply reproached himself and felt extreme shame. The bhikṣuṇī said, "Venerable sir, you should not give rise to such self-reproach and resentment. As the Buddha said:
'After my parinirvāṇa, those sentient beings of the first day will surpass those of the second day; those of the third day [will surpass those of the second]...'"

Such people become increasingly base and inferior. In this way, through successive generations, their merit and virtue decline, they become foolish and dull-witted, and their wholesome qualities wither away.

How much more so now for the Venerable One, who lived a hundred years after the Buddha; even though he performed acts that were not in accordance with proper decorum, what is there to be surprised about?
Later, at another time, Kūṭadanta gathered the assembly and preached the Dharma, discussing how giving and precepts lead to rebirth in the heavens.

In this discourse, he reviled sensual desires as impure and taught that renunciation is virtuous. The Māra King became sorrowful and terrified, fearing that his realm would become empty. He then came to disrupt the assembly’s resolve;
while the Dharma was being preached, he rained down gold and jewels, showered flowers and necklaces, and manifested as a white elephant adorned with the seven treasures.
He further appeared as a woman, exquisitely beautiful and extraordinary, such that the entire assembly gazed at her and lost all intention to listen to the Dharma. At that time—
During these three days, he expounded the flavor of the profound Dharma, yet not a single person attained the Path.
Guptaka entered meditative absorption to observe the cause of this. Māra again placed a necklace of pearl flowers upon his head;
the Venerable One, knowing this was the work of Māra, transformed three corpses—namely those of a snake, a dog, and a human—into flower garlands. He caused Māra to approach and addressed him:

He said, "You have given me this garland; I feel deeply grateful for your generous gift. Now, I shall return it to you as a gift in kind. Māra was greatly delighted and stretched out his neck to receive it.
Having received it, he saw that the corpse was covered in worms and boils, putrid and foul-smelling, difficult even to approach.

He exerted all his supernatural powers to remove it, but could not dislodge it. Leaping into the air toward the assembly of devas, he sought release but could not find it. He then went to the Brahma realm.
"O King, seek deliverance from this corpse. The Brahma King replied, "As for the supernatural power exercised by a disciple of the One of Ten Powers, what can I do?

Even the conflagration at the end of an eon or the fierce winds of Saṃvarta could not effect such deliverance. It is like one who has fallen to the ground and must be supported back up by the very ground.
If you take refuge in Upagupta, it may be possible to be delivered. Māra then accepted the Brahma King’s instruction and departed.

He prostrated himself before the Venerable One with his five limbs touching the ground and said, "O Virtuous One, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment and sat beneath the King of Trees, I led my retinue there to harass and disturb him;
we were beyond counting. Yet he did not utter a single harsh word nor did he show us contempt.
You, an Arhat, possess little power of compassion and patience that you allow yourself to be insulted and humiliated before gods and men. The Venerable One replied, "You..."

To compare a śrāvaka with a Tathāgata is like wishing to equate a mustard seed with Mount Sumeru, the light of a firefly with the radiance of the sun and moon, or the water in a cow’s footprint with the volume of the great ocean. The Great Compassion of a Tathāgata cannot be requited;
yet I am now narrow-minded and inferior, possessing little compassion or patience, and have thus insulted you. You must no longer cause further harm to the True Dharma. You should...
"I shall explain it for you. You have previously beheld the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata; you should now manifest it for me.

The Māra said, "I shall manifest the body of a Buddha; do not pay homage to me. The Māra entered the forest and transformed his appearance to resemble that of a Buddha, complete with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, radiating brilliance, with a serene and majestic demeanor.
He then transformed himself into a bhikṣu, surrounded by a retinue before and behind like a flock of geese.
The king hurriedly emerged from the forest. Upon seeing him, Guptaka spoke this verse:
"Alas, impermanence! Lacking any heart of compassion, It can destroy such a sublime and wondrous physical form."
Having spoken these verses, he gazed with single-minded devotion, his eyes never turning away for a moment. With a heart full of exultation, he further spoke in verse as praise:
"How wonderful! This pure karma Can bring forth such a marvelous fruit; It was not created by a sovereign god."
Nor was it obtained without cause; his face is like the color of purple gold.

His eyes are pure like blue lotuses, his upright form surpasses the sun and moon. He is as wondrous and marvelous as a grove of flowers, as deep and still as the great ocean, and as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
His steady gait is like that of a lion, and his glance is like that of a bull king.
"Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have purified your body, speech, and mind.
For this reason, you have obtained such a sublime body that even enemies rejoice upon seeing it; how much more so should I not celebrate it?
Having spoken this verse, he unconsciously prostrated himself. The Māra-king was struck with alarm and fear, immediately returned to his original form, and asked: "For what reason [did you do this]?"
Thus he replied, "Pāpīyan, I know that the World-Honored One has long since entered parinirvāṇa. Seeing this form and appearance, joy arose within me, and for that reason I paid him homage.

When the men and women of the city, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, heard that the Venerable One had subdued Māra, they all gathered like clouds to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
Of those hundreds of thousands of millions of people, eighteen thousand attained the first fruit of enlightenment.
One thousand attained arhatship. From that time forward, those he converted were immeasurable. At that time, King Aśoka attained indestructible faith in the Triple Gem.
He frequently accompanied the Venerable One to visit sacred sites, converting and delivering immeasurable sentient beings at every location;
all of them attained arhatship. For each person who attained the Way, one tally was placed; each tally was four inches long. When they reached one...
There was a stone chamber, six *zhang* high, and its length and breadth were likewise.

Thereupon, his fame filled Jambudvīpa, and the world all called him the Buddha Without Marks (*animitta-buddha*). When his work of transformation was complete and he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he addressed the great assembly:
"Seven days from now, I shall pass into extinction. At that time, he gathered one hundred thousand *arhats* and various students who maintained pure discipline.

As for the precepts, they are beyond counting. He immediately manifested eighteen transformations, causing the four classes of beings to give rise to great faith and attain parinirvāṇa in *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Using the tally-sticks from within his room, he performed the cremation; one hundred thousand arhats likewise entered nirvāṇa.
It was like a great elephant departing, followed by its young (and so forth). These are the five aforementioned [miracles].

The Master followed in his footsteps to transmit the teachings; therefore, they are known as the Five Masters of Successive Generations. The preceding section concludes the exposition on the lineage of the Five Masters.

Second, regarding the explanation of the origins of the various schools, this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the differences between the five schools; second, following their respective tenets.

The Treatise on the Wheels (*Cakravāda*). This work extensively clarifies the origins of the schisms among the twenty schools. First, regarding the explanation of the five schools: however, various sūtras and śāstras present differing accounts.

I shall now briefly set forth two or three examples to provide a general understanding of the path. According to the *Śāsana-vinaya-samādhi-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Robes for the Fivefold Saṃgha," it says:
"During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu named Rājuka who frequently engaged in the distribution [of robes]."

Wei Ze returned empty-handed. The Buddha, knowing his past deeds and wishing to manifest both calamity and fortune while clarifying the precepts, commanded the assembly of monks to divide into five groups, each wearing robes of one of the five colors, and ordered them to go on alms rounds day by day following one group.

Thus, they followed the ritual observances of their respective groups until they attained liberation. Later, they were known as those who each venerated the color of the robes they wore. Sarvāstivāda.

The Mahīśāsaka school is broad in its learning, quick-witted, and proficient; they understand the path of wisdom and the transformation through the Dharma, and they should wear saffron-colored *kāṣāyas*.
The Dharmaguptaka school reverently upholds the heavy precepts and adjudicates according to the rules and laws, and they should wear black-colored *kāṣāyas*. As for the Kāśyapīya school...
Those who are diligent, energetic, and resolute in rescuing and protecting sentient beings should wear saffron-colored (*mūlāna*) *kāṣāyas*.
Those of the Mahīśāsaka school, who contemplate deeply and penetrate subtle mysteries to fully elucidate profound principles, should wear blue *kāṣāyas*.

Those of the Mahāsāṃghika school, who diligently study the various sūtras and expound their meanings and principles, should wear yellow *kāṣāyas*. It was because the Buddha had gone on alms-round in Rājagṛha that...
[The Buddha] granted this, so that the bhikṣus might know there is karmic retribution. He then divided them into five groups and commanded each group to go out for alms one by one;
however, they obtained nothing at all. This was the case for all five groups. The Buddha then ordered Rāhu to sweep and sprinkle the temple grounds, while the others were invited to receive food.
For one day, he did not perform those tasks, and Śāriputra requested food on his behalf.
While eating on the road, he overturned his alms bowl; as all the food was lost, he could not eat. He then said, "Since my merit is so meager, what need is there for me to remain long?
Thereupon, he entered nirvana while eating sand and drinking water. [The Master] privately remarked: "Although this is the portion of a monk, it is divided into five types of robes."

The training in the precepts remains the same, and there shall be no discord or contention regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The reason for this is known from the *Daśasvapna-sūtra of King Aśoka*, which states:

"In a dream, he saw a white woolen cloth descend from heaven and, upon reaching the ground, divide into five sections. At that time, the king was distressed and came to question the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, 'This is not a matter concerning the king; it concerns my Dharma. After my parinirvāṇa, among the assembly of my disciples..."
The Vinaya was divided by me into five schools. Since it is stated that this occurred after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, it was not divided while he was present;

rather, during the Buddha's lifetime, there were only prophetic declarations, but the division into five sections had not yet been made. For now, I shall list the names of the five schools based on various sūtras.

According to the *Yijing sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), the five schools are: first, the Sarvāstivāda school (wearing crimson robes); second, the Mahīśāsaka school (wearing black robes).
1) The Kāśyapīya school (wears saffron-colored robes). 2) The Mahīśāsaka school (wears blue-colored robes). 3) The Dharmaguptaka school (wears crimson-colored robes).
4) The Sarvāstivāda school (wears black-colored robes). 5) The Mahāsāṃghika school (wears yellow-colored robes). Regarding the five schools mentioned in the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
1) The Mahāsāṃghika school (wears yellow-colored robes). 2) The Tāmraśātīya school (wears red-colored robes). 3) The Sarvāstivāda school (wears black-colored robes). 4) The Kāśyapīya school.
(The Dharmaguptaka school) wears garments of mulan color. The Mahāsāṃghika school wears garments of blue color. Regarding the five schools mentioned in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
first, the Dharmaguptaka school; second, the Sarvāstivāda school; third, the Kāśyapīya school; fourth, the Mahīśāsaka school;
fifth, the Vātsīputrīya school; sixth, the Mahāsāṃghika school. Question: This sūtra has already listed the names of six schools; for what reason does it [now] speak of...?
Regarding the five schools (*pañca-nikāya*), there have been many interpretations since antiquity; for now, I shall provide a single explanation.

Since the *Mahāsāṃghika* were able to extensively survey the scriptures of all five schools, it is clear that they did not adhere exclusively to a single tenet system. Therefore, according to their own tradition, they simply refer to them as "the five schools.
The brief explanation of the names and meanings of the five schools is now complete. Next, I shall clarify the meaning of the twenty schools and list their names, following the *Śāsanāvatāra*.
The treatise states: More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king named King Aśoka in the city of Kusumapura in the kingdom of Magadha, who ruled over Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the Buddhist Saṅgha was first split due to a disagreement among the four assemblies regarding the five points of Mahādeva;
they divided into two schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika, and second, the Sthavira.
Section. The treatise states: "Precisely during this second century, from within the Mahāsāṃghika school, two schools emerged:
first, the Ekavyāvahārika; second, the Lokottaravāda; third, the Kukkuṭika. Furthermore, from within the Mahāsāṃghika, yet another school emerged."
The school named Bahuśrutīya. Next, from within the Mahāsāṃghika, one further school emerged, named Prajñaptivāda. Subsequently, three more schools emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika:
first, the Caitika; second, the Aparaśaila; and third, the Uttaraśaila (the section on the schisms of the Mahāsāṃghika is hereby concluded).
Following that, for such a period of time, the Sthavira remained as a single flavor in harmony for three hundred years.
At the beginning of the year, there was a dispute that divided [the community] into two: first, the Sarvāstivāda; second, the Haimavata (which is another name for the Sthavira).
Subsequently, from the Sarvāstivāda, one school emerged, named the Vātsīputrīya. Furthermore, from the Vātsīputrīya, four schools emerged:
first, the Dharmottarīya; second, the Bhadrayānīya; third, the Saṃmitīya; [and fourth, the Mahīśāsaka].
[The] Kāśyapīya school. Fourth, the Mahīśāsaka school. Next, from the Sarvāstivāda school, one further school emerged, named the Mahīśāsaka school.
Next, from the Mahīśāsaka school, one further school emerged, named the Dharmaguptaka school.
Next, from the Sarvāstivāda school, one further school emerged, named the Kāśyapīya school. Then, at the beginning of the fourth century, from the Sarvāstivāda...
There is the Sarvāstivāda school. A branch that emerged from it is called the Sautrāntika, also known as the Saṃkrāntika.

In this manner, the Sthavira school split off to form eleven schools. Among the five schools and twenty sub-sects mentioned above, the present *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* corresponds to the Mahīśāsaka school;
the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* corresponds to the Tāmraśāṭīya school; and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* [corresponds to the]... [text truncated].
According to the Dharmaguptaka school, as well as the twenty schools of the Dharmaguptaka lineage—this concludes the general explanation of the third period of division.

Regarding the fourth point, the differences in the eras of translation for the Vinaya texts: although the precepts and their doctrines were transmitted previously, the original Vinaya texts had not yet [been translated].

It arrived. Some were translated as standalone *karmavācanās*, while others were translated separately as the "Essence of the Precepts" (*Śīlacittopadeśa*), being sufficient for the needs of the time and not yet requiring extensive detail.
It was only later that the Tripiṭaka masters translated the full Vinaya texts. Of the five schools prevalent in the Western Regions, only four reached this land.

Among them, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) consists of sixty-one fascicles; it was translated by the Indian monk Puṇyatāra, whose name means "Flower of Merit" in the language of Qin.
In the sixth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the original text was recited and brought forth; Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated it, as recorded in the second [section] of the *Ji*.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* consists of sixty fascicles. The Śramaṇa Zhi Falin of the Jin state traveled west across the shifting sands.

He set out for India with the long-term goal of reaching it, traveling via Khotan where he met the Kashmiri śramaṇa Buddhayaśas—a master of the Mahāsāṃghika school and a Vinaya-dhara—whose name means "Awakened Clarity" (Jue Ming) in the Qin language.
Upon arriving in Chang’an, in the twelfth year of the Hongshi era, he recited the Vinaya Piṭaka.
At that time, more than three hundred śramaṇas who upheld the Vinaya were assembled, and the translation was produced at Zhong Temple in Chang’an under the patronage of the Liang state.
The *śramaṇa* Zhu Fonian of the province translated the Sanskrit; the monks Daoyun and Daohan of the Qin state acted as scribes.
Translated together with Changhan, this person delighted in expansion, and thus the phrasing is quite rich. Therefore, Master Zhao said:

"I requested the Mahāyāna Vinaya Master at Shiyang Monastery to newly produce the Vinaya-piṭaka; its beginning and end are precise and exhaustive, as if one were beholding the original enactment. Regarding the Sangha...
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* consists of forty fascicles. There was a śramaṇa from Pingyang named Shi Faxian, who traveled far to India.
At the Devavimāna Monastery south of the Aśoka Stūpa in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Magadha, he transcribed the original text in its entirety and brought it back to the land of Jin.
On the eleventh month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of Jin, at the Daochang Monastery in Yangdu, [he translated it].
Translated by the monk Buddhavarman of the kingdom of Kāpiśī—known in the Jin language as Juéxián—from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* in thirty fascicles.
The Sanskrit original was also brought from India by Faxian.

It was translated at Longguang Monastery in Yangzhou during the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty (423 CE) by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra—known in the Song language as Juéshòu—and the śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng.
Translated by Sheng. The above concludes the section on the differences in the eras of translation.
Fifth, regarding the delimitation [of the teachings] according to the Piṭakas, and the explanation of the title of the established school:
this present Vinaya scripture, among the Three Piṭakas, is comprised within the second, the Vinaya Piṭaka. Its specific name, as it flowed eastward, is the Vinaya Piṭaka. All...
Not few are those masters who established the fundamental tenets; not few are the schools that expounded the essence of the teachings. To summarize them, there are briefly nine schools.
A verse says: The schools of Cessation, Action, Receiving, Following, and Cessation of Evil; The Teaching, Practice, Cause, Effect, and Regulation throughout the One Vehicle.
The seventh [section] concerns the eight precepts of wholesome cessation; the ninth concerns the three wheels as the fundamental doctrine for establishing and refuting these various tenets.

These meanings have been explained in detail in the commentaries. However, the Vinaya Master Nanshan now takes the three wheels as his primary principle, asserting that the World-Honored One’s entire career of transformation did not transcend these three wheels. This is because the ignorant minds of the common people have not yet understood the correct [teaching].

[Objection: Although [the Buddha] proclaims [the Dharma], it is as if for the deaf and blind; therefore, he must manifest wonders to startle the ears and eyes, causing them to submit with faith that he is a sage.
Thus, the wheel of supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda) is required because they lack faith.
Second, once beings have developed faith and their bodies submit, if he does not show them the words of the Dharma, there will be no way for wisdom to open. Therefore, the second [wheel] follows.

To speak of the Wheel of the Dharma (dharmacakra) is not yet to have attained liberation. Nevertheless, through faith and understanding, clarity arises; yet afflictions and delusions remain like knots.

One cannot claim purification through mere verbal explanation. The meaning must rely upon practice, so that realization may be achieved within oneself. Therefore, there must be the Wheel of Mindfulness (smṛticakra).

Now, this training in the precepts (śīla-śikṣā) is subsumed under the latter wheel. How is this known? As described in the sūtras, the former [wheel] necessarily manifests wonders to cause [the truth] to appear, thereby inspiring faith.
The subsequent exposition of the Dharma is not like that regarding the precepts. The latter are established based on transgressions and do not depend on the six matters such as the emission of light;

rather, they follow the characteristics of observance and violation, making the specific instances easy to understand. Therefore, it is said that the "Three Wheels" constitute the primary tenet. If one were to discuss the fundamental tenets of this *Commentary* specifically, they consist of four factors:
the essence of the Dharma, its characteristics, its practice, and its application. Next, regarding the explanation of the title: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is, in fact, the Dharma.
This is still the teaching transmitted and received from our former masters. Regarding the categories of this teaching, there are differences in their names and meanings. Why is this so?

For instance, "Four-Part" (*Caturvarga*) is a specific designation within the broader category, while "Vinaya" (*Lü*) is the general name encompassing all internal divisions. Without the specific, the general cannot be manifested.

Therefore, the headings of the four divisions (*caturvarga*) are first indicated; for without the general [classification], there would be no way to manifest the specific. Consequently, the name of the Vinaya is subsequently revealed.
Regarding the distinct appellation within the [general] category: the "Four Divisions" is the specific name of one division among the five schools (*pañcanikāya*).

If one were to state the name based on the founder who established it, one should say *Dharmaguptaka*, which is translated here as "Dharma-Excellence" (*Fashang*), also as "Dharma-Protection" (*Fahu*), and likewise as "Dharma."
Mirror. Now, regarding the title of this work, it is called the *Caturvarga* (Four Divisions). According to the original text, the division is as follows:
the Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra constitutes the first division; from the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya down to the two methods of receiving and reciting [the precepts] constitutes the second division;

from the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) down to the *Dharmakhandhaka* constitutes the third division; and following the rules for dwellings (*śayanāsana*), there are two *Khandhakas*, together with the *Mahā- and Kṣudraka-vastus*.

The *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Precepts), along with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, was compiled by the five hundred and seven hundred [monks] respectively. Together with the various *Ekottara* (Incremental) sections, these texts form a single body of literature;
as this Vinaya collection constitutes the fourth division, it is called the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya). "Vinaya" means "dharma" (law/teaching); it is named after its instructional content.

It determines the gravity of offenses, what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes upholding or violating the rules; without the Vinaya, there would be no certainty. Thus, "vinaya" is glossed as "dharma. [This concludes] the *Śaṅfan* (Elimination of the Redundant).

Regarding the "Supplement" (*Bùquè*): the phrase "above, clarifying the *Sifen lü*" refers to the name of that specific Vinaya school. From the character "delete" (*shān*) downward is the intention of the present compiler.
The commentary states: "To excise redundant wording is called 'Deleting the Redundant' (*Shānfán*); to augment what was omitted is called 'Supplementing the Deficiencies' (*Bùquè*).
"Delete" (*shān*) is pronounced as *suǒjiān*. As for the "Procedures" (*Xíngshì*): the intent of this compendium lies in its practical application; it is not without [purpose].
This is the "Gate of Arising Contemplation. Therefore, it is called the *Xingshi* (Practices) [and so forth]. The author of the *Chao* (Excerpts) has directly extracted the essential passages;

the words do not follow a sequential order, nor does he concern himself with formal topical chapters (*yìzhāng*). Thus, it is called a *chao*, which carries the meaning of being inferior or fragmentary. As for the term *xù* (Preface), it means to narrate, to originate from, or to lead to;

that is, to narrate the origins and purpose of these excerpts. It is not that the author failed to provide a title to distinguish his work; however, when he first composed this *chao*, he had not yet...

The name of Daoxuan is inscribed [at the beginning]. Later, when the Vinaya Master Li of Xiangzhou saw this *Chao* (Excerpts), he copied one volume and constantly studied it, saying, "This *Chao* was composed by the Vinaya Master Shou.
Only later did he realize it was the work of Vinaya Master Daoxuan; he then marked the author's name to distinguish it clearly.
Thus it is said: "The author is not without [recognition]," and so forth. As for "Jingzhao," it is where the Son of Heaven resides.
The place where he resided was the capital city. As for Chongyisi Temple, it was the monastery where Xuan initially composed his commentaries.
"Śramaṇa" refers to one who has stilled the mind and reached the fundamental source; thus he is called a śramaṇa. "Śākya" indicates his clan lineage. "Daoxuan" designates his personal name.
"Zhuanshu" (author/composer) clarifies that these are the words he himself wrote; therefore, it is titled *Sifen lü shanfan* (The Four-Part Vinaya with the Elimination of Redundancy).
Preface to the *Chang-a-hsing-shih-ch'ao* (The Supplementary Record of Ritual Practice). [Note: The author is not unnamed; his name is clearly distinguished.

Sixth, regarding the analysis and explanation according to the text, this is divided into four parts: first, the explanation of the preface; second, a brief listing of the titles of the thirty chapters;
third, the explanation of the ten gates; and fourth, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the thirty chapters. Regarding the first:
In the preface to the commentary, it is further divided into three sections.

First, from the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the virtue of the precepts is inconceivable" down to "the various scriptures cease their chanting," it clarifies the meaning of the relative superiority and inferiority of the three trainings as they contrast with one another.

Second, from the passage beginning with "When the Great Master was in the world" down to "distinguishing between similarities and differences," it clarifies the meaning of how the transmission of the Dharma by teacher and disciple flourished or declined. Third...

The third section, from "From oneself... down to "...the rise or fall of the intent of the unifying teaching," clarifies the removal of doubts and the resolution of stagnation in composing this present text;
it is the formal introduction to the meaning and purpose of this commentary (*chao*). Within these three sections, there is further a division into two.

From the beginning down to "its legacy remains unaltered," the first section clarifies that this is correct; from "reaching the age of the Semblance Dharma" downward, the second section clarifies that it is incorrect.
These two sections differ; what follows now is the first.

Now, as for the virtue of the precepts: it is the very starting point of all speech. Regarding the virtue of the precepts, there are many passages extolling them throughout the various sūtras and śāstras.
The precepts serve as the foundational basis for all wholesome deeds and stand at the forefront of the Three Vehicles. They constitute the correct path for proceeding toward Bodhi.

It is the excellent rule for transcending birth and death; it is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma and the guiding path for practitioners. Therefore, it is called the virtue of the precepts (*śīla-guṇa*).

Regarding the statement that it is "inconceivable," there are two meanings: first, the inconceivability of its essence (*svabhāva*); second, the inconceivability of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). As for the inconceivability of its essence:

the essence of the unconditioned precept (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*) is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*). It is the primary foundation of all myriad virtues and the direct cause for the Three Vehicles. Thus...

It is said that "the essence is inconceivable. Regarding the statement that "the characteristics are inconceivable": from the essence, practice arises; practice then employs provisional characteristics for expression.

These characteristics pervade the Dharma-realm and extend across realms as numerous as grains of sand. Since every single realm gives rise to various forms of discipline (*saṃvara*), and this pervasion is so vast, it is called "inconceivable characteristics.
"Surpassing all forms like a crown" is a direct praise of the supreme dignity of the precepts (*śīla*). It borrows the metaphor of head-ornaments, specifically a crown.

This person is one whose head is adorned. Among the various features such as clothing and other ornaments that embellish the human body, the crown occupies the most preeminent position among all such images.
Now, this precept occupies the foremost place above concentration, wisdom, and the myriad virtues; therefore, it is metaphorically compared to a crown.

The "multitude of forms" refers to the myriad virtues such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because precepts can give rise to concentration and wisdom, and because they are that upon which concentration and wisdom rely, their merit transcends the two [other] trainings;
thus it is said they "crown and transcend all forms. Regarding "serving as the guide for the five vehicles," this means acting as a teacher and model.
The three vehicles, together with humans and devas, constitute the five vehicles. "Gui" (軌) means a model; it is correctly defined as a track or path. "Dao" (導) means to lead.

Now, this clarifies that the precepts are precisely the foundation of the five vehicles. If one can uphold them, one may escape the three miserable realms and attain the fruits of the human and deva vehicles, as well as the three vehicles.
Therefore, it is said thus. Regarding the phrase "truly the boat and rudder of the Triple Gem": "shi" (寔) means "actually" or "truly. [End of section.]

It is so. It is so. This also takes up the meaning of "is" (shi). It clarifies that the precepts can transport the practitioner across the great ocean of birth and death to the noble stages of the Three Vehicles;
they are thus metaphorically likened to a boat. "Boat" (zhou) is the general name for a vessel, while "ship" (hang) is a specific designation for a boat.
This precisely clarifies that sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of desire and have no means of rescue; the Buddha therefore reveals the Triple Gem to them.
It causes them to take refuge and look up, enabling them to cross the vast expanse of the ocean of craving by boarding the vessel of precepts and meditation. Thus it is said:

"The merit of establishing and cultivating concentration and wisdom based on the teachings is peerless. This means that if one can establish practice in reliance upon these Vinaya teachings, it is only then that concentration and wisdom arise therefrom.
Since the precepts come first and their merit surpasses that of concentration and wisdom, they are said to be peerless.

Therefore, the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "By relying on this precept, one attains the various dhyāna-concentrations as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
To attribute the achievement back to its source, it is said that nothing can equal it. Regarding the statement, "To maintain the Buddha-dharma, the various scriptures cease their chanting":
maintaining the Buddha-dharma cannot be accomplished without the precepts; thus the text says, "The Vinaya-piṭaka is the life-span of the Buddha-dharma. Vinaya...
When the *Pitaka* is preserved, the Buddha-dharma will abide. "The various scriptures" refers to the remaining two *piṭakas*.

The preceding section concludes the analysis of the relative superiority and inferiority of the three trainings as they contrast with one another. From this point onward, the discussion focuses specifically on the *Vinaya-piṭaka* to extol the efficacy of the precepts.
As for the fact that since the Great Master was in the world he has especially propagated this scripture: it is because the Buddha taught the sūtras and the formal instructions (*śāsana*).
Unlike other teachings which are expounded without distinction of time, place, or person, this Vinaya instruction is not so;

it is restricted to the Buddha’s own discourse, must take place within the Saṃgha, and is intended solely for the internal assembly. Thus, it can open the gate of non-secrecy and reveal the profound arts of the secret [teachings].

Therefore, it extensively spreads the net of the doctrine and establishes its great protocols, demonstrating the two principles of lightness and gravity, and clarifying the two practices of cessation and action. It distinguishes...

At that time, [the teaching] was selected for specific locations and not presented to the laity; hence it is called "partial propagation" (*piānhóng*). As for the phrase "reaching down to the four reliances" (*yuánjí sìyī*):
*yuán* means "to reach" or "thereby," and *jí* means "at" or "in. Since the time when the Buddha was present, all propagated and proclaimed the Dharma themselves;

now, to clarify that after his passing, the four reliances appeared in the world and likewise propagated and proclaimed the Dharma without cessation. Regarding these four reliances: in general discussion there are three distinctions, namely: person...

This is the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*). To practice the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) consists of: constantly begging for food, sitting at the foot of a tree, wearing rag-robes, and using medicinal decoctions that have become putrid.
The four reliances of the Dharma are: relying on the Dharma and not on the person; relying on wisdom and not on consciousness; relying on the meaning and not on the words;

and relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*). The four reliances regarding persons are discussed by combining the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna perspectives.

Regarding the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) of the Mahāyāna, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: the awakening of the eight types of great persons (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*) is the first reliance;
the two fruits [of the stream-enterer and once-returner] attained in an instant is the second; the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is the third; and the arhat is the fourth.
