When explained according to the Hīnayāna, the practitioners of the initial seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya-puruṣa*) are the first; the remaining three are identical to those listed for the Mahāyāna above. "Yi" (遺) means "to bestow."
This means that after the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, he left behind this teaching for the sake of the bhikṣus. "To replace" (ti) means to alter, to extinguish, to depart, to cease, or to await.
This clarifies that at this time, this teaching was neither abandoned nor altered.

"Wind" (feng) refers to the Buddha’s teaching. Wind has the power to bend the grass; the teaching has the function of eliminating what is non-virtuous. Therefore, it is called the "bequeathed wind" (yifeng).
There is no substitution.
The preceding section clarified the virtue of the Buddha’s presence and his sustaining power after his parinirvāṇa; from this point onward, it clarifies its decline.

Regarding the phrase "reaching the age of the Semblance Dharma" (*xiangji*): *dai* (逮) means "to reach" or "to arrive at. *Xiang* (像) means "semblance," and *ji* (季) means "the end" or "the final period. During the True Dharma (*zhengfa*), one is able to attain reality.

Because it is merely similar [to the True Dharma], it is called the "Semblance Dharma" (*xiangfa*). This clarifies that the time has become distant from the Sage, and that the teachings have suffered the loss of decline.

Regarding the "end of the Semblance Age" (*xiangji*): if nuns are able to practice the Eight Respectful Precepts, they currently belong to the final stage of the Semblance Dharma period; hence it is called the "end of the Semblance Age.
If nuns do not practice the Eight Respectful Precepts, this period then belongs to the limits of the Final Dharma (*mofa*). Therefore, the character "end" (*ji*) is used.

There are two interpretations. Regarding the phrase "at times it becomes diluted and corrupt": one interpretation states that "diluted" (*jiāo*) means "thin," and "corrupt" (*é) refers to an object lacking sharp edges;
it is called "corrupt" because it is neither square nor round. Another interpretation holds that "corrupt" means "excessive. "Becomes" (*zhuǎn*) refers to change and transformation.
Regarding the phrase "clashing at the tips of lips and tongues": "tip" (*fēng*) refers to the edge of a weapon's blade, carrying the sense of being sharp and keen. Jì says:
Nowadays, those who comment on the Buddha-dharma all employ a mind of victory and defeat, establishing right and wrong against one another and harming each other with their tongues;
thus it is said they "vie for supremacy between lips and tongue. Though they speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) with their mouths, their conduct remains within the realm of existence (*bhava*).
Unable to practice in accordance with the teachings, they merely lodge themselves upon their lips and tongues. As an ancient master said: "Words precede the flying dragon; conduct [follows]."

This refers to what follows the "lame tortoise. Regarding the phrase "discussing matters that do not take form": "drum" (gu) signifies movement. This clarifies that movement itself is the discussion of things that do not manifest.
One moves the lips and tongue to discourse loftily on profound principles, claiming that sin and merit have no master and that form and emptiness are both extinguished.
Because the characteristics of the principle of *tathatā* are so profound, they cannot be seen or heard; therefore, they are said to be "without form" (*abimba*). Form—
It is because they manifest [only appearances]. Furthermore, it is said that their empty discourse on the ultimate principle is like the sound of a drum;

when one examines their karmic conduct, the mind has not yet realized or known [the truth], and within, there is absolutely no reality. They merely employ provisional designations to fail to manifest the principle of namelessness and formlessness, just as the sound of a drum is empty and insubstantial within. Therefore, it is so called.

Regarding the phrase, "Thus, those who heard the transmission of the teaching through nine generations from Zhēn-lǐng," the following clarifies the flow of the teaching to the Eastern Land and the benefits or losses incurred in its preservation.
*Zhēn* refers to Zhèndàn (China). *Lǐng* refers to the Muztagh (Pamir) Mountains. The region east of these mountains is called the country of Zhèndàn.
It is named *Zhèn* because when the sun first rises, it shines upon the eastern corner; hence it is called Zhèndàn. This explains the transmission of the teaching.
Thus it is said: "The transmission of the Teaching to Zhenglǐng. Regarding those who have heard of this through nine dynasties:
from the night dream of Emperor Ming of the Han during the fifth year of the Yongping era until the present time, the Buddhist Dharma has been transmitted to the East for nine successive dynasties.
As for what is called "nine," these refer to the nine names of the Han, Wei, Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, and Tang. This refers to the eminent monks of former ages.

As for the renowned monks and others, although their wisdom, arts, and supernatural powers were preeminent, they were unable to sustain the Buddha-dharma because they could not inspire faith in sentient beings at the proper time,
nor did they rely on the Vinaya to provide instruction when necessary; therefore, it is said that they possessed merely "wisdom and arts," and that these have already ceased.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to clarify and manifest [one's] conduct and demeanor" (*xingyi*): the two characters "desiring to clarify" (*yuming*) serve as a heading for the subsequent clauses.

This means that for those possessing the aforementioned wisdom and skill, it is impossible for them to "desire to clarify and manifest their conduct and demeanor," "desire to clarify and rectify the semblance-teachings" (*xiangjiao*), or "desire to clarify and establish exemplary models.
As for "conduct and demeanor": "conduct" (*xing*) refers to the practice of the precepts (*śīla*), while "demeanor" (*yi*) refers to formal ritual protocols (*vidhi*). "Rectifying" (*kuang*) is...
"Rescuing" means correcting. "To transmit the eternal models": "eternal" (*yi*) means constant; it is also the name of a vessel. "Models" (*fan*) refers to that which follows the law;

it signifies a standard pattern and a regulatory rule. This means that by taking these constant laws of the Vinaya teachings, one transmits and disseminates the instructions for future generations—this is called "instructing those of later learning.
"To restore the profound guiding cord that has already snapped" is a metaphorical explanation that follows below.
Just as a net has a main cord that can keep its meshes in order, so too the net of the Buddha’s Dharma uses the precepts as its cord.

If one does not uphold the precepts, the cord is severed; when the cord is severed, the net of the Buddha’s Dharma falls into disorder. If there is anyone who can maintain this net of the teaching, [they shall succeed].

Not allowing the Buddha-dharma to be severed or extinguished—this is called "restringing the profound guiding cord. Regarding the phrase "having planted the great banner when it was already toppling":
this clarifies that within the world, there are markers such as *stūpa* banners (*caitya-ketu*) at specific locations which serve as signs of distinction.
Just as at a ferry crossing one erects a great banner, if people lose their way and fail to find the crossing, they can look toward this banner from afar to know its location and direction. If...
When the marker that points the way suddenly falls, one becomes lost regarding the destination it indicated. Suppose there were a person who could once again set this marker upright;

"Repeated Doubts. This refers to those who, apart from the individuals listed above who have examined the rise and fall of the general principles of the teaching and the truth or falsity of various doctrines, possess no further capacity;

because these are elaborately composed treatises on meaning that are not suited for timely application, they are termed "flowery rhetoric. *Ji* (機) refers to karmic conditions (*pratyaya*). *Dou* (逗) means to meet or adapt to.

although the ancient masters produced the formal texts of the *karmavācanā*, they did not set forth the characteristics of what is correct (*yǒng*) or incorrect (*fēi*).

Lì says: "When words have not yet been manifested, they are called *fěi* (斐). 'Mìng' (命) means to summon. 'Zhíbǐ' (直筆) refers to one who does not rely on conventional literary flourishes;

"Comprising the essential texts of various schools" means including within this compendium the essential passages from the Vinayas of all the schools.

This means that within the various sūtras, śāstras, and vinayas, there are principles concerning long-term [observances]. I have recorded them all in their entirety to assist in forming the knowledge and insight of this present compendium (*chao*).

Regarding "The Dharma": this refers to the subsequent section on various essential practices (*zāyàngxíngpiān*). It is intended to provide relief for those new students who labor over their studies.
It is said: "If one completes the study of this *Chao* (Digest), all ritual forms and regulations will be fully understood;
there will be no need to seek them elsewhere, and thus one's efforts will not be wasted."
However, regarding those who agree with me, he strikes at their major points. Zhi Li says: "Those whose views accord with mine are able to proclaim that my words are most excellent and most good;
it is like one person singing while another claps their hands, which is why it is called 'striking the major beat' (*dajie*).
As for divergent doctrines, he rejects their prolixity of text," meaning that those whose emotional views differ from his find fault with the verbosity of my excerpts.
The text says: "Why is it necessary to explain this so elaborately? It would suffice to record three or five instances of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) for practical application;

therefore, it is said that the text is verbose. The *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) states: "This dismisses [the need for] such usage. The *Sancang* (Three Cang Lexicons) says: "'Chì' (斥) means to push aside, or to rebuke, or to eliminate.

Regarding the phrase "certainly not urgent words," etc., it refers to the conditions for receiving the supreme method of "Welcome" (*svāgata*), as well as the essence of the reception at its conclusion.
It is not appropriate for the present age; thus it is called "not urgent. If I were to discuss this at length, it would not accord with the intent of this *chao* (abridgment).

Therefore, it is said to be "that which is avoided. Regarding the phrase "now, *tu*, *duo*, etc.": *duo* (徒) and *du* (各) are reversed [in the original]; they mean "to measure. As for *tu* (圖), the *Guangyi* states: "To measure; to deliberate."
This is also a calculation. Regarding the commitment to "both parsimony and restraint": "parsimony" (shěng) means reduction; see the *Zìlín* dictionary, where it is glossed as jiǎn (reduction).
"Restraint" (yuē) means limitation and scarcity. Because there is both parsimony and [simplicity], there is no prolixity; because there is both restraint and [moderation], there is no excess.

"Providing emergency aid for those who are unprepared": "Emergency" refers to newly ordained monks and nuns who are at a loss in every situation and do not recognize the characteristics of the teachings;

thus they immediately commit offenses, making their holy life difficult to maintain—a situation as precarious as being suspended upside down. This present *Chao* (Digest) demonstrates the proper methods so that one may avoid the fault of transgression;

this is called "providing emergency aid. Regarding "being prepared for the unexpected": when there is suddenly a need due to circumstances, understanding arises simply by reading the text; this is called being prepared.

"Provisions for emergencies" (be zuǒ): as explained below regarding guiding the secular world, transforming the regions, and matters such as the passing away of people and objects—when such events suddenly arrive, one prepares for them in advance.
Therefore, it is called "provisions for emergencies."

If one's contemplation does not suffice for the circumstances of the time, there will inevitably be a deficiency regarding the practice and the teaching. "Contemplation" refers to mental engagement (*ālambana*).

"Does not suffice" means it is not abundant or sufficient. "Practice" refers to ethical conduct (*śīla*). "Teaching" refers to the instruction that can express [the truth]. This means that my contemplation has fallen short;
since I have failed to reach the practice expressed by the teaching that can express it, it is said that there is a deficiency regarding the practice and the teaching. Thus, it is abbreviated.

Regarding the statement, "To broaden what follows by indicating the intended meaning," there are two interpretations. The first says: "Although I have now composed this commentary, it merely provides a brief indication;
there remains that which is not fully exhausted. I entrust the detailed elucidation of the preface to scholars of future generations."
It further states: "In this present digest (*chao*), the essential purport is briefly indicated; the detailed exposition will be clarified in the subsequent thirty sections.
Regarding the phrase 'the upper volume encompasses various affairs to establish ritual efficacy': 'encompassing' (*she*) means to unify; 'various' (*zhong*) refers to the *saṃgha*."

This refers to the monastic affairs that govern the Sangha; hence, they are called "public duties" (*saṃghakārya*). Regarding the middle fascicle, which establishes the repentance for the observance and violation of the essence of the precepts:

as for the "essence of the precepts," it refers to the unmanifest substance (*avijñapti*) at the time of receiving them. As for "observance and violation," it refers to the two types of observance and the two types of violation within the course of practice.

As for "establishing repentance," it refers to repenting for the offenses of the six categories (*ṣaḍvarga*). Since the middle fascicle exhaustively discusses these matters, the lower fascicle follows.
Regarding "arising by relying on matters as required for practice": "required for practice" refers to various matters such as the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) of robes and medicine.

"Arising by relying on matters" refers to practices such as leading the laity, teaching the methods of transformation, receiving the five or eight precepts, as well as the rites of tending to the sick and attending to the deceased;
all these arise in reliance upon matters such as illness and death. Therefore, it is said they "arise by relying on matters. (From the lower fascicle)

This matter has been fully discussed. Therefore, it is said that "perception is without confusion. This refers to the detailed and careful examination without disorder within the thirty sections mentioned below.
*Wen* (紊) is pronounced *yun* (運) in reverse; the *Shangshu* states it means "disorder" (*luan*).
"However, as the objects and matters are truly numerous" refers to the intent behind the titles of the thirty chapters that follow. "Objects" (*jing*) refers to sentient and non-sentient entities;

"matters" (*shi*) refers to such activities as the distribution of robes (*cīvara*), the formal announcement (*pravāraṇā*), and so forth. Since these objects and matters are not identical, they are said to be "truly numerous.
Now, in selecting categories according to their mutual affinity to serve as headings for the titles—for instance, the general topic of "delimiting the boundary" (*sīmā-bandha*).
There are seven types: three for the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), three for the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and the ordination platform (*sīman*) as the seventh.

Here, we directly state their names as "The Method for Binding the Boundary. Although there are these seven aspects, they are subsumed under a single name; the remaining twenty-nine chapters can be understood by listing them. This is similar to the exposition of the *Poṣadha*:
there is the mental recitation of the *Poṣadha* and the communal recitation according to the formal procedures (*yathāvidhi*). Now...
This accords with the formal protocol of conventional discourse; hence it is said that "things of a similar category follow one another.

As for that which governs the grand outline, this refers to the purpose of the ten topical sections (daśamukha) that follow. Here, the "grand outline" refers to the overall significance of these ten sections.
Fearing that those who have not yet fully grasped the details might remain confused, the term "branches" (tiao) refers to the titles of the thirty chapters.
This refers to each individual item. "Stream" (liú) refers to the categories of matters explained under each chapter.

That is to say, within the thirty sections and their respective streams, there are instances where the texts of other schools are utilized, as well as differences in gravity regarding the origins of the teachings' emergence;

these constitute the general purport of the main outline. Since this was not fully detailed within the thirty sections, the *Shimen bian tong* (Discerning the System in Ten Sections) was composed. Specifically:
These ten gates are called the "Great Outline" (*dàgāng*). They serve as the main ropes that govern the thirty subordinate gates, which are like the fine hairs of a net.
This is because, fearing that within the thirty gates one might not yet recognize their overarching structure, these ten gates are presented to provide clarity.
"Fang" (方) signifies constancy; constancy signifies excellence. Furthermore, "fang" signifies what is appropriate. "Jing" (鏡) means illumination. "Xiao" (曉) means to awaken.

This means "to clarify" and "to illuminate. Regarding "remote elucidation" (*yuanquan*): speaking in terms of the proximate, it refers to describing these ten gates, which then illuminate the meaning within the thirty gates below.
Because these ten gates rely upon the two types of observances and the two types of transgressions within the thirty gates below, they are called "remote elucidation."
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle One, Part One;
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle One, Part Two.
The first section, the extensive explanation of the meaning of the preface, is hereby completed. From this point forward is the second section: a brief enumeration of its three parts.
These are the titles of the ten chapters. As for the thirty chapters, they are grouped into verses:
* Establishing the Number of Monks and Distinguishing the Precepts; * The Net of Precepts, Receiving the Teacher’s Rituals, and the Chapter on *Pravāraṇā*;
* Following Offenses, the Six Robes, and the Four Alms Bowls; * Purification, Relics and Images, and the Chapter on Lay Guests; * Miscellaneous Matters, Illness, and the Sections on Bhikṣuṇīs.
The above concludes the second section, which briefly lists the titles of the thirty chapters. From here on follows the third section, the formal explanation of the meanings of the ten gates.
Regarding the first gate, "The Purpose for Which the Teaching Arose," this section is divided into two major parts; the first part, ending with the word "upward," is general.
"Since the rise of the 'Manifest Teaching' (Mingjiao), this refers to the general meaning of the rise of the Manifest Teaching.

Second, from 'From now on, based on our own school' onwards, it clarifies that within our own school there are inherently distinct meanings. Within this general meaning, there are three specific parts:

first, up to the point 'for people,' it clarifies the intention behind establishing precepts according to specific circumstances; second, from 'in opposition to non-Buddhists' onwards, it addresses those non-Buddhists."

Regarding the absence of fixed rules: this clarifies the intent behind the established precepts. Third, regarding "responding to divergent schools": this concerns governing the Dharma in relation to other schools;
the examples apply universally even where there is no standard, thereby clarifying the intent behind the established precepts.

Regarding the "Supreme Person" (*zhiren*) appearing in the world: the Buddha is called the Supreme Person because he is the one who has reached the ultimate limit; thus, he is termed the "Supreme Person.

Only the Buddha alone may be so titled, for he alone has completely exhausted the source of suffering. Regarding "benefiting beings through skillful means" (*yiwu youfang*): "means" (*fang*) refers to the Dharma.

Since the Buddha appeared in the world, his preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is entirely termed "beneficial"; therefore, it is said that he benefits beings through skillful means. This is according to their capacities (*suiji*).

If one were to say that the established teachings and principles are not bestowed in vain, it means that when the Buddha taught the myriad dharmas, it was entirely for the benefit of sentient beings and was not a hollow bestowal.

Being well-acquainted with their nature and characteristics, he taught according to what was appropriate for each individual's faculties and capacities; if one desired the states of humans or devas, he would then teach the five precepts or the eight precepts.
For those who wish to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, he immediately teaches the great bhikṣu’s *apraṇihita-vinaya*.

For those who should hear of the Three Vehicles, he teaches the parables of the three carts and so forth. For those who should hear of the One Vehicle, he brings the three back to the one. He speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

therefore, it is said that he establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings. Since all these are intended to lead them to Bodhi, it is said that they are not bestowed in vain. As the Treatise says: "Relying on Great Compassion..."
Regarding the explanation of the Vinaya through its gates, the first fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* clarifies this, stating:

"The Sūtra is taught based on the Ten Powers; the Vinaya is taught based on Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*); and the Abhidharma is taught based on Fearlessness. As for the gate of Great Compassion, as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata possesses three kinds of compassion. The first is compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambanā maitrī*). This takes five [categories of beings] as its object..."

The first is compassion with sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), which wishes to bestow happiness upon them. The second is compassion with phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), which desires to provide sentient beings with whatever things they require.

The third is unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), which does not dwell on the characteristics of phenomena or the characteristics of sentient beings; this is called unconditioned compassion.
It is based on these three gateways that the Buddha taught the Vinaya; therefore, it is said, "relying on the gateway of great compassion," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "therefore, the Vinaya says": the Vinaya refers to the sixtieth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which states: "The Buddha was staying in the country of Vatsa.

He asked the bhikṣus, 'With what intention do you think that I preach the Dharma for you? The bhikṣus replied, 'World-Honored One, it is because of Your Great Compassion that You preach the Dharma for us.
Therefore, it says, 'because of compassionate mindfulness,' and so forth."

The second [point] is for the sake of those who, being outside the fold, lack a dharma by which to abide. It is said that "they have no dharma by which to abide" because non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) possess no dharma that can serve as a standard;
it does not mean they lack false dharmas. This is stated to manifest that the Buddha’s Dharma is supreme and his Way is exalted.

Because the Buddha is the Great Teacher of the three realms, a person of celestial and human veneration, and one to whom none can equal him, he is uniquely honored in the world; therefore, it is so called.

The Honored One among Men has taught a Dharma that can serve as a standard for transforming beings; by relying upon it for practice, one may transcend the state of an ordinary person and become a sage.
Such a Dharma is worthy of being treasured and esteemed, for it differs from those other views; therefore, it is said that "the Way is lofty."

Regarding the phrase "as for whatever is prescribed in the Vinaya below," the *Vinayottaragrantha* states: "For what reason did the World-Honored One prescribe the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?

It was to subdue the three poisons so that they might be exhausted; thus he prescribed the training in higher ethics. Through this training, the mind becomes clear and these three poisons are exhausted; concentration and wisdom further become luminous.
When delusions are exhausted and liberation is fulfilled, one cuts off the limits of all suffering; this is called the 'extraordinary method' (*visiṣṭopāya*). Therefore, the text says:"
Regarding the phrase "if one does not compile and conclude," "text" refers to the text of the five hundred-fold compilation (*pañcaśata-saṃgīti*) of the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.
That text states: "Do not allow the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to utter further words," and so forth. "Further words" refers to the claim of the non-Buddhists:

"Now that the Śramaṇa Gautama has entered parinirvāṇa, his Dharma and Vinaya shall also perish completely. It was for this reason that Kāśyapa universally addressed the great assembly to conduct the compilation (*saṃgīti*).
"Fa-zang" [is used] to conclude the remaining discourse. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of non-Buddhists maintaining that there is no self-nature (*anātman*).
Third, as for "coming forth to respond to other schools": this is the third section below, which concerns the intention for arising in response to the doctrines of other schools.

Regarding the statement that "the tenets are largely diverse": from the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until four hundred years later, there were many divergences among the five schools, the eighteen schools, and so forth; therefore, it is said.

Furthermore, regarding the relative elaborateness or brevity of the *Sarvāstivāda* Prātimokṣa Sūtra: within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* Prātimokṣa, there are twelve precepts concerning the wearing of the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) and the three robes (*tricīvara*) in a neat and orderly manner;
thus, it is considered elaborate. It lacks the precept on not showing disrespect to stupas and the precepts concerning chewing tooth-sticks (*dantakāṣṭha*) and so forth;

thus, it is considered brief. Hence, it is said to be "elaborate and brief. As for the phrase "the essence of the indication is not yet complete," "indication" (*zhi*) refers to pointing toward or gesturing toward [the object].
"Body" refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*). This school asserts that both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) take form (*rūpa*) as their essence.

This school [of the Sarvāstivāda] holds that the unmanifest precept takes that which is neither form nor mind (*arūpācitta*) as its essence. This means that the former school’s conceptualization of the essence of the precepts was not yet complete; hence the statement.
Regarding "engaging with the laity and fixing [the precepts] according to time": this refers to bestowing the five or eight precepts upon laypeople, which is termed "engaging with the laity.

The five precepts must be maintained for the duration of one's life, and the eight precepts must be observed for one day and one night; neither extension nor reduction is permitted. This constitutes "fixing [the precepts] according to time.

When receiving the five precepts, one must receive all five; it is not permitted to receive only one, two, or three. When receiving the eight precepts, one must receive all eight. It is not permitted...
It can be increased or decreased; this is the fixed standard for counting. Although the Sarvāstivādins maintain this principle, it contradicts their own fundamental Vinaya.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in the section on leather, the lay follower Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went to sea with a group of merchants to gather treasures.
The boat was tossed by the waves and lost its way; his companions perished while he alone survived.

On his return journey, he passed through the city of hungry ghosts and came to the foot of a tree, where he saw a man and a woman of handsome appearance, wearing celestial jeweled crowns, enjoying themselves together.

When the night had passed and the woman vanished, dogs immediately arrived and devoured the flesh of the man and woman. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked in wonder, "For what reason has this occurred? They replied, "In a former life, we were butchers."
“Son, Kātyāyana converted me. I said, ‘My ancestors have always practiced this occupation; how can I refrain from doing it?
He then instructed me, saying, ‘Since you slaughter during the day, you may observe the precepts at night. It was because of this that my karmic retribution in this life is as it is.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went forward again and arrived beneath another tree, where he saw a man and a woman enjoying themselves during the day, as described in detail previously. This...
Because of his excessive lust, Kātyāyana transformed him, saying: "Since you were greedy for lust at night, you ought to have observed the precepts during the day;

therefore, we now experience pleasure by day and suffering by night. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa returned and related in detail what he had seen. Consequently, he went to Kātyāyana, left the household life, and received the precepts.

According to this Vinaya, there is also the practice of receiving the precepts in parts. As for the principle of "governing" (or "administering") the Dharma, it applies universally where there is no fixed standard. "Governing" refers to the act of upholding [the discipline].

It is "according to the master. "Dharma" refers here to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action). If one performs a single motion (*jñapti*), adding a second motion (*jñaptidvitīya*) or even many motions is permissible;

if one performs a second motion, adding a fourth motion (*jñapticaturtha*) or even adding many formal ritual actions (*karmavācanā*) is also permissible. One may only increase [the number of motions], one may not decrease it.
Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed standard.

Now, regarding those of the Dharmaguptaka school who maintain that their legal procedures (*dharma*) are orderly, they establish: for one person, there is only the *cittānuvartana* (mental) method; for two persons, the *pratyakṣa* (face-to-face) method;
and for four or more persons, the *saṃghakarma* (formal act of the community) method. If there are fewer than these, it is not accomplished; this is called "the orderliness of person and dharma.
Furthermore, there are many differing explanations as recorded. Regarding the "manifold applications of ritual practice," this refers to employing the methods to provide relief.

At that time, there were many expedient means for inducing others to cultivate goodness. Bin said: "According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* school, the five precepts and ten precepts must be received for the duration of one's life.
Only the eight precepts may be observed for varying lengths of time according to the occasion.
One may be granted anywhere from one precept up to eight precepts, regardless of whether it is for a year or a month; the sole requirement is that they be maintained before death."

This is for the sake of cultivating wholesome qualities and awakening faith. Regarding the meaning of "manifest" (*khyāna*) and "restricted" (*saṃkṣepa*) in the establishment of the teachings: "manifest" means clear or explicit; "restricted" means limited or fixed.
This refers to the three types of *karmavācanā*—the single, the double, and the fourfold proclamation.

These texts must be recited clearly before the assembly; thus they are termed "manifest. They may not be increased or diminished, as they are strictly limited to these forms; hence they are called "restricted."

"Regarding 'above, it clarifies the intent for the arising of the teaching,' this concludes the text of the preceding three sections; it is the general intention for the arising of the Great Teaching of the School.
Now, regarding 'discerning according to our own school,' this introduces the following text, which consists of five sections that may be sought out according to the text."
Question: The previous statement was made in response to other schools; this current one is made by relying on our own school to provide a clarification. What is the difference between them? Answer:
The previous response to other schools was intended to demonstrate how the teachings of the *Caturvarga-vinaya* differ from those of other sects.
This current explanation, which relies on our own school, differs because it clarifies the underlying intent for the emergence of the *Caturvarga-vinaya* teachings.

Now, the teaching does not arise in isolation; this means that if there were no receptive conditions (*indriya-pratyaya*), the Buddha would not have preached it. Hence it is said that "the teaching does not arise in isolation.
To say that its arising must depend on persons means that when the disease of outflows (*āsrava*) arises, the medicinal Dharma accordingly applies to it.

For example, when Sūdanī returned home to beg for food and committed an act of impurity, the First Precept was established because of that. Furthermore, it was because of a bhikṣu in the forest... [that the next rule was established].
...and so forth. Regarding the formulation of precepts for the monk Dhanika and his like, it is said that they are all based on specific individuals; thus, it is called [the "person-based" approach].

As for "gathering and guiding," "hong" (弘) means extensively, and "ji" (濟) means to rescue or deliver. This phrasing is identical to the previous rule regarding the meaning of employing various methods.
The phrase "valuing the attainment of its original purport" clarifies the Buddha’s intent in establishing the teachings: it values the preservation of the ultimate goal of severing delusions.

One attains the benefit of the Way and proceeds toward Nirvana by relying on the teaching; this is for the sake of attaining the primary referent (*mūla-abhidheya*), and the primary referent is precisely Nirvana.

Regarding the statement that it is difficult to examine the details of the injunctions: "details" (*tiao*) refers to branches, and "threads" (*xu*) refers to the ends of a line. The Buddha’s intention in establishing the teaching was to cause [beings] to recognize the direction of the fundamental referent;
as for the secondary branches and their sequential order, they are truly difficult to trace. However, once the root is attained, there is no need [for the branches].

At the end of the treatise it says: "The reason for establishing [rules] such as 'opening' and so forth is as follows: when times are lean, permitting eight matters is called 'opening'; when times are prosperous, returning to prohibitions is called 'regulation.
Furthermore, for the sake of the five types of spiritual capacities, there are 'openings' and 'regulations' regarding the three robes and the one hundred and one monastic requisites;

all are for the sake of human beings. Therefore it says: "To manifest the intent of maintaining and violating [the precepts], the sincere intention lies in being without fault. Here, "sincere" (*liàng*) means "lofty" (*gāo*). Loftiness arises from...
This refers to the characteristics [of precepts]. It clarifies the characteristics of upholding and violating [the precepts], with the intention of ensuring there are no transgressions.

Therefore it is said: "Regarding the nature of prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śīla*)," for example, digging the earth or destroying living beings; their essence does not violate reason, but they obstruct and disrupt the cultivation of the path and invite worldly censure and slander.

Thus they are called "prohibitions. Because they can obstruct the right path, they are termed "prohibiting evil. Regarding "natural precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*), such as the ten [unwholesome actions]...

Unwholesome states (*akuśala*) and the like are by nature contrary to reason; regardless of whether a Great Sage has established a prohibition or not, if one performs such contrary actions, one will experience bitter fruits.
Therefore, they are called "inherently evil" (*prakṛti-duḥśīla*). Because these inherently evil states are prohibited, they are termed "natural precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*).

This inherent evil can obstruct merit, while the previously mentioned [prohibited] evil can obstruct the Path; thus, the Buddha mandated their abandonment. This inherent evil applies to both those governed by the transformative (*vinaya*) and the prohibitive (*prātimokṣa*) disciplines.

As with killing, sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth, the Sūtras further define these as transgressions of the paths of karma (*karmapatha*), while the Vinaya regulations further define them as offenses such as *pārājika*.
Therefore, it is said that they "pervade both transformation and regulation. Regarding prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) that arise due to specific faults:

this refers to cases where non-Buddhists or laypeople reckon that plants and trees possess life; the Buddha, because of this, established the prohibition, saying: [as in the case of the prohibition against digging the earth].

Regarding the statement that the nature of the precepts (śīla) is "gentle in wording but urgent in meaning," Jì explains: for example, when one commits sexual misconduct under duress from an enemy, the opening [of the rule] permits union with the object;

this is the gentleness. However, the prohibition against pleasure at the three times [of the act] is the urgency of the meaning. This means that for all the major precepts, there are corresponding texts that provide such openings.
This refers to the passages concerning exceptions found beneath the various precepts. Although the text speaks of an "exception" (*kai*), in reality, it constitutes an offense (*betsubam*).

For example, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct: if one is coerced by an enemy, an exception is granted for engaging with the object. Yet, even though engaging with the object is permitted, if one experiences pleasure during any of the three stages [of the act], an offense is still incurred.
Therefore, it is said that "although there is an exception, in reality, an offense is incurred. Regarding the term *hikishi* (slander): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *si*...
"Zhe" (者) means "it is"; "wen" (文) means "manifest. "Since these are the fundamental [principles]" and so forth refers to the conclusion of the preceding two passages.
Therefore, "hence we know" and so forth is a sentence that universally concludes the preceding text.

Regarding the phrase "the prohibitive precepts are initially established as restrictions," this refers, for example, to the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). This is an initial restriction; however, if there are conditions for generating wholesome states (*kuśala*) or extinguishing unwholesome ones (*akuśala*), one is permitted to leave for a day.
This constitutes an exception (*anujñā*). Regarding the phrase "if the fault of making an exception arises," this refers, for example, to the three robes (*tricīvara*).

This is an initial restriction, but later, due to the suffering of cold, the keeping of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) is permitted. Thus it is said: "If there is benefit, an exception is made. Since this is due to such an exception, [the fault does not arise].

"Storing [possessions] in excess invites censure and obstructs the Path; this is called 'the fault of opening [the prohibition]. Consequently, the rule of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification) was established. Thus it is said:
'Because the fault of opening arose, it was once again made subject to regulation. Is this not for the sake of preserving the transformation of the world and so forth?
This phrase serves to clarify the meaning of the preceding text. It means that because laypeople might disparage the Sangha, those born later would inevitably fall into hell."

The Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings and in order to establish the teachings, spoke thus. His great benevolence in establishing the teachings intends solely to examine those who have erred.

This section below generally concludes the intent behind the emergence of the teachings on both prohibitive (pratiṣedha) and natural (prakṛti-sāvadya) precepts. Regarding "examining those who have erred": "Examining" means, as Master Ci says, [to investigate their faults].
"Seal" (*yin*) carries the meaning of closure and confinement. Master Ying stated that "to inspect" (*jian*) means to restrain. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states:
"To inspect" means to prohibit. "Lapses" (*shi*) refers to transgressions; specifically, these are the transgressions of body and speech.

Regarding the statement that the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* establishes both the "permissive" (*śithila*) and the "strict" (*tīvra*) regulations equally, the treatise explains it as follows. According to the traditional transmission:

for a bhikṣu who wishes to engage in sexual intercourse, being permitted to relinquish the precepts and return home is the permissive regulation; whereas not being permitted [to do so] even with an animal is the strict regulation. This refers to the absence of pleasure during the three times [of the act].

Regarding theft, the view that one does not commit an offense if there is no perception of ownership is the permissive regulation; whereas not being permitted to take even grass or wood is the strict regulation.
"Urgent": To kill a human while perceiving them as a non-human is "non-offensive," which is lax; from the lowest level of an ant downward, not killing is "urgent. Regarding falsehood:
if at the time of speaking the person does not understand, there is no offense, which is lax; down to mere joking, it constitutes an offense, which is "urgent."
Therefore, it is said that the two modalities of laxity and urgency are fully established.

As for the statement that one should "seek them out to apply them universally," this refers to the fact that all two hundred and fifty precepts possess these two modalities of laxity and urgency; one should now employ these two modalities to apply them universally across all precepts.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of "prohibiting the movement toward intrinsic nature" (遮性往分).

Second, regarding the point that "the teaching, by means of both opening and prohibiting, universally applies to the two periods [past and future]," this refers to the fact that within the teachings there are both openings and prohibitions.

Now, based on these texts concerning openings and prohibitions, we investigate the intent behind the arising of the teachings. These teachings apply universally to the two periods of the present and the future; as it is said in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: [text follows].
Although I have established a rule, if it is not considered pure in other regions, it should not be applied.
Even if it was not established by me, one should practice what is beneficial in other regions.

Regarding those rules that were established and then reopened, or reopened and then re-established—such as the eight matters permitted during times of scarcity, which were permitted in times of famine but prohibited again when harvests were plentiful—this teaching, though established while the Buddha was still in the world, nevertheless applies universally even to later times.
Because it is brought forth for practical application, it is said that this "teaches for the future. Regarding the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, "Although these were prescribed by me...
they should not be used," the term "other regions" (*yifang*) refers to areas outside of the five regions of India. For example, in Western countries, cow dung is used as a means of purification;
although this was prescribed by the Buddha, it is considered impure in the borderlands and therefore may not be used there.
Although this was not established by me, it is something that cannot but be practiced.

For example, when a king decrees that the Sangha may not enter cities and such places, there are circumstances within the Buddha’s teachings that permit entry into villages after making an announcement. Therefore, it is said that while this was not established by me, it is due to the king’s prohibition.
"One must rely on the King’s teaching; therefore it is said that one cannot but practice it. This is what is called the 'teaching while in the world' of the Tathāgata.
This means that the fivefold teaching was personally proclaimed by the Buddha himself; hence it is called the "teaching while in the world."
As for the mutual integration and reciprocal inclusion of these two teachings: what the *Pañcavargika* calls "that" is what the *Caturvargika* calls "this.
The present teaching of the *Pañcavargika* and the future teaching of the *Caturvargika* are able to communicate with one another; hence it is said that they mutually include both "this" and "that."

Third, regarding the fact that the teachings are also heard repeatedly according to the strength or weakness of one's capacity: "strength and weakness" refers to the fact that the faculties (indriya) have superior, middling, and inferior levels;

thus they are called "strong and weak. Because those of inferior faculties are weak, what was permitted previously is permitted again; hence it is called "hearing repeatedly. For example, after the permission to keep extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) was granted, a further ten-day period was permitted for declaring them pure (*śuddhi-ārocana*).
Furthermore, even if one forgets this, another permission is granted so that no offense is incurred; thus it is said to be "heard repeatedly. To "hear" means to be permitted.

Furthermore, regarding the regulations, "deeply preventing" and "delimiting" refer to the following: using water free of insects is "deeply preventing," while drinking water that contains insects is "delimiting.
Therefore it is said: "The mountain and the world differ according to practice.

For instance, in a *araṇya* (wilderness) where there are no people, one is permitted to cook food oneself and is also permitted to receive food from a cow; however, within a village settlement, these are not allowed. Hence it is called "the mountain."
The worlds are not the same. "Mountains" refers to *araṇya* (forest hermitages), while "worlds" refers to villages. Thus concludes the preceding explanation of the third point:
that the retributive existence (*vipākabhava*) has varying strengths, and that the teaching is likewise subject to being heard repeatedly.
Regarding the phrase "Fourth, taking spiritual awakening as primary," etc.: When the Great Sage first established the teachings, there was originally no divergent path.

It was because the spiritual understanding of later generations naturally differed that their entry into awakening according to their respective capacities became diverse, resulting in the distinctions between the five schools and even the eighteen sects.
Since their views were already different, the gates of the teaching became separated by differences of gravity and importance; therefore, it is said that spiritual awakening is primary.

Regarding "light and heavy": according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, four coins and three small pieces constitute a grave offense, whereas according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it constitutes a light offense, and so forth.
As for the phrase "the differing tenets of the five schools," this sentence concludes the meaning that the capacities and realizations of those awakened to the Dharma differ.

Fifth, regarding the correspondence between matter (*vastu*) and dharma: for example, the three robes and one bowl are "matter," while receiving and maintaining them according to the rules is "dharma.
Applying this dharma to the aforementioned matter is what is meant by "correspondence. Since there is matter, there must be dharma;
because dharma is required in response to matter, this teaching arose. As for "dharma being merely a model": "dharma" refers to all *karmavācanās* (formal ecclesiastical acts).
"Ma" means to polish. "Kai" means that which is correct. "Shi" refers to the formal method. Regarding "those who deviate from the intent": "intent" refers to the Buddha’s intention;

if one deviates from the Buddha’s original intended method, the ritual act is not accomplished, and the matter is likewise not accomplished. Regarding "the matter pervades both emotion and nature": this clarifies the matters to which the Dharma is applied.
"Emotion" (qing) refers to the category of sentient beings, such as those receiving precepts, undergoing disciplinary treatment, or being expelled. "Nature" (xing) refers to...
The five elements are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. Such things as the boundaries of a *sīmā*, the *kaṭhina* robe, and the robes of the deceased are all insentient matters.
Regarding the establishment of gain and loss according to the object: it is said that gain and loss are established according to both sentient and insentient objects;
to maintain [the precepts] is "gain," and to violate them is "loss. Therefore, they are called "gain and loss. Alternatively, they may be based upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

The conditions (*pratyaya*) are namely: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. Regarding those of a wholesome nature: for example, a bhikṣu pulling grass from atop a stūpa, or preaching the Dharma to a woman beyond the permitted limit.
Regarding those of an unwholesome nature: for example, striking, beating, or killing humans or animals with a mind of anger. Regarding those of a neutral nature:
for example, failing to restrain the mind, damaging living plants or trees, digging the earth, and so forth; or acting in accordance with worldly censure.
Regarding "arising": for example, begging for food at improper times, wandering during the summer retreat, or not accepting offered food—all such acts are subject to reproach.
Therefore, it is said that they arise in accordance with worldly censure.

Regarding the phrase "briefly citing several articles," this refers to the five examples mentioned above. As for the expression "knowing slightly before proceeding," the *Ervih* (爾疋) states that "to proceed" (*yì*) means to advance, to arrive, or to reach.
This means that the five articles cited above refer to knowing slightly the source of the formulated precepts (*śikṣāpada*) and the place to which one proceeds;
that is to say, the "mud and water" (*nièyuè*) held in one's mind, which is the destination.

This is the intended meaning. "Direction" (*fang*) refers to a specific location. "To summarize and encompass" means to comprehensively grasp the discourse on the beginning and end of the emergence of the transformative teachings.
Upon observing the intent behind the emergence of these teachings, it is simply to cause sentient beings to reach the path of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
"What is meant by 'the learner' (śaikṣa)? This is posed as a provisional question in order to explain the meaning of "learning" and to set forth the origins from which the teaching arose;
hence the phrase "what is it. Regarding those who seek the four fruits: one plants the causes over successive lifetimes before finally realizing the four fruits.

At the very minimum, one realizes the first fruit after three lifetimes while maintaining the precepts; this refers to those of sharp faculties. Alternatively, one may maintain the precepts for seven lifetimes, or pass through six.
Having practiced for ten kalpas, one finally attains the status of a *śrāvaka* foremost among disciples, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others.

Regarding the phrase "merely following previous matters," this clarifies that although each of the subsequent thirty sections has its own intended purpose for regulation, these purposes are all explained in response to specific preceding actions;
they do not represent the fundamental intent behind the establishment of the Great Teacher’s teachings. One should seek [this intent] by examining the individual articles.
"Knowing the root" means that while the following thirty chapters are the branches, this teaching arising through a single gate is the root.

If one seeks the branches of the following thirty gates without understanding their underlying intent, one must seek this gate; only then will one recognize the fundamental purpose of the formulation.
The extensive explanation of the first section, "The Meaning of the Teaching Arising," is hereby concluded.
Regarding the second point, the intention behind establishing the categories of light and heavy according to the Vinaya teachings:

the reason this section is introduced is that, since within the subsequent chapters there are both light and heavy offenses regarding observance and violation, it is feared that people might not discern them. Therefore, this section is established to clarify the distinctions between them.

As for the phrase "it is truly difficult to adjudicate": determining and distinguishing between what is heavy and what is light is something only a Buddha can know; such is the case for the monks and nuns of the final age.

Because one does not recognize the penetration or obstruction of the faculties and the teachings, speech is difficult. To trace the source of that teaching capable of bestowing [benefit], it is none other than the Buddha;
the Teacher is also the Buddha. Those for whom it is intended are persons of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

Regarding the phrase "the medicine and the disease strike one another," this clarifies the mutual resonance between the faculties and the teaching; hence it is said, "the medicine and the disease strike one another. How could this be severed by mere sentiment?

Regarding the word "etcetera" (等): my own intention is this. It clarifies that the Buddha, having fully exhausted the capacities [of sentient beings], recognizes the gravity or lightness [of their offenses]. People today differ from the Buddha;
therefore, they cannot adjudicate between gravity and lightness. Hence it is said: "How could one possibly decide based on mere sentiment," and so forth.

"Although it is 're-examining the distant markers' (yuǎnbǐāo), it is in fact for the benefit of future descendants. 'Descendants' (yì) refers to the end; 'descendants' also implies distance. 'Examine' (hè) means reality;
'markers' (biāo) means what is looked toward, that is, the Teaching. This clarifies that the intent of the established teachings reaches far back through distant generations;
hence they are called 'distant markers. Since this is already evident in the text itself, why rely on further proof? Here, "text" (wén) refers to the Vinaya text. Now, I shall introduce this...
In brief, there are seven points. These two perspectives on lightness and gravity do not exceed these seven types of meaning.
If one understands these seven articles, the significance of lightness and gravity can be understood.
Regarding "the gradual and sudden arising of revulsion": *xing* (興) means to arise; *yan* (厭) means satiety or weariness. To clarify this by citing an example:
if one gives rise to a mind of revulsion toward wholesome states and simultaneously violates all precepts, it is called "sudden"; the offense incurred is grave.

If, however, one violates them one by one according to their sequence—violating one, two, or three—it is called "gradual"; the offense incurred is light. This is based on the gradual arising of a mind of revulsion toward wholesome states.

First, clarifying the meaning of lightness and heaviness. Second, regarding the section on establishing the formal classification of karmic actions: it is stated that because the Buddha thoroughly understood the nature of karma’s lightness and heaviness, he established the precepts;
furthermore, he classified offenses based upon these very karmic actions, and thus there are differences in their relative weight. For example, regarding the precept against killing a human being:
because humans possess much wisdom and are vessels for the Path, the retribution for the precept is superior; therefore, one who kills a human incurs a *pārājika* offense. [In contrast,] animals...
Those born into this world are not vessels for the Path; they are deluded and ignorant. Through the bonds of killing, one falls into transgression, even down to the minor offenses.

Regarding the gravity of the primary karma according to its binding nature, it is said that the results of the three types of retribution differ. As stated in the *Maudgalyāyana-questions-on-retribution-sutra*:

regarding the first offense of *pārājika* (defeat), if one falls into hell, their lifespan there will be sixty thousand years, equivalent to the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven in human terms.
The interval is nine hundred twenty-one billion sixty thousand years.

Thus, the six groups of offenses differ in the lightness or heaviness of their retributions, just as the five, eight, ten, and full precepts result in rebirth among humans, devas, or śrāvakas; however, this differs when one upholds the bodhisattva precepts.

Up until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, this is considered weighty; therefore, it is said that the retributive fruits differ. Regarding the superiority or inferiority of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), let us speak first in terms of the four precepts of the first section.

If one commits sexual misconduct with an object belonging to any of the three realms of existence, one incurs a grave offense in all cases. However, regarding the [remaining] three precepts below, there is a gradation of superiority and inferiority.

For instance, stealing the property of a human being constitutes a grave offense, whereas stealing from a non-human or an animal results in offenses of progressively lighter gravity, such as *sthūlātyaya* or *duṣkṛta*. The same applies to killing.

Regarding humans, the offense is grave; regarding non-animals, it is a *pāyattika* (Lan-ti), which is progressively lighter. Regarding false speech, it is grave for humans, whereas for non-animals it is a *dukkaṭa* (Lan-ji).

These distinctions in the gravity of the offense are all based on the superiority or inferiority of the realms (*gati*). Superiority implies length [of duration], while inferiority arises from brevity.

As for the five ways in which the arising of emotion is either false or real: take, for instance, the precept against killing; [the cases include] perceiving a human as a non-human, or perceiving a non-human as a human.

If it is a false [intention], the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a light offense. If a person forms the perception that another is a person, this is a real [intention] and the offense is grave.

Regarding theft, if one takes what belongs to no owner while perceiving it as belonging to an owner, this is a false [intention]; the preparatory offense is a *sthūlātyaya* and is light. If it is an object belonging to an owner and one perceives it as such, this is a real [intention].

The gravity of the offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is significant; therefore, it is said that the arising of emotions may be either false or real. Regarding the mutual establishment of prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) and allowances (*anujñā*):

Master Li states that in the case of a great falsehood (*mahāvadyavāda*), the prohibition as a *pārājika* is grave, whereas the allowance for speaking in jest—which still constitutes an offense—is light.

Thus, one knows that both prohibitions and allowances possess degrees of gravity. It is also like the prohibition against staying overnight separated from one's three robes (*tricīvara*), where the downfall (*pāyattika*) is grave; however, if [the circumstances differ]...

One may obtain [the robe] through meeting, opening, or relinquishing; however, to be separated from one's robe when such conditions are lacking constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). Regarding the seventh point, "distinguishing differences based on conduct":

as with the aforementioned superior person dwelling in an araṇya (wilderness), they are permitted to be separated from their robes for six nights; whereas for an inferior person dwelling in a village (*grāma*), separation from the robes is not permitted.
"Village" refers to the settlement (*grāma*), and "seclusion" refers to the araṇya. This explains the gravity or lightness of the offense based on conduct.

Regarding "the fundamental intention behind the establishment of the Vinaya": this refers to the fact that when the Buddha originally established the teachings, his underlying intent concerning their gravity did not exceed these seven types of meaning;
these seven constitute the original purport of the Vinaya. As for "the essential substance of the principles for adjudication": [it refers to...]

If one wishes to determine the gravity or lightness [of an offense], the principle must rely upon the essential substance of this school. These seven items constitute that essential substance of gravity and lightness;
therefore, it is said that "one relies on the essential substance for determination. The preceding seven sections, though differing, collectively complete the explanation of the second section:
the gate of the meaning of the gravity and lightness of the formulated teachings (*śikṣāpada*).
Regarding the third section, the intent of the "Judgment of Matters Based on the Teachings" (*jiao-pandu*) is as follows.

The purpose of this chapter is to clarify that when performing ritual acts or adjudicating offenses, one must recognize the fundamental tenets of one's own school. Fearing that others might arbitrarily engage in forced interpretations or erroneously cite other traditions, this chapter has been composed.

As for "matters," these refer to the three robes and one alms bowl, the binding and releasing of various boundaries (*sīmā*), the formal assembly (*pravāraṇā*), and the distribution of the belongings of the deceased.

"Robes" and "affairs" are both termed "confronting matters. Regarding the phrase "to judge the matter by means of the teachings": since there are already the aforementioned matters, there is, in principle, the application of the Dharma;

this Dharma is precisely the teaching. One examines the matter by means of the teaching; therefore, it is called "judging the matter by means of the teachings. "Judging" (pan) means to decide or determine; "matter" (chu) refers to the disposition or settlement.
For instance, speaking in terms of confronting the property of the deceased, one must determine right and wrong and settle the relative gravity of the items.
It is indivisible yet divided; thus, it is said that this refers to the intention of the judgment.
Regarding the statement, "The Buddha-dharma has flowed eastward for nearly six hundred years": it is called "flowing eastward" because it originated in the West and came to this land.

"Nearly six hundred" (幾六百): the character *jǐ* (幾) is pronounced *qí* (其); *jiǔ* (久) is explained as meaning "nearby" or "approximate. This clarifies that the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward from the time of the Han dynasty.

Regarding the dream last night: up until the present Zhenguan era, less than two or three years have passed since it occurred; thus, six hundred years have not yet been completed. Hence, it is said to be "nearly six hundred years.
As for those who judge right from wrong and compete to seal their own positions while opposing others:

it is like the case in the past when some relied on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to borrow robes and bowls for full ordination, yet they recited the *Caturvargika-vinaya* karmavācanā and judged that [the former] to be wrong. This is what is meant by "competing to seal."

Regarding "identity and difference": "feng" (seal) refers to being closed off. This means that one clings to what is held within their breast, blocking it so that it cannot be opened or communicated; hence it is called "competing for equality.

This truly arises because those who investigate do not recognize the fundamental principle—that is, each person receives the precepts according to their own respective school, yet when it comes to practice...
At the time of performing ritual acts, they do not recognize the fundamental tenets of their own school; consequently, they engage in disputes over similarities and differences.

This is simply because they fail to understand the essential purpose of their own tradition. Jie (Jizang) said: "Without knowing the tenets of the five schools, one arbitrarily uses the tenets of one's own school to determine the transgressions and observances of others.
Thus it is said, "not recognizing the tenets," and so forth. It is said that those who perform ritual acts are muddled regarding the fundamental intent.

This means that even those who perform the rites within their own specific section may still be bewildered when determining the gravity or lightness of an offense, failing to recognize the characteristics of what is light or heavy within that very section;
thus it is said they are "confused regarding their own course. "Confusion" here implies darkness. One must perform the rites according to the school of one's original ordination.
If one were now to take the *Mahāsāṃghika* text on the wearing of robes and apply it to this present section for practice, it would be called being "confused regarding [one's own tradition]."
This is the fundamental intent.

Regarding the statement that "one who upholds the teaching must wear the true texts," "wearing" refers to carrying them upon oneself. This means consulting the texts of the Vinaya-piṭaka so as not to become a false teacher.
Since one carries the true texts, one understands the essential principles; because one understands the essential principles, one's conduct and practice do not fall into confusion. Because...
Because one is not confused or distracted, one does not incur the shame of others’ ridicule, slander, or humiliation.

Regarding the phrase "to sink into derision" (*chīzé*): "to sink" (*lún*) means to submerge, to drown, or to be submerged. Regarding "derision" (*chī*): according to the *Bópǐ*, it means to treat lightly; according to the *Zìshū*, it means to laugh.
Master Ying states that "derision" (pronounced *sǐzhī fǎn*) refers to contemptuous mockery. Here, by clearly adhering to the authentic texts, one avoids both light ridicule and heavy [reproach].
This is an excessive criticism.

How could it be that those who clarify the *Sui* (隨) school elsewhere maintain that its basis for receiving the precepts is originally the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*), yet in their current practice they still rely on the observance of the *Four-Part Vinaya*, and if the text and meaning of the *Four-Part Vinaya* are complete, they simply employ it? How could they possibly employ the *Ten Recitation Vinaya* (*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*) instead?
This is merely to clarify and resolve the textual passages.

As for the phrase "fearing that [the reader] may not yet understand the great outline (*mahā-koṭi*)": this refers to the fundamental purport and essential tenets previously explained, which are termed the "great outline.
Although the above has provided a general summary—a concise and approximate description of these great outlines—it is still feared that people of the present day may remain in doubt.

[The previous explanation] is finished. Therefore, it is said: "I still fear you may not understand. Now, wishing to provide clear and explicit instruction, it is said: "Furthermore, I shall show its limits (*pramāṇa*). My own interpretation is as follows: "Furthermore, I shall show its limits" refers generally to this present section. "Lest one should incur transgression" (*tuō lí qiān shī*): *tuō* (脫) is an indeclinable particle; furthermore, *tuō* means "error. *Lí* (罹) [is pronounced with the initial *l* and final *-i*] means "to be caught in a net. To seek to clarify the relative gravity of offenses and violations by adhering exclusively to this single school while misguiding others is to cause their remorse for past sins to remain unextinguished, thereby incurring sin oneself and causing them further transgression;
both fall into the net of guilt. To say that this applies only to the ignorant who do not study clarifies what has been stated above regarding oneself.

Regarding the Dharma they have studied, they judge others' observance or violation of the precepts; not only do they fail to cause the transgressions of others to be cleared away, but they further increase their own offense of ignorance for failing to study.
Therefore, they are called "deluded. Delusion is precisely ignorance.
Regarding the statement, "Now, by establishing a comprehensive fixed framework (*dingge*), we collectively achieve a standard for comparison," *Sheng* says:

This clarifies that the previous [position] adhered to a single corner [of the doctrine], recognizing only its own school while failing to recognize other sects. Now, thirty sections are established to comprehensively reveal all schools, with each section producing the names of ten consciousnesses from the *Mahāsāṃghika* and other traditions;
this is called a "fixed framework. "Framework" (*ge*) means "correct" (*zheng*). That is to say, by citing various schools, we collectively establish this.
Each school individually demonstrates its own name, which is precisely to establish the definitive standard. Regarding the collective establishment of a comparative benchmark:

when one now adjudicates matters according to the textual teachings of this *Dharmaguptaka* school, if the specific circumstances differ, one then cites the common practices of various schools to collectively establish the ritual procedures for this single school.

This ensures that everything is complete and clear; thus it is said, "it forms a comparative standard" (*jiao-zhun*). "Comparative" (*jiao*) means clarity; "standard" (*zhun*) means evenness, measurement, or (according to the *Erlie* glossary) literary expression.
Regarding the phrase "once one opens the articles and the collar," this refers to the thirty sections below as the "articles" and designates this present section as the "collar.

This is intended to clarify the matters regarding the scope of the provisional teachings (*jiaojiao*) within those thirty sections, by citing texts from various divisions (*bu*) as a general overview.

Regarding the abandonment of transgressions, the observance of precepts, the primary substance of the vow and its secondary practices, the contradictions and non-contradictions between light and heavy offenses, and the meanings of equality and inequality—I feared that confusion might arise, so I have cited the texts, yet they remained obstructed within my mind.
By illuminating them with this present section, once one has opened this gate, all doubts and obstructions will be entirely removed;
this is called "vast and clear observation. "Explanation" (*śe*) means to eliminate, to discard, and to resolve. "Observation" (*guān*) means to illuminate.

Regarding the fourth [section], which employs the textual meanings of various schools: since all thirty sections utilize texts from other schools, this section has been introduced so that one might not fear failing to grasp their overall intent.
As stated in the preceding preface, "encompassing the authentic texts of different schools and summarizing the teachings of various scriptures," this refers precisely to this section.
"Fundamentally, it is originally a single text. This means that when one traces the Buddha’s establishment of the precepts, they were originally but a single text.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa compiled the Dharma-piṭaka through oral recitation. It was transmitted successively by five masters across different generations, without any divergent views arising;

hence it is said, "fundamentally, it is originally a single text. However, as for the differences in the awakening of sentient beings' faculties, this is an interpretation based on the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
The tradition states that after one hundred years, [the teachings] were divided into five schools; after two hundred years, into twelve schools;
and after four hundred years, into eighteen schools. Regarding the division into five schools:

while Upagupta was still in the world, King Aśoka and the great master of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-śāstra* discussed the Buddha-dharma together. At that time, the various individuals held differing views based on their own personal perspectives.
There was partiality and dogmatic attachment; Kūṭadanta could not adjudicate what was correct, and consequently, this Piṭaka was divided into these five canons.
Thus it is said that "the capacities for awakening differ," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "those who establish their own peaks": a high mountain is called a "peak" (yue).
Likewise, the various five masters each clung to their own views, which is termed "calculation" (ji)—meaning they were attached to their own calculations and desires—and each claimed, "This is mine."
Regarding their views: each claims its own position is high and preeminent; thus, they are said to be "like mountains.
As for those who compete to adopt the texts of the Mahāsāṃghika (the Great Assembly), at the time of the first council, they were divided into two sections:

the Sthavira (Elders) and the Mahāsāṃghika. The city interior was the Sthavira section, while the city exterior was the Mahāsāṃghika section. As for that Sthavira section, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa, five...

The masters transmitted and upheld [the teachings] until, after more than one hundred years had passed, they split into five schools. What is referred to here as the "Mahāsāṃghika" (Great Assembly) school is the former Sthavira school;
it is called the Mahāsāṃghika because its followers were numerous, and not because of the "Great Assembly" that held the council outside the city mentioned in the previous discussion.
Here, the wording of the *Chao* (Excerpts) is overly broad.

Regarding the two precepts concerning physical contact, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* generally classifies them as *sthūlātyaya*. The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If the intent is directed toward a male, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the intent is directed toward a female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.

Therefore, it is said that the gravity of offenses differs in their respective scopes. Regarding the distinction between observance and violation: for instance, in the demarcation of a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*... [text fragment ends]

the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) mentions storehouses; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Great Assembly Vinaya) mentions multi-storied pavilions; the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Great Commentary) mentions the "boundary of the path of practice" (*caryā-mārga-sīmā*);

Therefore, it is said that "existence and non-existence alternate. Regarding "the abandonment and the arising manifesting each other": this is as in the case of the demarcation of a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*). Both the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) contain textual accounts of this, yet their treatments regarding its abandonment and arising differ.

therefore, they are said to "mutually manifest" [the teaching]. Second, regarding "following the original": re-enactment is termed "following the original," such as the enactment within the forest, which concerns the same offense committed by those approaching [a nun]. Third, regarding "the words of the Dharma Master":
this refers to the explicitness of the text through the fourfold application of meaning. Now, citing the intent of this treatise, I wish to adopt the meaning of the fourth phrase.

"Applying the meaning" fulfills the intent of the present section. Regarding the phrase "and the extensive explanations by the Tripiṭaka masters and others," the term "others" refers to the Tripiṭaka teachings themselves, not to specific individuals.

As for the phrase "equal to the text and phrases," the term "equal" means that he establishes the explanation of the fourth point, the "functioning of the text. However, as for the reason why these four dharmas from within this treatise are cited here:

This is the section on the method of interpreting the meaning of the texts from other schools; it correctly takes up the meaning of the fourth phrase as a skillful means to apply the text concerning "usage" (*yòng*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "However, the task of the treasury of practice is truly difficult," "practice" (*xíng*) refers to taking up [virtues], while "treasury" (*zàng*) refers to relinquishing [defilements]. One who desires...

Since it was previously clarified that adopting and discarding are not easy matters, I now wish to clarify my own adoption [of the teachings] beyond [other systems].

This refers to those within this school for whom both the text and its meaning are complete. What follows below is precisely the explanation and exposition of the Great Exposition (*Mahāvyākhyāna*). Regarding "both text and meaning being complete":

This is an unresolved teaching. After the emergence of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* teachings, all such practices were prohibited.

Because these unresolved teachings in the Vinaya existed prior to the time when the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* abolished them, it is said that "the matter remained unresolved prior to the abolition. According to another interpretation, there is no textual basis for this.

This is called "correspondence of meaning and force. Therefore, one takes the text of the *Sarvāstivāda* to establish the practice of maintaining the robe according to the *Dharmaguptaka*.

Regarding "necessarily [considering] urgency or laxity, heaviness or lightness," for instance, in the case of receiving the robe for a period of days, the *Sarvāstivāda* rule of thirty-nine nights until the completion of the *kaṭhina* ceremony is "lax" (*śithila*), whereas the *Dharmaguptaka*...
Regarding the three grades of urgency based on conditions: the *Mahīśāsaka* rule that one must protect one's robes by attending a single session throughout the night is considered lax;
