according to the *Dharmaguptaka*, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, which is light. Regarding the distinction between what is and is not a formal rule: the *Sarvāstivāda* states that receiving the precepts when the preceptor is not present is [an invalid case]. Fourth.

The *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya) considers [the case of] receiving the precepts while borrowing robes to be invalid; the *Mahīśāsaka* (Five-Part Vinaya) considers it valid. The *Mahīśāsaka* considers [the case of] a layperson receiving the precepts to be invalid;

This refers precisely to the present passage. Therefore, as for the listing of four explanations in the text, it means that within the Vinaya text there are four major detailed expositions (mahā-vastu), which are clarified in the *Caturvagga-vastu* (The Section on the Fourfold Group).
First, someone says: "I have heard such words from the presence of the Buddha.
Second, [hearing] from a harmonious Saṃgha consisting of four or more persons. Third, [hearing] from a group of many persons consisting of three or fewer.
Regarding "hearing": when one hears from a single person, one should not immediately believe it. One should examine whether it accords with the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
One should say: "Does what the Venerable One has said accord with the Dharma or not? (and so forth).

Now, these four modes of hearing are cited to clarify the application of the phrase "if the words and phrases [of the teaching] are equal"; if they are not equal, one should not accept them. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Regarding the meaning of "seal" (*mòyìn*): it is the same as the extensive explanation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The term "seal" differs; its various explanations are not fixed. Regarding "movement that accords with the compass and the rule" (*guīyóu*): "compass" (*guī*) means round, standard, or square; "rule" (*yóu*) means method. This refers to movement that accords with methods and standards.
Regarding "why would the principle be obscured? (*lǐ hé huìmò*): "obscured" (*huì*) means dark. This refers to my current composition of this text.
This means that its textual meaning is clear and manifest, as it is not obscured or lost; thus it is so called.

If one does not reflect upon and examine the various schools but instead adheres dogmatically to a single corner—meaning that one fails to see the explicit texts of the various schools and directly adopts only a single passage from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*—"mirror" (*jing*) refers to clarity, and "illumination" (*zhao*) refers to the meaning.
"Examining" (*lan*) refers to seeing. If one engages with matters in this way, then one's understanding will not be comprehensive.
"Affairs" refers to matters such as holding robes or adding medicinal ingredients. "The affairs are not comprehensive" means that there is no textual record for the preceding matter;
hence it is called "not comprehensive. This refers, for example, to the first master who merely held [the object] in his hand without uttering a word;
this is what is meant by being "not comprehensive. Regarding the phrase "the text has nothing to rely upon," Zhi Li says: "As stated below, the first master said, 'I have collated...'"
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is no textual basis for the practice of holding medicine with one's robes; therefore, one simply holds it in hand.

To point mutual faults at one another out of delusion truly arises from a lack of formal instruction. This means that those who adopt the practices of other schools point to those who do not as being deluded.
Those who do not accept [the teaching] point to those who do as being deluded. Such mutual refutations arise because they have failed to penetrate the various teachings;
thus it is said: "It is truly due to the absence of the teaching."

Regarding the statement that the textual limits for the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) are restrictive, [Dao]li says: "The *Caturvargika* holds that if one's robes and bowl are incomplete, this constitutes a limit where the precepts cannot be obtained;
such cases are not to be accepted. This refers to the textual passage concerning robes in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya)."
Regarding "either two Vinayas": within this school, one Vinaya is treated as primary, while the other three Vinayas are collectively treated as a single Vinaya;

thus, they are referred to as "two Vinayas. Regarding "both text and meaning being clearly elucidated": for instance, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Caturvargika-vinaya* are called "the two Vinayas.

Since both contain the textual passages concerning the fifteenth-day and the monthly observances, they are said to be "doubly clear. One may then freely adopt from them according to the tenets of one's own school. [End of] personal [note].

Regarding this passage, there are two interpretations. The first interpretation holds that when performing the ritual, one must personally consult the sacred teachings; thus, it is intended to exhort future generations.

The second interpretation maintains that this sentence precisely expresses the author’s own intent. By stating, "I now take [the teachings] from other schools," he indicates that he has personally consulted them himself rather than relying on hearsay;
therefore, it is said that among the six masters, one or two texts are explicit. Third...

The Master’s intention is as follows: in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, the section on the renunciation of the precepts merely states that the renunciation is not valid when performed before a mad person;

however, it does not clarify whether [the presence of such a person] counts toward the quorum. Since the meaning ought to be established by the Vinaya texts yet remains unresolved therein, this Master relies upon the explicit text of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Daśādhyāya-vinaya) to extensively clarify the characteristics of what constitutes a sufficient and what an insufficient quorum, thereby employing the rules of another school (*nikāya*). As for why other schools do not possess this specific teaching, it is because... [text ends].

The Master likewise did not adopt the fourth method of chanting the precepts by means of melodic singing. Although the textual evidence for practices such as the demarcation of pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is clear, he did not employ them because they were discarded by other schools. Thus, he did not use them.
"Others are also consulted" means that "consultation" (sān) arises from similarity; it is also called "intermingling" (zá).

Regarding the phrase "gains and losses depend on the occasion and knowing the time," this clarifies that the views held by various masters differ. If one adopts the textual applications of external [non-Buddhist] traditions, it is termed a "gain."
Not adopting external texts is called a failure. Regarding the phrase "according to capacity" (*suiji*), both success and failure are termed "according to capacity.
To adopt external texts is called succeeding according to capacity; if one does not adopt them, this is also called failing according to capacity.

Thus, these instances of success and failure, as well as adoption and rejection, are all in accordance with what is appropriate for the occasion. Nevertheless, because its application requires knowledge of the proper time, [one must act accordingly].

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the fifth section, "Resolving and Unifying the Textual Meaning": the intent behind this passage is as follows. In the preceding section, it was stated that there are certain meanings for which no textual evidence exists, yet there are matters for which no texts exist.
Now, in order to resolve and unify this original intent, the following passage cites the fact that the eras [in question] are remote and distant, and so forth.
Now, as for the statement that "the principle fundamentally transcends names," this clarifies that the ultimate principle of *tathatā* (suchness) fundamentally transcends names and language;
because the path of speech is severed, it is said to "transcend names. Therefore, when a name is established to mark its ultimate tenet, this refers to using a name to summon forth the principle.
For instance, although all names and designations function to explain the principle, even though the true principle transcends names and language, it nonetheless requires reliance upon them.

Only through names and conventions can one cognize the principle. Just as the moon, though not the finger itself, is ultimately seen by relying on the finger, if one does not now designate names, one will not know the ultimate limit of the principle—such as *tathatā* (thusness), *nirvāṇa* (extinction), *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), *pāra* (the other shore), or *sukha* (bliss).
Liberation is likewise a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). If these names were not established, by what means could the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) be expressed?
Therefore, it is said that "names are established" and so forth. As for "names manifesting in accordance with phenomena," "phenomena" refers here to both sentient and non-sentient things.

Names are provisionally formulated in relation to these phenomena; because these are the dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are called such. Thus, this text is prepared in correspondence with phenomena.

Regarding matters such as the formal demarcation of boundaries for robes and bowls (*cīvara-pātra-sīmā-bandha*) or the retreat during the rains (*varṣā*), there are indeed texts for receiving and upholding [the precepts], as well as texts for binding and releasing them.
However, when one examines this Vinaya Piṭaka and finds that both its words and its matters are comprehensive, this examination arises from certainty.

That is to say, the teachings within the Vinaya are complete in their application to both specific matters and the underlying principles; hence it is said that "both words and matters are comprehensive. The term "myaò-miào" (miao-miao) describes a state of profound depth and remoteness.

"Voice and color" refers to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. It must rely upon vocal sound; "voice" (*sheng*) signifies the teaching, while "color" (*cai*) signifies form—that is, the subtle and wondrous form of the Buddha’s body.
Regarding "the Dharma perishing as time shifts": because the period since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is remote and distant, and the Dharma perishes according to the passage of time, it is said:
Bin said, "In recent times, there was an evil king in the Western Regions who destroyed the Buddha-Dharma. At that time, there was an elder..."
He was one whose heart was deeply moved by the lamentable state of the world, as there were no monks available for him to make offerings to.

Suddenly, while on the road, he encountered an elderly monk and immediately invited him home, where he prepared a porridge made of pure milk. When the monk took a single mouthful, he appeared sorrowful and distressed. The elder, finding this strange, asked, "Is the porridge not good?"
The monk replied, "Does the elder recognize me? I am a son of the Buddha, Rāhula. The reason for my grief is this:
although this porridge is made entirely of milk, I perceive its flavor to be inferior to the porridge boiled with pure water during the Buddha’s lifetime;
its taste was superior to this. The water used when the Buddha was present was more excellent than the milk of today. It is because I reflect upon this that I weep."

From this, it may be inferred that the "Dharma-water" has likewise diminished. Thus it is said: "Matters are largely incomplete. Since the Dharma is fundamentally supported by matters, now that the Dharma is insufficient, matters are consequently deficient.
For example, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lacks texts concerning the "holding of robes" (*cīvara-dhāraṇa*) and so forth, such that one cannot discern the prior procedures for holding robes;
hence they are called "incomplete. Furthermore, regarding the "five masters" and so on, this refers to the differing tenets of the five schools.

Now, in synthesizing these to achieve a comprehensive vision, my own view is this: the Vinaya of the five schools contains contradictions in both word and meaning, and their standards for gravity and lightness are mutually inconsistent.

They cannot be reconciled through mere sentiment, nor can they be resolved through intellectual interpretation alone. Since ancient times, those who have clung to these disputes have continued them through successive generations.
It is not so. Now, they are all comprehensively integrated; therefore, it is said that this constitutes a "great view.

If one were to claim that both the text and the meaning are deficient, and thus cites one case as an analogy for all others—stating, for instance, that regarding the precept against eating at improper times, there is neither a textual provision for an exception nor a logical basis for an exception—and that since this one case is thus, all other precepts are likewise so—this argument is incorrect. (As stated in the *Jingzhong*)

Regarding this section, the outline is divided into four parts. From the beginning up to this point, these are synthesized to provide a general overview for the purpose of clarifying the definitive universal application and to discern the intent of all the schools (*nikāya*).

This means that although the original canon possessed [these texts], they were missing due to various conditions; it is not that they did not originally exist, but rather they are now restored through this universal application.
This summarizes the sectarian tenets to fulfill the preceding requirement of supplementing what was missing. The second part concerns those instances where both the text and its meaning are missing.
The final four phrases correctly distinguish whether the application of the decision is appropriate or not. There are four such phrases.
Regarding the first, the phrase where both the text and the meaning are deficient need not be adopted. Next, there are three phrases, all of which are judged as requiring adoption.

Third, although it is indeed difficult to establish or discard the definitive application of both text and meaning, the difficulty lies in clearly demonstrating that definitive application. Fourth, the passage beginning with "Therefore, the Vinaya says... cites the scriptural text as proof.

Regarding the meaning of "difficult to resolve": as for the second point, "if both text and meaning are deficient," this means that if within these five schools both the text and meaning are deficient, it is not appropriate to adopt the text from another school.

The general intent of this section is that, among the four *dharmaguptaka* schools, where text and meaning are mutually deficient, one should take the text and meaning from various other schools to complete this particular school. Since the text and meaning...
Both [text and meaning] are missing. Why must one take the text from another school? Therefore, it is known that this passage should not be adopted. To cite one example as representative of many:

within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, both text and meaning are missing; since there are many precepts, I shall take the single precept against eating at improper times (*vikāla-bhojana*) as an illustration for all the other precepts—this is what is meant by the phrase (which is the explanation given in the *Da-jue-ji*).
Or, when something exists according to principle and thereby establishes a prior matter, such as the practice of keeping robes (*cīvara-dhāraṇa*).
This is an example of explaining medicinal substances. Although the principles are inherently present, they must be established to complete the matter of maintaining robes (*cīvara*).

Therefore, the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is taken to establish this school’s practice of maintaining robes. Thus it is said: "In some cases, although the wording is complete, there may be deficiencies in the meaning. In such instances, the intent of other schools is also adopted;
for example, regarding the five kinds of formal food (*pañca-prakāra-bhojana*), although the wording is complete, the meaning is deficient. This is as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Because the original teachings have been lost, we now take the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to definitively establish the meaning of the four missing sections; hence it is said that "the meaning is established.

As for the commentators, they previously used the intent of the *Sudarsana-vinaya* as a provisional interpretation. Alternatively, although the meaning must necessarily be established, there is no explicit textual authority within the specific school (or division) itself.

Regarding the width and narrowness of the establishment of a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) merely states that one must travel back and forth within a single day.

Now, according to the principles of this [present] interpretation, we adopt the measurement of three *yojanas* from the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Therefore, it is said: "This is to cease further slander. This means that we do not adopt the passage from the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) concerning the addition of medicine or the carrying of robes;
otherwise, outsiders would immediately say: "The teachings within your school are insufficient, for there are explicit texts currently existing in other schools."
"Why do you not accept it? This is because [the opponent] is one who clings to their own preconceptions and guards their own position like a person waiting for a hare at a stump.

However, as the textual meaning is decisively clear, it is truly difficult to reject or establish [an alternative]. This correctly concludes the preceding passage. Regarding "opening and closing" (*kai-sha*), these refer to permission and prohibition.
Otherwise, there would be an accumulation of faults within one's own mind; thus, that which is of no benefit to the external realm is [the case] if one does not understand the decisive resolution.

The meaning of "penetrating" [the intent] is as follows: to uphold the Dharma and apply it to another person without benefiting oneself or the other—meaning that the prior matter is not accomplished and one further incurs an offense—is what is meant.

Therefore, the Vinaya states, "where the text and meaning are identical," which refers to the twelve additional articles in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. There are four propositions; the first proposition is: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a commentary on a specific section of the Vinaya regarding legal procedures and the consequences of improper application.*
Regarding the phrase "the text and meaning are identical": this refers to cases where both the Bhikṣu and Bhikṣuṇī divisions each have five categories [of offenses].
Regarding the second point, "the text is identical while the meaning differs": this refers to the practice of using water containing insects. Because it equally protects life, the text is the same;

yet, as for the meaning expressed, they differ—such as in the calculation of fetal months and intercalary months. That is to say, the precept on reducing years did not permit the inclusion of fetal and intercalary months, whereas in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Receiving the Precepts), it does.

There is also the opening for the *garbha-vyantara* (intercalary month). Although these two texts are identical in wording, their meanings differ. Regarding the reduction of years [for ordination], it is not yet an opening;
however, within the *Upādhyāya-pātayantika*, there is an opening for the disciple to obtain the precepts. Thus, the meaning differs.

As for the fourth case where both the text and the meaning differ, it is like the different precepts for monks and nuns. Furthermore, regarding those that follow the Sūtras and Vinaya, such as the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is that which gives rise to nirvāṇa.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are three matters: first, the "original incident," which refers to Sudinna;

second, the "formulation of the precept," which means that based on this original incident, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and established the prohibitions; third, the "subsequent formulation," which refers to [the rules] within the forest.

This is the established rule. Regarding the "Two-Part Vinaya": this refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, whose initial section lists the fundamental precepts for the two assemblies of monks and nuns.
Furthermore, regarding the "exegesis of the Vinaya" (*vinayārtha-vyākhyāna*): this refers to the entire *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as a single canonical collection known by the general name *Vinaya*.
This means that after the fundamental precepts are first listed at the beginning of that Vinaya, each one is subsequently cited and explained; what is thus explained applies universally.
This is because it is the *vinaya*. "Increasing by one" (*ekottara*) refers to the *Ekottarika-āgama* (the *Ten Recitations Ekottara*).

This means from one up to ten; because one is added to each preceding number, it is called "increasing by one. Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, and what is light and what is heavy: for example, the five primary colors are termed "impure."
"Not permitted to wear" is termed *pratikṣepa* (prohibition). If it is not one of the five primary colors, it is pure; if its wearing is permitted, that is an *anujñā* (allowance).

An allowance is light, whereas a prohibition is heavy; thus they are called "light and heavy. Regarding the phrase "these are impure prohibitions," etc., this refers to the text of that Vinaya itself.
Regarding the phrase "weighing such things as the beginning and the end," etc., this refers to the preceding and following passages of that same Vinaya.

A bhikṣu who is able to know the five characteristics: first, the origin; second, the formulation of the precept; third, the subsequent application; fourth, the discernment of the characteristics; and fifth, the exceptions. Regarding the discernment of the characteristics:
it refers to [the measurement] of even a hair’s breadth and so forth. Regarding the exceptions: those such as mental derangement or insanity are all termed "exceptions.
One who does not look to the countenance of others possesses clear understanding within themselves and has no doubt or fear in their heart; how could they possibly look [to others]?

Regarding the phrase "Its colors are as stated above; the text is abbreviated, and for details it is as explained therein," this means that in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* there are five characteristics.
The first three are abbreviated as above, corresponding to the three matters in the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*. The latter two characteristics are as explained in detail in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*;
hence the statement.

Regarding the meaning of the sixth section, "The Teaching and Its Referent": The preceding section resolved the ambiguity by allowing for the inclusion of various schools so that the texts might be complete;
however, it was not yet known what those texts actually refer to. This section exists for that reason. "Teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to the means of expression (*vācaka*).
"Referent" (*vācya*) refers to the two types of retention (*dhāraṇī*) and the two types of transgression (*āpatti*).
The texts that explain the teachings refer specifically to the Vinaya texts. Their primary purport concerns upholding and violating the precepts; therefore, it is said:
"This work clarifies only upholding and violating."
Regarding the statement that "the objects [of discipline] pertain to both the internal and external": this refers to the two modes of conduct, observance (*dhāraṇa*) and transgression (*āpatti*).

One may take the internal mind as the object of observance or transgression, or one may take external phenomena as the object of observance or transgression; therefore it is said [that they are both]. "Internal" refers to the mind that performs the action (*karmasamutthāna-citta*).

This means that among the four mental aggregates—consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*)—one performs the first three. These belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state and cannot constitute karma. [Karma is constituted only when] it flows into the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*).
The mind, according to whether it performs good or evil, subsequently constitutes the formation of karma. Regarding what is called "forming karma": what kind of karma is formed?
It refers to the karma of upholding or violating the precepts. When the three poisons arise within, this is violation;

taking these poisons as the object, when one gives rise to the three virtues within, this is termed "upholding," which means taking the virtuous mind as the object of upholding. These two objects are both bound together within the active mind.
It is not the three types of non-defined (avyākṛta) mentioned previously. Therefore it is said: "The external refers to circumstances that are favorable or adverse.

"Circumstances" (qing) refers to the realm of sentient beings; "matters" (shi) refers to the realm of non-sentient things. Within these two realms, there are both observances and transgressions; hence, they are termed "favorable and adverse.

To ensure that the practice of the teachings conforms to them from beginning to end without transgression: "teachings" (jiao) refers to the Vinaya teachings, while "practice" (xing) refers to mental conduct.

As for "following" (*xún*): Shen says that "following" means "circling," which signifies the sense of being uninterrupted. Sheng says that "following" means "traversing. It refers simply to applying the teachings to one's practice;
to traverse the characteristics [of the precepts] such that they do not correspond with conditions for transgression is what is called "maintaining" them.
Ci says that "following" has the meaning of "correspondence"; it means to correspond with the teachings, speaking of being without transgression from beginning to end.

"Beginning" refers to the moment one first receives full ordination (*upasampadā*). "End" refers to the exhaustion of a single lifetime’s retribution. To maintain its purity and brilliance is called "non-transgression.

As for those who have not studied the Dharma since birth and have heard nothing of it: this is termed "since birth" from the time they first received ordination; it does not mean from the moment they emerged from their parents' wombs.

Such individuals do not recognize the characteristics of what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed, nor the gravity or lightness of offenses, nor the distinctions between what is permitted, what is prohibited, and what is right or wrong.
Therefore, it is said that one has not heard the Dharma. How is it known that from the time one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) onward is called being "born"?
A verse in the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "One born through the Buddha's precepts is truly born; just like Aṅgulimāla, as the Tathāgata prophesied.
As for the phrase "this includes both merit and punishment," it refers to a newly ordained person who, not knowing the characteristics of the teachings, sees grass upon a stūpa.

If one hopes to gain merit by cleaning a stupa or pulling weeds, yet that hope violates the Buddha’s teachings, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense; therefore, it is said to be both merit and punishment.

Regarding the reality or unreality of the circumstances: among the nine categories of training rules, if one recognizes the object (*vatthu*) and recognizes the offense (*āpatti*), the root offense is established—this is what is meant by "reality.
If one does not recognize the object, does not recognize the offense, or is in doubt, the root offense is likewise established; this is termed "circumstance" (*sattika*).
"Empty. Regarding "the reality or unreality of the matter": among the five propositions concerning the object and the perception, in the first and second propositions the object is real;

in the third proposition, both reality and unreality can be discerned—such as when a non-human or an animal comes to take one's place. In the first proposition, the offense is *pārājika*; in the latter [third] proposition, the offense is *sthūlātyaya*.

Although *pārājika* and *sthūlātyaya* differ, they are both violations; hence it is said, "without distinction," etc. This is called the general designation for "observance and violation," meaning that broadly speaking...

Regarding the circumstances, one clarifies the nature of their observance or violation; however, because the relative gravity of these acts has not yet been distinguished, they are termed "general" (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
As for "binding the primary offenses," this refers to the formal adjudication of the primary offenses within the five categories (*pañca-varga*).

Regarding "exhaustively investigating the various punishments," this means that when sentencing a crime, one must first thoroughly examine its gravity. "Binding the preparatory acts" (*prayoga*) and so forth refers to gathering [the relevant factors].

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) constitutes the offense for the result (*phala*). First, one must inquire into the nature of the transgression and observe where that transgression corresponds with the teaching—is it corresponding to the preparatory stage, or is it corresponding to the point of the result?

This is the principle of weighing and verifying the actual facts of the case. Regarding "attaining lightness or heaviness according to reason and teaching": "reason" (*yukti*) refers to the violation of the path of action (*karmapatha*) against reason.

Regarding "offenses": "teaching" refers to offenses incurred by violating the formal precepts (*śikṣāpada*). That is to say, violating the principle is grave, while violating the teaching is light. Now, in adjudicating cases, one must skillfully discern this gravity and lightness;

only then can one distinguish between the two boundaries of principle and teaching, whereby the adjudication becomes crystal clear. "Weedy" (*wú*) means that the ground is overgrown with weeds and filth.
This refers to having already investigated and ascertained the actual facts so that they correspond with the teaching; thus, one may judge whether there has been an observance or a violation.
There is no fault of over-extending the categories. This is termed "distinguishing observance and violation" (*dhāraṇa-āpatti-vibhāga*). This is spoken in terms of their respective antidotes;
therefore, it is said that observance and violation are explained separately.

Regarding the intent behind the establishment of the universal and specific teachings for the seven groups of monastics and laypeople: the seven groups consist of the five classes of ordained practitioners and the lay followers.
The two assemblies are called the seven divisions. As for "teachings," they refer to the two types of instruction: the transformative (*hua*) and the regulatory (*zhi*).

Regarding the fact that there are many paths in the teachings that reveal principle: this means that the Buddha established teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, all for the purpose of revealing the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Since the capacities of sentient beings differ individually, the teachings also vary according to those capacities; thus, there are many paths. Nevertheless...
It does not go beyond the two gates of transformation (*vaipulya*) and regulation (*vinaya*); hence it is said that "the great divisions are twofold.

As for "generally clarifying cause and effect," this means generally clarifying how the two causes of good and evil evoke the two results of suffering and happiness—namely, that practicing good and cultivating merit brings reward, while committing evil incurs retribution;
and that through patience one gains an upright appearance, while by refraining from killing one attains longevity, and so forth. Hence it is called "general" (*fan*).
This refers to clarity and so forth. Regarding "the consciousness that discerns the heterodox and the orthodox," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This is the Buddha’s teaching; this is Māra’s teaching.
To store the eight impure things is heterodox; not to store them is orthodox. Those who store them are the retinue of Māra."

Those who are not disciples of the Buddha and do not believe in cause and effect are heterodox; taking refuge in the Triple Gem is orthodox, as explained in detail in the "Heterodoxy and Orthodoxy" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the classification of karmic actions that are profound and difficult to discern—for instance, in the *Parinirmita-vinaya* (Transformation Teachings), it merely states that one should not kill living beings without distinguishing between the categories of light and heavy offenses regarding killing. Now, I wish to classify these lighter [offenses].
Because one does not know the weight of karma, it is said to be difficult to know.

That which makes its retribution manifest, clear, and easy to describe is, for example, when a person who observes the five, eight, or ten wholesome precepts attains rebirth among humans or devas. By directly observing the cause, one knows the future retribution.
Therefore, it is said that [the teachings] are clear and easy to describe.
Regarding the phrase "the two types of disciplinary teachings" (*xingjiao*): Master Nanshan said, "As for 'disciplinary teachings,' one gives rise to understanding based on the teachings;

because they cannot be accomplished without practice, they are called 'disciplinary teachings' (*xingjiao*). They are also called 'prescriptive teachings' (*zhijiao*), for the teachings arise from prescriptions; thus they are called 'prescriptive teachings'. [The section on] Concentration (*dìng*)...
Regarding the principles of acceptance and rejection: if one acts in accordance with the teachings and the Dharma, it is called "acceptance" (taking).

If one acts in contravention of the teachings and is contrary to the Dharma, it is not to be practiced; this is called "rejection. As for establishing the fundamental framework: the five categories and seven groups of offenses constitute the framework.

Resolving doubts and obstructions refers to uncertainties regarding transgressions or observances, and doubts concerning the gravity of an offense, which have remained unresolved and stagnant for many years.
When one does not understand a matter, upon seeing a single passage of the Vinaya text, understanding is immediately attained; hence it is said that this "resolves doubts and obstructions.

Regarding the phrase "pointing to specific matters and explaining them in detail," this refers to the teaching of practice (*pratipatti-śāsana*). In each and every precept, one points to each specific case and explains it in detail.

This differs from the general explanations found in the preceding *pariyāya-śāsana* (doctrinal teachings), where matters such as sexual misconduct and theft do not explicitly specify the object or the locus of the offense. In the present Vinaya teachings, these are made explicit.

Regarding the distinctions in the gravity of offenses within the three realms of existence, because one has fully understood and mastered them, it is said that there is no need for further deliberation.

As for cases where an offense is subject to a double penalty, such as those who commit the transgressions of killing or stealing, they are penalized with both the violation of the precepts and the resulting karmic offense.
Furthermore, because one additional offense from the *karmapatha* is added, it is called "a double charge" (*zaike*). "Charge" (*ke*) refers to punishment.
Thus, the two teachings circulate in such a way that they are not without overlap. Jì says:

Within the *Huàjiào* (Teaching of Transformation) there is also the *Zhìjiào* (Teaching of Regulation), and within the *Zhìjiào* there is also the *Huàjiào*; therefore, they are said to overlap. What are these? For example, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*...
The *Kāśyapa-parivarta* is surely not merely a teaching of transformation (*huàjiào*). Within it, the meaning of the precepts and discipline (*śīla-vinaya*) is clearly elucidated.

Furthermore, in the *Pravrajyāvastu* (Section on Receiving the Precepts) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it first clarifies how the Tathāgata converted the five bhikṣus, such as Aññā-Koṇḍañña, and preached the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths and Twelve Aspects, up to the three wheels used to convert non-Buddhists and others.
Is this not an instance where teachings of transformation also exist within the teachings of regulation (*zhìjiào*)? Therefore, it is said:
It is not that there is no confusion between them; rather, when the fundamental principles are cited for judgment, the道理 (principle/reason) becomes self-evident. This means:

the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teachings) take principle as their core tenet (*zong*), clarifying gain and loss by way of the mind; it is also said that they take mental action (*manas-karman*) as their core tenet.

The *Xing-jiao* (Practice Teachings), however, take phenomena as their core tenet, clarifying gain and loss by way of bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*). Since it was stated above that these two are mutually confusable in their circulation, this [distinction] is now cited.
The second point concerns the principles for distinguishing between the two categories [of transgression and observance]. This is why it is said that they "manifest themselves.

That is to say, when the internal mind relies upon principle (li) as its basis for either contrariety or compliance, it constitutes a "thesis" (zong). For instance, if the internal mind arises in contravention of principle, one commits an offense;

if the mind arises in accordance with principle, one maintains observance. Since the establishment of both observance and transgression arises by relying upon principle, it is said that they "rely upon" (tuo) it.

Principle constitutes the fundamental tenet; this refers to the teaching of transformation (*pariṇāma-śāsana*). As for "externally employing acts such as giving," this clarifies the teaching of practice (*caryā-śāsana*).

Even if one stirs the mind while the body and speech remain motionless, one has not yet violated the teaching of practice. It is only upon the movement of body and speech that one can be subject to censure or punishment.
Therefore, it is said: "If one necessarily guards body and speech, then one relies upon the teaching of practice."

Regarding the phrase "therefore the sutra says": this refers to the explicit text of the *Sūtra on Good Birth*. The reason for further dividing it is that this serves as the introduction to the meaning now being elucidated.
Although various teachings clarify the two systems of transformation (*huà*) and regulation (*zhì*), fearing that people may not be proficient in them, I have made this distinction.

I have composed this single section because I fear that those who are confused regarding the essential nature of the two teachings might mistake the *Huàjiào* (Transformation Teaching) for having the prevention of internal thoughts as its doctrinal essence,

while the *Zhìjiào* (Regulation Teaching) has only the prevention of the seven branches of misconduct as its doctrinal essence. Fearing that later generations might become deluded by such distinctions, I have further divided them.

This refers to those who falsely describe the right and wrong of karmic actions. For example, there are those who rely on the *vinaya* (prescriptive teachings) and hold that killing an animal incurs a *pāyattika* offense;

yet, once the transgression has been confessed, they remain ignorant of the nature of the karmic path and falsely claim their own purity. Furthermore, there are monks and nuns who rely on the *sūtra* (transformative teachings) and think:
"If one sees a suffering sentient being and kills it, one ought to gain merit. What fault could there be? Although this does not constitute a formal karmic path..."
Unaware that this corresponds to the conditions set forth in the Vinaya, one incurs the offense of violating the teachings by falsely claiming, "I am pure.
Therefore, it is said: "Yong" means long; "juan" means to eliminate, to remove, or to select. This refers to eliminating the source of the aforementioned false view.

Regarding the eighth point, concerning the mutual accessibility or obstruction between monks and nuns: as for "accessibility" (*tong*), Master Li states that in cases such as receiving precepts or repenting for offenses, the *saṃgha* is mutually accessible, and thus it is called "accessible.
As for all other matters, such as the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā*) or the formal determination of time (*divasagrahaṇa*), these may only be performed within their respective assemblies;
they cannot be done interchangeably. This is termed "obstruction" (*se*).

"Those with identical precepts and identical regulations whose matters and dharmas are the same" refers, for example, to the precepts shared by monks and nuns within the five categories (*pañcāpattinikāya*); these are all termed "identical precepts.

Regarding "peaceful conduct," "inviting criticism" (*pravāraṇā*), "receiving [the robe]," and "confession," these are all "identical regulations. As for "matters and dharmas being the same": "matters" refers to sentient and non-sentient things;

the matters themselves—such as extra robes and alms bowls—are identical. "Dharmas" refers to the *karmavācanā*, the face-to-face method, and the mental recitation method; these are identical and are termed "matters."
"The characteristics of the dharmas are identical" means that the procedures and ritual protocols are fully contained within the various sections;

this is established as clear, for rituals such as *an-shi* (the invitation for confession) and others are all included within the thirty sections, and one may apply them in detail according to one's discretion.

"Hidden and difficult to know, they are fully contained in the *Suixiang*" means that in the subsequent explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the section on the precepts, the specific names and characteristics of the precepts for both the monastic and lay communities are explained in detail.
Therefore, it is said that they are fully present within their respective characteristics (*sui-xiang*).

As for what is meant by "lightness and heaviness being different": for example, a *bhikṣuṇī* incurs a *pārājika* offense through physical contact, whereas a *bhikṣu* incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the case of seminal emission, a *bhikṣu* incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, while a *bhikṣuṇī* incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* fails to observe the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), she incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, whereas a *bhikṣu* incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Hence, it is said that lightness and heaviness differ. There is also the mutual presence or absence [of these offenses].

Regarding "deficiencies": there are precepts that the Saṃgha lacks which the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha possesses, such as the rule against washing more than three joints [of a garment], the four rules concerning solitary [conduct], the rule regarding addressing people, and the rules concerning spinning and weaving;

these exist only for nuns and not for monks. Conversely, there are rules such as those against teaching [the Dharma] without permission and those against going out at dusk which the nuns lack while the monks possess;

thus it is said that they are mutually deficient. Regarding "the offense is the same but the conditions differ," Gao says: for example, the offense of giving food to non-Buddhists is the same, yet the conditions differ.

There are differences. When a monk gives [an alms-bowl] to an ordained non-Buddhist, or a nun gives it to an ordained or lay non-Buddhist, all incur an offense. Furthermore, regarding the precept on keeping an extra bowl:

for a monk, the rule is relaxed such that failing to declare it within ten days constitutes an offense; for a nun, if she does not declare it upon receiving it, she incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) immediately.
Thus, while the nature of the offense is the same, the conditions for its allowance differ; therefore, it is said that "the offenses are the same, but the conditions differ."

Regarding the phrase "this merely distinguishes their categories," it means that for now two positions are distinguished; there are similarities and differences, mutual absences, and variations in gravity and so forth.

However, the underlying reason for these differences has not yet been clarified. Furthermore, the purpose behind the terminology used has not yet been made manifest—namely, the reasons why the precepts for monks and nuns differ in terms of presence and absence.
This is fully explained in the *Great Commentary* (Dàshù), such as in the commentary by Master Shou.
In the middle [section], the reasons for this are explained in detail.
Regarding the "three assemblies" under the ninth section: the śikṣamāṇā, the śrāmaṇera, and the śrāmaṇerī are what constitute the three.

If one considers that the substance of the precepts (*śīla-dravya*) is the same as that of the great monks (*bhikṣu*) because there is no separate agent [of ordination], it clarifies that the measure of the unmanifest precept-substance (*avijñapti-śīla-dravya*) produced is identical to that of the great monks.
Therefore, it is said below that "the categories of conduct are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Gratitude) states:

"The ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera and the full precepts of a bhikṣu are fundamentally and eternally one; they are given different names according to the occasion, just as the leaves of a tree differ between spring and summer."
It is green in spring, yellow in autumn, and white in winter; though its names differ according to the season, the leaf of the tree remains one and the same from beginning to end.
The precepts are likewise always a single precept, yet they appear different according to the occasion. Bin said:

"If, at the time of receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts, one simultaneously generates the unmanifest (avijñapti) precept-body as the bhikṣus do, then once the śrāmaṇera has received the full ordination (upasampadā), [the former state ceases]."
Furthermore, one should not receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). This also contradicts the text of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. That treatise states:

"When a lay follower (*upāsaka*) receives the novice discipline (*śrāmaṇera-saṃvara*), he does not abandon the five precepts; rather, upon receiving the ten precepts, he then accomplishes fifteen disciplines.
When a novice receives the bhikṣu discipline, he then accomplishes two hundred and sixty-five disciplines. Since the treatise is thus explicit, [your position is untenable].

Question: If it is said that at the stage of the ten precepts one only obtains fifteen types of restraint, and their number is only increased upon reaching the stage of full ordination, how can it be that a śrāmaṇera universally conditions and universally generates [the non-informative action]?

Answer: The treatise bases itself on the ten precepts to establish the nature of a śrāmaṇera; it does not exclude the universal conditioning and universal generation of the non-informative action. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the differences in external practices (*bāhya-caryā*): [Master] Sheng says that because there are five virtues, ten numbers, and so forth, as well as the *an-śi* (invitation) and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, it is said that there are differences in what is adopted and what is discarded.

For example, if one destroys living plants for the purpose of making offerings to the Triple Gem, this is permitted (*kṛta-anujñā*). In other cases where such a condition does not exist, it is prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*).

What is prohibited is called "discarding" (*tyāga*); what is permitted is called "adopting" (*ādāna*). It is also said that "maintaining" is called adopting, while violating it is called... [omitted].
It means "abandonment.
Regarding the "six dharmas of a śikṣamāṇā" and so forth, these are foreign terms. Here, *śikṣā* is translated as "learning the dharma" (*xuéfǎ*) and *mānā* as "woman" (*nǚ*).
Therefore, it is called a "woman learning the dharma" (*xuéfǎ nǚ*). This refers to one who learns the six dharmas and guards against the four grave offenses. As for the six dharmas:
The verse says: "Touching with a defiled mind, stealing four *kārsāpaṇas*, taking the life of an animal, and minor false speech; fifth, eating at improper times;

sixth, drinking alcohol—those who train in these together with the three groups [of renunciants] constitute the first. The great monks (*bhikṣu*) and great nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) form two; the two groups of novices (*śrāmaṇera*) form the third.
Śaṅghabhadra says: "Monks and nuns form one; novices form the second; and novice nuns form the third. Therefore...
It is said that they share the same training rules as the other three assemblies.
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü) as the fundamental school: the Mahāsāṃghika school—foreigners call it *Mahāsāṃghika*, which here means "Great Assembly"—is this [school].
Those who performed the first council within the city are called the Sthavira school; [it was led] by Kāśyapa.
The name "Elder" (Sthavira) was derived from those who were senior among the assembly. Since the multitude numbered five hundred, they were called the Mahāsāṃghika;
thus, this Sthavira school is what is referred to as the Mahāsāṃghika. It is not, in fact, the Mahāsāṃghika that convened outside the city.
These five schools of today all emerged from the former Mahāsāṃghika of the Sthaviras; therefore, they are called the Saṃmitīya. The Mahāsāṃghika outside the city is not [the same].
It is the root of the four [divisions]. This is why the Mahāsāṃghika is regarded as the fundamental source of the five schools.
According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is called the Mahāsāṃghika because it extensively surveys and comprehensively examines the scriptures of the five schools;

since it is said to "comprehensively survey the five schools," it is clear that it does not belong to the number of the five schools, and is therefore judged to be the fundamental school. If one follows the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-śāstra* (or *Śāstra on the Wheel of Doctrines*), [it is likewise established as the root].
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that at the beginning, [the Saṃgha] was divided into two schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira.

Among these, the Sthavira school is the root of the four divisions (*caturvarga*). Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are themselves the roots of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the other [divisions].
As for the "two treatises," they refer to the treatises of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the term "foolish thicket" (*yūzō*): some say that one person lacking wisdom is called a "fool," while ten people gathered in one place are called a "thicket.
As for the phrase "my wisdom is like the glow of a firefly," this is a word of humility. It means saying, "My wisdom is like the light of a firefly;
using my understanding to assist in the Buddha’s transformation of beings is like the light of a firefly assisting the sun. Sōshin (Shin) says: "If a firefly were to emerge during the day..."

Then it has no light. When it emerges at night, it possesses a slight, faint glow. I am likewise so. During the time of the True Dharma, I did not dare to assist in the Buddha’s transformation of beings;
even had I sought to assist, I would have lacked the power. This is like a firefly emerging during the day—it has no light.
Now, in this final age, I assist in the Buddha’s propagation of the teaching according to my capacity, like a firefly emerging at night that seems to possess a slight glow. Therefore it is said:
It is like the glow of fireflies. Regarding those called "negligent" (*sū-yōng*):
they are called "negligent" (*sū*) because they do not draw near to the Buddha-dharma; they are called "common" (*yōng*) because they possess neither letters nor martial prowess.

As Master Ying said: "Common" refers to those who are habitually dull and deficient. Their minds lack self-restraint and vigilance; their mouths utter no words of the Dharma; and they take evil people as friends. This is what is meant by [the term].

Regarding the term "ordinary" (*yōng*): "to slight and insult" (*qīngwǔ*) refers to the words of the *Yóu* (the Way/Method). The *Sāncāng* states that "insult" (*wǔ*) means arrogance. "The *Yóu*" refers to the Dharma. This means:

"How would I dare to slight or insult the words of the Dharma? As for "frivolous discourse" (*xìlùn*): if one says that [reality] is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, this is termed frivolous discourse and slander.
Regarding the phrase "having a lineage of learning" (*xué yǒu suǒchéng*) and so forth: this means that I personally received [the teachings] from the Vinaya Master Shou.

I have listened to and studied the Vinaya more than twenty times. Regarding "a lineage must know the source" (*chéng bì zhī běn*): this means that the succession has been passed down from master to master without interruption; thus it is called a "lineage" (*chéng*).
Because one personally knows the original intent behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the precepts, it is said that "a lineage must know the source. Every citation...

"First adding a verification" means that within this present compendium, when citing various sutras, śāstras, and the commentaries of past masters, one must first cross-examine and verify whether they are accurate before subsequently citing them;
hence the phrase "first adding a verification," and so forth.

Regarding the many points established for the purpose of setting aside [the rule] under each individual matter: as in the Vinaya, where for a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense, an exception is made...
Regarding the practice of repentance (*śikṣā-manatva*): Ancient masters judged that if one has committed an offense but has not yet concealed it, repentance is permitted;

however, if it was previously concealed and one fails to repent, it is not. Today, we set aside this interpretation. We maintain that at the time of confession, one must fully disclose everything so as to be eligible for repentance; this principle must be established.

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the Vinaya stating "going to another place," ancient commentators explained this as "walking to another room. This interpretation must also be discarded. Our current explanation is as follows: [The text continues with the modern interpretation of the Vinaya rules.]

This refers to going outside the boundary; this point must be established. Such matters are not limited to these alone. Therefore, it is said that "under each individual matter," the various masters' emotional views are manifold and extensive.

For instance, the ancients established five types of attaining the precepts (*śīla*), providing extensive explanations on the conditions for receiving them, the essence of what is received, and the timing of the arising of the precepts.
In the present day, as the necessary conditions are lacking, much of what has been described is of no benefit; thus, it is considered prolix and extensive.
Therefore it is said that "sentiments and views are manifold and extensive.

Regarding the statement that "the teachings of the Vinaya and Abhidharma are difficult to understand in their logical characteristics": "teachings" refers to the Vinaya teachings, meaning that the treatises explain the Vinaya; these are called "teachings" when they extend to other treatises as well.

As for what is "difficult to understand," it is as found in various treatises where, for instance, one speaks of the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), or the active (*kṛta*) and the non-active (*akṛta*).

Regarding informative and non-informative [action], the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Informative precepts take form (*rūpa*) as their essence; non-informative [action] takes that which is neither form nor mind as its essence.

Such a doctrinal determination and interpretation is difficult to discern in its underlying principles; only those who have a comprehensive understanding of the treatises are able to fully comprehend it.
Therefore, it is said that they are difficult to understand.

As for the fact that the cited and abridged evidentiary texts were often not recorded in full detail, I have now taken the complete passages from the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras within this compendium (*chao*) and described them in their entirety.
Whatever words are relevant, I have immediately cited and brought them forward to enter into this school. Should you wish to know the beginning and end of these matters, [you shall find them here].
For instance, the precept concerning the schism of the Sangha despite being exhorted to desist is so extensive from beginning to end that it does not pertain to current practice.
If one wishes to exhaustively investigate its origins, that would not be the intent of this *Chao* (Abridged Commentary).
Regarding the phrase "useful according to the occasion," this refers to cases such as when one must address matters like *ān*, *zì*, *qǐ*, or *qǐng* in relation to receiving [precepts].

One simply consults the text and applies it accordingly, without the need to consult others. How could there be further doubt regarding transgressions or merit? Since one relies on the ritual procedures and follows the text, what is there to doubt?
As for "transgressions or merit"—that is, the offenses of violation and the merit of observance—how could one doubt the observance or the violation?
"Non-urgent matters" refers to flowery rhetoric. "The true doctrine is overgrown with weeds" points to the *Chao* (Excerpts) as the true doctrine;
it means that if one further adds non-urgent texts, they become desolate and defiled. This causes later practitioners to use them while remaining confused and failing to understand their meaning;
hence the phrase "the analogy of the birds and mice," which illustrates the distinction between the genuine and the false, just as the bat is a bird [that is not].

The mouse cannot be caught; the mouse cannot be caught. If unnecessary passages were added to this draft, it would ultimately result in those who perform the rites in the future being unable to distinguish between the true and the false. Therefore, the birds and the mouse are used as metaphors.
Regarding these ten items that collectively bind all the sections: they constitute the comprehensive conclusion of the preceding ten gates.
That is to say, these ten gates serve as the governing framework for differentiation, horizontally encompassing the thirty gates that follow.
Regarding the phrase "one who dwells within the ocean of the Buddha," from the character "夫" (fú) onwards, the intent of the three fascicles is established.
"Dwelling" (zhái) means to reside; it refers to residing with one's body within the ocean of the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, it says: "One who partakes of and savors the flow of the Dharma."
This means that the mind submits to the water of the Way; hence it is said: "The physical form occupies the rank of the Sangha. Here, "occupies" (*cè*) refers to intermingling or insertion.
Regarding the statement "the practices consist of only three positions," this refers to the current three fascicles, which encompass the entirety of the practices of these three positions.
"Thoroughly understanding and mastering the observance and violation [of precepts], even to the point of possessing their essence and characteristics" refers to the middle fascicle.

It extensively elucidates the essential nature and characteristics of the precept-substance (*śīla-ātman*), as well as the characteristics of the individual precepts; therefore, it is said that "essence and characteristics are complete. "External virtues manifesting their function" refers to thoroughly understanding and mastering the observance and violation [of precepts], as detailed in the middle fascicle;
only then can one uphold the Dharma for the sake of the times and skillfully fashion things, which is why it is said that "external virtues manifest."
"Regarding the phrase 'the framework is preserved': this means that the upper scroll contains the framework of the Buddha-dharma, which comprehensively encompasses all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The lower scroll, however, consists of the mesh; it is that which is held and sustained by the framework. If one lifts the framework, the tips of the hairs [of the net] follow;

if one raises the main cord, the meshes are orderly. Regarding the phrase 'the two virtues of self and others are accomplished through many paths,' this clarifies the text of the lower scroll, wherein various practices..."
It concerns beneficial things and self-benefit. For instance, guiding worldly affairs and transforming others is benefiting others, whereas practices such as the dhūtas are one's own virtues;

thus, it is called "the two virtues of self and other. Question: In the preceding preface, you clarified the intent of the three fascicles by first explaining the upper fascicle, followed by the middle and lower.
Why, here, do you first explain the middle fascicle and then the upper and lower? Answer: There is a great reason for this.

The reason why that which was explained in the preceding introduction clarifies the general sequence of the communal dharma (*saṃgha-dharma*) is that it first elucidates the maintenance of the community’s conduct, and only thereafter elucidates the specific practices of receiving the precepts and repentance.

As for what is clarified here, placing the middle fascicle at the beginning is intended to show that one's own practice is the foundation for establishing oneself; once this essential nature and form are established, one is then able to uphold the practices of the upper fascicle.
The Dharma of the Saṃgha is why it is explained first in the middle fascicle.
Now, as for those matters where the categories correspond and are even more difficult to measure or estimate, Master Ying says that "ni" (擬) means "xiang" (向), meaning to face toward;

the *Shuowen Jiezi* says "ni" means "du" (度), meaning to measure, and "bi" (比), meaning to compare. "Lei" (類) means "li" (例), meaning precedent or category. For instance, regarding the matter of receiving the precepts, there is the category of receiving the precepts.
Just as with the matter of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), there are categories of boundary-establishment.

Now, if one does not follow such categorical precedents when assigning names and titles, but merely explains in a disorganized manner, it will be difficult to investigate; this is what is meant by that statement.

If one were to provide a lengthy, diffuse exposition for each point rather than engaging in focused discussion—as Master Sheng says—if these ten gates were further expanded into a long discourse with each explained diffusely, it would result in thirty gates below.
Regarding the meaning of this matter, its depths cannot be fully exhausted; therefore, it is said that one should be sparing in discussion. "Discuss" (*tǎo*) is derived from "to govern" (*zhì*).

To cause the main sections to be raised and the general principles to be upheld so that the minor details naturally fall into order—these ten gates shall be called the "general principles" (*gānglǐng*).
All the various matters contained within the thirty subsequent gates are entirely the "minor details" (*màomù*). If one understands these ten gates as the general principles, [the rest follows].
The following thirty chapters, with their titles clearly manifest, record the principles and methods.

Regarding "following matters and relying [on them]," this refers to exhorting the monastic community to be diligent in upholding the precepts, thereby forever departing from the defiled currents of broken discipline and attaining liberation in serene tranquility.
Thus concludes the third section, the general explanation of the meaning of the ten gates.
Section One: Establishing the Tenet and Manifesting Virtue.

In order to explain this section, it is divided into two major parts: first, establishing the tenet; second, citing texts to establish virtue. Regarding the first part, there are further two subdivisions.
From the beginning up to the point "the wheel of Dharma shall not be turned again," it clarifies that among the multitude, the person who has left the household life is distinct in two ways.

Practice. There are those who rely [on the teaching] and those who do not, which brings about either loss or benefit. I exhort you to abandon loss and follow benefit, so that the teaching may be practiced.

Second, from "From now on, I shall briefly indicate the essence of the school and its modes of practice" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the essence of the school. Regarding the first part, there are two further divisions.
From the beginning up to "The rise and fall depend on the person," it clarifies how the two teachings—collective and individual—are neglected, resulting in the loss and disappearance of the Dharma.
The second section, from "Following those who deeply revere and protect the Dharma" onwards, clarifies the benefits of establishing and practicing based on the two teachings.

Within the first part, there are further two sections: the first clarifies that the pure assembly’s teaching does not tolerate what is improper; it employs metaphors to reveal the meanings of exhortation, interpretation, and so forth.

Second, from "Being lax leads to confusion and entrusting [the community] to those who disrupt the Dharma administration" onwards, it clarifies that when an unrighteous leader governs the conduct of the assembly, it clearly demonstrates the loss resulting from such decline.
Within the first section, there are four parts; the first presents both the teaching and the analogy together.

This clarifies that the assembly does not tolerate what is improper, nor does it allow for overnight stays or transgressions (*buxu* [不宿] refers to collective practice; *buyue* [不越] refers to individual practice.

The reason these two types of practice are specifically cited here is that the two categories of collective and individual practice encompass all forms of practice). Second, from the passage "Therefore, ordinary people join the ranks" (*gufan ceyu*) downwards, the text exhorts the fulfillment of the aforementioned principles of not staying overnight and not transgressing.

It states that one must strictly observe pure prohibitions and allow no room for what is improper, thereby exhorting the principle of not staying overnight by purifying the mind through the Way (*dào*).
"Water and so forth, up to being unstained by the world," and so on, encourages the fulfillment of the aforementioned principle of not exceeding limits.

This is because if one is stained by the world, one violates the boundaries of the noble precepts. Regarding the third point, "Precisely because it is contrary to the Dharma, there is no way to illuminate one’s deportment," and so forth, this explains the reason why one does not stay overnight and does not exceed limits.
To ensure that one neither transgresses nor stays overnight is for the purpose of illuminating the Path.
To manifest this virtue, the fourth [section] further explains the second intention behind the exhortation for those of shallow understanding in the degenerate age and below.
What is the intent of such earnest exhortation as to say that there is "no room for non-[virtue]" and "no defilement in the world"? The explanation states:

For those of shallow understanding and mediocre vision in the degenerate age, many—though they wear the robes and join the ranks of the black-clad—do not act in accordance with the Vinaya. If one does not earnestly exhort them, it will allow [for their transgression].
It is not a defiled world; therefore, one must exhort [others] toward it. (Of the four sections, this is the first. Within this section:

The phrase "the ocean of the Vinaya is profound and deep" raises both the dharma and its metaphor simultaneously. ("Vinaya" is the dharma; "ocean" is the metaphor. "Chong" (沖) means empty and vast. Question: Why is the Vinaya compared to the ocean? Answer:
It is said that within the ocean there are eight inconceivable qualities, and within the precepts there are likewise [eight].
Because it possesses eight kinds of inconceivability, it is used as a metaphor. "Tongling (津通) the myriad phenomena" means to moisten; it also carries the sense of "crossing over.
This refers to how the great ocean reaches out to the boundless, serving as a place for the salvation of all people and things. The *vinaya* (disciplinary code) is likewise:
its compassionate moisture reaches the realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, moistening the sprouts of sentient beings as they traverse the stream of birth and death to reach *nirvāṇa*.

It is the shore of the vessel, the place for crossing over; therefore it is said that it connects with the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*). The myriad phenomena are precisely the myriad virtues (*kuśala-dharma*).
Although it encompasses all things without exception, it does not harbor corpses.

This means that just as the great ocean possesses eight inconceivable qualities—such as being able to contain all things without exception yet never harboring a corpse—the ocean of the Vinaya is likewise. Although its universal grace flows forth...
It encompasses all myriad things, yet it never harbors the corpse of one who has committed a grave offense until death; if such a person exists, they are expelled through *karmavācanā*.
Therefore, it is said that this is like "not harboring a corpse. Regarding the phrase "the waves and clouds surge from the mountains, yet the tide does not exceed its limit":

"surging" (*téng*) refers to the galloping of horses; "mountain" (*yuè*) refers to a peak that is extremely steep and lofty. This means that while the billows of the great ocean surge upward like mountains, [the tide remains within its bounds].
Mountains rise as clouds do, yet the tides never exceed their limits; the ocean is likewise.

Now, when treating those monks or nuns who have committed grave offenses (*pārājika*) or those who have committed the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), its majestic power, and its efficacy are largely the same as the waves of that sea.
However, if there are monks or nuns who have committed a grave offense, one must not illegally strike or punish them with a staff; rather, one may only...

By means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), they are expelled and placed outside the assembly; thus it is said that this is like the tide not overstepping its limit.

Therefore, for anyone who has entered the profound gate [of the Dharma], there is no room for what is improper. This serves as an exhortation to fulfill the principle of "not harboring a corpse" mentioned above:
namely, that those who occupy a position within the Triple Gem and wish to enter the gate of profound and wondrous concentration and wisdom ought not to do so [if they are unfit].

This refers to those who have committed grave offenses and are not persons of the Dharma. Therefore, it says, "Those who bathe their minds in the water of the Way," and so forth. This is intended to encourage the fulfillment of the aforementioned principle of not exceeding limits.

It means that monastics—both monks and nuns—who have left the household life to enter the Way, maintain a pure mind and uphold the prohibitive precepts, do not delight in the pleasures of humans or devas, but seek the bliss of world-transcendence;
hence it is said, "Thus they are able to increase virtue for the age," and so on, up to "even..."

"Transcending the net of worldly dust" summarizes the preceding two phrases. This refers to those who purify their minds, strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts, and aspire to the path of renunciation;
whose virtue and character are fully realized within, and whose excellent reputation is heard abroad; who are able to engender goodness in others and serve as guides for sentient beings;
and who, moreover, swiftly escape the love-net of the six sense objects and five desires. Therefore, it is said: "Virtue benefits the age, while their traces transcend the net of worldly dust."

"Also. *Chao* (transcendence) means "to emerge. "Precisely because there is nothing by which to manifest virtue" explains the reason for the two preceding phrases, "not lodging a corpse" and "not exceeding the limit.
This means that if one does not cultivate the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*) according to the Vinaya rules, one's external demeanor will be unsightly;
how then could it produce wholesome states in sentient beings? If the inner mind lacks the Way, by what means could its virtue be manifested?

This refers to external virtue. Therefore, it is said that without the Dharma and the Path, one cannot bring forth the brilliance of one’s ritual deportment and virtue. The preceding section distinguished attainment;
the following section distinguishes failure.

As for the phrase "those of shallow understanding in this degenerate age," the following clarifies those who destroy the Dharma—meaning those who, despite having received and attained the Buddha's precepts, [act contrary to them].
Yet, lacking the heart to protect the Dharma, they cause it to perish—swiftly and utterly. Regarding the phrase "the decadent end" (*jiàomò*) cited in the text: *jiào* means "thin" or "diluted.

It refers to those of a thin and diluted character during the final age. As for "those of common vision": *yōng* means shallow and superficial. [The term] "skin" (*pí*) refers to the outer layer of the body;

[the text] says "fū" (a particle). Regarding "participating in the black robes" (*cān zīfú*): *cān* implies being together with or mixed with. *Zī* means black. Their learning is not based on the profound and far-reaching scriptures.
One who has accumulated years of study is said to be "far-reaching" (*jingyuan*). As for those of shallow understanding mentioned above, they are unable to seek out a teacher over a long period;
therefore it is said: "Since the emotions are both remote and wild," and so forth. Not being intimate with the Buddha-dharma is called "remote" (*shu*);

having the mind outside of principle is called "wild" (*ye*). "Wild" carries the meaning of "unrestrained. This means that the emotions are constantly dissipated and unrestrained, having no fixed mindfulness toward the Dharma; hence, they are called "remote and wild."
Regarding the phrase "it is better to investigate the essential truth": "寧" (néng) means "better than" or "rather than," derived from the sense of "peaceful" or "certain.

This means that if one does not associate with those who uphold the Dharma and Vinaya, one will not advance toward the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and how could one know the path to liberation? The path to liberation is called the "essential truth. Regarding the phrase "those who harbor attachments and cling like to a stump":
"封" (fēng) means "to close off" or "to confine," referring to the confinement of a deluded mind. As for "clinging like to a stump," it refers to [the persistence of] plants and trees.

This refers to the "root" (mūla). In the Song dynasty, there was a man who pursued a hare and struck a tree stump, dying on the spot. Later, he remained there all day long, waiting for another hare to come.

People of the time called him "one who waits for a hare by guarding a stump. To say that one's resolve is cut off and all hope is lost means that although one has received the precepts, one does not realize that the precepts are the cause of Bodhi;
furthermore, one does not cultivate concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) for the sake of liberation.

Because of these benefits, it is said: "To sever the mind that seeks narrow expectations and has no one to whom it first resorts" means that once the precepts have been received, one considers the fruit to be fulfilled.
Furthermore, because the words uttered therein lack ultimate purpose, it is said: "The *Erlpi* (爾疋) states that 'yi' (詣) arises from 'jin' (進).
To 'zao' (造), 'zou' (奏), 'yi' (詣), and 'jin' (進) share this same meaning. Although the intent discusses the Way, it is not different from the mundane; this refers to having received [the precepts].

When precepts are maintained in the body, one speaks of the excellent merits of these precepts as if discussing the Way; yet this is merely a pursuit of fame and profit, having no desire at all for liberation from birth and death.
Therefore, it is said that such a person is no different from the laity. Furthermore, when worldly discourse is discussed, who is able to embody its true meaning?
The preceding sentence clarified that even those who study do not yet know it; now, the following clarifies that among those who do not study, who indeed could?
"By whom? It refers to those who discourse on worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*). Furthermore, who else could truly embody these precepts and laws?

As for the passage 'allowing for confusion and negligence, such that prosperity or decline depends upon the person,' this clarifies that if the leader of a non-Dharmic assembly governs the community with improper conduct, there will be the loss of extinction.
In this text, 'allowing' (*rong*) means to receive; 'negligence' (*wei*) means to entrust, to be deluded, or to be at ease."
This means that by admitting such unrighteous and meritless persons and indiscriminately installing them in the position of a Dharma master, one brings disorder to the Buddha-dharma;
hence, it is called a "disorderer of the Dharma office" (*luàn fǎsī*). Regarding the phrase "indulging in arbitrary seizure and plunder," *sì* (肆) denotes license or unrestraint.

This refers to those who, having usurped the position of a Dharma master, do not act according to the teachings of the Dharma, but instead let their bodies and speech run wild, harboring love and hatred toward their disciples. As for hatred...
Thus, one commits a minor offense but receives a severe judgment; conversely, out of affection, one commits a grave offense but receives a light judgment.

This is termed "indulgence and deprivation. Regarding affection, it is indulgence; regarding hatred, it is deprivation. As for the phrase "exclusively practicing violent oppression," "exclusively" means being singularly intent or arbitrary.

It refers to inflicting irrational punishment upon the object of one's anger; hence it is called "exclusively practicing violent oppression. Such conduct is not even consistent with worldly propriety.
