Excessive accounts must be excised and called "refutations" (*bó*). When long-standing views share the same name, excessive accounts are called "differences. Hence, it is said "sameness and difference. Regarding the term "exhaustive investigation":
"exhaustive" (*qióng*) means to investigate thoroughly; "investigation" (*hè*) means to examine minutely.

Long-standing views must be recorded to assist those of broad knowledge. Master Ying says: "To assist" (*fǔ*) means to aid; "broad" (*bó*) means extensive. This refers to aiding the vision of one who possesses extensive knowledge, clarifying [the meaning].
I have recorded all instances of the principle of "long duration" found within the various sūtras, śāstras, and vinayas to assist in forming the knowledge and insight of this present compendium.
This is analogous to how Confucius established the rites; for instance, the *Liji* (Book of Rites) fully incorporates the three ritual systems, stating:
"Adopt the calendar of Xia, ride the chariot of Yin, and wear the cap of Zhou. Thus, taking the thirteenth month as the first month of the year is likewise [a synthesis of long-standing traditions].
This follows the calendar system of the Xia dynasty. In the Zhou system, the eleventh month was the first month of the year.

The carriage here is that of the Yin dynasty, while the crown and cap are those of the Zhou; these are all adopted because they represent what is most excellent, hence the saying: "That which is superior must be recorded.

Regarding the phrase "excessive accounts must be pruned," this refers to the fact that many of the former virtuous masters have included superfluous descriptions, such as the account of the "apricot seed soup" (xingzi tang).

Non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*) is a point of confusion. Furthermore, sugarcane is a timely medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*), yet there is confusion regarding those who treat it as non-timely medicine.
Now, these various confusions are being eliminated: sugarcane is a timely medicine; when its juice is pressed and purified, it becomes non-timely medicine;
when made into rock sugar (*śarkarā*), it is for seven days; when made into ash, it is for the duration of one's life. Another interpretation states that other masters say this applies elsewhere.

To apply this [rule] to one staying in a separate room is an over-extension (*làn*). To seize a lost treasure constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; to seize what is not lost constitutes only a *duṣkṛta*.

This analytical judgment is also termed an "over-extension. Regarding the phrase "employing it to achieve a comprehensive meaning," this refers to my observation of the various treatises composed by former masters;
they all harbor biases regarding superiority and inferiority and contain many over-extended explanations, which cause my mind to remain constantly unsettled.

"I regret that my understanding was not yet unimpeded; this meant my mind was congested and obstructed. Today, by composing this commentary (*chao*), I have excised its redundant accounts to fulfill my original intention.
Since my intent is now unimpeded, it is said: 'To accomplish the unimpeded meaning. Ji said: 'I do not restrict myself to a single text.'"
Now, by synthesizing the various sections into a single compilation, this manual has been completed; thus, it is said to convey the comprehensive meaning.
In cases where elaborate text is employed to clarify practical applications—as in the section on Receiving Precepts—the matters involved are so extensive that detailed exposition is necessary.

For instance, it first clarifies that there are five types of those who receive ordination and six types of preceptors they face, and further elucidates eight kinds of preparatory regulations. Is this not [the case]?
This is an elaborate exposition. It is so called because it clarifies the practical application of the precepts for laypeople.

Furthermore, regarding the detailed explanations provided for the rules on possessing precious objects, stealing, destroying living beings, and eating in a group, these are extensively elucidated because people are prone to violate them;
they clarify the matters concerning theft for laypeople so that they may put them into practice. Sengshen says: "This section corresponds to the many listings above."

Regarding the phrasing of these discursive expressions: I do not claim that my elaborate text differs from your discursive style; rather, it is intended solely to clarify the practical application within the various categories of ritual matters.

As for instances where [the text] is abbreviated or modified according to similar types—for example, although there are thirty-nine distinct types of *śuddhaka-karman* (single-announcement *karmavācanā*), the present digest (*chao*) directly cites only the single method of the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) to explain its essential characteristics and the number of its constituent phrases. Furthermore, as for the additions...

The omissions differ; the rest should all be treated according to this principle. Furthermore, regarding the three types of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the four types of *pravāsanīya-karman*, and the seven methods for disciplining individuals—since these matters are rare, I have only explained the first, the *tāḍana-karman* (reproach), and have omitted the rest. Shen says:

"This phrase corresponds to the section on *ekakarma* (single *karman*) above. Although I have only briefly indicated it, its meaning follows along with [the previous discussion]; it is not like your single heading. Or...

Regarding "the text is severed but connected by meaning": "text" refers to the monastic codes (vinaya). For instance, across various schools, there is no textual passage for the ritual of dissolving the *sīmā* (boundary) or for receiving the seven-day permit (*saptāha-karman*).
In such cases, one applies the meaning and function of the text for receiving the half-month permit; this is to be understood as being in accordance with the Dharma.

As for the dissolution of the *sīmā*, since the meaning is the reverse of its establishment, it is called "connected by meaning. The *Shenjie* (Deep Explanation) states: "In the text of the relevant school, [the passage] is severed, yet the meaning..."

This refers to taking textual passages from other schools (nikāya) and connecting them [to one's own]. For example, regarding the addition of medicinal substances to robes or the counting of those who are insane or intoxicated: although the text does not fully contain these details, their meaning is inherently present.

Now, taking such points from another school is called "connecting by way of meaning" (*artha-saṃbandha*). Furthermore, as for the path of water and the element of water (*āpa-dhātu*), although there is no explicit text on this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Caturvargika*), how could the matter itself not exist?
Therefore, one takes the textual passages from other schools and connects them by way of meaning. [The author] privately remarks: "This should refer to..."

In the present excerpt, there are instances where the text is interrupted, such as in the section on receiving the precepts (*śīla*). In that passage, it states that the person receiving the precepts must first be granted the śrāmaṇera precepts;
however, the specific ritual for this is not established within the text itself. It merely says that one "must obtain a portion of the dharma.
This is a textual omission, yet the meaning is fully implied. It is only in the subsequent section on the śrāmaṇera that the actual ritual for bestowing the śrāmaṇera precepts is set forth.

Alternatively, regarding those who raise objections and pose hypothetical questions: it should be understood that the present *Chao* (Excerpts) itself contains the answers. For example, a question asks:
"Regarding the four types of nuns, why are three among those who are insane not counted? Is it because they do not count due to their own declaration, or because they are deficient by nature?
Furthermore, another question asks: "The natural boundary (*jñapti-kṣetra*) is sixty-three paces wide; is this measured from one side of the body as sixty [paces]?"
"Three steps. Does this mean taking [the distance] from the four sides of the body? Or, as in the question regarding the natural realm (*dharmadhātu*), does it refer to being square or circular?

These are all interrogative phrases used for rhetorical inquiry. When such instances of beginning and end reflecting one another, and the hidden and the manifest appearing alternately, are said to "conclude the preceding text," it is expressed by the word "thus" (*evam*).
"Beginning and end" refers to the words within the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*); the preceding part constitutes the beginning.
The latter constitutes the end. Having a beginning but lacking an end, or lacking a beginning but having an end, is called "mutual reflection" (*jiaoying*).
Because these two texts clarify each other in contrast, it is named "mutual reflection. "Reflection" (*ying*) means illuminating from the side; see Pan Yue’s *Pomegranate Rhapsody*. Shen says:

within this *Chao* (Excerpts) itself, there is mutual reflection. For example, in the section on "Counting the Quorum," more than sixty people who do not meet the quorum requirements are excluded; below that is the *Karmavācanā*.
It is not further elaborated upon in the text. This is also like the ten kinds of conditions explained in the *Karmavācanā*; in all subsequent *karmas*, these are not further clarified.
For example, when one within the Saṃgha slanders another with a *pārājika* offense, the characteristics of the transgression and the full set of conditions are listed;

subsequently, among the nine [categories], when one slanders another with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one directly points to the relevant conditions for the offense established within the thirteen [rules] to seek understanding. As for the former...
The beginning serves as the start, and the end serves as the conclusion. Now, one must use existence to reflect non-existence, and use what precedes to reflect what follows;

therefore, it is said that "the beginning and end mutually reflect one another. Sheng says: "As in the *Zu-shu* (Supplementing Numbers) chapter, where both substance and object are negated, it is said:

'If one knows [the number], it is insufficient; if one does not know it, it becomes sufficient. This refers to the time of granting consent (*chanda*). In that *Yu-yu* (Granting Consent) chapter, it says: 'One declares for oneself...'"

Therefore, it is not for the use of the Saṃgha. If one does not speak for oneself, yet conforms with the assembly within the context of the ritual characteristics—as in the case of being counted toward the quorum because the Saṃgha knows it—this also does not constitute holding a *chanda* (consent).

This is because in the act of giving *chanda*, there is "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) due to speaking for oneself, whereas here there is "concealment" (*gūhana*) because there is no knowledge by the Saṃgha.

In the case of being counted toward the quorum, there is "manifestation" because there is knowledge by the Saṃgha, whereas there is "concealment" because there is no speaking for oneself. Hence, it is called "concealed."
This indicates that they were produced from one another.

Regarding the phrase "including the current *karmavācanā*," Fazhao states: "The claim that this refers to the title of the *karmavācanā* he himself composed, titled 'Dharmaguptaka,' is likely incorrect.
It should rather refer to the *karmavācanā* contained within the *Vinayavibhaṣā* itself, as each section therein presents its own *karmavācanā*."
"Polishing" refers to such matters as receiving the precepts and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; these are common practices currently in circulation, hence they are called "current practices.
Regarding "the right and wrong of various affairs": this means clarifying the attainment or failure of legal rules amidst urgent and essential administrative tasks;

thus they are called "right and wrong. For example, if the conditions for receiving the precepts on a given day are met, it is called "right"; if the conditions are lacking, it is called "wrong. As for "guiding the laity with correct ritual": [this refers to...]

Regarding the statement, "This preface [introduces] the sections on guiding the laity, transforming the world, ritual protocols, the five and eight precepts, entering monasteries, and other such legal rules," Fazang says:
"This refers to the section below this preface concerning the various essential practices.
Regarding the phrase, "To provide a means for the novice practitioner to avoid laborious effort," Fazang says: "If one has read through this compendium..."
Regarding all ritual methods and modes of conduct, what is there that is not understood? There is no need to seek elsewhere, nor will one waste effort or incur loss.
However, as for those who claim to agree with me yet strike at my fundamental principles, they say: "Only those who share my views can join in the chant."

To say "greatly good, greatly good" is like being cognizant of the musical melody. It is like one person singing while another claps their hands, so that they harmonize with each other and attain the proper rhythm.
Some say it is as described in the prose-poem by Zuo Taizhong: "The lady of Ba plucks the strings; the maiden of Han strikes the rhythm.
Furthermore, it is as Liu Yimin said in his letter to Master Zhao: "Recently, I have already received the various teachings..."
This refers to those who repeatedly clap their hands in rhythm. It is also like when the Prince of Chen (Cao Zhi) played the lute;
everyone who recognized the melody clapped their hands in harmony, believing they shared the same vision. Sheng said:
As Pei Xuanxin stated, Chen Fan, whose courtesy name was Wulong, served as a Regional Inspector. Under his jurisdiction was Xu Ru, the young son of Xu Ruo. Whenever they discussed current affairs...
In ancient times, there was a couch belonging to [Cao] Long that was always suspended high up, such that no one was able to ascend it. Only when Xu Ruzi arrived would he alone ascend it;
when Ruzi departed, the couch would be lowered. People of the time said, "Xu Ruzi lowers the couch of Master Chen"—this refers to this very thing. Yuanlong’s son was Mo.
Xu Ruzi, styled Zili, would prepare his mat and seat to engage in lofty discourse, debating the past and present with such integrity that he appeared truly upright.

When sitting in the same hall, those present would clap their hands and strike their palms in rhythm, singing out words of praise and acclaiming his eloquence as excellent. Today, if one were to censure him for the profusion of his writings, it would be because "the melody is so high that those who can join in harmony are few.
It is like a skilled lute player performing in a marketplace; when playing melodies such as "The Radiant Spring" or "The White Snow," they find no one to harmonize with them.

There were three or five people who sang the "Bari" melody. Those who joined in harmony numbered in the tens of thousands. This illustrates the saying: "The higher the song, the fewer those who can harmonize.
It is said that Song Yu addressed the King of Chu, saying: "There was a guest who sang in the city of Ying. At first, he sang 'Xialiren Bari';
those in the capital who joined in harmony numbered several thousand. When he sang 'Yang'e' and 'Xielu', [those in the capital...]"
Those who joined in harmony with him numbered several hundred. When he played "Yangchun" and "Baixue," those in the kingdom who joined in harmony numbered several dozen.
When he modulated the *shang* and *yu* notes and interspersed them with the flowing *zhi*, those in the kingdom who joined in harmony did not exceed a few people.
Thus, as the music became more sublime, those who could harmonize with it became fewer. Furthermore, the *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "When Boya played the zither, Ziziqi..."
He waited for him to listen. When his mind was set upon Mount Tai, Ziqi said, "How magnificent!
It is like Mount Tai. When his mind was set upon flowing water, Ziqi said, "How vast! It is like flowing water. After Ziqi died, Boya broke his zither and snapped its strings.

He never again played the lute for the rest of his life, believing that there was no one in the world who could truly appreciate his music. Regarding divergent doctrines, he rejected those whose texts were overly prolix;
those whose perspectives differed from his, he criticized, saying: "I suspect you find my excerpts too wordy. Why is it necessary to speak with such verbosity?"
One need only record three or five instances of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures); this will suffice for practical application. Thus it is said that "redundant text is excluded.
"Excluded" (*chì*) here refers to setting aside due to remoteness; it also means to point out or reject. The *Hànshū* states: "The imperial carriage excludes [the need for] carriages and horses.

The *Yìnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) says: "To exclude" means not to employ. This refers to the case where the imperial carriage does not employ carriages and horses, and those who ride carriages and horses do not [employ the carriage].
*Yù*. The contemporary Chan master Mingzuo saw this commentary and said: "What is the use of this? The text is too verbose and extensive;

it is a case of different names leading to divergent explanations. The *Sāncāng* states: "The character *chì* means to push away, and also to rebuke. Others say that the pronunciation of this character is *dīng* and is rare.
Furthermore, "yī" (移) means to move or intrude. The character below is written as "gān" (干), meaning: "I am already at home; what need is there for you to come and intrude upon me?
The upper part of the character depicts a house, and the lower part represents a wall. As for the phrase "Who would delight in such prolixity?

(文繁誰所樂之者), it refers back to the preceding line. It means: "Prolixity is not what I delight in; however, fearing that my practice might not be comprehensive, and with no other choice, I must describe it."
This is so. Why? If one were to abridge and omit the general outlines for practical application, there would always be insufficiency.

This means that my current *chao* (extract) must fully synthesize all the various sections (*nikāyas*), taking passages from external schools regarding the wearing of robes and other matters to ensure sufficient utility.

If it were further abridged, I fear it would be the same as the aforementioned person who recites the *karmavācanā* by rote alone. One must certainly avoid making horizontal evaluations of non-urgent texts.

The phrase "that which is avoided by the *Chao*" expresses the intention of the author regarding the preceding sentence. It clarifies that if the transgressions are too brief, the application of the ritual is insufficient;
yet if they are too numerous, this is what the *Chao* seeks to avoid. What, then, are these "non-urgent" words?

They clarify that while in former times there were conditions for receiving the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) and the higher ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), in the final age such conditions no longer exist. Thus, the teaching has become obsolete; therefore, it is termed "non-urgent. If I...
To discuss this at length is not the intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts); therefore, it is called "that which is avoided. To avoid means to shun.
If one were to further engage in such tangential arguments on this matter, how would it differ from the previous multitude of those who employ flowery rhetoric? Some have said:

"This sentence specifically targets and rebukes the aforementioned multitude of those who employ flowery rhetoric and those whose writings merely collect meanings. This clarifies that these collections of meaning and flowery rhetoric do not serve the essential needs of the times.
This is called "not urgent.

Now, regarding the present [method of] "taking the middle": this means eliminating both the redundant and the overly brief, retaining only the one correct "middle. To delineate it is called a "diagram" (tu).

"Measure" (*liàng*) means "to gauge" (*dù*). Master Ying says: According to the *Zhào dìng gǔwén huànshū*, the character [口/面] (pronounced *dá hú* in the second form) has the lower radical pronounced *tú gè*.
The *Guǎngpǐ* states: "[口/面] means to measure (*dù*), to deliberate (*yì*), and also to calculate (*jì*). To measure (*dù*) means to gauge (*liáng*).

This clarifies that this present digest (*chāo*) is neither prolix nor abridged; it is called "taking the middle course. Regarding the effort to be both concise and frugal: "concise" (*shěng*)... [text ends].

"Jian" (減) means to reduce. See the *Zilin* (Word Forest), where "jian" is glossed with the phonetic transcription *gan'an* (緘黯). "Yue" (約) means to limit; it also means to diminish. Because they are both comprehensive and parsimonious, they are not prolix;

because they are both comprehensive and concise, they are not excessive. Someone has said: "The three types of *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) admit no further increase or decrease—this is 'conciseness' (*yue*).
Not engaging in flowery rhetoric—this is 'parsimony' (*sheng*). As the following text states: "The intent of establishing the teaching lies in being manifest and concise. This refers to...

This is the meaning. Regarding "providing for emergencies and preparing for sudden events": "emergency" refers to newly ordained monks and nuns who, when confronted by any matter, are like people facing a wall;

they do not recognize the characteristics of the teachings and immediately commit offenses. The difficulty of maintaining the *brahmacarya* (pure conduct) is as urgent as being suspended upside down, much like an infant who relies entirely on nursing.

There is no emergency more pressing than this. Now, this *Chao* (Excerpts) demonstrates the textual norms (*wenguī*) to avoid the faults of violation and destruction; thus, it is called "rescue" (*jiu*).
"Emergency Preparedness. When there is suddenly some occasion requiring one to consult the texts, they are immediately understood; thus it is called "emergency preparedness.

For instance, matters such as guiding the laity, transforming the local customs, and the distribution of the deceased's property often arrive with sudden urgency. The *Chao* (the manual) prepares for these, which is why it is said to provide for emergencies and ensure preparedness.
If one’s reflection does not attend to the timing and circumstances of affairs, there will be a deficiency in the expression of practice. "Reflection" refers to the process of mental engagement;

it means that when the power of one's mind and spiritual thought fail to reach a certain point, there is a deficiency in the expression pertaining to the category of practice. "Practice" refers to ethical conduct (*śīla*), while "expression" refers to the teaching that expresses it.

The teaching is the expresser (*vācaka*), and practice is the expressed (*vācya*). Since the expresser has been lost, the expressed— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
"The expression also perishes. This is the humble statement of the author of this *Chao* (Commentary). Furthermore, it is explained:
"In this present *Chao* of mine, I fear that regarding matters not belonging to the mind, there is a deficiency in the teachings (*śāsana*) that can express them;

and not only is there a deficiency in the teachings that can express them, there is also a deficiency in the practices (*caryā*) that are expressed by them. Therefore, it is said that 'practice and expression are deficient. This is simply because my spirit, emotions, and reflections—"
To reach that state would be to lack the exposition of practice (*caryā*). Exposition is precisely the teaching (*śāsana*). This means:

"If I do not understand the teaching which is the expositor, then the practice which is the exposited will also be lacking. Thus it is said. Regarding the brief indication of the essential intent (*tātparya*) for the sake of expansion later on, there are two interpretations.
The first states: "Although I am now composing this commentary (*kośa*), I shall merely provide a brief indication..."

[The preceding] has been concluded. There remains that which is not yet exhausted; it is entrusted to scholars of the future to provide a comprehensive and detailed commentary on the preface. Furthermore, it is said:

"In this present preface to the *Chao*, I have briefly set forth the intended meaning of the core doctrine; the full exposition shall be clarified within the subsequent thirty sections. Shen [Dao] remarked:

"Since my own knowledge is insufficient and the matters to be addressed are many, I shall for now briefly cite the essential points, hoping that future generations will explain them extensively on their own."

The "Three Sections on Meaning" (*Gisho Sanbu*) refers to the three fascicles of the text. The first fascicle clarifies the communal regulations (*sōhō*); the middle fascicle clarifies personal practice (*jigyō*);
and the lower fascicle clarifies miscellaneous essential practices (*zatsumu yōgyō*). The first fascicle, then, subsumes the communal affairs and establishes the protocols for their implementation.
"Śa" (攝) means to unify; "zhòng" (眾) refers to the Saṃgha. "Wùshì" (務事) refers to the administrative affairs and ritual ceremonies of the Saṃgha; hence it is called "zhòngwù" (眾務).
It clarifies the *karmavācanā* (羯磨); as its success or failure follows established rules, it is called "yí" (儀).

In the middle fascicle, regarding the establishment of repentance based on the substance of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) and their observance or violation, this clarifies the nature of the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma generated at the time of receiving the precepts, in accordance with the intermediate [stages].

"Second, the practice of both upholding and violating. 'Upholding' refers to guarding and maintaining with single-minded diligence; 'violating' refers to the completion of an offense through the presence of its constituent conditions.

Once violated, the Sages permit purification through repentance, as discussed exhaustively in the middle fascicle; hence this statement. Question: Within the "Receiving" [section], both the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the essence (*tattva*) are present.

In the middle fascicle, the essence is clarified but the conditions are not. Within the "Following" [section], there is both upholding and violating. One ought to speak of upholding and not of violating. Answer: Regarding the conditions, the essence, and upholding... [the text continues].

The offenses arise in mutual dependence; logically, they should be explained in one place. However, because the formal reception of precepts requires the Saṃgha as a condition, they are discussed in the upper fascicle under the "Dharmas of the Assembly.
If that is so, since the confession of heavy offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) and the remorse for residual offenses (*śeṣa*) are both performed by the assembly, why are they placed in the middle fascicle?

The answer is that while confession may apply to both the Saṃgha and individuals, the formal reception of precepts is exclusively an act of the assembly. That is to say, the confession of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses must involve the Saṃgha, whereas the confession of *pāyattika* and *duṣkṛta* offenses applies only to individuals.

This was composed by a person. Regarding the section in the lower fascicle titled "Arising from Entrusting Matters According to Circumstances": this refers to matters such as the purification of robes and medicine, all of which are termed "essential practices" (*yàoxíng*).
As for the phrase "arising from entrusting matters," it refers to the methods for guiding the laity and transforming them: receiving the five or eight precepts;
and because bhikṣus may fall ill or pass away while living together, the establishment of rules for nursing the sick and conducting funeral rites—all of these are based upon the occasion of illness.

It arises based on phenomena; hence it is said that it "relies upon phenomena to arise. Regarding the phrase "without confusion in perception," this refers to the detailed and orderly examination within the thirty gates discussed below.
Some say that "wen" (紊) means "disorderly threads"; its pronunciation is *yun* (運) with the tone *fan* (反), as in the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), which uses it to mean "chaos."
"However, as objects and matters are truly manifold" means that this statement was intended to provide the titles for the thirty sections on their arising.

"Objects" (*viṣaya*) refers to the external realms of sentient and non-sentient beings encountered; "matters" (*vastu*) refers to the practice performed in relation to those objects, such as the *cīvaradāna* (distribution of robes) or the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony), which are termed "matters.

Therefore, when wisdom encounters an object, there is necessarily a corresponding matter. Furthermore, "matter" may also refer to *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts). Among the four types of disputes...

There is the *adhikaraṇa-śāma* (settlement of disputes), which takes the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) as its object. To clarify this, throughout the following thirty chapters, there are none that do not concern objective matters (*viṣaya-vastu*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that all sentient and non-sentient things constitute the "object" (*viṣaya*), while "matter" (*vastu*) refers to matters concerning persons and the Dharma. For example, receiving the precepts, killing, stealing, and so forth are matters concerning sentient beings;
non-sentient matters include the *pravāraṇā*, destroying living plants, digging the earth, and so on. Since such objective matters are numerous, their measure [is vast].

"Difficult to categorize" refers to the application of appropriate analogies; "analogous" (*ni*) also means comparison. Now, taking categories that follow one another to serve as headings for titles—for instance, regarding the *sīmā-bandha* (establishment of boundaries), there are five types in total:
three types of *mahāsīmā* (great boundaries) and three types of *kṣudrasīmā* (small boundaries), together with the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field), making seven.
Here, we simply provide the title "The Method for Establishing Boundaries. Although there are seven types of boundaries, they are grouped together as one.

The title [of this work] is [to be understood by] analogy with the other twenty-nine chapters, which can be understood in the same way. For example, regarding the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts), there are both the mental recitation (*cittānuvartana-poṣadha*) and the communal recitation according to the formal procedures (*sammukhavinaya-poṣadha*);
yet here they are combined under the single heading "The Formal Procedure for the Poṣadha. Thus it is said that "things of the same category follow one another."
As for "summarizing its general outline," this refers to the purpose of the ten sections that follow; here, "general outline" refers to the meaning of these ten sections as the overarching framework.

The phrase "fearing that the detailed ramifications may not be fully understood" means that beneath each of the thirty sections there are various branches and categories, which might not yet be thoroughly comprehended;
thus, the general outline and essential intent are further encompassed crosswise by these ten sections.
There are thirty sections. One thereby understands that within each of these thirty sections, the meaning of ten further sections is contained.

This means that each is fully equipped with the intent for the arising of the teaching, the intent regarding gravity and lightness, the application of the textual meanings of various divisions, and so forth. As for the "major outlines," they refer precisely to the meaning of these ten sections.

As for the "branching currents," "branches" refers to the titles of the thirty chapters—that is, the specific matters of each individual chapter. "Currents" refers to the contents beneath each chapter.

This is the matter of the "Outline" (*dàgāng*). It means that within the categories and sub-sections of my thirty topics (*triṃśan-mukha*), there are instances where the texts of other schools are utilized, as well as variations in weight and the reasons for the arising of the teachings;
such is the general purport of the outline. Since this is not yet fully detailed within the thirty topics, I have composed the "Discernment of the System" (*biàn tǒng*) in ten topics.
These ten topics are precisely what is called the "Outline," which serves as the governing framework for the following three [sections].
The ten gates are the hair-ends of the subject matter. I fear that within the thirty gates, you may not yet recognize their great structural framework;
therefore, I present them by means of the ten gates. One must call these ten gates the "framework" (*kang*). As for "the square mirror clearly elucidating the distant":

"square" (*fang*) arises from the constant (*chang*); the constant arises from the supreme (*sheng*). Furthermore, "square" arises from the appropriate (*dang*). "Mirror" (*jing*) means illumination, like a mirror suspended in a high hall.
The myriad phenomena thus appear. "To understand" means to comprehend; it means to clarify. "Far-reaching exposition" refers to the path of Bodhi.
The intention is to employ the meaning of these ten gates to illuminate the thirty chapters that follow, such that there is no dharma that is not encompassed.

One might ask: for what reason did the Buddha establish these teaching gates? It is truly because there must be a destination to be reached—far, to attain the fruit of Nirvana; near, to summon [the benefits].

Because it results in the superior retributions of humans and devas, it is called "distant exposition" (*yuanquan*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that within the formulation of the precepts, the manifest characteristics are not immediately revealed;

rather, they exist beyond the literal text, expounding the meaning of severing delusions—this is termed "distant exposition. Thus the text says: "In order to subdue the three poisons and bring them to an end, the training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is established.
Another interpretation holds that "distant exposition" means, speaking briefly, that by describing these ten gates, one then illuminates [the truth].

This refers to the meaning within the thirty sections below the "Mirror. By means of these ten sections, the two types of observance and the two types of transgression within the thirty sections below are encompassed;
this is termed "remote explanation" (*yuanquan*).
The first part, the extensive explanation of the meaning of the preface, is now complete. From this point onward is the second part, which briefly lists the titles of its thirty chapters.
Question: Since it was stated above that "the ten gates provide a comprehensive outline," one would expect the ten gates to be explained immediately following the preface.
Why, then, are the titles of the thirty chapters listed first, while the ten gates appear only later? Answer: This is due to the flow of the text (*vṛtti*).
It begins with "Arising and Ceasing. Logically, it should conclude with "Cessation. The reason for this is that the preceding text could not have omitted this point.

Now, following the principle that "like things follow like," we establish these names at the beginning. Thus, the titles of the thirty chapters have already been presented in their sequence of arising.
Therefore, the current arrangement of the sections follows the order of the text on their arising. These thirty chapters are summarized in verse as follows:

The thirty chapters arise as follows: "Distinguishing the Number of Monks" (1), "Discerning the Precepts" (2), "The Ritual for Receiving Teachers" (3), "The Chapter on Restraint and the *Prātimokṣa*" (4), "The Six Robes and Four Alms Bowls" (5), "Purification" (6), "The Image Hall" (7), "Provisions for Lay Guests" (8), "Illness" (9), "Miscellaneous Matters" (10), and "The Bhikṣuṇī Section" (11).
These have been handed down from antiquity; when lecturing, one proceeds to the beginning of each subsequent chapter and presents them individually.

The underlying principle is now briefly clarified in advance; when the time comes, one may adopt either position as appropriate. Now, in establishing the teaching, it is essential first to recognize the fundamental tenet (*śāstra-mūla*).

What this tenet elucidates is precisely the discussion of observance and transgression. Since moral virtue becomes most exalted by conforming to observance and avoiding transgression, it was necessary to include the first chapter, "Establishing the Tenet and Manifesting Virtue.
Furthermore, once the virtue of the precepts is fully prepared, there must be [the practice of] bestowing...

This is for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings and delivering them across the sea of suffering, and for presiding over the assembly at the appropriate times. Among all forms of presiding, none precedes the performance of formal ritual procedures (*dharmakarma*).
At the commencement of such procedures, it is first necessary to assemble the Saṃgha; therefore, the second section concerns the general and specific requirements for assembling the Saṃgha.

Although the assembly is generally convened, the distinction between purity and impurity has not yet been clarified. That which is pure accords with the Dharma, whereas that which is impure need not even be mentioned; thus, the third section clarifies this point.

This is the characteristic of being sufficient in number. However, although the assembly is complete, there is a fear that within it there may be divisions or opposition. When pure monks gather like clouds, their bodies and speech are harmonious and detailed;

when defiled monks disperse like stars, they act according to the occasion, whether speaking or remaining silent. If the pure assembly is discordant or contentious, the ritual procedure cannot be accomplished; therefore, the rules for a "separate assembly" (*bhinnasaṃgha*) are appended.

Yet, although the monks may gather in splendor, they must be distinguished as sufficient or insufficient. However, since human emotions and circumstances are difficult to keep constant, this is clarified [herein].
Regarding the rules of conduct: if there are obstacles due to external conditions, the Sages permitted a relaxed mind to demonstrate that no discord exists;

thus, there is the fourth section, "On Receiving Desires. These four sections are collectively titled "The Human" (*pudgala*). Since the human body is such as it is, one is capable of upholding the True Dharma.

As the great essentials of the Dharma do not exceed the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures), there is the fifth section, "Comprehensive Discussion of *Karmavācanā*. It is further said: "Above [this]..."

Those who can uphold the Dharma must clearly understand the Dharma they uphold and practice the conduct of maintenance. Since the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) establish its major categories, there is the "Chapter on *Karmavācanā*.
However, the great methods of *karmavācanā* vary according to specific tasks; the conditions to which they apply encompass both sentient and non-sentient realms.
Next, it is explained that the formal establishment of boundaries (*sīmābandha*) specifically applies to non-sentient objects; therefore, there is this "Chapter on Establishing Boundaries."

It continues: Furthermore, it explains the great dharma of *karmavācanā*. Since the *karmavācanā* relies upon the boundary (*sīmā*) as its foundation, there is the sixth method: the rite of establishing the boundary.

Now that the characteristics of the boundary are clear and the site upon which it depends has been established, one must immediately propagate the True Dharma to extinguish evil and give rise to good.

Regarding the methods for extinguishing evil, nothing surpasses the three types of formal accusations (*tri-udghāta*) and the four types of expulsion (*catur-niḥsaraṇa*). These are the ritual protocols for maintaining the Saṃgha and governing the community.
This is the fundamental framework of our tradition; hence, there is the seventh chapter, "The Great Outline of the Monastic Net.

Now, since the Sangha’s capacity to propagate the Dharma and extinguish evil has already been established, and their internal virtues and external conduct are capable of engendering goodness in sentient beings, the very root of such goodness is none other than the reception of the precepts.

Therefore, the eighth chapter, "Clarifying the Reception of Precepts," follows next. Furthermore, the essence of receiving the precepts is to maintain them with such resolve that one would rather die than transgress them. Yet, should circumstances or difficulties arise—

Regarding the objects of the precepts (*viṣaya*), there may arise violations or breaches; the Noble Ones have opened the way for restoration to purity, so that one’s coming and going may remain without blemish—hence, the method for relinquishing the precepts is appended.

Furthermore, as for the formal acceptance and maintenance of the robes and bowl (*cīvara-pātra*), it is not appropriate to neglect or forget them; moreover, they serve to prevent the offenses of the six classes (*ṣaḍ-āpatti*)—hence, the method of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) is appended.

Nevertheless, although one has received the Noble Dharma, if one does not yet understand how to protect and maintain it, confusion will arise in every encounter; thus, one must rely upon a teacher and mentor to bring it to completion.

The benefit has already been shown; to demonstrate the departure from delusion, there is the ninth chapter, "The Mutual Inclusion of Teacher and Disciple. Thus, the positions of teacher and disciple are established.
The characteristics of the precepts must be understood. If they were not proclaimed every half-month, there would be no means to admonish the assembly at the proper time;

therefore, the section on the recitation of the precepts (*Poṣadha*) is explained next in sequence. Now that the assembly has heard the precepts, they should be courageous, diligent, and focused, and it is only right that they remain in quietude for three months and advance in their practice for ninety days.
If they wander about without restraint, they will harm things and incur reproach; therefore, the rule for the rainy season retreat (*Varṣā*) was established to ensure stability.

One sits to cultivate the Way; therefore, the tenth section clarifies the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). Now, the restrictions of the *varṣā* must not be entered or left according to one’s own whims.

However, if there should suddenly arise circumstances that benefit both oneself and others, it is essential to calculate [the necessity]; the Sage did not prohibit such cases when they were deemed permissible.

Since the rules for remaining [in retreat] have already been established, there must likewise be a formal procedure for departing; therefore, the ritual for requesting an extension of the retreat period (*āpatti-dina*) is appended here.

Furthermore, because one dwells together for ninety days and resides collectively for three months, there is constant apprehension over the long duration that many transgressions may occur; thus, one should mutually confess and apologize, allowing the Saṃgha to freely raise and address any faults.

Therefore, the twelfth section, the *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Exhortation) text, follows. Now, when the virtues of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) are complete and the *pravāraṇā* is performed without fault, the Saṃgha is individually pure and exalted, and they are entitled to receive the benefits.
Since the great merit of the *kaṭhina* robe provides protection for practitioners, the *kaṭhina* robe rules are appended.
These twelve chapters above belong to the first volume, which collectively elucidates the monastic laws (*saṃghadharma*) and their various applications.
Although this applies generally to individuals, it subsumes the derivative under the fundamental and is collectively termed "various duties.

From the section on the retribution for the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) onwards, there should be four chapters belonging to the second fascicle, which are specifically concerned with the conduct of the individual.

Now, in order to clarify what constitutes observance and violation so that one may abandon transgressions and achieve perfected conduct, it is necessary first to demonstrate the depth and shallowness of the retribution for violations, thereby inducing feelings of joy or remorse. Therefore, regarding the individual precepts...

First, let us clarify the names and the retributions for the categories of offenses (āpatti). Once one understands the distinctions between the fruits of retribution resulting from upholding or violating these rules—namely, gain and loss—one must then manifest their characteristics according to their respective positions and provide a detailed commentary and explanation.
Therefore, there is the chapter "Explaining the Characteristics of Each Precept" (*Suijie shixiang pian*). Now, within this section on each precept:

Although the outward manifestations are clear, the great direction of mind and object remains obscure; thus, the following chapter is universally applied as a comprehensive summary, titled "The Method for Maintaining and Violating Precepts.

Now that the two aspects of maintaining and violating—their names and essences—have been clarified, those of superior capacity will protect and maintain them with single-minded diligence, while those of middling capacity, having committed a violation, are able to repent.
Through repentance, they restore their original purity and return to the state of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*). However...
The ritual procedures for repentance have established precedents within the Vinaya; therefore, it is followed by the section on the "Repentance of the Six Classes of Offenses.

The fourteen chapters below belong to the lower volume, which concerns matters arising according to specific circumstances and based upon particular events. The middle volume clearly elucidates the rules of observance and transgression, thereby purifying both body and mind.
Once body and mind are purified, one is fit to receive robes and food; when eating, it fills the interior so as to dispel [hunger].

When the vital energy (*prāṇa*) is depleted, clothing serves as an external resource to shield one from the suffering of cold; thus, there come the two chapters on clothing, both general and specific.

Although the upper body may be sufficiently covered by garments, one must further require food to fill the mouth; therefore, next is explained the chapter on receiving and purifying the four types of medicinal food.

The preceding section has clarified the four types of medicine; the essential substance of food has already been established. However, one must have a vessel to contain it, and as for the essentials of holding and maintaining [these provisions], nothing surpasses the bowl (*pātra*).

Therefore, there is this chapter on the regulations and permissions concerning bowls. Now, the alms-bowl is the appropriate vessel; the Buddha ordained that it be kept with one’s person to be used for the purpose of begging for alms.
It is like the wings of a bird, following conditions along the long path; whether departing or staying, it is without hindrance. Yet, as for those of middling or inferior capacity...

Unable to endure this teaching, [the Buddha] established the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*), so that [monastics] might ultimately perish in ditches and ravines. The Sage then permitted dwellings and household requisites;

thus, the "Method for the Fivefold Arrangement of Utensils" is appended here. However, when the principles of food and clothing are sufficient and the needs regarding dwellings are fully met, if one’s acceptance of offerings deviates from proper ritual, it conversely becomes a source of transgression and burden.

Therefore, there is the chapter on "Managing Offerings in Accordance with the Dharma. Having already explained the contemplation of food in detail, [one proceeds to] the practice of detachment from defilement.

Accomplishment is achieved when the burden of transgressions does not arise. One sits in quietude to cultivate the Way, and through the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification), one becomes preeminent and beyond compare.

Thus, there was Kāśyapa, who wore robes made of discarded rags and for whom the Buddha personally shared his seat; and Huìxiān, who restricted his food and was renowned as a person worthy of offerings. For these reasons, there is the chapter on *dhūta*.

However, although one cultivates these practices oneself, one must remain cautious and respectful. Fearing that one might rely on superior merit to become self-important and look down upon others, [the following] is provided:

Chapter on Paying Homage to the Monastic Image. Once the protocols for reverence are established, ritual propriety will permeate the times; one’s every movement and pause will be worthy of observation, thereby inspiring faith in the people.
Since many seek to invoke blessings, it is necessary to establish a formal standard. If one lacks a model when facing specific circumstances, seeing such conduct will not give rise to goodness;

therefore, there is this chapter on the Rules for Accepting Invitations. However, although the forms of monastics and laypeople differ, and though their blessings and wisdom are distinct, they rely upon one another in both body and mind.
Having attained peace and received their material provisions, one must repay them with the medicine of the Dharma; this principle requires guidance, for which a proper method must be found.

Thus, there is the chapter on "Methods for Guiding the Laity and Transforming Them. Although the seven groups of followers observe their respective codes of conduct and a single region is thereby purified and solemn, one fears that when those from foreign lands come to gaze upon us—whether as guests observing our transformation or as long-term residents or new arrivals—there may be no distinction between host and guest.
It is logically necessary to receive them with hospitality; this is the resonance of the righteous principle.

His fame spread far and wide; thus, there exists the chapter on "The Host and the Guest" (*Zhugui xiangdai pian*). Although the etiquette between host and guest is already known in its successes and failures, the fragile form and illusory substance are subject to constant birth and extinction.
The hundred-and-one afflictions easily invade, and the four snakes are difficult to nourish. Yet, one dwells together with companions of the Way.

Successively providing offerings and service, when the retribution is exhausted and conditions depart, the deceased body must be buried; thus there is the chapter on "Attending the Sick and Seeing Them Off at Death.
Although the preceding [chapters] have been categorized according to specific matters, miscellaneous duties still abound. How could what the Sage has taught be permitted to be omitted?

Therefore, a chapter is established to clarify essential miscellaneous practices; thus there is the chapter on "Various Essential Practices. These aforementioned sections constitute the primary [content].

Regarding the karma of the Saṃgha, there are two distinct sets of practices. As for the ritual protocols of the Great Saṃgha (bhikṣus), those in lower positions must rely upon them; thus, one must clearly understand these rules. For this reason, there is the chapter on the "Distinct Practices of Śrāmaṇeras.
Although the aforementioned [rules] are based on the precepts, there is a distinction between those who have received full ordination and those who have not;

yet, they are all male positions. However, as for the Bhikṣuṇīs, women are naturally timid and weak, and they become confused in every matter. If their ritual models were not proclaimed and shown, by what means could they recognize the principles of practice? Therefore, there is [the following].
The Section on the Separate Practices of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha: The preceding sections have merely compiled the practices of a single school to form a coherent whole.

As for the distinct traditions of the various schools, they are not without differing tenets. If one does not briefly examine their characteristics, there is a fear that future practitioners will harbor doubts;
therefore, this final section describes the similarities and differences among the various schools, hence its title.

The second section, the brief explanation of the titles of the thirty chapters, is hereby concluded. From this point forward is the third section, the formal explanation of the meanings of the ten gates.

First, regarding the intent behind the emergence of the teaching within this gate, it is divided into four general parts; the first is the introduction concerning the period when the Buddha was in the world.

There are four distinct purposes: first, the purpose for establishing the Vinaya teachings in response to [non-Buddhist] systems; second, the purpose for the compilation of the teachings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa in response to non-Buddhists;

third, the purpose for establishing the teachings in response to dualistic doctrines; and fourth, the purpose for establishing the teachings of this specific school. These constitute the four distinctions.
This may be sought according to the text. Furthermore, another interpretation states that within this section there are two major divisions.
First, from the beginning up to "then," it generally clarifies the emergence of the teaching; this is the general meaning regarding the emergence of the teaching.

Second, from "now, based on our own school" onwards, it clarifies that once the teaching has emerged, our own school inherently contains specific distinctions. Within the first part concerning the general meaning, there are further [subdivisions]:
There are three distinct parts. First, from "To those who have attained the human state" onwards, it clarifies the intention behind establishing the precepts in response to specific capacities.

Second, from "In contrast to non-Buddhists" onwards, it reveals how the extensive teachings differ from the non-existent dharmas of those outsiders, thereby manifesting the intention that our own school possesses the true Dharma.

Third, from "In contrast to other schools" onwards, it clarifies that the extensive teachings apply to many capacities; each may practice according to their own station and both shall obtain benefit. Nevertheless, the intention of our own school is the most supreme.
The concluding passage is elegant.

Now, regarding the "Supreme Person" (*zhiren*) who appears in the world: it is the Buddha who is called the Supreme Person, for he is the person of ultimate perfection; thus he is termed the "Supreme Person.

Only the Buddha alone may be designated as the Supreme Person, because he alone has completely exhausted the source of suffering. Furthermore, it is said that he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Furthermore, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he appears in the world. His birth in the royal palace and his realization of the Way through the eight phases of manifestation are called "arising" (*xing*).
"Arising" implies "origination. The Dharma-body is formless; it assumes form for the sake of all things. To show itself as being identical to sentient beings, it makes itself visible.

Its traces—coming and going—are called "arising" because they manifest in response. That which benefits beings has its "method" (*fang*), for this method derives from the Dharma. Once the Buddha has thus arisen in the world...
He preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, employing skillful means that are all called beneficial; thus it is said that he has a method for benefiting things.

To say that he establishes teachings according to capacities and that there is no empty bestowal of principle means that the Buddha’s methods of teaching are all for the benefit of sentient beings and are never bestowed in vain.

Being well-acquainted with both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he acts in accordance with what is appropriate for each individual's faculties and potential. If one desires the realms of humans and devas, he immediately teaches the five [precepts].
Eighth: For those who wish to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, he immediately expounds the Great Bhikṣu’s *apraṇihita-vinaya*.

To those who should hear of the Three Vehicles, he immediately expounds the parables of the three carts and so forth. To those who should hear of the One Vehicle, he then brings the Three back to the One. He speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

therefore it is said that he establishes the teachings according to the capacities of beings. Since all are intended to be led to Bodhi, it is said that these are not bestowed in vain. The Buddha possesses two kinds of wisdom.

This refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If it is fundamental wisdom, it constantly takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object without wavering.

If it is subsequently attained wisdom, it flows forth to transform the three realms, delivering sentient beings and manifesting various bodies to convert them. Furthermore, it is explained that this is how the Vinaya teachings arose.

One must prioritize benefiting all things. However, because sentient beings are mired in desire, and the root of desire is what is called the "self-mind" (*ātman*), the Great Sage, in accordance with their inclinations, revealed the Dharma of the supreme mind.
Thus, the mind is the root from which desire arises; to extinguish desire, one must necessarily still the source of the mind.

Stillness of mind arises through clear and luminous wisdom (*prajñā*); the arising of wisdom depends upon the development of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the achievement of concentration does not come about without the power of the precepts (*śīla*).

It is not expansive. Thus we know that the arising of this teaching is spoken according to the capacities of beings (*sattva*). Furthermore, the interpretation that the establishment of teachings according to capacity means there is no principle of bestowing them in vain is as follows:
it is like a great physician of the world who uses medicine to save the sick; because he correctly identifies the illness, there is none that does not receive benefit.

Likewise, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, knows the faculties and understands the teachings; he applies the Dharma to the faculties, and there is none that is not beneficial. Therefore, there is no bestowing in vain. [Excluding...]

The Buddha alone is capable; no one else can do so. For example, when Śāriputra taught the son of a goldsmith the meditation on bones (*asthi-smṛti*) and the son of a washerman the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), they were rebuked by the Buddha because they did not understand the [students'] capacities.

It should be known that the son of the goldsmith ought to have been taught counting the breath, while the son of the washerman ought to have been taught the meditation on bones. Furthermore, regarding the teaching of instruction according to capacity: as it is taught [in the scriptures]...

There are differences between the extensive and the concise, due to the varying capacities of sentient beings—some being sharp and others dull. For instance, when first attaining enlightenment, the capacity of those to be converted was sharp;
thus, he taught only the concise doctrine, which they were able to uphold and maintain without requiring the extensive teaching to reveal the specific names and categories.

This refers, for example, to the verses of the seven Buddhas found at the end of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which are collectively termed the "concise teaching. Later, as the faculties of sentient beings gradually became duller, [he taught extensively].

The teachings on the five categories of offenses and so forth have been explained; as previously stated in the *Jiexing* (Addition) fascicle, the four Buddhas established the extensive [rules], while two Buddhas established the abbreviated [rules].
This concludes the discussion on the meaning of increase and decrease regarding what was established by the two Buddhas. The treatise states:

"To speak of the Vinaya according to the gate of great compassion" clarifies that among the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the Tathāgata, through the mind of great compassion, opened the door of non-secrecy and revealed the profound methods of the secret [teachings].
The secret formulas were bestowed privately, and the inner assembly was granted special favors. The reason for this passage not being explained to the laity is that it is both secret and superior;
such is its intended meaning. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, in its first fascicle, clarifies this, stating:
"The Sūtras are taught based on the Ten Powers; the Vinaya is taught based on Great Compassion; and the Abhidharma is taught based on Fearlessness."
Furthermore, in my own view, the Buddha possesses great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth.
Regarding what is called the "gate of great loving-kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*), as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "The Tathāgata’s loving-kindness is of three kinds:

first, loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambanā maitrī*), which takes as its object sentient beings formed by the five aggregates and vows to grant them happiness; second, loving-kindness directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambanā maitrī*), which takes as its object the necessities required by all sentient beings..."

To desire to give [benefit] to things—these three are the "objectless compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*). It does not dwell upon the characteristics of dharmas nor the characteristics of sentient beings;

this is called objectless compassion. The full text of the sutra is not transcribed here; such is merely the interpretation provided by the commentators. Furthermore, another explanation holds that there are three types of compassion:

first, compassion directed toward sentient beings, which takes as its object the conventionally designated sentient beings consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); second, compassion directed toward dharmas...

This refers to the dharmas that are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Third, "unconditioned compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*) means that both sentient beings and dharmas are entirely without reality.
Thus, the Vinaya states:
"Because the World-Honored One regards them with loving-kindness, he preaches the Dharma for them. This refers to the sixtieth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The scroll says: The Buddha was in the kingdom of Vatsa.
He asked the bhikṣus, "Do you think that I preach the Dharma for you because of [providing] clothing, food, bedding, seats, and mats? The bhikṣus replied, "No.
The Buddha said, "With what intention do you say that I preach the Dharma for you? The bhikṣus answered, "World-Honored One, it is because of Your Great Compassion that You [preach] for us."
This is the Ear for Preaching the Dharma.

Second, it is intended for those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who claim that no Dharma exists and dwell therein. This concludes the second section, which clarifies the purpose of the compilation (saṃgīti).
It may also clarify that while the Buddha was still in this world, these teachings were promulgated in response to the non-Buddhists. How is this known? Therefore, now...

The text states: "Therefore, this precept was established. How could it be that the compilers of the canon established it? Regarding the statement that there is "no dharma," this refers to the absence of any dharma that can serve as a standard for guidance;
it does not mean that there are no unwholesome dharmas. Examples include such practices as scorching the body with five fires, leaping from cliffs, or throwing oneself into fire.
As their own established rules state: "If one commits sexual misconduct, one must not have intercourse with the wife of one's teacher; as for other women..."
In all such cases, there is no offense. Regarding theft, one must simply not steal the teacher’s gold; doing so incurs a grave offense. Regarding killing, one must simply not kill an ox;
as for other acts of theft or killing, there is no offense at all. These instances are all cases of individuals who abide by their own arbitrary standards.
This precept was established to manifest that the Buddha is the Honored One among men and his Way is sublime.

Because the Buddha is the Great Teacher of the three realms, a celestial being honored by men, and without equal—being uniquely venerable in the world—he is called the "Honored One among Men" (*puruṣottama*). The Dharma he has taught is able to serve as a standard for the excellence of all things;
by relying upon it for practice, one can transcend the mundane and become a sage. Such a Dharma is truly worthy of being treasured.
Noble. Because it differs from those various heterodox teachings, it is said that "the Way is lofty.
Observe that among the regulations set forth in the *Vinaya*, all those who harbor heterodox arts are excluded. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (Supplementary Text on the Vinaya) states:

"For what reason did the World-Honored One establish the training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)? It was to subdue the three poisons so they might be exhausted; thus he established the training in higher morality. This intention clarifies [the distinction].

Exhausting these three poisons, concentration and wisdom are further clarified; when delusion is exhausted and liberation is perfected, one cuts off the limits of all suffering—this is called a "different method" (*visama-vidhi*).
Furthermore, it is said that "whatever is prescribed" refers to all that was established by the Buddha. There is a distinct intention here:

for instance, the five, eight, ten, and full precepts are clearly established according to the capacities of beings. Taking their remote intent, they all lead to Bodhi; this is a "different method. Moreover,

[Commentary: Because the Buddha established the precept against destroying living beings or digging the earth, kings and ministers ceased their [harassment], and they were no longer permitted to conscript bhikṣus for labor;

this is what is meant by "extraordinary methods" (*visesa-dharma*). Regarding the self-explanation: observing the meaning of the current text, the term "extraordinary methods" refers to being distinct from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
As the Vinaya states: King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha, yet he [the king] came and went together with the non-Buddhists who gathered on the eighth and fifteenth days. I...
Because [the Buddha] received offerings, he consequently established the rule of reciting the precepts every half-month, which is not shared with non-Buddhists;
thus it is called a "different method" (*visama*). Furthermore, within each individual precept, none are held in common with non-Buddhists; therefore, they are called "different methods.

For example, the five categories and seven groups [of offenses] do not exist among non-Buddhists at all. This is how we know it: the present text states that "different methods" refers to being different from non-Buddhists.
This can be understood by examining the intent of the following sentence. Thus, the text of the subsequent passage states:

"If one does not compile and conclude [the teachings], it will cause non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to produce further [objectionable] remarks. This makes it clear that the words of "heterodox arts" refer specifically to those of the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, the text says: "If one does not compile and conclude, it will cause non-Buddhists to produce further remarks. This refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), fascicle five.
This is the Chinese text from the *Shata-bandhana-saṃgīti*. Its origins may be sought in detail in the Vinaya texts. Regarding the source of the *Sifenbiechao*, the *Yuan* (Commentary) states:

"When the Tathāgata was in the world, he taught according to the capacities of beings, benefiting them as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Now that he has entered parinirvāṇa and passed away, [the teachings must be compiled]."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "I entrust [this teaching] to Kāśyapa, Upāli, and Ānanda, desiring that you compile the Buddha’s sincere words and record them upon bamboo and silk for the benefit of future generations.
My intention is for its circulation; if it is not compiled, the teachings will fall into ruin."
Furthermore, it would invite slander. As stated in the latter part of the Vinaya:

"Do not allow non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to have further cause for criticism, saying that the Dharma and Vinaya of the Śramaṇa Gautama are like smoke and fire—when the fire is extinguished, the smoke vanishes. During the Buddha’s lifetime, all bhikṣus studied the precepts together.
Now that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, there are none who possess the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). For this reason, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, addressing the great assembly:
"The Tathāgata having passed away, the world is without a teacher; we grieve at the loss of our guide and benefit, and have no one to whom we may turn for counsel.

With a profound sense of reverence for the Dharma, he commanded that the Dharma-piṭaka be compiled to repay the Buddha’s kindness and ensure that the Dharma would not perish. Thus, atop Mount Sumeru, he struck the gavel and recited these verses.
He assembled these arhats and exhorted them not to enter parinirvāṇa, but rather to compile the Dharma-piṭaka as a way to repay the Buddha’s kindness.

This was intended so that the Buddha’s teachings might circulate through the final age and silence the lingering claims of non-Buddhist paths. The preceding explanation of the meaning of how non-Buddhists have no dharma in which to abide is now complete.
Third, regarding the arrival [of this treatise] to counter opposing schools: this is the third section below, which sets forth the intent to address the doctrines of external (non-Buddhist) schools.
As for the phrase "many distinctions," it is as stated in the *Karmavācanā-prastāva*: "In the beginning, there was the distinction between the two schools and the five schools;

in the middle, there were the divisions of the eighteen and the five hundred. This means that the fundamental [schools] were only the two: the Sthavira and the Mahāsāṃghika. One hundred years later...
It was divided into twelve schools; after two hundred years, it was divided into twelve;
after four hundred years, it was divided into eighteen schools, including the root school, making twenty schools in total. As for those called the Sthaviras (Elders):
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa selected five hundred *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training) from Jambudvīpa and convened a council at Rājagṛha. Kāśyapa was then advanced in years.
At that time, those residing at the head of the assembly were thus named the Sthavira (Elders) School. Later, there were minor sages from other regions who had not heard of this council;
they held their own recitation outside the city, and as their number was great, they were called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) School.

Thus we know that at the time of the recitation, the community had already split into two schools. Therefore, it is proclaimed: "As for the original division of the Sthaviras and Mahāsāṃghikas at the first recitation..."

Regarding the schools: more than a hundred years after the five divisions and eighteen streams were established, although they were divided into five divisions and eighteen streams, if one considers those that have been transmitted and are currently practiced in the world, there are only the five divisions.
Furthermore, these five divisions all originated from the Sthavira school;

because they subsequently split and diverged so as not to remain a single entity, they are said to be "many distinct [branches]. One may consult the diagram of the schismatic divisions at the appropriate time.
Regarding the recitation at the time of the lecture:
for instance, as for the abbreviated *Prātimokṣa* of the Sarvāstivāda school, it clarifies that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-prātimokṣa* contains the fault of being excessively verbose.
For example, within the *Saiksa* rules, it explains the proper manner of wearing the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) and the three robes (*tricīvara*).
There are twelve precepts; this is considered detailed. Omitting the precepts regarding not showing disrespect to stupas, chewing tooth-sticks, and so forth, is also called "abbreviated.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is not like this; it simply states, "Wear the inner robe neatly," which encompasses everything without exception. Jì says:
"In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Shisong jieben), when the number of precepts among the *Saiksa-dharmas* does not reach one hundred, it is called 'abbreviated. Within its *Pāyantika* section..."
The ninety-first *pācittiya* is called "prolixity. Now, I shall examine this at length and refute it. However, within this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is likewise both prolixity and brevity.
For example, regarding the *niḥsargika-pācittiya* rules for bhikṣuṇīs: when a bhikṣuṇī applies fragrant oil or sesame paste to her body, seven precepts are established in total.
First, applying fragrant oil oneself; second, applying sesame paste oneself; third, having a mahā-bhikṣuṇī apply it; fourth, having a śrāmaṇerī... [text continues]

[If one] applies [it with] a brush, or employs a śrāmaṇerī to apply it as the fifth, or employs a laywoman (*avadātavastrā*) to apply it as the sixth, or employs a female heretic (*tīrthikī*) to apply it as the seventh—all these constitute a *pāyattika*.

Is this not indeed prolix? If only the destruction of living beings and the digging of the earth were combined into a single precept—whether done by oneself or taught to another—yet now multiple precepts are established based on the specific objects involved, is this not prolixity? As for the statement that "the substance of the finger is not yet complete":

Lì says: "The 'indicator' (zhǐ) refers to the school (zōng). It is also called the 'indicative teaching' (jiàozhǐ). The indicator arises from the mind. 'Essence' (tǐ) refers to the essence of the precepts (jièti).
This clarifies that within this school, both the manifest (biǎo) and unmanifest (wúbiǎo) precepts take form (sè) as their essence.

He says: since the manifest is the cause and the unmanifest is the fruit, and since the cause is form, why would the fruit not be form? This school does not hold such a view; the active precept (zuòjiè) is form, but the non-active (wúzuò) is not."
Regarding "form and mind": form can be afflicted and destroyed by having shape, segments, and spatial location, whereas the essence of non-action (avijñapti) is not so;

therefore, that [other] school is criticized as being incomplete. As for the phrase "pointing with the finger," it must be understood as "making a finger with the hand"; this means that because the precept-essence (śīla-tattva) of that school is not yet perfected, it is said thus.
"Adapting to worldly conventions to fix the duration" refers to receiving the five or eight precepts from laypeople, which is called...

This is for the purpose of conforming to worldly conventions. The five precepts must be observed for a lifetime; the eight precepts must be observed for one day and one night. One is not permitted to extend the duration.
This is the fixed determination of the time. Regarding the number: when receiving the five, one must receive all five; one may not receive only one, two, or three.

When receiving the eight, one must receive all eight; they may not be increased or decreased. This is the fixed determination of the number. Daolüe says: "As clarified in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, when receiving the five or eight precepts, one must receive them in their entirety."
[Objection: It is so. [The opponent] then raises a challenge: "Why does the Sūtra speak of 'one part' up to 'the full amount' regarding an *upāsaka*?

[Response: This refers to the quantity of precepts one maintains; thus it speaks of "one part," "two parts," and so forth. It does not mean that there are only one or two [categories] within the act of undertaking the vows.

Although the Sarvāstivādins maintain this interpretation, it contradicts their own Vinaya. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in the section on the Leather Rules (*Carman-dharma*), Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa...
The upāsaka was traveling with a group of merchants into the sea to gather treasures. When their ship was wrecked, they lost their way; his companions died, but he alone survived and returned.
Passing through the city of hungry ghosts (preta), he came to the foot of a tree where he saw a man and a woman of handsome appearance, wearing celestial jewel crowns, enjoying themselves together.
When the night passed and the woman vanished, dogs immediately came and devoured the flesh of the man and woman. Ayyu was struck with wonder.
Question: For what reason was it thus? Answer: "In the past, I was a butcher. Kātyāyana transformed me, and I said, 'My ancestors have always practiced this occupation;
how can I stop? He then instructed me, saying, 'Since you slaughter during the day, you may observe the precepts at night.
Because of this, such is the karmic retribution in my present life. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa walked forward and again reached the foot of a tree, where he saw...
Men and women enjoyed themselves during the day, as described in detail previously. This was due to their fondness for sexual indulgence.

Kātyāyana transformed his appearance and said, "Since you are greedy for lust at night, you ought to observe the precepts during the day. Consequently, we now experience pleasure by day and suffering by night. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa returned and related all that he had seen;
thereupon, he went to Kātyāyana, left the household life, and received the precepts. According to this Vinaya, there is also the practice of receiving the precepts partially, though it is common.

Treatise, Chapter One. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 124. Various great masters of the treatises gathered at this passage. First, the *Vibhāṣā* asks: "How is such an exposition to be reconciled?
That is to say, if one does not admit that [the precepts] are received separately for day and night, as stated in the aforementioned Vinaya text, how is it to be reconciled?
The answer is: "That is comprised within 'excellent conduct' (*sucarita*), not a formal restraint (*saṃvara*). It is the fruit of receiving excellent conduct, not [the fruit of] restraint."
