hence it is said to be incomplete. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the five masters gathered [the fragments]": the *Fangyan* (Explanations of Words) states that "gathering" (*jùn*) refers to picking up or collecting objects;
it is also said that to gather means to collect what has been left behind. Jing says: "While the Tathāgata was in the world, and during the hundred years after his parinirvāṇa..."
Prior to this period, their views were without divergence; however, after a hundred years had passed, the five masters held differing opinions.
Each of them, from within the Great Vinaya Piṭaka, selected those passages that accorded with their own views and compiled them into distinct schools.

Those that did not agree were set aside and not recorded, resulting in the division into five schools. Regarding these five masters, the tradition of the ancient virtuous ones maintains that they were all brothers of Kātyāyanīputra.
My son, there is no authoritative teaching to rely upon. Now, examining this closely, it is clear that these five masters were not entirely disciples of Kūṭadanta;

some were, while others were not. According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (or *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*), the sources from which the names of the five schools emerged are each distinct and different.
How could their founders all have been disciples of Kūṭadanta? In the past, when the sūtras and śāstras were not yet complete, ancient scholars made arbitrary judgments.
This is because they have failed to reach the original source of the various schools' tenets and thus arbitrarily impose their own judgments.

Furthermore, regarding those who, due to errors in translation, have falsely constructed their own systems: for instance, there was once a Tripiṭaka Master from a foreign land who came to this region to translate the *Siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*.
The Tripiṭaka Master of this land did not understand its language, and the other [foreign] Master likewise did not understand [the local one's]. This is why...

A Tripiṭaka Master from a foreign land was about to sprinkle water upon Youdu (Youdou). Youdu immediately manifested a display of vigor (*visphūrjana*), pointing it out and saying, "Such is this matter.
From this, the Tripiṭaka Master of this region realized its meaning and called it the *bai* (pronounced *tusha hai*) samādhi.
Later scholars of great talent changed its name to the *visphūrjana* samādhi. Based on this, one can see that translation is truly difficult; therefore—
It is possible that there may have been errors in the interpretation. Furthermore, even when the ancient texts of Confucianism were translated, they were still flawed;

if the colloquial language of the present day is already inconsistent in its transmission, how much more so is this the case when ordinary people and sages belong to different categories and the East and West are separated by vast distances? To truly understand Sanskrit, one must become proficient in correct translation.
Having read the *Cangjie* and *Erya* only superficially and having gained a rough familiarity with seal and clerical scripts, one is then able to attempt translations.
To say "to construct" (*gòu*) means to frame or build up. Since the original translations already miss the mark, one then proceeds to establish their own methods based on mere personal fancy;

therefore, it is said that they "arbitrarily construct. Jì says: "Nevertheless, I do not wish to speak of the shortcomings of the ancients; however, as for the points where the ancients' translations went astray—"

There was none. It was only when the Tripitaka Master translated the scriptures during the Tang dynasty that the principles were somewhat fully exhausted. For instance, in the old version of the *Vimalakīrti*, it says:
"He is unmoved by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru. Now, [the new version] states: "He is unmoved by the eight winds, like the king of mountains.

Since "praise and blame" are merely specific names for two of the eight winds, this would omit the other six types; how then could it be called complete? It is also like [the treatment of] various sutras—
First: All ancient editions state that the Buddha was in Śrāvastī and so forth. According to the Sanskrit manuscripts, all contain the term *bhagavat*;
the translators omitted it and simply said "Buddha. Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The term *bhaga* functions according to six meanings:
first, the meaning of sovereignty; second, the meaning of brilliance; third, the meaning of majesty; fourth, the meaning of renown; fifth, the meaning of auspiciousness..."
The meaning of *śrī* (auspiciousness). The meaning of *bhagavat* (the Blessed One) consists of six aspects of nobility. As a verse says:

"Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), brilliance (*tejas*), and beauty (*darśanīyatā*), Fame (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*prabhutva*): These six distinct meanings Should be known as collectively termed 'Bhaga'. The prose commentary explains:
"Because the Tathāgatas are forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*), they possess the meaning of sovereignty. [They possess] Nirvāṇa..."
Because it is refined by the fire of wisdom, it possesses the meaning of "blazing. Because it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, it possesses the meaning of "exquisite beauty.
Because all supreme qualities are perfected and there is nothing unknown, it possesses the meaning of "renown.
Because all the world approaches, makes offerings to, and praises it, it possesses the meaning of "auspiciousness. It possesses the one...

Because he constantly gives rise to skillful means out of all virtues to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without ever becoming weary or negligent, he possesses the meaning of "Bhagavat" (the Venerable).
Alternatively, because he destroys the four Māras and their enmity, he is called Bhagavat. Thus, this single name serves as a general designation for his manifold virtues.

For this reason, this title is placed at the beginning of all sūtras. It is sometimes rendered as *bhagavān* or *bhagavat*, both of which are merely different phonetic shifts of the same Sanskrit term.

When the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated the scriptures, he frequently employed both terms together, saying "Buddha Bhagavān. Regarding this, there are four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first is one who is a Buddha but not a Bhagavān;
this refers to those in the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and realized the two types of nirvāṇa. Thus it is named.
First, there are those who are Buddhas but do not cultivate merit; therefore, they are not Bhagavāns. Second, there are those who are Bhagavāns but not Buddhas;
these are the great Bodhisattvas who have cultivated all merits but have not yet entered parinirvāṇa. Third, there are those who are neither; these are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

If one uses only the term "Buddha," it would erroneously include the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). If one uses only the term "Bhagavān," it would erroneously include Bodhisattvas. Therefore, both terms are established together.

There is no longer the confusion caused by the first two [errors]. However, in the Sanskrit original, the term *bhagavat* is used alone; it is only when adding the word "Buddha" that the meaning of the True Dharma (Paramārtha) is fully realized.

Thus, the Tripitaka Masters of the Tang dynasty all used the single term *bāgavàn*. When ancient translators directly rendered it as "Buddha," was this not a failure to convey such a significant portion of its intended meaning?
Therefore, it is said that the translation repeatedly lost the original intent. Furthermore, errors may arise from scribal omissions and transpositions.

For instance, as for the texts of one division of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the wording is often incomplete because the recension brought from the East by the scholar Paramārtha was transcribed on the spot as it was translated.
Valuing the preservation of a single copy, there was no leisure for cross-referencing or verification; soon thereafter, he returned to the West.
Consequently, these texts were not widely circulated or utilized, and thus many parts are missing.
Regarding the phrase "abundant entanglements of thought" (*fenlü xiāngduō*): "entanglement" (*fēn*) refers to confusion and disorder; "thought" (*lǜ*) refers to doubt and hesitation.

This clarifies that since the aforementioned various faults are already present, when one reaches the time of investigation, the mind becomes cluttered and the intellect filled with uncertainty. One cannot resolve matters and knows nothing of their underlying principles;
such persistent stagnation makes it difficult for the mind to reach a definitive understanding. Now, to synthesize these points in order to facilitate a comprehensive vision:

Lì said: "Although the Vinaya-piṭaka contains mutual omissions and deficiencies, these all result from the differing personal views of the five masters, as well as errors and omissions during transcription.
Nevertheless, the original source of the Great Canon was one; it is now being harmonized here. Where the text is complete, I supplement it with the meaning;
where the text of a particular section is insufficient, I draw from other schools; and where the text is absent in both, I rely on the meaning."

This is an example of a comprehensive resolution (*tongjue*). It differs from the localized attachments of various masters, who are unable to provide a comprehensive understanding of the views. My present synthesis is called the "Great View" (*dajian*).

Furthermore, another interpretation is that "comprehensive Great View" refers to what is clarified below: when both the text and its meaning are deficient, one cites a single instance to serve as an analogy for all others;
this is called the "Comprehensive Great View. Alternatively, when a principle exists and brings about a result, this too is the "Comprehensive Great View."
Furthermore, if in some instances the wording appears [in the text] but the meaning is deficient, one should resolve it by means of the meaning;

this is also called "penetrating the great vision. Some explain that "penetrating the great vision" refers to the fact that the personal views (*dṛṣṭi*) of the five preceding masters were not in accord.
This is not called a great view; it is merely called a small view. Now, by synthesizing these five into one, this constitutes a great view.

Furthermore, I personally believe that the Vinayas of the five schools are like spears and shields in their words and meanings; their severity and leniency contradict one another, such that they cannot be reconciled through mere sentiment nor resolved through intellectual interpretation.

Since antiquity, scholars have clung to their disputes, which have persisted for generations without being extinguished. By now synthesizing and harmonizing them all, I therefore say this constitutes a great [view].
It is indeed seen.

If both the text and the meaning are lacking, and one instance is cited as an illustration for all others, [Seng]li says: "For example, regarding the precept against eating at improper times, there is no text permitting exceptions, nor is there any underlying principle for such exceptions.
Since this one case is thus, other precepts are to be treated accordingly. Furthermore, it is like the first precept, which was [established] because of being harmed by an enemy.
Regarding "coercion": if there is no pleasure during the three stages [of sexual intercourse], there is no offense; this is both the scriptural text and its meaning.

If one were to say that because there is pleasure during the three stages, it is permitted and thus not an offense, this would lack both scriptural authority and logical meaning. Furthermore, regarding the precept against great falsehood: for those who have left the household life, speech must accord with reality.

If one lacks the factors of the Path within yet deceives others by claiming to have attained sainthood (*ārya*), a grave offense is prescribed; the offense is completed the moment the words are finished. If one were to say that the offense is not [completed] even when the words are finished...
Regarding the omission of rules on offenses (*saṃvara-āpatti*): it is a case where both the text and the meaning are missing. Sengshen says:
"For example, in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there is a prohibition against nuns keeping female attendants (*karmadāna*). In this [present] Vinaya, however, both the text and the meaning are missing.

Again, for example, in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, it is stated that a messenger of suffering may not remain for more than two months. Furthermore, in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, one who violates royal regulations commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Also, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, they do not..."

One must not permit the conferring of precepts in the midst of clouds and mist or darkness when identifying the recipient is impossible; there is no textual basis for this in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), and its meaning is likewise lacking.

Now, this [point] is resolved by taking the texts of other schools to interpret this Vinaya. Furthermore, regarding the care of the sick, it is both textually and logically required that one who possesses the necessary virtues be rewarded with the three robes (*tricīvara*) for their labor.
If one rewards someone who lacks such virtues, it is not permitted by the text, nor is it consistent with principle.

Upon examination, it is likewise not appropriate to grant a reward; therefore, it is said that both the text and the meaning are deficient. Alternatively, regarding cases where a matter is accomplished based on principle, [Dao]li states:
"For example, in the original Dharma, there is no textual provision for a *bhikṣuṇī* going among the *bhikṣu* community to receive ordination and having an ordination preceptor (*karmācārya*).

Since it is required by principle that one should have such a preceptor, one must rely on this principle to request one, thereby accomplishing the rite of ordination. Furthermore, as in the case of the two hundred..."

Regarding the fifty precepts: among the twenty-six precepts listed in the Vinaya, there are cases where the object (境) and the perception (想) are specified; for the remaining precepts, they are not so listed, yet it is logically consistent that they should exist.

For instance, in the case of eating at an improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*), there are instances involving the perception of it being the proper time, the perception of it being the improper time, or doubt, and so forth.

Furthermore, as will be established in the meaning of the following text, the seven types of "impropriety" (*asamyak*) all exist according to logical necessity. Alternatively, regarding those cases where the text is complete but the meaning is deficient, it is stated: "For example..."

Regarding the distribution of the deceased’s robes, the three *kāṣāyas* and six articles are listed in detail; these are to be given collectively to the attendant who cared for the patient. Such a person must possess virtuous qualities.
Since the present individual does not possess such qualities, it is logically improper to reward him; therefore, it is said that there is a deficiency in principle (*artha*).

As for the statement, "one settles it according to principle," this clarifies that if one possesses virtue and principle, one is fit to be rewarded; if one lacks virtue and principle, one is unfit to be rewarded.
Therefore it is said. Shen says: "In the text for establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), the cardinal directions are chanted in unison; their names are complete within the text.

However, the intermediate directions (*vidiś*) are not mentioned, which is a deficiency in terms of meaning. Now, they must be established according to the principle. One chants starting from the corners, so that the names are determined by the underlying meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the *karmavācanā* for receiving the sun, while the Vinaya text is complete, although the names are present in the text, it does not clarify that [the boundary] may be re-established.

Regarding the precepts: one must not receive them repeatedly; this is termed a deficiency in meaning. Since the meaning is thus incomplete, various masters have each maintained that repeated reception is not permitted.
Now, the meaning must be definitively established: whenever the conditions arise, one may receive them again.
This is why it is said [in the treatise]: "Because taking principle as the standard. As for the phrase "Cí says," this refers to the aforementioned passage from the *Sudarsana-vibhasa-sastra*.

It is said: "To apply [the rule] by means of one's own judgment" refers precisely to this principle. Or, there may be cases where a meaning must necessarily be established even though there is no explicit text in the relevant section; as the preceding preface states:

"Sometimes the text is broken, yet the meaning connects them," which is like the example of the deaf and mute being insufficient [to determine the standard]. One must then resort to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Furthermore, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely says it should be a distance that can be traversed in a single day; now, according to our interpretation...
It is said that taking three hundred *yojanas* as the measure, according to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, is intended to quell further slander.

This means that if one did not adopt the passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning the addition of medicine and the wearing of robes, outsiders would claim: "The teachings within your own school are insufficient."

The external schools possess clear and explicit texts; why then are they not accepted? This is likely because you are one who clings to narrow-mindedness and guards like a person waiting for a hare at a stump.

Nevertheless, since the textual meanings are decisively interconnected, it is truly difficult to establish or reject them. This precisely concludes the preceding section. Therefore, it was said above:
"Now, we synthesize these altogether to form a grand vision. Yet, the various schools differ in their degrees of gravity, as in the case of the four coins and three pennies.
And so forth. Now, if one were to abolish that and establish this, or abolish this and establish that, it would be difficult to reach a definitive resolution.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that this is a praise of the fact that the meaning of the present method is difficult to practice. Moreover, the *Śāṅgīti* says: "For instance, within the single-announcement (*ekajñapti*) of the *karmavācanā*, it is divided into two."
In the second sentence, both the root and the condition are cited together. By the fourth sentence, only the root is cited, and the condition is no longer cited.
Now, if the root were to still cite the condition, this would be redundant; thus, this superfluous phrase is discarded, and the citation of the root alone is established.
Such a process of discarding and establishing is truly difficult; hence it is said: "Unless one is profoundly clear regarding the characteristics of the Vinaya, one cannot [do this well]."

"To master what is permitted and what is prohibited" means that "permitted" refers to what is allowed, while "prohibited" refers to what is restricted. Otherwise, there will be entanglements for one's own mind;

thus, it would be of no benefit to the external realm. This means that if one does not skillfully master the distinctions between what is permitted and prohibited as described above, nor clearly understand the characteristics of the teachings, [one will fail].

When passing judgment on another’s offense, it may happen that one who is heavy is punished lightly or one who is light is punished heavily, thereby preventing the other from repenting their transgression while causing oneself to incur further fault;

this is a case of burdening both oneself and others. Furthermore, it is explained that if one does not understand the intent of decisive resolution and applies the law to the person before them, it benefits neither self nor other;
this means the matter at hand is not settled, and one also incurs guilt.

It is so. Therefore, the Vinaya states that where the text and meaning are identical: among the twelve additional articles of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when the Buddha was in the country of Vatsa, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You bhikṣus, you should be harmonious and joyful; within the Abhidharma, plant [the seeds of merit]."
Regarding the various types of contentious speech, one should say: "The words spoken by the Elder are consistent with their meaning;
you should not dispute them. Second, if it is further said: "The phrasing differs but the meaning is the same; do not engage in strife. Third, if it is further said:
"The words spoken by the Elder are identical in phrasing but differ in meaning; you should not dispute them. Fourth, if it is further said: "The words spoken by the Elder..."
It is said that both the text and its meaning differ; do not engage in mutual strife. If the Saṃgha is thus united, should a dispute arise, they should reconcile.
One should observe it in this way. Such is the scriptural text (*vinaya*). Regarding the *Liyi jie* (Exegesis of the Commentary), it states: This clarifies that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to adjudicate a matter, do not contend with one another; do not give rise to disputes. The first phrase says: "Text and meaning..."

Regarding "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*): for example, the two divisions of the Saṅgha—the monks and the nuns—each have five categories [of offenses]. One who establishes the formal argument (*viniścaya-vādī*) says that the text and its meaning correspond;

one who debates the meaning (*artha-vādī*) says that the status of male and female is distinct. Since these two explanations are divided, both the text and the meaning fail to correspond, and thus a dispute arises.
Regarding the second statement, the one who establishes the formal argument says: although the wording differs slightly, the meaning is the same, just as when using [the term] "drinking."

Regarding "insect-infested water": because both serve equally to protect life. Regarding the two types of sitting mats—those used in private and those used in public: because both serve equally to protect the property of the Saṃgha.

Regarding acts such as striking or beating: because both serve equally to prevent killing and harassment. The proponent of the [first] argument says: "Since the phrasing is different, how can the meaning be the same?

Why then do you give rise to this dispute? The third proponent of the argument says: "Although the phrasing is the same, the meanings expressed are different, just as in the case of counting the fetus."
Regarding the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) and the increase or decrease within the seventeen [days] of benefit and loss, the proponents of the treatise say:

"Since the texts are identical, how can there be a difference in meaning that gives rise to such dispute? This refers to the case of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) with a reduction in years.

In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there is an allowance for the intercalary month and the embryo (*garbha*); likewise, in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, the allowance for the intercalary month and the embryo is also clarified. Although these two texts are the same, their meanings differ.
The reduction of years for the precepts is intended to exempt the preceptor from the offense of falling (pācittiya); within the Khandhaka, it is for the sake of the disciple obtaining the precepts;

thus, the meaning is different. Regarding "increasing by seventeen benefits and reducing": this refers to how, in the passage on increasing by seventeen concerning the five qualities for censuring faults, one benefits without reducing.
This statement is consistent with what is said in the increase by twelve regarding the person who censures faults.
One should reflect regarding the person against whom the charge is brought: "I have incurred but little affliction; there is no harm to them, and they will receive benefit.

If one can cause them to abandon unwholesome states and perform wholesome dharmas, then one should indeed bring forth the charge. These two statements are identical in meaning, both being called "benefit."
How are they distinguished? It is said that among the twelve increases, one who is free from affliction toward oneself is included;
and among the seventeen virtues of benefit, one who is free from affliction regarding what has been raised is so called. Furthermore, Li says: "The proponent of the thesis (shuyi zhe) states..."
Harsh speech and the like are grave offenses by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), whereas matchmaking and the like are light offenses by prohibition (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). The *Lunyi* (Expositor) says:

"Since these belong to the same category (*ekādhikaraṇa*), how can there be such a difference in gravity? The fourth statement, made by the *Shuyi* (Proponent), says: "The wording and the meaning are both different. The *Lunyi* says:
"They categorize them under a single heading and then engage in dispute by making arbitrary comparisons. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The *Shuyi* says..."

The phrasing and the meaning are both different, just as the precepts for monks and nuns differ. The proponents of the formal discussion (*vāda*) say: "Since these are both the teachings of the Sage, the phrasing and meaning are not different;
yet you have given rise to this dispute. The guest says: "The proponent of the established position (*siddhānta*) says: For instance, the Four Truths have four distinct meanings;

therefore, it is said that both the phrasing and the meaning are different. The proponents of the formal discussion say: "If the four meanings are already different, they ought not to share the same name."
The Truths. Although the names "truth" (*satya*) and "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and "origination" (*samudaya*) are the same, their referential meanings differ.

Furthermore, although the four are equally named "truths," since suffering and origination are both contaminated (*sāsrava*), do cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) likewise share the quality of being contaminated? It is for this reason that a dispute arises. In the Vinaya, there are four propositions.

First, the phrasing and meaning correspond; second, the phrasing differs but the meaning is the same; third, the phrasing is the same but the meaning differs; fourth, both phrasing and meaning differ.

Regarding the inversion of the second and third phrases in the *Chao* (Commentary), it was intended to take the word "sound" (*śabda*). Why, then, are the four phrases from the Vinaya text cited here?
It is because the preceding section praised the definitive penetration of both phrasing and meaning as difficult [to master]; thus, the four phrases from the Vinaya have been cited.

This is the root of the dispute, difficult to resolve. One person says they are the same; another says they are different. Since it is difficult to reach a definitive conclusion, it is also like the intent of this present school.
As for the detailed analysis of the pros and cons that need not be laboriously explained, this refers to the text of the Vinaya.

I shall clarify the similarities and differences myself; I will not laboriously recount the entire commentary. This refers to the passage concerning the "twelve increases," which is as previously cited.
However, in determining what is right and wrong:

the two instances of "maintaining" (*dharana*) are correct, while the two instances of "violating" (*āpatti*) are incorrect. Thus it is said. Furthermore, one should recognize the accompanying [circumstances].
The "texts of the sūtras" refers to the vinayas that follow the sūtras, such as the *Śālistamba*, the *Upāsakasaṃvara*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
The *Nirvāṇa* extensively elucidates the eight kinds of impurity and other such categories.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are three aspects [to the formulation of a precept]: first, the origin (*nidāna*), which refers to the occasion when Sūpananda returned to his native village to beg for food;
thus it is called the "origin. Second, the formal promulgation of the precept (*prajñapti*), which means that based on this origin, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and established the prohibition.
Third, the subsequent application (*anuprajñapti*), meaning that although the precept had been promulgated following the initial incident, this particular individual had not yet spoken [of it].

There are three categories. To prevent transgressions from being exhausted in the past or future, later, due to Bhaṣaja, he lived together with the lay community; they reported his fault to the Buddha, and he likewise established the *pārājika* offense.
This completes the core of the precepts (*śīla-mūla*), which is why it is called "binding according to circumstances" (*anuprati-bandha*).

As for the two sets of Vinaya, this refers to the listing of the core precepts for the two assemblies of monks and nuns at the beginning of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. They are known there as the *Dvividha-prātimokṣa*; the author of the *Chao* (the *Vinayamātṛkā-ṭīkā*) has changed [the terminology].

This refers to the *Vinaya* (Precepts and Discipline) and the *Arthaviniścaya* (Exegesis of Meaning). Examining the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it first lists the two sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, followed by the explanation of the expanded texts from one to ten;

hence it is called "Incremental" (*Ekottarika*). Next, it provides an exegesis, citing each point from the aforementioned two sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and explaining them in successive order;
hence it is called "Exegesis of Meaning. This is also similar to the *Caturvargika-vinaya-vibhaṅga*.
"Similar Vinaya" refers to the entire *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) as a single collection within the Great Canon, which is collectively termed "Vinaya.

It may also be described continuously as "along with the Exegesis of the Vinaya," for upon examining that Vinaya, one finds that following the initial listing of the core precepts (*śīla-sūtra*), each is subsequently cited and explained;
since all that is explained constitutes the Vinaya, it is so called. As for the "Ekottarika" (Incremental), the ten... [text ends]
In the recitation of the Vinaya, there are various passages that are no different from those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
From one to ten, because one is added at each stage, it is called "Incremental by One" (*Ekottarika*). Bin says: "As for 'Incremental by One,' the text of the first section is the initial 'one';

all subsequent passages increase by means of this one, hence it is called 'Incremental by One. The text states that 'one' is taken as the basis, and by adding one to that one, [the sequence proceeds]."
Regarding the term "Ekottara" (Increasing by One) and the terms "allowance and prohibition" (*kai-sha*) and "lightness and heaviness": for example, the five primary colors are called "impure.

Not permitting their use is termed a "prohibition" (*sha*); that which is not among the five primary colors is "pure," and permitting its use is termed an "allowance" (*kai*). An allowance is light, while a prohibition is heavy.
Thus, there are degrees of gravity. Regarding "impurity, prohibition, and so forth": within that Vinaya, there are further categories of pure and impure.
If colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white are impure, they are prohibited; if these colors are altered to become "dyed colors" (kāsāya), they are termed pure and are not prohibited.
It is further stated that at five years of age one attains purity by being released from dependence; at twenty years of age one attains purity by receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*);
with four bhikṣus, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is called purity; and with five bhikṣus, the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) is called purity.

To deviate from these is termed impurity. The meaning of purity and impurity explained in the text is extremely extensive. This refers to those who have already applied themselves after deliberating upon such matters from beginning to end. Regarding that text:
The *Zhongzibing* (Self-Clarification) states: "In this way, one should deliberate upon the relative weight of the root and the branch before putting [the robe] into use.

One should use what has been dyed the prescribed color (*vaivarṇya*); one should not use what is not dyed the prescribed color. One should use what is not prohibited; one should not use what is prohibited.

Regarding 'root and branch,' the meaning of that text is to have one examine the preceding and succeeding sections of the Vinaya: the preceding is the root, and the succeeding is the branch. Alternatively, it may also refer to the origin."
The name is the root; the interpretation of the meaning, as well as purity and impurity, are the branches. One should calculate that the intention [of the author] must be understood in this way;
this is the sense of definitively reconciling the meanings of the preceding and following contexts.

A bhikṣu who is able to know the five characteristics [is one who understands the boundary]. First, the basis of origination; second, the establishment of the boundary; third, the following of the establishment; fourth, the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*); and fifth, the opening of exceptions. Regarding the "discernment of characteristics":

it refers to entering [the boundary] even as much as the tip of a hair, or departing from one's original location; when these are clearly understood, this is called the discernment of characteristics.

When the mind and its objects are confused or forgotten, or due to joking and laughter, or states of insanity and mental derangement—all such cases are termed "openings" (*mukta*). It is not [otherwise].

Regarding the phrase "looking at his face," the *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* explains it itself as follows: "Since one already possesses clear understanding and a mind free from doubt or fear, how could one further look at another's facial expression? Thus it is said.

The meaning clarifies that once the five signs (*pañca-nimitta*) are recognized and one is able to skillfully resolve and penetrate them, there is no need to question others or deferentially observe their countenances.
Some say it is like when there is dust and grime on the upper and lower parts of a person's face; then one [reaches out] to wipe it away.

To look at oneself in a mirror is called "looking at one's own face. If one knows there is grime on one's face, yet asks another person about the matter at hand, this is called "looking at another's face.
Now, if you understand the teaching as explained before, you will take up the mirror and have no need to ask others;
if you do not understand the teaching, you rely on the countenances of others—this is what is meant by "looking at another's face. Jie said: "The Vinaya teachings are called the 'five locations'."

Seeking means observing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth, up to the discernment of characteristics and the opening of understanding; through these, one knows what is authentic and what is spurious.

The teachings of the *Sūtras* are called "seeking by sequence," meaning that by observing the scriptural text—if there is a systematic order and a sequential progression of questions and answers—one knows whether it is an authentic or a spurious scripture.
The *Abhidharma* is called "seeking by analysis" (*vibhaṅga-paryeṣaṇā*), and is also termed "thorough analysis. Regarding the text:

"Concise as above; detailed as explained therein" means that the five characteristics in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* are such that the first three are concise and correspond to the passage on the "three matters" in the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*.
As for the phrase "detailed as explained therein," it refers to the extensive explanation of the five characteristics found within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.

Regarding the meaning of what is expressed by the sixth [category], the teaching is the expressive agent (*vācaka*), which expresses the practice of the precepts (*śīla-caryā*). This practice is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

The characteristics of that which is expressed do not exceed two matters: timely transgression and untimely transgression. These two observances and two transgressions encompass the entirety of practice;
because these two observances and two transgressions constitute the intended meaning of what is expressed, it is called "the meaning of what is expressed by the teaching."
Regarding the texts that explain the teachings, although these texts are vast and extensive, their primary intent is solely to clarify what constitutes observance and transgression.

To clarify the teachings that express this meaning is precisely the Vinaya Piṭaka. Although this Vinaya Piṭaka is indeed expansive, its underlying purport does not go beyond observance and transgression.

Therefore, it is said that "stopping" clarifies the maintenance and violation [of precepts]. As in the *Vinaya-mūla*, the preceding two sections on the precepts for monks and nuns constitute "stopping-maintenance" (*zhi-chi*), while violating them is termed "active-violation" (*zuo-fan*).
The subsequent twenty *khandakas* constitute "active-maintenance" (*zuo-chi*), and violating them is termed "stopping-violation" (*zhi-fan*).

Regarding the statement that "the objects encompass both internal and external," this means that the two practices of maintenance and violation may take either the internal mind as the object of maintenance and violation, or...

External matters constitute the objects of transgression and non-transgression; internal refers to the karmic formations of the active mind. Within the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the first is matter (*rūpa*) and the latter four are mind (*citta*).
Among these four mental factors, they are consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*); [the latter] precedes the former three minds.

This belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It cannot constitute karma; it flows into the mind of volitional formation (*saṃskāra-citta*). Only when one subsequently performs good or evil does it become bound karma (*karmabandha*).
As for what is called "bound karma," what kind of karma is bound? It refers to the karma of transgression. The arising of the three poisons within is the transgression;

taking these poisons as the object of transgression, the internal arising of the three poisons constitutes the offense. Conversely, the cessation of these three poisons is termed "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*); that is, taking a virtuous mind as the upholding.
These are the objects [of transgression]. These two types of objects are both bound to the mind of action (*citta-saṃskāra*) and are not the first three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*).

"External" refers to the favorability or unfavorability of sentient beings and insentient things. Liangbi states: "Sentient beings are the category of sentient objects; insentient things are the category of non-sentient objects.

Regarding these two types of objects—sentient and insentient—there are both cases of holding [the precept] and cases of violating it. For example, in the case of the precept against killing, there is a violation regarding sentient beings.
This is called an offense (*āpatti*). If one does not kill, it is called observance (*dhāraṇā*) by way of conformity.

If, for instance, one destroys living beings or accepts food [from them], this is called an offense by way of contravening the actual matter; conversely, not destroying living beings and so forth is called observance by way of conformity.

Now, I shall provide a direct and single explanation to make it easy to understand: regarding both the subjective intention (*citta*) and the objective matter (*vastu*), if one contravenes the teaching, it is called an offense; within the teaching—

If one acts in accordance [with the teaching], it is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇā*). This is because, in all cases, one's own mind may either conflict with or accord with the circumstances previously encountered;

thus it is said. Provided that the practice and the teaching follow one another from beginning to end without transgression: "practice" refers to mental conduct, and "teaching" refers to the Vinaya instruction.

When these two proceed in mutual succession, if the mind remains in harmony and free of contradiction, it is called "upholding. All of this means that the mind performs the action through its conduct. It does not... [text ends].

To violate its teachings: for instance, as it is taught that one must not destroy living beings or dig the earth, now, in accordance with practice, following the teachings without contradiction—this is the meaning of this passage.
Shen says: "Circulating" (*xun*) means "to go around in a circle," which refers to the sense of being uninterrupted. Sheng says: "Circulating" (*xun*) means "to traverse.

It simply means taking the teachings and applying them to practice; those instances where one traverses [the path] such that one does not correspond with conditions for transgression are all [included].

"Name" means "to maintain. The Compassionate Cloud [Master] follows this sense of "correspondence. To correspond with the teaching means to correspond with the formation of an offense through the presence of its constituent conditions as set forth in the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "no offense from beginning to end": "beginning" refers to the initial reception of full ordination;

"end" refers to the exhaustion of the karmic retribution of a single lifetime. To maintain this with purity and brilliance is called being "without offense. If one has not studied the Dharma since birth...

Regarding those who have not heard [the Dharma]: this refers to those who, having first received full ordination within the Buddha-dharma, are said to be "born" [into the Sangha], yet are not born from the womb of their parents.

If they study the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they do not recognize the characteristics of what is maintained and what is transgressed, nor the gravity of offenses, nor the distinctions between what is permitted and what is prohibited, or what is correct and what is erroneous.
This means that one has not heard the Dharma. How is it known that one who has left the household life and received full ordination is called "one who has been born"?
It is as stated in a verse from the *Vinayamātṛkā*: "One who is born through the Buddha’s precepts is truly born, just like Aṅgulimāla."
This is what the Tathāgata has prophesied. Aṅgulimāla was instructed by a false teacher to kill a thousand people and make a garland of their fingers;
later, he left the household life. At that time, King Prasenajit sought him out with the intent to kill, and he came to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said to the king: "That man, from birth, had never killed a person... (and so forth).

As in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, this shall be left for the expositor to explain when the time comes. Regarding the meaning of cultivating good and evil, which encompasses both merit and retribution:

it is like a newly ordained person who, not knowing the rules of the teaching, sees grass growing on a stupa and pulls it out with a pure heart, hoping to gain merit; yet, because he violates the Buddha's teachings, he incurs transgression.
"Ti. Now, we do not discuss a virtuous mind; rather, if one violates the teachings, one incurs an offense regardless.

Regarding the phrase 'without asking whether the matter is false or real,' my own view is that this may be clarified through the nine propositions concerning what can be learned within the section on observance and violation (shichifan pian). These are: knowing the matter and knowing the violation."

Furthermore, when one commits the root offense, it is termed "real" (*satya*). As for "false" (*mṛṣā*), this refers to cases where one does not recognize the matter, does not recognize the transgression, or harbors doubt;
these also constitute the commission of the root offense and are termed "false. To this is added the fault of ignorance due to a lack of training (*aśikṣitājñāna*):

because the matter is something that ought to be learned, one fails to recognize it due to a lack of training. The Sage does not exempt such persons from liability. This interpretation accords with the text; this is termed "intentional" (*saṃcetanika*).

Regarding the reality or unreality [of the object]: what constitutes the reality or unreality of the act? Take, for example, the five propositions concerning the perception of an object. In the first proposition, killing a human while perceiving them as a non-human is a case where the object is real.
If, however, a non-human or a headless corpse comes to occupy that place, and one kills it while the mind perceives it as a human, one likewise incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
Although the *pārājika* (defeat) and *thullaccaya* differ, both are indeed offenses. Therefore, it is said: "one does not inquire into the factual reality."

"Sentiment" (*qing*) refers to reality and unreality. Regarding the statement "this is the general name for observing and violating" (*chih-fan*): Master Li says this establishes the preceding context.

That is to say, it generally addresses matters of sentiment within the broader tradition to clarify what constitutes observance and violation, yet it does not yet distinguish the characteristics of their gravity, the boundaries of violations, or the distinctions between cause and effect;
these will be clarified below according to the specific chapters (*pian*).
"Regarding 'if one summarizes the primary offenses of the five categories': this refers to summarizing the primary offenses of the five categories (*pañca-varga*).

Since the preceding section has already generally clarified the maintenance and violation of the precepts without specifically addressing them according to the categories and clusters (*varga-piṭaka*), and because one now wishes to clarify them individually according to the categories and clusters, this first paragraph introduces the following text.
Regarding 'exhausting all disciplinary punishments': this means that when adjudicating the names of offenses, one must first question [the offender] regarding..."
Regarding the person [who commits an offense]: is it a *pārājika* (defeat), a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), or is it abiding in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*)?

If one has reached the point of fruition (*phala*), then it is grave and there is no longer a preparatory stage; if one has not yet reached fruition, it is light. One must thoroughly investigate its gravity or lightness by clarifying it according to the *vibhaṅga* (sections of the precepts).
As for "binding the preparatory stages to constitute the karmic fruit," this means taking the preparatory stages as the offense of the fruition itself.

If the action is not completed, one merely incurs the offense of the preparatory stage (*upāya*). Because it is a preparatory stage, it can be expiated; however, once the fruit [of the full offense] is reached, it cannot be expiated.
One must inquire into the nature of the transgression and observe where that transgression corresponds with the teaching:

does it correspond to the preparatory stage, or does it correspond to the stage of the fruit? Therefore, it is said that "lightness and heaviness are determined by principle and teaching. This concludes the section on the "Weeds."
It is also called "máng" (weed). Furthermore, it is said that when weeds defile the ground, they are called "wú" (overgrown).

This means that once the actual facts have been verified and found to correspond with the teachings, there will be no error of over-extended judgment when determining one's adherence to or violation of the precepts. This is what is meant by "adherence and violation. This refers to the application of remedies;
therefore, it is said that "adherence and violation are explained separately. Alternatively, it may be understood as being explained in relation to specific matters; hence [the term].
It is said: "The distinct names are 'upholding' and 'violating.
*Sifen lü chao pi*, Scroll 2, end;
*Sifen lü chao pi*, Scroll 3, beginning.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Temple in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
The Seventh Section: The General and Specific Intent of the Establishment of the Sevenfold Teachings for the Clergy and Laity.

Regarding the seventh section on the general and specific intent of the establishment of the sevenfold teachings for the clergy and laity: there are the five groups of the ordained and the two groups of the laity.

These are known as the seven divisions. What is called "teaching" (jiao) refers to the words that express [the meaning]; taken collectively across the three piṭakas, they are all equally termed "teaching.

Although the teachings are numerous, they do not exceed two types: the transformative teaching (huajiao) and the disciplinary teaching (zhijiao). The transformative teaching is universal, applying to both monastics and laypeople;

the disciplinary teaching is specific, being restricted to monks and nuns. Within the transformative teaching, the two karmas of good and evil causes and effects are explained in general terms. The teaching...

It is called "Transformative Teaching" (*huàjiào*) because it transforms beings to cause them to cultivate the path of renunciation. It is called "Regulatory Teaching" (*zhìjiào*) because it consists of the five categories and seven groups [of precepts] which prohibit and restrain non-virtuous conditions;
since the teaching arises from such regulations, it is called "regulatory. Regarding "universal" and "restricted":

this means that the Transformative Teaching is universal across the seven classes of followers, whereas the Regulatory Teaching is restricted to the five classes of monastics. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that within the "universal," there is exclusively what is universal, with nothing else.

Regarding the restricted [rules]: if there is restriction within them, there is also pervasion. For example, within the *vinaya* (prescriptive teachings), it is permitted for one to receive the five or eight precepts from a layperson;

this is such a case. Furthermore, within the restricted, there is further restriction. For instance, although the *vinaya* applies equally to both monks and nuns, if one has committed a transgression against the boundaries (*ānantarya*) or possesses one of the thirteen obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*), one cannot receive the full ordination.
Likewise, if a monk or nun commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), they are excluded from monastic affairs. Therefore, within the restricted, there is yet further restriction.
There is a specific scope.

As for the teaching that reveals the principle, its many paths refer to the Buddha’s establishment of teachings according to the capacities of beings; all are intended to reveal the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because the capacities of sentient beings differ, the teachings are differentiated according to those capacities; thus, there are many paths. Although this is so...
There are many paths, yet they do not exceed the two gates of transformation (*hua*) and regulation (*zhi*); these encompass all [teachings] without exception.

The first refers to the "Transformative Teachings" (*huajiao*). Master Nanshan said: "In works such as the *Āgamas*, there is the unfolding and exposition of guidance and transformation, intended to cause one to recognize the nature of causes and effects—both false and correct—and the nature of karma.
These words are without obstruction, and their meaning extends to both monastics and laypeople; the essence of this teaching is to transform people so that they may attain enlightenment."

It is understood through wisdom; therefore, it is called the "Transformative Teaching" (Hua-jiao). Now, this Transformative Teaching is subsumed within the Piṭaka of the Tripiṭaka, specifically the Sūtra Piṭaka.
It is sometimes called *sūtra* and sometimes called *sūtrānta*; both are merely different phonetic transcriptions of the same Sanskrit term. The Dongta [Master] says:

The claim that *sūtra* is a corruption is incorrect. However, *dru*, *tṛ*, and *tāra* are sounds of a single phonetic transformation (*ekavartana*) that possess varying degrees of lightness and heaviness.

Just as within the *Siddham* syllabary there are fourteen or sixteen types of phonetic transformations, and within a single transformation there are themselves several varieties of heavy and light shifts—how could it be a corruption?
It merely refers generally to those who clarify cause and effect. That is to say, "but... [the text continues].
Generally clarifying the two causes of good and evil and their resulting fruits of suffering and happiness: practicing good brings merit; committing evil incurs retribution.

Such examples as "patience leads to physical beauty" and "refraining from killing leads to longevity" are all instances of general clarification. Regarding the discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox, it is as stated in the sutras:
"This is the Buddha’s teaching; this is the Māra’s teaching. For instance, if one keeps the eight impure things, that is heterodox.
Not maintaining these [views] is correct; those who maintain them are the retinue of Māra and not disciples of the Buddha.

Furthermore, not believing in cause and effect is heterodox, while taking refuge in the Three Jewels is correct, as explained at length in the "Heterodoxy and Orthodoxy" (Xiézhèng) chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

As for evaluating those whose conduct and karma are profound and difficult to discern—take, for instance, the teachings of transformation (*pariṇāmanā-śāsana*): they simply state that one should not kill living beings, without distinguishing between types of killing.
Birth has gates of lightness and heaviness. Now, wishing to weigh these karmas of lightness and heaviness, it is said they are difficult to know.
Furthermore, if a thief does not state whether the amount taken was five *kārsāpaṇas* or less than five, then the boundary for the formation of the karma cannot be known.

However, within the *vinaya* teachings, there are clearly established boundaries such as those for the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. In these *dharmaparyāya* (transformative) teachings, one discusses only the good and evil present within the mind.

One may give rise to the three poisons and four inversions, or one may give rise to thoughts of compassion and meditative concentration; these exist only within the mind, and their external manifestations are difficult to discern.
If one relies on the *vaipulya* (transformative) teachings, it is difficult to know the signs of the lightness or heaviness of one's offenses and blessings.

To clarify the retribution of future lives so that it is evident and easy to describe, one observes the present cause to know the future fruit, and examines the present fruit to know the past cause. This is as in the case of killing.

One receives the retribution of a short lifespan. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This is killing; this is the retribution for killing. This is harsh speech; this is the retribution for harsh speech. This is sexual misconduct;

this is the retribution for sexual misconduct," and so forth. Furthermore, by observing the five precepts one is born among humans, and by practicing the ten wholesome actions one is born in the heavens.
If one does not receive the five precepts, one will fall into the three miserable realms in the future. If one cannot endure suffering, one will certainly be ugly in future lives.
By observing the present causes, one knows the future retributions; therefore, it is said that [the Vinaya] is clear and easy to explain.

Second, as for the claim that the practice of the teachings is restricted solely to the internal assembly (the monastic community): Li states that the Great Canon of the Vinaya governs the five classes of renunciants;

from the first step of initiating practice until the final attainment of the benefit of the Path, one acts in accordance with the words. It is simply because one acts according to the words [of the Vinaya].

This is why the textual expressions that enable such communication are categorized as the Teaching of Practice (*xingjiao*). Hence it is said so. It is also called the Teaching of Regulation (*zhìjiao*).
Because this door of teaching issues injunctions to the fivefold assembly, permitting them to act without transgression, it is called the Teaching of Regulation.

Master Nanshan said: "As for what is called the Teaching of Practice: one relies on the teaching to give rise to understanding; without practice, it is not accomplished. Hence it is called the Teaching of Practice. Furthermore, it is called the Teaching of Regulation because the teaching..."
Because it is established through regulation, it is called "regulated teaching" (*zhìjiào*). As for determining what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected:

if one follows the teachings in accordance with the Dharma, that which may be practiced is termed "adopted" (*qǔ*); if one violates the teachings and acts contrary to the Dharma, that which may not be practiced is termed "rejected" (*shě*). Furthermore, it says:

"Taking and abandoning" has the meaning of gain and loss. For example, at the time of receiving the precepts: if one intends for [the precepts] to last through the three periods of existence and the conditions and causes are complete, then obtaining the precepts is "taking.
If the opposite occurs and the reception of the precepts is not achieved, it is called "loss," which must be abandoned.
Regarding the establishment of its fundamental principles: "Gang" (綱) refers to a main rope; it is the primary cord of a net. "Chi" (致) refers to the intent; it is also the mind.
"Principles. This refers to taking the five categories (*pañcavarga*) and seven groups (*saptasaṃghādisesa*) as the fundamental principles.

It is further stated that within the Buddha-dharma, such practices as establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*), receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) are all fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the resolution of doubts and obstructions, some say it is as stated in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*: "One who can know the five characteristics is said to understand the Vinaya. If one is able to...
One who clearly understands the characteristics of the two divisions of the Vinaya must resolve any questions that arise.

Furthermore, "resolving doubts and obstructions" refers to cases where one is uncertain regarding transgressions or observances, or uncertain as to whether an offense is light or heavy; such uncertainties may persist for many years, leaving matters unresolved.

Upon seeing the Vinaya texts once, one’s understanding becomes thoroughly penetrating; thus it is said that they "resolve doubts and obstructions. Regarding the phrase "pointing to matters to explain them in detail, with no need for repeated reading":
"reading" (lǎn) is synonymous with "seeing" (jiàn). For instance, within the Great Vinaya Piṭaka, there are the Monastic and Nun Precept Texts (*Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra* and *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla-sūtra*).
The ritual procedures for practice are easy to understand; all are accessible to study. This clarifies the conditions of transgression (*āpatti*) and provides guidance on their application.

For instance, it is said that killing a human being incurs a *pārājika* offense, while killing an animal incurs a *thullaccaya* offense; however, there is no offense if one lacks the intentional mind.

Such explanations all refer to specific preceding cases, making the distinctions clear and distinct; there is no need for further elaboration. This means that each individual precept refers to each specific case, providing a detailed and thorough exposition.

It is proclaimed that this differs from the previous teachings of transformation (*pariṇāmita-śāsana*), which spoke generally of sexual misconduct and theft without clarifying the objects, the locus of the offense, and so forth.

However, the present teachings of practice (*pratipatti-śāsana*) clearly reveal these objects—the relative superiority or inferiority of the three realms of existence (*gati*)—as well as the specific distinctions and limits regarding the commission of offenses, such that one may understand them completely upon merely opening [this text].
There is no need for repeated examination. Regarding matters that involve the fault of a double classification: this clarifies the transgression.

In the context of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), those offenses that constitute violations of the essential precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), such as killing or stealing, are classified as both a violation of the precept and an additional offense of the path of action (*karmapatha*). This is the meaning of the classification and punishment.

Ji said: "It refers to the meaning of committing [an offense] repeatedly; hence it is called 'a second charge' (*zàikē*). For example, if one commits a *pārājika* offense previously and later commits another *pārājika*, it is therefore called a 'second charge.
Thus, the two teachings (Buddhism and Confucianism) revolve around each other and are not without points of overlap. Master Ying said: "'Revolving' (*xúnhuán*) means circling or returning."
"Coming," "circling," and "pervading" illustrate that the two teachings have mutual interpenetration, like the appearance of two rings hooked together.

Although they are hooked together, they ultimately remain distinct from one another; this is intended to clarify that while the teachings of transformation and practice may overlap, they are nonetheless separate.
However, their principles are distinct. As for what is said regarding their confusion: take, for example, the killing of an animal. Both teachings clarify that one incurs guilt;
yet, in the *Huajiao* (Teaching of Transformation), only the sin of the karmic path (*karmapatha*) is clarified, without mention of the transgression of violating a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

In the *Zhijiao* (Teaching of Regulation), one first incurs the guilt of violating the prohibitory teaching and subsequently receives the sin of the karmic path. This is precisely the meaning of "confusion. Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
As in the two teachings of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and prohibition (*vinaya*), when one gives rise to the mind to create good or evil, the mind may be subject to confusion.

In the Mahāyāna, the mind is restrained; in the Hīnayāna, the mind is likewise restrained. Therefore, regarding mental intention in the Vinaya, it is said: "The mind conceives thus. However, in the Mahāyāna, an offense is incurred as soon as the mind alone arises;
in the Hīnayāna, an offense is only formally established once there is the intention to move the body or speech. Nevertheless, these two teachings are identical in their prevention of the mind.

It is merely that body and speech are provisionally distinguished; therefore, they are said to be "intermingled" (*làn*). Jì says: Within the *Huàjiào* (Teachings of Transformation) there are also *Zhìjiào* (Teachings of Regulation), and within the *Zhìjiào* there are also *Huàjiào*;
hence it is said they are mutually intermingled. What are these? For instance, the *Nirvāṇa*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, and *Śāriputraparipṛcchā* (Yìjiào)—are these not *Huàjiào*?
Yet within them, the meaning of the precepts and regulations is clearly elucidated. Furthermore, as in the *Sifen lü shòjì jiàn* (The *Karmavācanā* for Receiving Precepts in the Four-Part Vinaya)...

[The section on] "Deliverance" (Du). First, it clarifies how the Tathāgata delivered the five *koṭī* of people, such as the Pañcavaggiya, by preaching the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths in twelve aspects, up to the deliverance of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) through the three wheels.
Is this not evidence that within the *vinaya* (prescriptive teachings) there is also transformation (*pariṇāmanā*)? Therefore, it is said that there is no confusion [between the two].

When the fundamental principle is raised to judge the matter, the truth becomes manifest: [the author] establishes that the *pariṇāmanā-śāsana* (transformative teachings) takes principle (*li*) as its primary purpose (*zong*). Regarding...

The mind clarifies gain and loss; it is also said that taking mental karma as the primary principle (*zong*) clarifies gain and loss. When practice and teaching take phenomenal matters as the primary principle, they employ bodily and verbal karma to clarify gain and loss.
Since it was previously stated that these [principles] circulate and overlap with one another, now these two principles are raised for distinction.

Because the underlying logic is thereby differentiated, it is said that "it manifests itself. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, raising the primary principle to judge means that before the body has moved...

[The text continues: "However, if a thought merely arises, one violates the *dharmatā-śāsana* (teaching on transformation) but has not yet committed an offense against the *prajñapti-śāsana* (prescriptive teaching). If one gives rise to the intent to move body or speech, then one violates the *prajñapti-śāsana*.
Such are the two schools [of interpretation]. Now, if one violates the *prajñapti-śāsana*, one incurs two offenses:

namely, the offense of violating the teaching and the offense of the *karmapatha* (path of action). If one violates the *dharmatā-śāsana*, one incurs only one offense: this is the offense of the *karmapatha*. Therefore, it is said that 'the principle is naturally...'"
This means "to manifest.

It refers to the case where the internal mind takes opposition or conformity as its basis, entrusting itself to principle (*li*) as its thesis (*zong*). The preceding text states: "By citing the thesis to judge, the principle manifests of itself.

If one asks how it manifests of itself and wishes to understand its meaning, it is therefore said: "It means that the internal mind has opposition," and so forth. This means that within the internal mind there is opposition.

Regarding the two states of mind arising from following or opposing one's emotions: they take as their fundamental principle the truth of entrusting oneself to the single coming of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If one gives rise to a mind that contravenes this principle, it is called an offense; if one gives rise to a mind that accords with this principle, it constitutes observance.

It is simply said that when an evil mind arises and contravenes the True Principle, one immediately incurs the karmic guilt of violating the principle. This is the fundamental tenet of the *Hua-jiao* (Transformative Teaching). This...

This is merely termed "breaking the Mahāyāna precept of signlessness. Because the Mahāyāna restricts transgressions to the mind, it is said that the internal mind’s compliance or opposition takes the principle as its core;
this is cited as belonging to the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teaching). I privately remark:

the *Hua-jiao*’s regulation of the mind means that if an evil thought arises within the internal mind and opposes the principle, one immediately incurs a karmic path (*karmapatha*). This is the essential purport of the *Hua-jiao*. As for external conduct...

Regarding the statement that "one must necessarily guard the body, speech, and so forth when performing acts of giving," this clarifies that the practice of the teaching pertains exclusively to the immobility of body and speech.
Even if one gives rise to a thought, it does not yet constitute a violation of the teaching; it is only when there is actual movement of body or speech that one may be subject to formal censure.

However, regarding those who violate the *Hua-jiao* (Transformative Teaching) and receive only the retribution for the *karmic path* (*karmapatha*), yet further incur the offense of transgressing the weighty prohibitions established by the Sage through the *Xing-jiao* (Practice Teaching), the *Jie-shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"That which is elucidated in the *Hua-jiao* refers to the nature of offenses as karma (*karmasvabhāva-avadya*). One who violates them possesses only two meanings:

first, it is an evil conduct that contravenes principle; second, it is capable of obstructing the Path. It must possess these two meanings. If one commits an offense after the Buddha has promulgated the extensive teachings of the *Xing-jiao*..."

It possesses three meanings. Two of these do not differ from what was stated previously; there is the offense of violating the Buddha’s precepts. Regarding the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*) mentioned above, the treatise explains:

"Action" (*karman*) refers to the mind (*citta*); because the mind proceeds through [the body and speech], it is called a "path of action. As for the citation from the Sūtra, according to the *Śrāddhakarman-sūtra*, Chapter on Precepts:
"There were two people who together committed a single offense. One had received the precepts, while the other had not..."
Regarding the precepts: for one who has already received the precepts, an offense is grave; for one who has not received the precepts, an offense is light.
Why is this? Because it constitutes a violation of the Buddha’s word.

The phrase "the words and texts are clear in their own breadth" refers comprehensively to all the textual passages within the various teachings. The reason for further dividing them is to clarify the intent of the present section.
Although the various teachings elucidate both the *huà* (transformative) and *zhì* (regulative) schools, it is feared that people may not be proficient in them.

Therefore, I have made this distinction regarding this single gate. Fearing that those who might be confused about the fundamental essence of the two teachings would mistake the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teaching) for having the prevention of the internal mind as its teaching-essence, and the *Zhi-jiao* (Regulation Teaching) for having the prevention of the seven branches [of misconduct] alone as its teaching-essence, I have made this distinction.
Because I fear that later generations might become confused, I have further divided [the categories]. Regarding those who falsely describe the right and wrong of karmic actions, they claim:

"I fear someone might say that if a Vinaya Master kills an ox, he commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), which is no different from killing grass or trees; therefore, by killing grass, one also incurs a *thullaccaya*.

Now, if we together perform repentance for this *thullaccaya* offense, both offenses will be extinguished. They do not realize that although the collective retribution may be extinguished, the individual...

The retribution has not yet been exhausted. Since they do not recognize the transgression of the path of karma, they simply state that their sin is extinguished; this is called falsely describing right and wrong.

Furthermore, regarding the false description of the right and wrong of karmic actions, Sheng says: for example, a person who follows the prescriptive teachings (vinaya) may commit the offense of *thullaccaya* by killing an animal, yet being unaware of the existence of the path of karma, they falsely claim their own purity. There are also monks and nuns [who act similarly].
Regarding those who rely on the *Hua-jiao* (Transformative Teaching): seeing sentient beings undergoing suffering, they claim that killing them ought to bring merit; what fault could there be?

Although this does not constitute a formal karmic path (*karmapatha*), they fail to realize that by failing to comply with the prohibitions within the *Zhi-jiao* (Regulatory Teaching), they incur an offense against the teachings (*āpatti-viruddha*).

They falsely declare themselves to be pure. "Permanently" (*yong*) means for a long time; "to dispel" (*juan*) means to eliminate. This refers to eliminating the aforementioned false view of self-declaration.
This is the reason.
Regarding the eighth point, the meaning of the "passage and obstruction" (*tong-se*) of the ritual procedures for the two communities of monks and nuns:

"passage" refers to those matters where the precepts and regulations are identical, such as the rainy season retreat (*an-gu*), the invitation at the end of the retreat (*zi-zi*), the recitation of the precepts (*shuo-jie*), and the establishment of boundaries (*jie-jie*). In these cases, monks and nuns employ them in common, as their principles overlap; thus they are so named.

It is said that "unobstructed" (*tōng*) and "obstructed" (*sè*) refer to things being mutually present or mutually absent; the dharmas such as formal instruction (*shanjie*) are examples of this. Regarding the establishment of what is unobstructed or obstructed in practice:

for instance, in the receiving of precepts or the confession of offenses, the *saṃgha* may collectively perform them, and the name "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*) is mutually applicable—this is called "unobstructed.

As for other matters such as the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*) or the reception of the day [of the lunar month], these can only be performed by the respective assemblies facing one another; they cannot be mutually shared, and thus are termed "obstructed."

Regarding "identical precepts and identical regulations with identical matters and dharmas": this refers to the four *pārājika* offenses and so forth. Among the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), all those shared by both monks and nuns are termed "identical precepts.
The procedures for the *pravarana*, *jītakarman*, and the formal reception of the precepts are all instances of identical regulations.

As for the phrase "identical matters and dharmas," "matters" refers to objects, whether animate or inanimate; thus, items such as extra robes and alms bowls are identical for both. "Dharmas" refers to the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), as well as the face-to-face (*sammukha*) and mental (*manasikāra*) procedures, are all collectively termed "procedural dharmas" (*kriyādharma*) because their nature and function are identical.

Regarding the detailed application of these protocols according to specific matters, they are fully contained within the various sections; this is clearly established. As for those that share the same procedural dharma, such as the rituals for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) and so forth.
Furthermore, within the thirty gates, one may apply them as desired with detailed consideration; the only difference is that "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*) is substituted [for "monk"].

Regarding the discernment of the characteristics of offenses (*āpatti-lakṣaṇa*), the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* itself provides the internal classification: this refers to the fact that within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtras* of the two assemblies, the characteristics of observance and violation are clarified by each assembly itself;

thus, they differ from one another. As for the statement, "Hidden and difficult to know, it is fully contained in the *Anuvyañjana*," Zhiyi says: "The following is the *Anuvyañjana* (the section on individual precepts)."

Regarding the "Explanation of Characteristics" (Xiangzhong): this provides a detailed explanation of the names and characteristics of the precepts for both the monastic community of monks and the community of nuns.

Although the explanation of characteristics is presented primarily through the lens of the monks' precepts, those aspects of the nuns' precepts that share the same names and characteristics are likewise all included within the "Explanations of Characteristics" (Suixiang) pertaining to the great monks.
Therefore, it is said that they are fully contained within the "Explanations of Characteristics."

Regarding the precepts categorized by status (*yue-wei*): this refers to the fact that the two classes of monks and nuns are distinct; hence, they are said to be "categorized by status. Regarding the difference in gravity:

for example, in the case of physical contact (*mochu*), a nun incurs a *pārājika* offense while a monk incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the case of emission (*lou-shi*), a monk incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* while a nun incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

In the case of failing to observe the rains retreat (*bu-anju*), a nun incurs a *sthūlātyaya* while a monk incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Hence, it is said that "the gravity differs. Regarding the mutual absence or presence [of offenses]: as for the monks...

The three precepts concerning washing, the four precepts concerning being alone, and the precept regarding addressing others by name while spinning or weaving belong exclusively to the nuns and not to the monks.
The three precepts concerning giving instruction without permission and staying until sunset, as well as the two precepts concerning dwellings, belong to the monks and not to the nuns;

thus it is said that there are mutual deficiencies between the two groups. Regarding the differences in the causes for transgressing these rules, Gao says: "It is like providing food to non-Buddhists."

Regarding the precepts: although the transgressions are identical, the conditions for their application differ. For example, when it comes to the offense of associating with non-Buddhist renunciants, monks incur the offense, whereas nuns incur the offense regardless of whether the non-Buddhists are renunciants or householders.
Furthermore, regarding the precept on possessing an alms bowl: for monks, the offense is incurred if they do not declare their intention within ten days;

for nuns, the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is incurred if they do not declare it on the very day the bowl enters their hands. Thus, while the nature of the offense is the same, the conditions for its allowance differ; hence it is said:

The causes for the offenses differ. Li says: "When the offense is the same but the conditions differ," it is as in the case where both the *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (offense of refusal) and the *pātra-pūrṇa-bhakṣaṇa* (offense of eating from a full bowl) constitute a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), yet the conditions for their exemption differ.
Bin says: The Saṃgha has the *atiritta-kappa* (rule of leftover food), whereas the *pratikṣepaṇa* is separately prescribed;

the Bhikṣuṇīs lack the *atiritta-kappa*, so they are governed by a single combined precept. Because the Saṃgha has this additional rule, it is said that "the conditions for exemption differ. Furthermore, [there is] the reduction...
Regarding the annual precept: as for the differences in the conditions for receiving it, for a *bhikṣuṇī* and a *śikṣamāṇā*, the formal procedure (*dharmakarma*) is performed;
