Since they are not permitted to leave, it is like great stones pressing down upon grass so that its heads cannot emerge. Furthermore, the Upādhyāya explains it thus: "It is like the kings, ministers, and high officials of a state."
It is called the "burden of the flat rock" (pan-shi zhi ren) because it signifies the succession of heirs being taken up so that they remain eternally firm and immovable;
its meaning is like a flat rock, hence the name "burden of the flat rock.

By analogy, the ignorant leaders of the assembly and masters of the Dharma within this Sangha are also called the "burden of the flat rock," for in their adjudication of censure, release, or removal, they do not rely on the holy teachings, and subsequently give rise to new students who bring corruption to this Dharma.
The Master therefore said, "He is distressed by the flat rock. Shen said, "In the *Yi* there is the hexagram Kun (Obstruction).

The commentary says: "Advancing, one treads upon thorns; retreating, one is further distressed by the flat rock. When the forces of Yin and Yang are blocked and do not flow through, it is called the hexagram Kun.

It is like the officials of today who first act with heterodoxy and commit evil; when they are subsequently investigated and brought to justice, they advance only to be punished by the law and retreat by losing their official rank. Now...

The Dharma Lord [has taught]: "If one indulges in or seizes upon things according to one's own whims, then at the end of life, one will fall away from the fruits of the Path and lose the superior rewards of humans and devas, regressing into the three miserable realms;
this is like the hexagram Kun (困). Regarding 'the Vinaya strictly cutting off the bridle and bit':
in the body it is called the bridle, and in the mouth it is called the bit; these are simply the bridle and bit of a horse. This is intended to clarify that for those who are newly learning..."

Regarding the characteristics of the teachings on consciousness: they do not rely upon the precepts and discipline, allowing body and speech to run wild and commit various transgressions, much like a horse without a bridle.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] is "severed. Here, the term "bridle" (*jibi*) is used directly to designate the precepts and discipline. Thus, a sutra says:
"The prohibitions established by the Buddha are like a monkey caught in a chain, or like a sharp bit and rein"—this is precisely their meaning. This is the profound guiding cord of the True Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "lest one should fall headlong," Master Li explains: "Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) serves as the profound mainstay, while the precepts are the profound cord.

Because of the precepts, concentration (*samādhi*) arises; through concentration, wisdom arises. Now, since the precepts have been violated, concentration and wisdom do not arise; therefore, it is said that one would 'fall headlong. Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
The precepts alone are designated as the "Mysterious Mainstay" (*xuán gāng*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "lest it be overturned and fall," it is as the Sūtra says:
"If my disciples practice them in succession, then the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body will remain eternally present and never perish.

Now, since they do not rely on the teachings to practice and the succession has been severed, no one is able to continue it; therefore, it is said that the Mysterious Mainstay has been overturned and fallen.
Therefore, we know that the rise and decline [of the Dharma] depends on people. The *Erlü* (爾疋) states: "Rise (*xing*) comes from 'arising' (*qi*); decline (*ti*) means 'abandonment' (*fei*).
This single phrase serves as a general conclusion to the preceding text. The character "rise" concludes the passage concerning how the traces [of the Buddha] transcend the net of worldly dust;

the character "decline" concludes the preceding passages concerning the degenerate age and its end. Regarding the question, "Will the Wheel of the Dharma not turn again, even though the protection of the Dharma is so deeply revered? Jì (Jizang) says:

If one can act for the sake of sentient beings without being exclusively intent on violence and oppression, and causes one's disciples and later generations to go abroad to study, not creating obstacles like a solid rock for them, with the intention that they pursue learning to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddha—this is precisely the profound veneration and protection of the Dharma.
Master Li said: "As described above, those who have bathed their minds in the water of the Way and whose traces transcend the net of worldly dust..."
If one can practice in accordance with the teachings, this is itself the further turning of the Wheel of Dharma; why lament that the Sun of the Buddha does not shine again?
As a sutra says: "You should know that this is your Great Teacher; were I in the world, it would be no different from this."
Thus, the Wheel of Dharma has turned once more in Jambudvīpa, and the light of the Way shines again for a thousand years.
As for the brief indication of the essence of the school and so forth herein, this precisely gives rise to the four types [of teachings] that follow; these constitute its essential doctrine.
When it says, "Those who come later and wish to establish [the teaching] have a basis," it means that those future students who desire to manifest and establish [the truth] should...
Relying upon these four kinds [of supports] means to depend upon them; "to depend" (tuo) signifies to attach oneself to.

Now, as for precepts taking the vessel as their function, it is established that the body is the vessel for the precepts. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "That which serves as the basis for merit is called a vessel.
Since vessels have large and small capacities, the precepts likewise have large and small degrees; hence, they are called "precepts" (jie).
This refers to following the capacity of the vessel. For example, the five precepts correspond to the vessel of a human;
the ten precepts correspond to the vessel of a deva; the two hundred and fifty precepts are the vessel of a śrāvaka; and the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts are the vessel of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, it is explained that because there are superior, middling, and inferior grades of mind at the time of receiving them, one accordingly obtains precepts of these three grades; thus they are called "following the vessel."
Ciyun said: "This precept accords with the capacity and expectations of sentient beings, just as a vessel holds objects without discriminating between fragrance and stench.

Whether one seeks human blessings, superior fruits, or other such goals, the resulting grade of the precept is realized according to those expectations; therefore, it is called 'according to the vessel'. Jì said:
"As for the precepts, they accord with the size of the roots and vessels of sentient beings; according to the amount received, one attains the precepts accordingly."
They are also not the same. For example, if an ordinary person’s vessel is small, they receive the five or eight precepts; if the vessel is large, they receive the full precepts.
Thus it is said that "merit is achieved according to the vessel. When a practitioner takes "receiving" as their aim, this refers to the person who can receive the Dharma being transmitted.
For instance, during the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four proclamations), one receives [the precepts] in the span of a single thought-moment.

The sublime Dharma dwells within his breast. As for being able to thoroughly purify body and mind and receiving [the precepts] in accordance with conditions: this means that having no physical obstructions or impediments constitutes a pure body;
vowing to sever evil conditions and objects, and giving rise to a mind that yearns for and seeks the essential path of liberation with a superior grade of resolve, is called a pure mind.
Regarding the phrase "receiving in accordance with conditions," it means that the preceptor-monks are pure and the robes and bowl are complete.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) is accomplished; it resides entirely within the conditions (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, it can purify the vessel of one's body. The presence of the aspiration for [attainment] is called the "cause" (*hetu*).
Taking this internal cause and casting it against the preceding and succeeding conditions, because the causes and conditions are complete, it is logical that the precepts should arise.

Since the cause does not conflict with the conditions, it is said that "one receives them in accordance with the conditions. As for the statement regarding the path of attaining correspondence: since...
It is a vessel for purifying the mind that receives [the precepts] according to conditions.

When this precept is generated through the correspondence of both internal causes and external conditions, it then accords with the goodness of non-action (avijñapti-śīla). This very path of correspondence is the essence of the precept of non-action.
"Kè" (克) means "to be able. Furthermore, as explained in detail below: what is used to serve as the pure vessel for the Path?
This is precisely what is called the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*) thus generated; because it can correspond with the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*), it is termed the "Path of Correspondence.

This means that since one receives [the precepts] by taking them as one's object, one then corresponds with non-action (*avijñapti*), and subsequently achieves the Buddha-path. (Both interpretations are excellent.
As for the phrase "if the mind lacks a distant aspiration, even a hair’s breadth of deviation," this refers to the absence of a mind that maintains the precepts and severs delusions.
Not knowing that this dharma of the precepts can lead to the fruit of supreme tranquility, one lacks the aspiration to seek it; this is called "lacking a distant aim.

To say there is a discrepancy of even a hair's breadth refers to the manifestation of incomplete causes and conditions. A slight discrepancy in these causes and conditions constitutes the limit of not obtaining the precepts.

Furthermore, even if the causes and conditions are complete, at the time of the *jñapti-caturtha* (the formal motion and three proclamations), if the mind focuses on other wholesome matters and does not focus [on the precepts], [the precepts are not obtained].
One must cultivate a mind that severs evil regarding the objects of the three periods of time. A single moment’s deviation constitutes a failure to attain the limits of the precepts;
as it is said, "A deviation of a hair's breadth results in a loss of a thousand li. Thus, regarding the phrase "merely defiling the flow of the Dharma" and so forth:

this means that if the recipient lacks the proper intention, the ritual performance is performed in vain and yields no benefit. Therefore, it is called "merely defiling the flow of the Dharma. It asks: with what, then, can one serve as a pure vessel for the Way?
As for this: Precepts are that upon which all myriad virtues depend for their arising; concentration and wisdom rely upon them to emerge.

Because they are able to contain and store [virtue], they are metaphorically compared to a vessel and thus named "precepts" (*śīla*). They can hold the merit of the myriad virtues, and are therefore called the "vessel of the Way. Thus, a sutra says:
"If this precept did not exist, all virtuous merits would fail to arise"—this is precisely its meaning. As for the meaning of being "a good field for the world," where does it reside?

It means that taking the tonsure and dyeing of robes as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and upholding the precepts as its nature (*svabhāva*), when both nature and characteristic are complete, one is fit to be a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Now, since having received the precepts, one has failed [to maintain them], where does the meaning of being a field of merit reside? "An" (安) means "peacefully" or "certainly. Thus, the wisdom...
The treatise states: "To be a fertile field for the world is truly due to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*). The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* says:
"If one cannot eliminate the inversion of self, one shall not receive even a cup of water or a single robe. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also says:
"One who has not left home for the sake of liberation shall not receive [offerings] according to the monastic order. The meaning is clear from these passages.
Regarding the phrase "those who purify their physical conduct and are members of the assembly" (*xingtu*): "assembly" (*tu*) refers to the community of followers in the present time.

Because this group maintains the precepts (*śīla*) in their practice, they are called "practitioners of the path" (*xingtu*). Now, desiring to receive the precepts and enter this fellowship, one vows to protect and uphold them, preferring death over transgression;

hence, it is said "to purify the body. This intends to clarify that such individuals enter the gate of practice with solemnity; though their bodies remain within this assembly of practitioners, [they do so with a purified mind].

What does the mind do? It is said to aspire to the fruit of the Buddha-way and nirvana. Therefore it is said: "To purify one's bodily conduct while remaining far removed from the aspiration for the perfect fruit.
Regarding the statement "one should not falsely contrive," this clarifies that those who receive the precepts seek bodhi from afar.
If one merely hopes for the pleasures of humans and devas, it is called "vain fabrication. If one hopes for the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), this too is vain fabrication.

"Fabrication" (zào) means to proceed toward, to arrive at, or to reach. Regarding the phrase "concentrating one's will and gathering the mind," Master Ying says: "Concentration" (zhuān) means self-sufficiency.
"Yi" (also) means "to entrust" or "to rely upon. It is also said to mean "one. "Lü" (concern) refers to mindfulness and thought;
it means to focus one's single mind upon the precepts and wholesome dharmas. Regarding the phrase "causing one to enter into non-obstruction," Cí (Cíxián) says:

"To cultivate with single-minded devotion, intending to enter into the true principle of perfect quiescence and nirvana, which is formless and universally penetrating, leaving no place for obstruction. [The author] privately comments: It is simply...

This is the sincere resolve. By taking the merit of one’s preceptual goodness as its object, it causes that merit to correspond with one’s own mind, so as to directly accord with it, directly enter into it, and directly bring it forth, ensuring there is no further obstruction in the interim.

Furthermore, it is explained that the very name of the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) precept-essence is "unobstructed. This is because, within the Satyasiddhi school, that which is neither form nor mind is taken as its essence. Therefore...
It is called "unobstructed. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, since precepts are of the nature of form (*rūpa*), they would possess obstruction.

Therefore, the Sūtra states, "though it has no form or color," which refers to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifying that the essence of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) is devoid of such qualities. Now, this sūtra is cited [here].

This establishes the meaning of being "unimpeded" (*wu-zhi*) mentioned above. According to the intent of this passage, the previous explanation of the meaning of "unimpeded" is appropriate when using the latter interpretation.

However, as the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) follow many paths and are not limited to a single track—whereas "track" (*yì*) has two pronunciations, one being *yì* (yì)—the *Zītǒng* states:

This is an error. "Yi" (pronounced with the *tié* and *jié* finals) refers to a carriage track; it is used here in that sense. To speak of "many paths" is to clarify this in terms of the characteristics of the objects [of discipline].

Since these objects encompass both sentient and non-sentient beings and extend throughout the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are called "many paths. They are also referred to as the two types of observance—cessation and action—and the two types of transgression—violation and non-violation.

They are also called prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) and natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). They are also called the five, eight, ten, and full precepts. They are also called the superior and intermediate [precepts].

Because there are grades such as the inferior and so forth, it is said that there are many paths; they do not constitute a single track. This is like a road formed by the wheels of chariots treading upon the ground:
a thousand chariots share the same track because the size of the chariots is uniform. If the chariots were of different sizes, the rear chariot would be crushed by the front one.
Since they are of equal size, they can share the same track for a thousand *li*. The characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) are not like this.

Even with many different paths, they do not differ from the tracks of a carriage. As for the mind having limitations such that its apprehension differs, this refers to minds of superior, middling, and inferior grades;
accordingly, one also apprehends precepts of superior, middling, and inferior grades. It is also said: "One may take the five, eight, ten, or full [precepts] according to one's desire;
whichever precept one receives, that is what is obtained. It is also said: "For those of the three vehicles, according to..."
The reception [of the precepts] is not uniform. If names are manifested according to the objects [of the precepts], there would be an infinite number;
that is to say, with respect to the *dharmadhātu*, whether sentient or non-sentient, all are objects from which the precepts are generated.

If the numerical designations of the precepts were to be manifested based on such objects, then the precepts would possess an inexhaustible number of names. Furthermore, according to the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot), the *Guypu* (Broad Lexicon) states: [text follows].
The "pivot" (*śū*) is the socket of a door. It is also said to be the master of movement and turning; that is, it is the fundamental basis.
Just as a door can only move and turn when it has a pivot, one must understand that these [four] gates necessarily depend upon one another. Now, these four dharmas are likewise essential;
they are compared to the pivot. Therefore, it is said: "For the time being, based on the essential pivot, I shall briefly set forth these four kinds."

Regarding the statement that "discussing the rules of dharma does not limit one to either ordinary person or sage," this means that whether one is an ordinary person or a sage, this precept-dharma is universally applicable.
For instance, even a sage received these precepts; such was Dharmarāja (沓婆摩羅), who went forth at fourteen and realized arhatship at sixteen.
Upon reaching twenty years of age, he received the full ordination through the *karmavācanā* ceremony. This is an example of a sage who likewise possessed them.

Therefore, it is said that [this method] is not restricted to the noble ones (*ārya*). As for the term "ordinary" (*prākṛta*), it refers to all present-day bhikṣus who receive ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
To say "directly clarifying this dharma as leading to the path of liberation" means that I shall now no longer discuss the reasons why it is not restricted to ordinary or noble persons;
rather, I shall simply clarify the meaning of the precept-dharma itself. Hence, it is said "directly clarifying."
This is the Dharma. To say that it "can certainly serve as a guide for establishing the path to liberation" means that this precept-dharma can be followed and taken as a standard;
it enables one to transcend birth and death and accomplish the untainted (anāsrava) path. It is essential to cause the recipient to believe and know that such a thing exists.

This means that the person receiving the precepts must have faith and knowledge that this noble Dharma (āryadharma) dwells within their body, and by mounting it, they can attain liberation from birth and death.
That is to say, it does not restrict itself to ordinary persons or sages; anyone who receives these precepts has them dwelling in their body.
It is precisely because these precepts abide in the body that they are called the "noble Dharma. One must necessarily have faith and knowledge that this dharma of the precepts exists.
Regarding the statement that "what is now received is called 'holy dharma' (*āryadharma*) in reference to its already accomplished state," Ciyun explains:

This dharma is said to be "already accomplished" because it is attained at the conclusion of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). It is called "holy dharma" because it serves as the foundation for the holy path (*āryamārga*) and is capable of bringing about holiness.
Furthermore, "already accomplished" clarifies that this precept-dharma is able to lead one toward the holy; thus, from the perspective of attaining the fruit, it is so named.

It is already accomplished. Because it is already accomplished as the noble, it is only then called the "Noble Dharma" (*āryadharma*). That is to say, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas rely upon this dharma of precepts to attain *bodhi*;

therefore, it is named the "Noble Dharma. Now, although those who currently receive it have not yet attained the state of a noble one, from the perspective of the cause looking toward the fruit, [it is so named].

It is called the "Noble Dharma" (āryadharma). Furthermore, it is explained that because noble ones (ārya) ride upon this dharma of precepts to attain the fruit of sainthood, we know that what is now received is itself the Noble Dharma.
This is stated with reference to those who have already become noble ones; therefore, it says, "speaking from the perspective of those who have already attained [sainthood]."
Shen also says: "Although both ordinary persons and sages universally possess this dharma" refers back to the preceding text.

"Speaking in terms of what has already been accomplished" clarifies that those among the present monastic community who have received it—having fulfilled the requisite conditions and obtained the precepts—are being discussed; hence, it is said, "speaking in terms of what has already been accomplished."

"Only those who turn back from that cycle of birth and death and ascend to take their place among the ranks of the Saṃgha" clarifies that whereas in the past they were within birth and death, following the current of saṃsāra far along its course, they have now resolved to distance themselves from it and take their place within the position of the Saṃgha;
hence, it is called "ascending to take one's place" (*yǎng chè*). To look upward is called "ascending.

The previous phrase, "turning back from that birth and death," refers to descending; the present phrase, "ascending to take one's place," carries the meaning of ascending. This is the establishment of one's resolve.
Regarding the commitment to dwell loftily beyond all burdens: this refers solely to returning from that cycle of birth and death and transcending afflictions;
such is called establishing one's resolve and commitment. "Burden" (*lei*) here refers to the karmic burden of birth and death.

Since one possesses the mind to sever evil, cultivate good, and return from birth and death, this mind ascends high above the three realms and finds its habitation outside the dust of worldly burdens; therefore, it is called "lofty."

It means "to dwell aloof" and so forth. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: now, when one resolves to take the precepts, with the aspiration to transcend the triple world and take leave of the four currents, this is called "dwelling high above and beyond all burdens.
Regarding the necessity of first cultivating this mind, it is said: "If one gives rise to such a mind established by the aforementioned resolve, one must necessarily cultivate this mind beforehand.
One should further give rise to a mind of the highest grade (*uttama-kṣānti*) in preparation for [the path].

Regarding the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada-viśuddha-śīla*): if, when the time arrives, even the teacher and the monastic community who intend to instruct them are themselves insincere, how can they teach others to give rise to this mind?

As for "attaining accomplishment according to the person," this means that whether ten or a hundred people receive the precepts simultaneously, those who possess the capacity for growth and who turn back from birth and death to give rise to the highest-grade mind will receive and attain those precepts.
This is called "accomplishment. If this mind is absent, there is no accomplishment. It is said that as long as there is someone who nurtures this mind, it does not matter how many people there are;
therefore, it is called "accomplishment according to the person. Master Ci said: "It refers to those who seek the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]."

Alternatively, for those who aspire to the stage of a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or others, they shall immediately attain their goal according to what each person’s mind aspires to; hence it is said that "accomplishment follows the person.

Regarding "practicing the holy conduct and abiding in its essence": once one has received the holy dharma of the *karmavācanā* and completed the attainment of the precepts, [one abides in the essence].
One must immediately practice according to the Dharma; this is called "Noble Conduct" (*ārya-caryā*). Therefore, it is said that practicing noble conduct constitutes the essence of abiding.

As for what is called "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma," Paramārtha says: once one has received these noble dharmas and they reside within one's person, every movement and action must be protected and maintained;
this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma. The preceding explanation of the meaning of the precepts is now complete.

Second, the clarification of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*). Regarding the clarification of the essential nature of the karma produced, according to the *Tonglun* (Comprehensive Treatise), Ciyun states:
"The *Tonglun* refers to treatises that encompass the Vinaya, such as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

When these clarify the essential nature of the karma produced by what has been received, they distinguish it in terms of 'informative' (*vijñapti*) and 'non-informative' (*avijñapti*) action to define its essential nature, because it is the karma that initiates the body and speech. As the treatise says: "Action" (*karman*) refers to bodily movement; the body...
Regarding the expedient means: when the bodily movement has ceased and there is no longer an agent, that which coexists with other consciousnesses is called "non-action" (*avijñapti*).

Thus, one should know that "action" (*vijñapti*) and "non-action" are distinguished in terms of their activity. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Alternatively, they are distinguished in terms of activity as 'action' and 'non-action.'"

Lì says: "This passage refers generally to various treatises. For instance, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) take matter (*rūpa*) as the essence of their karmic substance.

In contrast, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* holds that manifest precepts (*karmapatha-vijñapti*) constitute the essence of the karmic substance of matter, whereas non-manifest action constitutes the essence of the karmic substance as being neither matter nor mind."
These treatises all clarify the nature of the karma produced; thus they are so described. If one were to explain this extensively as it is here, it would not be clear for the present context.
For now, I shall directly clarify the mind capable of receiving [the vow]:

at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, one produces the substance of non-informative action (*avijñapti*). The meaning of this substance of karma is that which is produced; however, there is no leisure to discuss it further at present.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the mind capable of receiving [the precepts] is what is called the "precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*). Now, to directly manifest and plainly state the characteristics of this receiving mind:

this is made clear through the following explanation. In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, one merely distinguishes the substance of the karma produced and clarifies its object, but does not distinguish the subjective agent.
Here, however, we take the side of the receiving mind itself as the precept-substance. It says:
"Mind" refers to the mind that seeks the precepts; because this mind gives rise to the essence of non-action (*avijñapti*), it is precisely this mind that is designated as the "essence.
As for "characteristics," one must rely upon this mind to be able to take external characteristics as objects.

What are these characteristics? They are the characteristics of the dharma-realm, the sands of the Ganges, the two truths, and so forth. Because the mind takes these characteristics as its objects, they are called "mental characteristics. This is explained in relation to this [point].
Both aspects of the meaning constitute the essence of the precepts; therefore, it is said that one directly expresses the mental characteristics capable of receiving them.
When it refers to "dharmas such as the dharma-realm, the sands of the Ganges, and the two truths," this means the dharmas that the practitioner is able to receive within their own mind.

The two truths are precisely emptiness and existence: emptiness is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and existence is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). For what reason are these two employed?
The truths constitute the objective sphere of the precepts. To clarify this, first consider the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the principle of cessation and *nirvāṇa*.

For instance, if one slanders the holy teaching by claiming it was not spoken by the Buddha, or if one speaks of the principle of cessation and *nirvāṇa* as not being ultimate quiescence, one incurs a grave offense. Now, conversely, these [teachings] become sources of merit and enter the gateway of the precepts.
As for conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it refers to turning away from that cycle of birth and death, severing all evils, and abstaining from killing, stealing, and so forth. This...
All are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and all constitute the objects of the precepts; therefore, they are called the "Two Truths. Regarding "one's own solemn vow to apply skillful means":
this refers to the solemn vow to sever evil and cultivate good, even at the cost of death rather than transgressing.

"Applying skillful means" refers to such practices as kneeling on the mat, joining the palms in worship, and entreating with compassion for the conferral [of the precepts]; these are all applications of skillful means. As for "compassion, reflection, clear wisdom," and so forth:
The *Guangyi* states that "ce" (惻) means sorrow. The *Shuowen* states that "ce" arises from pain. "Si" (思) refers to contemplation.
This clarifies that at the time of receiving the precepts, one should compassionately regard all sentient beings so as not to give rise to various evils such as killing or stealing.
It means: both myself and all sentient beings have long drifted through birth and death, creating various karmic offenses; now we feel pain for our past delusions.

Therefore, it is said that one must have "compassionate reflection. Regarding the term "clear wisdom" (*vidyā-prajñā*): it means that one must rely upon clear wisdom to be able to feel deep sorrow for sentient beings within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
If one were ignorant and deluded, how could such a mind arise? Furthermore, *Śaṅgharakṣita* says:

the term "clear wisdom" is used because one must understand that this dharma of the precepts is the root of all virtues and is capable of producing great fruits; thus, because one knows its superior efficacy, [this mind] arises.
With a superior mind (*adhi-citta*), one receives this precept, cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and practices wisdom (*prajñā*) in order to realize the Right Path.

To repay the Buddha’s grace above and to transform all sentient beings below is called "clear wisdom" (*vidyā-prajñā*). One must clearly understand that the Buddha’s precepts possess such merit and benefit;
because one understands them with distinct clarity, it is called clear wisdom. Only by generating the mind in this way can one correspond with the essence of non-action (*avijñapti*).
Therefore it is said: "To mysteriously accord with the prior dharma. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "to mysteriously accord with the prior dharma": "mysteriously" (ming) refers to darkness (an).

This means that if one possesses both compassionate empathy and clear wisdom, and establishes one's resolve in this manner, one will necessarily and mysteriously—darkly—accord with the fourfold pure noble dharma.
What is "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*)? It refers to the meeting with principle; therefore, it is called correspondence.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding dharmas," this refers to the textual passages on the precepts from the preceding section as the preceding dharmas. Alternatively, it may refer by anticipation to the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) within the Teaching.
To cause this mind of formal commitment to correspond with those sublime dharmas, one must first resolve to give rise to this mind of upholding the precepts.
This refers to the correspondence with the wondrous Dharma that is as vast as the dust motes of the dharma-realm.

Regarding the meaning of "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) within that Dharma: it arises by virtue of conditions; therefore, it is called "dependent origination. It is also termed "dependently established," meaning it is formed through the convergence of conditions.
Therefore, it is called "conditioned arising" (*pratyaya-siddha*). Master Li states:

"When the recipient possesses the requisite mind, the robes and bowl are complete, the preceptor and the monastic community are pure, and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is accomplished—specifically, at the conclusion of the third proclamation—in a single kṣaṇa, one realizes this essence of non-action (*avijñapti*) within the dharmas of the dust-mote-like dharma-realm, both sentient and insentient; this is what is meant by the principle of dependent origination."
Shōyu further explains: This precept is a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). However, the mind seeking the precept, the vow, and so forth are the *hetu* (causes);
the preceptor, the monastic robes, the alms bowl, the ritual procedure (*karma*), and so forth are the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions).

When these two types of factors interact and the causes and conditions harmoniously coincide until the conclusion of the third *karma*, this precept is provisionally induced and brought forth upon those two types of phenomena; this is termed "condition" (*pratyaya*).

This refers to the arising of the meaning [of the precepts]. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Regarding those dharmas" means that, according to the intent of this passage, it points to the aforementioned dharmas such as the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the sands of the Ganges (*gaṅgā-vāluka*), and the two truths (*satya-dvaya*), which are termed "those.
That is to say, it means that the essence of the precepts (*śīla-bhāva*) is produced upon the basis of all these objects.
When the third *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is completed, one attains all the dharmas of the precepts; their arising and being focused upon within body and mind is called "origination" (*nidāna*).

This means that by virtue of the conditions of the teacher, the Sangha, the robes, the bowl, and the *karmavācanā*, together with the internal causes and conditions such as the mind's aspiration, the Dharma arises.
Thus, on the basis of all objects, the merit of virtuous precepts is produced; this is termed "arising. Therefore it is said:
This is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Regarding the statement that "that which is received and held in the mind is called the precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*):

it means that for one who is about to receive the precepts, the very mind capable of receiving them constitutes the precept-substance. Question: What is the difference between this gate of the precept-substance and the aforementioned gate of the precept-dharma (*dharma*)?
Answer: If we discuss the dharma itself, it exists spontaneously regardless of whether one receives it or not; it is capable of bringing about liberation.

Regarding the Way: if one discusses its essence (*tī*), it is this dharma attained by giving rise [to it] through body and speech; because it resides within the person, it is called the "essence. Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā Commentary) states:
"The essence of the precepts (*śīla-tī*) is the receiving of the noble dharma within the heart and mind; that is, the dharma itself is the essence of the precepts thus received.

Examining the meaning of this passage, the essence is defined from the perspective of the capacity to receive, while that which is received is the dharma (this is the point of agreement with the *Śata-śāstra*).
Regarding the "practice of the threefold training in morality": this refers to practicing in reliance upon the precepts, which is termed "the practice of morality.

Having already clarified above the dharma of the precepts and the essence of the precepts—both of which pertain to the act of receiving them—this section now distinguishes how, within the course of following the practice, one is extensively able to exert and advance the mental activities.

Since the essence of the precepts has already been received and resides within the person, this section now extensively cultivates skillful means, acting in accordance with the precepts; thus the meaning is consistent.
Therefore, it is called "precept-practice" (*śīla-carita*). "Holding it in the mind": "holding" (*bing*) means to grasp. This refers to grasping it within the mind.
As for this character, the upper part is the head of the character for grain (*ye*), and the lower part is the ancient form of the character for hand (*shou*).

It means to hold grain with the hand; thus it is named "to hold. If two such holdings are joined together, it is named "to join" (*jian*). This means to grasp the grain with both the left and right hands simultaneously. It must be so.
"Those who must extensively cultivate skillful means" refers to those who do not transgress any precepts;

this is entirely due to possessing skillful means and maintaining a mind of protective upholding, whereby they remain unstained when confronted with sense objects. Thus, the subsequent text states: "If one’s radiant and pure consciousness encounters the five sensory objects, the arising of desire and defilement is due to the aforementioned skillful means.
Zhencheng (Shen) comments: "This refers to the extensive cultivation of the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*)."
What are the four? First, to employ skillful means so that unarisen wholesome states arise; second, to cause already arisen wholesome states to increase further and further;
third, to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising; and fourth, to extinguish already arisen unwholesome states—this is the method of repentance and purification.
To examine the body and speech and so forth refers to guarding against the seven non-virtues of body and speech; this is called *śīla* (precept).

Furthermore, regarding the "practice of majestic deportment" (*īryāpatha*): this clarifies that the aforementioned examination of body and speech, which is capable of prevention, is termed "precept" (*śīla*).

Its characteristics are coarse. Now, however, one may observe the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—at the level of subtle majesty. Hence it is called the "practice of majestic deportment.
That one can "refine the will and focus exclusively on the sublime, admiring the former sages," is due to the power of capability. This clarifies the Buddhas.
The Arhats and others all upheld this precept and were thus able to attain liberation from birth and death. By virtue of this merit of the precept, they subdued Māra and achieved the Way.
I also emulate them; therefore, it is said that one "highly admires the former sages. Regarding the phrase "maintaining the mind so that subsequent actions accord with what preceded":

this clarifies that when one first resolved to receive the precepts, one vowed to uphold them without transgression; now that one has already received them, one is able to remain in accordance with that prior commitment.

It does not contradict one's original mind; therefore, it is said that "the meaning accords with what precedes. The scripture states, "Although it is not something to be contacted," which some say refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

This clarifies that although the essence of the unconditioned precept (*anabhisaṃskṛta-śīla*) is neither form nor mind, if one practices skillful means to guard and uphold it, the body attains purity.
Because it is neither form nor mind, it is said to be "not something that can be contacted."

Regarding the passage from "The four clarify the characteristics of the precepts" up to "reaching the equality of dharmas," Li states: "If explained directly, it refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts;
if discussed more extensively, then all objects—whether sentient or insentient—are the characteristics of the precepts. (I fear this interpretation may not be correct.)
Now, regarding "the manifestation of precepts according to the occasion" (where the characteristics of the precepts are summarized and their meanings precisely distinguished):

it is said that to act in accordance with the Dharma whenever one moves refers to such things as not grasping precious objects, not touching women, not lodging with women, and not eating at improper times—all of these are called acting in accordance with the Dharma whenever one moves.
In all four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one accords with the Dharma. Because of this accordance with the Dharma, virtuous qualities manifest externally;
one's physical appearance becomes pure and capable of inspiring faith in sentient beings. Thus, these virtuous qualities shine forth, and this is termed the "mark of precept" (śīla-nimitta).

Regarding the phrase "the fundamental basis for the emergence of the Way," it means that the paths of the Three Vehicles all rely upon these four precepts as their root to emerge from birth and death.

Regarding the phrase "the ultimate goal of accomplishing the fruit," it means that by taking these four precepts as the primary principle (*zong*), one is able to accomplish the four fruits of arhatship as well as the fruit of Buddhahood.
For example, while the five precepts take human rebirth as the ultimate fruit, the ten [precepts]...
Skillfully employing the heavens as the ultimate fruit—these four articles herein constitute the ultimate fruit among the Śrāvakas.

That is to say, the foundation of all ultimate fruits depends entirely upon the precepts (*śīla*). Since the precepts are pure, one is able to accumulate the arising of samādhi, give rise to wisdom, and sever delusions, ultimately attaining the benefits of the Path.
Therefore, it is said: "The root basis for departing from the world; the ultimate principle for those who have accomplished the fruit."
Therefore, regarding the statement "marked at the beginning of the *Shō* (Commentary) and elsewhere": "marked" (*hyō*) means from the outside.
This indicates that these four dharmas are placed at the very start of the *Shō*; hence the phrase. As for the statement "now, where the mind is entrusted":

this means to cause future generations to entrust their minds to these four articles, so that they may know for themselves that those who wear the sacred Dharma upon their persons are surely capable of serving as fields of merit for the six realms of existence, thereby continuing and exalting the Buddha's [teachings].
Regarding the phrase "the merit of erecting the banner of the Dharma is inconceivable," etc.: "shao" (紹) means to succeed to; "long" (隆) means flourishing.

Since the seeds of the Three Jewels—the field of merit for the six realms of existence—and so forth possess such vast merit, it cannot be exhausted by the mind’s reflection or the mouth’s deliberation.
When it asks, "How could mere discourse exhaust it? it clarifies that since the mind’s reflection falls short, verbal expression likewise cannot reach it.
"It is difficult to fathom. This concludes the preceding text. Regarding the statement "directly citing the words of the Sage as a sincere proof," [Master] Li says:

"The phrase 'concluding the preceding' also gives rise to what follows. To say that 'directly citing the words of the Sage' is the conclusion of the above, while 'sincere proof' gives rise to what follows, is incorrect;
it is merely a general introductory passage intended to cause those who uphold the Dharma to be lofty."
Regarding the scholar (*shì*) who is meticulous and reflective, Lì states: "To have a beginning and an end is called being a scholar.
From one to ten, the number reaches its conclusion. One is the beginning; ten is the end. Because he acts from the bottom up starting with one, he is called a scholar. Róng says:
"Indeed, there is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to necessarily have an end. Only the sage, perhaps, has both a beginning and an end. Zhèng Xuán says: [The same].
To distinguish between right and wrong and understand the principles of meaning—this is called being a "scholar" (*śi*).
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the first theme: the essential nature of the doctrine. From here on follows the second section:

the gate of citing texts to establish virtue. Regarding the clarification of the matters of a *bhikṣu*: it is established that the affairs of a *bhikṣu* involve discerning great difficulties. If one relies upon...
To teach and practice, to receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts, to be able to transform oneself and others, and to discern the characteristics of phenomena—this is called "discernment.

If one violates the prohibitive precepts, extensively commits unrighteous acts, and is unfamiliar with the characteristics of phenomena, such that they do not even count as a member of the Saṃgha, this is called being a "non-discerning bhikṣu.
Regarding those who conceal and destroy the True Dharma and instead plant the seeds of suffering, it is established that since they have contravened the holy teachings, they [shall] be left to...
The meaning of "upholding" is severed; it causes the Buddha-dharma to decline. This is truly because there is no one to propagate it, hence it is said that it will be extinguished.

At the time of receiving the precepts, one is solely intent upon severing evil and cultivating good, hoping to transcend birth and death. If one had not received them, there would be no precepts to violate;
yet now, having received them but failing to uphold them, one falls into hell at death—is this not to plant the karma of suffering in reverse? Now, to summarize comprehensively:
Regarding "the authentic texts spoken by the One Transformation": this means that apocryphal scriptures are excluded and not cited; therefore, they are called "authentic texts.
Regarding "precepts as the presiding lord of the ten thousand practices toward enlightenment": this clarifies that the precepts are the primary foundation of all practices.

Since the ten thousand practices arise from the precepts, which occupy the central position and stand at the head, they are called the "presiding lord. Thus, a sutra says: "If one wishes to be born in heaven, etc., one must..."
Regarding the phrase "one must protect the feet of the precepts," some say this refers to the *Sūtra of Birth from Goodness* (*Śrīgarbha-sūtra*).

The Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta states that according to the Sanskrit original, it should be called "traces of the precepts" (*śīla-pada*) rather than "feet of the precepts. The Sanskrit term is *pāda*, which is translated as "foot"; however, if one says *pādāṅguṣṭha*, it refers to the "toe."
This is translated as "trace" (jì). Since the Sanskrit original states *padā* (or *paddhati*), it is clearly known to be a trace.

Regarding the term "precepts" (*śīla*): former Buddhas studied these precept-dharmas and attained the fruits of sainthood; later people follow these prior traces and study them, and likewise attain the fruits of the Path.
Therefore, they are called "traces. Jì says: "Observing this explanation, there is also reason in it; one must not take [the previous view] exclusively."
You dismiss the Tripiṭaka; yet even a horse that travels a thousand li occasionally stumbles. Who among men is without fault? One should employ what is most substantial.

Since he was able to endure the hardships of traveling tens of thousands of li to that distant land to obtain these sūtras and śāstras and bring them here to teach and transform sentient beings, how could you not have at least a modicum of faith?
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "The precepts are the root of practice and the basis for abiding," which is illustrated by the following analogy:
Regarding "ground" (bhūmi): according to the *Śubhavyūha-sūtra*, it states that the precepts are the primary foundational ground of the path to bodhi;
thus they are called "precepts. Such precepts are also called the "first ground," the "level ground," the "equal ground," and the "ground of loving-kindness."
It is also called the Ground of Compassion, and it is also called the Footprint of the Buddha. It is named the root of all merits, and it is also called the Field of Merit.
For these reasons, the wise should uphold it and not violate the precepts. This concludes the preceding explanation of the meaning of praising the precepts according to the Sūtras of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the statement that "the multi-storied pavilion of the factors of enlightenment takes precepts as its pillars": Bin says that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment support one another to achieve the Way;

this is likened to a multi-storied pavilion, with the precepts serving as the pillars of this structure. Regarding the statement that "the city of meditative concentration takes precepts as its outer coffin":
when crossing the river of birth and death, the precepts serve as the bridge. Regarding the statement that "entering the assembly of virtuous people takes precepts as the seal": [Eight]...

The straight and upright field is the precepts as its strong embankment. Just as water does not remain in a field that lacks an embankment, so too, if there is no pure precept, the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) will not abide.
[Master] Li states: "Entering the assembly of virtuous people" refers to the noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles, who are called the assembly of virtuous people.
"Those who need it should look at it so that their precepts do not become weak. This means that in that treatise, there are many passages praising the precepts;
if one sees those texts, one will become courageous and diligent, always joyfully protecting and upholding them, and thus the precepts will not become weak.
*Vibhāṣā* is translated here as "Following Analysis. This refers to the analysis and explanation provided following the text of the *Vinaya*.
It is also translated as "Extensive Explanation. These are treatises composed by Arhats to explain the *Sūtras* and *Vinaya*, equivalent to the commentaries (*zhangsū*) of this region.
Regarding the statement that *śīla* (precepts) is also called "conduct" (*caryā*), see the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

It is said that "śīla" means "the practitioner. Just as a person with feet is able to travel to other lands, so too a practitioner who possesses the feet of śīla is able to travel to the wholesome realms and reach nirvāṇa. It is also called "keeping one's word."
That treatise explains: To say that *śīla* means "keeping one's word" is a conventional expression of worldly discourse.
If a person well guards their *śīla*, they are said to be one who keeps their word; if a person cannot well guard their *śīla*, that person does not keep their word.
Therefore, in worldly discourse, *śīla* is termed "keeping one's word. [Daolun] says: "Originally received..."
"Vowing to uphold": this means that one can now maintain [the precepts] in accordance with one's practice, not contradicting one's original resolve; hence it is called "keeping faith.
As for the statement that it is also called a "vessel," the commentary on that treatise explains: because it is the locus upon which all these meritorious qualities depend, it is called a "vessel."
*Śīla* means "coolness," referring to the absence of the heat of broken precepts and the heat of the three evil realms.
The twenty-fifth fascicle of that treatise asks: "What is the meaning of *śīla*? It answers: "The meaning of coolness is the meaning of *śīla*. Why is this?

Broken precepts cause the body and mind to suffer from feverish affliction; upholding the precepts causes the body and mind to be cool. Furthermore, the twenty-fourth fascicle provides another explanation.
It is said: "Those who break the precepts suffer heat within the three evil realms; those who uphold the precepts experience coolness among humans and devas.
Master Ying (pronounced ling) says this refers to the sense of awakening and understanding. It is also said to describe the state of being cool and pure. Master Li says the pronunciation is ling.
This means that the dharma of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is cool and refreshing, free from the affliction of oppressive heat; therefore, it is called "cool.
Regarding the three evil realms—namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—they are also called "good dreams. The commentary on that treatise explains:

*śīla* is called "dream" because those who maintain ethical discipline do not experience mental or physical fever, and thus constantly obtain good dreams. Master Li states: "Those who maintain ethical discipline are protected by the devas."

One always has auspicious dreams. It is also called "the practitioner" (*śikṣaka*). That treatise explains: *śīla* means "practice" (*śikṣā*), because one who maintains the precepts practices the dharma of the precepts well.
It is also called "the one in concentration" (*samāhita*). That treatise explains:

*śīla* means "concentration" (*samādhi*), because if one abides by the precepts, the mind easily becomes concentrated. It is also said: "When *śīla* is pure, *samādhi* manifests before one. It is also called...
Regarding the phrase "a pool for the bathing of the multitude of noble ones," that treatise explains: *śīla* means "pool. As the Buddha said in a verse:
"The Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the pool of precepts are pure and free from blemish; the noble ones bathe in it without getting wet, and they will surely reach the further shore.
Regarding the phrase "or called 'ornaments' and so forth," that treatise explains: *śīla* is like an ornament. There are those who adorn themselves with ornaments, and there are...
That which is pleasing in youth is not pleasing in middle age or old age; that which is pleasing in middle age is not pleasing in old age;

and that which is pleasing in old age is not pleasing in youth or middle age. However, for one adorned with the necklace of the precepts (*śīla-kaṇṭhika*), there is constant beauty throughout all three stages of life.
It is said: "Worldly people adorn their bodies with incense, flowers, and necklaces, whereas monastics who have left the household life take the precepts as their necklace."
Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: The Buddha said to the Bodhisattvas, "There are four kinds of necklaces for adornment:
first, the necklace of ethical discipline; second, the necklace of meditative concentration; third, the necklace of wisdom; and fourth, the necklace of dhāraṇīs.
Thus, the *Bodhisattva-śīla Sūtra* says: "Ethical discipline is like the sun and the moon, and it is also like a pearl necklace."
The meaning is that "a multitude of subtle-dust Bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment" by means of this.

It is also called a "mirror. That treatise explains it thus: "Furthermore, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is like a mirror. If the mirror is bright and pure, reflections appear within it; for one whose precepts are pure, the reflection of non-self appears. Longchi says:

"Because the precepts are pure, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arises; concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*); through concentration, one contemplates the body as being without [self]."
The mark of self (*ātman*) can be apprehended. Furthermore, regarding what is called "majestic power" (*anubhāva*), that treatise explains: moreover, the term *śīla* refers to majestic power.
That the Tathāgata possesses majestic power throughout the trichiliocosm is entirely due to the power of *śīla*.
Why is this? Because his precepts are without deficiency or transgression. As for the phrase "the rest is like the account of driving away the dragon," it is from the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*.
The Sūtras and Śāstras together clarify that seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a wicked nāga king named Ariya in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
By nature he was violent and malevolent, and thus he wrought calamities, afflicting the people of the land until they were all distressed by him.
Not far from his dwelling place was a saṃghārāma where five hundred arhats were then gathered together.
The assembly entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and each exerted their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) to drive this dragon away from the borders of the kingdom.
However, this dragon possessed great majesty and power; although five hundred arhats moved the earth with their supernormal powers, they were unable to move the dragon.
At that time, there was an Arhat named Jīvaka who arrived last. Then the other Arhats related this entire matter to Jīvaka.
Jīvaka did not enter meditative concentration; he simply snapped his fingers three times and said, "Virtuous ones, go far away.
When the dragon heard the sound of the finger-snapping, it immediately departed to a distance. Then the Arhats spoke to Jīvaka...

[The Dragon King] spoke at length: "By what power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*) did you cause this dragon to depart? Both you and I have attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

Even though I exerted all my supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), I could not move him. Why, Venerable One, did you snap your fingers three times to cause him to go forth and enter far into the great ocean?
Yāmātṛ replied: "As for the power of my snapping my fingers, it was simply because I am still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
Since that time, I have been cautious regarding the precepts and have guarded against *duṣkṛta* offenses as if they were no different from the four *pārājika* transgressions.
By the power of my ethical discipline (*śīla*), I have caused this nāga to depart; therefore, *śīla* is said to possess "majesty" and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the head of ethical discipline can see the various forms of the Truth of Suffering," that treatise explains: furthermore, the term *śīla* means "head," just as a person has [a head].
With a head, one is able to see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, taste flavors, feel tangibles, and cognize mental phenomena.

Likewise, a practitioner who possesses the head of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to see the forms of the Truth of Suffering and so forth, hear the meanings of the sets of names and so forth, and smell and perceive the fragrance of the flowers of the mind.

Having experienced the taste of the three types of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi) through renunciation, the state of non-action, and tranquility, one awakens to the touch of dhyāna, samādhi, and liberation, and understands the general and specific characteristics of phenomena such as the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). For this reason, śīla is called the "head."
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says: "As far as being able to reach nirvāṇa, etc. That treatise states:
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says that the meaning of *śīla* (virtue) is the sense of being unbroken. Just as a person with unbroken feet is able to go wherever they wish to go.
A practitioner who acts in this manner, because they do not violate the *śīla*, is able to reach *nirvāṇa*. As for the name "Ghoṣaka," it refers to a person;
in the treatise, the words of this individual are extensively cited.

The preceding section concludes the explanation from the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna, which extols the excellence of the precepts. From here on, we shall next clarify the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, which extensively praise those same precepts.

Regarding the passage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that speaks of "fully receiving and upholding the teachings on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) and so forth," according to the explanation in the "Chapter on the Dharma" (*Dharmavyūha-parivarta*), there are three successive expositions of its meaning. I shall now attempt to set them forth. Namely, with respect to the three...
Because they plant the three jewels, there are three sections. The first states: "They enable sentient beings to generate the bodhicitta, ensuring that the Buddha-jewel is not interrupted;
they reveal and expound the profound treasury of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, ensuring that the Dharma-jewel is not interrupted."
Upholding all teachings on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) so that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted; the second verse says:

praising the great vows (namely, those vowed by Bodhisattvas) so that the Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted; discerning and revealing the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) so that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted;
and practicing the six points of harmonious respect so that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted. The third verse says: planting the seeds of the Buddha.

In the field of sentient beings, they cause the sprout of perfect enlightenment to grow, ensuring that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted. They protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, ensuring that the Jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted.
They skillfully guide the great assembly with hearts free from anxiety or regret, ensuring that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.

Within these three phases, there are respective gradations. First, regarding the Jewel of the Buddha, its gradations shall be clarified: in the first phase, one is able to cause [others] to generate the aspiration for Bodhi.
Focus the mind and strive toward the fruit of Buddhahood. In the second section, the great vows are praised; this praises the arousal of the vow of practice, causing one to cultivate it.
In the third section, the seeds of the Buddha are sown within the field of sentient beings, forming the seeds of practice.

Next, regarding the manifestation of the stages and ranks within the Jewel of the Dharma: the first section expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures, which constitute the teaching. The second...
In the first section, it is shown that dependent origination is the principle of the Dharma. In the third section, the preservation of the treasury of the Dharma is the practice of the Dharma.

Regarding the subsequent presentation of the stages of the Sangha Jewel: in the first section, those who receive and uphold the laws of dignified conduct (vīrya-dharma) represent the skillful means of monastic practice.
In the second section, those who cultivate the six points of harmony represent the non-contradiction of perfected practice. In the third section...
This is because he skillfully guides the great assembly, having matured his own virtues and gathered others through conversion.
Regarding the phrase "as with other Buddhas and so forth," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, fascicle nineteen, contains the "Chapter on Protecting the Dharma" (*Dharmapālana-parivarta*), which states:
"When this sutra was being preached, at that time, great bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions came from other lands and assembled to discuss the Way."
Thus he spoke on the meaning of the Dharma. At that time, the Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have established prohibitive precepts for the sake of such beings of the five corruptions.

We pray only that the Tathāgata, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, shall further establish prohibitive precepts—namely, the precept of body, the precept of speech, and the precept of mind—stating that one must not accept or store any evil things whatsoever."
Regarding the pure precepts established in other Buddha-lands, the Buddha said, "Stop, stop! The Buddha knows the proper time himself;

as long as the causes and conditions have not yet arisen, the Tathāgata does not preemptively establish prohibitions and precepts. When this sutra was preached, it was in the twelfth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment.
There is now a transcribed version that uses the character for "king" (王); many who transmit it explain it thus: "Just like a virtuous king, all..."

He established strict regulations, forbidding the commission of transgressions and so forth. These are all human words; those who claim that the original character was "king" (王) have been mistaken for a very long time.

This is clearly evidenced by what is said in the *Ten Gates* (*Shimen lun*): "Transcriptions contain errors and omissions, and these have been passed down through tradition in a corrupted manner. These words are self-evident.
Regarding the phrase "one shall not become a scabby jackal," the *Sātyaka-nirgrantha-putra Sūtra* states:

There was a Sātyaka-nirgrantha-putra who, together with eighty thousand *nirgranthas*, traveled through various kingdoms to teach and transform sentient beings. In due course, they arrived at the city of Ujjayinī.
At that time, the ruler of the country was named Yan-chi (Ugra). The king held him in high esteem and welcomed him to receive his teachings.
That man extensively expounded various Dharma-gates for the king. Next, he described for the king the fame, merit, physical marks, and beneficial qualities of the śramaṇa Gautama.
The king asked from where such a Dharma-body is obtained. The Nirgrantha replied:
"It takes precepts as its foundation and upholding the precepts as its beginning. If one does not uphold the precepts, one will not even obtain [the state of] a mere scab."
"If even the body of a jackal [is thus transformed], how much more so can one obtain a body of merit?

Great King, you should know that because of the purity of their precepts, they do not sever the lineage of the Dharma nor the lineage of the Saṃgha; because of the purity of their precepts, their merit is immeasurable. Having heard this, the King gave rise to the bodhicitta (and so forth).
Regarding those who possess physical beauty, noble lineage, and extensive learning: "Physical beauty" (*rūpa*) refers to a handsome countenance as well as physical vigor;
"noble lineage" (*kula*) refers to high-ranking families and great clans; and "extensive learning" (*bahuśruta*) refers to a clear understanding of worldly scriptures, up to the Sūtras and Śāstras.

Yet, they are unable to maintain the precepts—this can be understood through analogy. As for "birds and beasts": those that fly are called birds (*pakṣin*), and those that run are called beasts (*mṛga*). Although they may have broad knowledge...
The sacred teaching is called "much learning. If one cannot act in accordance with the teaching, it is like a parrot mimicking the sound of a crow's foot.
Therefore, a sutra says: "For example, it is like a dead man wearing a golden necklace; so too is one who is learned but violates the precepts while receiving the offerings of others.
For this reason, I cite it again.

Regarding the instruction to "recite this as the core of one's heart": previously, it was already clarified that those who uphold or violate [the precepts] receive different retributions; these words are essential and profound.
Now they are presented once more, and thus it is said that they are repeatedly cited with persistent and earnest exhortation. Therefore, it says, "let them recite this as the core of their hearts.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the Mahāyāna sūtras.

Although dwelling in the mountains and practicing austerities may lead to nothing at all, the essential and correct path is solely the Eightfold Noble Path, which encompasses all practices and leaves none unexhausted.
Within the Eightfold Noble Path, there are right precepts, right concentration, and right wisdom.
Now, although this person has attained concentration, this concentration was not produced by relying on the Buddha’s precepts; it is called "wrong concentration. It is named...

Defiled wisdom cannot realize the true fruit; therefore, it is said to be empty and yielding nothing. Regarding the statement that for one who upholds the precepts, at the time of death, the "wind-knives" dismember the body and so forth:

consulting the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it says that when a person who upholds the precepts reaches the end of their life, the "knives of wind" dismember the body and the sinews and vessels are severed.
Yet, knowing for themselves that their observance of the precepts was pure, their minds are free from fear. As it is said:
He spoke in verse: "In the midst of great and grievous illness, the precepts are the excellent medicine; in the midst of great terror, the precepts are the protection;
in the darkness of death, the precepts are the bright lamp; in the midst of the evil realms, the precepts are the bridge; in the waters of the sea of death, the precepts are the great ship.
Regarding the phrase "the wind-blade dissects the body," the Sūtra says: "At the time of death, those whose complexion turns black will certainly fall [into the lower realms]."
If the color is blue, one falls into hell; if yellow, one falls among the animals; if it is red or white as usual, one is born among humans;
and if it is twice as red or white as usual and handsome, one attains birth in the heavens. These are the signs of the wind-sword (vāyu-śastra).
Regarding the statement that the thirty-two marks of the earth-holding [Buddha] are all obtained through the cause of upholding the precepts without distinction:

Jì (Jie) says that among these thirty-two causes, there are both general causes and specific causes. For example, as clarified in the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), the mark of the invisible crown of the head has "absence of arrogance" as its cause;
likewise, even the webbed fingers have their respective matters as their causes—all of which are termed "specific."
This is the cause. If one upholds the precepts, it is the general cause for the thirty-two marks.

Regarding the thirty-two marks: first, the soles of the feet are level like the bottom of a casket; second, there are wheel-spokes on the soles of the feet; third, the fingers and toes are slender and long;

fourth, the heels are broad and long; fifth, the body is straight; sixth, the fingers and toes are webbed; seventh, the hands and feet are soft; eighth, the ankles are even and inconspicuous; ninth...
10. The mark of body hairs curling upward; 11. The mark of shoulders like those of a deer king; 12. The mark of his body being perfectly rounded; 13. The mark of hands reaching below the knees; 14.
The mark of having a fleshy protuberance on the crown of the head; 15. The mark of having a sheathed organ like that of a horse; 16. The mark of skin that is fine and soft.
Sixteenth, the body hairs curl to the right. Seventeenth, the body is golden-hued and constantly radiant. Eighteenth, all parts of the body are fully developed.
Nineteenth, the voice is soft and gentle. Twentieth, the collarbones are well-filled. Twenty-first, the upper body is like that of a lion.
Twenty-two: His arms and elbows are slender. Twenty-three: He has forty teeth that are white, clean, even, and closely set.

Twenty-four: He possesses the mark of four canine teeth. Twenty-five: His cheeks are like those of a lion. Twenty-six: Among all tastes, he perceives the supreme taste. Twenty-seven: His tongue is broad and long. Twenty-eight:
He possesses a beautiful Brahma-voice. Twenty-nine: The eyelashes of his eyes are deep blue. Thirty: His two armpits are...
[The thirty-two marks are as follows: ... [omitted] ... Thirty-first, his eyes blink like those of a bull king. Thirty-second, he has the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
These are the thirty-two marks. Such marks as these are all obtained through the observance of the precepts. Therefore it is said: "The thirty-two marks have no differentiated causes;
they are all obtained through the observance of the precepts. (This citation is from the *Chuyiming ji*).
Regarding the two chapters on "Praising the Precepts" and "The Retribution of the Precepts" extensively listed in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* as being fully explained therein:
these two chapters exist in the fourteenth fascicle of that treatise. The first, the chapter on Praising the Precepts, states:
"A brief praise of a small portion of the *śīla*. *Śīla* is the very foundation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). *Śīla* is a heap of the jewels of merit. Furthermore...
This is the abode of merit; it is like the great earth upon which all things depend.
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) enables people to transcend birth and death, just as a sturdy boat can carry one across the great ocean.

Ethical discipline can extinguish the afflictions of the defilements, just as excellent medicine can eliminate various diseases. Furthermore, ethical discipline can deliver people from all evil realms, just as crossing deep waters results in reaching a safe shore.
Bridges. Such various [examples] praising the efficacy of *śīla* (ethical discipline) follow the same principle; as the text would become too voluminous, they are not recorded here.
Next is the "Chapter on the Retribution of Precepts," which clarifies that a Bodhisattva who is able to purify *śīla* attains the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*, i.e., the Second Ground).

He constantly acts as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin-rāja*), transforming people through the ten wholesome paths of action, and the seven treasures appear spontaneously. The text extensively explains the characteristics of these seven treasures in detail.

Regarding matters such as these, the power of their merit and benefit is extensive and not recorded here. The above four sections complete the general explanation of the meaning of the first gate, the Teaching of Transformation (Hua-jiao).
From this point forward, the second gate, the Teaching of Regulation (Zhi-jiao), is correctly elucidated. One should not harbor doubts or regrets, nor seek clarification from others.
As for the person: if they clearly uphold the precepts and their understanding of the sacred teachings is thorough, there is no need to consult others.
They may travel and transform beings in all directions without encountering obstacles. Lì said: "The Buddha-dharma of the ten directions is identical in principle and without distinction.

If one does not understand the sacred teachings, there will be much fear wherever one goes; if one acts in accordance with the teachings, traveling through various regions will leave one free from timidity. Jì said: "If one is clear..."
He was well-versed in the Vinaya and understood all matters pertaining to the Sangha. When traveling on the road, he encountered others;

regarding all *karmavācanā* procedures, the recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*), and the performance of ritual acts, he understood how to perform them, and his mind was free from obstruction. It is said that if one were to answer that they do not understand, the heart would harbor fear.
Thus it is called [the "fearless" state].

Regarding the first point, "the firmness of the category of precepts," Lü [Xun] says: Although there are five items in number, they may be condensed into three categories. The first concerns one's own practice;

the subsequent three concern the conduct of governing the community. When these two types of conduct are perfected, one is then able to uphold the Dharma and apply it to the times, ensuring that it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years.

Therefore, with this final phrase, one establishes the True Dharma. By practicing mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, and so forth, one causes the precepts to be pure and prevents them from being destroyed by conditions;
thus it is said that "the category of precepts is firm. Second, those who break the precepts are the opposite of those who uphold them;
in meaning, they are like enemies. Because one’s inner mind is pure, it surpasses theirs; thus it is said that "one is virtuously superior to all enemies. Third, since there is none...
Regarding flaws and defects: when adjudicating matters among the assembly, his mind is free from fear or hesitation; thus it is said that he is "decisive and fearless.

Fourth, because he clearly understands what constitutes an offense and what does not, he can resolve the doubts and stagnations of others; thus it is said that he is "skillfully able to provide clarification and resolution.

Fifth, if one does not uphold the precepts, the Dharma will not endure for long—this meaning is easy to understand. Furthermore, regarding the attainment of the ten benefits, as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: first, the gathering of the Saṃgha; second...

1. To cause the Saṃgha to rejoice; 2. To cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; 3. To inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; 4. To cause those who already believe to increase in their faith; 5.

To bring those who are difficult to discipline into submissiveness; 6. To grant peace and happiness to those who possess a sense of shame and remorse; 7. To sever the outflows (*āsrava*) of the present;
8. To sever the outflows of the future; 9. To cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time. The meaning of these ten benefits is extensive.
The section on the causes for the arising of the teaching as presented in the first fascicle has already been explained.
As for the phrase "even so for the three periods of time," the past, present, and future are what are termed the "three periods of time."
