Furthermore, the remaining nine directions are set forth. Regarding the eighth condition, it generally admits both success and failure. If the assembly for the *poṣadha* possesses deficiencies, the rite is not accomplished;
this pertains merely to the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*). In reality, by performing the recitation of purity (*śīla-viśuddhi*), one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) for violating the teaching.

If the boundary markers (*sīmā-nimitta*) are slightly deficient, the boundary is not established, because the boundary is determined according to the markers cited during the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*). Fifth.

Regarding the establishment and abolition [of rules]: it is said that the conditions established by ancient masters appear and disappear inconsistently. For example, Master Yuàn of the Northern Liáng school, relying on the *guṇavastuka* (robe of merit) procedure, established six conditions:

first, the assembly of the Saṃgha; second, harmony; third, the selection of the person; fourth, the taking of the *chanda* (consent); fifth, the inquiry into the conditions; and sixth, the response to the intent.

Yet, as for the reliance upon a specific boundary (*sīmā*), he did not reveal this at all. Consequently, those who rely solely on the text end up [performing the rite] within a "natural" (*svabhāva*) boundary.
To proceed immediately to receive the precepts upon reaching the site is the first error, which has persisted without correction to this day.

According to the Vinaya masters of the Xiangbu school, these are generally categorized as seven, or sometimes six or five: first, the provisional boundary; second, the presiding Sangha; third, the exclusion of other assemblies; fourth, the transmission of consent and purity;
fifth, the origin of the formal act; sixth, the sequence of questions and answers; and seventh, the actual performance of the rite. These constitute the combined conditions.

The same root text has its branches and stems confused; the questions and answers are divided among people, and the titles and characteristics are each distinct, such that their meanings cannot be reconciled as one.

Furthermore, it is said that the person appointed [to oversee the assembly] must possess six qualities, for there is no basis [for such a requirement] in the original text. Regarding the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding), five factors are required because of the absence of the *chanda* (consent/vote).

Now, if it is said that the *chanda* is not listed, how can one know that the boundary-binding lacks the *chanda*? Therefore, it is impossible to omit it. These ten reasons above are what distinguish this from others.
The Master [said]: "It is not that I dare to seek difference for its own sake; rather, the principle itself cannot be the same. A brief exposition is thus concluded.
The foregoing ten sections on differences complete the general explanation of the meaning of the first section, 'The Gate of Requisite Conditions for the Performance of Rituals.'"

Second, regarding the clarification of the universal and restricted application of established rules (*vidhi-prajñapti*): Shen says that among the various formal procedures (*karma*) and those performed in the presence of another (*pratyekam-śiras*), when applied to times when no one else is present, those that may be performed through mental recitation (*citta-manasikāra*) are called "universal" (*sāmānya*).
If they can only be performed through mental recitation and do not apply to the aforementioned two cases, they are called "restricted" (*pratiniyata*).

Regarding the first point, the scope of mutual inclusion (*anyonya-saṃgraha*): Shen says that "mutual inclusion" corresponds to the character "universal" (*tong*), while "scope" (*fenqi*) corresponds to the character "restricted" (*ju*). Ji says: [The text continues...]
Regarding the section on mutual inclusion and assistance: first, by citing the *dharmas*, it includes the eight kinds of *karmans*.
Second, by citing the *vastus* (matters), it includes all matters subject to *karmans*, whether animate or inanimate. Third, by citing the persons, it includes the entire Saṃgha;
there are seven distinctions within the Saṃgha, beginning with a single person and ending with a Saṃgha of twenty persons. Fourth, by citing the boundary (*sīmā*), it...

All ritual procedures (*vidhi*) are subsumed within spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Spontaneity consists of various collections of emptiness (*śūnyatā-rāśi*), and ritual procedures likewise possess distinctions of magnitude.
Second, regarding the specific presentation of formation and destruction: phenomena do not arise in isolation; they ultimately require four conditions (*pratyaya*).

According to their respective meanings, these are clarified as being no more than seven types. The meaning of these seven types will be explained extensively below. Since there are already two gates of differentiation, now...
This refers to the first [category].

"One dharma" refers to the procedures for the mind-to-mind (*cittānuvartana*) and face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) assemblies. "Two matters" refers to the specific matters addressed by the *karmavācanā*, such as receiving the precepts or confessing offenses.
"Three persons" refers to the monastic assemblies ranging from a single person up to a group of twenty persons.

Furthermore, as for the four boundaries (*sīmā*): they are established by formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*) and arise naturally. For now, I shall briefly indicate them; below, each will be cited and explained in detail. Regarding "matters that are minor":
this refers to the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and the confession of light offenses (*duṣkṛta*), which are minor matters. Or, regarding "a boundary where there are no people":

this refers to cases such as receiving a robe (*cīvara*), which is a rite performed before a single person (*pratimukha-dharma*), whereas the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is a rite for the assembly (*saṃgha-dharma*). Because there are no people within the boundary, these [minor rites] are permitted.

Regarding "mental recollection" (*manasikāra*): as for the cases where one's own practice results in no transgression of the precepts, even when ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) are not formally completed, consider, for example, a bhikṣu who possesses robes that must be formally dedicated (*deśanā*).
If he were to fail to do so, he would commit an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), which constitutes a transgression of the precepts.

However, because there is no one present within the boundary (*sīmā*), the Buddha permitted him to perform the dedication through mental recollection, thereby ensuring he incurs no guilt. This is what is meant by "no transgression of the precepts. As it says:

Receiving the robe and declaring its purity (*śuddhi*) is called "accomplishing it through one's own action. The above has completed the explanation of the meaning of mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Below, the method of face-to-face declaration (*pratyakṣa-vākya*) is clarified. This refers to cases where the conditions for mental recollection do not apply, as well as instances where there is no Saṃgha within the boundary (*sīmā*); these require a face-to-face declaration. Regarding the phrase "and where there is no Saṃgha within the boundary": [This refers to] when the conditions for mental recollection are absent, and because there is no Saṃgha present within the designated boundary, one must perform the rite through a face-to-face declaration; this is simply what is meant by "face-to-face" (*pratyakṣa*). As for the expression "and where there is no Saṃgha within the boundary":

[This indicates that] even if one is within a boundary, if no members of the Saṃgha are present, the procedure must be carried out by addressing another person directly. Thus, it is termed a "face-to-face" rite. As for the phrase "and where there is no Saṃgha within the boundary": [It means] when the specific circumstances for mental recollection are not met, and furthermore, because no monks are available within the limits of the *sīmā*, the rite is necessarily performed by means of a direct, face-to-face communication with another qualified individual. This constitutes what is known as a "mere face-to-face" (*kevala-pratyakṣa*) procedure. The mention of "and where there is no Saṃgha within the boundary" serves to clarify the scope of this requirement.

This clarifies the *saṃghadharma-pratimukha* (the face-to-face method for a group). This applies generally to two, three, or up to four persons, as explained below, including cases where they jointly perform the ritual acts;
this is precisely what is meant by the *saṃghadharma-pratimukha*. For instance, it is permitted for two or three persons to perform it together.
Regarding the statement that "it may involve as few as four people," this refers to the time of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).

If there are only four people present, one cannot perform formal acts (*saṃghakarma*) by way of face-to-face consultation, because one person serves as the fivefold virtue (*pañcavarga-guṇa*) and the other three do not constitute a *saṃgha*. However, if it is for the purpose of reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), four people suffice.
Furthermore, in the case of confessing a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, four people merely perform the formal act appropriate for a group of many.

Regarding the "two assemblies' method of face-to-face confession" being the same as the aforementioned "method of the assembly" for mental recitation (*cittamanasikāra*): this refers to the same four types of methods mentioned previously.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "That which was originally performed by the Saṃgha, because there is no one present within the boundary (*sīmā*), the mental recitation is now permitted. What, then, is mental recitation?

This refers to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the distribution of gifts received by the Saṃgha, and the clothing of deceased persons, and so forth.

As for matters that are minor or trivial, such as the confession and relinquishment of an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), one harmonizes the Saṃgha with a single motion (*jñapti*). For example, when one wishes to go forth (*pravrajyā*), one grants the shaving of the hair with a single motion;
likewise, one relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe with a single motion.

"Or those that are performed regularly" refers to the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of the Precepts) and the *Jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion consisting of a single announcement) for the *Pravāraṇā*.

Based on these matters such as the *Poṣadha*, they are indeed important affairs; however, because they are performed regularly, there is no need for excessive diligence, and one simply performs the single announcement (*jñapti*).
Or, regarding "those that are strictly prescribed as being accomplished by a single proclamation to the Saṃgha," this refers to other types of speech and physical contact.

This refers to the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure). It was established because the monk Channa engaged in both verbal and physical frivolity—namely, lewd jesting and agitation—which disturbed the community and caused him to constantly violate the rules regarding speech and silence.
Since his conduct had fallen into disorder, a formal regulation was enacted through a motion (*jñapti*) and a decision (*niścaya*), and the name was changed to *anyavāda* (speaking otherwise).
The same applies to causing provocation. Regarding "frivolity of body," it refers to cases such as when the Saṃgha is sitting and he stands, or when the Saṃgha is standing and he sits, and so forth.
Regarding "frivolity of speech," it refers to repeatedly seeking to provoke the Saṃgha; when the Saṃgha performs a formal act of admonition (*karmavācanā*), he asks, "With whom are you speaking?
What matter are you discussing? and so forth. When the Saṃgha asks him, "From where have you come? he replies, "I have come from the past. [When asked] "What...? he replies... [and so on].

[The questioner] says: "Where does it go? [The respondent] answers: "It goes to the future. The Buddha ordered that a *jñapti* (formal motion) be established to prohibit it. Once prohibited, to do it again constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;

prior to the establishment of the *jñapti*, doing it constitutes only a *duṣkṛta*. Jing says: "As in the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), when the Saṃgha establishes a regulation by means of a *jñapti*, entering the marketplace is not permitted."
Regarding the phrase "because the matters are intertwined, their meaning must be harmonized," and so forth, up to "the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one proclamation)," Li states:

"This means that the matters are intermingled and overlap between the Great and Small [Vehicles]. Because there is a 'small' element, they are called 'intertwined. For example, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for requesting the day [for a ceremony] is 'small' when performed for an individual;
whereas the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for establishing or dissolving various boundaries (*sīmā*) is 'large' as it is performed for the Saṃgha. Shen states: "[It refers to] the single..."
A *jñapti* (motion) concerns minor matters. When it proceeds to a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), it involves major matters;

therefore, [the assembly] must come together. Regarding matters that range from small to large where the circumstances may be inconsistent: it is said that receiving the precepts is a major matter, while repenting for a grave offense is a minor matter.

Censure and admonition also range from small to large; for example, admonishing those who have split the Saṃgha or their associates is a major admonition, whereas admonishing those who live in close association is a minor one.

"Small. Regarding the administration of these measures (*karma*), there are also large and small types. The three *utkṣepaṇīya* (suspensions) are large; the four *pravāsanīya* (expulsions) are small. Jì says:

However, according to Lì’s commentary (*Sū*), the three types of *karmavācanā* are further subdivided into nine: namely, the single *jñapti* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion and one proclamation), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations).

Fourth: each is divided into three grades. When the formalities (*rūpa*) and the Dharma (*dharma*) coincide, benefiting an individual, yet harmony is somewhat difficult to achieve, it is judged the "middle grade. When there are superfluous words or provocation—since such acts disturb the Sangha—the fault of the intention is grave, and harmony is extremely difficult to achieve; this is judged the "upper grade. [This concludes] the *jñapti*. The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion followed by one proclamation) is as follows: first, the motion is made; second, the proclamation is made. This is called the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. It is also called the *jñapti-anuśrāvaṇa-karman* (the motion-and-repeated-announcement rite). Regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, there are two types: first, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the sake of the Saṃgha; second, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the sake of an individual. Regarding the three grades: those involving the binding or releasing of various boundaries (*sīmā*) and matters essential to the community where the reconciliation of feelings is easiest are called the "lower grade.

Those that involve being dispatched by the day, where duties are performed both for the community and for oneself—whether exclusively for private ends—where the reconciliation of feelings is somewhat more difficult, are called the "middle grade.

Those such as the six-year separation from one's robes, where the matter is performed solely for private ends and the reconciliation of feelings is most difficult, are called the "upper grade. [The *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and third proclamation) is used for] the three [lower grades].

Regarding the "categories": as in the *Smṛtivinaya* (Recollection Vinaya), this refers to a pure person who is slandered—namely, Dharmatāla. The Saṃgha performs a recollection [ceremony] to certify that he has not committed an offense.
Because the assembly collectively knows that Dharmatāla is pure, it is easy for their minds to be harmonized. As for the term "lower":

because the *Amūḍhavinaya* (Vinaya for those not insane) was committed while one was mad, the Noble Ones have declared it non-offensive. From the time the madness ceased, he did not commit it again. Now, he is...
He cites an example: when the Saṃgha performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) in this manner, it serves as proof that he has not committed an offense.

This is because although he was previously insane, one perceives only his outward appearance; who can discern whether his insanity is real or false? Therefore, since the current state of mind is somewhat difficult to harmonize, it is called "the middle. Regarding the "place of the offense" (*āpattisthāna*):

because what was cited previously contradicts what follows, or because what was cited previously is heavy while what follows is light, the wording is indeterminate and the matter is most difficult to fully comprehend.

Harmonizing with human sentiments is extremely difficult; it is termed "superior grade. To speak of sentiments and appearances being discordant means that [procedures] such as expulsion (*pārājika*), formal censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), reconciliation (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*), and suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) are contrary to sentiment.

The establishment of these disciplinary methods constitutes a divergence from the common way. Conversely, receiving the precepts, repenting of offenses, and requesting [formal] acts are in accord with sentiment.

One who wishes to clarify the four types of legal procedures (*dharmas*) does not entirely oppose sentiment; therefore, the term "appears" (*yōng*) is used. "Appears" implies that while there may be some degree of opposition, it is not absolute.

This refers to the meaning of "indefiniteness. Jì (Jie) says: "In terms of the *saṃgha* that administers the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*), their mental views may differ; hence it is called 'discordance. For example, some say:
'If one teaches another to plant flowers and fruits from their own seeds, or if these are offered as general offerings, this is a virtuous matter—why trouble oneself with formal censure or expulsion?
Others say: 'This is defiling the household and must be disciplined. Because of such differences in speech and view, it is termed indefinite."

This refers to a discrepancy in the terminology. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the *jñapti-caturtha* and so forth," Zhìlì states: "In all these cases, the matter consists of three grades; thus, the rule is halved.

For example, the allowance for receiving the precepts with a group of five persons in border regions is due to halving the number based on the distinction between the Central Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*) and the borders.

This is similar to the three grades of days for receiving [the *poṣadha*], or the category of *karmavācanā* being divided into three according to the specific matter at hand. As for the phrase "halving based on the Central Kingdom and the borders," it refers to the usage in the Central Kingdom.
Ten people [are required for a formal act]; in these frontier regions, half of those from the Central Kingdom are used, so there are only five people.
Regarding the three grades of receiving the day, these are likewise halved: the fifteenth day is half of the month-unit, and the seventh day is half of the fortnight-unit.

Regarding the three [grades] based on the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) corresponding to the matter at hand, this also means they are halved; the two-part proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*) is half of the four-part proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha*).

Half of that is the *jñapti* (single motion), which is half of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation) category. These are all reduced according to the lightness of the matter; thus, the ritual procedure (*dharma*) is proportionally diminished.

If one includes the previous two categories, there are one hundred and eighty-four procedures. The "previous two" refer to the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) and the *manasikāra* (mental recitation).

Furthermore, there are three types of *cittavijñapti* (mental recitation) performed alone; seven types of *cittavijñapti* performed with a counterpart (*pratimukha-cittavijñapti*); four types of *cittavijñapti* involving the community (*saṃgha-karma-cittavijñapti*);
and four types of *cittavijñapti* involving the community with a counterpart. These together constitute eighteen. As for those performed with a counterpart alone, there are thirty-two.

Adding these eighteen to those [thirty-two], there are fifty. When these fifty are applied to the one hundred and thirty-four *dharmas* of the various rules, it should total one hundred and eighty-four *dharmas*.
However, in the text concerning the *pratideśanīya* (confession) procedures, only thirty-one *dharmas* are listed.
Now, excluding the *bhikṣuṇī*'s announcement of entry into a monastery and the *bhikṣuṇī*'s request for instruction, only twenty-nine *dharmas* remain. Furthermore, taking...

Eating before or after [the prescribed time], visiting the homes of others, receiving *pālika-ra-cīvara* (translated as "miscellaneous robes" or "auxiliary robes"), and relinquishing them—these constitute three [additional rules].
Together with the previous twenty-nine, these total thirty-two.
The response states: "This is a general indication; it is not fixed according to the number. The intent of this reply is as follows:

Regarding the common expression "the hundred-and-one *karmavācanās*," it does not mean that their number is strictly one hundred and one. It is rather like the "one hundred and one articles for the body," which may simply consist of exactly one hundred and one items.
However, "hundred" is merely the conventional term for the limit of a count. Thus, the *Karmasūtra-ṭīkā* says: "As is commonly transmitted, 'hundred'..."
This is the collective name for these numbers. Since each matter involves exactly one *karmavācanā*, they are called the "one hundred and one *karmas*.

As there are one hundred and one *karmas* within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is said that the *Daśabhāṇavāra* may also be cited. Thus, according to the *Karmavastu-śāstra*, there are one hundred and one:
namely, twenty-four *jñapti* (single motion), forty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), and thirty *jñapti-caturtha* (motion followed by three proclamations).
"Examine this one gate minutely from top to bottom and across its breadth, so that there may be no discrepancy or duality.

This means that one should take this one gate and apply it as a heading to all subsequent sections, such as the accounts of receiving the precepts, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and so forth. These matters will be further clarified within the texts themselves;

one need only look to this one gate to determine whether they are established or failed, thereby recognizing their characteristics. As for the phrase "so that there may be no discrepancy or duality," "shu" (庶) here functions as an expression of hope or expectation.
Lì says: "To have 'duality' (èr) means that because there is a difference, duality arises. Had there been no difference, it would have remained as one.
Yīngshī says: "'Èr' means two. The *Erlǐ* says 'èr' means doubt; it means having two minds, both of which are full of uncertainty."
The answer regarding the "fourfold and threefold [vows]" and the "layperson’s exposition of the Dharma" refers to the period before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) was established.
At that time, one received the precepts through the "threefold formula," which is precisely the Three Refuges (*triśaraṇa*). Initially, one received the precepts via the Three Refuges;

later, because there were no *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, there was no one to provide instruction. Consequently, they violated the precepts, engaged in various unlawful acts, and wore their robes in a disordered manner when begging for alms.
They eat contrary to the Dharma; they accept impure food in various places; and during the great and small meals, they shout and clamor loudly like the assembly customs of the Brahmins.
For this reason, the Buddha ordained the establishment of preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya), and the conferral of the precepts through formal ritual (karmavācanā).

Regarding the first three refuges: since those who receive them through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) encounter many procedural requirements, they may doubt whether their previous reception was valid.
They report this to the Buddha, and the Buddha says: "Receiving by means of the three utterances is called a well-performed and lawful ritual; it is indeed the conferral of the precepts.

As for the statement that "even within the discourse for laypeople, when it reaches the words 'this is the ritual' (*karmavācanā*), etc.," this refers to the *Poṣadha-vastu* (The Section on the Uposatha).
In the middle [section], bestowing the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts upon laypeople and so forth are all termed *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts).

To clarify that since *karmavācanā* is defined as "accomplishing a matter," why would such matters be restricted to either the Great or Small Vehicles? This is like the method of mental recitation (*manasikāra*), which also distinguishes various communal procedures (*saṃghakarma*);
this refers precisely to what is called "communal procedure by mental recitation."
The explanation of the meaning of the *dharmas* is now complete. From this point forward, the explanation proceeds by way of the actual matters (*vastu*).

Regarding the matters to which the *karmavācanā* applies, they are not explained again here; that is to say, these are the matters to which the *karmavācanā* applies. As previously listed, there are one hundred and eighty-four *dharmas* in total;
accordingly, one hundred and eighty-four matters must likewise be listed. This is because the enumeration of the *dharmas* has already been concluded.
It does not further clarify the specific matters to which [the rules] apply; it simply demonstrates that they are incorrect.

Furthermore, it says that *karmavācanā* is the dharma, and dharma must contain the matter (*vastu*), while the matter must contain the dharma. This passage merely clarifies the dharma and does not further present the characteristics of the matter.

In the subsequent chapters, those matters will be revealed of themselves, as in the explanations of the procedures for the *pravāraṇā* and the confession (*pratideśanā*). Question: Regarding the statement here that "it is not further clarified," this—

The meaning of the text seems to indicate that the matter has already been clarified previously. The response concludes that the matter has already been settled within the first section, "The Section on Weighing Previous Matters," and the eighth section, "The Section on Stating One’s Original Intent," among the ten preceding sections.

Regarding those matters that apply to both sentient and insentient objects: for example, relinquishing, repentance, disciplinary treatment, banishment, and receiving the precepts pertain to sentient beings; whereas the binding and releasing of various boundaries (*sīmā*) pertain to insentient things.
As for the statement that "if there is a discrepancy in even a single condition, all [acts] fail to be accomplished," this is indeed the case in the present text.

This explains the meaning of the differences in conditions (*pratyaya*). From the passage beginning with "From what... onwards, it specifically explains the meaning of the differences in conditions. Jì says:

For instance, in the midst of worldly affairs, one may receive the precepts for another; provided that there are no obstacles or impediments regarding one's own person and that one already possesses the robes and bowl.

This refers to the actuality of the external object. Within insentient things, for instance, the boundary markers established according to the teachings when performing a ritual demarcation (*sīmābandha*) are likewise actual external objects;
therefore, it is said that both are combined as being real. If one were to deviate from this, it would be termed "a discrepancy within a single cognitive object."

Regarding "the *karmavācanā* for non-concealment and concealment," etc.: if one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and subsequently performs confession (*pratideśanā*), why would it be necessary to grant the *parivāsa* (concealment) discipline?
This refers to cases where the Buddha judged an action to be invalid because the medicine and the illness were incompatible;

such as the instances cited in Campā involving the three types of formal accusations (*tṛtiya-karma*) and the four types of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karma*). With respect to those subject to the three accusations, there are twenty-one [cases].
No. The seven permutations formed are like the twenty-one "non-cases" (*apaiśunya*). These are precisely the instances where the confession is not appropriate.

Regarding the twenty-one non-cases: taking "not seeing," "not confessing," and "not relinquishing" as three; "not seeing" and "not confessing" as four; "not confessing" and "not relinquishing" as five;
"not relinquishing" and "not seeing" as six; combining these three into one makes seven; and multiplying this by three results in twenty-one. This is what is meant.

Regarding the twenty-one "non-[valid] acts" (*akṛtya*): those that are "non-[valid]" are transformed into "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*) by reversing them. For offenses, one reverses the first two; for "not seeing [the offense]," one reverses the latter two (and so forth).

Regarding the failure of the *karmavācanā* for the two types of rooms (*vihāra*) due to obstacles among non-sentient objects: since it was stated above that these pertain to the objects upon which the ritual is performed.
"Penetrating both the sentient and the insentient. The following section explains the insentient. Regarding rooms with an owner or rooms without an owner:

it must be free from obstruction and difficulty for the *sthāpanā-karman* (the formal act of assignment) to be valid. If either one or both [of these conditions] are present, even if the *sthāpanā-karman* is performed, it shall not be accomplished.

As for the requirement that both items must be present regarding the separation from robes (*cīvara-vippavāsa*), this is established to clarify that there may be cases where the robes are heavy due to illness.

This is called "possessing two items. When the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is performed, it is successfully accomplished. Although the robe for one who is ill is light and the robe for one who is not ill is heavy, the addition of the ritual formula (*adhivāsanā*) is not accomplished [in the latter case].
As for the staff (*daṇḍa*), it is permitted for those who are old or sick; specifically, there must be both physical illness and old age for it to be called "possessing" (*samanvāgata*).

This does not mean simply casting down the staff; rather, one must formally request it. There is very clear textual evidence for this in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*). Some have explained it as follows:
It is said: "To cast down one's staff at ordinary times requires that one must first seek the Dharma; this is a great falsehood. This is the interpretation of Jie.

The intention of Nanshan was that for those who are aged or infirm, the casting down of the staff is permitted. Nowadays, people are not ill, nor are they frail and weak; yet they constantly lean on long staffs, making a display of being great beings.
This encourages arrogance and directly violates the ritual rules; such behavior is also not permitted. Furthermore, it is as [stated] in the *San*... [text truncated].

Regarding the "Householder's Step": a "bowl-net" (*patraloka*) is a carrying pouch; using it also constitutes an offense under this rule. According to the Buddhist teachings, the bowl is to be held only in the hands.
The explanation of the meaning of the matter is now complete. From here on, the subject is clarified by way of persons.

As for the "three types of persons" mentioned below, they are: the Saṃgha, many individuals, and a single individual. Within the Saṃgha, there are four categories as previously explained [in the section on] "Assembling the Saṃgha."

The section on the "Middle" concludes the exposition on the meaning of the fourfold demarcations for the *saṃgha*. These four types are the *saṃghas* of four persons, five persons, ten persons, and twenty persons.

Thus, it should be known that there are four within the *saṃgha*; this [section] does not repeat those explanations, but directly sets forth the rules (*dharma*) and procedures (*karma*) for groups of three and one person.
Regarding the determination that certain rules and matters are not permitted, [the author] states: "As for the above..."

Regarding the four types of *saṃgha*, they may only exercise the formal procedures (*dharmas*) of the *saṃgha*; they may not perform those that are "only in the presence of another" (*pratimukha*) or "only by mental recollection" (*manasikāra*).

As for these *dharmas* and their corresponding matters (*vastu*), if one were to employ these two types of procedure using the aforementioned four types of *saṃgha*, it would be categorically incorrect. Some say:

"Dharma" refers to such things as the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, while "matter" refers to such things as the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and the purification of the site (*śuddhasthāna*). Within the matter itself there is still dharma; thus, the dharma is subsumed under the matter.
Therefore, it receives the name of "matter" (*vastu*). Alternatively, because the matter is subsumed under the dharma, it receives the name of "dharma.
Regarding the establishment of two dharmas within groups of two or three persons: "establishment" refers to the *dvika-saṃgha* (a community of two) and the *trika-saṃgha* (a community of three).

These may perform only the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations), the *pratyekamukha* (face-to-face) method, or the *saṃgha-pratyekamukha* (community face-to-face) method. When two persons perform [the act], they employ only the *pratyekamukha* method; when three persons perform it, they employ the *saṃgha-pratyekamukha* method.
Therefore it is said thus. Regarding the requirement that monks from both boundaries must assemble when there are none present, even to the point of having to change the ritual procedure:
this is a matter of the natural application of the rite; it is essential that everyone assemble so that there is no "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).

If there are persons within the two boundaries, they are subsumed under the fundamental communal dharma (*mūla-saṃgha-dharma*), and one may not perform the rite in the presence of only a few individuals. As for the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, one must consult those nearby.

According to the precepts for the presiding master of the confession (*kṣamāpaka*), when receiving an invitation from another, one must question those nearby; this is not the time for the actual confession of offenses.

There are also cases where questioning is universally required: as clarified in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the ninety *pāyattika* (single-downfall) rules, if one is in a concealed place, one must question those nearby, and the same applies within a fathom’s distance in an open space. The above clarifies that for the ninety *pāyattikas*, questioning is not required.

This was merely a provisional judgment. Now, we clarify that for the confession of the thirty-nine or forty offenses, one must simply inquire of the boundary; therefore, it is said that "in all cases one must inquire.
Some say there are also cases where "in all cases one must inquire," meaning that while the inquiries differ, there is simply a general inquiry applicable in some instances and not in others.
If the offense occurred in a concealed place, one uses the specific inquiry; hence it is said, "in all cases one must inquire. If, however, it occurred in an exposed place...

Upon further investigation, there is no need to inquire; therefore, it is said that this does not involve formal inquiry. If one holds the robe and performs the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity) without distinguishing between the general and the specific, it means that one need not question those nearby.
This would mean there is no communication at all, so why even mention it? Hence, it is said that "one does not distinguish between the general and the specific.

Furthermore, another interpretation states: if one holds the robe and performs the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* without distinguishing between the general and the specific, it clearly establishes the act of holding the robe.
In such cases, one must never ask about the boundaries. Since there is no regulation within the boundary requiring that everything be asked about, it is said that "the general is not discussed.
Furthermore, since there is no separate selection of five or three items to be asked about together, it is said that "the particular is not discussed.

If it is a *cittānuvartana* (a mental act) that is entirely non-procedural, this refers to the *cittānuvartana-dharma*; one simply performs it oneself and need never ask another person at all. Some say:
Regarding the practice of mental recollection (*cittamanasikāra-dharma*): if one is to perform it in the presence of another person, it is not appropriate for that occasion.

When there is a specific matter that must be performed according to circumstances, this is called the practice of mental recollection—such as the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or the confession of minor offenses (*laghu-āpatti*).
These should be performed immediately upon encountering the conditions, without the need to consult a person nearby.
If one refers to what is upheld according to the aforementioned method, Jì says: "This refers to the four great categories previously mentioned:

first, the Dharma; second, the matter; third, the person; and fourth, the boundary. Since we are now returning to the text on the 'Dharma' within the first category, it is said to be 'within the Dharma.

Lìmíng says: "As clarified in the previous section on the delimitation of mutual inclusion. Lìjiě says: "This is correct. If one performs [the rite] by means of the *cittamātra* (mind-only) method..."
Regarding "whether identical or distinct": this means that when performing these rites, there is no fault of having a separate assembly.
Fourth, regarding the boundaries (*sīmā*): the four natural boundaries are the wilderness (*araṇya*), the village (*grāma*), the path (*adhva*), and the water boundary (*udaka-sīmā*).

Within these four types of boundaries, if one applies the formal procedures of the community (*saṃgha-dharma*), one may only perform the rite of binding the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). Furthermore, among the miscellaneous rules for groups of one, two, three, or several individuals, [the same applies].
Lì says: The procedures for distributing deceased property, the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), and so forth, are called "miscellaneous dharmas.

Although these are communal dharmas, if there are currently no [other] people present, one may perform them through *pratimukha-vijñapti* (face-to-face declaration) or *manasikāra* (mental recitation). One may also perform them spontaneously on the ground.

Regarding the statement that four people may jointly perform the *pravāraṇā*, it must be that they all assemble; Lì clarifies that this applies when there are four people within the boundary who wish to perform the *pravāraṇā*. Even if...

This is performed in the presence of another person; therefore, it may take place within the open space (prakṛti-sthāna). It may also involve two people, which refers to the distinction between the Saṃgha and the individual.

As for the statement that "the dharma applies to three types," this refers to the mental recitation (cittotpāda), the presence of another person (pratyakṣa), and the formal procedure of the assembly (saṃgha-karma).

Regarding the phrase "a number of people" in the context of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*: the text states that one should demarcate it by saying, "I bind this area as far as the seating places of so many bhikṣus. Hence, it is called "a number of people.

As for the statement that these three minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) are provisionally established due to difficulties, allowing them to perform only a single ritual (*ekadharma*) and not being of long-term duration, Jì explains:
when the three minor boundaries are being demarcated, the wording for each is different; therefore, they can only each perform a single ritual.

They must not be used interchangeably. For example, once a small boundary (*sīmā*) has been established for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one may no longer perform other rites such as the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) within it;
one may only perform a single rite at a time, which must then be dissolved. Therefore, it is said that "only one rite may be performed."

Regarding the fourth point, "The *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) up to the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) all have both accessibility and restriction; they may be understood according to their respective characteristics":

Jing says that for the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, begging for a bowl, the relinquishment of vows, and the robes of a deceased person, if there are no difficulties (*an-āpatti*), one may not remain within the *śīmaṇḍala*; these must be performed within the *mahā-sīmā*. Therefore, it is said they are "restricted.

If there are difficulties, then they are "accessible. However, regarding the acceptance of a day’s extension (*divasa-grahaṇa*) and the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha-vimocana*), one may never [perform them] within [the *śīmaṇḍala*].

Regarding the *śīmaṇḍala* (ordination platform): this refers to "blocking" (*saṃvṛta*). This is a general discussion. If, as previously mentioned, one first enters the *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and subsequently establishes the boundary (*sīmābandha*), it is indefinite according to the number of days accepted by the two boundaries;

the other two cases are definite. Some say that acts such as the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), begging for a bowl (*pātra-yācana*), and the ritual of relinquishing and confessing (*pratyaya-pratideśana*) must be performed within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), which is termed "blocking.
Other matters are common to both boundaries, which is termed "unrestricted" (*asaṃvṛta*). Regarding this point, Master Li says: "Within these..."

There are both cases where [the procedure] applies universally and cases where it is restricted. As it is said: when there is no difficulty and one is permitted to perform the act within the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (the ritual enclosure), this is called "universal" (*tōng*).

When there is no such permission and the act is restricted to the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary), this is called "restricted" (*sè*). Furthermore, it is said: regarding the eight procedures following the begging for a bowl and the confession of transgressions, those that require the original *mahāsīmā* are termed "restricted.

This refers specifically to the restrictions pertaining to the *mahāsīmā*. As for other matters not listed here, the application of the rite extends to both the *śikṣādattaka-maṇḍala* (the training enclosure) and the *mahāsīmā*.

This is called "passage" (*tong*). Thus we know that when one performs [the ritual] within a restricted great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it is called "blocking" (*se*); when one performs it so as to connect two places, it is called "passage. Some say:

just as in the *karmavācanā* for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), there are cases where the rite is performed upon natural ground (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) and cases where it is performed upon consecrated ground (*kṛtrima-bhūmi*);
this refers to the boundaries for food and clothing. This is what is meant by "passage. As for other *karmas*, they require consecrated ground.
Dibing said, "It is 'obstructed' (sè). This interpretation is excellent. What was stated above regarding begging for a bowl and performing a confession (*śamatha*) refers to one specific matter;

it does not mean that one must understand the confession involving the forfeiture of clothing or wealth. Bin said, "In this practice of begging for a bowl and performing a confession, the offender is penalized by being required to use the old [bowl] while holding the new.
His fine item is confiscated and sent to the monastic kitchen, while a single inferior one is retained and passed around among the monks until the very worst is selected to be given to him."

The order to take possession of it has already been revoked and it has been brought into the kitchen. Since there is no kitchen on the site, performing the ritual procedures on the site is not permitted.

Regarding the "Dharma for the Deceased's Robes": this refers to the light belongings of the deceased; as their benefit extends throughout the ten directions, they may not be divided exclusively on the site. As for "receiving the [summer] days":
because the site does not permit the Sangha to reside there, and since residence is not permitted, one must not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) therein. Why?
It is permissible to receive [the precepts] on the upper level. Regarding the dissolution of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha-vimocana*):

since neither the binding nor the dissolution of a boundary is permitted at a distance, how could one dissolve the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) from within the ritual enclosure? As for the binding of the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*), it is established so as to include the robes of the people within the same location;
however, the ritual enclosure is not a place where the Saṃgha resides—how, then, could one include the robes therein? Furthermore, the robe-boundary arises in reference to the Great Boundary.

(If explained, the meaning is the same). Regarding the "pure ground" (*śuddhasthāna*): it was originally intended to prevent [food] from being kept overnight or cooked [on that spot]. Since no monks reside on the threshing floor (*khalasthāna*), what need is there to formally designate it as pure?

Furthermore, the pure ground is established based upon the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). As for receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, it was originally permitted for those who had labored during the summer retreat;

since the threshing floor is not a place where one dwells during the rains retreat, [the rule does not apply]. [Commentary: This brief analysis here does not exhaust the underlying principles. According to the *Lì shū* (Commentary by Lì), there is further...

The formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for dealing with those who are insane, the four-month suspension of the *pātra* (bowl), the eight qualities for not paying respects to a family under training (*śikṣādattaka*), and the demarcation of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) are all restricted to the great boundary itself.

The formal act for the construction of a dwelling is performed at a separate site so that the assembly may collectively take notice; thus, even in the *Cīvaravastu*, it is not permitted [to perform it within the monastery].
Guest monks from other regions come to this place for their allotted portions; therefore, the fixed boundary is established according to the original residence.

Since those who are insane or mentally deranged may or may not attend the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the *karmavācanā* is granted to them. However, the site does not permit the recitation of the *pravāraṇā*;

how then can the procedure for the insane be granted there? As for the four months, it is a trial for non-Buddhists. Once they have followed the community and demonstrated that their faith is complete, they must be granted [ordination].

Regarding the ordination site: since it is not a place where the Saṃgha resides, how can one perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) there? How could one dwell together for the four months [of the rainy season retreat] in such a place?

As for the "upturned bowl" (*pātra-nyubja*): this was established so that the assembly would not go to the site to perform rituals; however, because the assembly did not know [the situation], [this rule was made]. Regarding the "eight qualities":

if a person possessing these eight qualities reports to a household whose bowl has been turned upside down, they inform the layperson to restrain the Saṃgha from going. They dispatch a person to report to that [household], desiring to...

[The author] offers a revised explanation: If [the ritual] is performed in the courtyard, since the monks do not know [of it], they will not cease their visits later on; as for those who do not prostrate, this is because it was performed for the sake of the *saṃgha*.

If it is performed in the courtyard, the community of nuns does not know [of it], fearing that if they were to see these monks later, they might still show them respect. Regarding "families under discipline" (*śikṣādattaka*):...

When performing the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), one must not depart; it is necessary that the assembly be collectively informed. A separate regulation applies within the precincts (*kṣetra*); if the assembly departs, [the rite] will surely cease.
The preceding explanation of the meaning of mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*) is now complete. Below, the meaning of accomplishment and failure (*siddhi-vibhāga*) is clarified.

Regarding the statement that "dharmas do not arise in isolation and must ultimately rely on four conditions": these refer to the aforementioned ten conditions condensed into four—namely, person (*pudgala*), dharma, matter (*vastu*), and boundary (*sīmā*). These four...
The above has clarified what is correct. From here on, what follows clarifies what is incorrect. Regarding "formation and destruction": that which is "is" is formation;

that which is "is not" is called destruction. Although the characteristics of destruction are many, they do not exceed seven types. In the Vinaya, these are categorized according to the *jñapti* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three proclamations).

The seven types of invalidity (*asādhū*) regarding the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) and the mental recitation (*cittotpāda*) have not yet been explained. Now, according to the interpretation established by the author of this *Chao*, there are generally seven forms of invalidity.
Since the mental recitation is already designated as a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*), why should its invalidity alone not be distinguished? It is simply that the Vinaya text is deficient here.
This is precisely what is meant in the Preface: "The text is broken, but the meaning connects it. Now, we shall address this through the three categories of person, dharma, and matter.
It consists of three single [actions], three pairs, and one combination, making seven; this is to distinguish what is improper.

That is to say, when performing these rites in the presence of others, they should originally be performed alone by oneself through mental recitation (*manasikāra*); yet now they are being performed in the presence of others.

This is a case of human error. When one's speech is not clear and the ritual does not accord with the teaching, it is because the Dharma that is to be contemplated must necessarily be spoken aloud so that one may hear it oneself;
now that the recitation is indistinct, this constitutes a ritual performance that does not accord with its teaching.

Regarding each of the matters such as the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti) being contrary to the Dharma: among these six recollections, there are instances of accepting invitations [for meals] and eating in a separate assembly, as well as the possession of robes and alms bowls.

[Deficiency]. Regarding the age and summer retreats at the time of receiving [the precepts]: these pertain to the factual details. Every day one recites the formal declaration (*vācanā*), the facts must be stated truthfully in accordance with the teachings.

Now, however, one makes false declarations—stating the dark fortnight as the bright, or that robes are complete when they are deficient. Because such speech is falsely presented, it is called a "deficiency in the facts."

Regarding the statement that "the number is the same as above, but each has its own distinct characteristic according to the specific matter and the corresponding rule," this refers to the preceding text.

Explaining it in terms of the rules (*dharma*), there are seven types of procedures for the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) and the *manasikāra* (mental recollection): namely, the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat), the *viśuddhi* (purification of impurities), the acceptance of medicine, and the acceptance of the seven-day [period].
Because one receives the three robes and performs the ritual of relinquishing and receiving the alms bowl and so forth, it is said that "the number is the same as above.
As these matters arise, there are corresponding dharmas; thus it is said that "each dharma corresponding to a matter has its own distinct characteristic."

"Regarding 'not relying on another': there are persons within the *dhātu* (monastic community) who perform [the ritual] without relying on a person present before them; therefore, it is called a 'non-person' (*pudgala*).

Another interpretation states that during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one does not rely on a master of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) [to perform the retreat]. Jì explains: this means performing it without facing a person, and does not refer to relying on a fifth Vinaya master.
Regarding 'the time is not the summer limit and there are difficulties due to circumstances': this refers to the four months."

The sixteenth day is the beginning of the summer season; yet now, on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, one enters the *anvaya* (rainy-season retreat). Therefore, it is called "inappropriate. Regarding the term "difficulties," these refer to lions, tigers, and wolves.

As for the statement that "within the boundary, a separate assembly commits the six classes of offenses," this clarifies that the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is fundamentally a communal dharma (*saṃghadharma*).

Because there were no people present, the practice of mental recitation (*manasikāra*) was permitted as an exception. Now, since there are people within the boundary, to perform mental recitation alone is therefore improper.

This would result in the fault of violating human propriety. Furthermore, the purpose for which the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of the Precepts) was originally established was to purify those who are pure; now, having committed offenses against the six classes of transgressions (*ṣaḍ-varga*), one should not recite the precepts.

Indeed, the Vinaya texts state: "One who has committed an offense is unfit to hear [the recitation]; one who has committed an offense is unfit to recite. This is clearly established by the fact that the threefold proclamation is not made.

Regarding the text for the mental recitation (*manasikāra-poṣadha*), it says: "I, bhikṣu so-and-so, am pure," yet this must still be proclaimed three times. If it were now proclaimed only once, it would be incorrect.

Regarding the point that "this practice is improper" because the requisites are incomplete: this means that one must first sweep and clean, then prepare flowers, counting-sticks (*śalākā*), scented water, and so forth, and ring the bell to await guests.
Only if no one arrives should one direct the mind toward the task. Since we do not follow this procedure now, it is called "improper in terms of the matter.

Regarding the statement that "the time is not the True Dharma," [the Master] established that performing the rite at dawn is called "not the True Dharma," because it does not wait for [the arrival of others].

Regarding the "guest bhikṣu," it is further explained as referring to the improper time of the day: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days are called "time," while any other time than these is "improper."

Regarding the statement, "There is one who censures; this censure belongs to a person, not to the dharma": The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) asks: "If the censure does not cease the non-dharma, how does this differ from the censure of a person who has already been censured?

The answer is: Censure is clarified in terms of the person (*pudgala*), because their intentions (*citta*) differ; thus, it constitutes a *bhedasamgha* (a schismatic assembly). Censure is not ceased in terms of the dharma (*dharma*);

since the differences and similarities are carefully maintained during its performance, it falls under the category of non-dharma within the ritual procedure. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that when a person of virtue (*guṇin*) utters words, their meaning...

One must abide [in accordance with the Dharma]. To abide is to be distinct [from the transgression]. Regarding "the Dharma cannot be negated" (meaning that if one abides immediately upon hearing the reprimand, it is merely a case of a separate assembly;

thus it is called "distinct," referring only to the person and not the Dharma, hence "the Dharma cannot be negated"): if one does not abide, it contradicts the Dharma, and both person and Dharma are negated (meaning that the person who previously reprimanded was not authorized to do so—this belongs to the negation of the person;

now, having heard the reprimand yet not ceasing—is also a negation of the Dharma; therefore, it is said that both person and Dharma are negated). The Commentary further states: "The one who is authorized to reprimand and the one who reprimands are those capable of destroying the Dharma."
This refers to being apart from the assembly. Upon hearing a rebuke, one should stop; yet even stopping is not [necessarily] correct, for it depends on whether the person is at fault.

If one does not stop, then the person is right and the dharma is wrong. However, since the Dharma is propagated through persons, if there is a rebuke, one must stay. To say, "I am leaving because I heard a rebuke," and then leave, is to follow the person and abandon the Dharma;
to stay is to follow the Dharma and abandon the person. This is spoken out of an inability to endure [the situation], for the meaning is not established independently; therefore, this is the Dharma.

This is a failure. Therefore, Lì said: "To discuss 'reproving' (āha) in general, it contains two meanings: first, reproving because of a divergence in sentiment, whereby the reproving constitutes a separate assembly;

second, reproving because of a commonality in sentiment, whereby the reproving constitutes a case where the reproving does not cease (the former meaning refers to the person being wrong, while the latter refers to the dharma being wrong). It is further stated:"
Regarding those who criticize through *karma* (formal acts): whether one criticizes oneself or speaks to a bystander, this also constitutes criticism. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu within the same boundary, or even one who causes his neighbor to hear it, this constitutes criticism.

According to this text, although one may not criticize directly in the presence of the person performing the formal act, merely discussing with a neighbor whether [the act] is valid or not also falls within the limit of criticism; that is, it constitutes an offense.
These all refer to the time when one is formally reciting the *karmavācanā*. Regarding the five primary colors: blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
As for "dyed with superior [dyes]," this refers to true vermilion and true purple. Regarding "impure materials," these are those obtained through the five types of improper trade and commerce.
Thus, it is known that if one makes robes from wealth acquired through trade and an improper livelihood, the ritual addition of the *dharmas* (the formal consecration) will not be valid.

Regarding the five-member *pañcavargīya* dharma procedure where four persons hold the formal act and the fifth person receives the *chanda* (consent): this refers to five persons within the boundary (*sīmā*). All must assemble;
one person expresses the *chanda*, while the remaining four perform the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, it is said that [if fewer than five are present] the number of persons is deficient. "Mutually recounting [faults]" means knowing that another has committed an offense but not bringing it forward. "Speech is not clear" refers to the actual...
Regarding the time for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination): it means that the words spoken were not clear. Regarding "the time is not the end of summer," etc.:

this refers to the Buddha’s instruction that one should perform the *pravāraṇā* after the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is completed; to perform it now while the summer has not yet ended is improper. As for the statement "the assembly lacks the necessary conditions": [it refers to the following].

This means that if the Saṃgha encounters difficult circumstances, an extension of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is permitted; however, to perform it now when no such difficulty exists constitutes an error regarding the matter (*vastu*).

As for "the assembly within the boundary being separate and the individuals not being pure," this clarifies the confession of a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). One must face those of pure precepts;

because one has violated the precepts, one cannot receive the absolution of offenses from others—this is called an error regarding the person (*pudgala*). "Those whose gravity [of offense] is equal according to the Dharma" refers to those who are appropriate to the measure.
Regarding robes: one should perform a *pāyattika* (提) confession; one must not measure a robe, for which a *duṣkṛta* (吉) confession is required.

To now perform a *pāyattika* confession for all of these is called "the method of treating the heavy and light as identical. Another interpretation holds that the fundamental *pāyattika* is heavy, while the concealment (*chādana*) of it is light.

Alternatively, the fundamental act and its concealment are heavy, while that which arises from them is light. Furthermore, the Sūtra states that a silent lie (*mṛṣāvāda*) is heavy, while that which arises from it is light. Now...

Thus, they perform the confession simultaneously, without enumerating names or characteristics, but directly merging [the offenses] into a single repentance; hence it is said that "heavy and light offenses follow the same method" and "observance and violation are not distinguished.

Zhi Liang clarifies: that which has already undergone *shuōjìng* (purification by declaration) is observance (*chí*) and not violation (*fàn*), whereas that which has not yet undergone *shuōjìng* is violation and not observance.
Since these are now confused and both are to be entirely relinquished, it is said they are "not distinguished. Alternatively, this may refer to relinquishing based on the violation itself.
[This refers to] robes. To say one has committed an offense when they have not yet worn them, while claiming it is an offense for wearing them, is as follows:

if the *sūtra* states that one commits an offense by remaining silent during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), yet one falsely claims to have committed an offense even though the recitation has not yet occurred—that is this case. It is also like the rule regarding the separation from the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*);

one should list each item as it is separated. Now, simply stating "one has separated from the three robes" is the correct way. As for the phrase "to speak falsely," it means to state things with deceptive words.

This means that while robes are not subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), to now say they are subject to forfeiture is a false statement. Regarding the phrase "the property is not fit for forfeiture," Master Li states that it should belong to the *dharmas* (the Sangha).
However, from the perspective of the substance of the property itself, it is pure and thus not fit for forfeiture; therefore, this is termed a "fault of the matter" (*vastu-doṣa*).
As the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* says: "When robe-material is scattered and its status as defiled or pure has not yet been distinguished, it is generally brought into forfeiture."

This matter is improper. Furthermore, it is like trading two types of precious goods; they should simply be returned to their owners. Now, to relinquish them to the Saṃgha is called an "improper relinquishment.

Regarding the text that requests the silk robe, it merely requires that it be cut and destroyed; it does not permit its relinquishment to another person. To now bring it forward for relinquishment is why it is termed "improper.
As for the phrase "failing to disclose transgressions," this refers to the two faults of *sthūlātyaya* and *pāyattika*, which have not been disclosed.

To the question of "how much," it is said that a *dhātu* (boundary) is not a constructed dharma; this means that while one is in a natural state, one may abruptly perform a *karmavācanā*. Regarding "the gathering of robes and utensils not occurring":

if one commits the offense of possessing extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), yet only discards seven or eight, they are therefore said to be "not gathered. As for "the class of those who falsely and arbitrarily entrust [robes] to others":

this refers to saying, "I have committed the offense of possessing extra robes; I have mentally relinquished them to such-and-such a bhikṣu," while the mental attachment is fundamentally never severed.

Lizhen said: "At the time of relinquishing [the robes] for confession, if one's clothing and possessions are not yet exhausted, and one subsequently encounters an item previously forgotten, one should say:
'I intended to give this to others; since I originally had no intention [to keep it], let this relinquished robe return to defile the object that was forgotten.'"

Regarding the statement that "among the seven types of white [robes], one must assemble at the boundary markers (*sīmā*) even if they do not reach the natural limits (*prakṛti-sīmā*)," Jing said: "Markers" refers to the intended boundaries for establishing a formal demarcation;
"natural limits" refers to the actual geographical extent of the territory. This means that the markers may be wide while the natural limits are narrow, and thus one must assemble at the markers.

If one assembles naturally [at the limits] without having reached the markers, one commits the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). This statement is made on the basis of a case where the markers are wide and the natural limits are narrow; if the markers are narrow...

"Exhaustive inclusion" (*jìnbiāo*) means to include everything. "Surrounding the entire monastery" means taking the monastery itself as the boundary marker. This "boundary" refers to the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*).

According to the ancient masters, it would suffice to have exhaustive inclusion; why then is exhaustive marking necessary? Because before the formal rite (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, there is no offense for being apart from the assembly (*pṛthag-varga-doṣa*).

The author of the *Śāstra* (the *Chao*), acting out of urgency, therefore established the requirement for exhaustive marking. According to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, all within a radius of three *yojanas* must assemble.

The meaning can be understood. [I] privately remark: The *Liaolun* (Treatise on Understanding) is distinct; the author of the *Chao* (Commentary) has erroneously applied it here. This shall be refuted extensively below.

Regarding "one who is subject to censure" (*āpattipratideśaka*), this excludes others who are being disciplined, such as those undergoing the seven types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*), who are termed "those not subject to censure.

*Li* says: "In this context, 'censure' refers to censure because the sentiments are discordant; such censure constitutes a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*). As for the subsequent text stating that 'the censure does not cease,' it refers to the sentiments..."

They were censured for being identical [to the offense]. Because the officiant did not say, "I am [the one committing this]," and the censure did not stop upon hearing it, it fell under the category of a non-offense regarding the dharma;

this is termed "non-offense due to censure not stopping. Regarding the phrase "the ritual procedure was obscure and relied upon [others], and furthermore the censure did not stop," etc., this establishes the clarification:

since the proclamation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) was not clear, it caused the time of performing the ritual to lack a basis for reference, such that the boundaries could not be known, as if in the dark.

This is a metaphorical representation. Furthermore, it is said: "Not knowing the location of the marker, one falsely points to mountains and valleys, and indiscriminately assigns it to forests and trees.

Regarding the fact that the three categories—the marker (*lakṣaṇa*), the signified (*lakṣya*), and the essence (*svabhāva*)—are confused into a single disorder, [the master] Li establishes: "Walls, trees, rocks, and so forth are the markers;
these are what is proclaimed as the signs (*lakṣaṇa*). If one proclaims from within, the marker is outside the sign; if from without..."

The "proclamation" (*cāng*) is marked within the boundary marks (*xiàng*). Regarding the "substance" (*tǐ*), it refers to the ground where the ritual is performed. The *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "That which the proclaimer relies upon is called the 'mark' (*biāo*);

that which is recorded in the karmavācanā is called the 'boundary mark' (*xiàng*); the ground where the ritual action is performed is called the 'substance' (*tǐ*). Nowadays, these three types are not understood, and their names are confused.
As for "not knowing the distinction between this and that," when one looks from the mark toward the boundary mark, the mark is [the point of reference].
This characteristic is that; it is designated by means of that characteristic. That characteristic is this; this designation is that.

Regarding the phrase "the two boundaries intersect," this refers to the case where the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the Precept Platform (*sīmaṇḍala*) overlap, such that there is no naturally vacant space (*ākāśa*) between them to serve as a demarcation.
Therefore it is said. It may also be done by summarizing two separate *pṛthak-vāsa* (separate dwellings), which is permissible. Regarding "repeatedly binding in an alternating manner":
this refers to a case where, after the preceding person has already performed the binding, the succeeding person, unaware of this, performs another binding on top of it;

thus, these repeated bindings are performed alternately before and after, hence they are called "alternating. As for "distant chanting and remote binding do not achieve [the result]," etc., this clarifies that there is...

If a person has already completed the demarcation of the boundary site (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) and then attempts to establish a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) from within it at a distance, this is not valid. Furthermore,
if a person first establishes three types of markers and then sits within the great boundary to first establish the boundary site from a distance,
this is also contrary to the Dharma and is not valid.
Regarding the phrase "although there are five hundred people," Jing says: This is a concessive statement; it merely mentions five hundred as an illustration.
As for the statement that within each person there are more than fifty dharmas, Li Ming explains that this is as clarified in the text concerning the counting of the members.

When all sections are combined and the individuals are distinguished, there should be sixty-three people in total. The fact that it now says "more than fifty" means that there are thirteen [additional] people; this is the meaning.

[This is] established. My own view is as follows: In the text concerning those who do not count [toward the quorum], four types of monks who perform penance for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are listed—namely, those practicing *parivāsa*, those undergoing *mūlāpakarṣa*, those undergoing the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*), and those undergoing the rehabilitation from guilt (*āvarhaṇa*).
Furthermore, the three types mentioned in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* are also considered to not count toward the quorum; thus, there are sixty-three such cases.

This constitutes the general principle regarding those who do not count. However, if we consider the matter of receiving the precepts, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) allows for exceptions.

Regarding the disciplinary procedures for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: one should undergo formal ordination from another; this serves as a favorable condition for generating wholesome roots and provides relief for prior obligations.
Since this text clearly states that ordination excludes the seven [categories], there are consequently more than fifty types [of offenses]. (This interpretation is excellent).

As for the eightfold regulations concerning the advance and cessation of the preparatory stage (*pūrvakarma*), it is established that they are explicitly clarified within the section on ordination (*upasaṃpadā-vastu*). While there are eight preliminary gates listed in the table of contents, when it comes to the actual time of ordination, it constitutes the ninth.

Section on the Gate. The verse says: "Please set aside the appointment to go and summon; request the formal motion (*karmavācanā*) for inspection. Upon reaching the actual conferral of the precepts, one shall see it;
here we clarify that within the eight gates, although there is a sequence of preparatory arrangements, at the time of the actual conferral, one simply recites the formal motion.

Therefore, it is said that 'adhering to the text leaves nothing to chance. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that both the eight types of preparatory arrangements and the actual conferral itself are not known by those who do not understand the Dharma."

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the dharmas are self-established and do not intermingle or circulate: it is established that *ming* (the trigram for fire) and *shu* (the trigram for earth) form three, while *li* (the trigram for fire) divides into eight.

All of these are based on the number of persons within the boundaries [of the ritual space] to determine which dharma may be administered; according to the number of persons, each is mutually established and does not intermingle.

It is "universal" (*sāmānya*). It is further said: for example, the *jñapti-caturtha* (fourth motion) rite does not include other rites such as mental recollection (*cetanā*) or face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) procedures;

likewise, the mere mental recollection rite does not universally include other face-to-face or mental recollection rites. Furthermore, how could that which is originally a face-to-face rite be treated as a rite for the entire community (*saṃgha*)?
Originally there were only three [categories]; they are divided into eight aspects based on their specific conditions (*pratyaya*). This is the distinction.

Regarding the phrase "the various *saṃgha*-dharmas are many, yet some apply universally": this means that if one performs them solely through mental recollection (*manasikāra*) or solely by facing another person (*pratyekamukha*), there is no separate *saṃgha*.

As for the remaining *saṃgha*-dharmas performed by facing another or those performed through mental recollection, if there are people within the boundary (*sīmā*), they constitute a separate *saṃgha*;

if there are no people within the boundary, there is no separate *saṃgha*. Because their presence or absence is not fixed, it is said that "some apply universally. The word "or" (*vā*) is a term indicating uncertainty.

This is also the case. To clarify the aforementioned eight dharmas: when a *sīmā* (boundary) is devoid of persons, these eight are established through separation. If there were persons within the *sīmā*, they would simply be subsumed under the three dharmas.
If there were persons within the *sīmā* and it were further divided into eight, there would be the fault of constituting a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*). Therefore, it is so stated.

The preceding numerous sections have concluded the general explanation of the second gate, the process of formation and destruction (*saṃvarta-vivarta*). From this point onward, the main text of the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) will be explained.
Regarding the statement, "To see even a single character added or omitted and to deem it illegal," the *Lilong* clarifies that the intent of the *Chao* is as follows:
"If I do not fully clarify what is permissible and what is obstructed, I fear others might see a single character added or omitted and doubt its legitimacy."
The Dharma. However, success or failure truly depends on a single word; yet one must not be as inflexible as a fixed zither string, but must know the proper context.

Regarding the formal ritual (karmavācanā) itself, nothing may be added or subtracted. As for the circumstances and matters recorded in the proclamation, there is no fault in increasing or decreasing them.

To say that one "must not be like a parrot" refers to borrowing from external matters. For example, when a heavenly thunderclap occurs, a hundred birds are startled at once, and ten thousand city walls all [tremble].

"Gu! Thus it is said, "Echoing like thunder. Those who employ this term today wish to clarify that when one observes another adding or subtracting even a single character, one must know the specific context;
one must not merely echo others, meaning that one must not arbitrarily add or subtract anything at all.
Regarding the phrase "never having altered the presence or absence [of elements]": take, for instance, the text of the *jñapti-karman* for receiving the seven-day leave.
If there is a matter concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, and one has received the seven-day leave, should a circumstance arise requiring nursing care, one must immediately alter the text.

This involves removing the "absence" of matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha from the text and adding the "presence" of the matter of nursing care. Because people do not understand how to make such modifications, it is said that they have "never" done so. Thus it is stated.

"Retuning" (*zhang*) refers to a situation such as when the strings of a lute are too tight; they must be retuned again. This term is used here by way of metaphor. As the *Book of Documents* says, "Rarely are [strings] retuned," which is precisely the point.
