"Bhikṣu" refers to the words used when calling someone forward. Regarding the phrase "as Master You says" cited below, this refers to Master Li.
From "as Master You says" down to "therefore it is necessary to collect [these points]," all are the words of ancient masters. From "if one follows the principle, it is not so" onwards...

This is the language of the commentator [Daoxuan]. *Ce* states: "The boundary markers are broad while the territory is narrow; Master Yuan also required that the collection be made according to the full extent of the markers.

Master Li, however, based it on the full extent of the territory. Regarding the previous statement, "If one has already left the boundary, one performs the ritual act to bind it," this refers to cases within a three-yojana radius where there are monks who are summoned to come;
if they do not come, one must leave the boundary and only then perform the ritual. (Check the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*).
The text says: There was a certain residence where the monks had already completed both the earlier and later retreats (*pūrvavāsa* and *paścimavāsa*).

When the days [of the retreat] had passed and a difficult situation arose—whether it be the danger of bandits, the danger of kings, the threat to life, the violation of precepts, or an abundance of water with many insects such that even after straining it one could not obtain pure water—and they wished to go to another monastery to avoid these various dangers, they may go within three *yojanas*. If there is... [one... there.
"O Bhikṣus, whether they are summoned to come, or have departed beyond the boundary, one performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to establish the boundary.

The meaning of this passage in the *Cīvara-vastu* is distinct; it refers specifically to avoiding danger. Upon reaching that monastery, one summons the people within that monastery to establish the boundary together.

That monastery is three *yojanas* away from the original site of danger; how could this possibly mean assembling the Saṃgha within a radius of three *yojanas*? It simply means going to that other place.
Within the vihāra, one calls for them to assemble. If they are unwilling to assemble, once they have been made to depart, one should then proceed to demarcate a boundary of three yojanas.
"There being no authoritative teaching to rely upon" means that it is not mentioned in the Vinaya; this is what is meant by "no authoritative teaching to rely upon.
This refutes the tenets of the ancient masters. Your statement that "one does not take the marker as the assembly point because there is no authoritative teaching to rely upon" refers to this.

If there is a village within the boundary markers, even though it is naturally included and one does not wish to include the village, or even if the bhikṣus within the village do not need to assemble outside, Ji says:
"This clarifies the case of establishing a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) at a forest hermitage (araṇya). Since the boundary is vast and expansive, there may be a settlement in its midst;
thus, it is called a 'village. Now, because one does not wish to include this village, one proclaims the village and excludes it. Regarding this:
Once the boundaries of the village monastery are fully established, it can be designated as a "clustered settlement" (*grāma*) and is thus distinct from the boundary of an *araṇya*.
Why, then, would one need to assemble outside? The original intention was simply not to include the village; therefore, the internal boundary was proclaimed and excluded.

It was not because monks were present within that it had to be proclaimed. Had it not been proclaimed as "outside," there would have been no fault of being a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), for [the village] is a settlement.
This is because the *sīmā* (boundary) and the *araṇya-sīmā* (wilderness boundary) are distinct. Furthermore, regarding the statement that monks within a village need not assemble outside, Jing says:

"Because the village and its monastery precincts (*sīmā*) surround one another, they do not assemble within the village; thus, they do not commit the offense of forming a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Regarding those who dwell separately within an enclosure, Li says: "For example, if there are many separate residences within a single settlement, each establishes its own boundary. Now, suppose there is a person..."

Furthermore, it is more appropriate to completely delimit a large cluster of settlements as a single boundary (*sīmā*). One should then each proclaim the internal markers (*antarlakṣaṇa*), excluding all minor boundaries, and subsequently proclaim the external markers to establish it.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a bowl filled with grain. This may be sought in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The explanation of the meaning of assembling the Saṃgha is hereby concluded.

Regarding the two cases where one may not receive *chanda* (consent), there are three meanings: First, "The boundary (*sīmā*) is the foundation of the assembly" means that some say this refers to subsequent legal acts (*dharmas*).
Other legal acts are the branches of the assembly and all arise based on the subsequent [boundary]; therefore, the granting of *chanda* is permitted [in those cases].

Second, "Because the natural ground is weak, it cannot sustain the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)" means that it is established and clarified that *chanda* should originally accompany the ritual; however, because the natural ground is weak...

It is weak; however, if one can uphold the legal procedure (*dharma*) of two or three people, it will certainly not prevail over the formal act (*karmavācanā*). Why then labor to announce one's consent (*chanda*)?

If it were the legal procedure of separate individuals, it likewise would not prevail over the formal act. Therefore, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) states: "Because of where the consent resides..."

If one must attend to monastic affairs, one’s strength will naturally become depleted and one will be unable to sustain it. Some say that the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) was originally opened [for such purposes];

however, the *chanda* (consent) is a secondary condition that necessarily arises in dependence upon the Sangha. Because the boundary is a formal ritual act (*dharmakarma*) and is thus powerful, it subsumes the *chanda*.

Third, regarding the instruction to know the boundaries up to the protection of robes and so forth: if the condition of *chanda* were opened, one would ultimately not be thoroughly proficient [in the ritual]. Thus, the *Karmasūtra-ṭīkā* states: [text follows]
It is said: "The boundaries must be delimited. If one has established the *kṣānti* (consent) for opening [the boundary], one must never fail to request full authorization;

therefore, they must be gathered together. Lì says: "There are three meanings for explaining 'no *kṣānti* when establishing a boundary. The first is identical to the *Jiaoding* and can be understood. The second states:

'Because the natural ground is weak and cannot sustain the *karmavācanā*, etc. This means that since no boundary has yet been established, within the natural state, the ritual procedure (*dharmakriyā*) is weak and thus does not encompass [the area]."

Regarding the *chanda* (consent): other *karmas* (formal acts) are performed based upon the boundary (*sīmā*), and because they are mandatory, they include the requirement for consent. Thirdly, it serves to make known the limits of the boundary so as not to obstruct the affairs of the Saṃgha;

furthermore, it eliminates the difficulties of violating the summer retreat or being separated from one's robes. The *Cai* (策) states: "However, these three points are merely matters of human sentiment.

Since one knows that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) does not permit the granting of consent, why bother to investigate further? If one seeks its underlying reason, it is according to [the precedent of] others..."

Section. Regarding the *sīmā* (boundary), there are also rules concerning desire; thus, they differ according to circumstances and cannot be harmonized. As for "protecting the summer retreat" (*varṣā-rakṣā*), it means dwelling in *anvaya* (residence) within a boundary; one must recognize its limits.
As for "separate assemblies" (*pṛthag-jana*), this refers not only to separate assemblies regarding the Dharma, but also to separate assemblies regarding food;

both are defined by the existence of a distinction within the boundary, while outside the boundary, there is no offense. As for "protecting food," this refers to the food belonging to the permanently resident Sangha. It does not...

If one has stepped outside the boundary and suddenly finds that the *kṣetra* (monastic precinct) is large while the *sīmā* (boundary) is small, and one returns the food to the room, would this not constitute an offense of theft?

This interpretation is unreasonable, as it has already been refuted by the previous interlocutor (*pūrvapakṣin*). This is actually a case of establishing a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) based on the boundary. As for "protecting the robe," it refers to establishing a robe-holding boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) based on the [monastic] precinct.
Thus far, the meaning of the first section, the "Gate of Establishing Conditions" (*pratyayapratiṣṭhāpanadvāra*), has been explained.

Regarding the second point, "the noble method of formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*) and so forth," Bin said: "The person who proclaims the boundaries (*sīmā*) may not perform the *karma*, and the person performing the *karma* may not proclaim the boundaries.

This is because when the ritual is being conducted, the proclaimer of the boundaries is formally cited, saying: 'The bhikṣu of this residence shall proclaim the characteristics of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) for the Saṃgha.
How could one possibly cite oneself? Furthermore, the Vinaya texts do not prescribe a formal rule for the method of proclaiming the boundaries."
Three times. This is merely for the sake of current practice. Master Sù (Sōng) performed it only once.

Furthermore, as for the instruction to have someone pierce through a wall while chanting, there is no scriptural authority for this in any of the Nikāyas; one must understand that this is an unauthorized innovation.

Jì stated: "I personally asked the Nanshan Ācārya, who said: 'The three repetitions are not required. It is only because one fears the chanter may be unclear that three repetitions are mandated. Based on this...
In the Vinaya, it is sufficient to perform [the ritual] only once. Furthermore, when chanting the boundaries (*sīmā*), one must not utter the names [of individuals].

Moreover, at the time of performing the *karmavācanā* to establish the boundary, one likewise must not recite or chant the names of those who mark the boundaries; this indicates that there is no separate purpose for them.

If one were to utter their names, there would be fear that people might harbor doubts, thinking the boundary was established specifically for that individual alone. However, according to the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the ritual is performed by uttering names, whereas the *Caturvargika-vinaya*...

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the names [of those granting consent] are not all recited. Lü says: The text regarding the addition of the ritual formula states, “Those who dwell in the same residence and perform the same *poṣadha* (confession of offenses) shall, when asked, announce the matter and grant their consent (*chanda*).
For other matters, this would not be valid. Now, since this text mentions the *poṣadha*, it is analogous to announcing a specific matter;

thus, one should specifically obtain the *poṣadha*. The intent of this question is as follows: just as with the announcement of consent, if one says, “I grant my consent for that specific matter,” then [it is not valid].

It is used to apply to other matters; that is to say, it refers to the specific matter undertaken by the Saṃgha. Now, since this boundary-establishment (sīmā-bandha) is called "reciting the precepts together" (*ekato poṣadha*), it is likewise a boundary established by reference to a specific matter.
Should it not follow that one may only perform the recitation of the precepts here, and that it does not extend to the performance of other legal acts (*karmas*)?

Answer: This difference in sequence causes there to be success and failure. That is to say, when speaking of designating an object (*vastu*), the designation of the dharma comes first and the performance of the *karmavācanā* comes later;

therefore, it does not succeed. Now, in the case of designating an object to establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*), one first states, "Within these four boundaries, I establish a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*)," and only afterwards does one designate the object, saying, "For the sake of a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*. Although this is so now...
This is a clarification. However, since the Buddha established these rules at different times, how can they be reconciled? [The questioner] asks:

"In the context of establishing the *sīmā* (boundary), why is it not stated that they share 'the same recitation of the precepts' (*ekapoṣadha*)? The answer is: The *sīmā* was originally established as an exception for cases where the assembly is too large to gather together;

thus, it was separately opened up. The recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), however, is a universal regulation based fundamentally upon a residential site (*āvāsa*). Since a *sīmā* is not a residential site, it is therefore not said that they are "the same."

Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*): it is asked whether these two dharmas require the assembly of monks at a *sīmā* (boundary), whereas other dharmas do not.

The answer is: these two are not included among the dharmas that bind the entire Saṃgha; rather, they are intended for those whose conduct is pure. Therefore, the regulations are established so that all within and outside the boundary may participate equally.

As for the *karmavācanā* and other such dharmas, they apply to many different circumstances and are not restricted by time; they frequently involve separate duties, and thus if [the assembly] were to be opened...
If they assemble together only to disperse again, it merely serves as a preliminary opening but ultimately yields no subsequent benefit.
Therefore, when performing the ritual, if there are persons from different boundaries present, they shall not assemble in both places.

From this point onward, the meaning of the *sīmā* (ordination precinct) is correctly elucidated. Regarding the instruction that one must exercise meticulous care for the matter to be successfully accomplished:
when one wishes to establish a *sīmā* or a *mahāsīmā*, it is essential to erect three layers of boundary markers (*liṅga*).

If these are neglected or omitted, the performance of the ritual within will not be valid, resulting in the failure to receive the precepts. Therefore, the preceding text states: "It is simply because the three characteristics are difficult to clarify."

Fearing that the Dharma might not be thoroughly practiced, I have briefly cited diagrams for illustration. However, the purpose of chanting the ritual procedures according to these diagrams is to clarify the confusion of those with miscellaneous learning;
this is precisely their meaning. As for the term "subtle mind," it distinguishes it from the coarse mind. "Accomplishing matters" means that all affairs are in accordance with the Dharma.
From this point onward, the text formally cites the diagrams to instruct the assembly.

Regarding the note beneath the diagram stating, "and so forth for other directions, following this model," this means that while the north and south have been cited as examples, the east, west, and the four intermediate directions must likewise follow this model.

Regarding the note stating, "once the ritual of demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*) has been performed, one should mark the distances and so forth according to their actual characteristics," this means that once the boundary has been established, there are specific procedures for each case.

Regarding the ritual matters: they should be assembled according to the signs indicated by the ritual procedures; it is not necessary to rely on the natural cardinal directions. As for the distance between the five signs:
this refers to cases where villages cannot be distinguished, which I shall now cite as examples; there are other cases where villages can be distinguished.
The five types of characteristics for forest hermitages—whether with obstacles or without—and for traveling on roads or within water-boundaries, follow this same principle.
If one completes two dharmas such that they do not interfere with both locations, this refers to the delimitation of a *sīmā* (precept field) and a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary).
The two types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) are concluded. Subsequently, where there are monks in both locations, they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the statement that "if one clarifies the external boundaries, one must chant them outside the courtyard," this means that since the boundary markers (*sīmā-sthāpana*) have already been posted against the wall, when now chanting the external boundaries of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), one must necessarily chant from outside the wall.
If one were to chant from within, it would conflict with the interior of the great boundary.

They coincide; therefore, it is not permitted. Furthermore, regarding the prohibition against entering a large courtyard wall to announce [the boundary], this is because its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be seen.
Zhi Liang states: "It is like an earthen wall, perhaps five or six feet wide; one announces that the center beneath the wall constitutes the characteristic.
Therefore, it is said that it is 'not seen'. Jie agrees with this explanation.
If one does not rely on this explanation for seating, it shall likewise be deemed invalid in other places;
that is to say, if one does not understand this diagram, it shall also be deemed invalid to apply it by analogy in other distinct locations.
Regarding the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that "one should first demarcate the boundary for the precepts" (*śīlā-maṇḍala*), the *Shoushu* (Commentary by Shou) states:

This refers to the procedure in that Vinaya where one first demarcates the area outside the boundary, and subsequently, due to the threat of bandits, returns to the monastery grounds to demarcate it; thus, one must first demarcate the boundary for the precepts.
This refers to the binding of a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). If a great boundary already exists, one may first relinquish it, and after the site has been demarcated, bind another great boundary.

According to the intent of this text, it accords with what is maintained in the *Commentary* (*Shō*); however, it differs from the meaning of the question-and-answer section within that same *Commentary*.
Regarding these five sections of the text: [the *Vinayamātṛkā*] states that after causing the abandonment of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one should then establish the precinct (*sīman*).

The *Chao* (Excerpts) immediately says, "Having abandoned it, one should establish it again," which refers to abandoning the precinct and then establishing it again. Is this not an error? Li says: "One should first establish the great boundary."
The boundary of the *sīmā* (field) is established later because the field is to be situated within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
However, this principle should also be understood as generally applicable, since when establishing the great boundary, one still leaves space for the *sīmā* and the open ground.

That the present *Chao* (Commentary) does not permit this is because, although there is no explicit text in our own school, both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mātṛkā* state that one first establishes the field and subsequently establishes the great boundary; we must now follow that precedent. (*Vinayamātṛkā*)
Regarding the statement that the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* explains it in the same way, Tanyao says:

"In the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, one should first demarcate the food zone (*bhojana-sīmā*), next demarcate the boundary for the ritual site (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), then demarcate the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and finally demarcate the robe-holding zone (*cīvara-dhāraṇa-sīmā*).
When one wishes to dissolve them, one first dissolves the robe-holding zone, next dissolves the great boundary, then dissolves the ritual site boundary, and finally dissolves the food zone."
Even now, there are those who first establish the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). Jì states that this refers to Master Lì; it is also a tradition inherited from the ancients.

The ancients relied on the sequence of the Vinaya texts, which state: "Because the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept platform) is established within the *mahā-sīmā*, one first establishes the *mahā-sīmā* at a time prior to when the *śīla-maṇḍala* was permitted in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, there were specific circumstances under which the establishment [of the *śīla-maṇḍala*] was permitted.

Regarding the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field): the textual passage concerning the *śīmaṇḍala* appears later [in the Vinaya]. Ancient commentators have stated that the field is situated after the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), yet they failed to investigate the underlying meaning.

Although the *nidāna* (origin story) instructs that the field be established within the *mahā-sīmā*, this is because the subsequent formal act (*karmavācanā*) of establishing the great boundary encircles the field;
thus, the field resides within the great boundary. If one adheres strictly to the *nidāna*, it is like the precept against drinking alcohol.
Sagata was sleeping drunk on the road and was rebuked by the laity; this served as the causal basis [for the rule].

It may also be that one drinks within one's own room, in which case it should not constitute a *thullaccaya* offense. Furthermore, just as Sūdena took his former wife as the causal basis, how could one discuss "new" or "old" when the matter arises in the present?
Moreover, regarding the ancient practice of observing the days, one must first observe the seven-day period, followed by the half-month, and finally the month.
This also follows the sequence of the Vinaya texts. In the present time, one accepts [the site] as soon as the conditions arise; how, then, can this sequence be discussed? The Guest said:

"The meaning of the Commentary is that one should first establish the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) and only afterwards establish the enclosure (sīma-koṭṭaka). This means that after having made the threefold markers..."
First, the external boundaries of the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*) are announced; next, the internal boundaries are announced, namely the reserved area and the open space, etc.

Only after the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has bound the great precinct may one gather within the field to bind the field itself. This does not mean that once the great precinct has been fully bound, one subsequently binds the field upon it.

However, regarding those who say that because the subsequent rite cannot be accomplished, it must be dissolved: this is clarified by establishing the subsequent rite. That is to say, there are persons who receive [ordination] therein.

If one does not repent their transgressions through the precepts, then they merely rely on chance. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "To encounter blessings without due merit; hence it is so called.
Some say that "jiǎo" (僥) means "to encounter," and "xìng" (倖) means "to celebrate.

Master Ying says: "Jiǎoxìng" refers to obtaining something that is not one's rightful due. The *Xiǎopǐ* (Small Lexicon) says: "Obtaining something not one's due is called 'xìng'. This is intended to clarify...
First, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is established; afterwards, the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) is established. Within this [latter], receiving the precepts is not permitted.

However, if one does not know that the great boundary was established first and the platform afterwards, the situation is the same as before the Buddha had promulgated the regulations; thus, the attainment of the precepts is permitted.
It is because there is this path of ignorance that the attainment of the precepts is opened up; hence it is so said.

Regarding the statement that "having chanted the three marks in total, one performs two types of *karmavācanā*," this refers to the practice of certain masters who, while performing the ritual within the precincts, chant the three sets of marks in full and thereby establish the *śīmaṇḍala* (boundary), while simultaneously establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) from a distance within that same *śīmaṇḍala*.
Hence it is said that "two layers of *karmavācanā* are performed in full. As for the previous mention of those who do not assemble within the boundary, this refers to those who...

This is the complete natural assembly. Alternatively, there may be cases where, after the three characteristics have been proclaimed throughout the boundary, one subsequently adds the ritual procedure within the boundary.
This refers to a person performing the rite who proclaims the three characteristics at a single time; this is contrary to the Dharma.

One must first proclaim the single characteristic outside the *karmavācanā* site (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), and then immediately add the ritual procedure to bind it. Regarding the phrase "adding the procedure according to the boundary," although the procedure is added...
This is like saying that the proclamation of the boundaries is incorrect; this is actually a proclamation made within the natural boundary (*dharmatā-sīmā*).

It is said that while the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) remains validly established, it is simply the ritual site (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) that fails to be established. Alternatively, regarding "binding the site from afar within the great boundary":

this refers to a teacher who, having proclaimed the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*) within the great boundary, immediately binds the site from a distance. Only when each person proclaims and each person binds does the rite achieve success.
Because the boundaries are distinct, the formal act of binding (*bandhana*) is not accomplished.

The same may be understood for other cases. From this point onward, its characteristics are clarified. Once the boundary has been bound, four or five monks who understand the characteristics of the Dharma should remain seated;
they go to bind [the boundary] so as to avoid overburdening the assembly. If [all]...
The more one proceeds, the better it becomes. First, to clarify that there are two different ways of chanting the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):

the first involves chanting the internal characteristics three times, followed by chanting the external characteristics three times, and finally concluding with both together; that is, after having separately chanted the internal and external characteristics once each.
Tie it all around accordingly.

Composed by Dajue of Huayan Temple in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Regarding the statement in the Vinaya texts that "one does not add words" and so forth, Jingyun says:

"If one simply says, 'Within these four sides,' and so on, the meaning is naturally understood. The intention is that within the four-sided boundary, the phrasing is universally applicable. [The text continues: "...outside."
The boundary marks (*sīmā*) are also within the four directions; the inner boundary marks (*antaḥ-sīmā*) are likewise within the four directions.
This is simply stating that they are within the four directional boundaries, which already encompasses both [the outer and inner]. Why, then, is it necessary to add the word "inner" (*antaḥ*)?

Therefore, at the end of the Wei dynasty, Master Guang, who was a clear exponent of the Vinaya school and held the high esteem of the monastic community, always had a thousand people present whenever he gave lectures. Later, while performing the ritual of delimiting the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), he [encountered] another...
They debated the meaning of the character "internal" (nei) within this [term], yet the dispute remained unresolved. At that time, a young novice emerged and spoke, saying:

"If one considers characteristics (xiang) in relation to characteristics, then characteristics have internal and external aspects; but if one considers the substance (ti) in relation to characteristics, the substance must necessarily be within the characteristics.
Thereupon, [the opponents] were silenced. However, after a long while they replied, "It should also be like this. Thus we know that there is no need to add the character [nei].

"Regarding 'assembling the saṃgha within a different great boundary' (mahā-sīmā): this means that while a great boundary is free from difficulties and requires the assembly of monks within five *li*, the present case involves such difficulties and thus limits it to seven *paṇḍa*.

Therefore, it is said to be 'different from the great boundary. In response to this, regarding the statement "there is no difference from the *Caturvargika-vinaya* up to the point where the ease or difficulty of arrival is clearly seen," *Sengyou* states:
"The *Samantapāsādikā* says: 'If there are difficulties in an araṇya, [the boundary] extends for seven *paṇḍa*.'"
The *Lüji seng* (Collection on the Assembly of Monks) states that according to the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), when there is an obstacle, one must establish three minor boundaries (*sīman*).

Since there is the textual passage concerning the *qīpántuó* (seven *pāṇṭa*), we now follow the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Observations) regarding the seven *pāṇṭa*. As both texts state that these two situations are equally obstacles, they are said to be no different.
This interpretation is incorrect. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Some say that because difficult circumstances have arisen, there is no need to rely on the formal boundary (*sīmā*);

rather, wherever the assembly gathers and sits shall serve as the fixed location. Therefore, the text cites: 'The seating area is already full,' etc. (The meaning of this is that the master directs them to assemble at the designated sitting area)."

[This] does not employ the seven spirits). Furthermore, there are masters who say that such citations are not of correct authority and cannot be relied upon; one must instead rely on the Vinaya texts, which do not permit departing the boundary without formal consent.

One should quickly re-establish the boundary, clearly knowing that otherwise it would be feared to be equivalent to a "natural" (unconsecrated) area. Thus, it is evident that the boundary is used as the limit.
Since it is stated that there are difficult circumstances, this does not compare with ordinary cases; one should instead employ the seven *paṇḍa* measure as prescribed in the *Jianlun*.
This is because the text of that [work] states "disagreement," which is identical to the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya). As for the current statement that it is no different from the *Sifenlü*:
The *Shanjianwen* (Text on Good Observation) states: "In the Āraṇya, there is a boundary for difficult circumstances;
the smallest [area] is seven *paṭala*s in circumference. One *paṭala* is twenty-eight cubits (*hasta*). If those who do not consent are outside, one may perform ritual acts [there].
The *Sifen* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) also says: 'If they do not consent and have not yet left the boundary, quickly establish it. Therefore, it is said that there is no difference. Jì also says:"

Regarding the fact that these four parts are not different: the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) states that those who do not agree may perform ritual acts outside [the boundary], and thus it is said they are "not different.
Calculating the total, there are seven *pan* (units), which equals fifty-eight paces, four chi, and eight cun.

Xuanwen asked: "In the case of the country of Kauśāmbī, they were likewise not in harmony. How can it be that they are permitted to speak separately while remaining in the same location? The answer is: this is not the same [case].
In those cases, the matter and the manifestation would be at variance; thus, it would not accord with the meaning of the Saṃgha. Therefore, a separate explanation is provided.
By citing the case where the manifestation of shared activity is distinct, one may issue a reprimand for failing to recognize the matter; hence, a separate formal act (karmavācanā) is established.

Regarding the statement that "it must be within a village and does not permit [the following] etc.," this means that within a village, one does not establish a small boundary (sīmā) during times of difficulty. This refers to a secluded spot within a village, such as behind a wall.
It is difficult for the shadows of walls to provide concealment. If a bhikṣu hides in a layperson’s house within the seven-fold enclosure, he constitutes a separate assembly;
even if an evil bhikṣu arrives, he cannot see him. In an araṇya, however, one is exposed and not hidden, making visibility neither difficult nor easy; therefore, this [rule] is waived.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the principle regarding the distance for assembling the Saṃgha. The following second section clarifies the absence of fixed boundaries.

To say that "the boundary-substance is constituted simply according to the number of persons" means that there are no demarcating signs; rather, the sitting places themselves constitute the substance. Thus, the characteristic and the substance are one and the same.

Regarding the matters of these individuals performing rituals such as establishing small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) for receiving the precepts or for designating the limits of monasteries (*ārāma*), "establishing" refers to what the ancient masters said:

among these three types of small boundaries, if it is a small boundary for receiving the precepts, one must establish the physical characteristics of the monastery; if it is a small boundary for the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, [the requirements differ].

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* small boundary (*kṣudrakṣetra*), these two do not require the establishment of physical boundary markers (*sīmāliṅga*). They must simply be aligned with the seating area; drawing [the cord] or releasing it [from a fixed point] is incorrect.
Now, in both cases, there are no limits of a physical enclosure. Jì (Jizang) says:

"In the old traditions of the [Vinaya] schools, those who did not understand the teachings would, when it came time to confer the precepts, frequently establish a small boundary within laypeople's homes for their master-monks to receive the precepts, yet they did not even align the bodies [of the candidates] when establishing the boundary."
Nor did they erect boundary markers; they simply extended their forearms forward and hooked them together, saying, "We establish a boundary as far as this distance.
People of the time called this the "Forearm-Hook Boundary Ordination" (*wanguan jie*).
When newly ordained persons arrived in Jinzhou, Tongzhou, or Puzhou, they were often teased by others, who would say, "Did you not receive the ordination within that Forearm-Hook Boundary?"
The initial statement, "the monks have gathered in one place," refers to the conferral of precepts under difficult circumstances.

The middle statement, "so many bhikṣus have gathered," refers to the recitation of the *Poṣadha* under difficult circumstances. The final statement, "the seating places for the bhikṣus are already full," refers to the *Pravāraṇā*.

Regarding the reference to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other texts: Master Li states that the *Pini yiyi* (Vinaya-saṃgraha) and the *Yuan lüshi* (Master Yuan, the Vinaya Master) say that a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) must have marked boundaries (*nimitta*).

That master cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which says that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed outside the distance of one *vyāma* from the sitting area; based on this, it is clearly known that there must be marked boundaries.

However, the present *Chao* (the *Sifenlü xingshichao*) differs from this, stating that the "small boundary" in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* refers to the text of that Vinaya regarding the matter of performing the confession of abandonment (*pratyāpatti*).

Because it is difficult for the Saṃgha to assemble within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), and because there is no designated site for ordination (sīmā-maṇḍala), it is permitted to separately establish a small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā) outside the great boundary.

The procedure is the same as the method for the great boundary and the ordination site used for gathering the Saṃgha; however, because that which is established is small, it is called a "small boundary.

One establishes its markers and delimits it, leaving a space of one *vyāma* open outside the seating area; this is termed a "small boundary. It must not be confused with the three types of small boundaries mentioned previously.

Now, I wish to refute the Master’s erroneous adherence to the view that these are the "three small [boundaries]. If one were to take the name "small" as the basis for designating them as the three small boundaries, then one could likewise call the *kṣetra-maṇḍala* (the ordination site) a "small boundary";

would it therefore be the same as those three small boundaries? By refuting the ancient masters here, I clarify that one should not establish [boundaries] based on such formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "opening space for one person’s share," Jì says: "This is according to the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*), which instructs that it should be done in this way.
This means that once the boundary has been established, if the master-monks wish to accommodate those of superior or inferior status, even half a body's space will suffice.

When the ancients established the rules, there were also instances where they permitted the establishment of a boundary at a small portion of the seating area; however, they would set aside a separate small space, like the handle of an iron cauldron, so that the recipients might [be accommodated].
To take the middle [case] as the basis for receiving [the precepts] is also untenable now. Suppose a wicked person suddenly appears and rebukes one from a position of authority; what then?
If one were to say that self-indulgence (*prātimokṣa*) is permissible in such circumstances because it is not necessarily so in all cases, this refers to "self-indulgence in difficult matters.

To insist that one must sit in a complete circle is merely human convention and need not be strictly so. This is the intended meaning of the ancient masters; therefore, it is called "human application" (*pudgala-prayoga*).
This concludes [the preceding section]. Below, the concluding dharma is clarified. Regarding the statement that "there are three other distinct realms":

this means that what has been explained above consists solely of the realms where persons and dharmas are mutually identical; these are merely cases of internal identity within their own respective realms.
From here on, there are further three realms that differ from those above. To clarify them once more, it says, "there are others. Li (Lì) states: "The Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*)."

There are four [types]. Sometimes three types are mentioned: first, the identity of persons and the Dharma within the same boundary (*sīmā*), meaning that while the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the distribution of offerings (*lābha*) are distinct, they are nonetheless identical within their respective boundaries;
this is the common practice of the present day. Second, the identity of both the Dharma and the food within the same boundary;
this refers to when there were previously two separate boundaries, one possessing the Dharma but lacking food, and the other possessing food but lacking the Dharma, which have now been unified.

1. Resolving the common bonds while sharing the same recitation and the same benefits; alternatively, this is called "merging two dharmas" where the food is shared. 2. Three dharmas being shared while the food is separate within different boundaries (*sīmā*).

This means that previously there were two distinct boundaries where the dharma and the food were each separate; now, each resolves their common bonds, shares the same recitation, and has separate benefits.

This is also called "merging two [dharmas]" where only the dharma is shared. 3. Food is shared while the dharma is separate. This also refers to two boundaries that were previously distinct; now, they are separately recited.
The "commonality of precepts and material gains" is also called the "commonality of two single-meal foods. Regarding this latter boundary, there is no matter of formal binding or releasing;
it simply refers to the guarding of the dwelling place. It is bound by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) so that food may be shared.

Although its *karman* text resembles the method for binding a boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*), it does not proclaim the boundary markers (*nimitta*) nor does it recite the boundary markers. Judging by reason, it would not be appropriate to call it [a boundary-binding].
Regarding the *dhātu* (elements/spheres): although they are enumerated as four, they are designated by the name "element" because they share the common characteristic of being fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Alternatively, at times the great elements (*mahā-dhātu*) are enumerated as only three; this is simply because the latter [of the four] is not discussed here. Some say that the first two are combined to include the latter, thereby forming three; however, this is not a correct interpretation.
As for the statement, "The distinct [factors] are explained separately, while those with identical benefit and desire are explained together," this— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
The names "Dharma" and "Food" share the same realm; this refers to the second point in the aforementioned commentary on the *Śāstra*.

Since the former [pair] was distinct, whereas the latter intends for them to be identical, it is because the Dharma and Food were previously deficient in relation to one another, while now they are mutually required.

Taking the Dharma as the means to sustain the mind and taking Food as the method to sustain the body—since mind and body are the very instruments of the Way, how could any teaching not apply when the karmic conditions arise? Therefore, the Buddha permitted it.
Resolve each separately from the joint bond.

Second, regarding the separate explanation of distinct benefits while the explanation is joint: this refers to the same food within distinct boundaries (*sīmā*), which is precisely what was explained above as the third case.
Because the benefits for both parties are abundant, there is no [conflict] regarding a single residence; this is the purpose of those who have gone forth. By means of...
The Dharma comes first. As the end of one’s life approaches, the Dharmakāya shall be established; it must necessarily depend on this. Therefore, the Buddha permitted it.

Regarding the third point, the separate explanation of distinct benefits and desires versus the separate explanation of shared benefits: this is called "sharing food but having different boundaries regarding the Dharma" (*śikṣā-samāna-dharmānya-deśa*).

This refers to the fourth case in the *Śīla-vibhaṅga*. Here, there is no method for interpreting the Dharma; rather, it concerns the harmonizing of the Saṃgha by sending food to provide relief to other locations. This...
"‘The Dharma is nearly exhausted’ (*daijin*): ‘nearly’ (*dai*) means to escape, to perish, or to approach. The *Mao Shi* says: ‘It is nearly. The *Guangshu* says:
‘Nearly means ruin. Zheng Xuan says: ‘Nearly means almost (*ji*). Almost means proximity.”*

From this point downward, the method for disbanding [the boundaries] is explained. If there is a *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) and one first disbands the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), it is established as being like putting on clothes:

when putting them on, one first puts on the inner layer and then the outer; this is an analogy for the time of binding [the boundary]. When taking them off, one first removes the outer layer and then the inner.
This is an analogy for the time of dissolving a boundary (*sīmā*).
Regarding the practice of using the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) ritual to dissolve it found in the older *Karmavācanā* texts, this was the procedure of Master Guṇabhadra (*Guang*). Why is this so?
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Therefore, Master Guṇabhadra produced the *karmavācanā* text," and the sub-commentary (*vṛtti*) says: "This is a single *karmavācanā*."
This universally resolves both boundaries; according to their respective sizes, there is no further partial restriction. As for the objection:

"If the current practice differs from this, why is it not permitted to recite the *Poṣadha* on the *Sīmāmaṇḍala*, and how can one proceed with the formal resolution? This clarifies that ancient masters used the text for resolving the *Mahāsīmā* to resolve the *Śīlāmaṇḍala*.

The current method does not follow this resolution. In the text for resolving the *Mahāsīmā*, it states: "In a single residential area (*ekavihāra*), there is a single *Poṣadha* recitation. Now, regarding the *Śīlāmaṇḍala*...
"Regarding the site: originally, the recitation of the precepts was not permitted there; how then could one employ that text?

As for the statement, 'Now, according to difficult circumstances, the formal act of binding is reversed to become one of releasing,' this refers to the three small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*). When reversing the binding to release them, now, following this principle, if one wishes to release the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept-site), it is sufficient simply to reverse the binding to release it.
To say 'the principle is pervasive and the text is compliant' means that it is both logically consistent and in accord with the Vinaya text."
It is not a contradiction.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that one must not build a dwelling on the boundary of the *śīla-maṇḍala*, an examination of that treatise reveals:
"If a powerful king builds a dwelling upon the boundary of the *śīla-maṇḍala*, it is called a 'difficult dwelling. One should ensure that he does not cause any obstruction to our *poṣadha*."

If [the construction] continues despite being forbidden three times by such means as [the recitation of] the *Āryā*, a conscientious (*hrīmān*) bhikṣu shall demolish this dwelling, leaving only the Buddha-hall and the Bodhi tree. Once demolished, it must not be used;

rather, the materials shall be collected in order and sent to the resident bhikṣus (according to the intent of that text, this refers to the construction of a dwelling that causes obstruction). This is clearly established, just as with the sacrificial altars and suburban sacrifices of a state.

There is a suburban altar (*jiaotan*). It is located seven *li* south of the capital. Sacrifices to the celestial deities (*tian shen*) are performed upon it; thus it is called the "Suburban Altar. A distance of seven *li* from the city wall is termed the "suburb" (*jiao*);

at two or three *li* it is termed the "farmland" (*tǎng*; the character is read as *yíng* in the ancient pronunciation); at three or seven *li* it is termed the "forest" (*lín*); and at four or seven *li* it is termed the "wilderness" (*yě*).
The *Erlǐ* states: "That which is outside the town is called the suburb. According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, lands for residential use were assigned to the territory of the near suburbs. (Zheng [Xuan...])
Xuán said: "The *Sīmǎ Fǎ* states: 'One hundred *lǐ* from the royal capital is called the *jiāo*; two hundred *lǐ* is the *zhōu*; three hundred *lǐ* is the *yě*.
A Confucian scholar remarked: 'Jiāo means "exchange. This refers to when the lords of small states come in person;

the high ministers of the state then go out to welcome them, and thus there is an exchange at this location. It is one hundred *lǐ* from the capital. [This is] the textual explanation. The Southern Suburb (*Nánjiāo*) is for the sacrifice to Heaven; the Northern Suburb..."
They sacrifice to the Earth because it is within this [earth] that they communicate with Heaven. It is also called a *śīlā-maṇḍala* (precept platform).
In the western lands, there is the country of Northern Tukhāra, also known as the country of Udyāna, where a precept platform is erected fourteen feet high, consisting of three tiers.

This is in accordance with the Dharma. This can be clarified by reference to the altar of a pure official: it is constructed on the southern mountain using accumulated fragrant mud, extending upward from the water's edge.
Regarding the "untying of the three small boundaries" in the same manner as the previous method of binding: this refers to untying them by reversing the procedure of binding.
The preceding section has concluded the explanation of the second meaning: the gate of practice according to the stages (*sthāna*).

From here on, the third meaning—the existence or non-existence of the arising of dharmas—is correctly elucidated. Regarding the statement that "by performing wholesome dharmas, one immediately gives rise to wholesome non-action," the proponent establishes as follows:

If one performs an evil deed, it gives rise to unmanifest (avijñapti) evil; now, this boundary-binding (sīmābandha) is the performance of wholesome dharmas, and thus it gives rise to wholesome unmanifest karma.
As for the statement that it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha):

it is established that among the five aggregates, the first three are neutral (avyākṛta), while the aggregate of formations is determinate (vyākṛta) and capable of constituting the causes for wholesome or unwholesome karma. This present method of boundary-binding is a wholesome karma.
This is a mind of wholesome conduct. Because of this mind of wholesome conduct, one attains the stage of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and wholesome dharmas arise therein.
Question: Since this stage is indeterminate, how can it give rise to wholesome [dharmas], which are determinate? Answer:

Although the stage is indeterminate and does not itself distinguish between good and evil, because the mind is determinate, it imparts its wholesome quality to that stage; thus, it enables this stage to possess [wholesomeness].

Regarding the statement, "Wholesome dharmas arise; it does not mean they are connected to the neutral (*avyākṛta*) stage, nor that they do not reach one another," the *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Ritual) asks:

"What is the neutral? It is that which is subsumed under non-sentient things. However, at the place where the boundary is established, it is not that the mind does not arise; the ground is a result of reliance (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Ji said: "Sentient beings experience retribution, and this abides here; that is to say, the earth is the place upon which sentient beings rely.
For instance, a virtuous mind invites a pure land, while evil karma evokes a defiled realm—is the earth not, therefore, a 'retributive support' (*niśraya-vipāka*)?

Even clothing, food, and material offerings are all subsumed under retributive supports. How could it be that there is a phenomenon relying on the earth according to the power of one's mental karma? Therefore, it is pervasive."

Within the headings, there is always the force of karma (*karmabala*). This is as stated in the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: "By the power of the realm (*dhātu*), one is protected by benevolent deities.
Regarding the statement that they are not mutually unrelated, some say it refers to the reaching of the light-phase (*āloka-nimitta*). Master Li says: To take a metaphor, it is like water and waves.
Apart from water there are no waves; apart from breaking [the water] there is no water. Water has moisture as its nature; waves have movement as their nature. Their...

Although their natures are distinct, they ultimately depend upon one another. This is like the relationship between resultant form (*vipākavarṇa*) and conditioned form (*prāyogikavarṇa*): they are neither identical nor separate.
When there is movement, it is called conditioned form; the body of maturation is called resultant form. Conditioned form does not arise of itself.
That which moves by depending on the retributive form (vipākaja-rūpa) is called the form of skillful means (upāya-rūpa).

Since the retribution has no separate substance, that which is moved by the body and speech is itself designated as the retributive form. Because they stand in mutual dependence, they cannot be said to be two.

However, while the form of skillful means permeates all three natures (trividha-svabhāva), the retributive form is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta); therefore, they cannot be said to be one. Ultimately, they must rely upon and depend on one another.
However, virtuous dharmas must necessarily rely upon the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

Although the earth-element itself is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is solely by virtue of the Saṃgha performing the ritual action that virtuous dharmas arise within the boundaries established by the markers. Outside these markers, there are no virtuous dharmas.

Just as the nature of waves and the nature of water, though two distinct natures, are able to combine with one another, so too, although my own nature as the earth-element is indeterminate, what hindrance is there to its [combining with]...?
Because it is conjoined with the wholesome that is determinate (*niyata*), it is said that they are not mutually unattainable.

Regarding the former statement, "There is no dharma that arises, up to and including not discussing whether dharmas arise or not," this refers to a person mentioned in the *Jielü mo-shu* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*).
Some say this was Master Li; others claim it was Master Yuan. Upon examining Master Li’s *Jielü mo-shu*, it says:
Formerly, Xie [Jizang] followed the *Sudarsana-śāstra* and claimed that it appears as if dharmas arise; my current interpretation is not so.

For example, when a practitioner performs an action, "non-informative" (*avijñapti*) karma is produced and co-exists with the practitioner’s mind. This means that within the sphere of the mind there is an attainment (*prāpti*) that can be acquired; therefore, karma exists.
This present demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*) is not for the sake of anything else. It is capable of acting upon that which is sentient; how could it act upon that which is non-sentient?
What dharma would arise [therein], and who would be bound by it? A guest explains this point, saying: "Generally speaking, what is called 'unmanifest' (*avijñapti*) refers to bodily and vocal karma.
How could a non-sentient thing achieve unmanifest karma? If that is so, how should one interpret the *Sudarsana* [Sūtra]? The answer is: this is within the scope of the restriction.

This does not mean that a separate dharma arises; rather, it refers to the location where the boundaries (*dhātu*) converge. To cite the Vinaya text from the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on Settling Disputes):
"What is the manifestation of the boundary? It refers to those who perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) within [the boundary] and are subject to its restrictions.

This means it is the place where the ritual action is performed, distinguishing it from what is natural (*prakṛti*), as there is no separate dharma that arises. One should understand other categories such as the boundaries for robes and medicine in this same way; they are merely...

In the past, when performing ritual acts (*karmavācanā*), one incurred no transgression; this was not because a formal dharma arose. Regarding the mention of robes, medicine, and bowls, Master Bin said:

"Although there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) upon the physical objects themselves, within the bodies of those performing the ritual, the non-informative matter of maintaining the precepts (*śīla-avijñapti*) also arises.

It is the same with the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*): although there is no non-informative matter on the ground that is being delimited, within the bodies of those performing the ritual..."

It also gives rise to the non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of the merit of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*). As clarified in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this refers to the establishment of a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) as previously described;
it is like the case where the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* establish the inclusion of a village protected by benevolent deities. This passage is cited as proof.
"Knowing that dharmas arise; if no dharmas arise, the good deity Nātha protects them. 'The minor dharmas are extinguished'—this is the title of the sutra.
Regarding 'when the kalpa-fire arises,' Zhencheng (Shen) says: this commentary clarifies that one is not burned by the kalpa-fire; this refers to a *kṣudrakalpa* (minor kalpa).
If it were a *mahākalpa* (great kalpa), heaven and earth would be utterly incinerated; this is not merely a matter of words. For now, this explains the minor kalpa."

It is fire. Within one great kalpa, there are eighty small kalpas: namely, twenty small kalpas of formation, twenty small kalpas of abiding, twenty small kalpas of destruction, and twenty small kalpas of emptiness. This continues until even the diamond [vajra] becomes the foundation of earth.
Lì Míng states: The terrestrial yakṣas and bhūtas move upon the earth as if birds fly through the sky;

yet, when they reach a place where a boundary has been established, they are unable to proceed. This is because, once the boundary is completed, the Wheel of Vajra (vajramaṇḍala) extends to its limits, and wholesome dharmas arise therein.
At this point, one may cite the *Gantong zhuan* (Account of Spiritual Resonance) regarding the efficacy of the boundary for precepts (*jiechang*), as follows [and so forth].
The preceding explanation of the three sections is now complete. From here on, the fourth section—concerning the characteristics of whether the boundary is maintained or lost—is properly elucidated.
Regarding the case where various bhikṣus leave the monastic quarters with the intention not to return: it is established that they maintain the intention within the monastery.

If one does not return and loses it immediately upon leaving the gate, [the forfeiture] is established. However, if one only forms the intention to relinquish it after having already left the monastery, the forfeiture is not established;
for a remote relinquishment outside the boundary is not valid.
Regarding the previous statement by *Sudṛśa* that [the boundary] is not lost, etc.: the intent of this question is as follows.

*Sudṛśa* previously stated that even if one builds a three-story house above or digs down to the water’s edge, the boundary is not lost. Why, then, is it now said to be lost after staying overnight and failing to return?

This statement that it is "lost" implies the intention of not returning and the mental state of abandoning the boundary; this explanation serves to resolve the contradiction with the treatise of Jñānaprasthāna.
It is as follows: if one forms the intention not to relinquish [the site], it is the same as the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* regarding non-forfeiture;
if one forms the intention of permanent relinquishment, it is the same as the *Jñānaprasthāna* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Regarding the statement that "a previously treated monastery does not forfeit its status as a pure ground," this serves as proof that the relinquishment performed previously does not result in forfeiture. According to the text in the *Bhaiṣajya-khandhaka*, it says: "At that time, the bhikṣus..."

Not knowing where the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) was located, the Buddha said: "It should be demarcated. If one suspects that there was previously a pure ground, it should be released and then demarcated anew.
At that time, while restoring an old monastery, they did not know whether it could be made into a pure ground. The Buddha said: "It may be so made."

(Commentary: Since it is stated that one does not know which part is pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), it is clearly understood that this place has previously been devoid of human footprints, thereby revealing it to be an ancient monastery (*pūrvārāma*).
Furthermore, regarding the second sentence—whether, within an ancient monastery, a bhikṣu who is unaware [of its status] may establish it as pure ground—it is directly ruled that he may indeed do so.
This makes it clear that the legal boundaries (*sīmā*) of the ancient monastery have not been lost; they were previously established by relying upon the physical site itself.
Because it is established through purification (*pariśuddhi*). Since purification exists by virtue of being within a boundary (*sīmā*), the boundary itself cannot be non-existent.

If, when performing the ritual of relinquishment (*utsarga*), both the robes and the persons are lost along with the boundary, this clarifies that the two boundaries for robes and food depend upon the establishment of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
Now, if one dissolves that great boundary, since the basis (*āśraya*) has vanished, that which depends upon it (*āśrita*) naturally disappears of its own accord. This treatise discusses this...
This fundamentally encompasses the boundary of the Saṃgha; therefore, it is called the "human boundary" (*pudgala-dhātu*). The above clarifies the meaning of "loss.

Regarding the first point—that abandoning the pure ground through an illegal and malicious mind does not constitute a valid precedent—the establishment of this [argument] cites these words to prove that, as stated in the preceding text, the boundary is not lost when abandoned with a malicious mind.
It is also like the case where a bhikṣu touches the food of the Saṃgha with a malicious mind; the Buddha said: "It is not [an offense]."
This constitutes a transgression of contact; however, only the one who makes physical contact incurs the offense. In the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā*, there are six types of non-loss [of the boundary].
By combining this fourth [case], "loss of the boundary marks," with the fifth, "loss of the original site through space," into one, there arises the view that mutual binding results in no loss.

Because they are seen as distinct, there are no separate assemblies for the two; they are explained separately within the same realm, yet the Buddha’s judgment establishes that [the act] is accomplished.

Furthermore, there is the mutual binding of the heterodox and the orthodox without loss, as well as this evil mind among the monks and nuns, both inside and outside—these constitute the six [cases]. Regarding the four ways the characteristics of the boundary (*sīmā*) are lost, as described in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian lun):
this refers to cases such as when water washes away the boundary markers to form a pit and so forth; in such instances, the boundary is not lost. Fifth is the fundamental emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Regarding "the place" (*sthāna*): it means that because one does not form the intention to abandon it, there is no lapse of the limit [of the precept]. The *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) explains:
"The original place of the void" refers to digging the earth to make it empty.

Regarding the prohibition against "interlacing" (xiānchā): Jingyun says this refers to a lack of reverence and deference, and is therefore not permitted. There are two interpretations of the term *li* (standing/establishing).

The first states that "interlacing" means being unable to pass each other [on the path]; for example, when a *bhikṣuṇī* establishes a boundary (*sīmā*) within the territory of the *bhikṣus*, she must do so by formally designating it as the "territory of the *bhikṣus*.

She may not have half of it within the *bhikṣus'* territory and half within the "natural" (*prakṛti*) territory. The same applies when a *bhikṣu* [establishes a boundary] within the territory of the *bhikṣuṇīs*.

When performing the formal act of boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandha*), one must likewise determine it by referring to the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary. Jì states that the *Nanshan Jiemoluoshi* (Nanshan Commentary on the Karmavācanā) says:
"The boundaries must not overlap, for fear of being excluded from the *saṃgha*, as this would not fulfill the principle of sharing the same Dharma.

This meaning clarifies that if a *bhikṣuṇī* is to determine a boundary upon the *bhikṣu* boundary, she must do so in a manner that conforms to the *bhikṣu* boundary. If the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary were larger than the *bhikṣu* boundary, then when the *bhikṣuṇīs* sit [within it]...

There is the possibility of meaning that one exists outside the boundary of the *saṃgha*. When receiving full ordination as a *śrāmaṇerī*, the two assemblies (*ubhayasaṃgha*) do not encompass one another;
thus, it does not constitute the characteristic of being of the same dharma as the *bhikṣu* *saṃgha*.

If the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary were smaller than the *bhikṣu* boundary, then when the *bhikṣus* are seated, there would be the possibility of being outside the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary; this likewise is not the characteristic of the two assemblies sharing the same dharma. For these reasons...

Therefore, it is necessary that they mutually agree. Furthermore, it is said: "The *saṃgha* does not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a *bhikṣuṇī*, nor does the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha* perform it for a *bhikṣu*;

hence, it is called 'mutually crossing' (*xiāngchā*), which means 'reciprocal'. If one follows the later interpretation, the character [used] would be inconsistent; it should instead be the character "difference" (*chā*).

However, the *Wǔbǎiwèn fǎ* (Five Hundred Questions on the Dharma) cannot be relied upon as a clear standard for the principles of the Dharma. It deviates from the fundamental tenets in its determination of offenses, such that the gravity of the transgressions is suddenly rendered either too light or too heavy. Thus, the statement...

It is said: "Bimokṣa" is a vulgar term. Hui-guan compiled and recorded it, and the people of the capital vied to copy it; the paper became as precious as jade. The first six chapters of the commentary are hereby concluded.
○ Chapter Seven: The Great Outline of the Monastic Net.

The preceding chapter elucidated the *dhātu* (monastic boundaries), which is the place upon which the Saṃgha relies. Once the physical site has been established, it is further necessary to propagate the True Dharma and to guide the assembly of the times.
To illuminate and manifest the lineage for future generations and to sustain the teachings throughout the ages, one must rely upon the practice of the teachings;

only then can the Great Dharma be made radiant and far-reaching. It is for this reason that this present chapter follows. Regarding the "Great Outline of the Monastic Net," this is a metaphor borrowed from the secular world.
The main cord of a net can straighten its mesh; this present treatise is the governing framework for the legal net of the monastic community.

The essential principles of the abbot are called the "main cord" (*kang*), while the rules for minute conduct are the "mesh. It may also be said that this is the guiding principle for the mesh of the monastic assembly;
hence it is so named. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The large rope used to hold a net is called the 'main cord' (*kang*). This refers to the monastic law.
If there is discord, confusion, and a loss of order, by upholding this single chapter, there is no dharma that is not brought into alignment. Thus, the preceding preface states:

"To repair the dark silken cord that has already snapped"—this refers precisely to this meaning. Jì says: "The 'three fundamental principles' mentioned here regarding the various leaders also include the monastic network."

The net is sustained by its main ropes; the net is the assembly of monks (*saṃgha*). This is because the leaders of the assembly are able to uphold the *saṃgha*, just as the main ropes are able to sustain the net.
Shen says: Within this introduction, the text is divided into three sections.

From the beginning up to "the light of the sun of wisdom is gloriously spread," it clarifies how the Three Jewels are established through reliance on and maintenance of the Teaching. Second, from "If the Dharma transcends the common mind... [and so forth].

From "Upon arrival, one must surely follow the Holy Dharma" down to the end of the preface, it clarifies that violating the teachings and destroying the Dharma brings about suffering as one's own retribution. From "From now on, I wish...
onwards, it clarifies that if one wishes to compile the Dharma to rectify the times, one must propagate the Holy Teachings and once again illuminate the transformative influence of the Way.
There are three stages, of which this is the first.

Regarding the necessity of establishing and propagating the Dharma through one's own sphere of activity: it is established that one must clearly maintain the teachings and institute regulations in accordance with them within one's own region.
One must ensure that the established rules accord with the sacred teachings; if the regulations one establishes do not conform to the sacred teachings, it is termed "obstruction.

Because the teachings of the Tripiṭaka are universally shared throughout the ten directions, if one acts in accordance with them, there will be universal penetration everywhere. Therefore, it is said that "establishing the Dharma requires universality.

Regarding the phrase "residing in the assembly and adjudicating," "establishing" means to clarify; "residing" refers to dwelling. This clarifies that one who dwells in the assembly serves as the leader and sustainer, exercising the power of judgment and resolution.

Right and wrong must necessarily rely upon the Vinaya teachings. This is because the teachings provide the standard models; thus, the rules and regulations are fixed, and their meaning cannot deviate from them.
Regarding the phrase "distant regions and foreign lands," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "region" (*yu*) means "state" (*bang*). The *Guangpi* states:
"State" (*bōngyì*) refers to the name of a country. To say "the mind is uplifted toward something" clarifies that there is a specific dwelling place.

If one establishes [the teaching] extensively according to the *Vinaya*, one can cause those in distant regions to be reverently devoted and to look up with sincere veneration, just like the sun and moon; therefore, it is said that "the mind is uplifted toward something.

As for practitioners within the boundaries who settle their minds and advance in their practice, this is due to the regulations established by the community leaders through their transformative influence.
At that time, by acting in accordance with the teachings, one is able to provide shelter for future lives and settle the mind to advance in the work of the Path.

If one does not rely on the teachings to establish proper conduct, causing disputes and controversies to proliferate, how could one possibly settle the mind and progress in the cultivation of the Buddha-way?
"If one governs the assembly in this manner, what task would not be accomplished?"—this refers to such a case; it merely concludes the preceding section. "Govern" (yu) means to manage or regulate.

Furthermore, it is intended to clarify that the superior transforms the inferior just as the wind bends the grass. If the senior monks (upādhyāya) now act in accordance with the teachings, how could the junior monks not follow?
This is all due to the transformative influence of being bent by the wind.

As for the phrase "who would not serve him," it is intended to clarify that those who can act in accordance with the teachings—whether lay or ordained, noble or humble—who would not look up to, revere, and honor them? How much less so among the monastic community alone!
Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): if one establishes the Dharma based on these teachings, why should it be limited merely to the assembly of monks being grand and impressive to behold?
It is also intended to cause them to cease worldly attachments and turn toward the principle of Bodhi. Only then can they support the tree of the Path and glorify the sun of wisdom.
This means that not only do they personally cease worldly involvement and return to the Truth within, but they are further able to externally radiate the brilliance of the sun of wisdom.

As it was previously stated, "profoundly honoring and protecting the Dharma," what concern could there be that the Sun of the Buddha would not shine once more, or that the Wheel of the Dharma would not turn again?

The "Tree of the Path" (Bodhi tree) is a metaphor for the Buddha-dharma, which is able to provide shade and shelter for sentient beings, freeing them from the scorching heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the term *fúshū* (扶疏): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the appearance of tree branches and twigs spreading out in all directions.
From this point onward, the second section clarifies the meaning of violating the teachings and thereby inviting the retribution of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "if a law exceeds ordinary sentiment," it means that when one follows worldly customs and common practice rather than relying on the holy teachings, trusting only in one's own whims and exercising personal judgment to establish laws, it is said that "the law exceeds ordinary sentiment.
To say it does not rely on the Vinaya is to mean it has no authoritative basis; such penal codes are as base as the vulgar.
Regarding "vulgar": [Master] Li states that imposing fines in money and grain is termed a "punitive decree" (ke-fa), which is identical to the vulgar customs of the common people.
Ji says: "Even good worldly people do not establish teachings in this manner; it is because of such vulgar customs that this teaching exists.

Inflicting punishments with staves and whips, using coarse shackles and heavy clubs, and meting out penalties at will—this constitutes the heavy and coarse nature of the net of the teaching. As for those subjected to it, there is much clamor and disorder. [Master] Li states:
That is to say: when one who establishes regulations does so in a manner contrary to the Dharma, and those subject to them do not comply, there is consequently clamor and disorder.

Furthermore, when one teaches what is not the Dharma and arbitrarily governs others, people will not submit; they will instead harbor mutual resentment and litigate, which constitutes clamor and disorder.
Regarding "falling into hell as if shot by an arrow," Jì says: it is like a spear being released from a hand; it must inevitably reach the ground.
This person is likewise; when his life is cut short, he will inevitably fall into hell. It is established that one hundred thousand people cannot dwell together [with him].
Furthermore, a monastic residence must necessarily share both the Dharma and the food; since there is now no Dharma, it is logically impossible for him to remain.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "When a master keeps a disciple, if there is no mutual support through the Dharma-food (*dharmāhāra*), the disciple must depart regardless of whether it is day or night.
The meaning of this is clear.

From here below is the third section, which correctly elucidates the profound radiance of the Way’s transformation. It ensures that the regulations (*vinaya*) and the teachings (*śāsana*) are in accord.
The term "etc. clarifies that in establishing the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-karman*) now, they must correspond with the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka, as seen in the following passage:

the seven types of *karmans* for disciplining individuals correspond to these teachings. Regarding the phrase "the meaning and the timing coincide," it clarifies that in establishing regulations, one must necessarily know the proper time;
for instance, even in cases such as reprimand (*tarjanīya*), one must know the appropriate time, and in censuring faults, one must likewise know the proper time.

This is because it does not deviate from the underlying principle; hence these words were spoken. Some say: "The regulations now established are both appropriate for the times and consistent with the principles of righteousness" (this interpretation is excellent).
Regarding "not establishing what is not a regulation," this means that regulations which are contrary to the Dharma are not instituted.
Regarding "that which is a regulation is put into practice," this clarifies that regulations which accord with the Dharma are currently being implemented.

The three preceding sections have concluded the general explanation of the meaning of the introduction. This was for the purpose of severing those who would destroy the lineage of the Triple Gem and rob sentient beings of their eyes.
In that great assembly, the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:

"If in a future age there should be one of my disciples who possesses abundant wealth and many treasures, who has great power and is a close favorite of the king, yet whom the entire great assembly does not [recognize]..."
"You should discipline such persons as these who are capable of being expelled and corrected.
If members of the four castes—the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras—cannot discipline them, they shall sever the lineage of my Three Jewels and extinguish the torch of the Dharma."
They destroy the Dharma-ship and rob sentient beings of their eyes. It is as if one person were to rob everyone of their sight.
What do you think? Is this offense great or not? "It is very great, World-Honored One; it is beyond measure. The Buddha said:

"If there are members of the four castes who possess great power, and seeing my Dharma perish, they abandon it and fail to protect it, the offense they incur shall likewise be such as this. Although [they may claim]..."
Regarding the statement that the merit of having cultivated precepts, generosity, and wisdom over immeasurable lifetimes will be lost:

the Buddha told the Great King, "If there is a sovereign who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, has cultivated precepts, generosity, and wisdom, yet upon seeing the extinction of my Dharma, abandons it rather than protecting it, then all such immeasurable roots of goodness he has planted will be entirely lost.
In his kingdom, three kinds of calamities shall arise: first, the high price of grain; second, warfare."

The three pestilences will afflict him, and all benevolent deities will utterly abandon him. His royal edicts will not be obeyed by the people, and he will be constantly harassed and oppressed by neighboring states.
Winds and rains will fail to come at their proper times, and those close to him, both inside and out, will all conspire together to rebel.
