From the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no further speech. As for the Intermediate Dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*):

In the state of "without vitarka and with vicāra," the Brahmā Heaven is without speech. Since those who govern people there do not speak now, it is called the "Dharma of Brahmā," meaning they are like Brahmā in their silence.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although Brahmā Heaven lacks *vitarka* (applied thought) but possesses *vicāra* (sustained thought), it nevertheless takes speech as its pleasure.
Only from the Second Dhyāna upward are both *vitarka* and *vicāra* absent; therefore, [the inhabitants] do not speak. This refers to Brahmā Heaven.

Regarding those with offenses within [the realm], they are governed by the "silent dharma" (tūṣṇīka-dharma); hence the statement. As for the claim that this also extends to the form realm (rūpadhātu), it is because within the form realm, speech exists only in the first dhyāna;
therefore, it is said that it "also extends," and so forth. Master Sheng says: "In the meditative stages of the Brahma-heavens, there is no dharma of speech;
now, one governs them by means of the silent dharma. Calculating according to principle, from the second dhyāna upward, there should be no dharma of speech. Great!
Since even those from Brahmā-rāja downwards possess speech, it is treated as "non-speech" [in this context], following the text of the *Shuchao*. Master Bin says:

"Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of speech. Whenever one wishes to produce speech, there must first be the expedient means of investigation and analysis within the mind."

Only after this should one speak. It is further stated: for offenses from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward, if the person does not acknowledge both the fact (*vastu*) and the offense (*āpatti*), they are to be treated according to this Brahma-punishment (*brahmadanda*).
As for the "treatment of a wicked horse" mentioned in the subsequent text, it applies specifically when one has committed a *pārājika* offense and neither the fact nor the offense is acknowledged.
This refers to the "treatment of a wicked horse. It means that when a person refuses to acknowledge or confess their faults, one must cite specific instances and bring forth their transgressions;
only when they are about to commit a *pārājika* offense does one apply the treatment of a wicked horse. Regarding the three methods of discipline (*vinaya*), it is said:
first, gentle discipline; second, forceful discipline; and third, both gentle and forceful discipline; hence they are called the "three kinds. This is like...
Regarding "killing those who are undisciplined": this means that one first admonishes them with both gentle and firm words.
If they do not comply, one then treats them with the discipline of not speaking to them; thus, one "kills" them.
From this point onward, the meaning of the rules for expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) is clarified. Regarding the phrase "one may not dwell together or engage in communal affairs":

"dwelling together" refers to the two types of communal dwelling, namely the *poṣadha* (confession) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticize). "Affairs" refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts). This applies to the entire Saṃgha.
Regarding other *karmas*, one must likewise not perform their ritual affairs in common with them.

The reason for knowing that *karma* refers to these matters is that among the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), there is the dispute concerning matters (*vastu-adhikaraṇa*), which refers precisely to those disputes arising on account of *karma*.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya* that when the great assembly knows [the offense], there is no need for the offender to speak of it themselves, whereas the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* requires the offender to speak of it themselves—up to the account of Maudgalyāyana being rebuked—it may be asked:

why do these two texts contradict one another? The explanation is as follows: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* applies to cases where the five virtues [of the witnesses] are lacking or the three roots [of knowledge] are not clear;

therefore, the offender must speak of it themselves. The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*, however, is based on cases where the three roots are clearly established; therefore, [it does not require self-accusation].

If one speaks falsely, one merely incurs the *tshangs-pa'i phrin-las* (brahmadaṇḍa). Regarding the statement that Maudgalyāyana was rebuked during the recitation [of the precepts], according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is said:
Formerly, when the Buddha himself recited the precepts, there was a king who fashioned a golden lotus petal for the Buddha.
At the time of the *poṣadha*, the Buddha sat upon it and the bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform the *poṣadha*. Then, a golden lotus petal fell to the ground.
There was a bhikṣu who, acting according to his own will, tucked [a garment] under his arm. The Buddha remained seated in silence and did not perform the *poṣadha*.

When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda requested the Buddha to speak [the precepts]. As the middle and latter watches of the night passed, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "The assembly of monks has sat for a long time;
I pray that the Buddha will recite the precepts. The Buddha said, "The assembly is not pure. At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "Who is it that is impure?"
He then entered meditative concentration and observed that this evil bhikṣu was sitting among the assembly with his body concealed.
He went to where he was, seized him with his left hand, dragged him out to the door, and pushed him out with his right hand, saying: "From this day forward, you are no longer a śramaṇa.
The Buddha rebuked Maudgalyāyana, saying, "You must wait for him to speak for himself. Because of these words of the Buddha, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward..."
"You all should recite the precepts yourselves. The reason the Buddha does not recite them himself is that he has five hundred *vajra*-wielders at his side;
if, when the three questions for purity are asked, anyone fails to disclose their transgressions as they truly are, the *vajras* will strike them with their maces and crush them into fine dust.
Master Li said: "According to the meaning of this passage, it differs significantly from what was stated previously; I shall now explain it."
It is said: If one commits an offense within the mind and the three roots have not yet manifested, one must rely on the Vinaya texts and wait for the person’s own confession.

However, if one openly commits an offense, such as by keeping a wife and raising children, what need is there for a confession? One may, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, directly expel them from the community.
The purpose for which the *Śāstra* (Commentary) cites these two passages is as follows:

"The great assembly tolerates it, yet oneself and others alike are defiled" means that when one’s own person has violated the precepts, their substance is ruined and they are no longer a monk (*saṃgha*).

They are unfit to hear the recitation of the precepts and do not partake in the benefits and offerings of the *saṃgha*. Upon death, they enter the evil realms; this is called being "defiled by oneself. Yet, in this present life, they still improperly remain among the monks.

If one who presides over the ritual lacks the required number for the quorum, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) will not be accomplished, thereby misleading the assembly of monks; this is termed "corrupting others.
The above explanation of the first section—the two teachings of transformation (*vinaya*) and regulation (*śāsana*), clarifying their distinct characteristics—is now complete.

Second, regarding the regulations for the Saṃgha concerning communal meals, the conditions for their accessibility or obstruction are as follows: being pure in precepts and timely is termed "accessibility.

Conversely, if one has broken the precepts despite being timely, or possesses virtue but is untimely, this constitutes "obstruction. As for those who have committed grave offenses, been imprisoned, and then obtained release through an amnesty:
this refers to a bhikṣu who, having committed a grave offense, is confined by the leader of the community in an empty room, awaiting the arrival of a national amnesty.
To release him is called unlawful. Within the Buddha-dharma, how could such a thing exist? First, it is improper to bind, confine, or imprison him; second, it is not a matter for royal pardon.
As for "escaping by means of bribes," the *Shuowen* states: "To accept wealth while perverting the law is called *bó* (bribery).
It also says: "To offer wealth as a substitute for perverting the law. This is intended to clarify that although he has committed a grave offense and been imprisoned...
Regarding "prison": it refers to cases where one brings much money or valuables, and a monk, together with the community leaders or virtuous elders (*bhadanta*), seeks to secure one's release.

Regarding "seizing the property of thieves" or "seeking profit from profit," this refers to the regulations established by the Sangha: if there is private property belonging to a monk that has been stolen by thieves...
To seize it later is contrary to the Dharma; this is called "a thief seizing a thief.

Regarding the phrase "seeking profit through profit," this refers to those such as flower-gathering mendicants who preach the Dharma for others to cause them to abandon stinginess, yet subsequently seek wealth and property for themselves.
As Ci-yun said: "It is like a knowledgeable official who, on behalf of another, petitions a case and gives goods to the magistrate, while keeping the remainder for himself."

This is it. Regarding the phrase "not allowing those of the same dharma to follow as cited later," this refers to the various passages below that state "having no power, having no companion, one departs alone," and so forth.

It is like the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states: "If one does not [remain], one goes elsewhere after making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the Saṃgha. This means "if not, one goes to another place."
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning the enactment of illegal regulations, even down to the case where only three persons are permitted:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, at one time the bhikṣus of Campā were disputing with one another; those living together did not know [the truth], and one person accused another, and so on until many people were involved.
Regarding a large assembly: the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward, I authorize the practice of *dṛṣṭy-aniñjya* (the refusal to consent based on one's view).
As for *dṛṣṭy-aniñjya*: if within the Saṃgha there is a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that is contrary to the Dharma, those who have the power should intervene and say:
'Venerable elders, this is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; it should not be performed. [However,] if the person before you is wicked and possesses great power..."
If one fears that it will be difficult for them to grant their consent (*chanda*) to me, they should express their refusal to see (*dṛṣṭy-akāma*).

They should speak thus: "This is an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*); I cannot endure it. Having expressed their refusal to see, they should do so three times. When expressing this refusal to see, one must not go before that person to do so;
one should do so before a person who is in agreement. One may not perform the refusal to see before a group; it may be done before two or three people.
If others perform [an act] and one has already given their formal consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma and then departs, they are at fault.

If there is an illegal decision being made within the Saṃgha, and one neither objects, nor gives consent, nor expresses a lack of approval based on one's view, one commits an offense of violation of the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).

If one thinks, "I shall act according to my own karma," like a fire burning a house, and protects oneself by maintaining mental composure, there is no offense. This is called "not seeing" [the fault].

This refers to "desire. My personal interpretation is as follows: The previous statement that one "cannot have many performers" means that regarding the act of expressing disagreement (*na-kāma*), it is permitted for only three people to perform it, but not four.
Therefore, it is said that there cannot be a multitude. The *Karmavācanā-vṛtti* states:
"Expressing disagreement" refers to the lack of consensus among the six types of harmony; since it constitutes a difference of view, it does not carry the meaning of concordant harmony.
Question: Why not explain in full the arising of desire? Answer: If one were to explain "desire" in its entirety, desire is precisely the harmony of the passions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* (Mo-lun) stating that when a monk sees an illegal act and is unable to admonish it alone, he should remain silent as previously described:

this was already addressed in the preceding section on the General Exposition of Karmavācanā, where the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* cites the case of a bhikṣu who sees an illegal matter involving three, four, or five [monks].
If one is accompanied [by others], they may be admonished; if alone, it is unnecessary. One who violates an unlawful regulation incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The explanation of the meaning of "unlawful regulation" is hereby concluded.
Although certain rules were established by me in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that others may not practice elsewhere—

such as when there was a renunciant during the Buddha’s lifetime whom the Buddha ordered to shave his hair, yet today kings do not permit it, and thus it is said one should not practice it— Master Jing says:

"Just as the Buddha prohibited wandering after the summer retreat (*varṣā*), under current royal regulations, if one leaves the monastery for ten days without a valid reason, one is judged to have returned to lay life."

Furthermore, one must not practice [this]. Thus the commentary states: "The secular king established regulations for the Sangha that do not rely on the original scriptures"—this is precisely their meaning.
Regarding the punishment of Śāriputra for standing during the day: checking the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says that when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he established various rules for the bhikṣus.

The Buddha had finished establishing the dimensions for the *niṣīdana*. While the bhikṣus were gathered in the lecture hall, they discussed the matter together, saying, "The Buddha has prescribed the size of the *niṣīdana*.
If it is spread out where one sits, the two knees are not covered; if it is spread over the two knees, the sitting area is not covered.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Who is the senior elder (*sthavira*) among the Saṃgha? They replied: [Name].
“Śāriputra,” the Buddha said to Śāriputra, “many fellow practitioners of the holy life have been making this discussion.
Why did you listen in silence? You shall now be punished: stand upright in the middle of the day. Śāriputra accepted the punishment and immediately stood in the middle of the day.
The bhikṣus each went to the Buddha’s presence to confess their transgression regarding Śāriputra and to ask for forgiveness. The Buddha said, “The sun, the moon, and the stars...”
"One's past karma may still be turned back, but Śāriputra’s mind could not be turned back. Because he accepted my punishment, his mind was firm and unshakable.
[It is said that] in the past he had once been a snake... (and so forth). Jì remarked: "Śāriputra was a great general of the Wheel of Dharma;
if he had faults, they were still punished. Now, as for the monks and nuns of this final age, if they possess even a single practice or a single ability, at all times—"

To transgress the collective command is, in principle, not to rely upon the teaching. Question: For what reason, among the five hundred śrāvakas, are Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana alone designated as the "Great Generals of the Dharma Wheel"?
Answer: Because Devadatta broke the Saṃgha by destroying the Dharma Wheel, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were the foremost pair;
their power was able to suppress and eliminate [the schism], restoring harmony on that very day. For this reason, they are called the Great Generals. As it is said:
Now, when the Great General of the state is able to defeat the enemy, he is called the "Great General.
Devadatta, who split the Sangha and usurped the title of Buddha, is a great whale-like adversary; he is a thief who destroys the Wheel of Dharma. Śāriputra was able to subdue him.
Therefore, he is called the Great General. Furthermore, it is explained that Śāriputra was constantly able to subdue [opponents] when the Buddha preached the Dharma. As a sutra says:
"The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, is able to follow the Buddha in turning the Dharma. Thus, he is called the Great General of the Dharma Wheel.

Regarding the aforementioned instructions on the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-vidhi*) and formal procedures (*dharma-krama*): these constitute the Dharma-compliant regulations and must be observed according to principle.
As for rules established that are contrary to the Dharma, there is no fault even if they are transgressed. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the monastic regulations.

Second, regarding the discussion of what is permitted and what is obstructed in relation to the food of the Saṃgha: first, it is clarified in terms of the monastic and the lay; next, within the monastic community, it is clarified in terms of those who uphold and those who violate the precepts;

furthermore, among those who uphold them, it is clarified in terms of the proper time. In all these cases, there are both permissions and obstructions, for the [proper] time is a permission while the improper time is an obstruction.
Regarding "whether alms can be obtained or not": when the Buddha was in the world, all bhikṣus practiced begging for food, and the Buddha did so as well.

This refers to begging for alms. It is not only the case for bhikṣus; indeed, the Buddha himself begged for alms. Furthermore, there are four reasons for this: first, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for all Buddhas of the three periods of time to beg for alms;
second, it is to sustain the body and support one’s person, thereby providing benefit for one's own progress on the Path;
third, it is to provide merit and benefit to the donor as a reciprocal gift; and fourth, it is so that his śrāvaka disciples may emulate this established model.
Regarding the phrase "the methods of the ancient masters for rectifying the multitude" and so forth: "rectifying" (*kuāng*) means to correct.

This refers to the *Sìgào* (Monastery Edict) of Dharma Master Língyòu of Zhǐxiàng Monastery during the Cháng'ān period of the Sui dynasty. That monk was skilled at divination; it happened that he lived during the suppression of the Buddha-dharma by the Northern Zhou.

He continued to take refuge from the chaos in the Southern Mountains. At that time, by imperial decree, the monastic community was subjected to a thorough search, and all were ordered to return to lay life.
Those who refused were commanded to shave their heads deeply. Daoyou, however, donned secular clothing and remained in the mountains with his disciples.

Whenever he went out to practice divination, he used the money obtained to purchase rice, providing for his followers. Later, during the reign of the Sui dynasty, he was granted permission to be reinstated as a monk.
Tong was included among the number of the Ten Great Virtues (*daśa-mahāpuṇya*). Consequently, he established Zhixiang Monastery on the mountain where his original residence had been.
The Dharma Master personally composed the monastic regulations for the temple, stating: "Monks' temples must not keep female attendants (*karmadāna*).
Bin said: "Master Lingyou is the Upādhyāya of Master Xiu. [Another] said: "He is the Upādhyāya of Master Xuanzang. You originally resided in the capital.
The Master was born to a woman who sold *zhui* (a type of grain) in the Western Market. At thirteen years of age, he still resembled a young child.
He would play at tossing coins (*lianqian*) in the Western Market, attracting hundreds of onlookers. At that time, there was a Chan master walking through the market who happened to see this boy;
his clothes were extremely tattered, yet as he stood atop a well-railing tossing coins, he struck them one hundred times without missing a single throw.
It fell. [The boy] realized it was a wondrous object and went to ask where it had been. Daoyou said, "It was recently at such-and-such a street corner.
He immediately called out to him, saying, "Will you be able to go and leave the household life with me? He replied, "It depends on my mother. The Chan Master took him along to ask his mother.

The mother said, "Our family is poor; having given birth to this child, how could he possibly leave the household life? Furthermore, we have no means to support him. The Chan Master urged her earnestly. His mother—
He immediately granted permission, thinking, "What is the use of knowing [this] if it is of no benefit? On the following day, the Meditation Master came in person to take the garments.
Upon arriving at the temple, he brought a wall-beating iron mallet and ordered [Hui]you to grind it on a stone, saying, "I wish to make an axe.
You then began grinding it. For sixteen or seventeen days, he did not rest for even a moment. When one side was somewhat like an axe blade, the Master came.

Upon observing him, [the Master] recognized his resolve and intended to dismiss him immediately, saying, "I shall no longer employ you. The youth would not stop; [the Master] had already prepared an axe [to punish him].
How could he now regret it? He set the limit that once [the punishment] was completed, it would be final. The Master deeply respected and cherished him.

Later, he was taught the sutras and treatises, reaching mastery in everything. His fame spread throughout the world. By nature and in his conduct, he vowed never to look upon the face of a woman. When he was stricken by illness and at the point of death...

He died. A nun sister came to visit him; seeing him from afar, she entered the room and found him turned away with his face toward the wall. Furthermore, Dharma Master Jingying Yuan was a disciple of Huizhou.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, when he recited the *chanda* (consent) but did not emerge, Huizhou came out and went straight to the head of the hall.
His robes were coarse and tattered; no one recognized him, and none showed him respect. When it came time for the assembly to recite the *kāṣāya* (the precepts), he stopped them, saying:
"Huiyuan is currently reading a commentary in his room. This is a matter of Dharma practice; when the community of monks recites the precepts, how could this be the speech of a demon?"
The messenger reported this immediately, and Huiyuan came running, weeping and repenting his error. Only then did the assembly realize that he was the Venerable Huiyuan.

When it was said that "the temple is the realm where the Sangha cultivates the Way," it meant that the Sangha relies upon the temple to practice the Way, just as a king governs a nation by relying on the six great cities as his domain.
The commentary states: "Those who are laypeople (*avadātavasana*) and those among the clergy who can observe the fasts may also [participate]."
Lì (Lì Ming) says: Because one is able to observe the fast (*upavāsa*), this serves as the cause for attaining the Way in the future and becoming a renunciant.

Therefore, the opening of the five portions of food does not possess these characteristics [of the formal precept]. This is explained in detail in the section on the precept against stealing according to its specific manifestations (*anuvyañjana-śīla*).

Only those who act in accordance with the Way, like Hùfǎ (Hùfǎng), may rely upon it. Lì says: "Rèn" (to allow/rely) means "dàng" (to be fit/appropriate; pronounced in the departing tone). That is to say:
One should act according to the principles of the Way. For instance, when monks arrive, the bell is struck at the proper time; likewise, laypeople who come to observe the fast are also provided for.
This is called acting in accordance with the Dharma, and is therefore termed "relying on the Way. To deviate from this and not rely on the methods of the Way is called "not protecting the Dharma.

When it is said today that one "protects the Dharma together," it refers to the mutual dependence of the monastic and the laity, like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. If [this is not so]...

Regarding the giving of food: because the two great [monks] were criticized by the laity, they were permitted to give while observing the fast. If one were to give everything without exception, the laity would again say, "The Buddha-dharma ought to be like this.
Now, if one establishes an agreement regarding what is permitted and what is restricted, then they will likewise be able to protect the Dharma together.
Regarding the statement "not damaging the affairs of the donor": this means that because one acts in accordance with the principles of reason, one does not damage the affairs of the donor.
"Affairs" refers to the four types of material offerings. "Tān-yuè" (檀越) is a Sanskrit term; in this language, it means "donor" (dānapati).
"If this clarifies right and wrong by itself" concludes the preceding summary. Regarding "those who fear the manifold sufferings of the four enemies":

*māra* in Sanskrit means "the slayer," so called because it destroys the goodness of humans; in meaning, it is like an enemy. To speak of "the four enemies" is an explanation based on a numerical compound (*dvigu*).
First is the *kleśa-māra* (affliction demon), which refers to all afflictions such as greed that arise internally and are capable of harming [one].

First, the Māra of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-māra*). Second, the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), which refers to the mutual destruction and cessation of the five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).

Third, the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), which refers to the characteristic of impermanent cessation that can destroy the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Fourth, the Māra of the devas (*devaputra-māra*), who dwells in the sixth heaven of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the pinnacle of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Possessing great power, he delights in destroying the goodness of others; seeing a person enter the Path, he comes to disturb and confuse them, fearing their cultivation.

The Way unifies correctness; transforming others to be the same as oneself empties one’s objective realm. Among the four [māras], the first is the cause of birth and death, and the last is the condition for birth and death.
The two māras of the aggregates (*skandha*) and death are the fruits of birth and death. Furthermore, to clarify this in terms of the beginning and end, as well as the internal and external:
at the very moment of receiving birth, one inherits the body of the out-flowing five aggregates, which is called the *skandha-māra*—this is termed the "beginning."

The destruction of the physical form and the exhaustion of life is called the "death-māra" (*mṛtyu-māra*), which marks the end. The arising of the three poisons within is called the "affliction-māra" (*kleśa-māra*).

Because one externally encounters the "heavenly māra" (*devaputra-māra*), it is said to be "internal and external. Now, regarding the statement "fearing the four enemies," this refers to the period before leaving the household life;
out of fear of these māras, one leaves the household life. Having left the household life, one is then able to cause the māras to fear. Both interpretations apply to the preceding [context].

This is well understood. Therefore, the Commentary states: After leaving the household life, one attains the Way by means of the ten armies; thus, one destroys the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) by attaining the Dharma-body;

one destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) by attaining the path free from outflows (*anāsravamārga*); one destroys the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*) by attaining the immovable samādhi (*aniñjyasamādhi*);
and one destroys the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*). As for the ten armies: desire is the first army, continuing up to self-exaltation and the disparagement of others.

There are ten [points]. The remainder can be understood. Regarding the "three realms," these are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding "taking leave of the six kin," Master Ying says they are father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and children. Regarding the "five desires," these are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

Regarding "jealousy and narrow-mindedness" (*jì xiá*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "jealousy" (*jì*) means to avoid mentioning [something] (*huì*), and it also means "to loathe" (pronounced *wù gù*). This is seen in the *Maoshi*.
When we speak today of people who are narrow-minded, we mean to clarify that such individuals loathe hearing of fame that extends far and wide;

thus they are called "narrow-minded. Some editions read the character *jú* (constrained) instead of *jì*; would this not be laughable? Regarding "laughable" (*chī*): the *Guǎpǐ* states that "chī" means "to treat lightly. Others say it means "to laugh."
"Exposing the teeth is called *chi* (stinginess).

The commentary states that those who practice stinginess regarding food and eat alone are those whose karma leads them to become hungry ghosts (*preta*). This is intended to clarify that the causes for becoming a hungry ghost all stem from the habit of stinginess.
Once fallen into this realm, their retributive lifespan is vast and far-reaching. As recorded in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha Sūtra*, there was an arhat named Jñānottara.
Accompanied by his disciples, he traveled north toward India and arrived at a city of stone chambers. Upon reaching the outskirts of the city, his countenance turned somber.
He entered the city to beg for food; having finished eating, he exited through the city gate, his expression still somber.
His disciples then asked, "For what reason are you so sorrowful? He replied, "Just now, by the side of the city, I saw the son of a hungry ghost, who spoke to me, saying:"
"I have been by the city for seventy years. My mother entered the city for my sake to seek food, yet she never once obtained any. Now I am hungry and thirsty;
I pray that the Venerable One will enter and see my mother, and tell her to come quickly. I then entered the city and saw the mother of the hungry ghosts.
I said to her, "Your son is famished and exhausted; he longs to see you. She immediately replied to me, "I have entered this..."
In this city for over seventy years, due to my own meager merit, I have recently given birth.
Emaciated by hunger and lacking strength, although there was impure food consisting of pus, blood, mucus, saliva, and filth, those with great power took it first and I could not obtain any.
Now, having finally obtained a single mouthful of impurity, I wish to send it to my child; yet at the gate stands a powerful ghost. Furthermore—
"I am not permitted to go out. I pray that the Venerable One will take pity on me and bring me out with you, so that mother and son may see one another and eat this impurity.
The Venerable One then led him out of the city; mother and son met and ate the impurity together.
The Venerable One asked the ghost, "How long have you lived here? He replied, "I have seen this city form and perish seven times. The Venerable One sighed in admiration.
He said: "The lifespan of hungry ghosts is long, and their suffering is great. After the disciple had asked this, he felt weary of and detached from birth and death (and so forth).
This is like the shallow understanding of the vulgar; even a man of worldly knowledge who has attained insight still prioritizes concern for the Way over concern for greed.
That this bhikṣu would pose such a question is merely to be categorized with the vulgar—speaking of the shortcomings of a petty person.
Regarding "huái" (懷): the *Erlǐ* states that "suǒ" (瑣) means small; "suǒyù" (瑣玉) refers to broken jade, signifying the loss of wholeness.

This is like the growth and flourishing of heaven and earth, serving as a metaphor for the boundlessness of what is attained. As for "shānhǎi" (山海), it signifies that one's enjoyment is inexhaustible.
Therefore, regarding the statement in the *Buddhapiṭaka* that "even a single portion within the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa [white tuft]" and so forth:
in that sūtra, the Buddha told Śāriputra, "I now declare to you clearly: this True Dharma of mine will not remain long in the world. Why is this?

Because the merit and roots of goodness of sentient beings have been exhausted, and the age of turbidity is drawing near; they should cultivate revulsion toward worldly things and seek their own true benefit."
"O mind, you should apply yourself with diligent effort so that you may quickly attain the fruits of the Path. In my Dharma, there are no difficulties;
one need not concern oneself with clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. If one practices the Way with single-minded devotion, devas and humans alike will all offer their support with one heart.
Even if devas and humans were to neglect you, as long as you can remain single-minded and diligently practice the Way, you will ultimately have no need for clothing."
They shall have whatever food they require. Why is this? The treasury of merit of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and inexhaustible.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, even if one were to take but a single part from among hundreds of thousands of billions of parts within his ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair between the eyebrows) to provide for the śarīra relics and his disciples—even if all the people of the world were to leave the household life together and practice the Dharma as required—within those hundreds of thousands of billions [of parts],...
[It is] divided, yet not all of it is exhausted. The Tathāgata is likewise possessed of immeasurable merit. These bhikṣus should reflect in this manner;
they should not practice various forms of wrong livelihood or evil dharmas regarding the requisites they require.
Regarding the phrase "like a box and its lid fitting together," Sheng said: "The Sangha relies on the Way to receive offerings, which is like the box;

the donor gives for the sake of the Way, which is like the lid. Because these two correspond to one another, they are said to be 'fitting. Why worry about exhaustion? As for the term 'deprivation' (kui):"
Zheng Xuan says: "Kui" means deficiency. The *Shichuan* (Commentary on the Odes) says: "Kui" means exhaustion. This is as stated in the *Liji*: "Having wealth, one does not let it become kui.
Regarding the commentary's phrase "the meaning of practicing giving universally": "shī" (giving) refers to the act of providing. One does not discriminate between the noble and the humble;

the noble are provided with fine things, while the humble are provided with coarse things. Therefore, it is said: "One takes only after having fulfilled the righteous principle. [The term] "shuō" (to preach/explain) refers to the rotting of monastic grain.

This karmic offense is grave. As recorded in the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), when the Buddha and Ānanda entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, there was a large, deep pit outside the city walls.
The people of the city carried excrement and urine to discard into this pit.
When the heavens sent down foul rainwater, it too flowed into the pit. Within it lived a worm whose form resembled a human, possessing many hands and feet. From afar...
He saw the Tathāgata, who had raised his head above the water and was gazing at the Tathāgata with tears filling his eyes.
Having seen this, the Tathāgata felt pity and compassion, yet he appeared sorrowful and displeased. He immediately returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. At that time, Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Regarding the worm seen earlier in the excrement, what karmic actions did it perform in its previous life to be born in these waters? For how long has it been there? Furthermore, where..."
"At that time, you shall attain liberation. The Buddha said, "Listen well, all of you. In the past, immeasurable thousands of kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world.
Having completed his work of teaching and transforming beings, after his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka), a brāhmaṇa constructed a monastery (vihāra)."
While making offerings to the assembly of monks, a donor sent a great quantity of ghee and oil. At that time, some visiting bhikṣus arrived.

The administrative officer, the *karmadāna*, became angry and resentful; resenting the large amount of oil that had been brought, he concealed the ghee and oil, withholding them and not giving them to the visitors.
The assembly asked, "Why did you not pass on the ghee, oil, and honey? The *karmadāna* replied, "You guest bhikṣus said, 'This is a gift from a donor for the *saṃgha* present here.
At that time, the *karmadāna* was fierce, evil, and terrifying; he immediately cursed them, saying, "Why do you not eat excrement and urine?
Why do you come to me and demand ghee and oil? Because of these words, they were changed; from that time onward, [they acted accordingly].
For ninety billion kalpas, he constantly sat amidst such pouring water. The *karmadāna* (steward) of that time was this very insect (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "the path has not yet been traversed while the matter is obstructed": this clarifies the four types of offerings.
If these were cut off, it would be called an obstruction to the matter; now, one simply practices the Way without worrying about whether [the offerings] have been exhausted.
Regarding those who are people of supreme compassion: this refers to laypeople who, unable to observe the fast, refrain from giving food.

This is to uphold the Buddha’s teachings and to protect the Dharma of the Sangha. If one were to eat while not fasting and thus cause others to fall into hell through negligence, one would not be a person of compassion.
By not providing food, one ensures that sentient beings do not fall into the three evil realms due to such circumstances; this is called great compassion.
How tragic! To defile the Three Refuges means that if one bestows [the precepts] without inquiring whether [the recipient] is fit or unfit, the monastic and the laity become indistinguishable;

what then can serve as an object of refuge and reverence? To fail to recognize the boundaries of the honorable and superior, thereby giving rise to thoughts of contempt, is precisely the meaning of "defiling.
To be "enmeshed by the net of self-delusion" means not understanding the teachings on transgression and merit; this is to be ignorant of the proper timing and circumstances.
This refers to using a net.
According to the teachings, it should be prepared as described in the section on "following characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*).

As in the section on the precept against stealing, when wicked bandits arrive, one should prepare [the defense] at that time, regardless of their number. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this applies even to wicked bandits, donors, public artisans, and so forth.

If kings or ministers possess the power to cause harm or benefit, one should provide them with food and drink. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is improper to give to those who can cause harm while withholding from those who can benefit;
such an act constitutes a violation of the rules for defiling a household. The explanation of the meaning of what is permitted and what is prohibited is hereby concluded.

Second, regarding the citation of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*), there are three levels in total: namely, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).

Regarding the statement that "when the *saṃgha* eats, one should perform four gestures": *Saṃgha* here is translated as "the great assembly," meaning that when the monastic community (*saṃgha*) eats, these gestures must be performed.

As the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika-śāstra* (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhāṣika-śāstra), fascicle seven, states: "When it is time for the *saṃgha* to eat, one should perform four kinds of gestures. First..."
First, strike the *gandī*; second, blow the conch; third, beat the drum; fourth, proclaim the announcement so that it may be heard and known within the boundary.

These four types of signs must necessarily have fixed limits; one must not at times strike the *gandī* and at other times beat the drum and blow the conch, causing the ritual procedures to become confused and lacking definite rules, thereby failing to establish the monastic dharma.
If these four signs are not performed, yet one consumes the monastery’s food offerings...
This is impure and is called "stealing the *saṃghī*. *Saṃghī* is a Sanskrit term; the distinction lies between masculine and feminine sounds.
When pronounced with a masculine sound, it is called *saṃghī*; when pronounced with a feminine sound, it is called *saṃgī*, or sometimes *saṃgha*.

These differences also reflect the lightness or heaviness of the vocal tones. *Gī* (third tone), *gī* (first tone), *ka* (third tone), *ga* (first tone), *qí* (first tone), *jīn* (third tone)—all of these belong to the Siddham script.
In this chapter: first, the term *varga* (chapter/section) is translated as "assembly" (*gaṇa*). Regarding those who commit an offense even while intending to prevent it by making a formal gesture:
nowadays, when striking the bell at dawn, one must first open the monastery gate; to strike the bell while the gate remains closed is contrary to the Dharma.
As for the statement that each has its beginning and end, and that the *Mahāsāṃghika* school maintains the same *poṣadha* until purity is attained without fault, this refers to the following:

This dharma concerns the boundaries for communal versus separate meals. Since the meals are taken separately, each group should strike their own bell to assemble; there is no fault in not assembling with one another.
Regarding the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it states that when fruit is found in an empty monastery, the *gandī* (wooden gong) should be struck for those who eat.

This clarifies that this applies specifically to the two times of eating—morning and noon—and is not appropriate for improper times (*vikāla*). Some say that it may be done at both proper and improper times, but this is not so.
It is also permissible to take fruit at that time and press it to make a juice. If one says this is not allowed, where could one escape the fault regarding tea and soup nowadays?
As for the instruction "at least three claps of hands," it means one should strike them three times.
The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Regarding the rules for the communal meal (*saṃgha-bhakta*), there should be a fixed limit, whether it be much or little.
Jing says: "This refers to times of scarcity; both increasing or decreasing [the portion] constitutes the offense of theft" (and so forth).

During the Xianheng era, when the National Teacher Nanshan was at the Qingguan Daochang in the capital, there was a famine that year. At that location, there were about fifty monks, and each day they received a ration of rice.
Four *dou* [of grain] are to be provided for the assembly of disciples. Regardless of how many monks come and go, the limit is strictly these four *dou*.

This is the current interpretation. Regarding the case of mistakenly receiving an extra portion of cake, Jing says: "This applies to both times of plenty and scarcity; in either case, one commits an offense.

Since the administrator has established a fixed limit, even receiving an extra portion by mistake constitutes the transgression of theft. How much more so, then, would there be no guilt in demanding more than that?"
The Vinaya states that when an evil bhikṣu arrives, one should not give him food. Someone asked:

"If laypeople who observe the fasts are permitted to receive food, and since those who have broken the precepts are still members of the Saṃgha and can likewise observe the fasts now, why may they not be given food? The explanation says:

"That laypeople who observe the fasts possess the karma for future transcendence of the world is clear; by the same principle, it should also be understood regarding those of the class who have broken the precepts."
To bypass the ordained order of monks when selecting guests is, conversely, to violate that order. In this regard, it is clarified that there is a monastery;
if one bypasses the order of monks during the hall ceremony (*saṅgha-krama*) to select someone from among those staying in the quarters, all such individuals commit the offense of theft.

Furthermore, because this dwelling is not called a "monastery" (*saṃghārāma*), the selection of guests and hosts does not carry the same meaning as communal harmony (*sāmagrī*). This is a natural precept (*prakṛti-śīla*); its violation constitutes the grave offense of theft, resulting in karmic retribution.
Furthermore, it is profound. Thus, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: While Maudgalyāyana was traveling along a road, he saw a sentient being whose body was extremely large.
Upon its head it bore a copper cauldron that was blazing intensely; molten copper filled the cauldron and poured over its body as it traveled through the air, wailing and crying out in distress.
The Buddha said: "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this was a renunciant who served as an administrator for the Saṅgha..."
When a donor gave food and drink to be distributed among the Sangha, there were many visiting bhikṣus at that time.
Because the administrators did not share [the offerings] with them, they waited until the guests had departed before dividing it. Due to this cause, for immeasurable years they fell into hell.
They undergo great suffering and distress. Having escaped that, they again receive this body. Furthermore, one sees another sentient being whose tongue is long and wide;
blazing iron nails are driven haphazardly into its tongue as it travels through the air, weeping and wailing. The Buddha said:
"In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a renunciant bhikṣu who served as a *karmadāna* (steward). This *karmadāna* rebuked a visiting bhikṣu, saying:"
"This place is impoverished; we cannot provide for one another. Venerable elders, each may go as you please to seek a place of abundance and joy.
Because of these words, those who had previously resided there all departed, and future guests did not come.

Due to this stinginess, they fell into the great hells and underwent all manner of suffering. Having finally escaped from there, they again received this body—this is what is meant by "selecting" [the body].

Regarding the point that severing the relationship between guest and host is not the same as the meaning of being in harmony with the Saṃgha: the Saṃgha possesses the six kinds of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*). Since [the person in question] does not share in the common benefit, the meaning of being a member of the Saṃgha is also deficient.

Concerning those who are weary of and distressed by birth and death, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* verse states: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise, abide, undergo transformation, and perish. Thus it is explained.
It is said: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) each possess four characteristics, namely: arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and destruction (*bhaṅga*).

Because they originate within the world, they have arisen; because their own functions are established, they have endured; because their momentum declines, they have changed; and because they perish, they are destroyed.
Furthermore, one should contemplate this body from the feet to the crown of the head as being filled with various kinds of impurities and foulness.

Observing this form to be like a fierce wind scattering a heap of sand until it vanishes in an instant—one who contemplates in this way obtains the seed of the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

Becoming weary of and disenchanted with that cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) without taking pleasure in it, one obtains the seed of the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Having become disenchanted with birth and death, he correctly directed himself toward nirvana and attained the seeds of the signless door of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
Furthermore, in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, it is said that seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was the Venerable Gijjha who had personally attained arhatship.

He was highly esteemed by the people of the kingdom and resided in Kaśmīra. At that time, two bhikṣus from South India, having heard that Jīvaka (Jñeyadatta) possessed great majestic virtue, traveled a long distance to pay their respects and visit him.
Upon reaching his dwelling, they passed beneath a tree on the way and saw a bhikṣu there.
His physical form was extremely emaciated. He was tending a fire before the hearth. The two men asked him, "Do you know Jīvaka?
Where is his dwelling? He immediately pointed out the location. When they went forward and saw the bhikṣu who had previously been tending the fire, they wondered at the reason for this:
"Since he possesses such renown and virtue, why does he naturally tend a fire? The Venerable One replied, "I contemplate the suffering of birth and death in the past."
"If even my own head, hands, and feet could be burned for the sake of the Sangha, I would do so; how much more so the burning of firewood?
The two men then asked, "What were the painful circumstances of your past births and deaths?

He replied, "I recall that throughout five hundred lifetimes among dogs, I was constantly tormented by hunger and thirst. Only on two occasions did I obtain full satisfaction: once when I encountered a drunken man..."
A man vomited wine onto the ground and attained peaceful satiety. Second, he encountered a husband and wife who lived together for their livelihood;
the husband had gone to the fields, and the wife had gone out on account of her young child. At that time, I entered to steal their rice.

Because the mouth of their rice vessel was small, although my head managed to enter, it was difficult to withdraw. Although I obtained one full meal, I subsequently suffered great hardship. The husband returned...
The field was returned. He then had the dog’s head cut off and placed inside a vessel. At that time, two bhikṣus heard this account;
weary of the suffering of birth and death, they attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

Furthermore, Śākyamuni Tathāgata recalled a past life when he was a worm in Jambudvīpa, boring through the great earth of Jambu as if sifting through it with a sieve. Possessing few desires and tranquility, he cultivated mindfulness.
Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: Although those who have left the household life have not yet attained the Way, they take seclusion as their medicine.

For laypeople dwelling amidst the clamor of female beauty and worldly distractions, there is ultimately no peace or happiness. Furthermore, if one practices seclusion, the mind easily becomes tranquil;
like water that is not disturbed, it naturally becomes clear and limpid. Moreover, this method of seclusion is for the sake of the [beings] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is praised by the Buddha. How is this known to be so? When the Buddha saw bhikṣus sitting in meditation within a village settlement, his mind was not pleased;
yet when he saw bhikṣus sleeping in a secluded place (araṇya), he rejoiced. This is because being near a village settlement involves many distracting conditions.
One whose mind is distracted from meditative concentration fails to attain what should be attained and fails to realize what should be realized.
Even if one sleeps or lies down in an empty place and takes a brief rest, if one subsequently arises to seek concentration, one can gather the scattered mind and thereby attain liberation.

Furthermore, in an empty place, there are no signs such as forms, and thus afflictions are easily severed; it is like fire that naturally extinguishes when there is no fuel. What is called "mindfulness of concentration" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
This refers to the [meditative] bases. As for "concentration," it refers to the four dhyānas, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments; these are left to the speaker [to elaborate].

Regarding "guarding the precepts with shame and remorse," the Satyaka-nirgrantha Sūtra states: "For those who wish to leave behind birth and death and reach nirvāṇa in peace and security, all Tathāgatas have said that maintaining the precepts is foremost.
The precepts are like pure ground, capable of producing the flowers of all virtues. It also says:
Just as a fierce, blazing fire can burn away all evil weeds, for this reason one must protect the precepts. Regarding "shame and remorse" (*hrī-apatrāpya*):
one feels shame before kings, parents, teachers, and the Sangha; that the grace of their faithful offerings is difficult to repay and difficult to requite. Furthermore, one feels shame and remorse.
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly instruct me, yet I am unable to practice accordingly. For this reason, the Sūtra states:
"Those who lack a sense of shame and remorse are no different from birds and beasts. However, it is sufficient that five persons remain pure and uphold the Dharma according to the Law;

this clarifies that as long as these five persons who maintain the Vinaya exist in the world, they can perform the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the reception of precepts, thereby enabling the Buddha-Dharma to endure.
It remains for a long time without perishing.
Regarding the phrase "waiting upon the king and others," according to the *Suixiang* (隨相), one may use nineteen coins to provide offerings for the king and his ministers.

If more than this is used, it is necessary in principle to inform the assembly. The various points discussed above, though differing in detail, all collectively explain the second section concerning monastic regulations.
The discussion on the principles of the gate of "openness and closure" regarding communal meals is hereby concluded.
From this point forward, we shall properly clarify the third section, which explains matters according to the dharma and in relation to specific times.

That which must be performed before the *poṣadha* (confession of offenses) when the Saṃgha cannot reach harmony includes, for example, the formal authorization (*jñapti*) to receive the day’s duration, the appointment of the steward (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), and the distribution of the property of the deceased.

If one raises a charge that is groundless and leaves no remainder, it is because the four pārājika offenses have been committed; thus, one’s connection to the community is severed, which in meaning is like having one's head cut off—hence it is called "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*).
Because the three grounds [for accusation] have not been manifested, it is called "groundless" (*amūlaka*). Although the person who makes the accusation has raised the charge, it is not established.

This refers to the obstruction of such an accusation; therefore, the path is not established as being obstructed. As for the phrase "to punish the offense of slander," [in the case of] slandering someone of *pārājika* status, it must be...

[The offense] is treated as *śeṣa* (residual); [if it is] slanderous, it is treated as *pāyattika*. Regarding the statement that "the text does not clarify whether the facts of the case are true or false," Hui-li says:
"In that text, it does not say that one must inquire into whether the person being accused has actually committed an offense or not. If there is an offense, it is called 'false.

However, it simply requires that the person making the accusation not have cultivated the three roots [of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion]; in all such cases, the charge of slander is established. Hui-ji says: "As for that person who..."

One who is constantly remembered and constantly comes may not be separated from others; therefore, it is unnecessary to grant them the formal act (*dharma*). Even if granted, it would be merely nominal.

Whether they come or do not come, this one case requires the granting of the *karmavācanā*, because since their presence is uncertain, the formal act must be used to bind them. It is established as the "insane *karmavācanā*.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a person cannot be found after searching, the formal act must be granted remotely. According to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it must be performed in their presence; [this is done by] the motion (*jñapti*).

Second, it must be granted to them. Furthermore, it is necessary that the one who is insane know that the Saṃgha is performing the ritual for his sake; if he does not know this, it is not accomplished.
According to the Vinaya, if one actually has an illness but adds [the pretext] of a legal procedure, it only succeeds as a fraudulent act. In principle, fraud is not permissible.
The following clarifies the meaning in response to the specific cases. Regarding "the devas and nāgas concur and praise": Master Ying explains that "xie" (叶) means harmony, agreement, or accord.
As for the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that "a bhikṣu’s robes are impure and subject to reproach by non-humans," this establishes that there are many kinds of impurity.
First, it refers to the impurity of the robe's substance itself; that is, clothing and wealth obtained through wrong livelihood, such as through trade and selling. Furthermore...

Although it may be the substance of what is in accordance with the Dharma, if one does not undertake its formal acceptance or fails to observe the rules regarding duration and so forth, it is also called impure.
Furthermore, although one may avoid these two faults, if it is made of a vessel with many flaws, it is also called impure; in both cases, it is censured by non-human beings.

Regarding the recitation of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (or *saṃghabhadra*): In the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, there was the householder Śrīgupta, who, having been instigated by a non-Buddhist, intended to kill the Buddha by offering him food mixed with poison for the Buddha and the Saṃgha. The Buddha knew of this immediately;

he instructed the monks to wait until the *saṃghabhadra* had been recited before consuming the meal, and then he spoke this verse in the presence of the elder: "Standing before the elder, I shall recite the *saṃghabhadra*."
[The meal] was finished. All poisons were eliminated. "You all may eat as much as you wish. Once he had spoken this verse, the food transformed into something sweet and delicious.
The circumstances of this are somewhat extensive; one may consult that treatise for further details. Master Li states: "This is precisely the method for providing equal offerings.

Regarding the instruction that when laypeople come, one should give them food and preach the Dharma for them, Master Li clarifies that one should explain to them that 'meritorious food is difficult to digest,' thereby demonstrating [the gravity of the matter]."
The cause and effect [of this matter] (I fear does not admit of such an interpretation). It should follow the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: one who is capable of observing the fast should provide food;
once they have eaten, one should preach the Dharma to them and confer the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, and so forth.
Regarding "one who brings disgrace to the family through *pai*-style speech" (*pai* is pronounced with the *pi* rhyme): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "mockery.

According to this, a *pai* is what performers do—acting out jests to amuse themselves. The *Sancang* states that a *pai* is "whistling. Others say it refers to the performance of *pai-xie* (comic satire).
This is according to the precedent of the leader of the procession.
As for other superior dyed colors, these refer to true crimson and pure purple.

Regarding the "five dharmas for entering the assembly and knowing how to sit and rise" mentioned in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, in the section on the "addition of five [dharmas]" below, the Buddha addressed the monks:
Monks, when entering the midst of the Saṃgha, there are five preliminary practices one should observe: first, one should maintain a mind of loving-kindness;

second, one should humble oneself like a cloth used for wiping dust; third, one should know well how to sit and rise—upon seeing a senior elder (sthavira), one should not remain seated comfortably, and upon seeing a junior monk, one should not stand up;
fourth, having entered the midst of the Saṃgha, one should not engage in miscellaneous talk concerning worldly matters; fifth, [one should observe] what is seen...
If there is a matter within the Saṃgha that can be endured, yet one’s mind cannot endure it, one should remain silent.
A bhikṣu should first possess these five qualities before entering the midst of the Saṃgha; if explained in detail, they will appear in the text below.
Regarding "jacket pleats" (*zhe*): the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states that a *zhe* resembles a short tunic (*ru*) with large sleeves and a decorative border (*lan*) at the hem.

As stated in the memorial from the Great Jing'ai Temple in the Eastern Capital: the temple master regulates the assembly; neither the ordained monks nor the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) are permitted to wear trousers.

He dispatches his household members to conduct successive inspections, and those caught wearing them are stripped and placed in the outer storehouse. This is conducted according to the established regulations.
"Retaining the defiled and expelling the pure, while birth and death have no end": women are a defiled realm; to support them is called "retaining.
When a pure monk withdraws from the Path and is banished, it is called "expelling. This is intended to clarify that keeping women within the monastery is what causes a bhikṣu to retain defilement.
If they commit a grave offense through mutual defilement, they shall be expelled and return to lay life; this is called "departing from purity.

Consequently, when this person's retribution for hellish sins is exhausted, they emerge as animals and the like, thereby losing the fruits of the Path of the Three Vehicles. Hence it is said: "Birth and death have no end."
Regarding the frequent confusion between monastics and laypeople due to the failure to demarcate pure areas (*śuddhasthāna*), Shenxiu stated:

"It is a confusion when one falsely claims that an area within a monastery is a 'pure area of a donor' (*dānapati-śuddha*) when it has not been formally demarcated as such. For example, regarding all food and drink in the East and West Chan Temples established during the Sui dynasty..."
All of this is provided as an offering by the state; originally, it did not belong to the monks. This is termed "pure for the donor" (*dānapati-śuddha*).

If one were to claim that places like Guoqing Temple today—which was also established by the Sui dynasty—have no food offerings and that everything there is merely monastic food, yet still assert it is "pure for the donor," such a claim would be confused.
Therefore, it is said that the distinction between the clergy and the laity is conflated. To speak of the "Way" (*dao*) refers to its practice.
The Dharma is bound by the *jñapti-dvitīya* [formal motion]. Therefore, it is so called.
Regarding the phrase "the flow and succession of non-restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*)," the verse from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The flow and succession constitute Virtuous and non-virtuous precepts; Toward all sentient beings, There is restraint and non-restraint. The commentary explains: "The *prātimokṣa* restraint..."
"Vow" (saṃvara) refers to receiving the precepts toward all sentient beings; it is the non-interruption of the precepts at all times.
"Non-vow" (asaṃvara) refers to abiding in an evil vow; it is the non-interruption of evil precepts toward all sentient beings at all times.

This includes, for example, sheep-butchers, poultry-raisers, pig-breeders, bird-catchers, fishermen, hunters, thieves, and executioners. An "executioner" (sūnika) is one who kills people to make a living. This...
This is an example of such cases. For instance, consider a sheep-butcher: although he does not kill other sentient beings, he incurs non-restraint (asaṃvara) with respect to all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because if any sentient being were to appear before him in the form of a sheep, he would give rise to a mind of harm toward them all;
for it is possible for any sentient being to become a sheep. Furthermore, even if [he does not actually do so], [the non-restraint remains].

Regarding the logic of sheep-slaughterers: since they harbor harmful intent even toward those [animals], they incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Just as one who dwells in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) extends the perception of benevolence universally, it should be understood that the same applies to those dwelling in other forms of non-restraint.
[The author] establishes this to clarify that there exists such a thing as "evil discipline" (*duḥśīla*).
It flows constantly from moment to moment; it arises perpetually without effort. It is just like when one receives the precepts of a virtuous restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*):

once they have been generated, even while one enters into the midst of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the wholesome continues to increase without interruption. Therefore, it is called "continuous" (*saṃtati*).
If there are those who do not maintain or adorn the Buddha halls, stupas, and temples, consider how in secular life parents are taught to revere the ancestral temple;

even Ding Lan’s wooden mother would show a smiling face when he returned from his duties. Now that I have left the household life, if I do not encounter a true Buddha and yet fail to revere the sacred images, from whom shall my teacher receive [the Dharma]?

Liuming, these days many monks and nuns commit this transgression; they merely cultivate— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "but cultivate" (但修). The translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.*
They decorate their own quarters and vie with one another to make them splendid, yet within the Buddha hall, the dust and filth are beyond description.
Though they claim to have shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes to become disciples of the Buddha, how could such be the way of serving one's teacher? Other matters may be inferred from this.
As for those who gather at the temple gate instead of assembling at the proper time—such as the ranks of junior monks and ignorant elders—they mostly congregate at the gate.

In a monastery, observe the conduct of the men and women as they go about their business; some lean against the gate or sit and stand there. When the temple bell is struck for the ritual of worshipping the Buddha, not a single person may come.
Thus it is said that "they do not assemble at the proper time. This is truly due to the presiding masters being unskilled in guiding and gathering the community—a most lamentable state of affairs.

Regarding the terms "Elder" (Upādhyāya) and the "Three Teachers," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The one who is foremost among people is called an Elder; this does not refer exclusively to those with white hair."
The "three masters" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the two instructors (*ācārya*); these are called the three.

As for the phrase "if other monks do not come, they are all treated according to this analogy," it means that even those who are critically ill are still sent to be gathered [at the assembly], let alone those who are otherwise free from ailment;
it is logically necessary that they attend. From this point downward begins the fifth major section, which correctly elucidates the method of instruction.

Regarding the practice of first desiring [the offender's] confession before offering admonition: this means that one must first go to a secluded place and ask the person who has committed the transgression, saying:
"Venerable sir, since you have committed such-and-such an offense, can it be confessed? For the precepts are subtle while people are coarse;

they are difficult to maintain and easy to violate—who could be without fault? It is valued that one may confess early. If the person replies, "I have indeed committed it," and the assembly is permitted to discipline them, only then...
One can treat it; therefore, it is called "taking up desire. This is merely another name for "seeking to hear [the Dharma].
As for the phrase "a single thought of evil" and so forth in other sutras, these "other sutras" refer specifically to the *Śīlasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Regarding the passage in the Vinaya concerning Ānanda’s white hair and so forth:

consulting the Vinaya text, it says that Ānanda had sixty disciples, all of whom were young and wished to abandon the precepts and return home. Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "This assembly is about to perish;
you, being young, do not realize this. Ānanda replied, "Venerable One, my head has already shown white hairs. Why [do you say this] to me, Kāśyapa?"
"Is it because you cannot avoid being young? Kāśyapa replied, "You associate with young bhikṣus;

you do not properly restrain your sense faculties; you do not know moderation in eating; during the first and last watches of the night, you are unable to practice diligently; you visit every household, merely acting like a grain-thresher;
your followers shall surely be lost. Furthermore, the *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merit) states that Kāśyapa often referred to Ānanda as...
The novice Ānanda had a sister who was a nun; upon hearing these words from Kāśyapa, she became greatly resentful, saying, "Ānanda is intelligent and profoundly learned;
why do you call him a 'child'? Kāśyapa replied to the nun, "Ānanda has two things that are shameful:
it is precisely because Ānanda urged the Buddha to ordain women that the Dharma will perish five hundred years sooner."
First: Furthermore, Ānanda had sixty disciples; recently, thirty bhikṣus returned to lay life.
Now, according to the Buddha’s dharma for ordaining disciples: if one who has left home comes seeking the Way with faith, they should be tested for seven days;
if a follower of an external path comes seeking the Way, they should be tested for four months. Yet Ānanda ordained them as soon as they arrived. This is [the first point].
Secondly, it was because they felt ashamed. As for why these thirty bhikṣus returned home:

previously, they had heard that Ānanda was foremost among the ninety-six types of practitioners in the equality of wisdom (*samatājñāna*). They sought ordination from Ānanda with the desire to study this equality of wisdom.
However, because Ānanda did not explain the equality of wisdom to them, their original intention was not fulfilled, and so they returned. Thus they returned.
They must have slandered Ānanda, claiming he lacked "equalizing wisdom" (samatājñāna). Because this bhikṣuṇī harbored a heart of malice toward Kāśyapa, she entered hell in her very body.
Some say that "equalizing wisdom" is conventional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna);

it is also called "subsequently attained wisdom" (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) and is likewise termed "equalizing wisdom. One must first realize fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), and only thereafter realize conventional wisdom.
One must first realize fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and subsequently, from that very foundation, flow forth conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). A guest remarked:

"The old name for this was 'equality-wisdom' (*samatā-jñāna*); in the new sūtras and śāstras, it is called 'conventional wisdom. This is because conventional wisdom universally takes all phenomena as its object."
Therefore, names such as "equal" are established. Ji says: Kāśyapa was the preceptor (upādhyāya) of Ānanda, and that Ānanda received the full ordination through the *karmavācanā* ceremony.
As for the statement above regarding one who does not know contentment with food, this does not refer to greed for wealth and profit; rather, it refers to a craving for the Dharma (*dharmarāga*).
The treatise explains that this means craving extensive learning and broad knowledge, so called because he had not yet realized the stage of *aśaikṣa*. The Vinaya text states:
"One who does not know contentment in eating is a 'grain-consuming worm. As for the statement that even those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) were still subject to reproach:
regarding the term 'those beyond training' used here in the text, at the time Kāśyapa rebuked him, he was still a learner (*śaikṣa*);
it was only at the time of the Council (*saṃgīti*) that he realized arhatship."
"May it be understood according to the preceding text" refers to what was stated in the Preface above: "In propagating the teachings in a region, the established laws must be universal;

when presiding over an assembly to adjudicate matters, one must rely upon the Vinaya teachings. This is precisely its meaning. The explanation of the Seven Sections [of the Prātimokṣa] is hereby concluded.

Chapter Eight: The Collection of Circumstances for Receiving the Precepts.

The preceding chapters have collectively elucidated the monastic laws, manifesting their virtues and functions, detailing the sequence of administration, and providing the structural framework for the Buddha-dharma.
He presides over all practices; his virtue and morality are fully cultivated within, making him capable of generating goodness in others.

Regarding the method for generating goodness, none is more primary than receiving the precepts. Therefore, this chapter has come forth. Furthermore, having explained the preceding "Chapter on the Monastic Hierarchy," one eliminates excess and removes abuses;
by adhering to these rules, one becomes capable of wielding authority and applying it to affairs. Although affairs have many paths, they do not exceed the generation of goodness and...
The method for extinguishing evil and giving rise to goodness is precisely the reception of the precepts.

Therefore, following the regulations for the monastic administration, the reception of the precepts is now clarified so that the transmission of instructions has a source and the teachings do not decline. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"If my disciples practice this from one to another, then the Dharma-body will remain eternally present and never perish. Regarding the intent behind the regulation, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

To begin with, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he did not wish to increase the various realms of existence (*bhava*), but sought rather the extinction of desire; thus he established the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*).
Now, morality is the primary foundation for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and the root of all practices. If this root is not established, upon what else can one rely?

It is simply because during the Buddha’s lifetime, those with sharp faculties were in accord with his diligent efforts and thus attained realization (the "deluded" being those who required the precepts). In these latter times, however, the era is degenerate and the people are insincere; thus the Sage’s regulations allow for certain conditions, and those conditions...

When conditions assemble, the work of practice is accomplished; when conditions disperse, the virtue of the precepts cannot be established. One must rely on conditions to determine whether success will be attained.

The Great Sage proclaimed that if there are deficiencies in the various conditions, one may receive the precepts yet fail to obtain their fruit. Therefore, it is necessary to strike the palms together and manifest the ritual with full exposure; this is certainly not in vain. Thus, I now explain this clearly.
Furthermore, it is said that among the primary duties of one who has left the household life, the precepts alone are supreme and exalted; therefore, they are established.

Regarding the conditions for receiving [the precepts], this clarifies their principles. Master Li stated: "Although there are five types of conditions for receiving [the precepts], if we speak of the final age, there is only the single method of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

Among the five ways of receiving—namely, *svāgata* (welcoming), *uttamadharmā* (superior dharma), the three refuges and eight precepts (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), and *karmavācanā*—only the single reception by *karmavācanā* possesses six superior qualities.
First, it is long-lasting, meaning it extends through both the present and the future. Second, its location is universal, encompassing all three regions."

Excluding Uttarakuru, [the three continents] include both men and women; the four ranks encompass both ordinary beings and sages; the fifth point concerns those to whom it applies, who are innumerable;

the sixth concerns those who mostly perform the ritual while seated. Bin said: "This refers to the simultaneous and separate assembly of monks in the three continents for the purpose of conferring the precepts upon individuals.
By these various principles, the beginning and end of the Buddha-dharma take the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) as its fundamental core.

It is able to continue the Three Jewels and perform boundless benefit; it possesses the merit of sustaining [the Dharma], and no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is greater than this, which is why it is said to be supreme.

Among the other four types of ordination (*upasampadā*), the single ordination by "Welcome" (*svāgata*) lasted until the end at the Twin Sala Trees. As for the other three types of ordination, they ceased during the intermediate period.

Furthermore, they were restricted to Jambudvīpa and did not encompass the other three continents. There are differences in rank between ordinary beings and sages, and their retribution is limited to the male and female genders. In contrast—
Regarding the first six meanings, each lacks mutual completeness and the merit of their succession is slight; therefore, they are called the "four minor" [meanings].

Now, we establish [the meaning] according to what is preeminent, which clarifies only the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). As for the phrase "the gathering of conditions for receiving the precepts," Xuanchao says:
