when one first gives rise to the essential vow and the conditions gather to form the requisite assembly, taking the dharma into one's own mind is termed "receiving"; this is precisely the moment of reception, wherein the mind guards against external objects, which is termed [the "reception"].
Jielì (Jie-li) said: "When one first resolves upon the essential vow and establishes the will for accomplishment, taking the Dharma into one's heart—this is termed 'receiving' [the precepts].

Because this receiving involves a long-term, preventative protection, it is designated as 'precepts' (*śīla*). A Vinaya Master asked: 'The unmanifested (*avijñapti*) lasts for the duration of one's life; it can be called a long-term preventative protection.

But once the manifested (*vijñapti*) precept has already fallen away, how can it be called a long-term preventative protection? He replied: 'The unmanifested arises from the manifested; therefore, the two..."*
They are both suspended as a defense. Furthermore, it is said: to establish a solemn vow and commitment, internalizing the Dharma within the mind, is called "receiving" (śīla).

Because they both serve the function of prohibiting what is improper, they are designated as "precepts" (vinaya). Therefore, it is called "receiving the precepts. As for the term "convergence of conditions": the teacher, the monastic community, the robes and bowl, and the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* constitute the conditions.
When these ten types of arrangements gather together in one place, it is called "convergence. This refers to the proclamation of the ritual procedures.

To "touch" [the precepts] is what is called the Dharma; therefore, it is said: "The Dharma of the assembly of conditions for receiving the precepts. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the assembly of conditions for receiving the precepts":

this refers to the mind that is capable of receiving them. "Mind-precepts" refers to the Dharma that is received. "Conditions" (pratyaya) clarifies that this receiving of the precepts arises from conditions.
"Assembly" (samudaya) means the gathering together of many conditions; it is so named because they assemble. Furthermore, as for the term "conditions," it is as follows:

The recipients listed above are five in number, while those corresponding to them are six; both constitute the conditions (*pratyaya*). It is further stated that there are five kinds of conditions according to the Vinaya: first, the "Come Hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*);

second, the "Superior Dharma," also known as the "Breaking of the Fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*); third, the "Threefold Utterance" (*tri-vācikā*); and fourth, the "Eightfold Respectful Observances" (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
This is the fifth *karmavācanā*. Regarding the term "Come, O Worthy One" (*ehi bhikṣu*): this refers to one who has already attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

Such a person, impelled by the power of past virtuous karma, arrives just as a Buddha has appeared in the world. Upon hearing the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, they realize the first fruit of the Path and seek ordination out of compassion.

The Buddha commands them, "Come," and they immediately receive the precepts. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "When the 'Come, O Bhikṣu' is spoken, the hair and beard fall away of their own accord, and the saffron robe [appears]."

Clad in robes, his deportment was composed and orderly, as if he were one who had studied the Dharma for twenty years. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Having chanted 'Sādhu' (well done), eight matters follow him.
Second, regarding the "superior Dharma" (*uttara-dharma*): its position lies in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The Vinaya says:

"If a person cultivates the path and attains arhatship, they are then called one who has gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*); this is the precept. That untainted, true Dharma transcends the realm of learning (*śaikṣa*). He attained [this].

The Dharma is supreme; therefore, it is called the "Superior Dharma" (uttaradharma). If one speaks of "destroying the fetters," this refers to a person whose delusions are exhausted and whose understanding is complete, who has given rise to the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) and reached the ultimate limit of correct principle.
Such a person naturally induces the precepts; thus, they are named according to what was destroyed, and are said to have "destroyed the fetters and proclivities" (saṃyojana-anuśaya).

Regarding the "three words and three phrases," this refers to those situated at the level of the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and above. Such individuals encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, yet they hear [the teaching] without seeing [the Buddha].
They meet an Arhat who bestows upon them the Three Refuges and causes them to realize full ordination (*upasampadā*). This is truly because their accumulation of practice has not been long.
Before attaining the rank of a noble one (*ārya*), she had a prior connection with that Arhat; relying on this, she was permitted to go forth by means of the "threefold utterance.

Thus it is said. Regarding the four and eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*): although she was at the stage of a woman who had already attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and deeply loathed birth and death, seeking to go forth, she was restrained and not permitted because there would have been no benefit for the broad propagation of the Way or for distant transformation. She returned to Śrāvastī to... herself.
Having shaved his hair and donned the robes, he stood leaning against the monastic quarters. At that time, Ānanda made three requests, and the Tathāgata preached the Dharma of Reverence for him.

He then dispatched Ānanda to transmit and receive it, commanding him to honor and uphold it, and to practice it fully according to the instructions; thus, he immediately felt the power of the precepts. This is why he was so named.
This, then, was the occasion for receiving [the precepts], involving only the Buddha and Ānanda. That person was the Buddha’s maternal aunt, who requested the Buddha to come forth.
At home, the Buddha initially did not permit it. The Buddha said, "If women are allowed to enter my Dharma, there will be much decline and diminution.
It is like a household that has many daughters and few sons; one should know that such a family will soon face ruin. When women enter my Buddha-Dharma, it is just the same.
Ānanda requested this again and again, citing how the Buddhas of the three periods of time had all ordained women. Furthermore—
Regarding the mention of the fourfold assembly: all Buddhas are fully possessed of the fourfold assembly, namely bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of maternal nurturing: seven days after the Buddha was born, his mother passed away; he was then nourished and raised by the breast milk of Mahāprajāpatī.
"One should repay their kindness by permitting them to enter the Path. The Buddha said, "If I had not appeared in the world, they would not have known even the names of the Three Jewels.
Now that they recognize and take refuge in the Three Jewels, they have already fulfilled their debt of gratitude; how much more so since they have already realized the first fruit [of the path].

Ānanda entreated the Buddha earnestly, and the Buddha immediately ordered that the Eight Weighty Rules be transmitted to her. If she can fully observe them, she may be allowed to enter the Path. Thus it was with Pāṭācapurikā.

Having received the Eightfold Respectful Precepts, she declared, "I shall receive them upon my head. She then addressed Ānanda, saying, "I pray that you will petition the Buddha once more on my behalf:

how can a nun of even a hundred years' seniority prostrate at the feet of a monk who has only recently received the precepts? I beg that she be permitted to pay respects according to the sequence of their *varṣa* (years since ordination). The Buddha said:
If one were to perform prostrations according to the order of seniority by summer retreat, such a thing would be impossible. As for the five-word *karmavācanā*, this is what is being clarified here.

Although this method of receiving the precepts applies universally to both ordinary persons and sages, because the roots of goodness are so thin and meager in this present degenerate age, it is difficult for the aspiration for the Path to arise;
thus, one must rely on ten monks performing the ritual to achieve its fulfillment. The *Karmasūtra* states: "For such individuals..."

By relying on strong conditions to support those weak causes, one is then able to generate the precepts. With the Sangha as the objective condition, the category of precepts is generated at the moment the words are spoken.

Because the capacity to confer [the precepts] is concealed and the focus is placed upon that which is conferred, it is so named. Regarding the statement "the method for relinquishing the precepts is appended": [it follows].
It does not mean that after receiving [the precepts], one must necessarily abandon them.

Regarding what the original mind aspired to and vowed to uphold, there is a fear that a practitioner might, over time, become negligent in their practice, grow weary of the ritual of the Path, or set their will upon worldly customs;

or perhaps they may encounter difficult circumstances beyond their control, leading them to commit transgressions while still wearing the precepts, which can obstruct the Path. For this reason, the Sages permitted the relinquishing [of the precepts], so that one may come and go [freely].
There is no obstruction; it does not preclude one's subsequent entry into the Path. Regarding the inclusion of the Six Recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti):

after having received the precepts, one must constantly maintain mindfulness regarding the robes and alms bowl that one upholds. Since there is nothing more essential than this for fully guarding against the six classes of offenses, they are appended here.
Regarding the phrase "transcending the vulgar, base, and defiled stream," Master Ying explains that "base" (*bi*) arises from "crude" (*lou*). The *Guangpi* states: "The base is shame.
This is intended to clarify that the ordinary worldling follows the stream of birth and death; the six objects of sense and the five desires are, in their very essence, defiled.
The practitioner who is bound by defilements causes their body and mind to become impure; therefore, it is called "filth. Now, this received body can carry one far out to the shore of Nirvana;

therefore, it is called [the vessel]. Jì says: If one possesses extremely dull faculties, by maintaining the precepts without transgression for seven lifetimes, one will immediately attain the fruit of Srotāpanna.
This is the natural order of principle. If one possesses sharp faculties, one will necessarily realize [the fruit] after three or five lifetimes.

This is the first fruit. Regarding the phrase "entering the precious rank of the assembly of sages," it means that once one has received the precepts, one enters the immediate rank of the Sangha Jewel through its maintenance;
furthermore, it signifies entering the ultimate rank of the sages of the three vehicles' bodhi.

Regarding the phrase "Since the aspiration is increasingly vast," "vast" (*bō*) implies breadth. This clarifies that at the time of receiving [the precepts], one generates a magnanimous mind, such as that which transcends the ranks of ordinary beings and enters the stage of the sages.
Regarding the statement "therefore, the objects of focus are increasingly numerous":

since the aforementioned mind that takes objects is already broad, the realms that serve as its objects are necessarily many; this refers to focusing on the myriad realms of both sentient and insentient beings.
There is a mind that severs evil and cultivates good, which must universally pervade the Dharma-realm. Thus, the *Śubhavyūha-sūtra* says:

"Sentient beings, the great earth, grasses, trees, and the boundless void," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the term "extensively many" (*mi duō*), there are five types of objects countered based on the methods of receiving and maintaining [the precepts], and six types of objects countered.
Therefore, it is called "extensively many. All of these are conditions (*pratyaya*). This is the essential point of the ritual practice.

"Difficult" (*nán*) means "that which is to be" (*yǒu suǒ*). It is said thus because one wishes to clarify that since the goodness generated is already vast, the Dharma to be practiced is consequently difficult;

hence, it is called "difficult. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that when the subject (*néng*) encounters the object (*suǒ*), the manifold conditions are already so numerous that performing the ritual procedure is difficult;

therefore, it is termed "difficult. Regarding the phrase "because it is difficult to know, the principle must be examined in detail," this means that since the undertaking is already great, one must now establish [the method].
The Dharma examines the causes of right and wrong regarding one's preceptors and teachers.

Yet, worldly passions and defilements frequently obscure the teachings; it is said that the preceptors and teachers of the present age are attached to the six sense objects and defiled by forms, sounds, and so forth, such that they cannot clearly understand the holy teachings and remain muddled within the net of the Dharma. To serve as a teacher or a master is truly easy.

Regarding the "actual difficulty": it is established that if one maintains pure precepts, has a broad understanding of the Tripiṭaka, and possesses both the Dharma and the material support (āmiṣa) to sustain others, such a person may serve as a teacher;

for them, upholding and governing the precepts is easy. However, if one violates the precepts, acts contrary to the Dharma, does not understand the holy teachings, and lacks the support of both Dharma and material sustenance, it is difficult for them to act as a teacher now.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that even if one possesses sufficient conduct and understanding to fulfill the required number [of qualifications], [it remains difficult].
To accord with the virtue of the teacher, it is easy to receive [the precepts] at a single session on the ritual platform;

however, it is difficult to subsequently provide instruction during the course of practice so that one may perfect the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). As for those who merely follow established customs and fail to reflect upon the need for reform or innovation:

the *Zilin* (Forest of Characters) states that "to go down along water" is called *yán*, meaning to follow the current. Lì (Lì Yù) says: "To follow the current is called *yán*; to go against the current is called *suí*."
Tracing back to the present day, the monks of this final age do not contemplate following the current of the Buddha-dharma or acting in accordance with the teachings;

they merely delight in practicing worldly customs and habitual routines. For instance, they receive the robe and bowl as if borrowing them, and such a tradition has been passed down in this manner—this is what is called "practicing worldly custom."
Now, this must be corrected. For instance, among the laity, those who possess discernment know that at age fifty, the errors of forty-nine years are still apparent;
how much more so for one who studies the Way, yet harbors attachments and refuses to suddenly abandon what came before? This is utterly unacceptable.

Regarding those who disrupt the True Teaching, it is clearly established that they are like *mahallakas* (senior monks) acting as teachers for others, failing to understand past matters, yet claiming in their own words: "I..."
This is the Mahāyāna; how could it be limited to such a minor teaching?

To call this "disturbing the true doctrine" refers to those who cling to the literal text and recite it with pedantic precision. They close their eyes and recite the *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) with meticulous care, never altering whether something is present or absent, and failing to recognize what is correct or incorrect;
thus they remain mentally attached to them. Or, regarding those who were previously subject to prohibitions and were unfit for the monastic laws, they claim that they [are now capable].
If the person receiving the precepts has obstacles or impediments that hinder the arising of the precepts, it would not accord with the teachings of the Dharma.

The *Jie jiemoluoshi* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) states: "Now, the precepts are the root of generating goodness, the source of extinguishing evil, and the sublime cause for proceeding toward Nirvana."

It is the root from which concentration and wisdom arise. Since the Dharma is so refined and sublime, it is not easily received. For example, if one wishes to invite a great king, one must first thoroughly clean the palace;
now, in inviting the Great King of the Precepts, it is likewise necessary to purify the vessel of the body.

If there are no grave obstacles before and no minor hindrances behind, and if one accords with the teachings, then the precepts possess the meaning of being able to be realized; otherwise, they are received in vain.

It is of no benefit; it merely causes toil for oneself and others. One who cannot engender faith is like a teacher or monk who has transgressed the precepts and whose deportment is disordered, such that they are unable to cause the recipient to give rise to faith.

"To exhaust one's life for the sake of the Way" means to establish clarity. "The Way's instruction is great" refers to exhausting one's life for the sake of the Great [Way]. It is also explained as "emptiness.

Emptiness is exhaustion. "In future lives one will likewise encounter such [conditions]" means that in a future life one will again meet with such teachers and monks, yet will not receive the precepts, because in this present life one acted unrighteously toward other teachers and monks.

Regarding "relying on the capacity of the recipient": receiving the precepts according to this method possesses, in principle, the limit for attaining them. The preceding explanation of the meaning of the introduction is complete.

As for the difficulty regarding the remaining paths [of rebirth], the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "This excludes the other four destinies (*gati*). Although the heavenly realm possesses superior retributive fruition, it is merely attached to..."

Those who delight in much [sensual pleasure] find it difficult to cultivate the path because they have no aspiration for it; those who cultivate while harboring doubt find it difficult because the path lies in the realization of correctness, and due to their doubt, they lack the capacity for it;
those in hell find it difficult because their suffering is so great that burning affliction assails their hearts. Thus, the treatise says: "The intermediate state (antarābhava) body in hell..."
It is like a mass of molten iron, burning with the torment of heat; no metaphor can suffice for such suffering. How could one who harbors such [afflictions] come to receive the precepts?
Because ghosts and spirits are deceitful, false, and possess evil minds that disturb and afflict sentient beings, their retribution as animals is inferior.

They are gathered among the foolish and ignorant, and thus cannot bring glory or benefit to the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, the Buddha stated in the Vinaya that animals have nothing to grow toward or benefit from within my Dharma.

Only those in the human realm can receive the precepts, because their suffering is lighter than that of the lower realms, their pleasure is superior to that of the heavens above, and they possess sufficient strength of intellect and mindfulness to honor the path of practice.
Furthermore, regarding the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, [these exist] in the desire realm...

It possesses [wisdom]. Because this is the stage of scattering (*vikṣepa-bhūmi*), it possesses the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are the two types of wisdom—wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī*) and wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*)—but there is no wisdom of reflection.
Because this is the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*), as soon as the mind is raised, one enters concentration; therefore, there is no wisdom of reflection.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only wisdom derived from cultivation, and the two types of wisdom—wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from reflection—are absent. Because there is no form, there is no faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*); therefore, there is no wisdom derived from hearing. Furthermore...

This is a state of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*); therefore, there is no wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmaya-prajñā*). Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one is less than seventy years old and unable to perform the duties, the *Lì* (Lìbǎo) states:
"Although by age they should be instructed, because their physical capacity is insufficient, they are not permitted.

Regarding those over seventy who have passed the time for ordination, the *Lì* counters this by citing the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), where the Buddha permitted the ordination of the bhikṣu Fúzēng (Puṇyavardhana), who was one hundred years old.
"Domestic affairs may be sought out and utilized" (and so forth).
Second, regarding "those with complete faculties," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Because their appearance alone is dignified and upright, it gladdens the hearts of sentient beings."

In all matters of propagation and elucidation, it is easier for people to receive the teaching when they behold its outward forms. If these are not concise and streamlined, they will bring disgrace upon the monastic community.

The Vinaya states: "Only when the six sense faculties are all pure should one be fit to receive the Dharma. For instance, if the eye is focused on a single object, more than twenty other forms cannot be endured simultaneously.
Those who are deaf, mute, or insane do not generate the precepts; among the six sense faculties, if the faculty of hearing is impaired, one cannot hear the sound of the *karmavācanā*.

One cannot. The mute person lacks the faculty of the tongue and is thus unable to request the precepts; furthermore, because they lack the merit of recitation and upholding the teachings, they have no share in the Way, and so they cannot receive them.

The insane person has a disordered mind and is incapable of receiving the teaching with intentionality; moreover, they lack the resolve to receive and uphold it. Since these three faculties are impaired, they are judged to be ineligible.
As for the others, there are cases where they may or may not be eligible due to various circumstances. Master Shen said: "Among the six faculties, the ear..."

The three faculties of tongue, mind, and [ear] are as can be understood from above. As for the remaining faculties—eye, nose, and body—although they may be impaired, their function can still be obtained.

Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Among the three faculties beginning with the ear, these are superior for advancing on the Path. This is because one listens to the Dharma through the ear; the mind takes both the false and the correct as its objects, and when doubt arises, it is resolved through penetration."

It is not that the tongue lacks clarity; rather, because these three [faculties] are deficient, one does not attain the limit. As for the others, although they are capable of begging and capable of maintaining [the precepts], they generally fall within the prohibitions;
yet the attainment [of the precepts] lies within the scope of what is permitted.

Regarding the purification of the vessel for the three bodies (*trikāya*), the *Karmasūtra-vṛtti* states: "Since one has become a vessel for the Way, it must be pure before it can be fit [for the task].
Just as if one wishes to invite a king, one must first adorn the residence; what is received now is the invitation of the Dharma King, and thus the vessel of the Way must be purified."
Only then is one fit to receive the Dharma. It is like a clean cloth that easily takes dye; if it is first stained with impurities, the subsequent reception will not be accomplished.
The *Lì Jīemó Sū* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) states: "The vessel of the body must be pure, free from the thirteen grave offenses and other such transgressions.

Now, the Dharma of the precepts is pure and subtle, the supreme cause for exiting the mundane world. Since the Dharma is so refined and wondrous, its reception is not easily achieved. Regarding this reception...

It is not that the body alone can achieve it. Therefore, the body is regarded as the vessel for receiving the Way, while the mind is the master that receives the Dharma. When both body and mind are perfectly pure, one has attained the precepts;

this has already been stated. However, if one harbors internal obstacles or impediments within, the vessel of the body is impure, and even if all external conditions are complete, [the precepts cannot be received].
It is merely laborious and of no benefit; for one's entire life, one is cut off from the possibility [of ordination]. It obstructs the arising of the precepts and is termed a "difficulty.
Fourth, the "endowment with the characteristics of a renunciant" refers to having a form identical [to that of a monk].

The fifth, the method for attaining a small portion, is the identity with the Dharma. The ocean of Dharma does not open instantaneously; rather, expedient means are gradually revealed to make faith and delight firm and stable.
Regarding these five conditions above, they are not divided into two categories. The first four must be fully present; without these conditions, [attainment] is not accomplished.

After receiving [the precepts], one must possess the requisite implements; if they are not complete, one incurs both the offense of violating the precepts and the fault of transgression. The above concludes the explanation of the first point, that there are five meanings regarding the "one who can receive.
Regarding the second point, that there are six factors concerning the "one who is faced," the ancient masters established seven factors. This present *Chao* (Excerpts) abbreviates the seventh.
Sixth. The sixth condition states that [the ritual] must take place during the time when the Buddha-dharma exists;

that is to say, if the Buddha-dharma has already ceased, all *karmavācanā* procedures as well as the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) will not be accomplished. The masters of the *Poṣadha-vibhāṣā* commentaries also explain:

"With respect to what has not yet been performed, it is not accomplished; with respect to what has already been performed, it is not lost. Although this condition is omitted in the manuscript, its inclusion here is also appropriate.
Therefore, the sixth [consciousness] must exist during the period of the Buddha-dharma. Question: For how long shall the Buddha-dharma endure? Answer:
According to the texts of the holy teachings, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) lasts five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) one thousand, and the final period ten thousand.

However, when the masters of Nanshan (Daoxuan) recount the duration for which the Śrāvakas abide in the Dharma, they cite an extreme longevity of sixty thousand years (the source of this figure remains unclear). Furthermore, according to the biographies, there were five hundred Arhats in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when they wished to assemble and compose a treatise, they deliberated together as to which land possessed the most necessary resources for its creation.
They saw that in the land of Kaśmīra there was much provision for offerings, though it lacked fine monasteries. At that time, there was a pond in which lived a nāga;
because of the spiritual merit of that site, the arhats approached the nāga and requested the use of the pond’s grounds.
They set out to build a monastery (ārāma), but the nāga was reluctant and would not grant it. There was an elder who requested a single seat;
the nāga immediately granted it. The elder entered the pool and sat within it. Since the nāga had already given his consent, he could not take it back and so withdrew elsewhere.
As he was departing, he said: "I now offer this pool to the great virtuous ones to be used for constructing a monastery. If, in the future, the Buddha-dharma should perish..."
"At that time, the earth shall return to me. There, the Arhats will build a monastery and extensively compose various treatises;

it was at this very spot that the *Sārvāstivāda-śāstra* was composed. Now, within this monastery, there is gradually moisture; in the place where the five requisites were kept, the water reaches as high as the ankles.
Thus we know that the Buddha-dharma will not endure for long and is about to perish. Since there are six distinct sections [of the canon], this is now the first."

Regarding those who immediately establish a small boundary outside the monastery to receive [the precepts], it is said that establishing three small boundaries in the absence of obstacles is invalid and constitutes an illegal act.
This is for two reasons: first, because there are no obstacles; and second, because even if obstacles were present, it would still be improper to erect markers and proclaim the boundaries.
The phrase "as clarified above" refers to the preceding section on the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).

Regarding the passage, "Many people boarded boats in the middle of the river to perform the ritual; when asked the reason, they replied as follows," the *Sārvastivāda-śāstra-śiṣya-paramparā* (The Lineage of the Sārvastivāda Masters and Disciples) states:
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Huizhao of Qiyuan Temple received the full precepts (*upasampadā*) once again from the Indian monk Saṃghavarman.
At that time, the Dharma Master Huiyi of Qiyuan Temple was by nature upright and straightforward; upon seeing Saṃghavarman...
...and so forth. [Guṇavarman] was about to confer full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), but because their dispositions differed, they said in anger:

"The Great Dharma has flowed eastward, yet the lineages of its transmission are not one. The former sages and eminent philosophers all shared established conventions; to suddenly alter them—how can this harmonize the minds of the assembly? Guṇavarman replied:

"We have together renounced the secular world for the sole purpose of propagating the Dharma. Since the Dharma must necessarily be transmitted according to its textual phrasing, how could we contravene the sentiments of the assembly? (and so on). Yì then questioned him:
[The questioner] said: "During the lifetime of Guṇavarman, the *poṣadha* and other monastic affairs were always conducted within the monastery.

When it came to receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), for what reason was it performed exclusively outside the town? In terms of perfecting wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), why is there such a difference? [The answer: "The matter of receiving the precepts is of great gravity."
This differs from other matters. If these [precepts] were not fulfilled, one would incur only a minor offense (duṣkṛta), which would cause no great harm and could be expiated through confession.

However, as for perpetuating the lineage of the Buddha and consuming the offerings of the faithful, the precepts are the very foundation. If the reception [of the precepts] is not validly accomplished, one is not a renunciant;
it becomes the source of karmic obstructions and leads to the extinction of the Great Dharma. Therefore, this differs from other ritual matters. Master Yì bowed his head in joyful submission.
Having no further words to say, he then sent his disciples Huiji, Jingming, and Faming—three men—to cross the Cai River at Zhuyang.
There, they received the precepts on board a boat. At that time, Dharma Master Rui of Shixing Temple offered this critique:
"Beholding the good, one fears one cannot attain it; seeing the evil, one recoils as if from hot water. Master Yi stands apart amidst those who conform. Less than ten days had passed when...

Furthermore, it repeats what was different [in the previous section], likely to mock his initial delusion (the *Chao* records that someone asked for the reason; the answer states: "The 'equal' [passages] are all the questions and answers from the preceding text").
Those who serve as a field of merit for the world are those who have received full ordination. This clarifies that they act as a field of merit for humans and devas;

their ability to increase the merit of others and to digest the offerings of others is entirely due to the power of maintaining the precepts. Recently, I observed Master Huayan reprimanding several great virtuous ones.
Whenever they entered the inner palace, the Emperor would always grant them audience, yet he would allow only one attendant to enter with them, while many others were frequently brought along.

For śrāmaṇeras to enter [the palace] is entirely contrary to the Dharma. Since śrāmaṇeras possess no precepts, how could they possibly digest the hundreds or fifty pieces of silk offered by other states?
Furthermore, since śrāmaṇeras possess no precepts, if they were to enter the inner palace, they would inevitably commit transgressions:
upon seeing the precious possessions of others, they would steal them; upon seeing beautiful women, they would become lustful. Would this not bring disgrace upon the Great Virtuous Ones?
Yes. However, although these admonitions are very powerful, there is nothing that can be done as the Venerable Ones do not accept the words.

Second, regarding those capable of presiding over the legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) of the Saṃgha—namely, the formal motion and the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations)—if the Saṃgha is incomplete, it is not valid.

In border regions where the Saṃgha is absent, an exception is made for five persons who uphold the Vinaya to be eligible for ordination; this refers to the disciple of Kātyāyana named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, who resided [there].
In the kingdom of Upananda, he sought a preceptor-monk for three years before finally receiving the precepts. Daoli said: "This caused Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to receive the precepts only after three years;
because of this, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha then permitted that from now on, in border regions, five persons may be allowed to confer the precepts.
As for the statement that 'one who upholds the Vinaya may perform it,' Jie asked: 'In the Central Kingdom, ten persons are required; why does [the text] not mention that one must uphold the Vinaya?'"
The reason why it is stated that "only those in the border regions who maintain the Vinaya may perform [this act]" is that in the border regions, those who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous;

thus, it is necessary to specify that they must maintain the Vinaya. In the central lands (*madhyadeśa*), however, the monastic community is entirely pure, and therefore this is not mentioned. These are the points listed in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Ten Recitations).
The Vinaya asks: "If there are ten people in a border region, would it suffice for five of them to receive the full ordination? The answer is:

"They would indeed obtain the name of having received the full precepts, but the Saṃgha incurs an offense of censure. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*) is likewise. Based on this, it appears that the number is fixed according to the specific location.
Regarding the phrase "there is no other expedient means to permit a separate assembly": because they belong to the same boundary (*sīmā*), everyone must assemble in full.
If anyone does not come, the conferral of the precepts is not accomplished. As for "inversion" and "omission": performing the *karmavācanā* first and the *jñapti* later is called inversion;
the dropping of textual phrases is called omission.

Regarding the sixth point, the fulfillment of requisite conditions, the *Jiemo shu* states: "Internally rejoicing in the sublime Dharma and externally relying upon the sublime ritual, body and mind depend upon one another like a fish and water.
Whether these are naturally present or must be borrowed, if they are lacking, the conditions are not fulfilled."

Regarding the phrase "because it cannot be accomplished without a [proper] mind": when one wishes to receive the precepts, it is a matter of principle that one must earnestly and respectfully request them; only then is the full ordination accomplished.
If one acts with negligence and does not make the request, according to the underlying meaning, there can be no attainment of the precepts.

"Mind not corresponding to the object" means that while the preceptor, the robes, and the bowl are objects that accord with the Dharma, the recipient lacks the intention that accords with these objects.

This is what is meant by "the object not corresponding to the mind," which refers to a case where the recipient possesses the aspiration to receive the precepts and sever evil, yet the preceptor is not pure.
Regarding the statement that "if there is a sincere mind, there is unmanifest action (*avijñapti*)," this...
This clarifies the person capable of receiving [the precepts]. If one possesses earnestness, then the unconditioned (avijñapti) precepts will arise.

Regarding the necessity of a recipient who first accords with the aforementioned conditions, one may rely on the five conditions listed in circumambulation. This concludes the general explanation of the first section:
the gate of accomplishing the reception through the possession of conditions.
Within the second section on the addition of dharmas (*dharmopasaṃhāra*), there are ten parts in total. In the preceding general discussion of *karma*, seven types of non-validity were clarified.

Regarding the "eight kinds of preparatory treatment" (*parikarman*): this refers to the fact that within these ten parts, excluding the first part—the section on the ten novice precepts (*śrāmaṇera-daśaśīla*)—and the section on receiving [the precepts] within the formal assembly, there are only eight sections of preparatory treatment;
these pertain to the period prior to the actual reception. Furthermore, it is said: beginning from...

Regarding the request for the teacher to conclude the ninefold procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations) involving the coming and going [of the candidate]: this specifically excludes the *śrāmaṇera*, as it requires the text of the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*).

Since the limit for obtaining ordination would necessarily be lacking [without it], it is not discussed here. As for the nine procedures: first, requesting the teacher; second, establishing the place for the recipient; third, appointing the instructor (*śikṣācārya*);

fourth, going to see and question [the candidate]; fifth, calling [the candidate] into the assembly; sixth, instructing [the candidate] to make the formal request; seventh, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).

The motion (*jñapti*). Eight: examining for impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*). Nine: the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). The verse says: "Requesting, setting aside, appointing, going, summoning, begging, the motion, and the examination of the *karman*.
As in the preceding section," which is explained as clarified above in the general discussion of *karman*.
That which is elucidated by the four Vinayas refers to the texts of the four schools of Vinaya: the *Dharmaguptaka*, the *Mahīśāsaka*, the *Sarvāstivāda*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

This differs from the approach of non-Buddhist outsiders who receive [precepts] all at once; rather, those currently granted the ten precepts are so because it is feared that those receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) might be unable to maintain them.
Therefore, they are granted [the precepts] gradually to refine their faculties and capacities, a process similar to that of the *śikṣamāṇā* (probationary nun).

The Dharma proceeds by gradual stages. Regarding the statement that it is "like the great ocean, gradually deepening as one enters," the sixth fascicle of the *Baoen jing* (*Sūtra on Requiting Kindness*) states:

Upāli asked the Buddha, "If one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*), one thereby encompasses the ten precepts; why then must one first receive the ten precepts and subsequently receive the great precepts?
The Buddha said, "Although they are obtained simultaneously, in order to cultivate and habituate oneself to the Buddha-dharma, one must [proceed in this manner]."
The sequence is as follows: first, one uses the ten precepts to discipline oneself; faith and joy gradually increase, and the roots of goodness grow deeper.
Next, one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Through this sequence, one attains the flavor of the Buddha-dharma, developing a profound joy that is firm and difficult to cause to regress.
It is like traveling across the great ocean, entering deeper and deeper by degrees; entering the ocean of Dharma is likewise so.
The text asks: "Who requested the Venerable One to ordain me and others? Regarding this, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

There was a bhikṣu who, after having received full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, committed many evils and failed to observe the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*).
At that time, there were bhikṣus of few desires and contentment who rebuked him, saying: "How is it that you commit various evil deeds and do not observe the rules of decorum? Thus it continues.
The Buddha replied, "Who requested the Venerable One to grant me the precepts? Who requested the Venerable One to act as my upādhyāya?

At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward, if one has not requested someone to act as upādhyāya and has not begged for the precepts, one must not be granted full ordination (upasampadā).
Should anyone grant it, they shall incur a duṣkṛta offense."

Regarding those who should practice as described above: as stated in the "Great Outline of the Monastic Network" (*Sengwang dagang pian*), whenever one enters among the Sangha, the Vinaya prescribes five dharmas:
baring the right shoulder, removing leather sandals, prostrating at the feet of the monks, placing the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms.

Regarding the formula "Venerable Sirs, please attend to me with one mind; I, [Name], etc.," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states that it consists of five phrases, the first of which is "Venerable Sirs."

1. “Virtuous One, please attend to me with single-mindedness” means to request that he focus his attention exclusively on this. 2. “I, [Name], up to and including the Preceptor” clarifies the object of one’s prayer. 3.
“I pray that the Virtuous One will act as my [Preceptor] and so forth” expresses the fulfillment of one’s fundamental hope through compassion.

4. “May I, by relying upon him, receive full ordination” refers to the fact that the three trainings arise from such reliance. 5. “Out of compassion” means that having already set forth what is held in one’s heart, one only wishes for it to be heard.
[The candidate] consents. [The preceptor] replies, "So be it" (*keryo*). This collectively accepts the request and grants permission to act as preceptor.

Within the phrase "so be it," "so" (*ka*) is a response of assent for an inferior, while "be it" (*ryō*) is the formal courtesy due to a superior. To say both "so be it" together is a failure to understand the nuances of speech;
it is entirely improper.
The instruction, "Teach you purity; do not be negligent," and so forth, is not merely a matter of ritual practice (*vastu*), but also contains the extensive teaching of the Dharma (*dharma*).
Regarding "purity": one should revere the *Prātimokṣa* and maintain the three types of action (*trikarma*). Regarding "do not be negligent":

since negligence is the source of all transgressions, one should restrain the faculties of the emotions and distance oneself from the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). Among the four responses, the ancient masters say:

Although the Vinaya lists four types of responses, a single response may suffice for any one of them. The author of the *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The intent is that these apply universally to all four, collectively forming a single response.
The first is a term of assent; the latter three are subsumed within it, as their meanings are interconnected. Regarding the ten further methods of responding mentioned in the text below:
This is explained in detail in the lower section of the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*. It states: "The ten modes of answering are: first, 'able'; second, 'acceptable'; third, 'it is'; fourth, 'practice';
fifth, 'heedfulness'; sixth, 'good'; seventh, 'excellent'; eighth, 'arise'; ninth, 'depart'; and tenth, 'give.
These are the ten modes of answering."

Regarding the statement that "the preceptor may lack virtue" and so forth, Master Li explains: although one requests [ordination] at the time of receiving the ten precepts, it may be that the preceptor has violated the precepts;
hence, he is said to "lack virtue. Therefore, one must now exercise discernment regarding whether he possesses virtue or not, and should request another person [to serve as preceptor].

Regarding the statement "therefore, he requested twice," Jì said: "The first refers to when he was a śrāmaṇera, requesting face-to-face; and now, at the time of receiving full ordination, he again requests face-to-face.
Thus, it is called 'two face-to-face requests.'"
Regarding the phrase "requesting the seven witnesses," etc.: such a person is called a *bhadanta* (Venerable One) and is also termed a *upādhyāya* (Preceptor).

In the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, he is referred to as the *karmācārya* (Master of the Ordination Platform). As for the procedure for requesting him according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the preceding text states that one should first perform the sequence of instruction by prostrating head-to-foot before each member of the Saṃgha;
only after this should one request him. This must be done when there is a large assembly of monks.

Regarding those who have not yet reached [full] ordination: since there must be many people, one should simply request those specifically designated as "Venerable Ones" (bhadanta); the others need not be requested.
As for the question of why this does not encompass all cases, Jia Kui’s commentary on the *Guoyu* states:

"It clarifies that once a bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), he may no longer dwell together with the two types of saṃgha—those performing the *poṣadha* and the *karmavācanā*—and he does not count toward the quorum of the saṃgha. Now it is known that he has committed [an offense].

The section on the "grave offenses" concludes. This refers to those who are not of the same dharma; they cannot participate in the joint certification of *karmavācanā*. What, then, is not encompassed by this term "knowing"?
It means that once one knows an offense is grave, one should not participate in any *karmavācanā*—how could it be limited to the recitation of the precepts alone?

Master Ying says: "To encompass (*gai*) means to be complete. According to the local dialects, "gai" derives from "to include" (*bao*). Regarding the ten masters in relation to one another, it is based on whether they know of an offense.

[The offense] is grave. Even if one commits an offense from the "Lower Section" (of the *Prātimokṣa*), it is still permissible according to the Dharma. However, from the perspective of the recipient, if they know well that the preceptor has committed a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), then that person lacks the virtue of a preceptor.

As for the case where the reception [of the precepts] is not accomplished because of being forced: Jing says this means that if the disciple’s *upādhyāya* has violated the precepts and does not possess the virtue of a preceptor, and the disciple has no intention to receive them from him, then the reception is not accomplished.
Furthermore, as is the case nowadays, if the person receiving the precepts sets their mind upon another person [as their preceptor], [the reception is likewise not accomplished].

Regarding the preceptor (upādhyāya): if the administrator or the presiding master of the altar coerces others into serving as preceptors, one may not accept them against one's will, as this is done without a sincere intention.

Therefore, regarding the preceptor with nine years of seniority (*navavārṣika-upādhyāya*): if one establishes a preceptor with nine years of seniority as the one from whom the precept is received, and that teacher commits an offense, [the recipient] does not obtain the precept;
if it is a preceptor with eight years of seniority, one likewise cannot obtain the precept. In both cases, it is equally a transgression.
"Venerable of great virtue" (*śuòdé*): "great" (*shuò*) means large. The *Fāngyán* (Dialectal Lexicon) states that in the region between Qi and Song, they call "large" *shuò*.
*Shuò* also implies excellence. One who has reached seven *varṣa* (summer retreats) or more may serve as a *karmācārya*; this is according to the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*.
Regarding the *vinaya-ācāra* and the seven witnesses, five *varṣas* are required; for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), seven *varṣas* are required—this differs from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.
From this point onward, the conditions for generating the precepts are taught. Regarding "causing a mind of compassion to arise toward all objects," the *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:
"Within the superior mind (*adhimukti-citta*), to rescue all sentient beings is the root of goodness of loving-kindness; this refers to the Buddha-mind. First, the objects of focus are clarified:
this means that, initially, the objects of focus are explained as pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Subsequently, the scope of the mind is clarified.
"This" refers to the mind that acts as the perceiving subject.
The separate excerpt consisting of more than thirty sheets refers to a monk in the capital who recorded the mental states associated with the objects of the precepts during their reception.
It consists of more than thirty sheets of paper. Whenever there is one who wishes to receive the precepts, they are made to recite it from memory.
The Nanshan Ācārya was constantly hailed as the "Buddha of the Final Age" because he was able to skillfully guide and instruct sentient beings.

Regarding the equality of the two truths—emptiness and existence—and the principle of cessation for both the animate and inanimate: from the Buddhas above down to the three miserable realms below, all are the path of the animate; mountains, rivers, and so forth...

The great earth is termed "insentient" (*niṣceṣṭa*). Regarding the statement that there are two truths, emptiness and existence: it is established that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is emptiness, while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is existence.
These two truths are referred to by various names in the sūtras: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* call them the worldly truth and the ultimate truth;

the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-alaṃkāra Sūtra* calls them the truth of existence and non-existence; and the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Rājavavādaka*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* call them the ultimate and the conventional.
The Two Truths are also called the Two Truths of Emptiness and Existence (*śūnyatā-saṃvṛti*). Regarding the statement that there are the Two Truths of Existence and Non-existence:

existence refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and non-existence refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the statement that the principle of cessation is *nirvāṇa*: there are four kinds of *nirvāṇa*.

First is *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*, which is the fact that all sentient beings share the same fundamental nature. Second is *apratisthita-nirvāṇa*, which refers to the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting transformations for the sake of sentient beings.
This is correct. The "three" and "four" refer to those with remainder and those without remainder; all are cases where one incurs offense through slander and lack of faith.

Now, by reversing this into "good," the precept is formally established. Regarding "texts, scrolls, images, stupas, and temples," these are the scriptural canons of the Tripiṭaka as ordained by the Buddha;
since one incurs an offense based on failing to study them, they constitute the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of this precept. It is said that one ought to establish images, stupas, and temples.
Faith. It is through faith that one believes these dharmas exist; because one gives rise to a mind of reverence, one generates the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

This is as in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, where there is the precept regarding the veneration of stūpas. Furthermore, it is because destroying stūpas or monasteries all incurs the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave transgression).

Regarding the statement that "the Dharma-realm is the measure and constitutes the essence of the precepts" (*śīla-tattva*), this means that [the Dharma-realm] is properly the object of the precepts (*śīla-viṣaya*). That it is now called the "essence" is because the precepts are generated from this object; thus it is designated.

It is the essence. Regarding the term "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because it is the characteristic upon which the sublime Dharma of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas relies.
The commentary says: Because all phenomena constitute the nature of the precepts, they are called the Dharmadhātu.
Regarding the phrase "the ocean waters are boundless," this refers to [the consumption of] alcohol, water containing insects for drinking, and likewise to the theft of water.

Therefore, water in all such cases constitutes the object of the precept. For example, if someone sells water, whether for five or three coins per load, if one acts with the intent to steal it, it is entirely a transgression.

A person who has newly received the precepts and whose virtue is equal to that of the Buddha does so because, with respect to the realm that pervades the Dharma-realm, they possess a mind of upholding and maintenance, and all wholesome dharmas arise together;

thus, their virtue is equal to the Buddha's. Furthermore, since they have not yet committed any transgressions upon first receiving the precepts, the essence of their precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is radiant and pure, identical to that of the Buddha.
Now that one knows this person’s virtue is equal to the Buddha’s, one must not treat them with contempt; rather, one should receive [the teachings] from such a person.

Regarding matters such as performing prostrations and giving commands, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duolun) relates that in the past there was a bhikṣu who was destined to attain arhatship, yet he was obstructed from reaching the exhaustion of outflows by the karmic residue of having been a wheel-turning monarch.
The Buddha, wishing to remove this obstacle, immediately became a bhikṣu for his sake.
The merit of a single *pūrvakalpa* of a wheel-turning monarch is extinguished all at once, and one immediately attains non-attachment.
For this reason, if one provides for the deficiencies of a newly ordained person, the merit of one's own extinction is not small.

Regarding the *campaka* flower: Paramārtha states that its original Sanskrit name is *campaka*, which translates here as "yellow flower. It has a mild fragrance and is abundant in the Western Regions.

As for the statement that one who breaks the precepts is superior to a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*): the views of non-Buddhists are heterodox and deviate from the truth, and they have not yet exhausted the cycle of birth and death.
Although one who breaks the precepts may fall into hell, there is still a distant prospect of eventual liberation.

Next, the section beginning with "next, cause [them] to generate the precepts" constitutes the second segment, which clarifies the magnitude of the mind that serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*).
It states that one who generates a superior grade of mind shall obtain a superior grade of precept; this establishes that the precept is the fruit resulting from the cause of a single grade of mind.
Regarding the statement that the precepts of an Arhat are of an inferior grade (*hīna-prakāra*): this means that when such a person received the precepts, they generated an inferior state of mind;

subsequently, through diligent application and cultivation of the path, they realized the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*). Yet their precepts remain of an inferior grade because the state of mind generated at that time was fixed as being of one particular grade.

Regarding the *Vibhaṅga* and other texts, Falin states: "There is only one fascicle. It is clear within the Vinaya text that with an inferior grade of mind, one cannot attain the middle or superior grades;
the mention of the two superior grades in the *Shuochao* (Commentary) is the interpretation of the author of that commentary. Bin says: "This *Vibhaṅga* is a Mahāyāna text;
it does not fully accord [with the Sarvāstivāda], so there is no need to cite it. As for the statement that "all sentient beings cherish their own lives," this...
The former clarifies the salvation of the body, but not yet the salvation of the mind. Regarding the middle grade of mind, it says "to resolve the doubts of sentient beings";
this is indeed the salvation of the mind. Since doubt arises from the mind, to speak now of resolving the doubts of sentient beings is to save the mind.

Regarding those who seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa* and so forth by means of accomplishing the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*) and entering the three gates of liberation (*tri-vimokṣa-mukha*), it is established and clarified that these three clusters of precepts bring about the realization of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
First, the vow to sever all evil, wherein there is no evil that is not severed, is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
In the future, this brings about the realization of the *dharmakāya* bodhi. Second, the vow to cultivate all good...
There is no good that is not cultivated; this is the precept of restraining oneself (saṃvara-śīla). It brings about the realization of the Reward Body Buddha (saṃbhoga-kāya) in the future.

Third, the vow to deliver all sentient beings—there is no sentient being who is not delivered—is the precept of gathering sentient beings (sattva-saṃgraha-śīla). It brings about the realization of the Transformation Body Buddha (nirmāṇa-kāya) in the future.
Regarding the phrase "entering the three gates of liberation," Fazhi says: the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha), the gate of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha)...
The Gate of Emptiness, the Gate of Signlessness, and the Gate of Wishlessness. The Buddha transforms sentient beings by relying upon the Gate of Emptiness.

These are also called the three samādhis; in the new sutras and śāstras, they are termed *samādhi*. According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these three gates of liberation represent the principle of the Hīnayāna;
thus, in that text, the śrāvakas describe themselves as merely contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s Dharma and so forth, his mind finds no joy or delight. According to Liu Qiu’s commentary, he takes the three emptinesses (*tri-śūnyatā*) as the ultimate limit;
yet, when it comes to roaming the spirit and saving sentient beings, not a single thought of seeking pleasure arises within the path of the Bodhisattva.

Now, the designation "three emptinesses" arises from the exhaustion of all burdens. The first [emptiness] is so called because one is hindered by existence (*bhava*); for this reason, one realizes that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty. The second...

They delight in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, they speak of emptiness as being signless (*animitta*). Thirdly, they take the simultaneous elimination of both grasping [at existence] and [grasping at] emptiness to be the ultimate.

Consequently, they wish to destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) by practicing them; yet, they are further led to the realization that no formations are to be performed. When their practice is exhausted and their minds are extinguished, this is what is termed the "ultimate" of the Hīnayāna.
Jì stated: "The three gates of liberation exist within the Mahāyāna, but do not exist within the Hīnayāna. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Contemplate emptiness and..."
"Equality" refers to the Śrāvaka’s own description: "In the past, I too aspired to the three gates of liberation, yet I was unwilling to practice them.
Therefore, it is said that he merely contemplates equality.

Regarding the statement that "generating the mind [of awakening] in this way is still a perverted thought," Fazhao establishes that if generating it in this manner is already perverse, how much more so for one who does not generate it at all? Such a person is entirely possessed of perverted views; how then could they possibly generate the superior grade of precepts? As for the ordinary person who, as a beginner, speaks with a perverted mind, Cizongyun says:

"Although they perform such wholesome deeds, because they do so with a mind that grasps at attainment, it is called a 'perverted mind. Fazhao comments: "Even though they have generated the mind [of awakening], they have not yet attained the true path. Because they have not yet attained the true path, their minds are perverted. Because their minds are perverted, they cannot generate the superior grade of precepts. Because they cannot generate the superior grade of precepts, they cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi* states:

'If a bodhisattva generates the mind while harboring the view of a self, or generates the mind while harboring the view of a sentient being, or generates the mind while harboring the view of a life-force, or generates the mind while harboring the view of a person—this is called generating the mind with a perverted mind. It is for this reason that the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* says: 'If one generates the mind with a perverted mind, one will fall into the evil paths. (From *Fahua xuanyi shiqian*, fascicle 10)
Ordinary beings possess the nature of afflictions and constantly employ the coarse minds of the six consciousnesses; this攀緣 (pān-yuan) and contemplation is called the "coarse mind.

If one enters meditative concentration to contemplate, this is the "subtle mind. If one takes True Suchness (tathatā) as the object of focus, it is then called the "outflow-free mind" (anāsrava-citta); this is the "correct mind."

The absence of meditative absorption and the emergence from it constitute a coarse mind; to engage in discursive investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) with such objective referents is called a mind of false views and a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) mind.

Although one may now be at the very beginning of training, because this is still a false mind, it is so described. Regarding the statement that an Anāgāmin speaks from within a state of pride (*māna*):

Ciyun says that while this person has eliminated the afflictions of the Truths (*satyadarśana-heya*), they still possess the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and their afflictions have not yet been eradicated due to craving.
Because the afflictions of anger and pride remain, it is said that "pride and so forth" [are present]. A guest [commentator] says:

In the *Tattvasiddhi* school, a practitioner may at times give rise to the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) due to distracted mindfulness. However, in the Sarvāstivāda school, although the conceit of self is generally abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it does not manifest.
Thus, the nineteenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Since the conceit of self is augmented by the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."

Because the view of self has been completely severed, it cannot arise in the Noble Ones (*ārya*). This is the intention of the *Tattvasiddhi* school, which maintains that the view of self still exists for those in the first fruit;
therefore, the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) can also manifest. The Mahāyāna school explains this as stated in the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"However, the tenets held by the various schools are briefly of two kinds: first, the innate (*sahaja*); second, the conceptual (*vikalpita*)."

The innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is subtle and therefore difficult to sever; it can only be eliminated by repeatedly cultivating the superior contemplation of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) during the subsequent path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Thus, one knows that when [the text] speaks of "still having grasping at a self" within the pride of an *anāgāmin*, it refers to this innate affliction (*sahaja-kleśa*). The intellectually acquired grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*), being coarse, is easy to sever;

at the initial moment of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), by contemplating the true suchness of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā-tathatā*) regarding all phenomena, one is able to eliminate it. Therefore, it is severed at the initial path of seeing.

There is one form of self-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*), which clearly indicates that [the preceding] conceptual elaborations are largely exhausted. It is established that this person has completely severed the coarse afflictions of the desire realm, yet still possesses the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*).

What are these five lower fetters? They are: restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*);

they are also called craving for the form realm (*rūpatṛṣṇā*) and craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*). Because these five exist, only by severing them all can one attain the state of an Arhat.

Although these five fetters exist, pride is the most prevalent. Whatever words they speak are all uttered with a mind of pride; therefore, it is said that their speech arises from within a state of pride.
Regarding the speech of those who bear the name of Arhat: as Ciyun says, their afflictions are entirely exhausted, yet they merely conform to worldly names and language without any attachment.
Liming states: such a person has severed the seeds and fruits of the three realms, and their entanglements are completely...

Exhausted. Not returning to the three realms. One contemplates the world as like an illusion; it possesses only names and designations. Whatever speech is uttered is merely in accordance with the Dharma of truth through names and language;
therefore, it is called "speech of names and designations. It is also termed "worldly conventional speech" (*loka-prasiddha-vāk*). As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 32:
"What is meant by 'worldly conventional speech'? It is as the Buddha has taught: men and women, great and small, coming and going..."
"Come, sit, lie down; vehicles, houses, gold, jars, clothing, sentient beings; permanence, bliss, self, purity; armies, forests, cities—these are conjured by illusion and then dispersed.
These are called worldly conventional expressions. The commentary explains: "In accordance with worldly convention, one speaks of 'man,' 'woman,' and so forth."
This is what is called "worldly conventional discourse.
Regarding the statement that Master Guang also made such a judgment: this refers to Vinaya Master Guang of the Northern Qi, the *Sengtong* (Patriarchal Head of the Sangha).

As for the various masters such as Bin and others, Nanshan [Daoxuan] judged the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to belong to the Mahāyāna school because he saw that the original text states: "If one wishes to seek the Buddha-way," and so forth. Furthermore...

"May we together attain the Buddha-way," and so forth; or "I exhort you to become a son of the Buddha," and so forth. Therefore, one must cause them to resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind. Examining these words closely now, they reveal a great error.
The *Nanshan Jie-mo-su* (Nanshan’s Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "Tapussa was weary of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); this shows he knew it was not secure.

(If one wishes to know the affairs of the Saṃgha, one seeks a secure method; this clearly shows that Arhats of both the Great and Small Vehicles are not secure. He bestowed [the merit] upon sentient beings to bring about the Buddha-way, knowing that other [vehicles] were not directed toward it."

(The end of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "Bestow [merit] upon all sentient beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way. This clarifies that one may turn toward Buddhahood. To summon one another as children of the Buddha means there is no distinct vehicle (*yāna*).

(The preface to the Vinaya says: "The children of the Buddha are likewise; they practice the foundations of the prohibitive precepts. To discard robes and not regard them as important means knowing the mind to be empty and pervasive. (When the Buddha praised the *dhūta* practices, monks discarded their robes until they formed great piles.

That the realm of dust is not perceived by the sense organs means that consciousness (*vijñāna*) realizes the ultimate meaning. (In the *Tattvasiddhi* school, it is held that seeing is by consciousness and not by the sense organ; other schools hold that the organ and consciousness act in conjunction.)
[This is] seeing. These two paths are precisely the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the mind that takes it as its object (*ālambaka-citta-mātra*).

As for the statement that "the perceived realm is clear and pure, and one should not wait until the moment [of death] to speak of generating the resolve [for enlightenment]," this establishes clarity;
because one can awaken to what is held within, all sentient and non-sentient realms become clearly visible.

Regarding the instruction to place [the candidate] where they can be seen by the eyes but not heard by the ears: this is established for two reasons. First, at the time of receiving the precepts, one must not be placed beyond the range of sight and hearing;

otherwise, the reception of the precepts will not be valid. Second, prior to the reception, one is placed beyond the range of hearing so as to avoid overhearing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual proclamation).
One is then placed within the range of sight so that any potential transgressions may be observed. This applies unless [the candidate] is outside the boundary (*sīmā*).

Regarding the recipient of full ordination (*upasampadā*): it is established that this clearly explains the time of receiving [the precepts], specifically when the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is being performed.

Even if one is within the range of sight or hearing, or even if one is outside the boundary (*sīmā*), the precepts are not obtained. As for the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*’s allowance—stating that because of the arising of faults, one may be placed outside the ordination platform (*sīmaṇḍala*)—that Vinaya states:
"If a bhikṣu borrows another’s robes and bowl to receive full ordination, and after having received it, the other bhikṣus call him to join them..."
As he was going and coming, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl to beg for food, a newly ordained monk replied, "I have no robes or bowl.
The bhikṣu said, "Do you not know that the Buddha has established a rule that one may not receive the precepts without robes and a bowl? He replied, "I know this;
I simply borrowed the robes and bowl, and am now returning them. When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
The candidate for ordination should be taken to a location outside the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), where they are within sight but beyond the range of hearing.

The *karmavācanā* master, assuming his dignified demeanor, shall go there and inquire. [The candidate] should rise from their seat; he shall ask whether their robes and bowl are complete, and so forth (as detailed).

Regarding the phrase "following the text of the *Śrāmaṇera-vidhi*": some maintain that this refers to following the text on the five categories of the higher [stages] (this interpretation is incorrect).
Others say it refers to the text concerning the non-attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*) outside of the higher realms.

Regarding the instruction that one should be stationed in two places: this means that if the questioning takes place within the assembly of novice *śrāmaṇeras*, one is stationed in both locations for fear that those not yet questioned might hear [the answers] later and fail to show respect. As for standing there with one's robes and bowl:

the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states, "In the two postures of walking and standing, the mind is restless and distracted; sitting is tranquil and still, yet it is not yet sufficient [for the purpose]."
"Respectfully. Thus, the term "waiting for the assembly" (*wàng-sēng*) is established to signify the act of looking up with focused attention.
Regarding the phrase "causing the recipient to feel shame, delay, and so forth," this is established to clarify that at that time, one was sent before the assembly to remove one's robes.
Seeing that the śrāmaṇera had an illness on his body and was unwilling to remove his clothes, thereby delaying and obstructing the matter of receiving the precepts, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the interrogation regarding the obstacles and impediments shall take place outside the boundary; there is no need to remove one's clothes."
Regarding the case where many people participate in a general question-and-answer session, it is established and clarified that if the answer is given generally, one may become a *śrāmaṇera*.

This applies even to ten or a hundred people, provided they are on the same ritual platform (*maṇḍala*); all may participate together. This is permissible because there is no separate group of monks coming and going.

Furthermore, it is also permissible if there are no monks within the assembly who temporarily leave the boundary; however, if those who have temporarily left return, they must once again [perform the necessary rites].

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "Jingyun": when appointing a Master of Deportment (Veyyāvaccakara), one asks, "Who is able to do this? If one answers, "I am able," without stating one's name, it is not valid.

This is because within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), it is essential to record the individual's name. [The question] "Is it I? may be used. As for "going to the place of the recipient," this refers specifically to the location where the śrāmaṇera is.

Among the various forms of opposition and refutation (*pratiṣedha*), there are those that are permissible and those that are not. It is established that while a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) is invariably impermissible, opposition is not fixed.
For example, if one fails to address the preceptor by name or by one's own name, it is certainly impermissible;
however, if one is in debt, it becomes permissible upon forming the intention to repay it, and it is also permissible for a deaf person to hear a loud voice.
If one refers to the Vinaya-mūla-sūtra (the Fundamental Text of the Vinaya), the question concerns only the thirteen [grounds for disqualification] and so forth.

This means that while the *Upasampadā-khandhaka* (Chapter on Ordination) of the Vinaya-mūla-sūtra fully enumerates the thirteen *antarāyika-dharma* (obstructing factors), providing their origin stories (*nidāna*) and explanations—stating that if such factors exist, ordination shall not be conferred again—yet when one reaches the actual ritual text for the formal procedure of ordination, it only inquires about the various prohibitions (*parivāsa*), and the matters of the thirteen obstructing factors are not seen to be asked about there. This is a mutual omission within the Vinaya texts, and not...

This is logically untenable. Now, judging by the meaning, one first asks regarding the "repeated difficulties" (*punar-vāda*) and then asks regarding the "light obstructions" (*mṛdu-pratibandha*); thus it is said that the questions regarding the obstructions precede.

For those who recite and study in a muddled manner, it is established as clear that the ancients merely recited directly, closing their eyes and reciting with haste, while the person before them [did not respond].
"I do not understand. I shall now treat this differently; I must explain each point one by one so that the person before me may recognize what exists and what does not.
Jie said, "When the ancients were questioned, it was not only the recipient who did not understand; even the questioner himself did not understand the meaning."
He then said to the recipient: "When I question you, answer only that there is no [preceptor]. Close your eyes and answer quickly.

When it comes to asking whose name the Upādhyāya is, you must likewise answer: 'I have never heard of him; an old monk from the Bingfen region conferred the precepts upon me while intoxicated with wine.
A short time later, we ascended the altar, and one person became so drunk and exhausted that he could not even leave the platform. But...

There were nine people, yet one was missing. The presiding elder (upādhyāya) immediately said, "Take a bundle of grass, stand it upright at the bottom of the row, and thread a *kāṣāya* robe through it to serve as the tenth person.
Now, in the exchange of questions and answers between host and guest, both parties must fully comprehend the meaning.
I have seen someone lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* where a debater asked: "Since you speak of 'joy in the Dharma' (*dharmaprīti*) and 'delight in meditation' (*dhyānārāma*),"

Regarding "food": it is not yet known how its scope compares to that of the three *ni*s. What are their respective characteristics? As for the "high seat," one remains perplexed, not knowing what it refers to.
Answer: The three *ni*s are namely *pūjani*, *khādani*, and *śayyāni*. Furthermore, I saw a question posed to a Vinaya master which says:

The *Yimoditi* (Upāli) and others all state that these were offenses committed through the "gate of the face" (*mukha-dvāra*). Why, then, are their degrees of gravity different? Following the section on the "offenses of one side" (*ekadeśa-āpatti*), there are thirteen items herein.
According to the Commentary (*Śāstra*), there are first five gates for a preliminary analysis: 1. The intent behind the formulation of the precepts;
