As for the statement "because one asks within the *karmavācanā* assembly, there is no need to appoint another person" and so forth, the *Lì nán* (Polishing the Difficulties) says: "If..."

Regarding the statement that one need not appoint [an official] when questioning within the assembly, the procedure for the five virtues of *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is likewise a formal act of question and answer performed before the assembly.
Why, then, must [an official] necessarily be appointed? The answer is simply that the sages established different rules. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"When the Preceptor of the Precepts is present in the assembly, there is no need to appoint [another]; the Council of Five Hundred was also a matter of question and answer within the assembly. Why, then, must [an official] be appointed?"
[Question: Why must there be an appointment? [Answer: Because the task of compiling the *Saṃgīti* (Council) is a great matter for the Saṅgha, and the sentiments of the multitude are not uniform;

therefore, it is necessary to designate who shall ask and who shall answer. For this reason, an appointment is required. However, in the present case, this Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīlācārya*) acts as an individual; since the request for his service has already been settled, an appointment is not required.

"Regarding 'there being no prior occasion': this means that in the Vinaya, one merely inquires about various obstacles; there is no occasion for presenting the three robes (*tricīvara*) by name to offer consolation.
It is only through oral tradition that this practice is performed. 'Good son, listen: now is the time of true sincerity'—Lì says that sincerity arises from reality.
This refers to the time when the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is born; therefore, it is called the 'time of true sincerity. Previously, it was the birth of the conventional."
This is not a time for insincerity; therefore, the matter of receiving the precepts is grave and admits of no falsehood. Thus, one must say "real" when it is real, and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "If you do not answer truthfully, you will deceive devas and humans, and you will also deceive the Tathāgata," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) says:
"Because the Dharma of the precepts reaches from the lowly to the exalted, to receive them without the proper conditions is to have a substance that violates the ritual protocol; it is deception."
The depth of delusion extends even to pervasiveness. The commentary states:

"All [proceeding] according to existence or non-existence, etc. Now, one who wishes to receive the precepts does so fundamentally for the sake of creating the causes and conditions for attaining the Way.

Regarding the questions and answers concerning impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*), one must rely entirely on the facts. If one further engages in falsehood and deception, it will deeply invite culpability; this is not merely a matter of deceiving others in the present.

The preceptor-monk himself would likewise be unable to receive the precepts. Thus concludes the explanation of the first section, the Gate of Expedient Means regarding the Origin of Conditions, consisting of ten distinct parts.
Now begins the second major section, which correctly elucidates the substance of receiving the precepts.

Regarding the phrase "when this time arrives" and so forth: it is established that what has been explained above—the recipient, the object of reception, and the ten kinds of dharmas—are all the preliminary preparations for receiving the precepts;

they do not yet constitute the essence of the arising of the precept. From here below, the text correctly elucidates the sacred teaching being upheld, which brings forth the essence of the karmic act.
"Only those with profound precepts are supremely good. Ciyun says: "When the roots of the precepts are deep and firm, it is called 'profound precepts.

Since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas alike possess these precepts, they are called 'supremely good' (*śubha*). Lì says: 'Because they will give rise to the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit in the future, they are named 'supremely good.'"
Regarding "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time," the Commentary states: this refers to possessing majestic power (*pratāpa*). As for the term *nirvāṇa*, it is synonymous with *niepan*.

The "three liberations" are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. The "three aggregates" are the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of gathering wholesome qualities, and the aggregate of benefiting sentient beings.
To give rise to such a mind is called the "superior grade."

Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "If this dharma of precepts possessed form, color, and so forth... This refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*. When the *Karmavibhaṅga-vyākhyā* cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* as proof, it is citing the *Sammitīya-vinaya*.
Those who are ordinary and foolish possess shallow wisdom; how could they possibly generate true insight?

Were it not for the instruction of those who have studied for a long time, one would remain as ignorant of these precepts as if in darkness. Since the primary duty of the renunciant is [the practice of the precepts], those who have never harbored great aspirations will certainly find it difficult to accommodate them.

This contains profound significance. Regarding the statement, "Now, for you, I perform the *karmavācanā* of the noble Dharma (*āryadharma*), even unto the wholesome Dharma (*kuśaladharma*), which infuses your body and mind," the commentary states:
"This clarifies that the noble Dharma relies upon conditions; when the conditions are fulfilled and the Dharma is complete, it suffices as the primary retribution (*pratyātmavipāka*)."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen: this so-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from such-and-such," and so forth—this *karmavācanā* text has already been fully explained in the preceding section on the general analysis of *karmas*. Since the matter is of great importance, it is now explained once more so that students may attain understanding.
Regarding the initial statement, "Venerable Saṃgha, listen": this refers to addressing the assembly and commanding them to listen.
This causes the ear-consciousness to arise; it should accord with the Dharma of the Saṃgha. Second, "this so-and-so" refers to the previous inquiry: "What is your name?
"From so-and-so one seeks to receive full ordination" refers to the previous inquiry regarding the name of the preceptor: "Who is your *upādhyāya*?
From this point downward, the specific circumstances and personal situation are recorded; that is to say, "from so-and-so one seeks full ordination."
This is the formal citation of the conditions (*nidāna*). It means that the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is the condition for obtaining the precepts. Thus, the Vinaya states:
"If there is no preceptor, or if the preceptor has violated the precepts, or if he is not present, it is not called the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

From this point, "Now, so-and-so requests the community of monks to receive full ordination" cites the previous threefold formula for requesting the precepts; this cites the petitioner's own intention, as before.

In the petition for renunciation (*yācanā*), after these words have been spoken, this petition is now recorded and incorporated into the formal ritual motion (*karmavācana*). This constitutes its essential intent.

The phrase "from [the candidate] X, who has personally declared himself pure and free from all obstacles" records the previous text concerning the inquiry into the thirteen obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*).
The phrase "having reached twenty years of age" records the previous inquiry: "Has your age reached twenty or not?"

1. "The three robes and alms bowl are complete" is the formal restatement of the matter at hand. 2. "If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with forbearance" refers to the harmonious assembly of the Saṃgha;
it means that the proceedings must not be in discord and that the Saṃgha should grant its collective consent.

3. "The Saṃgha now confers full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] acting as the preceptor" is a reiteration of the essential meaning of the second sentence of the formal motion (*jñapti*), establishing the decision.
"Jiu" (to settle) means to accept it as a fact. This merely reiterates its fundamental basis and does not detail the specific circumstances.
To state "five times in this manner" is to inform the assembly so that they may know.
"Do not allow the mind to sink; it should be uplifted by applying the mind to reverent contemplation. Here, "sinking" refers to states such as drowsiness and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Uplifting" refers to the pursuit of objects through applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), as well as the recollection of worldly affairs.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"—this is an address to the assembly to listen again. Since the matter is no small one, attend closely to the conditions and the characteristics of the sound.
From "this [person], so-and-so" down to "who among the elders consents," this is identical in meaning to the second phrase of the previous formal announcement (*jñapti*).

It establishes the conditions and the fundamental basis; that is to say, the Saṃgha now confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon so-and-so. One must therefore deliberate upon whether it is appropriate or not. Thus, "who... [is asked].
The elders consent. The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor.
Whoever does not consent, let them speak. This is the fourth phrase of the formal announcement (*jñapti*), restating the fundamental basis of the matter.

The specific details of the circumstances are not recorded here, as the purpose is to establish the definitive judgment of accomplishment. Regarding the statement above that "the second and third [proclamations] are likewise," if there were only one, the matter would not be fully accomplished;
if there were many, the ritual would become confused. Therefore, this is established as a fixed limit according to the rules.
The passage from "this assembly has already consented" onwards is the concluding exhortation; it is not the essential body (*kāya*) of the formal act (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding the question of whether the Sangha has achieved [the necessary conditions]: if one performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) without first inquiring whether they have been achieved, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This is simply based on this statement; it differs from the extensive explanation above because if one were to elaborate further, it would cause the recipient to give rise to arrogance toward the teacher.
The monks were again weary and indolent. "One who was previously saved by compassion" refers to the recipient as having been [the donor] in a prior life.

"Having maintained it thus" means that one has already ceased [unwholesome conduct]. Below this, the text clarifies the number of recipients, the recording of the time and season, the methods for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), and matters such as the morning and evening [rituals].
Regarding the statement, "Having properly received the precepts, one stands to measure the shadow with the length of one's own feet," [Master] Li says:

"This refers to measuring the shadow at the time of midday, as it is now. One stands in the sun and measures how many feet long the shadow of the body is. As for the phrase "indicating the times of spring and winter," Li says:
"After receiving the precepts, one must be taught that within the Buddha-dharma there are only three seasons; this is not the same as the current [four-season] system."
In the secular world there are four seasons, namely spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Regarding the "number of members," Master Li says that it refers to the number of people present;

it describes the characteristics of the assembly as they gather for the subsequent seasonal recitation. Regarding the "four reliances" (*catur-śaraṇa*), they encompass persons, teachings, and activities extensively.
The explanation of the meaning of the preceding introduction is hereby concluded. The meaning of the four grave offenses (pārājika) is as usual.

Regarding the phrase "it does not necessarily require a preceptor": as for the method of explaining the characteristics [of the offenses], any other person may do so; it does not necessarily require a *upādhyāya* or a *karmavācanā* master.
Regarding the statement, "This newly ordained person is similar to those who were outside the boundary (*sīmā*)," the intent of this question is as follows:

When the preceptor (*śāstṛ*) goes outside to pose the formal inquiries (*praśna*), he returns and again performs the communal reconciliation with the Saṃgha. Now, this recipient of the ordination is likewise one who has come from outside;

why, then, is there no further communal reconciliation? The answer is: "One who newly arises at that very place. Because they become a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) upon this very altar, they are said to have "newly arisen. Thus it is concluded.
The following clarifies that the characteristics of the teaching constitute dependent origination.
Regarding the phrase "first establishing the four root offenses and so forth," it means that prior to their formal establishment, there were those who had received the precepts;

having emerged from the ordination platform, they were walking behind their preceptor when they encountered former wives on the road. The former wives asked, "Where have you come from? and they replied:

Since my ordination and reception of the full precepts, I have repeatedly committed improper acts together with [my companions]. Later, when my teacher asked me, "Where have you come from? I fully reported the aforementioned matters.
My Upādhyāya rebuked me, saying, "Leave! You are no longer a bhikṣu. The disciple spoke in anger, saying, "Why did you not tell me sooner?
It was on account of this that the Buddha established the rule: first, one must explain the four pārājika offenses. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is thus:
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses may be compared to those of the lower stream":
this refers to individuals of middling faculties who must still train as noble learners (*śaikṣa*); how could they possibly be compared to those of the lower stream?
When those elsewhere were training for the fruits of the great śramaṇa, because the Venerable Upāli had grown old and passed away, there was a lack of instruction and admonition.
As for the term "śramaṇa," it means one who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source; therefore, he is called a śramaṇa.

The following clarifies the procedures for receiving robes, alms bowls, and other items. Regarding the instruction that one should be made to perform a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) confession for what was previously abandoned:

it is asked, "A *śrāmaṇera* incurs a *duṣkṛta* for keeping an extra robe; why then does a *bhikṣu* not incur a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense)? The explanation says: although the physical status has changed, the essential nature of the offense has not changed;
therefore, one must confess according to the original *duṣkṛta*.

The following clarifies the method of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). Regarding the "six recollections," Lü states: "In these six dharmas, binding the mind so as not to forget them is called 'recollection' (*anusmṛti*).

The essence of recollection is not six; it becomes six according to conditions. Because one generates recollection toward these six, they are termed the 'six recollections. Bin states: "There are six according to conditions;
the six are the objects of focus (*ālambana*), and recollection is the subjective faculty that focuses upon them. If one follows the various sections of Lü’s commentary:

[This is a] detailed analysis. For now, I shall not further elaborate on the explicit prevention of offenses. Speaking generally, all six [types of mindfulness] prevent transgressions of the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).

This is because by failing to maintain these recollections, one would each commit a *duṣkṛta*. If we discuss their specific prevention, the first recollection prevents two *duṣkṛtas*: first, [the offense of] not knowing the date and month when asked by a layperson;

second, [the offense of] knowing [the time] yet failing to announce it when the day and season for the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) arrive. The second recollection prevents one [offense].

1. One mindfulness to prevent the *pācittiya* offense of "taking from a house in front" (i.e., taking what has been left behind by a household). 2. Three mindfulnesses to prevent the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses:

as explained in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, receiving offerings after the summer retreat has ended constitutes the offense of theft (*steya*). 3. Four mindfulnesses to prevent the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense of keeping extra robes, the *pāyattika* offenses regarding impure items, and so forth, as well as the *pācittiya* offense of having one set of the three robes incomplete.

4. Five mindfulnesses to prevent the *pācittiya* offense of forming a separate assembly (*bhedana-gaṇa*), the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of causing schism in the Saṃgha, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of persisting in opposition despite the Saṃgha’s three-fold admonition, and the *sthūlātyaya* offense of persisting in opposition despite a private admonition.

"Ti. The sixth mindfulness prevents *pāyattika* offenses. It is for the purpose of knowing whether one is ill or not ill, such as when sitting down to receive food or when receiving food from a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), and so forth.
Regarding the second mindfulness, Lì (the commentator) says: "This mindfulness must be recited three times, because it prevents many offenses. That is to say, if one is fundamentally unmindful:

[1] *duṣkṛta* for turning toward the next house after leaving the previous house; [2] *pāyattika* for turning away from the next house after leaving the previous house; [3] *duṣkṛta* for turning toward the previous house after leaving the next house. Now, [one must be mindful]."
The same applies here. Thus far, the analysis of the offenses has been concluded. Since there are differences regarding the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), this is now the first.

Regarding the statement that it is appropriate for both monastics and laypeople to know [the date] together: Lì Míng replied that when addressing a layperson, one may simply say "on such-and-such day of the first month," and it is permissible not to specify whether it is the waxing or waning phase.
Jì said: "The white month is the essence of white silver; the black month is..."
The essence of lapis lazuli takes the form of the moon, which is exceptionally circular. Half is white and half is black;

from the first day until the fifteenth day, the white increases and the black decreases, hence it is called the "white month" (śuklapakṣa). From the sixteenth day until the thirtieth day, the black increases and the white decreases, hence it is called the "black month" (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
If one entirely does not accept an invitation, this refers to a person of the "three colors" who completely refuses all invitations;
such is the person who does not accept individual invitations. If one accepts an invitation, this refers to the second type of person who accepts individual invitations.
If there is an invitation, this refers to the third type of person who has many invitations and is permitted to relinquish them.

Regarding the knowledge of the time of ordination and the number of years since one's full ordination (*kṣānti*), the Master [Daoxuan] says: The *Fengsu tong* states that in the Han dynasty it was called *lâ* (臘).
"Lâ" derives from "hunting" (*liè*); it refers to taking game to sacrifice to one's ancestors. This is the name for the festival at the end of the year for worshipping the deities.

The sūtras and vinayas state that *lâ* carries the meaning of "year. Alternatively, it is said that *lâ* means "to join" (*jiē*); it signifies the joining of the new with the old. [Daoshi] further explains: It is like the state...
At the end of the year, the ruler releases the high officials to hunt; this marks the conclusion of the year.

When heaven and earth are at peace and the five grains have ripened in abundance, the month that concludes the year is called the "Là" (臘) month. It is in this very month that one hunts birds and beasts to sacrifice in the seven ancestral temples;
the food resulting from this is called "là-shí" (臘食). By analogy with this principle, it is understood that the various bhikṣus have performed meritorious service during the summer retreat. Five...
Bestowing rewards for labor is in principle the same as the *khaḍga* meal; thus it is called "summer *khaḍga*" and so forth.
Regarding the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* stating that when the Buddha ordained bhikṣus, eight items were permitted to accompany them:

upon examining the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it says that as for the "well-coming" (*svāgata*) bhikṣu, there was a layperson who came to the Buddha’s presence desiring to seek ordination, and the Tathāgata immediately examined his faculties and conditions.

Being fully endowed [with the marks], those who were ready to be delivered were summoned with the words, "Come, O Bhikṣu. Consequently, their hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and they became bhikṣus.
The Buddha extended his golden-hued hand and, with a Brahma-voice, called out, "Come, O Bhikṣu! Cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) joyfully within my Dharma;
quickly exhaust the source of suffering. Before the Buddha had finished speaking, they became bhikṣus and attained full ordination (upasaṃpadā), possessing the three robes.
As well as a clay alms-bowl, which he suspended over his left shoulder; the color of the bowl was like that of a blue *utpala* flower, and his *kāṣāya* robe was as bright as a red lotus.
He was fully equipped with a needle, thread, an axe, and a water-strainer. These eight items are the standard requisites for those who have left the household life;
he used them naturally, his deportment being perfectly complete. This was the Buddha acting as a *śramaṇera*.

The Upādhyāya is also the Preceptor (Śāstr). From the time the Tathāgata first attained the Way until his Parinirvāṇa, there were one thousand three hundred and forty-one Bhikṣus who entered the order by the "Come, Bhikṣu" (Ehi Bhikṣu) formula;
these alone were ordained by the Buddha himself. All others were ordained through the Three Refuges, the Higher Dharma, or the Karmavācanā rite, and their number was boundless.

Regarding the confusion between bhikṣus and non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), the Buddha instructed that one should ask: "At what time and in what month [did you receive the precepts]? and so forth. This establishes the following:
if a non-Buddhist has secretly entered into the Buddhist Dharma and is conflating himself with the monastic community, one should ask when he received the precepts.
If he claims it was during the autumn, one knows him to be a non-Buddhist, because within the Buddhist Dharma there are only three seasons, which differ from those of the secular world.

He was a human being. Thus, the *Xinshu* states: "The reason for listing the three seasons of spring, summer, and winter—and further, the white and black months—is that because the positions of the monastic and the lay differ, the calculation of time is likewise altered. For the laity, the year has four seasons;

for the monastics, the year has only three periods, as the autumnal equinox is omitted. However, regarding the commencement of these three seasons, winter is placed at the beginning to signify the absence of [defilement].
This is the constant practice. It causes those with a mind to enter the Way through contemplation at this time; there is no room for negligence or idleness.

As for providing the [text] after one has received the precepts, it is like the case where, upon the completion of receiving the precepts, each person is given the Six Mindfulnesses (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and so forth.
The above concludes the general explanation of the meaning of the "Gate of the Gathering of Conditions for Receiving Precepts for the First Time."

Second, the explanation of the relinquishing of the precepts. From the beginning up to this point, the conditions for receiving [the precepts] have been explained in general. Fearing that there might be circumstances necessitating their abandonment, the Great Sage permitted their relinquishment.

Since receiving and relinquishing are opposites, the latter is explained next. According to the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface), it is said: "In the past, people remarked that the precept against sexual misconduct is difficult to practice over a long period."

Such matters cannot be abandoned abruptly, nor do they obstruct the attainment of the first fruit (*ādyaphala*); therefore, it is permitted to relinquish the precepts in order to accomplish these tasks.

This is not the case for killing or stealing, and the same applies to the training in repentance (*śikṣādattaka*). Now, my interpretation is that this is not so; the principle encompasses all such cases. We know that the training in repentance applies universally because:
Below, the text adds four lines: "If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī has not yet committed a pārājika offense, they shall never commit one;

if it is seen that they have no intention of concealment at all, they may perform repentance according to the Dharma. Lì says: "According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, there are four kinds of relinquishment:

namely, through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), death, the severing of the roots of goodness, and the emergence of both sexual organs. Relinquishment by formal ritual occurs because it contradicts the original vow."

Regarding "abandoning at the end of life": because the basis no longer remains. Regarding "one who has severed the roots of goodness": because the original basis is lost. Regarding "one with both sexual organs": because the physical support is dual.
Some say that this applies even to one with wrong views who has plucked out a single hair, or even to one wearing yellow robes.
Li asked: Generally speaking, when one speaks of "abandoning the precepts," does it mean abandoning the wholesome precepts already produced, or does it refer to the causal aspect?

Regarding the abandonment of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precept-body: the answer is that since the wholesome precepts already produced act as causes to inevitably induce their fruits, they are not abandoned;

rather, it is only the unmanifest precept-body that is abandoned. The original vow undertaken at the time of reception results in an unmanifest state that continues spontaneously throughout one's life.

Now, through a mind of revulsion and renunciation, one causes the unmanifest to no longer arise in succession; this is called "abandoning the precepts. To speak in terms of principle, there are first the precept-dharma (*śīladharma*).

Second is the karma of morality (*śīla-karman*). If one discusses the relinquishing of morality, morality is relinquished but the karma is not; this is because the status of being a cause is established. If one discusses the attainment of the fruit, the karma is relinquished but the dharma is not lost;

this is because the fruit arises while the cause has ceased. Question: If one does not relinquish already-arisen wholesome states, what is the meaning of the principle that through repentance they are resolved?

Should one not then eliminate those evils that have already arisen? Answer: Wholesome states arise in accordance with the principle, whereas evil arises in opposition to the principle. [Wholesome states] accord with...
The power of principle is strong; that which has already arisen is not relinquished. Because it contradicts principle, its power is weak, and thus it may be expiated and removed.

According to the Vinaya texts, there are nineteen ways of relinquishing [the precepts]. In the Vinaya’s section on the precept against sexual misconduct, there are explicit clarifications. Now, they are summarized in verse:

"Relinquishing the Three Jewels, the two teachers, Fellow practitioners, the precepts, and the study; Accepting a layperson, Saimi, Or becoming an outsider—these are non-śramaṇas. (The first two lines refer to relinquishing through weariness; the latter two...)
[The phrase] "sentence-prayer" (or "clause-entreaty") [refers to] renunciation. The *Xinshu* states: In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the bhikṣu Saṃghama subdued Māra seven times;
subsequently, he received the precepts again and attained the fruit of Arhatship. From this point forward, the renunciation of the precepts is permitted up to seven times;

if it exceeds this, it is contrary to the Dharma. Bin says: This refers to the subduing of the affliction-māra (*kleśa-māra*). Because he was oppressed by afflictions, he renounced the precepts. Gao says: It was because he was pressed by afflictions.
To abandon the precepts seven times is what constitutes being subdued by Māra. How, then, could this be the subduing of Māra?
Now, it may also be understood that receiving the precepts seven times is itself termed "subduing Māra."

Regarding the fact that there is no formal procedure for nuns to relinquish their precepts: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that nuns have no such method for relinquishing the precepts; even those who have transformed into males may still go forth.

This is because there are no obstacles to their coming and going. It is established that when one first comes to seek refuge with the Buddha and goes forth, this initial arrival is in accordance with the Dharma; subsequently, [one listens to...]
To renounce the precepts and return home without carrying the burden of transgressions is to depart in accordance with the Dharma; it is without obstruction.

This ensures that while remaining a layperson, one commits no faults and does not give rise to reproach or disgrace. Master Li said: "If one does not renounce the precepts yet engages in improper conduct as a layperson, one will incur the censure and blame of worldly people.

Since renunciation is now permitted, this is the principle of being without fault while remaining a layperson. Some say: "It allows for [the possibility of] becoming a person of the two lower realms."
This is said because of the multitude [of preceding explanations]. The explanation of the eight chapters above is now complete.
*Sifen lü chao pi*, Volume Five, Part One;
*Sifen lü chao pi*, Volume Five, Part Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Chapter Nine: The Mutual Support of Teacher and Disciple.
Although one has received the sacred Dharma and taken it to heart as described above, those who are newly initiated do not yet understand how to protect and maintain it. Upon contact—

When delusion arises regarding affairs, one must rely upon a master to consult and receive their dharma instructions; thereby, one achieves personal benefit. If one does not receive both material sustenance and the dharma from a teacher, how can the life of wisdom survive?
Without someone to provide instruction and admonition, one will immediately commit evil when facing perilous circumstances.

Nothing is more dangerous than this. Therefore, the Great Sage established the rule that one must rely on a teacher for five years of study; thus, the dharma-body and the life of wisdom will surely [endure].

Because it is that upon which one relies, this chapter is established following the section on "Receiving [the Precepts]. Lì said: "A person who has newly received the precepts has not yet become proficient or enlightened;

they should follow their teacher to consult and receive instruction in order to achieve their own benefit. If they suddenly leave their teacher and depart, they will not receive the teacher's guidance and encouragement, and will remain mired in confusion and stagnation."

The transgression of violating the teachings is profound. Regarding the terms "teacher" (*shi*) and "disciple" (*zi*): the *Yupian* states that one who instructs others is called a teacher. Zheng Xuan says that one who instructs others in the Way is called a teacher.
Ying Shi says that "teacher and disciple" refers to followers; "disciple" (*zi*) means to employ, and it also means to take [instruction].
Laozi says: "The good person is the teacher of the not-good person; the not-good person is the resource (*zi*) for the good person. Here, "resource" (*zi*) is as follows:
It refers to material resources (*sambhāra*). Lì (Lì Yǒng) says: "A teacher (*shī*) is like a father; he is the master, and is also called a craftsman (*jiàng*), meaning one who fashions things.
Regarding "resources" (*zī*): the *Guǎngpǐ* states that "resources" mean "to employ. This refers to the disciple taking the Dharma from the teacher. Furthermore, "resources" also means "to bestow.

This character *zī* is used in two directions, applying to both teacher and disciple: it signifies that the teacher is able to instruct according to the characteristics of the Dharma, thereby... [enabling the disciple].
The strengthening and solidification of practice and understanding is "giving" (yǔ). That the disciple is able to rely on the teachings to practice is "receiving" (qǔ).

The teacher sustains the disciple with the food of the Dharma, while the disciple serves and supports the teacher with reverence; as they mutually benefit one another, it is said that they "sustain each other" (xiāngshè).

If we were to explain this directly: one who instructs and admonishes others through the Dharma is called a "teacher" (śāstr). One who receives and accepts the instruction of the Dharma is called a "supporter" (upastambha).

As for the term "mutual support," it refers to the practice of the common observances mentioned below; because they instruct and admonish one another, it is said that they "mutually support" each other. (This interpretation is also excellent.)
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-dharma increases, expands, and so forth," this is a passage from the Vinaya text. The *Chao* (Commentary) cites it as the opening of this preface. Yanli says:

"The Buddha-dharma increases, expands, and so forth" means that because of the instructions and admonitions, the Dharma-body is not destroyed; because [monks] look after one another, the vessel of the Path is not impaired.
Therefore, it is said that it "abides for a long time, increasing, expanding, and so forth. As for the phrase "master and disciples supporting one another":
Master Ying says: "Disciple" (*tu*) means a class or category. The *Zhuangzi* says, "The disciples of Confucius. Sima Biao states: "Disciple" refers to a student.
As for the phrase "truly because of," it means that because masters and disciples sustain one another, the Buddha-dharma abides long and increases;
this is called "vast and great. If there were no benefit from the successive transmission of practice by masters and disciples, the Buddha-dharma would perish.

It is called "not vast. Regarding the term "mutual inclusion" (*xiāngshè*), the *Jiemo shū* (Commentary on the Karma-vastu) states: "The master possesses the diligence of caring for and protecting [the disciple], while the disciple possesses the resolve of honoring and following [the master];
therefore, it is called 'mutual inclusion. Regarding the phrase "mutually encouraging one another" (*xiāng hù dūnyù*) and so forth, the *Erlǐ* (Classic of Rites) states:
"To 'encourage' (*dùn*) means to exhort and urge one another; it is also faith. Cí (Cíyún) says: "To 'encourage' (*dùn*) also carries the meaning of exerting effort," meaning that they mutually...
"Exhorting with vigor" means to strengthen the mind through effort. "Encountering" is like two people meeting and mutually encouraging one another;

it clarifies that teacher and disciple rely upon each other, just as those traveling together have shared practices by which they each lead and inspire one another to advance in their spiritual cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "relieving both through wealth and Dharma," this is clearly established: "wealth" refers to providing sustenance such as food and clothing, while "Dharma" refers to instructing with teachings and admonitions. However...
Not only does the teacher instruct the disciple through these two matters, but the disciple also exhorts and encourages the teacher through these same two matters.
If there is a lack of clothing and food, one then repays the teacher’s kindness through offerings; this refers to the "Dharma for Practicing Together" mentioned in the following section.

For example, the śrāmaṇera Cūḍapanthaka did not receive the full precepts in order to repay his teacher’s kindness. Thus, the sixteenth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "The Venerable Śā..."
"Ānanda, three times each day and night, I survey the world with my divine eye to deliver those who are ready for deliverance.

At that time, there were some merchants traveling together with a dog. When they reached the middle of their journey, the merchants halted to rest, and the dog then stole the flesh from among the merchants."
At that time, the crowd beat the dog and abandoned it in the wilderness, then departed.
Śāriputra, seeing this from afar with his divine eye, gave him food and taught him the subtle and wondrous Dharma. When he passed away, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Śrāvastī;
his name was Cunda. When he reached the age of seven, he was entrusted to Śāriputra to be ordained as a monk.
Having cultivated the path and attained the fruit of Arhatship, he used his own power of wisdom to observe his past lives.

He had been a starving dog who, through the grace of his preceptor Śāriputra, was now to serve him for the remainder of his life by providing whatever was required. He manifested as a śrāmaṇera, yet did not receive the precepts.
Regarding the phrase "long practice and firm virtue," it means that because his conduct and merit were steadfast and solid, they are described as "long and firm. This refers to all...

*Rais* (賴斯) means "to rely" (*rai*) and "to be protected" (*su*). It refers to the master and disciple being mutually sustained as one. This signifies that their practice and virtue are firm and stable, having been protected by the power of the master.
Regarding the phrase "the profound teaching has declined," it is established that "profound" (*xuan*) arises from "wondrous" (*miao*). This refers to the wondrous and profound teachings.
As for "decline" (*lingchi*), it is because there is no mutual sustenance between teacher and disciple. "Decline" does not carry the meaning of being overtaken by illness or vigor.
Some say: "Ling" means "above," and "chi" means "not advancing. It is like a person wishing to ascend high into the void; it is difficult to rise further ahead, which is what is meant.
"Declining. This is intended to clarify that in the final age, the Buddha-dharma is difficult to propagate; it is likened to a decline.

Regarding the phrase "the wind of wisdom is fanned closed," my own interpretation is as follows: Now, "wind" carries the meaning of "fanning and moving. When there is no wind, there is this absence of fanning.
Currently, the Buddhist teaching does not prevail among these people; thus, there is a mutual absence of the wind of wisdom, which is why it is so stated.
"Shutting the fan" refers to this. Regarding the phrase "the common folk harbor contempt and arrogance," *Lì* explains that "contempt arises from slighting.

This clarifies that such customs have persisted for a long time; the common people harbor worldly sentiments, treating the net of the teachings with disdain and looking down upon the masters and monks.

As for the statement "the Way issues from what is not the Dharma," *Lì* clarifies that the Way is propagated by people; since the people are not according to the Dharma, the Way lacks its support and perishes accordingly. Thus, the *Lun-yü* says:
"Man can broaden the Way; it is not the Way that broadens man. "Broaden" (*hong*) means to make great. When the Way resides within the person, this is precisely that meaning.
This refers to cases such as ordained monks and nuns who do not follow the teachings in their conduct; thus it is said, "The Way emerges from non-dharma.

Regarding the phrase "all due to the teacher lacking guidance and exhortation," etc., this below serves to conclude the preceding text. It says that above, the wind of wisdom has covered the fan of the profound...
Regarding the teaching that those who transgress the Way and depart from the Dharma do so due to the fault of teacher and disciple:

it is because there was no guidance and attraction from the teacher, and thus the disciple failed to follow and honor him. As for the term "leading" (*shuài*), it corresponds to the teacher’s word (pronounced *suǒ lǜ*); it means to lead and conduct [others], or to guide.
Regarding the phrase "the two of them abandon one another," etc.: when the teacher abandons the disciple and the disciple abandons the teacher, these are called "the two of them."
The teacher has no dharma-food to sustain the disciple, and the disciple is unable to receive and follow the teacher’s dharma-instructions; thus it is said they have "mutually abandoned" one another.
Regarding the phrase "flowing into vulgar realms," the *Guangpi* states: "Vulgar (*bi*) means shame; it also means lowly.
This clarifies that once teachers and disciples have mutually abandoned one another, they extensively commit various transgressions and frequently enter nunneries and taverns—these are vulgar realms.
As for the phrase, "How could one wish to cause the Way to shine?"—this establishes clarity. As seen above, such a relationship between master and disciple lacks any formal succession;
how, then, could they uphold the Buddha-dharma and propagate its transformative influence? Such a thing is impossible. Therefore, it is said: "How could one wish to cause [the Way] to shine?"
Regarding the phrase "therefore, rescuing from the urgency of being suspended upside-down," Fazhi states: A newly ordained person is like an infant;
if not given milk, they will surely die. This is the meaning of being "suspended upside-down. It clarifies that if one does not now bestow the Dharma [upon them], [the same consequence will follow].

Unable to comprehend the net of the teachings, they violate the prohibitions and precepts, thereby losing the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body; this is what is meant by being "suspended upside down. Regarding the statement that one is granted the means for both safety and peril:
when newly receiving the precepts, one encounters matters and gives rise to delusion; facing the pit of transgression is like treading upon the edge of a precipice.
Now, the Master rescues them with the Dharma, providing security amidst their peril. He causes them to take up the two types of observances and avoid the two types of transgressions.
One must abandon [faults] and gather, guide, and instruct [disciples]; this is the meaning of "method" (*fang*). Method arises from the Dharma (*fa*). Some say:

"This present chapter transmits the ritual procedures for the mutual guidance between teacher and disciple; thus the True Dharma shall no longer decline or fall into peril, but will abide in eternal peace for a thousand years.
My own view is that the passage beginning with "From the former rescue... serves as the introduction to the purpose of this chapter. It says: "Fortunately..."
This is a term of aspiration; it is also glossed as "favor. The preceding explanation of the meaning of the preface is now complete.
As for this term having no direct equivalent, it is because such a category did not previously exist here [in China], so it is unknown how it should be translated.

If it were like water and fire, which both exist in both places, their names would differ, yet they could be translated as counterparts. Now, regarding the phrase "the power that gives rise to correct practice," this refers to—

"Yi" (義) is a translation of the term *artha*. Regarding "seeing guilt where there is no guilt," this clarifies that although a disciple practices in accordance with the teachings and appears outwardly pure and blameless, the teacher, upon close examination, perceives that they are guilty; thus it is said.

Because one forcibly perceives guilt within what is actually blameless, one reprimands them. According to the *Kṣudrakavastu-vinaya* (*Jianjian lun*), one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was Aśoka.

"O King, since ascending the throne, for three years you have served only non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika). It was only upon reaching the fourth year that you came to believe in the Buddha-dharma.
Later, while providing food for the non-Buddhists and Brahmins, the King saw these two groups from afar atop his palace;

looking around at their left and right, he saw they possessed no Dharma-practice whatsoever, so he ordered them to be driven out. Furthermore, from atop the palace, he saw a single śrāmaṇera from afar."
His name was Gauda. As he passed before the palace, his gait was level and upright, and his deportment was complete.

The King thought to himself, "This man’s movements—his bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—are so orderly and dignified; he must possess the noble Dharma. With a heart of faith and joy, the King immediately dispatched three ministers.
He went to summon the śrāmaṇera. The king immediately gave him food. When he had finished eating, he preached the Dharma for the king.

Upon hearing the Dharma, the king was filled with joy and said to the śrāmaṇera, "I wish to offer you precious jewels. The śrāmaṇera replied, "Excellent! I shall give them back to my teacher. The king asked, "Who is your teacher?
He answered, "One who sees no fault where there is no fault, yet reproaches me for seeing what is not a fault—this is my teacher. The king asked again, "What is his name?"

The *ācārya* replied: "One who instructs and causes me to understand within the wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) is my *ācārya*. Regarding the statement "as explained in the treatises," the *Samantapāsādikā*, fascicle seven, states:
"Upādhyāya is a foreign term; in the Han language, it means 'one who knows what constitutes an offense and what does not constitute an offense.
This is called an upādhyāya. The same is stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) in the section on the disciple’s censure of the upādhyāya.
Ji said: "The Vinaya states: 'Whether my preceptor knows me as practicing according to the Dharma or does not know me as practicing according to the Dharma;

whether my preceptor knows that I have committed an offense or does not know that I have committed an offense. Based on this text, it corresponds to the aforementioned *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) regarding knowing whether there is an offense or no offense."
The meaning is the same; therefore, it is said "also. Regarding *upādhyāya* and so forth, this Sanskrit pronunciation is slightly corrupted.

According to the *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karma-vastu), in the Central Indian original, it is *upādhyāya*. Translated into the language of Tang, it is called "one upon whom one relies for learning" (*yixue*).
Because they rely on this person to study the Way of Renunciation, translations from antiquity have often been mixed with the languages of the barbarians.

When the Hu (barbarians) transmit the language of Heaven (Sanskrit), they fail to capture its true sounds and meanings; thus, errors and distortions arise. For instance, "Upādhyāya" is translated as "Heshang. According to the interpretation of people of old, it means "the most supreme among equals."

This is a word-for-word explanation. Not knowing the original phonetics, others have further interpreted it as "power-birth" (*balotpāda*), claiming it means "generating the power of disciples" through reliance on the production of the Sage.
While this captures the distant meaning, it misses the proximate terminology.

The *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* by Paramārtha states *upādhyāya*, which is somewhat closer to the Sanskrit sound, yet still deviates from the rules of phonology (*śabdavidyā*). I personally attended the translation and inquired exhaustively regarding the original source.
Regarding the term *upādhyāya*: "Ūpādāye" is correct here. Yancong of the Sui dynasty wrote "Dūbōdìyé," which is phonetically similar.
It is traditionally said that "Upādhyāya" means "one who gives strength" (*balajanaka*). This is the interpretation of Vinaya Master Yun, as cited in the *Cè* (策).
The *ācārya* is the teacher of correct practice. The *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states that the terms "ben" and "sui" were transmitted erroneously and abbreviated.
According to the authentic Sanskrit pronunciation, it is *ācārya*; in the Tang translation, it is rendered as "Professor" (Jiàoshòushī). Yàn Zōng’s translation as *ācāliye* is phonetically similar.
As for non-Buddhists also designating their teachers as *upādhyāya*, Lìmíng notes that among all ninety-six types [of heterodox schools]...
Non-Buddhists all address their teacher as "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor); this is not limited to the Buddha-dharma alone.
To say that "understanding arises from me" is also expressed as "the precepts arise from me," whereby one is called a "disciple. Some say:
if one says the precepts arise from me, it refers specifically to the Upādhyāya; thus one may say the precepts arise from me. However, as for others...
Regarding the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) and the *karmācārya* (preceptor of ritual action), it can simply be said that "understanding arises from me. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

a disciple serves his teacher just as a younger brother serves his elder brother in secular society, or as a son serves his father; thus, he is called a "disciple" (*śiṣya*). Moreover, the *upādhyāya* may also be said to cause the precepts to arise from himself.
This is because there are two kinds of precepts: first, the precepts received through formal ordination; second, [the precepts arising from understanding].
Regarding the precepts: although one cannot generate the formal reception of the precepts based on a *ācārya* (preceptor), that person shall provide instruction for the rest of one's life.
Furthermore, because one can generate the conformity to the precepts (*anuśīla*), it may also be said that "the precepts arise from me."
Regarding the phrase "Śukarāja and others": this sutra is titled after its protagonist. When the Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain, there was the son of an elder named Śukarāja.
Rising early, he groomed his hair, bathed, and donned exquisite, fine garments.

He then performed four prostrations toward each of the six directions—east, west, south, north, above, and below—at each of the six periods of the day. Just then, as the Buddha entered the city for alms, [Śukarāja] saw him from afar and went toward him.
Question: Why do you perform prostrations with six limbs? To what dharma does this correspond? He replied: My father taught me to do so;
I did not know to which dharma it corresponds. Now that my father has passed away, I dare not disobey him. The Buddha said:
Your father taught you to prostrate with six intentions, not to prostrate with the body. The Buddha then explained it for him, as recorded separately in another transcription.
Regarding the phrase "enabling the True Dharma to abide for a long time," it is through respect that the True Dharma is made to increase and expand;
conversely, if this is lacking, the Dharma will perish. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the definitions and meanings of the terms "teacher" and "disciple."
Regarding those who do not rely [on others]: there are six types in the *Caturvargika*, one in the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and one in the *Pañcavargika*;
these constitute the eight types of persons.

First, "one who delights in tranquility" refers to a disciple who wishes to practice meditation in seclusion, such as by dwelling in the mountains; hence, they are called "one who delights in tranquility. Second, "one who maintains... [the text continues].
Regarding the protection of a dwelling place: for instance, if there is no monk who knows the Dharma in a monastery in a certain region, it must rely upon this disciple to maintain it.

If [the disciple] were to leave, the property of the Saṃgha would fall into ruin and waste; therefore, for the sake of its protection, the Buddha has permitted [this arrangement] even if there is no formal reliance (niśraya).
Third, regarding those who are ill: this refers to one who, being ill, is unable to rely upon others.
"If one fears dying of hunger, one should see the upādhyāya every day. The Vinaya states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a famine and food was scarce.
At that time, a bhikṣu who had not yet completed five years of seniority and was required to receive formal dependence (niśraya) went to the home of his relatives.
After staying for four or five days, he took his leave and wished to depart. His relatives asked him, "For what reason are you leaving? He replied:
"Because I must rely upon [a preceptor]," a kinsman said, "Venerable One, at this time there is famine, or there may be famine;
what use is there in relying [on one]? The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "In times of famine, you may go to see your upādhyāya every day and receive permission to stay, coming back each day. If you cannot come every day, you may go..."
On the fifth day. If one cannot come on the fifth day, one should come at the time of the *poṣadha*.

If one cannot come at the *poṣadha*, one must come to see the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) by the time of the *pravāraṇa*, even if it is two and a half *yojanas* away. Regarding the distance of "two and a half *yojanas*": [it refers to the maximum distance from which one may travel].

It is understood that one may reside in a place two and a half *yojanas* away from one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) during the rainy season retreat (*varṣa*). At the conclusion of the summer, one should come to request instruction and admonition.
One who dwells with the thought of relying [on a teacher] as if they were a master merely avoids the offense of not relying [on a teacher];
however, it does not constitute the formal practice of reliance (*niśraya-dharma*). This must be understood.

Second, regarding the requirement to rely upon ten persons: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are eight; the ninth and tenth are mutually [included] in the text of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Regarding the fourth point, the preceptor’s relinquishing of the right to ordain others: it is established that whether for a monk or a nun, if one wishes to ordain a śrāmaṇera or confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon another, one must request the right to ordain others from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should deliberate and, if the candidate is deemed capable, grant the formal motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Regarding the permission to maintain a retinue of disciples: although this present preceptor has previously attained the Dharma, he now abandons it and does not maintain a retinue, delighting instead in practices such as seated meditation (*dhyāna*).
Consequently, the disciple must rely upon another person. Sixth, regarding a disciple who does not delight in their current residence and seeks superior conditions:
this disciple does not find satisfaction under the care of this present preceptor and wishes to seek out a better teacher.

Regarding those who surpass their upādhyāya, this is explained in terms of the *vinaya* (teachings on conduct). Master Li states: "For now, this is explained according to the *vinaya*; if one were to explain it according to the *vaipulya* (transformative teachings), even the Buddha has a teacher, namely the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "those in the Mahāsāṃghika who do not well understand the *vinaya*," if one consults the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says: "If a bhikṣu..."
The bhikṣuṇī does not well understand the Dharma, nor does she well understand the Vinaya, nor is she skilled at establishing herself, nor can she establish others.

Such a bhikṣu, throughout his life, relies [on another]—as the *Chao* text notes, there are only three [cases] with one missing. One whose resolve is not upright and correct establishes the following clarification:

this person, upon seeing an offense, immediately confesses it and claims, "I know [the rules]. However, since they repeatedly commit offenses and repeatedly confess them, this is not skillful; rather, one should be single-mindedly diligent so as not to commit them. Therefore, [the text] returns to...

One must rely upon it, for it is not upright and correct. Because one frequently transgresses, there is much repentance; were it upright and correct, one would be able to maintain it with single-minded diligence and refrain from transgression.

Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned seven persons," this refers to the ten types of persons mentioned above. Although all must rely [on a teacher], the present discussion specifically examines the meaning of who *must* rely on one.
Among these, the first seven require it because they have not yet completed five years of residence (*pañca-varṣa*).

As for the latter three, although they have exceeded five years, they must still rely on a teacher because they lack knowledge. Regarding the statement that "virtue and conduct must both be complete," Wǎilì asked: "Virtue..."

How does this differ from "practice" (*caryā*)? The answer is: "practice" refers to the initial cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*), while "virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to the ultimate fulfillment of completion.

It is only when both virtue and practice are fully possessed that one is permitted to be released from formal reliance (*niśraya*). Regarding the loss of reliance after five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*), as explained according to the scriptural characteristics:

Jing says, this refers to a case where there is no superior person residing in the same location. If one takes up the exemption from reliance, it extends even to the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

"Only then may one depart. This means that within the context of the provisional teachings (*yiao*), those who are five years old and possess wisdom are permitted to depart; however, regarding the essence of practice (*xingti*), it is not yet appropriate to depart.
Only when the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*) is established in the following section is departure permitted.

Regarding the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*): guarding against what is improper and ceasing evil is called morality (*śīla*). Calming the mind through meditative concentration is called concentration (*samādhi*). Contemplating and illuminating emptiness and existence is called wisdom (*prajñā*).

The exhaustion of karmic burdens and the disappearance of delusions is called liberation (*vimukti*). To clearly and thoroughly recognize this state of one's own liberation is called the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

This refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). Regarding the statement that "the Buddha also has teachers, as is understood through various teachings," this means it refers to passages from the *Vaipulya* (transformative) teachings and so forth.
The explanation of the meaning of "conforming to the Dharma" is hereby concluded.
Second, explaining reliance upon correct practice. *Lei* says: "Relying" (*yi*) means to depend upon; "abiding" (*zhi*) means to dwell.

Therefore, it is called "reliance and abiding" (*yizhi*). Regarding the seven types of common practices (*sādhāraṇa-pratipatti*): these refer to the mutual conduct between teacher and disciple, which is termed "common practice. The verse on the seven dharmas states:

Regarding the phrase "not performing [acts] so as to cause the Saṃgha to resolve [the issue], repentance for the *śeṣaka* offense, tending to the sick, moving to another location, removing doubts, abandoning evil, and providing protection—these are the two or three types of distinct practices and dharmas":
first, the declaration of matters to avoid transgressions; second, receiving the Dharma to sustain the body;
third, repaying kindness through offerings. These meanings will be explained in detail below.
If an evil view arises, it refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which denies cause and effect. Because this view is evil, it is called an "evil view.

One should cause such wrong view to be abandoned so that one may abide in right view; thus it is said that one "abides in wholesome view. Regarding the "increase of the training in higher ethics" and so forth:

The Vinaya states: What is the training in higher morality? If a bhikṣu fully maintains the *prātimokṣa* precepts, accomplishes dignified deportment, and out of fear and caution treats even minor precepts as heavy as a vajra, training equally in all the precepts—this is called the training in higher morality.

What is the training in the higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*)? If a bhikṣu is able to abandon evil and so forth, up to attaining entry into the fourth dhyāna, this is called the training in the higher mind.

What is the training in the higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*)? If a bhikṣu knows the truth of suffering as it really is, and knows [the truths of] the origin, cessation, and the path, this is called the training in the higher wisdom.

The *Śūshù* (Commentary on the Preface) states: "The training in the higher morality begins with the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), where one applies oneself exclusively..."

Maintaining [the precepts], one awakens to and attains the emptiness of arising; through understanding, the [precepts] are perfected and the category of morality becomes firm, surpassing what came before.

Therefore, it is called the "increased training in morality" (*śīla-śikṣā*). As for "manifesting principle and tranquility," Master Bin says: among the seven stages of expedient means, those with the four roots of goodness (*catur-anuloma-kṣānti*) are called the "four present patiences.

Having severed all agitation and movement, this is the beginning of the accomplishment of the category of concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*). Therefore, it is called the "increased training in mind" (*citta-śikṣā*). Entering into non-existence...

Having transcended signs, one realizes the emptiness of true reality and the state free from outflows (*anāsrava*). Bin said: "This is entering the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*); such a person is one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Therefore it is said: 'Having entered the vision of signlessness and gone beyond. Because one is decisively clear and lucid, it is called 'increasing the training in wisdom' (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). The *Saṃyukta Āgama* says:
"If a bhikṣu dwells in the *Prātimokṣa*, is complete in his dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), and perceives even the slightest fault with fear, he [should] receive..."
To uphold the training in the precepts is called the higher training in virtue (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).

If a bhikṣu, having abandoned unwholesome and evil states, dwells having attained the first dhyāna—accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness—and so on up to dwelling having attained the fourth dhyāna, this is called the higher training in wisdom (*adhijñāna-śikṣā*).
If a bhikṣu knows this noble truth of suffering as it really is, and [knows] the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path.

To know this as it truly is—this is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). As for what is called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), this is the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*);
because concentration is that which disciplines the mind, it is termed "mind-training. A guest asked:

"Regarding these terms—the training in higher morality, higher mind, and higher wisdom—if we consider morality, there is the *prātimokṣa* with outflows (*sāsrava*), the morality of the four dhyānas, and the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*). As for concentration..."

There are contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*) and uncontaminated concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*), as well as mundane dhyānas (*laukika-dhyāna*) and supramundane dhyānas (*lokottara-dhyāna*).

Wisdom (*prajñā*) likewise includes contaminated wisdom, uncontaminated wisdom, wisdom obtained through retribution (*vipākaja-prajñā*), wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayi-prajñā*), wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayi-prajñā*), and wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayi-prajñā*).
Since these distinctions exist, what kind of morality, what kind of concentration, and what kind of wisdom are those being cultivated now? The answer is as listed above in general.
There are many types [of training], all of which must be studied. To speak of their essential nature according to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma:

based on gradual cultivation, first, the *prātimokṣa* precepts constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*). Second, the fundamental four dhyānas constitute the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).

Third, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that enters the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) and so forth constitutes the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). This can be understood by reciting the scriptures.
The explanation of the meaning of "protection of the Dharma" (*dharmarakṣā*) is now complete. Below, the protection of robes and food (*cīvarapiṇḍapātarakṣā*) is clarified.

If a student who relies upon a preceptor (*niśraya-ācārya*) intends to take his robes and bowl to stay overnight outside the boundary, it is established that by staying overnight outside the boundary, he immediately loses the latter two protections.

Upon returning, he may request another person to serve as his preceptor. If he does not go outside the boundary but simply requests another person [while remaining within], it will not succeed in removing the disciple's dependence.
Regarding the three poisons of greed and so forth, the *Cīvaravastu* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) states:

It refers to a teacher who, by relying upon him, can skillfully teach the Dharma to his disciples, thereby eliminating greed, hatred, and delusion. Such a teacher is the most supreme and excellent, comparable to obtaining curd from milk.
From curd one obtains butter; from butter one obtains clarified butter (*ghṛta*); clarified butter is the most supreme and most excellent.
The above concludes the explanation of the meaning of the seven types of collective practice. From here on, the three types of distinct practices are correctly elucidated.

Regarding "the three types of interwoven [practices]," this is the text from the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (The Vinaya of the Four Parts), specifically the section on the *Poṣadha-kaṇḍa*. It concerns the performance of the four positions.

Regarding these: first, one is as it is while the other two are not, which constitutes a state; second, two are as they are while the other is not, which constitutes a state; third, all three are neither as they are nor otherwise, which constitutes a state;
fourth, all three are as they are, which constitutes a state. First, the companion is as it is while the destination and the task are not;

second, the destination is as it is while the companion and the task are not; third, the task is as it is while the companion and the destination are not; fourth, the companion and the destination are as they are while the task is not; fifth, the destination and the task...

1. Like the companion, but not like the matter; 2. Like the place, but not like the companion; 3. Like the place, but not like the matter; 4. Like the matter, but not like the place; 5. Like the matter, but not like the companion; 6. Like the companion, but not like the place; 7. Neither like the companion nor like the matter; 8. Like both the companion and the matter.
Only the final phrase is permissible; the preceding seven are not. The Vinaya text lacks the sixth phrase, which is "like the place, but not like the other two.

The *Śū* (Commentary) judges that it was omitted from the Vinaya. Gao says: It is not merely omitted; by principle, it ought not to exist. For if the companion is like [the rule] and the matter is like [the rule], how could...
"One may go to an improper place;
it is the same for the non-timely announcement (*akāla-śilākṣepa*). This means that today’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is likewise subject to the non-timely announcement.

One should simply omit the phrase "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind," and instead say, "I have arrived at such-and-such city, such-and-such village, or the house of such-and-such person," and so forth. This is the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*).

Regarding those who attend the assembly: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that when a junior bhikṣu takes leave of his upādhyāya or ācārya, wishing to travel abroad, the upādhyāya or ācārya should ask, "Who is your companion?
He should then answer with the name of his companion.
If that companion bhikṣu does not know the *poṣadha*, does not know the *poṣadha-karman*, does not know how to recite the *prātimokṣa*, or does not know how to attend the assembly...
The preceptor should retain [the candidate]. Regarding the method for the assembly:

on the six days of the monthly fast—namely, the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days—on these days, healthy bhikṣus should gather in one place to preach the Dharma.
If non-Buddhists come to debate, the bhikṣus should challenge them according to the Dharma.
"Rebuke and subdue; do not harbor anger or speak harshly. This is called the Dharma of the Assembly Seat. Jì said:
"The 'Assembly Seat' refers to the seat within the place where the assembly is convened; that is, the place where offerings of food are set forth."
Regarding the term *jīn* (紉): the *Zilin* (Lexicon of Characters) states it is pronounced *zhēn* (with the second tone). It means "rope.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If a barber comes," etc., a consultation of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (*Qishi*) states: If the Upādhyāya or Ācārya has entered a village and a barber arrives wishing to shave [the head], one should inform another elder bhikṣu, saying, "I wish to have my hair shaved.
When the teacher returns from the village, one should again inform the teacher, saying: [as follows].
"Announcing to the other elders" does not refer to the person being addressed for the purpose of shaving their hair;

rather, according to the intent of the text, it applies equally to one who shaves for another or one who receives the service of being shaved by another. From this point onward, the method for a disciple’s offering is clarified.
When one intends to perform the act of dyeing robes, they must announce the matter in general; the procedure is like that for lighting a fire or fetching water and fuel—all [must be announced].
This is the business of those who are defiled; hence it is called "pervasive. Furthermore, one must report each instance individually.
Regarding the phrase "because they are able to establish themselves," this means that they not only establish themselves but are also able to establish others.
The following section clearly explains the method by which the two masters provide guidance. First, regarding the intention behind the reliance [on a teacher]:

for those who have newly received the precepts and have just entered the Buddha-dharma and so forth, Master Li says: "A person who has newly received the precepts is like an infant amidst the graves of the past.

If they are not instructed and nurtured in their mind and spirit, it will be difficult for their Dharma-body to be established; they must rely on one of virtuous character and depend upon such a person to receive instruction."

Therefore, the Vinaya states that when newly ordained bhikṣus have no one to instruct them, they do not maintain dignified deportment, they beg for food improperly, they accept impure food at various places, and they shout loudly and clamorously during the great and small meals, like the assemblies of Brahmins (and so forth).
[The question arises: "Upon what shall the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom rely? Jì replied: "Ordinary persons..."

One relies on consciousness; the noble ones rely on wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is precisely insight (*prajñā*); therefore, wisdom alone is life. Regarding the allowance in the Vinaya for washing one's feet and drinking water:

it is clearly established that when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu who, upon arriving at a place, had no leisure to drink water and immediately requested to stay as a dependent disciple (*niśraya*).
Being extremely exhausted from his journey, he reported this matter to the Buddha, whereupon the Buddha permitted the washing of feet and the drinking of water.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If one does not rely [on the Sangha] by drinking water, eating rice, and so forth, one commits the offense of theft every day.
Jing says: "This does not mean that one directly commits theft; rather, because one does not rely [on them], there is no one to provide instruction, and thus one loses the Dharma.

When one uses the Sangha’s bedding and furniture and causes them to be damaged, it is on this basis that the offense of theft is established. It is not that one directly commits theft simply because of the failure to rely [on them]. Li says:

Because one fails to recognize the characteristics of the teachings and thus violates the precepts, such a person is a breaker of the precepts and is unfit to receive the offerings and sustenance of the Sangha.

This matter is equivalent to committing theft; therefore, the twentieth section below, the "Chapter on Bestowing Treatment upon the Gift," states: "Receiving offerings while breaking the precepts is like a thief who has stolen. This is precisely that meaning.

Furthermore, if one has passed ten years since ordination (*daśavarṣa*) but does not recite the precepts, the offense is the same as that of one who lacks a formal reliance (*aniśraya*). This refers to:
This constitutes the same offense of theft committed day after day.
First, the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) is the one who shaves the hair. Fifth, the *niśraya-ācārya* (preceptor of reliance):

this *niśraya-ācārya* must have a minimum of ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). This differs slightly from the aforementioned four types; whereas for the former four, five or six years of seniority is sufficient.
Regarding the phrase "with those of equal seniority" (*he-shang*): it means that if one is of the same age as another of equal seniority, they should not sit on the same bed.
This is the meaning of the worldly saying: "One who is twice one's age or older is treated like a father. This applies except in the case of the *niśraya* (the preceptor).

This means that one who relies on a substitute for the position of preceptor (upādhyāya) performs duties identical to those of a preceptor; however, he must have ten years more seniority than oneself.
He cannot be like the four types of ācāryas mentioned previously; therefore, he is excluded [from that category].
Regarding the question of what harm there is in receiving such a title: it means that even one who has not yet completed five years of summer retreat may still be called an *ācārya*.

This is illustrated by the case of an *upādhyāya* with nine years of seniority, who is clearly recognized as having received the precepts; thus, if my current *ācārya*, though not yet having completed five years, is addressed as *ācārya*, what possible harm or detriment could there be?
Regarding the phrase "What are his attendants like, etc.? it means that one takes his disciples as one's own attendants.

As for the statement "If there are none at all, only then may one rely upon him," this means that only when there are no aforementioned disputes or conflicts can one request him to be one's preceptor of reliance (*niśrayācārya*).
Regarding "accomplishing five qualities," it means that only when a teacher possesses these five qualities may he be requested [to serve as preceptor].
Second, regarding "reverence": this refers to a teacher who is by nature humble and is highly capable of showing respect to others. Fifth, regarding "delighting in dwelling":

Master Li states that if one is constantly rushing about and traveling, one cannot rely [on the teacher]; it is only when one dwells constantly in one place that one becomes capable [of reliance]. Master Ji says:
"Delighting in dwelling" (the character *zhu* pronounced as *zhù*) means possessing the food of the Dharma; the disciple relies upon this to practice and study, thereby accomplishing the Dharma-body.
Because he stands [firmly], it is called "dwelling in joy.

Regarding the phrase "long-term benefit for the fruits of the śramaṇa and so forth," this means that the teacher can instruct the disciple to study the Tripiṭaka and swiftly realize the four fruits [of the path].
Master Bin says: "At the very least, one must maintain the precepts for three lifetimes; some say one must maintain them without violation for seven lifetimes."
Only then does one realize the first fruit [of the path]. Now, there are those who uphold the precepts and bring their practice to maturity without finding it difficult;

this is entirely due to the force of habitual cultivation from past lives. Even great Arhats such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had to undergo practice for sixty minor kalpas before they could become the foremost among the śrāvakas.
If one practices the bodhisattva path and realizes great enlightenment (mahābodhi), one must likewise pass through...

Only after three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* does one finally attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the phrase "one who breaks the precepts, views, and dignified conduct" (*vinaya-dṛṣṭi-īryāpatha-bhramśin*):

this clarifies that those who have broken the precepts, as well as those with the sixty-two types of views (*dviṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*)—such as those who have destroyed right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)—are unfit to be relied upon as teachers.
As for the passage concerning the two-year-old bhikṣu taking a one-year-old disciple, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there was a person named Vatsa...

A bhikṣu who had been ordained for two years took a disciple who had been ordained for one year and went to where the World-Honored One was. The Buddha, knowing [the situation], asked him intentionally:
"What kind of bhikṣu is this? Vāsaṃtapura replied, "He is my disciple. The Buddha asked, "How many years have you been ordained now? He replied, "Two years.
Again he asked, "How many years has the disciple been ordained? He replied, "One year. The World-Honored One then rebuked him in countless ways.
