Regarding the passage on "language": "Your body has not yet weaned itself from milk; you ought to receive instruction from others. How can you instruct others?
For this reason, it was established that those who are ten years of age or older and possess wisdom are permitted to bestow full ordination upon others.

Regarding the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), it states that if a teacher lacks unlawful conduct—such as luring away disciples or committing grave offenses—the master is exempt from blame. Jing says: "This refers to the reduction of the strength of one's provisions."

If one calculates this, it constitutes five instances of a grave offense (*pārājika*). Regarding the statement that the death of an aged and sick bhikṣu was the cause [for the rule], the *Wǔbǎi wèn* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"In the past, there was an aged bhikṣu who had only one śrāmaṇera. He was lured away by others, leaving him with no one to look after him;
before long, he passed away. Because of this, the precept was established: one must not lure away another's śrāmaṇera. To lure one away is an immediate grave offense."
Regarding the two divisions of the Vinaya: it is established that these are the Vinayas for the two communities of monks and nuns.
As for the method of requesting a preceptor when the *upādhyāya* has passed away: to provide an analogy, it is like a newborn infant who immediately requires...
When an infant loses its parents, it must seek a wet nurse; now that the Upādhyāya has passed away, one ought to rely upon another, for in principle this is equivalent to having a wet nurse.
Regarding the fact that the ritual for being received by the five teachers is largely the same as the previous ritual: this means it is identical to the ritual for the *upādhyāya* mentioned above.
As for the instruction in the Tripiṭaka three times daily and the ceremony for requesting instruction from the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*):
ten or twenty persons simultaneously prostrate to the teacher, then kneel together, and one person among them speaks these words: "Venerable Sir, please take heed; I, the disciple [Name],..."

"Excellent! I request your instructions and teachings; I pray that you will grant me your guidance out of your compassionate mercy. (One version says this. The Master then extensively demonstrated the characteristics of the teachings until the end, at which point he should say:
"Draw near to virtuous friends, distance yourself from evil associates, practice the Path with diligent effort, and be cautious and never negligent.
The disciple replies: "I shall receive and uphold this upon my head. Regarding the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*): it refers to the five...

The aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The five aggregates are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); they belong to the bodies of sentient beings. As for the eighteen elements:

there are the six external objects (*viṣaya*), the six internal faculties (*indriya*), and the intermediate discrimination, called the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*)—namely, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
These three groups of six constitute the eighteen. As for the twelve bases: they consist of the six objects entering into the six faculties.

Sometimes, when referring to the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they are explained from a single perspective; however, because both the subject and the object are revealed together, there are twelve.

As for the statement that one is called a "teacher" (*śāstṛ*) during the time of receiving the scriptures, reciting them together, or practicing seated meditation—this refers to the occasion when the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) recites together with a disciple.
Should the disciple be unable to inquire [about the meaning] immediately, the preceptor must then provide instruction and admonition.
Regarding the current practice of listening to lectures on meditation (*dhyāna*) until it becomes cumbersome: [Dao]li explains that "fasting" (*zhāi*) means "to align" (*qí*).

This refers to the master and disciples aligning together to listen to the lecture and returning [together], such that separate instructions are not required. This is because there is concern that the proceedings might become overly complex.

The same applies to those who sit together in meditation (*zhuàn*). If one does not practice and does not recite, what benefit is there in setting up [the ritual] in vain? [Dao]li explains the above as follows:
If it becomes overly cumbersome and burdensome, people will certainly not follow such practices; why then establish such empty invitations?

As for "the one who has descended from the seat remains solitary and serene," this is intended to clarify that at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, when ordinations are frequently held in the two capitals, the relationship between teacher and disciple is like that of master and student while on the ordination platform;
however, once the ceremony is concluded and they have descended from the seat and returned to their quarters, the relationship between teacher and disciple [ends].

"Abandoning. This means they are solitary and separate from one another. Another interpretation is that one takes only a single senior elder (*upādhyāya*) as one's preceptor, regardless of whether he possesses virtuous qualities;
even if a junior elder possesses such virtues, no one will request him for initiation. Therefore, it is said that "one is solitary and alone.

Regarding the phrase "originally there is no mutual inclusion," Ciyun says this refers to the fact that between teacher and disciple, there is no mutual inclusion of both parties. It may also be accepted [in this sense].
Having received the precepts, he immediately departed; the master lacked both the support of wealth and the support of the Dharma.

As for the statement that it is "roughly like a wild horse," the *Zhuangzi* says this refers to dust and grime; it is merely drifting vapor that appears to exist yet is difficult to grasp. This serves as a metaphor for receiving the precepts at the ordination platform.
It appears to be the relationship between teacher and disciple; yet after receiving [the transmission], they part ways. The principle of "teacher" cannot be grasped.
To say that "receiving" is like a mirage is to speak from the perspective of its ultimate nature—it is indeed like a mirage.

Just as a mirage in the heat appears to be water but lacks reality, this serves as a metaphor for the teacher and disciple at the time of reception, the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), and the Dharma: they appear to be mutually encompassing one another, yet later, when they depart...
They do not know one another; their situation is like a mirage where water cannot be found. Seeking the meaning of this relationship between teacher and disciple, it likewise cannot be found.
As for the phrase "if a bhikṣu [is] with the Great Master," the "Great Master" refers to the Upādhyāya. To revere him and humble one's own mind—this is the meaning.
This should be understood.

One must not detain a disciple for a minor matter: that is to say, when a disciple wishes to travel to another region to study and accumulate superior merit, one must not detain them for a trivial reason.
If it concerns matters such as bandits plundering [the area], it is established that if the disciple has been robbed by bandits, [one may detain them].
Regarding the phrase "as recorded in the *Chao*": the Master must seek money to redeem [the disciple]. The preceptor should then use skillful means to bring him back.
If he is brought back after having been kidnapped, the Master commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). If the disciple steals himself out on his own, there is no offense for the thief.

Furthermore, in the present day, if a disciple suddenly encounters disaster and is imprisoned in a region of drifting yellow sand, the Master must devise a plan to secure his release; otherwise, he incurs an offense.
The following clarifies the dharma for an aged disciple. Regarding the phrase "does not accept [instruction]," the commentary states: "one does not practice according to what was taught.

This differs slightly from the teacher's instruction in its contradiction with the subsequent text. Lì asks: "This 'difficulty in conversing'—how does it differ from the previous phrase 'not accepting instruction'? Answer:

"Difficulty in conversing" refers to a situation where one consistently resists the teacher’s admonitions. The "not accepting instruction" mentioned previously refers to [the case where] one accepts the teacher’s... [text truncated]
Having spoken thus, he subsequently failed to act according to his words; this is why there is a distinction.

As for those who delight in going to look at turtles and tortoises, Bin said: "Such people are mostly distracted; they take pleasure in looking at them and thereby neglect the cultivation of the Way."
Therefore, one should reprove him. If we follow the passage in the *Upāliparipṛcchā* regarding the increase of five items, it states: "One must not go to the homes of those who catch fish or turtles.
This refers to households with evil vows (*akuśalasaṃvara*), and he is reproved because such conduct invites public censure.
Regarding the passage in the *Śīla-sūtra* stating that one is even more culpable than a butcher, a consultation of the *Sujāta-sūtra* reveals that the Buddha said to the elder Sujāta:
"It would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings, than to maintain and support a wicked disciple who cannot be tamed.
Why is this? Such evil discipline brings calamity only upon oneself; whereas maintaining a wicked [disciple]..."
Disciples who are unable to provide instruction and admonition cause immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil and slander immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas;

they destroy the Saṃgha and cause many sentient beings to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution. For this reason, their offense is more grave than that of those with evil vows (such as butchers).
Master Li says: "Butchers do not destroy the True Dharma nor sever the seed of the Buddha, just as Aṅgulimāla killed a thousand people."

It should be understood that those who later see the Buddha and attain the Way, yet harbor evil disciples whom they fail to instruct and admonish, will destroy the True Wheel of Dharma, cause the Jewel of the Sangha to be severed, and upon death enter the evil realms.
Regarding the statement that they subsequently fall among the dragons and so forth, a consultation of the *Wu-bai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states:

"In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who took on disciples. These disciples committed many unrighteous acts; when their lives ended, they were reborn among the dragons."
The Dragon Dharma is to undergo confession once every seven days. At the time of confession, fire burns his body until the flesh is consumed and only the bones remain;
immediately thereafter, he recovers, only for the fire to burn him again. Unable to endure such suffering, he reflects to himself: "By what transgression have I come to suffer thus?
He then contemplates his past lives and sees that he was originally a śramaṇa who did not maintain the prohibitory precepts, nor did his teacher [instruct him].

He then conceived a poisonous thought, feeling anger toward his original teacher and intending to harm him. Later, he met his teacher while traveling by ship with five hundred merchants across the sea.
The nāga emerged from the water and seized the bow of the ship. The people immediately asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a nāga. They asked, "Why have you seized the ship? He replied, "If you [would] let this [person] down..."
“Kauṭilya, release him and let him go. What concern of yours is this bhikṣu? He replied, “He was originally my teacher.
Since he did not instruct or admonish me, I am now suffering great pain. Having no other recourse, I intended to throw him into the water.”
The bhikṣu said, "I shall enter the water myself," and he immediately threw himself into the water and died.

Regarding the statement that one must possess five faults before being rebuked, the *Shoushu* says: as mentioned above, first, there is no gradualness; second, there is no sense of shame; third, one does not accept instruction;
fourth, it is contrary to dignified decorum (*airyāpatha*); and fifth, there is a lack of reverence. Having thus completed the questioning above—
The following section clearly presents the answer. What is its meaning? Regarding the passage in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* concerning "a young bhikṣu unacquainted with the Dharma and Vinaya" and so forth:
consulting that sutra, it says that when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there were many bhikṣus who entered the city to beg for alms.
Among them was a young bhikṣu who had not long since left the household life and was unacquainted with the Vinaya rules.
When it was time for almsround, he did not know the proper order of precedence. Seeing this, the other bhikṣus spoke to him with reason: "You are young and have not long been ordained."
"Those who beg for alms without knowing the law and without observing proper sequence will experience disadvantageous suffering for a long night.
Thus he spoke to them a second and a third time, yet he could not make them desist. Then, after the meal, the bhikṣus returned and reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "It is as if in a desolate marsh there were a great lake, and within it a great..."
A nāga-elephant, having extracted lotus roots from a marsh, washed away the mud, and then eaten them, became plump, vigorous, and at ease.
At that time, there was a small elephant of a different breed, whose body was thin and small; it emulated that nāga-elephant.
He pulled out the lotus root, but was unable to wash it clean; he ate it with the mud still clinging to it.
Because he could not digest it, his body became neither plump nor joyful, but grew increasingly emaciated and weak until he died from this cause, or suffered a death as painful as that.

Such was the case with an elder bhikṣu who had long studied the Path, who took no pleasure in lustful play, who had long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya) praised by the Great Master, and who resided in towns and villages.
He begs for alms, well-guarding his body and speech, properly restraining his sense faculties, and focusing his mind with mindfulness. He is able to inspire faith in living beings.
If he obtains wealth, profit, clothing, or food and drink, his mind is not stained by attachment; he does not crave them, does not relish them, is not deluded by them, and does not become negligent.

He perceives their faults and perils, and perceives the way of transcendence from them, and only then does he eat. Having eaten, his body and mind are joyful and contented; he attains a healthy complexion and physical strength.
By these causes and conditions, one always attains peace and happiness. That young bhikṣu, having left the household life not long ago, was not yet familiar with the Dharma and Vinaya.

Relying on a village, he put on his robes and took up his bowl to enter the town for alms; he did not properly guard his body, did not maintain the gates of the senses, and was not single-mindedly attentive.
He could not cause those without faith to believe, nor could he prevent those who believed from changing their minds. If he obtained wealth...
Regarding the four requisites of robes, bedding, food, and drink, he becomes stained by attachment and pursues them with greed.

Failing to perceive their faults and failings, and failing to perceive the way of transcendence, he consumes food with a mind of sensual craving; yet this cannot bring him strength, joy, peace, or happiness. It is because of such food that—
They turn toward death, or experience suffering equivalent to death. What is called "death" refers to abandoning the precepts and returning to secular life, thereby losing the true Dharma and Vinaya.
What is called "suffering equivalent to death" refers to violating the true Dharma and Vinaya while failing to recognize the characteristics of offenses and not knowing how to eliminate them.
Therefore it is said. The Buddha then spoke these verses:
"The dragon-elephant pulls up the lotus root, Washes it with water, and eats it. The elephant of a different breed imitates him And eats it together with the mud.
Because of eating it mixed with mud, He becomes emaciated and sick, and eventually dies."

Regarding the previous statement on "greed, delusion, and heedlessness," Ciyun says that this refers to the unrestrained indulgence in the objects of the six sense faculties, such as forms, sounds, odors, and tastes.
Regarding the phrase "fire erupting from within first incinerates one's own body," Jì says that the arising of anger within is called the eruption of fire; it is capable of—

This burns one's own merit; hence it is said that "one first incinerates oneself. To give way to anger at present and thereby harm another is equivalent to eating filth and first defiling one's own mouth.

Regarding the phrase "purifying past transgressions by relying on the path of renunciation," some say that the teacher relies on the path of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*) to purify the person's prior faults.
Others maintain that it means to reprimand [the offender] by relying on the path of the Noble Teachings (*ārya-śāsana*).
His disciples are pure and free from the faults of unrighteousness; hence they are said to be "pure in transgression. (Note:
Regarding "because of extreme gravity of transgression," it is not only the commission of a fault that constitutes gravity;
even if a fault committed is light, if the object of the offense is grave, this same treatment must also be applied. To say "you may go" means to depart beyond the boundaries of the monastery.
Regarding the statement that "a bodhisattva who attains the stage of the pure mind (śuddhacitta-bhūmi) acquires non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna)," the *Shen* commentary states:
"Only from the seventh stage upward does one attain non-conceptual wisdom; this is termed 'pure mind.'"

Regarding the "Purification Sutra" cited as prescribing three hundred strokes for punishment: this refers to what that sutra states—that for a grave offense one receives three hundred blows, for a middling offense two hundred, and for a minor offense one hundred;
all of these clearly specify that the blows are administered to a bhikṣu.

Regarding the statement that one must not even brandish a staff toward animals, Jì remarked: "In these times, those who ride donkeys or horses already commit an unrighteous act by mounting upon their backs;
to further beat them is exceedingly cruel and devoid of compassion."
Regarding "those who have committed offenses and are punished by dismissal" (*chù*): Master [Dao]sheng says that *chù* means to depart or to be expelled. To clarify:

it is like when an official of the Imperial Court commits an offense and is demoted to a minor post in a remote prefecture; this is called "dismissal. It clarifies that those who have committed transgressions today are banished outside the community and may no longer dwell together;
the meaning is identical to being "expelled and demoted," as explained in the *Dichizhi chao* (copious notes on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*), and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "the offense is equal to shedding the blood of ten billion Buddhas," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, in the *Candragarbha-parivarta*, states:

At that time, Kauṇḍinya asked the Buddha, "If there is one who has their hair shaved for the sake of the Buddha and wears the saffron robes, yet does not receive the prohibitive precepts, or receives them but violates and destroys them, and one then harasses, reviles, beats, or binds such a person—how much offense does this incur? The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! Do not ask."
When this matter was asked, Brahmā Śikhin immediately rose and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that you will explain it for us.
The Buddha replied, "I shall now explain it briefly for you. Suppose there were a person who shed the blood of ten thousand koṭis of Buddhas; would the transgression of such a person be great?
Brahmā said, "If a person sheds the blood of even a single Buddha, they incur a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense and fall [into hell]."
[The sin of] the Avīci Great Hell; how much more so for shedding the blood of ten thousand billion Buddhas? The Buddha said:

"If there are those who disturb, revile, beat, or bind one wearing the *kāṣāya*, even if that person has not received the precepts or has violated them, their sin is greater than that [of shedding the blood of the Buddhas].
Although this person lacks the precepts or has broken them, they are still able to show the path to *nirvāṇa* to all devas and humans. This person has already, in three..."
Among the jewels [of the Sangha], they attain reverent faith in their hearts, surpassing all ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders and surpassing all those who have not left the household life.
If there are kings, ministers, or judicial officials who see someone within my Dharma...
If those who have gone forth commit great sinful deeds—such as sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or lying—they should simply be expelled from the boundaries of the kingdom according to the Dharma;
they are not permitted to remain in the monastery, nor may they participate in monastic affairs or share in monastic benefits.
They must never be whipped, nor may they be reviled through verbal karma. If anyone punishes them for violating the law, that person falls away from the Path and is distanced from it.
The merit of all humans and devas will inevitably lead to the Avīci Hell, let alone the act of whipping. This is because one who fully upholds the precepts possesses a mind of restraint.

Thus, the *Jie xin shu* (Commentary on the Mind of Precepts) states: "Regarding the shedding of a Buddha’s blood, although there is no offense according to the literal appearance [of the act], it constitutes a grave offense because a transformation Buddha lacks a mind and cannot be afflicted by sentient beings;
yet, it damages the basis upon which the Dharma-body relies. The principles for the benefit or harm of the Dharma and the Sangha follow this same precedent from beginning to end.
However, as for the breaking of the precepts and the bhikṣu who is without precepts now, their transgression is weightier than shedding the blood of ten thousand billion Buddhas.
Is this not because one’s physical form and robes serve as the outward sign of the holy path? If one treats them with contempt or slights them, the Three Jewels are simultaneously destroyed;

therefore, the offense is grave. (Regarding the "beginning and end" mentioned above: based on the present state, the physical form, the scriptures, and the tonsure are the "end," while the fundamental meaning is the "beginning," which can be understood). Daolun said: "Tie-daò (Devadatta) produced [the offense of] one Buddha-body."
If shedding the blood of a single [Arhat] leads to entry into Avīci for one kalpa, how much more so for the blood of ten billion Buddhas?

Regarding the statement that those who fall back from the Path will inevitably enter Avīci, this refers to falling back from the Path oneself due to striking a monk, and subsequently entering Avīci. Thus, the subsequent passage says:
"Birth and grasping become obscure; one is indiscriminately self-deceived. Based on this, striking [a monk] out of anger is, in fact, self-harm.

It is like a person with a mouth full of blood; this person first defiles their own mouth. How can one expect every previous person’s karmic actions to accord with one's own? One must restrain the mind and suppress its impulses.
If one happens to encounter something unwholesome, one must certainly practice forbearance and forgiveness. Thus, an ancient master spoke in verse:
"One's own mind constantly drives oneself, yet throughout the day it does not accord with one's heart. When others drive themselves, how could they ever accord with my heart?"
If one performs this contemplation, one will certainly not give rise to anger or strike another person.
Regarding the instruction that "this child should be taught later, even to the point of commanding him not to do so," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Qishi) states:

When a disciple is subject to monastic discipline—such as being formally accused (*tri-udghāta*) or expelled (*catur-nissāraṇa*)—the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the instructor (*ācārya*) must, on behalf of the disciple, offer apologies to all other people. Long...
"I have seen this text myself; now that I have abandoned such conduct and am following the Dharma, how could an ordinary person, being foolish, be without fault?
This child has studied late and truly possesses these faults. Today I shall instruct him so that he will never do it again.
Having thus pleased the assembly, he requested the Saṃgha to revoke the *karmavācanā* (formal act).
Regarding "not pointing out their transgressions and not rebuking them," *Li* says: Rebuking the evil of a disciple involves three factors of the Great Dharma:

first, the disciple must be present; second, the transgression must be manifested in the present; and third, the method of rebuke must be manifested (such as saying, "Go away," or "I will not speak with you").

When these three factors are complete, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma"; otherwise, it is contrary to the Dharma. This applies if one has been subject to disciplinary action and has not yet performed repentance.

Regarding "refusing and then receiving provisions and so forth," Kyōryoku says: This clarifies that one incurs an offense by providing service and making someone work after having already rebuked them, even though they have not yet repented.

That is to say, one originally performed the third method of rebuke (saying, "Do not perform services for me"), yet now, instead of bestowing joy, one turns them into a servant, thereby increasing their provocation and distress;
thus, one incurs an offense. If one performs other forms of rebuke and then provides service...

There is no offense. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If one is reprimanded by others with minor reproaches, yet does not perform services such as those for the *upādhyāya* or other administrative duties, one incurs an offense.
This means that if one was originally subject to a second-level reprimand (such as being told, "Do not enter my room;
you may stay at the monastery and provide service from outside"), and although one is permitted to perform such tasks, fails to do so out of resentment, one thereby incurs an offense.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, "a co-practitioner disciple" refers to one for whom the preceptor (upādhyāya) has conferred full ordination; such a person is called a co-practitioner disciple.
The following clarifies the "dependent disciple" (niśraya-śiṣya); this is one who requests [the preceptor] to be their teacher at a later time.

Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* passage concerning those who wish to subdue others by stripping them of their robes and leaving them naked, an examination of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* reveals the following:

At one time, the group of six bhikṣus had a śrāmaṇera with pubic hair who, having committed minor offenses against his teacher’s wishes, was immediately stripped naked and rebuked as something people would not find pleasing.
This matter was reported to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should not subdue a śrāmaṇera for a minor offense."
Maitreya, when performing a disciplinary subjugation (*nigraha*), one should leave him with at least one garment.

What is meant here by "one should not perform a disciplinary subjugation for a minor matter" is that one should not strip someone of their clothes and leave them naked to carry out other forms of disciplinary action for a trivial reason.
Regarding the four methods for declining an invitation and the subsequent instruction that "the preceptor should deliberate upon those bhikṣus," a question is raised:
since the preceptor lacks knowledge and cannot increase one's wholesome qualities, how can he further deliberate upon the person before him? The answer is as follows:

when it was stated above that he "cannot increase wholesome dharmas," this does not mean that the preceptor possesses no knowledge at all; rather, it means that while he understands the sūtras and śāstras, he is not conversant with the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Therefore, he did not understand the practice of maintaining disciples. Regarding the passage "one should not dwell with those who provide food but do not provide the Dharma," the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface) states:
"The reason for this is that the intent of leaving the household life is fundamentally to seek the Dharma; one does not hope for food or clothing. Since the teacher lacks virtue..."

He was unable to instruct me in the Dharma to nourish my mind and spirit, causing me to give rise to understanding and practice; he merely accepted me in name, utterly lacking the benefit of a master’s guidance.
Therefore, I must take my leave and depart, seeking instead a virtuous teacher to consult regarding his teachings and instructions.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is largely the same [as other versions], though there is a distinction regarding the "abiding in pleasure" and "abiding in suffering. This means that when both the Dharma and food are present, it is an abiding in pleasure;

when the Dharma is present but food is lacking, it is an abiding in suffering. Regarding the phrase "I call you to come and take wine," Huilin stated: "Upon examining the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it is actually 'I call my daughter to come.

In the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth fascicles, there are many instances of ritual practices (*vidhi*), as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*: [Insert relevant excerpt from the *Śāstra* here.]

"Regarding those who do not accept [the confession], they are to be dealt with according to the Dharma. This means that if a preceptor does not accept the disciple’s confession, one must rely on the *kṣudraka-dharma* (minor rules) to punish the preceptor for his offense.

First, regarding "I am a preceptor who does not know the Dharma according to the rule," *Lì* says: this refers to the methods of requesting instruction, admonition, and reporting matters, which he does not perform.

This explains the method for instructing and guiding disciples. Second, "I am not as [virtuous] as the Upādhyāya" refers to those who do not practice the aforementioned Dharma and are unaware that they should be instructed and exhorted at the proper time.
Third, "I have violated the precepts, yet the Upādhyāya has abandoned me and neither taught nor rebuked me."

That is to say, they willfully practice what is contrary to the Dharma. Fourth, if they commit an offense and do not recognize it, this means they do not discern the characteristics or the gravity of the transgression.
Fifth, if they commit an offense and do not know how to repent, this means they do not understand the methods for eliminating the offense.
"As for the statement, 'I am you and you are me,' this is established as clear proof. Since he has rebuked me, I should be his disciple and he should be my teacher.
Regarding the instruction to depart based on the two types of teachers: if the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) does not accept one's words, one should abandon him and go far away;
if it is the resident teacher (*niśraya-ācārya*), one should take one's robes and bowl and go beyond the boundary for one night."

[The preceding section] was equal [to the previous]. Below, the dharma of losing one’s preceptor is clarified. Regarding the statement that “there is one type of preceptor for whom there is no sense of loss,” this is because [the preceptor] is the basis upon which the attainment of the precepts depends;

therefore, [the relationship] is not lost. As for the phrase “or perhaps lacking virtue,” this establishes the clarification: if a preceptor commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), he is termed “lacking virtue.”

Furthermore, if the teacher is subject to monastic disciplinary action but does not lose [the status of] being a *niśraya* (reliant), this means that while he loses one lower method of instruction, he does not lose the two higher methods.
Regarding the case where the disciple is subject to monastic disciplinary action yet neither [of the three statuses] is lost, this is evident from the text. [The section on] "Opening" follows.

Regarding "no offense of compliance": this refers to when a disciple has been disciplined by the Saṃgha, and another person observes them; such an observer commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) of compliance.
However, because the two teachers provide instruction and speak with them, the offense of compliance is waived.
Regarding the case where one who has resolved to leave the boundary loses their *niśraya* (dependence) upon returning on that very day: the *Śū* (Commentary) raises an objection, stating:

"If it were the case that when a preceptor and disciple resolve to leave the boundary together and return on that same day—without having spent a night away—they lose their *niśraya*, then could one also rely on the boundary for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and the protection of robes?
Even if one resolves to leave the boundary and returns on the same day, would one not thereby lose the robes and break the summer retreat? The answer follows.

This is not analogous. Regarding dependence (*niśraya*), there is a loss [of the relationship] because both parties possess the intention to relinquish it: the teacher resolves to relinquish the disciple, and the disciple resolves to relinquish the teacher.

As for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and the robes (*cīvara*), they are lost solely through one’s own intention to relinquish them; this is because in the former case—concerning non-sentient objects—there is no intention to relinquish on the part of the object itself.

It is not lost. Furthermore, regarding robes and the summer retreat (*varṣā*), loss is determined by the appearance of dawn; regarding the formal reliance (*niśraya*), loss occurs immediately upon crossing the boundary.

It is further said that for the summer retreat and robes, loss is established based on the night spent away; for the formal reliance, loss is established based on the mind. Therefore, they are not comparable.

Moreover, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) for distinguishing between the formal reliance, robes, and the summer retreat: first, when separated by one night but not otherwise, the formal reliance is lost, while the robes and the summer retreat are not lost.
Among the three types [of non-transgression], there is "separation by two nights but not by mind," which refers to not losing the summer retreat due to encountering difficulties.

There is also "not losing the place of dependence," such as when a disciple of the *Sudarsana* follows his teacher on a journey; while holding the teacher's robe for him, he happens upon someone preaching the Dharma.

Because the disciple was eager to hear the Dharma, there was no offense of abandoning the reliance (*niśraya*), yet the teacher lost his robe; this is an example of both losing [the robe] through separation.

One may understand that in the fourth case, both do not lose it through separation. Lì asked: "Why does the loss of reliance through mental separation (*citta-viccheda*) not require a lapse of one night, whereas the summer robe (*varṣā-śāṭī*) is not like that?
The answer is: Reliance involves an emotional connection; because both parties mutually intend to abandon it, the reliance is lost. If...

If one does not form the intention to relinquish both, the [robe] is lost only after staying apart overnight. Regarding the separation from the robe and the *anvāsa* (summer retreat), it is precisely when one has the thought "I shall relinquish this" that it is lost;
since the other [the monastery] lacks the thought of relinquishment, it must be that both the mind and the night are separated for it to be lost. Question:

If there is no offense in losing the *niśraya* (place of dependence) through separation, why is there an offense in staying overnight separated from the summer robes? Answer: The *niśraya* is permitted to be left behind; once one has arrived at another location, [the offense arises].

The Buddha established the rule for requesting a new preceptor (*niśraya*) and departing in accordance with the teaching; if one loses [the robe] in this way, there is no offense. However, the Buddha prohibited being separated from one's robe and breaking the summer retreat (*varṣā*);

therefore, if one loses [the robe] or breaks [the retreat] through such separation, there is an offense. Question: Why is the offense for losing the robe heavy, while the offense for breaking the summer retreat is light?

Answer: The three robes are the formal attire; as they are essential for sustaining the body, they are treated with gravity. During the rains retreat (*varṣā*), it is difficult to break [the robe] without causing harm and without interrupting one's cultivation;
therefore, the offense for breaking [the vow] is light.
1. Regarding those who die: they lose all three types of dharma—namely, the dharma of requesting instruction, the dharma of relying on others for support, and the dharma of receiving formal teaching.

2. Regarding those who go far away: they lose the lower two dharmas. 3. Regarding those who abandon the path: they lose all three dharmas. 4. Regarding those who commit a grave offense: they lose the lower two dharmas. 5.
Regarding those whose teacher has issued a reprimand: they lose the lower one dharma. 6. Regarding those who enter the ordination platform (*sīmā*): it is established that they lose [the dharmas].
Regarding the latter two dharmas, Lì (Lìzǔ) says: "One loses [the status] immediately upon entering, without waiting for the passage of a night.

Why is this so? Because these are places where separate practices are performed; since those who are young and ignorant might be led astray by others, they lose it immediately upon entry, without waiting for the night to pass.
This differs from those outside the boundary (*sīmā*), who do not perform separate practices and thus lose their status only after the night has passed. This should be understood. (7)
One who has completed five years of residence loses the two lower dharmas. Regarding "one who sees his original upādhyāya," the established view states that he loses the two lower dharmas.
Regarding "one who returns to his original upādhyāya and dwells under his gaze," he loses the two lower dharmas. Śāriputra asked:

"What is the difference between seeing one's original upādhyāya and returning to one's original upādhyāya to dwell under his gaze? The answer provides two interpretations: [the first concerns] the original upādhyāya; [the second concerns] the supplementary upādhyāya.
Regarding the "empty place": because there is no emptiness to be supplemented, one sees the root [preceptor] and thus loses [the status]. As for "one who resides under the eye of the Upādhyāya":

previously, having abandoned the keeping of disciples, one saw [them] and did not lose [the status]; now, by taking them back into care, one loses it immediately upon residing under the eye. Another interpretation:
"seeing the original Upādhyāya" means that the teacher went on a distant journey and has now returned; "residing under the eye" means the disciple comes from outside.
Regarding the returning to one's *kṣetra* (preceptor): initially, the intention was merely for a temporary return; later, upon reaching the teacher’s residence, it became permanent.

Therefore, when the one currently residing [with him] asks about losing the *śīla*, if one says they have lost their *niśraya* (dependence), what further dharmas are lost? The answer is: there are three kinds of dharmas. One loses the two lower dharmas;
the upper one dharma, which is requested, is never lost from beginning to end, just like the *upādhyāya*. Because one obtains the precepts by depending on him, there is no mutual loss.
Regarding the meaning: it is permissible to rely [on a teacher]. Once one has requested [instruction], the method of requesting remains constant; therefore, one does not lose it.

This clarifies that because the teacher possesses virtue, one does not lose [the reliance]. If one follows the interpretation of Vinaya Master Yuan, it is not so; he states that "losing the reliance" means:
All three factors are lost simultaneously. How is this known? As stated in the latter part of the Vinaya:

if a disciple is fierce and evil, or otherwise difficult to instruct, the *niśraya-ācārya* (preceptor) must go outside the boundary for one night and then return; at that point, the *niśraya* is lost.

Or, if the preceptor lacks virtue and is incapable [of providing guidance], another disciple may go outside the boundary for one night and, upon returning, rely upon another person as their preceptor. Thus, it is known that there are three ways in which the relationship is lost.

"The Dharma is lost" refers to a teacher who lacks virtue; such a person will certainly develop a mind of abandonment toward the gate [of the teaching], and for this reason, the three dharmas are all lost.
If one considers the loss of reliance on the teaching, it clarifies that the aforementioned five types are all cases of losing the teaching.
If one considers it in terms of practice, it means that the fivefold Dharma-body must first be established before [the teacher] can then be lost.
Chapter Ten, Part One: The Proper Ritual for the Recitation of the Precepts.

Having clarified the principles governing the relationship between teacher and disciple, and having already set forth the methods of instruction, it is now necessary to rely upon the protection of the teachings and to clearly recognize the characteristics of the precepts.

By proclaiming them every half-month, one admonishes body and mind and encourages the assembly at this time, so that they may correspond to their spiritual practice. Therefore, this chapter [is presented].

It is said: "The commentaries and sub-commentaries of various schools, as well as the *Khandakas* of the Vinaya texts, all place this section immediately after the preceding [section on] receiving [the precepts].

However, the reason the Vinaya texts state that there are no four persons within a boundary (*sīmā*) and thus require face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*) or even mental recitation (*manasikāra*) for the *Poṣadha*, is simply because they were in a state of emergency.

Yet, according to the intent of the present *Chao* (Commentary), if one lacks the instruction and guidance of a teacher, one will immediately commit transgressions; therefore, it is not appropriate to hear [the precepts in such circumstances]."

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*): after receiving them, one must first establish the relationship between teacher and disciple; once the ritual for teacher and disciple is perfected, one may then properly engage with the Dharma. This is why the present text exists.
As for what is called "reciting the precepts" (*poṣadha-vācanā*), it is said that this means to expound the sacred intent and clearly proclaim the five categories of offenses.

When the teaching is manifested through speech, it is termed "recitation. This very act of explaining serves as a warning and exhortation for body and speech; because it has the function of prohibiting what is improper, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).
Within this, following the holy teachings of the Buddha, the rules and procedures for the time of recitation are explained in detail; thus it is called the "Correct Ritual" (*zhèngyí*).

Furthermore, it is said that "correct" (*zhèng*) refers to distinguishing [this] from heterodox teachings, while "ritual" (*yí*) refers to the orderly sequence of the performance of the rite. Because it may be taken as a model for practice, it is termed a "dharma" (*fǎ*);
hence it is titled the "Section on the Correct Ritual for Reciting the Precepts."
Regarding the note stating "Pure Abode" (*śuddhāvāsa*) and so forth, the *Lü* (Vinaya) establishes that because the recitation of the precepts is a dharma for pure communal residence,
those who have committed an offense within the Vinaya are not permitted to hear the recitation of the precepts.
Regarding the phrase "the essential discipline (*naiṣkramya-śīla*) and so forth," according to an examination of that text, it says:

"As for *poṣadha*, depending on the differences in local dialects, it is also called *fǎn* (turning), and it is also called *cháng* (constant). What is termed *poṣadha* is the dialect of the kingdom of Kośala;
its meaning is translated as 'purity' (*viśuddhi*). If translated correctly, it should be called 'good lodging' (*sukha-vasati*). Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*..."
It says: "This person possesses a virtuous mind and is free from dwelling with those who have broken the precepts; therefore, it is so called. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To sincerely repent today, such that the body is pure, the speech is pure, and the mind is pure, and to receive and practice the eight precepts—this is what is called *poṣadha* (the Uposatha)."
In the language of Qin, this means "Good Abiding" (*Bhadrapada*). Regarding the note on "the twofold increase of merit": it establishes clarity;
because the precepts are pure, the myriad virtues and merits arise based upon them and increase more and more. Regarding the note on "U" meaning "to sever": it refers to severing all evil karma.

This causes the precepts to be pure. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "That which can sever what has been transgressed, and can sever all unwholesome dharmas such as the afflictions, is all called *poṣadha*.
Regarding the note that *poṭṭhapāda* means "increase," it refers to the increase of the merit of wholesome dharmas.
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The meaning of *poṣadha* is translated as 'abandoning evil,' because it realizes wholesome dharmas. (*Dharmasaṃgraha*)

As for "assembling" (*ju*), Zhi Liang states that it refers to the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), meaning that regardless of whether one is within or outside the boundary (*sīmā*), the Sangha gathers together. Furthermore, he says that "assembling" means to assemble all merits.
Regarding the commentary on "knowing what is appropriate," Zhi Liang states that it refers to knowing and preparing the various requisites, such as flowers and counting sticks (*śalākā*).

He further explains that by performing the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-uddeśa*), one comes to know the gravity [of offenses], or to confess and repent, or to recognize them once they have been known.

"Not to commit transgressions" accords with the meaning of "pure abiding. Regarding the phrase "it is appropriate to perform [the ritual]," this clarifies that the exposition of this *śīla-dharma* (precept-law) is what is appropriate for a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, it states that one must know the appropriateness of the time and circumstances—whether there are obstacles or no obstacles, and whether it is appropriate to be extensive or concise.
Regarding the commentary on "identical" and "co-residing" (*sādhivihāra*), the Master Li states that these refer to the Saṃgha collectively performing these acts together.

Master Sheng says that since the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is identical, it does not matter whether the Saṃgha is unified or divided, as they perform them in common. As for the term "co-residing," Master Li clarifies that this refers to those who are pure by not violating the precepts dwelling together;
that is, they dwell together within the sphere of pure Dharma. Those who have committed grave offenses (*pārājika*) and the like are not permitted [to co-reside].

They dwell together within both the *poṣadha* (recitation of precepts) and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures). Now, because they are free from transgressions, they dwell together and perform the *poṣadha*.

Furthermore, it is said that they "dwell together" because they reside within the same boundary (*sīmā*). Regarding the note on "transforming into karma and so forth," the established view is that once one has seen one's offense and performed repentance, they act together;
this is the transformation of impurity into purity. Another interpretation holds that the *poṣadha* itself is the transformative dharma.
It is a wheel. To say it is "constant" (nitya) means that it is the practice regularly followed by the Saṃgha and must not be interrupted. Sheng says:
Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively established this Dharma, and the Dharma of the preceding Buddha and the succeeding Buddha is no different, it is called constant.
Regarding the commentary on "nurturing" (*puṣṭi*) and "concord" (*sāmagrī*), it is established that "nurturing" refers to the cultivation of merit.
Furthermore, as for "concord," it means that the Saṃgha must possess the six kinds of concord before it may properly perform this *poṣadha* rite.
The commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* designates the eight precepts as the *poṣadha-saṃvara*.

According to an examination of the treatise, the term "precept" (*śīla*) is referred to as "restraint" (*saṃvara*), specifically the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*. Regarding the "eight precepts," the text states:

Those precepts: first, the śrāmaṇera precepts; second, the śikṣamāṇā precepts; third, the śrāmaṇerī precepts; fourth, the upāsaka precepts;
fifth, the upāsikā precepts; sixth, the upavāsa precepts. These eight types of protection are called the prātimokṣa precepts.
How does one become an upāsaka, and so forth, up to becoming a bhikṣu? The verse answers:
"Five, eight, ten, and all: because of undertaking the avoidance of evil states.

Commentary: Because one undertakes and maintains the avoidance of the five things to be shunned—namely, sexual misconduct, theft, killing, lying, and intoxicants—one is an upāsaka, an upavāsastha, a śrāmaṇera, or a bhikṣu.
If a person abides in the restraint of an upāsaka regarding the eight things to be avoided (the eight precepts), that person abides in the restraint of an upavāsa.
If one undertakes the avoidance of the ten things to be distanced from, that person abides in the restraint of a śrāmaṇera.
Regarding the ten things to be avoided, these consist of the previous eight plus the undertaking of abstaining from accepting and possessing gold and silver.

...and so forth, completing the ten [precepts]. Because one undertakes and maintains the distancing from the two types of action—bodily and vocal—one who does so abides in the *bhikṣu-saṃvara* (monastic restraint) and the others.
Bin says: In the correct Sanskrit, it is called *upāsaka*, which is translated as "lay follower" (*jìnshì*;

referring to those who observe the five precepts). The Sanskrit term *upavāsa* is translated as "near-dweller" (*jìnzhù*; referring to those who observe the eight precepts). Since these two names are distinct, they are not [the same].
One who observes the eight precepts is called an *upāsaka*. The *Nanshan Lishi* (Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain) states in his *Text on the Eight Precepts*:
"I, [Name], up to taking refuge in the Sangha, for one day and one night, am an *upāsaka* of pure conduct. Its meaning should properly be expressed as *upavāsa*, which accords with the teaching.
Personally, I say that this interpretation is wonderfully consistent with the old *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; it rests in the mind.

Regarding the statement that "that which is called 'protection' (ārakṣā) residing in body and speech is called 'precept' (śīla)": this establishes the point. The *poṣadha* (Uposatha) is precisely the examination and restraint of body and speech to make them pure.

Because it is able to examine and restrain the mind, the mind itself is the protection (*ārakṣā*). Therefore, the *poṣadha* is designated as "protection. The reason for using these words here is that the intention lies in this very point.
As for the reference in the commentary on the Vinaya regarding the *poṣadha* rules in a single location and so forth, this refers to the Vinaya.
The middle section clarifies the matters concerning the *poṣadha*. Gathering together in one place is called the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*; this is also the *poṣadha* itself.
The explanation of the commentary's meaning is now complete.
The general outline of the Buddha-dharma refers to the precepts as the foundation for gathering the Saṃgha and maintaining its discipline.
Therefore, according to the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma remains in the world without perishing by means of pure bhikṣus reciting the precepts. As in the past, the Buddha himself recited the precepts;

later, due to specific circumstances, he entrusted this task to the senior monks (sthaviras) of the Saṃgha. It is precisely through this duty that the Buddha-dharma maintains its order and continuity. Thus it is said.
It was intended that the Great Sage himself would proclaim [the teaching]. Furthermore, it was said: "I shall not enter parinirvāṇa; I will come once every half-month.

If one were to preach constantly every half-month now, it would enable the True Dharma (Saddharma) to abide for a long time. Because this can sustain the life-span of the Buddha-dharma, it is called the "Great Outline" (mahā-vidhi).

Regarding the terms "upholding the True and Semblance," "True" refers precisely to the True Dharma, while "Semblance" refers to the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma). As for "rectifying" (kuāng), it means...
This is correct; it is also a form of salvation. Master Ying stated: "Wei" (維) means to connect or link; it also means to sustain or maintain, and furthermore, to bind or fasten.

This clarifies that regarding both the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), if one wishes to rectify monastic affairs and ensure their maintenance continues without interruption, it must necessarily be through the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
It is rare for those who are honored and esteemed to be treated with such contempt and disdain. Liuming stated:

"If we examine the monks and nuns of the present day, if they perform the *śīla-vyākhyāna* (recitation of the precepts) only once or twice a year, it seems as though they value it highly; yet if it were held regularly every half-month, they would mostly harbor feelings of disdain and negligence.
Liang said: "For one who has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), if they recite the precepts eight hundred times, the offense of *pārājika* will be extinguished. Therefore—

One should know that this is a method for extinguishing transgressions. It is not intended to be explained in detail before a multitude, but rather recited privately within one’s chamber; it simply requires eight hundred recitations.

Thus, in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), there was during the Qi dynasty the monk Shi Sengyun, who was eloquent and discerning, possessing a thorough mastery of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
He was highly esteemed and attached to the Qi court's lectures, constantly serving as the presiding master. During the Qi era, the Three Jewels flourished in Ye, and Sengyun became renowned.
He resided at Baoming Monastery. Embracing all principles, on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, as the time for the recitation of the precepts approached, the assembly gathered in the hall.

The head of the community at Yunju addressed the congregation, saying: "The core of the precepts is to prevent wrongdoing; everyone can recite them. Why trouble the assembly by hearing them repeatedly?
It would be better to have one monk expound upon their meaning so that those who come later may attain awakening. Thus he spoke. Clouds gathered.
He regulated the times, and none dared to oppose him; the multitude all followed his lead. By the end of summer, the recitation of the precepts had been suspended for some time.

On the morning of the fifteenth day of the seventh month, as he was about to ascend the grass seat, he lost sight of Yun’s whereabouts. The great assembly had not yet received the new-year ordination.
The assembly broke up and dispersed in haste, rushing out in all directions to search for him. They found him about three *li* from the temple inside an ancient tomb;
his entire body was covered in blood, as if it had been sliced by a blade. When they questioned him as to how this had happened, he said:

"A man wielding a great sword three feet long appeared with a fierce and wrathful countenance. He rebuked me, saying that I had altered the *poṣadha* ceremony and falsely assumed the role of a master in debate. [He struck me] with his sword..."
His body was emaciated, and his agonizing pain was unbearable. He was brought back to the monastery, where he practiced repentance with utmost sincerity for ten years.
He made it his constant practice to recite the precepts, perform the *poṣadha*, and read various sutras. On the day of his death, a rare fragrance welcomed him;

his countenance remained undisturbed, and he passed away with joy. As for those who are superficial and lacking in discernment, they immediately claim that the method of reciting the precepts is common to both ordinary people and sages.

One must not treat [the Dharma] with contempt or negligence. During the Northern Qi dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Fan of Da Jue Monastery. His conduct surpassed the standard patterns of human relations, and his virtue outshone the expectations of the multitude.

He lectured extensively on the various Mahayana and Hinayana sutras, vinayas, and śāstras. Whenever he gave a lecture, many flocks of birds would soar and gather beside the hall, vying with one another to come and listen to the Dharma.
At that time, there were outsiders who spoke ill of and slandered the Dharma Master; yet those who harbored evil intentions were all transformed by his goodness.
The deity died and was restored to life. The Dharma Master had several thousand disciples who practiced his teachings.
Later, while traveling, he stayed overnight at another temple. On the night of the fifteenth day, he gathered with a junior monk and established a formal doctrinal position (*sthāpanā*).
As the assembly raised various challenges and objections, a benevolent deity asked the one seated on the high seat: "What day is this, that you are merely lecturing on the sutras? He then...
The monk Yi replied, "Today is the fifteenth day, the day for the recitation of the precepts. He then struck the bhikṣu on the high seat with his hand and dragged him to the ground.
Going further to the place of the *sthavira*, he said, "What day is this, that you do not recite the precepts?
Again, he struck him on the neck with his hand, causing him to fall to the floor at once. The great assembly was struck with terror and dispersed in all directions at once. From that time onward...
That the *poṣadha* was not abandoned for half a month—their disposition can be known from this. Master Li says:

"Because they harbor transgressions within their persons, they feel shame for their own defiled conduct and do not wish to hear the pure Dharma. Thus, the *Xinshu* states: 'Defiled people do not delight in hearing the pure Dharma.
Therefore, within the Vinaya, there are instances of prohibiting the *poṣadha* and prohibiting the *pravāraṇā*; the principle is the same as this. That is to say, the person..."
Once defiled, one does not wish to hear the pure Dharma. If this was so even during the Buddha’s lifetime, how much more so in the final age?

Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty compiled the *Jingzhu zi* (The Son of Pure Abiding) in twenty fascicles, establishing a method for lay precept-observance (*poṣadha*) that is in every respect identical to the *poṣadha* rites within the monastic community, with the sole exception that one recites the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
This tradition has been handed down as the interpretation for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; one should consult the *Jingzhu* [for details].
My son, you have not seen the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha*; perhaps you should compile them separately.
Regarding the "Śramaṇa Puzhao" and others: "Śramaṇa" is a general name for a bhikṣu, while "Kāpisi" (Kaishi) is a beautiful epithet used to praise him.
Jì says that his path was peaceful and direct, and he compiled this Dharma; indeed, he arranged all the Buddha-dharmas and practiced them.
Regarding the ritual protocols (*vidhi*), when the later sūtras and vinayas arrived, they were found to be in perfect accord with those established by Dao’an.

Furthermore, regardless of whether a sūtra was Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, he invariably structured it into three chapters: the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*samyaktva*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*).

This, too, was Dao’an’s initial innovation. Thus, Master Lingyou sighed, saying: "Master Dao’an cleared the wilderness to establish ritual protocols; one knows, therefore, that Dao’an was no ordinary man. Daoli said: "Dao’an..."
Although the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha* had been established, at that time no one practiced them.
It was not until Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu that the method of Dao’an was first put into practice. This Huiyuan was a fellow student who had served together with Fotudeng;
after Fotudeng passed away, Dao’an was the most senior among his disciples. He then dispatched Huiyuan to Mount Luofu, and as he passed by Mount Kuang, the mountain deity detained him.

"Regarding the term 'Zhuzun' (Master Who Abides in the Clouds): this title was established by Fu Jian for [Hui]an. As for the statement that one can directly accept and apply it without relying on textual evidence:

this is called "the non-impairment of the dharma of reciting the precepts. If the Saṃgha has committed transgressions, then it is improper to recite and improper to listen;

this is called "the impairment of the dharma of reciting the precepts. Some say: "Precisely because the Saṃgha is pure and without transgression, or because those with transgressions have immediately repented, it is universally appropriate [to proceed]."

Pure dwelling: because the precepts are pure, concentration and wisdom can be expected. The True Dharma continues and does not cease because of this; thus, the characteristics of its long endurance are propagated through this means.

When it comes to the time for instruction, if there is no reflection to cleanse and purify oneself, or if one is incapable of repentance, and furthermore does not rely on remorse, then when those gathered together hear such talk, it will all conflict with their minds, increasing their affliction, agitation, and distress. If one cannot help but proceed in this way, [the fault remains].
If one comes to understand this principle yet feels ashamed of not being counted among the ranks, such talk is insufficient for sustaining the teachings.
Or, if one hears nothing at all, a lifetime will be spent in vain. Examples such as these do not contribute to the long endurance of the True Dharma.

As for those who have realized the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and the ultimate holy life (*brahmacarya*), this clearly explains the method for guarding the precepts: if one can, every half-month, examine and scrutinize one’s own body and speech with single-minded devotion...

To maintain [the precepts] with diligence, remaining pure and unoffending, is called the first white dharma (*śukladharma*). To immediately repent and eliminate transgressions once they have occurred, thereby escaping their causal faults, is called the second white dharma.
If one has committed an offense but conceals it and does not confess, this is called black dharma (*kṛṣṇadharma*).

In some manuscript copies of the *Chao* (Excerpts), it reads "afflictions have feeling" (*kleśāḥ sa-vedakāḥ*). This refers to the totality of phenomena (*sarva-dharma*). I have personally examined the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which states:

"Having abandoned all evil and unwholesome dharmas, as well as afflictions and craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), one realizes the white dharmas (*avadāta-dharma*). The term "feeling" (*vedaka*) mentioned here [in the *Chao*] refers to this.

This is mostly an error. Thus, the aforementioned ten gates state: "Errors and omissions in transcription; transmission through successive generations that has become confused"—this is precisely the meaning.
Second, regarding "before and after meals," this refers to the periods before and after the midday meal. Third, regarding "whether by day or by night," this concerns...

As for the instruction that "one should cause [them] to bathe," this refers to when a *bhikṣu* who has witnessed a disaster enters the boundary; he then says: "Venerable Sir, since you have already..."

Only at this time, which is also the end of the summer retreat (*grīṣma*), is it the time for the invitation to admonition (*pravāraṇā*). However, there are only two [fortnights] of postponement;
if one were to postpone it further to three, it would enter the winter season (*hemanta*). Since the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) corresponds to this, there are likewise two postponements.

If there were perhaps three, it might be confused with the *pravāraṇā*, and thus there are only two postponements. Regarding what is called "confusion with the *pravāraṇā*," it is feared that people’s minds might lead them to think that the [recitation of the precepts] is...
"Since the precepts already have three [stages], my own *prātimokṣa* (self-indulgence) should likewise be subject to three stages of rejection (*pratyākhyāna*), and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no textual passage stating that the Dharma perishes if the recitation is not performed three times. Hui-li said: 'The tradition inherited from antiquity holds that if the *poṣadha* is not performed for three cycles, the Buddha-dharma will perish;
however, it is now said that this meaning does not exist, and it is merely a widespread, erroneous transmission of the past. The people of former times thought as follows...'"

The Vinaya clarifies that there are two occasions for the increase of the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts), but only two increases are permitted; it must not reach three. This is because it is said that if the *poṣadha* is not recited three times, the Buddha-dharma will perish.
However, according to the intent of the Vinaya, this is not the case. It is merely out of fear of confusing the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticism) that it does not reach three.

The *pravāraṇā* must be established at the end of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). If the increase were to reach three, one would have entered the winter season, and thus it would be improper to perform the *pravāraṇā*. Therefore, there are only two.
[The number of recitations] increases. According to principle, there is no fault in reciting the *Poṣadha* up to three times.

However, following common sentiment, it is thought that since there are three increases for the *Poṣadha*, the *Pravāraṇā* should likewise be deferred three times. Fearing such confusion, the two methods of the *Pravāraṇā* are taught, opening only two deferrals;
thus it is said, "fearing confusion regarding the *Pravāraṇā*. Li asks: Why is the *Poṣadha* recited at the end of the month? It is a metaphor for hearing the precepts.

The "sign" (lakṣaṇa) serves to manifest the elimination of unwholesome dharmas and the fulfillment of the practice of restraint (śīla-dhāraṇa). Furthermore, the mention of the "half-month" is intended to demonstrate the gradual increase of merit and the completion of the practice of observance (samādāna-dhāraṇa).

As for the statement that "the Dharma is extinguished when one does not attain the fruits of the noble ones" (āryaphala), this is meant to rescue the aforementioned claim that the Dharma is extinguished;
it means that the previous assertion—that the Dharma of the recitation of the precepts (prātimokṣa) is extinguished—is incorrect. It does not, however, preclude the occurrence of strife.
Regarding "contention": the failure to attain the fruits of the Path is what is meant by the "extinction of the Dharma.
As for Ānanda’s doubt concerning the bhikṣu Ghoṣila, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the bhikṣu Ghoṣila had a lay donor (*dānapati*) who fell ill.
The donor said to the bhikṣu, "I have two young sons; the cleverer one, I have already told you where my treasure is hidden. These were the two young sons.
When they had grown up, the elder brother showed them the location of the treasure. After the donor had passed away, the children gradually grew older.
When Ghoṣila saw these two young boys, the elder brother immediately pointed out the place where the treasure was. The one who did not receive it wept and went into the monastery, saying to Ānanda:
"Venerable Sir, look at this bhikṣu Ghoṣila; he has taken both [shares] of my father’s inheritance."
[The portion] was combined and given to one person. At that time, Ānanda said to Ghoṣila, "You should depart;
you should not participate in the *poṣadha* together with me. For six *poṣadha* ceremonies, Ānanda did not join him.

Later, after Ānanda had inquired thoroughly and fully understood the circumstances, he said to Ghoṣila, "You have not committed even a *duṣkṛta* offense. The Saṃgha has merely harbored mutual suspicion for twenty years."
Regarding this, according to that Vinaya: In the village of Pukkara, there was a monk who observed the *poṣadha* together with a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) monk.
At that time, the forest-dwelling monk possessed great renown, while the village-dwelling monk saw an opportunity for gain and offerings.
A mind of jealousy arose. Then, on the fourteenth day, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu entered a village and said to the village bhikṣus, "Let us perform the poṣadha together.
The village bhikṣus replied, "The poṣadha shall be performed on the fifteenth day.
The forest-dweller then departed. After he had left, the village bhikṣus immediately performed the poṣadha. When the next day arrived, the forest-dwelling bhikṣu...
"Kāśyapa came wishing to perform the *poṣadha* together with us," [the monks] replied, "but we have already finished the *poṣadha*.

They then said to the forest-dwelling (*araṇya*) bhikṣu, "You have violated the *poṣadha*. We shall no longer share the Dharma or the food with you. From that time forward, the forest-dwelling bhikṣu...
Every fourteenth and fifteenth day, he would come; thus it continued for twenty years, and the *poṣadha* was not performed.
At that time, there was a benevolent deity who held the forest-dwelling (*araṇya*) bhikṣu in high esteem.

He went to Mount Cetiya and informed the bhikṣu Cetiya-Dhava of the aforementioned matter in full detail. Having heard this, the Venerable Cetiya immediately went to the village, while the benevolent deity returned.
He said to the bhikṣu of the white aranya: "The Venerable Śuddhipanthaka is currently in the village;
you may go there to pay him your respects. Having arrived and paid his respects, Śuddhipanthaka asked: "Have you abandoned the *poṣadha*? He replied:

"For twenty years, when it was the fourteenth-day *poṣadha*, I have come on the fourteenth day; when it was the fifteenth-day *poṣadha*, I have come on the fifteenth day. Is this abandoning it, or not?"
[The monks] rebelled. Sudinna said, "You have followed the Buddha’s Dharma; however, for twenty years, all the *karmavācanā* (formal acts) performed by the monks of this village have been invalid.
Their reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*) cannot be called 'reception of ordination,' and their *karmavācanā* cannot be called 'karmavācanā.'"

Regarding the question asked by a *dānapati* concerning the number of monks when it is unknown: Sengyou states that laypeople in the Western Regions (India) always inquire about the number of monks once the *poṣadha* recitation has concluded.
This is because they wish to know that the community is pure so that they may generate merit by providing either wealth or food; for this reason, they come to ask about the number.
Regarding the statement that "the counting sticks (śalākā) were as short as five fingers," some say this must refer to the Buddha’s own fingers, for they would have been one chi long;
yet if measured by human fingers, they would total only five cun, which is far too short. As for the phrase "so many bhikṣus, so many śrāmaṇeras, and so many renunciants in harmony":
"śrāmaṇera" refers to those who share the same dharma as a śrāmaṇera, while "renunciant" refers to those who share the same outward form.
Regarding the distributor of *śalākā*: one takes these blades of grass to serve as counting sticks (*śalākā*), and it is for this reason that they are so named.
According to the science of phonology (*śabdavidyā*), they are called *śalākābhāga* in foreign lands, which is translated here as "counting stick" (*chou*).
Regarding the passage in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* concerning laypeople scattering flowers upon monks seated on high seats:
it is established that if a layperson scatters flowers over a monk, the Buddha permits it; however, if a monk scatters flowers over another monk, the Buddha does not allow it.
Furthermore, there is a fifth section where a monk scatters flowers upon a high seat, and the Buddha says this should not be done. Additionally, there are laypeople...

For the sake of making an offering to the Dharma, he scattered flowers over the high seat. The bhikṣu did not permit this and spoke with resentment, saying, "He is unworthy of receiving such offerings.
He then informed the Buddha, saying, "When a layperson scatters [flowers], let it be as they wish. If they fall upon the head or the robes of a bhikṣu, they should be brushed away;
if they fall upon the high seat, there is no harm."

Regarding the phrase "the miscellaneous minor rules are difficult to maintain," Jing states: "The four *pārājika*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, and the ninety *pāyattika* are all termed 'miscellaneous minor rules' (*kṣudrānukṣudra-vinaya*).
According to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), it says: "'Miscellaneous minor rules' refers to those from the two *aniyata* down to the *śaikṣa* rules."

Some say that, excluding the four root precepts, all those from the second category downward are "miscellaneous fragments," consisting of five hundred and seven hundred rules, including those common to the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*.
Jì says: according to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, at the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, one should recite the *prātimokṣa* texts of both orders in their entirety.

Regarding the statement that one incurs an offense by speaking the names of the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*) to those who are not fully ordained, Śaṅghabhadra says: this does not mean that one incurs an offense by speaking the names of all five categories in general.

When it says "one incurs an offense," it refers specifically to the names of the offenses for particular acts, such as sexual misconduct (*maithuna*), killing (*vadha*), touching (*sparśana*), and causing injury (*kṣata*).
As for the statement that "all offenders incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)," this means that for a śrāmaṇera, offenses across all five categories are equally considered *duṣkṛta*.
Now, if one sees someone committing an act belonging to the five categories [of offenses], one should say to them: "By committing this act, you have incurred a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

This is because, according to the rules for each individual precept, the text establishes the *duṣkṛta* offense for a *śrāmaṇera*. Furthermore, it says: "One who commits all [offenses] is a *śrāmaṇera*.

This means that although they may commit offenses from all five categories, they collectively incur only one *duṣkṛta*; therefore, they are called "one who commits all [offenses]. To clarify, one must not speak of [the commission of] a *pārājika* (defeat) to such a person.
The name *caṇḍāla* (殘蘭提) is used as a designation for one who has committed a *sthūlātyaya* (向道吉羅).
If various circumstantial matters arise, it is established that these refer to conditions such as the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*).

Regarding all *karmavācanā* (羯磨) procedures, which are generally performed prior to the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, Master Li states: "In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the bhikṣus first recite the precepts and subsequently perform the various *karmas*. (6)
When the group of bhikṣus had finished reciting the precepts, they immediately rose and departed, refusing to remain in harmony with the Saṃgha for the performance of various *karmas*.

They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should first perform the various *karmas*, and only then recite the precepts. Since the precepts are that which bind the Saṃgha together, one must not allow them to depart.
Regarding the manner of recitation: while the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* does not permit chanting in a melodic style, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* allows it. (2)
The Vinaya rules are contrary [to worldly practice]. Now, those who wish to harmonize and assemble [the community] must employ a melodic chant;

however, one must not exceed the proper limits. Thus, when reciting the precepts within the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, if the melodic chant exceeds these limits, the Buddha declared that it should not be done so.

He subsequently explained that there are five faults in such melodic chanting, as clarified in the *Śīlanirdeśa-khandhaka* of the *Caturvarga-vinaya*. This will be presented below in this commentary (*chao*). Based on this, now...
When reciting the precepts, one must not exceed the limit by drawing out the voice too long.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one who knows the method of the *poṣadha* and completes the offerings is so called because if a bhikṣu understands the characteristics of the teachings and masters the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha*, he is worthy of receiving offerings;
that is to say, he knows the time for the recitation and understands the detailed or abbreviated methods of the flower-counting sticks (*puṣpa-śalākā*).
The conditions for consciousness abiding together in purity or impurity, and the gravity of the characteristics of transgressions, are termed the *poṣadha* (confession) dharma.
Below, three types of procedures for the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) are explained. Regarding the *poṣadha* hall in the Central Kingdom (India):

it is established that in those countries, monasteries are large and the number of monks is great—whether five hundred, one thousand, or two thousand—and the buildings are likewise numerous; when the time arrives, they assemble at these locations.
It is difficult to know [the procedure]. Listen as I announce the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for binding a single location into a great hall.
