When the time for the recitation of the precepts arrives and the community of monks has gathered like clouds, the method of binding is stated in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), in the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
The Saṃgha now establishes this place as a Poṣadha Hall. The motion is thus: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
The Saṃgha now establishes this place as a Poṣadha Hall. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha establishing this place as a Poṣadha Hall, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak. The Saṃgha has consented and completed the establishment of this place as a Poṣadha Hall. The Saṃgha...
Because they have endured in silence, this matter is thus upheld. Once the *karmavācanā* has been concluded, the *Poṣadha* is always recited at this location.

Regarding the phrase "among those of high rank, there are times when they further offer comfort": this establishes that among those of high rank, it is not the case that all do so; rather, it occurs only occasionally.

For example, since the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was the *Kǎotáng* (Hall of Examinations) within the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Shěng*). Within that hall, there were eight rows [of seats]. During the Song...

When the time for the formal examination arrives, those of the rank of Great Officer (Dafu) of the fifth grade and above, as well as the Governors (Zhumu) and Regional Inspectors (Cishi), are permitted to sit upon them.

Furthermore, it is said that the eight rows of seats within the Examination Hall are called the "Eight Seats" (Bazuo); these are the seats where the two Vice Presidents (Puyeshi) and the six Ministers of State (Shangshu) sit.

Thus, there are eight [categories]. Regarding the "Hall of the Secretariat" (Shangshu Ting) in the present day, Ji said: "In ancient times, those of the third rank and above were titled 'Dafu' (Grand Master).
During the early Tang dynasty, for instance, officials from the Yuanshenbu (Ministry of Personnel) and above were all designated as Dafu.

In the current state, when foreign guests are received at court, they are seated upon purple mats spread across the floor. On one side are the *gelang* (officials), who are Han officials; on the other side are the foreign guests.
The guests face one another and sit opposite each other; neither sits upon a bed. When a sage presides at the Chengtian Gate (the Hall of Receiving Heaven), he observes their manner of taking food.
According to this, even today the state still preserves these ancient customs. As for those who employ both methods simultaneously:

it is said that mats are spread before the beds, and while the monks sit on the beds, the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) distributes the counting sticks (*cau*) upon the mats on the floor, thus utilizing both locations at once.
It is for the sake of convenience that they are said to be used together. However, regarding the original practice, there were many inconveniences. Master Li stated:
"Relying on the custom of sitting on mats as practiced in the Western Regions was indeed inconvenient; one must follow the standards of the present time."

Third, regarding the elder who informs the Saṃgha on the day of the recitation of the Prātimokṣa: this is established as clear. This formal announcement (*jñapti*) should be made by the elder to the assembly.

The rest is as in the *Saṃghakārikā*. It says there: "Every time the morning for the recitation arrives, let the administrative officer (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) take note of the members of the Saṃgha—whom is present and whom is absent;
how many are healthy and how many are ill; how many can be brought [to the assembly] with assistance, and how many may grant their consent (*chanda*)?"
Up until the time when the leader of the assembly instructs them, on the day of the *poṣadha*, he shall inspect each dwelling room in turn and offer consolation to those who are ill and so forth.

If there is a *śrāmaṇera* who has a reason to grant his consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma, it should be made clear that the wording for granting consent differs slightly from that used for the *bhikṣu* community.
It should be stated: "Venerable sirs, listen. The *śrāmaṇera* [name], regarding the legal business of the Saṃgha, grants his consent and purity. One should say "the *śrāmaṇera*."
Regarding "not returning constitutes a separate assembly": this refers to a separate assembly of śrāmaṇeras, not concerning the great saṃgha.

As for the uposatha of these śrāmaṇeras, there are two different ways of arranging it: either the śrāmaṇeras assemble separately on their own as one distinct group, or they enter among the monks to perform the ritual together with them.

Regarding the aforementioned "fivefold respectful observance of the ritual," this refers to such things as not falling asleep, nor crossing one's arms over the chest or placing hands on the hips, as previously mentioned.

As for the phrase "this is what remains of the ultimate instruction" (*parama-śāsana*): because the formal rule (*śāsana*) mandates that this be performed regularly every half-month, it constitutes the vision of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Even when sudden obstacles arise, the rule still prescribes a brief recitation; it must certainly not be omitted. Therefore, it is called the "ultimate instruction. If one were to transgress it...

Regarding the offense: whether within or outside the boundary, one must issue a command for all to assemble; those who have heard of it or harbor doubts must seek clarification. Therefore, this is called the "Root of Gathering the Sangha.

As for *pánqíng* (槃檠), the character *qíng* is pronounced as the opposite of *jìng* (奇竟反); it resembles a high-legged stand with folded legs, which was once seen in the capital. Regarding the incense burner and counting-tablet stand (*xiānglú chóuàn*):

some say that when the assembly is large and the counting-tablets (*chóu*) are numerous, it is difficult to hold them all in hand; thus, they should be placed upon the table at intervals. Furthermore, one may also bathe [the tablets] on the table.
It is a tally. In the present age, people are few; it is not necessarily required to use a board. The character for *guàn* (盥) is written as 盥 and pronounced *guǎn*.
To wash one's hands is called *guàn*; this is a pictographic character. The "mortar" (*jiù*) represents the two hands, each with three dots representing the fingers.
The center is water; the vessel is for holding water. Regarding the term "foolish old man" (*yǒushǒu*):
it is explained that an elderly person who is ignorant is called an "old man" (*shǒu*). This is an interpretation based on meaning. According to the *Fāngyán*:
"In the regions between Dōng, Qí, and Lǔ, anyone who is venerable is called an 'old man' (*shǒu*; pronounced *sū zǒu*)."
The method for striking the gong for silence is as explained in the "Miscellaneous Items" section, specifically in the aforementioned second chapter on the "Requisites for the Assembly.
A guest remarked: "When striking for silence, one must not allow any lingering sound that would cause the assembly to become distracted.

Furthermore, when distributing or collecting the voting sticks (*śalākā*), tradition dictates that they must not be allowed to fall to the ground; if a stick falls, it signifies that someone within this assembly will die."
However, as it corresponds to a misconception, such a thing often occurs.
The commentary states that "collecting" (*shou*) refers to one who gathers the various implements;

this means collecting the counting sticks (*śalākā*), and waiting until the recitation of the *Poṣadha* is finished to collect the articles for the Sangha’s offerings, which are the items required for the *poṣadha*. The commentary further notes that this is based on the preceding text.

Regarding those who have already completed [the ritual]: it is established that there is no need to chant further. To say "and receive the tally for the offerings" (*bìng gòngyǎng shōu chóu*) means that since it is stated that "the small ones are collected and guarded," the inclusion is already exhaustive.
As for the aforementioned "offerings and receiving the tally," this simply refers to holding the incense burner before the Buddha.
The "Junior Master" (*xiǎoshī*) who receives offerings is like the person currently assigned to arrange seats; the intent is the same.
Furthermore, he is the one who follows the *vinaya-dhara* (*weina*) to collect the tally-sticks (*chóu*). When this announcement is made, both of these two individuals must be summoned.

In current practice at the two capitals, it is said: "Who among the assembly is the junior? Let the junior one collect and guard [the sticks]" (after saying this three times), and then the offering for collecting the tally-sticks is performed.
The statement "it is not restricted to the noble ones" establishes the clarification. The aforementioned person’s interpretation—that this indeed refers to inviting Piṇḍola—is correct;

however, one should fear that other members of the assembly might not attend and thus ought to further investigate. It is not for the purpose of specifically summoning Piṇḍola that it is said "it is not restricted to the noble ones.
Nevertheless, in reality, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the holy assemblies of the Three Vehicles all equally observe this dharma; therefore, [the text says] "highly."

In the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is recorded that during the Wei dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Tanwuwei at Rongjue Temple in the capital of Luoyang. His secular surname was Dong, and he was a native of Wuan.

Possessing spiritual insight, he penetrated the subtle mysteries; he absorbed and dwelt upon the profound secrets. Having received the transformative influence of the Way from his youth, his fame spread throughout both the court and the common world.
He was broadly versed in both the profound mysteries and Confucian classics, and he was particularly well-versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Yet, he held worldly affairs in utter disdain and intended to renounce the four types of offerings to devote himself to the practice of giving and the encouragement of instruction, making the precepts his primary concern. His influence moved the hearts of sentient beings, and his reputation spread like clouds.
Once, while reciting the precepts at Chongzun Temple in Handan, there were over a thousand followers in attendance, all of whom were his constant disciples. This occurred in the fourth month.

On the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony on the thirtieth, as the counting sticks were distributed and tallied according to the number of those present, there were more than sixty people in excess of the usual count.
Seated at the very head of the assembly, he was deeply perplexed by this anomaly. Since no outsiders had arrived, he harbored doubts throughout the entire night.
When he investigated again the following morning, someone saw them coming from west of the city of Handan; they were all eminent masters of extraordinary character, clad in [monastic] robes.
He wore his formal robes and walked with a graceful and elegant gait.

There were also those seen coming from the east side of Mount Gu, or encountered on the road, all of whom said they were going to Chongzun Temple to listen to the monks recite the precepts. Such was the case in various stages and groups.

Examining their ages, they supported one another; the number of people exactly reached sixty. Thus it was known that the assembly had grasped the Sage’s mind, which caused the spiritual essence to descend from afar.

Most notably, his virtue permeated the Buddhist tradition, and he repeatedly fulfilled the expectations of the monastic community. Later, he resided at Yonggak-sa Temple, where he was exceptionally skilled at propagating the teachings and guiding others.
He attained a profound mastery of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. With a congregation of a thousand monks, his daily practice was constant and tireless.
Dai. When the Indian śramaṇa Bodhiruci saw him, he prostrated before him and titled him the "Bodhisattva of the Eastern Land.
He once read the *Mahāyāna-yìzhāng* (Treatise on the Meaning of Mahāyāna) composed by Zhìzuì; every time he did so, he snapped his fingers in admiration of its excellence.
He transcribed it into Sanskrit characters and sent it to the Western Regions. Those who read it there all faced the east to pay homage to him, regarding him as a sage.

Regarding the three Vinayas of the Mahāsāṃghika school—namely, the *Pañcavargika*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and the *Vinaya* itself—all of them previously recited this [formula]. Now, we follow the ritual procedures of our own school;
thus, their respective Prātimokṣas state: "When those who have not yet received the precepts have already departed," and so forth.
This means that in the Prātimokṣa texts of the three Vinayas belonging to other schools, all contain these words: "Those who have not received the precepts have already departed."
Regarding the statement, "There is no need to mention that those who are not pure shall depart," etc., Ciyun says: This was established as a rule by the ancients.

When chanting the name of a *śrāmaṇera*, they would immediately say, "Those who are not pure, depart! This saying arose because it is improper for one who has committed an offense to recite the precepts together with others.
Now, this is not the same; according to both our own school and other schools, neither maintains this view. There is no need to say that those who are impure must depart.
When the preceptor reaches the time for reciting the precepts, there are naturally three inquiries: "In this matter, are you pure? If it comes to this point, [the procedure continues].
If one can still perform the confession through mental recollection and immediately hear the precepts, why is it necessary to chant them out beforehand?

Regarding the practice where all the monks simultaneously follow the ritual of the presiding elder (upādhyāya), Zhiji said: "In the present day, there are those who see the presiding elder kneeling cross-legged while they themselves sit upright and at ease;
this is a great violation of the Dharma. It is not even equal to secular etiquette; one should observe and adopt [the proper standard]."
In the past, when officials of the prefectures and counties sat at the same table as a Regional Inspector (Cishi), they all looked up to him with great reverence.
As soon as they saw the high official rise, they would immediately follow suit; at a single command to sit, they would all take their seats.
Nowadays, when a young disciple is told by his master to sit, he instead declines out of modesty and refuses; this is a violation of propriety. When told to sit, one must simply sit.
"One must not return to one's seat while awaiting the completion of the offerings. This is clearly established by Master Nanshan:

one should only return to one's seat once the waiting for the seated position has concluded. If one is elderly or ill and unable to remain in the *mutu-kai* (interlocking kneeling) posture, returning to one's seat is permitted.

It is also acceptable in the present day for the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) to return to his seat after the formal announcement (*kṣānti-vākya*). To fail to follow this instruction constitutes a transgression against the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that [the assembly] was as pure as the full moon: according to that Vinaya, when Devadatta had split the Saṃgha and proceeded toward Gayā City to establish his own uposatha, the Buddha sent Ānanda to summon him, saying, "The World-Honored One calls for you. Devadatta replied, "I will not go."
"From this day forward, there shall be no sharing with the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; no sharing in the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, or *karmas*.
From this day forward, whether one wishes to study or not study the *prātimokṣa* shall be according to my will. Having heard this, Ānanda thought to himself:
"How strange! Such evil words have been uttered. Will he not destroy the Saṃgha? He reported all these matters in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha then ordered him to summon [the offender] once more.
This was repeated three times. When the faction of Devadatta had finished their *poṣadha* ceremony, Ānanda heard of it and said, "How extraordinary!
They have already brought about a schism in the Saṃgha. He reported this in full to the Blessed One. Having heard this, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Pure as the full moon, pure is the attainment of the *poṣadha*. Only when the actions of body and speech are pure does one truly merit the *poṣadha*.
Having said these words, he spoke to Ānanda: "The non-Dharma practitioners have already finished their *poṣadha*; those who follow the Dharma should now perform it."
Regarding the *poṣadha*:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one may simply take the next seat; this is what is meant by "standing. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one should instead invite the senior monk (*sthavira*);
if he declines, saying he is unable, one proceeds directly to where the capable person is. The instruction from above to "inquire of the next seat" is precisely the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

Regarding the term *bhāṇaka* as used according to the Dharma: the *Yuyao lüyi yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of the Vinaya) states that *bhāṇaka* refers to what those who uphold the Vinaya call "chanting" (*gēsong*), and it is also called "laudatory verses" (*zànjié*).
Now, it is said that this is the language of the country of Uvvi (Udyāna). *Bai* (唄) is translated as "cessation" (*zhǐ*), and *ni* (匿) is translated as... [text fragment].

"Cutting off" (*chadan*) refers to ceasing all evil; "cutting off" (*duan*) refers to being able to sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, *ni* is translated as "resting," meaning to rest from all labors and duties.
According to the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, "half-chant" (*banbei jiluo*) refers to that which expresses the meaning incompletely, hence it is called "half-chant.
For example, the two verses in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* praising the Buddha’s three bodies, such as the phrase "the wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata."
"Even unto the peerless and inconceivable" praises the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
"The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so" praises the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body); both his form and his mind are without end.
"All dharmas are eternally abiding" praises the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* (dharma body); it is that upon which all dharmas rely, eternally abiding and profoundly serene. Now...
At that time, there was a person who would recite only a single verse; thus it is called "half-chant" (bàn bèi). [This applies to all cases accordingly.
As for having one person represent the assembly, Master An instructed each individual to remain at their own seat, holding an incense burner to make offerings.
Now, because this would be too prolix, it is required that one person perform [the ritual] before the Buddha.

Since there is no distinct virtue (*bhedaguṇa*) that can be demonstrated—meaning that while the teaching of nuns requires the total possession of ten virtues and twenty years of seniority (*viṃśativarṣā*), which constitutes a specific virtue within the total number of virtues—the person seated below has not yet fulfilled [these requirements]; therefore, it is said that "there is no distinct virtue. "Distinct" refers to...
Regarding the general and specific terminology: the ten virtues constitute the general category, while each individual virtue constitutes the specific.
The commentary states, "For now, only one or two passages from the Vinaya texts have been cited," etc. The *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) says:

"The reason for having the Elder issue the formal injunction is that in this present degenerate age, the extensive methods are lacking; therefore, the abbreviated method is currently practiced by means of the leading bhikṣu of the assembly."

The maintenance of the Dharma duties is the primary responsibility; whenever matters arise, there is nothing that is not attended to with care. As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states, this is to act as a substitute for the Buddha’s place.
Nowadays, one often sees those lacking in learning and knowledge who, despite being advanced in years, sit at the head of the assembly yet fail to act according to the Dharma.

They cause nuns to return empty-handed without ever offering a response. Those who understand this feel a shared sense of shame. This applies to both hosts and guests alike upon the seat of the *Poṣadha* ceremony; it is the duty of the virtuous.
The foolish gather together; how can you disparage yourself? What I have said here regarding the instructions for nuns, up to the point of "do not be negligent," is merely a general outline.
If you have leisure time, we shall discuss it further as the occasion arises; how could it be limited to this alone?
The nun who had been instructed to come the following day and deliver the message did so; she took her leave and returned to the monastery.

She assembled the community of monks and requested their formal consent (*saṃgha-kāma*). Once the ritual chanting was completed, she sent the nun to announce: "Venerable Elder of the Great Saṃgha, there is now a brief instruction."
Having heard these words, the assembly of nuns rose together, straightening their bodies and standing upright. Once standing, they fully proclaimed the brief instruction of the Elder.

Having proclaimed it, they cried out in a loud voice, "We receive and uphold this! They prostrated to the Buddha and dispersed. If one were to proclaim it while sitting upright, it would be a great breach of decorum.

The answer states: "Regarding the *karmavācanā* of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the *karman* is the dharma (the formal procedure), while the recitation of the precepts is the matter (the substance).

Only when both the matter and the dharma are addressed together is the rite completed. The commentary explains that the term "recitation" (*poṣadha*) is used generically, regardless of whether the specific details regarding the participants are fully understood. This refers to the word *poṣadha*.
This serves to distinguish between the practices of the monastic and the lay. For instance, the five and eight precepts and so forth are all termed *poṣadha*.

Now, if one speaks of the *śīlanirdeśa-karman* (the ritual for reciting the precepts), it is intended to distinguish this from the *poṣadha* rites of the monastic community (*saṃgha*). This is because the ritual of *karman* is not a practice performed by the laity.

If one did not mention *karman*, then the distinction between the monastic and the lay would be confused and indistinct; thus, it would be unclear which side [the rite] belongs to. This [rite] belongs to the monastic community. That...
This pertains to secular matters.
If, upon reaching the brief instruction (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*), one strikes the bell to assemble the *śrāmaṇeras*, this refers to the Seven Buddhas’ Verses.
One must wait until the recitation of the Seven Buddhas’ teachings is complete before rising; if one rises before it is finished, one incurs the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa-doṣa*).
Because this abbreviated instruction serves to gather the Saṃgha, even those who possess full decorum and have leisure for polite courtesy are included. Jì says:

"To present one's words before the Buddha and express thanks to the assembly is called 'polite courtesy' (cíxùn). Now, when performing the *bèi* chant to lead [the ceremony], it allows the Preceptor (*śīlācārya*) to have leisure;
therefore, it is named 'leisure' (*xiá*)."

Regarding the phrase "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy," etc., Ji [Jizang] says: This is a verse of self-congratulation; it is precisely the text of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Because the language of the ancients was plain and substantial, he used the term "joy" (*kuài*). In the new translation of the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is bliss."
The joy of hearing the Dharma; the joy of the harmony of the great assembly; the joy of sentient beings being free from suffering.
Regarding the phrase "whether many or equal, even after the recitation of the precepts has been completed, one must cause them to recite again, etc.":

this means that if visiting *bhikṣus* arrive after the recitation of the precepts has finished, if they are equal in number or more numerous, it is necessary to recite [the precepts] for them once more; if they are fewer, it is not necessary. Within this, the "great" [refers to...]
There are several verses (as follows).
Regarding the commentary stating that the words of this verse originate from the Āgamas, according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
Ānanda said to Kāśyapa, "The *Ekottarika Āgama* gives birth to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all other dharmas; they all arise from this. For now, let this suffice.
Regarding the *Ekottarika Āgama*, I privately remarked that when compiling the habitual practices (*vāsanā*), it would have been appropriate to compile this sutra first.
Indeed, within a single verse, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and all dharmas are produced. Kāśyapa asked, "What is this verse?
and Ānanda immediately recited the ancient verse: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
The commentary explains: "Commit no evil" means to be fully endowed with the precepts and to maintain pure conduct. "Perform all that is good" means to purify the mind.

"Purify one's own intention" means to eliminate false and inverted views; this is the teaching of all Buddhas. By removing deluded and confused thoughts, since one's precepts are pure, how could one's intention not be pure?
When the intention is pure, there are no inversions. Because there are no inversions— [one attains liberation].
When deluded conceptions are extinguished, the fruits of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are then accomplished. Since these fruits have been accomplished, are they not indeed all dharmas?
As for the Buddha’s entrustment (*parindanā*), it is called "entrustment" because he successively transmits [the teaching] to others.

Regarding the "defiled pure consciousness" (*śuddha-vijñāna*): it is established that the wholesome karma practiced by one who has left the household life to cultivate the Path perfumes the seeds within consciousness, with the distant aspiration for liberation.
Since one now does not rely on the teachings to practice, it is called "defiled. According to the old translations, there should be eight consciousnesses;
according to the new translations, there are nine, of which this is the last, named the "pure consciousness."
If, after performing repentance, one’s mind is still not at ease, one has already committed a grave offense and becomes a *śikṣādattaka* śrāmaṇera.

If, for the sake of forcing the recitation of the precepts so that one may hear them once they are finished, one repents by means of a *jñapti* (single motion) according to the ritual procedures of the present day—does the offense thereby cease?
Our current judgment is that it does not cease, because the original Vinaya text states: "By oneself... [and so forth].

"Should repent" (dāng chàn) means that at a later time one should repent again. Nanshan’s judgment of "extinction" (miè) suggests that when reciting the Vinaya, the character *dāng* (當) should be pronounced with a departing tone (*qù yīn*), meaning it refers to repenting according to the rule.
Master Bin now examines this and finds it not so; for the Tripiṭaka-master also allows for further repentance through the presence of pure dharmas (*báifǎ*).

When the entire Saṃgha assembles, there must be no one who has granted their consent (*yù*) [to be absent], and furthermore, those who have committed the same offense must be excluded—four such cases in total.
As for the *yī* (barbarian): one must clearly recognize the characteristics [of the offense] and must not perform a formal declaration (*śukra*).

If someone has given their consent (*chanda*), and the woman says she is pure, or if one trusts that she is pure, one should still proceed to the confession; one must not perform a formal declaration.

If one does not trust her, she must be summoned and formally accused, because since she has committed an offense, it is improper to speak of her as being in agreement. One must not make a false declaration. Nowadays, there are those whose offenses are mixed with doubt.

[The text] omits [the following]: "To grant consent (*chandadāna*) when it is not unanimous, yet to proceed with this formal motion (*jñapti*), hoping thereby to extinguish the offense—this is extremely unreasonable.
Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāv āpattayaḥ*) and so forth, *Lì* says: First, "the king" refers to a king coming to arrest a bhikṣu. Second, "the bandit" refers to...
"Coming to seize and bind" refers to bhikṣus. "The three fires" refers to fires coming to burn the monastery. "The four great waters" refers to floods swelling and drifting away the *saṃghārāma*.
"The five illnesses" refers to the illness of the preceptor for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, which creates an obstacle to the recitation.

"The six human difficulties" refers to cases such as when there are many laypeople (*avadātavasana*) residing at the dwelling place, thereby obstructing the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. "Non-humans" refers to ghosts.
Divine spirits cause agitation for the bhikṣus. Regarding the "difficulties of the eight evil creatures," these refer to venomous snakes, centipedes, mosquitoes, ants, and the like.
In all such cases, one must not raise one's voice; rather, one should recite the precepts with mental intention and verbal speech.

As for the statement, "Today the precepts are being recited," since there are the aforementioned difficulties, a bhikṣu must not chant the precepts in a loud voice. Regarding "noble persons," this refers to kings, ministers, and others of high status.

The aforementioned "eight difficulties" (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ) refers to a citation from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. Regarding the statement that there may be living grass on the ground, it is out of fear that damaging such life would incur the offense of *pāyattika*.

As for the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that when thieves arrive during the recitation of the precepts, one should recite the sūtra in a continuous stream, a consultation of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In a forest hermitage (*araṇya*)..."
"O monks, on the fifteenth day of the month, during the *poṣadha* ceremony for the recitation of the precepts, a bandit arrived.
When the monks saw him, they stopped and did not recite the precepts. The bandit asked, 'Why are you silent? They replied, 'What we are about to say should not be heard by laypeople.
The bandit said, 'Is what you are saying not the word of the Buddha? They replied, 'It is the word of the Buddha. The bandit said, 'Since it is the word of the Buddha, who would not [listen]...'"
"You should listen! You have all gathered here now; this must surely be a discussion that will not be to my benefit. He then beat the bhikṣus and seized their robes and bowls.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, if bandits should come, you should immediately recite other sūtras so as not to let [the recitation] be interrupted.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when bandits arrive during the time of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), the bhikṣus should continue the recitation until the ninth [section].
The tenth supplementary passage states: "Once it has been cut, there is a *pāyattika*; once it has been broken, there is a *pāyattika*.
While he was reciting, a thief arrived. The reciter stood silent; after a short while, the thief departed. He began reciting again, and this occurred up to three times.
The thief thought to himself, 'This wicked śramaṇa, by making such a statement, will surely cut me or break me! He then struck the bhikṣu. Afterward...
He informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "When the bandits arrive, you should recite other sūtras instead.

If the bandits already know the monks' methods and say, 'Śramaṇa, I already know [your recitation]; you may simply continue with what you have been reciting before,' you should recite it hurriedly so that the verses and phrases are indistinct, thereby ensuring they do not understand."
"First, 'abbreviated extraction' refers to taking the titles of the eight chapters. For example, saying: 'These four *pārājika* rules, as the Sangha has constantly heard; ...
up to these four *prātideśanīya* rules, as the Sangha has constantly heard. To say 'abbreviated omission' means omitting the specific names and categories within the chapters.
For instance, omitting the names of sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth; or, for example, when dealing with the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, simply stating five or six of them and concluding."
As for the others, they do not explicitly state "the Sangha constantly hears," but rather omit this term; thus it is said that they follow the various category-names found within each section.

However, in reality, "omission" (lueque) simply carries the sense of abbreviation and exclusion. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "exclusion" (lüeque) refers to omitting and removing phrases such as "weakened by the precepts" (jie li), and instead stating directly "committing impure conduct" (fan bujing xing); this too is called "omission."

Regarding the observation of timing when the urgency of matters is unequal, according to the Vinaya, there are generally two types: first, proceeding from the slow to the urgent, which is called "abbreviating by discarding" (*lueque*);
second, proceeding from the urgent to the slow, which is called "abbreviating by taking up" (*lüequ*). As for "proceeding from the urgent to the slow":

There are three sets of five, which together constitute fifteen types. Regarding the first five, Bin says: Although those of former times recited these fifteen types as a brief summary, they did not understand their underlying reasons.
I shall now describe them. For instance, suppose the formal *poṣadha* ceremony is being held at Zhuangyan Temple when news arrives that a disaster is approaching from the north.
The monks immediately consult one another regarding whether the disaster is near or far. Someone then replies: [The first type].
It was said: "The official inquiry is about to arrive at the north gate. The monk immediately said, "You may recite the Preface; for the rest, you may simply say, 'As the Sangha has always heard it.

This is what is meant by intending to recite only the Preface as the first abridgment. Later, on another occasion, when a similar inquiry arose as before, they deliberated together and intended to recite only the Preface.
Once the Preface had been finished, the inquiry had still not arrived, so they further recited the Four Grave Offenses as the second abridgment.
Later, at another time, there was again a threat as before; they deliberated together and intended only to recite up to the end of the *Nidāna*, but the threat had not yet arrived.
They continued reciting until the thirteenth [section], which constitutes the third abridgment (*saṃkṣipta*). Later, at another time, there was again a threat as before;
they recited up to the end of the *Nidāna*, but the threat had still not arrived. They further recited the two *Aniyata* rules, which constitutes the fourth abridgment. Later, at another time...

At that time, having likewise finished reciting the introduction as before, and while the obstacle had not yet arrived, they further recited thirty [precepts] to constitute the fifth abbreviated version. Regarding the next five:

when the time for the formal recitation of the precepts has come and it is heard that an obstacle is approaching from some distance, the assembly of monks deliberates together, saying, "We may recite the introduction and the four grave offenses.

This means that, having observed whether the obstacle is far or near, one intends to recite only those; this constitutes the first abbreviated version. Before the obstacle has actually arrived, they further recite...
The thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] rules constitute the second [section]. Reciting the two *aniyata* rules again constitutes the third. The thirty [naiḥsargika-pāyattika] rules constitute the fourth.

The ninety [pāyattika] rules constitute the fifth abridgment. Regarding the subsequent reduction to five [sections]: this refers to when the Saṃgha hears that a threat is approaching from afar; they consult together and plan to recite only the introduction, the four *parājika*, and the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa].
When the recitation is finished, the threat finally arrives. This is the first abridgment. Subsequently, at another time, they likewise planned to recite only the introduction.

The four *pārājika* rules constitute the thirteenth [section]. Having finished reciting them, the difficult questions have not yet arrived; therefore, one further recites the two *aniyata* rules as a summary of two.
The remaining phrases are to be understood accordingly. The two *aniyata* rules constitute the summary of two; the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules constitute the summary of three;

the ninety *pāyattika* rules constitute the fourth; and the four *pratideśanīya* rules constitute the fifth. These fifteen types are called "abbreviated extraction," meaning that before the difficult questions arrive, they are gradually extracted.
Yeli said: "For the *bhikṣuṇī*, there are only two sets of five, because there are no two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, and because there are only two *adhika* (additional) rules.

Consider this. Regarding the fact that for the *bhikṣuṇī* there are only two sets of five: Bin says, 'The first is the *nidāna* (introduction); the second extends to the eight *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules; the third extends to the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

the fourth extends to the thirty [rules]; and the fifth extends to the *pāyattika*. The second set of five extends to the eight *pratideśanīya* (confessional) rules. This may be inferred accordingly. Bin.
It is said: "The ancients called this 'proceeding from the urgent to the relaxed. This is a great way of naming. Question: Why does it not include the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules? Answer:

The precepts consist of five categories (*pañca-varga*). If one were to include the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, it would no longer be called "abbreviated" (*laghu*), but would instead be termed "extensive" (*vistara*).

Furthermore, even within the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmā vinayasya saṃgrahāya*), if a difficulty arises, one must simply proceed directly; one may not abbreviate them. Second, [the category] proceeding from the relaxed to...
Regarding "Urgency" (*āpatti*) and "Abbreviation": there are seven types of abbreviation. First is "going straight ahead. Suppose the difficulty is still somewhat relaxed;
one has been reciting extensively from the beginning and manages to reach the end of the *Pratideśanīya* rules when the difficulty suddenly arrives.

Being unable to recite the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, one abbreviates them—this is the second type of abbreviation. Third, suppose one has recited from the introduction up to the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules when the difficulty suddenly arrives, and one abbreviates...

First, from the *Pratideśanīya* [downward], two sections are omitted; this constitutes the second abridgment (*saṃkṣepa*). Third, after reciting from the beginning up to the end of the thirty *Śaikṣa* rules, once the objections have been raised, ninety rules are omitted;
this constitutes the third abridgment. Fourth, from the beginning up to the end of the two *Aniyata* rules, thirty rules are omitted; this constitutes the fourth abridgment.
5. From the end of the Preface (Nidāna) up to the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; the objections then arise, and the two Aniyata rules are omitted—this constitutes the fifth abridgment.

6. From the end of the recitation of the Preface up to the four Parājika rules; the objections arise, and the thirteen [Saṃghāvaśeṣa] rules are omitted—this constitutes the sixth abridgment. 7. Reciting only from the beginning up to the end of the Preface.

When difficulties arise, they arrive immediately. One must not recite the four *pārājika* rules; rather, one omits the four *pārājikas*, which constitutes the "Seven Omissions. This is called the "Seven Omissions.
If the difficulties are imminent and one cannot recite the introduction (*nidāna*), the assembly disperses. In that case, one says: "Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth day;
each of you should rectify your body, speech, and mind," and then they disperse. This is called "going straight away. Lì (Lì Daoyuan) said: "For nuns, there are no two *aniyata* rules; however—"

There are six abridgments, the first being "going straight ahead. All are said to be difficult to approach closely; this refers to the abbreviation of the subsequent text. However, according to tradition, the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*) may not be abbreviated.
Since the seven methods for settling disputes belong to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (or *pācittiya*) category, they should also be permitted to be abbreviated;

it is simply that tradition does not abbreviate them. Jì says: "Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes, they are already abbreviated from the outset. One cannot abbreviate what is already abbreviated; therefore, they must be stated in full."
This refers to recitation. If one proceeds from the previous extensive recitation, once the *Śaikṣa-dharmas* have been completed, it constitutes an "extensive" version and is not called "abbreviated.
However, according to the intent of the present *Chao*, which states that titles are abbreviated and categories are omitted, the meaning is slightly different;
thus, it differs from these fifteen types.
Regarding the statement "each one is individually titled and collectively concluded": this refers to both collective conclusions and individual conclusions; either may be employed.

A "collective conclusion" (*tōketsu*) occurs when, after reciting the titles of all the sections (*honsoku*), one concludes them collectively by saying, "The Sangha has constantly heard [this]," and so forth.

An "individual conclusion" (*bekketsu*) refers to concluding each section immediately after reciting its title, saying, "The Sangha has constantly heard [this]. For example, after saying, "This is the Four Pārājika [Offenses]," one concludes with, "The Sangha has constantly heard [this]."

"Thirteen types of monks, such as those who have heard [the Dharma] constantly," and so forth, are examples of this. Regarding the statement, "Now, according to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*," Master Li establishes that from the character "this" (此) down to the character "also" (也) constitutes the actual text of the treatise.

There are also cases where the brief conditions are established and not explained in detail, yet they universally remedy transgressions; this is clearly evident. Since there are brief conditions, an extensive explanation is not permitted;
the matter must be treated concisely. Now, these are not explained at all, as they universally remedy the offense of the Saṃgha for violating the teachings.
The preceding explanation of the meaning of the Saṃgha’s recitation of the Prātimokṣa is complete.

Regarding the statements "some say it must be confessed" or "some say one may proceed once others are present," Vinītadeva explains: This refers to a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) that constitutes a grave transgression.
Since he is staying alone and is pressed to recite the *Poṣadha*, he does not know whether he should proceed or not; furthermore, there is no textual authority in the *Vinaya* [addressing this].

If it were a light *duṣkṛta*, the *Vinaya* would require him to perform a mental confession (*cittavipratisāra*) and then the *Poṣadha* could be recited. However, since this is a grave *duṣkṛta*, the *Vinaya* requires it to be confessed before another person.
At present, one dwells alone; however, the Vinaya does not clarify this rule. Consequently, some masters advocate for confession (*āviṣkaraṇa*), while others say one should wait for another person.
Now, according to the general principle accepted by all, one must indeed confess. Therefore, it is said: "Now, following the general interpretation.
The meaning of this general interpretation is as follows in the subsequent text.

Regarding the statement in the *Five Hundred Questions* that "one should repent before the Sangha of the four directions after having recited the confession three times," [the commentator] Li explains:
according to the monastic laws of the present day, this refers to repenting before the Sangha of the four directions.

This clarifies that since one is living alone, on the day of the *Poṣadha* (confession ceremony), one should purify body, speech, and mind, join the palms toward the noble and holy Sangha of the ten directions, and speak the words of repentance for the offenses committed. (Three times)
Having finished the exposition, one may then recite the *Śīlaskandha* (Precepts Text). The preceding section concludes the explanation of the ten chapters.
Chapter Eleven, Part One: "Exertion in Cultivation during the Retreat.

Since the assembly has already heard the precepts and understands what constitutes their observance and violation, and has gained a rough knowledge of their names and models, when it comes to discussing the departure from transgressions, it is entirely due to...

One must exercise restraint and self-control; how much more so now that the summer retreat is approaching! This is precisely why one must be courageous and diligent, focusing single-mindedly on cultivating the path of practice.

For this is the essential task of those who have left the mundane world: it cannot be accomplished if the mind is distracted and scattered. The perfect cause of the Eightfold Noble Path is easily achieved through restrained reflection. Thus, the teaching was established in accordance with the timing of the season.
This text was composed because the rules for the summer retreat were established to limit the period to ninety days, during which one practices the Threefold Training. Furthermore, it says:

"The preceding section identified the characteristics [of the mind] and provided general admonitions for its protection. Now that the time has arrived for the summer season, there are sacred regulations for those who have left secular life to pursue the Way.

Yet, instead of this, people are scattered by non-virtuous activities; they follow the laws of their local villages and fields, chasing after the dust of sensory passions, and thus fall headlong into calamity."
The abyss is such that there is no thought of returning to one's tracks. Therefore, the Great Sage used the Dharma as a barrier to prevent such wandering;

by constantly abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and finding security in his dwelling, he was finally able to advance toward the Way. Thus, following those [preceding sections], this chapter follows.
Next, the names are explained. To settle the mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is called "peace" (*an*); to designate a place where one relies for residence is called "abiding" (*ju*).

Furthermore, it is said that the tranquility of body and mind is called "peace," while not moving from the place of reliance is called "abiding. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "To collect and quiet the physical form and mind is called 'peace';

to vow to remain in a dwelling is called 'abiding. The *Shou-su* (Preface to the Commentary) states: "Explaining according to the Dharma, the path that departs from peril and suffering is called 'peace'; [the mind...]"
Regarding the term *āśraya* (dwelling): the *Cangjie pian* states that "peace" (*an*) means "stillness. The *Erya* states that peace arises from "stopping," and it is also said to mean "stability.

Regarding the phrase "exerting cultivation" (*ce xiu*): Master Li says it refers to vigorously applying the three karmas to advance in the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Master Sheng says that since one is currently in the summer retreat, one should diligently apply the three karmas to advance in mental practice; thus it is so called. It is also referred to as "exerting cultivation."
This refers to the cultivation of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*): causing unarisen wholesome states to arise; causing arisen wholesome states to increase;
preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising; and eliminating arisen unwholesome states. Therefore, it is so called. Regarding the attachment to the "Dharma of Receiving the Sun":

one should fear that the duration of a single summer retreat may be too long, and that there might be occasions for generating wholesome states or extinguishing unwholesome ones [that require immediate action]. It is only right that one should go to rescue and deliver [beings] in such circumstances. This is the principle.

Regarding "staying": once one has established oneself by observing the prescribed rules (*dharmas*), one must still act in accordance with those rules. Restriction serves to prevent transgressions, while permission serves to facilitate benefit.
Since these restrictions and permissions function as conditions (*pratyaya*), the procedure for receiving an extension of time (*ādiśanadharma*) is appended here.

Now, as for "dwelling in stillness and contemplating the subtle": contemplation arises from reflection; "subtle" means wondrous. That which is the untainted, true wisdom and is not seen by ordinary people is called "subtle.
"Stillness" refers to tranquility; being tranquil in body and mind, one contemplates the subtle and wondrous True Principle.

This is the essential method for exiting the world; therefore, it is called the correct track of the Way. "Taking days to pursue merit": merit arises from its fruit. Taking [the days of] the ninety...
If one diligently cultivates precepts and meditative concentration during the day, there will be daily progress and the realization of superior fruits.
Even if the fruit has not yet been attained, it is nonetheless a cause for the state of fruition, for one will certainly obtain the benefits of the Path.

Regarding "relying on conditions and taking up residence," this means either depending on a village, a hamlet, or a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), or depending on places such as mountain caves; these are simply indeterminate, following the conditions of the time. Thus it is said.
"Whose resolve is solely intent upon benefit": "Resolve" (志) refers to the mind (意). The mind is directed toward benefiting others and aspiring to the path of liberation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
"Restrained throughout the three seasons" means that during spring, winter, and summer alike, one is not permitted to wander about without purpose or neglect the practice of cultivation.

Although this restriction applies to all three seasons, because the summer months are excessive [in heat], they are specifically prohibited and regulated. Regarding the statement "the sentiment lies within the three excesses," it refers to the following passage.

This refers to the manifestation of those faults. Conversely, these faults become three benefits. First, regarding "wandering about aimlessly, which hinders the cultivation of the practice for transcendence":
this means that monastics who have left the household life are guests cast out from the three realms, intending to attain *nirvāṇa*.

If they do not now cultivate the practice of one who has left the household life but instead merely engage in wandering, it is said that this hinders the cultivation of the practice for transcendence. Second, injury...

Regarding the point that "violating the life-force of sentient beings deeply contradicts compassion," [Dao]li establishes this as follows: At the time one first receives the precepts, one makes a solemn vow and commitment toward all sentient beings to abandon the thought of killing.
If one now harms them, it violates that original compassionate mind. Third, regarding the point that "it invites worldly censure," [Dao]li establishes this as follows:
Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) rebuke him, saying: "Even birds and beasts still have nests and dens; yet the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, constantly [neglect their own]"... [text fragmentary].
While wandering about, he tramples upon living beings without any compassion in his heart, yet he claims aloud, "I know the True Dharma.
Looking at him now, what True Dharma could there be? Furthermore, worldly people and non-Buddhists reckon that plants and trees possess life;
seeing a bhikṣu trample and injure them, they claim it is the taking of life. It is for this reason that he is rebuked.
"However, it is not that these various reasons for abandoning [the retreat] and protecting one's life are non-existent. This means:

although the establishment of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) was based on the aforementioned reasons—such as obstacles to the Path and the inciting of public censure—it is not that these circumstances do not exist at all. Indeed, they apply throughout all three seasons; however, when it comes to the loss of life, this is particularly prevalent during the summer.
Therefore, the intention behind sitting out the summer retreat now is precisely to protect one's life. Regarding the phrase "the fault lies in not requesting": this clearly establishes that since...

To transgress the teachings constitutes the commission of an offense; it is not something one can escape by means of petitioning. As the Sūtra says: "Except for past calamities, which cannot be escaped through petition. This interpretation is superficial.
Since one has already committed an offense by violating the teachings, one incurs the fault of one's own making; this offense is not something obtained through petitioning.
This is also like the meaning of "bringing this responsibility upon oneself. Regarding the phrase "perpetually flowing in the sea of suffering," "perpetual" (yǒng) is a term for "long-term.

To tread upon and injure the lives of sentient beings violates the established teachings and incurs a *thullaccaya* offense; furthermore, there is the karmic path [of killing]. If one does not observe the *varṣā* retreat during the summer, one violates the teachings and commits a *dukkaṭa* offense, resulting in rebirth in hell (*niraya*) as a retribution in this life.
When will one ever see deliverance from it? Thus it is said. The explanation of the meaning of the preface is hereby complete.
The initial section is divided into five parts: the first is the commencement of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), and the last is the receiving of the [extra] days.
Now, within the context of the *varṣā*, it is divided into five gates.
One must not undertake the *varṣā* residence upon a tree, because the Buddha prohibited climbing trees higher than the height of a person’s head.

Regarding "sufficient protection against water and rain," the *Lìjiè* (礪解) explains that this does not refer to the feet of hands and feet; rather, it refers to the meaning of being able to avoid water and rain by means of [a shelter].

As for those such as cowherds or oil-pressers, *Lìmíng* clarifies that one must rely on them only if they are constantly present in the *araṇya* (wilderness/monastery) as cowherds for one, two, or three years; if they are there only temporarily, it is not permissible.
Regarding those who have resided for a long time: one may not rely upon them [as permanent residents]. If such a person moves away, the bhikṣu must follow them out.

This applies equally to those on oil-pressing sites, timber-cutting sites, and ships. Lì (礪) says: "Those who rely on a ship must be permanent residents of the ship, and not merely temporary visitors."
It is permissible to calculate that one has completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*) by staying for the duration. Regarding the statement that the text is unclear:

upon examining the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it says within the section on the rainy-season retreat (*anvāsa*) that the Buddha permitted monks to observe the retreat in reliance upon cowherds, woodcutters, or boatmen;
if they must move during the interval, they should depart following those [protectors]. Furthermore, it says that monks may observe the retreat in reliance upon a village.
If a village is divided into two parts, one should remain where the provisions and necessities are fully supplied.

During the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), if one must relocate, one may go wherever it is necessary to go. Such is the text of the Vinaya. This is established and clarified; as for that which is not clear within the text:

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) states that for those such as the person mentioned above, there is no explicit mention of the intention to dwell long-term or the intention not to dwell long-term;

it merely says that one obtains the basis for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Furthermore, it does not say whether one obtains the summer retreat or not, but simply says "one follows [the person] in departing.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü) states regarding those who rely on others as described above: according to this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one must first have the intention to dwell before one can obtain the basis for the *varṣā* by relying on them; one merely follows [them].

Regarding those who have faith and joy and for whom food and clothing are abundant: according to the *Wufen lü* (Pañcavargika-vinaya), at one time there was a bhikṣu who entered the rainy season retreat with a group of merchants.
Suddenly, the merchants departed. The bhikṣu did not know what to do and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to follow them. The merchants divided themselves into two groups.
The bhikṣu did not know which group to follow and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If one group has faith and joy..."
They depart with their abundant provisions and enjoyments. This applies even to those who tend cattle and sheep, those who build rafts, or those who travel by boat, as explained above.
It is said: "Those who have faith and devotion" refers to those who, once the others have dispersed in the four directions, follow those bhikṣus whom they revere, trust, and respect.
Furthermore, they follow those who possess excellent clothing, food, and drink in abundance; they do not break the summer retreat.
[This refers to] the two periods: before the sixteenth day of the first summer month and after the sixteenth day of the fifth month. This briefly cites the sixteenth day of the first summer month;
thus, one should know that both the preceding and following sixteenth days are valid for entering the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Therefore, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā* states: "The preceding and following [periods] each reach the sixteenth day."
"The eastern sky has already turned red" means that the fifteenth day of the lunar month has ended and the dawn light has fully appeared; this is precisely the summer period (*grīṣma*).
This statement is made to refute those who rely on the *Śāriputra-vinaya-śāstra* (the *Shisong shu*). That text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not make such a claim;

rather, it was later commentators who established this practice. It states that one must ensure the fifteenth day and the boundaries have been reached, and that the allocation of rooms and quarters is completed.
The *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is established on the sixteenth day. Those who arrive only on the sixteenth day do not establish the retreat;

therefore, the *Sifen jieben su* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya Karmavācanā) refutes this, stating: "If one performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) on the fifteenth day, that is the final day of spring and is not called 'entering the summer retreat.

The present *Chao* (Commentary) cites the *Liao lun su* (Commentary on the Vinayamātṛkā) and the *Sifen* [Vinaya] to refute the tenets of the masters of the *Shisong* (Ten Recitation Vinaya), asserting that it must be the sixteenth day."

If one enters the boundary before the division of day and night has ended, even if only one foot has crossed the boundary, it constitutes the formal establishment of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

Regarding the term "separate dwelling" (*pratyekavāsa*) as referring to the *poṣadha* boundary: this means that when the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for gathering the Saṃgha is currently being demarcated, all such areas are designated as separate dwellings.
This realm is not that realm; therefore, it is called "separate dwelling" (*pratyekavāsa*). Because one gives rise to the intention to dwell within this realm, it is called "settling" (*vāsa*).

Regarding the first point, "a village too far away," the Commentary states: "If one must wait for physical sustenance or rely on material provisions, seeking them from afar will hinder one's practice."
Therefore, these are not permitted. Second, regarding those places too close to cities: cities are crowded and chaotic, while the path of pure cultivation is often contrary to such environments;

thus, they conflict with one another. Regarding these two aforementioned locations, although they may not be ideal for the *an-gan* (rainy-season retreat), if there is already a monastery (*vihāra*) in that place, how could it not constitute a valid *an-gan*?
Third, regarding those places with many mosquitoes, ants, and the like: the lives of creatures such as mosquitoes and ants are fragile, yet those who harm them are numerous. Or...
They devour the physical remains, having no intention to choose or discriminate. Jì said: "At Shíbì Temple in Bīngzhōu, there were an extreme number of fleas.
An old master would constantly make a silk bag and sleep inside it at night; otherwise, he could not sleep at all. His junior disciples teased him, saying:
'If you had not come to spend the summer retreat at Shíbì Temple, how many times would the fleas have carried you away from your bed during the night?'"

Regarding the "four types of people who cannot be relied upon," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "A person requires a virtuous friend as the foundation for the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Although both may be called 'good,' they are not necessarily compatible; therefore, one must exercise discernment. Furthermore, [the teacher] must possess five virtues:

first, being free from impediments in answering questions. Thus it is said, 'to cause those who have not heard to hear. This clarifies the person who relies [on the teacher], whose mind harbors doubts and seeks [instruction]."
Regarding "one who hears and understands": this refers to the person upon whom [the teaching] relies, namely, the one who is able to instruct and cause others to hear.

Regarding "having already heard, causing [others] to be purified": this means that once the person who relies [upon the teacher] has heard, the person upon whom they rely causes that relying person to become purified.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Second, generating faith in accordance with what is taught. Regarding "being able to resolve doubts": this refers to the person who relies [upon the teacher].

Regarding such a person, whether one doubts whether [an offense] is light or heavy, or doubts whether it exists or does not exist, the person upon whom one relies is able to resolve these matters. The *Sū* (Commentary) states:
"Resolving doubts as they arise is the third. As for the phrase "able to cause thorough penetration," the *Sū* states: "Being unimpeded in question and answer is the fourth."
Regarding the statement "removing wrong views and attaining right view," the *Shu* (Commentary) says: "Distinguishing between the peripheral and the correct, one is free from all false attachments;

this is the fifth [requirement]. Regarding the fifth, "there being no donor," the *Shu* says: "The body is not like a gourd that remains tied up and is not eaten. One must first have medicine and food to alleviate hunger and emptiness.
If these are lacking morning and evening, then [the precept] cannot be bound. The *Sifen lü mudejia* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya Mātṛkā) is largely the same as this treatise.
Regarding this, Fazang states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is identical to this *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*; therefore, I shall not cite its text again.

As for the statement in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* that 'one should not dwell in a deep mountain forest where there are fearsome non-human beings,' an investigation of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* reveals:
There was once a bhikṣu in the kingdom of Kośala who lived alone in a deep mountain forest. At that time, a non-human female came and spoke to the bhikṣu..."
The bhikṣu said, "Come and engage in sexual desire with me. The bhikṣu replied, "I am one who has severed desire.
The woman said, "If you do not comply, I shall ruin your profits and bring you misfortune and distress. The bhikṣu said, "Do as you wish;
I will never engage in sexual desire with you. When it was midnight and the bhikṣu was lying down, the woman folded her patched robe and took hold of the bhikṣu.
He lay down beside a lady within the royal palace. When the king saw him, he asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
He then answered the king in detail regarding the matter. The king immediately released him. The bhikṣus heard of this and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, one should not dwell in such places as deep mountains or terrifying locations where there are no people. Furthermore, there was another...
The causes and conditions for the bhikṣu were as described above. A female ghost seized the bhikṣu and placed him inside a wine jar in a tavern.
Thereupon the Buddha said: "A bhikṣu should not dwell in deep forests, empty places, or fearsome, uninhabited locations."

Regarding the "Great Exposition on the Methods and Applications for the Summer Retreat (Varṣā)" in the sixth fascicle of the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, according to an examination of that treatise, it says:

When a bhikṣu seeks a place for the summer retreat—whether it be a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) or beneath a tree—he should first go there to inspect whether there are bedding and seating materials (*śayanāsana*).
He should also check whether the location is free from disturbances such as noise, and whether it is devoid of lions, tigers, wolves, mosquitoes, and gadflies.
"Are there no dangers from bandits and the like? Can one dwell here in peace until the end of the retreat?
Is food and drink available as desired? Can medicine be obtained for those who are ill? Are fellow residents trustworthy?
Can whatever is required be obtained as wished? Can one practice the path in safety? Do you dwell, stay, sit, and lie down together with them?"
"Will I not create obstacles? Will they not abandon me when I am ill? Having thus deliberated on these various matters and prepared accordingly, one then enters the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Furthermore, one observes whether there are none among the assembly who are prone to violent quarreling, whether they will not give rise to ill will toward oneself, and whether there are those within the assembly who understand the Vinaya.
This is called the method for entering the rains retreat. Thus it is said.
Regarding whether the *upadhivāra* (distribution of duties) should be performed for the *sthavira* (senior monk) and others during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:

"Within the assembly during the *varṣā*, the *sthavira* should inquire about the location of the boundary markers (*sīmā*) of the great enclosure (*mahāsīma*). He should also inquire about the locations for the storage of robes and food, as well as the location for the *poṣadha* ceremony."

The method for reciting the *Poṣadha*: Appointing a person to recite the precepts; appointing a person to offer prayers of blessing (*svastyayana*); appointing a person to manage affairs; appointing a *śrāmaṇera* (monastic attendant) for the Saṃgha;

and for the monks who go outside the boundary, [granting them] a period of seven days, fifteen days, or one month by means of a formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) regarding the location.

Furthermore, one should inspect the rooms and bedding to see who is using them in accordance with the Dharma and who is not; those who use them in accordance with the Dharma should be instructed, exhorted, and benefited.
One should rejoice and praise those who act in accordance with the Dharma. For those whose conduct is not in accordance with the Dharma, one should admonish them to bring it to mind, saying:
"Venerable sir, you ought to utilize the property of the Sangha in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "so much time has already passed" and so forth, the *Lishi* (Establishment) says:
"The Elder, having comforted the great assembly, causes them to realize impermanence; the days and months pass swiftly, seasons change and years shift, and impermanence approaches in secret."

Diligently cultivate the Path. Birth and death are to be feared; there should be no negligence. Such a senior elder (sthavira) is truly a parent to the Saṃgha and is also called a teacher of the Saṃgha.
This is called the Dharma of a senior elder.

The above concludes the explanation regarding the meaning of the first point concerning what is permissible and impermissible. Below this, the sequence of the ritual procedures for the formal act of binding (saṃghāvaśeṣa) is clarified.

Regarding the statement, "There must never be a case where one does not rely on the same formal act [of confession], otherwise it is a duṣkṛta (minor offense)": this establishes that if the Great Saṃgha does not remain in a state of concord, a duṣkṛta is incurred. This applies during the three periods [of the day].
If one wanders without a formal invitation (*niśraya*), it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for all.

As for the question, "If a nun is unwell, why is the period fixed at only three months?"—the intent of this inquiry is: since the summer retreat consists of four months, for what reason is it fixed at only three?
There are three points in the answer below. Regarding the opening of the final month to provide robes for the body: this refers to the month of Kārttika.

As for the statement that there are three types of *vassa* (rainy-season retreats) in the Vinaya, Master Li states: "Among the various masters of old, there were those who did not establish a middle *vassa*."

Regarding those who reside [in retreat]: although the *An-gan-ken-do* (The Chapter on the Summer Retreat) clarifies only the preceding and succeeding retreats, it does not clarify the method for a middle retreat.

In the "Increase of Three" (*Zeng-san*) section of the text, there are three periods of retreat, namely: the preceding, the middle, and the succeeding. Therefore, the *Karma-shu* (Commentary on the Ritual Procedures) states:

"The 'Increase of Three' fully clarifies the preceding, middle, and succeeding [periods]. Based on the fixed divisions of time, these consist of one day at the beginning, one day at the end, and two days in the middle.
On the nineteenth day, within the *Khandhaka*, it is merely clarified that they each resided for three months before and after [the rains retreat], with no intermediate period.
Therefore, the subsequent text of this *Khandhaka* states: "On the fifteenth day, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana wished to enter the rainy season retreat (*vassa*) in the presence of the Buddha."

They departed from their place of residence and only arrived after seventeen days. Not knowing what to do, they asked the Buddha, who said, "I permit you to observe the later *anvārohaṇa* (postponed retreat).
According to the characteristics [of this rule], the former [retreat] lasts for only one day, while the remaining thirty days constitute the later retreat.

It is not that they look forward to the beginning and thus merely name it "later," which would result in the middle period being omitted. Some say that according to the three additional passages in the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
There are three types of *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat): the early, the middle, and the late. Within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, singing and performance are like weeping;
dancing is like madness; and frivolous laughter is like that of a child.

Some take these three types of *varṣā* to be distinct methods for settling the mind, asserting that the actual *varṣā* does not occur only during the first and last days of each period. [The Master] granted permission for the *varṣā* during all three periods. It is said:
I have briefly examined the text of the seal. Great wisdom follows the meaning. An ancient said:

"In my observation of this Vinaya, regarding the method for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*), there are only two days—before and after—by which the retreat is established. If that is so, why does the *Triparivarta* (Three-Section) Sūtra state: "There are three kinds of rains retreats:
the early retreat, the middle retreat, and the late retreat"? The answer is: the subsequent passage of that text states, "In the Noble Dharma..."
In the Vinaya, singing and playing are likened to weeping, dancing to the behavior of a madman, and laughing to that of a small child.

Examining the force of this textual passage, one who dwells in stillness through right mindfulness is said to be in "summer retreat" (*an-gu*). One first contemplates singing, then dancing in the middle, and finally laughing at the end;

thus it is called the "three-fold summer retreat. This does not refer to the ninety-day retreat method. Nowadays, there are also those who support this interpretation based on such a view. Now, let us examine this in detail.
This is merely a convoluted interpretation of the explicit text, falsely attempting to communicate one's own views.

Since the *Gāthā* and other such passages lack any characteristic of the preceding or following rainy-season retreats (*varṣā*), they are simply texts concerning distinct sections; they need not be correlated with the three types of rainy-season retreats.
The *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, fascicle five, states directly that it is part of the Bhikṣu-dharma that one must neither dance oneself nor teach others to dance; this was not permitted by the Buddha.
[The Buddha] listened. The group of six bhikṣus sang, danced, and performed as entertainers. The Buddha heard of this and prohibited all bhikṣus from singing, dancing, or performing as entertainers.
There was another instance where the group of six bhikṣus ran about like a capering horse; the Buddha did not permit this.

Dancing is the work of ignorant children; singing resembles the sound of weeping; laughing with bared teeth is the appearance of a madman. None of these are things a bhikṣu should do. (The Commentary states:
They lack the three *anvārohaṇa* (supplementary periods) and are not mutually affiliated. Thus, one knows that the extended period ends on the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
One may perform the formal boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandhana*) every day. It is clear, therefore, that there are three *anuvāsa* (summer retreats) within the summer season.
However, upon examining the original text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it did not originate in the kingdoms of Khotan or Kucha. Vimalākṣa was a native of Kucha;
he made this statement based on the new version of the Vinaya. If one were to say that other schools entirely lack the passage concerning Zhong'an:
If one were to harmonize this Vinaya with other schools, how could the various schools each have their own distinct tenets? Gao said:

"However, regarding the three periods for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there has been common dispute since ancient times. Upon reaching my own resolution, when seeking it through the meaning of the doctrine, there are only two periods."

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lacks the text concerning the three periods [of the rainy season retreat] (this is the first proof). The various Vinayas of the external schools all recognize only the two periods, before and after [the summer] (this is the second proof).

Only the *Pañcaśata-praśna* permits the three periods, yet it is not sufficient to rely upon as a standard. Furthermore, the text regarding the "increase of three" (*zengsan*) was originally not intended as a rule for the summer retreat;
rather, it specifically concerns the three distinct periods for the cultivation of the mind. Therefore, it says there are "three kinds of *an-gu* (retreats)."

In the *Ekottarika-āgama* (Zengyi Ahan jing), among the three [sections] concerning the three types of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreats)—that is, the three within the summer—it is not stated in the section on the two [types of retreat] that there are two kinds of *varṣā*, namely the earlier and the later (this is the third proof). Furthermore, it says:

"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived on the seventeenth day; the Buddha ordered them to enter the later retreat. This clearly shows that since they could not reach the earlier retreat, the Buddha ordered them to wait for the later one, until the fifth [day].

The sixteenth day of the month (the fourth proof). Furthermore, the "forgetting the completion" and the "boundary" are both provisions of leniency (*kai-mon*). Because there was no time to perform the formal ritual (*kaji*), the leniency allows for forgetting the completion.
If one obtains the continuity of the *sīmā*-binding and it is called "established within" (*chū-an*), why would it be necessary to grant leniency for forgetting the completion and the boundary?

Granting leniency only for "established within" is surely not essential? (The fifth proof). Moreover, in the subsequent section of this *Khandhaka*, it says: "Accepting an invitation from another to observe the rains retreat."
In the section concerning the postponement of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), all the enumerated phrases state "the fifteenth day.

Regarding the *poṣadha* within and outside the boundary, or going to the place of retreat on the sixteenth day, since these refer to the time of the *poṣadha*, it is clear that this refers only to the middle of the fourth month or the middle of the fifth month.
If one were to establish the retreat in the middle [of the month], there would be no *poṣadha* against which it could be compared. (This is the sixth proof.)

Regarding the statement, "The middle [period] is not distinguished, for the principle is self-evident," [Dao]li says: It is like measuring the capacity of a bowl; between three *dou* and three and a half *dou*, the meaning can be understood even if the intermediate amount is not specified.
