As for receiving [the authorization] from the five groups of monks, the established view is that the Buddha ordained the five groups to observe the summer retreat by mutually authorizing one another; it is not otherwise.

This refers to a bhikṣu facing the four lower assemblies. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "If one calculates that performing [the ritual] with those who are not qualified is insufficient, how can one receive [it] from them?
This established rule applies universally; the text is like the example of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) for the five assemblies. Each follows their respective status. It further states:
"The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* now follows the four assemblies; how could this be the authentic teaching? The text is not fit for use. Someone says: "One simply informs [them]."

The fourfold assembly knows my movements; how could it be better not to inform them? Thus, [the former view] is still superior. Now, the interpretation is not so. The establishment of the Dharma must be fixed.

How could there be a bhikṣu who acts as a witness for a bhikṣuṇī? In such a case, the principle is defeated. If one wishes to apply this universally, one need only perform the mental recitation (cittamanasikāra).
If one insists on ensuring harmony, one may verbally announce the location, but one must never take this as the formal procedure for receiving the *poṣadha* day (āpattipariśuddhi). Lì says:

Regarding the three lower assemblies (śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, and śikṣamāṇā), although they are subject to the regulation of the rains retreat (varṣā), if they have a reason to go outside the boundary, there is no procedure for receiving an extension of days (*anujñā*).

Because their years [of ordination] are not counted [in the same way as full bhikṣus], the procedure for receiving an extension of days is not considered; nevertheless, even when departing, they must still announce their departure.
Regarding the point that this differs from the ancient masters who held that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and so forth could only be performed after seven days had passed:

Hui-li states that former teachers said one first received the seven-day period, then the fifteen-day period, and finally the one-month period; throughout a single summer retreat (*varṣā*), one must not exceed these three methods.
The present [text] does not agree with this. Daolì says that former teachers stated that one must first [observe] seven days, followed by fifteen days.
One month later, following this same sequence: if one has already accepted [the robe] for fifteen days, one may not further accept it for seven days, because the longer period subsumes the shorter.

This is like the *kaṭhina* (merit-cloth) of five months, which subsumes the *kārttika* [month]; or as with the *pārvana* (full-moon) cloth, where the collection for ten days and so forth is permitted.
However, the current interpretation is not thus. This is because, like the *kaṭhina*, the time is fixed; furthermore, both possess the five benefits (*pañcānuśaṃsa*).
Regarding the "one-month robe," it is determined by taking the acquisition of the robe as the standard; it is permitted for one extra length, and there is no other basis for this.

Therefore, these two cases are established as fixed permissions, wherein the long [period] subsumes the short. Now, regarding this "receiving of days," it is distinguished according to specific circumstances; since those circumstances vary in duration, [the rules differ].

The sequence of priority is not fixed; how could one definitively establish that the short must come first and the long last? Therefore, the correct explanation is as follows: the three grades of days for receiving [the precepts] vary in length according to circumstances.
Depending on what is required beforehand, if there is a long circumstance, one first performs the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to receive them; or if there is first a short circumstance.

First, one receives the seven-day period. Regarding the three types of matters, each has its own priority and sequence. If this is so, why does the text say "the method for receiving [a period] exceeding seven days"?
Answer: This refers to cases where the preceding matter cannot be completed within seven days; it is called "exceeding" because the matter itself has passed its deadline.

Furthermore, it is called "exceeding" because the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been transgressed. It does not mean that once the seven days have already elapsed, it is termed "exceeding seven days. Question again: Why?

Regarding the statement that one does not exceed fifteen days: this refers to the two rules of the half-month and the month in contrast to the seven-day rule, as both possess two types of transgressions (transgression of the matter and transgression of the rule).
If one compares the fifteen-day and the month-day periods with one another, there is only a transgression of the matter, but no transgression of the rule;
therefore, it is not said that one exceeds fifteen days. [Question: When one simultaneously receives the month-day rule, what is the case?
Regarding the statement that it does not exceed half a month: the answer is that for seven days it is an individual matter, while the remainder is entirely a communal rule (*saṃghadharma*).

It simply says "exceeding seven days," which makes it clear that the other two [periods] both require a formal motion with announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Since they are equally communal rules, the specific division is not mentioned. Furthermore, it is asked:
if one now receives the practice for half a month or one month, and it happens to be a small month (*kṣudramāsa*), how should it be counted? The answer is: according to the Vinaya text.
Regarding the addition of the half-month period: if based on the fifteenth day, one does not distinguish between the long and short months, but rather counts the days for the return;

this is as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the thirty-nine nights. If one receives [the rains retreat] for one month, it must follow the long and short months and cannot be calculated by days;
as the Vinaya says, "staying for three months," etc., the short month is included therein.

Regarding the fourth point, the inclusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha*): examine this section of the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā*. It refutes the errors of the ancient masters who claimed there was such inclusion of characteristics, stating:
"If one has completed the seven-day period [of the *saptāha-karman*], only then may one hear the *karmavācanā* for receiving days; if one receives the seven-day [period]..."
If the [seven-day period] has not yet been exhausted or has not yet been used, and one undergoes another *karmavācanā* (formal act) to receive further days, then the previous seven-day rule ceases.
However, if the previous *karmavācanā* for receiving seven days has not yet been exhausted, one may not receive further seven days, because the force of the previous *karmavācanā* remains.
The seven-day rule does not arise [in this case]. For now, I shall describe how that master establishes his position; next, I will explain the text.

When the Vinaya states, "If one cannot return within seven days, one is permitted to receive [the *poṣadha*] for fifteen days," etc., this refers to the adherence of the ancient masters to the scriptural text.
It means that if the day for which the previous *karmavācanā* was received has already expired, only then may one receive the seven-day rule. This is because within a single body...
Because two dharmas are manifested simultaneously, it is said that one cannot return to receive the seven-day period on the same day.

Furthermore, if one has not yet completed the seven days, one must again employ the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). Yet, since the seven days have not yet expired, how can one already perform the *karmavācanā* for receiving [the precepts]?

This clearly shows they mutually encompass one another. The author of the *Chao* (Commentary) explains that this principle is not without merit; however, as they originally constitute a single circumstance, there should be no discrepancy in their duration.
The two methods may be judged as before. Now, regarding the distinct conditions of the preceding and succeeding [periods], each relies on the day of its respective undertaking.

If the preceding method has been applied to a matter, and that matter has not yet ceased, how could one lose the method? It is like being afflicted by an illness where one must take ghee; as long as both conditions have not yet subsided, the oral method remains in effect accordingly.
The Vinaya lists three grades of methods for undertaking [the precepts], which differ from one another; all are based on various conditions and cannot be undertaken at will. Therefore...

It does not wait for that very day; by precedent, it is collected within seven days. It is clearly understood that one uses the Dharma to collect conditions, and according to the rules of those conditions, they exist accordingly.
This above is how the *Jie-mo-shu* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) refutes [the opposing view].

If one must wait until the previous *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is exhausted before being permitted to receive the seven-day [passage], this is also the view of the ancient masters; it represents the intention of one school.

The author of the *Chao* (Commentary), fearing confusion regarding the simultaneous application of both the occasion (*pratyaya*) and the dharma, states below that thirty-seven days are not permitted to be used concurrently.

The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) clarifies that the dharma is not lost as long as the days are fulfilled, provided one reaches the boundary (*sīmā*) for lodging. It is said that many [erroneous views] exist in comparison.
Regarding the phrase "receiving [the precepts] for one month is insufficient," etc., this is the commentary-master’s (Chaozhu) interpretation of the ancient masters' meaning.
It means that when you say "one cannot have two dharmas in a single body," it refers to the fact that within a single object of focus (*ālambana*), two dharmas cannot rely upon one another;
thus, one must practice for a full thirty-seven days. Since these must necessarily be different objects of focus, why would they not be permissible?
Regarding the offense of a grave transgression committed by a *sajñapti* (one who claims seniority) when accepting offerings during his own summer retreat:

it is established that if someone brings an object to offer to the Saṃgha and asks for a monk with ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), and this bhikṣu actually has nine years of seniority but claims to have ten, he commits a grave offense upon receiving the object.
Regarding the statement that "one should not pay homage to those who earn a living by making Buddha images," as explained extensively in the subsequent text: this establishes the principle.

Within the section on the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*) among the *pratideśanīya* offenses, it clarifies the establishment of the interpretation; within the section on the precept against selling [sacred items], it clarifies one's own doubts.

According to this principle, if one acts on behalf of a great monastery or for various other monastic matters, it is clear that the aforementioned occasions—such as those concerning the Buddha-dharma and so forth—are all for one's own sake.

Now, by analogy, when acting for the sake of the monastery’s monks or its Buddhist affairs, receiving a *sūryodaya* (permission to leave) and going outside the boundary every day is logically beyond doubt.
Question: At present, if one acts for the sake of the monastery and submits a petition to the local authorities, may one receive a *sūryodaya* and go?
"No. Among the four regions [of his realm], the people of a bordering kingdom of King Prasenajit have rebelled. The king has personally led his army to go and suppress them.
All the offerings previously provided by the king for the Buddha and the Saṅgha—robes, food, drink, and all necessary requisites—"

There was a minister who lacked faith and devotion, and he seized [the property] and refused to give it back. The bhikṣus wished to go and inform the king, but they reflected that the road was so far that they would not be able to return on the same day.
The Buddha said, "In such a matter as this, I allow you to go for the duration of the day.

Furthermore, when King Prasenajit went forth on a military expedition, there was a minister who lacked faith and harbored a jealous and evil mind, wishing to dig a channel through the Jetavana. Compared to...
The Master [Kāśyapa] wished to go and inform the King, but he reflected that the road was too far for him to return on the same day. The Buddha permitted him to depart for seven days.
According to this text, we know that one may receive the *saptāha* (seven-day) leave when there is a formal petition regarding matters concerning the Saṃgha.

As for "personally undertaking the management of Buddha images and the like," this does not mean creating images for the monastic community, nor is it for the sake of laypeople; rather, it is solely for the purpose of seeking merit for oneself.
Therefore, it is so constructed. If it is not in accordance with the Dharma, one may not receive the *jñapti* (authorization) either, because it is done for the sake of profit.
Regarding those who, desiring to give a gift to the Saṃgha, do not understand the proper procedure and thus request a bhikṣu to instruct them—saying, "I wish to give property to the bhikṣus;
please come and receive the authorization (*jñapti*) to take it"—the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks: "For whom [is this]?"

"Receiving for seven nights" refers to the question posed by Upāli in that Vinaya. "For the sake of the seven assemblies, bestowing merit, receiving days, and so forth" means that the seven assemblies act as the hosts.
The two hundred and forty-two conditions listed in the subsequent text are all instances of this condition;
they are all conditions pertaining to the seven-day period. Regarding the phrase "sending a messenger or not sending a messenger," it refers to whether the person before one sends a messenger or not.
If a messenger is sent, both [the messenger and the recipient] may go. This is the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations). In the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), it is not so;

one must send a messenger to summon [the recipient] before one may receive the *divasa* (day of grace). If one hears of a death while on the way, it is established that the original purpose of receiving the *divasa* was to go there to attend to the sick.

Since one has heard that the person has died and the conditions for the journey have ceased, one returns. To say "one who reverses the precepts" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) refers to the former person who has reversed their precepts through wrong views.

Because one sees [the deceased] being reborn, there is no need to go. Another interpretation is that because one hears that they have died, one returns; this is called "returning from the realm" (*pratyāgamanam*).
As for "difficulties arising," it means that if one encounters the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) on the road, one must retreat and return.
Whether one's parents and ministers are believers or non-believers is not to be questioned;

this is because the kindness of parents is profound, having given birth to and raised this physical body, and because the power and influence of ministers can cause either harm or benefit. Even if they lack faith and devotion, one should go to transform them so that they may believe;
if they already possess faith and devotion, it is all the more necessary to go.
Regarding what was stated above concerning life-threatening dangers during the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), it is said that these robes, alms bowl, and medicinal herbs constitute a life threat;

by extension, this is also permitted in cases of threats to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, one may also point to the two aforementioned [categories], such as malevolent spirits, evil beasts, and the inability to obtain food or drink at will—anything that necessarily creates an obstacle to one's life.
The Buddha’s words permitting departure are recorded in the text; this is to be understood according to the transgression [rules].
Regarding the precept of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and so forth, it is established as follows: as in the *Triṃśaka*, if one loses the three robes, one may receive two;
if one loses two, one may receive two. To receive more than that is called "lack of contentment. As for the term "contentment," there are two interpretations:
first, contentment for householders; second, contentment for renunciants. Regarding contentment for householders, it is said:
Laypeople give out of a sense of loss; they lose three things and give back three. They act in accordance with the original intention of the layperson’s gift, which is itself contentment.
One must be cautious regarding householders; therefore, it is said that householders possess contentment. As for what is called "contentment in those who have left the home life," it is as follows:
Losing three [robes] means one receives two; losing two means one receives one. Now, this text is cited to clarify that even if one loses the three robes, one still obtains two;
how much more so when one possesses extra robes in abundance? Why then would one die rather than seek out the three robes again? Therefore, receiving them on a daily basis is not permitted.

Regarding the statement "abandoning what is prohibited and taking up what is permitted": possessing extra robes is permitted, whereas the three robes are prescribed as mandatory. Now, they are lacking...
Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), this refers to those who habitually keep many extra ones.

In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is a passage concerning those who quarrel within the same boundary (*sīmā*) because of oneself; this establishes that [the offense applies to] the monks of this very boundary.

Because of my presence here, they are fighting; furthermore, there may be strife among the monks of that realm, which must be pacified by me. The Buddha permitted me to go directly without having to observe the formal period of *posadha*.

Since the previous disputes among the monks were immeasurable and could not be restricted by a fixed time limit, one now observes the period according to the specific purpose (*artha*), which does not violate the fundamental principle.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "One observes the period according to the circumstances; this does not harm the great principle."

It is so. Below this is the section on the schism of the Saṃgha and its reconciliation. Within the Vinaya there are eight statements, divided into two sections. The full text of the Vinaya lists these two sections;
the first section contains four statements clarifying that the monks of this boundary are split because of me, and for the sake of reconciliation they depart.
This refers to moving from here to there; it is not necessary to return. Regarding the "four statements," they are: first, schism through seeing; second, schism through hearing.

Because there are distinct categories for those who have seen and heard, there are monks and nuns for each; thus, they form four [combinations]. In the subsequent section, regarding the schism of the Saṃgha in different realms, there are likewise four propositions:
first, the desire to cause a schism; second, having already caused a schism; each of these is applied to both monks and nuns, forming four propositions in total.

This means that regarding the first two phrases, one hears that the monastic community (*saṃgha*) of another realm intends to cause a schism; regarding the latter two phrases, one hears that it has already been split.

In such cases, one must go to mediate and bring about reconciliation. One may then proceed directly there; having reconciled the matter before midday, one may return on the afternoon of that same day.

If one returns by dawn after finishing at dusk, or if one stays and does not return, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is broken after one night has passed, because the original location was fundamentally free from any calamity.

This is different. In the preceding section, the summer retreat is completed by moving there. Therefore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if two difficulties coincide with the preceding section for harmonizing the Saṃgha, from the very day one departs, one must diligently seek a place to settle.
Even if one diligently seeks a place and has not yet found it, staying overnight wherever one passes does not constitute a breach of the summer retreat, because this is not due to mental negligence.
Conversely, if one breaches the retreat in this way, then once a dwelling place is secured, the rules of the summer retreat apply.

Once it has been accomplished, one must not abruptly return or cross the boundary. If there is a necessary reason, one must receive a formal authorization for the duration of days (*jīrì*), as explained in the *Chao* (in extenso).

This is the interpretation of Li. Regarding the statement that "receiving [the precepts] according to circumstances does not violate the great principle," Li means that one should observe the disputing parties beforehand.
What kind of person is this? If they are a disciple or follower of my school, then they will receive my [teachings on] arising and ceasing without requiring many days.
As for those who receive them by observing prior conditions, they do not harm the fundamental principles of the Great Community.

Regarding the phrase "except for other causes and conditions such as robes, bowls, medicine, and grass," this establishes that one must not rely upon the aforementioned five conditions as a pretext for food and drink.
If one seeks food and drink while specifically relying on those five conditions, the formal procedure for receiving the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna* (authorization for the day) is not valid.

However, if there is a separate cause and condition—such as a serious illness requiring medicine—one may indeed receive it. Even if one does so for that purpose, the *vinaya* rules regarding begging apply.

Regarding the formal determination of offenses and so forth: begging for wheat constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Therefore, according to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu begging for living seeds commits a *duṣkṛta*.

As for "indirectly soliciting through private entreaties," this refers to instructing a layperson to say, "When the silkworms are ready, please invite the poor monk [to come]," or begging for cotton and the like.
In such cases, both the agent and the object are improper; even begging for cotton constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If the request for permission is not granted, and if it concerns one's parents or others as described in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this means that according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*,
regardless of whether the parents have faith or lack faith, if one can personally go— or send a messenger—

to turn them around through one's power so that they gain faith and produce wholesome roots, one may depart. Regarding "others," the established interpretation states these are high ministers or teachers.
[This refers to] the *saṃgha* and so forth.

Second, regarding the separation and combination of matters: it is established that when there are many conditions or matters, and each receives the day [of the observance] individually, this is called "separation" (*li*).

When the various conditions combine to receive [the observance], and the conditions are recorded all at once as they enter into the formal procedure (*dharma*), this is called "combination" (*he*). As for the statement that one may receive the day through combination, it refers to the *karma* (formal ritual).

The *Moshu* (Commentary on the *Vinayamātṛkā*) states: "If there are two separate occasions for the *khaḍga-viśāla* [seven-day] period, each being seven days, they cannot be combined to form a single *pākṣika-saptāha* (fortnightly seven-day) observance.
Since this practice is performed by individuals separately, one may only receive the seven-day period before and after [the fortnight]. This principle applies to all such cases.
If both occasions are three days, whether they overlap or alternate, they may be treated like the seven-day period and used concurrently by both parties. Or [it says]: "Or [if it is] *khaḍga*..."

This is a case of separate conditions (*pṛthak-pratyaya*); the King represents the collective conditions (*sāmagrī-pratyaya*). Regarding the dharma of receiving [the precepts] according to one's status, they likewise cannot be combined for use.

As for the statement that "confessing many *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses follows the same rule," this clarifies that within the procedure for confessing *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, if one commits ten offenses and simultaneously performs the six-night penance (*ṣaḍ-rātra*) along with concealment (*pracchādana*), it is termed "combination" (*saṃyoga*).
Now, it is clarified that the same applies to the days of receiving [the precepts]: one may record multiple conditions at once.
It is also permissible to receive [the precepts] together and then go to that place to employ them.

Regarding the "three types of receiving [precepts] by anticipation" (*sāmantaka-samādāna*) and so forth, Sthiramati states that because one takes the present as the object-condition (*ālambana*), one may receive them by anticipation. As for the phrase "constructing conditions through mental fabrication": [it refers to the fact that] although the object does not yet exist, one generates a conceptual representation of it and thereby establishes the conditions for its reception.
"Establishing" (*li*) means that since the matter is not yet real, one fabricates it from thin air as a pretext. This may refer to saying "ten days," "fifteen days," or "one month," and so forth.
"Fabricating" (*kou*) means to construct or frame. Or, it refers to relying on past sayings to imitate what is not yet real. Regarding this, [the commentator] says:

suppose a layperson comes and says, "You should invite a bhikṣu to perform the path of practice and repentance," yet no specific time has been fixed; later, he holds [the invitation] in comparison... [and so on].

"Qiu, suddenly receiving the *jìrì* (seven-day pass) when it has not yet gone [into effect], is for the name to exceed the reality. As for the statement that 'the words are hollow because the matter is empty, and the limit is recklessly extended over days, falsely established,' Lì says:
'I have seen in the *Shísòng lǜ* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya) that the ritual practice of the masters was like this:

once the *ān-jū* (rainy-season retreat) was completed, they would immediately receive the seven-day pass and place it within [the retreat], intending to use it later when there was a need. Now it is not like this, because the matter has not yet arisen; thus the name [is applied prematurely].'"
The matter is unfounded. Since the duration of the event is not yet known, to immediately accept a seven-day period is merely to establish a limit.
To receive the days in advance and wait for the event to occur before putting them to use—is this not a frivolous arrangement? Furthermore, the interpretation relies upon and cites ancient words.
Even if one accepts [the period] for seven days, this matter is false; for one does not yet know the length of the event, and thus it is merely a provisional limit.
To immediately accept seven days, or even up to half a month and so forth, is to arbitrarily establish these numbers of days.

Regarding the statement that "there must be an original cause (*hetu-pratyaya*); what fault is there in using [the remaining days] in common?"—this means that, for example, if one has received the seven-day period and goes beyond the boundary for the sake of monastic affairs (*saṃghakārya*), and having used three days, returns;
since the original cause—the monastic affairs—still remains, if one goes out again later, it is not necessary to receive the days anew. What fault is there in simply using the previous days?

Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) that "one uses the remainder of the night after making a formal announcement (*jñapti*)," according to an examination of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, it says:
The bhikṣus received the seven-night permission to go to a village. Before the seven nights had expired and before their business was finished, they returned.
Not knowing what to do, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Use the remaining nights. I have established the rule of the seven nights;

if two nights have already passed and there are several nights remaining, one may receive [the permission] to go beyond the boundary" (as stated in the Vinaya text). [The commentary] says: it must be that the original conditions have not yet...

[The author] replies: "Now, returning [to the original point] is for the sake of the fundamental cause. As for the statement 'it does not mean a different matter' and so forth, this was said in response to the ancient masters.

The ancient masters—that is, those mentioned in the *Shoushu*—stated: 'Since there is already the receiving of the Dharma which belongs to oneself, it is simply a matter of acting according to the Dharma.'"
They may be used interchangeably without impairment. Now, [the author] refutes this master; thus it is said, "it is not as [you] claim," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "not the previously mentioned conditions of the Three Jewels or other miscellaneous conditions," [the commentator] Liang states:

the former refers to the matter of the Three Jewels belonging to the Zhang family, while the latter refers to the matter of the Three Jewels belonging to the Wang family. As for the phrase "and other miscellaneous conditions," Liang states: [this refers to] giving.
Repentance refers to the arising of good and the extinguishing of evil, and so forth.

If, according to principle, one family’s common conditions should be included, it is established that this clarifies the original reception of the *jñapti* (formal authorization) for the purpose of preaching the Dharma to the Zhang family, as well as for repenting of offenses, making offerings, and so on.
If one originally knew that there were such numerous matters, then the *jñapti* was received [for them].

Because it is permitted, one may obtain the *pārivāsika* (the status of being on probation) for common use. Regarding "furthermore, this is for generating wholesome states": the meaning of the preceding question is as follows.

If a monk in this realm receives a *pārivāsika* period and travels to another realm for matters concerning the Three Jewels and so forth, or for the sake of others who are ill, or to travel east or west in search of medicine and the like—will he be permitted?
It is said that "furthermore" (*mi*) because these are legitimate causes, and the sacred teachings permit them. Thus, it says "furthermore."
This is virtuous.

Regarding the Vinaya regulation concerning the two types of invitations: both the invitation according to the monastic order (*saṃgha-krama*) and the individual invitation (*pṛthag-nimantraṇa*) permit the receiving of the day. If one follows the Vinaya text, the individual invitation is further permitted;
however, if one follows various sūtras, the individual invitation is not allowed, because it deprives the monks of the ten directions of their rightful benefit and constitutes the offense of theft.
Regarding the statement that "one who is entitled to a meal by turn in the monastic assembly (*saṃgha-krama*) may not accept an individual invitation" and so forth:

this means that if it was originally an invitation for the monastic assembly, and one now accepts it after another has relinquished their claim, then one may go on the appointed day; this is because the donor made no specific distinction.

However, if it was originally an individual invitation, and one now accepts it after it has been relinquished to oneself, one may not go on the appointed day; this is because the donor lacked the [original] intention.

Regarding the ancient practice of opening three periods for the *varṣā* (summer retreat), it was established that one first receives the seven-day period, followed by the half-month, and finally the month;
beyond these, it was not permitted. However, nowadays this is not so; provided that the prior conditions are in accordance with the Dharma, all [periods] may be received.
Vinaya Master Li also refuted the attachments of the ancient masters, stating: "The ancients said..."
First one takes the seven-day [vow], then the fifteen-day, then the month-long, and so forth in this sequence.
If one has already undertaken the fifteen-day vow, one may not further undertake the seven-day vow; for the longer encompasses the shorter, as has already been explained above (etc.).
Regarding the statement that there are extensive citations and refutations as described in the *Śū* (Commentary): the *Jie-mo shu* (Karmavācanā Commentary) states: "Some say:

'The establishment of the practice of the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) takes the cultivation of the Path as its primary purpose. Since three options are permitted according to urgency to meet the necessities of the time, how could one receive it again? There is no such principle.'"
Therefore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, for the purpose of preventing schisms in the Saṃgha, it is permitted to accept a period of seven nights, but not two periods of seven nights;
even after accepting up to thirty-nine nights, one may break the *anvāya* (rainy-season retreat) and depart. This is a clear textual authority. Some say:

"The cultivation of the Path is a matter of urgency; why must one be restricted by staying? If a necessary cause arises, one may open the way as desired. Now, I shall explain this through both reasoning and the text.

[The text] establishes [the rule]. Regarding the first interpretation, which allows for the general case: as previously mentioned, when a donor invites one to accept the seven-day [period], there may subsequently be matters concerning the Triple Gem that must be managed.
How could it not be permitted? It is clear that it is indeed permissible. If this is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) allow only the first seven days?

Our current explanation is that the original prohibition was not intended to be strange or restrictive; perhaps it was because, regarding a single matter, one would not repeat the seven-day period twice. How could it have been intended to prohibit different matters?

Is it not permitted to receive [the precepts]? From the perspective of the Dharma, they appear to be weighty; yet from the perspective of the matter or the conditions, there is no difference between the former and the latter—how then can they be considered weighty?

It is not as weighty as receiving them for the sake of one's parents. Furthermore, when one has received the precepts for the sake of one's parents and travels to that place, even if the allotted time is exhausted, it is still permissible to remain there.
If a donor now receives the precepts and is forbidden from going immediately, how does this compare to the case where one stays and simply does not receive them?
It is permissible. If one says that it would be difficult to obtain the summer retreat (*varṣā*) because the period for staying has expired, then [the rule] is relaxed:

if parents command one to return, or if one must go to attend to the affairs of the Three Jewels (*triratna*) which have not yet been concluded, then even if one has already received the [initial] seven-day leave, what prevents one from going again? To go back and forth repeatedly would cause great harm. How could this not be permitted?
Furthermore, if there are official matters requiring two or three days, and one has already received a seven-day leave, how could one possibly not go? Thus it is direct.

Go! It is better to receive [the formal authorization] in addition. The original intent of the summer retreat (varṣā) is that one should not travel for no reason; however, when a major circumstance arises, one may go after receiving [authorization] according to the Dharma.
This is not a case of going solely for the sake of a donor; how could it be appropriate to prohibit it alone? In the Vinaya, the seven-day period is permitted in addition to the immediate [return];

this is a general text and does not apply exclusively to a single matter—is this not a case of redundancy? As for the enumeration of circumstances, it includes parents, elder brothers, and elder sisters, and so forth.
He set out for that place. His elder brother had already invited him previously, and his father subsequently summoned him again; how could he not have gone?
In the Vinaya, it simply states that the Buddha had not yet permitted such a thing, so he went on this business and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit it.

Just as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, where one may receive a day’s extension during the summer retreat based on eighteen grounds, or if there are others, nineteen are also permissible—just as entering a village at an improper time is permitted.

The Buddha established the rule for entrusting one to go [on a journey]. How could it be that what was permitted earlier is not allowed later? If this were so, how would one reconcile this with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations)? The answer is:
that text’s prohibition against the "two seven-nights" refers to the fact that one cannot simultaneously state both "two" and "seven nights.

Therefore, it does not preclude those who go at different times; they may still do so. As for the listing of more than twenty conditions in the Vinaya, it is clearly established that these are all instances of the seven-day [passage].
Regarding the conditions: because the matter had not yet become manifest, the Buddha had not yet permitted departure; it was not said that one may not go again.

Regarding the four cases where parents have faith and devotion, the established view is as follows: first, the father has faith but the mother does not; second, the mother has faith but the father does not;
third, both parents have faith; fourth, neither parent has faith. In all four permutations, one may receive the permission for the day.
[The Buddha said: "Go. However, according to the Vinaya texts, it is not so. At that time, there was a faithful minister who invited a bhikṣu, saying, 'Venerable Sir, please come;
I wish to see you. The bhikṣu thought to himself, 'The place is far away and I will not be able to return on the same day.
The Buddha has not yet permitted me to go for such a matter. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: 'From this day forward, I permit such a person to receive the seven-day [pass].'"
1. He departs; whether it be beneficial or not, he returns within seven days. 2. There is another case involving a minister who lacks faith and devotion;
it is the same. 3. There is another case involving parents who lack faith; it is the same. 4. There is another case involving parents who have faith and devotion and make a request; it is the same.
Regarding the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that whether there is an invitation or not, one may even accept a seven-day leave.
This indicates that the *Pañcavargika* differs from the *Caturvargika*; according to the *Caturvargika*, one may only go if there is an invitation.
Regarding the listing of "more than seven nights" in the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya), Master Li states that within the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Buddha:
"For whom is the seven-night [permission] received? The Buddha replied: "It is received for the sake of bestowing merit upon the seven classes of followers.
He then listed twenty-two conditions for *upāsakas*, twenty-two conditions for *upāsikās*, and likewise twenty [conditions] for *śrāmaṇeras*.
There are two conditions. For a śrāmaṇerī, twenty-two conditions are also enumerated; for a śikṣamāṇā, twenty-two conditions are enumerated;
for one undergoing penance (śikṣādattaka), twenty-three conditions are enumerated; for a female undergoing penance (śikṣādattakā bhikṣuṇī), twenty-three conditions are enumerated;
for a bhikṣu, twenty-three conditions are enumerated; and for a bhikṣuṇī, twenty-three conditions are enumerated. Altogether, there are two hundred and forty-two conditions.
These are all matters concerning the seven-night period. If they are in accordance with the Dharma, it is permitted for them to depart.

If, according to the *Saṃghabhedavastu*, it appears that a matter may not be repeated if it is similar to one already settled, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "At that time, a dispute arose among the monks of a different boundary.

Knowing that it could not be extinguished there, they sent a messenger to the monks residing nearby, requesting them to come and adjudicate this matter. They should immediately go and adjudicate it. If the Saṃgha has already established [a settlement]..."
Residing [in the rainy season retreat], one may receive permission to depart for seven nights; if those seven nights are exhausted, one may receive permission to depart for thirty-nine nights;
if those thirty-nine nights are exhausted, one should break the retreat and assemble at one place to receive [the formal conclusion].

This matter is settled according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching as a resolution. The intent of the *Chao* (Commentary) states: "This is because the matter of resolving through harmony is difficult."
[One] knows [this]. Therefore, the breaking of the summer retreat (varṣā) is permitted; this does not mean that receiving [the precepts] again is not allowed.

Examining the intent of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it appears that regarding a single matter, receiving [the precepts] again is not permitted. The text, moreover, is not explicit. If, however, it concerns different matters, one certainly knows that receiving them again is possible.

The principle is like that of ghee and oil: because the illnesses are different, although both are for seven days, one may add the medicinal preparation and take them together. However, the ancients...
The Master’s statement that "one summer [of residence] permits the reception of the three dharmas" is based precisely upon this text from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

The Guest says: "The ancient masters have cited the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in vain as proof; this is because the schools differ and their tenets diverge, so there is no need to attempt a reconciliation.

For instance, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* speaks of the completion of the task, while the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* speaks of thirty-nine nights; these are entirely inconsistent with this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Why must one cite those [texts] to harmonize them?"

The *Saṃgha-vinaya* permits receiving [the *uposatha*] a second time; therefore, I shall now provide the correct explanation. If there is a cause that arises, what fault is there in receiving it again?

Now, regarding the passage on "not being invited" which is more lenient than the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, one may go for the sake of the day whether one sends a messenger or does not send a messenger, whereas in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one must send a messenger to be permitted.
Thus it is said: "The wording is not explicit, but the principle must be clearly understood."

This refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which, regarding a single matter similar [to the case at hand], does not permit receiving [the precepts] repeatedly; thus, it is stricter than the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.
Furthermore, there is a textual passage concerning "not requesting" (*apraśna*), which is more lenient than the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. Now, I shall harmonize these two texts:
although the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not permit receiving them repeatedly, its wording is not explicit, and moreover, the aforementioned "not requesting" passage is lenient. Since these two...
The textual passages vary between being broad and restrictive. Now, it is clearly explained that receiving [the precepts] again is without fault.
Regarding the statement in the *Vyākhyā* on the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra* (Liaolun) that "one may receive [them]," this means:

whereas previous scholars did not permit receiving the seven-day [precepts] a second time—stating that one first takes the seven days, then the half-month, and then the month—the present view is not so; according to the *Vyākhyā* on the *Vinayaviniścaya-śāstra*.

Among these, there are nine phrases, all of which concern receiving [the precepts] repeatedly. Examining the *Shu* (Commentary), it says: The verse of the treatise states, "If there is an obstacle for seven days, one may travel at will.
The commentary on the three types of nine categories explains: For example, during the period of *an-guo* (rainy-season retreat), one may go outside the boundary due to three reasons:
first, being invited by someone for a specific cause; second, going outside the boundary because an emergency has arisen; and third, [the third reason].
There are circumstances under which one may leave the boundary at will. Each of these three [cases] has three sub-types, thus forming nine categories.

Regarding these nine categories, each triad is divided into three. As for the first triad: (1) having previously established a seven-day limit for a specific matter, one subsequently establishes another seven-day limit;
(2) having previously established a seven-day limit for a specific matter, one subsequently establishes a limit due to an emergency; (3) having previously established a specific matter...
The seven-day condition (*saptāha-kaṭhina*). Subsequently, it becomes the condition of *yathāsammuti* (as-agreed). Regarding the second set of three cases:

first, there is a matter where it initially becomes a condition of difficulty (*sa-vighna*) and subsequently becomes a condition of difficulty; second, there is a matter where it initially becomes a condition of difficulty and subsequently becomes a seven-day condition;
third, there is a matter where it initially becomes a condition of difficulty and subsequently becomes a *yathāsammuti* condition. Regarding the third set of three cases: first, there is a matter...

First, there is the case where the *yathāsamaya* (at-will) condition is established first, and subsequently the *saptāha* (seven-day) condition is established. Second, there is the case where the *yathāsamaya* condition is established first, and subsequently the *saptāha* condition is established.
Third, there is the case where the *yathāsamaya* condition is established first, and subsequently the *sa-vipatti* (with difficulty) condition is established.

These are the enumerated categories; now, they shall be explained one by one according to the Commentary (*ṭīkā*). Regarding the first category—where the *saptāha* condition is established first and the *saptāha* condition is established later:

Having initially received a seven-day leave to depart the boundary for the sake of one's parents, relatives, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), fellow students, virtuous friends, or others who are ill, as well as for receiving offerings or reconciling with the Saṃgha, one must return to the original boundary on the seventh day.

If on the eighth day there should arise further circumstances such as those mentioned above, one may again receive a seven-day leave to go. If one has already previously requested a seven-day leave to depart the boundary...

If one uses three days and the prior conditions have ceased, one should return to the original location. If there are other conditions, one may remain outside the boundary for the remaining three nights;
these latter three nights are all valid because one has already stayed overnight for seven days in total.

This means that although one initially requested seven days to stay outside the boundary, once the matter for those three days is concluded, if further causes and conditions arise, one is permitted to use the remainder.

Three nights may be spent [outside the boundary], but one must not separately receive another seven-day period. Once the latter three nights are exhausted, one must return to stay within the original boundary before one may again request a seven-day period;
this is because the seven-day period has a fixed duration. Second, regarding the case where there was a prior seven-day period followed by an obstacle:

if there was previously a cause or condition for receiving a seven-day period to go outside the boundary, once the business is concluded, one should return to the original location. As for that original location...
This refers to one who, when the eight calamities such as water or fire arise, nevertheless goes to dwell elsewhere. Third, regarding "first [leaving] seven days before, then returning at will":
having first received the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary, one should return to the place of retreat (*varṣā*) once the business is finished.

This is because that place of retreat lacks good spiritual friends, or is noisy and distracting, thereby hindering the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), or lacks good medicine and food, causing the four great elements to become weak.
This is a violation. For this reason, one should instead go to dwell in the presence of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and others; this is called "acting according to one's inclination.

Although there is such a reason that permits departing at will, staying for even a single night constitutes a breach of the *anagga* (rainy-season retreat). This is because, despite the existence of such a reason, [the rule] remains in effect.

Therefore, one incurs no offense. If there is no such cause, to leave the retreat at will constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Although the retreat has been broken, the summer rains-retreat is not lost;
the duration of the summer is calculated by days and months, regardless of whether one was in retreat or not. Fourth, there were previously established grounds for hardship.
Regarding the subsequent case where a danger arises: first, one goes outside the boundary due to a threat from bandits, but before a night has passed, the bandits depart on that very day.
The bhikṣu should immediately return; however, he then hears that a fire danger has broken out and consequently goes to stay in another location. This is the case.

The reason one must discuss this in terms of not having spent the night is that if the *anvārohaṇa* (the period following the breaking of the rains retreat) has already passed, there is no need for further discussion;
the same applies to all such persons who depart later. Fifth, regarding those who first encountered difficulties and subsequently [received] the seven-day [permission]:

they previously left the boundary due to an emergency, and once the difficulty subsided, they returned to their original location. Subsequently, due to the circumstances of an invitation from a *dānapati*, they were invited to go for seven days.

Furthermore, these obstacles pertain specifically to that very day; upon hearing of the stillness, one should return immediately, and it goes without saying that this should not be delayed until the following night.

Sixth, regarding those who first encounter an obstacle and subsequently perform the *svacchanda* (as they please): this refers to first departing the boundary for the sake of an urgent matter, and later proceeding to the dwelling of a virtuous friend because of the absence of such a person.
Seventh, regarding those who first perform the *svacchanda* and subsequently perform the *svacchanda*: this refers to first [departing] due to the absence of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

[And so forth. One may leave the boundary at will without having spent the night outside. Upon hearing that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is at one's original location, one should immediately return to that original location.
Furthermore, if there are causes and conditions for noise and disturbance, one may instead go to stay elsewhere; this is the case. Eighth, "first [the *pravāraṇā*] at will, then seven days":
first, due to the cause and condition of not having a good spiritual friend, one leaves the boundary; later, one hears that a spiritual friend has come to one's original location.

He immediately returned to his original location. This refers to the case where there is still an invitation from a donor (*dānapati*); he accepts it and leaves the boundary for seven days. Ninth: "First the *svacchanda* (as one pleases), then an obstacle arises.
First, due to the lack of favorable conditions for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he leaves the boundary.
Later, hearing that a spiritual friend has come to the place of retreat, he returns to his original retreat site. Suddenly, an obstacle arises at that place, and he [immediately] goes...
This refers to dwelling in other places. Now, this *Chao* (Excerpts) cites only the meaning of the first sentence to take up the sense of receiving [the precepts] repeatedly.
Regarding the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, the record states: he was a native of Ujjayinī who came to this region during the Chen and Liang dynasties;

he translated thirty-four scriptures and treatises, totaling one hundred and forty-one fascicles. However, Paramārtha would sometimes spread out his sitting mat and sit in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka*).
He walked across the water; if he wished to cross to the shore by boat, he would sometimes use lotus leaves as a raft to ferry himself across.

Such instances of his supernatural wonders were exceedingly numerous. Bin said: "This man’s broad knowledge of past and present was peerless. He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and he understood the Vinaya of the eighteen schools.
Among the Tripiṭaka masters of the Tang, he alone was able to subdue this man. This account originated from [him].

From the Western Regions, he traveled afar to propagate the teachings. Upon first arriving at the capital of Yangdu, he encountered the rebellion of Hou Jing; the Liang ruler was besieged and died of starvation.
He then proceeded to the Chen dynasty, where the Chen ruler held him in deep respect and requested that he undertake translations. He began by translating the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

It was titled the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-śāstra*. At that time, there were two gatekeeper teachers, Wujing and Baijing, who submitted a memorial stating that the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-śāstra* he had translated was not well-known in the kingdom.
The Chen ruler consequently expelled him, and he returned to the Western Regions. Upon reaching Guangzhou, he passed away.
While traveling westward on a merchant vessel, he encountered a rising storm that blew the ship back to Guangzhou.

The local governor, Ouyang Yi, invited him to his residence to provide offerings and wished for him to engage in translation work. He first requested a demonstration of supernatural powers, saying, "I have heard that Kumārajīva once swallowed a needle;
I hope you, Master, will show us some minor feat of spiritual art. He replied, "It is very easy. A needle is small and easy to swallow. Thereupon, he [sought]—
He unearthed a cartload of them with his hoe and swallowed them whole. In a short while, they had accumulated into a mound within the western garden of the residence.
Jingyi was struck with wonder and bowed his head, praising him as excellent. The Tripiṭaka Master replied, "This minor feat is not difficult enough to be considered remarkable.

The Great Men of the West feel ashamed to perform such things. He then requested that the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (She da cheng lun) and the *Śāstra on the Tenets of the Schools* (Bu zhi lun) be translated.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and other treatises each have their respective commentaries (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s transformation pervades the three thousand [worlds]," this means that the Buddha’s transformative activity encompasses the three thousandfold world system.

The treatise states: "In one set of four continents, there is one Mount Sumeru, one set of four great oceans, one Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*) surrounding them, and one sun and one moon; this is called one world. Counting by this standard, until—

One thousand [worlds] constitute a small chiliocosm. Counting from this number to one thousand again constitutes a medium chiliocosm. Counting from this number to one thousand once more constitutes a great trichiliocosm.
It is within such a great trichiliocosm that a single Buddha appears in the world and reigns as the sovereign of the Path.
Regarding the practice of observing the seven-day *uposatha* on a single day at the end of summer: this is done provisionally because of the specific circumstance of the seven-day period.
If there is a circumstance of one month or half a month, one must likewise observe it according to that circumstance. Thus, Daolü said:

"Even if the three types of days do not exist, as long as the three types of circumstances exist, one must observe the precepts in accordance with those circumstances. The "three types" refers to the seven-day period.
"Half-month" means one month. During the summer retreat, there are only one or two remaining days when suddenly a circumstance arises;
whether it be for seven days, half a month, or one month, one receives the [permission] according to these three conditions.

If the road is near and one can return due to that circumstance—even if one stays overnight—the established rule states that although one has departed from this place of retreat by three or five *li*, one may return to the boundary on the same day, provided one returns before the morning meal (*prātar-bhakta*). This is because of the donor.

Regarding the circumstances of being summoned by a superior, it is also permitted to accept [an invitation] for seven days; it is not necessarily required that the distance be great. This is called "not having arrived in time.
One may only depart after accepting the days [of leave] once one has returned on the very same day.
Regarding the phrase "provided that the conditions for these three dharmas arise," the ancient masters spoke erroneously, saying:

"The seven-day, half-month, and one-month periods—these three dharmas of receiving [food] are permitted for nuns to use, provided there is a valid reason; as long as it accords with these three dharmas, they may all be received.

They then cite an objection, saying: "As for the monastic community, all 'one hundred and one' *karmavācanās* are permitted in the presence of the *saṃgha*, yet for nuns there are no such texts. Now...
Since monks and nuns share [the same rules] in common, how could it be that the *jñapti-karman* for receiving [the robe] alone is suddenly forbidden?

We do not agree with this, as we have not seen a clear ruling to that effect in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Gao says: "By calculation of principle, the 'one hundred and one *karman*s' used by monks should all be applicable to the practice of nuns."

Why should the *Caturvargika-vinaya* alone be accepted as the sole authority while other sources are abruptly disallowed? Reason dictates that it should apply universally, including for nuns; there is no need to cite the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Śrī-vinaya) as proof.

The *Śrī-vinaya* merely records the *karmavācanā* for the completion of the ritual. Even according to my own *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Great Saṃgha may not rely upon it [for certain matters]; why then restrict it to nuns alone?

Therefore, the position established here is that nuns may employ the fortnightly and monthly procedures of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. This is logically sound and without fault. As for the claim that there is no textual basis in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: [this is incorrect].

Regarding the clear determination in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: it means that within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (the Four-Part Vinaya), there is no textual passage clarifying whether nuns may receive the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for extending the period [of the rains retreat] or not.
This serves as clear evidence that, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, nuns do not have the procedure for receiving the formal act for extending the period.
"Also rescuing other special circumstances" means that one may simply accept the seven-day period to also rescue prior matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
illness and so forth are such special circumstances.

Regarding "the eight matters being concluded," in the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā*, some say: if one does not return because the matter has been concluded, it does not constitute a violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). As...
The seven-day medicine and its analogues follow the same principles as the cases regarding the curing of insanity and the non-loss [of the summer retreat]. Thus, the *Lishi* commentary states:

"If one has accepted [the invitation] and goes out of the boundary, one must return once the business is concluded. If one does not return, one incurs a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*), yet the summer retreat is not immediately broken because the formal rule still applies—just as in the case of having granted consent (*chanda*) and then not returning after the business is finished.
In such cases, one must immediately employ the means to return, unless there are various obstacles."

[The opponent] says there is no fault in [the monk] coming. The author of the *Chao* (Commentary) refutes this, saying: "For example, in the *kāyastha-karman* (formal act) for those who wish [to leave], the matter is not recorded; whereas in the present *divasagrahaṇa-dharma* (method of receiving the day), the matter is recorded.
If the matter is added [later], the formal act is lost. This is also like the method for medicine: once the illness has ceased, it is of no further use.

Furthermore, this is not the same as the case of a madman, where one must request [permission]; therefore, why do you cite this recklessly? Lì’s explanation states: "My intention is that if one is deranged and does not come, it is not called 'separation' (*bīe*)."

After the assembly has finished reciting the *chanda* (consent), if a matter is concluded and [a monk] does not come, nor does he formally leave the assembly, it is difficult to argue that he must beg for the lifting of his status as one who is "insane" (*unmatta*).
Since he has not yet been lifted from that status, the legal efficacy (*dharma*) remains with him; therefore, this does not constitute leaving the assembly.

As for the recitation of *chanda*, it originally does not involve recording the specific circumstances of the consent within the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). Thus, when the circumstances have ceased, the legal efficacy remains. However, in the case of receiving the [extension of the] *poṣadha* day, one records the circumstances and enters them into the ritual procedure. Therefore...

"When conditions cease, the dharma perishes. This means that when the conditions set forth in the formal proclamation have ceased, there is no longer anything to bestow. This refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for receiving [the day].
Since the prior conditions such as the invitation and summons have now ceased, the ritual of the *karman* is likewise abolished; hence it is said that "there is nothing to bestow."

Regarding the statement that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* explicitly prohibits going [to perform the *pravāraṇā*], Śaṅguo says: "The previously cited passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra* states that whether one sends a messenger or does not send a messenger, both are permitted to receive [the invitation].

However, if one hears of death or the boundary being returned while en route, one should not go. As for the claim that the intent of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the same, the previously cited passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika* states:
"One must not take a detour when harmonizing with the Saṃgha; having reached there before midday, one should complete the harmonization by midday."

Thereafter, he immediately returned; had he remained, he would have lost his summer retreat—this is the point. The preceding many sections, though differing, all together conclude the explanation of the second section:
the gate of whether to proceed or not based on specific conditions.
From this point onward, the third addition of the ritual (*dharma*) is correctly explained. This *dharma* consists of three distinct types; the present section concerns the first.

Regarding the five kinds of persons mentioned in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, such as those who dwell alone and so forth: (1) those who dwell alone, (2) those in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), (3) those on a long journey, (4) those with chronic illness, and (5) those during times of famine.
For these five types of persons, when they dwell alone or in a secluded place, the Noble One has permitted them to receive [the food].
Day. If there are those who do not wait, the ritual procedure will not be accomplished; it violates the teachings and incurs guilt.
If there are śrāmaṇeras and the like, because they do not share the same status as the Dharma, one may only inform them verbally.

Regarding the tradition that this follows the formal announcement (*jñapti*) of the *Karmavācanā*: it is said that while none of the various schools possess a formal text for receiving the seven-day period, such a practice does exist.
Now, one proceeds by relying on the formal announcement within the *karmavācanā* for receiving days according to the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*).

Therefore, the ten gates in the preceding introduction state: "Or, based on principle, one accomplishes the matter"—this refers precisely to this meaning. Although there is no textual authority in the various schools, nevertheless...
It is logically appropriate that there should be [a distinction].

If there were no *dharmas* (procedural rules) to express the difference from the seven-day medicine, this would clarify that if the prior conditions (*pūrvapratyaya*) had ceased, the *karma* (formal ritual) would then be expressed as having lapsed;

however, if those conditions still persist, the *dharma* has not yet been lost. It is simply that once the period for receiving [the medicine] has expired, one must calculate the number of days based on the actual substance used.
Medicine is not like this. According to the Vinaya rules, after seven days have passed, regardless of whether it has been consumed or not, its efficacy as a medicinal treatment is lost.

This is because the illness undergoes a transformation every seven days. As for the fact that one does not perform the ritual of returning (*pratyāśraya*) for the days already received when the medicine has not yet been used, it is because the underlying conditions (*pratyaya*) still persist.

From the phrase "If that were so" (*yadi cet*) onwards is a further objection. The objection states: "If the medicine is lost when the illness transforms, then the medicine should [remain effective] while the illness persists."

As for the statement, "If one takes it for seven days and the solid disease is eliminated," this clarifies that when a disease reaches the seventh day, it undergoes a transformation; therefore, there is no need to continue taking it.
Even if the disease does not transform by the seventh day, further administration will provide no benefit, as the potency of the medicine is limited to seven days.
Because it is based on the day, the established rule limits it to seven days.

As for the claim that this differs from the "seven nights" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, although that [text] specifies seven nights, it is no different from the seven days of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
It must also be completed before the dawn of the seventh night and within the boundary; thus, one knows it is still only six nights. This is the established interpretation. Master Bin says:
"In that Vinaya, 'seven nights' refers to eight days by our reckoning. Regarding the phrase "the matter is concluded" (*kṛta-kṛtya*) in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

this means that one does not wait for a full month or half-month, but rather returns on the day the matter is finished according to the length of the preceding circumstances; this is called "the matter being concluded."

This is a *karmavācanā*. According to that Vinaya and other texts, chapter twenty-seven states: "Whether for one month or two months, from the formal announcement (*jñapti*) up to the occasion of the *pravāraṇā*, one should return [to the assembly] for the *pravāraṇā*.
To fail to return constitutes a transgression (*vaidhika*). However, if there are obstacles, there is no offense regarding the *pravāraṇā*.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) prescribes three methods for receiving the extension of time (*divasagrahaṇa*); the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü) is the same. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) prescribes two methods, namely the seven... [text ends].
The "three nights" refers to thirty-nine nights. The first section concludes the *pratimukha-dharma* (rules for individual confession).
The third section concerns the conditions for communal *dharma* (*saṃgha-dharma*), which, as before, are generally applicable. To clarify:

in the preceding *pratimukha* section, there are instances where multiple conditions are cited at once to receive [an ordination or precept], and these may be applied according to their specific use. Now, the same applies to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); it is said that they are generally applicable.

This refers to receiving [the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna*] based on multiple conditions. Lì (Lì Daoyuan) says: "However, monks from a different boundary (*sīmā*) may suffice for the monks of this boundary regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of receiving the day;

it does not differ from the allocation [of the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna*]. The principle is restricted to the monks within the same boundary. It is not the same as the 'preservation of the single person' (*cún dānrén*). Lì states:

'The ancient masters held that during one summer retreat, one could receive three types of legal acts (*dharma*) for the purpose of receiving the day, which was termed the 'preservation of the single. This has already been analyzed above. He then cites the seven-day [period]."
This causes one to assume that the masters of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* school maintain that only three types of periods are permitted, and that anything other than these is invalid.
These are: first, seven days; second, half a month; and third, one month. One may not receive them repeatedly.

If someone has previously completed the seven-day period, but subsequently a need for another seven-day period arises, they should instead perform the half-month rite. Furthermore, if one has suddenly already used half [of a period]...

The procedure for the full month is concluded. If further causes arise during the remaining half-month or the seven-day period, one then performs the procedure for a full month; thus it is said that "one draws it out to lengthen it.
This does not mean that one draws out the causes to make them long, but rather that one personally draws out the procedure itself to lengthen it.

Regarding the statement that "there are now four different versions of the *Jiāfǎ* (Addition of Precepts), with the ritual texts (*jīemówén*) of two schools being rarely seen," the first is the version of the *Jīemóběn* (Root Text of Rituals) produced by Tandi during the Cao Wei period;
the second is that produced by the Vinaya Master Jueming during the Yao Qin period.
The original texts of these two schools are currently missing from both traditions and are no longer seen in practice; hence it is said they are "rarely seen.

This means that the author of the *Chao* (the *Shan-chien-p'i-p'o-sha-ch'ao*) once saw a single copy of the text transmitted by them, but having hoped for more and still not finding it, he says they are rarely seen.
The third was produced by Master Kuang-t'ung of the Northern Qi dynasty; the fourth was produced by Master Yuan of the Northern Wei. Among these four masters, [Master] Li states:
The third master, Guangshi, added a request for permission (*yācanā-vākya*), arguing that since receiving the day [of ordination] is a common practice, a request must be made;
for among all *karmavācanās*, those that accord with common sentiment invariably include a request. However, this is not the case here.

Since the Vinaya does not establish it, one must not arbitrarily add to it. Therefore, the text states: "One should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) according to the method of making an announcement," meaning:

Regarding such a person, there is extensive analysis and discrimination concerning this matter in the *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā). It states: "For the first type of person, one adds the request for the *karmavācanā*, but does not record [the details] in the formal announcement (*nivedana*), fearing that it would constitute an augmentation of the ritual procedure (*dharmopacaya*).
This refers to the 'ancient *karmavācanā*,' which is the first master [of the three types].

As for the second type, although they are appointed and the words of the request are recited, according to the procedure for requesting *parivāsa* (probation), the details of the matter are recorded twice; once at the time of the assembly and again before the formal motion (*jñapti*) is made. The words of the request are then added. *Ren* (Endure/Consent) [is the concluding term].
After having heard [the recitation], one performs the ritual in brief; the *karmavācanā* is likewise. This compilation by Master Guang was widely practiced during the Wei dynasty.

The third master, however, follows only the procedure for requesting the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*); the formal announcement (*naya*) and the recitation of the matter are both complete, because the Vinaya text states that it must not be performed contrary to the method of formal announcement (*jñapti-dharma*).
If one now increases or decreases [the elements], it will not be valid. Generally, regarding these three compilations, the wording is restricted while the meaning remains consistent.

[This is] a general principle. Some have definitively judged that [the validity of the *varṣā*] depends on whether one has received [the invitation]; this is the judgment of Master Lì. The author of the *Chao* now explains that this is not so, for it merely follows the teachings.
Whether there is an increase in the request (*yācanā*) or a decrease in the request, each has its own basis; the general framework and regulations of the *karmavācanā* remain intact.

If one does not lose [the status] by relying on what was received, then the various masters of recent times who do not add the words of the request—reading directly according to the *Vinaya* as the rule established by the *Vinaya*—are correct. To add the request is...

[The Master] increased [the text], yet did not dare to use it arbitrarily. Question: Regarding the ritual for receiving the *jīva* (permission to leave the retreat), its purpose is to prevent the violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Since the summer retreat is a private obligation, if one does not request [permission], how could one be allowed to grant it recklessly? Therefore, the request is indeed necessary. Answer: One must rely on the teachings as the basis for what ordinary minds believe.

Since the Vinaya lacks a specific textual passage [for this], one cannot arbitrarily append it. This is not like the case of the staff-bag (*daṇḍakośa*), where the act of requesting was added as part of the ritual; for in that [case], the request was already contained within the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Because [the text] was requested [for translation], errors were introduced during the process of transcribing and transmitting it; this is not an instance of [the original] being inconsistent. I privately observe that while the *Vinaya* contains no text regarding requesting [permission for] a staff-bag (*daṇḍakośa*), this is an omission by the translators.
Across all sections of the various Vinayas, the branch-bag (*śākhā-kośa*) must always be requested; therefore, it was not added arbitrarily.

This is not the case for the "receiving of days" (*āpatti-dina-grahaṇa*), as none of the three Vinayas contain a text mandating that it be requested. The fourth master follows the textual authority of the Vinaya and does not add [anything].
Regarding the request for permission: the same applies to the preceptor; one must not add a formal request.

As for the statement that "the mind may follow its framework," this means that one should not insist on using a formal request. Rather, the presiding elder (upādhyāya) need only inform the Sangha, saying:
"At this time of intense heat, it is evident that the assembly is utterly exhausted. Now, as that bhikṣu has a certain matter [to attend to]..."
When the Saṃgha receives the day [for the observance], they may unify their minds and together uphold the holy teachings; thus it is said, "according to its framework.

As for the statement that those who recite and receive [the precepts] in accordance with the instructions, this means relying on the instructions of the Vinaya text, not requesting the formal motion internally, but directly reciting the *karmavācanā* according to the teaching.
Regarding the fact that there is no error in the essential substance of the *karmavācanā*, it is clearly established as follows:

although the initial request within the *vinaya* merely sets forth the circumstances of the matter, there is no error in the second and third phrases because they do not constitute the formal core (*mūla*) of the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding the fourth person who cites the text according to the Vinaya, this refers to the *yuan-shi* (preceptor of the vow) [as in the current *Jiaochao*, which agrees with this].
As for the prohibition against reciting "the fifteenth day" twice: Sheng says that one must not recite it twice because two fifteenth days constitute one month;
one must simply say, "I now receive one month. Another interpretation holds that one must not recite it twice because two fifteenth days constitute four [units of time].
This is the fifteenth [day]. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of the addition of the ritual formula (*adhikāra*).
What follows below correctly clarifies the characteristics of the formal discernment (*viniścaya*).

Regarding "receiving [the precepts] through a common object" (*samāna-ālambana*), this refers to many people who, for the sake of a single matter, may have the ritual formula added to them simultaneously by three persons; however, if the objects differ, they cannot undergo the *karmavācanā* (formal act) at the same time.
Regarding the *sīmā* (boundary) for the rains retreat (*varṣā*) and other minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*):
