it is established that a minor boundary is still a boundary for gathering the Saṃgha, such as the circular enclosure for separate residence (*pṛthagvāsa*).

However, because one’s original intention was based on the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and not this minor boundary, one may not receive the formal day-count (*divasagrahaṇa*) therein. If two boundaries are subsequently demarcated, they are the great boundary and the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field).

Even if one enters the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) without breaking the summer retreat (*varṣa*), yet becomes separated from one’s robes (*cīvara-vipravāsa*), it is established that the summer retreat is not broken because one previously resolved in one's mind to sit upon this ground;

furthermore, since the boundary (*sīmā*) was formally demarcated later, it is said that one is "separated from one's robes" because [the separation] occurs within the limits of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

When one designates the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) and then establishes a *cīvara-saṃvartana-sīmā* (robe-holding boundary), upon entering the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept arena), it is no longer a robe-holding boundary;

because they are naturally separated by the intervening space, they become distinct boundaries. If one does not establish a robe-holding boundary, although there is a precept arena, one protects the robe by relying on the *ārāma* (monastery grounds);
thus, even when entering the precept arena, the robe is not lost, because the *ārāma* is able to hold the robe, whereas the great boundary cannot.

Furthermore, if the original great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) was smaller than the monastery (*ārāma*), it is established that this monastery’s great boundary is small. Originally, the intention required reliance upon the monastery, not the boundary.
Now, performing the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) within the boundary does not constitute a valid reception of the day, because it is not the original [intention].

Because the *sīmā* (boundary) is the essential locus. If one wishes to observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one may designate the characteristics of the boundary and dwell in retreat based upon that boundary;

subsequently, one may receive the formal authorization for the days. In this way, the retreat is successfully established, because the boundary is strong while the monastery (*ārāma*) is weak; thus, one must necessarily rely upon the boundary.

Regarding the preceding phrase, the author of the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) provides the definitive interpretation. Lì asks: "If there are boundaries within a monastery, upon which location should one base the formal establishment [of the retreat]? Answer: There are two interpretations.
First, regarding the reliance on a village or a monastery (*ārāma*), the text for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) states: "In dependence upon such-and-such a village or such-and-such a monastery.

Furthermore, it is explained that one must rely upon a defined boundary (*sīmā*). We know that one relies upon a boundary because it serves to protect the limits of the summer retreat; as the text says: "If even one foot enters the boundary..."
This refers to the "Receiving the Sunrise" (Pravāraṇā), the "Departing from the Realm" (Sīmā-vimokṣaṇa), and so forth.

The preceding eleven chapters have now been concluded. **Chapter Twelve: The Essential Points of the Pravāraṇā (with the Appendix on the Kāṭhina-cīvara).** First, to clarify the purpose of this chapter:
In the preceding chapter, it was explained that during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one dwells together for ninety days; fearing that transgressions may have occurred, [the following is set forth].
Because one knows through self-inspection, it is necessary to personally declare the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) so that the Sangha may freely investigate and raise charges.

Therefore, this passage appears following the end of the *varṣā* retreat. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Having lived together for a long time, the nature of the mind is opened; only after refining the spirit can one face the true measure [of the Dharma].

Thus, one must declare one's own faults and publicly inform others of past conditions. If there is necessarily a matter requiring investigation and correction, it is not appropriate to remain silent. Consequently, it is able to...
Successively, because their conduct was pure, they lived together according to the Vinaya. Those who received the "dumb" method did so by falsely establishing a rule;

because of such speech, disputes arose, and they all practiced silence. What transgression could there be in this? The Buddha-dharma is not like that; one must recognize what is wrong as a matter of principle.

Those with innate knowledge are few, and one must certainly rely on virtuous friends. How could mere silence prevent one from committing faults? Therefore, the words of reprimand are identical to those of formal announcement (*jñapti*).

It is like a sheep; until death, it makes no sound. This [behavior] is merely stubborn and perverse—what further merit could it possibly produce? Therefore, the Buddha established this regulation so that they might mutually examine and correct one another.
For this reason, after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), this section was introduced. A guest said: "In the Vinaya there are two parables.

The first is the parable of the enemy, meaning that although they dwell together, they do not even speak with one another, being like enemies. The second is the parable of the white sheep, by which they live together..."

Dwelling in silence, one clears oneself of blame; thus it is likened to a white sheep. This means that during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), if one remains without speaking and fails to present a matter when there is something to be addressed, one resembles a white sheep.
It is as if one has seen a butcher leading a sheep to slaughter;
the sheep, knowing its death is near, sheds tears profusely yet makes no sound, even as it is slaughtered, hung upside down on a rack, and its body is cut away from behind until half of it is gone.
"Come! His life is not yet ended, yet he makes no sound. However, the karmic retribution of sentient beings is not fixed; what karma has caused this?
Now, upon careful examination, this is an official who beat a commoner and suppressed him unjustly, refusing to allow his case to be heard.
Therefore, this year’s retribution yields a corresponding fruit, likewise preventing the one with reason from being able to vindicate himself. This principle is certain. Thus it was said.
Regarding *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence): it is called *pravāraṇā* because one freely declares one's own transgressions, allowing the Saṃgha to raise them as faults.

Furthermore, it is said that it is so called because one freely allows one’s own body and mind to be subject to the Saṃgha’s imposition of penalties. As for the phrase "the essential core" (*zongyao*): this clarifies that *pravāraṇā* is the essential core of the practice for repenting transgressions.
Moreover, it is said that "core" (*zong*) means "venerable" (*zun*); for by being able to revere this dharma of *pravāraṇā*, one causes the wind of the Way to flourish.

It is constantly recited and designated as the essential [text]. Therefore, it is called the *Ziziyongyao* (Essentials of the *Pravāraṇā*). The commentary states: "The term *kāṭhina* and so forth is a Sanskrit sound;
translated, it means 'the robe of merit' (*guǒdé yī*). This is because one has cultivated the path for ninety days and performed meritorious service during the summer retreat."
The individual monks have no fault; they may freely receive the benefits. The protection of the *guṇavastra* (merit-cloth) is vast, and its merit extends to all practitioners.

For this reason, this dharma is appended [to the rules]. As for the explanation of its name: because one has rendered service by sitting through the summer retreat, one is rewarded with five benefits for that merit; hence it is called the *guṇavastra*, the "merit-cloth."

Regarding the phrase "refining the body and mind for ninety days," some maintain that it refers to practicing concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) throughout a single summer retreat, diligently and strenuously refining both body and mind.
(This interpretation is likely incorrect. The *Jielu su* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) states:

"Because they have cultivated the Path during these ninety days and have mutually refined their skills, as they are about to bid farewell and depart, it is necessary to allow the Saṃgha to raise [objections] so that one may acknowledge the duration of one's summer retreat; this has not yet occurred."

This is because of the beauty of its purity. The intended meaning is as follows: according to this intent of polishing, "refined" refers to the fact that the great assembly is intimately acquainted with one another and has fully mastered their own bodies and minds.

As for the statement that many people are deluded regarding themselves and do not perceive their own faults, it is established that worldly people see only the faults of others and fail to see their own.
Thus, the *Lüfa Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Vinaya) says: "Worldly people..."
This is the proof: one is ignorant; one sees only the faults of others but not one's own faults, and sees only one's own virtues but not the virtues of others.
As for "entrusting body and speech to another," this clarifies the commissioning of transgressions, which do not go beyond the two karmas of body and speech.

Fearing that what is committed by body and speech may manifest externally through the three faculties yet remain unseen due to one's own delusion, one therefore entrusts them to another to point out one's errors.
"Others" refers to those possessing the five virtues; it may also be understood generally as referring to the great assembly.

"Not being solitary" clarifies that one should not fear that there might be transgressions committed by oneself that go unnoticed, nor should one allow others to freely raise such points or offer correction.
After closing one's eyes in death, if one is reborn in the three miserable realms and loses all wholesome dharmas, this is called being "solitary and abandoned.

Now, by allowing others to administer punishment according to the teachings, one undergoes repentance and purification, and is constantly provided with the pure laws and regulations as companions; this is what it means to not be solitary.
Furthermore, one may fear that transgressions remain unseen;

yet, one should not allow others to freely expose them, fearing that by doing so they might commit a grave offense, be excluded from the monastic community, and be cast out as an outsider—this too would constitute being "solitary. As some say: if a person breaks the precepts, they are deceived by evil and are thus called "solitary.
Now, through the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) and repentance, one’s body and speech become pure and are no longer deceived by evil; this is called [being free from solitude].
It means "not being alone.

To "confide" (*kuan*) with those who share the same purpose is called "to pour forth one's confidences" (*tu kuan*). It is also said that "pouring forth the heart" (*shu xin*) is called "confidence" (*kuan*).

This clarifies that they have mutually agreed to pour forth their confidences and dwell together in the *an-ju* (rainy-season retreat). The *Guang pi* states: "Confidence arises from affection. The *Cang jie pian* states: "Confidence is sincerity and gravity."

The *Shuowen* states: "To 'intend' (欵) means that the mind has a desire. Regarding those whose obstacles to the Path are profound: having already committed offenses, they do not attain the fruits of sainthood;
being excluded from the Dharma, they have no share in the Path. This is called "obstructive evil karma being turbid and heavy," which is what is meant by "the obstacles are profound."

There are those who, through ignorance, engage in confused practice, asserting that "acting wickedly during the *pravāraṇā* constitutes confused practice. The preceding explanation of the introduction is concluded.

Regarding the statement, "Based on the intercalary month, one enters the rainy season retreat and performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month," this refers to the intercalary fourth, fifth, or sixth months.
As for the statement, "According to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, one performs the *pravāraṇā* after ninety days," [the author] asserts that if one originally knows...

If there is an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) and one does not rely upon it, the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is not established. What is clarified here is based on the original ignorance of the existence of an intercalary month, as has already been explained in the preceding chapter.
If the intercalary month falls in the seventh month and one takes the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation) in the preceding month, this is established as clear.

This refers to the sixteenth day of the fourth month; subsequently, when the *pravarana* is performed on the first day of the fifth month, there are sixteen people therein, but [only] those who... must [be present].

Because they reside for three months, they are permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) during the first seven months. My own view is that this text merely provides a general clarification regarding the timing of the *pravāraṇā* for the various groups.
According to the Vinaya, one should follow the *pravāraṇā* of those who settled early; therefore, it is necessary to state that they take the *pravāraṇā* of the preceding month.
This does not mean that the *pravāraṇā* occurs after the summer retreat has passed the intercalary month and the ninety-day count is complete.

This refers to the intercalary seventh month. It clarifies that if one establishes [the retreat] on or before the first day of the fifth month, one may go beyond the boundary until the *pravāraṇā* on the thirtieth day of the seventh month. Now is precisely the second day of the fifth month;

if one establishes it later than this, then by the thirtieth day of the seventh month, the summer retreat would still not be complete, as one would have stepped upon the intercalary month and would further be permitted to pass through it.
Once the month has passed, until the first day of the eighth month is reached, one may finally perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and depart from the boundary.
This is because an intercalary month is a "void" month and cannot be included in the calculation.
Regarding the second point, "increasing or decreasing the *pravāraṇā* due to disputes," as it is said in the section on the *poṣadha*: "As established in the *poṣadha*.
This means that just as it is established in the *poṣadha*, if an obstacle arises and enters the boundary, one must act in accordance with what was stated there; let it be the same here as well.
If one knows that the fourteenth day will arrive, the *pravāraṇā* must be performed on the thirteenth day. If one knows that the fifteenth day will arrive, [one should...]

The *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day is an abbreviated procedure. If [the monks] have already entered the boundary, they may have those entering for the bath leave the boundary immediately and establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) outside it to perform the *pravāraṇā* quickly.
If one cannot act in this manner, one should instead perform the single motion (*jñapti*).
One should wait for the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month to perform the *pravāraṇā*. If one does not depart before then, the *pravāraṇā* may be extended to the twenty-fifth day;

however, it may only be extended to the second [fifteenth], and not to the third. If it reaches the third, one must forcibly bring about reconciliation and perform it, as the winter season has begun and no further extension is permitted.
The Upādhyāya said: "In this context, there are three cases of 'withdrawing' and two cases of 'extending. One is the constant [observance on] the sixteenth day."
First, one takes the fifteenth day back [to the fourteenth]. Second, one always takes the fifteenth day back [to the fourteenth].
Third, one takes the fourteenth day back [to the thirteenth]. These are permitted because of disputes or difficulties; this is called "reduction" (*ūna*). Regarding the "two increases":
first, if the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) day arrives, it is increased until the thirtieth day of the seventh month; second, if [the dispute] still persists...
[The period] departs; it is further increased until the middle of the eighth month, reaching only these two increases and no more, because the winter season has begun.
Regarding the third point, "Practicing the Path with Joy and Extending the Days of the *Pravāraṇā*," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In a residence where there are many [monks]..."
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*) and practice the Path with diligence; you shall attain the realization of the higher fruits.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves, "If we were to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony today, we would have to move elsewhere, and we fear we might not obtain such bliss as this.

They immediately informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*). For the *pravāraṇā* in the fourth month, it should be said: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If the time is right for the Saṃgha...'"
"Venerable Sangha, please listen. The Sangha shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* now; when the fourth month is complete, we shall perform the *pravāraṇā*. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

This refers to the single-motion procedure for harmonizing the Sangha, awaiting the *pravāraṇā* until the middle of the eighth month. The commentary states: 'For ninety days one exerts oneself in cultivation to attain the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

Those liberated by waiting for the time (*samayavimukta*) become numerous in the final age. If one were to travel elsewhere, it would be difficult to obtain the various requisites; therefore, this motion is made.'"
Stop [this]. It coincides with the time when the *zhengfa* (correct dharma) is being performed.
Regarding the statement that "in the sequence of the increased *jishi yi* (clothing offered in haste)," it is clearly established in the *Lidudu wen* (Text on the Vinaya of the Liudu):

it simply states that the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) occurs on the fourteenth and fifteenth days; however, within the context of the *jishi yi*, the *pravāraṇā* takes place on the sixteenth day. Now, this is cited.
This text proves that there are three occasions for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, taking the sixteenth day as the fixed date. How is this known?

It is because when kings and great ministers provide robes as rewards to the Saṃgha during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) with the intention of offering them at its conclusion, they may have urgent reasons to travel far away.

He wished to offer it in advance to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus did not dare accept it as the summer retreat had not yet ended. They questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha asked, "How many days remain of the summer retreat?
They replied, "Ten days remain. The Buddha declared that since these circumstances existed, from this day forward he permitted acceptance during the ten days prior [to the end of the retreat];
this is called the "urgent offering robe" (*ātyayika-cīvara*). That is to say, from the sixth day of the seventh month onward, those who obtain it are permitted to accept it.
Beyond this, the recipient commits a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding the sequence:

if one obtains a robe on the sixth day of the seventh month, once the night of the fifteenth day of the seventh month has passed, exactly ten days have elapsed; by dawn on the sixteenth day, one would incur the offense of *atireka-cīvara* (excess robe).
This is because the Buddha has permitted [the retention] upon entering the month of Kārttika. If one exceeds this one-month period and it passes until the fifteenth day of the eighth month...

On the [first] day, one should perform the *śuddhika* (declaration of purity). If one obtains a robe on the seventh day of the seventh month, and the count reaches the ninth day, it then enters the *kārttika* period;

one should wait until the sixteenth day of the eighth month before performing the *śuddhika*. If one obtains a robe on the eighth day of the seventh month, and the count reaches the eighth day, it then enters the *kārttika* period;
one must wait until the seventeenth day of the eighth month before performing the *śuddhika*. In this manner, it proceeds gradually.
In sequence, when one obtains robes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, all the preceding days are counted.
Once the month of Kārttika has passed, the days of the "non-seasonal" period (*akālika*) are added. When the count reaches ten days, one must immediately perform the *śuddhi* (declaration of purity).
The days following the end of the month of Kārttika are termed "non-seasonal days," while the days prior to Kārttika, following the receipt of the robes, are added [to the count].

[This is] a numerical [calculation]. Therefore, it is said that they increase in sequence. Now, the reason this passage is cited in the *Chao* (Excerpts) is to clarify that the sixteenth day of the seventh month is the day of *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).

Since one receives the *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe-offering) on the sixth day of the seventh month and says, "The *pravāraṇā* is ten days away," it is clearly known that the sixteenth day is the day of *pravāraṇā*.
As for the statement, "The nuns perform *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day," this refers to...

Regarding the question of mutual dependence for the confession of faults (*pravāraṇā*), [the Vinaya] establishes that a *bhikṣuṇī* must first come among the *bhikṣus* to perform her *pravāraṇā*, and only after it is concluded may she return to the community of *bhikṣuṇīs* to perform her own *pravāraṇā*.

It should be understood that if she were to first complete her *pravāraṇā* among the *bhikṣuṇīs* and only later come to the *bhikṣus* to perform her *pravāraṇā*, this would invariably be contrary to the Dharma.
As for the statement that the specific period is fixed on the sixteenth day, [the Vinaya] establishes that although the *Vinaya* clarifies this...
The *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is held on the third day [of the fourth month]. If one were now to calculate and fix the date, it would be best to perform it on the sixteenth day.
This is because the Vinaya prescribes that the *pravāraṇā* occurs at the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and the sixteenth day is precisely when the summer retreat concludes.

Furthermore, it must be understood that if one is to receive the *śīlākā-cīvara* (robe for meritorious labor) or the *kaṭhina-cīvara* (robe of merit), it must be on the sixteenth day; if it were on the fifteenth day, one would not be permitted to receive them.
The recipient does not fulfill [the requirements]; it is merely called "out-of-season robe-cloth. This is what is meant by "an offering obtained by the Saṃgha out of season.
If there is an obstacle, as in the *Pañcaśata-praśna* regarding the monthly *pravāraṇā*:

from the middle of the seventh month until the middle of the eighth month, if an obstacle arises during this interval and one wishes to perform the *pravāraṇā* every day, one is unable to do so because of the obstacle. Upon reaching the middle of the eighth month, all [proceedings] take place.
One must not perform it; therefore, it is called the "Self-Admonition of One Month. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the timing for the self-admonition.
From here on, the text properly discusses the right and wrong of individuals.

"Waiting for the days to be complete" means that it reaches fulfillment on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. The above concludes the explanation of the meaning of the section on the assembly of conditions (*pratyaya-saṃnipāta*).

Below is the clarification of the method for the invitation to admonition (*pravāraṇā*). Regarding "three persons": it is established that from five persons upward, one may perform the formal ritual of motion and resolution (*jñapti-karman*).

The delegation of the five virtues is the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*). If there are four monks, they may only perform the face-to-face procedure (*pratyakṣavidhi*), which is termed the "law for a group" (*gaṇadharma*).
If there is only one monk, only the mental procedure (*manasikāradharma*) is permitted; therefore, it is said that [the minimum quorum] is three.
Regarding the phrase "the signs of pride while seated on the bed do not cease," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "To speak of 'leaving the bed' means to abandon one's arrogance.
As for the statement that "even śrāmaṇeras must assemble in the hall," Bin says: "In the present commentary (*chao*), it is stated that śrāmaṇeras must wait for the formal announcement."
Having departed, they go to a separate location to assemble for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together. The Tripiṭaka Master Jing alone states: "After midday has passed, the assembly gathers together;

first the *bhikṣu* community performs the *pravāraṇā*, followed by the *bhikṣuṇī* community, and then the three lower orders of the Saṃgha, each coming before the *bhikṣu* community to perform their own *pravāraṇā*.
(Commentary: According to reason, the lower orders should first assemble in one place; only after the higher order has completed its *pravāraṇā* should the lower orders be summoned.
The assembly enters the *saṃgha* for the *pravāraṇā*; the phrasing is the same as that of the *saṃgha*, and the meaning is likewise without error.

Regarding "one who possesses the two sets of five qualities," this means that within a single individual, there are two kinds of fivefold virtues. Thus, the *Karmavācanā-viniścaya* (Jie-mo-su) states:

"The conditions for appointing the five virtuous ones establish two types of virtue. First, regarding the virtue of *pravāraṇā*, one takes those who are free from attachment and so forth, because the assembly is diverse."

Right and wrong, defilement and purity, coexist; there must be no injustice or confusion that would bring disgrace upon the ranks of the Sangha. One who knows the timing and the Dharma cannot manifest [the truth] if they are not a worthy person;

therefore, such a person is required. Furthermore, regarding the selection of those with the five virtues to charge an offender: since the community prioritizes purity, how could one remain silent when transgressions are fully evident?
Therefore, one must be appointed to the position of accuser. This is the conduct of a virtuous person. As for "one who is disinterested," it means to provide relief...
Regarding "not [acting] out of affection": Ji says this means that when one commits an offense against those with whom one is intimate and close, one does not excuse it on account of that affection.

Regarding "not being angry": Ji says this means that toward those who are hateful and hostile, one does not seek out faults by picking at them like fine hair. Regarding "not being afraid": this means that even in the presence of those who are powerful and influential, one does not act out of timidity.

Regarding "knowing whether one is acting according to one's own will or not": this refers to knowing whether there are obstacles or no obstacles, and whether the practice should be extensive or concise.

This is appropriate. Regarding "knowing the time and not [acting] at an improper time," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "To raise up faults and settle disputes, there is nothing that is not in accord.
Jì explains: "Even if another has committed an offense, if one raises it before the disciples of others or in the presence of lay family members, this is to be ignorant of the proper time.
Therefore, the *Su* says: "In the presence of laypeople (*baiyi*) and novices (*shami*)."
One should not accuse a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) who does not possess full precepts; nor should one accuse when the assembly is fewer than four members.

Both of these cases are called "not knowing the proper time. The opposite is termed "knowing the proper time. Regarding "according to reality" (*yathābhūta*) and so forth: it means there is truth and no error, and there is a basis (*mūla*) and no confusion.

That is to say, for there to be an offense is one form of "reality"; furthermore, for the three bases [of accusation] not to be mutually contradictory is another form of "reality. This is "skillful" (*tīkṣṇa*).
"Benefiting others and so forth" means desiring to cause the person before one to become pure, so that their virtuous qualities may manifest outwardly.
"Gentle and soft and so forth" refers to comforting them with a compassionate mind, free from anger. Regarding "a compassionate mind does not employ hatred," Jì explains:

"Because one feels compassion for the person before one, one brings up their transgressions; how could one possibly harbor hatred? "The intention is to bring about harmony and the absence of strife" refers to the aforementioned understanding.
The phrase "at that time" corresponds to the term "equality. To say that there is no fault in [speaking of] transgressions corresponds to the preceding phrase "in accordance with reality.
To desire that the former person’s virtue in repentance be manifested outwardly corresponds to the preceding phrase "benefit.

Thus, being able to exhort and advise them so they leave behind resentment corresponds to the preceding phrase "gentleness. To speak of "compassion for beings and the granting of happiness" corresponds to the following section of the preceding [text].
These are phrases such as "the mind of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-citta*).

Regarding why two people are appointed [as *pañcavarga*] while the text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is not clear: Sengli (Seng-lü) states that the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely says to appoint five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*), but does not specify whether it be one or two persons.
Now, following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they act as substitutes for one another.
It is for this reason. For example, if there were one hundred thousand people, because of their great number, one might fear exhaustion and fatigue.

Some say that the text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is not explicit because its text prescribes appointing a single person alone as the presiding officer (*dharmavādin*), yet a single person has no place to perform the *pravāraṇā*.

Therefore, it is said that [the procedure] is not fully understood. Regarding the "two or more persons up to many" mentioned in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the established interpretation is as follows:
this does not mean that many people are appointed as the five virtuous qualities (*pañca-guṇa*) simultaneously and enter the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) at once.

Rather, because the Saṃgha is large, ten or twenty people may be appointed as the five virtuous qualities; they take turns performing the duties. At the time of the formal announcement of the appointment...

Only two persons may be selected at one time to enter the legal procedure [of *pravāraṇā*]. Regarding the requirement that two people must be appointed for the three thousand rules of decorum (*trīṇi sahasrāṇi īryāpathāni*):

this is because they perform the *pravāraṇā* facing one another. Since the fivefold virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) require that one’s faults not be pointed out by anyone other than a qualified person, and because those lacking such virtues have not been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is improper to perform the *pravāraṇā* in their presence.

Nowadays, there are many who perform the ritual by appointing individuals separately. This is clearly established: if six or more people are performing the rite, two *pañcavarga* (groups of five) must be appointed simultaneously.
If the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is performed sequentially, it is entirely contrary to the Dharma. For this reason, we have not seen such practices in the various schools (*nikāyas*).
Generally, those who are senior elders (*sthavira*) or possess great virtue are appointed; if an aged veteran acts as a member of the *pañcavarga*, he is honored by the assembly.
"Solemnity" refers to reverence.

"The youth reverses this" refers to the following clarification of the method for the five virtues (*pañca-śīla*). Regarding this *Prātimokṣa* rule on *pravāraṇā*, the opening for granting consent (*chanda*) differs from other schools.

This is established by clarifying that within the *Mahāsāṃghika* texts, the speaking of consent is not permitted, whereas all other schools permit it; the intention of the *Mahāsāṃghika* is thus to raise the matter as a formal accusation.

[The person] must be present in person. Fearing that they might rely on being inside a room [to avoid attendance], or fearing that the Saṃgha would investigate and discipline them, and fearing such evasions, *kāma* (consent) is not permitted.

Checking the *Jiǎnzhī* (Vinaya-mātṛkā), it says: "One must not give *kāma* for the *pravāraṇā*. If one is ill, one should be brought [to the assembly]. If one fears death, the Saṃgha should go to that person's location and perform the ritual.
If the illness is severe, the Saṃgha should go outside the boundary (*sīmā*) and perform the *pravāraṇā*. Lì asked: "When declaring *kāma*, is it not..."

It is appropriate to refer to the matters handled by the Saṃgha as "monastic affairs" (*saṃghakaraṇīya*). Regarding all such monastic affairs, one must invariably grant consent (*chanda*). If one were to refer to them by their specific content, it would be contrary to the Dharma.
Now, regarding the expression "granting consent for the *pravāraṇā*," why is it said that one grants consent for the *pravāraṇā*?

The answer is: it is because one is not permitted to refer to the specific matter. This principle is indeed correct. What is meant here by "granting consent for the *pravāraṇā*" is the declaration of one's own mental state, allowing the Saṃgha to exercise its authority (*pravāraṇā*) over oneself.
[Objection: "This is a transgression. It is fundamentally not something appropriate for the monastic community; this is an anomaly. [Response:

It is said that within the *pravāraṇā-karman* (the ritual of self-examination), there are likewise both general and specific aspects, as mentioned above. This means that within the general exposition of the *karman*, it is clarified that the response possesses both general and specific dimensions.

If one were now to answer by saying it is the *karma* of the *pravāraṇā*, that would be a general answer; if one says it is the *karma* for appointing the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*), that would be a specific answer.
When it comes to the time of the single-announcement (*jñapti*) for the five virtuous ones, one must again engage in questioning and answering.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen: today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding this, Master Jì explains that "today" is merely a conventional expression used in the monastic rules;
one should instead specify "on the [number]th day of the waxing moon" or "on the [number]th day of the waning moon," and so forth.

Regarding "sitting after distributing five blades of grass": the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states that this is done for fear of causing injury. When distributing the grass, one must not allow those of the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) to perform it;

rather, one should command a person from the lower seats to do so. Once the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made to the five virtuous ones, the distribution of the grass must immediately take place.

The grass is placed before [the candidate] and spread out, after which the body is moved to sit upon the grass. It is also called "long-life grass" (*dīrghāyu-grass*), and it is also called... [text ends].
There is also the *śara* grass. When proceeding with the grass, one calls for a boy or a layperson to kneel cross-legged while holding the grass.
The elder (*upādhyāya*) recites the verse: "The auspicious boy offers grass to the Buddha; having accepted it, the Tathāgata attained Perfect Enlightenment.
We bhikṣus shall emulate the Buddha’s wisdom, thus purifying our three karmas through this self-discipline (*pravāraṇā*). Having spoken thus, the bhikṣus receive the grass and proceed themselves.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Each of you should take a seat of grass; I wish to observe the *varṣā* (the rains retreat).
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha sat upon a seat of grass and addressed the bhikṣus: "You all should each sit upon seats of grass.
After the bhikṣus had sat upon their seats of grass, the Buddha remained silent for a while, observing the bhikṣus, and then commanded them, saying, "I wish to observe the *varṣā*."
"I have committed boundless faults; they are now in the hands of the assembly. Furthermore, have I not transgressed in body, speech, or mind? Thus he asked three times.
At that time, none of the bhikṣus replied, remaining silent. Then Śāriputra rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying, "O Bhagavān, regarding this assembly of bhikṣus..."
Contemplate the Tathāgata: he is without fault of body, speech, or mind. Why is this so? Because today the World-Honored One delivers those not yet delivered and liberates those not yet liberated;
he acts as eyes for the blind and as a great King of Physicians for the sick; he is the sole Honored One within the triple world.
"To provide a path for those who are deluded—for this reason, the Tathāgata has no fault regarding the multitude, nor does he have any transgression of body, speech, or mind.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "I now declare before the Tathāgata: am I without fault toward the Tathāgata and the Saṃgha?
The Buddha told him, "You are now entirely without transgression of body, speech, or mind. For this reason..."

"Furthermore, your wisdom is immeasurable; there is no one whose wisdom equals yours. You have attained the *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis*, and you are perfected in ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
You are able to subdue Māras and overcome non-Buddhists; all that you do is in accordance with the Dharma and never deviates from principle.
These five hundred bhikṣus, each observing the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat), are likewise so. (and so forth).

Regarding the first point, "The *pañcavāriyaka* (the one with five virtues) goes before the *sthavira* and spreads out a large sitting mat": this means that the *pañcavāriyaka* does not spread out grass mats;
therefore, it is necessary to spread out a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). If one were to spread out grass mats, a sitting mat would not be required.

The commentary states, "This is from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*," referring to the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which says: "If two persons act as the *pravāraṇā* officiants, one person receives the *pravāraṇā* from the *sthavira*..."
*Pravāraṇā*. One person stands before the seat of the *upādhyāya* (senior). Once the *upādhyāya* has finished speaking, the one below him speaks in turn.

In this manner, they proceed in succession until each reaches their own seat and performs the *pravāraṇā*. One must not wait until the entire Saṃgha has completed its *pravāraṇā* before performing one's own;
the above is entirely according to the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one mind," and so forth, constitutes the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). The *Karmasūtra* states: "The text consists of five phrases.

First, addressing the 'Venerable One' (*bhadanta*) is to formally inform the one of virtuous qualities (*pañcaguṇa*), requesting that he listen and grant his consent. For those of lesser rank, one says 'Elder' (*sthavira*).

Second, 'the Saṃgha today performs the invitation for self-examination' (*pravāraṇā*) refers to the time when the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*. Third, 'I, [name], also perform the self-examination' means that the subordinate responds to the superior."

Regarding the Dharma: even if one were to set forth faults, it would be at the discretion of the Sangha to raise them. Fourth, "If one sees, hears, or suspects... and below: "I possess the three roots [of seeing, hearing, and suspecting];
please show me compassion and grant me repentance. Fifth, "I see my transgression... and below: "By repenting according to what I have heard, may I achieve purity and excellence.

As for why these are recited three times: it expresses the earnestness of one’s upward petition and entrustment; it is not a matter of frivolous or excessive reliance. According to Li’s commentary, these words also consist of five phrases.
First, regarding the address "Venerable One" (*bhadanta*): this term is applied regardless of seniority when addressing one who possesses the five virtues;
it is a word of praise and commendation. Second, by citing that the same is observed throughout the ten directions, it says: "The Saṃgha today performs the *pravāraṇā*.

Third, by looking up to established precedents, it expresses reliance on the monastic law, saying: "I, [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*. Fourth, it involves the proclamation of one's own faults and the request for [correction].
He requests that his faults be pointed out and prays for instruction; thus it says, "If one sees, hears, or suspects [a fault]," etc.
Having praised his request for correction, it states that for a virtuous elder (bhadanta-sthavira), there is no harm in complying.

Fifth, to manifest one's own faults and repent them so that one's conduct may become pure, it says, "If I see a fault," etc., expressing one's diligent effort in this manner up to three times. The term "virtuous elder" refers to the *karmadāna*.
The *Moshu* (Commentary on the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*) states: "The previous instance where 'Venerable One' (*bhadanta*) is mentioned alone refers only to the five virtuous qualities.

The subsequent double citation is due to the utmost gravity and respect, as it concerns the *saṃgha*. How is this known? Because within the *Vinaya*, one must not perform the *pravāraṇā* in a whisper or speak too hurriedly during the *pravāraṇā*;
therefore, it is performed before the *saṃgha* so that the names and categories may be known. In principle, it must be clear and distinct, intended for the universal purity of the assembly."

According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, those who are great are called "Venerable" (*bhadanta*), while those who are junior are called "Elder" (*sthavira*). These two categories are established for the time being;

however, since the meaning applies across both senior and junior ranks, this must be further discussed. An Elder is necessarily great; thus, while in the Sūtras figures such as the Elder Śāriputra and the Venerable Ānanda are designated by their respective titles, in the Vinaya the usage is not fixed.
Here, I shall briefly explain it: one is called a "Venerable" because they are endowed with both practice and realization, whereas [an Elder] refers to [one distinguished by] age.
Virtue that is lofty and far-reaching is called "Elder" (sthavira)—this refers to those with many years of seniority (*varṣa*). This should be analyzed in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):

first, one who is a Great Virtuous One (*bhadanta*) but not an Elder—this is a youth endowed with both understanding and practice; second, one who is an Elder but not a Great Virtuous One—this is one of advanced age but shallow understanding;
third, one who is both—this is one of advanced age whose practice and understanding are profound; fourth, one who is neither—this is a youth lacking knowledge. The *Shoushu* states:
An ancient said: "The first instance of 'Venerable' (*bhadanta*) refers to one who possesses the five virtues.
The intermediate 'Venerable' refers to those in the assembly who are superior to oneself. The subsequent 'Elder' (*sthavira*) refers to those in the assembly who are inferior to oneself.
If this is the meaning, then whom does the highest-ranking *upādhyāya* call "Venerable," and whom do the lowest-ranking juniors call "Elder"? If...
The term "assembly" refers to both the ordinary and the noble. It is on this basis that one enters by proclaiming purity as a great śramaṇa; this principle is for now accepted.
The intent is to clarify that even the greatest *sthavira* (elder) is considered "junior" in relation to a noble one. If those in the final seats are "junior," whom could one call an *sthavira*?

How could a noble one be junior to a monk who has not yet completed his first summer retreat (*anupasaṃpanna*)? The commentary states: "This clarifies the smallest and lowest seat; he does not descend [to a lower rank]."
Noble ones are addressed as "Elder" (*sthavira*), because a noble one is not small. Furthermore, those who are small are also addressed as "Elder.
For what reason, among the ninety rules, is there the precept regarding expelling another from a room?
Since the group of seventeen was junior to the group of six, why did they address the group of six as, "Elder, you are our senior"? Also, during the Council of Seven Hundred, Revata...
"Summon all the *paramopadhāyaka-sthaviras* who act as *bhadanta-sthaviras*. Now, the explanation is as follows: one whose conduct is perfected is called a *bhadanta*;
one who is lofty in supervision, compassionate, wise, far-reaching in practice, and has vision that extends afar is designated a *sthavira*.

The titles "Bhadanta" and "Sthavira" used here—whether at the beginning, middle, or end of a statement—all refer to those endowed with the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) who are being addressed. Question: This...
If the meaning is as you say, then it would suffice simply to address him as "Venerable" (*bhadanta*); why is it necessary to further say "Elder" (*sthavira*)? Answer:

It is done out of a desire for earnestness in requesting the five virtuous qualities (*pañca-dharma*). Because he is being charged with an offense, one fears that [the Venerable] might not take it to heart;
therefore, one must call upon him repeatedly. If this were the case, why not say "Venerable Elder, Venerable Elder"? Either interpretation is acceptable; it is merely a matter of translation.

"Family" (*kula*) is merely a synonym for "household. Regarding the second interpretation: to repeat [the title] would be improper; furthermore, the meanings differ because they refer to distinct virtues.

If this is so, why can one not initially address him as "Elder" (*sthavira*)? Answer: If one were to address him as "Elder" at the outset, and then ask, "Why is 'Venerable' (*bhadanta*) not placed first?
the resulting difficulty would be endless. As for the person addressed by these two interpretations, he is one who possesses the five virtues within the assembly.
He was dispatched. Since he is said to possess the "five virtues" (*pañca-guṇa*), and virtue is the root, the virtues are mentioned first. The "far-reaching vision" is its auxiliary condition;
it is not the primary root, and therefore "uprightness" (*ajjava*) must be mentioned last. Question: Why is there no double invocation at the beginning, followed by a single call at the end? Answer:
At the beginning, when one has not yet made a formal request, a double invocation is unnecessary. In the middle, when one is formally seeking to appoint a guardian, the five virtues are raised.
This constitutes an offense; therefore, it is called a "grave summons.
The Vinaya provision that allows a sick person to remain wherever they find comfort refers to returning to one's original seat, not to returning to one's private room.

This immediately refutes the school’s tradition of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations). It is clearly established within the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that one must wait until the Sangha has finished its *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Both...
These five virtues are performed facing one another; now, this [procedure] is different from that. Upon reaching one's original seat, it must be performed.

Regarding the manner of advancing, it is not as described in the "Four-Person Procedure" (catur-varga-vidhi), but rather as clarified in the "Four-Person Face-to-Face Procedure" (catur-varga-mukha-mukha-vidhi) in the following text, which explains its advances and retreats.

From this point onward, the text correctly explains the procedure for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) for *bhikṣuṇīs*. Regarding the statement that it is not necessary to ask the *bhikṣuṇīs* whether [an offense] exists during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*):
this refers to the time of the *poṣadha*, when one asks, "Who has sent a *bhikṣuṇī* here to request instruction?

This regulation requires such a question so that a person may be appointed to go and provide instruction, thereby ensuring the purity of the *bhikṣuṇī* community and benefiting both sides. As for the present *pravāraṇā*...

This nun has come to request that the Saṃgha raise her faults. Since the Noble One did not establish a rule regarding whether she should be questioned as to whether she has come or not, there is no need to question her.
As for other matters concerning the specific rules for nuns, these meanings are clarified in the "Chapter on the Separate Conduct of the Nun Community."

Regarding the statement that "within the *Saṃghāṭī-śikṣā*, there was originally no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), yet it also required one to speak of the *chanda* (consent) according to circumstances":

this clarifies that when a nun comes into the midst of the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* to request the person who shall provide the instruction, the Elder among the great monks briefly instructs her with such phrases as "Do not be negligent," and so forth.
These words are then repeated back to the assembly of nuns. If there are nuns who do not come, they must still communicate their consent (*chanda*). Based on this, it is also [the case].

There is no formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*). The purpose of citing this passage now is to clarify that when a nun comes into the midst of the *saṃgha* for the invitation to self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) so as to request the monks to point out her faults, if the *saṃgha* does not assemble accordingly, she must then communicate her intention (*chanda*).
Regarding the fact that a nun commits a grave offense by traveling alone beyond the boundary: this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghadisesa) offense, which is termed "grave.
However, as for appointing a nun to come into the midst of the monks for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), one need only perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to appoint a single competent nun;

the others may be appointed orally as her companions. At present, on the night of the sixteenth day of the seventh month, before the appearance of the dawn light, the community of nuns comes into the midst of the monks.

This is entirely contrary to the Dharma. Since the night-watch of the fifteenth day has not yet ended, those who rise during the night and depart will all break their summer retreat and be separated from their robes.
Why must one leave so urgently at night? (I have often seen this happen).

Furthermore, when the assembly gathers at midnight and the departure has not yet been announced, one may say, "Two or three nuns are coming. This is to act in accordance with the instructions. The above clarifies the departure of nuns.
The section on the completion of the rules regarding offenses concludes.

Regarding the fourth point, the "Brief Explanation," the *Shu* (Commentary) states: When the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Administrator) performs the ritual and a sudden emergency arises, if he were to recite the full text alone, it would disturb the assembly.

Therefore, if a person of virtue is present, he makes a formal announcement (*bai*) to inform them; then, at one time, two pairs of individuals from both sides confess their transgressions to one another. This...

This refers to performing [the ritual] without being in the presence of the five virtuous qualities (*pañca-guṇa*). If one is in the presence of the five virtuous qualities, there are two brief procedures: namely, the single recitation and the double recitation.

When in the presence of the original five virtuous qualities, one should know for oneself the appropriate pace—whether slow or rapid—and adjust according to the time and the matter at hand; it is not necessary to announce and seek permission (*ārocana*). This applies when not in the presence of the five virtuous qualities.

There are three abbreviated methods for reciting the *karmavācanā* (formal proclamation) to modify the assembly. First, after one *jñapti* (motion), each pair faces one another and recites three times;

thus, a group of one hundred becomes fifty pairs, with both members of each pair reciting three times simultaneously. Next, after one *jñapti*, each member faces their respective counterpart and recites twice.
The final "threefold announcement" (tri-śrāvaṇa) refers to each person announcing it once in turn. The Upādhyāya said: "These three announcements should properly be combined into one;
[Dharma]lì divided them into three. This is what is meant by the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* when it says: "Some divide them into three announcements; now they are combined into one."

Regarding the prohibition against speaking in secret or engaging in self-indulgent chatter during the *pravāraṇā*: this matter arose concerning the group of six bhikṣus, who either spoke in whispers or spoke with hurried haste during the *pravāraṇā*.
The Buddha declared that such conduct was contrary to the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "performing in reverse order," [Dao]li states that this means proceeding from the bottom upward.

Regarding the statement "placing persons in rows as if serving food," this refers to placing one person of fivefold virtue (wude) at the head of a single row, or placing one person of fivefold virtue at the head of two or three rows.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneously and by skipping while chanting in total," [Dao]li says this means not following the sequential order, but rather skipping over it.
It is performed as follows: having performed it before the first *pañcavarga* (group of five virtuous ones) who is seated at the head, the second *pañcavarga* should stand before the next seat.
To now bypass that next seat and proceed before the third seat is called "transgressing" (*chao*).

Furthermore, regarding the term "reciting collectively," this means speaking simultaneously; thus it is called "collective recitation. The citation from the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*) refers to a textual error in the *Shu-yao-chao*. This is the matter.
The *Shi lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) states that one should descend from the senior monk (*sthavira*) in successive order; one must not place people in separate rows.

It is like the method for serving food: one must not skip over anyone, nor may one announce it collectively by saying, "All virtuous monks (*bhadanta saṃgha*), please speak of any offenses you have seen, heard, or suspected during the *pravāraṇā*.
The text of the Vinaya simply provides these words.
"The procedure for the motion is the same as before" means that the wording of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is identical to that which preceded it.

Regarding the "six kinds of abbreviated explanations" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, they are as explained previously; that is to say, there are two types of abbreviations when addressing those possessing the five virtues (*pañcaguṇa*).

The first [type of] *prātimokṣa* involves two recitations before five virtuous elders; the second involves one recitation before one person. This manual (*chao*) does not include the text for the second type of recitation, yet it ought to be present there.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* performed with a single formal announcement (*jñapti*), there are three abbreviated forms, namely: the threefold recitation, the twofold recitation, and the single recitation.
This is the first explanation. Together with the subsequent "difficulties" (nān) that proceed directly and urgently, they constitute the sixth.
These distinctions arise because the arrival of the difficulties varies in terms of distance; thus, there are these six different types.

Regarding "binding a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) and performing the *pravāraṇā* while seated in a circle": this clarifies that the members of the Saṃgha sit facing one another, with the one possessing the five virtues (*pañcavarga-dharma*) at the center, receiving the *pravāraṇā* from all four directions.
The above four sections constitute the complete explanation of the first section.
Next, the *pañcavargīya-saṃghadharma* (the legal procedure for a community of five) is explained. Question: Above, the *ṣaḍvargīya* (six-membered) was explained; here, the five-membered is explained.
Since both are equally *saṃghadharma*, why are they divided into separate sections? Answer: There is a specific reason for this, intended to clarify the distinctions.

Fearing that those unacquainted with the teachings might be confused—wherein a boundary (*sīmā*) may consist of five persons, one of whom declares the *chanda* (consent), whereas if there are six persons in a boundary, one declares the *chanda* and the remaining five constitute the *saṃgha*.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is accomplished by appointing those possessing the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*). If there are five persons, one person expresses their consent (*chanda*), while the remaining four, though they constitute the *saṃgha*, are merely those capable of performing the rite;
there is no other person available to be appointed as one possessing the five virtues.

If one were to appoint a single person as one possessing the five virtues, it would not be established at all, because three [of the total] would not constitute the *saṃgha*. Furthermore, even if all five persons have assembled, there is still fear that one...

At that time, two [cases] were presented together; two of the names entered the Dharma, while the remaining three were not members of the Saṃgha. Therefore, it was again not established. It merely resulted in a discrepancy between the preceding and succeeding [parts].
Thus, this section is now established in order to distinguish [the cases] from one another.
If five persons within the boundary do not disclose their consent (*chanda*), it means that among four persons performing the *pravāraṇā*, they may not receive the consent of a fifth person;

because four persons assembled in the hall cannot perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) or appoint those with the five virtues, they can only carry out the rite for face-to-face communication (*pratyakṣa-dharma*).

Since the *pratimokṣa* (confession before another) is a procedure for individuals, how could one receive a formal consent (*chanda*)? Furthermore, although this is fundamentally a procedure for a community (*saṃghakarma*), now that four persons have assembled, it is a *pratimokṣa* procedure for a group;
yet since there are still people within the boundary (*sīmā*), it constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*). Therefore, this [consent] belongs to the person and is invalid.
The ritual procedure is not accomplished.
From this point downward, the text correctly explains the method for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) of a community of four monks.

As for the phrase "merely entering into the category of *sthūlātyaya*," this refers to one who has committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense, up to and including a *pārājika*, and has been brought before the community, yet has not yet reached [the point of formal confession].

Regarding the treatment: if one is startled by a difficult circumstance, it is termed "entering into the confession of a *sthūlātyaya*. This means that once the offense has become manifest, the teaching states that one has committed it;

hence it is called "entering into the confession" (*sāmghātiśeṣa*). Furthermore, even if one has merely committed an offense oneself and the assembly does not yet know of it, it is still termed "entering into the confession of a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to the remaining *sāmghātiśeṣa* offenses and the *pārājika* offenses.

"One should not obstruct the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults)" means that those who have committed an offense and have already been formally accused by others are ineligible for the *pravāraṇā*.

As for the rest who are without fault, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the usual procedure. One must not, because another has committed an offense, cause the rest of the Saṃgha to cease and fail to perform the *pravāraṇā*.

Since both are equally comprised within the *saṃgha-dharmas* that purify conduct and their functions are identical, it is established that both the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) and the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) are *saṃgha-dharmas* for purifying conduct.
The recitation of the precepts prevents non-virtues not yet arisen, while the *pravāraṇā* prevents faults already arisen.

Since the prevention of faults is one and the same, they are said to be equally *saṃgha-dharmas* for purifying conduct. If, during the seat of the recitation of the precepts, one recalls having [committed a fault]...

Regarding offenses, the Noble One has commanded that one must confess them with mindfulness; thus, one immediately attains the hearing of the precepts. It is the same for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination):
if one recalls having committed an offense, one must likewise confess it before the *pravāraṇā* can be performed.

Regarding the statement, "If it is not true, the offense is determined according to the transgression; for three [instances], it is a *thullaccaya*": this clarifies that while the substance is actually impure, one declares it pure in the presence of others;

therefore, it constitutes a deliberate falsehood (*musāvāda*). For each of the three utterances, there is a *thullaccaya*, which differs from the case of silent deception during the *poṣadha*, where one incurs only a *dukkaṭa*.

The following clarifies the rules for a single person (*ekapudgala*). Regarding the statement, "If one commits a *duṣkṛta* (or worse) intentionally, there is no sense of disciplinary punishment, and since it must be confessed, it does not accord with the rules for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony," this phrasing here is somewhat inverted.

What is intended to be clarified is that if one commits such an intentional *duṣkṛta*, one must first perform a mental confession (*manasā deśanā*); only after that can one proceed with the mental self-exhortation (*manasā pravāraṇā*).

"Self-Confession" (*pravāraṇā*) means that once an offense has been committed, one must confess it before another person; since there is currently no such person present, one may only perform a formal disclosure.
As for the phrase "the rest follows the former," it refers to the wording of the self-confession performed through mental recollection as previously described.

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) ritual. The following section clarifies the third point: the analysis of difficult cases. The response states that within the *saṃgha*, there is the principle of formal censure (*codanā*) and suspension (*utkṣepana*);
furthermore, when the ritual is augmented, it can be made complete. This clarifies that during the *saṃgha-pravāraṇā*, one may censure a person who has committed an offense.

If they have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), they are immediately subjected to banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*). If they have committed a residual offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), they may undergo the six-night *parivāsa* (probation) followed by reintegration.

Regarding offenses such as *pārājika* down to *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*, all may be subject to disciplinary treatment (*daṇḍakarma*). This is because the number of monks required for the assembly does not necessarily have to be complete;

it is said that they may be "admissible" (*yogya*) even if incomplete. As for the confession of a grave *sthūlātyaya*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) specifies that a great assembly of eight persons is required.

If there are now only six or seven persons, then it is still insufficient. Although individual monks may perform acts of discipline, censure, or formal restraint (*saṃvṛti*), they are unable to achieve the full efficacy of the rite.
"Exhausted" means that since the number of people present is few, even if they commit an offense, if it is a *thullaccaya* or a *pācittiya*, they can be subject to disciplinary punishment;

however, if it is a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a heavy *dukkaṭa*, they cannot be purified through confession because the number of people is insufficient. Therefore, it is said that "the governance is not yet complete."

Regarding the statement that "the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is itself the recitation of the precepts": the recitation of the precepts is for the purpose of knowing the characteristics of the precepts so as to prevent unarisen transgressions;

the *pravāraṇā* is for the purpose of removing transgressions already arisen so as to achieve the beauty of purity. Although there is a difference between what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred, their meaning in terms of purity is the same; therefore, it is so called.
"Returning to the same procedure as previously explained for face-to-face confession" refers to what was stated above: "Three persons, Great Virtues, attend to me with one mind;
today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*, and so forth."

The answer is: "One may not break the summer retreat by being separated from one's robes. This clarifies that when the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is completed on the fifteenth day of the first half of the month, one must leave the boundary on that very day to break the summer retreat.
Since the night-watch of the fifteenth day has not yet ended, one is only permitted to leave the boundary after the appearance of the morning light (*aruṇodaya*).

Regarding the term "being separated from one's robe": this means that since the summer retreat was not successfully completed, one does not obtain the five privileges; how then could one be permitted to be separated from one's robe? The same applies to receiving [permission] to go out of the boundary on a day of departure.

As for the answer stating that the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] does not permit it: this clarifies that the *Mahāsāṃghika* differs from the *Dharmaguptaka*. The *Dharmaguptaka-vibhaṅga* states: "In this place..."

Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat): if one receives a formal authorization (*jñapti*) to go to another location, it is also permissible to perform the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation) at that other location.

This applies even if one moves during the summer so as to reside for more days in another place, receive robes and other requisites there, and—contrary to the essential rule of returning to the original location for *pravāraṇā*—perform the *pravāraṇā* at that other site.
One must understand deeply that this constitutes an offense (*āpatti*).
Answer: Regarding the Vinaya rule that one may receive goods on other days provided they are sufficient, the intent of the following response is as follows:

"Obtained" here refers to what the Saṃgha obtains during that specific time. If it is property present before the assembly at that time, it is strictly not permissible; for such property is considered "present before the assembly."
Because it possesses four characteristics: first, the determination of time, meaning that the ordination is received on the same day, the sixteenth of the seventh month;

second, the determination of place, which restricts it to those observing the rains retreat within this specific boundary; third, the determination of persons, which restricts it to those currently residing together as the practitioners of the preceding retreat;

and fourth, the determination of the dharma, meaning that there is no need to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), as the allotment is made simply by counting the number of people. Thus, one should know [the rules for] the subsequent retreat.
The residents did not obtain these items. As for the statement that "one now obtains a share of the robes," this refers to the time when the Sangha receives an offering;

it makes no distinction between those who have already entered the retreat and those who have not, nor between one's own boundary and another's, as the gift is offered universally to the entire community of monks.

Regarding the rule that "if one divides the rooms and bedding, it is also permitted to accept them for the sake of the future," the commentary states: this clarifies the case of those entering the later retreat (*paścimā vārṣikā*); although the day has not yet...

It is sufficient. One may receive the robes. Regarding the bringing forward of rooms, bedding, and furniture: this clarifies that after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, the winter quarters and other such allotments are divided.
Those who entered the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*) and whose summer period is not yet complete may also receive these rooms, bedding, and furniture in advance.

If one does not receive them in a timely manner, there is a fear that by the end of one's own summer retreat, the Sangha will no longer be able to divide the rooms; therefore, it is said "for the sake of [preparing for] what has not yet occurred."
This refers to receiving [the bedding] for the sake of the future. The guest (the *atithi*) explains it in the same way. Another commentary states:

regarding the phrase "receiving for the sake of the future," the subsequent section of the *Aniyata-khandhaka* (or *Varṣā-vastu*) relates that when the summer retreat had not yet concluded, they hesitated and did not dare to receive the bedding. The Buddha said, "I allow you to receive it for the sake of the future."

This means it is necessary for the future. Furthermore, Sheng asked: "In the Vinaya texts, it is said that those who completed the earlier summer retreat may travel after the summer is over, and because of the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they divide the rooms and quarters.
May those who entered the later summer retreat, though their term is not yet full, also divide them?"

The Buddha said, "I permit you to receive [the bedding] for the sake of the future. Why is this so? When rooms are currently being distributed, one may not receive them prematurely if they are not yet full.
Since it is for the winter season, looking from the present toward the winter constitutes receiving them for the future; therefore, I permit it."
Regarding the one who instructs the person granting the *pravāraṇā*: the established view is that even one designated as a "five-virtue" (*pañca-guṇa*) *pravāraṇā*-giver may provide instruction.
As for the question "What is an elder?": this clarifies that it refers specifically to a senior disciple, not to anyone else.
When Kāśyapa rebuked him, saying "you are young," he meant that you are young in understanding; because your understanding is deficient, you are called "young."

Regarding "the *pravāraṇā* (formal invitation to criticize) for those who have stayed longer during the rainy season retreat": this refers to the *pravāraṇā* performed by the majority of those who entered the retreat early.

Regarding "committing an offense by not departing at the conclusion of the retreat," the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states: "There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who had accepted invitations from donors for the rainy season retreat.
When the days of the retreat were complete, the bhikṣuṇīs did not depart because the food and drink were delicious; consequently, the donors felt resentment."

[The monks] became weary and tired. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "When the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded, if one stays beyond [the designated time] by even one day, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
for a *mahābhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This refers to those who were observing the retreat in a lay residence. If there is a valid reason and one does not depart, there is no offense."

"It must be within the monastery; there is no need for it to be otherwise. 'If one does not set a limit,' etc., refers to when a donor, out of a sense of pride, invites a bhikṣu without restricting the invitation to a single summer retreat.
As for 'a place other than where one has accepted an invitation,' this refers to locations such as within the monastery or among mountain crags.
Regarding 'one obtains five merits by doing the opposite,' these refer to [the absence of] fear of being robbed, longing for relatives, and so forth."
This is a point of concern.
The preceding many sections have been different; this concludes the general explanation of the first topic, the Dharma of *pravāraṇā*.
From here below is the second section, which correctly clarifies the five benefits as rewards for the merit of observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Regarding the *kāṭhina* robe: this is...

In the Sanskrit language, this is translated as the "Robe of Merit" (*guṇa-vattha*). According to the Chinese lexicons, regarding the character *ka* (pronounced with the *ju* and *qie* finals, or as an upper tone):

the small variety is called *ge*, while the large variety is called *chi*; *ge* refers specifically to *ge-bu* (hemp cloth). As for the term "robe," it refers exclusively to the three robes (*tricīvara*). First, to clarify the intent behind its introduction:

because of the preceding *an-guo* (summer retreat), one advances in their practice; through the summer sitting, merit is achieved; and since the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) was performed without fault, a fine reputation has spread far and wide.

Pure both internally and externally, it moves the hearts of sentient beings. At such a time, it brings forth much merit and bestowal. The Sages have opened up five benefits, rewarding virtue and supporting merit.
Does not the worldly say, "He who has merit is rewarded"? It is for this reason that these words were written. Regarding the note on "firm and solid":
it is said that once one has received this robe, one can cause the five benefits to become firm and solid; that is to say, the five benefits shall not be destroyed.

The *Lì* (Commentary) says: "Solid and substantial" means that there are many robes offered as gifts; because one constructs this robe by selecting those that are durable and superior, it is called "solid and substantial.
Furthermore, the *Liaolùn shū* (Commentary on the Vinaya-saṃgraha) says: "Kaṭhina is that which can procure many robes.
If a person accepts the kaṭhina robe, whatever robes a donor offers shall all belong to this person. Since this person already possesses many robes, the robes will not be spoiled."
Because it is indestructible, it is called "solid" (*kaṭhina*). Furthermore, when the *kaṭhina* robe is being made, this robe is composed of many materials;
therefore, it is called "solid. All solid substances are termed *kaṭhina*. Even the powerful influence of afflictions (*kleśa*) is also called *kaṭhina*.
Moreover, just as a person whose mind is gripped by anger or desire finds it difficult to relinquish them, such a person is also designated as *kaṭhina*.

"Chixin" refers to a person. It means that there are no garments that have become worn out or ruined; this is because, by receiving these five benefits, one is permitted to possess many extra robes (*cīvara*) without committing the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If there is no wear or ruin, it would mean that—had it not been for the receipt of these garments—one would have committed the offense of forfeiture by possessing an extra robe beyond the limit.

This is precisely what is meant by "worn out. The commentary notes that it is also called "difficult to sustain" (*durlabha-jīvita*). The *Liaolun shu* (Commentary on the Vinaya-mātṛkā) explains: [text follows].
This is what is meant by "poverty. A poor person lacks the means of livelihood and finds it difficult to sustain themselves; therefore, it is said that they are "difficult to support.

If a poor person can manage to extract even one or two pieces of cloth and offer them as this *kaṭhina* robe, the merit and karmic fruit thereof surpass the gift of a mass of robes as vast as Mount Sumeru.
When the Buddha demonstrated the making of this robe, the poor person likewise...
One should practice giving within this [community]. Because it is intended to lead impoverished people to practice giving within this community, it is specifically named after those poor people;
thus, it is called the "garment for those who find it difficult to live. The commentary states that some call it the "firm garment" (*dṛḍha-cīvara*);

this carries the same meaning as the previous term "solid" (*sāra*), because it can cause the five precepts to become firm. The commentary further states that some name it the "sheltering garment"; this refers to the ten [precepts].
In the recitation, the *kaṭhina* robe is designated as "protection" (*āvāsana*). This is intended to clarify that this garment provides protection for the five benefits.
It is also called the "robe of merit" (*guṇa-cīvara*); as Li states, if one receives this robe, it can generate the merit of the five benefits.

It is called thus because its name is manifested through its merit. However, among the five benefits, the statement regarding "being permitted to stay apart from the three robes" does not mean that one is entirely permitted to separate from all three robes;

rather, it is an allowance specifically for separating from the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe). This is because, within the *nidāna* (contextual origin), the *saṃghāṭī* was heavy, whereas there is no textual provision for an allowance to separate from the two lower robes.
"Up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one may receive robes on every day.
This establishes that from the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month—within these thirty days—one may receive robes on each and every day.
If the first day of the month is still the sixteenth day of the seventh month, [the Master] Daoli says: "In the Buddha-dharma, there are only three seasons.
For example, the sixteenth day of the fourth month is the first day of summer; yet now it is said to be the sixteenth day of the seventh month."
This is the first day of the fourth month of summer. If it were the second or third day, it would correspond to the seventeenth or eighteenth day of the seventh month.
Regarding the phrase "up to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is likewise," the word "up to" (乃至) is used because there are intervening days omitted;
that is to say, from the seventeenth, eighteenth, and [nineteenth] days of the seventh month onwards, until the [fifteenth day of the eighth month].
On the fifteenth day, one receives the robe according to the date; it must be accepted on that very day and may not be kept overnight. Therefore, it is said to be "likewise.
