According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are thirty days for receiving and thirty days for relinquishing; those who obtain only the four-month benefit should examine this.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Regarding the receiving of the *kaṭhina* robe, there are thirty days; the relinquishing likewise has thirty days.
If one enters the summer retreat on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, one receives [the *kaṭhina*] on that date and relinquishes it on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month.

If one receives it from the seventeenth day of the seventh month up to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one relinquishes it from the sixteenth day of the eleventh month up to the tenth [day of the twelfth month]."

It is relinquished on the fourteenth day of the second month. If it is the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*), it is undertaken on the sixteenth day of the eighth month and relinquished on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month (this refers only to the dates for obtaining the four benefits). In the *Dharmaguptaka* school, it is not so;

the undertaking lasts for thirty days, beginning from the sixteenth day of the seventh month and ending on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, during which one may undertake it every day. As for the relinquishing, there is only one [date].
The day refers specifically to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. Although the period for undertaking [the precepts] lasts thirty days, the period for relinquishing them lasts only one day;
thus, it can be understood that the number of intervening days gradually decreases.
Regarding the statement that one must calculate the full duration according to the number of days of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) and may not include an intercalary month:
this means that once the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted, if an intercalary month occurs, one should simply count five months starting from the day the retreat is completed;
the intercalary month is not to be included.
"Obtaining it not by means of signs" refers to manifesting signs such as cold or heat. "Obtaining it not by means of incitement" means agitating others so that they give;

for example, saying, "The Zhang family has finished acquiring a piece of cloth," with the desire to make them give. Obtaining an object in this manner does not constitute the making of a *kaṭhina* robe.
Regarding the statement, "If one makes it pure (*viśuddha*) without [incurring] the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), it accords with the Dharma," this is what is established.

If one has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), one may not make [the robe]; however, if it is an extra robe that has been formally purified (*viśuddha*), one may do so. Bin said:

Regarding those who have not forfeited but have performed the purification, the traditional interpretation handed down from former times states: this refers to cases where one has previously committed an offense involving forfeiture, such that even though one now performs the purification...

It is also unfit for use. Now, the explanation is not so. This refers to the non-offense regarding the relinquishment of robes (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*), as well as all other instances where purification (*pariśuddhi*) has been performed;

in all such cases, one may proceed with them. The reason for this knowledge is that, in contrast to the subsequent passage which clarifies that within what is *adharma* (unlawful), failing to perform purification constitutes an offense of relinquishment and downfall (*pācittiya*), we know that this current passage clarifies what is *dharma* (lawful)—that is, it concerns non-offenses of relinquishment and downfall as well as the performance of purification. Thus it is said:
Regarding "five strips and ten intervals": this refers specifically to the five-strip robe for the sake of illustration; the others should be understood by analogy. All must conform to the Dharma.
As for the statement "if it exceeds this number of strips," this refers to the seven-strip robe, the nine-strip robe, the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and so forth.
If one goes to a cemetery to retrieve a corpse that has been intentionally decayed or covered over, Ji says:
"This is like the case of reinterment; it refers to changing the clothing on the corpse. It is just as when Empress Wu died and was interred in the same tomb as Emperor Gaozong.

When they opened the Emperor’s coffin, it was found to have been lined with a stone sarcophagus filled with mercury. Consequently, her physical form remained white as usual, unchanged. As for the Duke of Taiping:
The Master said: "One should separately make new robes and completely replace those that are old; these 'old' ones refer precisely to these very robes. The commentary states:

"Regarding the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this does not refer to the clothing of the dead; rather, it refers to what has been picked up from the streets and successfully completed [as a robe].
Furthermore, a cloth that has covered a corpse does not qualify as [a *pāṃśukūla*], nor does one that has already been used to receive the *kaṭhina* robe.
Regarding the phrase "having completed [the robe]," *Lì* (Lìzǔ) says: "Last year, when the *kaṭhina* robe was about to be made, it was finished; now it is being made once again.
Regarding the phrase "if one folds leaves," *Lì* says: "This refers to the *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe), which has folded layers (*śatapattra*) placed upon it."

If one has received a robe during the period for urgent offerings (*ātyayika-cīvara*), one stands and says: "The 'timely robe' (*kālika-cīvara*) refers to the end of the summer retreat, from the sixteenth day of the seventh month onwards;
this is the robe for rewarding labor. As for those who practice it nowadays, they all claim that one may receive it as an urgent offering.
However, if this urgent offering was originally received outside of the [prescribed] time, or if at the time of its original reception, one intended—

Regarding the making of a *kaṭhina* robe (merit-cloth): it is indeed not permitted. As for what is said here regarding "obtaining" it, this refers to when one originally received the cloth without the intention to make it into a *kaṭhina* robe, but later unexpectedly had it made into a *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha; thus, it is obtained.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may make the three robes (*tricīvara*) from cloth that has never been used before.

This establishes that when a bhikṣu makes new three robes, he is permitted to do so provided they have not yet been worn; however, if they have already touched his body even once, he may no longer make them.
If one abandons the five matters for the sake of craving the five benefits and thus fails to accomplish them, it is established that this is clear:
if one accepts [the precepts] out of desire for the five benefits and does not do so with a mind intended to increase the merit of the donor, the acceptance is not accomplished.
Regarding the *Shanjian lü* (Sudarsana-vinaya), it states that the seven classes of practitioners may accept the *kaṭhina* robe, but it asks:

"As for the aforementioned rule that when the *guṇa-kaṭhina* robe is sent, it must be accepted on that very day and may not remain overnight, since it is now said that monks and nuns may act as donors, does this not imply that the robe was made within the boundary (*sīmā*)?"
Answer: Although one is within the boundary, there is no fault provided that the robe has not yet been given to the Saṃgha.
If it is taken out to be made into a *kaṭhina* robe, it must be received on that very day. Ji said: "Among the robes of the seven classes of followers, there are the robes of the two lay classes;
how could these be suitable for making a *kaṭhina* robe? This refers to the cloth worn upon the bodies of laypeople, which is taken and cut to be fashioned [into a robe].

Furthermore, if one receives even one or two of the three robes from among them, it means that when a layperson brings robes as an offering, one may accept and designate as *kaṭhina* one robe, two robes, or all three robes; it is not necessary to possess all three robes.
If a layperson says, "Take this robe and give it to the keeper of robes," one must also comply with their intention. It is the same for the five groups [of monastics] when they are producing [robes].
Lì said: "According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, among the three robes, one may produce a single robe according to whether it is of superior, middling, or inferior quality;
it is not necessary to produce all of them, but one may simply produce one now. He further said: "At most, one may produce the three robes. If...

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is essential that the *saṃghāṭī* be made of cut pieces for the formal acceptance (*upasaṃpadā*) to be valid; if the two lower robes are not so made, the acceptance is not valid.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that if the dimensions are reduced, the acceptance is likewise not valid. This concludes the explanation regarding the substance of the robes and the meaning of their validity or invalidity.
Third, regarding the distinction of persons: Li states that if one classifies those who may receive this robe according to person, it must be a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*.
This is because the three lower assemblies are not practitioners of the full path;

their labor is not weighty, and furthermore, they have no *saṃghāṭī* robes for which [the present case] serves as a substitute (the origin story [of the rule] was established because the *saṃghāṭī* is heavy, thus permitting this exception). How do we know now that the lower assemblies are not permitted to receive this robe?
Thus, in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), it is recorded that four bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇera were about to conclude their *varṣā* retreat.

[The bhikṣus] conferred the full ordination upon the śrāmaṇera so that they might reach the required number of five to receive the *kaṭhina* robe. Consequently, the newly ordained one also became eligible to receive the robe. The same applies to the case of one bhikṣu and four śrāmaṇeras.

This clearly demonstrates that śrāmaṇeras do not possess the formal procedure for receiving the *kaṭhina*. Nevertheless, this must be understood as being contingent upon the *varṣā* retreat within the context of those possessing full ordination (*upasampadā*).

One who has not entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*) may not receive [the robe]. Within the period of the rains retreat, one must restrict it to those who have entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*).
Even if one has entered the earlier retreat, if they have violated the retreat, they may not receive the robe.

Furthermore, regarding those who have not violated the retreat, even if they possess the *saṃghāṭī*, it must be within the boundary (*sīmā*) and before the Saṃgha; only then does one become a recipient of the robe. (From the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*).
One who is undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) may not receive robes; it must be five or more persons who may receive them, while four or fewer may not.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One does not receive [them] before the Saṃgha."

The *Shu* (Commentary) states that regarding one who gives their consent (*chanda*), [Daoshi] Li says: "This clarifies that if such a person is present, the acceptance [of the robe] is not accomplished.

That is to say, this person who gives consent does not obtain the five privileges, nor do they count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, if there are obstacles or if one lacks the *saṃghāṭī*, Li says:
"A person subject to the thirteen impediments is unfit to receive the *kaṭhina* robe, nor may they obtain the five privileges. This is profound.

Another interpretation states: "If there are difficulties within the boundary (*sīmā*), one may not receive the *kaṭhina* robe. *Ce* says: "If the eight difficulties arise, then one may not receive the *kaṭhina* robe.

Another interpretation states: "Even if it is the earlier retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*), because the summer retreat is broken by difficulties during the summer and one departs the boundary, the procedure for receiving [the robe] is not accomplished.
This interpretation is likely incorrect; if one does not have the *saṃghāṭī*, [one cannot receive it].

Regarding "the validity of the acceptance": because within the context of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), the primary purpose is the weight of the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe), one is permitted to accept the *guṇa-cīvara* (meritorious robe) so as to open up its five benefits (*pañca-lābha*).
Since these benefits cannot be obtained if the *saṃghāṭī* is lacking, the acceptance is not valid. As for the remaining two robes, whether they are missing or not, neither is considered excellent.
Regarding the phrase "and that [person] being outside the boundary," this establishes that although it is the earlier *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

If a person is outside the boundary when the Saṃgha is formally receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, this person does not obtain the five privileges. Furthermore, monks from another boundary may not receive it either;
this is because, although people from another boundary may come here to perform the ritual for the Saṃgha, they do not belong to this specific assembly.

However, the people of this realm do not receive the benefits. Regarding the various realms of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), when monks wish to receive robes and other items, according to an investigation of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, it says:
Upāli asked the Buddha: "When the monks have completed their rainy season retreat (*varṣa*), many monasteries may collectively establish a single boundary (*sīmā*) to receive the *kaṭhina* robe.
After receiving the robe, they relinquish this great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). Having relinquished it, they then relinquish the *kaṭhina*."

[Question: Regarding robes, do all bhikṣus come to be said to have relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe? [Answer: Yes; those who relinquish it have accomplished the relinquishment, while those who do not relinquish it have not.
[Commentary: The above clarifies that monks from various different territories (*sīmā*) wish to collectively receive [the *kaṭhina*].
Not knowing by what means this could be accomplished, the Buddha ordered each to relinquish their respective original territory so that they might collectively receive it together.

Regarding "renunciation": if renunciation is accomplished, those who do not renounce rely on the five benefits (*pañcānuśaṃsa*). This is established as clear: once the robe has been collectively accepted, it is immediately released.

The previous boundary for accepting robes is dissolved, and each person separately establishes a new boundary, whereby each is permitted to receive the five benefits. If that is the case for the Saṃgha of that boundary...

In this context, one’s own relinquishment constitutes a valid relinquishment; however, for other realms where relinquishment has not yet been formally declared, it does not constitute a valid relinquishment, and thus it is said that one must rely on the benefits [of the precepts].

A *śrāmaṇera* who undergoes training through repentance (*śikṣādattaka*) is precisely a person who has committed a grave offense and is undergoing training through repentance. Because those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a formal expulsion (*pārājika*), or similar transgressions possess an impure body, they are ineligible to receive [the precepts].

The preceding section has concluded the discussion on those who receive the robes. Below, the text correctly clarifies the person who holds them. This refers to one who knows with perfect clarity what may and may not be received; such a person is established as the "holder of the robe.

He must possess five virtues and must know that those who have broken their summer retreat (*varṣa*), those who have not observed the *anvārohana* (the supplementary retreat), and those who lack the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) and other requisites are not permitted to receive them.
Conversely, those who do not fall into these categories are permitted to receive them; therefore, it is said: "knowing what may be received and what may not."
"It is received.

Regarding "the rest is the same as the distribution of light items," this clarifies that the distribution of these articles is identical to the distribution of the deceased bhikṣu’s property. Light items should be divided;
heavy items belong to the permanently resident Sangha (*sthavira-saṃgha*). This refers to the end of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), when laypeople often obtain both light and heavy items.

This concerns items given to the Saṃgha. Sengzhao states: "This refers to what is obtained during the [proper] time; therefore, there is a dual classification based on whether the items are light or heavy.
In the present day, this mostly occurs on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. When one obtains clothing or other requisites, they are simply termed 'non-time' items for those present;
thus, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, they must all be divided among those present. Furthermore, if a donor brings items to offer during the [proper] time..."

One must inquire about the donor’s intention: is the gift intended for those who have entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer retreat) within this specific boundary, or is it offered generally to the monastic community (*saṃgha*) of both monks and nuns throughout the entire region?
If the answer is that it is for those entering the retreat within this boundary, it is termed a "present-time offering" (*pratyakṣadāna*), which is precisely what is clarified in the current text.
However, if one says that the disciple offers it generally to all those entering the retreat, regardless of whether they are early or late entrants—[then it is otherwise].
This refers to the alms received by the Saṃgha during the [rainy season] period. It must be divided only after performing a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to establish the limits.
Regarding what was mentioned above concerning "alms for those present at the time," no *karmavācanā* is required because it is determined by four fixed factors:

first, the time is fixed, being restricted to the sixteenth day of the seventh month; second, the location is fixed, being restricted to this specific boundary (*sīmā*); third, the persons are fixed, being restricted to those who have entered the prior retreat (*pūrvavarṣika*).
Furthermore, regarding the four fixed rules (*dharmas*): it is simply a matter of several people consulting one another and distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*).

Although ancient masters also maintained that the *karmavācanā* ritual must be performed, the author of the *Śāstra* (the *Chao*) does not include this. If a donor says, "I am keeping these three robes;

give them all to the one who keeps the robes," it is clearly established that one must follow the donor's intent. Nevertheless, if one already possesses the three robes oneself, one may act according to that [donor's] wish; however, if...
Regarding heavy objects, they definitely fall under the category of permanent property (*saṃghika*).
The *Vyākhyāna on the Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "At the time of the initial *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), those who wish to receive [robes] and so forth establish a clear rule:
if someone says during the summer, 'If robes should arrive later, I am willing to accept them,' the Saṃgha must deliberate upon this person. What [kind of person is this]?
"Similar to [the above]," etc. If the person is wicked, one must not entrust them with it.
From this point onward, the fourth method for receiving robes is correctly explained.

Regarding the statement that "sixteen thousand bhikṣus surrounded [the Buddha]," the *Lì* (立) commentary states that because their minds were reverent, they gathered around to observe and contemplate. The *Jiànjiàn lùn* (檢見論) says: "The Dharma..."
The Master said: "Why are you so earnest regarding the *kaṭhina* robe? Because it was praised by the Buddha.
Long ago, there was a Buddha named Padma Tathāgata. He had a śrāvaka disciple named Sujāta who had begun making a *kaṭhina* robe but had not yet finished it.
Then, Padma Tathāgata, surrounded by sixteen thousand bhikṣus, together with him, made the *kaṭhina*."
Regarding the phrase "that robe...
thus five patches, etc.": this clarifies that, fearing it might come undone, one must make four horizontal seams;
two at each end and three in the center.
The Elder addressed the assembly, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today the community of monks is receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.

Having recited this *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion), he informed the Saṃgha that they wished to receive the *kaṭhina* robe; thereafter, he immediately performed the *karman* for appointing the person to hold the robe, as may be found in the text.
Lì asked: "In the procedure for the *pravāraṇā*, why is the appointment made first and the formal motion (*jñapti*) follows? Why is it different in this procedure for receiving the robe?"

First there is the announcement (*jñapti*), followed by the appointment (*niyoga*). This is because it is performed for the sake of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*). First there is the appointment, and afterwards the announcement.

Receiving the robe is an exception; if one does not receive it, there is no fault. Because it is not known whether one will receive it or not, it is necessary to first announce and then appoint. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen:
the robes and other items obtainable by the Saṃgha at this residence..."—this is the core of the *karmavācanā* text. At this time, the fundamental matter regarding the robes is set forth.
The "robe for rewarding labor" (*śāngláo yī*) refers to a robe that is currently available for distribution.

Since it is now to be designated as a *kaṭhina* (功德衣) robe, the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the matter is immediately set forth: "The Saṃgha now takes this robe and gives it to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Bhikṣu so-and-so shall take this robe and, on behalf of the Saṃgha, receive it and make it into a *kaṭhina* robe," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "one who maintains [the robe] at this dwelling place," the *Lìjiè* (Exegesis on the Grinding) explains:

This is to demonstrate that such a person is not entitled to the benefit of the robe, as the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding this robe is specifically entrusted to him. Master Bīn says: However, when performing the ritual, one must carefully select those participating in the formal act;
it should be performed in the center of the assembled Saṃgha. If, for instance, there are many rows of benches in the hall, the formal act should be performed upon the central row of benches.

In such a case, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) performed by the person previously seated on the bed is valid; however, because the person subsequently using the bed sits with their back turned toward the former, the procedure is not accomplished.

Furthermore, if one does not distinguish those who have already performed the ritual from those sitting in the same place—such as those separated by a boundary, those who are not part of the preceding *anvārohaṇa* (summer retreat), or those who have broken the summer retreat—the count of persons eligible to receive the robe would be corrupted by including individuals who do not qualify.
If those who are entitled to receive [the robes] sit intermingled with others, or if they are separated by a threshold or an open space,
such that the persons entitled to receive the robes are each beyond arm’s reach of one another, the ritual is not valid.
"This robe the community of monks shall accept to make into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe the community of monks now accepts to make into a *kaṭhina* robe;
this robe the community of monks has already accepted to make into a *kaṭhina* robe. These were established as the three recitations.

In the Vinaya, Upāli immediately asked the Buddha regarding these nine phrases concerning the acceptance of the robe: "The phrase 'shall accept' refers to the future; the next phrase [refers to the present]..."
"Receiving now" refers to the present; "having already received" refers to the past. Since these phrases are stated three times, are they not nine?
This is because there are three [phrases] for each of the three time periods. Question: In which time period does one receive the *kaṭhina* robe? Answer:

The Buddha spoke of nine phrases for the sake of completeness, Venerable Upāli; however, one does not receive the *kaṭhina* robe by means of the three phrases of the past, nor by means of the [three phrases of the future].
The three phrases regarding the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe in the future are precisely the three phrases for accepting the *kaṭhina* robe in the present.
Why is this? Because the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; therefore, one accepts the *kaṭhina* robe in the present.
Those bhikṣus should speak as follows: "The recipient has properly received it. (Lì says: This clarifies the assembly.)
The Saṃgha accepts it. To demonstrate that the holding of the robe accords with the Dharma, it says, "it has been well accepted.

Regarding the statement, "Whatever merit and reputation herein belong to me," this is established for clarity: because the person holding the robe does not receive the five benefits, and those benefits belong to the bhikṣus, it is said that the reputation belongs to me.
As for the phrase "merit and reputation": "gong" (功) refers to labor or service, and "de" (德) refers to virtue.
These are the virtues of practice; "renown" refers to these five benefits. Because one attains these five benefits, there is no occurrence of breaking the precepts;
as virtuous qualities shine forth brilliantly, it is called "renown. Lì says: since the merits of these five benefits are free from fault, [they are so named].
Its beautiful resonance manifests outwardly; therefore, it is called "renown. Because it causes me to obtain these five benefits, its name belongs to me.
To answer "yes" means, as the *Lì* (Commentary) says, that the person holding the robe speaks words of agreement and compliance.
Furthermore, regarding the detailed explanation of the forfeiture of essential requisites, this refers to the eight types and ten types mentioned in the subsequent text.

As for the various methods of forfeiture found in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, according to an examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika* text itself, there are ten types of forfeiture: first, forfeiture upon the completion of [the making of] a robe.
1. Abandonment upon receiving; 2. Abandonment when finished; 3. Abandonment upon hearing; 4. Abandonment through a transgression;

5. Abandonment through pregnancy; 6. Abandonment through loss; 7. Abandonment through departure; 8. Abandonment when time has passed; 9. Abandonment upon completion. Regarding the first, "abandonment upon completion": while receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, one forms this thought:
"When my robe-making is finished, I shall relinquish the *kaṭhina*. Once the robe is made, [it is abandoned].

First, "abandonment by name": it is so called because at the very moment of receiving [the robe], one abandons the *kaṭhina*. Second, "abandonment upon receiving": one forms this thought, "At the time I receive this robe, I shall abandon the *kaṭhina*";
because it is abandoned at the very moment of receiving the robe, it is so called. Third, "abandonment at the end of the period":

one forms this thought, "For such a length of time, I shall maintain the *kaṭhina*, and once that period is fulfilled, I shall abandon it"; because it is abandoned immediately upon the completion of the stipulated time, it is so called.

Regarding the fourth, "abandonment through hearing": one forms this thought: "I heard that when my preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya) were abandoning the *kaṭhina* robe, I too shall abandon it.
Later, hearing the preceptor and teacher say, "Today the Saṃgha abandons the *kaṭhina* robe," at that moment it is called abandoned;
thus it is said. Regarding the fifth, "abandonment through [the robe] being given away": one forms this thought: "I have already given this robe to another."

Regarding the "abandonment by relinquishing" (*nissaggiya*): after the *kaṭhina* robe has been formally sent out, it is said to be "abandoned" because it is immediately designated as discarded. Regarding the "abandonment by destruction":
after having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, one says of one's own accord in the interim, "I now abandon the *kaṭhina* robe. At the moment these words are spoken, [the *kaṭhina* is abandoned].
It is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) because it is so designated. Regarding the seventh abandonment, one forms this thought:
"If this robe becomes torn or ruined in the interim and is no longer present, I shall abandon [the *kaṭhina*]; if the subsequent robe becomes torn or ruined and is lost, I shall abandon it.

It is called "abandonment" because it is so designated. Regarding the eighth abandonment, one forms this thought: "While I am staying here, when I go out, I shall abandon the *kaṭhina* robe. If, at the time of going out...
"Leaving" refers to what is called "renouncing"; thus it is said. Regarding "renouncing after nine times have passed":

if one does not renounce on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, but reaches the sixteenth day, it is then called "renouncing," and one incurs the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*; thus it is said. Tenth is "ultimate renunciation."
On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, it should be relinquished. One person among the assembly of monks should make this proclamation:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the kaṭhina robe. This is said because it is recited three times in this manner. Regarding the eight types and ten types [of relinquishment] in other schools, Master Li states:

"The ten types appear in the *Cīvara-vastu* (Text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*), as has already been explained above; the eight types appear in the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Mother of the Vinaya)."

The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] is divided into four parts. Within the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, there are eight types of relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*). The first six are relinquishments through formal commitment (*samaya-pratyākhyāna*); the latter two are relinquishments through ritual action (*karmavācanā-pratyākhyāna*).

1. Relinquishment by departure (*gata-pratyākhyāna*). 2. Relinquishment upon completion (*paryavasita-pratyākhyāna*). 3. Relinquishment before completion (*aparyavasita-pratyākhyāna*). 4. Relinquishment by loss (*naṣṭa-pratyākhyāna*). The verse says: Departure, completion, non-completion, loss, and expectation;

hearing, silent knowledge, and the five combined expectations—these constitute relinquishment. Sixth is relinquishment by hearing (*śruta-pratyākhyāna*); seventh is relinquishment by silent acquiescence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva-pratyākhyāna*) (also called...).

Regarding "renunciation by going out of bounds" (*sīmātikrānta-tyāga*): there are eight ways of renouncing through one's own arrival and communal agreement. First, concerning "renunciation by departing": this refers to the time when one has not yet accepted the benefit (*lābha*).
One forms the following mental resolve: "If I remain here to make the robe, I shall accept the benefit;

if I go out of bounds, I shall not accept the benefit. Therefore, one does not make the robe now. When one departs from the boundary, because this action accords with that original intention, it constitutes renunciation.

Lì says: "Regarding 'resolving the mind' (*yàoxīn*): it may refer to resolving the mind at the time of actually leaving the boundary, or it may refer to resolving the mind at the original time of receiving the robe.
It is called this because as soon as one makes a firm decision to depart, the virtuous robe (*déyī*) is lost.

The following sections are all Lì’s explanations based on the Vinaya texts. "Second, 'abandoning'" means that originally there was no intention to abandon [the robe] by departing via the aforementioned gate; therefore, although...

"Leaving the boundary does not constitute relinquishment. This refers to a case where one lacks the two lower robes and seeks the materials for obtaining robes, intending to make them within this boundary.
One's original formal resolve (*samādāna*) was: "If I make the robes and receive the benefit [of the robe-material], yet once the robes are finished, I shall not accept the benefit.

Later, when the robes are completed, one fulfills that original resolve; this is called "relinquishment by completion. For this reason, it is not said that one lacks the three robes, but only that one lacks [the specific condition].

Regarding the "two lower robes": this means that such a person must already possess a *saṃghāṭī*. If the *saṃghāṭī* is lacking, it is fundamentally not permissible for them to receive the *kaṭhina* robe.
Therefore, only the two lower robes are mentioned. Master Bin said: "Although we now speak of the two lower robes, this is based on the specific circumstances;

nevertheless, it would also be appropriate to mention the making of a *kūṭa* (patch). Regarding "not relinquishing the three before the end": this also refers to the absence of the aforementioned [conditions].

The intention to leave [the robes] behind persists even after one has crossed the boundary; that is, this person leaves two robes and their materials within the boundary, and at the time of crossing the boundary, makes a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying:
"I shall return and make [a robe]; if I do not have the leisure to make it, I will not return to the place where the robes are.
Once he has reached the outside, he reflects: "I am also unable to make the robe, as it would hinder my practice of the Path."
Once the mental resolve has been severed and no longer maintained, one does not return to the original location; therefore, it is called "incomplete relinquishment.
Because this essential condition existed from the beginning, even an incomplete relinquishment constitutes a valid renunciation. Regarding the fourth type of loss through relinquishment:

it refers to the mental resolve at the time of receiving [the *kaṭhina* robe], wherein one originally received the *kaṭhina* robe for the purpose of making a garment. Now, in this mountain monastery, there are many thieves and robbers; if one loses either of the two robes or their value—
If one does nothing, then no benefit is received. Later, when the object is stolen by another and taken away, if it accords with one's original intention, one relinquishes it;
this is therefore called "loss and relinquishment. For such a person, there is likewise no essential distinction between whether the previous [act] has been completed or not completed.
Thus, although the ritual (*dharma*) and its completion may not constitute a formal relinquishment, there is only the loss of the merit. Therefore, one now returns to the original requirement.

It is said: "First, one relinquishes. Regarding the relinquishment through the severance of the five expectations, this also refers to the absence of the necessity for coming and going as mentioned above.
When receiving the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe), one makes a formal resolve (*niyama*), saying: "I wish to make the two lower robes; I shall go to such-and-such a village, and shall not go further.

Even if one goes to that village first, the request [for the robe] is not invalidated; rather, it remains valid because the original resolve was made at many points during that time. If one subsequently goes elsewhere...

Village. It is also as before: if the request is not fulfilled, it is immediately lost. The Vinaya also states: "Loss through the continuation of expectation. This refers to the original intention, saying:

"I wish to go to such-and-such a place to seek clothing and wealth. If I do not obtain clothing at that expected location, but there is another location where I continue to have expectations, I shall not relinquish my claim to the profit.
However, if my expectation for the former location is severed and I have no further expectation for the latter, I shall relinquish the profit."

"Subsequently reaching the point where expectation ceases" means that there is no further expectation to continue. This refers to having gone out to beg for alms and arriving at a previous house where nothing was obtained;

this constitutes a severance. Since there is subsequently no place where expectation can resume, one returns to the original intention; therefore, it is called "abandonment through the cessation of expectation. Sixth, "abandonment upon hearing":

this also refers to the fact that originally there was no fixed intention regarding the completion of the journey, and thus one does not abandon [the vow] upon completing the journey. It simply means that once the robe has been accepted, [one maintains] the original intention.

The mind has gone beyond the boundary. If one hears that the Sangha is relinquishing [the robe], thinking, "I too shall relinquish the robe," and subsequently hears that the Sangha has indeed relinquished it, thereby fulfilling the original intention of the mind, this is called "hearing the relinquishment.
This hearing applies to both the real and the unreal. A guest asked: "It suffices that one hears of the relinquishment for the [robe] to be lost;

it does not matter whether the person before one actually relinquished it or did not. Even if it is a false report, upon hearing it, the [robe] is lost. Question: "If one hears that the Sangha has relinquished [it]..."

Regarding "one who has heard the essential matter": if the Sangha has already completed the relinquishment, why wait for the essential intention (*āśaya*)? Furthermore, if the essential intention were not required, then upon hearing [the announcement], the [right to] the robe would not be lost.
Now, to explain "hearing": it means hearing that a specific individual within the Sangha did not receive the benefit of the robe.

Therefore, this is called "the robe being issued from the Sangha. As for the word "issued" (*niṣṛta*), it is a synonym for "relinquished" or "lost. This is the interpretation of Li; its intent clarifies the location where the virtuous robe is received.
There was a virtuous elder (*bhadanta*) of great renown and high esteem. A certain bhikṣu made a solemn vow, saying: "If this elder accepts a gain, I shall accept a gain;
if this person renounces the gain, I too shall not accept a gain. Once that man had gone outside the boundary to seek wealth, he later heard that the elder had already renounced the gain.
Thereupon, he gave rein to his original evil intent. Therefore it is said: "Hearing of the renunciation" (Lì says: as above).

Six matters (if there is no intentional resolve, there are six cases of non-forfeiture). Seventh, having accepted [the precepts], one leaves the boundary and the Saṃgha is in harmony and relinquishes them; this is also called "relinquishment by remaining hidden."

This refers to a person who, having accepted [the benefits], has gone outside the boundary (*sīmā*). While inside the boundary, the community of monks, led by the presiding elder, grants the five privileges (*pañcavastu*) to him;

however, he becomes distracted and does not cultivate the practice of the Path. Consequently, the Sangha assembles in harmony and relinquishes [the privileges]. That person, being outside the boundary, is unaware and loses [the benefits] on his own. If he does not know that they have been relinquished, there is no offense regarding the acceptance of the benefits.

This is the eighth case of relinquishment through harmony (*saṃghasāmagrī-pratiniḥsarga*). It means that after having accepted [them], one goes outside the boundary and, having departed, does not return at all.
Because the intention was ultimately firm, even though he departed later, whether the time had elapsed or not, neither case resulted in the loss [of the formal act].

Since he returned to within the boundary and was unable to receive benefits, he abandoned [the act] in harmony with the Saṃgha; therefore, it is called "abandonment through harmony" (*saṃghasāmagrī-pratyākhyāna*). The *Liaojian* states: "The six cases above constitute abandonment through the firmness of intention;

the two cases below constitute abandonment through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*)". It further says that in each case, although they contravene one's original intention, all are established as abandonment.
Among these eight types, the first six are so called because they contradict one's original intention.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the various meanings of relinquishing robes. From this point forward, the names and characteristics of the five benefits are clarified.
This refers to the meaning of the inclusion of the timely (*kāla*) and the untimely (*akāla*). The commentary states:

"Regarding the inclusion of the timely and the untimely, this has already been explained above in the section on the gradual increase [of robes] concerning the robe given in haste (*ātyayika-cīvara*). If there is a *kaṭhina* robe, it is from the middle of the seventh month onwards."

The entire period from the beginning until the next [period] is called "proper time" (*kāla*). The period before the middle of the seventh month and after the middle of the twelfth month is called "improper time" (*akāla*).
This means that proper time naturally encompasses proper time, and improper time naturally encompasses improper time; thus they are said to be mutually inclusive.

Regarding "proper time encompassing proper time," this refers to obtaining extra robes during a period of proper time and being required to perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification by declaration) within that same period of proper time. Improper time likewise naturally encompasses [itself].

"Non-seasonal" refers to the sequence of increased urgency regarding the offering of robes (*akālacīvara*). This meaning will be explained below, within the section on the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, at the end of the explanation for the precept concerning the robe offered in times of urgency.
A detailed citation from the *Shoushu* (Commentary by Shou) explaining this is provided as follows, which shall be clarified later.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of how the characteristics of "timely" (*kāla*) and "untimely" (*akāla*) robes subsume one another: Ji states that for the sake of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), those [robes] are designated as "timely robes.
If they are obtained during the [prescribed] time, they must be formally declared within that same time; one may not combine them with days outside of that period.

If the robe is obtained at an untimely moment, it is subsumed by its own characteristic of being untimely; likewise, one may not discuss it in conjunction with days of the [prescribed] time. This concludes the preceding section.

Beginning with the proclamation of the fundamental tenets and the manifestation of virtues, and concluding with the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) which is the essential core, there are twelve sections of text;

these constitute the communal (*saṃgha*) dharmas. Although among them there are not lacking the methods for individuals, such as those performed in the presence of another or by mental recollection (*manasikāra*), they all serve to accomplish the practice of communal dharmas.
If one now takes up the fundamental tenets to encompass them, they all fall within the meaning of being gathered into the net of communal dharmas.
Commentary on the *Sifenlü Chao*, Fascicle Six, Part One; Fascicle Six, Part Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Names of the *Piñjū* (Articles of the Code).

From the beginning, where the fundamental principles were established, until the conclusion with the *Pravāraṇā*, there have been twelve chapters; these clarify the *Saṃghadharma* (Rules for the Community) to completion.

Although these are termed "rules for the community," they are also permitted to be maintained by individuals through face-to-face (*pratimukha*) or mental (*manasikāra*) procedures when the assembly is incomplete. Now, following the root...

This is subsumed under the fundamental [category]. Since it pertains exclusively to the administration of the *saṃgha*’s legal procedures (*dharmas*), it is called "the laws of the assembly" (*saṃghadharma*).

Alternatively, this section may be designated as the "Treatise on the Fundamental Principles," as its meaning encompasses both the communal and the individual. Only from the "Section on Assembling the Saṃgha" onwards is it properly termed "the laws of the assembly.

From this present section onward, the text clarifies the methods for the individual practitioner’s own conduct; thus, the preface states: "The first volume subsumes the communal affairs, wherein the performance of functions follows established ritual. The middle...

This middle fascicle follows the precept essence (*śīla-tattva*), establishing the methods for observance, violation, and repentance; thus, from this section onward constitutes the middle fascicle. Furthermore, it is said:

"The preceding fascicle has already clarified the accomplishment of active observance (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) and conduct, yet the method of prohibitive observance (*vārita-dhāraṇa*) and the characteristics of prohibitive observance have not been distinguished.

Since these cannot precede the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, we shall now, based upon the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, explain their manifestations; therefore, we first clarify the names and essences of the categories of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*)."
This chapter was composed because [the author] wished to cause practitioners to harbor a sense of weariness toward and detachment from the retributive fruits of karma.

Thus, as Ciyun said: "The preceding volume has already completed the exposition of the various practices; one must now further clarify the specific practices. In principle, one must understand and master what constitutes upholding and violating the precepts, and extensively reveal their allowances and prohibitions.
There should follow a text concerning the characteristics of purity; to clarify these characteristics, one must first recognize the categories of the *pien* (offenses) and *ju* (aggregates)."
This is to distinguish between the names and the retributive fruits; therefore, this chapter is explained first. To explain the title:

regarding the statement that the *piān* (sections) and *jù* (clusters) are called "retribution" (*bào*), the *piān* refers to the five sections (*pañca-varga*) and the *jù* refers to the seven clusters (*sapta-nikāya*), as is extensively clarified in the text. As for the characteristics of these sections and clusters:

if one violates them in accordance with these categories, one shall incur the faculty of suffering; hence the name. The *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The *piān* are the chapters and divisions..."
"Jiaming" (Elegant Name) refers to the specific title of a section. "Pian" (Chapter) is the name for a fascicle. Prior to the Han dynasty, paper did not yet exist;
bamboo, wood, and silk were used instead, and records were inscribed upon them. It was during the Later Han that Cai Lun invented paper.

Using plain and simple materials, ancient books were written on bamboo slips; even if there were but a single chapter, they would be bound together with leather thongs and designated as a "pian" (fascicle).
We now follow this principle and provide it with this name. As for what is called a "collection," an ancient commentator explained that the various offenses are not merely one.
Gathered together in one place, it is called a "heap" (*piṇḍa*). The commentary explains: "The ancients termed it a 'heap' because they bound the offenses together according to their names.

Thus, the *Liwen* asks: "Since there is no separate text for the *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses, why are they called a 'heap'? The answer is: "They are called a 'heap' because they are contained within the great heap."
Alternatively, they may be gathered under a single name. If one were to cite a single name and issue a summons, then there would be no *sthūlātyaya* left unexhausted.

(The intent of this question refutes the ancient interpretation. The ancients explained that "gathering" means to assemble various offenses in one place. However, one may only say they are gathered under a single name; one cannot say they are gathered in one place. Thus, the *Xin shu* says:
"If it were as the former interpretation regarding *sthūlātyaya* and 'evil speech,' where would they be gathered? Furthermore, it is like not relying on others during the summer retreat."

Regarding those who commit offenses leading to *pāyattika* (falling away): these are not included within the *śīla-mūla* (Roots of the Precepts), up to and including being dealt with according to the Dharma;

their manifestations are limitless and are not subsumed under the *śīla-mūla*. Where, then, are they gathered? Therefore, this is not the same as in the past. Now, they are merely categorized by name, yet there are no offenses that are not fully accounted for; the meaning is thus understandable.

As for "names," this refers to the specific categories of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, and *pratideśanīya*. As for "retribution," it is discussed in terms of the commission of the offense.
The retributions differ in degree of severity. For a violation of the *pārājika* (defeats), one is reborn in hell for nine hundred twenty-one billion sixty thousand years.
For the four lower categories of offenses, the successive stages of retribution are as described in the *Maudgalyāyana-questions-on-retribution-for-offenses Sūtra* cited below.
Therefore it is said that the title of this chapter is "Recompense.

That it serves as a fertile field for the world is truly due to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*); this means that it exists because of the presence of the unmanifest precept-essence (*avijñapti-śīla-tattva*).
Upholding untainted purity is the field for worldly beings to cultivate merit. If one is able to practice giving within this field, one will certainly obtain the benefit of a reciprocal reward;
because the field is pure, it can cause the seeds and sprouts of virtue to grow.
If one lacks these precepts, even one’s own various virtuous merits will not arise—how then could one produce the merit of others? Therefore, as for worldly people...
Those who are not fields of merit are so because they lack the precepts.

Because monks and nuns possess the precepts, they are able to cultivate and give rise to samādhi, develop wisdom, sever delusions, and ultimately obtain the benefits of the Path. Since the holy ones of the Three Vehicles all receive these precepts, a sutra says:
"With pure precepts and wisdom, one immediately attains the foremost Path. Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "The precepts are like the bright sun."
The moon is also like a pearl in a necklace; through it, the multitude of bodhisattvas achieves perfect enlightenment.
Because they have accomplished conduct free from defilement and possess the causal seeds of the Three Vehicles, it is called a "fertile field.

Just as in the world’s fields of merit, where there is no sandy wasteland or weeds, one is able to sow seeds that will surely grow into magnificent sprouts. It is said: "Now, at the beginning of this chapter, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is first expounded."

What is his intention? It is because he wishes to clarify the names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) of upholding and violating the precepts that he first discusses their essential nature (*tattva*).

Only when there is an essential nature can one discuss violations; if there were no essential nature as a basis, there would be no transgression. Thus, he sets forth the reasons for his fundamental tenets (*mūla-siddhānta*); these principles are not recounted in vain.

Regarding the statement that "upholding the prohibitive precepts constitutes the nature [of a field of merit] and shaving the hair constitutes its characteristic," this is intended to clarify that only when both nature and characteristic are complete can one be properly called a *puṇyakṣetra* (field of merit).
If one takes only the characteristic—as with non-Buddhists who also shave their hair—it does not qualify as a field of merit because they lack the precepts.
The *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* states: "Wearing the *kāṣāya* robe is the characteristic of liberation for all Buddhas; it is also called..."
It is the great banner of the True Dharma; it is also the banner of the flavor of liberation in the Mahāyāna. The meaning is this:

according to the characteristics of this banner, whether one is a field of merit by virtue of being upright, or lacks precepts and is a breaker of them, both are fit to be called a "field. However, in the latter case, the benefit and merit are diminished, and thus it cannot be called a "fertile field" (kṣetra).
Therefore, the text below says: "Blessing arises from a pure field; the Path arises from few desires. Now, regarding nature and characteristics...
Only these two constitute the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Now, regarding the phrase "if one makes the mind as pure as ice," "ice" implies firmness and "pure" implies clarity.

By firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts with a pure mind free from defilement, one is able to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it is said that this generates the seeds of goodness. This clarifies the present.
Monks and nuns: if their conduct is like ice and frost and their minds are like clear water, they are fit to serve as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Regarding the statement that "jade moistens its virtue," this is to clarify that jade is lustrous, beautiful, and highly prized by people. Jade possesses ten virtues, as clarified in other records.
Now, if the precepts of monks and nuns are pure and clean, they are esteemed by all beings; like jade, they are worthy of honor. Therefore, it is said:
This is virtue. This virtue is worthy of being treasured; it is as precious as jade. Therefore, it is said that "jade moistens its virtue.

Because jade can moisten things, it is used as a metaphor for the virtue of the precepts (*śīla*), which likewise can moisten things and provide a conduit for the myriad phenomena. Ji said: "The nature of jade is luminous and moist.
Wearing it makes the body lustrous and supple. One may observe that those in the jade trade nowadays soak the jade in water during the winter months with their hands..."

"Not crippled" means that they are able to produce the seeds of goodness and are called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). This concludes the preceding text, establishing the meaning of being a "virtuous field for the world.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples is fully endowed with the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, and the aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; these four pairs and eight classes are worthy of receiving offerings.
To make offerings to, revere, and serve them is the unsurpassed field of merit in the world. It is like a fertile field that has been plowed, tilled, and made supple;
if one sows seeds at the proper time and irrigates it until it is rich and lush, the harvest will surely be abundant. The Sangha as a field of merit is likewise:
with the plow of wisdom, they till out the roots of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and with the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they cultivate and soften it. [The donor] gives... (dāna).
If one takes even a small measure of grain from a faithful donor’s gift and irrigates it with the water of a mind of mindfulness, generosity, reverence, and purity,
one will obtain immeasurable worldly happiness and the fruits of the Three Vehicles in either this life or future lives—
just as the bhikṣu Bakula did when, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he offered a single *harītakī* fruit to the Saṃgha and, for ninety-one kalpas, [resided] among gods and humans.

In the interim, he experienced the fruits of merit and bliss, remaining forever free from illness. Now, having encountered Śākyamuni Buddha, he left the household life, exhausted his outflows, and attained the state of an Arhat.
Furthermore, it was like the case of the bhikṣu Viśākha (Twenty-Crore-Ears):

during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he built a dwelling and covered the floor with materials to offer to the Saṃgha; for ninety-one kalpas, he experienced the fruits of merit and bliss among gods and humans.

As for the fruit [of his merit]: when he was born, his feet did not touch the ground, and the hair on the soles of his feet was two inches long. Later, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Among all the disciples, he was foremost in diligence. Thus, through such a small gift, he obtained a great reward.
Therefore, one should know that the Saṃgha is the unsurpassed field of merit. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there was once the son of an elder in the kingdom of Campā.
(Shoulongna, whose family name was Sifen). His household was wealthy and prosperous. From beneath his feet grew hair that was golden in color and four inches long.
When he walked, he would spread a cloth mat upon the ground and tread upon it as he went. Later, he came to where the Buddha was;

seeing the World-Honored One sitting in the open air from afar, he immediately withdrew his cloth mat and approached treading directly upon the ground. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "This youth... (9)
For eleven kalpas, his feet have never trodden upon the ground.

Because he now beholds me with reverence, he once spread a single white cotton cloth upon the earth to make offerings to the Saṃgha during a past life; as a result of that karmic fruit, for ninety-one kalpas...

Having been born among gods and humans, he had never before trodden upon the ground. When the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he immediately left the household life and applied himself with diligence to ascetic practice.
At the place where he walked in the Śītavana (Cemetery Forest), his blood flowed and stained the earth until it resembled a slaughterhouse.

Consequently, the Buddha permitted the wearing of leather sandals; otherwise, those who would reject [such things]—meaning those who do not seek to purify their minds as described above, like the smooth luster of jade—would be acting contrary to this.

Because of such qualities, it is said that this is not so. Rather, it is said because they indulge the three poisons and the four inversions of affliction, thereby rejecting and refusing the Buddha’s teaching.
"Indulge" (zòng) means to allow oneself license; "reject" (jù) means to oppose or resist, which is also called to defy (kàng).

This refers to indulging in ordinary worldly sentiments while opposing and violating the sacred teachings. Regarding the phrase "one brings calamity upon oneself," the *Erbǐ* states: "To bring" (yí) means to leave behind; "to leave behind" (yí) means to bestow.
Furthermore, *yi* (貽) means "to summon" or "to invite. *I* (伊) is a particle used to introduce a statement; it also means "you," "deeply," or "intimately. *Qi* (戚) means "sorrow" or "affliction.
This clarifies that one who violates the teachings summons their own suffering; it is not bestowed by another.

Regarding the phrase "thereby summoning the transgressions of the six categories," this refers to the matter of faults and errors. That is to say, whatever offense one commits, one will inevitably be ensnared by that violation.

The net completes their transgressions; this is the formal adjudication within the six categories of offenses (*ṣaṭ-nikāya*). Regarding the statement that they enter the eightfold hells of retribution, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 19, states:
"There are eight great hells surrounding one another. As for the "eight great" [hells], they are: first, the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell; second, the Kālasūtra (Black Rope) Hell;
third, the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell; fourth, the Raurava (Crying Out) Hell; fifth, the Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out) Hell; sixth, the Tapana (Heating) Hell... [and so forth].
Seven: the Great Burning Hell; Eight: the Avīci Hell. Each of these great hells is surrounded by sixteen minor hells.
Regarding these sixteen minor hells, the verse says: Black, Boiling, Nails, Hunger, Thirst, Copper, Many Stones, Pus, and Measurement.
Ash, Iron, *Jin*, Wolf, and Sword; Cold Ice, the sixteenth. First is Black Sand; second, Boiling Excrement; third, Five Hundred Nails;
fourth, Hunger; fifth, Thirst; sixth, Copper Cauldron; seventh, Many Copper Cauldrons; eighth, Stone Mill; ninth, Pus and Blood; tenth, Measuring Fire;
eleventh, Ash River; twelfth, Iron Balls; thirteenth, Axes and Hatchets; fourteenth, Wolves; fifteenth, Swords.
The Tree Hell. Regarding the sixteen Cold Ice Hells and the Thought Hell (*saṃjñā-naraka*):

since these sixteen minor hells surround [the main hell], and even the Avīci Hell possesses these same sixteen, their names are identical to those mentioned previously; thus, they constitute one hundred and thirty-six hells in total.
Furthermore, according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, this is likewise the case; the names are largely the same, with the exception that the initial "Thought Hell" is changed [to "Great Thought Hell"].
It is called the Saṃjīva Hell, followed by the Avīci Hell, which is renamed the Abhi Hell.
This Abhi Hell is located at the very bottom beneath Jambudvīpa; immediately above it is the Saṃghāta (Fire-Burning) Hell.
Thus, starting from the top, these are the seven hells. Each individual hell has four gates. This is the first [section].
Each gate has four retinues, totaling sixteen retinues. Including the principal [hell] itself and its retinues, there are seventeen.
Since the Avīci hell already possesses these seventeen, the other seven hells likewise each possess seventeen; thus, in total, there are one hundred and thirty-six.
The differences in the suffering experienced therein are as recorded in detail elsewhere (*etc.*). Furthermore, according to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*...
This is obscure in the sutra and is likewise the same as the present commentary (*chao*). As for what is called "two eights," this merely takes the number of attendants.
Regarding the term "hell" (*dìyù*): the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Sanskrit term is *niraya*, which in the language of Qin means "place of no going.
This is because sentient beings born there have no place to go, no place of reliance, and no place of refuge; hence it is so called. Now, regarding the term "earth" (*dì*)...
"Prison" (*yù*) is the name used here [in this region]. Xuān says that hells (*dìyù*) are for the most part located beneath the earth.
There are eight major realms, each surrounded by sixteen secondary ones. Because these prisons are situated underground, they are called "earth-hells.

Regarding the term "prison," the Zhou dynasty called it *língyǔ*. The *Zhou Lǐ* states: "The Three Kings had prisons. Later, it was also designated as "yellow sand" (*huángshā*). This is clarified in the Five Articles.

Regarding the statement that "the transgressions and the observance of the precepts are accomplished of themselves": this means that the five categories (*pañca-āpatti*) and seven groups (*sapta-saṃghāvaśeṣa*) are termed "transgressive dharmas.

If one does not now trouble oneself with these transgressive dharmas, then the observance of the precepts is thereby accomplished. Thus, the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) says: "The five categories clarify the transgressions..."

"Raising up those who have transgressed the law" refers to those who violate the precepts they uphold. "The self-completion of the practice of non-transgression" clarifies the practice of not violating the rules.

To violate the law while claiming to fulfill it contradicts the intent of the Sage’s regulations; conversely, to follow the law while committing a transgression likewise contradicts the intent of the Sage’s regulations.

Regarding the statement, "The seven groups [of offenses] manifest what is upheld, while the various transgressions obscure and lose what is upheld," Master Li states: Within these seven groups, each manifests the Dharma that is to be upheld. If...
If one upholds these teachings in accordance with them, the two transgressions will naturally vanish into obscurity. "Zhang" (彰) means clarity; it means manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "newly learned ones are for the most part foolish and dull-witted" (*xīn xué bì duō yú lǔ zhě*): in the *Erlü* (爾疋), *bì* (卛) is glossed as "movement," while here *bì* (卛) is glossed as "totality.

To lack wisdom is called "foolish" (*yú*); to be dull and obtuse is "dull-witted" (*lǔ*). The *Lúnyǔ* says, "Chái was foolish; Shānshǐ Zēngshān was dull-witted. Kǒng Ànguó explained that "dull-witted" (*lǔ*)— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

"Insentient" (*dùn*). Regarding the phrase "not yet knowing the regulations and so forth," Master Lì explains that this refers to not knowing the regulations for the five categories (*wǔpiān*) and seven groups (*qījù*) concerning the observance and violation of the precepts.
As for the phrase "how could one discern the constitutional statutes" (*xiànzhāng*), the *Erlǐ* states: "Constitution" (*xiàn*) is defined as law; "statutes" (*zhāng*) derive from chapters.

To cite, to contract, and to resolve matters according to their characteristics—all these possess legal statutes and chapters. Regarding the phrase "following the precepts while being as ignorant as wandering in mist," this refers to those who are newly learning.

This refers to those who do not recognize the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). They remain in total darkness, unable to distinguish between the names of the *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *duṣkṛta* offenses;

they are like one wandering through a mist. Thus it is said. Regarding the statement that the retribution for offenses is "like observing the ocean": this clarifies that it is as if looking at objects within the vast sea from afar;
one might say it is a ship, or a mountain, or a bird, yet ultimately one cannot discern their falsehood or truth. This makes it clear.

As for "learning": how could one recognize the characteristics of transgressions? One cannot know the gravity of the retribution incurred by violating the precepts. Regarding the phrase "following the current to flow on forever" (*shunliu changshi*): "shì" (逝) means to go away.

Because of the aforementioned failure to recognize the characteristics of the precepts and ignorance of the retribution for sins, one follows the six sense objects and the five desires, constantly proceeding toward their realms.

Becoming addicted and immersed in defiled attachment, one does not know how to turn back from delusion to return to the source. The term "shun" (順) implies that one must live out [the consequences] accordingly.
This is the current of death; one journeys far away toward the sea of suffering.

To say that one forgets the way home while craving a drop of honey is to use honey as a metaphor for the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), as clarified in the sutras through various analogies such as the well, the four snakes, the three dragons, the two rats, and the five dogs, and so forth.

"Forgetting the way home" means losing right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and failing to know how to return to its source. This refers to monks and nuns who violate the prohibitive precepts yet continue to receive offerings.
Regarding "nurturing," the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: When a bhikṣu receives alms from others, if he does not act in accordance with the Dharma, he falls because of that gift.

This means that while consuming the food given by others, he fails to cultivate the Path according to the Dharma and allows his mind to become lax and dissolute; consequently, he shall fall into the three miserable realms.

If there were no retribution to be experienced in the three miserable realms, this body would immediately decompose in the belly and food would be expelled; the clothes one wears would likewise fall away from the body.
As for the statement that "karma follows the mind and retribution is formed according to the mind," it means that the mind is able to create karma by instigating the actions of body and speech.
Whether one performs good or evil, it is all driven by the mind. If there is no intention (*cetanā*) and other conditions are present, although an act is performed, it does not constitute an offense.
It is only when the mind necessarily acts that an act is either maintained as virtuous or committed as an offense; this refers to the mind serving as the cause of karma.

As for the statement that "retribution follows the completion of the mind," this indicates that the fruit recompenses the cause. Because the mind constitutes the causes of good and evil, the resulting retribution bears the fruits of suffering or joy. This is certain.

Regarding the statement, "First, the causes and conditions are set forth to extensively clarify the characteristics and names [of the offenses]," Master Li states: "The five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) are exclusively resultant offenses (*phala-āpatti*), whereas the seven groups (*sapta-varga*) encompass both cause and result.
That is to say, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is called the cause, and the consummation (*niṣṭhā*) is termed the result. This interpretation is not tenable.

It should rather be understood as having two distinct intentions within this section: first, explaining the names and characteristics of the five categories and seven groups as the "cause," and subsequently...
The second section states: "Second, explaining the retribution for the offenses committed is called 'fruit' (one may understand this by examining the text itself).

Shen says: "First, setting forth cause and effect serves as the introduction to this chapter. He further says: "'Extensively clarifying the characteristics and names' serves as the introduction to the subsequent chapter on 'Explaining Characteristics.

However, this is likely not the case; rather, it is merely an introduction to the intent within the present chapter. This means that characteristics and names also exist within the causes, as is cited below.
The *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and others are examples of this; thus it is said that they "extensively clarify the characteristics and names. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:

first, regarding the exposition of cause and effect, being able to uphold or being able to violate [the precepts] constitutes the cause, while the resulting retribution of suffering or pleasure constitutes the effect.

"Observing the effect to know the cause" refers to the extensive explanation in the following text of how violating the precepts invites the fruit of suffering; this is intended to lead practitioners to observe these evil fruits so that they do not commit them.
This is the evil cause; one must diligently protect and uphold it.
As for why the retribution and karmic offenses for violating the precepts at the beginning and middle [stages] are so extremely great, this is brought up to resolve doubts.

People may harbor the suspicion: "Why is the offense of violating the precepts so suddenly grave rather than light? Now, it is said that this is solely because the precepts are capable of giving rise to...

Excellent. Its substance pervades as many realms as there are motes of dust, and it is further able to sustain the Buddha-dharma; because it is superior to all else, even the commission of an offense against it is grave.

As for the statement that "the power of merit established through the protection of the precepts is the strongest among those that give rise to goodness," the precepts serve as the foundation of all myriad virtues.
A sutra says: "If one lacks these precepts, no wholesome merits will arise. It further states: "The precepts are the correct conformity [to the Dharma]."
It is the root of liberation. Furthermore, it is said that when one possesses pure precepts and wisdom, one immediately attains the foremost path;

therefore, it is called the most excellent among the production of wholesome qualities (*kuśala*). Regarding the statement that its merit in establishing [the Dharma] is powerful: the Vinaya is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma.

Its merit in establishing [the tradition] surpasses that of the other two Piṭakas. Thus, the preceding introduction states: "To maintain and uphold the Buddha-dharma, it is the primary reliance for the cessation of [unwholesome] discourse," and so forth. Moreover, the treatise says:
Because there were Vinaya masters who upheld the discipline, the Buddha-dharma remained in the world for five thousand years. Is this not a powerful achievement?
It is precisely because of this that those who disparage it incur a heavy retribution.

Regarding the statement, "That which is in the mind is called 'protection' (*saṃvara*) and so forth," Master Bin says: In the new sūtras and śāstras, it is termed "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*), and it is also called "protection.
In the older sūtras and śāstras, there was only the name "protection. As for that which is called "faculties," it refers to the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth.

Regarding "restraint" (*saṃvara*): it has the meaning of protection. That is to say, guarding the six sense faculties through mindfulness, wisdom, and equanimity is called "restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvara*).
Paramārtha’s commentary explains that the old term "guardian" (*rakṣā*) refers to its ability to block unwholesome matters and gather wholesome matters;

its ability to guard the gates of the six sense faculties so that karma and afflictions do not enter; its ability to protect the practitioner so that they do not fall into the four realms of existence; and its ability to...
It guards the practitioner, causing them to exit the stage of ordinary beings and enter the stage of the noble ones. Because of these many meanings, it is called "protection" (*rakṣā*).

This meaning will be explained in detail later in the section on "Observance and Transgression" (*śīla-āpatti-varga*). As for the statement that what exists in body and speech is called "precept" (*śīla*):
this means that externally restraining the seven non-virtues of body and speech is termed "precept. There may be protection without necessarily having a precept; until—

Regarding the statement that these must be "restraints" (*saṃvara*) and so forth: the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* distinguishes between that which is called "precept" (*śīla*) regarding the departure from evil of body and speech, and that which is called "restraint" regarding the departure from evil of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
That which is not a precept is necessarily not a restraint; however, that which is not a restraint is not necessarily not a precept.

The reason for this is that if one initiates action through body or speech, one necessarily gives rise to improper mental application (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); thus, what is not a precept is necessarily not a restraint. If improper mental application arises...

It is not necessarily the case that [non-restraint] involves the actual initiation of body and speech. If it does not initiate body and speech, it is merely non-restraint (*arakṣā*) and does not pertain to non-precept (*aśīla*).

The same applies to restraint (*rakṣā*): precept (*śīla*) is necessarily restraint, but restraint is not necessarily precept. One should formulate this as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first permutation is:

that which is restraint but not precept, such as laypeople (*avadātavasana*) who possess mindfulness, wisdom, and equanimity, yet have not extended these to prevent wrongdoing through body and speech.
The guest said: "The interpretations of former masters have held that where there is protection (*rakṣā*), there must be precepts (*śīla*).

This is because many virtuous laypeople, though they give rise to wholesome thoughts, lack precepts within their bodies and possess only this protection; hence it is said that 'there may be protection without necessarily being precepts.

For ordained monks and nuns who obtain the precepts, these must arise from protection; hence it is said that 'where there are precepts, there must necessarily be protection. My current interpretation is not so."

However, according to the intent of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and so forth constitute "restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvara*). Because these are the restraint of the faculties, it is called "restraint of the faculties";

this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, this is termed "protection" (*ārakṣā*); this protection is the proximate cause for the initiation of karma.

However, this does not yet constitute the initiation of karma; that is to say, although one possesses this restraint (*saṃvara*), if one has not yet prevented misconduct of body and speech, it cannot be called "precept" (*śīla*).
Therefore, it is said that there need not necessarily be precepts. If body and speech do not commit various evils, this must be due to the preceding thought of wisdom and the mind of relinquishment;

therefore, it is said that where there are precepts, there must be restraint. Second, there are cases where there are precepts but no restraint: although one possesses the essence of having received the vows, one gives rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
However, there is no mental protection; because one does not move body or speech, it is not necessarily the case that this is not precept (*śīla*).

The third [category] is both protection and precept, for it is through the power of wholesome mental attention and so forth that one can prevent non-virtue from flowing into body and speech. The fourth is neither precept nor protection;

if one moves or initiates action of body or speech, one will inevitably give rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). Therefore, among these four propositions, the *Chao* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*) cites only the first and the third.

These are three or two phrases. Regarding the term "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) mentioned above, the *Śāstra* commentary states: it refers to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). It means to mindfully contemplate the merit of the precepts and not give rise to erroneous thoughts.
The Wise One explains that discerning the precepts—viewing them as a life-preserving float, feet, or a flight of stairs—is able to bring about the fruit of the future;

thus, one does not give rise to erroneous wisdom. Regarding "equanimity" (*upekṣā*): it is the state where the mind is impartial, having departed from sorrow, joy, and so forth; therefore, it is called equanimity. Question:
