What is the intended meaning of "abandoning sorrow and joy"? Answer: If there is no mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one gives rise to greed because of joy toward agreeable objects, and further gives rise to anger because of sorrow toward disagreeable objects.

Since greed and anger thus give rise to two transgressions, by knowing how to prevent sorrow and joy, the two modes of greed and anger do not arise, and thus virtuous conduct is accomplished. Question: What constitutes the essence of this restraint? Answer: If...
According to the Saṃmitīya school, its essence consists of three factors: right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), and right equanimity (*samyak-upekṣā*).

To clearly remember an object is called mindfulness; this refers to the ability to retain what was originally perceived. To discern virtues and faults is called wisdom; this refers to the ability to investigate and differentiate.
Equanimity is the state of mental impartiality that is free from the two categories of greed and sorrow. As stated above, it is free from both sorrow and joy.
“Sorrow” (*daurmanasya*) belongs to the category of the affliction of hatred (*dveṣa*). “Joy” (*saumanasya*) belongs to the category of the affliction of greed (*lobha*).

Because of joy, greed frequently arises; because of sorrow, hatred frequently arises. Once greed and hatred have arisen, how can one protect the precepts? “Category” (*pakṣa*) refers to a class or type.

For example, anger, resentment, malice, vexation, envy, and so forth, are the classes belonging to the family of hatred; therefore, they are collectively termed “sorrow. Greed, lust, and concealment... [the text continues].
Pride and the like are all termed "joy" (*muditā*). Regarding the statement that one who possesses precepts must necessarily possess protection (*ārakṣā*), Sthiramati asserts:
A bhikṣu’s ability to restrain the seven types of misconduct of body and speech is called "precept"; it is so named because it necessarily relies on the internal mind to protect the body and speech.

This refers to the third phrase of the *Vyākhyāyukti*. As for the passage in the sutra where the Buddha praises those who have attained the protection of the precepts, consult the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Tattvārtha-śāstra).
The *shu* (commentary) refers to various sutras. It does not specify the names of the sutras, perhaps because they had not yet been translated.

Ciyun states that this refers generally to all sutras, as they all praise the precepts, rather than specifically pointing to a single sutra. Within this sutra, there are eight parables, all of which praise these precepts.
The first is the parable of the king begetting a son; this clarifies that one is able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas.
Son, by virtue of these precepts, you will certainly attain Buddhahood and subsequently become a noble one (ārya).

Just as a prince who is beloved by the people succeeds to the royal throne, so too shall one who has obtained the protection of the precepts succeed to the rank of a Buddha; therefore, he is loved by all people.
Second, regarding the analogy of the moon’s radiance: it is said that once one possesses the protection of the precepts, they gradually become perfected, like the waxing moon. Subsequently...
One attains concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; thus, the fivefold Dharma-body is perfected. Regarding the analogy of the three wish-fulfilling jewels:
this refers to a person who certainly hopes and certainly achieves results. By obtaining these jewels, one can influence all things, and whatever is wished for will surely be attained.

Likewise, one who obtains the protection of the precepts—if they wish to be born in the superior bliss of the human or celestial realms, or to attain the fruits of the paths of the Three Vehicles—will surely obtain them according to their wishes.
Ji said: "The priceless pearl is, moreover, distinct from the wish-fulfilling jewel.
To say it is 'priceless' means that among men there is no one capable of determining its price. Nevertheless, the pearl itself provides its own valuation.

That is to say, when someone wishes to sell this pearl, they carry it into the marketplace upon a pure vessel; when the multitude desires to buy it, they immediately offer clothing, goods, and money."
[He] covered it with wealth, yet the pearls continued to emerge from atop the jewels; the clothing and goods were all scattered. The buyer then repeatedly covered them with more items.
If the price was not yet sufficient, the pearls would continue to emerge; once the price was sufficient, the pearls would no longer come out.

This established the price; thus, one knows that the pearls themselves set their own value. According to the *Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, it says: "The Golden-Winged Bird..."
As for their karmic retribution, they feed exclusively upon nāgas. On the first day, in Jambudvīpa, they eat one nāga king and five hundred small nāgas.
On the second day, in Pūrvavideha, they eat one nāga king and five hundred small nāgas.
On the third day, in Aparagoyānī, they eat one nāga king and five hundred small nāgas. On the fourth day, again in Uttarakuru...
It devours one dragon king and five hundred minor dragons; thus it continues in rotation until eighty thousand years have passed, at which point the bird dies.
At the time of its death, certain signs appear. What are these signs? It is that the dragons emit poison so that the bird has no means of obtaining food.
Pressed by hunger, the bird wanders in distress seeking food, yet it is utterly unable to find any. It roams among the mountains, but finds nothing at all.
He was at peace. He traveled to Mount Vajra and stayed there for a short while. From Mount Vajra he descended directly to the edge of the great waters;

from the edge of the great waters he reached the edge of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Blown by that wind, he returned to Mount Vajra. This occurred seven times in succession. Only then did his life end.
The flesh of the bird was completely dispersed, leaving only the heart remaining. That heart descended straight down, just as before, seven times.
[The bird] returned, and then settled atop Mount Vajra. The Nanda Dragon King took this bird’s heart and made it into a bright pearl (*maṇi*).

When a Wheel-Turning King obtains it, it becomes a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, pearls come from within the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, and from within the brains of snakes;
dragon pearls come from within the brains of dragons; and wish-fulfilling jewels originate from the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha. If [this is] the Dharma...
When [the relics] have not yet been exhausted, all the śarīras and so forth transform into cintāmaṇi jewels. This is like ice that has passed a thousand years, which transforms into crystal beads.
Because of this, it clarifies that "hǔpò" (amber) is a name for a jewel. The *Guǎngpǐ* states: "Hǔpò is the name of a jewel. The *Hànshū* states:
"The kingdom of Jibin possesses hǔpò. The *Bówùzhì* states: "Cypress and pine trees, having entered the earth for a thousand years, transform [into this]."
It is *fuling* (Ganoderma). After a thousand years, *fuling* transforms into amber, also known as "red pearl" (*hongzhu*). The *Guang wuzhi* states: "Amber grows within the earth;
no grasses or trees grow upon its surface or beside it. It reaches depths of eight or nine feet and can be as large as a *hu* (one bushel)."
The outer skin is pared away, and from within, amber is produced. It contains a resinous juice that is initially like peach gum; once it solidifies and hardens, it becomes amber.
The people of that region take it and fashion it into bowls and vessels. Fourth, regarding the analogy of the prince:

this clarifies that self-love differs from the first category [of love for others], whereas the former refers to the affection and respect of others. Fifth, regarding the analogy of the person with one eye: Master Li states:

Suppose there is a person with two eyes; though they cherish them, if one is lost, the other still remains. However, if one has but a single eye, the protection and cherishing of it is even more intense.
If that one eye is lost, one sees nothing at all. The guarding of the precepts is like having a single eye: if they are lost, one does not see the path to Nirvana.
As for the parable of the six poor men who cherish their meager provisions, it means that such provisions are able to sustain the physical body.
The precepts are able to sustain the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.
Regarding the "two sensual objects," Jì states that these refer to palace ladies and handmaidens; the remaining two can be understood accordingly.
Eighth, "like a sick person obtaining excellent medicine" clarifies that the precepts can eliminate evil, just as medicine can eliminate illness. Thus far...
The explanation of the primary doctrinal gate concerning the transgressions of the precepts is hereby concluded.

Regarding the classification of the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and seven groups (*sapta-saṃghāvaśeṣa*) according to their meaning: the names of the "five categories" within the *vibhaṅga* are themselves designations for the various groups (*saṃgha*).

This is because the two offenses of *sthūlātyaya* and *pāyattika* contain both cause and effect within their substance; as they are diverse and difficult to distinguish individually, they are collectively designated by the name "group. However...
Within the category of *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses), there is further division into two types: those committed by body are termed *duṣkṛta*, and those committed by speech are termed *durbhāṣita*.

Thus, it is said that they are distinguished according to their meaning based on these categories. Regarding the statement that the formal determination of offenses is limited to six rules, this means that although *duṣkṛta* offenses are divided into two groups, they do not depart from body and speech;
since the method of repentance for *duṣkṛta* is the same, they are collectively designated as *duṣkṛta*.
Therefore, when the formal rules for assigning offenses are combined into one, there are only six categories (*ṣaḍ-varga*). Thus it is said: "The Dharma is formally established with six names.

Regarding the fact that these six names have no direct translations [into Chinese], this is because the Buddha transformed beings in the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa) by establishing precepts according to circumstances, thereby establishing the names of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *pāyattika*.
Since these specific designations did not previously exist in the local [Chinese] context, they could not be translated; rather, they were adopted as they were.

The underlying meaning is translated as follows: For instance, when terms such as *anavaśeṣa*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* are mentioned, these names are established based solely on their semantic significance;

they are not literal translations. Why did the Buddha establish exactly five categories of offenses—neither four nor six? Regarding this, various explanations are provided in the commentaries (*śāstra*). One master states:
"Because there are five types of medicinal substances, five categories were established. This refers to the four *pārājika* (defeats) and the *śikṣādattaka* (probationary training).

The method of repentance (*deśanā*) is called "medicine. Residual offenses (*śeṣa-āpatti*) are treated with medicines such as *mānatva* and so forth. The *pātayantika* is treated by reciting it three times before another person;

the *pratideśanīya* is treated by reciting it once; the *duṣkṛta* is treated by mental reflection (*cetanā*). According to the Vinaya masters, the four lower categories of offenses are subject to repentance, and thus the method of repentance is termed "medicine.

However, since the *pārājika* is irreparable, how can it be termed "medicine"? The answer is: although one has committed a *pārājika*, if there is no concealment (*an-āvr̥ti*), one may still train [in the precepts].

"Repentance (*deśanā*) is the name of a medicine. [Objection: "If that is so, then formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya*) for offenses involving concealment should also be called a medicine. [Response: "Although killing and healing differ, it does not preclude both from being medicines.
The method of repentance is like a medicine for treating a disease; the method of formal exclusion is like a poisonous drug used to kill a person. [Question:

"There should be seven medicines corresponding to the seven classes of offenses (*saptakaṣāya*). [Response: "The classes of offenses are actually only six, because *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and *durbhāṣita* (ill-spoken) are identical in their essential nature."

Therefore, *sthūlātyaya* (蘭) is also treated the same as *pāyattika* (提). They share a single medicinal remedy (*bhaiṣajya*), meaning that *sthūlātyaya* and *pāyattika* are both repented before another person (*pratideśanīya*). Thus, although there are seven classes of offenses (*sapta-varga*), there are only five medicinal remedies.

If this is so, then among the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*), those for resolving multiple disputes should be excluded. Answer: The characteristics of the dharmas differ; they should be categorized into three examples.

First, there are many remedies but few ailments, such as the seven methods for settling disputes which remove four types of contention (*catur-adhikaraṇa*). Second, there are few remedies but many ailments, such as the four wheels (*catuścakra*) which move eight [objects].

[Question: Difficult. [Answer: The three medicines and the illnesses are equal, just as there are five medicines for the five categories [of offenses]. Regarding the "four wheels" and the "eight difficulties," let us first state them in verse:

The three miserable realms, the northern continent, and long life; Being before or after [the Buddha], lack of intelligence, and defective faculties. A favorable place subdues the first five; Meeting [the Buddha] fulfills the vow, planting the remaining three. Gao says:
Since the Bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni currently exists in the world, it is not called the difficulty of being before or after the Buddha. As for the Dharma...

It is only when [the faculties] have been extinguished that it is difficult. As for those born deaf or born blind who are combined [in one person], being merely deaf or merely blind, as well as others with incomplete faculties, is not difficult.
This is because one who is deaf but not blind does not neglect bowing to the Buddha, and one who is blind but not deaf does not neglect listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, another master explains this according to secular regulations governing the Path, such as the five penal laws; in secular society there are five...

The punishments are execution by beheading, strangulation, banishment, penal servitude, and flogging. Based on these five punishments, the five chapters were established. Now, [the critic] refutes this, saying:

"These five punishments were established according to the customs of this land; how can they be compared to the Buddha’s ordained precepts? It would be improper to equate them with local customs. Furthermore, Sanskrit and Chinese are vastly different, yet you have hastily attempted to compare them.
Moreover, one master explains that the Tathāgata established the teachings according to the specific circumstances of the time, and thus it was appropriate to establish these five."
Section. Thus, five names were established. Now, upon careful examination, the latter master’s [position] is the most excellent.
It is like a person's face: having two eyes, one hand, and one nose is simply according to what is convenient; why must one inquire into the reason for their specific number?

Therefore, in the *Vibhāṣā*, whenever the Venerable Pārśva explained a meaning, he would always say: "It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that one should be established; two, three, or four are likewise."
It is so. Having already briefly listed the six names above, this is now the first.

Regarding the explanation of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses through the three meanings of "extremely evil" (*parama-pāpaka*) according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the established view is that the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* explains these *pārājika* offenses by means of three meanings.
Here, the text first indicates those three meanings, which will subsequently be cited and explained one by one. Within that explanation, the latter phrase is explained first.
Next, the explanation of the preceding two points may be sought. First, regarding "those who have fallen away from the fruits of the path and lack a share [in them]":

Bin says that this does not mean they have already attained the fruits of the path and now lost them; rather, it refers to those who ought to have attained them but did not, and thus are said to have "fallen away. Li states:

If one violates this precept, one will certainly fall into the evil realms; this is termed "retrogression and submergence" (*pai-mo*), whereby one does not attain the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that one has "no share.
Alternatively, "having no share" may mean having no share in the fruits of the Path, which is precisely retrogression and submergence.

The latter interpretation is superior. If one follows the former interpretation, there would be a contradiction with the third point below; since this passage clarifies that retrogression and submergence refers to falling into the evil realms, [the former view] should not [be maintained].
Furthermore, there are three subsequent points concerning the meaning of "falling away" (*pātayantika*). This concludes the first heading. Below, there are two more:

second, "not living in communion" (*asāṃvāsika*), and third, "falling away. These are the headings for the three chapters. "No longer entering into the two types of Saṃgha" refers to the two types of [Saṃgha]:
the *karmasaṃgha* (the community for formal acts) and the *pravāraṇāsaṃgha* (the community for the invitation ceremony).
Regarding "falling into a state of defeat by fighting with Māra," the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Pārājika" means falling into an undesirable state.
It is like two people fighting together, where one wins and the other loses. A bhikṣu receives the precepts with the desire to transcend birth and death.
One fights against the four māras; if one violates this precept, one falls into defeat. Question: Violating any of the five categories of precepts results in falling into defeat;

why is this precept alone singled out for such a name? Answer: When the other four categories of precepts are violated, one likewise falls into defeat at that moment, yet through immediate repentance, the violation is extinguished and one does not fall into permanent defeat. Therefore, they do not receive this name. It is like an enemy with a sword—

If one cuts another person but does not sever their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), although it may be called "victory," it is not ultimate victory. If the life-faculty is severed, it is termed "definitive victory.
Committing the four categories of offenses is like the life-faculty being severed; thus, committing these four grave offenses is equivalent to the severing of the life-faculty.

Regarding the statement, "The four *pārājika* offenses are like severing a person's head; even though they are called 'practicing the Dharma,' it is not for the sake of its application," this establishes the clarification.
This citation of the text from the *Caturvarga-vinaya* serves to explain the first phrase among the three meanings previously set forth in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

As for the statement, "This is named according to the practice of the Dharma rather than its application," the Master [Dao]li states: The previous mention of "severing the head" was because he was no longer a *bhikṣu*; this [present case]...

From the perspective of the division of the Path (*mārga-bhāga*), it is useless. Therefore, the metaphor of "severing the head" in the following passage is stated with reference to not attaining the fruits of sainthood (*ārya-phala*);

thus, it serves as an illustrative citation. Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is "no remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) for a *pārājika* offense, Lì (Lì) maintains that what follows below cites the fourfold division (*caturvarga*) to explain the second phrase within the *Skt.
Saṃghāṭi-vinaya*. Thus, the verse says: "All those who perform evil deeds," and so forth; this is...
The introductory verses for encouraging faith at the beginning of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* are the words of Dharmagupta. They say:
"For example, just as a corpse is not accepted by the great ocean and, driven by violent winds, is cast upon the shore; so too are those who perform evil deeds not accepted by the assembly.
For this reason, one should uphold the precepts; one must not speak [of them otherwise]."

Regarding the phrase "those who co-reside with the two types of *saṃgha* in matters of precepts and *karmavācanā*," this explains the preceding passage concerning those who do not enter the ranks of the two types of *saṃgha*.

As for the dispute over whether one possesses or lacks the precepts, [the author] states: "Ancient masters each clung to their own views regarding the words 'possessing precepts' and 'lacking precepts';
therefore, it is called a 'dispute. One teacher says: "One loses the precepts by committing a grave offense (*pārājika*). The reason for knowing this is that a single precept serves as...
"Ti. The various precepts are like water. If one precept is violated, where do the other precepts remain? Furthermore, another master says:

"Violating a grave offense does not result in the loss of the precepts. The reason for this is known by consulting the Vinaya: if one strikes or slanders a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense, the same *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) is incurred.

If [the victim] were without the precepts, striking him would merely be a minor *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Moreover, the explanation regarding "contentious debate" is as found in the thirty-first fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Within this [sūtra], there are twenty-two pairs of contentious arguments. Regarding the bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense, the question of whether he possesses the precepts or lacks them constitutes one such pair of contentious arguments.
Thus, these twenty-two pairs of contentious arguments from that sūtra were raised by the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa to question the Buddha:
"Since you already know well the faculties of sentient beings, why do you not provide a definitive teaching? Why is it that people fall into contention? The Buddha—

He answered each point one by one: "I speak of the indeterminate for the sake of conditions; according to the capacities of beings, I provide two kinds of teachings—those of loss and those of non-loss.
At times, within a single name, I speak of immeasurable names; within a single meaning, I speak of immeasurable names.
All this is for the purpose of taming all sentient beings. My disciples, failing to understand my intention, take these as literal truth, and consequently give rise to [false views]."

[The following is] the *Vivāda* (Discourse on Controversy) [and so forth]. Its eighteenth pair of controversies states: "Some say that even after a bhikṣu has committed the four pārājika offenses, the bhikṣu-precepts still remain;
others say they do not remain" (this is the question posed by Kāśyapa). The Buddha later provides the answer in the text: "In the sūtras, I have made this statement:
'If there is a bhikṣu who, having committed the four pārājika offenses, is no longer called a bhikṣu; he is called a "ruined bhikṣu. " [End of excerpt]
A bhikṣu who has fallen away can no longer produce the seeds of the sprouts of goodness;

he is like a scorched seed that does not bear fruit, or like a tāla tree that, once cut down, never grows again. It is the same with a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense. Such is the case for my disciples.
Having heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed: "The Tathāgata has said that once bhikṣus have committed a grave transgression, they lose their bhikṣu precepts.
Furthermore, in another sutra, I spoke to Cunda of four kinds of bhikṣus: first, those who have ultimately reached the Way;
second, those who show the Way; third, those who receive the Way; and fourth, those who defile the Way. Those who commit the four grave offenses are...
This is a defilement of the Path. When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:

"The Tathāgata has said that even after the bhikṣus have committed the four grave offenses (pārājika), they do not lose their prohibitive precepts. The *Rongshu* commentary states: The first part clarifies that the commission of the grave precepts is spoken of as a loss for the sake of provisional teaching;
the latter part, taught for the sake of Cunda, explains that there is indeed no loss. As for those who ultimately reach the Path, they are the Arhats.
It is "Han" (China). To exhaustively sever the two obstacles is called "ultimate arrival. The "one who shows the Way" refers to those of the three fruits [of the śrāvaka path].

However, by correctly showing this to others, it causes them to study from the stage of the *srotāpanna-pratipannaka* downward. This is because they have received the noble path within their own bodies.

As for the "defiler of the Way," this refers to one who violates the precepts. It appears that the author of the *Yi-yi* (Commentary on Doubts) specifically points to this passage to direct the author of the *Niepan-shu* (Commentary on Nirvāṇa) to interpret this.
Twenty-two pairs of contentious arguments. These exclusively cite the various Vinayas of the schools, as well as the names of various masters and the tenets held by the eighteen schools, stating:
"For instance, the Vātsīputrīya school makes this assertion; the Sarvāstivāda school makes such a citation," and so forth.

Each definition differs; hence it is called "disputed discourse" (and so forth regarding the definitions). The Guest says: The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 66, states that the *Cunda-sūtra* also speaks thus:
"There are four kinds of śramaṇas, and there is no fifth. The first is the śramaṇa who has surpassed the path (*abhibhū-mārga-śramaṇa*)."

Second is the teacher of the path; third is the one who lives by the path; fourth is the defiler of the path. It should be understood that among these, the śramaṇa of the supreme path is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, because he has awakened to it by himself.

It should be known that all Pratyekabuddhas are likewise [supreme in their path], for they have awakened to the path through their own realization. (Because they awaken to the path, their path is most excellent.)

The "Śramaṇa who demonstrates the Path" refers to the Venerable Śāriputra, because he is peerless and without equal, because he is a general of the Great Dharma, and because he is always able to follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of the Dharma;
it should be known that all śrāvakas beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are likewise so (those beyond training have already accomplished their own practice and should only deliver others).
The "Śramaṇa who proclaims the Path" refers to the Venerable Ānanda; although he dwells on the stage of one still in training (*śaikṣa*), he is nonetheless equal to those beyond training.

The learner (*śaikṣa*) who has heard much and retains what he has heard, and who is endowed with pure precepts and prohibitions—all such learners should be known to be likewise (meaning that for a person on the path of learning, the noble path within their body still must gradually grow, just as life grows;
therefore, it is called the "life-path"). As for the "śramaṇa who defiles the path," this refers to one who does not proclaim himself a *bhikṣu* [of the true] lineage.

Those who delight in stealing the wealth and property of others [are reborn in] the Mahāraurava [hell]—this is translated as "Greatly Stupid and Dull," meaning they possess no consciousness whatsoever (formerly translated as *mahalla*; some say *mahalla* is translated as "curd-whey," though its source is unknown).

Regarding the point that within the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* it is understood that there are those who possess precepts and are not without them, the verse of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
The Prātimokṣa restraint is relinquished at four times: through formal renunciation, death, the severance of the roots of goodness, and the arising of both [sexual] organs.
The commentary explains: "Renunciation" refers to the relinquishing of the precepts; as the *Abhidharmakośa* states, this is because it is contrary to the act of undertaking them.

"Death" refers to the cessation of one's species; as the *Abhidharmakośa* states, this is because the basis has been abandoned. "Severance of the roots of goodness," etc., refers to the cutting off of the roots of goodness and...
This refers to the arising of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "For one who has severed the roots of goodness, it is because the cause has been severed;

for one in whom both organs have arisen, it is because the basis has been transformed. The Vinaya-holders say: "When the Dharma is about to perish, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the establishment of boundaries (*sīmābandha*), and all ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) will cease.
The Abhidharmikas state: "When the Dharma is about to perish, the previously received vows of discipline continue to arise in succession and are not abandoned."

Those who have never obtained the vows do not obtain them; therefore, it is said that "all [vows] cease. Some say that committing a root offense (āpatti) constitutes the abandonment of the vows, but this is not so.

If one were to lose the precepts by committing a root offense, then after returning to lay life following such a fundamental transgression, one should be able to go forth again, because the precepts would have already been abandoned. Now, the correct explanation is that regarding the commission of a root offense...
Regarding the *prātimokṣa* precepts, one is a bhikṣu; regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts, one is not a bhikṣu. (The above is from the *Śāstra*; the *Chao* states:

"Whether or not one possesses the precepts" refers to this debate, or it may point to this passage in the *Śāstra*). Since it is stated that [the loss of the precepts occurs] through wrong view, the emergence of both sexual organs, death, and renunciation, and does not permit the loss of the precepts through committing a grave offense (*pārājika*), it follows that [the loss] resides solely in these four types of renunciation.
According to the second fascicle of the *Dharmatrāta-abhidharma*, these five [grounds for loss] are maintained.

"Relinquishment" (*prahāṇa*) refers to the relinquishment that occurs when the fifth [condition], the disappearance of the True Dharma (*saddharma-antardhāna*), is added; this is not included here, as it has already been refuted previously.

Regarding "that which has never been attained," one cannot receive it again once it has been lost. As for "that which was previously received and not relinquished," the *Yogācārabhūmi* (13) establishes five types of relinquishment by adding "relinquishment through committing a grave offense" (*gurudharmāpatti-prahāṇa*).

Question: Why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* not include "relinquishment through committing a grave offense," while the Vinaya states that once a grave offense has been committed, [the status of a monk] is no longer [valid]?
Regarding the monk, that commentary explains as follows: When the Buddha says one is "not a monk," he means they are not a monk in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

That is to say, having committed an offense of the first category (*āpatti*), one remains a monk with respect to the *prātimokṣa* restraint, but is no longer a monk with respect to the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraint.

This constitutes a violation of the precepts, not a forfeiture of the vows; therefore, it is said that "there is still precept, it is not non-existent. If one discusses repeated offenses, this is clear from the Vinaya itself.
Regarding "abandonment," the Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu commits any one of these rules, it is the same as if he had committed them previously and subsequently. This is its meaning.

As for the statement that this Prātimokṣa precept is established based on the distinction of objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), it means that with respect to each individual object, [the offenses] are distinct.

It is called the *Prātimokṣa* (Individual Liberation) precepts because they prevent wrongdoing and attain liberation. When these precepts are generated, they arise individually according to each specific object;

thus, if one commits an offense now, it likewise occurs individually according to each object, rather than occurring all at once. As for the statement that twenty-one precepts are generated regarding the body of a woman, this is from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
This is merely taking the precept against sexual misconduct as an example, based on the seven poisons applied across the three [types of objects].

The "wound-entrances" (kṣata-dvāra) thus total twenty-one. Regarding the "seven poisons" (sapta-viṣa), this refers to the three poisons of affliction (kleśa) arranged as three singles, three doubles, and one combination.
Regarding the "fourteen for men," this means the seven poisons applied across the two wound-entrances.

This is based solely on the precept against sexual misconduct; as for theft, killing, and lying, they shall be discussed below. From the remaining types of sexual misconduct up to the formal recitation of the essence of the vows (samādāna-śarīra).
This refers to the moment when one originally received the precepts: at that time, the essence of the non-informative (avijñapti) was generated, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Although one may now defile a single object of sexual misconduct, other objects remain undefiled; it remains eternally pure and majestic. Since it has not been destroyed or violated, it is said to accord with the original essence of the reception.

Regarding "beating or slandering a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense," this cites the Vinaya text as proof. A bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense still possesses the precepts; they are not without them. If one beats or slanders [such a person]...
Regarding laypeople who lack the precepts, the Vinaya establishes that this constitutes a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
The answer is: if they have performed repentance and are fundamentally pure, they should properly be counted in the quorum;

if they are permitted to participate in the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) or the *Pravāraṇā* (Invitation), one should specifically respond to the aforementioned statement by saying, "They are included in the count," though this does not mean they are actually fit for the functions of the Saṃgha. This is because, when no other persons are present, the performance of these two dharmas is permitted.

There are no textual passages opening up other dharmas as well. Nevertheless, this person is in fact pure in essence and should properly count toward the quorum; however, due to the gravity of their mental transgressions, they are unfit for the functions of the Saṃgha.

In view of their own practice, they are pure and not defiled. As for the phrase "not coming when summoned at will," it means that when the Saṃgha performs formal acts (*karmavācanā*), their failure to attend does not constitute a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*).
Regarding the method of repentance mentioned below, within the section on repenting for the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga*), it quotes the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other vinayas, stating:

"After one has committed a grave offense and undergone the training for repentance (*śikṣādattaka*), the bhikṣu’s food is impure; they [the śikṣādattaka] likewise do not call it pure food. That food is impure, and the bhikṣu is likewise impure.
Since it is stated that both share this impurity, how could this person not be a bhikṣu? Furthermore, it quotes the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* regarding the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

The four methods for repentance have been explained. Those called "bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts" and so forth—regarding the term *huángshè* (惶懾), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *shè* (懾) means the mind being submissive;
the *Erbǐ* (爾疋) states that *shè* arises from fear. As for the phrase "constantly pure and dignified," *yǎn* (儼) refers to an appearance of reverence.

If one first purifies the consciousness and then engages with the five sensory objects, it is established that if one first gives rise to a mind of contemplative practice and subsequently encounters the five objects such as forms and sounds, one will not be defiled;
this is like the case where, through the perfection of the meditation on impurity, one does not crave the beauty of women upon encountering them.
If one possesses compassion, few desires, and has perfected contemplation, then one will not engage in killing or stealing.

This is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the elder Anupama saw all women as being like white bones, like swords, poison, or venomous snakes, and so forth. Regarding why the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are cited but the mental object (*dharma-viṣaya*) is not:

the explanation is that while the mental object is apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) exercise restraint and protection primarily over the body.

[The character] "mouth" [indicates that] one does not restrain the mind; therefore, it is not clear. This is merely my own interpretation. Regarding the phrase "concealing one's own illness," Master Li says:
to commit an offense and neither disclose it nor repent, but only to know how to conceal it—just as a person who has an illness does not let others see it, covering it with a garment;
hence it is called "concealing an illness. Although bystanders understand how to treat it, they do not see its origin.

It increases [the harm] until death arrives. To say that both wealth and the Dharma are lost means that sharing the same surplus of benefit is called "wealth," while sharing the same recitation of the precepts is called "Dharma.

Since both are severed, it is said they are "lost together. To recklessly consume [offerings] such that both oneself and others incur debt means that by eating the faithful offerings of others while violating the precepts, one fails to digest them;
the retribution in the future will be extreme suffering, and furthermore, it causes the donors' merit to be lost.
Virtue diminishes; therefore, it is said that both self and others are at fault. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Both the donor and the recipient commit an offense of falling.

Therefore, it is called "receiving [the precepts] in vain. As for the term "using," it refers to those who improperly join the ranks of the Sangha, defiling the pure assembly and inviting karmic retribution from the unseen realm.

Furthermore, they mistakenly cause the Sangha’s administration of the Dharma to fail in its purpose; this too is a case where both self and others are at fault. This is [the nature of] such receiving.

The two characters [“shou” (receives) and “yong” (uses)] correspond to the statement that both wealth and the Dharma have perished. “Shou” belongs to the character for wealth, and “yong” belongs to the character for the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase “as when one obtains death in four locations within the human body,” Jing says: first, the crown of the head; second, the throat; third, the heart; and fourth, the waist.
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, only two locations for obtaining death are clarified; thus, in that treatise, fascicle twenty-seven...
Question: Why is it that when the head or the waist is severed, one dies immediately, whereas when the hands, feet, or other limbs are severed, one does not die?

Answer: The head and the waist are the two primary sites for the cessation of life; therefore, when they are severed, death occurs. The hands and feet are not so. Furthermore, sentient beings of the desire realm subsist upon *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food).
The throat is the passage for this food, and the abdomen is the locus of its support; therefore, when these two locations are severed, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases.

It is severed. Furthermore, the head is the locus of the various sense organs, such as the eyes (meaning that within the head, the five material sense organs are present; these five material sense organs correspond to the five bases among the twelve bases).

When it is severed, the various organs, such as the eyes, are destroyed. The abdomen is the locus where the vital wind (āśvāsa-praśvāsa) resides. When the waist and abdomen are severed, they are destroyed, and the vital wind has no support.
Therefore, when these two locations are severed, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is immediately severed.
Regarding those who have left the household life and uphold the fundamental precepts, it is established that these refer to the four grave and eight secondary precepts of the monks and nuns.
According to the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "If there are sons or daughters of noble family who, with deep faith, take refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma..."
Whether they aspire to the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Mahāyāna, they shall go forth in my Dharma,
receive full ordination, possess supreme faith, guard the four root offenses and other transgressions,

and always exert themselves with diligence and heroic perseverance without ceasing; they shall never receive the offerings of gods and humans in vain, and among the three vehicles, according to their [aspirations]...
He desires it. Why? Because he is resolved to seek liberation; even at the cost of his life, he shall never violate it.
Furthermore, it is asked: why are these called root offenses? It is said that if a person commits such evil deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the evil realms.
Since performing such actions constitutes the root of the miserable paths, they are called root offenses.
Regarding the "four subsequent [offenses] explained separately," this refers to what is clarified in the following section on the distinct practices of the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha.

As for "crimes with identical names that involve repeated commission," this refers to the four offenses—sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying—in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya). These four are all identical in name as *pārājika* (defeats);

thus, there is the possibility of repeated commission. This means that if one first commits sexual misconduct and incurs a *pārājika*, and subsequently commits theft and likewise incurs a *pārājika*, these belong to the same category.
Regarding "no gravity": as previously stated, if one commits sexual misconduct and incurs a *pārājika* offense, but later commits it again, [according to some schools] it is merely a *duṣkṛta*.

However, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this is not so; when the name and category are identical, both instances constitute a grave offense. Why is it called a "category" (*jāti*)? "Category" carries the meaning of a "class.

Furthermore, because the offense arises from this, and because it is capable of generating an offense, it is called a "category. As for the statement that "this refers to the first section," it means:

Only for the first category (pārājika) is there no re-offense of the same kind; however, for the four lower categories, there are indeed re-offenses of the same kind. This is no different from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding those who commit offenses requiring formal training (*śikṣādattaka*) or the saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, this refers to cases where many saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses have been committed and one proceeds through the stages of repentance accordingly.
Thus, it is known that this constitutes a grave offense. Master Li states: "The previous interpretation is not incapable of being cited.

The earlier mention of committing 'many saṃghāvaśeṣa' offenses refers to those of the same category. As for the statement 'the rest is as explained in other sections,' this points to the further clarification found in the 'Section on Separate Practices' within the various sections below."

Regarding the statement that the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Miaofa lianhua jing lü piposha) speaks of five sections (*bhāṇaka*) and so forth: this means that the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* refers to a "chapter" (*piān*) as a "section.
Sengli states that "section" (*bhāṇaka*) is a specific term for a class of similar works. As for the remark that these are called "chapters" (*piān*) here, Hui-li says:

"Chapter" is a name from this land [China], as has already been explained previously. Originally, these were called "chapters" in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. During the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty, foreign...
The Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakāla arrived in Luoyang and established the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) for receiving the precepts.

He produced the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-hṛdaya*, which follows the terminology of this land and is titled "Chapters" (*pīya*). In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, however, only the categories of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*) are established, consisting of five types of transgressions.

There are five types of *śikṣāpada* (precepts). Now, according to the tradition of the commentators on the treatises (*śāstra*), the term "chapter" (*pien*) refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, as it follows the arrival of each subject matter.
However, if we establish the name based on its original meaning: "section" (*bu*) refers to what the *Vinayavibhaṅga* calls the "original name of a section" within the Vinaya.

First, regarding the establishment of the fundamental meaning: it clarifies that the three preceding preparatory offenses (*pūrvaprayoga-āpatti*) can bring about the accomplishment of the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*).

This refers to the fruit of an action where one intends to commit a grave offense but fails to do so; it pertains to the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) prior to the act. These three types of offenses can be expiated.

However, regarding those that can bring about the fundamental (*maula*) offense, they are therefore said to have the "meaning of accomplishing the fundamental. Second, the meaning of "conforming to the fundamental" refers to the result being achieved based on the cause.
This clarifies that the offenses of the three preliminary stages conform to the fundamental and cannot be expiated; hence, they are called "conforming [to the fundamental]."
This follows the fundamental [precepts].

Regarding the sixteen offenses of *pārājika* (defeats), Lì says: "Since the fruits of the five and seven [offenses] are established based on their causes, they are designated as 'preparatory' (*prayoga*) and 'grave' (*sthūlātyaya*).
In the *Liaosong*, it is stated that for each of the four *pārājika* precepts, there are three preparatory stages; this discusses the root."
The original offenses are four; four times four makes sixteen.

Regarding those offenses that do not constitute *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) but must be confessed before another person: this refers to cases where one touches [a woman] for the sake of amusement and thereby incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Now, if one intends to commit sexual misconduct with the original intent, although there is physical contact, it is only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). This *thullaccaya* is a preliminary (*upakkama*) to a *pārājika* (defeat) offense; it is not the actual fruit-offense itself.
If, however, one touches another for the sake of amusement, one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* (offense requiring suspension); this *saṅghādisesa* is the fruit-offense, not a preliminary to a *pārājika*.

This is because the original intent was merely to touch in order to obtain pleasure, and not to proceed further toward sexual intercourse; therefore, it is called the "fruit. Question: Touching with the body is nearly as grave as [sexual misconduct]; why is it only a *saṅghādisesa*?
It is not the preparatory stage (*upāya*). Theft is also close to being grave, yet it constitutes the preparatory stage because one must rely on four factors to commit the five types of theft;

however, these four are not themselves grave. In the case of great sexual misconduct (*maithuna*), one does not rely on physical contact; therefore, contact is not the preparatory stage. Thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

"The commission of sexual misconduct does not rely on another, as in the case of one's own three [orifices]. It further states: "In theft, there is a continuity that completes the gravity; therefore, it is designated by the name 'preparatory stage'. (Note: The final character "再" appears to be a scribal error or fragment).
Touching does not constitute a major offense of lust; how, then, could it be ultimate? As the Vinaya states regarding stealing less than five [measures] twice:

the Buddha declared that this constitutes a *pārājika* through continuity. To say that this offense is confessed before another person is clearly established as meaning confession before the Saṃgha, not before a single individual.
The first three skillful means (*upāya*) are all for the sake of accomplishment. [Dao]li states that this explains the meaning of accomplishing the fundamental [precepts].

[Daoshi] Ji says that Vinaya Master Yuan does not permit this; he maintains that within the skillful means, there is an offense at every step—that is, he does not permit the existence of a *thullaccaya* offense within the progressive process of the skillful means.
Now, regarding what is called "establishing an offense" (*āpatti-pratisaṃyoga*), it depends on two things: first, the cessation of the mind; second, the... [text fragment ends].
When the deed is completed, there may be a formal adjudication. In the midst of progress toward an action, these two conditions do not exist; how, then, could one incur a formal offense?
Now, when one intends the mind and creates an object, but the matter is not yet finalized, how can one suddenly discuss and impose a penalty for an infraction therein?
One may only acquire unwholesome karma at every step, but one can never formally adjudicate the name of the offense. If, within the preparatory stage (upāya), [one were to incur an offense]...
If one dwells [in the preparatory stage] without performing the preceding root action, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. Thus, the Vinaya states: "If it is accomplished, it is a *pārājika*;

if not accomplished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This is precisely what that means. Master Yuan praised the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) and termed them the "seven non-accomplishments" (*saptāsiddhi*).

Because they involve the performance of the root action, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* of non-accomplishment. Li and Xuan et al. termed these the "seven expedient means," but Master Yuan did not permit this; he did not approve of it.

In the "Chapter on Committing Offenses During the Preparatory Stage," it is required that one wait for the cessation of the mind before an offense can be established; otherwise, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). My intention is that whenever it is said an offense is established, it must wait for two conditions:
first, the cessation of the mind, and second, the completion of the act. In the midst of the process of proceeding toward an action, these two conditions are absent;
how, then, could an offense be established? It is just as when Sudatta proceeded toward the Buddha's dwelling; with every step, he increased his merit in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore...

It is granted that one who violates the precepts increases in evil with every step, yet incurs no formal designation of "guilt. This takes the unwholesome act of contravening principle as the very substance of "progression" (*abhyupagama*).
Now, [the opponent] objects (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Since the fruit [of Buddhahood] lacks a name when Sudatta saw the Buddha, it must be granted that there is no designation of 'merit' within the cause.

Now, since this contradicts the Buddha’s regulations and the fruit possesses a designation, one should grant that "progression" possesses a designation of "transgression" (i.e., guilt). [Furthermore, this also contradicts the *Śāstra*; such as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and others...]

It is said that "at every step there is a *mālatī* flower"). Regarding the previous statement, "like Sudatta and others," this refers to when Sudatta was traveling from his home to the Buddha’s dwelling and passed by a celestial temple on the way.
At that time, a heavenly deity spoke from mid-air, saying:
"Suppose there were a person adorned with necklaces, possessing a hundred fragrant elephants, a hundred jeweled chariots, and a hundred cast-gold figures, all of which one were to offer..."
Giving and making offerings are not equal to a person who takes a single step toward the presence of the Tathāgata;
for that teacher leads their intention toward the Buddha, and there is the merit of every step taken in accordance with principle.

Regarding the statement "the previous three are all incapable of repentance, which follows the meaning of the fundamental [nature]," this explains the aforementioned meaning of following the fundamental nature. As for the phrase "the remaining three follow this category," it means:
The three [offenses] of stealing, killing, and lying.

Regarding the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* that "only when completed" constitutes [an offense], this means that while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that failure to complete [the act] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, it does not explain the distance or proximity of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), the gravity of the *sthūlātyaya*, or the presence of initial transgression (*āpatti*).
Now, according to the *Vinayottaragrantha* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is clear that there is a distant [preparatory effort].

The proximate preparatory acts (*upakrama*) differ. If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in distinguishing the gravity of *sthūlātyaya* offenses, it means that the subsequent preparatory act is a light *sthūlātyaya*, the proximate preparatory act is a heavy *sthūlātyaya*, and the remote preparatory act is a *duṣkṛta*. However, within that *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are three grades of confession for *sthūlātyaya*:
first, before a great assembly; second, before a small assembly; and third, before a single person. As for the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, it establishes only one grade.

This refers to the two preceding preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*), both of which constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing). Since there is only one *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) for the immediate preparation (*āsannaprayoga*), it is said to be "one category.

Regarding the statement that "the substance (*tattva*) applies to both," [Master] Li states: although the names *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta* differ, their substance is one; thus, they apply to both the Vinaya and the Śāstra texts, which is why it is called "both.

Specifically, in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā*, the subsequent preparation is a heavy *duṣkṛta*, whereas in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. However, as for the name...
Although they differ, the essence of the offense is of one kind; both are confessed before a single person. The explanation of the meaning of the *pārājika* category is thus concluded.

Second, regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category: it is established that these are offenses with a remainder (*avaśeṣa*), which are eliminated through the Saṃgha; therefore, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the establishment of the name based on the object (*viṣaya*): the Saṃgha is the object toward whom the confession is made; "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the name for the essence of the offense.
One should say that the name is established based on both the object and the essence: the Saṃgha is the object of confession, and "remainder" is the essence of the offense.

Furthermore, the name should be formed according to the meaning of the object; the object is likewise the Saṃgha. "Meaning" refers to the fact that this offense possesses the sense of having a remainder.

Regarding the statement that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) clearly explains the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses as being "superior" (*ūrdhva*), this establishes the explanation; the name *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is the same as the explanation found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, the phrase "there are others who name it based on the non-interruption of the practice of the Dharma" clarifies that once the confession is completed, one returns to the status of a regular monk for communal use; hence it is so called.
Regarding the phrase "it is necessary to save them early," Jì explains that this refers to the statement in the *Vinaya Preface*: "There are thirteen cases where salvation is possible;

for the others, it is unnecessary. As for the expression "forcibly granting *parivāsa*," this is translated as "concealment" (*paryuṣita*). It is named after the emotional transgression that is to be remedied.

This clarifies that once a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has been committed, even if the offender has no intention of repenting, if the Saṃgha forcibly applies the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) to them, it is still permissible.
Purification through confession is not like this. It requires emerging from one's own mind; because of the gravity of the transgression, one must certainly wash the heart with remorse.
If one lacks such intent, even if the Saṃgha forcibly applies the ritual, the dharma is not established. "Neighbor" means proximity.
Touching, coarse speech, and the atmosphere of a house of lust—if one can do these things, there will surely be the commission of a grave offense.
Regarding the bhikṣuṇīs, there are seventeen rules: six are different and seven are the same. The six [rules] combined with the seven make thirteen; this is based on the thirteen rules for monks.
To explain them specifically in relation to the seventeen rules for bhikṣuṇīs, there are ten differences and seven similarities. As for the ten differences, the verse says:

1. Speaking of persons; 2. Crossing over thieves; 3. Unauthorized release outside the boundary; 4. Eating tainted food alone and encouraging others to do so; 5. Associating with [the laity] and violating admonitions;

6. Slandering the Saṃgha and violating admonitions; 7. Anger regarding precious objects; 8. Initiating disputes within the Saṃgha and violating admonitions; 9. Speaking of persons; 10. Crossing over thieves; 11. A woman; 12. Unauthorized release outside the boundary; 13. Unauthorized release outside the boundary.
1. The third: accusing others. 2. The fourth: the four solitary acts—namely, crossing water alone, traveling alone, staying overnight alone, and entering a village alone.

3. The fifth: accepting food from a man with a lustful mind. 4. The sixth: encouraging another to accept food from a man with a lustful mind. 5. The seventh: associating closely [with a monk] in violation of a formal admonition. 6. The eighth:

slandering the Saṃgha and encouraging close association in violation of a formal admonition. 7. The ninth: being angry and abandoning the Triple Gem in violation of a formal admonition. 8. The tenth: instigating the four types of disputes and slandering the Saṃgha.
Regarding the "seven offenses identical to those of the monks" that follow the refusal of admonition: first is matchmaking; second and third are the two types of groundless and groundless slander;

and the four instances of refusing admonition make seven. The verse says: "Matchmaking, slander with or without basis, schism, assisting a schismatic, and violating the nature [of the precepts]—these seven correspond to the preceding ten;
these are the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for nuns. Regarding the "six offenses distinct from those of the monks": these are emission, touching, the two types of coarse speech, and so forth.
The second is the offense of using a private room. The verse says: "Emission and touching; the two coarse offenses and the two rooms.

Regarding why the Sangha’s offense for emission is heavy while that of a nun is light, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) explains: "Women's afflictions and defilements are heavy; they are difficult to restrain and difficult to control.

If one were to impose a grave offense upon them, it would cause suffering and distress to sentient beings. It further states: "When a woman acts in a secluded place, her suffering overflows; as for a man..."

The Master did not reveal [the details], because he was able to reveal them according to each specific circumstance. Regarding the single precept on physical contact, the offense is grave for nuns and light for monks;

this is because nuns have a nature more prone to afflictions and delusions. Once they have accepted being touched or grasped, they will inevitably be subjected to harassment and oppression, thereby committing a great transgression. Within the category of preparatory offenses (*upakrama*),...
The prohibition and the gravity of the offense are designated as "husband" (puruṣa) and "grasping. There is certainly no violation or destruction [of the precept] here;

it does not require the prevention of defilement, but merely concerns the boundary of the limit, and thus the prohibition applies to what is light. Second, regarding coarse speech, the offense is grave for monks and light for nuns:

because men are by nature fierce and shameless, the meaning of such speech occurs frequently, and thus it is grave; because women are by nature soft and modest, such speech occurs rarely, and thus it is light. The same applies to the two cases concerning buildings.

The reason they differ is that the *saṃgha* consists of many members; thus, traveling alone to construct a dwelling involves numerous matters and is therefore grave. For a nun, it is the reverse of this and is therefore light.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, when two people build together, they do not sleep alone; consequently, there is no fixed measure for the dwelling.
Even if there is an excess, it is minor rather than grave.
Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and so forth: these are alternative names for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. They differ according to the various explanations in the *Abhidharma*;
such variations arise because of the lightness or heaviness of the Sanskrit pronunciation. As for the statement that there are fifty-two offenses, there are three preliminary stages (*prayoga*).
Combined with the root [text], they form four; thus there are several [versions].
As for the statement "this is the name of the Saṃmitīya school" and so forth, it means that the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Liao lun) states:
"Saṃghāṭiśasā" is a name within the Saṃmitīya school. Since the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains the Saṃmitīya school, it says so. It is said that there are three [parts].
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to establishing clarity. Regarding the "single meaning of things," this is the same as the Sarvāstivāda school;

that is to say, the definition of the *saṃgha* is based on the sameness of precepts and views, rather than on meditative concentration and wisdom. The second [meaning] is the "saving meaning. The third is the "ultimate meaning," which will be explained in the text below.
The Sarvāstivāda school calls this the *Saṃghabhedavastu*, and the Saṃmitīya school agrees with this.
"Et cetera" refers to the Sarvāstivādins, who maintain that there is only one meaning, which is identical to the first meaning in the Saṃmitīya school.
Regarding the statement "because they see the assembly in harmony," this should be understood as the explanation provided in the *Liaoshu* (Explanatory Commentary). As for "the assembly":
This refers to the Saṃgha. It must possess identical right view; thus it is said to be "by way of view. Furthermore, they must share an identical precept and must be in harmony.

This is the meaning of "Saṃgha. Now, while the Saṃgha possesses the six points of concord (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*), for the sake of explaining the meaning of "Saṃgha," only the two names of precept and view are cited here.
The statement that these two must be identical and not necessarily [identical in] concentration and wisdom is intended to refute the various [erroneous] schools. Many...

The community of practitioners (*saṃgha*) possesses three meanings: first, precepts and views; second, meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and third, wisdom (*prajñā*). If these three are identical, it is then called by the meaning of *saṃgha*.
While many schools define the essence of the *saṃgha* through wisdom and discrimination, the present case is not so.

It does not depend on concentration and wisdom, but rather, by merely possessing precepts and views, the meaning of *saṃgha* is established. As for the current statement that these two are different, it means:
Because their precepts and views differ, they deviate from the meaning of the *saṃgha*. The above has been an explanation of the term *saṃgha*.

Regarding the three meanings—the first of which was explained previously—there are three meanings within the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sanskrit: *saṃghātiśeṣa*). The first, the meaning of *saṃgha*, has already been explained above.
The second is the meaning of "rescue" (*avaśeṣa*), and the third is the meaning of "superiority. These points should be understood as the explanation of the meaning of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
[The section on] *sthūlātyaya* is concluded. Regarding the term *sthūla* (great), the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* states that it is called "great" because its characteristics are coarse and heavy.

Regarding the word *vāraṇa* (obstruction), the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* clarifies that the "path" (*mārga*) is that which is obstructed, while the "offense" (*āpatti*) is that which obstructs; because by committing this offense, one is able to obstruct the path. Thus it is explained.
Lì said: "As for what is called 'breaking the precepts obstructing the Path,' what kind of path does it obstruct? It means it obstructs the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness [samādhis]; and the fruits from that of the Srotāpanna up to the Arhat."

This also explains the obstruction from a remote perspective. Since one whose ethical discipline (*śīla*) is impure cannot cultivate and give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor can they develop wisdom (*prajñā*) to sever afflictions and ultimately attain the benefits of the Path, it is therefore said to be an obstruction to the Path.

That which "can bring about the offenses of the first two categories" means that it can serve as the cause for the two categories of *pārājika* (defeat) and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting); this refers to the preparatory effort (*prayoga*). "The first" refers to the first category.
The second refers to the section on *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension from the community). "Two" refers to the collective summary.

Furthermore, regarding the translation as "grave offenses," some say this is because [acts such as] causing schism in the Saṃgha, shedding blood [of a Buddha], or committing parricide are considered grave offenses.

First, regarding the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of a grave offense: this refers to the cause of the offense. There are both light and heavy [degrees]. The distant preliminary stage is light, while the proximate preliminary stage is heavy.
Second, regarding that which can sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): this refers to the independent fruit (*maula-phala*). This also has light and heavy degrees.

For example, causing a schism in the Sangha or shedding blood constitutes a grave offense of *ānantarya* (immediate retribution) or a serious *sthūlātyaya*; however, seeing the Buddha while naked, or [seeing] human skin and a stone bowl, is minor.

This is because causing a schism in the Sangha or shedding blood severs the roots of goodness. As for what is called a "transgression," it refers to one who does not act in accordance with the Buddha’s precepts;
this is a sinful transgression. Jì said: "This is not a 'transgression' in the sense of being a sin; it is simply 'excessive'."
This is the meaning. It refers to transcending the boundaries of the precepts; hence the name. As will be illustrated by the following metaphors, the meaning becomes self-evident.
Regarding the phrase "like a cow breaking through a fence," it establishes that *sthūlātyaya* (a grave offense) is the cause for [further transgression].

It is like the aforementioned cow breaking the fence, which serves as the cause for subsequent cows; the subsequent cows pass through because of the preceding one. Likewise, the prior commission of a *sthūlātyaya* leads to...

The subsequent offense constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat). The preceding ox breaking the fence is a metaphor for committing a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); the subsequent ox getting through is a metaphor for committing a fundamental heavy offense (*mūla-guru*).

Regarding the statement that "the name 'offense' (*atīta*) also applies equally," this means that while the preceding ox breaking the fence is called an "offense" and the subsequent ox is likewise called an "offense"—that is, although both the commission of a *sthūlātyaya* and a *pāyattika* (or other minor offenses) are generally termed "offenses"—there are nonetheless degrees of lightness and heaviness among these offenses. According to the *Liao shu* (Commentary on the Vinaya): [text follows].

However, the term "transgression" (*āpatti*) applies to all offenses; yet because this particular offense is coarse, it is designated by the name "transgression. An initial violation constitutes a transgression, while subsequent instances take their name from that first one.

This is like the case where the first ox crossing a boundary receives the designation "crossing the boundary," and subsequent oxen, following the first, also receive the designation "crossing the boundary.

Now, to explain the intent of the commentary: although all seven classes of offenses (*saptāpatti-nikāya*) fail to conform to what was established by the Buddha, [this specific case is singled out for its gravity].

One practices by means of the precepts; therefore, it is said that [the term] also extends to all offenses. Regarding the statement that "this offense is the first": this refers to its capacity to serve as the preliminary (*pūrvāṅga*) for the first two categories of grave offenses.

Because of these preceding preliminaries, one subsequently commits the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*); hence it is called "the first. As for the statement that "offenses extend to both primary and derivative":

the independent offenses (*mukhyāpatti*) are the primary ones. Lì (礪) says: "For example, those who assist in the schism of the Saṃgha, such as providing skins, alms-bowls, or appearing naked [in public]."
It is called the "ultimate pārājika" (究竞兰) and is also termed the "independent" (独头). If it serves as a means for another, it is called "derived" (从);
this is the causal pārājika, which is precisely the resultant pārājika.

Regarding the statement that "the substance [of the offenses] encompasses both light and heavy": as explained below, this applies generally to both light and heavy categories, and within the causes, it fully discusses the principles of light and heavy causes and effects;
a detailed explanation follows later. As for the Vinaya’s enumeration of seven groups (sapta-varga) or six groups (ṣaḍ-varga), which together include the *sthūlātyaya* and other offenses:

This refers to the Vinaya’s explanation of the six and seven [categories of offenses]. Although they differ individually, the *pārājika* (Pāli: *pārājika*; Chinese: 蘭) must necessarily occupy a fixed position within the numerical sequence.

Whether it is placed at the beginning or the end has its underlying reasons; "抑" (*yì*) here signifies "to stop," "to limit," or "to examine. That is to say, when the *pārājika* is placed below the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Skt.;

Chinese: 殘), it is called "upper"; when placed below the *prāyaścittika-naiḥsargika* (Skt.; Chinese: 提舍尼), it is called "lower. Its placement is not arbitrary; there is a reason for it. Therefore, it is said that there "is" [a cause].
Because of this, those that are heavy reside above, while those that are light reside below; they cannot emerge simultaneously, and thus appear either before or after.

According to the interpretation of Li, [the first three] are causes, while [the latter five] are effects. This is so because they are established for the sake of others and because others are established by them.
The commentary states: "As a means for the sake of others, they therefore reside in the third aggregate. Hence it is said: "for the sake of establishing others."

This refers to the means by which another is brought to the *pārājika* offense. Regarding "five for the sake of the fruit": this refers to the *phala-pāṇa* (fruit-garland) that stands alone, which is situated in the fifth category (*nikāya*).
Since the *duṣkṛta* (transgression) is used as the cause for this *phala-pāṇa*, it is said, "because it is accomplished by another, it is thus indicated.
Here, the *duṣkṛta* is referred to as "another" (*para*).

Alternatively, those [offenses] which follow after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and are subsumed under the category of "precepts" (*śīla*) refer to the coarse transgressions of the first three groups, which are termed "precepts," while the subtle transgressions of the lower four groups are called "dignified conduct" (*īryāpatha*).
Regarding the phrase "such as the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the first two categories, whether distant or proximate," my own view is as follows:

This statement is not yet precise; it is merely a provisional judgment. That is to say, regarding the first two sections, the preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*)—both distant and proximate—encompass offenses of varying degrees of gravity.
The proximate preparatory stage of the second section is equivalent to the distant preparatory stage of the first section, whereas the distant preparatory stage of the second section is light.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Light [offenses] are such as the distant preparatory stages of the second section, and so forth."

Thus, one should know that the words used here still leave room for further interpretation. This is merely a provisional judgment regarding the two sections on "barbarians" (*yi*) and "cruelty" (*can*), each of which has two preparatory stages (*upāya*).
It states that these are "grave" offenses, though it has not yet been possible to distinguish them in detail. Regarding the distant preparatory stages of the two sections, they are said to be "light.
This refers to those who use human hair while naked—that is, exposing their bodies before the Buddha or using human hair as a cord.

Regarding the statement that "precepts (*śīla*) and deportment (*airyāpathika*) are mentioned both generally and specifically": although these two names differ, they mutually manifest their respective categories.
They are explained by distinguishing them individually; yet, if discussed generally, all seven [types of transgressions] can be termed "deportment.
For example, when one commits the offenses of killing or stealing, is this not indeed a lack of proper deportment? As the Buddha rebuked Sūdena, saying: "You are lacking in deportment."

[The term] "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*) does not refer exclusively to pure conduct; rather, this is the general name for dignified deportment. Speaking in terms of the precepts, all seven categories are collectively termed "precepts.
For instance, when one speaks of the "two hundred and fifty precepts," how could one exclude the lower four groups? Even the commission of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is called "breaking the precepts.
Thus, within the opening passages of the lower sections, it is also stated: "At first, before the precepts were established," and so forth. Therefore, we know that [the term refers to the precepts].

"Name" (*ming*) refers to the general category. Thus, Lü [Xingfu] said: "If one discusses this generally, all five classes of rules that can effect correction possess the function of preventing wrongdoing;

they are collectively designated as 'precepts' (*jie*). Therefore, the subsequent text speaks of them together, mentioning both 'the initial transgression of a precept' and 'the establishment of a rule for a bhikṣu.

If we rely on the physical and verbal movements, postures, and ritual protocols, these are all termed 'dignified conduct' (*wei yi*). Hence, the subsequent text mentions 'non-dignified conduct' (*fei wei yi*) and so forth."

Let us first divide these into two categories. The faults prevented by the former two are coarse; thus, their antidotes are called *śīla* (precepts). The violations of the latter three are subtle; thus, their antidotes are termed *īryāpatha* (dignified conduct).

Regarding the distinction between them, the Vinaya text states within the section on prohibitions: "If someone brings forward another’s offense, the Buddha ordered that one should interrogate them thoroughly:
'Is it a breach of the precepts (*śīla*)? Or is it a breach of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*)? If they say it is a breach of the precepts, [one asks]: 'Which precept has been broken?'"
Regarding the precepts: are they *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or *sthūlātyaya*? Or if one says they violate the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*), what kind of decorum do they violate?
Are they *pāyattika* or *duṣkṛta*? Based on this, it is clearly known that the preceding section concerns the precepts (*śīla*), while the subsequent section concerns decorum (*airyāpathika*).
This is explained according to their specific distinctions.
Regarding the classification of those that are uniform and mixed: these refer to the *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *prāyaścittika*. These four are uniform.
There are three senses of "uniformity": first, uniformity of name, as they share the same names such as *pārājika* and so forth;

second, uniformity of substance (*dravya*), as in the case of the four grave offenses (*catur-ānantarya*), where the nature of the transgression has no degrees of lightness or heaviness, and their retribution likewise lacks gradations, being identical in measure—nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty [kalpas].

They are all "thousand-year" offenses. Although they differ in their categorization—such as the *Cankṣepa* (Residual) and other sections—their essential nature (*tattva*) is uniform insofar as they constitute offenses for violating the teachings.
