The character is composed of the radical "flesh" (肉). The *Liji* says, "His son was not *xiao*," which refers to this very point. This is a "compound ideographic" character (*huìyì zì*).
With "small" (小) below "flesh," it signifies a son born who resembles his father. When a person's offspring resembles the father, it is called *xiao*; thus, a son is termed "small flesh.
Since a son who resembles his father is called *xiao*, [it follows that] when Yao begot Prince Zhu, he did not resemble his father.
Such a person is called unworthy. Now, those who act contrary to the Dharma are unable to carry on the lineage, just as an unworthy son cannot fulfill his filial duty.

As for those who recklessly claim to have found refuge in the Mahāyāna and so forth: since the Nirvāṇa Sūtra was first transmitted to the East, we have ceased our attachment to the three kinds of meat and have internalized these supreme teachings.
We have long maintained a vegetarian diet without weariness, yet they conversely claim that this is merely the Hīnayāna, while they themselves indulge in fish and meat with ease.
Lips. To call this the practice of a bodhisattva is, in fact, the karma of a rākṣasa; what, then, can be called a bodhisattva?

Have you not heard the ultimate teachings of the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras? According to Tiantai, there are six kinds of bodhisattvas: first, the bodhisattva of principle-nature (*li-xing*), which refers to all sentient beings;
second, the bodhisattva of name (*ming-zi*), which refers to those who have heard the sutras (referring here to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*); third...

1. Bodhisattvas of Contemplative Practice refers to those who have first resolved their minds [for enlightenment]. 2. Bodhisattvas of Similarity refers to those in the thirty stages of mind (the *triṃśat-cittotpāda*).
3. Bodhisattvas of True Part refers to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). 4. Ultimate Bodhisattvas is the designation for the Buddha as a Bodhisattva.

Now, as for unworthy persons, they do not hinder the fact that one is among the number of Bodhisattvas of the rational nature (*dharmatā-bodhisattva*). Regarding those who speak lightly of the True Sūtras:
"True Sūtras" refers to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, as stated by Ciyun. Those who hold their own teaching in high esteem claim that the doctrine they study is the Mahāyāna;
that is, they are students of the Mahāyāna Vinaya as taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. Examining the text of that sūtra, it clarifies the entirety of the Great [Vehicle].
This is the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*). The text states: "The Mahāyāna is able to give birth to all dharmas, just as Lake Anavatapta gives rise to the eight great rivers;
in this way, the Great Vehicle encompasses all wholesome dharmas. There are six points regarding this: first, the abiding of the True Dharma; second, the extinction of the True Dharma;
third, the *Prātimokṣa*; fourth, the *Vinaya*; fifth, going forth (*pravrajyā*); and sixth, receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The full precepts are all for the sake of the Mahāyāna. That which causes the True Dharma to abide is that which causes the Mahāyāna to abide; that which causes the Mahāyāna to abide is precisely that which causes the True Dharma to abide.
That which causes the True Dharma to perish is that which causes the Mahāyāna to perish; that which causes the Mahāyāna to perish is precisely that which causes the True Dharma to perish.
The Prātimokṣa and the Vinaya—these two dharmas are identical in meaning though different in name. The Vinaya is precisely the Mahāyāna training. Why is this?
Because it is based upon leaving the household life and receiving full ordination (upasampadā); therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna code of majestic decorum (vṛtta-śīla).
This Vinaya is for those who have left the household life; it is the receiving of the full precepts. Regarding the eighty sections, Zhìlì states: "Wisdom..."
The treatise clarifies that at the time of the First Council, Upāli ascended the high seat eighty times during a single summer retreat to recite the Vinaya Piṭaka;

this is called the "Eighty Sections" (Aśīti-bhāga) and is also known as the "Eighty Recitations" (Aśīti-saṃgīti). This is precisely the *Śīla-pāramitā* (Perfection of Ethical Discipline), which translates as "precepts" (*śīla*) and is one among the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Are these Six Perfections not the study of the Hīnayāna? The *Śatadharma-upamāsūtra* (Hundred Simile Sutra), lower fascicle, states: "For example..."

It was as if there were a teacher with two disciples. The teacher suffered from a foot ailment and sent his two disciples away, instructing them that each should attend to one foot, massaging it at the appropriate times.

These two disciples constantly harbored mutual hatred and jealousy. When one disciple went out, the other disciple seized the very foot he was supposed to massage and struck it with a stone until it was broken. When the first disciple returned, he was enraged by what had happened. Furthermore—
They seize the person by the foot they are pressing and immediately break it apart. It is the same with the disciples of the Buddha’s Dharma:
those who study the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) texts do not concern themselves with the Hīnayāna, and those who study the Hīnayāna likewise do not concern themselves with the Vaipulya.
Consequently, the scriptural canons of the Great Sage are lost in both directions. (The preceding statement that "it does not concern the Hīnayāna" refers to the denial of the true nature.)

Regarding the statement that "even if a Bodhisattva establishes teachings, they remain unstained by their influence": this refers to a Bodhisattva who has attained the Stage of Pure Mind—that is, a Bodhisattva from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
For the sake of skillful means and benefiting others, such a Bodhisattva may fully engage in the ten non-virtuous actions, including killing;

yet, because they lack any defiled intention within, they "blend with the light" without being "defiled by the dust. Therefore, it is said that they remain "unstained by their influence," as explained in the previous fascicle.
This refers to the *Ākarṣaṇa-śāstra*. Its meaning is that although a Bodhisattva who has attained the pure mind may engage in acts such as taking life, he himself incurs no defiled fault.

Regarding the phrase "the great being at the initial stage" (*ādikarmika-mahāsattva*) and so forth: this refers to those who act with the aforementioned conditions; they are those from the first bhūmi upward who are permitted to practice this dharma.
If one is a Bodhisattva prior to the bhūmis, they are called a "great being at the initial stage. This must be identical to the sound [of the teaching].

Regarding the hearing of the Vinaya precepts: one must not transform [others] through contrary practices. This means that while one has not yet been able to abandon defilement, one merely severs the afflictions partially.

For example, as in the saying: "If I do not kill, I bestow the lives of all sentient beings. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, upholding the precepts can give rise to the dāna-pāramitā (perfection of giving).
There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; and third, the gift of fearlessness. By means of...
Regarding their observance of the precepts: they restrain themselves and do not encroach upon the wealth and property of any sentient being;
this is called the giving of material wealth to sentient beings. Furthermore, those who see them admire their conduct. Moreover, they preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain awakening.
Furthermore, by maintaining pure precepts, they serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings, enabling all beings to obtain immeasurable blessings. Thus one plants [the seeds of merit].
This is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Furthermore, all sentient beings fear death; to maintain the precepts and refrain from harming them is the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).
Master Ci said: "In general, there are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), which only provides external sustenance;

second, the gift of Dharma, which sustains the spiritual faculties; and third, the gift of fearlessness, which consists of non-killing and so forth, and bestows life itself. This concludes the discussion.

Regarding the phrase "In fact, etc.," Ciyun [Zhiyi] states: "The principle is fundamentally beyond words; it cannot be discussed through speech. To be free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and so forth is the true essence of this principle.

Yet these people forcibly generate conceptual distinctions regarding this principle, saying that 'the characteristics of the precepts are like empty space,' thereby leading those who uphold them into delusion and confusion.
Because they engage in conceptualization outside of the principle, it is said that their errors exceed the reality. I, however, believe this is not the case; it is merely internal...
It is of no practical use. To speak of the truth of formlessness with one's mouth while that speech exceeds what the mind perceives is mere verbal praise—a mere embellishment.
As for "having a dignified appearance," this refers only to the formal deportment at the time of receiving initiation upon the ritual platform; it does not give rise to [true realization].

Regarding the formation of the precept-substance (*śīla-skandha*), the fact that all one’s actions are none other than the precepts and so forth clarifies that throughout Śākyamuni’s single dispensation—throughout the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma—all established rituals and regulations are exclusively the Dharma of the *śrāvakas*. There were no Bodhisattva-saṃghas;

therefore, although Maitreya and Mañjuśrī were Bodhisattvas in mind, their physical appearance was identical to that of the *śrāvaka* monks in their tonsured ordination and observance of the precepts. This remains the case unto this day.

Together they have inherited this tradition. Such was the transformative ritual of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. If you now revile it, whom do you claim to follow as your teacher? By which Buddha were you transformed?
You exhaust yourself in vain effort, yet fail to recognize the fundamental source. If you give rise to wholesome states and receive benefit—even claiming, "I am a follower of the Mahāyāna"—Xuan said:
"In governing the study of the gates [of learning], nothing is propagated without the precepts; one must maintain them with mutual goodness."

Without the precepts, one cannot be established. Therefore, it is said that "benefit and reputation reach one another" and that during the summer retreat, one attends the assembly hall with reverence for the teacher’s transmission and the venerable models.

One hastens to the ritual platform and diligently wears the belt; is this not because of a greedy determination and courageous resolve? One seizes upon the precepts and honors them as teachers, yet one's conduct cuts off the essential principles of the Way.
One abandons the precepts to fill the ditches and ravines, focusing one's will solely on the fundamental poisons of acceptance and rejection, which are close at hand within the mind. This...
How deeply deluded they are! Regarding the analogy of the *liǎo-ǔ* (rat-bird) bhikṣu and so forth: according to the *Fózàng jīng* (Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra), the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"For example, a eunuch is neither male nor female; a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts is likewise.
He is not called a householder, nor is he called one who has left the home-life. After his life ends, he goes straight to hell. Furthermore, it is like a bat that wishes to catch..."
When it is time for the bird, it enters its hole and becomes a mouse; when it wishes to catch a mouse, it flies through the air and becomes a bird.
Yet in reality, it possesses no utility as a great bird; its body is foul and filthy, and it delights only in darkness and obscurity. The bhikṣu who violates the precepts is just like this.
They neither participate in the *poṣadha* nor the *pravāraṇa*; they do not enter the service of kings, yet they are called neither laypeople (*avadātavasana*) nor renunciants (*pravrajita*).
Like the charred remains of a corpse or burnt wood, they are no longer fit for use.

Lacking the aggregates of morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they produce no virtuous sounds—no sounds of morality, concentration, or wisdom—but only the foul and evil cries of those who have broken the precepts.
Regarding sound, the *Śāstra* states that they take up robes, food, and drink as offerings, yet day and night they engage in frivolous laughter and speech;
their actions of body, speech, and mind cannot be purified, and they delight in darkness like the bat. The *Sutra of Bequeathed Teachings* also says:
They are neither practitioners of the Way nor laypeople; they have no proper name. Regarding the phrase "a donkey wearing a lion's skin," the *Daśacakra Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "If there are sentient beings who give rise to coarse, evil, and foolish speech, yet claim to be wise;
who do not abandon false views and crave fame; who cannot restrain their body, speech, and mind, and whose minds constantly dwell on evil—"
First, they possess compassion, yet they do not reflect upon their own faults, but instead dwell on censuring the deficiencies of others;

their minds lack tranquility, yet they claim to be followers of the Mahāyāna and praise the Mahāyāna, teaching others to read and recite it while remaining themselves unsubdued regarding the Mahāyāna path.
Such persons find it difficult to obtain a human body and lose the fruits of the two vehicles, constantly tending toward the evil realms.
Those who possess wisdom do not wish to associate with them, declaring: "I am of the Mahāyāna.

It is like a donkey wearing a lion’s skin, which considers itself a lion. Someone seeing it from afar might also think it is a lion; as long as the donkey has not yet brayed, no one can distinguish it.
Once it has let out its voice, everyone near and far knows it is not a real lion. Thus do people perceive [them].
Having said this, they all spat upon him, saying, "This is a wretched, evil donkey, not a lion. People such as these are just like that.
Having committed the ten unwholesome deeds, they incinerate the human race; they are not vessels for the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*. They ruin the seeds [of the Dharma].
Who would be deluded by their words, thinking, "I am of the Mahāyāna"? The Buddha then spoke a verse: "The perverse and stubborn take delight in breaking the precepts. If they hear..."
He praises the Mahāyāna. Who is called a bodhisattva? It is like a donkey wearing a lion’s skin. As for the extensive denunciation and criticism, what need is there to state it explicitly?
This means that since the sūtra itself extensively criticizes [the opponent], what further need is there to describe it?
Those who are newly trained and thus deluded by external dust are exemplified by Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha and his conversion of five hundred newly trained disciples;
how could those who have studied for a long time follow such delusion? The explanation of the thirteen chapters is hereby concluded.
Commentary on the *Sifenlü Chao* (Excerpts from the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), Scroll Six, End; Scroll Seven, Beginning.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Chapter Fourteen: Explaining the Characteristics of the Individual Precepts (*Suijie Shixiang Pian*).

First, regarding the intent of this section: the preceding chapter has already clarified the essential outlines of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; however, it merely explained their titles.

As for the sections below, the various characteristics and categories are extremely numerous, and thus they must be further analyzed. Regarding these individual characteristics, the regulations are now shown in detail.
To further clarify the recognition [of these matters], this chapter has been composed. It is also said:

"The preceding chapters have already clarified the names and characteristics of the various categories of precepts (*śīla-skandha*), the karmic retribution for violations, and the stages of karma, serving as a clear mirror for the mind and eyes. This is intended to enable practitioners to maintain the precepts without transgression.

However, while the general characteristics of what constitutes holding or violating the precepts are established, the details of practice are still numerous. If these were not presented with specific detail according to each case, the practice of maintaining them would be difficult to establish; therefore, this chapter [is written]."

It comes forth. Furthermore, it may be said that this was originally intended to explain this treatise; thus, the names and categories of the articles [of the Vinaya] were first clarified as the purpose for which the preceding section appeared.
This section arises in response to that. Regarding the phrase "explaining the characteristics according to the precepts" (*suíjiè shìxiàng*), Master Lì states:

it means to explain the specific characteristics (*xiàngmào*) of each of the two hundred and fifty precepts one by one—that is, to explain their observance and violation, their gravity and lightness, their allowance and prohibition, and their pervasiveness and obstruction.

This is the characteristic [of the precepts]. I believe this is not the case. In the present treatise, the four dharmas—the precept law (*śīladharma*), the precept essence (*śīlatattva*), the precept practice (*śīlacaryā*), and the precept characteristics (*śīlalakṣaṇa*)—are fully elucidated.

If one were to establish only the "understanding" (*adhimukti*), it would fail to encompass these four exhaustively; therefore, I shall now provide an explanation. That which consists of the formal vow of the resolve and the ritual procedures at the altar is called "receiving" (*samādāna*).

Following the reception, one practices protection in relation to objective conditions, accords with the original essence of what was received, and exerts diligence in the three karmas to prevent [transgressions].
The seven non-prohibitions are called "conformity" (*anuvartana*). Since the characteristics of one who conforms are numerous, I shall now explain their manifestations; thus it is said.

If one interprets it in this way, even the inclusion of the *dharmas* (precepts) and the *dharma-body* (the essence of the precepts) would not be exhaustive. This is because the *dharmas* and the essence fundamentally belong to the category of "receiving" (*upasaṃpadā*), and are not matters pertaining to conformity.
Alternatively, the primary intent of the section is to clarify the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), as well as the *dharma*, the essence, and the practice.
Third, the distinctions are established based on their mutual relationship. If one explains it in this manner, there is no contradiction even with the preceding exposition.
As for the "sub-commentary" (zhuzi), it refers to the reason for composing this section as generated by the author of the *Chao* (the *Zongjing Lu*) himself.

Regarding the section titled "Commentary on the Section of Rules": In the Vinaya, the *Prātimokṣa* for monks and nuns is listed first to clarify what is to be observed (*śīla*) and what constitutes an offense (*āpatti*).

This is followed by the twenty *Khandakas*, which clarify what constitutes observance and what constitutes the cessation of offenses. Although the two categories of observance and offense are thus divided, there were still points that remained incomplete.

Therefore, Upāli further cited each individual rule from the preceding text to question the Buddha, and the Buddha answered each one; this is called the "Section of Rules" (*Vibhaṅga*). This is because...

Upāli was the master who transmitted and upheld [the Dharma]. Regarding all matters of doubt, he consulted and resolved each one individually, ensuring that others would recognize the characteristics [of the precepts] and uphold them.

Thus, by inquiring into the modes of conduct—whether an act constitutes an offense or not—he resolved doubts, removed obstructions, and made everything clearly understood; hence it is called the *tiao-bu* (sections/chapters).

When it says "to rectify the root" regarding those who have not yet fully mastered the offenses and non-offenses, this refers to the two preceding sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* within the Vinaya text, as well as...

The *Khandhaka* constitutes the fundamental text (*mūla*). Since the matters of observance and violation are not fully detailed within the fundamental text, there are the texts of the *Vibhaṅga* (Articles and Sections);
thus it is said that these are "further listed. For what reason are the meanings of the *Vibhaṅga* cited?

It is because one wishes to clarify that the purpose of this chapter on "Explaining the Characteristics" is identical in meaning to the *Vibhaṅga* of the Vinaya. Regarding the annotation, "Now, for the sake of those for whom the various chapters are insufficient," etc., it means:

Although the twenty-nine chapters from the beginning to the end clarify the observance and violation of precepts, it is feared that they may not have encompassed everything that has come down to us; therefore, this one chapter was established.
Thus, it is said that a separate section was created as a distinct category.

Regarding the "two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus," according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, when including the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (methods for settling disputes), and so forth, they precisely total two hundred and fifty.
For now, we shall follow this enumeration and explain their characteristics accordingly. As for the note stating that they are "immeasurable and boundless" in their detailed exposition:

since precepts arise from objects (*viṣaya*), and these objects encompass both sentient and non-sentient beings across myriad categories as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how could there be any limit?

This is the measure. The commentary states that those living at home do not possess *śīla*. This clarifies that although laypeople may receive the five or eight precepts, they only guard four branches of body and speech;
therefore, it is said they do not possess them fully. Monks and nuns who have left the household life fully guard seven branches of body and speech;
thus, they possess the *śīla-pāramitā*. What is called the "perfection of morality" (*śīla-pāramitā*) is precisely the *śīla-pāramitā*. *Śīla* is morality; *pāra* is...
Pāramitā means "reaching the other shore. To reach the other shore is the meaning of "crossing over.

Regarding the phrase "practicing in reliance upon this," it refers to practicing in reliance upon these two hundred and fifty precepts as they are designated; one recognizes and maintains the characteristics of grave and light transgressions, as well as the various categories of offenses—hence the term "categories and characteristics" (*zhongxiang*).
As for the phrase "thereby giving rise to concentration and wisdom": through the precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is able to arise.
Wisdom destroys the afflictions; therefore, it is called "cutting and pruning. Regarding the statement "darkness concerning the object of focus (*ālambana*) and so forth," this establishes clarity:

the mind is the subject that focuses, and the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) are the objects of focus. If one does not recognize these characteristics, this is darkness regarding the object of focus, which destroys pure precepts and is termed "defiled delusion.

As for the statement "one will subsequently sink further into the miserable realms (*durgati*)," one originally receives the precepts with the hope of becoming free from defilement and attaining the Path.
Furthermore, because one now follows along with objects of perception due to ignorance and thus transgresses against them, how can one turn back from birth and death?

Instead, one proceeds toward the three miserable realms; hence it is said, "sinking and wandering in the paths of suffering. Regarding "manifesting characteristics based on the teachings," this means manifesting the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts by relying on the Vinaya teachings now.
As for the phrase "may there be no calamities or harms," Zheng Xuan stated: "Shu (庶) arises from the multitude. Moreover—
The term "shu" (庶) means "hope" (*wang*). It is also glossed as "to cause" (*shi*).

Regarding the phrase "directly stating whether one advances or declines," this refers to a general discussion of the mind and its objects, as found in the "Lower Section on Rules. Here, however, we discuss directly the characteristics of maintaining or violating the precepts:

if the conditions are fully met and a violation occurs, it is called "advancing" (*jin*); if the conditions are lacking and no violation occurs, it is called "declining" (*fei*). Sheng says: "Advancing" means...
"Good" refers to upholding [the precepts]; "bad" refers to violating them.
The statement that "the precepts are the vessel for crossing birth and death" takes the sense of transporting and delivering across as its meaning; thus they are called a "vessel.

The meaning of this "vessel" has already been explained at length in the introduction. Regarding the phrase "the essential tenet of the renunciant," "tenet" (zong) derives from "master" (zhu); it signifies what is honored.
It means that one must certainly respect the precepts. For the five groups of monastics—both ordained monks and nuns—must constantly and diligently cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.

The Eightfold Noble Path consists of the Three Trainings: morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Since morality stands at the head of these, it is called the "essential core.

Regarding the statement, "The recipient takes the entire *dharmadhātu* as the measure, while those who uphold them are as numerous as the rhinoceros-like [sages]," the commentary states that a rhinoceros is singular.
The horn appears but once in a thousand years; it is extremely difficult to find. Alternatively, one may distinguish between the *qilin* (unicorn) and the horn: the horn refers to the horn of an ox.
As it is said, "Students are like the hair on an ox's body, while those who achieve realization are like the horns of an ox.

This clarifies that although disciples in this final age of the Dharma receive the teachings in numbers as vast as the measure of the *dharmadhātu*, those who uphold them are as rare as the *qilin* or the horn. Even so, they are still said to be numerous at present.

As for this, it means that those who possess the horn-like [solitary] nature (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa) are still more numerous than those who uphold [the precepts], while those who uphold them are still fewer than those with the horn-like nature.

Regarding "not yet understanding the primary designation": the precepts are the designator (vyañjaka), which designates untainted true wisdom; thus, true wisdom is termed the "primary designation. Alternatively, one may discuss this in terms of what is proximate:

they designate the two types of upholding and the two types of transgression. By abandoning faults and evil and proceeding toward the good, if the practice of upholding is perfected, [true wisdom is attained].
Reaching the state where there is no further transgression is what is called the "original exposition" (*mūla-pratipādana*). The meaning is this:

originally, the Buddha established the precepts to restrain body and speech, to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and ultimately to obtain the benefit of the Path. When the wisdom of awakening reaches its ultimate limit, the pure and wondrous *bodhi* constitutes the original exposition.

Because they do not recognize the purport of this teaching, they give rise to defilement in accordance with the six sense objects and the five desires; hence it is said, "defilement arises following the objects.
Defilement refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), which can pollute the pure and wondrous bodhi because they are impurities; thus it is called "giving rise to defilement.

Regarding the phrase "venerated by sages and worthies," [Master] Li states that during the Buddha’s lifetime, the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles should naturally have followed and honored [this teaching], and after his passing, all Arhats likewise did so.
First, the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* is established. Since even the noble ones (āryas) hold this in high esteem and revere it, how could ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) not observe its precepts?

"Revere" (*qīn*) means to look up to with veneration; "sequence" (*xù*) refers to the account of origins. "Restraint" (*yì*) means to cease. As for the phrase "the upright pen unfolds," this has already been explained within the introduction.

This is precisely that which embodies the path of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*). It is clearly established that by means of the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the four-part motion), one receives this [ordination].
