It is called "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*); it is not the essence of the precept-body consisting of manifest or unmanifest restraint. However, "disciplining" (*vinaya*) refers to the practice that is expressed [by the term].

According to the *Śrāddhaparivarta* (Chapter Seven of the *Upāsakaśīla-sūtra*), it says: "Furthermore, 'precept' is called 'training. One trains in disciplining the mind and the various faculties through wisdom;

therefore, it is called 'training'" (above is the scriptural passage). This means that one disciplines the mind by being free from desire, and disciplines wisdom by being free from... [ignorance/delusion].
Because of ignorance, one tames the sense faculties; because of their being well-guarded, this reveals the restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).

As for its essence being wholesome rather than unwholesome or neutral: in terms of the three natures, it is obtained as having the nature of wholesomeness, and not from anything else—neither the unwholesome nor the neutral—which can give rise to and obtain the precepts.
Regarding the statement that "because the nature [of precepts] extends to both good and evil, the category of evil discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*) likewise extends universally," Zhiyi clarifies:

If precepts are of the nature [of the mind], then since this nature extends to both good and evil, when one receives good precepts, one restrains evil from arising and brings the good precepts to fulfillment; this is called the "good nature.

Because at the time of receiving them, they are vowed toward objects as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is said that they "extend universally. This is also the case when one receives evil precepts.
It prohibits the arising of good and causes unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*) to be accomplished, increasing them moment by moment;
because its commitment is universal, it also pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. If one reverses the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*), the principle is the same.
Above, one prohibited good while practicing evil, which is also called "precept" (*śīla*); now, if one reverses this, one prohibits evil while practicing good. This is stated because...

Regarding the statement that "the name 'precept' (śīla) is established based on the teaching," Jì explains: this refers to the preceding passage. To call the precepts "restraint" (saṃvara) is to establish the name based on the teaching.
"Restraint" (lü) means the teaching; "discipline" (yí) means dignified deportment (īryāpatha). Therefore, it is said that the name is established based on the teaching.

It is not that the character for "precept" (*śīla*) is defined as "teaching. Precepts are, in fact, practice. Now, if one speaks of "evil discipline" (*akuśala-vinaya*) and names it "evil precept," is this not a case of receiving a name based on its teaching?
However, when viewed from the perspective of what a person actually practices, the precept is itself the practice.

Regarding the designation of this cause by means of its fruit: this refers to establishing the name of the fruit upon the cause. Only the *prātimokṣa* as principle (*nyāya*) is its cause; it is not yet its fruit.
Now, when one says that *mokṣa* is translated as "fruit," this is the manifestation of the name of the fruit within the context of the cause.
Therefore, Li said: *Prātimokṣa* is here called "liberation in each instance" (*prati-prati-mokṣa*), yet it is termed "precept" (*śīla*).

Furthermore, although the precepts are not liberation themselves, they are capable of producing the fruit of liberation. Because the fruit is designated according to its cause, the precepts are called "liberation.
Therefore, a sutra states: "The precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation; thus they are named *pratimokṣa* (individual liberation)."
Ji said: "It is like when people speak of a persimmon tree or a pear tree; the tree itself is not the pear or the persimmon, but it is the cause of the pear and persimmon because it can produce them.
The persimmon is the fruit. Now, when one speaks of a 'pear tree,' this is also a case of designating the fruit by its name within the context of the cause."

The explanation of the meaning of *śīla* (precepts) above is now complete; below, the meaning of *vimukti* (liberation) is clarified. Regarding the designation "partial liberation" (*aṃśika-vimukti*) used in proximity to clarify the name:
it is established that *mokṣa* (liberation) refers to [the stage] up to the attainment of *bodhi*. This is ultimate liberation (*atyanta-vimukti*).

Regarding the phrase "now, liberation according to one's capacity": this refers to being exempt from the three miserable realms and attaining the benefits and happiness of the human and celestial realms; hence it is called "according to one's capacity.

This interpretation is somewhat loose and does not accord with the present text. It should rather be understood as referring, for the time being, to the two hundred and fifty precepts, which are capable of preventing the seven types of misconduct.

This is called "partial liberation" (*prādeśika-vimukti*). For instance, regarding the first precept: by abstaining from sexual misconduct, one guards against internal desire; because desire does not arise, it is called "liberation.
Furthermore, as in the regulation against drinking alcohol, with respect to the aspect of not drinking, this is the abandonment of evil, which is likewise termed "liberation.

As for the phrase "restraining the acquisition of virtuous qualities" up to "because of following the precepts, one is freed from entanglements with respect to those [objects]," and so forth: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the available portion.]
This means that if one discusses the meaning of liberation from a distance, it is by virtue of the merit of the precepts that one ultimately achieves the benefit of the Path.

When delusions are exhausted and liberation is fulfilled, all myriad entanglements vanish; this is called "severing entanglements. Because of this power of the precepts, it is said that one attains sainthood through the precepts.

Fourth, regarding the differences in the conditions for undertaking [the precepts]: if we discuss the single method of receiving them through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) alone during the Final Age, this refers to the conditions for receiving the precepts.

Although there are five such conditions, the "receiving by coming forward" (*svāgata*) is restricted solely to being administered by a Buddha; the "receiving by the higher dharma" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) is restricted to those who have attained the fruits of sainthood.

The threefold formula was restricted to the eight years [prior to the First Council], while the Eight Respects were restricted solely to Mahāprajāpatī. Therefore, the five hundred Śākya women all received ordination through *karmavācanā*.

Since this single reception by *karmavācanā* remains applicable throughout the present degenerate age, it is said thus. Consequently, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The procedures for monks and nuns should be clearly understood.

There are ten conditions for receiving ordination: first, the 'Come hither' (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*); second, the 'breaking of fetters,' whereby one attains Arhatship and is spontaneously moved [to ordination]."

The precepts. Third, the three-fold verbal [ordination]: this refers to encountering an Arhat and receiving the Three Refuges; immediately, full ordination (*upasampadā*) is produced. Fourth, the five persons who maintain the Vinaya in the borderlands.
Fifth, the ten persons in the central lands (the above five are explained in terms of monks). Among the nuns, there are likewise five: first, the eight respects;

second, receiving [ordination] from a group of twenty; third, receiving by means of a messenger; fourth, those of younger age who have previously taken refuge—namely, those aged ten who have been married—and having completed [the requirements].

Twelve [types of ordination] involve receiving the precepts. Regarding the five directions, the principle is established that the ten-member assembly confers the precepts. As for these ten conditions above, if explained in terms of retribution (*vipāka*):

the "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) and the "shattering of fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*) apply to both monks and nuns; the "three-fold speech" (*tri-vākya*) is restricted to monks; the "eight respects" (*aṣṭau-gauravāḥ*) are for nuns; the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) applies to monks;

and the remainder may be understood accordingly. If explained in terms of time: the "Come hither," the "three-fold speech," and the "eight respects" are restricted to the Buddha’s own lifetime, while the "shattering of fetters" [applies to all times].

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it applies generally from after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. To clarify this in terms of location: the "Come hither" (*ehi*) ordination and the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) were restricted to Jambudvīpa, because the Buddha attained enlightenment there.

However, the *karmavācanā* for resolving the schism applies throughout the three continents. Nevertheless, of the various conditions mentioned above, they have almost entirely disappeared in the present age;
only the single reception of the *karmavācanā* is currently practiced and universally observed in this final dharma period.
That which must rely upon causes and depend upon conditions to be able to endure and be established: "endure" (cháng) is read with a level tone here.

The cause is the mind of the recipient, and this mind has three grades that differ. The attainment of the precepts likewise varies as superior, middling, or inferior, according to the state of mind at the time of reception.

When one takes all sentient and non-sentient objects as conditions and possesses a mind that intends to sever evil and cultivate good, this is called the "cause. As for "conditions," these refer to the preceptor and the *śramaṇera*, and so forth.
The Dharma: the establishment of the boundary is accomplished; the *karmavācanā* is without fault; the robes and bowl are already one's own, and so forth, as detailed in the preceding fascicle.
There are five [conditions] for the recipient and six [conditions] regarding the person addressed; these are all the requisite conditions.

The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states that there are five conditions: first, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) must act according to the Dharma; second, the two *ācāryas* must act according to the Dharma; third, the seven-membered Saṃgha must be pure;
fourth, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) must be accomplished; and fifth, the Saṃgha must be in harmony and grant their consent (*chanda*). Lì says:

Regarding the reception of the precepts through *karmavācanā*, what has been established since ancient times consists of four conditions. According to what is taught in the Vinaya, one understands the eight types of *bhikṣus*.

Regarding the term "bhikṣu through formal ritual" (*karmavācanā*): if one has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations), such that it is accomplished according to the Dharma (accomplishment through the causal conditions of the teaching);
if one has obtained a proper location (accomplishment through the causal conditions of the boundary, meaning not being separated from the assembly within the boundary);

and if one abides in the dharma of a bhikṣu (accomplishment through the causal conditions of having reached the required age and being free from physical impediments)—if these four conditions are fulfilled, one is a "Great Bhikṣu. Therefore, the present [text] is based on these four causal conditions.

Regarding the formal determination (*niyama*), it is entirely incomplete compared to the five conditions set forth in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*. Although that text enumerates five, when subsumed under the four conditions found in the Vinaya, they are comprised by only three:
the first and the second and third belong to the first condition, the "fulfillment of the quorum of the Saṃgha";
the fourth phrase belongs to the second condition, the "accomplishment of the teaching"; and the fifth phrase belongs to the third condition, the "not being a separate assembly."

Since it is sufficient to possess only these three [qualifications], this cannot be comprehensive. That is to say, regarding the phrase "the three faculties of the recipient are free from defilement, etc.," this establishes that among the ten preceptors, there must be no instance of breaking the precepts, such that the recipient might see, hear, or suspect such a thing.

If the disciple knows that among the ten preceptors there is one who has committed a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and if a feeling of aversion arises in their mind, then the reception of the precepts is not accomplished. If the ten preceptors look toward one another, they must... [text truncated]

If one knows that a grave offense (*pārājika*) has been committed, the ritual (*dharma*) is not valid. However, if one has committed an offense from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward, it is permissible for all to receive [the ordination].

Regarding the statement "one whose mind is not complete and who clearly knows it is wrong": this refers to the person receiving [ordination] who knows that the ten masters have committed a breach of the precepts, yet does not commit a grave offense.
This constitutes a deficiency in the dharma. The *Śāstra* states: "If the speech is deficient or the sequence of before and after is disordered...

According to the second fascicle of the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, it says: "That which renders a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) invalid is when the speech is deficient, or when the sequence of before and after is not orderly, or when the expression is not clear;
this is termed 'invalidation of the *karmavācanā*. Conversely, it is valid. [The text] establishes that there is addition or subtraction."

The written text states that this is called "incomplete," or alternatively, it refers to performing the *jñapti* (announcement) and other formalities after the *karman* (formal act), which is termed "out of sequence.

It further says that if one receives the five precepts while remaining a layperson, these five constitute the *vinaya* treatise. Below, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*Duolun*) is further cited to collectively corroborate this meaning.
The *Tujiji* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures) by Dharma Master Jingmai of the Tang Dynasty states: "Śramaṇa..."
Zhìyán was a native of Liangzhou. He had traveled to the Western Regions and returned with Sanskrit manuscripts.

In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, he translated the *Lalitavistara* and other sutras at Jiyuan Monastery in Yangdu. However, prior to his ordination as a monk, Zhìyán had received the five precepts and had committed some violations.
Later, when he received the full monastic precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*), he doubted whether he had attained them. Consequently, he crossed the sea and traveled to India.
Tudu consulted an Arhat, but the Arhat could not decide the matter. He then questioned Maitreya, who replied that he had obtained the precepts. Sengyan was deeply dissatisfied with this, saying:
"The first of the thirteen *ānantarya* (grave offenses) subsumes the remaining twelve; those that are identical [to it] are likewise excluded.

According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, the thirteen matters of the *ānantarya* are listed in full, no different from the Vinaya itself, and it states in all cases: "This person does not obtain [the precepts]."
[They] act as preceptors (*upādhyāya*). Therefore, the following passage states: "These thirteen kinds of persons are unfit to act as preceptors.
Why? Because these persons lack the precepts. Furthermore, regarding the statement that those who have lost all [levels of] dhyāna and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [precepts] cannot attain them:

this means that once one has violated the five, eight, ten, or full [sets of] precepts, one immediately obstructs the Path; thus, one does not evoke this outflow-free precept. [The Master] Li says: "Having violated the five..."
Eighth: One must receive these five precepts and the eight precepts at the proper time and in accordance with the Dharma; if they are violated, it constitutes an obstacle.

As stated in the *Sāṅghabhedavastu* (or *Śraddhākaragupta-sūtra*), when receiving the five or eight precepts, one must inquire regarding the prohibitions and obstacles (*parihāra*). If one has previously committed the five or eight heinous offenses (*ānantarya*) or the like, or if one's parents, children, or servants do not grant their permission, one may not receive them.
If one does not inquire regarding the prohibitions and obstacles, the reception is not valid. Now, [if] these are violated...
[The opponent] objects:

"Now, if there are causes and conditions for a lack of difficulty (*an-āpatti*), yet one binds a small boundary (*sīmā*) and receives [the full precepts], this too is contrary to the Dharma. Jing replies:

"In this case, one merely incurs an offense for violating the teaching (*śāsana-dūṣaṇa-āpatti*); however, the binding of the boundary is successfully accomplished, and the reception of the full precepts is also valid."

However, regarding those for whom the vow and the practice correspond (*yoga*), it is established that "vow" refers to the moment of undertaking [the precepts], because one vows to abandon evil and cultivate good.
"Practice" refers to the subsequent conduct, as this conduct accords with the preceding vow; hence they are said to be "corresponding.

Thus, when the Vinaya states, "One who shares the same precepts as the bhikṣus through the commonality of undertaking them," it is established that one may be called a bhikṣu by virtue of having received these precepts through the same *jñapti-caturtha* (fourth motion) procedure. This is the name [of such a person].
There is precept; yet there may be the transgression of precept. If one were like a worldly person who has never originally received [the precepts], there would be no precept to violate;

therefore, it is said that this is "contrary to the above. "Contrary to the above" means not being identical to the precepts. This principle applies equally to those who, though having received them, have failed to attain them.

Jing says: "Because the receiving and maintaining are identical"—this explains the identity of the precepts. Because one receives and maintains them identically with the Dharma-realm, attainment is possible.

Regarding morality (*śīla*) and the transgression of morality: if one does not undertake and maintain them together, it is called "having no morality. One who has no morality does not transgress, because there is no non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "At the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*, etc. This means that the intent of the question is as follows: the mind is of four kinds, namely—

Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states of mind], as well as the mindless state: at the conclusion of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), among these four types of mind, which eight specific minds constitute the limit of receiving the precepts, and which constitute the limit of not receiving them?
Answer: Those who universally receive the precepts do so through all four types of mind; thus, one receives the precepts in all cases. The meaning of the answer is this:
if, at the time of the formal announcement (*jñapti*), these four types of mind are present, it constitutes the limit of not receiving [the precepts]. However, if during the *karmavācanā*...
At the conclusion [of the ritual], these four states of mind are present, and in all cases one obtains the precepts.

To say that one possesses the aforementioned four states of mind is because there is no distinction between wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral minds, nor is there a state of non-mind (*acittaka*). Furthermore, this is not analogous to other instances of non-mind;

it is clearly established that one does not obtain the precepts while entering a wholesome mind, meaning that because one is focused on a specific wholesome object, one does not obtain the precepts. That is to say:
It is solely because of his practice of giving alms, his hosting of assemblies, and his cultivation of merit at the temple that [the precepts] were obtained.

If it were by virtue of a mind of virtuous discipline, why would there not be a limit to obtaining the precepts? As for an evil mind, an indeterminate mind, or a mindless state—these three types of minds do not lead to attainment in any circumstance whatsoever.

Therefore, it is said that this is not the same as other states of mindlessness. As for "mindlessness," this refers to such states as entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or being asleep.
As for "neutral mind" (*avyākṛtacitta*), this refers to a state where the mind is merely indifferent and does not take good or evil as its object.
Regarding the *prātimokṣa* precepts that exist while the Buddha is in the world: as long as the Buddha-dharma has not yet ceased, it is all considered "the time when the Buddha is in the world.
As for the so-called "dhyāna" and "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) precepts, Master Li establishes that dhyāna and the outflow-free state are two distinct types of precepts.

Within the stages from the first dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, there exists this wholesome quality of the precepts; because one refrains from committing evil based upon them, they are called "precepts. These are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).

This refers to karma; however, it also encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Laypeople and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also train in these precepts; therefore, the subsequent text states:

"As for other dhyāna-precepts, even non-Buddhists possess them" (this will be further explained below). Uncontaminated precepts are precisely the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*).
It is so called because it is associated with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). Only those from the stage of Arhat upward possess this precept;
those in the first three fruits have only partially severed the karma of outflows (*āsrava*) and have not yet attained this precept. Thus, the Vinaya states:

"If a person cultivates the path and attains the fruit of Arhatship, they are then said to have received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Furthermore, when an Arhat practices, they must resolve their mind [to maintain it].

One takes these precepts; once the fruit is realized, they are immediately attained. If one previously lacked an unwholesome mind, even if one has attained Arhatship, one has not yet attained these precepts and must receive them again later.
In the Vinaya, this is called the "Supreme Dharma" (uttama-dharma); it is also called "breaking the fetters" (saṃyojana-bheda). The *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* states:
"After casting off this body, never again committing evil is called the 'outflow-free precept' (anāsrava-śīla). Second is the outflow-bound liberation (sāsrava-vimukti).
Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*): [Master] Li states that the *prātimokṣa* precepts are contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma and are phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* says: "The precepts are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and contaminated karma; if they are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are termed uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.

Regarding the statement that "the other two are restricted and narrow in scope": Li states that the dhyāna-precepts and the uncontaminated precepts arise only with respect to sentient beings (*sattva*), and not with respect to non-sentient things (*asattva*).

Then it does not arise. Regarding the three types of liberation from the outflows (*āsrava-vimukti*) that arise from loving-kindness (*maitrī*): this refers to the mind that severs evil and cultivates good by taking the realm of sentient beings across the three periods of time as its object;
through this, one gives rise to and attains this precept. As for the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*), their remote causes are taken into account.

It is not that they lack a compassionate heart; rather, it is hoped that this has already been established. At the time of generating the precepts, one simply generates these precepts by being in accord with the Path;

a compassionate heart is not required. Regarding the four *mokṣa* (liberation) precepts that apply to the seven classes of followers—namely, the five, eight, ten, and full [precepts]—they are all equally termed *mokṣa*.
A guest asks: "If the precepts of the seven classes are all equally termed *mokṣa*, then [what of] the five, eight, ten, and full [precepts]?"

All are *mokṣa* (liberation). Thus, it is essential that from the appearance of a Buddha until the Dharma has not yet perished, this *mokṣa* exists; when a Buddha does not appear in the world, there is no *mokṣa*.
All noble ones (*ārya*) obtain the five precepts of non-action (*akaraṇa-śīla*), which refers to those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) being born in an evil land.

Not committing evil deeds and not violating the five precepts is called the "precept of non-action. If this were merely the *prātimokṣa* (vow of individual liberation), it should be abandoned at the end of one's life;
why then does it persist through successive births and still constitute the five precepts? Answer: In truth, the five precepts are indeed abandoned at the end of life.

However, because these five precepts induce a superior fruit in the future, they manifest as the very nature of the five precepts wherever one is reborn. Therefore, it is not that the original *prātimokṣa* has not been abandoned.
However, these five *akaraṇīya-śīlas* (precepts of non-doing) are logically newly acquired; they are not the *mokṣa* (liberation/vow) of one who has been reborn [in a previous life].

That is to say, these five types are also *sahaja-śīla* (innate precepts). Based on this principle, the *pratyekabuddhas* who appear in an age without a Buddha, as well as those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) who possess the five *akaraṇīya-śīlas*, are also called *mokṣa*, even though they do not rely upon an age with a Buddha.
This continues the succession of the Three Vehicles, the Triple Gem, and the Three...

Regarding the "Path" (mārga), [Master] Li said: "The two preceding 'threes' can be understood. As for the three paths: first, the path of training (*śaikṣa*); second, the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
and third, the path that is neither training nor beyond training. 'Training' refers to the first three fruits [of the śrāvaka]. 'Beyond training' refers to the Arhat.

Only those who are candidates for Arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*) are termed 'neither training nor beyond training. This means that if one looks toward the state of an Arhat, they are called 'training.'"

If one looks back from the perspective of the three preceding fruits, they are then called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*); hence it is so stated. Ciyun says: "The three paths refer to humans, devas, and asuras.
Without these precepts, one merely invites rebirth in the three miserable realms and cannot attain the states of humans, devas, or asuras. Bin says:

"The three paths refer to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). The first fruit is called the path of seeing; the second and third fruits are..."
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Arhatship is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Master Liang of Ren said: "The *Āgamas* speak of three:

the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. The *Renwang jing* speaks of three: namely, those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).

As for the statement that the other two are inferior because they lack capability, Daoli [Liu] says: the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) cannot continue the succession of the Three Vehicles, the Three Jewels, and the Three Paths."
The merit of abiding [in the dhyānas] is subtle; therefore, it is inferior. As for the claim that even non-Buddhists possess them:
this refers to the fact that non-Buddhists also have the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, such as those by which one is reborn in the two higher realms.
"Sunlight, Mount Sumeru, and the most excellent *mokṣa*": this refers to the combined metaphors above. Previously it was said that among all lights, the sun is foremost;
among mountains, Mount Sumeru is foremost; and among trainings, *mokṣa* (liberation) is foremost. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing): [text follows].
The Prātimokṣa is called the peerless training. Among all lights, the light of the sun is the king;
among all mountains, Sumeru is the greatest. Among all trainings in the world, the Prātimokṣa is the greatest.
This Dharma exists only when a Tathāgata appears in the world; if no Buddha appears in the world, there is no sentient being capable of establishing this Dharma.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "This precept does not exist within the Śrāvaka vehicle; it does not exist within the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
it does not exist within the Bodhisattva vehicle. It exists solely within the Buddha vehicle.
This is because only a Buddha can establish this precept, whereas others cannot. Thus concludes the explanation of the meaning of superiority and inferiority.

Regarding the six levels of gravity for receiving [precepts], there are two schools of thought within the text whose explanations differ; these will become clear upon examining the text itself. As for the statement that "a transgression is not a grave offense," Jing says:
"Only four [of the precepts] are cited because they are the foundation of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). If one breaks these precepts, there is no way for the Noble Path to arise.
Therefore, when one commits the second [offense], one incurs only a minor offense. Regarding the statement that "an Arhat acts intentionally with the mind..."

Regarding those of middling and inferior grades of precepts, the masters of that treatise cite this case of an Arhat with inferior-grade precepts to prove the principle that [precepts] do not arise again.

Now it is said that this is not so; rather, when this Arhat first received the precepts, his mind was of an inferior grade, yet as he progressed in practice, he eventually attained the fruit of sainthood.
This was not due to the state of mind at the time of receiving them.
Answer: This response clarifies that when the accompanying factors (*anuvartaka*) are not considered, the essential substance (*dravya*) of the undertaking is established.

If one is protected by specific vows and does not transgress them, yet the wholesome protection is slight and weak due to the accompanying factors, then even though the substance of the karma produced at the time of undertaking is not considered, the precept may still be formed as a single momentary mental state within a single grade of concentration.
This is established to clarify once again the meaning of the "inferior grade" of the Arhat’s precepts mentioned previously.

This refers to the mental intention (*cetanā*). It means that while the actual performance occurs at the time of receiving [the precepts], it is during the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) that one possesses minds of superior, middling, or inferior grades within a single moment;
thus, the precept is produced. It is determined by whichever grade of mind was present at that specific time, because the precept is the retribution for the cause of that particular grade of mind.

Since it begins from that single grade and does not increase even slightly, and because the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is not of the nature of mind but persists until the end of life, it follows the conduct.

Regarding those who hold that there is increase or decrease, [the author] establishes the following: The manifest (vijñapti) and the non-manifest (avijñapti) coexist with the physical form; they are neither matter (rūpa) nor mind (citta).

Once this precept has been received, it remains constant and unchanging throughout the entirety of one's life; thus, there is no increase or decrease in its essence. However, there is merely an increase or decrease according to whether one conforms to its practice.

Another interpretation is that this also refers to the non-informative (*avijñapti*) within the category of sensation (*vedanā*). If it were the non-informative within the category of formations (*saṃskāra*), there would be differences such as increase or decrease, subtlety or coarseness, superiority or inferiority, and robustness or emaciation.
Sengshen says: "Although the non-informative is not itself the mind, it follows the mind at the time of the informative act (*vijñapti*).

Since the mind at the time of the act is of a single grade, the non-informative also follows as a single grade; thus it persists until the end of the physical form. Therefore, it is called 'non-informative,' and it is not [the case that it changes]."

This is because the mind is exhausted when the physical form perishes. As for the statement that there is an increase or decrease according to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it means that the body naturally becomes robust or emaciated in accordance with one's conduct;
it does not refer to whether the received body is superior, middling, or inferior. This is cited as a single phrase to be read separately.

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* that "some say [the lower ones]," the established position (*siddhānta*) asserts that this treatise contains the principle of "repeated initiation" and "repeated transgression.

Regarding the statement that "the superior one receives the name," the established position asserts that if one receives the five precepts, one is named a full-fledged *upāsaka*; if one further receives the eight precepts, one is named a *śīlavat-upāsaka* (pure-conduct lay follower);
and if one further receives the ten precepts, one is then named a *śrāmaṇera*. Thus, from the subtle to the manifest, one receives names according to the superiority [of the vows].
This is because subsequent forms of undertaking [the precepts] are progressively superior. According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, "Chapter on the Sevenfold Good Restraints," it says:
Question: At what time can the restraints (saṃvara) be obtained? Answer: There are those who undertake the one-day precepts;
this is the first restraint. On that very day, they undertake the upāsaka precepts; this is the second restraint. On that very day, they leave the household life to become a śrāmaṇera.

This is the third restraint. On that very day, one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*); this is the fourth restraint. On that very day, one attains the dhyāna-precepts; this is the fifth restraint.

On that very day, one attains the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); this is the sixth restraint. On that very day, one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) state; this is the seventh restraint.
Wherever one attains the fruits of the path, one obtains the restraints, yet those previously obtained are not lost; it is simply...
The Victor receives the name [of this discipline]. (Commentary: Regarding "in accordance with the attainment of the fruits of the path":

this refers to attaining the mundane paths such as the four dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), as well as the untainted supramundane path and the fruits of the noble path (*āryamārgaphala*).

In such instances of attaining the fruits of the path, one should immediately obtain the discipline of concentration and the path (*samādhi-mārga-saṃvara*). Although one obtains such discipline of concentration and the path, yet fundamentally...
The substance of the five precepts and so forth that have been obtained is not lost even now. Although it is not lost, one is designated as a *bhikṣu* and so on based on the superior [vows].

Furthermore, it should be understood that while the five precepts may be designated by the name "śrāmaṇera," or a śrāmaṇera may be designated by the name "bhikṣu," one can never definitively obtain the full *bhikṣu* precepts from the designation of the "dhyāna-path" (*samādhi-mārga*). However, some say: "Seven..."

Regarding the "virtuous restraints," there are seven: the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts, the two restraints of meditative concentration and the path, and the restraint of abandonment.
They do not follow the tenets of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, but rather, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, within the formless realm...

"There is no restraint (saṃvara). Restraint is form (rūpa); since that [unmanifest action] is not form, there is no restraint in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—except for the seventh, which is the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyānasaṃvara) [meaning excluding the sixth among the seven]. Now, upon careful examination, this is not logical.

Following the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, since non-manifest action (avijñapti) has as its essential nature that which is neither form nor mind, there is indeed restraint even in the formless realm. One should not rely on the Sarvāstivāda school [to the exclusion of other views].

The *Chengshi lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra) also shares this same meaning. Regarding what is called "dhyāna-precepts" (*dhyāna-śīla*), it is established that these constitute the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If one cultivates contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karman*), one enters the first dhyāna; if one cultivates uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karman*), one enters the first fruit (*prathama-phala*).

What is now termed "dhyāna-precepts" refers to the preparatory means (*upāya*) for the four dhyānas; it is also called the "not-yet-arrived dhyāna" (*anāgamya-dhyāna*). If one progresses further in cultivation, one then enters the [first dhyāna].

Regarding "dhyāna" (meditative concentration), there is another interpretation by Master Li: the dhyāna-precepts are the four fundamental dhyānas. If one speaks of "concentration-concomitant" (samādhi-sahagata) [precepts], these refer specifically to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) preceding the four dhyānas;

they are termed "concentration-concomitant" because they exist when one has entered meditative absorption but cease to exist once one has emerged from it. Before reaching the four dhyānas, they are called "concentration-concomitant. Once one enters meditative absorption, they are present; once one emerges from meditative absorption, they are absent.

Since precept and concentration coexist, it is called "concentration-concomitant precept" (though this cannot yet be considered definitive). What is referred to as "concentration-precept" is termed "precept concomitant with concentration" (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*) in the newer sūtras and śāstras;
this refers to the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The four dhyānas belong to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

All [stages] from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and so forth belong to the preceding "dhyāna-precepts. The four formless absorptions belong to the formless realm, namely: the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and so on.

The concentrations are: the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, and the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Now, upon careful examination, it is clear that the previous explanation is irrational. Previously, "dhyāna-precepts" were mentioned, which refers to the four fundamental dhyānas;

subsequently, "concentration-precepts" were mentioned, which refers to the four formless absorptions (śūnyatā-samādhis) of the formless realm. How can one further speak of the four dhyānas? This would entail the fault of redundancy, as has already been set forth above.

Regarding what is called the "precept concurrent with the path" (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*): from the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) onwards, it is associated with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

At the time of realizing the fruit, the path and the precepts arise together; this is termed the "precept concurrent with the path. As for those at or below the third fruit, they have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), but have partially severed the afflictions and delusions.

There are those who have not yet obtained this precept; furthermore, there are even Arhats who, though they have attained that state, have not yet realized this precept—such as the śrāmaṇera Arhat, namely Śukloddāna (Junti) and others (and so forth).
Also, such was the case with Trapuṣa and others, who received it later through the formal ritual of *karmavācanā*.
The reason for this is that it depends on whether the resolve is essential or non-essential.

According to the *Sārvāstivāda-śāstrācārya-paramparā* (The Lineage of Masters and Disciples of the Sarvāstivāda), it is established that the purpose of this text is to implicitly refute the previous *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Why is it that, while belonging to the same school, some say there is "mūla" (root/origin) [of the precepts], whereas the previous *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the precepts do not arise repeatedly? Now, this transmission...
How, then, can one receive [the precepts] again? Jing said: "According to this biographical account, it is the same as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. There is the principle of 're-initiation.

As for the statement that one follows the sequence of one's original seniority (*vassa*), this refers to the time of the previous reception; provided that every matter was performed according to the Dharma. As for the recipient [of the new ordination], I fear..."

It is not of the highest grade; it is now received anew according to the sequence of one’s original *saṃghāṭī* (seniority). The opposite may be understood accordingly. Regarding "Huizhao and others of Jetavana Monastery":

Jetavana Monastery was in Yangzhou, which is present-day Jiangning County. This is because the Jin, Song, Liang, and Chen dynasties all had their capitals on the left bank of the Yangtze River (*jiangzuo*).

Later, once the Southern Dynasties were defeated, the capital was moved north of the river. According to the *Sarvāstivāda Masters and Disciples Biographies* (*Sapodu shizi zhuan*), it says: [text follows].
At that time, there were several dozen monks at Jetavana Monastery, including Huizhao and others, who had all received the precepts together.
Subsequently, two groups of people wished to receive the precepts in succession; however, as the summer retreat (an-ju) approached, they were temporarily halted [and so forth].
When someone asked for the reason behind this, the tradition records: At that time, Dharma Master Huiyi of Jetavana Monastery was highly esteemed and held great influence. By nature...
He was upright and resolute. Upon seeing that Saṃghavarman and others were being re-ordained into full ordination, he felt it was inconsistent with his own views and said in anger:

"The Great Dharma has flowed eastward, yet the lineages of its transmission are not one. The eminent sages and wise men of old all shared a common standard; how can there suddenly be such alterations?

This will surely cause discord among the assembly. Saṃghavarman replied: "The differences between the five schools are themselves a natural principle. We have together renounced the secular world for this very purpose."

To propagate the Dharma, the Dharma must necessarily be transmitted. Why then do you oppose the sentiments of the multitude? He asked: "Now, the precepts are not a visible form; their principle is inherently difficult to discern.

Yet, speaking from the perspective of actual practice, they are sufficient to give rise to deep doubt. Recently, I have seen those who receive the precepts again; some follow the order of their original seniority (*vassa*).

If one has already received them and obtained the precepts previously, then receiving them again would be inadmissible. If, however, one has only now first obtained them, then [the matter is different]..."
One should follow the order of seniority based on one's original ordination age. There followed further questions and answers (as detailed in the source).
The Master of Dharma Yi was so thoroughly convinced that he had no further words to say. He then had three disciples—Huiji, Jingming, and Faming—receive the precepts.

At that time, the Master Rui of Shixing Temple offered this critique: "In seeing evil, one is as cautious as if touching boiling water; in beholding goodness, one fears being unable to attain it. Yet Yi...

The Duke established himself as distinct from those with whom he could agree; yet before even ten days had passed, he returned to what he had previously found to be in accord. This was likely a satire on his initial confusion.
The preceding explanation of the sixth layer—the meaning of the penetration and obstruction of reception—is now complete.
I have heard someone say that this person was established as the Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. This man had previously studied the sūtras and śāstras, and later traveled to the kingdom of India.

Seeing that the reception of the precepts there was performed according to the Dharma, he falsely claimed that the precepts previously received by the monks and nuns of this land were not authentic from the beginning.
Having received full ordination there, he subsequently returned to China, bringing with him five...
More than one hundred scriptures and treatises were translated here. Upon his initial arrival, he saw that the monks of the land of Han all paid him homage.
However, the monks and nuns of this land lacked the precepts, as there had not yet been foreign *tripiṭaka* masters to propagate this teaching.

Originally, they had no monastic teachers at all and were thus entirely without the precepts. At present, if one were to receive the precepts, it would not be necessary to inquire about the teacher, the robes, or the alms bowl.
Because the conditions and so forth are fully present, it is said that there was previously nothing from which to begin.

Even if one who receives [the precepts] now slightly deviates [from the norm], provided the conditions are complete, this is precisely what Xuanzang meant. He meant that since this land has previously lacked good masters and monks, if one were to receive [the precepts] now, it would be a case of "deviating from the conditions" (guai yuan ju).
However, if one simply maintains the mind of revering the precepts and suddenly attains them, what more could be asked?

[Objection: Do not discuss conditions such as teachers or preceptors; [the recipient] simply does not possess them. (The above is all the words of Xuanzang). The guest asks: On what basis can it be verified that the monks and nuns of this land possess the precepts? Therefore, the Record of Master Nanshan states:

"In the third year of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, an Unrestricted Great Assembly was held within the palace. Emperor Wen asked: 'There is no means by which the monks and nuns of this land obtain the precepts.'"* *(Note:

This passage refers to the historical debate regarding the validity of ordination in China prior to the formal introduction of Indian masters and the establishment of the *śīla*-transmission lineage.)*

"How can this be known? The various venerable ones all remained silent and gave no answer. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who requested to travel to the Western Regions to inquire about the origins of receiving the precepts.
Upon arriving in Northern India, he encountered an arhat and asked him, "Do the monks and nuns of China receive the precepts?
The arhat replied, "I am but a minor sage; I do not know whether they receive them or not. He then spoke further to the bhikṣu.
He said, "Stay here for a moment. I shall now go on your behalf to ask Maitreya whether you have received the precepts.
Thereupon, he entered into meditative concentration and ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven, asking: "I am but a minor sage; I do not know whether those in the borderlands obtain the precepts or not.
Therefore, I have come to ask your reverence. Maitreya replied, "Those in the borderlands do obtain the precepts. He then requested a verification, and immediately took—
He took the golden flower and made this vow: "If the monks and nuns of the borderlands are able to receive the precepts, may this golden flower enter the hand of an Arhat;
if they are not, may the golden flower not enter. Once he had finished his vow, the golden flower immediately entered the palm of his hand, appearing as a shadow one chi in length.
When such a wondrous sign occurred, he felt great joy within. Maitreya then said to him: "Go down to China and compare [the teachings] there."

"At the place where the Master resides, I too shall make a vow. If the ordination of the monks and nuns of China is to be rendered non-empty, I pray only that this golden flower may enter the hands of the Bhikṣu.
Having thus completed his vow according to the instructions, he pressed the flower with his hand; the flower entered the Bhikṣu’s palm, appearing there as a shadow one chi in length.
Since the auspicious response was such as this, when he wished to return to his own country, Kāpiśī subsequently came into being.
A deity manifested its body and speech, saying: "The road is vast and distant, fraught with many perils and hardships. I shall escort you, my disciple, so that you may reach that land.
Before they had yet arrived, golden flowers appeared as reflections in the air before the palace of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty.
The Emperor asked the Grand Astrologer, "What strange omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "The Buddha-dharma from the Western lands is coming here."
It was not even a full month later when, while the bhikṣu held a golden flower in his palm, on the day he arrived, the golden flower in the sky immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
When they were about to set out from the territory of Han, there were over eighty people in total;
some, their devotion to the Sage so profound, remained in that region, while others met with calamities and passed away. Only one person remained, following the great flower with all his heart.
Seeking out ancient traces, he arrived in the land of Qin. Upon suddenly hearing these words, he could not help but sigh deeply. [The commentary] states:

"From this point downward, these are the words spoken by the Ācārya of the Southern Mountains. The *Sancang* (Three Cang Lexicons) states: "Quèi" (pronounced kǔ kuì) refers to a sigh; it is also called a sound of lamentation.
This means that having heard this speech from Xuanzang, his feelings were filled with indignation, and he could not help but—
"Great Sigh. This means: "What kind of words are these? Regarding the passage, "The thunder shakes the earth, yet the deaf do not hear it," Master Ying says:
The character *tíng* (霆) has three pronunciations: *ding*, *ting*, and *tǐng*. The *Erlǚ* states: "A swift clap of thunder is called *tíng*. The *Shuowén* says: "It is the residual sound of thunder;
that by which all things are brought forth. *Tíng* is also lightning. Guo Pu says: "It refers to the sudden and violent intensity of thunder."

It is called *tíng*. In the *Cāngjié piān*, it is said to be *pǐlè* (thunderclap). Regarding the statement that "the seven luminaries adorn the heavens," *Lì* says: "Adorn" (*lì*) means magnificent adornment;
this refers to the sun, moon, and stars being magnificently arrayed in the heavens. According to the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the Buddha told Brahmā:
"As for the seven luminaries, the one in the east is the comet (*huìxīng*). The *Shū* (Book of Documents) states: "Wood is the planet Jupiter (*suìxīng*)," which is this very one. At that time...
People call the planet of the dawn *Shu* (Jupiter); it is the southern *yinghuo* star. The *Shu* says: "The fire star is the *yinghuo* star. The western planet is *Taibai* (Venus);
the *Shu* says: "Metal and wood are *Taibai*. The northern planet is *Chenxing* (Mercury), also called the *changxing* (fixed star).
The *Shu* says: "Water is called *chenxing*. The central planet is *Zhenshi* (Saturn); the *Shu* says: "Earth is called *zhenshi*. These five—
Together with the sun and moon, these constitute seven. Another interpretation states: the star *Śravaṇā* (始星) in the east is called *Sāketu* (歲星) in the language of Han;
the star *Tiṣya* (明星) in the south is called *Aṅgāraka* (熒惑星); the star *Uśanas* (金星) in the west is called *Venus* (太白星); the star *Anurādhā* (輔星) in the north is called *Budha* (辰星);
and the honored star in the center is called *Bṛhaspati* (鎮星). Even if there were confusion regarding the objects of perception, [the author] establishes this as follows: "This..."

Regarding Master Mingxi, during his time, there may have been instances where precepts were broken or practices were contrary to the Dharma; this was due to the confusion surrounding the objects of the ritual.

However, provided that the recipient did not possess the three roots of evil and that among the ten monks there were likewise none with the three roots of evil, the ordination was valid according to the Vinaya.
Therefore, it is said that even within the Dharma, there are clear and decisive instructions.
Regarding the "night dream of Emperor Ming of the Han": this refers to the third sovereign of the Later Han, Emperor Ming, who ascended the throne in the first year of the Yongping era.
In the fifth year of Yongping, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man and consequently dispatched Cai Yin and others to the Western Regions to inquire about and seek out the Buddha-dharma.
In the tenth year of Yongping, Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived in the land of Han; in the eleventh year of Yongping, Dharmaratna arrived.
When two Arhats arrived with the scriptures borne upon a white horse, they reached Luoyang and established the Baima Temple (White Horse Monastery).

This is the very Baima Temple located outside the present-day Eastern Gate. When the temple was first established, there were not enough people to ordain as monks; therefore, they merely received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
This continued until the sixth year of the Yongkang era of Emperor Huan, the tenth sovereign, when in total— (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary at the end, ending abruptly with "總經一".)

For a hundred years, they transmitted [the teachings] to one another using only the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. After Emperor Huan passed away, during the reign of the eleventh sovereign of the Han,
Emperor Ling, who ascended the throne in the Jianning era, five śramaṇas from Northern India—
Zhi Falin, Zhi Qian, Zhu Fahu, Zhu Daosheng, and Zhi Loujiachen— arrived in this land and received the full ordination from the great monks.
Regarding the precepts: from that time onward, the transmission of the dharma of the precepts began, yet no formal Vinaya texts existed.

Only the *Ji-fa* (Branch Dharma) and the *Kou-song-jie-ben* (Oral Recitation of the Precept Text) in one fascicle, along with the *Jie-mo* (Karma/Ordination Ritual) in one fascicle, circulated in the world. Today, there exists an ancient manuscript of the *Jie-mo*.
...and the *Śīlaprakṛti* (The Root of Precepts). These were both produced by the Dharmaguptaka school.

From that time onward, fifty-five years passed until the third year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty (the son of Cao Cao). At that time, there was Dharmakāla (alternatively written as Kāla) from Central India;

this is translated as "Dharma-time. This man was comprehensive and sagacious, and his physical appearance was magnificent and extraordinary. Upon reading through a text once, he fully grasped both its words and their meaning.

He was proficient in the four Vedas and excelled in the treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). Regarding diagrams, prophecies, and the transformations of destiny, there was nothing he did not encompass.

Believing himself to be without peer in the world, he entered a monastic dwelling and unexpectedly encountered the *Dharmaguptaka-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Not knowing its profound purport, he marveled at the depth of the Buddha-dharma and subsequently left the household life.
He recited the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*). Later, he arrived at Xuchang.
Observing the monastic community within the territory of Wei, they were entirely devoid of Vinaya discipline. From the time [the scriptures] first arrived until now, twenty-eight years have passed;
adding the previous fifty-five years, a total of eighty-three years has elapsed.

In the second year of the Jiaping era of Emperor Feidi of Wei, he again assembled Indian monks in Luoyang and, using the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), received the full ordination once more with the great assembly of monks. He employed only ten monks for this, and also translated...
The *Sengqi jieben* (Sāṃghāṭī-śīla-mūla) in one fascicle. Regarding the current commentary’s statement that [the transmission] reached the beginning of the Cao Wei dynasty:
this refers to the reason for the subsequent re-administration of the precepts, specifically the reason why the five individuals including Fa Ling were bypassed when the precepts were conferred.

From the time Buddhism first flowed eastward until the second year of the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty, one hundred and eighty-three years had passed; it was only then that the Vinaya regulations became complete. Calculating from the Great... [text ends].
The Sangha first received [the precepts] from the eleventh reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, starting from the Jianning era down to the second year of the Kaiyuan period of the Great Tang,
totaling exactly five hundred and forty-seven years. As for the time since the re-ordination of the great bhikṣus,
it has been four hundred and sixty years from the second year of the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty down to the second year of the Kaiyuan period of the Great Tang.

Five years later, during the period when Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddha-dharma, ten individuals, including Dharma Master Lingyu and others, hid themselves in the home of General Jinmoti (pronounced *jū* [with the *ju* rhyme] *guān* [with the *guàn* rhyme]). When the Dharma was first revived by Da Sui, only nine of them were obtained;

they conferred the precepts upon others (because one person, Yuan Xingxin, had committed a transgression in the interim, there were thus only nine). They abandoned their former erroneous practices and produced the *Sengqi jieben xinxue chao* (Abridged Commentary on the Heart of the Mahāsāṃghika Precepts), among other works.
The preceding section on the method for monks to undergo the *zhai* (fasting) and repentance rites together with those of the ancestral shrines is now concluded.
Below follows the explanation of the method for nuns to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Regarding the translator of the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* and other scriptures, it is established that this is the *Sujāta-sūtra*, titled the *Sujāta-upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*. Translated by Yang [Xuanzhi].
The "State" (zhou) refers to present-day Jiangning. Regarding the eight nuns from Siṃhala (Lion) Country, Master Daolun stated:
"Originally there were ten nuns who set out intending to come to the land of Han to receive the full precepts as nuns; however, two nuns died along the way, so only these eight arrived here.
The account given in the *Shanfang yeyu* does not fully capture the facts. I shall now provide a more complete explanation. [Regarding] the bhikṣuṇīs...

Regarding the origins of its initial reception: after the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, there were also nuns who sought to receive the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇī-śīla*) from the ordained monks (*bhikṣu*).
Zhi Falin replied to them, "According to the Buddha's teachings, the ordination of bhikṣus by a group of five persons is only permitted in frontier regions."
The nuns were not permitted to enter. Weeping with tears, the nuns withdrew.
From that time forward, fifty-three years passed until the end of the Han dynasty and the beginning of the Wei dynasty, when two bhikṣuṇīs from the kingdom of East India arrived in Chang’an.

The substance of its formation merely follows the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Because the mental consciousness is able to sustain it, it is said to "coexist with other consciousnesses.

This is intended to clarify that although the arousal of the precept arises from body and speech, the apprehension of the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is solely the function of the mental consciousness.

It is capable of receiving this dharma. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: at that time, it is the consciousness of a wholesome mind associated with body and speech that brings forth this precept.
Later, when one enters into a consciousness that is either unwholesome or neutral (*avyākṛta*), the non-informative (*avijñapti*) remains undestroyed.

In relation to the unwholesome or neutral states, it is considered a "distinct" consciousness; thus it is said that the non-informative precept can coexist simultaneously with the unwholesome or neutral. Master Bin agrees with this interpretation. Therefore...
