Because it is an action that accompanies the physical form and is practiced through a perpetual vow, it is called a "true action" (*karma*). Verbal instructions to strike or beat are distinct conditions; those previously accepted and practiced are auxiliary actions.
As the movement arises, it is simultaneous with the performance (*kriyā-sahabhū*). As long as the instrument—the whip—is not discarded, it is termed [a non-restraint].
The matter lies in this: as one acts, one induces karma; is this not following from its function? Since evil thoughts do not cease, they are also concomitant with the mind.
Therefore, by citing a single condition, one immediately encompasses all eight types of karma; the rest may be understood by analogy.
Fifth, non-manifest action (avijñapti) arises from different conditions and lacks an agent. Master Bin says: For example, one may wish to kill someone but does not wield a blade or staff;
instead, one uses a finger-seal (*mudrā*) or writes a letter to effect the killing. Although this is equally a bodily action (*kāyakarman*), the specific matter differs.

Therefore, it is said that non-manifest action can be produced through different conditions. Second is mutual conditionality: for instance, using a finger-seal or a written sign to commit a great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*). This...
That is, bodily action (kāyakarman) accomplishes vocal action (vākkarman), or as in the case of praising someone to death, vocal action accomplishes bodily action.

Since these are produced interchangeably, they are called "mutually conditioned" (anyonyapratyaya). Previous masters, failing to understand the distinct characteristics of these different conditions, have consequently become confused, asserting that bodily action can produce vocal action and so forth.
[Vasubandhu] says: For example, suppose someone in a crowd says, "Whoever has attained arhatship, stand up!"
"Standing. This refers to when an ordinary bhikṣu stands up. Falsehood fundamentally originates from speech; now, the body manifests signs.

By manifesting the body, one expresses the karma of speech, which immediately gives rise to the non-informative (avijñapti) aspect of speech. The Guest says: "It is like using a finger-seal or using physical gestures to compose a letter;
thus committing a great falsehood is itself bodily karma, which establishes vocal karma and gives rise to the non-informative aspect of speech. It is created by the mouth."

Regarding bodily action (*kāyakarman*): Bin says that according to the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*, "The Lord's verbal command—when the ṛṣi felt aversion in his mind—the Lord, who is the king, issues a verbal decree to kill someone, thereby giving rise to the non-informative (*avijñapti*) of the body.

As for the "ṛṣi," this refers to the ṛṣi of the country of Daṇḍaka who gave rise to aversion; consequently, the entire nation perished. This is an instance where killing was accomplished through mental action (*manaskarman*). Furthermore, it is said:
A lion kills beasts; a strong man slays men. This is also a case where vocal karma constitutes bodily karma.
The Sarvāstivāda school does not accept this principle; however, the Mahāyāna Sautrāntika and the *Tattvasiddhi* schools all accept that vocal karma directly constitutes the act of killing.

There are extensive mutual refutations on this point, as detailed in the third fascicle of the *Bin-chao*. The commentary states: "When one beyond training (aśaikṣa) puts on robes, it is the body that performs [the action]."

This is an action of speech (*vākkarman*). To deceive the shallow by means of the deep refers to the bodily action (*kāyakarman*) created through speech; killing is that very action. [The commentary] states:

"To deceive the shallow by means of the deep" is as follows: if someone asks, "Is this river deep? and a bhikṣu, knowing it is deep, reports that it is shallow, and the person immediately crosses and drowns, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Although killing itself is a bodily action, in this case, because one causes death by deceiving with words, it gives rise to a bodily action.

In our school, there is no such thing as "action" (karma) in the sense of a substance. If one follows the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and posits that body and speech mutually produce [action], it is clearly established that this is identical to the aforementioned view that bodily action produces vocal karma and vocal action produces bodily karma.
The sixth [type of] auxiliary condition is that which lacks an agent, such as the bodily and vocal actions of another person being employed to accomplish one's own bodily and vocal actions;
it is just like sending a messenger to perform a task.

Seventh is the "non-manifestation resulting from a formal vow" (*samādāna-avijñapti*). This is established as follows: for example, when a person resolves their mind, thinking, "I shall hold a ritual assembly next year, fashion a Buddha image, and transcribe scriptures," once this resolve has been made, the non-manifestation constantly arises.
It continues until the end of the period specified by that vow, at which point the non-manifestation finally ceases. (This interpretation differs from that of Master Bin.)
Therefore, Master Bin says it is also called "the unmanifested state of the middle. This refers to such things as the night-day [vows], the middle [vows], and formal commitments.
"Night-day" refers to the eight precepts. "The middle" includes both wholesome and unwholesome states;

that is to say, although they may be wholesome karmas, they are not *saṃvara* (restraint), or although they may be unwholesome karmas, they are not *duḥśīla* (immorality). Because they abide in a neutral middle, they are called "the middle. — Tong Lushi.

It says: "Good [action] is not a purely pure mind; evil [action] is not a deeply entrenched entanglement; therefore, it is called 'abiding in the middle'. Now, examining this closely, it appears the meaning was not understood, and thus this statement was made.
There were ancients who established nine kinds of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), adding to them the non-informative action associated with vows.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, in its twelfth chapter on the nine types of karma, states: "If there is a person who makes a vow, vowing that I shall certainly..."

[The act of] giving, or the building of a stūpa or monastery—such a person will certainly attain the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Question: What is the difference between a vow (*praṇidhāna*) and a formal commitment (*samādāna*)? Answer:
Both what is currently being done and what is to be done in the future are collectively termed "vows. A formal commitment, however, is restricted solely to what is currently being done.
Based on this, one should say: if it is a formal commitment, it is necessarily a vow; yet there are vows that are not formal commitments, namely those intended for the future.
It should be understood in this way. Question: Since these vows are both capable of manifest action (*vijñapti*) and persist as prior events, what is the difference between them? Answer:
In the former case of manifest action, there is merely the arousal of the thought; in the present case, from the moment the thought is aroused, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) arises.
Commentary on the *Sifenlü Chao*, Volume Seven, Part One;
Commentary on the *Sifenlü Chao*, Volume Seven, Part Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.

The eighth is "non-informative action that follows the mind" (*cittānuparivartin avijñapti*). According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is termed "non-informative action following the mind" and is also called "non-informative action co-arising with the mind.
It is the activity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Other types of wholesome [action] do not possess this non-informative action that follows the mind.

Regarding the term "co-arising with the mind," it is called "co-arising with the mind" because it accompanies and pursues the mind simultaneously. Master Bin says: "The restraints of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the path (*mārga-saṃvara*) function in accordance with the mind."

Therefore, it is said that it co-exists with the mind. According to the intent of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, when there is a mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), this non-informative action (*avijñapti*) exists.

This differs from the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, as will be cited below. Thus, the Sarvāstivāda school states: "There are two kinds of restraint: that of dhyāna and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*)."

Regarding the path-consciousness (*mārga-citta*) in meditative absorption (*samādhi*): it is both accomplished (*samanvāgata*) and active (*samudācāra*). Regarding the path-consciousness outside of meditative absorption: it is only accomplished and not active.

As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* stating that [the unmanifest] "always exists" during entry and exit [from concentration], Sthiramati says: This refutes the aforementioned *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. It follows the mind of concentration and wisdom;
we do not here inquire whether one has entered or exited concentration. This unmanifest (*avijñapti*) always exists, though it may become more excellent upon entering concentration. It is not...

"It follows only the mind of meditative concentration and wisdom" means it follows only the mind of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Just as one dies here and is born there, all [phenomena] arise in accordance with it;
therefore, it is said to "follow the mind of birth and death. According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun), in the twelfth chapter, "On the Twelvefold Good Restraints," it says:

"The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) follows the movement of the mind, whereas the ethical restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*) does not follow the movement of the mind. A question is raised: "Some say that when one enters meditative absorption..."

There is the discipline (*saṃvara*) of dhyāna; it does not exist when one has emerged from meditative absorption. How is this so? Answer: It exists constantly both during entry into and emergence from absorption.

This person attains reality and does not perform unwholesome dharmas. Being the opposite of breaking the precepts, they constantly refrain from evil. Because their wholesome mind becomes increasingly superior, it should therefore exist constantly. Question:
If within the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) there is no dharma of breaking the precepts, with what is it opposed that it is called "wholesome"?
Regarding the restraint (*saṃvara*): The answer is that the Dharma is such that all sages and noble ones (*ārya*) attain wholesome restraint.

If there were a type of restraint that existed only because it was incompatible with breaking the precepts, then one would only obtain wholesome restraint from sentient beings who are capable of being harmed;

this would entail such a fault. Therefore, it is not so. The Guest (*Atithi*) says: "Since it is thus for the restraint associated with concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*), it should likewise be the same for the restraint associated with the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*). [The distinction is as follows:]...

If it were not so—that is, if it followed only the body—it would be established that this distinct Prātimokṣa-śīla, once produced and attained as non-informative (avijñapti), is called "concomitant with form" (rūpa-sahaja).

It would merely follow a single body; when the body perishes, the precept would cease. This is unlike meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), which follow the mind throughout birth and death.

Therefore, it is said that it is "not so. Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states: "The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) follows the movement of the mind; the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara) does not."

This refers to the activity of the mind. Regarding the statement that "Nirvana, the first fruit, and so forth" are established and clarified by citing this scriptural passage, it serves as proof that non-action (anabhisaṃskāra) follows the mind;

this [mind] is the mind of saṃsāra. If one were to say that non-action does not follow the mind of saṃsāra, then why would a person who has attained the first fruit not engage in [unwholesome] action when born in an evil land?
It is clearly known that this is because they rely upon the mind of past wholesome karma.
Regarding the statement that the first seven are both wholesome and unwholesome: among the eight types of karma mentioned above, the first seven encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;

only the eighth, which "follows the mind," is restricted to wholesome karma. Regarding the statement that these are "dharmas bound to the desire realm": even though the first seven among the eight are wholesome karma, [they are still bound to the desire realm].

This is because one has not yet departed from the desire realm; it is still a phenomenon bound by the desire realm. For example, if one practices morality directly without the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this is a phenomenon bound by the desire realm.

Later, regarding non-informative action (*avijñapti*), if it is mundane dhyāna and so forth, it is established that since concentration and wisdom are present, the karma of non-informative action is wholesome.
However, concentration and wisdom encompass both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the out-flow-free (*anāsrava*).
If one cultivates only mundane dhyāna—namely, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*)—one will be reborn in the two higher realms:

the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is like the mundane wholesome practices cultivated by non-Buddhists; such mundane dhyāna is called "wrong concentration" (*mithyāsamādhi*).

On the other hand, regarding the supramundane dharmas that are not karma belonging to the three realms, it is established and clarified: if one cultivates supramundane dhyāna, untainted concentration (*anāsravasamādhi*), and untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*), then one [attains liberation].
When both phenomena and emptiness are extinguished through the principle of contemplation, one enters the stage of the fourth fruit; hence it is said that this is "not karma of the three realms.

This means that only upon entering the fourth fruit is one truly called "not of the karma of the three realms. Alternatively, it may refer generally to all four fruits, as they all consist of the cultivation of untainted (anāsrava) wisdom.
The five preceding sections, which differ from one another, all explain the first gate: the characteristics of the essence of the precepts.
The explanation of the meaning is complete.

Regarding the second point, the identity or difference between "receiving" (shou) and "following" (sui), Li states: "In the past, the meanings of receiving and following were understood as one, like a single shield that can ward off many enemies.
This section is established to refute that interpretation. As for the terms "receiving" and "following," the *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) says: "It first arises..."
One makes a formal commitment; when the conditions are assembled and complete, and the Dharma is taken into one's heart, this is called "receiving" (śīla).

This merely involves making a vow at the ritual site to intend to uphold [the precepts], but no actual practice has yet occurred. Once the vow has been made, from that time until the end of one's life, whenever an object of the precepts arises, one immediately guards and maintains it in accordance with the mind of the vow.
Because one acts in accord with this, it is called "following" (anuvartana). Receiving is restricted to the wholesome.
The Dharma [of the precepts] is not established as being "concomitant" (*anuvartin*) when it is defiled. This is because both observance and violation depend upon the formal undertaking (*samādāna*).

Just as the ten thousand vows and practices depend on one another like the wheel and the wing of a bird, observance may be termed "undertaking," but how could violation be termed "concomitant"? Answer: There are two types of "concomitance," which differ in terms of observance and violation.

Both arise subsequent to the formal undertaking; their activities encompass both good and evil, yet all conform to that undertaking. Therefore, they are designated by the name "concomitant precepts" (*anuvartana-śīla*).

Regarding the term "conformity" (*anuvartana*): there are four kinds of conformity. First is conformity through diligent non-transgression. This conforms to the original undertaking of the precepts. Master Bin said:

"After once receiving them, throughout the duration of one's physical existence, one never transgresses even for a moment; because one follows the teaching consistently from start to finish, it is called 'diligence.
Such people are rare—who can embody this meaning? Examples include Jīvaka and others. As for the remaining arhats..."

Although one does not intentionally commit offenses, there may still be accidental ones. For example, if one forgets an instruction and enters a village, even those beyond training (aśaikṣa) may still err;

they immediately repent and apologize. Although this is called "white dharma" (kuśala-dharma), it is not called "exclusive diligence. Such a person belongs to the second category. Second, having committed an offense, one is able to repent and comply accordingly.
This compliance is partial and contrary to the original vows, because by repenting for an offense of the first category (pārājika), one no longer returns to the original state.

Third is the "conformity" (*anuvṛtti*) of non-intentional protection; although there is no transgression regarding the object, it constitutes a violation of the training rules because it lacks active application.

Fourth is the "conformity" of the ability to transgress without remorse; although this conformity may be either complete or deficient in its practice, it constitutes a transgression because it contradicts what was received [in the vows].

Therefore, regarding conduct subsequent to the reception [of the vows], whether it be maintenance or transgression, it is collectively termed "conforming to the precepts" (*śikṣā-anuvartana*). Do not...

[The offense] does not arise based on the nature of the transgression itself, but rather from the act of upholding or violating the precepts. A guest asked: "If upholding [the precepts] accords with the essence of what is received, it may be called 'conforming' (*anuvartana*).

However, violating them does not accord with what is received; should it therefore not be called 'conforming'? He replied: "Once remorse has been produced, it constitutes conformity. If that were so, how could one who has committed an offense of the first category (pārājika) produce remorse? It is because one trains in remorse that it is considered conformity.
If that were so, then for one who conceals [an offense], since there is no remorse, would it not follow that conformity is not established? He replied: "It is an offense..."

Regarding "concomitance" (*anuvartana*): it is called "concomitant" because it follows along with [the primary action]. If considered according to its essential nature (*svabhāva*), an actual transgression is not concomitant.

What is now discussed regarding their similarities and differences first concerns the non-informative (*avijñapti*) within the undertaking (*samādāna*) and the non-informative within the concomitance; there are five similarities and four differences. Next, the informative (*vijñapti*) within the undertaking is explained.
Regarding "and that which is produced in accordance with [the vow]," there are five points the same and four points different.

As for the phrase "two kinds of non-informative action" (*avijñapti*) and so forth, it refers generally to the time of undertaking the precepts, wherein one acquires a single form of non-informative action, as well as the non-informative action produced in accordance with [the vow].
Regarding the two identical meanings, Sthiramati states that the non-informative action within the undertaking is intended to prevent the seven misdeeds of body and speech.
"Non-manifestation (avijñapti) within the 'conformity' [vow] also prevents the seven non-virtuous actions of body and speech; thus it is so called. The *Ce* (*Cai*) states:

"Both the 'reception' and the 'conformity' of non-manifestation are alike in not depending on conditions for their discernment; because they possess the sense of being spontaneously and constantly present, they are so called. Regarding the fourth point, "enemy-like opposition and equal prevention of non-virtue," *Li* says:
"Because it opposes non-virtue and restrains it, it is called 'enemy-like opposition and prevention of non-virtue. However, although within the 'reception' [vow], it has not yet..."

There is that which is not subject to confrontation. Based on the original intent of the undertaking, one prepares to confront what is improper and thereby prevents it; thus, the meaning is taken from the original source, and it is termed "confrontation" (*pratipakṣa*) and so forth. Lì says:

Within the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) of the undertaking, there is already a suspension of the prevention of wrongdoing before any action has actually occurred. Within the non-manifest of the subsequent observance, one confronts the specific matter to prevent wrongdoing, whereby the practice becomes pure and bright.

This raises the question: since wrongdoing does not yet exist in the suspension, how can there be a confrontation? It is precisely because of the confrontation that the subsequent observance occurs. The undertaking...

"What is the use? [The answer is: "There is no such undertaking (*samādāna*); it does not follow accordingly because it shares the same remedy (*pratipakṣa*). (According to the meaning of the text, this refers to being named as an adversary;
it prevents wrongdoing. Jing says: "Adversaries prevent [wrongdoing] by not sharing the same undertaking; within this, the essence of non-action (*avijñapti*) exists in relation to the object.

This clarifies that because there is non-action within the undertaking, one prevents wrongdoing by following that non-action. (This interpretation is also excellent. The *Karmasūtra* states: "By means of the undertaking..."

The period of the essential nature (*tattva-rūpa*) does not involve following [the non-restraint] in order to prevent it; rather, it is for the sake of protecting the basis of the faculties (*indriya*). Thus, the original essence possesses the capacity to prevent what is non-virtuous.

This capacity truly follows along with the active conduct (*caryā*), arising as a protection for the basis; they are mutually dependent and supportive. Regarding the phrase "equal to the non-active within the following," this refers to applying a remedy toward what is non-virtuous, making it equal to the active.
This "non-active" is not the non-active that is co-existent with the active; it refers to the arising of a counter-measure against the prevention [of non-virtue].

There is thus a wholesome *vijñapti* (informative action) that arises simultaneously with its substance. Once the functional activity has ceased, this wholesome [state] remains constant—meaning that while performing this [action], the non-informative (*avijñapti*) state continues for the duration of one lifetime.
Therefore, this karma is designated as "concomitant non-informative" (*anuvartaka-avijñapti*), because it is not opposed [to the original act] and is similar to the undertaking (*samādāna*).

If one follows the ancient masters who claim there is no non-informative [action], asserting that it exists only after the activity has ceased, then this would not be a preventive restraint (*saṃvara*), but merely a "prohibitive precept" (*pratikṣepa-śīla*). Now, karma possesses causes.

Only then does the fruit become established. How could the fruit suddenly arrive once the cause has already ceased? When seeking the ultimate principle through reasoning, both positions involve conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one says they occur simultaneously, there is the fault of identity; if one says they occur sequentially, there is the fault of the cause being absent. Thus, when sought in either way, neither can be established.
Therefore, we provisionally follow worldly convention, as there is nothing superior to this. Fifth, regarding the "many categories being identical," the proponent states:

As in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, the attainment of precepts can arise repeatedly; for example, within a single day, one may receive seven types of precepts, and their manifestation occurs repeatedly.

This is called "multiple varieties" (*aneka-prakāra*). Furthermore, if one previously possessed a low-grade mind and attained low-grade precepts, and later receives them again, there arises a middle or superior grade;

this refers to the multiple varieties of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) within the act of receiving. Regarding these multiple varieties according to the middle grade, it means that there are those who are robust and those who are emaciated.
Therefore, it is said that there are "many varieties. Furthermore, the explanations are made according to the specific matters involved, each being distinct and different.

For example, such practices as the formal declaration of purity (*śuddhi*) regarding robes, the *ānanda* (joy), and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) are all considered "many varieties," which is why it is so called. Lì says: "This one section is treated as a separate section."

It is said that within the *prātimokṣa* (restraint) there is no non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), because it recompenses the causal mind of a single grade. Thus, the non-manifest action within the *prātimokṣa* is equal in meaning to that single grade;
however, the non-manifest action within the *anuvartana* (conformity) possesses degrees of superiority and inferiority. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* also states:

"The *prātimokṣa* is one, while the *anuvartana* is many, for in that school [of thought], repetition is not permitted. This refers only to the practice of conformity, which encompasses both superiority and inferiority. (Regarding the phrase "according to the above": this explains the attainment of sameness and difference within this particular section.)

Regarding the statement that within the "following" (anuvartana) there is no separate initiation of practice nor simultaneous cultivation, this means that as it is said: when the *poṣadha* is being recited, one may not perform the *pravāraṇā*;
when the *śuddhi* is being declared, one may not accept food. One must act through successive stages. This is not the case with the "undertaking" (*samādāna*). As for "initiation":

At one time, the restraint is attained instantaneously, pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, the Commentary states: "The undertaking is merely a formal vow; it is the desire not to commit evil amidst the myriad objects of experience.

Since the dharma-realm serves as its measure, is this not a universal arousal? However, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) that accords with actual conduct is formed gradually and cannot arise instantaneously;
thus, it is termed "distinct" (*pratyeka*). Second, regarding the difference in duration: within the undertaking, the non-informative remains suspended [in anticipation].

"Resolving for the duration of one's entire life" means that at the time of receiving the precepts, one makes a formal commitment to maintain them for as long as one lives, abandoning evil and practicing good.

Although during this period one may enter states of unwholesome or neutral mind, the non-informative (avijñapti) nature of the precept remains constantly present; therefore, it is called "long-lasting. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:

"The essence of the undertaking continues until the end of life; because the fundamental precepts are not lost even when the four types of minds arise in succession, it is 'broad. This refers to the non-informative [nature] within the intermediate state."

Regarding the statement that "expedient means consist of both form and mind," this establishes the following: when one practices in accordance with specific objects and moves the body or speaks, this is called expedient means as form (*rūpa*).

When the mental faculty contemplates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), this is called expedient means as mind (*citta*). To take the example of holding a robe: other cases may be understood by analogy.

Physically grasping the robe while kneeling and verbally reciting the prescribed phrases constitutes expedient means as form. Discerning the substance of the robe and clearly understanding its true nature constitutes expedient means as mind.
It is so called because of the mind. Since this karma of non-action (avijñapti) arises simultaneously with this form and mind, it ceases as soon as the object is dealt with;
therefore, it is said to be "short. Regarding the third point, that their breadth and narrowness differ, Fazhi says: "Within [the category of] feeling, there is no non-action."
After the initial moment of production, although one may enter the four types of mind or the three natures, the non-informative (avijñapti) remains without being lost;

therefore, it is called "broad. Within the category of "consequent" (anuvartin), it is restricted solely to the wholesome nature; if one enters into an unwholesome or neutral state, this constitutes a violation of the precepts.

How could there then be a wholesome non-informative action within that subsequent state? Therefore, it is called "narrow. Regarding the statement that the two [other] natures are narrow: these are the unwholesome and the neutral—these two states of mind.
In the middle [of the categories], there is no "following" (anuvartana) and no "unmanifest" (avijñapti); thus it is said. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:

"It is restricted solely to the nature of goodness (kuśala-dharma), as it prevents what is non-virtuous and protects the fundamental [precepts]. Since that which is evil or neutral does not accord with receiving [the precepts], it is not said to exist [in those cases] from a doctrinal standpoint;

therefore, it is called 'narrow'. Regarding the distinction between the four roots and the branches: "Receiving" (samādāna) is the root, while "following" (anuvartana) arises in dependence upon receiving; therefore, following is the branch. The *Vyākhyā* states: "Receiving..."
They constitute the root of practice; that which arises subsequently is termed the "branch.

There are two kinds of "action" (*kṛti*): namely, the two types of practice, *anuśrāvaṇa* (receiving) and *anuvartana* (following), both of which share the common name "action. The action within *anuśrāvaṇa* refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the consecration of the *maṇḍala*.

The action within *anuvartana* refers to the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) and so forth. As for the identity of their names, it refers to these two practices of *anuśrāvaṇa* and *anuvartana*.
They share the same name. Regarding the identity of their meaning: this refers to the common prevention of the seven types of non-virtue of body and speech.

Bin says that "identity" means prevention, taking the distancing from evil as its significance. Ce says that "identity" means the commonality of these formative activities; therefore, it is said that their meanings are identical. Regarding the identity of their substance:

this refers to the commonality of taking matter and mind as their substance. Within the category of sensation, matter and mind likewise constitute the substance, according to what is produced therein.

It also has form as its substance. Regarding the four types of "shortness" (samāna): for example, within the category of feeling (*vedanā*), when the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is concluded, one understands that it is short.

Within the category of conduct (*caryā*), as in the instruction on wearing robes, when the matter of the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, one likewise understands that it is short. The fifth is "narrowness" (*saṃkucita-samāna*), which refers to [the classification] among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

It must be restricted to the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala-dharma*) to be designated as "receiving the precepts. The subsequent [observance] is likewise restricted to the nature of the wholesome, because it does not apply to the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate);
therefore, it is called "narrow.

Regarding the distinction between "general abandonment" at the time of reception and "specific abandonment" during the subsequent observance: Sthiramati explains that at the time of reception, one makes a formal vow to abandon everything in its entirety.

Regarding the *anuprāpti* (concomitant) precepts, one may only practice them by distinguishing them according to specific objects. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "Among the received precepts, the *kriyā-śīla* (precepts of action) constitute a general cessation;
when the mind is aroused toward an object, there is a universal vow to restrain and prevent [unwholesome acts].

As for the *anuprāpti-kriyā-śīla*, since the practice arises in dependence upon objects, and these objects—whether material (*rūpa*) or mental (*citta*)—are inexhaustible, the practice only arises where the mind reaches. This very practice is then designated and termed 'concomitant' (*anuprāpti*)."

[The text] states: "Because the mind does not take two objects simultaneously, and because objects do not manifest all at once. Second, regarding "the root and the branches of receiving": this clarifies that receiving is the root and following is the branch.
Third, regarding "receiving as a preemptive defense and following as its antidote": the commentary says, "Receiving begins at the ritual site;
it may not be immediately manifest, but it serves as a preemptive restriction. Regarding "acting within following," this refers to [acting] in relation to the object.

[The section on] the "Cultivation" [of the fourfold restraint] ends with the single category of the one who has attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). According to the *Lì shù* (Commentary on the Li), it should be stated that the "four" refers to the multiplicity of distinctions;

that is, within the restraint of undertaking [the precepts], the mind is determined by a single grade of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Lì states: "This is the original undertaking of the one who has attained no-more-learning."

One generates a lower-grade mind; subsequently, through cultivation, one becomes an Arhat, yet the precepts remain of a lower grade. Therefore, it is said that "receiving and creating [the precepts] constitutes a single grade.

As for the phrase "due to the superiority or inferiority of the object," this refers to the fact that although one follows the intermediate grade in creating the precepts, they exist in many grades because they correspond to various objects.
This is because their relative quality differs. To take one example, that of wearing robes: if it is a silk robe, the object is inferior and the mind is faint;
this is the lower grade of upholding the precepts. If it is a cotton cloth robe, the mind is moderately intense; this is the middle grade of upholding or violating the precepts.

Even further, if it is a patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*), the object is superior and the mind is intense; this is the upper grade of upholding the precepts. Therefore, it is said that within the same category, there are many grades of preceptual observance.

Furthermore, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct: physical forms may be beautiful or ugly, and the mind may be light or heavy. If one encounters a beautiful object, it is difficult to guard the mind;

this is called a "superior object," and the mental intensity is correspondingly strong—this constitutes the highest grade of upholding the precept. If one encounters an ugly object, it is termed "inferior."

The mind is then indifferent; this is the lower grade of upholding the precepts. As for the statement that the mind is divided into three grades, it refers to the mental state associated with the formal observance (*saṃvara*) following the initial commitment.
Since the objects [of the precepts] differ in their degree of excellence, the mind likewise differs as superior, middling, or inferior; hence it is said to be "divided into three grades.
This does not contradict the fact that the original undertaking was made with a lower-grade mind; this clearly refers to the state of mind at the time of the undertaking. This...

The following section further explains the preceding text. It states that although the middle grade [of restraint] may not apply to the superior or middle grades, the original undertaking is based solely on a single grade of mind as its cause.

Thus, the commentary (*shu*) asks: "If the three grades to be prevented are distinct, while the precept capable of preventing them is of a single grade, how can it act as an adversary to prevent them?

The answer is: When the undertaking arises, a single grade of mind effects the total severance of all evil intentions. Since the causal mind is one, and because it is unmanifest (*avijñapti*), [the precept is able to prevent all].
There are not three [types of restraint]. Although the offenses to be prevented differ, the vow (*samvara*) alone cannot dispel them; it must rely upon the accompanying mind (*cittānuparivartin*).

Therefore, according to the gravity of the transgression, the mind likewise possesses degrees of excellence or inferiority. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although the arising [of the offense] differs, the prevention (*saṃvara*) depends upon the mind.

It is not the case that a heavy object cannot be dispelled by a light mind. There are indeed *duṣkṛta* (minor) offenses where the prevention is still frequently practiced; for this reason, one should not say [that the vow is ineffective].
The mind is differentiated by its gravity and lightness; this is clearly manifested through diligence and indolence.

That an Arhat may possess an inferior grade of precept (śīla) refers to the realization of the middle stage within the superior [attainment], which is determined from beginning to end by a single grade of mental cause. According to the fourth verse of the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*:

Regarding the reception of the Prātimokṣa vows, one should know that they are obtained through the instruction of another. Depending on whether the mind is inferior, middling, or superior, one obtains the three grades of restraint (*saṃvara*).

To explain: when receiving the Prātimokṣa vows, one should know they are obtained from the instruction of another—such as the full ordination (*upasampadā*) received through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of a motion and three proclamations), the "Come hither" (*ehibhikṣu*), the five persons in the borderlands, the ten persons in the central lands, and the three refuges; all of these are obtained from another.

Question: By what kind of disposition does one obtain the vow of restraint (*saṃvara*)? Answer: According to whether the mind is inferior, middling, or superior, one obtains the three grades of restraint.
What are these three grades? If one receives the *prātimokṣa* vows with an inferior mind, one obtains the inferior vow, because it is the fruit of an inferior mind.

If one attains goodness through supreme application, one becomes free from the three realms. Thus, for sentient beings who possess the seeds of the three vehicles, their respective lineages continue in succession.
That [precept] still functions as an inferior grade. If one receives the precepts with a middling state of mind, one obtains a middling-grade discipline (*saṃvara*).
If one practices goodness through supreme effort, yet does not abandon the precepts while committing various evil deeds, that [precept] functions as a middling-grade following.

If one receives the precepts with a superior state of mind, one obtains a superior discipline, which continues to function as a superior following throughout the succession of its lineage, even for years.

Young bhikṣus attain the higher restraint (*adhiśīla-saṃvara*). Although they may be arhats who have perfected the lower precepts—[where "higher" refers to the continuity of the species, meaning prior to the end of the continuity of a single life-form;

this is my own interpretation]—a question is raised: since an arhat has cultivated the path, transcended the three realms, and their afflictions (*kleśa*) are entirely exhausted, why is their restraint still of an inferior grade?
The answer is: because while they were ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they received the precepts in an inferior manner; even though they subsequently applied themselves with diligence...

One attains the fruit; however, according to the original precept, it remains of the lower grade (*mṛdu*), because the precept was repaid based on a single-grade mental cause from the original [moment].
As for the statement that a young bhikṣu possesses precepts of the upper grade (*adhimātra*), this is established by referring to a newly ordained person as "young.
This is because at the time of receiving the precepts, such a person generates an upper-grade mind. Thus, the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states: "Although even an..."
The Arhat still accomplishes the lower grade of precepts (Vibhāṣā 117). Question:
Is it possible for a newly ordained bhikṣu to accomplish the superior grade of restraint, while an Arhat accomplishes only the inferior grade of restraint? Answer: Yes;

that is to say, there is a newly ordained bhikṣu who, with a superior state of mind, initiates informative action (vijñapti-karman) and receives the various restraints, whereas the Arhat [accomplishes the inferior].
This refers to those from the Han dynasty onwards who, with minds of inferior grade, give rise to informative karma (*vijñapti-karman*) and receive various vows (*saṃvara*).
The above concludes the general explanation of the second section, the meaning of the gates concerning the similarities and differences in receiving [vows].

Regarding those who uphold [the precepts] with courageous diligence, there is a fourfold division within the gateway of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*). This section below corresponds precisely to the third part:

the segment on the breadth or narrowness of the objective sphere (*ālambana*) for the arousal of the mind of precept-giving (*śīla-cittotpāda*). That is to say, it clarifies both the mind that takes the object (*ālambaka-citta*) and the objective sphere that is taken as the object (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

The mind that acts as the perceiver is restricted solely to the present; thus, it is called "narrow. The objects perceived (ālambana) extend across the three periods of time; thus, they are called "broad. Question:

Since the relationship between mind and object was already clarified in the section on feeling (*vedanā*) in the upper scroll, why is this explained again at length? Answer: The upper scroll treated the matter from the perspective of the time of experiencing feeling.
This briefly indicates the objects of focus and instructs on the mind that focuses upon them. The discussion in the present text is intended for those who have already received the teachings;

they must recognize the essential nature and characteristics [of the mind] so as to cause them to maintain their resolve with vigor. Regarding "vigor" (*li*), the *Erh-pi* (Dictionary of Synonyms) states: "To lead forward and mutually exhort one another."

Regarding the phrase "one who cuts up a corpse," [the Master] established the explanation as follows: For the time being, this is discussed from the perspective of an enemy's household, encompassing the three periods of time.

This refers to a present non-object (non-sentient matter). Because one was previously an enemy to this person, even though that person has already died, if one were now to destroy the corpse, the Buddha would still prohibit it as an offense.
Furthermore, the child of a present enemy is likewise a present object. My own thought is that this sentence clarifies the act of cutting up.

"A corpse. This refers to an object of the past, which accords with the current text. The Guest says: "For example, upon seeing an enemy who has already died, one might say, 'I am fortunate that he died of his own accord;
had he not died then, he would surely have been killed by me. This is what is meant by giving rise to an evil mind toward an object of the past.
As for the present enemy's son having the potential to be destroyed, this establishes him as an object of the present. Or...
While [the child] is still in the womb, one also takes that as a future object. Because he has been an enemy to his father, the father intends in his mind to kill his son;
he considers the son already born to be a present object, while the one in the womb is a future object. Regarding how all future objects can be understood by analogy, it is clearly established:
for example, seeing an enemy who is pregnant and intending to kill her upon the child's birth. Another interpretation states that it refers to when [the child] is not yet...

"All that comes" refers to all hostile objects. Bin said: "It is like seeing a man of Zhang's clan and, upon hearing that he has a feud with a man of the King's clan, immediately saying, 'That man of the King's clan should become my enemy'; one will certainly see him and kill me.
This is the arising of an evil mind toward a future object."
Regarding the statement, "As when a person makes offerings to those honored in the past," it means: suppose there is a person who makes offerings to past Buddhas such as Kāśyapa;
would they not obtain merit? Furthermore, by performing sacrifices to one's ancestors, one becomes a filial son.

This statement serves as proof that the object [of an action] extends across the three periods of time. As for the statement, "The same applies to the restraint (*saṃvara*)," it clarifies that because the precept is also generated with respect to past objects.
It is known that one obtains the restraint (*saṃvara*) from the perspective of sentient beings across the three periods of time.

Regarding the statement, "The threefold arousal of the precepts is obtained within the present continuous mind," this means that the mind capable of arousing [the precepts]—that which arouses and acquires the wholesome dharma of the precepts—is capable of arousing it only within the present mind.
Master Bin said: "If one follows the school of Dharmaguptaka, [it is not so]."
One does not receive the precepts within a mind of the past or future, because these are not sentient beings.

Furthermore, within the present mind, one cannot speak of it in terms of a single moment, because according to this school, a "sentient being" is a conventional designation for the continuity of the five aggregates—namely, consciousness, perception, feeling, mental formations, and volition.
They arise in succession. Since the five aggregates are not present within a single moment, one cannot say that there is a sentient being or that there is no sentient being;

thus, it is impossible to say who obtains the precepts. Therefore, this is spoken of in terms of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), provisionally designating the "present," which differs from the Sarvāstivāda school’s position that the five aggregates are fully present within a single *kṣaṇa*. Once the *kṣaṇa* has passed, it is no longer the present. (The above is based on the attainment [of the precepts]).
[This refers to] the person who observes the precepts being able to take the mind as an object. Now, when we speak of "continuity" (*saṃtati*), it is a continuity of conventional characteristics;

that is to say, moment by moment, having arisen, they perish and pass away. How, then, could there be actual continuity? Nevertheless, although they perish, we merely speak of "continuity" as a conventional designation. Thus, the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra* says:

Although all conditioned phenomena arise and perish moment by moment, they have no capacity to move from this place to another; it is only through the continuity of their conventional characteristics that one speaks of them as being able to perceive.
There is nothing in the present that cannot be prevented. It is established that if something has not yet arisen, it belongs to the future; it is not as if, having just [arisen]...
Once it has arisen, it immediately belongs to the past, because it does not abide from moment to moment. Therefore, Master Zhiyi said: "A swift flame passes a blade's edge;
the original flow crosses a sword's edge. A single hair upon that edge is constantly falling into what is already past or yet to come. Thus, we know that there is no present.
Regarding the statement that "the *vinaya* eliminates what has already arisen, while the precepts prevent what has not yet arisen," the same author explains:

Since faults and transgressions are eliminated by the *vinaya*, they have no relation to the prevention provided by the precepts. Why, then, is it said that the precepts prevent faults and transgressions? In fact, the precepts merely serve to prevent those transgressions that have not yet arisen.
Regarding the response, "Although the object is past, it is not the case that it is not past," this establishes the following: For example, if an enemy has already died, that object is indeed past.
However, if one forms the intention to sever [the corpse] while facing the present dead body, one incurs an offense. Thus, we know that it still constitutes a transgression.
Now, by refraining from the severance, one prevents a future transgression; therefore, it is said to be "not non-past. In the present, one must use the precepts as a defense.

This is not so; it is intended to prevent [the offense] from arising. If one destroys a corpse, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense. This clearly demonstrates that one knows the corpse is not one's own object;

this meaning proves that the precepts guard against what is improper regarding both the past and the future. Furthermore, regarding the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), even if the object is in the past, if one does not settle it with another, one incurs an offense.
This is precisely "what is improper in the future. Therefore, the present answer says: "Although you have taken..."
The *Vinaya* says: "This is for the eradication of faults and transgressions. Now I say: it is still merely the prevention of what has not yet occurred.

The above constitutes the established interpretation, which accords with the *Chao-wen*. Some say: "The *Vinaya* eradicates disputes that have already arisen," etc. This is the intended meaning of the question posed by the ancient masters:
"The seven *vinayas* eradicate disputes that have already arisen, while the *śīla* (precepts) prevent transgressions that have not yet arisen. Why is this so?"

Now, it is asked: "Does one say that the precepts prevent past transgressions? The answer intends to say: It is as you have questioned. When I now speak of "prevention," I mean the prevention of future transgressions.
As for my current explanation regarding "past transgressions," this means that while the *object* (境) is in the past, the "transgression" (非) is not something belonging to that past;

it is merely the object itself. For example, in the case of a disputed object, it is not a transgression on the part of my own house, but is simply the object itself. Now, I do not act for the sake of others.

"Extinct" (*nirodha*) means "not yet non-existent. For now, we shall take this "non-existence" and discuss it in relation to the object (*viṣaya*). Therefore, it is called "transgressing non-existence," though in reality it is not yet non-existent.
Now, I shall directly answer regarding the meaning of the precept (*śīla*), rather than the meaning of the Vinaya (*vinaya*).

This is because although you have brought up the Vinaya to raise an objection, you wish to establish that the Vinaya is for the purpose of preventing transgressions and non-existences. My current response is: although the object has passed away, the non-existence [of the transgression] is not itself a transgression.

The term "going" (*gata*) precisely refers to the meaning of *vinaya* (discipline). It also establishes the sense of preventing future transgressions (*anāgata-avadya*). Although this has been answered, its meaning is not yet exhaustive.

What preceded was merely an answer regarding the prevention of future transgressions. From the section beginning with "Furthermore, it is explained" (*punar aparaṃ vyākhyāyate*) onwards, it is only then that the prevention of past transgressions (*atīta-avadya*) is explained.
Therefore, the method for confession is further cited as the means to prevent past transgressions; that is to say, [the transgression] which has already arisen.
Regarding offenses: since their antidotes can effect confession, do these not prevent further transgressions? The *Jie-mo-su* (Vinaya-karmavācanā-vṛtti) states:

"As previously transmitted, 'the Vinaya extinguishes what has already arisen' refers to the seven types of Vinaya; 'the precepts prevent what has not yet arisen' refers to receiving the formal substance [of ordination] at the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).

This is a localized discussion. My current interpretation is that the Vinaya also removes both the arisen and the unarisen. What are these? They are, for example, the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).

"Regarding 'removal' (*paṭinissagga*): this refers to the complete cessation of what has already arisen. It is the clear contemplation and right abandonment [of that which] should have arisen but did not;
it is the severing of what was not [previously] present. The Upādhyāya said: 'This means that regarding the object of dispute, if it has already arisen, it belongs to the past.

Therefore, although the object is past, if there is currently a fault (*sāpattika*), one ought to apply the seven methods (*satta dhammā*). If one does not apply them, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. Thus, it is said that it is not the case that [the fault] is not past.'"
It is simply because one incurs an offense whether [the gift] is given or not that this serves to prevent future transgressions.
This point means that, as an ancient said, "The Vinaya prevents past transgressions," referring to the four types of disputes (*caturvivādamūla*), which are faults already arisen.

Now, my expressed intention is not so. I mean that the dispute belongs to another and is not mine; I should now grant the seven dharmas in hope of not granting them, which means it is not yet my fault.
Therefore, I say that "not" does not refer to the past.
Regarding the statement that "the offense is incurred in the present while taking the three periods of time as the object":

this means that at the time of receiving [the precepts], the mind that acts as the perceiver takes the objects of the three periods—past, future, and present—and thereby gives rise to the precepts. As for the actual attainment of the precepts, it occurs within a single moment of the present.
If one now violates this precept, one incurs an offense; however, this offense is incurred solely in relation to the present body of the bhikṣu. It cannot be attributed to past or future bodies.

As for the statement that "one may give rise to the thought and speak [of it] as arising throughout the three periods of time," this clarifies that although one obtains the precept by taking the objects of the three periods of time as its condition, one may only say that the precept arises from the three periods of time. One must not say that if one destroys the precept, [the offense applies to all three].
The world collectively incurs transgression; however, the incurring of transgression is restricted solely to the present.

The *Śāstra* states that compassion and giving are meritorious; this constitutes the established doctrine of the treatise. In the current text, the interpretations of two masters are cited. The first master says:
"Suppose a person practices giving throughout the three periods of time. Although there are no [sentient beings] in the past and future periods,"
Because the mind of one who enjoys a gift is universal toward those who give, one universally obtains the merit of giving for all sentient beings of the three periods of time.

It is said that the same applies to the precepts; because they universally bestow happiness upon those of the three periods of time, this is established by classifying the precepts as being like the aforementioned giving.
Just as giving obtains merit universally across the three periods of time, receiving the precepts likewise takes all sentient beings of the three periods of time as its object.

One obtains the precepts only when one possesses the mind that uproots suffering and bestows happiness; therefore, the meaning of giving (*dāna*) is cited here to prove that the knowledge of the precepts arises from the three periods of time.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the merit of compassion encompasses all things," Master Li states:

this is the interpretation of a certain master who holds that although the past has already passed and the future has not yet arrived, even though your giving extends through the three periods, it is only in the present that one obtains merit. This is because...
The karma of sentient beings benefits them only in the present; they do not receive its benefit in the past or future. How, then, could such [karma] produce merit?
This is not the case with the precepts (*śīla*), which necessarily depend upon the three periods of time, unlike material gifts. This teacher’s conception of the act of giving is somewhat different.

If one considers the arousal of the precepts, it is the same as the former teacher’s view. The former teacher says that the precepts may also be like this; the latter teacher says that the precepts are not so. Thus we know.
It is the same. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* establishes that there is an increase or decrease [of precepts] depending on whether one follows them with an evil mind.

It clarifies that if one harbors an evil mind, because of this one does not generate the attainment of the precepts; thus, there is indeed an increase or decrease. This is as stated in the following passage: "If an evil mind does not perish, the 'capable' and 'incapable' alternate and arise."
Regarding the statement, "Precepts arise from the three periods of time but prevent only the two periods of non-virtue," the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā Commentary) poses the following question:

"The precepts take objects of the three periods as their conditions; the present object is that which is being conditioned. Since this [present object] is itself non-virtuous, how can it be said that [the precepts] do not prevent it? The answer is:

"The conditioning occurs through a remote correspondence" (meaning that when one generates the precepts by taking the three periods as conditions, there is only the sense of a remote prevention). "The non-virtue has not yet arisen" (meaning that at the time one is conditioning the three periods, that non-virtue has not yet occurred). This is the aspiration and intent.

It eliminates [afflictions]. It does not obstruct the sense of taking an object (meaning that while one makes a commitment to prevent evil, what obstruction could there be in taking the three periods of time as an object?).

As for its prevention, it occurs precisely in opposition [to the unwholesome] (meaning that one can only prevent by facing what is contrary). The objects of the present are not definitively stated to be "unwholesome" (meaning that they do not abide from moment to moment). Thus, it exerts effort in establishing a remedy.

It is not that one is unable to prevent future non-virtue (meaning that by initiating contemplative practice, one causes non-virtue not to arise). To treat weakness as strength is not called "prevention.

Relying on the teachings to repent and purify is called "preventing past [non-virtue]" (meaning that since the guarding of the mind is weak, it is not called "prevention"; having committed an offense and then repented is called "preventing past transgression"). Therefore, there is no non-virtue in the present. Furthermore, it is asked:
the arousal of the precepts occurs only in the present; the objects they take as conditions span the three periods of time; yet their capacity for prevention is restricted to the past and future.
Question: If that is so, through repentance, for how many lifetimes is sin extinguished? Answer: As revealed in the sūtras and śāstras, repentance pertains to the three periods of time.

This is because past karma draws forth retribution in the future; as for the present, since it has not yet arisen and its specific varieties are not mentioned, [repentance] applies universally across the three periods.
The Vinaya regulations are not thus. One may only repent for what has already been committed; if one does not recognize the name or category [of the offense], the transgression is not extinguished.

Since there is no evil in the present—because the two minds of good and evil do not coexist—and because the name of the offense to be incurred has not yet been fixed, it is not permitted to record the name [of the offense] when entering the ritual of repentance.
Regarding the statement that "if one does not maintain the mind, one incurs sinful karma," [Hui]li explains: "If one accepts [the precepts] but does not maintain them, one immediately incurs sin.
Had one not accepted them previously, there would have been no precepts to violate; now, in relation to these precepts, this constitutes the causal basis for sinful karma.

Regarding the statement that "if there is right mindfulness, transgressions do not arise," [Hui]li says: "Because the mind was previously restrained, one subsequently does not commit violations; therefore, it is so called."

When the transgression has passed, it does not arise again. For example, if one achieves the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one will not commit sexual misconduct; through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one abandons killing; and through few desires, one abandons stealing, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "according to the secondary factors that support the primary sensation" (*anuvyañjana-upādāna*): this refers to how, within the course of practice, these factors assist the substance of that sensation.
As for the statement "if there were no such sensation, the secondary factors would have nothing to arise from," sensation is the root and the secondary factors are the branches. If...

Since the root has not yet been established, the branches have nothing to rely upon. The answer—that if one considers the substance of the vow (*samādāna*) alone, it cannot by itself prevent [unwholesome acts]—intends to say this:
if the substance of the vow were inherently capable of preventing what is non-virtuous, then your question as to why non-virtue arises could indeed be addressed.

However, it is precisely because the substance of the precept (*śīla*) cannot by itself prevent [transgression] that it is merely an instrument of prevention. If there is someone who exercises control over it, then it is capable [of restraint].
Preventing what is non-virtuous (*avadya*). If there were no one to govern it, one would be unable to prevent what is non-virtuous; thus, non-virtue would arise again.

Therefore, the text below cites bows, swords, and so forth to clarify that these are defensive implements. The nature of the vows (*samvara*) is likewise: they are merely tools for preventing what is non-virtuous, and only when governed by a person can they function effectively.
Regarding the term "city and moat" (*cheng-chi*): it is established that a "moat" (*chi*) refers to a trench (*qian*). This is as in the expression "city-trench.

As for the statement that the number of precepts generated at the four gates is as explained above, Zhiyi says: "This has already been clarified in the 'Method for Receiving Precepts' in the upper fascicle.

Regarding the phrase "saving oneself while benefiting others," the reason for clarifying this again now is the desire to cause one to recognize the essential nature and characteristics of the precepts more fully.
It is brief, yet it also enables those who see it to understand the same.
Regarding the "two truths of existence and non-existence," they are also called the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional; these two encompass all phenomena exhaustively.

As for the statement that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) among the four modes of birth (*yoni*) belongs to the transformative birth (*upapāduka*), this means that the intermediate state is included within the four modes of birth and is categorized as transformative birth, rather than being one of the six [realms].

Because they are subsumed within the realms of existence (*gati*), it is said that they exist outside the realms, such as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The *Karman-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Aside from those born in the six realms of existence, can the precepts still be generated?
It answers: "The Tathāgata is not subsumed within the realms; the intermediate state is likewise so. Thus, the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra* states:

"The four modes of birth encompass all realms of existence; the intermediate state is not subsumed within the realms. This is because "realm" (*gati*) carries the meaning of "arriving," whereas the intermediate state merely transmits consciousness [to its destination]. "Arrival" refers to reaching one's final destination.
[This is] according to the Commentary by the Master Shou. Question: Beyond the sentient beings of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), is there any further place where the precepts are generated?

Answer: Yes; it is said that the Tathāgata does not fall within the inclusion of the six destinies. Question: Excluding the Buddha, beyond the six destinies, is there any further place where the precepts are generated? Answer: Yes;

it is said that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) also generates the precepts, as it is not subsumed under the six destinies. Thus we know that the six destinies do not include the intermediate state.

Regarding the term "destinies" (*gati*): the commentary explains that while "birth" (*upapatti*) is broad in scope, "destiny" is narrow. If one says "all sentient beings," this includes those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

However, if one speaks of the "six destinies," it does not include the intermediate state. Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* asks: "The World-Honored One has spoken of birth and destinies;
does birth subsume the destinies, or do the destinies subsume birth? The commentary explains: The verse states, "Birth subsumes all destinies; it is not [subsumed by] the destinies."
It is subsumed under birth (*jāti*). That is to say, it increases within the state of birth (*antarābhava*); one should know that it is not subsumed under the destinies (*gati*). Question:

Why is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) not given the name "destiny"? Answer: "Destiny" has the meaning of "arrival. Here, the preceding aggregates have already ceased and the subsequent aggregates have not yet arrived;

it is the consciousness that transmigrates in the interval, abiding for a brief moment. Because it is not the actual retribution (*vipāka*), it is not given the name "destiny. Master Bin says: As previously listed among the various...

Regarding the statement in the *Cittasūtra* that "the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) increases," "increase" is another name for a distinct location; it refers to the fact that there are sixteen kinds of hells.

Ancient authorities have also said that the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) should likewise not include the Tathāgata. Examining this now according to the Mahāyāna, his manifestation in the royal palace was an emanation (*nirmāṇa*) and not real;
thus, such a principle may indeed apply. If one follows the perspective of manifested characteristics (*nirmāṇalakṣaṇa*), even the demonstration of taking birth is likewise [an emanation].
[They are] comprised within the destinies (*gati*). Therefore, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, a Bodhisattva in his final birth is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Even though he has already attained Buddhahood in this very life, he still possesses outflows (*sāsrava*). When a Bodhisattva enters the womb, he possesses correct awareness during three stages.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120, states that the Buddha was born from a womb; by this, it is also admitted that [the intermediate state] is comprised within the destinies. Ji says: "The statement above that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not..."

Regarding inclusion within the destinies (*gati*): according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which represents the tenets of the Hīnayāna, the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is subtle and can be perceived only by the divine eye;
therefore, it is not included among the destinies. However, according to the Mahāyāna, it is indeed included within the destinies.

For example, after a person dies, if they are to be reborn as a human, the form of the intermediate state resembles that of a small child; if they are to be reborn as an animal, the body of the intermediate state resembles that of an animal.
This refers to the appearance at birth. If one is to be reborn in the various minor hells, the form is like that of a hell, resembling a mass of fire.
Therefore, the treatise states: "The intermediate state (antarābhava) body in the hells is like a mass of molten iron, burning with the torment of heat.
Since no other analogy can be found, we know that after life has ended and before reaching the next destination, there is always an intermediate state for all beings.
It is as if there were a subsequent existence (*punarbhava*). However, for those born solely in the Avīci Hell, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

This is because at the moment of death, they are like a single blade thrust through a dense array of spears; thus, upon entering Avīci, there is no leisure to linger in the intermediate state. To explain the name of the intermediate state:

the present five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called the "prior aggregates," while the future aggregates are called the "subsequent aggregates. The dark path between them is named the intermediate state.

It is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). In the new sūtras and śāstras, it is termed the "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) between the first existence (*prathamabhava*) and the subsequent existence (*paścādbhava*). The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"The gods face upward; the three [others] are horizontal; the denizens of hell face downward. The "three" refers to humans, devas, and pretas.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* that "precepts are obtained from all sentient beings, such as those of meditative concentration," Baoliang says:

To give rise to the precepts, one must, upon the basis of the dharma-realm, take a vow before all sentient beings to abandon evil. If, toward even a single sentient being, one's evil intent is not fully exhausted, [the precepts are not obtained].

When one observes the precepts, [the afflictions] do not arise; this is the definition. Therefore, it is said that "one attains concentration" (*samādhi*). Jing says: From this point onward is the establishment of the thesis (*siddhānta*);
from the phrase "Why is this? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) follows the detailed explanation of each point. There are three types of theses: first, concerning sentient beings;
second, concerning function; and third, concerning divisions. "Divisions" refers to the seven branches of the body. "Causes" refers to the absence of the three poisons and the aforementioned...
This refers to the middling and inferior grades of mind. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it concerns the observance of the precepts (*śīla*).

These are all obtained from all objects, all factors, and all causes. Although they are obtained from these three, the manner of their acquisition differs; thus the verse says: "Protection is obtained with respect to sentient beings;
It is indeterminate regarding factors and causes. The commentary explains: Protection is obtained with respect to all sentient beings, not [only] from all [factors].

Regarding the phrase "sentient beings obtain [it] by parts" (the remaining meanings are the same as cited in the *Chao*), the expression "the causes for obtaining by parts are not fixed" explains the aforementioned meaning of "parts being indeterminate.
This means that the seven branches constitute the "parts" of the body; therefore, they are called "parts.

If one receives the full precepts (*upasampadā*), one must obtain them from all the parts—namely, the abandonment of the three bodily and four verbal transgressions. However, if one receives the five, eight, or ten precepts, one obtains them from only four parts.
"Three bodies and one mouth" is also called the "four limbs. As for the statement that "it cannot be obtained from a single type of sentient being," this is the explanation:
it means that one must obtain it from all sentient beings; it does not mean obtaining it from only one type of sentient being.

This means that all sentient beings, whether aquatic or terrestrial, within the trichiliocosm constitute the objective field of the precepts. If one's focus were partial or restricted, the precepts would not arise.
When a person attains the precepts through all their components, this constitutes the possession of the complete precepts, which fully prevent the offenses of the seven branches.

Therefore, it is called "all parts. There are those who attain [the precepts] through four parts; this refers to the five and eight precepts, which directly prohibit sexual misconduct, stealing, killing, and lying.
Because they consist of these four branches, they are so named.
Regarding "the cause being indeterminate": this explains the meaning of the indeterminate nature of the cause mentioned in the preceding text. There are two kinds of causes:
first, taking the absence of the three poisons as the cause; second, taking the three grades of mind as the cause.

If one were to establish that the three poisons—such as non-attachment—are the causes for the arising of the precepts and that these are obtained from all [beings], it would mean that the three poisons cannot be separated from one another and must be entirely severed.
It cannot be divided or severed. Because one obtains the precepts by exhausting [the process] through the three non-poisons, it is said that they are obtained from "all.
If one posits that there are superior, middling, and inferior grades of intention and so forth, this refers to the three grades of mind;

since these do not arise simultaneously, one can only follow the cause of whichever single grade of mind is produced, and the precept will correspond to the cause of that single grade of mind. If one were to say that all three grades of mind are produced simultaneously, then... [it would not be so].
Regarding the arousal of the precepts, it is therefore said that they are not obtained from "all" [beings]. This is because the three grades [of intention] do not arise simultaneously.

The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) provides a fourfold analysis: first, there are those who obtain the precepts with respect to all sentient beings, yet not by means of all constituent causes (*aṅga*).
This refers to receiving five, eight, ten, or fifty precepts according to a single grade.

Second, there are those who obtain the precepts with respect to all sentient beings through all aspects (sarvāṅga), but not through all causes; that is, they receive the bhikṣu precepts using only a single grade of cause.
Third, there are those who obtain the precepts with respect to all sentient beings through both all aspects and all causes; this refers to the three [grades] of the preceding and following [stages].
Regarding the meaning of the categories: there are those who receive the three kinds of great precepts (mahā-śīla) from all sentient beings by means of all causes, but not by means of all parts;
that is, receiving the five, eight, or ten precepts with the three grades of intention.
Regarding the statement that if one does not receive the precepts from all sentient beings, they would not exist:

this establishes the definitive explanation of the preceding passage, asserting that the precepts are definitively obtained from all sentient beings. It means that one must refrain from transgressions such as killing toward all sentient beings for the precepts to arise.

If there is a mind of capability or incapability [regarding certain beings], the precepts will not be generated; this is because capability and incapability alternate and arise [in relation to different objects]. Thus, the precepts [require universal application].

This entails the fault of increase and decrease. For instance, if one thinks, "I shall abstain from killing aquatic beings, but I shall not abstain from killing those on land," then the precept is not generated, because they arise interchangeably.
Since the precept is not generated, it is said that the precept does not exist. The Commentary states: "The precept is the foremost among the various practices;
how can one learn according to partial capacity while hoping to achieve great goodness? This is logically impossible. [This refers to] evil intent.

Regarding the phrase "because it does not die": this summarizes the preceding text as a whole. It means that because one who gives rise to wholesome states toward those who do not pervade [all beings] intends to cause them harm, it is said that "the evil intent does not die."

First, regarding "a certain sentient being," this refers to one who abstains from killing only in relation to specific beings—just as a butcher observes the precept against killing wild animals but not domestic ones, or a hunter observes the precept against domestic animals but cannot observe it regarding wild ones. Second, regarding "a certain portion," this refers to observing [the precept against] sexual misconduct but not [the precept against] killing, and so forth; however, this interpretation is preferable when considering the complete set of precepts (*śīla*). 1. A certain portion of the upāsakas and others. In the *Abhidharmakośa*, this is termed "a specific branch" (*ekadeśa-kārin*), and the meaning is similar.

2. At a certain place. This means that it can be maintained in another region but not in this land; or that it can be maintained within a city but not in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*). 3. At a certain time.
