The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* (Mulun) II states: "When a bhikṣu receives offerings from others, he uses them improperly."
One falls because of giving. Even if there were no retribution to be experienced in the three miserable realms, this body would have its belly burst open and food would spill out;
the clothes one wears would immediately fall away from the body, and so forth.

Third, regarding "that which is present before those who are present" (*pratyutpanna-pratyutpanna*): Xuanzang also translates this as "the property of the Saṃgha that is present within its own division.

This refers, for example, to personal requisites or food and clothing that are allocated to specific individuals; such matters are restricted to particular persons and do not constitute a collective *saṃgha*-bond.

Here, the term "present before those who are present" is used in contrast to the following category, "that which is obtained by the ten directions being present," where the latter term applies broadly to both internal and external [monastic] contexts. Thus:

It is said: "The ten directions. Because the establishment of the Dharma excludes partiality, it is called "present before one" (*pratyakṣa*). Now, since this meaning is restricted to the present, it is called "present before one.
Furthermore, because there must be an equitable distribution, it is again called "present before one"; thus, it is termed "present before one, present before one.

Some say: first, the object is present before one; second, the Saṃgha is present before one; hence, it is called "present before one, present before one. The following passage concerns the ten directions.
"Present" refers to persons belonging to the ten directions; "present before one" refers to material objects. [Dao]li asks: What are the characteristics of such an object?
For example, when a funeral feast is held and sutras are recited, if the offerings have not yet been distributed, they are still considered to belong to the original owners.

Because the objects still belong to the original owners, the offense is not incurred with respect to other individuals or the assembly of monks. This is also like when someone donates items for the *an-gu* (summer retreat) that have not yet...

[If it is] divided, if one steals [it], the offense is determined as grave (pārājika) with respect to the original owner. If many people share an object and one person guards it, the offense is also determined with respect to that guardian;
this is established as being indefinite—it may be a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If the thief steals from a guardian who is diligent and careful, then the offense is determined with respect to the many owners; it may even be less than five [shares], in which case it is a *thullaccaya*. If the guardian...

The primary offense is concealment. Thereafter, one must be cautious and prepared; if one causes damage to the protector (the Sangha), one incurs the grave offense of *pārājika*. This is because the calculation easily reaches the full five [factors].

Fourth, regarding "objects present before one from the ten directions" and so forth: this refers to things that pervade both the internal and external, for which a formal rule (*dharma*) is established to prevent their division; therefore, it is so named.
Regarding "the objects present before one from the ten directions": because the mind pervades both the internal and external, they are called "the ten directions";
because they are established as a formal dharma and restricted to a specific portion, they are subsumed within the "present," and thus further termed "present before one. This is why it is so stated.

If, prior to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), the offense incurred from the monks of the ten directions is light, this clarifies that while the disciplinary penalty (*vinaya*) is light, the karmic gravity is heavy. That is to say, although one is now charged with a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), in terms of the path of karma (*karmapatha*), it is heavy.
This refers to cases where the Sangha of the ten directions cannot be assembled and there is no place for confession.

If one has already performed the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) but the offense committed toward the present Sangha is grave, then the disciplinary action will be severe while the karmic retribution remains light; this is because the number of people can be limited and the resulting karma can be confessed.

If, at the time of death, the deceased entrusts property to another person by agreement, it is established that this refers to a case where the deceased’s belongings have already been designated for a specific recipient and the transfer has been settled, yet the items have not yet been delivered.

If someone steals these items, they incur a grave offense (pārājika) with respect to the intended recipient; this does not concern the affairs of the *saṃgha* present there. If the administrator suppresses [the gift] and...
Regarding "taking by force" and "entering into one's own possession," the gravity of the offense is determined by the value.
Consequently, some have said that stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha does not constitute theft; however, this refers to the claim of ancient masters.

When the group of six had already divided the property of the Saṃgha, Śāriputra and others went to seize it back; therefore, we know that those who divided it previously certainly did not commit theft.
If it were indeed theft, then Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others would not have felt justified in seizing it back.

By this analogy, one might think that if someone steals the property of the Saṃgha today, it does not constitute theft, and taking it back would be without fault. Now, I clarify that this is not so. As for Śāriputra’s seizure, it was because—

Because he understood the situation, he fully grasped that the six groups of monks did not intend to permanently enter his own fold; rather, it was merely a provisional stratagem, which is why they were divided.

Had it been a permanent division, taking [the property] back would have constituted a grave offense, as it would have been "a thief robbing a thief. The master Li also agrees with this interpretation of the ancient masters.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "If one steals property belonging to the Sangha, it may be confiscated in all cases. This is because the Sangha of ordinary and noble beings throughout the ten directions is universally the owner;
since no individual has formed the intention to relinquish it, and the owners' minds have not yet abandoned their claim, it is permissible to take it back."

Regarding the establishment of the gravity of offenses for the sake of temporary communal use: this refers to when the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks were in the village of Kauśāmbī and engaged in conduct that defiled the householders.

The Buddha ordered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to go and discipline the group of six. They immediately divided the property of the Saṃgha and entered it into their own possession, sending Maudgalyāyana and the others away so they would have no place to stay.
At that time, they temporarily devised this stratagem of dividing the goods, assigning them to four people for the purpose of providing a dwelling for those [monks].

There is no place for stability. Since internal wealth (inner possessions) has not been diminished, external traces are all the more clearly dispelled. This may serve as a brief clarification regarding the exclusion from the Sangha.
However, because this was originally not a permanent state, the offense is not established. The Vinaya relies on the original intention; based on that intention, a provisional ruling is made.
Yet Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra deeply discerned these circumstances and therefore immediately revoked it, allowing him to continue using his former attire.
"Other matters are as described in the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta* and other sections.

According to the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, in the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*, when the Buddha was preaching the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, countless nāgas came to where the Buddha was and wailed aloud, saying to the Buddha:
"Within our bodies now we endure great suffering and affliction; day and night we are constantly being bitten and eaten by various kinds of insects. We dwell in hot water..."
[In] the middle, there is not even a moment of happiness. The Buddha said, "In the past, you were once bhikṣus within the Buddha-dharma;

having violated the prohibitions and precepts, you fell into the hells for immeasurable kalpas and subsequently received the bodies of nāgas. Having heard the Buddha’s words, they sincerely repented their transgressions.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them. At that time, among the assembly, there were twenty-six koṭis of hungry nāgas who recalled the past.

Their bodies all shed tears. By the power of the Buddha, they all remembered their past lives and said in unison, "World-Honored One, we recall that in the past, although we left the household life within the Buddha-dharma, we committed various evil deeds. Some further spoke of remembering their former times.

Or there may be laypeople who have a close relationship with the Sangha due to various causes and conditions; or again, due to the cause and condition of coming and going to hear the Dharma, they possess further faith and offer food and drink.
At such times, I partake of it together with the Sangha according to the established order.

Or some might say, "I have previously consumed the flowers, fruits, food, and drink belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters. Or again, some might say, "I went to the monastery and distributed [the offerings]."
They give alms to the community of monks; or, because of performing prostrations, they eventually consume the food of the Sangha;

or again, they say, "In the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, I was once a layperson," or they say, "I was a layperson in the Dharma of Śikhin Buddha," and so on, up to "a layperson in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Thus, in the Dharmas of these seven Buddhas, there were laypeople respectively. Or, it may be due to visiting old friends and acquaintances.

Due to these causal conditions—whether coming and going for the sake of hearing the Dharma, or traveling back and forth between monasteries because faithful laypeople provide offerings of food and drink to the Saṃgha—a bhikṣu might receive such food and then divert it to me. Having obtained it, I eat it.
By virtue of this karmic cause, I have been burned and boiled in fire within the hells for immeasurable kalpas, drinking molten copper or swallowing it.
The iron ball [was cast]. Emerging from hell, he fell among the animals; casting off his animal body, he was born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), where he underwent all manner of suffering.
As his evil karma was not yet exhausted, he was born among these nāgas, where hot water rots his body, hot winds blow upon his frame, and there is the heat of hot earth, sand, excrement, and ashes.
He undergoes such suffering that it is unbearable. "I pray that the Buddha will rescue me. The Buddha told him:
O nāgas, compared to the karma of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the sin of this [karma] is like half [of it].
Nevertheless, the retribution for this sinful karma has not yet been fully exhausted. You should now together take the three refuges and cultivate goodness with a single mind.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, you will encounter the final Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa, named Ruci. In the world of that Buddha, your sins shall be extinguished. Thus spoke the Buddha.
Because it was spoken by the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, it is called the "Sūryagarbha Section. Candragarbha is likewise the name of a bodhisattva (as detailed in other records).

Regarding the account of the Tripitaka Master’s repayment of his debt, according to the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), it says: "For a long time he has owed property belonging to the Buddha..."

"How is it repaid? He replied, "It is repaid simply by returning the principal, because the Buddha neither enters nor exits; thus no additional repayment is added. Even though it was thus, he nevertheless entered hell.
Long ago, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu who was diligent and possessed comprehensive wisdom.
A certain brāhmaṇa, seeing the bhikṣu’s diligence, gave his daughter to the bhikṣu to become a *śrāmaṇerī* and practice the Way. The girl was already beautiful.

It is so. Later, this bhikṣu lost his mindfulness and committed impure acts, living together with others and using the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—ten million coins each—to provide for their clothing and food.
This bhikṣu was able to preach the Dharma and transform people, leading them to attain the fruits of the four paths.
Suddenly, he reflected that his transgressions were profound and heavy, and he desired to repay them. He went to the country of Dharmasāra and begged for [the means to do so].
He obtained some wealth and intended to repay it. While on the road in the mountains, he was bitten by a seven-step snake (the Buddha explained).

The bhikṣu knew that he would die after seven steps; thus, while still within six steps, he turned toward his disciple, entrusted him with the repayment of the goods, and sent him back to his native country, saying, "Once you have repaid the goods, return and report to me.
The disciple finished repaying the goods and returned to report.
Immediately, he walked seven steps and died, falling directly into the Avīci Hell. Upon first entering it, the heat was still mild and not yet intensely scorching.
Thinking it was a heated bathhouse, he raised his voice and chanted sūtras and made prayers of aspiration. When the various hell-demons heard these sūtra verses, several thousand attained liberation.
The wardens then raised their clubs and struck them; they died instantly and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

From this evidence, it is known that property belonging to the Buddha must not fail to be repaid; even though one may incur punishment for it, one will nonetheless be released upon the appropriate time. Question:
Within the category of theft, for what reason does stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha result in such immediate and heavy retribution? Answer:

It is explained that, according to the original intention of the Buddha, the establishment of permanent property for the Saṃgha was intended so that monks from the ten directions could travel and come and go without obstruction, thereby attaining peace and happiness in their practice.
The Way requires only that one shave one's head and dye one's robes; wherever one goes, one shall receive one’s share of offerings and distributions.
Therefore, we now permit those who wish to study and cultivate the Path to do so. Having left home for ten years, wherever they go, they will find food, drink, bedding, and dwellings.
By making full use of these provisions for the long journey, liberation may be expected. This is unlike a layperson traveling abroad to seek learning, who must provide for themselves.
Regarding grain, if one person carries three thousand *liang* and *guan* on their back, it will all be consumed within less than a month; thus, one must return empty-handed.
Because of such physical burdens, how can there ever be a day when one’s desired studies reach completion? A *bhikṣu* is not like this.
They obtain clothing and food wherever they go and dwell in peace while practicing the Way. This establishes them within the gateway of the Tathāgata’s great compassion;
all of this is the fruit of the Buddha’s retribution, which flows down as a protective shade for the disciples of the final dharma.

It is said that the Tathāgata’s original lifespan should have been one hundred and twenty years, yet he entered nirvana at eighty in order to leave behind a portion of his merit for the sake of future benefit.
He replied: "Because he provided for his disciples, he previously relinquished his life. His current statement regarding 'repaying the Buddha’s kindness' has this very meaning in mind.
Furthermore, food that remains permanently [in the Sangha] is the collective resource for the harmonious cultivation of the Way by the monastic community of the ten directions.

If one now steals from or damages it, one loses the benefit of harmony; such an act is equivalent to causing a schism in the Sangha, and thus the offense incurred is likewise grave—either a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
Therefore, as the sutra says: "I am able to save all those who commit the five heinous crimes; however, I do not save those who steal the property of the Sangha.
This is precisely that meaning. The preceding explanation of the first point, the meaning of misappropriation, is now complete.
Recorded up to this point at Shouji Monastery on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the first year of the Jingyun era. This preface is thus recorded.
The time was one of severe cold, leaving no room for reflection or deliberation; I shall await a leisurely day to further investigate and determine the details in full.
Should anyone seek this out, may they respectfully uphold my intent.
Recorded by the monk Dajue at the end of Volume Eight of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shao pi*).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
[Regarding] the two types of transgressing boundaries... [in the section on] clarifying the characteristics of transgressions, it is further divided into six parts:

first, objects belonging to an owner; second, ... (Note: The source text contains lacunae indicated by □□□□□□□□□□. The translation reflects the extant portions while acknowledging the missing characters.)

[The factors are: first, the perception that there is an owner; second, the intent to steal; third, the object being of significant value; fourth, the employment of means; fifth, the lifting [of the object]; and sixth, its removal from its original location.
Regarding the first [factor], among objects belonging to an owner, there are three major divisions:

first, stealing the property of the Triple Gem; second, stealing the property of humans; and third, stealing the property of non-humans. Within the first of these—stealing the property of the Triple Gem—it is further analyzed and divided into four parts.

First is misappropriation; second is mutual use; third is lending on interest; and fourth is using the property of the Triple Gem to provide for the methods of supporting both monastics and laypeople.
Within these four sections, the first meaning, that of misappropriation, has already been explained.
From this point onward, the text properly enters the second section, which extensively clarifies the meaning of mutual interchangeability. Within this section, it is further divided into four parts.

First, regarding the mutual interchangeability of the Three Jewels: the established view holds that the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha may be used interchangeably, resulting in a *tīr* offense. Second, regarding interchangeability within the same category:
the established view holds that such use results in a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning the *sīmā-sthāpaka* (temple administrator) misappropriating funds, extending through the full text as found in that Vinaya and other sources:
according to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it says: "If a bhikṣu acting as *sīmā-sthāpaka* has no property for a stūpa, but the Saṃgha does have property, he then forms this thought:"
The reason why devas and humans make offerings to the Saṃgha is that they all receive the grace of the Buddha. To make an offering to the Buddha is to make an offering to the Saṃgha.
If one takes property belonging to the Saṃgha to repair a stūpa, one attains *āpatti* (an offense). However, if the stūpa has property but the Saṃgha has none, one should form this thought:
"In making an offering to the Saṃgha, the Buddha is also included therein. Thus, by taking property from the stūpa to make an offering to the Saṃgha, one attains merit.

Regarding "Yi" (夷): The Guest says that this refers to the time when the Buddha was in the world; because he manifested as a human being, he was categorized as a human "yi. This has already been explained previously.
As for "Mamati," it is translated here as "the person who manages affairs."

Regarding "those who constantly reside in the *caitya* and have mutual needs": "constant residence" refers to the property of the *saṃgha* (the great assembly), while the *caitya* refers to the property of a separate room.
Below, it cites Ānanda’s acceptance of a separate room and the offering of the lady Āmrapālī as examples of what is called a *caitya*.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty stated that "caitya" is a corruption; its correct pronunciation is *cautu-ti-she*, which translates to "the four directions. The translator further explained:

The characters *qù* (to go) and *qiú* (to seek), as well as *zhāo* (to summon) and *zhà* (mulberry tree)—these two pairs of sounds are mutually interchangeable; it is because of this phonetic confusion that such an error occurred.
Regarding items belonging to a Buddha stūpa, even if they have been weathered by wind and rain, Master Li states:

since these are objects already used by the Buddha and are venerated by devas and humans, their status is equivalent to that of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, because they were offered with sincere devotion by donors, he does not permit them to be diverted [for other uses].
This is clear. The following further elucidates it.

Regarding the phrase "if, according to this, within the Buddha hall," etc., it means that based on the principle explained above—that the property of the Three Jewels must not be used interchangeably—it is said:
if the status of the Three Jewels is distinct and mutual use is not permitted, then [the same applies] within the Buddha hall now.

Regarding the placement of monastic seats: it is logically improper to place images of the Buddha in monastic quarters (*vihāra*). Nevertheless, if it does not hinder the use of the space by the monks, such a temporary arrangement is permitted.

Likewise, it is also permissible for monastic bedding to be placed in a Buddha hall, provided it does not hinder the use of the hall by the Buddha. Therefore, the following citation from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"One must not place the Buddha in a lower room," and so forth. This clearly shows that temporarily placing the Buddha in a room is also logically acceptable.
This is because rooms have distinctions of quality, which are designated as "upper" or "lower.

Regarding the question, "What is the nature of *cātudisa-sāṃghika* (property for the universal community)?"—the intent of this inquiry is to ask: what is the difference between *sāṃghika* (property belonging to the Saṅgha) and *cātudisa-sāṃghika*?

The answer states that the textual accounts in the *Āgama* scriptures are not definitive; however, according to principle, flowers, fruits, and the like constitute the *sāṃghika* property of the Saṅgha's ornaments.
These are items belonging to the *caitya*. A dwelling is a property of the *caitya* (the universal Sangha).

This refers to the sevenfold assembly of both monastics and laypeople who construct dwellings and offer them to the community of monks for the sake of all three periods of time, ensuring that the four types of offerings are never interrupted therein. It is intended for the itinerant monks of the ten directions to come and go;
thus it is named *caitya*. The *Karmavācanā-vṛtti* states: "The *caitya* monks' quarters" refers either to the sevenfold assembly...

For the sake of the Saṃgha of the four quarters, one should set aside separate rooms within the monastery; this is because there is a distinct provision for offerings for those who come to reside there.
As stated in the Vinaya texts, "how many rooms have abundant merit? refers to these [separate rooms]. "How many rooms lack abundant merit?

refers to the rooms where the Saṃgha resides permanently. Master Bin says: according to the tenth precept regarding the handling of lost property in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that Mother Viśākhā, having found some lost...
[The donor] took the jewels and offered them to the Sangha of the four directions. He said to Śāriputra, "These may be used to construct a *caitya* (or *cāturmahārājika*) monastic hall.

The Buddha said, "It is permitted to accept them. This is what is meant by a "monastic hall for the Sangha of the four directions. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty stated that *caitya* means "the four directions" in this language. Question:
If it is said that *caitya* refers to the property of the Sangha of the four directions, why does the first fascicle of the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* refer to it as "permanent property of the Sangha"?
Regarding the matter of the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*, it is difficult to distinguish it from other property because the permanent residence (*sthavira*) is itself the four quarters.

The response states: "The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* is a spurious scripture; how could it suffice as an obstacle? Daoliang said: "Now, Nanshan says that, according to this, dwellings and so forth are the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*;
this interpretation is certainly correct. He also cites the case of Viśākhā from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* as evidence. Therefore, we know that in the present time..."
Regarding the dwellings within a monastery, those not constructed with permanent funds are termed *caitya-vihāra* (monasteries for all).
Regarding the courtesan Āmrapālī, who was the first to offer her grove to the Buddha, Rong states that she was the wife of King Bimbisāra and the mother of Jīvaka;
she offered the grove to the Buddha, and it was thereby established as a *saṃghārāma*. According to the second fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, when the Buddha was traveling...
Upon arriving at Vaiśālī, he sat beneath a tree. There was a courtesan named Āmrapālī who, hearing that the Buddha had arrived there, went to pay him homage.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she gave rise to a heart of joy; she then received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
She addressed the Buddha, requesting that the Buddha and his disciples accept her invitation for the following day and stay overnight in her garden this very evening. The Buddha then...
He granted her request. When the time arrived the following day, the Buddha, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people, went to her home and took his seat.

The woman personally prepared and served the finest food; when they had finished eating, she took a golden pitcher, completed the ritual of offering water for washing, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"Among all the parks and groves in this city of Vaiśālī, this one is the most excellent. I now offer it to the World-Honored One."
“Venerable One, out of compassion for me, please accept [this]. The Buddha told the woman: “You may offer this grove to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, headed by the Buddha.

Why is this? As for all the groves, gardens, dwellings, robes, alms bowls, and the six requisites belonging to a Tathāgata, even the power of all the Māras, Śakras, Brahmās, and devas is incapable of receiving such an offering. At that time, the woman accepted the instruction.

Regarding the statement that "this very garden is offered to the Buddha as the foremost and to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters" (Wen Zheng’s reading is correct), and that flowers, fruits, and so forth are "Saṃgha-mālya items":
the traditional interpretation handed down from antiquity explains that those items which are permanently assigned for the use of the resident Saṃgha are called "Saṃgha-mālya items.
This refers to the passage in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* stating that by not violating Saṃgha-mālya items, one is reborn in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*). If one follows the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang:
The Dharma Master said: "The 'monk's garland' (saṃghamaṇḍalika) object refers to an offering made directly and face-to-face. Thus, the *Xinshu* says:
'As stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*, it refers to the donation of a lodging for the *cāturmahā-ārya-saṃgha*, which is precisely what is meant by a donation of a separate room.

As for the phrase 'this is a garland object' (*maṇḍalika*) in the sutra, this is a Sanskrit term; according to the Chinese (Tang) language, it means an 'object given face-to-face. It is like what is called today a 'layperson’s offering.'"
Regarding offerings to the Saṃgha: whether it be robes, medicine, or furniture for a dwelling, all such gifts are to be bestowed upon the Saṃgha present there.
As for the reason why the Buddha, while in the world, also shared a room with his disciples: this refers to when Rāhula was a śrāmaṇera;

because the bhikṣus were constrained by the Buddha’s established precepts that one must not stay overnight with those who are not fully ordained, they consequently drove Rāhula out and stayed overnight elsewhere.

In the latrine. At night, the World-Honored One saw him there and called him back to share a room for the night. Although he was summoned to return to the room to sleep, the World-Honored One remained seated facing him until dawn;

because this was a precept established in common with the bhikṣus, the Buddha did not dare to violate it. Among the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*), this is called "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*).
Furthermore, the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, a disciple of Kātyāyana, also shared a room with him, as described below.
Regarding the ninety rules, this is the detailed explanation of the precept concerning staying overnight with those who have not received full ordination.

As for "that which is obtained through distribution among the Sangha": although monastic property cannot be interchanged between the property of the Sangha and that of the Buddha or the Dharma, if an individual, according to the proper time, receives a portion from the head of the hall through distribution, that is his own share;
he may then take it to make offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma as he sees fit.

[The respondent] said: "It has been obtained. There is nothing further to report regarding the inquiry. Lil said: "A junior monk like myself does not know the boundaries of the Three Jewels regarding lost property.

If it is acquired by the Sangha, it may be used for the permanent assets (*sthaviraka*) of the monastery. If the labor was provided by the Sangha, one should deliberate upon the amount [of compensation].
Lil said: "This is a well belonging to the stūpa. At the time the well was constructed, the labor of the Sangha was also employed; how much money should be calculated [as compensation]?"
For example, when constructing a well in Puzhou east of the River, it may require twenty or thirty thousand [units of labor], and the effort expended is great.
A bucket is raised by means of a rope harnessed to a donkey. Later, when monks take this water, they stop once the value reaches a certain amount of money;
if the price exceeds five *qián*, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the bark, branches, and leaves that may be used by individual bhikṣus: this refers to cases where [the tree] is dead or decayed and no longer fit for communal use by the Saṃgha;

it permits an individual to take the leaves for dyeing and so forth. Alternatively, it may refer to cases where there is no resident Saṃgha using them, thus permitting an individual to take the leaves and so on.
Or, it may be because they are so abundant as to be limitless that their taking and use are permitted, much like a mountain monastery where [trees] are plentiful.
Regarding the location of trees: furthermore, because it must be pure and clean, its use is permitted. It is also permissible to borrow monastic items such as cauldrons, pots, and jars;
this means they must be new and clean, as they can be used because they have not been stained by red dye or grease.

If they have already been used in a monastic household, there is the offense of "evil contact" (*duṣṭasparśa*), and according to the principle, they may not be borrowed. Alternatively, one might be able to borrow and use monastic utensils.
According to the *Bhikṣu-vinaya*, one must not touch [the fire] with one's own hand;

rather, one should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") to use it for warming the *jantāghara* (sauna) and so forth. This is not a regular bathhouse; it refers to a separate room constructed during cold weather for lighting fires to obtain warmth.
In the present day, this region designates a bathhouse as a *jantāghara*, and this meaning is also appropriate here. In this context, it is permissible.
This refers to the taking of monastic property. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when bathing the monks, one must make a formal announcement because monastic property is being used.

The practice of the *karmadāna* (steward) making a morning proclamation is also consistent with this principle; it is improper not to announce it, as failure to do so constitutes the offense of theft (*steya*).

Regarding the statement that "one may not take more than what is required for a separate room," this refers to things such as the branches and leaves of trees currently belonging to the monastic quarters.
Since a separate room is already a pure dwelling, it is logically appropriate to use it; however, one must not take [wood] beyond the limit without purpose.

This is clearly stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. If the Saṃgha requires wood for use, or if there are trees located on obstructed land, or even if the donor does not permit its use—such as in the case of fish bones, thorns, and the like—this is explicitly clarified.
In the various monasteries of the Western Regions (India), most were established by laypeople.
"It is for the communal use of the Saṃgha; however, since the temple still belongs to the donor, this is being consulted [with him].

When asked about the donor, it was said: "In this region nowadays, such a practice is not permitted. As for pouring ash-water on a tree to kill it: one must first remove a small portion of the bark, and only then pour it.
Use cinnamon powder to plug the holes; [the tree] will die easily. It is best to prepare a dust-free ash-water."

Regarding the account that King Bimbisāra offered his garden to the Buddha and others, [the Vinaya] establishes this clearly: if the garden belonged to the Buddha, it would not be available for the use of the Dharma or the Saṃgha;
however, if it was given to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha obtained formal authorization (*jñapti-sāmagrī*) and it became available for the use of both the Dharma and the Buddha.

Regarding those who take hidden treasures for the purpose of providing offerings for lectures and the like, it is established that one may only take them if there is an iron seal above stating, "If you are performing a feast or giving a lecture, you may take as you please. If this is not the case, they belong to the original owner;
if there is no owner, they belong to the King, and thus may not be taken. However, the intended meaning of this passage on hidden treasures cited here is that although within the cache—
These are the properties of the Three Jewels. Hereafter, they may be used according to specific needs; it is not necessary to divide them into three distinct portions.

This proves that one cannot break [the community] into three parts based on the aforementioned text. Regarding "wealth and Dharma being the same": this refers to the fact that one does not commit a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Sharing the same offerings constitutes the sameness of wealth; sharing the same recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) constitutes the sameness of Dharma. If one commits a grave offense, then wealth and Dharma are no longer shared.

"Know that the offense incurred is immeasurable, as extensively described in the sūtras. This refers to what was cited above in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, which state:
"I shall not save those who steal the property of the Saṃgha."
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "As the *Chuan* (Biographies) says," [Dao]li establishes that the *Chuan* of Lingyan Monastery in Qizhou states:
There was a bhikṣu who, upon death, saw the entirety of hell. He then encountered the form of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, who led him to examine his own karmic records (*karmapustaka*).
Furthermore, for him, a stone casket was opened, revealing the karmic records of all the monks; on these were inscribed various instances of misappropriating the property of the Sangha, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "to examine for oneself and then adopt," Li states that "examine" (*yin*) means to scrutinize, and "adopt" (*can*) means to harmonize.

This clarifies that one should personally scrutinize whether one's karmic actions are appropriate or not before adopting them. There is also a reading where it is written as *yin* (pronounced *yu xīn*), meaning that one should personally examine whether [the practice] is pure or impure.
Regarding the second point, "mutual use within their respective categories": this term "within their respective categories" (dang-fen) is designated in contrast to the preceding section.

In the preceding section, it refers to the mutual interaction among the Three Jewels as a whole, wherein mutual use incurs offense. In the present section, however, it refers to Buddhas interacting with Buddhas alone, Dharmas with Dharmas alone, and Sanghas with Sanghas alone.

Therefore, it is said that they are mutually interchangeable within their respective categories. Regarding those cases where the principle and meaning can be applied by looking toward the preceding object, it is established that these mutual interchanges within their respective categories do not necessarily entail the same degree of offense.
Although Śākyamuni and Amitābha differ slightly, they both share the common meaning of "Buddha" and both constitute fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Although monastic dwellings and vehicles differ, they both share the common meaning of belonging to the Sangha. Hence, it is said that the principle and meaning can be applied. Now...

However, if one violates the intention of the donor, one incurs the offense of "mutual use" (*pārivāsika-āpatti*). This merely constitutes the formal determination (*sīmā-bandha*) of what is improper.

Furthermore, regarding the case where funds designated for the current temple maintenance are diverted to make the five robes (*pañca-cīvara*): the present mention of the "five robes" is based on the *nidāna* (origin story) concerning the Bhikṣuṇīs; for the Bhikṣus, it should be understood by analogy that it refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*).
In the Vinaya, this matter arose because the Bhikṣuṇī An-yin (Anupamā) went to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) in a village and was given [the funds directly].

When funds were being used to construct a monastery hall for the *saṃgha* present [in that location], a nun thought to herself: "If I use these materials to build a hall, there will be many complications and it will be difficult for me to obtain robes;

I should instead make the five robes. Later, when the layperson heard this, he became resentful. The Buddha established a rule that this constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

This was because the funds were intended specifically for the hall currently being built. However, if funds intended for a monastery hall for the *saṃgha* from the four directions are diverted [for personal use], one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
This is not what is being clarified here.

Regarding the statement that "the causes and effects of the forged sūtras created by humans are entirely contradictory," it is established and clarified as follows: Originally, one composed authentic sūtras; now, one has composed forged sūtras.

Since these were created by humans and were not spoken by the Buddha, they are no longer termed "interchangeable within their own category" (*dang-fen hu-yong*). Therefore, they are concluded as grave offenses (*zhong-yi*).

Because truth and falsehood are entirely contradictory, it is not termed "within the same category" (*sabhāga*). As the preceding text states: "If one who was originally a Buddha turns back to become a Bodhisattva, he still incurs a grave offense.
This is because the Bodhisattva is the causal body (*hetu-kāya*) and the Buddha is the resultant body (*phala-kāya*); furthermore, there is a distinction between teacher and disciple.
Thus, this too is not a case of mutual application within the same category, and therefore incurs the grave offense of *pārājika*. From this Bodhisattva downward, all are causal [bodies].

The results are entirely contrary; all [cases] that come before us are judged to incur heavy [retribution]. Regarding the distinction between merit and non-merit due to the mixture of the orthodox and the heterodox:
this means that the True Sūtras state that there is merit for those who produce what is orthodox, whereas there is no merit for those who produce what is heterodox, such as false sūtras;

thus it is said. Furthermore, producing a sūtra brings great merit, while producing a śāstra brings little merit. Moreover, there are two kinds of śāstras: namely, those produced by Bodhisattvas and those produced by Śrāvakas.

Whether composed by humans or others, there is likewise a distinction between that which is meritorious and that which is not. Thus far, we have compared the sūtras with the śāstras; in this regard, the sūtras are meritorious while the śāstras are not.
Nevertheless, the sūtras are divided into authentic and spurious, and are further distinguished as being composed by ordinary beings or by sages; therefore, their merit differs accordingly.

If the Buddha’s dharma-relics, wealth, and property in the eastern and western niches have designated owners, it is improper for them to be used by others as if they were ownerless. This is clearly established:
two donors each made offerings to the Buddha’s relics, wealth, and ritual implements in the eastern and western niches respectively;
mutual use is not permitted. If the donor is still living, such use is strictly forbidden. If the donor has died, there are two interpretations regarding the donor: [the first is that...]
Even though [the donor] has died, if a bhikṣu knows that the original donor’s intention was restricted and not general, he still may not exchange [the items].

Here, however, it is simply based on the case where the later bhikṣu does not know the original donor’s intention; therefore, he is permitted to use them generally. In this context, such an exchange within one's own share constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If there are no masters, disciples, or various ritual implements for offerings, one should instead attend upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Saṅgha, Vajrasattva, Siṃha, the Eight Divisions [of Spirits], and so forth.

Regarding the point that taking the form of birds or beasts incurs offense—except before the Buddha and similar instances—it is as when Amitābha transforms into a white crane, a peacock, a parrot, or a śarī bird;
when creating a *nirvāṇa* transformation tableau, one should likewise follow the scriptural texts.
The various classes of beings obtain [the fruit] immediately.

Regarding the *Sudarsana* (Good Vision): if a donor originally intended to give a garden or fruit trees for robes and medicinal requisites, but [the recipient] diverts them to food, it constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) according to the value.
This is clearly established: when there is a protector, the offense is committed in relation to that protector. Jing says: "This refers to giving to the permanent residence (*sthavira-saṃgha*)."
The Sangha [intends] these items for monastic robes; now, by acting contrary to the donor’s intention and making them into food, a grave offense is incurred.

If one intends to make them into heavy property for a monastic dwelling but diverts them to make monastic food, the offense is a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). Jing says: "This is because the donor's intention was not yet fixed, hence it is light.
If the intention to give were fixed, it should be treated as above and result in a grave offense. He further states: "This refers to the side of diminishing merit, whereby a *duṣkṛta* is incurred."
When a donor originally intends to build a monastery, there is long-lasting merit arising from non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Now, if this is redirected toward providing food, the deficiency lies in the absence of non-informative action;

because the merit is thus diminished, it is established that if one uses heavy items such as garden fruits for the Sangha’s meals, it is clearly explained in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* that when a donor gives a garden intending to provide clothing, redirecting it toward food results in a grave offense.
Now, since food and provisions are currently scarce and people wish to disperse, this permission for sale and purchase is granted.

As for the statement that "even the dwellings of the Saṃgha from the four directions may be used," it means that if one wishes to protect the residence because of a lack of food, one may sell the buildings and houses to obtain money to provide for the monks' meals.
Regarding the allowance to carry [the property] with oneself during times of turmoil caused by bandits, this refers to the Saṃgha.
Household bedding and other personal belongings should be returned to their original places once the period of disorder has ended.

If one wishes to offer worship to this image and transfer it to that image, it is like the case of the people of Xiangzhou who made Buddhas, each having a patron who commissioned a Buddha image and installed it within Jing Temple, setting up separate rooms and doors for its placement.
When the seasonal festivals arrived, they would each personally bring incense, flowers, food, and drink [to the respective images].
Regarding offerings: if the donor should suddenly die and their descendants cut off the lineage, that image will ultimately remain forever enduring hunger and thirst.

Furthermore, there are those who have slaves create images for them to be venerated within the temple; if a free person should know that this is a "slave Buddha," [they must treat it with due respect].
No one was willing to pay him homage.
Regarding the case in the *Five Hundred Questions* where a layperson offers food to a bhikṣu who has not yet been ordained, the text states:

"This person wishes to enter the Buddha-dharma and leave the household life; however, due to various matters involving the Saṃgha, they have not yet had the opportunity to receive the tonsure. [The layperson] informs the Saṃgha and gives [the food]."
Regarding food: if it is for an ordinary layperson who has not yet been ordained, one may not give them food without having informed the Saṃgha. According to that treatise, it asks:

"If a layperson throws themselves [into the order] seeking the Way but has not yet been ordained, may they receive food from the Saṃgha? It answers: "If they inform the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits it, they may; if they do not inform the Saṃgha, they commit a *pāyattika* offense."
Regarding the rule that if one requests food on behalf of the Saṃgha and informs the Saṃgha, who then grants permission to carry it along the road and so forth, [the commentator] Li states:

although the Saṃgha has been informed and there is consensus, one must still compensate [the donor] before it may be taken. Even if there is consensus but no compensation, or if there is compensation but no consensus, in neither case is it permitted.
However, "consensus" refers merely to seeking the Saṃgha’s authorization; it does not mean that compensation is unnecessary. If one reaches consensus but fails to compensate, one commits an offense.
"Severe. To repay [the debt] without harmony results in an inauspicious response (meaning one fears being too hasty). According to that treatise, it asks:

"If one requests a road for the sake of the *saṃgha*, may one personally consume the food belonging to the *saṃgha*? The answer is: "If, when departing, one first informs the *saṃgha* and the *saṃgha* grants permission, it is well.

If one does not inform them at first, but informs them upon returning, that is also well. If permission was not granted and one does not repay [the debt], one commits a grave offense. Jing says: "This applies generally."

This is a matter concerning both the monastic community and the laity. Suppose a donor provides rice for a meal for the Sangha, and after the monks have departed, the donor intends to offer it to subsequent monks.
According to that treatise, it asks: "If a donor provides rice for a meal for the Sangha, after the monks have left, may the donor use it to provide for subsequent monks?
May those later people eat it? It answers: "If the *gandi* (wooden gong) is struck, they may eat; if it is not struck, eating even a single meal constitutes a grave offense. This refers to the donor.
Regarding rice: if the food for a certain number of monks has not yet been finished, and that monk shares this remaining rice with others, it then belongs to the Sangha of the ten directions.

One who steals it incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; this is because the original donor was guarding it, and the gravity of the offense is determined in relation to this current guardian, not in relation to the previous [donation].
As for "committing a grave offense upon a single meal," this refers to a time when the price was high, such as five [units of currency].
"Money must be of low value, not even worth five [units], and thus light. There are further various interpretations, which I shall not elaborate upon at length (etc.).
As for the path, it is not a place for begging; when a monk carries food on the road, he need not necessarily make a display of it. This is what [Master] Li says.
One may only take [the food] away after informing the Saṃgha, provided there is no other place to obtain alms. Even after such notification, one must still repay the value.

By notifying the Saṃgha and seeking their permission, one merely avoids the offense of using it arbitrarily; however, upon returning from the journey, one must still repay it. Sengce said: "Many people do not accept this principle.

For instance, when hiring laborers, since they are given money and food in full, why would one need to restrict the scope of where those items can be used? This is the case with the bhikṣu here as well."

He is exclusively a messenger for the Saṃgha and has indeed rendered real service to the Saṃgha. Since he is not one who relies [on others] for his own sake, it is logically appropriate that he be given food;
there is no fault in this. Regarding the passage from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* concerning the guardian of the monastery:

this refers to the rule in the aforementioned *Sudarsana-śāstra* stating that one may take fruits from the garden to prepare food for the Saṃgha, for the purpose of protecting the dwelling place, as well as the procedure for informing and obtaining the consent of the monks of the four quarters before preparing the food and so forth. For these reasons...

If one had previously sought permission from the Saṃgha and was thus permitted to use [the property], then even if one now seeks permission from the Saṃgha while carrying food on the road, it would logically be permissible.
Huiliang said: "The above cases all concern what is permitted for the sake of the Saṃgha.

In the present day, when administrators act on behalf of the monastery's assembly by entering the imperial court or provincial offices, or traveling through prefectures and counties using the monastery’s permanent assets—such as people, livestock, boats, or carts—they all commit a grave offense. This is because...

The monks currently residing at this temple belong to the *pratyutpanna* (present) community; they do not pertain to the *sthavira* (permanent/endowment) property. While the permanent property extends throughout the ten directions, the present community is restricted to this specific location.
How can you cause others to provide for the livestock of the permanent property? Be careful, be careful!

Regarding the statement that "the bells are rung at each residence to announce the communal meal," this refers to the established practice that within the temple's estate and its various dwellings, a signal must be given;
subsequently, one need not fill [the bowls] individually, because the estate and the temple constitute a single household.

Regarding the *pāyantika* offense for [stealing] the property of the Saṃgha, whether human or animal-related: it is established that although the parties involved are distinct, they both belong equally to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*).

Therefore, one does not commit a grave offense; because the parties are different, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks: "As for the food belonging to the permanent endowment of the ten directions..."

For example, when steamed cakes, cooked rice, or the sound of a bell are used to summon [the assembly], all members of the *saṃgha* receive them. It is not known whether those from other temples may obtain the slaves or livestock;

the answer is that it is not permissible. The *saṃgha* possesses the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) and exists everywhere; however, humans and livestock belong to specific individuals, and in principle, they cannot be used for general purposes.
Since such usage is restricted, food is treated in the same way. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of mutual use within one's own category.

Regarding the mutual relationship between the three images and the jewels: "images" refers to the *dharmatā*-maintaining distinct-aspect Three Jewels, namely clay shrines, painted or sculpted statues, yellow scrolls with red bindings, and those who have shaved their heads and dyed their robes.
"Jewels" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Three Jewels of Essential Unity.
In the new sutras and treatises, these are termed the ultimate Three Jewels, while the former are termed the conventional Three Jewels.
Regarding the statement that "offering the Buddha-treasure by placing fingernails and hair within a stupa constitutes making offerings to the Dharma-body," Jing says:
Because the physical body and the two [other] bodies are distinct, this refers to an instance that already occurred while [the Buddha] was in the world.
"One portion is given to those who recite the sutras and expound the Dharma. The commentary states:

"Since it is through people that the Dharma is propagated, and the Dharma does not proclaim itself, but relies on people to spread and transmit it, one now accepts this offering and divides one portion to give to the expounders of the Dharma."
The Sangha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-saṃgha) refers to those who are without contradiction or dispute in principle and whose essence is eternally harmonious; hence the name.
It is also called the "Sangha of the Supreme Meaning" (viniścaya-saṃgha). Bin says: "If one steals these items, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
This is because the nature of the Sangha of the Supreme Meaning does not involve the appropriation of material goods. Nevertheless, this *duṣkṛta* is extremely grave and difficult to calculate."

Regarding the statement that "if one gives to the Saṃgha, both ordinary and noble beings alike receive equal portions," [Sthiramati] asserts that this refers precisely to giving to the present *sthavira-saṃgha* (the permanent monastic community).

Because ordinary and noble beings assemble together, it is called the "Saṃgha. This is because the substance of the property belonging to the permanent monastic community is available for the use and enjoyment of both ordinary and noble beings.
As for the phrase "the word 'with' (*yi*) is not appropriate," [Sthiramati] asserts that since this specific act of giving is not explicitly stated, yet the principle of this giving remains.

It is also a treasure. Furthermore, it is explained that because at the time of giving one does not definitively state, "I am giving to ordinary monks" or "I am giving to noble monks," it is said that the words have no fixed application.
Regarding "knowing well the passages and obstructions at the time of receiving offerings," it is established that one must clearly inquire of the donor:

"Do you offer the Three Jewels as principle (*li*), or do you offer the Three Jewels as phenomena (*shi*)? If the donor does not understand, one should explain both the principles of phenomena and principle—such as clay stupas, statues, and scrolls, as well as the ultimate principle of the single essence of the Three Jewels.
A guest says: At the time of receiving offerings, one must examine and verify the offering.
The donor is the primary authority. One must not rely solely on the donor’s words, for fear that they may not understand and thus misdirect the donated objects.

Therefore, the *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 60, states: "In the Jetavana, people from the four quarters of the realm who were ignorant of the Dharma all came to the great assembly."

There are those who practice giving. When a bhikṣu offers a prayer of aspiration, he praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, and Kumbhīra—these Three Jewels, which are countless, immeasurable, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).
Among them, some may hold the name of the Buddha, the name of the Dharma, or even the names of the incalculable ones.
Once the great assembly has dispersed, they return to their fields, villages, and hamlets during the remaining time.
"O bhikṣus, when you go out to beg for alms in various countries, there may be those who hold the name of the Buddha and say, 'The Buddha has come to give';

or even those who hold the name of the asaṃkhyeya [monks] and say, 'The asaṃkhyeya have come to give. The bhikṣus did not accept these offerings and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

'These are people from border regions who do not know that they are giving food specifically because of the bhikṣus; yet the names [they invoke] are equal to the Buddha and the Dharma. You should accept them as you please.'"
[Receiving] (the above is from the Vinaya text). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle six, states: "In all acts of giving, one should cause both the mind and the speech to be settled.
When the merit of giving is thus profound, it is also easy to distinguish. If one gives the Dharma-jewel, the speech must be settled. If one gives scriptures, the speech must also be settled.
If one gives to a Dharma-preacher or a person who recites the sutras, the speech must likewise be made settled. If one gives to the Saṃgha, it is also [the same]."
There are three kinds: the *saṃgha-lakṣa* (the year of the Saṃgha), the *pravāraṇā-lakṣa* (the year of the invitation), and the *mukha-dvāra-lakṣa* (the year of the face-gate).

Regarding these three kinds, one should distinguish them well. (The commentary states: "Saṃgha" refers to the permanent property of the Saṃgha of the four directions. "Pravāraṇā" refers to the items obtained by the monks at the time of the invitation ceremony. "Mukha-dvāra" refers to the food of the present Saṃgha of the ten directions. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 27, states:
The Buddha said, "When giving items, have one bhikṣu stand there to observe and know the distribution."
It is distinct. These are items belonging to the stūpa, items belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions, food items, and items that should be distributed.
Regarding the mutual [relationships] among the four types of items according to their characteristics: the former explained the mutual relationship between images and jewels;

hereafter, it explains that within the category of images themselves, there are likewise internal mutual relationships. Each of these is set forth individually under the four headings in the text. Shen says: "If the Buddha has used [them]..."
Regarding these items: the first category may never be moved or exchanged; the latter three may be modified according to circumstances, depending on whether it is permitted or not.
As for the prohibition against mutual exchange as stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, it is because—as previously mentioned—the Buddha-dharma has no owner and no one sets its price;
therefore, one knows that within this context, mutual exchange is not permitted. If the Buddha’s seat or sitting mat is offered by all devas and humans...

Regarding the phrase "one must not use [the items] while they are being maintained," *Li* (Liu) states that the garden refers to the Buddha’s flower and fruit groves, and the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) refers to the objects used by the Buddha.

This is intended to clarify that these are objects of the Buddha’s personal use, which are revered and honored by humans and devas. This is explained in the *Jie xin shu* (Commentary on the Precepts).
This also clarifies four kinds of distinctions. First, it clarifies that the objects used by the Buddha must not be interchanged;

they are always intended for offerings, which generate great merit in the world. Thus, the Vinaya states: "If these are the Buddha’s garden, seating mats, and so forth," because all devas and humans regard them as being of the same substance as the stūpa.
The reason they are not permitted to be exchanged is that they are none other than the Dharma-body itself.
The characteristics of these [objects] indicate that their status is profound and must not be treated lightly.
Second, regarding items belonging to the Buddha: the *Xinshu* (Commentary on the Mind) states, "These items belong to the Buddha;

the reason they may be exchanged is that the original donor intended them for general use by the Buddha, and thus they may be traded. This is not the same as the former case, where [the object] had already served as a mark of excellence."
It is settled that there is only one [rule]. Regarding the rule that property belonging to the Buddha may not be moved to another temple, or else one commits the offense of *pārājika* (abandonment):

Jing says, "This refers to the karmic bond incurred by violating the intention of the donor. Because the donor’s intention was restricted to this specific location, 'abandonment' (*parityāga*) means committing a grave offense (*guru-apatti*).

It is so called because the entire Saṃgha performs a *karma* (formal act) to expel the offender from the community. As for a bhikṣu working as a laborer to create Buddha images or copy scriptures, he may not receive any goods [for his own use].
Regarding "taking": *Lilü* (Establishment) states that if one uses this object, it is no different from using the property of the Buddha; one will certainly incur a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the third point, "making offerings with the property of the Buddha and so forth," the *Xinsu* (Commentary on the Mind) says: "If one exchanges [the property] for banners, flowers, and the like, the matter is identical to that which belongs to the property of the Buddha;
this may be sought through reasoning. Regarding "if there are many Buddha-banners and one desires other Buddhist services," *Lilü* states: "Because there are many banners..."
One may fashion banners into Buddha-robes or canopies, or use them to drape a Buddha’s bed, or make them into ritual mats; however, one must not tear or break them, but keep them joined together.
This is what is meant by "not transforming the essential substance. Regarding the offense incurred by destroying [an image] out of an evil mind:
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 63, it is said that if one paints an image of the Buddha and another person, because they find the image unattractive...
Destruction occurs because one person breaks [the Sangha] out of an evil mind; since their minds differ, one gains merit while the other incurs sin.
It is also like Devadatta and Jīvaka, both of whom drew blood from the Buddha’s body.
Although they are identical in the act of drawing blood, because their intentions differ, one incurs the sin of entering Avīci Hell for one kalpa, while the other gains merit and is reborn in heaven.
One kalpa. In reference to this cause, the joyful affairs of the physician Jīvaka are recounted.

According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, once in the past, Maudgalyāyana went up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven because one of his disciples was ill, in order to consult Jīvaka. It happened that all the devas were entering the Nandana Grove.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana stood by the side of the road, yet none of the devas looked back at him—not even Jīvaka.
When he arrived later, he saw Maudgalyāyana raising one hand as Jīvaka passed straight by in his carriage.

Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "This man was formerly of the human world and was my disciple; now he enjoys celestial bliss. Because he is attached to these heavenly pleasures, he has completely lost his original resolve.

He immediately employed his supernormal powers to restrain the carriage and bring it to a halt. Jīvaka descended from the carriage and prostrated at the feet of Maudgalyāyana. Then Maudgalyāyana [expounded] various causes and conditions...
Regarding this reproach, Jīvaka replied: "Because I am a disciple of great virtue among men, I raise my hand to offer greetings.
Have you ever seen such behavior among the devas? Having been born in heaven, they are attached to pleasure and thus lack self-mastery."
It was for this reason alone. Maudgalyāyana asked, "I have a disciple who is ill; how should he be treated?
Jīvaka replied, "The primary method is simply to abstain from food. On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana exhorted Śakra, saying, "A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter;
why do you not come near us more often to inquire about and receive the True Dharma? Desiring to resolve Maudgalyāyana’s concerns, Śakra dispatched a messenger.
The King commanded a certain son of heaven to come, calling him repeatedly three times; yet he still did not come.

This son of heaven had only one wife and one musical consort; because his attachment to sensual desire was so deep, although the King of Heaven’s command was weighty, he could not bring himself to sever those ties.
Later, having failed to obtain them, he finally came. Śakra immediately asked, "For what reason is this? He then answered with the truth.
Śakra addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying: "This devaputra has only one celestial maiden and one musical ensemble with which to amuse himself;

he cannot bring himself to renounce them. How much less could I, as the King of Devas, who have various palaces and towers, countless celestial maidens, naturally produced *sūdhā* food of a hundred flavors, and hundreds of thousands of musical ensembles with which to amuse myself—so absorbed that I forget the west while looking toward the east—even though I know of the Buddha?"
The world is difficult to encounter; the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Yet, being bound by the fetters of defiled pleasures, one cannot attain self-mastery. Knowing this, what can be done?

Regarding the "four offerings to the Buddha" and so forth, the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) states: These offerings to the Buddha are permitted for use by the attendants (*vaitālika*). This is the meaning.
Because they are both subsumed under the Buddhist community (*saṃgha*), as in the Sarvāstivāda school, even those who give to Dharma teachers, preach the Dharma, or recite the sūtras receive a share.
Furthermore, there are four distinctions regarding Dharma property: if it is an object for the communal use of the Dharma community, it may never be diverted or exchanged.
Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "First are objects for the use of the Dharma, such as paper, silk, bamboo, or wood;

these include scriptures and images, or boxes, cases, vessels, and bags that have previously contained them. Once it is determined that they shall be permanently dedicated [to the Sangha], they are not permitted to be diverted or transferred. This is fixed;

they are revered as identical to the sacred teachings, for they are all that which supports and maintains the principle of cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Thus, any harm or benefit to them is regarded as being toward *nirvāṇa* itself."
This gives rise to demerit or merit. Regarding the statement that "the remaining three types may or may not be obtained, as can be inferred from the above":

these three refer to ritual objects (dharmavastu)—namely, offerings to the Dharma, dedications to the Dharma, and gifts to the Dharma. These three are treated the same as objects for the Buddha; they are presented according to circumstances.
Therefore, it is said that whether the remaining three are obtained or not can be inferred from the above.
If these two types of permanent [offerings] were fixed to specific locations, they would be "permanent-permanent" and "permanently permanent throughout the ten directions";

thus they are called "two types. Since neither may be taken out of their boundaries at will, they are said to be "restricted to specific locations," as was already clarified above in the section on stealing monastic property.
Regarding the phrase "the two types may be used interchangeably; their mutual sharing and common use can be understood as above," Li [Lilou] says:

"This refers to whether, within the two aforementioned types of permanent property (*nitya-dharmya*), the communal property (*saṃghika*) and the property of the *Jantaghara* (or *Caitya*) may be used interchangeably, just as in that previous case. Shen [Shenxiu] says:

"This refers to the passage in the *Jianlun* concerning the guarding of the monastery: using the gardens and fruits belonging to the community of monks (*saṃgha*) to prepare food for the monks, and likewise using the monastic quarters..."
This refers to cases such as preparing food and the like.

If one discusses the two types of offenses arising from what is present (*pratyutpanna*), as explained above, within the context of stealing monastic property, it clarifies the distinction between what is given to those currently present and what is given to those present throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the phrase "offenses are mutual" (*zui xu*): for example, in the case of the property of a deceased bhikṣu, this is...
Regarding "the ten directions being present": when the currently present Sangha is brought forward, one does not perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) again;

rather, one directly distributes the property according to what is present before them—this is "mutual [appropriation]" (*miśra*). If the property was originally intended for those currently present within this specific boundary—meaning the donor restricted it solely to those currently in retreat within this realm—it is now universally summoned from the ten directions to be distributed;
this is "mixed usage" (*miśraprayoga*). This is discussed in terms of the gravity of the offense.

Regarding the statement that "the severing of two objects does not constitute a textual violation" and the simultaneous imposition of two offenses: Master Li says, "The term 'simultaneous imposition' expresses the intention of the Dharma school;

because one wishes for the meaning to be comprehensive and inclusive, it is called the 'simultaneous imposition of two offenses. This phrase arises from the preceding text concerning the two types of *pratyutpanna* (manifest) [offenses];
therefore, it is appropriate here. Master Bin says, "In contrast to this, this section clarifies the application of the holy precepts in this land."

Regarding monastic property: Sengchong stated that stealing the money of a Sage necessarily incurs a grave offense, as the person currently occupying the position of Elder serves as the actual owner of the goods.
However, if one steals the wealth of others who have entered parinirvāṇa, they are not the immediate owners; such an act merely results in karmic retribution.

Now, examining the Western regions (India), there was originally no such practice of giving [to a living elder], and since the scriptures lack explicit clarification on the matter, it is difficult to reach a definitive judgment. According to the principle of Sengchong’s ruling, the logic is as follows: [text continues].

Furthermore, this is not so. Originally, the offering was made to the noble Saṃgha, not exclusively to the *sthavira*. Moreover, although the offering has been relinquished, the noble ones may not necessarily arrive;
since money is an impure substance, if they were to accept it, they would have to hand it over to the donor themselves or perform the ritual of "purifying by declaration" (*śuddhivācanā*).

How could it be permitted to simply take possession of it? Once the matter is concluded, it must be distributed. Furthermore, regarding that general category of making offerings solely to the noble Saṃgha—who among the noble ones would actually receive it?
[The Buddha] came to take exclusive charge [of these items]. Now, examining these objects in detail, they still have no fixed owner. If one were to steal them, all would incur a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅);

if one has the perception that they belong to an owner, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (蘭) offense. Nevertheless, both this *sthūlātyaya* and the *duṣkṛta* karma are profoundly grave, because one gives rise to a thieving mind toward the field of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, as for these donated objects, the intention of the donor was not directed toward a specific recipient, nor have they been definitively assigned to a particular noble monk (*ārya-bhikṣu*). It may be...
One may purchase offerings for the noble Sangha, or alternatively, erect stupas and temples for the noble Sangha; in the sphere of the noble Sangha, the field of merit is universally accessible.

This differs from the practice of the past, which provided seats exclusively for the [ordinary] Sangha, and from the restriction that forbids using brocades and silks as seats for the noble Sangha—fearing such a view might not be correct.
Furthermore, this method of giving has been transmitted down through the ages; it must not be abruptly discarded in the present day.

[This practice] is abolished. Therefore, when receiving a gift, one should inform the donor, saying: "This object should be used to erect a stupa for the noble Saṃgha, or to create images and various ritual implements to make offerings to the noble Saṃgha.
If the donor asks, "How shall I proceed? one should reply, "Do as you wish; there is no fault in any [of these].

Furthermore, the judgment of Master Chong states: "Those who have entered parinirvāṇa receive the karmic retribution for theft. Now, upon detailed examination, although they have entered parinirvāṇa...
It is not only a matter of karmic retribution; it also violates the Vinaya, for all that is improper constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Yet this *duṣkṛta* is extremely deep and grave; even a *pārājika* offense cannot be compared to it.

In the *Saṃyukta-khandhaka*, when the lay devotees of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana erected a stūpa and made various offerings, the Buddha permitted them all. Regarding food offered to a stūpa, whether it be a *śrāmaṇera* or...
Upāsaka, if one is engaged in the construction [of a temple], one may consume [the provisions]. However, other ritual implements ought not, in principle, be diverted for other uses.
Nowadays, there are various divine images within temples; when laypeople seek merit from them, whatever objects belong to those [images] actually belong to non-humans (amanuṣya).
Such a matter is impermissible. Even if they are made within the temple, the teachings do not permit it. As for making [images] according to one's own wishes, that too—

Some say that if one has a need regarding the Three Jewels, one may cast divination sticks or consult the *gua* (hexagrams); if the result is favorable, one is permitted to use the item. Now, I examine this:
the Three Jewels should not be used as a source for obtaining provisions. If one seeks goods and does not receive them, it is well; however, if one takes them, it is improper.

Furthermore, regarding the practice in monasteries today of erecting nameplates where the items obtained through begging are assigned according to the names on the plates—this should not be done before the Buddha for the sake of the Sangha.
If one uses [a coin] that causes the donor to err, one also incurs the offense of mutual transgression.
Furthermore, although many temples nowadays commonly use currency, such common usage is permissible only in cases where it benefits the Three Jewels.

If one provides alcohol or meat—even for the sake of the Three Jewels—whether by soliciting them on someone's behalf or using them to purchase a staff with which to strike a *śrāmaṇera*, this diminishes the merit of the offering and instead incurs the fault of theft. If one steals...

Regarding these items: since the Three Jewels are collectively possessed, it is logically appropriate that one may obtain the karmic merit [of their protection]. However, there is a separate heavy offense for binding oneself as a protector of a specific [monastery]. Liang said:

"The high seat for preaching the Dharma and the funds of the permanent endowment (chángzhù) should not be used to construct [buildings], because they are not for the common enjoyment of the entire Saṃgha.
Since it is for the purpose of preaching the Dharma, it is permissible to use the funds. According to the rules for the distribution of donated property, this constitutes one exception."

Half [of the merit] is given to those who preach the Dharma and recite the sutras; thus, one knows that it is permissible to construct [images]. The second point, the meaning of mutual application, has been explained above.
Third, regarding the lending of property belonging to the Three Jewels: Zhi Li says, "This character is used in two ways; when giving property to others, it is called *tài*."

To borrow an object from another person is called *dài* (with the entering tone). According to this text, when opening a loan of the Three Jewels' property, one must simply ensure that the monks maintain clear and explicit written records.
Regarding the case in the *Śāṇakavāsi-sūtra* where a sick person repays a loan from the property of the Triple Gem tenfold:

according to the third fascicle of the *Śāṇakavāsi-sūtra*, if an ordained bodhisattva takes on a disciple who has left the household life, he should first instruct him in the dharma of heedfulness (*apramāda*).

When experiencing suffering or pleasure, they should always remain together. Even if the disciple becomes destitute and has needs, [the teacher] should provide for them beyond the six personal requisites (*ṣaḍ-pariṣkāra*). If there is... [text continues].
One should cherish [the sick person]. When they are ill, one should seek out whatever they require. While attending to the sick, one should not give rise to weariness.
