Reaching the second marker is auspicious in both cases. As for the remaining two markers: raising one constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), and raising one constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat).
If one intends to steal and uses a cord to mark out another's land, at the first cord placed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both ends are placed, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding the term "measuring the land with a cord," Jì says this refers to measuring the land with a bamboo bow; if one moves the bow forward to steal the land, one fears [this will result in a grave offense].
This is incorrect; it should rather refer to the measurement for marking the ground with a signpost.

As for the Vinaya statement, "if it is of a discolored hue," this means that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, all instances of discoloring through burning or burying constitute a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the case where one steals another's ox or horse and does not incur a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) because the animal has lifted only four feet:

according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes this horse and intends to go toward the east, but the horse goes instead toward the south, west, or north, he has not committed a *pārājika* offense.

If he intends to steal it toward the east and it departs for the east, he commits a *pārājika*. If there was no fixed direction and it departs wherever it may, [the offense occurs when] the horse lifts...

Fourth, regarding quadrupeds: if a bhikṣu steals a riding horse and the owner no longer sees it, and while the owner pursues it, neither the owner nor the bhikṣu has yet formed the thought that it is lost or acquired, it does not constitute a pārājika offense.
Regarding the phrase "like blowing objects into the air," it is established that if someone places clothing or other items upon a shield and the wind blows them up into the air,
passing over the boundary of a bhikṣu’s domain, and the bhikṣu uses a staff to strike them down or blows on them with his mouth to cause them to fall,

he incurs an offense according to their value. Regarding "stealing birds from curved hooks" and so forth, this refers to species such as chickens or hawks that are being raised and protected by others, whether they are flying...
If one enters a monastery, or flies across its boundary, or encounters a bhikṣu on the road, and with a thieving mind seizes [a bird] from it, one commits a formal offense (sāpattika).

According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), if one steals a bird in flight, pulling it by the left wing so that it passes over the right wing, and its tail reaches its head—whether moving up or down—the offense is grave.
If one uses a staff to block it, preventing it from following its intended direction, it is an *ānantarya* offense. The treatise further states: "There was a peacock..."

[The bird] flies through the air. A bhikṣu stands before it; the bird spreads its wings and stays still. When the bhikṣu departs, raising his hand to release [the bird], it is also an offense of *śuddha-pārājika*.

If he shakes the cage, or if he seizes the wing and pulls the tail so that it leaves the head’s position, it is an offense of *pārājika*. If he pulls the left wing past the right wing, it is an offense of *pārājika*.
The same applies to moving it up or down. Standing [in the commentary] it says: if a bird chick is kept in a cage and a bhikṣu steals the bird, the offense is incurred the moment it leaves the cage.

If one originally has no intention to take the cage, although the cage is closed and carried away, there is no offense; it is only when the bird has exited and left the cage that an offense is committed.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if one steals a boat, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) at the moment of unmooring; even if the rope is cut but the boat has not yet left [the mooring], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Even if it has left the boat but the rope is not yet cut, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*. If the rope is cut and the boat leaves its place, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). If it is in flowing water, it is a *pārājika* as soon as the boat is unmoored and leaves the stake.

It constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one sinks a boat with a malicious intent, or breaks it, or sets it adrift, it is a grave offense because one has destroyed or lost another's property.

*Śīla* states: "If one steals a boat, whether one pulls it by the stern past the bow, or pulls it by the bow past the stern, or turns it from the left side to the right side—all these constitute a grave offense.
The same applies to a cart. Regarding the term "crooked peg" (*kuṭaka*), the *Lilavati* explains it as a garment hanging on a wall.
Hooks, dragon-tooth pegs, and the like are examples of this. If one intends to steal a garment, the offense is committed as soon as the garment leaves the peg;

if one takes it away while still attached to the peg, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If the original intention was to steal both the garment and the peg, the offense is a *pārājika* (defeat) once the item is lifted off the wall.

As the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "This refers to stealing an object within a curved hook on a wall; the gravity of the offense depends on its separation from the peg. The same applies to stealing objects from within a cart or a boat.

If one intends to steal property from its original location, but does not steal a vehicle or boat—though one may travel by vehicle or boat—if the intermediate object has not yet been lifted, it constitutes a *ānantarya* (grave offense) of preparatory action (*prayoga*).
If the object is lifted and moved beyond the boundary of the boat, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). Jie says: "The crooked peg and the bird are one and the same matter."

It is like the birds raised within the royal gardens, all of which are kept upon perches. Regarding the phrase "cutting off the flow of water," the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Śariputra*) states:

"As for one who steals water: if one uses a tube to reach the hole and drinks until full, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); if one draws it out little by little repeatedly, there is a *pāyattika* (offense) for every mouthful.

If the vessel was previously sealed and one removes the cover with the intent to steal, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the moment of removal; when it pours into the vessel, there is a *pāyattika*. Regarding the pouring: [the text continues].

If one has severed [the stalk] and it is full, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one goes [to the field] before it is severed, and immediately gives rise to a mind of regret because one fears committing a grave offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to water, milk, curd, ghee, oil, and honey. Even if the rope is severed, as long as it has not been detached from the rope, it is all *duṣkṛta*.

If there is flowing water for irrigation, whether it is worth one *māṣaka* overnight, or even four or five *māṣakas*, if a bhikṣu—for the sake of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, or for himself—[takes it]...

If one, with a thieving mind, destroys a water channel so that the water flows into a field and fills it, the offense is *pārājika*. If one, with a jealous mind, destroys and discards the water, the offense is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (according to the *Sifen lü*, this is a grave offense).
Question: What offense is incurred for stealing the water from a pond? Answer: If the water is calculated by its functional capacity and the pond is filled [by the theft], the offense is grave.
Regarding the nets of others used to catch livestock: if one releases them out of a compassionate heart, one must still return the value. If one does not return it, the offense is grave.
The same applies to destroying tools. The *Daśottara-sūtra* states: "To destroy another's hunting net constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; to destroy it with a mind of compassion is meritorious.
The same applies to destroying bird-nets or prisons. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, releases a pig that has been tied up by another..."
The gravity of the offense is determined according to the amount of the value. If one releases [the creature] with a mind of compassion, there is no offense, but the value must be returned.

If a bhikṣu, with a compassionate mind, ties a rope around the animal using the original object as a substitute for the value and then releases it, there is no offense. This applies analogously to other birds, deer, and so forth.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) cites the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*) stating that there is no offense in destroying the implements used for killing; however, this should not be done. The *Ten-Recitation Vinaya* (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*) states that among the nets, [there is no offense in destroying] those intended for killing.

"Compassionate mind" constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "cutting off the flow" (*chinnasota*) and "water pouring down" (*udakavāha*) are treated as two distinct phrases. Regarding "cutting off the flow":

when objects such as bamboo or wood are floating downstream, if a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, seizes the wood, and the head of the log moves with the current until it reaches the tail, he commits a *pārājika* offense;
hence it is called "cutting off the flow. Regarding "water pouring down," it is explained as before. The commentary states: these should be combined into a single phrase. It is not [two].

"Extensive as in the original commentary (*ben shu*)" refers to the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa). According to the primary commentary, it quotes the *Jianlun* (Abhidharma-vijñānakāya-śāstra):

"If one, with a mind of anger, destroys another's tools for all their livelihoods, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing); one must return the value. If one does not return it, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*). The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"If one steals birds or wood from another's water, if one lifts them out of the water, one incurs a *pārājika*; if they float away [on their own]," [one does not].
Ti-lan-ji said: "There was a bhikṣu who made an agreement with another, saying, 'Let us steal the upper robe of a layperson together; if we obtain it, we shall divide it equally.
One of them went to take it, but by mistake he stole his own robe and brought it back. He then refused to give the other his half-share. The Buddha said:
'If the value is calculated to reach five [kārṣāpaṇas], one commits a pārājika offense.'"

Once caught in the net of the *bīla* thief, there is ultimately no escape. Xuān said: "Since one's status is not that of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), it is difficult to argue against the principle of debt;

as for the precepts of nature (*prakṛti-śīla*), there is no repentance, and one must ultimately repay the debt. For instance, the *Go-mukha* bhikṣu damaged but a single grain of rice, yet he had to undergo retribution for five hundred lifetimes;

even though he now encounters a Sage, his feet remain those of an ox. The Vinaya clarifies what is maintained and what is transgressed; although transgressions may be opened for repentance, repenting while violating [the precepts] is itself a violation.

If one teaches [the existence of] transgressions, how could the paths of karma be eliminated? One fears that those who are "not filial" (bùxiào)—*xiào* meaning "to resemble"—might fail to emulate their predecessors;
for "not filial" (*bùxiào*) means not resembling them. To use the character for "small" (*xiǎo*) below the character for "flesh" (*ròu*) is to say that a son does not resemble his father.

The preceding many sections have been different; this concludes the general explanation of the second point, the characteristics of the offense. Below this, the third section clarifies the rules for non-offenses (*anāpatti*).
As stated in the Vinaya, these include cases where one is "deranged, mentally disturbed, or afflicted by intense pain.

Regarding the seven qualities that constitute being a "close friend" as detailed in the Vinaya, Jì (Jizang) says: "This refers to Ānanda and the elder Luṭi being close friends. The above is the explanation.
The precept against stealing is concluded.
The third precept is that against taking life. The first two precepts serve as antidotes to greed; this precept serves to guard against the poison of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Hatred is able to plunder the wealth of virtue; as the Sūtra says, "There is no thief of merit greater than anger"—this is its meaning.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states the underlying intention for the prohibition against inflicting harm as follows: "The reason such harm is not permitted is that the human realm possesses a superior retribution, being summoned by wholesome causes;

thus, both body and mind are vessels for receiving the Way. For those who have left the household life, it is logically appropriate to embrace the four immeasurable minds and compassionately rescue the lives of sentient beings.

To now, on the contrary, harbor internal anger and resentment within one's heart and sever the continuity of another’s life is a profound violation of compassion; therefore, the Sage specifically prohibited this."
Regarding the term "killing": to sever the continuity of retribution is called killing. Furthermore, it is said that to sever the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is called killing.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings dwells within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If one destroys these five aggregates, it is called taking life."
If one kills a living being, one immediately falls into the evil realms. There are three aspects to form (*rūpa*): that which is past and present cannot be harmed;
it is called "killing" because one obstructs the future. Now, what we call a "living being" is the inhalation and exhalation of breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*).
To sever this inhalation and exhalation is therefore called "killing a living being. We Buddhas speak of "killing" in accordance with worldly convention. Our school also says: "[It is] the breath."

The wind is called "birth. Its interruption and non-continuation is called "killing. Now, it is detailed that this was taught by the Buddha to King Ajātaśatru. The subsiding of the wind is called "birth.
King Ajātaśatru was a layman who did not comprehend the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa); he claimed that the subsiding of the wind was what constituted birth.

The World-Honored One, accordingly, followed the principle of conforming to [the listener's] understanding and spoke in this manner. However, according to the ultimate truth, [it refers to] the kalala and so forth, which are the fundamental...
When [the faculties] are not yet fully developed, the vital winds do not circulate; would this not then be called "birth"? If it were not called birth, then taking life would be without fault.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states: "In the *kalala* and other stages, when the faculties are not yet fully developed, the vital winds do not circulate.

Thus, the correct interpretation now is that killing consists in the severing and destruction of the objective sphere of the aggregates (*skandha*). This is precisely what the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 118, says in response to a question: [Question: ... [text continues] ...
Among the various aggregates (*skandha*), which aggregate can be killed? Some say it is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because it can be struck by weapons and staves.

Others say it is all five aggregates, because when the aggregate of form is destroyed, the remaining four aggregates no longer function; just as when a jar is broken, the milk and so forth within it are also lost.
Here, the jar is a metaphor for the aggregate of form, and the milk is a metaphor for the other four aggregates. However, according to the Sarvāstivāda and Mahāyāna schools...
Within a single moment, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fully present. According to the Satyasiddhi school, a sentient being exists within the continuity of these five aggregates;
therefore, to destroy this continuity is called "killing. (Commentary: This refers to consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations arising in succession.
By destroying the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one causes consciousness, perception, and the others to arise no longer in succession; this is what is termed "killing."

Question: Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three periods of time, which period’s aggregates are killed? Answer: According to the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, there are two explanations.

The first interpretation states: one kills the future aggregates. Question: Since the future has not yet arrived, how can it be killed? Answer: It is because they abide in the present that one obstructs the conjunction of the various aggregates of the future;
this is what is called "killing. This is because, by obstructing the conditions for the arising of the conjunction of the aggregates, [the act of killing is accomplished].

One incurs the offense of killing (which is identical to *nirvāṇa*, for it is called "killing" because it obstructs the future). Furthermore, some say that one kills the aggregates (*skandha*) of the present and the future.
[The opponent asks: The future may be so; however, the present does not abide. Even if one does not kill them, they perish naturally; how, then, can there be killing?
Answer: To sever its functional power is what is called "killing. Although the preceding present aggregates cease without persisting, they cannot prevent the subsequent aggregates from continuing.
However, when the present aggregates cease without persisting, they are able to prevent the subsequent aggregates from continuing;

therefore, even regarding the present [aggregates], one incurs the offense of killing. (The above is the treatise. The two explanations in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* (*Zaxin lun*) are likewise the same. Regarding humans...
This refers to benevolence (*ren*). Benevolence arises from forbearance (*nin*). It means that when a person establishes their will, the priority is to preserve and nurture others;

thus it is said so. Jie says: "Supporting those above and receiving those below is called being human. This means that those of advanced age should support and receive the young, while the young, in turn, should look up to and rely upon the elders.
Therefore, it is called "supporting those above and receiving those below. Here, "receiving those below" refers to this [the youth], and "supporting those above" refers to this [the elder]. This...

This is a *huiyi* (picto-phonetic) character. That is why two are placed beside the "person" (*ren*); it is called "benevolence" (*ren*). When forms are compared, there is the meaning of "endurance" (*ren*). If one person dwells alone, what is there to endure? Formerly, there was a man who lived on a mountain of immortals to study endurance. He stayed in solitude without a companion, believing that his practice of endurance had been perfected. Someone came and asked him, "What dharma are you studying? He replied, "I am studying endurance. [The questioner] asked again: [...]*repeatedly* [asked]. The man said, "I have no one to endure against; how can I be said to have mastered endurance? The questioner said, "If you truly have no one to endure against, then you have not yet mastered endurance. You must go to a place where there are many people and live among them; only then will you know whether you have mastered endurance or not. The man followed this advice and went to a village to dwell among the people. There, he encountered someone who insulted and reviled him. At that time, the man felt great anger and resentment arise within him. He thought, "I have come here to study endurance, yet now I am filled with such anger and resentment. How can I say I have mastered endurance? He then returned to the mountain of immortals. The deity of the mountain asked him, "How is your practice of endurance going? The man replied, "I have not yet mastered endurance. The deity asked, "Why is that? The man explained the situation in detail. The deity said, "You still do not understand the true meaning of endurance. Endurance means being able to endure both the pleasant and the unpleasant. Now you have only endured insults and abuse; you have not yet endured praise and flattery. You must go back to the village and see if you can endure when someone praises and flatters you. The man went back to the village. There, someone praised and flattered him excessively. At that moment, the man felt great joy and pride arise within him. He thought, "I have come here to study endurance, yet now I am filled with such joy and pride. How can I say I have mastered endurance? He returned once more to the mountain of immortals. The deity of the mountain asked him, "How is your practice of endurance going? The man replied, "I have not yet mastered endurance. The deity asked, "Why is that? The man explained the situation in detail. The deity said, "You still do not understand the true meaning of endurance. Endurance means being able to endure both the pleasant and the unpleasant. Now you have only endured praise and flattery; you have not yet endured insults and abuse. You must go back to the village and see if you can endure when someone insults and abuses you. The man went back to the village. There, someone insulted and reviled him as before. At that time, the man felt neither anger nor resentment, nor did he feel joy or pride. His mind remained calm and equanimous. He realized that he had finally attained the true meaning of endurance. He returned to the mountain of immortals and reported this to the deity. The deity said, "Now you have truly mastered endurance. This is why the character for "benevolence" (*ren*) is composed of two people beside each other. It signifies that one must be able to endure both the pleasant and the unpleasant. If one dwells alone, how can there be the practice of endurance? Therefore, it is necessary to dwell among others to cultivate this virtue.

When they questioned one another, their anger became heavy and they reviled each other, saying, "You who study the Way should learn forbearance; you should learn forbearance. The precept is the practice that can subdue, while killing is the object to be prevented.

Since both the subject (the capacity to subdue) and the object (that which is to be prevented) are mentioned together, it is called the "precept against killing. However, killing itself is not the precept; rather, the precept prevents killing.
Killing is the object to be prevented, and the precept is the means of prevention. Therefore, it is called the "precept for not killing people."
The commentary states: "The initial consciousness in the womb is still like congealed mucus. The *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) explains:

this refers to the mind that first takes up the physical aggregates (*ātmabhāva*), which is the impurity of congealed mucus; it is the union of the male and female red and white vital essences (*śukra-śoṇita*).

Because the initial consciousness takes up residence therein, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says this refers to the stage of the *kalala*. As the *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: "Forty-nine days after entering the womb, it is called..."
After passing this stage of resembling a human, one is then called a human being. As stated in the *Pañcarājāsūtra*: "In the first week after conception, it is like thin curd;
in the second week, like thick curd; in the third week, like congealed curd; in the fourth week, like a mass of flesh;
in the fifth week, the five fetal membranes are formed; from the sixth week onward, the six sense organs unfold. (Note)
Regarding the phrase "up to the end of life" and so forth: this refers to the final consciousness. That is to say, at the moment of death, there is a single thought-moment accompanied by warmth;
this is the final consciousness. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The reason these two consciousnesses are mentioned is to exclude the thoughts of evil bhikṣus."
If one kills a human being, one incurs a grave offense. However, an embryo in the *kalala* stage is not yet a full human being; therefore, it is not termed a violation.

This is why the net [of the law] is cast broadly to encompass both the initial and subsequent stages. If there is a human being in the womb, as long as consciousness has taken up residence therein, any harm inflicted upon it constitutes no less than the ultimate penalty.
This is just as in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, where the principle regarding those who are "human" or "resemble humans" can be understood by its intent. The following text...
Regarding signs such as causing abortion:
concerning the manifestation of bodily forms, the *Vinaya* states that one manifests a physical form to cause [the victim] to fall into a great pit and die, and so forth.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Either causing them to fall into ditches or ravines out of fear, or manifesting signs of death," and so forth. *Lilun* (Treatise on Establishment) states: "Manifesting the body."

Regarding "signs" (*nimitta*): it refers to manifesting an unusual appearance—staring with wide eyes, protruding the tongue, and having a terrifying, gaunt countenance that strikes fear into others and induces thoughts of death.
As for "praising the signs of death with the mouth," this is termed "manifesting signs through speech" in the Vinaya; it means praising [death] so as to incite someone to seek it. *Liyun* states:
"Seeing another who is poor or ill, one encourages them to seek death; this refers to cases where the person follows such advice and dies. The *Jieshu* states: "Manifesting the signs of death."
This refers to those who, by means of speech, praise and encourage death; or those who, by means of loud voices, intimidate and cause death.
For example, there are those in the world who loathe their bodies and either throw themselves into fire or fall from cliffs, or use knives for dismemberment or ropes for hanging.

Those who do not recognize these as teachings join their palms and cry out "Excellent! or assist them in climbing mountains or provide them with ropes and equipment. This is precisely what constitutes praising [death].
Fu’s transgression of the law manifested through both body and speech; this is precisely such a case. Regarding "trapping, ensnaring, or even administering drugs," the Vinaya states:

"If one knows with certainty that a person traveling along a path will inevitably pass by a certain way, one should dig a deep pit in the middle of that path and fill it with fire, blades, poison, or thorns, causing them to fall into it and die.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Knowing that a person is traveling..."
"One must necessarily proceed along this path; therefore, he set a pitfall to cause his death. Regarding the term "leaning against and pushing aside" (*niṣkubjita*):

the Vinaya states that if one knows a person will certainly lean against or push aside a tree, a wall, or similar structure, one may then apply fire to the outside, or place a blade or a venomous snake there.

This refers to poisoning, stabbing, or using a mechanical device to cause someone to fall into [a pit] and die. Master Ying states that "fa" (pronounced *fu* with the second tone) means the triggering of a mechanism;

it refers to the primary trigger of the mechanism. The Vinaya text uses the character "bo" (pronounced *bu* with the fourth tone). The *Guangpi* states that "bo" means to remove or to discard; "bo" does not carry this meaning here.
Master Li states that having ascertained that a person is leaning against a certain place, one then applies a blade or a staff to that point of support.

This refers to death itself. It is like a person setting a snare. Regarding the phrase "providing the instruments of killing," some say this refers to places where executions are carried out in the world;
it is when a bhikṣu goes to observe them and provides ropes or cords to cause another’s death.
Regarding the phrase "giving medicine," it is established that nowadays, when monks or nuns induce abortions, they all commit a grave offense. Second is "killing by inciting others."
Lì said: "To 'watch oneself' at the time of killing means to instruct another person to apply their hand [to the act]. How does this differ from killing by dispatching a messenger? The answer is:
'instructing' refers to watching oneself, which is to instruct another person to apply their hand. As for 'killing by dispatching a messenger,' it is when a bhikṣu dispatches a messenger."
"Going to take such-and-such a person's life" refers to this. Regarding the phrase "if one instructs another to praise [death]," the *Lishi* (立) states:
"To cause a messenger to praise the king so that he may die early"—both the agent and the object are grave offenses. Some say:

"Sending words to that person to tell the victim, 'It would be better for you to die early,' generates many sins. Regarding "instructing a messenger," the *Lishi* states: "Instructing the messenger to dispatch the king’s man."
He killed a person of Zhao. He also instructed a predecessor to send an envoy to kill such-and-such a person.
Some take the character "jiao" (to instruct) and attach it to the preceding clause, interpreting it as simply sending an envoy to kill, indicating a specific direction or location to go and kill.

Regarding the envoy who went and returned, Master Li says: "He instructed a royal official to go and kill a person of Zhang. The royal official received the command and went there, but had not yet killed him."
Or, having failed to kill [the victim], he returns; being sought out again, he is sent once more. Thus he comes and goes. At the time when the life is severed, the offense is grave;

prior to the severance, for every instance of coming and going according to the number of dispatches, there is one *pārājika* offense. Regarding the term "grave dispatch," it is explained that: first, he dispatches a man named Zhang to go and kill;
immediately thereafter, he dispatches a man named Wang to go and kill; and even further, he dispatches a man named Li to go. In this manner, even if it occurs a hundred times...
A thousand people obtain the offense of *pārājika*, yet they do not commit it themselves; only the one at the beginning who can instruct and the one at the end who can kill incur the grave offense.
The first person is the instructor, and the last person is the instructed. Daolüe says: "From beginning to end, there is a grave offense; in the middle, there is only a light one.

This is because the first is not the instructor and the second is not the instructed, as the karmic act was not performed by them personally. Regarding what is called "indirect instigation": [it refers to this].
"Establishing" means: first, there is the instructor who commands Zhang to go and kill; Zhang then dispatches Wang; Wang again dispatches Li; Li again dispatches Zhao to go and kill.
In this manner, the process continues through hundreds and thousands of people, all of whom are considered heavy [in karmic responsibility] because they are all capable of instructing.
Although it is the very last person who actually wields the hand to take the life, he shares the same [responsibility] as the preceding hundred thousand.
All are single-layered. Regarding "seeking a man" and "teaching to seek a man," etc., this refers to seeking a man for the purpose of killing.
As for the phrase "teaching to seek a man," the Vinaya states: "Teaching another to seek.

In this context, who knows of such a person—one who can use a knife with skill, has long practiced and learned the methods of killing, and is capable of ending the life of a certain individual? [One] sends a letter to instruct [him].

Regarding "letters and the like," the Vinaya states that this refers to sending letters in which one incites another to seek death; the same applies to instructions for seeking a superior rebirth and so forth.

Question: To what category of karma does killing by means of sending a letter belong? Answer: It belongs to verbal karma (*vākkarma*). However, according to the masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, bodily, verbal, and mental karma can all mutually produce [results].
They cite a verse from the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* which says: "The sovereign... (My private commentary: This refers to the king.)
It is a verbal command to kill. Because one speaks words that express what the mind detests, it is known that the verbal and mental karmas together constitute the act of killing.
The Sarvāstivāda school does not accept this interpretation, stating: "When one speaks words while the mind harbors aversion, the person has not yet died."
The matter is not yet concluded. [One might argue that] evil spirits, protective deities, or ghosts strike down an entire nation, or that a person employed as an agent strikes down another;

how, then, can there be physical karma (*kāyakarman*)? The master Saṃghabhadra says: "If that were so, when a lion kills a beast by roaring, or a strong man kills a person by shouting 'Ha!', how could there be physical karma?

[Response: Because the physical force is so great that death occurs only upon the roar or the shout. If that were so, when a deep river is deceived as being shallow, how could there be physical [karma]?
[Question: Regarding karma: when one deceives another who has not yet died, it requires the person's body to enter the water; this too is bodily action (*kāyakarman*). [Objection:

If that is so, when one uses a spell to transport goods across a barrier, how can there be bodily action? [Response: It is maintained by the power of the spell. [Objection: If that is so, what about making a false statement through gestures (*liṅga*)?

"Is it not the case that [the killing] is accomplished by the body? Answer: "It is merely through the vocal karma of another who utters the words 'sit' or 'rise'; therefore, it is not bodily karma. (The commentary states: The above is the logical defense of the Sarvāstivādins. Now, examining this closely:

because the various masters hold that the bodily karma of the protective deity of the hermitage constitutes the act of killing, they consequently judge it to be the bodily karma of the hermit himself.
If this were so, the hermit would incur the sin of taking life committed by another; how could one allow for another to suppress me and force me to bear the guilt?
Is it so? To speak falsely by manifesting signs and praising another with one's own mouth is judged not to be my verbal karma (the rest is the same as the refutation above).
Now, the intention of the Sarvāstivādins should be further explained: they merely exclude mental karma from being capable of killing, for they do not judge my bodily karma based on another’s body.
That which is called bodily karma must not depend on anything else to be able to sever life. Now, the seer’s mind was incensed, and thus he relied upon another.

Therefore, one knows that mental action (*manas-karman*) cannot directly kill; thus, it relies upon another's body as a condition for killing, giving rise to an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) within the body of the seer, which constitutes bodily action.
Deceiving a shallow person at a deep river also relies upon that person’s entry into the water as a condition, giving rise to an unmanifest action of bodily action within my own body.
All other cases should be treated accordingly. This is not the same as the position established by the Mahāsāṃghika Sautrāntikas.

Indeed, it is universally accepted that the mental indignation of a relative directly constitutes the act of killing, without requiring the separate emission of an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) within the body.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* refuting the Hīnayāna schools states: "If [killing] occurs through the mere anger of a seer, how could it be so?
How then can the mental punishment of the Daṇḍaka forest and others become a great sin? (The commentary states: Paramārtha says that Daṇḍaka is the name of a king. At that time, there was a seer...
Before he had attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he already had a wife whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that she was peerless in the world.
Later, while that seer was among the gods and spirits of the Five Supernatural Powers Mountain, he would regularly have his wife prepare food and drink for them. King Tālajaṅgha—
While wandering for recreation in the mountains, he encountered the wife of an immortal. He asked, "Who is this? An attendant replied, "This is the wife of an immortal.

The King said, "Since the immortal has already transcended desire, what use has he for a wife? He immediately took her into his palace. When it was time for the immortal to eat, [the King provided him with food].
He looked for food but could not find it. When he asked where it was, someone replied, "The king has taken her away. The rishi went to the king's side and demanded his wife back.
The king refused to return her, saying, "You are a rishi; why do you need to keep a wife? The rishi said, "I provide her with food and drink.
Although he pleaded this repeatedly, the king would not return her. The rishi then became enraged, and during that very night, he caused sand and stones to rain down.
The king and all the people of the country died completely; in an instant, this land became a forest and mountains.

In such places as these, there was emptiness and stillness with no people. Since this resulted from the anger of the rishi, is it not the mental karma that constitutes the act of killing? The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
"The guardian spirits of the rishi, out of reverence for him, knew of his resentment and killed [the people]. This is then refuted: "The punishment by mind constitutes [the act]."
This is a great transgression. How is this so? (The meaning is explained as follows: Formerly, there was a noble one named Upāli who came to the place where the Sage [the Buddha] was.
The Buddha then asked him: "Have you ever heard that the Taṭakā Grove is entirely empty and silent?

The householder replied to the Buddha: "This sage is indignant. The Buddha said: "Householder, you should know that among the three types of punishment, mental punishment is the greatest; it is so because of a single thought-moment."
If one were to kill an entire nation, how could such a great transgression of bodily action be tolerated?

Since the Buddha cited this case of the Daṇḍaka forest to establish that mental punishment is primary, you of the Sarvāstivāda school—how can you insist that the seer was killed by a protective spirit or deity for the sake of the seer?

Question: Since the Mahāyāna and other schools admit that killing can be accomplished through the mind, why does the Sūtra state that the karmic path of killing a single living being is categorized entirely as physical?
Answer: This is determined according to the majority of cases; it means that most instances of killing are performed by the body, not that mental karma is incapable of killing.
Regarding the statement, "Among the three natures, [the one who] instructs another commits a grave offense," and so forth: this refers to the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

This clarifies that by employing a skillful means (*upāya*) through prior knowledge, once the messenger has been sent, even if the victim subsequently enters a wholesome or neutral state of mind, the perpetrator commits a grave offense (*ānantarya*) at the moment the person’s life is severed.

The initial question asks: "If one sends a messenger to receive the precepts, the precepts are only obtained once the messenger returns; why is this not applied as an analogy to cases of sending someone to kill or steal?

The answer is: At the time of receiving the precepts, there is a formal commitment (*samaya*). However, in the case of killing or stealing, the act is completed when the messenger carries out the instruction. Therefore, the gravity of the offense is determined by the completion of the action, regardless of the victim's subsequent mental state.
The meaning of "intention" (*cetanā*) is fulfillment; the meaning of [the prohibitions on] killing and stealing is destruction. Therefore, they do not coincide.

As for the statement "the rest is as explained in the subsequent section," this refers to the discussion on the nature of the object and perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) within the following "Chapter on Observance and Transgression. This [present passage] merely sets forth the characteristics of killing.
"Unwilling to extend" means being unwilling to stretch out [the limbs]. To forcibly massage another person and cause them to stretch until death occurs.
Regarding "a bhikṣu who knows the stars, the calendar, yin and yang, and so forth," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhāṣika*) states:

"If a bhikṣu is well-versed in astrology, the calendar, yin and yang, and the *Guo Yi* (Tortoise and Change), and understands the rise and fall of nations and the strategic formations of military forces, yet causes an expedition to be launched based on the words of that bhikṣu..."
When conquering a foreign land, all acts of killing and the acquisition of wealth and treasures constitute both the pārājika offenses of killing and stealing.

If a lay follower (upāsaka) joins others with a single mind to campaign against a foreign land for the sake of the king, should they destroy that enemy state and cause injury or death, [the same applies].

One may also acquire wealth and treasures; though one does not work with one's own hands, because of this shared intent, one likewise violates the two precepts against killing and stealing. Master Li states:

"This refers to the Upāsaka who observes the five or eight precepts. According to the *Śrāddhakarman-sūtra*, when receiving the five precepts, one must fully inquire regarding the prohibitions and obstacles.
If one asks whether one’s parents, king, wife, children, servants, or slaves consent, and they do not consent, one may not receive the precepts.
He asked about the king because he feared that the king might later go on military expeditions against foreign lands and thereby destroy the five precepts;
thus, he questioned the king at the time of receiving [the precepts] so that he might remember it later.

Regarding the case where one digs a pit for an animal and the animal dies, resulting in a *duṣkṛta* offense: this refers to the establishment of the preparatory offense (*prayoga*) against the human agent.
It does not mean that the *duṣkṛta* is incurred at the moment the animal dies; rather, there is no offense at the actual time of killing because the primary intention was not directed toward it.

As for digging a pit for an animal and the animal dying according to the Vinaya, the Vinaya establishes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. As for the statement that one incurs a *duṣkṛta* if a human dies, this likewise refers to the preparatory stage directed toward the animal.
Furthermore, when a person's life is severed, what fault can be recognized? This is because there was originally no intentional mind.

If one were originally possessed of a mind of arrogance (*māna*) and so forth, then within the category of specific arrogance (*viśeṣa-māna*), this constitutes "great arrogance" (*mahā-māna*). There are four types of specific arrogance: great arrogance consists of intending to kill beings of the three realms of existence;

small arrogance is restricted to killing beings of only one realm of existence without distinguishing between individuals such as Zhang or Wang; and [the next two] consist of intending to kill a single... [individual].
"Categories" (*gati*) include two types of persons, such as those of the Zhang and Wang clans; "minor offenses" (*duṣkṛta*) apply exclusively to persons of the Zhang clan.
Regarding the phrase "lightness or heaviness according to the object," this means that if a human dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense, whereas if an animal dies, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the phrase "those who follow along and beg from people for hand-towels, silk, and so forth," it is explained as follows: there was a bhikṣu who had violated the laws of the king.
Many other bhikṣus followed him to go and see him; these are called "those who follow along. A butcher then followed this group and begged them for hand-towels and other such items.
Regarding the case of one who commits suicide and incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, Master Li states that this refers to the formation of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*).

According to the principle applied to suicide, it should also incur a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), because at the moment life is severed, the body has already died and the *prātimokṣa* vows have ceased; thus, there is no basis for the transgression to take effect.
From this point downward, the text clarifies the rules concerning non-offenses.

The Fourth Precept: Prohibiting Grave Falsehood; Concerning the Prevention of Poison. Discussing this precept, it serves as an antidote to delusion (*moha*). First, the intent behind its establishment is clarified.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "However, the untainted path of the noble ones (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) is not realized by ordinary beings.

Because they have not attained it, they falsely claim to have realized it through deceptive talk, thereby confusing the minds of the multitude and deceiving the world in their desire to attract fame and profit for themselves."

To conceal one's own [faults], to be singularly attached to the Dharma without regard for the proper time—these are among the most extreme transgressions; therefore, they must be strictly regulated. Next, regarding the explanation of the name:

because the transgression is grave and the deception is profound, it is termed "Great" (*mahā-*). Furthermore, it is called "Great" in contrast to the initial minor false speech of the ninety [offenses].

Its essence is not a factual record, hence it is termed "false" (*mṛṣā*). Since the formation of karma resides in speech, it is termed "speech" (*vāc*). The practice capable of counteracting this is termed "precept" (*śīla*). Precept...

The "able" refers to that which prevents; the "false" refers to that which is prevented. Since both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is called the precept against great false speech (*mahāmṛṣāvāda-śīla*).

Regarding the nine conditions for its completion, they are as stated in the text. As for the deficiency of conditions, the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) states: "If the first condition is deficient, there may be three *sthūlātyaya* offenses;

it may also lack one or two [conditions] singly or in pairs, with nineteen variations for each case. If the second condition is deficient, there are six *sthūlātyaya* offenses, because there are three variations each for 'conceiving' (*saṃjñā*) and 'doubting' (*vicikitsā*)."

Furthermore, if the third condition—the object being unreal—is missing and one now regards it as real, there is absolutely no room for the offense of *pāyattika* (thullaccaya), as explained below in the section on the ninety rules concerning the precept regarding falsely claiming to have attained the Path (*mārga*).
(etc. If the fourth condition is missing, then even with overweening pride (*abhimāna*), there is no offense.
The fifth condition is lacking: there is a deceptive mind because one is currently playing; therefore, it is auspicious [for the offense not to be incurred]. The sixth condition is lacking:
the claim of having attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). Here, one speaks of human states. As the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

"If one says of oneself, 'I maintain pure precepts,' 'lust does not arise in me,' yet one does not recite the four Āgamas or the Vinaya, nor does one practice meditation or dwell in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), yet claims, 'I recite these' or 'I am such a person'—these are all *thullaccaya* (grave offenses). The sixth condition is lacking.
Regarding the seventh condition, "having personally testified," there may be those who possess merit and praise the Triple Gem; in such cases, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (pācittiya).

Or, because one says, "This is my teacher," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* for speaking falsely regarding what another has attained, doing so out of a desire for fame and profit and living by wrong livelihood.

If the eighth condition is missing—meaning one says they do not understand—it is a light *duṣkṛta*. If the ninth condition is missing—meaning the person before them does not hear it, or hears it but does not understand—it is likewise a light offense.
This is merely a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
If one manifests a physical sign, it is established as follows: while the community of monks is all seated, someone proclaims, "Let those who have attained Arhatship stand up."

If a bhikṣu knows himself to be an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) yet stands [as one who has attained realization], if the person before him believes it, he incurs a *pārājika*; if he doubts it, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
One should formulate four propositions: first, I doubt while the other is certain; second, the other doubts while I am certain; third, both I and the other doubt.
Fourth, the ultimate [result] regarding oneself and others. First, regarding "doubt concerning oneself": Suppose someone proclaims, "Let those who have attained Arhatship stand up!
A bhikṣu immediately stands up, having manifested the signs of attainment. He then harbors doubt within himself, wondering whether the person before him believes he has attained it or not.
This constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as it pertains to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Regarding "the ultimate [result] concerning others": the person before him sees him stand up.
The determination is that he is an Arhat (the preceding sentence concludes the *sthūlātyaya* of expedient concealment). Second, another suspects his own ultimate attainment:

for example, one says, "The one who has attained Arhatship is traveling east," and the bhikṣu immediately travels east; the person before him then develops the suspicion that this bhikṣu has indeed attained it.

It is because he has not attained it. That bhikṣu thinks to himself, "The person before me believes that I have attained arhatship," and thus says, "I have reached the ultimate" (this phrase is also *ālaṃ*).

Third is when both self and other are in doubt. For example, if one says, "Having attained arhatship, I put on my robes," and the bhikṣu immediately puts on his robes, the person before him gives rise to doubt:
"Has this bhikṣu attained it, or has he not? The bhikṣu himself also doubts whether the person before him [believes so].
"It is for the sake of faith; it is for the sake of lack of faith" (this phrase is also *laṅ*). Fourth, the case where both self and other reach the ultimate:

as when one who has attained arhatship walks south, and the bhikṣu likewise walks south. The former person believes he has attained arhatship, and the bhikṣu also says, "The former person believes I am an arhat.
This phrase constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the statement, "These [practices] such as the contemplation of impurity are minor dharmas," the established position is as follows: The intent of this question is to say that these dharmas pertain to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

They refer to the five stabilizing meditations (*pañca-vastūpasthāna*): namely, those with an abundance of sensual desire practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); those with an abundance of malice practice the meditation on loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*);

and so on, up to those with an abundance of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) who practice the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), and so forth. Since these are shallow and minor dharmas, they are described here.

What has been attained? Why is it that one commits a grave offense? The answer is: "This is the initial gateway to the nectar of immortality" means that attaining the principle nourishes the mind, harmonizing the spirit and satisfying the will;
its meaning is identical to that of nectar. When the principle penetrates spiritual understanding, it is called a "gateway.

To say that all sages enter through it means that one must necessarily enter the Path from the initial contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and proceed by gradual cultivation. This refers to the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta*).
Observation of impurity is initially called "shallow and near.
To say that one intends to speak of this [impurity] yet instead speaks of that which is all-encompassing and profound is like intending to speak to Mr. Zhang, but instead addressing someone else.
When a royal official comes to take his place, one may speak [of him] as a "barbarian" (yí). This is because although the King and the barbarian differ, they are both human beings.
The following clarifies that there is no violation of the law.
Regarding the establishment of the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) section: this section derives its name from both the object and the substance at the time of confession.

Because one who has committed this offense requests confession from the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha is the object that performs the confession, and "residual" (*avaśeṣa*) is the substance of the offense committed; therefore, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one wishes to establish the meaning vertically, it is as follows:

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: I shall now briefly set forth three gates. First is "Prohibitive and Natural" (*zhexing*). Among the thirteen [offenses], the two regarding matchmaking and the two regarding rooms are prohibitive precepts (*zhajie*).
The remaining ten precepts are natural precepts (*xingjie*), as their essence is unwholesome. Second is "Observance and Violation" (*chifan*).

This means that within the two [offenses] concerning rooms, both types of observance and violation are present, because they contain both the observance and violation of abstention (*zhi*) and the observance and violation of performance (*zuo*). The remaining ten...

First, regarding the precepts: there are those involving cessation and maintenance (*śīla-saṃvara*), and those involving commission and transgression (*āpatti*). Furthermore, these categories of cessation, maintenance, commission, and transgression may apply collectively to all thirteen precepts.

Third, concerning the similarities and differences between monks and nuns: regarding the seven precepts—namely, matchmaking, the two types of slander, and the four admonitions—monks and nuns incur offenses equally. However, as for the four admonitions...

Although the offenses incurred may be equal, each differs according to the assembly [of the transgressor]. For instance, in the case of plotting to slander the three precepts, both the objective and the offense are identical.
Regarding the six precepts, there is a difference between monks and nuns: for the offense of emission (*śukra-utsarga*), the penalty for monks is heavy while that for nuns is light.

The reason for this is that many say women’s afflictions (*kleśa*) are deep and heavy, making them difficult to restrain and control; if one were to impose heavy penalties upon them, it would result in further suffering for these sentient beings. Furthermore, as for women...

People often engage in private seclusion; because their conditions and powers are manifold, suffering flows forth in abundance, and thus [the offense] is light. For men it is not so; because they are able to extricate themselves according to the circumstances, it is heavy.
Regarding the single precept on touching: for a *bhikṣuṇī* it is heavy, while for a *bhikṣu* it is light. The reason for this is that the afflictions and passions of a *bhikṣuṇī* are more intense;

once she has been touched, she will inevitably be subjected to harassment and oppression, which may lead to great transgressions. Therefore, within the scope of skillful means, the rule is established.
When a nun shares a name with a man, if he were to touch her, there would certainly be no violation; thus, she does not require such profound protection.
Because it falls within the limits of her allotted sphere, a light offense is prescribed. Furthermore, women have a strong inclination toward physical contact.

The Vinaya contains the case of a woman who left her husband to follow another for the sake of touch, as illustrated by the story of the wise and the foolish woman tested with a woolen blanket: while the man departed, the woman remained because her heart was still attached. The same applies to the two types of rooms. [The Sangha...]

The gravity [of offenses] for nuns is lighter than that for monks. Because monks travel alone and construct dwellings, their activities are numerous; thus, their offenses are grave. For nuns, it is the reverse of this, and therefore their offenses are light.
It is established that this explanation of the characteristics [of the precepts] is currently based on the thirteen [offenses] of the monks to clarify them;

however, nuns have seventeen. Of these thirteen monk precepts, seven are identical to those of the nuns; as for the remaining ten precepts, they will be explained in detail within the separate section on the nuns' community.

[The commentary on] "Clarifying": First, regarding "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time," the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Now, the evil dharma of lustful desire is precisely the source of birth and death and the root obstacle to the Path.
It is logically appropriate to prohibit and sever it, so that the Brahma-conduct may be pure. For by violating this precept, how [can one attain purity]?"
Because it can maintain the Buddha-dharma, the True Dharma quickly perishes; now, because of this regulation, the True Dharma abides for a long time.
Second, to stop slander: the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle three, states: "The people of the world and the non-Buddhists constantly say:

'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, engage in impure practices and are no different from the laity. Third, to give rise to faith in devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits: the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.
It says: "If one performs this act, although it may be in a private and secluded place, devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits will all see it.
The commentary states: "Internal matter refers to that which experiences matter. The Vinaya says: "That which the mind receives and accepts is called 'feeling' (vedanā).
Matter associated with feeling is called 'matter experienced through feeling,' which is precisely the human body possessed by consciousness. Master Li states: "This is based on..."
First, those with mind-consciousness that can receive form are the categories of all sentient beings.

Second, external things that do not receive form refer to the forms of non-sentient entities; these are all external objects belonging to the category of the insentient, such as clothing, bamboo, wood, and so forth, which serve as objects for leakage.
These non-sentient objects cannot receive form. Third, internal and external form.
"Between" refers to the space between two forms. On one side is a sentient form; on the other side is an insentient form.
It is from between these two forms that the semen is emitted. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, "internal form" refers to one's own body, while "external form" refers to another's body.
Regarding the wind being the same as the water-element method: even air blown from the mouth qualifies as this wind. (Commentary)

Regarding the phrase "up to other objects": according to the Vinaya, this is stated in terms of the six sense objects; however, by extension of this principle, all ten thousand objects may serve as the object of an offense.
Therefore, the section on Observance and Transgression (Hch’im-p'ien) below states: "As with the precept against emission, one commits an offense through contact with the conditions."
What need is there for the perception of an object? Furthermore, it is said that the loss of [semen] is likewise; the object remains broad.
If there are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind, the first is bad dreams. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, there are four kinds of dreams:
first, dreams caused by the disharmony of the four great elements, such as seeing mountains collapse, the earth tremble, soaring through the void, or [seeing] tigers...

First, dreams resulting from external circumstances (*lángzé*). This refers to having previously seen something during the day—such as blue, yellow, red, or white, or men and women—and subsequently dreaming of it at night.

Second, dreams resulting from what was previously seen. Just as one might see blue, yellow, red, or white, or men and women during the day, one then dreams of them at night. Third, dreams resulting from deities. There may be benevolent or malevolent *devas* who manifest both auspicious and inauspicious dreams for a person.
Fourth, dreams resulting from the conceptualizing mind. If this person’s previous life was meritorious, they will have auspicious dreams; [for example,] reciting the sutras.

Regarding the worship of the Buddha and so forth: if one is an evildoer, one will see [visions] such as killing and stealing. The former two [types of visions] are unreal, as the sutras state they are "like dreams and illusions.
The latter two are real, as the sutras state that "one merely grasps the characteristics of the dream," as explained in the *Vaipulya* and the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*.
Master Bin said: "Some cite the four types of dreams from the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, but within this context, they are entirely useless. (2)
Regarding "the gods do not protect": the commentary states that a single king may have many people protecting him, whereas a poor person, though having many [relatives], has not a single protector.
If one person maintains the precepts, many gods will protect them; if one breaks the precepts, even if they are numerous, not a single god will protect them.
Regarding "the five joys that cause emission of semen": according to the Vinaya, there are seven types of semen, namely, blue...
Regarding yellow and so forth: when emerging [from concentration], there are likewise seven types of mind—namely, those intending to emerge with blue, yellow, and so on.
Since there are already seven minds for each of the primary colors, these seven times seven constitute forty-nine minds; adding the one general mind makes fifty minds.
With respect to the six objects, such as internal and external forms and so forth, there are fifty minds for each object. Thus, across the six objects...
These are the three hundred mental states. In the Vinaya, regarding the emission of semen, there are eleven factors;

for each of these factors, there are three hundred [mental states], totaling three thousand three hundred phrases, all of which constitute the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. (The following clarifies the circumstances of non-offense.)
The Second Precept: Regarding the Sexual Contact with Women. "Rubbing" (*mā*) refers to the physical stroking or caressing of the body.

"Contact" (*chù*) refers to the mutual encounter of two objects. "Woman" (*nǚrén*) distinguishes this from men. "Human" (*rén*) differentiates this from other realms of existence. Hence, it is called the precept against sexual contact with women.

Regarding the statement that "the establishment of this precept today serves as a companion and provides reliance," it means that for monastics who have left the household life, the wholesome Dharma serves as their companion.
According to reason, do not the remaining precepts likewise serve as companions? In fact, they can indeed serve as companions. As for the term "reliance" (*niśraya*):
"rely" (*ni*) means to depend upon or lean on; "relief" (*śraya*) means to trust in or take support from. This is the root of contention and dispute, namely... [comparison].
When the Buddha touched another man’s wife, her husband heard of it and felt an especially unbearable resentment; he would surely have entered into a dispute with the Bhikṣu.
It was not merely that she was seized, but that he was said to have committed a great evil—meaning that when a layman sees his woman being touched.
This refers to saying that a bhikṣu has also committed sexual misconduct; hence the statement.
Regarding the three types of physical contact: first, a bhikṣu goes and touches a woman; second, a woman comes and touches a bhikṣu.
The third [category] consists of mutual encounters, also termed "jointly established. There are three distinct segments, and this present case is the first.
Regarding the statement that "whether one experiences pleasure or not, it is all a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense," this refers specifically to a bhikṣu experiencing or not experiencing pleasure.

When formulated as propositions in contrast to this, there should be nine hundred and seventy-one permutations, as explained in the separate record. [In this case,] a woman comes and touches the bhikṣu.

Regarding the statement that "it is not necessary to have a lustful mind," Master Li states: this refers to women; it means that one need not possess a lustful mind [for the offense to be established].

As for the fact that this Vinaya text is not explicit, Master Li states: within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, only the offense of a *duṣkṛta* (minor transgression) for stirring up the mind is clarified, while the characteristics of committing an offense by moving the body are not explained.

Now, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (*Shisong lü*), moving the body constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension). This applies whether one previously had a defiled mind toward a woman or toward another woman.

Regarding the phrase "coming into contact," it is established that although the preceding and succeeding instances differ, the woman remains the same; therefore, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
In this case, there are two women involved. Seng-shen says: "There is only one woman; that is to say, the bhikṣu first gives rise to a defiled mind toward this woman."

Later, this woman came and touched the bhikṣu; he immediately committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense, and had he moved, it would have been a *pārājika*. This was not a different woman, but rather the same woman as before.
According to the principle, the profound interpretation of the meaning is extensive. Why is this so?

If one has no defiled mind toward the woman from before, and she comes to touch the bhikṣu, if he does not move his body and experience pleasure, there is only a minor transgression (*duṣkṛta*). It is only because he previously possessed a defiled mind [that the offense is more serious].
Because of the mind, one who experiences pleasure commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Furthermore, regarding this point where the Vinaya text is not explicit, [Master] Li states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely says that touching the two sexual organs constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, but it does not clarify that the intent must lie with the male side.

Now, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if the intent lies with the male, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the intent lies with the female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting). Thus, based on this...
A hermaphrodite possesses both male and female organs; therefore, when there is contact, the mind takes both the male and female locations as its object.

Regarding the four permutations of "perceiving the object" versus "not perceiving the object," [the commentator] establishes them as follows: first, perceiving the touch but not perceiving the *śeṣa*; second, not perceiving the *śeṣa*;
third, not perceiving the touch and not perceiving the *śeṣa*; fourth, perceiving the *śeṣa*. As for the offense of *śeṣa* in the first permutation, the text says:
Because each individual part of the body is [a limb], even touching the nails or hair constitutes an offense; it is likewise an offense.

Regarding "the mutual impairment of the bodily organs through contact," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a woman’s bodily organ is impaired, a bhikṣu who touches her commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣu’s bodily organ is impaired, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense by touching a woman. This refers to cases where both the male and female organs are decayed and ruined.

Regarding the statement that touching the body of one who cannot procreate constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), [the commentator] establishes that this refers to a barren woman (*vandhyā*) and one who is not male (*apumān*). Checking the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says:
"If a monk touches the body of a woman who cannot procreate, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. If a monk who is not male touches the body of a woman, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

The intent of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is that if a man who is a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) touches a woman, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension); this is because there was previously...
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth, it is established as follows: the original intention was to touch a woman, and the object before one was indeed a woman;
however, at the time of going to touch her, the thought changed midway such that one perceived her to be a man or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), even though the actual object remained a woman.
At the moment of physical contact, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This is because the original intent was declared and because the necessary conditions were fulfilled.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Qishi), it states: "If it is a *paṇḍaka* and a woman touches him, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. It also states: "If it is a man and a woman touches him, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Now, examining the commentary (*chao*), its interpretation is erroneous. Why does it say that there was an intention for the preparatory act (*prayoga*) previously, yet later the original intent was declared?

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): it is certainly not the case that this permits [the act]. Now, examining this in detail, it is because the *Jiwen* (Text on the Vinaya) does not permit the presence of perception or doubt regarding the precept;

thus, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. It does not permit taking the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) as [an excuse]. Even if a woman is perceived as a eunuch or a man, the one who touches her still incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

As for the statement that "touching results in five offenses, namely *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so forth," according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observation), it says: "The five offenses are: first..."
1. A *śrāmaṇerī* who touches a man incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. 2. A monk who touches a nun incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. 3.
A monk who touches a woman’s garment with his body incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. 4. A monk who touches a woman’s garment with his own garment incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
5. A monk who pinches another monk with his finger incurs a *pāyattika*. (The following clarifies the cases where there is no offense.)
"It is not that one does not commit other offenses" means that one commits an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the phrase "water does not flow and is cut off for a woman who has conceived a lustful mind," this refers to a bhikṣu who directs a lustful mind toward a woman.
If, while begging for alms, there is a beautiful woman who comes bringing food, according to the *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Meritorious Deeds):
"There was an aranyaka bhikṣu begging for alms who encountered the daughter of an elder; he begged food from the woman, and the bhikṣu gave it to her."
Both were handsome, and they both conceived feelings of desire for one another. As the bhikṣu received the food, his lustful mind became intense;

his hand shook, and as he cast the rice into his bowl, he spilled some onto the ground. The woman, surprised by this, laughed aloud. Seeing the whiteness of her teeth, the bhikṣu suddenly attained self-awareness and said:
"In a woman's mouth, there is nothing but bone. Just as the Buddha has taught, within a human body there are three [kinds of things].

There are one hundred and twenty bones, six hundred joints, seven hundred thousand vessels, and nine hundred thousand pores. Through one opening it enters and through nine openings it exits, leaking impurities;
there is not a single thing therein worth craving. Contemplating the female body as these thirty-six substances, his hair stood on end with horror.
He focused his mind in solitary reflection and immediately realized the emptiness of the body, attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*. He thought: "It was because of a woman that I [attained this]."

"One who perceives the Dharma is my true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). I must now repay their kindness by explaining to you, daughter, the method for contemplating the body that I have previously understood.
Upon hearing this, the woman’s mind was opened, and she also attained the first fruit of the path. From this it may be said that mindfulness of the body is supreme.
Regarding the fact that there are still many instances where the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Caturvargika-vinaya* differ, if we examine the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

there were some women who went to bathe in the Ajiravatī River. Suddenly, the river water rose, and the women were swept away by the current. When the bhikṣus saw this, they did not dare to rescue them.
The women said, "Venerable sirs, please rescue and take hold of us! The bhikṣus replied, "The Buddha has prescribed that we must not take hold of women. The women [continued]...
They said, "Venerable Sir, out of compassion and pity for us, where are those śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas? Seeing us being swept away by the water, why do they not rescue and seize us?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should rescue and seize them.

The bhikṣus then seized them, but when lustful thoughts arose, they released them again. The women said, "Do not release us! We must wait until we reach the shore. They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
Even if a lustful mind should arise, one should merely grasp a single part and not let go. Once on the shore, one must not touch her intentionally.
The Third Precept Regarding Harsh Speech to Women: First, the definition: sexual desire is base and evil, and being extremely unwholesome, it is termed "harsh" (*cauḍa*).
Now, its manifestation is explained: that which is expressed through the mouth is called "speech. "Woman" excludes men; "person" distinguishes [the object].

This is not [a case involving] an animal. This precept involves two layers of objective perception (*saṃjñā*): first, regarding a human female, there is the perception of her as a human female or doubt;
second, regarding coarse speech, there is the perception of it as coarse speech or doubt. A bhikṣu who is by nature prone to coarse speech says:

"Because of his natural disposition, even if he speaks coarsely to a woman, he does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs only a *sthūlātyaya*. According to the Vinaya, a "human female" must be one who possesses cognitive awareness.

Now, this statement is cited to clarify that it differs from the previous case regarding the object of physical contact. In the former case, the object included both the living and the dead, as well as those who were unconscious, asleep, or infants, all of which constituted an offense.
In this case, however, the object must be a living woman who possesses intelligence and the capacity to understand the intent of sexual desire;

therefore, the woman subject to this precept differs from the woman subject to the previous one. Regarding "vulgar speech" and "non-celibacy," according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), it says:

Regarding harsh speech: if one speaks ill of the anus or the urinary tract, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if one speaks of the good or bad qualities of other parts [of the body], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the consumption of ghee while wearing red garments and being naked: according to the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, it is said that at one time there was a bhikṣu.
He went to the house of a layperson where there was a woman who had consumed ghee and whose body was exposed. Upon seeing her, the bhikṣu said to her, "Have you consumed ghee?
She replied, "Venerable Sir, it is so; I have consumed ghee. The bhikṣu remained silent and became doubtful. The Buddha said, "If one speaks unclearly, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu wandering for alms who went to the house of a layperson at a time when a woman wearing red-colored garments had her body exposed.
Having seen her, the bhikṣu said to her, "You are wearing red clothing. She replied, "I am wearing red clothing. The bhikṣu remained silent, yet doubt arose within him.

The Buddha said, "Because it was not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Bin said: "The bhikṣu intended to refer to that woman’s form as 'clarified butter' (*ghṛta*) or as 'red clothing,' but because he did not clarify his meaning, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Had he understood [the distinction] clearly, it would have been a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This refers to the case of 'red clothing.'"
This case differs from the previous matter regarding the consumption of ghee; these are two separate women. [The Vinaya] states:
"If she had known that the bhikṣu’s words were a joke, it would have been a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Because she did not know they were a joke, it was a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "A bhikṣu saw a woman whose newly dyed robe was worn loosely. There was a bhikṣu begging for alms who arrived at a certain house. The woman..."
A man sat wearing a newly dyed robe, his body exposed. When a bhikṣu saw him, lust arose in his mind, and he said, "Sister, it is too red.
She replied, "Ācārya, this is a newly dyed robe. The bhikṣu gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha asked what his intention was, and he replied that it was a lustful mind. The Buddha sent a bhikṣu to ask the woman whether she understood [the meaning of the color]. The bhikṣu...

The Bhikṣu then questioned her about the preceding matter, and the woman answered him in full detail. Later, the Bhikṣu returned and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One who understands the meaning but not the phrasing commits an *āpatti* of concealment (*channa*);

one who understands the phrasing but not the meaning commits an *āpatti* of concealment; one who understands both the meaning and the phrasing commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; one who understands neither commits a *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding "meaning and phrasing," the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Head) states: "Phrasing refers to speech; meaning refers to principle. Speech issues forth to manifest matters completely."
