Yuan says: "Wei" (flavor) refers to the underlying meaning manifested by the words. It is called "wei" because it is the principle expressed beneath the speech. Regarding the various combinations: if both the flavor and the meaning are understood, it is *can* (remnant);

if they are mutually understood, it is *lan* (fragrance); if neither is understood, it is *yue* (transgression). If one follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which contains instances of mutual coarse speech directed toward one another, [the classification remains as stated].

"Establishing" means: it should be understood that if a bhikṣu speaks coarse words to a woman, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; likewise, if a bhikṣu receives coarse words from a woman, he also incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

This refers to a case where a woman speaks coarse words before a bhikṣu and, with a defiled mind, consents to them; this is also an identical offense. According to an examination of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this specific text is not found there;
it is likely that the compiler of the *Vinayavibhāṣā* has misidentified it. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "A bhikṣu is present... [text continues].
If a woman stands before a bhikṣu and praises his three orifices, saying that their form and color are upright and handsome, being neither too large nor too small;
or if she disparages those three orifices—whether he acts upon such matters as these according to her will, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a woman stands before a bhikṣu and praises his three orifices, saying that their form and color are upright and handsome, or disparages them by saying that the form and color of the three orifices are not good, and so on, until the bhikṣu...
Previously, when someone requested that one may act as one pleases regarding the three orifices, [the Buddha] said, "I grant this according to your wish.
In this case, if a bhikṣu complies with her mind and utters words—whether few or many—he commits an offense for every single word. The same applies to praising one's own body:

if a bhikṣu praises his own body in front of a woman to solicit desire, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; likewise, if a woman comes before the bhikṣu and praises herself [to solicit desire], it is the same.

The others are also remnants. Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) explains: "The lower [section] praises the bodily precept as being the same" means it is the same as this precept against coarse speech.
A woman must not have her life-force severed; she is one who possesses the wisdom to understand the language of sexual desire.

This is not the same as the upper bodily-contact precept for women, which applies whether the person is alive, dead, unconscious, or asleep. The lower section clarifies the conditions for non-offense.
Chapter Four: Praising One’s Own Body and Precepts; Restraining the Mind. This is established because the defilements of delusion are so deep and heavy that they entangle one another in succession.

To praise one's own body while harboring intentions of lustful desire is utterly improper for one who has left the household life to distance themselves from defilement. It is like fire burning within water—it is particularly contrary to what is appropriate and expected.

Because it invites ridicule and draws in disgrace, the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension from the community) is prescribed. As for the explanation of its name: it refers to one who is highly skillful at concealing [their faults] and praising themselves.
Their goodness is merely a pretense; their intent is focused solely on desire. They manifest an appearance of purity while their emotions run wild and dissolute.
They falsely claim to find joy and comfort, luring others into giving by speaking of their inner feelings. It is for this reason that they speak thus.

The Fifth Precept on Acting as a Matchmaker: This precept also involves two levels of objective perception (*jñapti*). These refer to perceiving a human woman as a human woman, as well as perceiving a marriage proposal as such, or harboring doubts regarding it.
"Matchmaking" (*mèi*) means to scheme; it refers to bringing together the affections of two parties to fulfill the rites of marriage.

It is called "good union" because it involves deliberating upon two lineages. Regarding the initial commentary’s question: "If one acts as a matchmaker for many men and women at once, how many offenses are incurred?
The answer states: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the number is indefinite. If one separately receives the words from each male family, one incurs multiple *duṣkṛta* (minor) offenses;
if one separately speaks to each female family, one incurs multiple *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offenses. If one gathers many families and [acts] all at once...

Report: One *śeṣa* offense. If one receives many [sexual advances] at once from a male party, there is one *pāyattika*. If one seeks them separately, there are many *dukkaṭas*. If one reports them all at once, it is one *śeṣa*.
If one receives, speaks of, and reports each instance separately, there are many *pāyattikas*, many *dukkaṭas*, and many *śeṣas*.
If one receives and speaks of them all at once, but reports them one by one, there is one *pāyattika*, one *dukkaṭa*, and one *śeṣa*. This excludes the two [specific] paths.
"Place" refers to the two passages for excrement and urine. As for acting as a matchmaker for other parts of the body, such as the mouth and so forth, one incurs only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Furthermore, it is said that acting as a matchmaker by means of the mouth also constitutes a *saṃghādisesa* (offense requiring suspension); however, the present text mentions only two locations as an abbreviation.

It ought to have stated "excluding the three [other] passages," yet because there is no instance of acting as a matchmaker through the mouth, it is not clarified here (*this remains uncertain*). One cannot [facilitate intercourse between] male and female...
This refers to eunuchs and barren women. Regarding the "formal act of two announcements" (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for appointing a person to act as a matchmaker for all cases of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:

this refers to the practice of monks acting as matchmakers as described in the *Śramaṇera-vinaya* (the *Sifen lü*) section on the *Vinayavibhaṅga*. If the Saṃgha acts in unison, each individual monk incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If the property of the Saṃgha is used to provide the means for matchmaking, one incurs a grave offense of theft (*steya*). Although such formal acts (*karman*) are not performed at present, [the underlying principles remain].

Because the multitude are in harmony, it is also included as a residual offense (*śeṣa*). If one acts as a matchmaker for those who have already conceived, according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it states:
"If a woman has conceived once and another woman has conceived once, and a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker between them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

[The commentator] Li says: "Seeing that another has conceived, one knows for certain that a child will be born; thus, acting as a matchmaker after this is permitted. [The commentator] Bin says: "Because the matter is extensive, the formal rule (*saṃvara*) is established only then."
This concludes the section on "Lan-ye" (Lanyā). Regarding the mention of "self-promotion," this refers to a bhikṣu personally inquiring at a woman's family with the intent of seeking her as a wife.
By combining these methods—speech, writing, signs, and seals—in various permutations, forty-four thousand eight hundred phrases are produced.

First, there are four permutations regarding pure speech: 1. One receives a message from the man's family and conveys it oneself; one goes to the woman's family and conveys it oneself; and one reports back to the man's family. 2.
One receives a message from the man's family and conveys it oneself; one goes to the woman's family and dispatches a messenger to convey the message.
1. To inform the groom’s family. 2. To personally receive the words of the groom’s family and dispatch a messenger with those words to the bride’s family. 3.

To personally receive the words of the groom’s family, dispatch a messenger with those words to the bride’s family, and then personally carry the message back to inform the groom’s family. 4. To personally receive the words of the groom’s family, dispatch a messenger with those words to the bride’s family, and dispatch another messenger with those words to inform the groom’s family.
The second section summarizes these into four propositions: 1. To personally receive the words of the groom’s family and personally carry the written document.

1. Going to the girl’s family, one personally carries a letter to inform the boy’s family. 2. Personally receiving a message from the boy’s family, one personally carries a letter to the girl’s family and dispatches a messenger with a letter to inform the boy’s family.
3. Personally receiving a message from the boy’s family, one dispatches a messenger with a letter to the girl’s family and personally carries a letter to inform the boy’s family.
4. Personally receiving a message from the boy’s family, one dispatches a messenger with a letter to the girl’s family.
Having thus reported to the groom’s family by means of a letter, and so forth, up to a signet ring, a hint, or a formal notice—each of these items has four permutations.
Four times four makes sixteen; since there are sixteen permutations for each single item, this constitutes four sets of sixteen, totaling sixty-four permutations.
Furthermore, when three items are combined to form a statement, there are likewise four segments. First.
Within the sections, there are three matters. Regarding the first section consisting of four phrases:

(1) personally receiving the message from the groom's family, going in person to inquire at the bride's family, and personally reporting back to the groom's family—in these three phrases, the phrase "personally maintaining [the communication]" is applied to each;

(2) personally receiving a letter from the groom's family, personally carrying the letter to the bride's family, and personally carrying the letter to report back to the groom's family; (3) personally receiving a signet seal from the groom's family.
Carrying one's own finger-seal (*mudrā*), one goes to the woman's family; carrying one's own finger-seal, one reports to the man's family.

Furthermore, setting aside the manifest signs (*nimitta*), if manifest signs are subsequently given, then excluding the four [methods] such as the finger-seal and so forth, they are returned to form a single phrase as before.
Within the section on "sending a messenger," there are four phrases of its own. Regarding the three matters, there are four phrases; thus, three times four [makes twelve].
This forms twelve phrases. Since one section contains twelve, four sections constitute forty-eight. Together with the previous sixty-four, they total one hundred and twelve phrases.
This applies even down to cases such as returning wives, illicit intercourse, eunuchs, the three paths, men, and the three realms of rebirth including animals;
for each of these, phrases are constructed as above. Furthermore, among women, there are twenty types.
Regarding women, there are those protected by their fathers, those protected by their mothers, and so forth, totaling forty-four thousand eight hundred phrases.

The text of the *Chao* does not manifest these characteristics; it contains only three matters. As for "finger-seals" (*mudrā*), the ancient interpretation takes the joints of the fingers to constitute the seal.
The guest said, "Not so. It is by the differences in the horizontal and vertical lines upon the fingers that good and evil, fortune and misfortune are all indicated.

If one shows a horizontal line for misfortune and a vertical line for fortune, and the lines manifest whether what is sought will be achieved or not, then one knows whether the bride's family has granted permission or not.
As for what is called 'manifesting signs,' it refers to when one has previously made an agreement with the families of the bride and groom; if one sees—"
"If I come wearing tattered clothes and carrying an empty bowl, one will immediately know that [the marriage] is not permitted and the wedding will not be consummated;
whereas seeing me wearing fine clothes and carrying a full bowl is a sign that what is sought will be harmoniously accomplished.

Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*’s exhortation for the wife to return early, the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) quotes the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If the master keeps many wives and distributes property unfairly, they will quarrel and contend."
If a woman privately solicits a bhikṣu and he mediates for them, it is an offense (pācittiya).
If a husband and wife are quarreling, it is not appropriate to mediate their reconciliation;
in all such cases, it is an offense (thullaccaya), because she fears her husband’s anger and is unable to reunite with him. The following clarifies when there is no offense.
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Eight, Part One;
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Eight, Part Two.

The Sixth Precept: The Prohibition Against Unowned Dwellings. First, explaining the intent of the regulation. For those who have left the household life, it is logically impossible to harbor attachments. Accordingly...

When affairs are about to be undertaken, one is then capable of practicing the Way. One accepts offerings from the faithful only when there is sufficient time; even if there is some management required, it ceases once one’s own needs are met.
Now, however, one acts on a vast scale, resulting in no small amount of toil and fatigue. Therefore, the Sage established this regulation. Next, regarding the explanation of the name:

because the body alone performs the work, it is called "without a master" (*amukhya*). Because one relies solely upon oneself, it is called "the Sangha does not assign authority. This greatly accords with the limits of the Dharma.

Therefore, it is called "excessive. Thus, it is said: "The precept against a monk without a patron constructing an excessively large dwelling. The origin of this transgression occurred among the monks in a vast wilderness;
because they constructed private dwellings and begged for materials without moderation, the laity became weary and disgusted, and their resentment extended even to the virtuous.
For this reason, when Kāśyapa later entered the village to beg for alms, the householders fled in terror, thinking, "A mendicant has come;
he will seek wealth and goods from us. Kāśyapa questioned them in wonder until their source was made clear. He returned and informed the World-Honored One, who immediately departed the boundary.
At dusk, non-human beings came again and said to the Buddha, "Because you cut down the sacred tree, you have harmed the children of the deity. The Buddha [responded] once more...
It merely mentions that non-humans came to inform [the Buddha]; it does not say that Kāśyapa did so for the sake of protecting people's minds.
Regarding "increasing the fetters of greed," Master Li states: since he begged for much, he consequently deviated from the path of having few desires and knowing contentment;
because of this affliction of greed, it is called "increasing the fetters of greed. Although the donor’s giving may be insatiable, the recipient should be aware of this.
Furthermore, in the *Vinaya-nidāna*, the Buddha recounts the story of how he once begged for feathers from birds (*etc.*). According to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"When the birds gathered at dusk, a bhikṣu said, 'You, Śakuntaka birds, each give me one feather;
I now require them. For a short while, the birds remained silent and still. Having no other choice, they each plucked a feather and placed it on the ground. At dawn, [he returned] again..."
When he begged, the birds immediately moved away to another place for one night. Not finding pleasure there, they soon returned.
The bhikṣu begged again, and each time they gave him [a piece of meat]. The birds thought to themselves: "This śramaṇa is strange; he delights in begging.
I fear that before long my feathers will all fall out and this piece of flesh will remain on the ground, leaving me unable to fly. What shall we do? And so...

They deliberated together, saying: "We should depart; it is no longer fitting for us to return. Those who disturb humans and non-humans have many affairs and beg incessantly, thereby destroying the deep faith of the laity;
hence they are said to 'disturb people. They cut down trees and destroy the trees of the spirits and deities, prematurely injuring their lives."
The "disturbance" refers to non-human beings (*amanuṣya*). Regarding the act of felling the tree alone, it establishes the disturbance of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
By cutting down this divine tree, one harms the children of the deity; this is the disturbance of the realm of non-humans. Worldly people rely on the shade and cool comfort provided by this tree;
according to the Vinaya, five hundred chariots can fit beneath this tree, and worldly people use it as a place of rest when passing by; this is the realm of humans. First.
All insects and birds rely upon it as their dwelling; this is the affliction of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).

Alternatively, those who engage in self-destructive conduct that violates the path of compassion devote themselves exclusively to building houses, neglecting the cultivation of the path to liberation (*nairyāṇika-karman*); this is called "self-destructive conduct. Bin says: "Alternatively, 'self-destructive' refers to..."
It is because it is a difficult location; there may be lions, tigers, and wolves that devour bhikṣus. To level the ground involves killing and injuring insects and ants;
this is called violating the path of compassion. The explanation of the meaning of these five faults is now complete.

Below, the conditions [for the offense] are correctly clarified. An offense is established through six conditions. Regarding the fourth condition—perceiving that which exceeds the limit as not having been formally assigned—the initial question asks:

"Does the formal act of assignment (*cāraṇa-karman*) prevent obstacles and difficulties? The answer is: "It does not prevent them. If that is so, one might argue that the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*) should likewise not prevent the possession of an extra robe.

To resolve this: if there were prevention of obstacles within this context, the original rule would not have permitted assignment; it is only because there is no such prevention that assignment is permitted. Therefore, regarding the assignment...

The *parikathā* (assignment) does not prevent difficulties; the *śuddhivāda* (declaration of purity) is a preemptive defense against exceeding the limit. Therefore, by means of the *śuddhivāda*, one can prevent the fault of "excess" (*atireka*).
This is precisely because the *parikathā* does not prevent difficulties—once the assignment is completed, difficulties may still arise—whereas the *śuddhivāda* directly prevents excess;

once the declaration of purity is completed, there will certainly be no fault of excess. For this reason, they are not concurrent. Regarding the fourfold permutations of objective and perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) for this precept, the first is "without an owner. The second...
It is not subject to formal disposal. Third, there is no obstruction; fourth, there is no difficulty.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-śāstra* that the final two instances of kneading clay constitute a light *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) because the task is not yet completed: this establishes the principle that it is because the matter has not been finalized.

This does not constitute a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). One must resolve to desist; even if one continues to knead clay, it is the same as the previous case and remains a minor offense (*śeṣa*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, "kneading clay" refers to using lumps of clay to cover a roof, not to plastering walls—this is how it should be understood.
If one’s own use of something is auspicious, it is established as clear that even if one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense oneself, if one subsequently uses it, it is again auspicious.
Leveling [the ground] like the surface of a drum, up to six spans in length and four spans in width, does not require requesting formal authorization (*jñapti*).
As for the statement that this *Sudarsana* text is smaller in measure than the *Caturvarga*, the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) says:
"The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* translated during the Song dynasty [uses] a *buddha-viddha-hasta* measuring two chi and four cun;
this corresponds to one chi of the era of the Northern Wei, which is equivalent to two chi of the Song dynasty’s own standard. So it is heard and transmitted.
Regarding Buddhism: proceeding from north to south, the Wei *chi* (foot) corresponds to what is called the "Buddha-span" (*bō-zé*; that is, the Buddha-span is based upon the Wei *chi*).

The reason why two *chi* are fixed as the standard for the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is that this Vinaya was translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty. At that time, Dao-sheng and Zhi-yen were both renowned scholars;
as they were well-versed in calendrical systems and astronomy, and also proficient in local dialects, they were able to bridge the gap between the East and the West to establish this standard.
Regarding the foot-rule and the scale, there is indeed a historical basis for this. The southern foot-rule was originally that used during the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan;

from the Qin, Han, and Wei dynasties onward, it underwent no alteration. When the Liu Yu clan moved south, this standard became permanently established. During the Yuan-Wei dynasty’s suppression of disorder, however, official records were burned and destroyed, leaving nothing to rely upon as a standard.
Consequently, in the Sui dynasty, they established the use of two ancient foot-rules. Observing the one-foot measure of the Wei today, it is identical to the "Miscellaneous Ordinances" of the Tang.
It is just as described above.
Regarding the statement that "an ordinary person is one and a half cubits [in height]," it says they stand at eight or nine inches [per cubit].

This is because, in the context of translating the scriptures, there were two nations—the Southern and the Northern. It is said that Jiangning was the Southern Dynasty and Luoyang was the Northern Dynasty; therefore, they are called the "two nations."
The Tripiṭaka masters of the Southern Dynasties, in their translations, mostly clarify the "small inch," which is the inch of the Zhou dynasty of the Ji period.

The Tripiṭaka masters of the Northern Dynasties, in their translations, mostly clarify the "large inch," which is the inch of the Wei dynasty. The current inch of the Tang is two inches [longer] than that; it is precisely the inch of the Wei dynasty.
To say they are "mutually contradictory" means that their meanings are in opposition. This refers to what is stated in the aforementioned Vinaya and Śāstras.

The *Vibhāṣā* states that the span (*vitasti*) is not fixed. There are internal contradictions within the *Śāstra*, and there are also contradictions within the *Vinaya*. When comparing the *Śāstra* with the *Vinaya*, further contradictions arise.
For example, according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, the Buddha’s span is three times the human span; according to the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, it is two feet four inches;

and according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is one and a half cubits for an ordinary person. These are all contradictions found within the *Śāstras*. Furthermore, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha’s span... [text truncated]
The hand-length is two chi according to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, while it is two chi and four cun according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. This constitutes a contradiction within the Vinaya.

Now, for the purpose of general calculation and reconciliation, it is appropriate to adopt the two chi measurement from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Although the various schools differ regarding the specific cubit (*śaku*) used, we shall take the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan as the standard.
"Ji" is a surname and "Zhou" is the dynastic name; because there were two [Zhou periods], the surname is specified to distinguish between them. At that time...
The *chi* used is the same as the small *chi* currently used in the South and Wu regions. The *ji-sheng* is the same as the small *dou* today; three *sheng* equal one *sheng* of the Tang dynasty.
The *ji-chen* is the same as the medicinal scale used today; it can be understood that three *liang* equal one *liang* of the Tang scale.
Regarding the meaning of "shield and spear" (*maodun*), the *Mozi* states: "There was a man from Chu who sold both shields and spears. He praised his spear, saying..."
"This spear is extremely sharp; there is nothing it cannot penetrate. He further praised his shield, saying, "This shield is extremely sturdy; nothing can penetrate it.
Someone said to him, "If I were to give you this spear, what would happen when it struck your shield? The man was unable to answer. "To sell" (*yù*) means to trade.
According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a spear (*máo*) is two zhang long and is mounted on a war chariot. A shield (*dùn*) is merely something to be recognized.
As for Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, this refers to Yang Guang. Regarding the posthumous title established after his death, Master Ying said:

"In Jiangdong, a fierce and blazing fire is called *yang*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Yang* means to dry; it means to roast. According to the text, *yang* means to face the fire; it refers to facing the fire while roasting things.
The *Guangyi* states: "*Yang* means heat. Li [Daoyuan] says: "The reason he is now called Emperor Yang is because of the Sui..."

At that time, there were frequent droughts; thus, this name was given. Another interpretation is as follows: The Later Sovereign of the Sui dynasty was unrighteous and frequently acted arbitrarily, manufacturing vinegar and poisons for the common people.

He diverted the Jin River to carve out a new canal, launched the expedition to Liaodong, and moved the capital to Yangdu. Consequently, at the end of the Daye era, the empire fell into chaos and turmoil;
no place remained secure, and the people’s hearts were tormented by heat and suffering. Because he lost his throne due to these causes, he was posthumously titled Emperor Yang.
Regarding the posthumous title (*shì*), the *Guīhuā Zhūcóng* states: its pronunciation is "shì," and it refers to the traces of one's conduct (*xíng*).

For those of the rank of Great Officer (*dàfū*) and above, after death, a title is established based on their conduct during life; this is called a posthumous title. It is essential that this name be conferred only after death.

Emperors, kings, and the Three Ducal Ministers are entitled to receive such titles, whereas ordinary commoners do not merit them. However, in the case of recluses and sages, they may also [receive them].
One may establish [posthumous titles] for them. For example, after Guo Linzong died, he was posthumously titled "Master Jingjie" (Silent Integrity).
Similarly, after Tao Yinyu (i.e., Tao Hongjing) died, he was posthumously titled "Master Zhenbai" (Upright Purity).

This is just as people of the world give a name to a son at three years of age, and at twenty—known as "weak-crown"—they establish a courtesy name (*zi*) to manifest his virtue. [This illustrates] the desire to clarify Emperor Yang’s broad learning.
He was well-versed in the Classics and Histories. He extensively permitted the use of various cubits and weights, and established the standard measures for *dou*, *sheng*, and *chi*.

These were modeled after the ancient systems of the Zhou dynasty, such as its cubits, weights, and *dou* measures. Prior to this, from the Zhou through the Qin, Han, Wei, and subsequent dynasties, these same cubits and weights had been employed.

However, when the Northern Wei dynasty suppressed disorder, the literary records were burned, leaving nothing upon which to rely. It was not until the reign of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty that they were first re-established, and they once again utilized these same cubits. During the Tang dynasty...
Regarding the phrase "ruling the realm" (*yu-ü*) and its dual application to the world: it is stated that "realm" (*ü*) is glossed as "to cover," while "employing" (*yung*) means "to be appropriate.
This clarifies that the current Tang dynasty employs both the large and small *chi* (feet) as standards; it is not restricted solely to the large scale.

The small *chi* and pecks (*dou*) used in the Southern Wu region are those currently prevalent in the world, and the small scales used by pharmacists have remained unchanged to this day. Furthermore, the present state administration has been deficient and parsimonious.
The measurements are equal; their scales all rely on the small cubit (xiǎochǐ), which accords with the principles of ritual law and calendrical calculation.

For instance, when taking the locations for acupuncture and moxibustion today and measuring their dimensions, if one were to use a large cubit (dàchǐ), they would not correspond at all. This is what is meant according to the treatises.

Someone says: "The *Shat-lun* (Treatise on the Six Heaps) is the standard. Jì says: "'Standard' (*shuai*) refers to the principle (*ze*). It is as stated in the *Qingzhong-yi-ji* (Record of the Rituals for Light and Heavy Matters), etc."
Since one has not yet mastered the two systems— the secular and the monastic— the secular system refers to the Tang *chi*, while the monastic system refers to the Zhou dynasty *chi* of King Ji.
The reason the Zhou *chi* is called the "monastic system" is that it is based on the ancient laws concerning the span of the cubit (*jieshou*) and the capacity of the peck (*dou*).
Regarding the phrase "the scripts and standards are not two," Falin states: "Script" refers to written documents and classical texts; "standard" refers to laws, methods, and regulations.
As for the discussion concerning the five different types of cubits used, Falin says: first is the Tang cubit, which is equivalent to two inches of the Jizhou (Western Zhou) cubit;
second is the Jizhou cubit, which is currently widely used in Jiangdong; third is the Luozhou cubit, which is longer than the Tang cubit.

The second is two *cun* (equivalent to four *cun* according to the scale of the Jizhou of King Ji; it is more than this). The fourth is the *luo-ge* scale of Shandong, which is four *cun* of the Tang scale;
this is stated according to the large scale (*da-chi*). If one discusses the scale of the Jizhou of King Ji, it should be six *cun* or more.

The fifth is the small scale of the Jizhou of King Ji used in Southern Wu (which is approximately eight *cun*). However, in the *Jie-shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there are only four types of scales mentioned. Now, having inquired about Southern Wu:
There is no such thing as the "small princess" (*mōshiki*) inch of the Zhou dynasty. Examining the explanation above in detail, these are all transmitted through dreams.
Regarding the three types of inches currently in use—namely, the second, the Tang inch, and the third, the Ragaku inch—the five characters in the *Shō* [the *Ryōbu Shichū Shō*] must be an error.
Third is cooperation. Regarding the phrase "weighing and measuring so that nothing is uneven": "weighing" (heng) means to level; it refers to the horizontal beam of a scale.
"Measuring" (liang) refers to the measurements of the bushel and the foot-rule. That these are used together throughout Jambudvīpa is not limited to the Zhou dynasty alone;

this is precisely the meaning of what was stated above regarding how the hundred kings did not alter these standards. That the foot-rule and the scale follow ancient precedent further illustrates the aforementioned point. Thus it is established.
That is to say: regarding this measure of the bowl, as for the statement that it is "three *dou*," this may be based on the large *dou*.
If one follows the large *dou*, then a bowl of the highest grade would be three *dou*; yet how could there be such a bowl if measured by the small *dou* of less than one *shi*?

This clarifies that the usage here refers to the small *dou* of the Zhou dynasty. Since the *dou* is thus determined, the *chi* (foot) and the scale (*cheng*) may be known accordingly; one must rely upon the ancient standards of the Zhou.

The principle is consistent with that of the *Zhou li*; thus, the meaning becomes even more manifest. As for the statement that "six chi make one bu," this does not refer to the large *chi*, but clearly refers to the small *chi*.
Regarding the sequence beginning with the *hu* and the *si*, this clarifies the origin of measurement. The *Suanjing* says: [text follows].
Measurement begins with the *hu*. The tip of a silkworm’s mouth first emerging is called a *hu*. Ten *hu* make one *si* (fibre); ten *si* make one *máo* (hair);
ten *máo* are called a *lí*; ten *lí* are called a *fēn*; ten *fēn* are called a *cùn*; ten *cùn* are called a *chí*; ten *chí* are called a *zhàng*;
ten *zhàng* are called a *yǐn*; forty *chí* are called a *pǐ*; and fifty *chí* are called a *duān*.
Regarding "the Guanzhong region," this refers to the capital within the passes. There are many distinct passes; to the direct east of the capital, within the borders of Huazhou, is Zhaoguan Pass.
To the northeast, in Puzhou, is Pujin Pass. Further along the Yellow River upstream to Longmen is Longmen Pass.
Continuing further along the river upstream to Suizhou is Yonghe Pass. Continuing further along the river upstream to Yinzhou...
The province has Mengmen Pass. Reaching the border of Shengzhou, there is Hehe Pass (the locations above are north of the capital).
To the northwest, between Zhuzhou and Weizhou, there is Longshan Pass. Further north, there is Shuili Pass. Entering the border of Lanzhou, there is Jincheng Pass.
Ascending eastward along the river to Huizhou, there is Huining Pass. Further west along the river, ascending westward—
Upon reaching Hezhou, there is Fenglin Pass. Going due west past Qizhou to Longzhou, there is Dazhen Pass.
There is also Anyi Pass facing southwest toward the road to Yizhou. South of Qizhou, there is San Pass. Upon reaching Fengzhou, there is Ganting Pass.
At the border of Lizhou, there is Bailao Pass, which faces southwest toward Liangzhou. These are the routes of the various prefectures.

There is Luogou Pass (bordered by mountains), facing south toward Bìzhōu and Kāizhōu; there is Ziniu Pass (located at the midpoint between the Ziwu Ridge of Zhōngnánshān), facing directly south along the road to Yùzhōu and Fángzhōu;
there is Yìgǔ Pass; and facing southeast toward Shāngzhōu until the border of Lántiān County, there is Lántiān Pass.
"Fǔ" means to assist; there are the Three Fǔ, as explained extensively in the preceding preface.

Regarding the "Reflecting Light on the Nine Generations": from the Han to the Tang, there were precisely nine generations. During that interval, various masters were unable to clearly comprehend these measures and weights;
I have standardized these proportions so that, looking back at the nine generations, they may be understood with clarity.
Regarding the measurements of the *chi* explained above, the Vinaya and the Śāstra contradict one another; their words and meanings are mutually opposed.

They cannot be reconciled through subjective sentiment, nor can they be resolved through extensive scholarship. Since antiquity, scholars have clung to their disputes, which have persisted for generations without being extinguished. Now, I have brought them into comprehensive harmony;
if this is not a brilliant illumination, what else could it be?
"Regarding the term 'within the light' (*myōnai*): this means that the measurement of the room is taken from within the room. Jie says:

'That which is inside the threshold is called "within the light," and that which is outside the threshold is called "beyond the light. This refers to the 'light' in the sense of illumination versus darkness.
As for 'the walls being one zhang and two chi high,' this refers to the height and depth being such as this. Regarding the 'grass cart,' this is merely cited as a contemporary example."
At that time, he was carrying a grass cart.
As for the Śītavana (Cold Forest), its proper name is Śītavana; this is called the "Cold Forest. That forest is secluded and cold.
It is named for this reason. It was located beside the city of Rājagṛha, where corpses were sent to be disposed of; it now generally refers to a place for abandoning the dead.
"Śītavana" (Cold Forest) takes its name from that location. Regarding "the site protected by King Jita":

some maintain that this refers to places such as the imperial gardens, parks, or mausoleums of the present-day state. As for "not accessible on all four sides with twelve ladders," there are twelve ladders, each ladder being one [unit].
One *kuan* (fist-span) is one *zhu* (cubit). One *zhu* is nineteen *chi*. Calculated in total, this is twelve *gang*; thus, there is ground measuring two *zhang*, two *chi*, and eight *cun*.

This clarifies that if the space on all four sides of the dwelling is not encroached upon by another's fields, gardens, and so forth, and if the intermediate space can accommodate the turning of a ladder of these twelve *gang*, as well as the passage of carts and horses, it is called "unobstructed. If the southern side borders water, it is not [an obstruction].

If a vehicle or ladder must pass through this [space], or if the northern edge abuts a mountain, or the eastern and western edges abut official gardens or trees belonging to graves such that a vehicle or ladder cannot turn around, these are all termed "obstructed places.
The citation from the *Samantapāsādikā* is as clarified above. If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* below:
If the four sides are only one *xun*—that is, seven feet—it is called "unobstructed. Regarding measurement, there are different categories.
If one must have a partition when dwelling therein, it is established that this applies to cases such as staying within a rocky cave or similar location.

If the area is so vast that it requires great effort and labor to manage, one must establish separate boundary zones (*sīmā*). Furthermore, this requires the formal authorization (*anujñā*) through a *saṃgha-karmavācanā* (monastic ritual).
It is established as clear that those who go there in groups of four are not permitted to perform the *karmavācanā*; the *karmavācanā* cannot be carried out by a group of four persons.
At most, it shall be limited to three people; they are to be sent to that place to carry out the distribution. Regarding the "four kinds of persons" such as those who have passed a year and so forth:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Ji-wen), it says: (1) If a bhikṣu leads other bhikṣus to designate a dwelling place, but it belongs to the Saṃgha of another boundary, it is not called "designation.
(2) If it was designated in advance during a previous year, it is not called "designation. (3) If [it is designated] by one person within the Saṃgha...
One does not construct a dwelling; nor, even if two or three people do not construct it while others all do, is this called "assigning" (the site) [three].
If it is a place that causes obstruction or difficulty, such a place is not called "assigning" [four].

The meaning of this text clarifies that monks from a different boundary (*sīmā*) may not come to perform the formal act of assignment (*jñapti-karman*) for the distribution of the site. Furthermore, one may not assign it across years. Moreover, one may not...
Regarding the instruction on obstructed or difficult locations and so forth, as for the phrase "one who has exceeded the year" (*ekābdika*), Ji states:

"The ancients transmitted a mistaken interpretation, saying that a monk aged eighty or above is called 'one who has exceeded the year. They claimed that since such a person is old, they are incapable of providing instruction to others.

This current [explanation] does not follow that interpretation; it means that although one requested the Dharma last year, one only begins the construction this year, and thus it is not accomplished."

The Upādhyāya said: "He requested the *dharmas* for many years before finally constructing [the hut]. This means that although he had requested the formal authorization (*anujñā*) from the Saṃgha, he did not build it for a year.

The *Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā* states: "If one has already requested the authorization while a śrāmaṇera, and only constructs the hut upon reaching the stage of a bhikṣu, this person does not need to request it again;
though their status differs, since they have already entrusted themselves to the Saṃgha, the person remains no different."
Therefore, it is not required. Furthermore, it is said that although individuals do not differ, there is a distinction between those who possess [the requisite qualities] and those who do not;

because the *saṃgha* may reside in different locations, one must again request [permission]. Second, regarding the *saṃgha* of another boundary (*sīmā*), this is as previously explained in the *Ji*. Third, regarding "many private rooms":

Zhi Liang states that because the sites for construction differ, one must request [permission from] the *saṃgha* of two other boundaries. This is because the number of people within the boundary of the private room is extremely large.
One must not allocate [the space] for others. A guest asked: "Suppose there are one hundred people within a single boundary (*sīmā*), and eighty people have already made it their private quarters;

may the remaining twenty people no longer make [their own quarters], and may the community of monks (*saṃgha*) not perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for them? [The Master replied: "It is not so."
Regarding the two places where construction is obstructed: it is improper to perform the formal authorization (*jñapti*) for construction in these two obstructed locations.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states: "It is permissible to perform [construction] in one place after authorization has been granted, but not in other places. The initial question asks: Does this method of authorization correspond to the person, or does it correspond to the location?
The answer is: It corresponds to the boundary (*sīmā*) and the assignment; this *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is...
It corresponds to the site; it does not correspond to the person. Why? The treatise states: "One may perform [the ritual] on a designated site, but not on any other site.

Question: If the dharma of designation corresponds to the site such that another person may not construct a dwelling upon it, then once the boundary has been established, it would likewise correspond to the site, and other people should likewise be unable to perform any *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) there. Answer:
When establishing a boundary (*sīmā*), if no one requests it and no individual's name is mentioned, the Dharma is not restricted;
thus, once this community has completed the establishment, other communities may perform the formal act of *jñapti-karman* (assignment).

However, if a person previously requested the grant of this place and it constitutes an obstruction to the Sangha, and furthermore, if a specific individual's name is mentioned and the formal act of *karman* is performed according to the rules, then it belongs specifically to that person and others may not perform it. Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "If..."
If a person builds an upper story upon this house and the owner of the house consents to its construction, there is no offense of unauthorized action (*anāpatti*),
because the building is constructed upon another's private dwelling and not upon the ground.

Regarding cases where the measurements mutually exceed or fall short of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sengcan) limits and so forth, the established explanation states that the Vinaya contains nine distinct permutations.

The "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*) is divided into three sets of three. The first three permutations are: 1. Exceeding the length and exceeding the width (an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for the robe; an offense of *pāyattika* for the cloth). 2. Exceeding the length and being within the [standard] width (an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for the robe; an offense of *pāyattika* for the cloth). 3.

Exceeding the length and falling short of the width (an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for the robe; no offense for the cloth). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, these involve an offense of *duṣkṛta* regarding the robe. The next three... [text continues].

Regarding the phrases: 1. Length as prescribed, width exceeding [the limit] (offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* regarding robe-material). 2. Length as prescribed, width as prescribed (no offense regarding robe-material).
3. Length as prescribed, width less than [the limit] (neither offense). As for the latter three phrases: 1.

Length less than [the limit], width exceeding [the limit] (offense regarding the dwelling, no offense regarding robe-material). 2. Length less than [the limit], width as prescribed (neither offense). 3. Length less than [the limit], width less than [the limit].

(There is no offense). This is because the rule for the dwelling (*vihāra*) was established based on exceeding the prescribed measure, whereas the rule for the robe was established based on conforming to the prescribed measure;

therefore, they are not the same. If it were the case that one commits an offense by calculating each person’s share and finding it to exceed the limit, then it would be clear that since the dwelling is large, even if many people build it together, if one calculates the number of people, there would still be excess beyond each individual’s portion, and those who completed the dwelling would incur the offense of "residual" (*śeṣa*).

Answer: Regarding the offense for constructing this dwelling, it is established that the dwelling is built by oneself; because the degree of affliction is profound, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense immediately upon the mutual transgression.
As for the long robe (*atirekacīvara*), its substance is not self-constructed; rather, the transgression arises solely from covetous accumulation.
Since the nature of the fault is light, an offense is incurred only when both conditions are met.
If one instructs another to perform an act and the instructed person commits an offense exceeding the prescribed limit, it is established that this statement applies the charge to both individuals;

the wording encompasses both, meaning that both the instructor and the instructed commit an offense, though there is a difference in the gravity of their offenses, and the actual nature of the transgression has not yet been specified.
Below, the text explains: "If it is the householder who is at fault, the skilled craftsman incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); the skilled craftsman thus belongs to the category of the instructed."

This is the teaching. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "If one instructs another to build a dwelling, one likewise incurs an offense, because one is causing another to construct something contrary to the Dharma.

Although the Vinaya merely mentions the person who receives the instruction, it does not specify the name of the offense incurred. The reason it is not fixed is that if the one who performs the act commits an excess, [the instructor is also implicated].
This is because the householder is grave while the skilled artisan is light. Lü (礪) says:

"If one instructs another to act and the instructor commits the offense, it is stated directly as an offense [of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*] because a single statement intends to encompass both. If one were to say 'he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*,' it would not include the *sthūlātyaya* of the artisan;
if one were to say 'he commits a *sthūlātyaya*,' it would not include the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* of the householder. Therefore, it is stated directly and generally."
[The preceding section] explains the offenses; the following clarifies the rules regarding non-offenses.
Regarding "not committing [an offense] for the sake of many members of the Saṃgha," Jing says: "This refers to 'many' in the sense of the Saṃgha as a whole, not to many individual persons.
The *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) states: "'Many people residing' refers to a dwelling intended for many people; it does not mean that many people jointly constructed it."

The Seventh Precept on Dwellings with Owners: This precept involves three layers of objective perception (*sañjñā*). Because the dwelling has an owner, there is no offense of exceeding the prescribed measure. Question:

Since both preceding and following rules concern dwellings, why are they divided into two separate precepts? Answer: Because they differ in terms of "few" and "many," they cannot be combined. Specifically: first, the distinction between having an owner and not having an owner;
second, the distinction between having a fixed measure and not having a fixed measure; and third, within the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), [the distinctions differ].
The characteristics of these two are distinct. Because there are these three differences, they are divided into two types of precepts.
Regarding the case where the Saṃgha incurs an offense if it does not permit a sale:

since this is private property, if another person wishes to travel far away, or if the owner has already assigned a portion to them, or intends to sell it, or give it to someone else—if the Saṃgha does not permit the sale, the Saṃgha incurs an offense. If [the owner] departs...
If it was not previously assigned, it belongs to the Saṃgha only after death (the following clarifies the non-offense).
The eighth precept: Slandering with groundless charges. The six precepts below are offenses common to both monks and nuns. First, to clarify the intent of the regulation:
Now, those who have left the household life dwell together, for whom harmony is paramount; they protect one another and are permitted not to cause mutual distress. Yet now...
Harboring anger, they recklessly fabricate grave matters to falsely accuse others. They thus ruin their own mental conduct, increase the cycle of birth and death, and extinguish the True Dharma.

Furthermore, they defile the virtuous and cast them outside the community; they afflict others for a lifetime and cause them to abandon the cultivation of right practice. Such deception is profound and grave, and thus requires a specific prohibition by the Sage.
If one lacks the three kinds of evidence within, it is called "baseless" (*amūlaka*). To falsely allege the four major offenses is termed [the offense of groundless accusation].
This is grave. To falsely fabricate and slanderously accuse another is called "slander. Groundless slander is not itself a precept; rather, it is that which the precepts guard against.
The precept is the "guardian" (the agent), while slander is that which is guarded against (the object). Since both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is so stated.

Among the circumstances [of this rule], the bhikṣu Dharmatāpa—known as Dabba in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*—left home at fourteen and attained arhatship at sixteen. At the time of distributing bedding and seats...

There was no need for lamps or candles. From the little finger of his left hand, the man emitted a great light; holding it with his right hand, he pointed toward the place where the bedding for the monks was kept.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, second fascicle, states: "He immediately entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi), emitting light from his left hand while pointing with his right hand to the location of the bedding.
At that time, people from distant regions, having heard of this virtue, all thought to themselves: "I shall go there to inquire [of him]."
The *Xun shi zun* (Inquiry of the World-Honored One) states that he also saw the *dhāraṇī* and manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). The *Jian lun* (Treatise on Vision) says:
"As for entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, this is the fourth dhyāna. Having arisen from this meditative concentration, he extended the second finger of his right hand to emit radiance."

In an instant, his fame filled the entire Jambudvīpa. O bhikṣus, when those from distant regions desired to equal his supernatural powers, Ṭhapa followed along with one bhikṣu for the purpose of establishing a dwelling place;
as for the dwelling places established by the remaining bhikṣus, they were all transformation bodies, no different from his true body.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: According to the principles of the Buddha-dharma, transgressions ought to be confessed, while merits [should be...]

Regarding the concealment of virtues: for what reason does he emit light? [It is] to manifest his own virtues. The answer is that there are two ways of manifesting virtue: first, for the sake of gain and fame;
second, for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings. If it is for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings, he acts with mastery according to the occasion.

There is no obstruction. As for the fact that light issued from the hand of Trapuṣa, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states there are eight causes and conditions by which light issues from the hand.
First, to stop slander and demonstrate that one is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.

For example, when a Brahmin woman slandered the Buddha, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records that the Brahmin woman Ciñcā tied a wooden bowl to her belly and slandered the Buddha, saying, "He has slept with me."

Because she had committed adultery, she became pregnant (the character used here is *shēn*). The Buddha replied, "I possess the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth;
how could such a thing be possible? Śāriputra, [the Buddha continued,] "Supernatural power was used because it was gnawed by mice; might the ten powers also be considered a manifestation of virtue?
Two bhikṣus who had ceased their studies and were practicing meditation saw those engaged in monastic affairs and conceived thoughts of contempt and disparagement. Fire then issued from their hands.
First, it was to extinguish the mind of competitiveness that looks down upon others with contempt.
Second, it was to subdue the arrogant minds of forest-dwelling bhikṣus who constantly claimed that city-dwelling bhikṣus are always in a state of distracted mind;

thus, although Upāli was amidst worldly affairs, he emitted light through his supernormal power to separate the monks' bedding, thereby humbling their arrogance. Fourth, it was to manifest the karmic fruit of diligent effort.
1. To encourage those who are indolent in their understanding; 2. To cause the roots of merit of the donors to increase; 3. To demonstrate that even when slandered, his mind does not waver; 4.
To manifest that the Saṃgha possesses great majestic power—since the distributor of bedding beds has such supernatural power, how much more so the other great virtuous ones?
How could they not be lofty and superior? 5. To cherish right livelihood and ensure it is not abandoned now.

[Fragmentary. He constantly dwells in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is also responsible for the bedding and requisites. Because the Sangha is harmonious and he is able to manage these matters, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"This man served as an administrator for the Sangha and constantly entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi*. With one hand he emitted light, and with the other he assigned the bedding and requisites.
At that time, five hundred visiting bhikṣus arrived; at night, Ṭhapaka [the steward] simultaneously illuminated all five hundred of them. One.
At that time, he was granted bedding and requisites (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "to protect one's own practice and cause the Dharma to endure for a long time," it is established that slandering others while having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense oneself is called "corrupting one's own practice.

Once one's practice is corrupted, one is unable to uphold the Dharma; thus, even if one were made to live for a thousand years, the Dharma would not avoid falling into ruin, as one lacks the capacity to sustain it.
In the past it was thus; now it is the opposite. Therefore, it is said that this causes the Dharma to abide for a long time.

To cause those who practice the Brahma-faring to dwell in peace while cultivating the Path means that although they are inwardly free from transgression, they are outwardly subjected to false accusations. This disturbs and confuses the worthy and virtuous, causing them to abandon their cultivation of the Path.
By establishing this precept now, they shall obtain the conditions of tranquility to cultivate the Path.

Regarding the statement that "slander is established through falsehood," the [opponent] asserts: if slander were to have falsehood as its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it would not be called slander;

therefore, at the time of slandering, one relies on a fabrication, and there is no separate offense of fabrication. Now, the Master of the *Chao* (the *Nanshan Shu*) maintains the general principle that there must be the intention to deceive the Sangha, which also entails the offense of fabrication.
This is like the case of killing one's father who is an Arhat: because the father has cultivated the Path and attained Arhatship, if one now...

To kill them constitutes one *ānantarya* (immediate) offense on account of violating the kindness of one's nurturer; it constitutes another *ānantarya* offense on account of destroying the world’s field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle 16:
King Udayana had a queen who was permitted by the king to leave the household life. She attained the stage of *anāgāmin* and was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Flying into the air, he exhorted the king to renounce the world. The king immediately abdicated his throne and, having entrusted it to the crown prince, left home to study the Way.
He dwelt beneath the trees in a forest to the left and right of the city. When the crown prince saw his father, he was constantly afraid that he would reclaim the throne.

At that time, the king-bhikṣu had never seen the Buddha and wished to go and pay him homage; having thought this, he set out but then forgot his sitting mat. After a short while, he returned to retrieve it.

When the son saw the king returning, he feared that the king would issue orders to kill everyone quickly—slaughtering all śramaṇas as well—and thus he urged the messenger to carry out the king’s command.
The bhikṣu said, "I have left the household life; what I seek I have not yet attained. Please grant me a brief respite. The messenger consented to this.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu applied himself diligently to contemplation and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. In this manner, after four such intervals, he attained the four fruits of *śrāmaṇya*.
He then said to the messenger, "You may do as you please. Return and tell your king: 'I did not covet the throne;
I returned for a moment because I had forgotten my sitting mat. If you kill me, you will be killing your father and killing an Arhat. Consider that you shall suffer great misery for a long night.
Having spoken, he submitted to death. The messenger returned and informed the king. When the king heard these words, blood flowed from his mouth.

[He] departed. Having been born in his physical body, he entered the great hells. At that time, King Bimbisāra and his neighboring states, having previously heard his teachings, had resolved to kill all śramaṇas;

fearing they might enter their own territories, they ordered men to guard the gates of all monasteries (vihāras). Now, to distinguish this meaning: it clarifies that at the time of slandering, there is also the offense of falsehood.
Lì says: "The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* does not list a separate offense for [this] *pārājika*. To this, the objection is raised: "As for my..."
If one intends to harm the owner by falsely killing an animal, one does not incur a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) for harming the owner, but incurs a *pāyattika* for taking life.
Answer: Slander is necessarily based on falsehood; there is no slander that is not false, and therefore it constitutes a single offense. Theft, however, is not fixed in this way:

there are cases where one harms the owner without resorting to killing, such as stealing cloth or silk; and there are cases where one harms the owner while also resorting to an animal. That is to say...

This refers, for example, to killing another's domestic animal. In this case, because the two objects [of the offenses] are distinct—the act of harming the owner and the act of taking life—one incurs two offenses.
Slander is not like this; it necessarily depends upon falsehood to be established, and thus incurs only one offense.

This is the intention of Master Li (Lì). Liang (Liáng) says: "One should formulate two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to distinguish them in relation to one another. The first is: harming the owner without killing the animal."

1. Stealing money or silk [is an offense of theft, but not slander]. 2. Killing livestock [is an offense of killing, but] not damaging the owner’s property; this refers to killing wild animals. 3. Damaging the owner’s property and killing livestock;

this refers to stealing and killing pigs or sheep. 4. Neither; this refers to taking objects that have no owner. Regarding the application of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) by contrasting [theft] with slander:

1. Falsehood that is not slander; this refers to those who act contrary to their perception. 2. Slander that is not falsehood (this category does not exist in principle). 3. [Falsehood that is also slander...]
To slander this is false; that which relies on characteristics is the [true] one. The fourth is "neither of both," the pure bhikṣu.
Since it lacks one phrase, it is not of the same category as theft.

"Excluding the three lower assemblies" refers to the two characters [at the beginning of the phrase]. This clarifies that the three lower assemblies are merely subsumed within the two divisions [of the Saṃgha].

Regarding the question in the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) as to why slandering the three lower assemblies is considered minor: the explanation states that the emotional gravity of such slander and harassment is slight, and it does not obstruct spiritual cultivation;

furthermore, the offense committed is minor, and the one who slanders is not subject to severe retribution. This is similar to cases of striking or robbing, where the distinction between the upper two [assemblies] and the lower three applies.

In that case, the [offense] for the three lower categories would be light. If so, why is it that among the offenses of "accusation" (*pārājika*), a *śrāmaṇera* is treated as equal to a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*)?

The answer is: it is because there is no difference in their being in opposition to the community (*saṃgha*). This is why the formal act of confession (*saṃvara*) is established equally for both the great and the small. If so, since being in opposition to the community is one and the same, [the offenses should be equal].

Regarding "those who follow along with the same offense": this refers to monks and nuns following one another. They are likewise subject to the collective agreement regarding the division of offenses into light and heavy.

As for the statement, "If a nun follows a suspended bhikṣu, she incurs a *pārājika*; if a monk follows, he incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* or *duṣkṛta*," the answer is: because a nun has formal instruction (*śikṣamāṇā*) that can be cited as a precedent, she incurs a *pārājika*; whereas for a monk, it is the reverse of the former case, and thus he incurs only a *duṣkṛta*.
It was further asked: "For what reason is it that slandering a nun is treated the same as [slandering] a full monk, while striking a nun is treated the same as [striking] a novice?
The answer was: "Striking is based on the inferiority of rank; slandering concerns the practice of cultivation. This differs from other Vinayas where striking and slandering carry the same offense.

Regarding the statement 'the mental conception [of the object] is considered pure, which does not hinder the fact that she is actually impure,' the established view says: although the person being slandered is actually impure, it is still possible to slander her."

Regarding a person, if one harbors a pure perception and slanders them, one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. It does not matter whether the object is pure or impure; provided that one harbors a pure perception and slanders them, an offense is committed.
According to the various interpretations in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there are differing views. The first states: "Even though he is a bhikṣu, his person must be pure.
This is because, as in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one who is not a bhikṣu in terms of having committed a *pārājika* offense may still be slandered with groundless charges and so forth. Furthermore...

It is like being expelled from a village or a dwelling; because one has committed an offense, one is deemed impure (*aśuci*). If that is so, why does the Vinaya text state: "That person is not pure; he who slanders him commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense"? The answer is:

this refers only to the commission of offenses belonging to the lower four categories (*catuḥpārājika*). If that is so, why is it said that striking [another] constitutes a grave offense of falling (*sthūlātyaya*)?

The answer is: regarding mutual provocation, the distinction is made according to the status of the act; regarding slander, the distinction is made according to the disciplinary penalty (*daṇḍa*). Therefore, the clear and the turbid must be distinguished. Furthermore...

One interpretation states that one who slanders [another] for being impure also commits an offense. Generally speaking, when discussing the monastic laws (*saṃghadharma*), one relies solely on what has been seen or heard;

therefore, to contradict what was seen as pure and to declare of another that they have committed an offense—thereby distressing oneself and others—is a crime equal to that of the turbid [offense]. It cannot be treated according to the specific circumstances [of the original case].
For instance, in the circumstances of the first precept, how could there be a nun? When the root precept says "a bhikṣu who is not a pārājika," etc., this is based on the *nidāna* (the origin story).
It is said: furthermore, regarding the phrase "in accordance with the sentiments and perceptions of the slanderer," why is it that slander is added? Therefore, the Vinaya states:

"If that person is not pure, and one slanders them by claiming they have committed an offense when they have not seen such a transgression, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense; this is like the characteristics of a heavy *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

The preceding explanations were derived from related contexts, yet they do not accord with what is stated in the *Vinaya* under the section on "Prohibitions" (*pratiṣedha-dharma*): "If one prohibits [an action] when there is none..."

If there were no remaining [factors], the negation would not be established; this serves to counteract the sin of slander. "Remaining" refers to the gravity [of the offense], while "agent" refers to one who has previously committed [the act].

How can it be said otherwise? Someone asked: "If that which is slandered is actually impure, yet the slanderer forms a perception of purity and says to others 'it is impure,' thereby incurring the *śeṣa* (residual) offense—if my object was actually not a human being, but I formed the mental conception of it as a human being..."
Regarding perception: if one commits murder according to one's perception, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If the victim is actually not a human being, yet I slander them as such because they are actually impure, but I maintain the perception of purity within my mind and maintain the perception of a human within my mind—if, while possessing the perception of purity, I declare them to be impure.
If one obtains the remains [of a non-human], should one also incur a *pārājika* offense for killing a non-human while perceiving them as a human?

If it is argued that the offense is established because slandering another is done with a mind of malicious intent, then since the mind of one who intends to kill a person is extremely evil, why would this not be a grave offense? In this case, the two are indeed equal.

Why is it that slandering one who is impure while perceiving them as pure constitutes a *pārājika* offense, whereas killing one who is not a human being while perceiving them as a human being has varying degrees of gravity?

In both cases of slandering and killing, the perception and the object are mutually contradictory; what principle explains this inequality in cause and effect? Answer: Slandering is defined by the falsity of the mind, whereas killing involves both the mind and the object being real. If one objects that [the offense] would be unestablished because there is no basis (*amūlaka*) or because the act was not completed, the established position is as follows: [The text continues: ...because the mind is directed toward the actual object, the offense is established even if the physical act is not fully completed.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there is no basis" and so forth, it is argued that since the intent is directed toward the actual person, the gravity of the offense is determined by the reality of the object and the nature of the mental state. Thus, although the external action may differ, the internal motivation—whether it be the false assertion of slandering or the lethal intent of killing—is what determines the karmic consequence. Therefore, the disparity in the causal relationship between these two offenses is logically consistent.

"Obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) means to bring forward [an accusation]. "Without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) refers to having committed a grave offense; within the monastic community, being severed from the legal status [of a monk] is called "without remainder.
This clarifies that although one has committed a sin without remainder, if the accuser has not yet verified the three bases (*trīṇi mūlāni*), the formal charge is not established.
One must instead be dealt with for the crime of slander. This principle is derived from the *Āvaraṇavastu* (Section on Obstructions).
"If it is not so, I shall not accept it. According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the Dharma Master says:
"The one who would slander [the teaching] goes before the Saṃgha and addresses the Saṃgha, saying: 'I pray that the Venerable Ones will joyfully uphold this for our sake.
The Saṃgha should then adjudicate this matter. If they say, 'The Saṃgha shall adjudicate this matter for us,' he should not delay. If it is so, I shall accept it."
"Accept it. If it is not so, I will not accept it. If one speaks these words, the Sangha should say to the slanderer:
"First, pay homage to the Buddha," and so forth, exactly as in the *Shuochao* (云云). Only after this should they question the slandered monk and adjudicate according to the Dharma.
This means that since the person who brought the charge was previously an untrustworthy individual, one must not immediately believe them.
He said: "One must first employ the aforementioned expedients. Once the mind has become supple, one may then summon the person who made the accusation and inquire into the facts of the matter.
If there is indeed an offense, one must punish the crime; if it is not true, one must immediately punish the slander according to the law."

The following clarifies the first [category], the non-offense regarding the reality of the act (*vastu*). 1. **Reality of the act**: This refers to actually committing sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or lying. 2. **Reality of the perception**:
This means that one actually perceives the person before oneself as having committed an offense and conceives the thought that they have sinned.

If one speaks in contradiction to this perception, then because the mental conception is false and erroneous, it constitutes slander. 3. **Reality of the fact**: As established, for example, in the case of killing a single person, there must still be...
This refers to the killing of Zhang Ren; it corresponds to the eleventh [offense] in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Thus, that text states:

"If one says of oneself, 'I killed my father,' and then slanders by saying, 'I killed my mother' or 'I committed a pārājika offense,' provided the four or three bases of cognition (*indriya*) do not correspond to reality:

if what was seen is called 'seen' and what was heard is called 'heard,' this is termed 'non-correspondence. If what was seen is called 'heard,' or what was heard is called 'doubtful,' both constitute slander. Li states: "Observing blue and so forth..."

To call this "seeing" (*darśana*). To receive echoes and consume sounds is called "hearing" (*śravaṇa*). The *Śāstra* states that visual consciousness arises concomitantly with seeing, and auditory consciousness arises concomitantly with hearing.
Following seeing and hearing, when one hesitates and cannot decide, and the mind lacks firm resolve, it is termed "doubt" (*vicikitsā*).

Regarding the fifth point, "the precepts do not contradict one another in reality": for example, if one says they have committed theft, yet falsely claims they have committed sexual misconduct, this is called a "contradiction. (Bīn)

It is said: Of these, the five above are actual [transgressions], while the four below may be so. Regarding the first, the "actual truth," it should be subsumed under the remaining categories as appropriate;
it should not be established separately.

The ninth [offense], the false accusation regarding the root precepts, has the same conditions for transgression and the same intent for its establishment as before; it differs only in that it concerns a false [accusation]. Lì asked:

Both are equally slanderous. Why are they divided into two precepts? Answer: If one considers the basis of groundlessness (*amūlaka*), since both arise simultaneously and are not distinct, logically they should have been formulated as a single rule.
However, the former case involves groundlessness, while the latter involves a false basis; therefore, they must be separated.

Furthermore, regarding the three bases for slandering another, each incurs a separate offense. Why are they combined under a single principle? If one considers the resulting offense, it is not necessarily [the same].
[The offense of] *pāyattika* should also be established as threefold; however, because there is no basis [for distinguishing them], they are equal in terms of the meaning of the offense incurred.

Furthermore, since it is possible for multiple people to witness a single transgression, they are formulated together. The origin story (*nidāna*) is as found in the Vinaya; when the time comes, it shall be entrusted to the expounder (and so forth).
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in the past, the Bhikṣu Dabba once served as the distributor of food (*bhojanapariṇāyaka*). At that time, there was...
There was a bhikṣu named Liànyuè who was an arhat. His appearance was upright and handsome as he walked along a road.

A certain woman saw him and gave rise to lustful attachment; she followed him with her gaze, unable to let him go. At that time, a man who knew about food saw this and, thinking they had previously engaged in illicit relations, spoke these words:
"This bhikṣu must have committed an evil act with this woman," thereby slandering the noble ones.
Therefore, he fell into hell. Once his retribution was exhausted, he emerged; by virtue of his original wholesome karma, he encountered a Buddha and attained the Way.

However, due to the power of residual karma, he suffered this slander. According to the *Saṃyukta-ratnapitaka-sūtra*, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a young bhikṣu with handsome features and a beautiful countenance.
Before he had returned from begging for alms, a woman, infatuated by his physical form and beauty, gazed at him.
The bhikṣu did not abandon his gaze. At that time, the bhikṣu Dhava was serving as the supervisor of the granaries.

He happened to see this woman following the bhikṣu and immediately slandered her, saying, "This woman must have had an illicit affair with that bhikṣu. Because of these causes and conditions, she fell into the three evil realms;
even until today, the residual karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, and she is still subjected to slander. Furthermore, in the past, under Kāśyapa...
When the Buddha was practicing the Way as a renunciant, he now attained Arhatship.

Regarding the first case of "different realms" (*visabhāga*): it refers to seeing a sheep engaging in sexual intercourse and immediately saying, "I saw a person leading an animal," thereby slandering the person;

since humans and animals are distinct, this is called a "different realm. Regarding the second case of "different offenses": it refers to seeing an offense of the minor category (*pāyantika*) and [accusing someone of] the first category [offense].
It is slander. Furthermore, it refers to seeing someone commit killing or stealing, yet slandering them by saying they have committed sexual misconduct. Regarding the third "different person":

the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that this refers to seeing a bhikṣu whose name and surname are identical to those of the person being slandered, and then using the fact that the former has committed an offense to slander the latter.

Regarding the fourth "different time": *Liyun* states that this refers to seeing an offense committed yesterday and claiming it was committed today, or even seeing it in the morning and [claiming it occurred at another time].
[This refers to] the evening. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Regarding the difference between the timing of being a layperson and a monastic:

if one commits an offense while a layperson, it is not considered a transgression at this [monastic] time. It further states: "If the person being slandered has committed an offense and there is no confusion, and the Sangha subsequently investigates and finds that the offense occurred at a different time, they shall likewise punish the slanderer.
Regarding the fifth point, "the echo": if a bhikṣu speaks of himself and hears the sound of his own voice, and then slanders based on that echoed sound.
