This also constitutes an offense. That is to say, if the person capable of slandering calls out in a mountain valley, "A certain bhikṣu has committed sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth," and another, following that echo, takes it as the basis and says, "I have heard this;
this bhikṣu has committed such offenses," this also constitutes slander.
The Tenth Precept: Against Causing a Schism in the Saṃgha Despite Being Admonished. The intent of the prohibition is as explained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) [and so forth].

To alter the true Dharma with false teachings and to divide the assembly into separate factions is called "causing a schism. To stubbornly persist and refuse to relinquish this course despite being admonished is termed "defying admonition.

The precept refers to the practice that serves as a protection. Now, causing a schism in the Saṃgha is not itself a *pārājika* offense; it becomes a *pārājika* only because of the act of defying admonition. There are two kinds of Saṃgha: if one divides the Saṃgha of the Dharma...

Breaking the *saṃgha* by means of the wheel constitutes a heavy *duṣkṛta*; breaking the *saṃgha* by means of the ritual (*karmavācanā*) constitutes a light *duṣkṛta*. According to the *Shoushu*, "The *saṃgha* encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, and in reality is immeasurable.
Now, for the sake of brevity, we shall present the essentials and divide it according to the teachings into two types: first, the *karmasaṃgha*.

Because it lacks manifesting superior virtues, it is designated as such based on its harmony with the ritual procedures of the *karmavācanā* teachings; thus it is called [the ritual *saṃgha*]. Second is the *dharmacakra-saṃgha*."
The Sangha. That which the Buddha taught as the pure doctrine, which accords with principle and serves as a guide for practitioners, is called the Dharma.
Because this very Dharma can destroy the fetters and latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), transforming the ordinary person into a noble one, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).

If explained according to its essence, the wheel has untainted emptiness-contemplation (*anāsrava-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) as its substance. The reason it is named a "wheel" is that it receives its name through metaphor, like the precious wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), because it is true...

Reality is the essence, as in the previously mentioned emptiness-contemplation, the untainted [dharmas], and so forth. What is now called "breaking" refers to breaking the dharma of the Ten Wheels school;

there is no separate Wheel-Dharma Sangha to be broken, for this dharma is the cause for the establishment of the Sangha. If one speaks of *karma*, it is the method for governing the Sangha and applies exclusively to the Great Sangha (bhikṣus).
Within a single boundary (*sīmā*), if the *karma* is performed separately by each group, it does not constitute a valid deliberation. Breaking this alone—
This refers to the schism of a *saṃgha* in terms of its formal ritual (*karman*), not the schism of the *saṃgha* as a substance.

This too is a cause for the establishment of the *saṃgha*. All of this is an analysis of "schism" (*bhedana*) based on the specific action. Regarding the substance of the *saṃgha*, the treatise states: "Some point to non-mind (*acitta*) as its substance.

However, when the Vinaya masters analyze the *saṃgha*, they regard it as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). It is formed by gathering four [monks]; apart from these four, there is no separate substance. Thus, the four individuals themselves are pointed to as the substance.

Therefore, the Vinaya states: "A *saṃgha* consists of four persons; if there are more than four, it is likewise so," and so forth. To distinguish the breaking of the *dharmacakra-saṃgha* according to the Dharma and its application:
the Eightfold Noble Path is designated as the wheel. The three factors of right speech, right action, and right livelihood belong to the category of morality (*śīla*) and constitute the hub.
The two factors of right view and right intention belong to the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) and constitute the spokes. Right mindfulness and... [text continues]
Concentration consists of two factors; it is the numerical category of the rim (*nemi*). Right effort is the numerical category of diligence (*vīrya*); it is the wheel’s rotation.

These four combined form a single therapeutic remedy (*pratipakṣa*) that can crush (*cūrṇayati*) birth and death; therefore, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). The verse says: The three—verbal action, livelihood, and morality—are the numerical categories of the hub (*nābhi*).

Right view and right intention are the numerical categories of the spokes (*ara*). Right mindfulness and right concentration are the numerical categories of the rim (*nemi*). Right effort is the numerical category of diligence.
He caused Devadatta to establish a false Triple Gem on Mount Gayā: he claimed for himself the status of the Buddha to replace the true Buddha-Gem;
he taught five false dharmas to replace the true Dharma-Gem of the Eightfold Path; and he established the four [groups] beginning with the three types of disciples to replace the true Sangha-Gem.
If one causes the Wheel of Dharma not to turn and the practice of meditation and recitation not to proceed within the trichiliocosm, this is called "breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha" (and so forth).
These offenses, from the precept against rejecting admonition down to the lower sections— meaning those in the third category of ninety [offenses] below, such as the case of Ariṣṭa— are as follows.
Regarding the bhikṣu Cunda, who claimed that sensual desire does not obstruct the path: there are also other individuals who offer admonitions, yet these are rarely employed in the world.

This clarifies the matter of violating such admonitions; even if a transgression occurs, one fails to offer an admonition. Since this practice is rare and was not observed at that time, it is now also omitted.
Therefore, it is said to be "rarely employed. Alternatively, there may be those who possess only the cause but have not yet realized the fruit; this refers to the following:

Regarding the matter of schism in the Saṃgha: since there is currently no Buddha, with whom could one compete for the sake of conversion? Therefore, there is no ultimate offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
If such a mind were now to arise, it might serve as a cause for the Saṃgha to fall into dispute and disharmony;

however, since the parricide of causing a schism in the Saṃgha is not established, the secondary offense of violating a formal admonition is likewise absent. Thus it is said that the result has not yet been determined. This applies specifically to the period when the Buddha is in the world.
Regarding this, it would be excellent to cite the verse from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Záxīn) below to explain this point. Thus, the verse from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:

"Before the boundaries have been established, After [the boundaries] have been established, Before the Muni has entered Parinirvāṇa, While the inner peace has not yet arisen, And when there is no 'first pair'— During these six periods, It is not called a 'schism of the Wheel of Dharma.
The commentary notes: "These two types of schisms of the Saṃgha" refers to the establishment of both the leader (*pradhāna*) and the companion (*sahāya*).

This constitutes two [factors]. For example, Devadatta is the principal, who breaks the Saṃgha and defies admonition; the three types of hearing and so forth are the companions, who assist in breaking the Saṃgha and defying admonition.
Regarding those who defile the community and are expelled for slander: [Master] Li states that this is a brief reference to the following text.

As for "it does not preclude that evil conduct actually constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense": Li says that "net" (*jāla*) refers to the Dharma. This clarifies that while the defiling of the community is indeed evil conduct, it is not itself a *pārājika* offense;

rather, because one violates the admonition of the Saṃgha, and since such admonition is the "Dharma-net," the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is incurred precisely due to that violation of the admonition. The offense arises from...
The violation of the dharma of admonition arises from below; admonition is the net of the Dharma, hence it is called "arising from the net.

This is intended to clarify that the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* arises from within the net of the teachings. Sengshen says: "In the final age, although bhikṣus commit evil deeds, there will be no one to provide admonition."

Although the practice of admonition has been abandoned, those who commit evil deeds will inevitably violate the net of the teachings. Since they have been ensnared by this net of the teachings, they consequently incur guilt.
Guilt arises from the net; thus it is said. This means that having committed evil deeds, one is caught in the net of conduct.
Furthermore, it is said that by performing such evil deeds in the presence of the laity, one destroys the laypeople's faith, causing both parties to incur guilt due to the bhikṣu’s misconduct.
Because one ensnares those before them with the net of sin, it is called "the net of birth. "Birth" refers to the class of ordinary people and sentient beings.

Alternatively, regarding the discernment of characteristics and matters that may be generally practiced, it is established as follows: for instance, in precepts such as those concerning defiling the household, planting flowers and fruits oneself, or causing others to plant them—these are all matters of discerning characteristics.
As for "matters that may be generally practiced," this refers to the fact that the flowers, fruits, and so forth mentioned in this sutra are matters that apply universally.
It is evil. If one plants seeds for the Buddha-dharma and the like, this is called a virtuous matter; it is "penetration. If one plants seeds for worldly people, this is an evil matter;
it is called "obstruction. Although I have now distinguished these characteristics of defiling the household, such characteristics possess both penetration and obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that "matters may be universally practiced," and so forth. [Master] Shen says: This clarifies the various matters of admonition.

Although they were all simultaneously abolished at the time, the reason I now distinguish their characteristics is to enable people to recognize what constitutes upholding or violating, advancing or declining, and to ensure that universal protection is maintained;
hence, it is called "universal practice. Or, as for those who may rely on them without committing an offense—what prevents such people from existing? For instance, regarding the breaking of...
Regarding monastic affairs, these will not exist in the final age, nor will there be matters requiring admonition.

Now, in clarifying their characteristics, I fear that those who engage in separate eating and separate *poṣadha* may still cause the schism of the Saṃgha. I shall now briefly clarify their characteristics so that those of broad understanding may recognize them;

thus, in their practice and protection, they may avoid transgression—hence it is called "universal application. Alternatively, the opening conditions are essential for the time; this is established as clear, as in the case of [the rule on] defilement.

Regarding the household precepts: since they have been opened for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, one may plant flowers and fruits and have others gather the flowers to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha.

As this is a matter of timely necessity, such an opening condition is indeed appropriate. Within the text concerning these permissions, it is stated that there is no fault and there is merit in gathering [flowers] to offer to the Buddha.
This is a matter of necessity at that time. Furthermore, as in the passage below concerning food and drink given to the sick, parents, and others, these constitute exceptions to the rule;
how could these not be matters of necessity? Again, regarding the *śeṣa* offense incurred for disregarding admonitions, the text of the exception states: "If the person who is able to admonish..."

If one violates the rules of sinful dharmas, there is no offense. Furthermore, if one breaks with an evil friend (pāpamitra) intending to perform an evil act, there is no sin in breaking [with them], nor is there an offense of causing a schism in the Sangha (saṃghabheda). These are all essential points.

The principle is that this must not be transgressed. This means that since the Great Master has concealed his traces at the Twin Śāla Trees, with whom can one now compete for the sake of transformation?
Since such a thing does not exist, it is said that it must not be transgressed. Now, I shall tentatively set them forth in order to enable those newly learning to recognize their characteristics.
First, to clarify the establishment of false Triple Gems: one should know that Devadatta claimed to be the Buddha, thereby supplanting the true Buddha-Gem, and preached the five heterodox dharmas.
[He] replaces the True Dharma Jewel; [he is] the fourth among those such as Tripuṣṭa and others who replace the True Saṃgha Jewel;

thus it is said. Regarding "the third *karmavācanā* having been completed": the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Ji) states that when Devadatta did not desist after being admonished three times, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Devadatta, in a past life, he already rejected such admonitions and encountered suffering. In the past, there was a brahmin..."
In the midst of a wilderness, a well was established for the sake of providing water. As evening approached, there was a pack of jackals that drank the remaining water from the pool.

Among them was a leader of the jackals who did not drink from the pool; instead, he thrust his head into a water-jar, and having drunk, he carried the jar aloft, smashed it, and with the mouth of the jar piercing through his head, he took this as his pleasure.
The other jackals admonished him, saying, "Do not do this! The leader of the jackals said: "I..."
He was merely seeking his own gratification and paid no heed to the affairs of others. In this manner, he broke fourteen jars; though admonished many times, he did not desist.
The owner of the well observed him and, thereupon, fashioned wooden jars that were so solid they were difficult to break, yet easy for him to insert his head into and difficult for it to emerge from.
He placed them by the well and waited with a staff in hand. At dusk, as before, [the man] drank his fill and was then struck down, but the jars could not be broken. The well—
The master, wielding a staff, struck and killed the jackal. A deva in the sky spoke this verse: "A wise person heeds the words of compassion;
one who is perverse does not accept counsel. By stubbornly persisting, he invited this calamity and lost his own life. Such is the foolish jackal."
"Having encountered this suffering of the wooden jar," the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "the leader of the jackals was Devadatta;
the pack of jackals are the present-day bhikṣus. This occurred in the past; now, refusing to accept admonition, he shall fall into the evil realms and suffer for a long night."

As explained in detail in the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa Sūtra), according to that work: Since the Buddha’s passing beneath the twin śāla trees, the sun of wisdom has set and the Wheel of Dharma has ceased its turning;

who then would strive to break it? Nevertheless, regarding the two factions of the heterodox and the orthodox, and the four reliances of person and dharma, the fierce winds of karma suddenly surge and the waves of the ocean of delusion are tossed in alarm.

A schism in the Saṃgha that breaks the Wheel of Dharma does not occur in this degenerate age; however, a schism in the Saṃgha concerning ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) may perhaps still occur at times. Therefore, the present [discussion] is based on...

This is refuted by two [points]. To distinguish between right and wrong, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "If in three directions there are at least eight [monks], the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is destroyed.
If in Jambudvīpa there are nine, the Wheel of Dharma is destroyed. Regarding the number nine: Devadatta, as a false Buddha, supplants the True Buddha-Jewel;

the five types of false teachings he propounded supplant the True Dharma-Jewel; and the three [groups] beginning with those who have heard [the Dharma], etc., totaling four, supplant the True Saṅgha-Jewel. (The above is based on the capacity [of the agents]).
[The term] "refutation" (*bhaṅga*). Regarding the four types of *saṃgha*-schisms (this refers to the object of refutation), it is for this reason that non-harmony constitutes a schism.

Why is this so? As for the Tathāgata not being included within the ten [categories]: the *Abhidharmakośa* states that a schism occurs elsewhere [than in his presence], not directly in the presence of the World-Honored One.
First, because the Tathāgata cannot be lightly provoked; second, because his verbal teachings are most worthy of trust and acceptance. Thus, the *Cittaviveka* says: "The Great Master..."

Within the assembly, because he lacks majestic radiance, [the schism] is first distinguished by location. The breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) occurs throughout the three directions; in the northern direction, the Dharma does not exist.

Since there are disciples of the Buddha in the three directions, they are able to preside over the *karmavācanā*. However, it should be understood that the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is restricted to the southern direction.

Second, regarding the number [of monks], it is as previously explained. Third, regarding the time: the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is restricted to the period when the Buddha is in the world. [The breaking of the wheel occurs] after his *parinirvāṇa*.

The *pāṭayantika* offense does not exist after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; however, the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) exists both during the Buddha’s lifetime and after his passing, as it possesses the same sense of "breaking" [the community]. Fourth, regarding the persons involved:
the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) must necessarily involve the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*), whereas the *karmavācanā* extends to the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).

Nevertheless, because the female body of a nun lacks the capacity for faith in the Buddha and because those in the three lower assemblies have not yet received full ordination, they are not eligible for the *karmavācanā*. One who breaks the *karmavācanā* does not require the title of "Buddha"; therefore, the *karmavācanā* applies to nuns as well.
There are [such persons]. Among the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*), one must be pure. Among those who are pure, one must be widely learned and possess great wisdom.

Among those with great wisdom, one must be a practitioner of insight (*dṛṣṭicarita*) rather than a practitioner of craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*). A practitioner of craving is weak; they do not reach a definitive conclusion regarding good and evil.

A practitioner of insight is resolute and fierce; they decisively and thoroughly discern good and evil. Thus, a verse in the *Cittaviveka* says: "Before and after the boundaries were established, the Muni had already attained Nirvāṇa."

[The Buddha] said: "When the *pāṃśu-skandha* (the 'mound of dust') has not yet arisen, and when the first pair [of disciples] does not exist—during these six periods, it is not called 'breaking the Wheel of Dharma'.

The commentary (*Śīla*) explains: "Regarding 'when the boundary has not been established,' this is because the person capable of breaking [the Saṃgha], who must perform the *karmavācanā*, requires that the formal act (*saṃghakarma*) take place within the boundary (*sīmā*)."

Those who are to be refuted include both those within and outside the Buddhist fold; however, the sense of "refutation" applies specifically to those who have accepted false teachings. Regarding the "former" and "latter" periods:

the former refers to when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, and the latter refers to the time he was about to enter parinirvāṇa. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The former is not long after the initial turning of the wheel of Dharma;
the latter is when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa. During these two periods, the great assembly was full of reverence.
Since they equally follow the single flavor, there is no contradiction. Thus, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* says: "The nine years at the Twin Trees clarify what was [taught] in the interim.
"The Muni has already entered Nirvāṇa" means that after his passing, there was no one to compete in conversion.

"When the tumor had not yet arisen" refers to Devadatta giving rise to evil precepts and evil views; this is called the "tumor. "And when there was no foremost pair" refers to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
These two constitute the first pair. Had these two not existed, even one capable of destroying [the Sangha] would not have been able to do so.

They exist only because the false and the correct manifest against one another. The *Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins* states: It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when the Sangha is divided during a meal, it shall be restored to harmony.
When Devadatta proclaimed the five heterodox dharmas, the proclamation reached as far as heaven and earth, throughout the three thousandfold world system.
In this world, the practice of meditation and recitation has ceased; among the worldly devas and humans, there is none who has awakened to the Way.

Heaven and earth are shrouded in darkness, as if at twilight, lacking harmony; heaven and earth are overturned. Therefore, it is necessary that the first two parties arise to break through [this state].
The following clarifies the non-transgression of the Dharma. Regarding two or three people who wish to perform an illegal *karmavācanā*:
it is established that a *karmavācanā* must be carried out by four persons; if only two or three are present, it is termed "illegal. There is no offense in breaking this [rule].

"Performing [the rite] for one without a residence" refers to performing the *karmavācanā* of banishment; it clarifies that the Saṃgha performs the banishment of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), an instructor (*ācārya*), or others.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: if it is broken, there is no offense. As for the statement that "if it is broken, this person does not commit an offense," it means that when the mind is correct and breaks what is false, or when there are non-dharmic conditions, an exemption from the offense is granted.
The Eleventh Precept: Assisting in the Schism of the Sangha in Defiance of Admonition. Regarding the explanation of the name:

when the Saṃgha performed a formal act (karmavācanā) to admonish Devadatta, his four companions acted as his shadow and echo, assisting him in accomplishing the schism. The Saṃgha subsequently offered admonitions, yet he rejected them and would not accept them; hence the name.

Regarding "the four companions who assist in breaking the Sangha through admonition": this refers to the three types of followers, such as those who have heard [the schism], and so forth—these four companions who assist in the breaking of the Sangha.
Regarding "admonishing the Sangha": it means that these four companions, in turn, admonish the Sangha, saying, "There is no need to perform the formal act;

what has been done by Devadatta is in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the discipline. It is called this because the Sangha is now formally admonishing these four companions. The three formal acts (*karmas*) are performed.
"Having committed it at the conclusion" means that one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*.
If one does not relinquish [the intention] during the course of any preceding *karmavācanā*, one commits one *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The Twelfth Precept on Corrupting Families, Expulsion, Slander, and Defying Monastic Admonition. The origin of this matter involved the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*). Previously residing in a village, they had originally sought material gain;

now, through their corrupt conduct that defiled families, they ruined the impartiality of the local people. Their transgression was so profound that the Saṃgha required to impose disciplinary punishment.

Therefore, the assembly of monks was commanded to go there to carry out the expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*). They immediately gave rise to slander, claiming that the monks were acting out of favoritism (*anunaya*).
[The Buddha said: "Hatred. At the time of the previous expulsion, six people committed the offense together; two fled and were not present in person, so they could not be expelled.
This is similar to [the case of] Bhaya. Pin said: "When he fled toward the royal road and the village, the Sangha did not punish him at that time because of the king's power."
It is called "fear resembling [that of] the king" because they were as if afraid of the king's power. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Śravaṇadatta and Mahīśadatta fled to the village of Rājapatha. Bin says: this refers to the path where the king habitually travels;
it is called the "royal road" (*rājapatha*), such as the area within a subsidiary city wall. Kālodāyin and Chanda went against...
He repented on the road, reformed his ways, and submitted; there was no offense remaining for which he could be punished.

He appeared to possess attachment (*rāga*), and the two, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, knelt before him in view [of the community], neither fleeing nor repenting. The Saṃgha performed an act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against him because he appeared to possess hatred (*dveṣa*).

For this reason, he slandered the Saṃgha, saying that they were possessed of attachment, hatred, fear, and so forth. If he were not admonished and exhorted, there would be no way for him to understand by himself.
Therefore, one must offer admonition so as to manifest that there is no flaw within. The Sangha is truly impartial;

since the Sangha has already adjudicated right and wrong for itself, yet [the offender] remains obstinate and refuses to relinquish their position, and having fulfilled the requirements for admonition contrary to the Dharma, they are charged with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Regarding the explanation of the terminology:

there are four kinds of illegality (1) based on households, (2) based on gain and offerings, (3) based on relatives and friends, and (4) based on the monastery (*saṃghārāma*). To defile the minds of pure persons is called "defiling a household. To expose such faults to the assembly is called [the offense of] "defiling a household."

"Expulsion" (*nissāraṇīya*): To falsely accuse someone of a crime they do not have is called "slander. To use reason to explain and persuade, yet to refuse and not comply, is called "defying admonition.

Thus it is said: "Slandering the Saṅgha is such [an offense]. This clarifies that while defiling a family is merely a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), because one slanders the Saṅgha and defies admonition, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).
If a bhikṣu takes flowers or fruit and gives them to a layperson (*gṛhapati*), it is established that this only clarifies the defilement of a family.
Regarding its characteristics: as for the matter of stealing, it has already been analyzed in the second precept on theft within the first section [of this work].

As for "performing bird calls" (*pai shuo zuo niao sheng*), *pai* is pronounced *pi* (with the tone reversed). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *pai* means "jesting"; furthermore, it also means "performance music.
Regarding "obtaining the four kinds of offerings or escaping various calamities," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this explains the meaning of residing in dependence upon a village. Text.

It is asked: What is meant by "dwelling in dependence upon a village"? If a bhikṣu obtains robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites within that village, this is called dwelling in dependence.

If he does not obtain these four requisites—robes, food, and so forth—but merely relies on the village to escape various hardships, this is also called dependence. Furthermore, if one does not rely on a village...
To avoid calamities. However, for one who dwells relying upon the boundary of a village, this is also called "dwelling by reliance.
[Master] Li states: "This is the intent of permitting reliance on a village. Master Li’s Commentary says: "There are two reasons for allowing reliance on a village:

first, the physical form has dependencies; it is only through provisional resources that it can be established. Therefore, clothing is required to shield the body and food to sustain the frame, so as to support the person while cultivating the Way."
This accomplishes one's own benefit. Second, it benefits the donor; by practicing giving toward the field of the Saṃgha, one obtains the merit of a reciprocal reward.

Because there are these two meanings, the reliance on a community (*āśraya-gaṇa*) is established. As for the statement "or to avoid various calamities," this refers to avoiding evil bandits, tigers, wolves, lions, and the like in the mountains.
If one is in a village, drinking alcohol or eating at improper times is not termed "defiling the household. This...

If one merely breaks the precepts oneself and thereby ruins the faith of the laity, this is not called "defiling the household," because the laypeople recognize through their worldly understanding that this is contrary to the Dharma.
However, if one destroys the laypeople's faith, respect, equanimity, and wholesome mind, this is indeed called conduct that defiles the household, and so forth.
The Thirteenth Precept on Refusing the Sangha and Defying Admonition. The incident originated with Channa—this is the same person as Chandaka—who was by nature perverse and obstinate.
Relying on his kinship within the Śākya clan, he treated the bhikṣus with contempt and arrogance. Furthermore, his mind was deluded as he committed offenses, yet he did not recognize his own faults.

Now that the Saṃgha has admonished him according to the Dharma, it would have been appropriate for him to submit and comply; instead, he sided with those of superior status and, relying on himself, continued to treat others with disdain.

The transgression of the underlying emotion is particularly grave; this is why it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Next, regarding the explanation of the name: to be perverse and self-opinionated is called "evil nature.

To stubbornly persist and refuse to comply, using the analogy of the harmony of the community, is called the precept against rejecting the Saṃgha and defying admonition. According to the *Jian lun* (Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra), it says:
Chanda did not accept the instruction of the bhikṣus. He said to the bhikṣus, "You should not instruct me;
I should instruct you. Why is this? The Buddha is my family Buddha. Why is this? I entered the mountains with the Buddha to study the Path."
I do not see even a single one of the elder monks who followed the Buddha as his attendant and, having attained the Path, turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, the Dharma is also my family’s Dharma; for this reason, I ought to instruct the elder Dharma-teachers. Question:
Why did Chanda not say that the Saṃgha is my family’s Saṃgha? Answer: Because he was quarreling with the assembly of monks, he did not say that the Saṃgha is [my family’s].
Regarding our own school’s *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the seventh fascicle states: "In the past, people already relied upon me to look down on others.
Formerly, there was a great Brahmin teacher who constantly instructed five hundred youths in the Brahmanical laws. These laws were not heard by those of low caste.

A slave born into the household, however, heard them because of those youths and was able to memorize them. Later, he fled to another country and studied the Brahmanical laws; having mastered them, [he became a teacher]."
Because he had heard [the teachings], he was able to retain everything he heard. His master was greatly pleased and gave him his daughter as a wife.

When the wife prepared food, she was constantly resentful and angry. The master of the slave went to seek refuge with him; the slave spoke privately, saying, "I am called 'Great Master'; he is my father.
I pray you do not reveal my situation, and I shall pay you the price for my service. The master of the slave replied, "You are truly my son. Send me away at once. 1.
At that time, his wife came secretly to pay homage at the feet of the brahmin and asked, "My husband is constantly dissatisfied with our food and drink;

I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will instruct me as to what my family originally used to eat. The master of the slave thought to himself, "To cause suffering to another's children"—and as he was about to leave, he taught her a verse, saying:
"Without kin, wandering through foreign lands, Deceiving all the people of the world, Coarse food is his constant meal; What need is there for fine food?"
"I dislike it. I give you this verse. When he was about to eat, the man recited it softly while turning his back.
Later, the wife tested him; after the slave heard it, he constantly spoke with a timid voice. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The master of the slave was I myself;
the slave was Udāyin (Chanda). At that time, he relied upon me to insult others; now he speaks in this same way. His words are contrary, yet their intent coincides."
The Sūtra instructs one to observe oneself, while the Vinaya requires one to offer admonition. Although these two texts appear contradictory, they are said to be "divergent in expression.

Yet, as both aim to abandon evil and aspire toward the fruits of the Path, they are said to be "concordant in intent. This Sūtra refers to the tenth chapter of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Thus, a verse from that scripture says:
"Regarding the speech of others, follow it without opposition; do not scrutinize whether others have acted or failed to act. At that time, the World-Honored One...
"Venerable One, you have spoken this verse solely for the sake of King Ajātaśatru.

Good son, it is also for those who wish to protect and uphold the unbroken precepts and achieve dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), yet perceive the faults of others, that this verse is spoken. (End of scriptural passage).
Regarding the six types of differences, it is established that these all concern the person being exhorted; when one observes the exhorter, there are six matters. Second, if...
Regarding the statement, "If one of dull faculties and lacking wisdom speaks without benefit, one should simply stop," Ji says: One should observe the person offering the admonition;
since they lack wisdom, one must say, "You should simply observe your own physical conduct and so forth; there is no need for you to admonish me.

Regarding the statement, "If one of sharp faculties and clever intelligence speaks with benefit, one should then admonish," this means that because the person offering the admonition possesses cleverness and sharp faculties...
Regarding wisdom: when one offers admonition, it must be done using the words of others. Third, if one has little learning or insight and their speech provides no benefit, they should stop;
one ought to say to them, "Since you have heard so little, why do you need to admonish me? You should simply observe your own conduct."

If one who has heard and seen extensively provides exhortation for the sake of what is beneficial and expansive, then the person being exhorted—who has likewise heard much and possesses expansive benefit—must accept the other's words.
Fourth, if one ceases [their practice] for the sake of gain and fame, the person capable of exhorting them...
If it is merely for the sake of fame and profit, and one originally lacks the intention to benefit others, then there is no need to follow their admonition.

Fifth, regarding "if for the sake of happiness in the present life, but desiring only to restrain oneself, one simply stops": this means that the person offering the admonition constantly dwells in solitary self-cultivation and finds joy in the Dharma for themselves;
thus, there is no need to accept their admonition, which is why it says "one simply stops. Another interpretation is that [the phrase] refers to happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*).
As for "Ciyun," this refers to when a person greedily engages in sitting meditation, reciting sutras, and so forth, ceasing whatever activity accords with their own inclinations.

As for "Binyun" saying, "For the sake of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*), one simply observes the body oneself": this is stated in terms of its general characteristics. To attain the Noble Path is called "happiness in the present life.
If explained according to specific characteristics, the fundamental dhyānas constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life; that is to say, upon entering meditative concentration, there is...
It is blissful, such as when the Buddha first attained the Way and experienced the bliss of liberation, and so forth.

Sixth, if one who has newly left the household life is still attached to wife and children, and the person offering admonition likewise possesses these same faults, there is no need to accept their words.

However, if one has long been immersed in the Buddha-dharma and so forth, it means that such a person must be admonished by others before they are capable of accepting their words. According to principle, this is so.
These four types of people must all be admonished. A guest said: "Regarding these four, there is no scriptural authority to rely upon;

they are merely established based on the intent of the ancient masters. First is the senior elder of long standing: this refers to those who, though currently many in number, are old monks who rely on their age to harbor an evil nature and use foul language and abuse.
Second is one who has long occupied the headship of the community: this refers to those who, even if not elderly by years, have long resided [in leadership].
1. Regarding those who are leaders of the assembly: since their virtue and reputation are already great, they often look down upon others; therefore, they too must be admonished. 2.

Regarding those of meager learning and shallow understanding who claim their wisdom surpasses others: this refers to those whose studies are extremely superficial yet consider themselves sufficient, and who compare their own virtue to that of the Buddha while dwelling in arrogance;
for this reason, they must be admonished. 3. Regarding those who gather with the eminent: as is common among people today, they occupy high positions and rely on their power.
Because one insults others, it is necessary to provide admonition; this refers to Channa within the context of the *śaikṣa* rules. Below, the non-offenses are clarified:
"If the matter is indeed so" means, as Li states, that one truly considers what one has done to be correct and thus lacks any emotional transgression.
This concludes the explanation of the second category, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules: the establishment [of this section] refers to the citation of the *Great Commentary* (*Da shu*), which provides a brief explanation in three sections:

first, the purpose and origin; second, the explanation of the names and the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, whether they apply to monks or nuns. First, regarding the explanation of the purpose: the prohibitions of the Noble Ones follow conditions and meander through myriad strands;

offenses arise due to persons, and the regulations subdue them as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. It is necessary to follow these according to the specific circumstances in order to encompass and cultivate [the path].
It is difficult to prepare for. If one does not mutually examine and scrutinize one another, there may be no sense of self-exhortation;

therefore, it is listed here. Second, regarding the explanation of the names and the identification of their essence: formerly it was said that because the private and the public are two distinct states, they are called "the two.

Among these, the four dharmas each lack a fixed standard, and are thus called "indeterminate" (aniyata). Regarding the "four dharmas," Lì says: first is the indeterminate offense, which refers to cases where one may commit a *pārājika* (defeat) offense.
Some commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; some commit a *pāyattika* offense; some commit all three together; or again, some commit two. This is because the specific gravity of the offenses differs.

The second case, "the indefinite accusation," means that since the offense committed is already indeterminate, one may raise the accusation based on what can be reliably stated as the facts; therefore, it is also called "indefinite."

Third, the uncertainty of self-accusation (*svavāda-aniyata*): Since the gravity of the offenses raised varies—whether minor or major—and since one must enumerate the specific crimes committed, how could there be a single standard?

It might even be argued that by self-accusation one does not incur an offense. Fourth, the uncertainty of the disciplinary penalty (*daṇḍa-aniyata*): If one confesses to a *pārājika* offense, one is punished with banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*);

if one confesses to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one is punished with the *parivāsa* penance, and so forth. Now, regarding what is called "uncertainty," these categories three and four originally did not exist; they were established in vain.

Regarding the treatment: although [the offense] occurs within two categories, the actual transgression has not yet been definitively established. The Vinaya states that "there is no fixed rule herein," which is why it is called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).
As for the explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), there are also many interpretations; I shall now briefly omit them all.

One master says that the three offenses recorded for private settings and the two offenses collected for public settings constitute the essence of the indeterminate. Xuan says this is not so; the essences of the three and two offenses differ both in name and category.
It is distinct. It is bundled together to form a single precept. The commentary explains: Sexual intercourse is a private rite commonly practiced in the secular world;

however, a bhikṣu is without a companion and remains alone. When he engages in coarse speech while in the company of a woman, it causes others to suspect and find it strange among the three categories of offenses.

Because the characteristics of the transgression are difficult to name, it is called "undetermined" (aniyata). The reason it must be prohibited is that when one who has left the household life wanders or enters a village settlement, due to...

When matters involve mutual defilement and disgrace, the damage incurred is no small matter; therefore, it is necessary to establish a regulation. Thus, three cases involving doubtful offenses are selected.
This state of doubt has not been regulated since ancient times; the teaching stipulates that the arising of doubt constitutes the essence of the precept (*śīla*).

If one were to take the three offenses as already established within the various categories (*varga*), why would it be necessary to specifically mention "the first" here? Therefore, the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: "As for..."
Why is this precept stated as indeterminate? The answer is: because there is actual transgression regarding matters in the future. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Since sitting in an improper place gives rise to a lack of faith, one should know that [the offense] is determined by doubt. Third, regarding whether monks and nuns exist [in the future]:
There are also many interpretations. Some say: "The rule was established that a bhikṣuṇī may not censure a bhikṣu; therefore, there was a laywoman who censured him on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī.

Since a bhikṣu may censure a bhikṣuṇī, there is no such case [of a laywoman censoring a bhikṣuṇī]. Others say: "Because it is prescribed that a bhikṣuṇī must have a companion, this precept does not exist [for her]. To this, an objection is raised:
Question: For what reason do nuns have precepts regarding sitting in private and so forth? The explanation states:

The reason these do not apply to nuns is that when a bhikṣu sits in a place where he might give rise to scandal with a woman, her husband may lose faith or even expel him; thus, the harm caused is profound, and the rule is therefore established for monks.
Although a nun sitting alone with a man may give rise to scandal, since a husband has no obligation to his wife, the fault is minor and no offense is incurred. Question.
Why is it said that she may be raised as a witness by a trustworthy laywoman (*upāsikā*)? The answer is: this applies to all seven assemblies (*saptanikāya*).

However, because the emotions and intentions of women are often deceptive and mostly unreal, one must rely on a "trustworthy" woman to be fit to serve as a witness. Regarding the term "trustworthy," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, a "faith-abiding *upāsikā*" possesses sixteen qualities of faith:
first, taking refuge in the Buddha; second, taking refuge in the Dharma; third, taking refuge in the Saṃgha; fourth, regarding...

1. Unwavering confidence in the Buddha; 2. unwavering confidence in the Dharma; 3. unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha; 4. unwavering confidence in the training; 5. unwavering confidence in the Dharma; 6. unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha; 7.
enabling the Saṅgha to obtain benefits not yet obtained; 8. enabling the Saṅgha to increase the benefits already obtained; 9.

causing the Saṅgha’s lack of reputation to become widely renowned; 10. causing the Saṅgha’s ill repute to be swiftly extinguished; 11. not following one's own desires; 12. [not following others' desires].
13. Not following anger; 14. Not following fear; 15. Not following delusion; 16. Being free from desire; 16. Accomplishing noble precepts.
If one can accomplish these sixteen dharmas, they are called a trustworthy upāsikā;
such is the mother of Viśākhā. The verse on the sixteen kinds of faith says: "The indestructible purity of the three refuges in the Triple Gem; not for personal profit..."

Regarding "unfailing purity" (*avetyaprasāda*)—which refers to the purity of faith that does not follow after desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, and which is accompanied by the noble precepts of one who has turned away from desire—it is precisely unfailing faith (*akṣobhya-prasāda*).
In the new sūtras and śāstras, these are called the "four verified purities" (*catur-avetyaprasāda*).

They are termed "verified purities" because they are purified through realization; alternatively, they are called "verified purities" because the verification itself is purity. The old name for this is "unfailing faith."

Faith that cannot be destroyed is called "indestructible faith" (*akṣayā śraddhā*). In the Mahāyāna school, it takes faith as its essence, with the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and precepts as its objects.
In the Sarvāstivāda school, it takes the two dharmas of untainted faith and precepts as its essence. The *Abhidharmakośa* likewise takes the two dharmas of faith and precepts as its essence;
all four [schools] maintain that these are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). The *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* names it after Mṛgāramātṛ. Mṛgāra is...
Her husband was named Mṛgāra, who revered his wife as he would his own mother; therefore, she was called Mṛgāramātṛ (Mother of Mṛgāra), who is none other than Viśākhā.
First, it is to stop those who would slander: this refers to the concern that sitting with a woman might invite external criticism and defamation.
Second, it is to eliminate strife and contention: this means that if a husband were to see [the couple], he might expel the bhikṣu; such an act is the root of conflict.
Regarding the sequence for severing the evil karma that obstructs the Path: this precept serves as the primary gateway to the house of transgression and is the gradual cause of sexual misconduct;
hence it is called "sequence. Sexual misconduct is the root of birth and death and obstructs the supramundane Dharma; hence it is called "obstructing the Path."

Regarding the fourth point, "the offense according to what is done": the commentary states that this refers to the fact that as one commits an offense among the five categories of transgressions, the formal charge is established accordingly;
it also refers to the case of "many women," which means that although there may be many women present, it is still considered a secluded place (*praticchanna*).

One must have a man present to avoid the fault of seclusion. As for the previous statement regarding "the absence of a third person," this likewise refers to a man. This is based on what is seen [in the Vinaya].
The commentary explains the two *aniyata* [offenses] as follows: it is said that "in private" means if one sits in a secluded place at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), it is a *pāyattika*.
If, after leaving, one returns and sits again, it is a *pāyattika* for each instance. If one sits together with many women, there are many *pāyattika* offenses.

"Extensive as in the preceding section" means, according to my own interpretation, that it refers to the explanation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata-āpatti*) within the preceding section on the categories of offenses (*śīlavarga*).
Here, however, only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the offenses are clarified. The explanation of the meaning of the two indeterminate offenses is hereby concluded.
The Third Section: Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Rules.

From here below begins the third section. Although the thirty rules are divided into two groups of ten based on their sequence and specific distinctions, the nature of the offenses is equal and the procedures for confession are identical;
thus, these one hundred and twenty precepts are combined into a single section. Question: Why are they divided?

Regarding the "prior and subsequent": the commentary explains that this is because, due to these material gains, one’s methods of receiving and accepting them become improper, thereby giving rise to offenses and destroying the Path.

If one wishes to cleanse the mind through repentance, it must be before a superior object [of confession] that the continuous flow of greedy thoughts can be severed and extinguished. Once the mental state has been relinquished, the obstructing karma must likewise be dispelled;
thus, the method for abandoning offenses is clarified. Since this procedure is difficult to perform, the thirty [saṃghāvaśeṣa] offenses are listed first. As for the ninety *pāyattika* (downfalls):

One merely regrets [the offense] toward another; by simply severing the continuity [of the transgression], it is considered washed away. Since the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is easy, it is listed next.
There is a specific reason for the principle of listing the difficult first and the easy last. Regarding the term *niḥsargika* (尼薩耆): *niḥsargika* is a Sanskrit sound;

in this land [China], it is called "abandonment" (*śe*). There are three kinds of abandonment: namely, the abandonment of material wealth, the abandonment of the mind, and the abandonment of the offense. Regarding *pāyattika* (波逸提), in this land...
Because they result in a downfall, they are called the "thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses. This is an analysis based on the inclusion of a number (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*). Chongpo says:

"Many ancient masters relied on the commentaries (*śāstra*) for their explanations, asserting that 'renunciation' (*naiḥsarga*) has three meanings. However, in my current interpretation, the text of the *śāstra* contains no such three meanings.

According to principle, one merely renounces the material object; therefore, it is termed 'renunciation. If one were to define 'renunciation' as the renouncing of the offense or the renouncing of the [defiled] mind, then it would be a mere..."

[The term] *ti* (提) should also be named *śe* (捨). Now, examining the fourth fascicle of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it says: "The robe has already been relinquished and the offense has already been confessed, yet the intention to possess [it] has not been severed.
If one further obtains a robe, this subsequent robe constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in relation to the previous robe. It further states:

"The robe has already been relinquished and the intention to possess it has been severed, but the offense has not yet been confessed. Even if one obtains robes over many days, the relinquishing of the robes requires a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense."

According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if the mind has not yet been severed, one incurs an offense by subsequently defiling [the robe]; furthermore, as long as the offense has not been confessed, one also defiles subsequent robes.

This differs from the case of a *pāyattika* (offense of simple negligence), where the mental offense has not yet been relinquished and thus lacks the sense of "defiling" [a subsequent act]. Therefore, it is known that the claim that "veneration destroys [the offense]" is unreasonable.

Regarding these thirty [rules], they are briefly distinguished by two categories: first, the difference between prohibitions and intrinsic offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); second, the distinction between monks and nuns. First, regarding prohibitions and intrinsic offenses:
one rule concerning the misappropriation of monastic property is an intrinsic offense; the remaining twenty-nine are prohibitions. Second, regarding the distinction between monks and nuns:
among the thirty, there are eighteen rules that both monks and nuns violate equally; thus, in the Vinaya, they are treated as single [rules].

The list of the *Prātimokṣa* contains twelve precepts that differ in three respects; thus, they are distinct for nuns. Regarding the first two precepts, there is a difference in their presence or absence:
as in the case of using rain-clothing before the prescribed time and the six-night limit in the *araṇya*, these two precepts exist for monks but not for nuns.

The reason it is not [a formal offense] is that the bathing robe is for regular use; since the Bhikṣuṇīs were granted this by the Buddha without any time limit, it does not fall under the scope of the prohibitions.

Furthermore, as Bhikṣuṇīs are women of weak constitution, they do not frequent forest hermitages (araṇya); therefore, there is no offense of separation. Second, regarding one precept: the offense is the same, though the conditions differ.

Regarding the long bowl, both monks and nuns fall into the same transgression; thus it is called a "common offense. However, the limit for monks is ten days, while for nuns it is restricted to one night;

thus they are said to have "different conditions. As for why this is so, the answer is: because monks possess many requisites, they are granted ten days to allow for the continuation of their distribution.

Furthermore, because the Saṃgha does not require a companion, they are permitted ten days to seek someone to perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity). For Bhikṣuṇīs, it is the reverse of this.

If that is so, when a Bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and has a companion with whom she may declare its purity, why should it not be the same as the ten-day period for the Saṃgha? Answer: A bowl is not the same as a robe.
If a bowl has not yet been completed, there is no offense regarding "excess" (*atireka*). Once the bowl is finished, one must immediately confess it.
Regarding robes, even if they are still under construction, there is always the fault of excess; therefore, if they cannot be finished after a single day of stitching, a ten-day period is permitted.

If that is so, why should an uncompleted robe not be treated similarly when there is a companion to whom one may confess it, as it is analogous to the case of a bowl? Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the ten-day period is opened specifically for robes.
This is stated with reference to those who possess only the three robes (*tricīvara*). Because it is permitted within ten days, there is no need for formal purification (*pariśuddhi*).

If one were to perform purification, it is likewise restricted to a single day. If this is so, why are they treated identically in the allowance? The answer is: once the initial permission has been granted, both cases remain identical until the tenth day.
Just as gruel is permitted for the sick, it is likewise so for those who are not ill. Within the three categories of existence, there are nine precepts whose gravity differs.

This refers to the five rules concerning bedding and requisites: taking a nun’s robe, washing an old one, and carrying or spreading one out. These result in a *pācittiya* offense for a nun and a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a monk; this is because such distinctions are made based on the frequency with which these acts occur.

Regarding the first precept on extra robes exceeding the limit: to store and accumulate them beyond the prescribed measure is called "extra" (*dīrgha*). To exceed the permitted period is therefore termed "exceeding the limit.
Alternatively, it is explained that anything outside the three robes is called "extra," and to fail to declare them when the time has passed is termed "exceeding the limit."
This is that which is to be guarded against; the precepts are that which can guard. Because both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is so called.

As for those who violate the Buddha’s four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), these practices of the four reliances are the proximate cause for *nirvāṇa*. At the time of first receiving the precepts, this was already explained in full, and all declared that they would uphold them.
Nowadays, many keep extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) without performing the ritual of purification (*śuddhi-vyavahāra*); therefore, it is said that they violate the rules.

Regarding the case where the length and breadth are either both excessive or both deficient such that no formal act (*karma*) is established, Master Li states that there are nine permutations in total, divided into three groups of three.

The first three phrases: 1. An offense of *thullaccaya* in the long [measure], an offense of *pācittiya* in the broad [measure]. 2. An offense of *thullaccaya* in the long [measure], as a *pācittiya* in the broad [measure]. 3.

An offense of *thullaccaya* in the long [measure], no offense in the broad [measure] due to reduction. The next three phrases: 1. As [the measure] in the long [measure], an offense of *thullaccaya* in the broad [measure].

2. As [the measure] in the long [measure], as a *pācittiya* in the broad [measure]. 3. No offense in the long [measure] due to reduction. In the final three phrases: 1. In the long [measure]... [text ends]
If the length is reduced while the width exceeds [the limit], there is no offense. Second, if the length is increased while the width is reduced, there is no offense.
Third, if both the length and the width are reduced, there is no offense. Among these nine cases, only four constitute an offense.
Regarding the fact that there is no offense when the three robes (*tricīvara*) have not been formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*) for more than a day:

Lì asked, "If the offense for not accepting the robes is light, while the offense for being separated from them is heavy, then might it also be the case that the offense for breaking the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is heavy, while the offense for not observing the rains-retreat (*anavasthāna*) is light? The answer was:

"The *anavasthāna* has a fixed time limit, whereas the acceptance of the robes has no such boundary. Therefore, failing to observe the retreat results in a heavy offense, while not accepting the robes is merely a minor transgression (*duṣkṛta*); however, breaking the retreat is a serious offense."

Because one does not abandon the cultivation of the Path, the offense for violating the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is light. However, if one is separated from them, the offense is heavy because the means of protection and sustenance are lacking.

Regarding the fact that there are no extra robes to be guarded against: this means that the three robes are what one is entitled to by rule; there is no further offense of possessing an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) that could be committed.
This is because the *śuddhika-dharma* (the rite of purification) was originally intended to prevent such faults. "I shall now use these as my three robes. Three...
Once the days for [keeping] robes have passed, there is no offense of excess; thus, the purification method (*viśuddhi-dharma*) is lost. Śaṅghabhadra says:

"Because there are three robes, they are compared to the three types of surplus, and thus the purification method exists to prevent excess. Now, since there are no three robes, it refers to the substance of the robe itself;

there is no further surplus to be prevented, so the purification method is lost. Therefore, it is said that there is no excess to be prevented. Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has a reason and obtains cloth and so forth...
As for the term "立" (Lì), it refers to the fact that this passage from the *Upoṣadha-vinaya* concerns only those who possess the three robes (*tricīvara*).
If one robe exceeds three or five cubits, "立" clarifies that among the three robes, two have already been completed and only one is lacking;

having now obtained the material for a robe, once the amount required for that single robe is accounted for, it is then designated as "clearly explained. This is based on the circumstance of being short of one robe.
Regarding the phrase "the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) on the full moon day is not cut," etc.: the intent of citing this *pāṃśukūla* as a challenge is to question the previous statement.

If one were to claim that taking a finger-breadth of cloth constitutes the robe itself, then one would avoid the fault of exceeding the limit [of extra robes]. Why, then, in the case of the *pāṃśukūla* on the full moon day, is it not cut and sewn?
If the day passes, it becomes an offense for having an extra robe. Regarding the term *zhan* (祖含反): the *Tōngsúwén* states that "to stitch a garment is called *zhan*"; *zhan* refers to fine bamboo.
Based on the above texts, the phrase "the first must be one's own" serves to distinguish it from the robes of others.

Even if the property of the Three Jewels is in one's possession, there is no offense once the day has passed. Regarding the statement that "that which is completed in one day" refers to the eleventh day:
if it were merely the tenth day, the offense of *atireka-cīvara* (excess robe) would not yet have occurred. This [interpretation] is incorrect. [The latter...]
"One day" means that because one receives and obtains the robe on the first day, it causes me to commit an offense.

If one had not received and obtained the robe on the first day, what would there be to offend against when the ninth day arrives? Thus, we know that it is because of obtaining the robe on the first day that the offense is committed.
[Vasubandhu] says: Because it is long and easy [to finish], it is completed in one day; the five-strip robe is completed in two days; the seven-strip robe...
The four-day robe is completed in four days; the great robe (saṃghāṭī) is completed in five days. Because it is made by exchanging long robes, it is completed in one day.
Jì describes this in the same way, stating: "This is from the treatise."

Regarding the phrase "if one forgets the necessary conditions," the Master Li establishes that this statement serves as proof that the act of making [the robe] does not pertain to one's own intention.
There are two meanings to "forgetting," which are discussed in terms of diligence and indolence: for the diligent, it is permitted; for the indolent, it is not permitted.

As for the commentary stating that items such as cotton wool do not require further explanation, Master Li says this refers to small amounts of cotton, like those used for stuffing the hands. If a large quantity does not constitute the characteristic of a robe, it is like a ladder.
Cotton and the like must be mentioned; the same applies to wool. If it is merely wool, there is no need to mention it;
however, once it has been made into felt, it must be mentioned, because people in the Western regions commonly wear felt garments. The *Xinshu* states:

"If the quantity of wool or cotton can be measured, it constitutes the characteristic of a robe (*cīvara*). Anything else that is not yet finished and whose dimensions are not fixed—such as a bundle of wool or cotton—is not so."
"Zhun" (屯) originally does not refer to clothing; how then could it be applied here to mean "to speak"?

Regarding the statement that "on the eleventh day, the ground was cleared," *Lì* refers to the "appearance of light" (*mingxiàng*). According to the *Jiàn lùn* (見論), the Western [Indic] pronunciation is *Arūṇa*, which here is called "appearance of light.
The *Duō lùn* (多論) states that the appearance of light has three kinds of colors. If the sun shines upon Jambudvīpa...

Regarding the *tṛśu* tree: its color is black in the east; when it illuminates the leaves of the tree, they appear green; and if it passes beyond the tree to illuminate the realm of Jambudvīpa, it appears white.
All three colors are manifestations of luminosity, yet the white is considered the primary one.
To say that "it is not to be measured" is the same as the previous case, meaning that according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Question: Regarding the case where that which defiles is of the proper measure (*pramāṇa*), how is that which is defiled [to be understood]? Vasumitra replies:
The intent of this question is whether, since the defiling agent is of the proper measure, the object being defiled—which is of improper measure—constitutes an offense or not. The answer means:

If the defiling agent is of the proper measure and the object being defiled is of any measure, one commits an offense and must relinquish it (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If the defiling agent is property of improper measure, while the object...

Regarding the question of whether the dyeing must be done according to the prescribed measure, the intended answer is that it should be dyed completely. This means that the agent which dyes (the dye) is what is not permitted by measure, while the object being dyed (the cloth) is what conforms to the measure.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, three parts for the needle and one part for the thread must all be declared as pure (*śuddha*); if one fails to do so, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

This implies that although robes and bowls may vary in size and offenses may vary in gravity, there is no instance where an act is not a transgression. Thus, it is said here that the major [offense] encompasses the minor.

Regarding "auspicious" (*kṣema*): this designation is not given because it is inherently so; rather, there is no intrinsic smallness or greatness to *kṣema*. It is called "great" in contrast to *tīrtha*, and since *kṣema* has no inherent smallness or greatness, it is called "small" in contrast to *tīrtha*.
Question: Regarding the possession of unsuitable items, the treatise discusses whether one commits an offense against the Vinaya or does not. How is this now to be reconciled?

Answer: Regarding the protection [of property], one may follow the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (the *Duolun*); regarding the adjudication of offenses, one should follow the lenient approach, which is identical to the Vinaya regulations.

The commentary states that the phrase "not living together" refers to the aforementioned passage from the *Jiwen* (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*), concerning two people who possess shared property that has not yet been divided.
If one has offered robes to the Saṃgha that have not yet been distributed, there is no offense for failing to provide them even after a long time.
Regarding the opening of five matters in border regions: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, in the country of Aparāntaka, there was a disciple of Mahākātyāyana named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
He resided in the Aparāntaka country, within a bend of Mount Kukkutapāda, and desired to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
After three years, he finally obtained an audience with the Buddha. He addressed the Upādhyāya, saying, "I wish to see the Tathāgata.

The Upādhyāya instructed him to go and report this to the World-Honored One while observing five precepts. Having arrived at Mount Kukkuṭapāda and paid homage to the Buddha, he was commanded by the Buddha to prepare a seat for a visiting bhikṣu.

That night, he stayed in the same quarters as the Buddha and spoke to the Buddha regarding the essentials of the Dharma. The Buddha praised him highly and further recounted the [account of his] Upādhyāya.
Regarding the aforementioned five matters: the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha at dawn the following morning and clarified these five matters.
That is to say, for the country of Aparāntaka and other frontier regions—such as those beyond the White Wood Strip (Śvetavālukā) in the east—all five matters were permitted.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it took three years for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to find a preceptor; according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, six years; according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, seven years; and according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, twelve years. —Bin.
He said: "This Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was a merchant; he is not Śrona. That Śrona is also named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, but they are identical only in name.
These two individuals were in different places. Śrona went forth from home and attained the Way in the presence of the Buddha himself.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, however, was a disciple of Cāṭakāyana who went forth and received the precepts in a border region before later seeing the Buddha. He continued:

Regarding the five matters: first, because the Sangha is sparse in remote regions, it is permitted for five people to receive the precepts while holding the Vinaya texts. Second, because there is much sand, it is permitted to wear sandals with double layers of straw.
Third, because it is very cold in remote regions, it is permitted to use bedding made of leather. Fourth, because there is much dust and dirt in remote regions, it is permitted to bathe frequently.

Fifth, because the Sangha is sparse in remote regions, when an extra robe enters one's possession, if the ten-day period is reached, one may perform the *śuddhika* (declaration of purity). Some say that...

Regarding the four matters concerning the exclusive allowance for frontier regions: as for the ten-day period for a long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) once it has entered one's possession, this was first established for the central lands and later extended to the frontier regions;
it was not exclusively established for the frontier regions. Reflect on this. Bin said:

"The causal origin (*nidāna*) of this precept is that Ānanda obtained a robe intending to offer it to Kāśyapa, but not knowing what to do, he asked the Buddha. The Buddha said: 'When will Kāśyapa return?'"
The response was: "Ten days hence, I shall return. Consequently, Ānanda’s rule regarding long robes (*atirekacīvara*)—that they do not constitute an offense within ten days—was established.

Yet, it is now further stated that Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa requested the opening of five matters, including that long robes must be formally purified (*viśuddhi*) within seven days once they have entered one's possession.

Why do these two textual sources differ in their basis? The explanation is as follows: Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa’s prior request for the opening of the five matters applied only to the border regions; however, [the present rule applies to] the central lands...

The country had not yet been opened for ten days. Later, through the connection with Ānanda, it was finally opened in the Middle Kingdom. From that time onward, both the Middle and the Border regions were opened for ten days.
Question: When Ānanda received the robe, he intended to offer it to Kāśyapa; since Kāśyapa was no longer present, he had no intention of keeping the robe.
Why would this constitute an offense of *aticāra* (excess)? Answer: It is simply because Ānanda’s mind of giving had not yet reached a final decision. Therefore, there is no offense.

Fearing that he might commit the offense of *aticāra* (excess), the Buddha permitted a ten-day period so that he might deliberate. This was because [the Buddha] originally feared that Kāśyapa would commit *aticāra*;

it was due to Kāśyapa’s ignorance regarding whether he had obtained the robe, and thus what constituted *aticāra*. Therefore, we know this was not an opening for Kāśyapa; hence the commentary (*shu*) asks: "Why was the ten-day period permitted?
It is because [it was] for the purpose of deliberating upon the distribution and entry [of the robe]; thus, we know this was an opening for Ānanda.
It is also like this. Regarding the statement that in other regions it is not necessarily an offense only upon physical possession, Master Li says:

one takes the text permitting [the practice] in frontier regions and compares it to the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa), using the Central Kingdom to refer to those other regions. This means that in the Central Kingdom, it is not necessary to physically possess the object for the ten-day period to be completed;

rather, if one forms the intention that it belongs to oneself and the ten days are complete, an offense is incurred. Since there is an exemption for frontier regions, it must necessarily involve [physical possession].

The offense is incurred only when ten days have fully elapsed since the garment was received by hand. In the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa), it does not depend on the garment being received by hand; rather, if one merely forms the thought that it is one's own, the offense is incurred once ten days have passed.
Therefore, the following citation from the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Vinayavibhāṣā*) with its four propositions establishes this meaning.

Some say that later, due to a request made to the Buddha, the rule for frontier regions was relaxed so that the count of ten days begins only after the garment has been received by hand. Prior to such a request, even if the garment has not yet [been received...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
[The robe] is obtained. However, within thirty days, one commits [an offense] (this is the definition). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviśa addressed the Buddha.

Of the five permissions granted, the first four are understandable; as for the fifth: if a bhikṣu here has finished making a robe and gives it to a bhikṣu in another location, even though the [receiving] bhikṣu knew of it beforehand, he does not commit the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) as long as the robe has not yet arrived.
(According to this text, it is understood that in the Central Kingdom [Madhyadeśa], there is no need for...)

[Otherwise, one] commits an offense. Regarding the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*’s statement on the "ten-day robe" (*daśāha-cīvara*), it asks: "What constitutes an offense? It is when [the robe] reaches the hands or the knees, etc. The commentary states:

"This clarifies the case of the border regions (*pratyantaka*). This text is presented in contrast to the preceding [discussion]; in the central regions (*madhyadeśa*), it is not necessarily required that one grasp [the robe] with the hands."

In this case, it constitutes an offense only when it enters the border regions. It requires that one must hold it with the hand until it reaches the shoulder or above the knee, and only after counting ten days does it become an offense.
If it merely belongs to oneself and has not yet reached the vicinity of the body, there is no offense.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the existence of a substance that is attained by the eye but not by the body:

it is like a person who places a gift on the ground and departs; although a bhikṣu has his hand there, he has not yet grasped it. Regarding the calculation [of days] up to clothing, ghee, and so forth:

this means that one begins counting from the day the clothing is obtained as "day one. When the count reaches ten days, one must perform the *śuddhi* (purification/declaration). One may also calculate [in this manner].
Regarding the calculation of "my own property": as for the term *sū* (cloth), Jing says that according to the *Liaolun*, one may add the designation [of ownership] from afar;
once seven days have passed, it constitutes the offense of *dīrgha* (excess). Second, regarding "that which reaches the body but not the eyes":

Li states that if an object is sent in the dark and a bhikṣu, having grasped it, places it inside a chest, this counts as the completion of the day and must be formally declared (*ārocana*). Third, regarding "that which reaches both the eyes and the body and is obtained."

Regarding "establishing" (*li*): it refers to when someone comes to offer property to the Triple Gem and instructs a bhikṣu to accept it; the guest does not form the intention that the object belongs to himself.

Although the object remains in the possession of the bhikṣu, one cannot calculate the number of days to determine an offense. Regarding "four cases where [the offense] exists but not both until it is obtained": this is what is established.
It is like sending an object in the dark, with the message: "A disciple offers this one item to the teacher; it is inside his bed.
If the bhikṣu neither sees it nor takes hold of it with his hand, he commits an offense after ten days have passed.

If one obtains the robe on the first day but does not obtain it on the second day, and so forth, the established [commentary] states: "The offense of forfeiture occurs after the second day; since the robe has not been obtained, it may be dyed.
According to the *Jie-zhu* (Commentary on the Precepts), there are eight cases where there is no offense.

First, "if one does not obtain the robe. Thus, we know that the first gate cited refers to the case of not obtaining the robe. Within the Vinaya, there are eight gates; the first concerns obtaining or not obtaining [the robe]. There are indeed [these eight].
Chapter Ten: Transposing and descending [the sequence] to form phrases results in forty-six phrases, up to the "leaping over," "skipping," and "reversing" [arrangements], and so forth.

Regarding the offense of having no object for the formal act of dedication (*pariṣkāra-vyavahāra*): this refers to the offense incurred when there is no basis for the loss or destruction of the pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*). Second, regarding the "intermediate pure gift":
