Master Li says that if one obtains a robe on the first day but has not yet performed the formal act of dedication, and then obtains another robe on the second day, and so on up to the tenth day...

If one obtains robes on successive days and holds them all for the purpose of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification by declaration), and the declaration reaches the eleventh day, then only the robe obtained on the first day constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If, however, one performs the *pariṇāmana* (dedication/gift) during the intervening days, none of those robes will be tainted by the offense. Regarding the third case, "giving to another," Xuan says:

if on the first day one has not yet performed the *śuddhi-vyavahāra*, and on the second through the tenth days one obtains robes and intends to give them to another person, then upon reaching the eleventh day, it is only [the first day's robe] that... [is affected].

Regarding the offense of forfeiture for wearing [a robe] for more than ten days: if one gives it away to another during the intervening period, there is no offense. As for the four cases of losing the robe, it is established as follows:

having obtained a robe on the first day but not yet performed the ritual of purification (*pariṣkāra*), if one obtains a robe on the second day or thereafter and subsequently loses it by the eleventh day, then only the robe obtained on the first day constitutes an offense of forfeiture;
there is no offense regarding those lost during the intervening period. Regarding the seven cases of the intention of close intimacy: this refers to obtaining a robe on the first day.

This refers to receiving for oneself. Regarding those obtained from the second day onward, this constitutes receiving for a close associate. Up until the eleventh day, only that which was obtained on the first day constitutes an offense;
receiving for another during the intervening days does not constitute an offense. Eighth, "if one forgets" means:
having obtained a robe on the first day without declaring it as pure (*śuddha*), one subsequently forgets about the robes obtained from the second day onward, until the eleventh day.
Regarding the offenses concerning robes on the first day of the month: those who forgot [the rules] were entirely without offense.
As for the one who previously committed an offense of defilement by keeping wealth with the intent to possess it, Lì (Lìlǜ) stated: "The person of the past was none other than Master Lìlǜ.

He said that he committed an offense of keeping extra robes (*dīrgha-cīvara*) because, having traded wealth among the five groups of practitioners to obtain additional robes, his intent to possess them did not cease; therefore, he committed an offense of defilement and had to relinquish them."

Regarding the subsequent new garment, one must again perform the act of relinquishment and confession (*pratideśanā*). This is because the prior intention of possession (*parigraha-citta*) can taint the subsequent garment.

As for the term "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*), Lì says it means "auspicious for wearing and using. He also says it means "it is auspicious to trade it for old [garments] at will. My current explanation, however, is not so; one simply confesses the previous *thullaccaya* offense.

From this point on, the substance of the robe is pure; it need not be relinquished. The Vinaya states: "Regarding the offense of *thullaccaya* (a grave offense), it refers to the previous *thullaccaya* concerning the robe.
Formerly, one should not have traded it hastily. Xuán explains: "The *thullaccaya* was incurred regarding the previous robe; formerly, the *thullaccaya* was incurred regarding the subsequent robe."

Regarding the statement that it is not so in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*), this commentator [Daoxuan] explains in his sub-commentary (*chao*) that this refutes the interpretation of former masters.
Since the *Śāstra* refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, he cites it here to refute the ancient views.

Second, as for the case where one first discards an object according to the prescribed measure and subsequently exchanges it for cloth to make two robes, etc., the proponent [of the alternative view] states: although the two preceding sentences were cited above, they merely follow from one another; therefore—
This must be clarified. It is precisely this meaning that must be clarified in the current text; it is for the sake of establishing the current text.
"Making two robes" refers to the two types of robes: those of proper measure and those of improper measure.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If one has not relinquished a *niḥsargika-pācittika* robe, one should not give it to others, nor should one use it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*) and so forth.

The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Jie-mo-su) states: "As for 'not being permitted to give it to others,' since one has committed an offense, the robe must be relinquished and purified; one should feel ashamed of this transgression."
When begging from a person as they are, one should restrain the fundamental mind; how could it depend on the material object? Therefore, by giving impure wealth, one will later receive defiled fruit.

If one certainly wishes to give it away, one should follow the rule for relinquishing what has been made, as prescribed in the Vinaya. It may not be used to make the three robes or dharma-garments, as it cannot withstand the required dyeing process;
thus, it is not permitted.

The following clarifies the non-transgression of the law. Regarding the phrase "if one forms the perception of loss, it is also explained as above": this means that because it is likewise unintentional, as in the previous case, keeping [the item] does not constitute an offense;
furthermore, a ten-day period is additionally granted. Zhen-shen says: "First, regarding items that have been purified (pariśuddha), one should direct the mind toward giving them to another."

If one subsequently regrets it and does not give it away, it constitutes the offense of theft, as stated in the Vinaya regarding taking back what has already been given. Furthermore, it must undergo the rite of *śuddhika* (purification);
otherwise, one falls into further transgression. Because it was obtained through theft, its principle is the same as that of newly acquired property.

"Taking up and wearing [an extra robe] results in the faults of transgression and loss through burning or drifting away. If one already possesses a long robe that has exceeded the limit, taking it up and wearing it does not constitute a transgression;
thus it is said. However, regarding the allowance for robes that have exceeded ten days or those separated from the body for even a single night, Master Li states:
this clarifies that within the context of a single robe, two offenses may be incurred on the same day—namely, the offense of a long robe and the offense of being separated from the robe."

It says: "When calculating the principle of relinquishment (*niḥsarga*), one merely relinquishes the overnight [excess]. Since there is no second offense regarding a single robe, one simply confesses the *pāyattika* for the prior violation of the long-robe rule.
The purpose of citing this passage here is to prove that when one has committed the offense of a long robe, one may fashion it into the three robes (*tricīvara*).
This treatise permits its fashioning because [the subject] does not possess the three robes; if one already possesses the robes, one may not use [this method]. — *Vinaya*.
A *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe acquired within the [monastic] boundary must not be given to others, nor may it be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*). Lü [Xinzhong] says:
"If a bhikṣu previously lacked the three robes and committed an offense regarding an extra robe, he may take this extra robe to serve as his three robes; he need not relinquish it.

However, if it is a robe obtained through trade or barter, it cannot be used as one of the three robes, because there is no surplus [of other robes] to provide protection. This is based on the original text.

"The three robes" refers to the answer to the preceding passage. "Now, first regarding the color of the robes" establishes the explanation; this is precisely clarifying the meaning of the present text.
Below, the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited concerning encounters with bandits and other matters, where one wears the five great primary colors;
this is done to apply the same principle as that found in the present text.

If another person gives him a robe that has not been formally purified (*viśuddha*), the guest says: "I have come merely to resolve my doubts through oral transmission. If another person gives him a small item, one might say there is no offense;
however, if another person makes a robe for him, it should constitute an offense. [The guest] explains: "There is likewise no offense. Liang says:
Former masters explained that since a robe is a heavy object (*guru-dravya*), it does not require formal purification (*viśuddhi-dāna*); therefore, it is not an offense.

Now it is said that this is not so; rather, because another gives it to me to wear as a cloak, there is no offense. Within the Vinaya text, there is further wording which the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) does not cite in full.
The Vinaya says: "If one takes and wears [it], when another gives it to wear—meaning another gives it to be worn as a cloak—'taking and wearing' is explained as before.
If another gives it to wear, the other commits the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), but because they give it to me to wear, I do not commit an offense."

This is also intended to resolve a doubt. This demonstrates that it differs from the case where another person commits the offense of possessing medicine for more than seven days (*dīrgha-bhaiṣajya*).

If such medicine were given to me, its consumption would not be permitted; for while the medicinal flavor is common [to all], if one person has committed the offense of long-term possession, another is not permitted to consume it.

However, clothing belongs to specific individuals; therefore, if another person commits the offense of long-term possession regarding clothing, I may wear it without fault. This is explained according to the analogy of a guest. "Established" (*li*) refers to what has already been received as a gift.
Therefore, it need not be confessed. However, if it is a piece of cloth or material for a robe, one must confess it, because such items are light [in value].
If the person entrusted with the robe is traveling far away, it is clearly established that both are living together;

once one person has received the robe and placed it in a chest, the companion who remains behind does not incur an offense by failing to confess, as they are separated by distance. This is due to the physical separation, not a fault of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "entrusting the robe," it refers to the person to whom it is entrusted. A commentary asks:

Why was it not permitted [from the beginning], but instead did one directly allow the keeping of extra robes and then establish the precept, explaining this as a skillful means? The answer is: The Buddha-dharma takes few desires as its foundation.

The precept was established to prohibit the keeping of extra robes because the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ; therefore, permission was granted later. This was merely established as a skillful means.
The Second Precept on Not Remaining Overnight Separated from the Three Robes. First, the intention behind the regulation is clarified.

The reason one is not permitted to remain overnight separated from one’s robes is that these three robes are, in essence, the dharma-appropriate vestments of all Buddhas of the three periods; they are essential for sustaining the body and cultivating the Path.
In principle, one’s robes must accompany the person like the two wings of a bird; it is not permitted for them to be separated even for a moment. One should always vow to uphold this practice.

Now, if the robes are placed here while the body dwells elsewhere, and cold or heat should suddenly arise, they will be difficult to obtain in an instant. Furthermore, lacking a guardian, they may be lost or stolen, which would result in no small distress.

Therefore, the Sage established the rule that when a person and their robes are in different places, it is called "separation" (*nissaggiya*). This is recorded in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (Western Tower).
It is often said: "It is better for a person's clothing to have distinct obstructions," because the obstruction caused by dyeing does not occupy a different location.

To spend the night is called "staying overnight"; if it is prolonged, the matter becomes lax; if it is shortened, it leads to distress. A one-day limit is set; once this has passed, one commits an offense. Thus it is said.

Regarding "the three robes and the obstacle of different persons," Ji says: The reason it does not say "different realms" (*sīmā*) but rather "different obstacles" (*vighna*) is that within a realm there may be obstacles;
even if one remains within the same realm, one cannot avoid the loss of the robes. Therefore, it does not mention the realm. The term "obstacle" is broad because it encompasses the realm;
thus, the passage in the text below stating "there is a realm-obstacle" is precisely this point. Fourth, regarding "not relinquishing when meeting": since...

One must not assemble [the robes], nor may one discard them from afar. Regarding the five cases where there is no underlying cause: these refer to when the robe is heavy, when one has obtained the formal authorization (*dhārmika-anujñā*), and during the month of Kārttika, and so forth.

Regarding the "three robes" and the "five robes": the five robes refer to the five robes worn by nuns, namely the *saṃkakṣikā* (arm-covering cloth) and the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), which are equivalent to the three robes [of monks] and must not be separated from overnight.
This differs from the interpretation of former scholars, who maintained that the ancients said: "To separate oneself from an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

They then cited an analogy, saying: "The Buddha permitted [the keeping of] one hundred and one [robes]; to separate oneself from them overnight constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. The Buddha likewise permitted extra robes. As [it is said]:...

Why is it not ancient? The current interpretation is otherwise: one receives and maintains [the robe] by adding the one hundred and one [rules]. Because it is separated from the original bond, it is auspicious. Regarding the long robe (*atireka-cīvara*), it is originally received and maintained;
however, because it is subject to the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite for a specific person, there is no offense if it is separated [from that person], as there is a basis [for its maintenance].

Furthermore, regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), this regulation applies universally to those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities; the Buddha ordained that people of these three grades all wear them.

Because they were so ordained by the Buddha, to be separated from them constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. However, for the one hundred and one [other items], separation merely incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Puṇyatara asked: "The three robes and the six requisites are equally means of sustaining the body; why is it that being separated from the three robes results in the loss of their formal acceptance and the commission of a *thullaccaya*, while the other robes and items are minor?"

What is the reason? The answer is: the restriction regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*) applies universally to all three grades [of practitioners]. If one were now to separate from them, it would be a grave offense against the rule and result in the loss of the formal undertaking (*parigraha*).
As for other articles such as clothing and utensils, their use is permitted for those of middle and lower grades when there is an insufficiency of resources for the path;

if one were now to separate from these, it differs from the case of what is permitted, and one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) without losing the formal undertaking. If that is so, since the alms bowl (*pātra*) is also subject to the primary restriction, why is it that separating from it does not incur such a penalty?

"Light [offense]. It does not lose the formal act of acceptance (*parigraha*). Answer: Because robes are broad in their utility as requisites, they are permitted to be separated from for a short time; therefore, violating this results in a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) and one loses the formal act of holding them.

As for the alms bowl, however, it has but a single function and its use is subject to temporal limits; because there is a necessity [to keep it], it is light [in offense], and thus one does not lose the formal act of acceptance.

Regarding the statement that "the 'one hundred and one' aids to the body permit the middle grade," Master Li says: "These constitute three grades. According to the *Xinsu*, there are six types of objects."

Chapter. As mentioned above, the power of the face-king of the superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*) is exceptionally extraordinary; as the fetal membrane grows along with him (that is, at the time of birth, a white woolen cloth emerges from his body).

Before relying on external requisites and when about to enter the Dharma, he vowed never to wear anything else. The Great Sage, knowing his capacity, permitted him to rely solely on this one [garment]. Thus, he was able to maintain inner stillness and cultivate the Way through its support.

(Later, at the time of his renunciation, the Sage commanded him to "Come," and this blanket transformed into a Dharma robe. Second, the power of his karmic retribution was particularly strong; he was capable of enduring cold and hardship.
He fashioned robes according to circumstances without regarding it as difficult. Therefore, the rule was established that he should possess three robes, all of which must be maintained.
The first [type] consists of those who maintain only the three robes (*tricīvara*). Although they are permitted to keep these three, their heads and feet remain exposed;

being weak in strength and feeble in spirit, they are oppressed by the suffering of cold, their mental state becomes distracted, and they lack the mindfulness to dwell in the Path. The Tathāgata, gauging their capacities, permitted them to possess the "one hundred and one" items (*ekottaraśata*) to serve as markers for their practice.
The fourth type consists of those whose physical constitution is frail and whose mental faculties are not sharp; they require warmth depending on the time and the place.

It must be good. If one receives provisions, one can advance in one's practice; otherwise, as with the aforementioned superior person, it would result in the regression of the Way. Therefore, the keeping of surplus items is permitted.

One may accept whatever is offered so that the donor may obtain merit, while this [recipient] gains the resources to support the Way. As for the fifth type of person, their power of karmic retribution is weakest;

they require substantial material goods to be able to alleviate suffering, maintain their bodies, and advance in their practice, thereby allowing for gradual progress. Therefore, [the keeping of such items] is permitted.

One who possesses bedding, vehicles, or heavy goods must keep them in accordance with the teachings; because such matters are weighty, they do not permit the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification by declaration).
As for the sixth person, he requires a dwelling adorned with various jewels before he can find peace of mind.

According to the *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), when the heavenly Subhūti spoke of coarse robes, he was unwilling to enter the Path and instead sought various jeweled mansions. The Buddha then ordered him to borrow one from a king.
All these ritual implements were used by the bhikṣus, and after staying there for one night, they attained the Way. The Buddha said: "You should know that awakening to the Way depends on the mind;

it is not restricted by outward form or clothing. From this day forward, those who require them shall be permitted to have them. Although the above was granted as a general permission, it was not for the sake of sustenance or reward.

The Tathāgata appears in the world to eliminate the root of the self-view (*ātman*). As stated in the *Lokadhātu-buddhagarbha-sūtra*: "If it were not for the purpose of eliminating the inversion of the self-view..."
In my Dharma, one must not use even a single cup of water or a single piece of robe-cloth for the sake of liberation from afflictions.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Even ten thousand [items] would not be considered too much. The practitioner should measure themselves:

according to their own station, where do they stand? Furthermore, as the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "If one lacks virtuous conduct yet accepts clothing and food, one will not fail to go to hell. Regarding robes...
"Then it would leave the body; eating it would simply break one's belly. These words are extreme. How can one deceive oneself? Li said:
"As the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states, a precept-breaking bhikṣu may not receive the offerings of the faithful, just like the son of a toll-collector. Furthermore, as the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* says:"

Just as if a single hair were divided into hundreds or thousands of parts, a precept-breaking bhikṣu cannot even digest one such portion of an offering, let alone the fourfold requisites of support (and so forth).
Jing asked: "Since during the month of Kārttika it is permitted to be separated from one's robes..."
"May one also be separated from the alms bowl? He replied, "One may not. Because there are three types of robes; if one is separated from one, two remain, which can still be worn.
The alms bowl, however, exists as only one; therefore, one may not be separated from it."
Regarding the "obstruction of different persons and robes" within this precept, there are six distinct conditions.

Now, focusing on the third condition—the obstruction of different persons and robes—I shall explain in detail the four types of obstructions and the fifteen natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*), providing an interpretation for each (and so forth).

Regarding the statement that "the three aforementioned obstructions apply equally across all realms," this clarifies that the obstruction of defilement (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstruction of sentient beings (*sattvāvaraṇa*), and the obstruction of separation (*vyavadhānāvaraṇa*)—these three do not exclude the *dharmadhātu* or the fifteen natural realms (*prakṛtadhātu*). If any of these three are present, one loses possession of the robe.
Regarding the argument that boundaries obstruct one another such that they do not interpenetrate, [Dao]li states:

"This boundary is not that boundary; this monastery (*ārāma*) is not that monastery; this tree is not that tree. Each is individually and separately encompassed; therefore, it is said that they do not interpenetrate.

All of these are analytical examinations of the four kinds of obstructions mentioned above. As for a *saṃghārāma* having a single boundary, [Dao]li asserts: since the three kinds of obstructions are absent...
However, this is also one of the *nīla*-categories (blue offenses).
Regarding "the body being exposed" and so forth: it is established that within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), a monk left his robe in a village and went to retrieve it;

upon his return, the fastening of the robe came undone, and the monk’s body was exposed, leading him to feel shame. Having reported this incident to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
One must not leave one's robes within a village. If one wishes to establish a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), one must first exclude the village (and so forth).

Regarding the five reasons for excluding the village: first, to avoid slander; second, to avoid strife and contention; third, to avoid giving rise to suspicion; fourth, to protect the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

and fifth, because a village is indeterminate while a robe-boundary is determinate. This is intended to clarify that there are these five faults within a village, and therefore one must not leave the robes there.

Regarding "robes": when intending to establish [the boundary], one excludes the village. As for the statement that the "settlement" (*grāma*) is indeterminate, it means that the village may sometimes come and sometimes go.
Within such a village, there are men and women who are aware of the four aforementioned faults concerning a *bhikṣu*. Regarding the term "slander" (*paiśunya*):
Master Ying says that the *Zilin* (Forest of Characters) records it as 誹 (pí). "Pí" means to slander; "slander" (*bàng*) means to defame. It is one's nature...

Regarding the phrase "their natures being at odds leads to much censure," this refers to the fact that their characteristics are diametrically opposed to those of women. Women take lustful desire as their nature;
they seek to flirt and coquet, thereby inducing one to commit unwholesome deeds. A bhikṣu, however, constantly maintains a mind of pure goodness and the protection of the precepts;
hence it is said they are "at odds. "At odds" (忤) means to oppose. Therefore, it is stated in the treatises: "A woman is an enemy to one who has left the household life."
The ancient masters said: "A 'village' (grāma) is defined as a place where men and women reside together; in such a place, one must not leave one's robes unattended.

If there are only women present, it is merely termed a 'place of defilement and obstruction' (rañjanāvaraṇa), which is subsumed under a single category. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* frequently defines a village as a dwelling where men and women live together."

Regarding the rule that if the path between water and land is cut off, one may be separated from one's robes without fault, Daoxian says: "When one later sees the robes again, one must perform the ritual procedure once more.

Regarding the rule in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that one should not grasp the door-key outside the monastery gate, Daoli says: "This is because, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, there is no 'sphere of influence' (*śakti-bhāga*) [extending beyond the gate]."
One must grasp the end of the lintel of the gate-house; because it is connected to the interior of the boundary, it is permitted that one does not lose the robe.

Regarding "the door-key": this means that if one does not enter the room, but simply holds the door-key hook in one's hand, one does not lose the robe, as one has mastery over opening and closing, and may enter at will.
Regarding "the twelve-rung ladder and so forth," this clearly explains the gate and doors.
Once closed, one may no longer enter. If such a ladder exists, one may ascend and descend to come and go for the purpose of meeting with fellow monks to exchange robes;
therefore, its opening is not considered a transgression.

Regarding the "equal boundaries of brothers," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the area where brothers share their boundaries is called a "family boundary" (*kula-sīmā*). If the elder brother...

Two brothers live as one family, yet they have established separate boundaries within the household. The elder brother does not allow the younger brother to enter his portion, and the younger brother does not allow the elder brother to enter his.
If a bhikṣu stays within the elder brother’s boundary while his robe is within the younger brother’s boundary, he loses his robe.
If someone says to the bhikṣu, “Laypeople are naturally at odds with one another; this does not obstruct the Dharma. You may stay as you please,” then at that time, it is according to [the rule].

Regarding the rule that "the robe remains where it was placed and is not lost": it is established that although these brothers live under the same roof, because their food, clothing, and business affairs are separate, if one is physically in the elder brother’s house while the robe is placed in the younger brother’s house, it is considered lost.

As for the phrase "when the king enters the boundary," this refers to when the king goes out; as the night watchmen patrol and shout, and the military forces stand in dense array, they obstruct the coming and going, which is termed an "obstruction of circumstances. The king...
If one accompanies a noble lady, or is otherwise subject to sensual attachment, or associates with illusionists, musicians, and the like, an objection is raised:
"The King obstructs the coming and going of bhikṣus; this is a hindrance of the passions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Illusionists, musicians, and such do not obstruct the coming and going [of bhikṣus];

how, then, can they be called hindrances of the passions? The explanation says: Although these people—illusionists and musicians—do not obstruct the coming and going, because they frequently engage in flirtatious behavior and are prone to seduction, [they constitute a hindrance].
It destroys the holy life; therefore, it is an obstacle for sentient beings. Ji said: "Illusion" refers to delusive bewilderment that dazzles and confuses the human mind.
For example, when Dharma Master Xuanzang entered the Western Regions, on a great festival day there, music was being performed.

While Xuanzang was upstairs in the tower searching through the scriptural texts, the Master Śīlabhadra called out to him, inviting him to come down and watch the music. Xuanzang replied: "I have traveled more than a million li from my home to seek [the Dharma]..."
The holy teaching is not something the mind delights in. Śīlabhadra advised him, saying, "It would be well for you to observe the local customs and transformations.
As they were traveling together, they saw a magician who had conjured a city named Gandhavatī (City of Fragrance).
Because the Western magicians travel from village to village seeking the fragrance of others' food and drink to perform their illusions, it is called Gandhavatī. This city...
Among them was a young boy. He was placed upon the head of one pestle, then another pestle was set beneath him;
in this manner, they were linked together in an endless succession of pestles, causing the boy to ascend into the sky. Furthermore, he was strictly admonished:
"Be careful not to steal the flowers and fruits of Śakra; he will surely kill you. In an instant, the boy rose higher and higher, entering the azure clouds until he gradually became invisible.
He saw it. After a short while, he saw [the head] beneath one foot; then he saw it beneath a hand; then he saw it beneath the head.
The Lord of Birth and Death then said, "This child stole celestial flowers and fruits and has been killed in this manner.

He then took up the head, hands, and feet and severed them, whereupon they immediately transformed back into a small child who ran away as before. Furthermore, he recently saw a phantom person in the west.
He went to the capital to sell a donkey. A buyer mounted the donkey and returned to his home. The next day, seeing it was merely a bundle of straw, he immediately pursued the owner of the donkey.
Traveling until they reached the eastern border of Xiliangzhou, he encountered the original owner and seized him.
The man said, "I have fields where I harvest grain; I will give you millet in exchange. He then waited for the other to reap the millet, thresh it, and measure it out.
[He] paid the money and hired a carriage to carry [the robes] back. When they reached the middle of the road, he looked at them and found they were entirely sand and earth.

Regarding the three obstacles that prevent entry into these two boundaries, it is established that within the two boundaries—both those established by ritual (*dharmakṛta*) and those existing naturally (*prakṛtistha*)—if there is an obstruction by sentient beings or defilements (*sattva-rāga-vyavadhāna*), one may not rely on the boundary to protect the robes; they must necessarily follow the person. Each of the two boundaries...

Regarding those who separately obtain the protection of robes: this refers to within the two realms of both formal ritual action (*kṛtaka*) and natural occurrence (*prakṛtika*), where there are no more than three obstacles;
each person individually obtains the protection of their robe.
Now, to clarify that there are naturally fifteen *dhātus*, the verse says:

"Blue-black, gathering, field, chariot, boat, Village, house, hall, storehouse, granary, Aranya, well, waterway, And likewise the island boundary— These fifteen kinds: the first eleven Appear in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*;
The latter four kinds are explained by other schools. Within the *Caturvarga*, these ten kinds of natural [boundaries]..."

This constitutes one hundred phrases. That is to say: "This mango grove is not that mango grove," "This mango grove is not that tree," "This mango grove is not that field," "This mango grove is not that chariot," and so forth;
these constitute ten phrases. Taking the tree as the subject, one likewise obtains ten phrases.
Thus, taking "evenly" (*ping*) as the head, each yields ten phrases, totaling one hundred.

Since the Vinaya text contains eleven types of boundaries (*sīmā*), why are only ten boundaries used to form these one hundred phrases? The answer is that the "araṇya" (wilderness) boundary is set apart and explained later in the Vinaya;
therefore, it is not included in this count. As for why it is necessary to compose these one hundred phrases, it is because [the text] was incomplete.
It must be stated thus. People might think that since both the monastery and the person are involved—where the person is in that [monastery] and the robe is here—one would not lose the robe.
Fearing such an attachment, it is necessary to say, "This monastery is not that monastery," and so forth. The same applies to the remaining phrases.

Regarding the statement that "each has four kinds," this refers to the establishment [of boundaries]. In both the *nīla* (blue) and *grāma* (village) realms, each takes four things—enclosures, walls, fences, and hedges—as its defining characteristics.

Therefore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a "distinguishable village" (*vibhajya-grāma*) refers precisely to such a village boundary. This means that if these four characteristics are complete, it is called "distinguishable.
An unenclosed area is called an enclosure (*prākāra*), while an enclosed area is called a wall (*kuḍya*). Furthermore, it is said that what is high is called a wall.

The low [enclosures] are called *yuan* (walls). Those made of wood are called *ze* (fences), and those made of bamboo are called *li* (hedges). Regarding "incomplete" (*bu-zhou*) walls or hedges that have buildings on them:
this refers to cases where there are only the buildings but no surrounding fences or the like; thus it is named "incomplete. Some people say:

"Having houses on all four sides" means that even if there are no four characteristics such as walls and so forth, but there are merely houses on all four sides, these also constitute the boundary marks for the two types of monastic villages (*saṃghagrāma*).
Therefore, it is said "having houses on all four sides" (this interpretation accords well with the text).

Regarding the statement that these various characteristics are incomplete and thus the boundaries of the *saṃghārāma* are destroyed because trees, carts, and thickets grow there—Hōryū states that this represents the interpretation of the former masters (*pūrvācārya*).
As for the phrase "there are various boundaries within the *saṃghārāma*," this is the text of the Vinaya. The ancient masters explained it as follows:
when the four characteristics are incomplete, it is called the destruction of the characteristics of the monastery; within such a place, there exist boundaries such as those of trees and carts.
Then it arises. This clarifies that there are several distinct boundaries (*sīmā*). Now, my intention is not as [others] claim.

If the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) do not pervade [the area], how can the monastery (*ārāma*) itself be called "ruined"? The trees, vehicles, and so forth within it are merely separate boundaries; how could one say that within a single monastery there are several distinct boundaries?
When the Vinaya speaks of "several boundaries," it refers only to the three aforementioned obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). If, within the boundary of a monastery, there exists...
Obstruction: Because a bhikṣu cannot travel freely back and forth, it is said that there are various boundaries within a monastery (ārāma).
According to the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials), the text states: "A monastery has one boundary" means that when surrounded by fences or walls, this is called one boundary.
If it were not all-encompassing, the power [of the boundary] would not reach both the rooms and the trees; therefore, this is clarified.

This section merely concerns a distinct boundary (*pṛthag-sīmā*) and is not called the "monastic village" (*saṃgha-grāma*) or the "two locations. From this point onward, the author of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā*) formally refutes the interpretation of the ancient masters.
Regarding the four marks of the monastic village boundary, they are not called the "boundary of the monastic village"; therein, the trees, vehicles, and so forth stand independently. Therefore...
It is said: "This refers to distinct boundaries. The ancient masters explained that "several boundaries within a monastic village" refers to trees, vehicles, and so forth.

Now, this commentary explains that "several" refers to the three obstructions. Although it refutes the interpretation of the ancient masters, one must recognize that the ancient masters' interpretation also possesses its own logic.

"Even so for dwellings, nunneries, villages, and the boundaries of travel"—this establishes the clarification. Within these nunneries and other such places, one protects one's robes according to the boundaries of the precincts.
If there are three obstacles regarding the robes that prevent one from coming and going, then [the protection] is lost.
As for the term "house" (*shè*), it is a variant of "eye"; people of the north call a house *shè*, while those of the south and Wu call it *shā*.
Regarding the construction of a house: according to the *Jiwen* (Text on the Solemn Rite), this boundary of the dwelling consists of twenty-five cubits extending outward from each of the four walls;
this constitutes the substance of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). If one follows the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), there is additionally a zone of influence (*śakti-bhāga*).
Regarding the third case, where the boundary of the tree is equal to the height of a person:
it is clarified that if the tree rises as high as a person, such that it does not obstruct the head, then one may keep one's robes there. This refers to the smallest possible extent;

that is, when one is seated below, if the area shaded by the branches and leaves is sufficient to accommodate the body, then one may keep one's robes there. This applies to a single tree; one need only rely upon the tree itself. If...
If there are different trees joined together without interruption such that the sun and sky are not visible between them, one obtains protection extending for one *krośa*.

If the branches of the trees grow unevenly or are otherwise long, it is said that one may protect one’s robes for a distance of either one *zhang* or ten *zhang*; this constitutes the forest boundary (*vana-sīmā*).

Regarding the statement that "the robe remains within the forest without being lost over a distance of fourteen cubits," this refers to the smallest possible forest, consisting of four trees joined together.

It is established that if people pass through such a forest without it constituting a boundary for the robe—such as men and women, performers of illusions, or individuals of distinct types—the defilements of sentient beings arise therein, and thus protection cannot be maintained by means of the forest. Therefore, it is said:

Regarding the "boundary of no clothing" (*anivāsana-sīmā*): it is said that in a great forest (*mahāvana*) where there are no obstacles, one stands [to establish the boundary] because the three impediments do not arise;
hence it is called "without obstacle. A "great forest" is defined as one *krośa*; a "small forest" is defined as fourteen cubits (*hasta*). These are the fixed limits.

If a forest is less than fourteen cubits, one may only follow the actual size of the physical entity; one must not rely on the measure of fourteen cubits as the standard for the substance of the forest.
If the body of a forest is larger than fourteen *hasta*, one must not rely on the extent of the forest itself for the purpose of defecating or urinating;
rather, one is limited to fourteen *hasta*. If the body of a forest is larger than one *krośa*, one may not rely on the forest's extent;

instead, the limit is fixed at one *krośa*. (This is the established oral decision of the masters; however, the meaning remains somewhat doubtful and requires further clarification. This is because the power [of the boundary] does not extend beyond that, and thus it is not a "garment-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*).
Regarding "narrow and small," [Master] Shen says: This passage from the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely cites the measurement of a small grove, calculated at fourteen *zhou*.

It does not mean that the boundary of the grove can only be of such a limited extent. If there are no obstacles, one must rely on the ten recensions (*daśa-bhāṇaka*) which take one *krośa* as the standard.
What is cited here regarding the four trees is stated in terms of the absolute minimum; if there were fewer than four trees, [the boundary could not be established].
One may be called a "tree," but one cannot be called a "forest.
Regarding the statement that the grapevine arbor extends twenty-five *hastas* in each of its four directions, it is established that grapes are climbing vines.
Within this context, it is said that taking twenty-five *hastas* outward from each side of the arbor constitutes the natural robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
The "substance" (tǐ) does not mean that the measurements must be made equal by constructing a frame.

If each of the four directions has a potential boundary (śe-fēn) of thirteen paces outside, then for structures such as multi-storied pavilions (lú-gé), one may likewise take twenty-five cubits (zhǒu) starting from the exterior of the pillars as the substance of the robe-boundary (yī-jie).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qí), the area outside the stairs of a multi-storied pavilion is each twenty-five cubits, constituting the robe-boundary. Regarding the tree-boundary (shù-jie), it is each [twenty-five cubits] away from...

Regarding leaves: an area extending twenty-five cubits from the exterior is called the "robe-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*). If a bhikṣu places his robe under a tree, it is lost once he is more than twenty-five cubits away.
For all vine arbors, an area of twenty-five cubits from the exterior constitutes the robe-boundary.
If one wears the robe upon a vine while staying overnight below it, or if the robe is beneath the vine while staying overnight above it, in both cases the robe is lost.
If the cord is attached to the body, one does not lose [the robe].
According to the commentators on the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if the robe is beneath a building or a tree while the body is above it, why is it lost?
It is lost because the robe is below and suddenly encounters obstacles such as sentient beings or defilements. However, if the body is below and the robe is above, one does not lose it.
This statement is not yet fully understood; it shall be further clarified below. What is meant here by "in this manner" is that, in all cases, there is no prior difficulty [regarding the order].
If there were indeed a prior difficulty, then whether the person is above and the robe below, or vice versa, both would fail.

[The proponent] says: because the body is above and the robe is below, one fears three obstructions; thus, in the darkness, [the position] fails. It is said that the robe is above and the body is below.
Regarding "not losing": it is established that when clothing falls, one can reach up and take it because of one's mastery; therefore, it is not lost.
As for the size of the towers and trees: the towers are like those of Śakra, measuring one *yojana*;
the trees are as large as the Jambū tree, reaching a height of one hundred *yojanas*.

Regarding the four types of boundaries: "standing" refers to the fact that outside the boundary of the Jetavana monastery, there is a sphere of influence extending twenty-five cubits plus one-quarter.

Regarding the five types of boundaries for carts and boats: this clarifies that both are on land; furthermore, because they involve staying [in place], it refers to the area within which one can turn around.
If the robe is inside the cart or boat and the person is also on the boat or cart, as long as one remains within the limit of the turning space, [the robe] is not lost. This is directed toward...
If a boat is on the water, the [robe] is lost as soon as it leaves the boat, because the water element is distinct. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"Regarding boats on land and carts at rest: if a bhikṣu places his robe on a boat and separates from the boat by more than twenty-five cubits, he loses the robe;
within that distance, he does not lose it."
Regarding the area reached by the staff of a carriage: if this person rides in a carriage drawn by oxen, he does not sit upon the backs of the oxen, but sits only within the carriage.
Using his staff to strike the oxen, there are many such carriages traveling together in front and behind.

Even if his body is in a front carriage and his robe is in a rear carriage, as long as the carriages are in mutual view and the oxen and the staff reach one another, it is called a single boundary (*sīmā*). It is not otherwise.
There is no fixed limit. Even if people’s robes are separated by a thousand wagons, as long as there is no obstacle between them, it is all termed a "robe-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*).

Regarding cases where many dwellings exist on water, such as boats and the like—for example, when many men and women are aboard a large carriage or other vessel—if a bhikṣu travels freely back and forth upon it, his robe is not lost. However, if there is sexual attachment...

If it is obstructed by such things, [the boundary] is lost. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle eight, states: "If a bhikṣu washes his robes and dries them on a boat, if the wind blows them all toward the outside, he commits an offense.
If half are inside the boat and half are outside the boat, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. Because they were not cut off, they must all be relinquished.
This is called the 'boat boundary' (*nau-sīmā*)."

Regarding the seventh, the *śānta-sīmā* (boundary of abandonment): it is established as a solitary dwelling (*ekakuṭī*) that lacks the characteristics of a separate enclosure (*prākāra*). Its enclosure boundary extends outward to include the functional range (*sīmā-bhūmi*).

If one refers to the characteristics of a village settlement (*grāma*), this will be explained extensively later; for now, it refers to the three types mentioned below. According to the *Sudarsana-vibhaṣā*, a village is defined as one that has no market;

this corresponds to the four propositions in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if there is a multi-storied building, a ladder, a staircase, or a path [connecting it to other structures], it is not considered a village.

Regarding the phrase "obtaining twenty-five *hasta* on the exterior": this refers to the assertion that on each of the four sides of the four walls of the multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), one obtains a full twenty-five *hasta*.
Now, from the base of the ladder-carriage downward, one further obtains twenty-five *hasta*;

that is, in whichever direction the ladder-carriage is placed, one obtains twenty-five *hasta*. On the remaining side where there is no ladder-carriage, it is not obtained. This is what is meant by "outside the path."
"Outside" refers to the area beyond the edge of the ladder-platform; this ladder-platform is simply a stepped path.
Measuring twenty-five cubits on all four sides from the base of the ladder-platform—this ladder is installed outside the gallery (this is stated again for the sake of a definitive decision).
Jing says: "Only one side outside the ladder-steps is accessible, not the other three sides. This is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding the boundaries of storehouses and granaries.
Regarding the phrase "defining the interior as the limit," this refers to the area inside the pillars.

In contrast to the aforementioned *Cīvara-vastu*, which states that twenty-five cubits beyond the wall constitute the substance of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* permits only the area within the walls; thus, these two texts do not agree.
Regarding the expression "defining the interior as the limit": the area inside the threshold is called the "illuminated interior" (*prakāśa-antaḥ*), while the area outside the threshold is...
This is what is meant by "clarifying the external. Regarding the statement that both are "unrestricted" (*ren-de*), Hui-liang says:

The *Mahāsāṃghika* (Sengqi) lacks the spatial divisions for storehouses and granaries found in the *Dharmaguptaka* (Si-fen); the *Dharmaguptaka* lacks the twenty-five cubits outside the pavilions found in the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

Because one now wishes for both the path and the practice to be obtained, it is called "unrestricted. Jing says: "Both are unrestricted" means that while the *Mahāsāṃghika* has pavilions, it lacks storehouses.
Regarding the storehouse: in the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya), there are storehouses but no upper stories. If one wishes to take from the four parts, one may take from the storehouses;
if one wishes to take from the *Mahāsāṃghika* (Saṃghāṭa), one may also take from the upper stories. Therefore, it is so stated. My own view is this:

although the *Dharmaguptaka* speaks in terms of the interior, the *Mahāsāṃghika* maintains that the "sphere of influence" (*śakti-bhāga*) extends twenty-five cubits outside. Now, I wish to rely on the sphere of influence of the *Dharmaguptaka*.
[The boundary] is divided. If one does not take the *saṃghī* [measure] of twenty-five *hastas*, this constitutes one "absence" (*abhāva*), which is permissible.

If one wishes to take the *saṃghī* [measure] of twenty-five *hastas*, there is no "sphere of influence" (*prabhāva*) belonging to the four-part [boundary]; this is again one "absence," and since it is permissible, it is said that "both absences permit acquisition.
This means that on one side there is no sphere of influence, and on the other side there is no [measure of] twenty-five *hastas*; therefore, it is said that "both absences permit acquisition."

Regarding the boundary of the upper dwelling (*upari-śālā*), as for the interpretation of "village" (*grāma*), it is established that while the *Caturvargika-vinaya* clearly explains the boundary of the dwelling without mentioning the village, the village and the household nonetheless serve as the basis for its definition;
therefore, one should follow the fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.

Regarding the phrase "this is a *kula* (village/settlement), not a *grha* (house)": [Dao]li establishes that there are two settlements (*kula*). These settlements are enclosed courtyards, resembling the wards of the two capitals.
Within each of these two settlements, there is one household. Now, one obtains the protection of the robe by relying on the settlement; it is not necessary to rely on the individual house.
Since the name of the "house" is subsumed and one simply relies on the settlement, it is said: "this is a *kula*, not a *grha*. [Daoshi] Jing says: "the two settlements..."
Each has its own single household; these are merely called "villages" (*grāma*) and are not called "household boundaries" (*kulapradeśa*).
The reason for this is that if there were two households facing one another, it would be called a "village. Since there are no other households facing each other here, it is not called a village.

Some say that the term "village" refers to the enclosure of the compound being complete and circular, whereas the term "household" refers to the distinction between the sovereign and his subjects. These two are households.

Regarding "not a collection" (*akalāpa*): it is established that there is only a single collection, and no distinct collections exist in relation to one another; they are merely designated as "families" (*kula*).

Now, as for what constitutes a "collection," it must necessarily involve two collections in mutual relation and dependence to receive the name "collection. In the present case, however, this refers to the family-protector’s robe.

Since the collection is large and contains two sections such as the *rāja* (king) and so forth, there is a concern regarding sentient beings becoming defiled or obstructed; therefore, [the rule] now relies upon...

Regarding the protection of robes within a household (*gṛha-ārakṣā*): one must not rely on a village (*grāma*). Because the name "village" is subsumed [within the term "household"], it is said that this refers to a household and not a village.
Third, as for "possessing both boundaries and having many households in two villages," the established interpretation is as follows:
when there are two villages situated opposite each other and each contains many households, one may rely on the households alone to protect one's robes.

Regarding the term "separate realm" (*pṛthag-dhātu*), the phrase "that which a hen cannot fly over" and so forth establishes that it is called a separate realm because it lies beyond the range of such influence.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (or *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), fascicle 4: "A village has both a single realm and separate realms. A contiguous village is called a single realm;
a non-contiguous village is called a separate realm. As for the phrase "non-contiguous village": [it refers to those where there is no physical connection].

This refers to the area reached by a flying chicken, the area reached by an arrow shot, the area where a person of modest conscience performs their bodily functions, and the area where men and women are distinguished.

If there is only one household in a village, even if a bhikṣu’s body is inside the house while his robe is in the area reached by an arrow shot, or if his robe is inside the house while his body is in the area reached by an arrow shot, in all such cases he does not lose [the robe]. If it is a village...

There are several households [within a settlement]. If one's robes remain at home while one's person is in a place reached by the range of an arrow, one loses the robes because the boundaries of the households are distinct.

Regarding villages on the four sides, if each has a single household and there is mutual contact through the turning of a cart or ladder, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya*), fascicle 4, states:
"As for 'villages that are contiguous,' this refers to villages on the four sides [of a central area] which..."
There are twelve rungs on a ladder that reaches four directions onto a wall, allowing one to ascend and descend.

If one lies down at the base of the ladder while placing one's robes in the four villages, one does not lose possession of the robes because the four sides of the ladder are interconnected; this is also based on the four villages each having only a single household.
Since the robes remain within whichever single household they happen to be in, one does not lose possession of them. If [it is] a village...
There are many households. If one's robe is inside a house, one loses possession of the robe.

Furthermore, within a village, even if there is only one household, if there is no ladder or stairway, and the robe is in a fourth village, one loses possession of the robe because they are not contiguous. Regarding "vehicles," the treatise further states:
there are also contiguous village boundaries; for example, where there are villages on both sides with a road between them wide enough for a vehicle.
When traveling, if the two ends of a carriage axle reach into a village, one may place one's robe at one end and remain at the other;
as long as both are on the carriage, the robe is not lost because they are connected by the vehicle.

Even if there is only one household in the village, if the robe is inside that house while one lies on the carriage, the robe is likewise not lost. However, if there is no carriage, [the condition] is not fulfilled.

If they touch one another, the robe is lost. Regarding the case where there is only one household in a village and the robe remains inside the house on a carriage or ladder, and it is not lost—Sengshen says:
"This belongs to the first of the four propositions in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If the robe is outside while the person is inside the house, it is likewise; this refers to the reversal of the preceding proposition, meaning the person is inside the house while the robe..."
Regarding those on the carriage ladder: because they do not lose [the robe] there either, it is said "it is likewise.

If one is among many families' robes inside a house, yet one's body is below the ladder and one loses [the robe], the Buddha stated that because there are many families, their mental perceptions differ and each has its own boundary;
furthermore, because of emotional obstruction or the possibility of defiled separation, one loses it. Shen says: "This sentence belongs to the preceding section in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*."
This consists of two statements.

Regarding the "one boundary" (*ekasīma*) and the "separate boundary" (*nānāsīma*) within a household, it is established that: when brothers have not yet divided their property and share the same activities, this is called the "one boundary.
If the brothers have divided their assets and have separate food and separate occupations, this is called the "separate boundary. Thus, this separate boundary is designated as such.
This constitutes a *kula-sīmā* (clan boundary). Furthermore, within a *kula-sīmā*, there are both a single boundary (*eka-sīmā*) and distinct boundaries (*pṛthak-sīmā*).
When brothers belong to a single clan but reside in separate dwellings that have no mutual connection, this is called a single boundary. As for what is called a distinct boundary:

it refers to the case where brothers, although they do not eat together, share the same places for preparing food, drawing water, and for defecation and urination; because they each come and go together [in these matters], it is so designated.

In places such as those for drawing water, there are distinct boundaries (*sīmā*). If one places one's robe at the water source while one's own body is in another room, one immediately loses possession of the robe;

therefore, it is called a "separate boundary. Alternatively, if the robe is within a household while one is in a place for relieving oneself (whether large or small), one likewise loses possession of the robe.
Thus, the subsequent passage states: "If one is in both places, one loses possession of the robe"—this is precisely that meaning. This is because one's body is...
The well-side and the clothing—these two are called the "two places" within the household.

Regarding the clan (*kula*), there are both those that constitute a single boundary (*ekasīma*) and those that constitute separate boundaries. Jing says: Although there are many people, because they share the same food and clothing, it is one boundary.

As for what is called a "separate boundary," Jing says: Although they dwell in the same location, because their portions are divided and their food and clothing are not shared, [it is a separate boundary].
It is the same; that is to say, it constitutes several distinct boundaries (*sīmā*). Although they differ, they share common locations for activities such as preparing food or drawing water.
Because many households come and go, these places where water is drawn and so forth are designated as separate boundaries. This refers to a case where one loses [the robe] in both locations:
the person is within the household, while the robe is at the place where water is drawn and so forth; hence the statement.
Regarding the passage concerning "four villages joined together, even to the point where hands and feet are each in separate boundaries," etc.:
according to this, when the boundaries of four villages are contiguous, a bhikṣu lies with his head on a pillow and his robe [nearby].

If the bhikṣu’s head is in one boundary, both hands are each in two different boundaries, and his feet are in one boundary, while the robe is beneath his head—if the robe becomes separated from the head, he loses [the benefit of] the robe. If, however, it is a cart...
In these four cases, if the upper part of the carriage yoke is in one boundary, the rear of the carriage is in another, the left wheel is in another, and the right wheel is in another;
or if one places the robe in front of the carriage and stays overnight behind it; or places the robe behind the carriage and stays overnight in front of it;

or places the robe on the left side of the carriage and stays overnight on the right side; or places the robe on the right side of the carriage and stays overnight on the left side—in all such instances, [the robe] is lost.
This refers to clothing.
As for those who share the same views and the same doctrines: "views" refers to the ninety-six types of views held by non-Buddhists;
"doctrines" refers to the treatises of non-Buddhists, such as the four Vedas and other such works. It is like those who engage in various jests while wandering through marketplaces and camps.

Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned," it refers to the following: when a bhikṣu stays at the residence of non-Buddhists, even though they share the same views and doctrines, there may be conjurers, actors, or kings who come and go and travel about there;
in such cases, this constitutes the fault of losing one's robe due to emotional attachment.

Regarding "places for drawing water" and so forth, these are as explained previously in the section on the boundary of the clan (*kulagocara*), because in places such as those for drawing water, there are many people with differing views.
If heterodox teachers and followers of other paths come and go, this place is lost because it constitutes a separate boundary (*sīmā*).
However, if they are of the same view as the [monks], such as those who follow the same path, there is no loss [of the boundary] even at places such as water sources.
Regarding the statement that "the above are all from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), yet there are no textual grounds [to support this] and they must be accepted as valid":

this means that from the section on the "abandonment of boundaries" (*sīmā-bandha*) upwards, the various permitted practices found therein do not exist within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Although these are texts belonging to other schools, they must be universally applied according to principle. "Valid" (*yǔn*) means "to trust" or "to believe."

Regarding the "eight types of boundaries," the Vinaya states they include "mostly exposed" and so forth; this refers to cases such as having a wall on one side while there are no walls on the other three sides.
The commentary notes that "one provisionally uses trees to measure the dimensions and so on" because in open wilderness *araṇya* locations, there are no natural demarcations.
Regarding the measurement by trees, one takes seven *dhanus* (bows) and so forth. This is like using a measuring rod to discuss space, even though space itself has no such measurements.

As for the inclusion of the "potential sphere" (*prabhāva-bhūmi*) of over seventy [bow-lengths], Jie (礪) says: "In total, there are only fifty-eight paces and a half, including the area where stones can be thrown;
this is because it constitutes the substance of the boundary (*sīmā*). This differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika*, which states seventy-three paces and a half."
Thus concludes the preceding explanation of the eleven kinds of robe-boundaries (*cīvara-sīmā*) according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding the passage in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* concerning a bhikṣu traveling on a road with his preceptor while carrying his robes: it means that the disciple, for the sake of his preceptor, carries the three robes.
While traveling on the road, if one is at a great distance from the teacher and the dawn appears, fearing that one might lose the robe, one should inform the Buddha.

The Buddha asked how far apart they were and instructed that even in such a case, a distance of forty-nine fathoms is permitted. This should be understood as referring to a broad and large road, such as the main thoroughfares of Chang’an.
However, if it is a narrow path where one side is pressed against water and the other side borders a forest hermitage (araṇya), then [the rule is different].
One may discuss the "lengthwise" [measurement], but one must not discuss the "width. Regarding the rule that one's body must remain within the boundary of the tree or the *araṇya* (wilderness):

this means that when it is said today that one carries the robe on the road and loses it upon raising one's head from under the pillow, it does not mean that both the body and the robe are together on the road.
Rather, it means that while the robe is on the road, the person's body is in the *araṇya*, beneath a tree, or elsewhere; having placed the robe there, one falls asleep with the head resting upon it.
When [the robe] is put on, it becomes manifest; because the boundaries are distinct, the robe is lost.

Regarding the phrase "if the disciple’s summer retreat is not yet complete," etc., this means that if one has not yet completed five years of seniority (pañca-varṣa), and while following the teacher encounters someone preaching the Dharma, if one’s mind is so intent on hearing the Dharma that one does not commit the offense of being separated from the teacher, the teacher alone incurs the loss of the robe.

Regarding the statement that "this meaning is explained in detail within the *Cakravartana-sīmā* (the realm of the turning wheel)," the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa* (Commentary on the Vinaya-śāstra) states: As for the "expedient means of the turning wheel":

A bhikṣu was practicing the dhūta austerity of staying outside the boundary. When night fell, he was unable to reach the boundary; fearing he would lose his robes, he walked to the gate of the monastery.
After walking a few paces, he did not know what to do. Out of compassion, the Buddha established an expedient means to permit him to take up a staff (*daṇḍa*) and follow it [into the boundary].
Usage of the Blue Line. What are the four types of boundary markers? They may be moats, fences, walls, or the like. One should measure them with this staff according to their height.
If a moat is used as a marker, that moat will necessarily have variations in size, shallowness, and depth; for instance, it may be wide and shallow.
If it is wide, measure its width; if it is narrow but deep, measure its depth. If the boundary is defined by a fence or wall, take the measurement from the top.
If all four boundaries are low and shallow, or if there are no features such as walls or moats, one may follow the edge of the territory.
There are large trees, bamboo, and so forth; take one that is extremely tall and use a staff to measure its height as the standard.
Place one end of this staff in the center of the cart and position the cart at the point where one’s body reaches when the first light of dawn appears, facing toward the edge of the temple gate.
Rotate this cart within the space between [the starting point] and the gate. If one end of the staff reaches the wall or enclosure, let this person [proceed].
One remains at the place where the sun rose yesterday. It is like a turning wheel or the end of a staff: if one brushes against this person, one does not lose the robe;
if one does not reach this person, one loses the robe. This is called the principle of the "turning wheel" (*cakravartana*) expedient.

If someone comes and goes while the robe is not carried with the body and is lost, it means it was lost because of the coming and going of those such as kings, musicians, or women. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Regarding the statement that "in a waterway, one may traverse a boundary of twenty-five *zhū*": the commentary states this is based on the *Cīvara-vastu*. This refers to shallow water where one does not board a boat;

if one can walk through such water for a distance of twenty-five *zhū*, it is termed the substance of a "robe-boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*). If the water is deep and one lowers a boat, the boat itself constitutes a separate boundary;
once one steps out of the boat, [the robe] is lost [to the original boundary].
Regarding the fifteen-well boundary (*pañcadaśa-kūpa-sīmā*), which according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is also twenty-five cubits (*hasta*) [on each side]:
Jing says that this refers to placing the robe near the well-railing; on all four sides, each measures twenty-five cubits.

If the robe is inside the well, it is not opened up [as a boundary]; one must connect it with a cord to avoid loss. Regarding underground pits (*kūpa*) and the like, the prohibition concerning robes applies; northerners frequently construct such [storage spaces].
He bored a hole beneath his dwelling. In the hot months, he would enter it to seek coolness; at other times, he would place food and drink there.
In winter it did not freeze, and in summer it did not spoil.
Regarding the statement that "none of the various schools [recognize] a sphere of influence (*prabhāva*)," the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials) says:

"It is simply that there is no sphere of influence. If this is so, why is it that for vehicles, staffs, boats, and so forth, the measure is twenty-five cubits? This refers to the substance of the boundary (*sīmā*), not the sphere of influence. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* likewise does not [mention a sphere of influence].

If this is so, why is it said that "the vehicle-boundary extends to where the staff reaches," and so on? These are all the substance of the boundary; they were never intended to be spheres of influence.

The same applies to matters such as the "sphere of influence" (*sīmā*) and the range of a village arrow. None of the other schools possess [this rule], except for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which alone provides it.
As for the mention of throwing stones found therein, which is treated as a separate matter, although that text clarifies the throwing of stones, it does not constitute a means of protection.
This refers to the spatial extent of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). Although the act of throwing a stone is the same in both cases, the underlying meaning differs.

According to the *Vibhaṅga* (Jian lun), which clarifies the precept against stealing, it explains the locations where theft occurs. Whether in a wilderness (*araṇya*) or a village (*grāma*), both are places where theft may take place;

if one takes property from within them, an offense is committed. What constitutes a "village boundary"? It is defined as taking [an object] and throwing it with all one's strength, provided one is neither infirm nor weak.
The village boundary extends as far as the place where a stone reaches when thrown from the dwelling; it does not extend to where the momentum of the stone continues after it has fallen.
If the village has no fence, the boundary is defined by the distance a stone thrown from the edge of the water surrounding the dwellings would fall.

Regarding those who do not share the Dharma boundary, this rule is established. (Furthermore, in the *Śramaṇera-śikṣāpada*, it says: "Within this boundary, one *pācittiya* offense occurs beyond the first stone-throw outside the house; beyond the second stone-throw, it is a *thullaccaya* offense. Only those who do not share the Dharma boundary are excluded.

[The text] clarifies: "Fifteen [units] are natural; furthermore, the *śakti-bhāga* (sphere of influence) is opened. Only for the *kṛta-karma* (formally established) boundary for the gathering of robes (*cīvara-saṃgraha*) is there no *śakti-bhāga*. Question:
Since both are boundaries for robes, why is it that the natural robe-boundary has a *śakti-bhāga*, whereas the formally established boundary has none?

Answer: Li replies: "One may open what has not yet been opened. (Originally, the rule was that one must carry [the robe] with oneself. Now, the permission to establish a boundary for gathering robes is already an opening of the text. Why should one further open its *śakti-bhāga*?)"

The response was: "Because there is a formal dharma, there is no [boundary]; because there is no formal dharma, there is [a boundary]. (To establish a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is called "having a formal dharma," and thus there is no *prabhāva* (influence/scope).
To establish a natural robe-boundary (*prakṛti-cīvara-sīmā*) is called "not having a formal dharma," and thus there is *prabhāva*.)
Regarding the statement that "a bhikṣu may have reasons [to stay], even to the point of borrowing lay clothing," according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Qishi), fascicle 8:
A bhikṣu, wearing his upper and lower robes, enters a village where a woman says to him, "I wish to make offerings to the images tonight;
you should help me prepare them. The bhikṣu then intends to return as the sun sets, but she earnestly requests him to stay overnight. If...
If there are monks at that residence who possess extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), one should temporarily borrow them to maintain possession. If there are no monks there, one may borrow from a nun;

if there is no nun either, one may borrow a robe or cloak from a layperson to perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*). After attaching a fastening cord (*guṇa*), one should then maintain possession.
If none of these options are available, one should return quickly to the monastery when the city gates open during the final watch of the night; do not let the time pass.

When one leaves the city and arrives at the gate of the monastery, if it has not yet opened, one should request that the gate be opened. If it cannot be opened, one should stand beneath the gatehouse.
If there is no gatehouse, one should insert one's hand into a hole; there are two kinds of holes: either a door-hole or a drainage-channel hole.
If it is a drainage-channel hole, one should first insert one's hands and feet; should there happen to be a snake or a viper, one should first [use]...
One should startle them with a staff. Then, one should insert the hand so that it joins with the garment. If there is no opening, one should enter by leaping over the wall or fence.
One should make a sign so that those inside recognize [the visitor], lest they suspect him of being a thief and cause alarm and agitation.

If entry cannot be gained, one should quickly take the garment; it is better to be without the garment than to commit a *vyatikrama* offense against the *vinaya*, for the light is exchanged for the heavy. Jing says: "If..."

If one does not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) and does not secure the fastening cord, the act of receiving and holding [the robe] is completed; however, one incurs an offense against the Dharma. The commentary notes:
"Because the door-beam is connected to the interior boundary, that Vinaya lacks the 'sphere of influence' (*pradeśa*);

therefore, taking this as the substance of the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), it is established that since one cannot advance further, if one merely stands beneath the door and grasps the beam with the hand, one does not lose possession of the robe. This is because that Vinaya text lacks the sphere of influence."
Because it is divided, one must grasp the beam. Sengshen says: "Opening the grasping of the beam" does not refer to the ritual boundary for gathering robes (*cīvara-sīmā*);
it is merely the boundary of the monastic village (*saṃgha-grāma*). If it were a ritual boundary, it would necessarily require the robes to be assembled. Furthermore, he explains:
"Taking twenty-five *hasta* as the substance of the robe boundary" refers to cases such as other wells or halls; it serves as the monastic village boundary.

Regarding the two boundaries (*sīmā*), the existence [of a separate *śakti*] is not opened up. Since the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are already complete for both the monastic community (*saṃgha*) and the village (*grāma*) boundaries, there is no further need for twenty-five cubits (*hasta*).
Furthermore, it is said that because the lintel of the gatehouse differs from that of the *Dharmaguptaka* school, one should know this;

however, this commentary contains an error. If it were to say that because there is no *śakti* (influence/scope), one must stand beneath the gate, or even within the hand-hole (*karṇa-koṭara*), then—four [points follow].
Since there is already a "sphere of influence" (*śakti-bhāga*) regarding the division [of space], it would follow that one need not insert one's hand into the opening.

Yet, with the temple gate closed and one’s body outside the door, how could it be of any benefit to employ [the action] within the sphere of influence when obstructed by such a barrier? How could one possibly avoid transgression simply because one is within the sphere of influence?

If one follows this statement, it must mean that if there are the three aforementioned obstructions within the boundary, even if one performs this rite, one will inevitably fail, provided the three obstructions exist within the boundary—namely, that the person above holds the beam.
According to this, since there are no three obstructions within the boundary, [the rite] is not lost.

If there are three kinds of obstructions and one’s body is within a boundary (*sīmā*), one must either remain with the robe or, if discarding it, ensure there is an obstruction within the boundary or that it is an object outside the boundary.
Objects outside the boundary refer to those where the paths of water or land are cut off due to urgent difficulties and other such circumstances;

therefore, they must be set aside at a distance. If one does not perform these three aforementioned actions, first, one must remain within the range of a stone’s throw, and second, it refers to sentient beings who are defiled.
Second, there must be physical obstruction, such as when one must grasp the robe with the hand. Third, there is remote relinquishment due to an intervening barrier.
