It is just as the Sūtra says: "There are some who consume nectar, yet their lives are harmed and they perish prematurely."
This refers to those who die prematurely. Regarding the initial stage of committing a grave offense of theft:

it is established that by engaging in the buying and selling of living beings and contending over the high or low price, there may be the transgression of a grave offense. The "eight venomous snakes" are the eight impurities (*aśuddha*).
As in the past, when a bhikṣu saw gold, he cried out: "O śramaṇa, this is a venomous snake! O śramaṇa, this is a venomous snake! and so forth. If one shares [these things] with the Saṃgha...

Regarding those who fall into hell due to violating the precepts, [Vasubandhu] establishes that if a monk shares residence and participates in the communal affairs (*saṃghakārya*) with such a person, performing the *karmavācanā* rituals together with them will not be valid;
this constitutes a violation of the Buddha’s teachings, and for that reason, they enter hell.

Regarding the "precepts for worldly peace" obtained through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), Vasubandhu maintains that acts such as digging the earth, destroying living beings, and eating at improper times are prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*). Therefore...

It is said that this is to cease worldly censure. Regarding "grave by nature" (*prakṛti-garuka*): examples include killing, sexual misconduct, and so forth. Because these are natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and constitute paths of action (*karmapatha*), they are called grave by nature.

As for prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*), they only come into existence through the formal ritual procedure (*karma*), and thus it is said they are obtained through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
If it refers to natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), they are said to exist constantly, regardless of whether the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed or not.

Regarding the "eight kinds of coins," according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), they are: first, gold; second, silver; third, copper; fourth, iron; fifth, white tin (*rañjana*); sixth, lead and tin; seventh, wood; and eighth, coins made of lacquer resin (*hu-jiao*).
The commentary states, "resembling [the real] by way of its image," which means it explains the aforementioned "resemblance in color. If one says...
"Gold and silver in their natural state": this is a dual citation of both the Sanskrit and the Chinese. In Sanskrit, "natural state" (*jāta*) corresponds here to "gold";
in Sanskrit, "state" (*ākṛti*) corresponds here to "silver. Regarding the *duṣkṛta* offense for keeping [them] by means of the five kinds of acquisition:

the established view is that if one possesses counterfeit gems—or, according to the passage below, if one has already accepted them through the five kinds of acceptance, such as acceptance by vessel, acceptance by body, and so forth—then one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. This also applies if one grasps gold leaf and the like.

Regarding those who fall [into an offense] yet do not violate this precept: this refers to the ninety-first precept concerning the handling of precious objects (*ratna*) after having committed [the preceding offense].

Regarding the statement in the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* that "impure things" such as gold, silver, and coins are called impure because they are touched: the Master [Dao]li says that gold and silver are called impure precisely because they must not be touched;
whereas other precious objects are called pure because they may be touched. The Master says these are "precious-like" (*ratnopama*) objects, such as copper.
Because iron and the like can be touched, they differ from coins and such; this is called "pure. Nevertheless, because one still may not wear them, they are also called "impure.
This refers to items resembling jewels that are designated as both pure and impure: from the perspective of being able to be touched, they are called pure;
from the perspective that one should not wear them, they are also called impure. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, gold, silver, and coins are termed "impure objects. It says:
"Other treasures" refers to items that are either pure or impure; this means such things as pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, and so forth.
Regarding "if they possess the proper characteristics," this means that although the inscriptions are clear and distinct, they are not currently used for their purpose—such as ancient coins.
If a bhikṣu should trade these for robes, alms bowls, or other requisites, he should accept and maintain them after having traded for them. Thus it is established.

From this point onward, there are two sections of text. This refers to having money and treasures. If one performs the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification) with respect to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such items), but the *kappiya-kāraka* does not understand the procedure, the act is not accomplished;
one consequently incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Even if one causes [the money] to be exchanged for robes and bowls, these robes and bowls must still be further exchanged [for other allowable items], because the original *pariśuddhi* was not validly performed. If, at that time, the *kappiya-kāraka* did understand the bhikṣu’s explanation...
Regarding "pure dharma" (śuddhadharma): one does not incur an offense of falling (pātayantika). Later, if one obtains clothing through trade, it may be added to [the existing stock];
therefore, it is said that "one should take and keep it. Although the aforementioned tradition maintains this interpretation, Master Jueyi does not agree with it. He now states:

since it was previously mentioned that the purification (viśuddhi) had been declared before a pure person (śuddhapudgala), if that pure person takes the item and returns it to the bhikṣu, it must be regarded as belonging to that person.
He receives the command and has the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) reward him for it. Furthermore, it is explained:

if that person is a bhikkhu and they trade robes, bowls, and so forth, one should hold [the money] for the purpose of trading with those who receive and possess them. This refers to the previously mentioned money that has been purified;

since it is now in the possession of a bhikkhu, if the attendant now wishes to use this money to purchase robes for the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu must hold this money and give it to the attendant to trade for the robes.
Alms bowl. Therefore it is said: "One should accept and maintain it by exchanging [money] for it.

This means that one should give the money to a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) and have them trade it for robes, which one then accepts and maintains oneself. The passage beginning with "If that upāsaka... clarifies that once the *kappiyakāraka* has taken the money away...

Having acquired the robe through trade, one must apply the formal ritual (*adhikāra*) to maintain it. (This interpretation makes the text extremely smooth and direct. [The commentary] states: "If that *upāsaka*... and so forth;

this refers to the completed sentence for declaring purity (*śuddhi*) in the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka*. The preceding text, however, constitutes the incomplete sentence for declaring purity in the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka*.
Regarding the second point, "the *kappiya-kāraka* says 'one may store items that are easily purified'": this means that the *kappiya-kāraka* causes...

A bhikṣu may accept pure items and keep them; he must then perform the ritual of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity). These two aforementioned methods both concern the breaking of this rule regarding knowledge of the Dharma.
According to the fourth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, there are two ways to declare the purity of money and treasures.
If a layperson brings money or treasures to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should simply say: "This is an impure object; I should not possess it. If it is pure...

It should be accepted; this is itself the purification (*pariśuddhi*). If a layperson says, "I give these jewels to the bhikṣu," and the bhikṣu says, "I should not keep them," and the *śucidāsa* (pure person) says, "Exchange them for pure items and keep them," then this constitutes the performance of purification.

If the layperson does not say to exchange them for pure items, and the bhikṣu himself does not declare them pure, but simply sets them aside on the ground—if there is another bhikṣu present, he should follow that [other] bhikṣu’s declaration of purity. Accordingly...

Regarding the duration of storage: if there is no other bhikṣu present, one must not accept [money or valuables]. To accept them constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, it is said:

"The method for the pure donation (*śuci-dāna*) of money and treasures is as follows: one should first seek out a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) who knows the Dharma and ensure they understand the meaning [of the following]:

'According to the dharma of us bhikṣus, we do not store money or treasures. I now appoint you, donor, as the master of purity (*śucy-adhipati*). Any money or treasures I subsequently obtain shall be entirely donated to you.'"

After having obtained a *śuddhika* (pure owner), when one obtains money or precious objects, one must declare them as pure (*śuddhi-uddeśa*) before the monks; it is not necessary to state the name of the *śuddhika*.
Once they have been declared pure, one may keep them for as long as desired. If the *śuddhika* dies or departs to another country, one should seek another *śuddhika*.

With the exception of money and precious objects, all other surplus property (*atireka-lābha*) must undergo the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) before the five groups of monks. (Following the intent of this text, the declaration of purity regarding money and precious objects is likewise performed before a monk.)
If coins should scatter, one may use bricks or tiles to toss them back in; this refers to the *parikarmika* (attendant) who is made to drop the money.

When the money is being dropped and some scatters, the bhikṣu’s hand must not touch it; however, it is permitted to strike the scattered coins with tiles or stones to cause them to roll back into the pit.
Regarding "one must not touch the four edges," etc., this is like the case of kings, princesses, or persons of noble and high status.
People often encounter such situations: when one offers food to the monks using a golden bowl, the bhikṣu may not receive it directly with his hands.
Instead, he instructs the donor to place it before him. At the moment of setting it down, the monk says, "I receive, I receive, I receive," and it is thereby considered received.
However, regarding the food within the vessel, one must not touch its inner or outer edges with the hands. As for the statement that "holding with the hand is praised," since this refers to gold...
Regarding bowls and other vessels, one must not praise them verbally by saying things such as, "This is a truly excellent vessel," nor is it permitted to handle them with the hands.

If one says, "Give this to a *śuddhaka-purusa* (pure person)," both parties commit an offense; since both the one who receives it directly and the one who causes another to receive it are equally guilty of a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If these items are to be distributed among the Sangha, it is said that they shall be divided according to the established order within the Sangha. This applies to other items resembling jewels as well as the "one hundred and one" requisites.
Regarding "objects up to those that cause regret for an offense of light transgression (*dukkaṭa*"): items such as counterfeit pearls are called "resembling jewels.

Because one keeps them without performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), one commits an offense of light transgression and is made to repent. [Master] Shen says: These words regarding the "one hundred and one items" do not refer to a person who maintains the one hundred and one items of the middle grade.
Since the ritual of acceptance has been added to the keeping of these one hundred and one items, there is absolutely no fault of possessing excess. Now, it is said:
Regarding "one who relinquishes": this refers to the person who possesses the extra items. It is called "the one hundred and one" because it refers to each individual item within that collection.
Regarding the two ways of declaring the purity (*śuci*) of money and gems: Jing says there are two types—first, monastics; second, laypeople—as in the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* cited previously.
As for "if one acquires them without speaking to either party, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*)," this means that both the bhikṣu and the attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) remain silent.
This refers to the following: previously, it was explained that whether a bhikṣu speaks or a lay attendant (upāsaka) utters the words, both are termed "declaring purity" (śuddhi-vyāhāra).
Now, however, since neither of them speaks, purity is not established. Jing says: "This indicates that there is a mind [of the donor] to accept and keep [the object].

As for "one may not give it to a śrāmaṇera," this means that his legal status is the same as a śrāmaṇera; he is not permitted to handle precious objects. Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited below.
This is the testimony. Regarding the passage in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning Maudgalyāyana and the novice Cūḍapanthaka:
According to that text, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Maudgalyāyana was sitting in meditation with the novice Cūḍapanthaka by the side of Lake Anavatapta after the midday meal.

At that time, the novice saw golden sand along the riverbank and thought, "I shall now take a great deal of this sand and place it beneath the World-Honored One’s water-jar. Maudgalyāyana... [text continues].
Having emerged from meditative absorption, Maudgalyāyana returned through the air by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). A novice had been seized by a non-human being (*amanuṣya*).
Maudgalyāyana turned back, called for the novice, and asked, "Why have you not come? The novice replied, "I could not go. He asked, "Is there something holding you back?
He replied, "I am holding this gold dust; you should discard it. Once it was discarded, he immediately departed through the air. The elder bhikṣu then took the novice [with him].
Regarding the story of Mīḍhila returning to his village: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who, taking a śrāmaṇera with him, was returning to visit his relatives.

On the way, they passed through a wilderness where a non-human being manifested as a dragon. The dragon circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, scattered flowers over him, and praised him, saying: "Excellent!
You have gained great benefit by renouncing the home life to go forth, not grasping gold, silver, or money. Thus it is compared.

The Venerable Kāśyapa arrived at the home of his relatives. After exchanging greetings, he was about to depart when the wife of a relative said, "As you are now returning, the road is long and you will likely suffer from lack of provisions.
You may take this money and go to the market to buy what you require. The śrāmaṇera accepted it, tied it to the corner of his robe, and departed.
On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera walking behind the bhikṣu and further transformed himself into a dragon and came forward.
He circumambulated the śrāmaṇera from the left, scattering clouds of dust over him, and spoke these words:

"You have lost a great benefit! Having left the household life to practice the Way, you yet carry money while walking. The śrāmaṇera then wept. The bhikṣu looked back and asked the śrāmaṇera, "For what reason do you weep?
He replied, "I do not recall having committed any fault; I am being distressed for no cause. The teacher said, "Is there something you are holding? He replied, "I am holding this money."
They came, and the Master ordered them to be discarded. Once discarded, non-human beings again made offerings as before. [The monks] reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for śrāmaṇeras to hold gold, silver, or money. This refers to those who, because their transgressions can be remedied, encounter retribution from the dark realms;
that is to say, the fault of the two śrāmaṇeras mentioned above. Since this fault is remediable, they encountered retribution from the dark realms.
If one cannot be cured in the present, then one will inevitably undergo retribution in the future by entering hell;
thus, one does not encounter this light reproof in the present. As for the case of the pool deity’s reproach, that too is something that can be cured.
Regarding the pool deity’s reproach, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 17: there was once a bhikṣu in a forest, by the side of a lotus pond.
While walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), he smelled the fragrance of lotuses; his nose perceived it and his mind became attached. The deity of the pond spoke:

"For what reason have you abandoned your place for pure meditative sitting in that forest grove to steal my fragrance? Because of this attachment to fragrance, the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all afflictions will lie dormant within you."
Now they have all awakened. At that time, another person came into the river, gathered many of its flowers, and dug up and pulled out the roots and stalks, departing with them in disarray.
The deity of the pond remained silent and said nothing. The bhikṣu said, "This person has ruined your pond and taken your flowers, yet you said nothing at all;
but when I was merely walking along the riverbank, you immediately scolded and reviled me."

"Stealing fragrance. The deity of the pond said, "Evil people of the world constantly dwell amidst the filth of sin and defilement; they are submerged head-deep in impurity, and I do not speak with them.
You are a good person practicing meditation, yet you have attached yourself to this fragrance, which ruins your virtuous practice.
For this reason, I rebuke you. It is like a white cloth, fresh and pure, upon which a black stain has fallen; it is seen by all. Such is that evil person."
It is like a speck of ink on black clothing that no one sees; who would ask about it? As for those who have not yet repented their remaining offenses, they will inevitably meet with public execution.
Ciyun said: "If one commits acts such as theft, one will certainly be subjected to corporal punishment by others without a doubt."
This refers to execution. It can also be understood as the sin of transgressing and failing to repent, which increases day and night in the present life.

Furthermore, it is explained that if one merely smells a fragrance for a moment, one may still incur divine retribution; how much more so for those who further commit illegal acts and grave offenses, who will certainly be expelled and destroyed.

Thus, it is said they are "publicly executed. Regarding the phrase "like a swollen cheek," the *Śata-avadāna-sūtra* (Hundred Parables Sutra) states: Long ago, there was a man who went to his wife’s family home and saw...
He [the husband] ate rice. He then went to that place and stole some rice to eat. When his wife came and saw her husband, she wished to speak with him;
however, with rice filling his mouth, he could not respond at all. Out of shame before his wife, he was unwilling to spit it out, and for this reason, he did not speak.
The wife wondered why he did not speak, so she felt his mouth with her hand and thought his mouth was swollen. She said to her father, "My husband has only just returned..."
He suffered from a swelling of the mouth and was unable to speak at all. His father immediately summoned a physician to treat him.
The physician said, "This illness is most grave; it can only be cured by lancing it with a knife. He then used a knife to incise and break open the man's mouth, whereupon rice emerged from within.
Thus the matter was revealed. People of the world are just like this: they commit various evil deeds.
Having violated the pure precepts, they conceal their transgressions and are unwilling to confess them; consequently, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
They are like those foolish people who, out of a minor sense of shame, refused to spit out the rice and instead had their mouths slit open with a knife to reveal their fault.

The following clarifies the circumstances under which there is no offense. Regarding "the conditions for exemption (kai-en) are as stated above," this means that within the preceding text of this very precept, there are already provisions for such exemptions.
Precept 19: Trading Jewels. Regarding "exchanging purified jewels (setsujō-hō) with others, etc.," Shen says: "If it is not..."

The purification of pure wealth has been explained. Having already committed the previous offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, if one now further exchanges it for other goods, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), because there is no double offense.

Regarding the statement that "one incurs a *pāyattika* when it is given to another," although one may bargain over the price—whether high or low—if the time of committing the offense is precisely when it is being given to another, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
This differs from the five points regarding the subsequent precept on exchanging robes.

Regarding this, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: First, they differ in terms of the persons involved. Trading precious objects constitutes an offense for all seven classes of practitioners; trading clothing constitutes an offense only for the two lay groups.

Second, regarding the act of trading precious objects—whether performed by oneself or instructed to another—it constitutes an offense for one’s own sake, except when acting for the Three Jewels; however, in the case of trading clothing, employing another person does not constitute an offense.

Third, regarding the trading of precious objects, the prohibition is absolute and no exception is made even for one’s own benefit; in contrast, the trading of clothing allows for the exchange of items such as ghee and oil. Fourth...

Regarding the relinquishment of robes and jewels, the procedures for monastics and laypeople differ. In the case of the five types of returning property to its original state, there is a distinction between what is "original" and what is not; thus, it is called "exchanging robes.

When one relinquishes and performs the *pratideśanā* (confession) of a robe, having returned the original robe, one may receive it again after it has been exchanged. However, when relinquishing and confessing the exchange of jewels, once the property has been given to a layperson, even if the property is later returned, one must first exchange it for pure items before they can be accepted;
otherwise, the original property is not fit to be received. What is now referred to as "exchanging robes" [is explained as follows].
The "precept against selling" refers specifically to the precept against trading. As for its origin: it arose because Baddhālī (Bhadanta) traded robes with non-Buddhists;

therefore, this act of trading robes is designated as the "precept against selling. Furthermore, when compared with the fourfold classification of the precept against possessing precious objects (*ratna-parigraha*), there are two cases:
first, possessing without trading, which refers to accepting money or gold offered by laypeople; second, trading without possessing, which refers to exchanging robes.
Money is a treasure. The first three cases are all [instances of] this; one buys gold with money and keeps it. The fourth case is neither, which refers to the bartering of clothing and food.

As for the distinction that there is no clothing or food [in the other cases], this is clearly established: this precept discusses only the direct exchange of gold, silver, and money, and does not discuss clothing or food.
The subsequent precept, however, discusses clothing and food; therefore, they are distinguished from one another. "The first is money-treasure" serves to exclude the remainder.
Regarding clothing, there is no offense. Second, as for those who exchange with one another, all such cases constitute a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

There are a total of forty-nine permutations regarding mutual trade; among these, the categories of money, gold, and silver are divided into seven: namely, three for gold, three for silver, and one for money.
There are three types of gold: first, already-formed gold, which refers to items that have already been fashioned into objects such as hairpins and bracelets;

second, unformed gold, which refers to gold ingots and the like—some commentators explain this as "gold ore," but we do not agree with that view, for since the raw material is still mixed with stone, it cannot yet be called gold;
third, both formed and unformed gold, which refers to [metal] that has undergone casting and hammering but remains [in its semi-finished state].
It has not yet been polished. Gao says: "That which is already formed" refers to rings, bracelets, and utensils; "that which is not yet formed" refers to raw silver ingots.

"That which is both formed and not yet formed" refers to [semi-finished items] such as *ting* vessels. The three categories within silver are likewise. Together with money, these constitute seven types.
Within these seven, they may be exchanged for one another; thus, there are seven for each category, totaling forty-nine. Regarding the first group of seven: the first is that which is already formed.
1. Trading with gold that has already been acquired for gold that has already been acquired. 2. Trading with gold that has already been acquired for gold that has not yet been acquired. 3.

Trading with gold that has already been acquired for gold that has already been acquired and not yet been acquired. 4. Trading with gold that has already been acquired for silver that has already been acquired. 5. Trading with gold that has already been acquired for silver that has not yet been acquired. 6.

Trading with gold that has already been acquired for silver that has already been acquired and not yet been acquired. 7. Trading with gold that has already been acquired for money. These seven phrases involve exclusively using...
Having already made gold the head, the subsequent seven phrases follow the same sequence as above;

that is, one takes the finished gold as the head and exchanges it for the remaining six [parts], and this applies likewise even when using silver or coins as the head. Next, one takes unrefined gold as the head.
One should say: "Unrefined gold is traded for unrefined gold; two [pieces of] unrefined gold are traded for refined gold, and so forth.
Next, taking refined and unrefined gold as the basis, one should say: "Refined and unrefined gold are traded for refined gold."
Second, regarding the exchange of finished and unfinished gold for finished gold, and so forth (as detailed).

If one exchanges finished and unfinished silver for finished and unfinished silver, first one should record them in pairs; next, one proceeds from the former, meaning starting with gold as the primary item.
If one takes silver as the primary item, one likewise records them in pairs, meaning recording the currency first, followed by starting from gold. It is not otherwise.
Regarding those who may approach two or three people, it is stated: "This precept is grave; one must repent within the Saṃgha. The following clarifies the rules for non-offenses.
The twentieth precept concerns buying and selling.
Regarding the accomplishment of the four noble lineages (*catur-ārya-vaṃśa*), these are the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*). First, [relying on] the household... [text fragment ends].
"Among the assemblies" means that it excludes the five groups of the ordained from committing an offense. Regarding the "double opening" according to other schools:

the *Śāriputrābhidharma* states that within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one may only instruct a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) to perform the exchange; however, according to other schools, one should have the lay attendant perform the exchange—this is the first opening.
Furthermore, if no lay attendant is available, the bhikṣu may also perform the exchange himself—this is the second opening. Therefore, it is called a "double opening. Nevertheless...
When a bhikṣu engages in trade, he must necessarily know the "pure speech" (sammukhībhūta-vāc). It is better to be a butcher;

for a butcher might universally wish that no one in the world kills, while he alone sells meat. Or, if one deals in salt, one might constantly wish that the four distant regions were in rebellion and the royal roads were blocked.
This refers, for example, to someone living in the city of Chang’an who possesses ten or five *shí* of salt, and then suddenly [encounters] the King...
The roads were blocked; carriages could not pass, and the paths to the four quarters were cut off. Since salt was so scarce, how could it have a price?

Regarding the statement in the *Five Hundred Questions* that "if one acquires goods through trade and gives them to another, one commits a *pāyattika* offense," Jing says: "This refers to the recipient committing the *pāyattika* offense because of the sin of trading for profit;
the same applies to the subsequent sentence. As for the phrase "in cases of extreme distress and the like," Li states: "If one is starving and has nothing..."
Regarding the place of eating: if this monk who earns his living by trade has a layperson prepare food with these goods, it is permitted for him to eat it.
However, that monk who earns his living must first declare before the assembly, "This is not my own property," and only then may he eat it.
If a bhikṣu engaged in livelihood does not make this statement, he commits an offense of falling (pāyattika) regarding the food of the Saṃgha.

If he gives these items as a gift to a layperson, and that layperson subsequently gives them back to the Saṃgha for the sake of obtaining food, it is permissible because the ownership has changed. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one exchanges similar goods for similar goods, [it is permissible].
Lì says: "Both the similar and the dissimilar result in a *pāyattika* offense. For example, trading a bowl for a bowl or a jar for a jar constitutes a *pāyattika*;
this is called 'the similar. If one trades a bowl for a jar or the like, it also results in a *pāyattika*; this is called 'the dissimilar.

As for items that may be relinquished—such as gold, silver, or purchased grain—if one obtains clothing from them, it is a *pāyattika*, and if one obtains food, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This clarifies that while keeping grain or rice incurs only a *duṣkṛta*, keeping clothing incurs a *pāyattika*."
Now, the degrees of gravity differ, just as previously explained regarding the eight types of impure goods, where there are variations in severity.
Here it is clarified that if one acquires goods by using money or grain, if one obtains clothing, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); if one obtains food, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

Regarding the three matters of buying, selling, and bartering in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which all result in a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation), the established view is that within the acts of buying and selling, they may contain the element of "selling" (*vikkaya*) or they may be direct transactions.

To purchase without seeking profit is called "buying" (*māi*). Sometimes one merely sells without engaging in trade; however, if one purchases for the sake of profit with the intent to sell later at a higher price, it is termed "trading" (*p'an*).
Each of these cases is subject to forfeiture. To raise the price to a high level is called "selling" (*mai*); to suppress the price to a low level is termed "buying.
Having purchased with the aim of profit and then selling is likewise called "trading"; these three are all subject to forfeiture. However, as for the case of trading...
Regarding the timing of the offense: if one intends to seek profit, the offense is committed at that very moment; it does not wait until the price has been raised.

Even if one sells at the regular market price at the time of the transaction, one still incurs the offense of trading. As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) stating that this refers to a single item, Cízhì says:

"If one receives a single garment and then engages in buying and selling, the offense is incurred simultaneously. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), however, calculates the offense based on each individual item.

Each object incurs its own offense. *Lì* (Lì) says: "In that Vinaya, 'selling' includes buying and selling. [The author] privately comments: This refers to the offense arising from both selling and buying with respect to a single object.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are three clauses. The first clause states: "If one buys out of greed for a thief, it is a *duṣkṛta* (*gīla*);
this means simply seeing a thief and buying [the goods], without intending to sell them later. Second, selling out of greed for a high price; this means..."
If one possesses a robe and alms bowl that were originally not intended for sale, but upon suddenly seeing them become highly valued, one proceeds to sell them, this is also permissible.

However, once the third purchase has been made and one intends to sell, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Now, examining this closely, it is evident that the offense arises with respect to a single object in the third instance.

In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is not so. Even if, at the time of purchase, one does not intend to resell, if one does not utter the "purification through knowledge" (*jñapti*) formula while bargaining over the price—high or low—one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
Alternatively, even if one is not greedy for a high price at the time of sale, if one does not utter the "purification through knowledge" formula, there is likewise a *thullaccaya*.
To buy and sell for the purpose of trade is certainly a *thullaccaya* offense. Now, examining the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding a single object and [its] differences...
Regarding the phrase "on the object," it means that both [the buyer and seller] incur an offense. As for the statement that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is "unclear" and so forth:

Master Li states that while the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) allows for the return [of goods] within seven days, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely says one may not return them without specifying the number of days; hence it is called "unclear.

Furthermore, it must be understood that these rules all concern a bhikṣu’s private buying and selling. Regarding the phrase "one must know the worthy and good listener who gives at the proper price," Master Li says: "In general..."
When a bhikṣu exchanges goods with the Saṃgha, the value must be equal. Now, this bhikṣu is of few desires, virtuous, and moreover impoverished;

therefore, it is permitted for him to give the value of the Saṃgha’s property directly, without the need for barter. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: At that time, there was a bhikṣu who held onto his robe.
The Saṃgha possessed a saṃghāṭī which he wished to exchange for. The other bhikṣus did not disperse [the robe].
He then informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to exchange it. If the price of the *kuśa* grass is higher, the monk should compensate the Sangha.

If the price of the *saṃghāṭī* is higher, the monk should compensate the Sangha. If he is poor and has no goods to compensate the Sangha, yet he is necessarily one of few desires and contented, I also permit him to give it to them.
It is the same for other robes. This is from the *Caturvargika Vinaya* (Sifen lü).

Regarding expensive robes that one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") to trade for: it is stated in the *Khandhaka*: "If there is a *kappiya-kāraka*, have the *kappiya-kāraka* trade for them;
if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, send a bhikṣu to trade for them, and there is no offense.

[However,] if a *kappiya-kāraka* is present and one does not send him to trade, but instead causes a bhikṣu to trade for them, it is a *thullaccaya* (the details are uncertain; await a consultation of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*). Regarding the four types of medicine, they are purified according to whether the substance is light or heavy.

Regarding "impure items" (*aśuci-vastu*) and so forth: according to the *Cīvara-vastu*, there are eight categories: first, medicines for the immediate moment; second, medicines for the night; third, medicines for seven days; fourth, medicines for as long as life lasts (*yāvaj-jīva*);
fifth, miscellaneous items; sixth, valuable items; seventh, impure items; and eighth, items that are both pure and impure. The meaning of the four types of medicine is clear.
As for the fifth, "miscellaneous items," these refer to the three robes, the six articles, and the cloth for covering sores.

Robes, rain-cloaks, *kaṇḍolaka* (a small bowl), water-strainers, mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), straw sandals, and various other items that ought to be kept are all termed "accessory articles" (*anugata-vastu*).
The *Śrīmālā-vyākhyā* states that there are two kinds of "accessories": first, those that may accompany the person; second, those that may accompany the path.
Not keeping the three robes and six articles constitutes an offense, for it violates the path by failing to maintain what is necessary. These are further categorized into two types.

The opposite of the above may be understood accordingly. Regarding "heavy objects," these refer to beds, bedding, cushions, pillows, all copper vessels, all wooden vessels, earthenware vessels, and so forth.
Regarding "impure objects," these refer to money, gold, silver, and the like; because a bhikṣu is not permitted to touch them, they are called impure objects.
Regarding "pure-impure objects," these refer to pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, and coral.
Items such as pears, jade, and other such precious objects may be touched but must not be worn; therefore, they are called "pure-impure" items (*śuddhāśuddha-vastu*).

If one uses a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for the proper time) to purchase a *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, or uses a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* to purchase a *vikālika* (medicine for the improper time), a *saptāhika* (seven-day medicine), or even any other item of value, it is an offense of *duṣkṛta* (misdeed) at the moment the impure speech is uttered;
upon obtaining the object, one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If one uses an item of value that is pure-impure...
The same applies to all such transactions involving goods. Regarding those who, for the sake of the Saṃgha’s monthly provisions, purchase oil, flour, and so forth:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one purchases oil, ghee, rice, beans, or flour for the Saṃgha’s monthly provisions, speaking impure words constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong speech). This is because it is done for the sake of the Saṃgha, the offense is merely a *duṣkṛta*.

However, if one does it for oneself, speaking impure words at that time is a *duṣkṛta*, but upon obtaining the goods, one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If one personally handles the goods...

Regarding "equal value": *Śīlapālita* states that if a bhikṣu sells an object and the other person asks for how much money it is worth, and the bhikṣu demands a higher price than the actual value, yet the other person gives the amount requested, he commits the offense of theft (*steya*). Regarding "using leftover food to trade for ghee, oil, and so forth":
*Śīlapālita* states that this refers specifically to the offense of trading; however, if one takes monastic food back to one's own quarters, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
However, this is not what is clarified here. Regarding the statement, "As for 'obtaining the gift,' it refers to the confession involving the relinquishment of everything," Jì says:
Since goods sold [in violation of the rules] constitute an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), they are not fit to be given; giving them would incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Now, if one wishes to give such items to another person, one must first relinquish them through confession before the Saṃgha; only after receiving them back from the Saṃgha may one then bestow them upon another person. The following clarifies this.
"One does not violate the law. One must not engage in trade with others" means that "others" refers to laypeople;

it is only permitted to trade with the five groups of monastics. Regarding the statement "having a *śuddhakarman* (pure person) conduct the trade," Zhi Sheng says this is a text that provides an exception.

Regarding the *Śāriputra Vinaya* stating that one may ask three times for a price, Zhi Sheng says that when dealing in trade with a layperson, it is permitted to discuss the high or low value of the price up to three times.
If one asks whether it is an offense before the transaction is completed, the answer is that it becomes an offense upon the third attempt;

by the fourth attempt, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle goods) ask [the price], such as "for this much [quantity] of goods, up to [this much] profit," and so forth. This establishes what is called the method for instructing a *kappiya-kāraka* to conduct trade.

Therefore, it is not an offense. The twenty-first precept concerning the keeping of an extra alms-bowl: the offenses for monks and nuns are the same in terms of the causal conditions, yet differ in their application. Because they fail to perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification), both commit the same offense of *pāyattika*;
hence it is said that the offenses are the same. For monks, a ten-day period is permitted; for nuns, it must be declared on the very day. This is because the conditions for the exemption differ.

Therefore, it is said that they differ in their conditions. Regarding the third point, "the bowl must be according to the prescribed measure and not 'joined with oil'": Lì asked, "If the measurement of a robe exceeds or falls short [of the standard], it still constitutes valid possession (*dhāraṇa*).
Why is it not the same for the bowl? Why must it necessarily be of the correct measure? The answer was: "Robes involve cutting and joining; bowls do not involve extending or shortening.

Therefore, if they exceed or fall short [the standard], they do not constitute valid possession. As for the term "joined with oil" (*tǒng yóu*), Lì explained: "'Joined' (*tǒng*) refers to having already formed the clay mold for the bowl and then..."

It should be made to have a luster; it is then used for burning and is not to be reused. This is similar to what is commonly seen in the northern regions, where the shape is like that of a lumped-together tile.
Regarding oil: perilla seeds are used for this purpose. Ancient masters often used iron bowls with oil, but these retain grease entirely; using them [for food] will inevitably result in an offense.

One who keeps such a bowl does not commit an offense even if it exceeds the limit, because it belongs to the category of "unlawful" (adharma) items and thus does not constitute a "long-term possession" offense (*atireka*). The rest is as [stated] above.

Regarding the precept on extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), there are eight clauses in detail concerning the enumeration of offenses and non-offenses; these are explained in the same manner as the commentary on the precept on extra robes.
Li states that the fifth condition refers to the five causes for [the robe being considered lost], namely the four conditions consisting of the perception of loss, seizure, and so forth.
This is not known through the conditions of the month of Kārttika or the five-month period.

If one obtains a bowl on the fifth day and it has already been subject to the threefold suspension (*ukkhepana*) and the disciplinary treatment (*kamma*), even if many days pass, there is no further offense of prolongation. If, after the suspension is lifted, one obtains [another bowl] again on the fifth day—thus asks the *Sūsū*.

Regarding why there are instances of encouraging an increase in the price for robes but none for alms bowls: the answer is that robes provide broad support for the body, so people often delight in encouraging an increase;

therefore, the Noble One established it as a grave offense (*pārājika*). Alms bowls have but a single use, and their function in supporting the body is narrow; thus, the occasion for encouraging an increase is rare.
Therefore, one incurs a minor offense (dukkaṭa). This is why it was not prescribed. Lì asked: "Why is it that one does not accept a *kaṭhina* bowl?
He replied: "As for robes, there are three types; because they are heavy to carry, the acceptance of the *guṇa-kaṭhina* robe is permitted so that one may stay overnight separated from them.
However, the bowl is singular and must be used constantly. How could one accept a *kaṭhina* bowl? Because the matter of carrying the bowl by means of [the *kaṭhina*] is impossible."

This is also the case. "Sharpening" refers to the intention. Regarding the five types of fine cloth, they are not permitted within the bowl; that is to say, one must not stay overnight separated from the bowl.
Furthermore, if there is an extra bowl, it must also undergo the ritual of purification (*śodhana*).

The Twenty-second Precept on Begging for Almsbowls: An offense occurs because of begging from one who is not a relative. If one begs from a relative, or if one obtains it by purchasing it oneself, there is no fault.

Regarding the five types of begging for a bowl that is "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*): this excludes other bowls that are either of improper measure or not in accordance with the Dharma; [begging for such] does not constitute an offense.
Regarding the phrase "because such instances are rare": this refers to practices such as the *poṣadha* (confession) ceremony, which are detailed in the Vinaya texts.
However, when performing these ceremonies, one must restrict them to the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). Lì says: "If one obtains many bowls through begging, they must all be confiscated;

the fine ones are to be returned to the monastic treasury, while the remaining inferior ones are to be distributed among the monks. The following clarifies the rules for non-offenses. If [the number] is reduced...

Regarding "leakage" (*āsrava*): "established" refers to [the bowl] being of the correct measure; "diminished" refers to being less than the standard measure. "Leakage" means it is cracked and leaking.

If one possesses a bowl that is already diminished in size, or one that is of the correct measure but leaks, begging for another does not constitute an offense. Furthermore, [the commentary] states deeply:

if the bowl is diminished by five [measures] yet leaks, or if it has more than five repairs yet does not leak, begging for another in either case does not constitute an offense. It is not necessary for both conditions to be met before the permission to beg is granted. Thus, as stated previously...
In the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra-vibhāṣā*, it is stated: "If five patches are reduced so that they do not leak, they may be joined into a single patch.
This should be understood. Regarding the twenty-third precept on having a non-relative weave: Jì says, "This precept was established because it harms the weaver;
the preceding eighth precept on encouraging the increase of robe value was established because it harms the owner of the thread. As for 'making a seam [or binding] entirely auspicious,' it should..."

The Master said: "Su" is pronounced as the opposite [of its usual meaning]. In the local dialects, it refers to a spinning wheel; in Zhao and Wei, it is called *lilü*, while people in Jiangdong call it a *weiche*.
Now, regarding "auspicious" (*mingji*): this means that one obtains thread from someone who is not a relative and has a relative spin it;
therefore, it is considered auspicious.
Exhortation to Weave: Precept 24. One should consult the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi) for its essential origins (*nidāna*).

As noted in the *Sengqi chao* [and so forth], one must clarify here the matter of Baddhananda dividing his robes with two elderly men, as may be found in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-chao*.
The Twenty-fifth Precept on Taking Robes by Force: Master Guangtong says this refers to the precept against forcibly taking back a robe that was previously given without clear agreement.

"Jian" (甄) means to exclude; it excludes those who are not of the same class of practitioners. This is because, according to the *Nidāna* (the account of the origin of the rule), the original intention was for them to practice together.
Now, as for those of lower status and inferior rank, they are not of the same class as bhikṣus. Lì asked:

"If a śrāmaṇera says he has committed no offense, why does he follow along when being expelled, thereby committing the same offense as the great saṃgha? He replied: "Regarding traveling together with [the bhikṣu] who provided the robe, the śrāmaṇera is not of the same class;

such an act is rare, and even if he is deprived [of his status], it is not frequent. As for 'following along,' the meaning is that although their interpretations differ, they equally violate the monastic law and cause harm."

There is no difference, as they are equally guilty of the offense. Regarding the two cases among the four statements: this refers to when both the giving and the taking are certain, and one commits the *pārājika* offense by seizing it.

Second, if the giving is certain but the taking is uncertain, yet one seizes it and obtains it, one commits the *pārājika*. Third, if the giving is uncertain but the taking is certain, one commits this offense by seizing it.
According to this text, in the previous section on the precept against stealing, regarding the seizure of a thief’s property, it says: "The owner has not decided to relinquish it; the thief..."
If one has already formed the thought that the object is definitively acquired, then taking it constitutes a grave offense (pārājika), which contradicts this present text.

Now, since it is stated here that the giver is not certain while the taker is certain, it is clear that the loss of the object occurs only when the intention to relinquish it has not yet been formed; even though the thief has made it his own, [the original owner’s claim remains].
Taking [an object] by force does not constitute a grave offense. Regarding the fourth case, taking and giving are both indeterminate; if one takes it by force, there is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

As for "all cases of taking and lifting [the object] without concealing it," the established view is that one takes it for the purpose of setting it aside or storing it, rather than taking it to claim ownership for oneself; therefore, no offense is committed. Vasubandhu says:
"All cases of taking and lifting without concealing it"—this "not concealing" refers to the act of lifting without concealment because it is done in the presence of the person before whom it occurs.
Regarding "concealing and setting aside" (*saṃnidhi*): if one has not yet committed an offense, it is an offense merely to move the object if one does not face [the recipient] directly;

it does not require the act of concealing and setting aside. The twenty-sixth precept concerning the seven-day limit for medicinal substances (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*). Regarding the five circumstances where there is no cause [for transgression]:

the Master [Daoxuan] claims these refer to the month of Kārttika and the five months [of the rainy season retreat]. Master Jueyi maintains that this is not so. As for the five benefits of the Kārttika month, we have never heard of an allowance to store long-term medicines during them. This is superior [to the former view].
It says: "This is identical to the eightfold opening conditions for the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe); therefore, it is so called. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The five types of *anivārya-dūṣaṇa* (unobstructed obstacles) mean that one may not go to take [the medicine] from within a clean kitchen; or, it is said that due to the eight calamities (*aṣṭā-vighna*), one cannot take it into one's hand, and so forth.
Furthermore, loss, seizure, the spoilage of the medicine, and the like are also such causes and conditions. Below this, the non-offense rules are clarified. If [the period] exceeds seven days...
Regarding "medicine": it means that once a bhikṣu has received medicine on the first day, he may receive different medicine on the second and third days;

this remains "seven-day medicine. Upon reaching the eighth day, because it is associated with the previous [period], it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Since the medicine from the first day was not declared pure (*pariśuddha*), he commits an offense of forfeiture.
Furthermore, the medicine received from the second day onwards is likewise affected by this transgression. Within the present text, there are three examples.
Regarding the term "initial": this refers to that which exceeds seven days. The "subsequent" clearly indicates the actual seven days.
The "final" refers to that which has not yet reached seven days, from six days down to a single day. If one now relinquishes the confession, one relinquishes all three of these to the Saṃgha.
When the Saṃgha returns later, that which exceeded seven days is given to the park-keeper; that which was exactly seven days may be given to others as appropriate.

Regarding "those not yet seven days old," this refers to returning these medicines to the bhikṣu for such uses as applying them to the feet. As for "medicines for the seventh day," Master Li states that these are those obtained on the following day.
If the previous medicine was kept for eight days, it constitutes an offense of *aticāra* (excess); although this medicine has only just been obtained for seven days, [it is distinct].

It has not yet been transgressed. Because it has been defiled, one must relinquish it; having performed the confession, it returns. One must relinquish it to another bhikṣu and may not eat it oneself.
If less than seven days have passed, one declares: "This medicine has only been in my possession for five or six days.

Because it was defiled and because it is recent, it may be returned to its original owner. A bhikṣu may apply it to doorways, windows, and so forth. (Check the Vinaya text yourself regarding the above.)

This refers to having finished discussing the forfeiture of residual medicine (*śeṣa-bhaiṣajya*) due to an offense. Regarding the term *hùxiàng* (戶向): according to the *Sāncāng*, "xiàng" means a north-facing window; it is also a window.
As for the current expression "to smear the *hùxiàng*," Jì says: one takes ghee and oil and smears them upon the paper on the window to make it bright.
This refers to the practice of sealing windows with waxed paper at the present time. Some say that regarding these seven-day medicines:

if they are stored for the purpose of taking them, there may be an offense of "retention" (*atireka*) beyond the limit; however, if they are stored not for the purpose of taking them, there is no offense of retention even if the days have passed.
Furthermore, if one has received seven-day medicine and it has been touched due to circumstances after five days have passed, one may again apply the rule for an additional seven days.
However, once six days have elapsed, even if it is touched, the application of the rule is no longer permitted.
The twenty-seventh precept: Seeking Rain-Clothing Before the [Proper] Time. Regarding this precept, the form of the garment is largely the same as that of the *amaṇḍalaka-antarvāsa*.
A question is raised at the outset: "What is the difference between 'seeking before the time' and the precept on begging for robes? The answer is that there are three kinds of differences.
First, the substance of the robes differs: this is a rain robe, whereas that is not a rain robe. Second, the conditions for its allowance differ:

this is solicited according to the specific time, such that to solicit outside of that time constitutes an offense; that has no temporal limit, except when four specific conditions are met. Third, there is a distinction between relatives and non-relatives.

In that case, the relative is not at fault; in this case, both are at fault. Regarding the four conditions that constitute an offense when using [the robe] before the [prescribed] time, as listed previously, the second condition states:
"obtained during the two periods. Zhen-shen says: "Anything obtained from the sixteenth day of the third month onwards is all termed 'during the period.
To receive it prior to this time constitutes an offense under the preceding precept, which is not what is being clarified here. As for the statement 'three cases of receiving before the time'..."
This refers to receiving [the precepts] by means of the formal proclamation made during the middle period; it does not mean that they are obtained from the side of the laity. Master Li says:

"It must be obtained during that specific time for there to be the transgression regarding prior usage. If one seeks them before that time, once they are obtained, one commits the preceding offense, but does not further commit the subsequent offense.
The Upādhyāya says: "Receiving before the time" means receiving them even before the first day of the fourth month has arrived. However...
Furthermore, this is not a request made prior to the [proper] time; rather, it is a request made after the [previous period] has passed.

Regarding the statement, "One should request on the sixteenth day of the third month for use on the first day of the fourth month," Zhen says: The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states, "When one month remains of spring, one should request a rain-bathing robe.
Thus, from the sixteenth day of the third month until the fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes "one month remaining of spring."

This refers to the month of Caitra (the fourth month). Regarding the statement that "on the first day of the fourth month [one] uses [it]," the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "One should use the bath every half-month.

This means that starting from the first day of the fourth month, there is exactly one half-month until the beginning of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). All of this refers to the permission granted for use during the first half-month prior to the summer retreat.

Śīlādhi quotes the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā* as saying: "If it is an intercalary third month, one should not seek [the bath] on the sixteenth day of the first three months; [it should be sought] in the latter three months."
One should seek [the rainy season robes] on the sixteenth day. If one does not know whether there is an intercalary month, there is no offense.

If it is the fourth intercalary month, those who enter the retreat on the sixteenth day of the preceding month may use the robe for rain from that very day until the sixteenth day of the seventh month, a period of one hundred and twenty days.

Because of the moisture and heat of the summer rains, and because one seeks to have a fixed period for the entire [robe], one may not seek to use it before including the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), as there would be no fixed period for the whole.

However, it is permitted to include the intercalary month when seeking its use. The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* states: "If one uses it even one day past this [fixed period], one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If one has already passed the initial period of seeking, then even if one further exceeds that and uses it beforehand, one only commits a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), for the substance of a single robe does not constitute a repeated offense."
"One may not accept [it] as the three robes, nor may one perform the *śuddhika-dāna* (pure gift)" means that one must not treat this robe according to the rules for the three robes.
"One may not perform the *śuddhika-dāna*" means that when it is being used for its primary purpose, there is no need to recite the *śuddhika-dāna* formula.
"One may not make it into the three robes or perform the *śuddhika-dāna*" refers specifically to the time of primary use; [the rule applies] only once the period of residence has been completed.
Regarding the rule against bathing naked: Saṅghabhadra states that one should wear a *śāṭī* (a lower garment) or other old clothes as an undergarment.
If the rain stops early and the filth and grime have been washed away, Saṅghabhadra clarifies that one may wear this garment while bathing in the rain;
if the bath is not yet finished when the rain ceases, and the filth on the body has not been entirely removed, one is further permitted to enter the river water wearing it.
Washing. As for the previous statement that one must not enter the water while wearing [the robes], it is because there was no such occasion [for doing so].

Regarding the term "bathing robe" (yuyi) being said to be "comprehensive" (tong), Master Li states: this robe may serve two purposes; namely, it is worn for bathing and also used to protect the three robes during rain, as both involve becoming wet.
Furthermore, it is called "comprehensive" because its name, "rain robe" (yuyi), necessitates being wet; thus, one should lightly sprinkle it with water.

Regarding the phrase "must make it damp," this means that one must necessarily wear [the bathing robe] at the time of bathing. Since one is now bathing while wearing other garments and has set aside the bathing robe, one must sprinkle water on it to make it damp.
The reason for doing so is that the bathing robe was originally intended for use during bathing; since it was not used at the time of bathing, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
By sprinkling water to make it damp, the meaning is equivalent to having already finished using it. This applies until the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

Regarding "that which is to be relinquished on the day": the established view is that once it has been relinquished, it must be formally announced; otherwise, one commits an offense of "excess" (*ātyaya*).

This robe may be accepted daily from the sixteenth day of the third month until the sixteenth day of the fourth month. According to this, at the time of acceptance, the formal announcement is also applicable.

While there is a scriptural text concerning the time of relinquishment—wherein one announces the relinquishment before the Saṃgha—there is no such text for the time of acceptance. Nevertheless, by logical necessity, it ought to exist. Now...

According to principle, one must announce it aloud for all to know; it need not necessarily be administered face-to-face. Below is the clarification of the rules regarding non-offenses. Chapter Twenty-eight:
The Precept on Receiving Urgent Alms-Clothing Prior to the [Regular] Time. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle five, states: "Regarding 'urgent alms-clothing' (*ātyayikacīvara*):"
If it is during a military expedition, or for a woman about to give birth—such urgent times of giving, once the time has passed, one no longer gives.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T.1425), fascicle 11, states: "Regarding 'urgent robes' (*ātyayikacīvara*):

if it is a man or a woman, whether lay or ordained, at the time of setting out on a campaign, returning from a campaign, at the time of death, when a woman returns [from her family], or when a merchant departs; the donor says to the bhikṣu: 'If today...'"

If one does not accept it, it is gone by the following day; this is called "urgent giving" (*ātyaya-dāna*). If one accepts it before the sixth day of the seventh month, it is called "accepting ahead of time.

If one obtains a robe on the sixth day of the seventh month and fails to perform the *aśuddha-dāna* (purification through distribution) by the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is called "keeping it beyond the limit.
The commentary states that these two precepts are established together yet differ in their application to a single robe: if one accepts it ahead of time, one commits an offense.

In principle, there can be no double offense; thus, there is no such thing as a "subsequent possession" offense arising from a prior transgression. If a subsequent possession offense is indeed not a transgression, then it is accepted [as such].

If it is not a transgression prior to the acceptance, yet becomes a transgression after the acceptance, then there is an offense. This does not mean that two offenses exist upon the substance of a single garment; therefore, it is said that they are not the same garment.
These are rain-clothing robes, which together constitute a single precept. One is the "prior transgression," and...
Regarding "receiving": one case concerns keeping [an item] after the [proper time] has passed; thus, two precepts are mentioned.

As for the statement that "if one receives it, one obtains it, but if one does not receive it, one loses it," this refers to when a donor wishes to travel far away and offers a gift in advance. At that moment, if one accepts it, one obtains it; if one does not accept it, it is lost forever.
This means that if one does not take it at the time of the offering, it will be difficult to obtain later. Regarding the "four cases of no basis" (catur-nirālamba), according to the four...
The commentary states: "Having lost, been robbed of, burned, or washed away" refers to circumstances where one lacks the three robes (*tricīvara*).

In such cases, one may receive [extra cloth] beyond the previous limit and use it as a formal robe (*tricīvara*). Since there are currently no such circumstances, it is said "without cause. Regarding the first and second points being the same as the aforementioned conditions:
(1) it is an urgent gift; (2) one knows it is an urgent gift; and (3) it is within ten days. If it is the sixth day of the seventh month...
"Receiving later" refers to receiving within ten days [of the *pravāraṇā*], which constitutes an "urgent robe" (*ātyayika-cīvara*). There is the offense of keeping it beyond the limit.

If one receives it on the fifth day of the seventh month, this constitutes receiving it prior to the [prescribed] time; having already committed the prior offense, there is no further offense of keeping it after the limit, because an offense is not committed twice over.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha permit receiving within ten days after the *pravāraṇā*, yet does not allow receiving prior to that time?

Answer: This refers to the case where the donor has no intention [to give immediately], having originally offered the gift for the sake of the summer labor. It was properly received during the appropriate season;

however, because there is now an urgent cause of distress, it is brought forward in advance to be presented to the Sangha. Thus, within ten days, it connects with the original time-period and remains identical to the original offering.
Therefore, receiving it within ten days is permitted. If one receives it after that period, it would not connect with the original time-period, and thus it would not be permissible.
Because it accords with the original intention of the donor, it is not permitted [to keep the robe beyond that time].

For example, if one obtains a robe on the sixth day of the seventh month, when the full ten days have elapsed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one must perform the *śuddhika* (purification) ceremony.

If one obtains it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the eleventh day has already entered the month of Kārttika, so purification is not required; however, by the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the period is deemed complete, and one must then perform the *śuddhika*.
If one does not declare it, it is considered kept beyond the permitted time.

Thus, if one obtains a robe on the seventh, eighth, or ninth day after the seven months have passed, and having exceeded the number of days in the *kārttika* month, one adds the preceding ten days, one must then perform the *viśuddhi* (declaration of purity).

If one does not so declare it, one commits an offense. What is now referred to as "within ten days" specifically points to these ten days. This explains in detail the distinction between the proper and improper times.
Regarding "the proper time" (*kāla*): Zhi Sheng explains that the month of Kārttika and the five months [of the rainy season] are called "time"; outside of these, all are called "improper time.

As for the "robe given as an urgent offering," it was originally intended to be given for the sake of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat); now, within ten days of the departure from that period, it is [considered timely].
That which is received in connection with the specific period of time is called a "timely robe" (*kālacīvara*). One may receive it on the sixth day of the seventh month;

once the month of Kārttika has passed, one must then perform the formal declaration of purity (*pāriśuddhi*). Other robes that are not "urgent gifts" (*akālacīvara*), such as "extra robes" (*atirekacīvara*) and the like, are not treated in this way.

If an extra robe is obtained during the [Kārttika] period, one must perform the declaration of purity immediately upon the completion of the month of Kārttika. However, if it is obtained prior to the month of Kārttika...
If one obtains [extra] robes, it is called "out-of-season" (*akālika*). Upon obtaining the robes, one may not bypass the *kārttika* month;

rather, one must calculate the days from the current season and add them to the preceding out-of-season days, such that by the tenth day, they must be formally declared. Regarding the five privileges of the *kārttika* period for those who do not perform the *viśuddhi* (purification/declaration), this is based on the fact that extra robes are obtained during the regular season;
thus, it permits their use before they have been declared. If robes are obtained prior to the regular season, only urgent necessity is permitted.

If one gives a single piece of cloth, one obtains a *mukhaṭikā*. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one obtains a long robe (*dīrghacīvara*).
During the [following] nine days, it must be formally declared. Following this precedent, the *Shoushu* (Opening Commentary) asks: "Why is it that robes are received outside of the proper time?
Why, beyond the five days after the first month, are nine additional days added for receiving them during the proper time? The answer is: It is not so.

When one receives robes at the proper time, one subsequently obtains the dispensation for [using them] outside the proper time. Now, since these were received at the proper time, how can there be a dispensation for [using them] outside the proper time?

If that were so, then receiving them outside the proper time should likewise not permit their use during the proper time. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it must be an urgent gift that is received outside the proper time.

Furthermore, nine additional days were added externally. Regarding those who receive [the robe] during the [designated] time, since this is not an urgent gift of cloth (*ātyayika-cīvara*), there is no limit on the time for its acceptance;

why then was it necessary to further authorize these nine days? Vimalakīrti asked: "In general, regarding an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), if one does not announce it within ten days, one commits an offense as soon as the dawn of the eleventh day breaks.
This urgent gift of cloth was received on the sixth day of the seventh month; when the ten days have ended and the sixteenth day arrives, at dawn—"
This constitutes an offense of transgression. Why, then, is it said that one may keep [extra robes] for one month or five months without offense? The answer is:

regarding long-term extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), if they do not connect with the designated time-period, there is only the initial allowance (*pūrvānujñā*) and no subsequent allowance (*paścād-anujñā*); therefore, one commits an offense.

However, in the case of these urgently offered robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), receiving them for ten days is the initial allowance, and entering the sixteenth day is the subsequent allowance; thus, the two periods connect.
Beyond this limit, there is no offense. If that is so, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one may be separated from one's robes and leave the *anvāsaṃvāsa* (rainy-season retreat);

as long as the dawn has not yet appeared, the violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā-bheda*) is not yet established. Being separated from one's robes until the sixteenth day is still within the permitted time for departure.

"There should be no offense of breaking [the summer retreat] or being separated [from one's robes]. Answer: Regarding the summer retreat and being separated from one's robes, there is only the subsequent permission; there is no prior authorization.

This is because on the night of the fifteenth day, one must still remain within the boundary (*sīmā*) to maintain the summer retreat and protect the robes. Therefore, they are not analogous. My private explanation is as follows:

the statement that "there is only the subsequent permission for the summer robes" means that only after the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is one permitted to go outside the boundary, and only then is one permitted to be separated [from them].
This refers to robes (*cīvara*). Prior to the *pravāraṇā*, there is no provision for relinquishing them.
If a long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) is connected to the time-period, then both before and after it are permitted. Prior to the *pravāraṇā*, there is the ordinary ten-day allowance;
after the *pravāraṇā*, there is further the *kārttika* allowance.

The Twenty-ninth Precept on the Separation of Robes in Difficult Forest Hermitages. Commentary: Question: What is the difference between this precept and the previous precept on the separation of robes? Why was it further established? Answer: It is simply that in the previous case, the village was peaceful and secure; one incurred the offense after staying for only one night. In this case, it is different. Furthermore, the previous precept concerned the three robes, whereas this one concerns the five robes. Moreover, the previous precept applied when one was separated from the robes by less than a *krośa* (one *li*), while this precept applies when one is separated by more than a *krośa*. Therefore, it was established separately. Regarding the term "difficult forest hermitage" (*nāṇa araṇya*): "Difficult" refers to places where there are many tigers, wolves, thieves, and robbers, or where the terrain is rugged and uneven, such as mountains, marshes, or deserts. "Forest hermitage" refers to locations where practitioners dwell, such as mountain caves, tree roots, or grass huts. "Separation" means being apart from one’s robes. "Robes" refers to the five types of robes permitted by the Buddha. "One day" (*ekāha*) means a single solar day. "Offense" (*āpatti*) means the transgression of the precept. This precept is established because, in difficult forest hermitages, one may be separated from one’s robes for a day or two due to various circumstances, such as being pursued by bandits or encountering dangerous terrain. If one were to incur an offense merely by staying overnight, it would be excessively restrictive. Therefore, it is permitted to remain separated for up to one day. However, if one stays for two nights, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one stays for three nights, one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community). Thus, the precept is established to provide a moderate allowance. If one is separated from the robes for one day, one must perform the ritual of returning them (*pratyānayana*) before the following dawn. If one fails to do so, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If one is separated for two days, one must perform the ritual of returning them before the third dawn. If one fails to do so, one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one is separated for three days, one must perform the ritual of returning them before the fourth dawn. If one fails to do so, one incurs the offense of *pārājika* (defeat). Therefore, one must be diligent and not negligent. If one is separated from the robes for one day, one must perform the ritual of returning them before the following dawn.
