This is as perilous and fearful as the offense committed after six nights have passed. The former case concerns those who are ordinary stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), for whom the *kaṭhina* robe is permitted;
this present case concerns those in times of difficulty, further combined with superior practice. "Superior practice" refers specifically to the *dhūta* (ascetic) observances.

One who does not receive the *kaṭhina* robe but possesses only the *kārttika* [robe] is different because it is not produced through formal ritual action. The Buddha established the net of his teachings: within the six nights, there is but one assembly; to exceed this is a transgression.
This time limit deviates from the holy intent; therefore, the offense of *thullaccaya* (提罪) is prescribed. Second, regarding "the non-seasonal period of winter":

this refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the eighth month until the middle of the twelfth month; this is the winter season. It does not mean that one is prohibited from being separated from one's robes during the summer. Liang states:
"The Master of the Commentary (Sanzang), Nanshan, and the ancient masters all judge that the summer robe and the winter robe are separate."
This is a point of divergence. Because the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is obscure, it has been misinterpreted since ancient times.

When compared with other schools—such as the citations from the *Mahīśāsaka*, *Sarvāstivāda*, and *Daśabhāṇavāra* vinayas provided below—they all refer to the period within the summer retreat. How then can the *Dharmaguptaka* alone be so difficult to reconcile? The Vinaya states:

"If a bhikṣu has completed the three months of the summer retreat, and the month of Kārttika is fulfilled" (the above is according to the Vinaya text). Some editions of the original text read: "If a bhikṣu [has completed] the three months of the summer... [The text continues].

The summer retreat (*varṣā*) concludes on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. Regarding this, the Master of the Commentary (Dōshō) states that it is called "fulfillment" because both the earlier and later retreats reach completion.
Nanshan (Daoxuan), however, arbitrarily added the character "already" (*yi*), stating: "It reaches fulfillment already on the fifteenth day of the eighth month."

Now, examining this in detail, neither interpretation captures the intended meaning. If it is claimed that one who has completed the three-month summer retreat is considered to have "previously entered" the retreat, then such a person ought to receive the five privileges of the *kārttika* month;

logically, they should be permitted to be separated from their robes. Why, then, would it be necessary for a difficulty to arise before the separation of robes is allowed? Consequently, [the author] provides the following explanation:
"This aranya [practice] lasts for six nights; this refers to those of superior practice, as they do not accept the five benefits.

Now, a detailed examination shows this is not so, for there is no such indication in the text, and it contradicts other schools. Therefore, the correct interpretation is as follows: "The three-month summer retreat" refers to the completion of the formal rite for entering the retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*).
"Reaching the full [term] on the fifteenth day of the eighth month" refers to the conclusion of the subsequent summer retreat (*paścimavarṣā*).

"Since [the beginning of] the summer retreat," refers to within the four months of the rainy season. Formerly, the Master’s intention was that [the period] after the fifteenth day of the eighth month was permissible;
now, it must be strictly defined as being before the fifteenth day of the eighth month. This must be established by citing evidence from various schools, as will be described below (etc.).
The Guest said: "It has been traditionally transmitted since ancient times that once the month of Kārttika is completed, it is no longer the 'unseasonable' time."

In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is stated that the six-night period is granted as an exception. Now, the Venerable Jing says: "This rule in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* grants a six-night extension for those who enter the later retreat (*paścima-varṣā*).

This is because those who entered the earlier retreat must depart once their summer has concluded, while those who enter later must remain until the end of the *kārttika* month to observe the rains retreat at this location.
Furthermore, as this month is frequently plagued by bandits and one may be dwelling alone, the six-night extension is granted; it does not concern the practice of the higher [stages]. However...
There is the term *kārttika*. Examining this Vinaya now, it is not restricted to the later [period] of the retreat. Thus, the *Nidāna* (Origin Story) states:

"When the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded, even though one has already completed the retreat, if one still dwells in an *araṇya*, this may also be described as having 'completed the *kārttika* and returned.

Because one is in an *araṇya*, the preceding precept text should state 'having completed and returned'; logically, it does not fall outside of 'completion. Yet Nanshan arbitrarily altered the precept text, saying:"

When the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded and the full period ends on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it would be a grave oversight if one were to depart from a remote location where there is suspicion or fear.
According to other Vinayas, this refers to the completion of the period; it does not refer to a time outside of that completion.

Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Treatise on the Five Divisions), fascicle 5, and the *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* (Eleventh Section of the Mahāsāṃghika), are entirely in agreement. The *Pañcavargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If [one is] nearby..."

The Buddha resided in an araṇya for the three-month summer retreat. Regarding the phrase "not yet having completed eight months," the *Śāriputra-Abhidharma* states: "The three-month retreat refers to the early retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*);

'not yet having completed eight months' refers to the late retreat (*paścimavarṣā*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the circumstances permitting [the late retreat] are not limited solely to cases of hardship.
He said: The Buddha told Upāli, "Go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to resolve the dispute with the Saṃgha. Upāli said, "My saṃghāṭī robe is heavy;
if I leave my robes behind now during the half-month of the rainy season retreat, I will incur the offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). The Buddha asked, "In how many days can you go and return?
Upāli replied, "Calculating two days for the journey there and two days for the return, it will take six days in total; I shall be able to go."

[The Buddha] returned and, consequently, permitted [the practice] for six nights. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If the three months of the summer retreat are not yet complete, and a bhikṣu is staying in an araṇya...
The commentary (*Śīla-bhāṣya*) explains: "The three months of the rainy season retreat (anvāsa) lasts from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
'Not yet complete' means that the fifteenth day of the eighth month has not yet arrived. 'A bhikṣu who has not reached the final month' refers to one in an araṇya..."

Regarding the passage "If one dwells in such a place" (all the preceding texts refer to the *pūrṇamāsa* [the full moon]; for what reason did the ancients misinterpret them?), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"At that time, there were 'eight-month bandits' who constantly waited to capture people and kill them as sacrifices to the gods. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, states:

"When more than fifteen days have passed, but the eighteenth day of the eighth month has not yet arrived" (referring to those who entered the *pūrvavarṣa* [early rains retreat] on the fifteenth day of the seventh month). It further notes: "In foreign lands, bandits and thieves appear occasionally; this occurs during these six nights."
[Interval. This is the time when the thieves set out. According to the eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

"If a bhikṣu has passed three months [of the rainy retreat] but has not yet reached eight months [and thus the year is not complete], and if that forest-dwelling bhikṣu is staying in a forest hermitage and experiences doubt or fear, this bhikṣu may, from among his three robes, take whichever single robe he wishes [to leave behind] within the boundary or at a layperson's house. This bhikṣu...

There is a cause and condition: going outside the boundary and staying apart from one’s robe for up to six nights. If one stays apart beyond this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. (The Vinaya itself explains:
"For one who has not yet completed the year," referring to the section on the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*). Furthermore, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains:

"When three months have passed" means that although there are four months in the summer season, even though three months have elapsed, for those in the later retreat, the days [of the fourth month] have not yet passed.

Because it is not full, it is said that "the eight months are not yet complete. Regarding the "five conditions of no [obstacles]": this refers to the absence of obstacles such as water, land, or the interruption of the path.

Another interpretation states it refers to the condition of the month of Kārttika. For those who are superior practitioners, they do not receive the *kāṭhina* robe, and thus there are no five months [of the rainy season].
Regarding the phrase "doubting the loss of a water vessel," Master Li says: it means there is doubt regarding thieves in the location, down to even the fear [of them].
This refers to the loss of a water vessel or similar item. As for entrusting items to a suspicious layperson:
it is because such people are untrustworthy and may be thieves that one leaves them with him; thus, it is known that the bhikṣu remains alone in the araṇya and will not come to commit theft.

Regarding the prohibition against wearing [the robes] singly: this means that the three robes (tricīvara) should normally be kept on one's person at all times; now, since it is permitted to leave one behind, the remaining two...
"One must necessarily follow [the robe] when entering villages and so forth; if one is attached to it with gravity, this is in accordance with the Dharma.

At present, wearing only a single garment is a great violation of the Dharma and is merely a matter of habitual custom. Regarding the clarification of the two conditions, Jing says: "First, in places where there is suspicion or fear, one is permitted to separate from the robe;

this is not limited by the number of days, as it follows the duration of the difficulty, whether long or short. Second, for matters such as the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, one is permitted [to separate from the robe] for six [days]."
There is one assembly at night, regardless of whether it is winter or summer; therefore, these are called the "two conditions.

These are all explicit passages from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, yet ancient masters erroneously clung to the notion that in a *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) where there is fear, one may only stay for six nights—meaning one assembly every six nights—without regard for the seasons.

This is truly because they did not see the explicit passages of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Furthermore, the *Caturvarga-vinaya-śīla-sūtra* merely states: "If there is suspicion, fear, or strangeness, one may depart for one [night]."

Regarding the single robe (*ekacīvara*): it does not yet state that there is a further circumstance permitting its separation from the body, nor does it specify the characteristics of such a circumstance.
Now, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, both circumstances apply (the previous mention of "two circumstances" refers to the text of the *Pañcavargika*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, during the three months of the summer retreat in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) that is a place of fear, it is permitted to leave one robe within a village without setting a time limit. Examining the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it says: "This was [decided] by Upāli at the Buddha’s command."

In other places, the Saṃgha settles disputes through communal harmony. Because the *saṃghāṭī* robe was heavy, the Buddha permitted its separation [from the body]. He asked how many days it would take to go there, settle the dispute, and return;
calculating that it would require six nights, he therefore permitted an absence of six nights. Later, in the *Poṣadha-vastu*, it is stated:
"A forest-dwelling bhikṣu, during the three months of the summer retreat, if there is fear or danger, may entrust one robe and wear it [elsewhere]."

In a village where there are families of ill repute, if such dangers do not exist, one may stay for only the previous six nights for the sake of other matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that during the summer retreat, if there are dangers, one is permitted to leave [the robes]; this refers to the passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cited above.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* does not permit leaving the robes during the summer retreat, requiring instead that one wait until the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* (second) retreat is completed, or even [allowing them to be] entrusted [to others].
Regarding the case where lay households do not set a time limit [for their protection], the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there were bandits who operated for eight months, constantly lying in wait to capture people and kill them as sacrifices to the gods. Upon reaching an *araṇya* (wilderness) dwelling, they intended to kill the bhikṣus. Hearing this, the bhikṣus each fled.
The bandits then intended to disperse to other places to seek [victims] separately. Among the bandits was one who had previously left the household life but had since abandoned the path.
He said to the crowd, "I have heard the Buddha's teaching that it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to be separated from his robe even for one night; let us simply guard them together.

When dawn approaches, we shall surely return. At that time, the bhikṣus feared they would commit the offense of being separated from their robes. Although they knew the bandits had not yet left, by the end of the night they all returned and were killed by the bandits.
Among them, those who did not die thought to themselves, "If only the Buddha had permitted me to [keep my robe] full..."

On the [blank] day of the eighth month, he sent one robe each to those living in white-clad households so that they would not encounter such calamities. He reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I allow the bhikṣus in forest retreats (araṇya) who have completed the three-month rains retreat, but whose eight months are not yet full, to stay for one night each [in the villages]."

There was a family wearing white garments who had entrusted their robes to another household, yet the monks did not go to see them at all; furthermore, the robes became damp, soiled, and infested with insects.
The monks reported this matter to the Buddha, who said, "You should go to look after them. The monks went to look after them repeatedly, which caused the householders to feel weary and disgusted.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, who said, "I allow you to go and look once every ten days. Furthermore, there were monks who had business regarding the stūpas.
Regarding monastic affairs, matters concerning one’s preceptors and instructors, as well as one’s own affairs or the affairs of others, it may be necessary to go outside the boundary.

Fearing that he might not be able to leave for the sake of his robes, a monk informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to leave for these matters for one night. When the monks went outside the boundary for one night and their business was not yet finished, they returned.
They informed the Buddha again, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to stay for six nights. If you exceed six nights, you commit an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Regarding the offense: as for the statement above that "the three-month *varṣā* has not yet reached eight months," the commentary below explains:
"The three-month *varṣā* refers to the earlier *varṣā*; 'not yet reaching eight months' refers to the later *varṣā*. The remaining meanings have already been explained as above.
It must be due to other specific circumstances that the six-night limit is prescribed. As cited above from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is no fixed time limit when there is an emergency;

however, in the present case, it is not an emergency. Rather, it is for the sake of causes such as work for the stūpa, work for the Saṃgha, or matters concerning one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*), which permit the separation from one’s robe for six nights.
Later, because certain monks in a village committed an offense, it was established that monks may leave their robes behind in the village.
A monk practicing the dhūta ascetic practices while residing in an araṇya fled when a village fire broke out, fearing his robes would be burned.
A layperson criticized him, saying, "This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas sees another's house on fire and runs there to plunder their property. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

If one opens [the text] at the section on the six-night period and looks, one will know that it is not there; thus, there is no cause for anxiety. However, to clarify why the ancient masters held erroneous attachments due to the lack of explicit signs:
it simply states that one may be separated from the six nights, but it does not say there is an obstacle (*āpatti*), nor does it establish a limit in days.

It does not mention other conditions for opening [the period] to six nights and so forth. Sheng says: "The ancient masters maintained that when there is doubt or fear, only the six-night period is opened;
if it exceeds this, one incurs an offense. Since the arising of the transgression is the same, once the restriction to six nights has been established, how can it be further opened?"
The text merely mentions conditions such as fear and does not open up other conditions. Although the ancient masters held this view, it contradicts the explicit fivefold textual evidence of others.
Regarding the phrase "the place reached by a thrown stone," it means that if one enters within the sphere of influence (*iśa-bhāga*), one obtains [the robe] and does not lose it.
If there are three obstructions, one must actually take it into hand. As for the statement "if one abandons the robe," the established position is that if one...

The assembly is convened. The permissions for *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), *manasikāra* (mental recitation), and remote relinquishment (*dūrasaṃjñā*) are established. Regarding the remaining rules concerning the separation from robes within the same village, the commentator states:

as for the permissive texts, such as the perception of being robbed, the perception of being burned or swept away by water, and the conditions of roads being cut off by water or land—clarifying what constitutes a loss and what does not—these are largely the same as the previous rule on the separation from robes.

The Thirty Precepts on Diverting Property Belonging to the Sangha. First, regarding the initial condition: "that which is generally permitted for the Sangha" refers to property that is broadly granted to the Sangha without yet distinguishing between what belongs to the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) and what is for immediate use (*pratyutpanna*).
To divert such property constitutes the actual offense of this precept. It is established that this refers to light items;

however, one must form the mental intention of regarding it as permitted for the Sangha. That is to say, if it has not been permitted for the Sangha, diverting it does not constitute an offense. Second, "for the sake of the Sangha."
Regarding the phrase "having made it not yet permitted for the Saṃgha," the established view is that this phrase refers to an object of great value.

Because the donor’s mind has not yet resolved to give it specifically to the Saṃgha, diverting it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); the preceding phrase, however, constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Nevertheless, masters of antiquity have disagreed regarding these two phrases.
Some say that both [terms] are *ti*. The formal pronouncement states that the second phrase is auspicious (*jī*); because it is a repeated return, the offense is auspicious.
If one says, "I have already given to the Saṃgha; I now give to the Venerable One," Ciyun says that the former act of giving was itself contrary to the Dharma.
There is no fault in receiving such offerings. It is like receiving an offering from a thief; one thereby regards the thief as the owner of the object.

If one gives it to someone so that they may constantly see and enjoy it, the established view is that this refers to Chan masters and others who are always in the monastery practicing the Way and paying homage to the Buddha, thereby enabling them to see it.

The commentary states: "According to the preceding offense. Shen says: "This refers to the third case; once permission has been granted to the Sangha, it is not permitted to assign it to a specific individual."

"Returning [the food] constitutes an offense of abandonment. My own interpretation is that this statement generally clarifies that wherever one consents [to receive food], if one subsequently diverts it to oneself, one commits an offense according to the specific circumstances;
it does not necessarily refer exclusively to a single textual passage. The *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials) quotes the *Vinaya-gāthā*, stating:

"If a donor invites the Sangha and the turn for a monk has not yet arrived, yet he says of himself, 'I should go,' this is a *pātayantika* offense for false speech. If it concerns food, one commits an offense by calculating its value. If it bypasses the turn..."

Regarding the assignment [of property]: this is an object specifically designated for a certain purpose. Furthermore, to bypass the proper order and act solely out of one's own will, thereby harming others, constitutes a grave offense.

If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of another person and causes the object to enter one's own possession, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). To divert the property of the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha* into one's own possession likewise constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If it is property belonging to the *saṃgha*, and one diverts it to a *stūpa*, it then belongs to that *stūpa*; there is no need to reclaim it, as it is [already accounted for] by way of merit.
Because they are the same, the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies equally to the monks of this community and those of that community, as explained above.

Regarding the transference of property belonging to animals, it is said that one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression) of the mind; this refers specifically to the case where a bond is formed with respect to the animals themselves.

It must be the property of an owner, and each animal is provided its own specific items; mutual exchange is not permitted. If one now transfers these goods to another [animal], one incurs a *pārājika* offense with respect to the owner, just as in the case of fodder for another horse.
Regarding flour, beans, and so forth—if one were to divert these, would it not be considered auspicious?

If one permits the exhortation toward what is evil, then those who break the precepts are called "evil," while the bhikṣus who uphold the precepts are called "good. In the third section, the text is divided into two parts.
The explanation of the meaning of the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules is hereby completed.
Commentary on the *Sifen lü chao*, Fascicle Nine, Part One; Fascicle Nine, Part Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.

There are sixty-nine precepts that monks and nuns commit equally; therefore, in the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, the core rules (śikṣāpada) are listed individually, with their commonalities with the monks clearly distinguished.
There are twenty-one precepts where the nuns differ from the monks, involving three types of differences. First, there are differences regarding what is permitted or prohibited:

there are three such precepts, namely, [the prohibition against] instructing nuns without authorization, preaching the Dharma until sunset, and reviling one's teacher. Since a nun does not hold the rank of a formal teacher, these apply.
Therefore, there are none. Second, whether light or heavy is not questioned; there are thirteen precepts. The verse says:

Making robes, holding [robes], sitting in concealment, the three periods, receiving [food], praising food, encouraging [others], sufficient [food], fine [food], ivory and horn, exceeding the measure, covering the three robes, many, and because they are included within the number of the great Saṃgha, they are heavy;
because the Bhikṣuṇīs are few, they are light. However, there are five types of robes: giving robes to a Bhikṣuṇī, making robes for a Bhikṣuṇī, and the three kinds.

Regarding the offenses of "excessive quantity" (atimātra): the three [offenses] within the five precepts for the five classes of beings share the same nature of offense but differ in their conditions (*pratyaya*). That is to say, regarding the offenses of "refusing an invitation" (*pravāraṇā*) and "eating after having finished" (*pūrva-bhakta*), the nature of the offense is the same, yet the conditions under which they are permitted differ.

Regarding the offense of giving food to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), although the nature of the offense is the same, the conditions for its occurrence differ. Regarding the precept against ordaining those who have not reached the required age, the conditions for receiving the precept differ.

Regarding the offense of an oversized bathing robe (*snāna-śāṭikā*), the conditions for the arising of the offense are the same, but the conditions for its application differ. Thirdly, regarding the differences among the various schools (*nikāya*): [the following points illustrate these variations].

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are ninety-one *pātayantika* rules. It lacks this precept against not accepting admonition; instead, it establishes separately the precept against disrespecting those who preach the Dharma.

Its rule regarding frivolous speech during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) resembles [the offense of] causing provocation, yet that [text] already possesses its own precept concerning responding to questions.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are ninety-one *pāyattika* offenses. It lacks the offense of not accepting admonition; it combines the offense of using water containing insects with the offense of drinking water containing insects into a single precept;

and it establishes separately the precept against entering a nun’s monastery and preaching the Dharma without permission. It also includes two minor precepts regarding the three teachers and the precept against diverting monastic property to an individual.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are ninety-two *pāyattika* offenses. It lacks the offense of not accepting admonition and the two offenses concerning causing fear.

The four precepts established separately for nuns are: preaching the Dharma [to monks], diverting the property of the Saṃgha to another person, not relinquishing what has been purified, and making the three robes from light materials.

Furthermore, the precept against frivolous speech is separated and established as the precept against causing provocation. According to the *Vimukti-vinaya*, there are ninety *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).

There are no other words [to add] here. These three precepts—sitting in private with a man, regretting a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) after having performed it together, and establishing a separate nunnery—are established separately.
The three [remaining] precepts are: preaching the Dharma to a layperson without being invited, diverting the property of the Sangha for oneself, and failing to show respect.

According to Master Guangtong, these ninety precepts are divided into nine sections. The first section, from the precept against lying to the precept against destroying the "village of spirits" (trees), contains eleven [precepts].
1. Regarding the precepts on guarding speech, restraining the mind, and controlling the body so as not to commit evil—skillfully harmonizing the conduct of the three karmas.

From the section on "speaking differently" down to "exceeding the measure for covering a roof," there are nine precepts; these clarify skillfully guiding others' minds, following and protecting the intentions of the assembly, and acting without causing disturbance.
2. From the section on "instructing a nun without authorization" down to "traveling together with a woman," there are ten precepts; these clarify avoiding suspicion from afar.

The fourth section concerns the practice of purity through detachment from doubt; it comprises seventeen precepts, beginning from "receiving a single meal" and extending down to "accepting an invitation for four months," which clarify the practice of moderation in internal sustenance, fewness of desires, and contentment.

The fifth section begins from "observing military arrays" and extends down to "the three colors for dyeing robes," comprising thirteen precepts that clarify the practice of fixing the mind on its object, remaining free from distraction, cultivating the path, and practicing non-attachment.
Sixth, from taking the life of a living being down to traveling with bandits, there are seven precepts. These clarify the practice of constant distancing and cultivating compassion for all beings.
Seventh, from claiming that sensual desires do not obstruct the Path down to listening to others' private conversations, there are six precepts.
These clarify the practice of deep-seated faith and understanding, and of reverently following the teachings. Eighth, from regretting having practiced in accordance with the Dharma...
From "The rootless and groundless slander" up to this point, there are seven precepts that clarify dwelling together in peace, harmony, and non-duality, and practicing in accordance with them.

From "Entering the royal palace by force" down to the end of this section, there are ten precepts that clarify the proper measure and restraint of clothing and external deportment, ensuring no transgressions are committed. Since there are thus nine distinct sections, this [section] is now the first.
The precepts for destroying rebirth come forth; there are eleven precepts that clearly explain guarding the mouth, restraining the mind, and ensuring the body does not commit evil.

One should skillfully regulate the conduct of the three karmas. Regarding the phrase "speaking false words": speech that does not correspond to reality is called "false" (*mṛṣā*); when this is manifested through the mouth, it is called "speech" (*vāda*).

To commit an offense without intention is called "accidental. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks: "If deception is grave when intentional, and an offense is light when done in jest, why do both cases of concealing an object result in the downfall (*pāyattika*) offense?

The answer is: False speech is not grave in terms of causing distress; it is because of the underlying state of mind that one incurs the downfall. In the case of jesting, one incurs a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

However, regarding the concealment of an object, the objective of causing distress is profound. Although there may be differences in gravity between the concealment itself and the resulting loss, in terms of the emotional distress caused to the other party, they are identical.

Therefore, both result in a downfall (*pārājika*). [The author] establishes that some refer to it as "minor falsehood" (*kṣudra-mṛṣāvāda*); it is called "minor" in contrast to the aforementioned "major falsehood. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five types of false speech:
namely, those involving a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *pāyattika*, and a *duṣkṛta*. To falsely claim to have attained [superhuman powers] is a *pārājika* falsehood.

To maliciously slander another with one of the four grave offenses is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* falsehood. The two preceding cases of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* falsehoods involve the preliminary stages (*prayoga*) that have not yet reached their culmination.
This concludes the section on lying that constitutes a *pārajika* offense. To slander another with a charge of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is called a *thullaccaya* (grave) lie.

Apart from these four types of lies, all other lies constitute an offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "the accumulation of the熏 (xūn, perfuming) of delusive karma" (*mṛṣāvāda-karma-vāsanā-ācaya*):

this clarifies that since beginningless kalpas, one has practiced this delusive karma, which has perfumed and formed seeds that accumulate within consciousness; hence, it is called the "accumulation of the perfuming of delusive karma."

Regarding the statement that "the seeds of consciousness are especially numerous," Liangbi (Lingbian) says: "This refers to the accumulation of the seeds of this beginningless deluded mind within the eighth consciousness.
Bin says: "However, concerning the meaning of consciousness, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha taught that there are nine consciousnesses.
The first six are as commonly known. The seventh is named the *ādāna-vijñāna*. The Tang Tripiṭaka Master translated *ādāna* as 'grasping' (*zhí*')."
*Héshí* (Holding Consciousness) is an alternative name for the eighth consciousness; it is not the same as the *zhēnzhì* (True Consciousness).

The eighth *ālíyè shí* (ālaya-vijñāna)—which the Tang Tripiṭaka Master names *ālāiyé shí*—is translated as *zàngshí* (Storehouse Consciousness); this is also an alternative name for the eighth consciousness.
Regarding the ninth *āmóluó shí* (amala-vijñāna), the Tang Tripiṭaka Master states: *āmóluó* means "stainless consciousness" (*wǔgòu shí*) in Chinese. It is [identical to] the Great...

This is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). According to Paramārtha’s translation of the *Nirnayāsaṃgraha-śāstra*, the ninth chapter of the "Nine Consciousnesses" section is titled "Amala-vijñāna.
Paramārtha’s translation states: "This has two kinds: first, the object of cognition (*ālambana*), which is True Suchness (*tathatā*)."

The second is called *mūla-avabodha* (fundamental awakening), which is the cognizing wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*). This consciousness encompasses both the subject that cognizes and the object that is cognized;

their union constitutes the essence of this consciousness. The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty explained: "By transforming the eighth consciousness, one attains the stainless consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*); there is no separate ninth [consciousness]."

The details are as found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other texts, which cannot be recounted here at length (the *Niyatārthadharmaparyāya-śāstra* is the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;

the Tripiṭaka Master of Tang stated that Paramārtha falsely added a "Chapter on the Nine Consciousnesses"). The eighth is named the *ālaya-vijñāna*, also called the *saṃbhāra-vijñāna* (the consciousness of containment), meaning it contains and stores the seeds of both good and evil.
It is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna* (store-consciousness) and the *gṛha-vijñāna* (dwelling-consciousness). The ninth is the pure white consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), which belongs to...
This is the Buddha. Now, it is said that the seeds of consciousness are even more numerous.

Therefore, "moving according to the realms of sensory objects and thus engaging in empty fabrications" means that one constantly engages in false speech and mental-oral activity following the realms of the six dusts and the six great elements, perpetually constructing and creating karma through empty delusions.
"Not contemplating the beginning of the reversal of the flow, but only wishing for the end of this life" means that there is no...
The beginning of the primordial source originates from True Suchness (*tathatā*). However, due to the arising of delusion, one deviates from the truth and fails to know how to return to the source.

If one now cuts off delusion and cultivates the truth, one will transcend the three realms and flow upstream against the current of birth and death, thereby realizing the original source of True Suchness;

hence it is so called. For example, a person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* is said to be "flowing upstream against the stream of birth and death," meaning they simply vow to bring their worldly life to an end.
"Until the end" means that throughout one's life in this world, one has constantly engaged in false speech and has not thought to reform it;

wishing to carry this through until the completion of one's life, one says "until the end of one's life. "To live in peace by means of this" refers to its application; that is, to employ this karma of false speech.
He settles his life with this; he may even use such false speech as a means to secure his own safety—hence these words.
As for those who must die, they stand [in their position] embracing this deluded karma until death arrives; it is only at the moment of death that it finally ceases—hence these words.

It is certainly not the case that one who practices falsehood can eliminate karmic suffering. The establishment of this point is as follows: since one has habitually practiced lying, how could one possibly eliminate the karma of the suffering of birth and death?
"Good" (liáng) means virtuous; it means faithful. Furthermore, regarding those who transgress against indeterminate objects:

this refers to objects for which there is no fixed standard of right or wrong. It depends solely upon the mental conception; to act in contradiction to one's conception constitutes a transgression, whereas to act in accordance with one's conception incurs no fault. Nevertheless, the object itself must not be false.
It is true; however, it is simply that the arising of the mind itself possesses both the real and the unreal. If the mind is unreal, this constitutes an offense.

It is said that as long as one violates the internal conceptual mind, external conditions are irrelevant. That is to say, regardless of whether the external object is favorable or unfavorable, if the mind violates [the precept], it is an offense.

However, the meaning of the correspondence or non-correspondence between the object and the mind is extremely difficult to grasp; it will be briefly set forth below. For instance, consider a case where the object is favorable but the mind is contrary.
This refers, for example, to one who has previously seen a person named Zhang, but while on the way, becomes confused in thought and mentally thinks they have not seen him.

Later, when asked by another whether they saw Mr. Zhang, they reply, "I saw him. This is precisely what constitutes an offense. In terms of the six mental states (*ṣaḍ-citta*), this constitutes one instance.

The meaning of these six mental states will be explained later. An offense is established through six conditions: first, it must be a human being; second, there must be the perception of that person as such. First... [end of fragment]

Question: Is there a distinction between *saṃjñā* (perception) and *jñāna* (cognition)? Answer: There are both similarities and differences. The mind that discerns an object is called cognition (*jñāna*).

That which penetrates the specific characteristics of the object is called perception (*saṃjñā*). They are similar because both are able to discern objects. As for their difference: cognition only discerns the object, whereas perception encompasses both delusion and awakening. Penetrating the specific characteristics of an object is called perception;
penetrating the specific characteristics of an object while being deluded is also called perception. When these characteristics are categorized exhaustively, they form four types.

Regarding the categories: the established explanation states that there are four possibilities: first, false speech that is neither divisive speech nor harsh speech; second, divisive speech that is neither false speech nor harsh speech;
third, harsh speech that is neither false speech nor divisive speech; fourth, all three together. As for the other three verbal actions:
This refers to false speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech; it should be understood that frivolous speech is excluded. Regarding "either combined or separate":

the first case means that there may be false speech alone without harsh speech, which constitutes separation; at other times, there may be both false speech and harsh speech, which constitutes combination.
As for the single category of frivolous speech being inseparable from the others, Master Li states: within the aforementioned three types of karma, frivolous speech is contained within all of them.

Within false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), there are also frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*), double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), and harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). This is by way of analogy with frivolous speech.

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, after explaining frivolous speech in detail, it states: "The other three vocal karmas are all abandoned [in that state], yet frivolous speech cannot be separated from them.

Regarding the passage in the *Śraddhākaragupta-sūtra* (or *Upāsakaśīla-sūtra*) which says, "Some people, regarding the ten paths of karma, even claim that there are no paths of karma," Master Liang (Liu Qian) cites this text as proof.

This comes to corroborate the four phrases in the preceding text; it may also be intended to show the combination and separation [of the factors]. Regarding the statement "simultaneously performing eight," Jing says:

this refers to the fact that the preceding and succeeding minds are accomplished simultaneously. Regarding the statement "up to eight matters," this means taking only the mind of malice (*vyāpāda*) to perform the three types of physical and four types of verbal actions mentioned previously.
This is because at the time of greed (*lobha*), there is no hatred (*dveṣa*) or delusion (*moha*); and at the time of delusion, there is no hatred and so forth.
Therefore, one can only obtain eight matters. Because greed and anger are mutually contradictory, they cannot arise simultaneously;

for greed arises toward a favorable object while anger arises toward an unfavorable object, and their characteristics do not coexist. Thus it is said that "one does not commit ten. Regarding these eight matters:

If categorized according to what one does for oneself, there are eight [offenses]; if discussed in terms of causing others to do so, there are only six. This is because the karma of sexual misconduct and delusion must necessarily be performed by oneself;

since their gratification resides within oneself, it is impossible to cause another to perform sexual misconduct on one's behalf. Regarding the denial of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-apavāda*), this arises from one's own mind.

As for the remaining offenses—killing, stealing, and lying—the agent and the object may both commit them together. [This is based on] the *Caturvargika* and *Pañcavargika* Vinayas, due to the Dharma Master.
Regarding "the bhikṣus," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a Dharma-master bhikṣu in Śrāvastī named Śāraṇa (known as Hastibala in the *Caturvargika*).
He was brilliant and possessed great eloquence; none among the fourfold assembly, nor among the non-Buddhist śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, could equal him.
Consequently, he took what was wrong to be right and what was right to be wrong; he claimed to know what he did not know and claimed not to know what he did know. Constantly...
With his incisive eloquence, he surpassed the speech of others. At that time, there were no monks who did not sigh in admiration and submit.

They asked him, "When you debated, did you intend it as a view, or was it a claim of knowledge, or was it not? He replied, "I truly claimed it was not; I spoke falsely only because I had taken a point of defeat upon myself.
The monks reported this transgression to the Buddha. The Buddha immediately established a precept regarding false speech within the Sangha.
Regarding the statement that "the gravity of the offense of speech exceeds that of a hundred arhats": an arhat is restricted to the status of a sage, and their number is limited to a hundred.

Within the *saṃgha*, however, both ordinary beings and sages are included, and their number is infinite; thus the meaning is clear. Furthermore, although an arhat is a sage, even if they were to engage in false speech in the presence of others...
Its meaning is difficult to believe and accept; yet ordinary monks receive it with deception, for they give rise to faith without doubt—hence its gravity.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha taught that there are ten offenses for speaking falsehoods: first, one’s breath becomes foul; second, benevolent deities distance themselves while non-humans find an opportunity;
third, even if one speaks the truth, people do not believe or accept it; fourth, when wise men deliberate on matters, one is never consulted or included. Fifth...

First, one will constantly be subjected to slander and foul reputations that spread throughout the world. Second, one will not be respected by others; even if one issues instructions, people will not accept or follow them.
Third, one will constantly experience much sorrow and anxiety. Fourth, one plants the karmic causes and conditions for slander.
Fifth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one shall fall into hell. Sixth, if one emerges as a human being again, one will constantly be slandered.

Regarding "slander": to establish a statement by tracing it back to its source is to provide a basis for one's words. For example, when preaching from a high seat, one should not say, "I myself have made this teaching;
these are my own words. One must trace it back to the Original Teacher (the Buddha) so that there is scriptural authority. Even if there were faults, they would then belong to the former person.

As for the phrase "the axe is in one's mouth," according to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), the Buddha said: "When a person is born into this world, an axe is already in their mouth."
In the middle [section], the Buddha himself recounted his past causes and conditions: "In the distant past, many kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Ārila.
Within that Buddha’s Dharma, there were two brothers who left the household life. The elder brother attained the fruit of Arhatship through the practice of dhyāna;

the younger brother mastered the Three Piṭakas through study and propagated the Buddha-Dharma. At that time, the fourfold assembly venerated both of them; however, the elder brother, by the power of the Noble Path..."
Consequently, gain and offerings were disproportionately abundant. At that time, there was a donor who gave a bolt of woolen cloth to the elder brother but did not give any to his younger brother.
Regarding food, drink, clothing, and all four requisites, everything was biased and unequal. The younger brother became envious and slandered him. At that time, there was another donor...
He dispatched a young woman to where his younger brother, the bhikṣu, was staying. That younger brother, the bhikṣu, said to the woman, "Give yourself to me, and slander that bhikṣu.
At first, the woman refused, saying, "How could one bring such a slander against that noble person?
Thereupon, that younger brother, the bhikṣu, used various skillful means to entice her mind, saying, "I shall obtain that woolen blanket for you and give it to you."
To prove her guilt, she simply said, "He committed sexual misconduct with me. She then went to her brother and obtained a woolen blanket (*kambala*) to give to him.
The woman immediately returned home. When her family asked, "Why have you been gone for so long? she replied, "That bhikṣu detained me at the mortar to play;
that is why I was delayed. She further added, "Give me this blanket. At that time, the people of the world all gave rise to doubt and suspicion regarding her brother, who was an arhat.
Seeing these two people committing great evil deeds, he immediately avoided them by going to another place. Then the Buddha said: "The younger bhikṣu was I myself;
the woman was Sundarī. Because I slandered a holy person in a previous life, even though I have now attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), I am still subjected to defamation.
Regarding the phrase in the Vinaya, "seen, heard, touched, or known," these four refer to the objects of perception; as for the verbal expression [of these], it is as follows...

All eight constitute offenses. Regarding "object and speech": for instance, seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing—these four are the objects. To deceive another by saying one has not seen, heard, touched, or cognized them is "speech.
Furthermore, when one has actually not seen, heard, touched, or cognized—this is the object—to deceive another by saying one has seen, heard, touched, or cognized them is "speech.
Therefore, it is called "object and speech. Within this context of seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing:

Speaking in terms of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), "seeing" and "hearing" correspond to visible forms and sounds. "Touch" refers to the three [objects] of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility;
that is, the nose, tongue, and body are all termed "touch. These three faculties perceive only proximate objects and are thus collectively designated as "touch."

Question: Regarding the objects of contact for the tongue and the body, their functioning can indeed be demonstrated. But when the nose perceives fragrance, how could it ever be said to "contact" its object? Answer:

It must rely upon the vital breath-wind (*prāṇavāyu*) to draw the fragrance to the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*). If the nose is congested, the breath-wind cannot circulate; unable to draw in the fragrance, one consequently does not smell it.
Thus, it is clear that the olfactory faculty itself is what contacts [the object]. As for the eyes and ears, they only perceive...
Regarding distant objects: if an object comes into contact with the eye, the eye is unable to see it.

Therefore, the treatise states that seeing occurs when five conditions are present—namely, depending on the eye (the cause), depending on space, depending on light, and depending on consciousness; this is called "seeing. The same applies to the ear:

it hears only external sounds, but does not hear sounds within the ear itself. Thus, a verse in the *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra* says: "The two objects are not perceived when they are too close," and so forth.
Furthermore, the prose commentary explains: "The two consciousnesses that do not perceive objects closely" refers to visual consciousness and auditory consciousness;

they do not perceive objects that are too close. For example, when a form is pressed against the eye, it is not seen; the same applies to the ear—if it is pressed, one does not hear. As for mental consciousness, it perceives both distant and near objects.

The remaining ones, which exclusively perceive objects closely, are olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness; these require the object to be proximate, as their support and objective condition must be contiguous.
Therefore, the commentary states: "Support" refers to the sense organ upon which consciousness relies; "condition" refers to the object upon which consciousness takes its support.

Only when there is no separation between the organ and the object can there be sensation. As the treatise says: "If one hears a sound and yet hears it as if it were within oneself, this is a disorder of the ear;
it is hearing external sounds [as internal]. The treatise further states: "Hearing requires four conditions: the ear, the sound, space, and consciousness. These enable hearing."
As for the remaining three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—they can be cognized provided they possess three conditions: first, the three respective sense organs must be unimpaired;
second, there must be contact between the object and its corresponding organ, such as the odor-object contacting the nose-organ, the flavor-object contacting the tongue-organ, and so forth.

The three factors that give rise to consciousness are the causes. Since consciousness possesses these three conditions, it is clear that it does not depend on the cause alone; rather, contact and the others function together. These three [conditions] only serve to apprehend the immediate object.
What is called "knowing" refers to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as it takes the objects of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as its domain;

this belongs to the category of knowing. According to the Vinaya texts, there are four types: seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing. There is also the state of having a perception (*saṃjñin*), which refers to the opposite of these four.

Furthermore, there are four [additional cases]. That is to say: saying one has seen when one has not seen; saying one has not seen when one has seen. The remaining examples may be understood by analogy.
Regarding this, the meaning of the "six minds" is established. The opening commentary states: "Citing eight objects to deceive another constitutes an offense. Within this, there are two parts.
First, regarding deception of another based on the four objects of what was not seen, heard, touched, or known, there are twenty-four permutations. Second, regarding what was seen and heard..."
Deceiving another through touch constitutes an offense; there are likewise twenty-four permutations.

In the Vinaya texts, regarding the statement "not seeing, not hearing, not touching, and not knowing," when one gives rise to a false claim based on this, it should be understood as deceiving another concerning the object of "not seeing. There are six permutations for this.

First, one does not actually see [the object], yet sees it as a deceptive path; this is a contradiction between both mind and object. Second, one does not actually see it, yet says "I do not see" while deceiving others;
this accords with the object but contradicts the mind. Third, one does not actually see it, yet internally gives rise to doubt, wondering "Did I see it, or did I not?
but when it comes to deceiving others, one says "I saw it" without hesitation; this is a contradiction between both mind and object. Fourth, one does not actually see it, yet doubts...
The mental state is as before. When one actually sees nothing and has no doubt, yet deceives others by saying "I did not see it," this is a contradiction between the object and the mind.
Fifth: one actually does not see and has no doubt, yet when deceiving others, says "I saw it with doubt"; here both the mind and the object are contradictory. Sixth:
one actually does not see and has no doubt, as before; yet when deceiving others, says "I saw it with doubt"; here the object accords with the mind.

This is incorrect. Based on the single factor of "not seeing," six permutations can be established. Proceeding down to the offense of *thullaccaya*, one should understand that for each of the three objects—hearing, touching, and knowing—there are likewise six permutations;
thus, there are twenty-four permutations in total. Now, the Vinaya text is well-suited to brevity;
it identifies the four objects—not seeing, not hearing, not touching, and not knowing—and applies them across the six mental states (*citta*), thereby resulting in another four sets of six.
The twenty-four phrases may be understood accordingly. Li states: "Among the six states of mind mentioned above, in the first, third, and fifth, both the mind and the object are contrary;
in the second, fourth, and sixth, the mind is contrary while the object is compliant. Regarding the phrase "what is seen differs," the *Commentary on the Mind* (*Xinshu*) says:

"While practicing within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one sees various evil images; yet when asked by others, one describes them differently from what was actually seen. This is why it is so called.
Lì says: "When, within the mind engaged in practice, one sees tigers and wolves, yet speaks of seeing Buddha-images, this answers the different versions of what was seen by others.

Regarding the difference in the definition of 'patience' (*kṣānti*): the *Xinshu* (Commentary on the Mind) states, 'To accept what is contrary and settle into suffering is called patience,' which refers to others’ pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*).

The *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) states, 'To experience a contrary object and settle the mind in the sensation of suffering is called patience,' which answers others’ [definition of] painful sensation."
This refers to "feeling" (*vedanā*). Regarding the differences found in the Vinaya concerning what is "delightful": seeking material wealth is termed "desire" (*kāma*);

the answer differs from the original by stating that one delights in the True Dharma (*saddharma*). This is like calling cold "heat" or enduring suffering and calling it "pleasure. Regarding differences in "conception" (*saṃjñā*):
the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) states this refers to conceiving an enemy as a friend. It may also refer to actually forming a perception of something while answering, "I did not see it."

It is so called because it contradicts one's perception and intention. Furthermore, regarding the "three times," this refers to the two preparatory stages (the preceding and succeeding) and the time of actual performance; thus, they are called three.
If one does not recall [the offense] during the preceding and succeeding stages, but recalls and recognizes it as false at the time of actual performance, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one does not maintain mindfulness while performing the act itself, it is still auspicious provided there is the preliminary application (*pūrvaprayoga*) and the subsequent mind of rejoicing (*pṛṣṭhacittānumodana*).

In contrast to this, there should be eight permutations: 1. There is a mind before [the act], but no mind during or after (one is auspicious). 2. There is a mind during [the act], but no mind before or after (one is neutral). 3.
There is a mind after [the act], but no mind before or during (one is auspicious). 4. There is a mind before and during [the act], but no mind after.

Regarding "not having seen or heard much": although one has actually not seen or heard, because one deceives another by saying, "In the past, I did not see or hear much," an offense is committed.
"Standing" means that although one has actually neither seen nor heard, one deceives another by saying, "I did not clearly or distinctly see or hear. Therefore, it is so called.
It is not so. According to the *Śāṅghabhedavastu* (or *Sāṃghika-vinaya*), if one says that one has not seen, heard, sensed, or known [something], it is likewise a false speech.
This does not constitute a complete inquiry regarding whether the object is a visible form (*rūpa*) or a faculty (*indriya*). Answer: The two schools differ. According to the *Tattvasiddhi* school:

It is consciousness alone that is able to see; "eye" is merely its name. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) maintains that it is the faculty (*indriya*) that sees, not consciousness (*vijñāna*).

As the verse in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "If the eye arises following [its object], it sees; the auditory element arises following [its object], it hears. Furthermore, another verse says: "The eye of its own category sees visible forms."
It is not that eye-consciousness sees; it is neither wisdom nor their conjunction. This is because they do not see manifest form. (Commentary:

"The eye as its own part" refers to the eye-faculty at the moment when consciousness arises; this is called "its own part. The eye and the eye-consciousness perform their respective functions together.
This is called "one's own" (*svaka*). In the new sūtras and śāstras, it is called "homogeneous eye" (*sabhāga-cakṣus*).

As for the statement that "it is not that eye-consciousness sees," this is the tenet established by the Sautrāntikas, because they hold that it is consciousness, not the eye, that sees. Furthermore, there is another school which holds that the wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with eye-consciousness is able to see form.
Yet another teacher of the Sautrāntika school offers a distinct interpretation, stating that the conjunction of the eye and eye-consciousness is what is called "seeing. Now, [the author] Sa...

Bhadanta and others all refute this, stating that it is because external forms are not seen. That is to say, when the mind and mental factors apprehend an object, there is no obstruction or separation.
If consciousness and so forth were to see the parts of the external [object], then it would follow that consciousness sees; therefore, this is not consistent with correct reasoning.
If one speaks by "breaking the signs" (*lakṣaṇa*), it is as follows: Suppose one goes to the western room and sees a certain bhikṣu repairing the dwelling;
later, upon returning to one's own room, someone asks, "Did you see so-and-so? One answers them, whether one saw him or not, simply saying, "That bhikṣu is very capable at manual labor.
This is called speaking by breaking the signs, and in this case, there is no offense. Jing says: Speaking by breaking the signs means [to speak] according to reality...
It is said thus. Someone remarked: "To shatter the mind that clings to views, one says that the nature of form is fundamentally non-existent;
what, then, is there to be seen? Jie replied: "Ordinary people cling to appearances and reckon that form is permanent. Now, by shattering these appearances, one declares that form is empty.
However, the bhikṣu’s eyes have not actually seen emptiness; this refutation is merely made in accordance with the teaching. Thus, there is no transgression. So it was said.
"Speaking with concealment" means speaking according to the facts. "Speaking in a different dialect" refers to using foreign sounds such as those of the Hu or Han;
the intention is to cause others not to understand, yet even if the words spoken are neither false nor unreal, it constitutes an offense. Master Shou says:
"That which is spoken according to a different script is called a 'different script sound'. Master Ci says: "A 'different script speech-sound' may involve making the voice loud or soft."

Not allowing the person before one to understand is called "a different original sound" (a variation on the original phrasing). Regarding "having them look at their fingernails," this refers to the established practice of saying:
"Donor, look for yourself. If one story is not sufficient and two stories are desired, and one now wishes to employ a skillful means (*upāya*), the response is:
"I see [the donor] while sitting; wait until he comes over. Then, rising, one replies: "I have just risen and have not yet seen him. This is the teaching of Jie.
It is said: People in the Western Regions use their fingernails as mirrors. If a butcher asks, "Do you see [the animals]?
a bhikṣu may reflect his own face in his fingernail and say, "I do not see pigs," and so forth; thus he commits no offense. This is indeed a skillful means.
The *Jī* text states: "If an animal from a butcher's house runs away, and someone asks a bhikṣu whether he has seen it, the bhikṣu must not speak falsely, nor may he point out its location.
He should say, 'Look at the markings on my fingernails. This is what the sutra means by "look at the fingernails."
The Hu (barbarian) pronunciation is the same as "not seeing.
Regarding the two [sections on] reviling the precepts: as for "inner dharmas" and "outer dharmas," etc., this means that the good and evil within the internal mind are called inner dharmas.
Because one perceives the external world, there is purity and impurity; these are called "external dharmas.
However, all sentient beings and the class of living creatures are called "internal dharmas. All non-sentient things, such as mountains, rivers, and the great ocean, are called "external dharmas.

Because the minds of sentient beings possess the causes of good and evil, they attract external objective retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*). The presence of beauty or ugliness within these supports is termed "conditions" (*pratyaya*), such as mountains.
The "River World" (Gāṅgā-loka) is so called because it is the realm upon which these sentient beings depend.

Regarding the passage in the Vinaya concerning animals who feel shame upon hearing insults—this refers to the story of two bulls competing for the right to pull a cart, where one was insulted by being told, "Your horns are broken. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun), in ancient times all animals were capable of speech;
at the beginning of the kalpa, there were only humans and devas, and the three evil realms did not yet exist, as they all originated from among the devas and humans.
"Come. This was spoken because of past habitual tendencies; it was not spoken now because [the beings] had mostly come from the three evil destinies.

Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which state that disparaging the four assemblies constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense: however, this precept involves the same causal conditions for both monks and nuns, yet differs in its application. For monks, it is restricted to those of the same class.
If a nun reviles a monk, both are guilty of a *duṣkṛta* offense; if a monk reviles a nun, he incurs a *pāyattika*. Regarding the "six categories":

these refer to (1) lineage, (2) occupation, (3) craft or skill, (4) those who have committed transgressions, (5) those with many fetters (*saṃyojana*), and (6) the bald, the blind, and the lowly—this refers to the enumeration of families.
There are three methods of verbal abuse: face-to-face abuse, metaphorical abuse, and comparative abuse. "You are an *āraṇyaka*... [and so forth].

If a practitioner of meditation is entirely auspicious, the *Xinshu* (Heart-Questions) asks: "Virtuous dharmas are good; reviling is evil. How can one incur an offense [for the latter]? The answer is given by way of the mind of the reviler:
they desire to slaughter and dismember [the other], yet later, seeing a minor fault, they cause it to be magnified.

You are a person of admonition (*yanruo*); why do you still cling? Even those who have abandoned clinging—the Arhats—still maintain their robes and alms bowls. Therefore, on account of a slight cause, [one should remain] hidden...
They incited one another to commit [the offense]. Since the transgression of the facts was not grave, the resulting *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) was also light.

Regarding the statement that "if the Upādhyāya or Ācārya is a *sthūlātyaya*," Jing says: "This is a light *sthūlātyaya*; it is lighter than a *pāyattika*, being reduced by one degree. According to the intent of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* text, one should say:
"If one reviles others with other middling or superior evil dharmas, this should be verified in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* as listed separately. There is a treasury of gold in the ground.

Regarding those who delight in fighting: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, in a past age, there was the son of a householder in the city of Vārāṇasī who had a slave named Amoyu. By nature he was fierce and evil.
At that time, the householder’s son was playing in a garden with several sons of Brahmins, while his attendants were all outside the garden gate. Then Amoyu was in the garden...
Outside the gate, he struck the various attendants. At that time, those attendants who were beaten by him each informed their masters.
All the sons of the brahmins came out and rebuked him. Then Amayū did not accept their words, but answered the sons of the brahmins, saying:
"I will not follow your words. If the son of my master comes to rebuke me, then I shall accept his words."

He continued beating him without ceasing. The victim immediately went to inform his master, Āmātya. Āmātya, who had previously attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), observed the site of the conflict and saw that beneath it lay a hidden treasure of gold and silver;
because the ground was inauspicious, it caused them to fight. He went there and rebuked them, and the slave immediately stopped.
There is also a sutra which clarifies that when there are "hidden corpses" (*pūtiśava*) within the earth, they are called "hidden treasures" (*nidhi*); such is the case for humans.
Dwelling in this place, many take pleasure in strife; they all share this same understanding.

Regarding Kāśyapa’s raising of the matter concerning the faults of the monks who had initiated construction, among the thirteen rules there was a bhikṣu who built a large dwelling and solicited alms from the village settlement, causing everyone to feel weary and disgusted.

Consequently, when Kāśyapa entered the village for alms, the lay devotees fled to avoid him. He pursued them to inquire into the reason, and later reported the matter to the Buddha. Upon hearing this, the Buddha...

Having spoken thus, he commanded that [the monk] be sent out of the boundary to stay overnight. That night, a non-human being came to inform the Buddha: "A bhikṣu cut down a tree and injured my child’s limbs.
Out of faith, I did not dare to harm him; may the Buddha take note of this.

The following morning, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked the bhikṣu who had built the hut. He spoke directly of how the non-human being had come to inform him the previous night, but he did not mention Kāśyapa.

Regarding "making a formal announcement": this is because the Buddha protected the minds of others; he caused Kāśyapa to leave the boundary so that the bhikṣu who was building the dwelling would not harbor doubts regarding Kāśyapa’s purity.

The following clarifies the non-offense according to the Dharma. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "If a bhikṣu speaks of another’s offense and the other bhikṣus recognize that person as being such...
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*’s section on the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), it states: "At the time of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*, there was a bhikṣu... [The text continues from here.]

“Kauṭṭhila, if a bhikṣu speaks of another bhikṣu’s offenses—whether he has seen, heard, or suspected them—and other bhikṣus know that this person who speaks of others’ offenses is impure in his bodily actions, being capable of sexual misconduct, theft, lying, destroying grass, eating at improper times, drinking alcohol, and so forth, then one should not trust the words of this bhikṣu when he treats others for their offenses.
The Saṃgha should say to him: ‘Venerable sir, do not be angry; do not quarrel; do not dispute.’”
"Do not speak to one another. The following text explains that the verbal karma of the person who brings forth the accusation is impure;

it is likewise stated that their bodily and verbal karma are both impure when they act in this way (and so forth). Jing says: "This refers to the fact that the bhikṣu capable of speaking possesses his own faults.
Even if the bhikṣu being spoken about actually has faults, because the person who speaks is by nature not pure, [the Saṃgha...]"
One must speak to the person capable of explaining it, saying: "Do not harbor anger, dispute, or engage in mutual recrimination.

Regarding the third precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*): as for the statement that there are no superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are seven kinds of abusive speech (*ākrośana*).
Within these seven [categories], there are three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—of abusive speech, according to which the degrees of offense are determined.

Now, if one engages in divisive speech (*paiśunya*), this constitutes transmitting the abuse of others; it merely creates a mind intent on separation. Who asks whether the abuse transmitted is superior or inferior?

By merely transmitting the three grades of abuse while harboring a mind of division, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This differs from the case of abusive speech itself, where the offense is differentiated according to its own internal grades. Now...
The commentator briefly summarizes the meaning of that passage; therefore, readers are all confused. One should consult the *Ji-chao* as provided elsewhere (and so forth).
Regarding the statement "having already spoken, one speaks again and falls [into an offense]," the Master said: "One transmits the words of another and repeatedly speaks them before others."
Repeatedly one incurs the offense. Below, the non-offenses are clarified.

Regarding the fourth precept on sleeping together with a woman: among the conditions for the offense, the first is "a human female. Liang states that according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, even a newborn who has not yet dried is an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi), fascicle ten, states: "The three realms of existence incur the same offense; if it is a cow..."

When a donkey or similar animal holds its head up, there is no offense; when it lies down with its head drooping, it is a *thullaccaya*. When a female dog stretches out its head, there is no offense; when it curls its head over to sleep, it is a *thullaccaya*.

When geese, chickens, and the like curl their heads under their wings, it is a *thullaccaya*. When an elephant stands upright, there is no offense; when it leans against something, it is a *thullaccaya*.

(Since this is the case for animals, it should be understood accordingly for non-humans. The *Cīvara-vastu* also states: "If many bhikṣus are sleeping inside a room, and a woman is holding her daughter..."
If any bhikṣu enters while asleep, he commits a *thullaccaya* offense. If the *karmadāna* (steward) or an administrator is aware of this, they should say:

"You must hold the child upright before entering. According to this, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, a young girl would not commit an offense; therefore, in the subsequent explanation of the characteristics [of the rule], it states that "a human female" refers to one who possesses intelligence and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed.
In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is recorded that a woman was staying in another's house, and a hole large enough for a kitten to enter existed there.
This constitutes an offense. Regarding the phrase "the four sides have enclosures and there is a roof above," Jingyun says: this refers to all the enclosures within a large hall;
even if there are separate partitions in the middle, because the enclosures and the roof are the same, it is also an offense.

The note states, "According to the *Śāstra*, it is not permitted," which refers to both the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra*; the details appear later in the text, namely, within one large hall, on all four sides...

There is an obstruction. If a separate small room is constructed in the middle, although there is a partition, one still commits an offense because it is encompassed by the four boundaries of the same large hall.
Second, regarding "the former dilapidated [room] without walls," the established interpretation states that this refers to a case where it is mostly obstructed, meaning it has walls on three sides.
The commentary notes: "That is, a long rectangular room with obstructions at both ends under the eaves," etc. Jing says: "This room..."
This refers only to cases where three sides have walls. Even if there is a separate door, it constitutes an offense because it is situated within the three obstructions;
this is not the same as the previous case of a chamber, which refers only to internal partitions within a hall. This, then, refers to all instances of being fully covered with many obstructions.

Now, if one extends the eaves of a room such that there are no obstructions at both ends, or if there is an obstruction at only one end, it is not an offense, because it does not constitute "many obstructions."
The characteristics of a "room" (śālā) are not established. By this standard, secular people’s halls and lower levels all constitute an offense. Third, "though covered, it is not complete":
this refers to being enclosed on all sides but with the two ends covered while the center remains uncovered. Fourth, "though the covering is complete, there are openings."
The sub-commentary states: "This refers to the upper chamber having openings. Jingyun says: "In the chambers preceding this one, there are generally many such openings;
the difference here is merely that it has only light-holes. This type is commonly seen in this region; the four sides of the chamber have no windows, but only the roof is opened."
"Taking the light" refers to this. Regarding "lying sideways," the Upādhyāya says: it means leaning to the east or leaning to the west;

whether leaning against a wall or leaning against a rope-bed, any lying down that is not with the body held upright is called "lying sideways. Thus, the *Yùnjí* (Rhyme Collection) states: "To lean (*yì*) is to rest against. This is precisely its meaning.
As for the rule that "if a bhikṣu lies down while a woman stands, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense," Jǐng says: although it is during the day...

Lying down is not subsumed under "staying overnight," but is rather subsumed under "sitting in seclusion. Even if both [a monk and a woman] sit or lie down together, one commits the offense of *pārājika* for sitting in seclusion.
An Arhat does not stay overnight with a woman, just as one would not stay with cooked food or drink. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Ānanda stayed overnight.
Distressed by the courtesan, he later returned to the Buddha’s presence and recounted these events in detail, as recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and said: "Although Aniruddha has attained arhatship and is free from desire, he should not sleep together with a woman.
Just as cooked food and drink are what people desire, so too do women desire men."
The precept was established because of this. The commentary states: "Those with flat-roofed houses in the Bing region" refers to the Bing-Fen commanderies, where such houses are commonly built.
They do not have ridgepoles; half [the roof] is entirely covered with earth, with a drainage ditch opened in the middle to discharge water.

They can be as long as ten or five bays, but the interior is not partitioned, remaining as a single unit. Ji says: "In the Bingzhou region, these houses are sometimes entirely [constructed in this manner]."
