A "dwelling" (*zhái*) is generally understood as a single house. One opens a single aperture in its center to admit light and allow passage through one door.
Furthermore, it is said that the principle is the same for multiple rooms sharing a single door, such as the shops along a road that all share one common entrance.
However, in this dwelling there are many guest rooms set aside. Although the guest rooms are separate, they all share a single entrance for coming and going.
If there is a woman within these rooms who has not yet reached full maturity, the bhikṣu commits an offense even if he is in a separate room.
Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Even if one makes a hut by hanging up a cloth, it is an offense. This applies when many rooms share a single entrance.
One also commits an offense. This excludes cases where there are separate doors. It is further stated:

if the four sides each open inward toward a single large central door for entry and exit, one also commits an offense (this refers specifically to shop-houses). If there are separate doors, there is no offense. It is further stated: if the houses are joined together.
"Large" refers to up to one *yojana*. To commit [the offense] together with another under a single roof also constitutes a violation.

Regarding "those who share the same precepts," this refers to those explicitly identified as capable of engaging in sexual misconduct within the subsequent section on the precept against traveling the same road with a woman. As for "you have no merit":
This means that by sleeping in the same place as you, I would incur an offense and cause a loss to your merit. Regarding the phrase "not concealing and not obstructing," there are nine clauses.

Because the characteristics of the dwelling are not fulfilled, these are permitted so as not to constitute an offense. As cited previously in the section on "Completing the Quorum," these nine clauses serve as proof.
When performing legal acts within this dwelling, if one is within arm's reach [of the others], one is exempt from the fault of being apart from the assembly and succeeds in completing the quorum.
Because the characteristics of a "room" are not established, the situation is the same as being in the open air.
Regarding the five precepts on sleeping together with one who is not fully ordained (*asaṃvṛta*): the first concerns a male who is not fully ordained.

According to the citation from the *Zhongming* (中冥), which refutes the former interpretation, it refers only to a man; there is no need to include a woman. If one sleeps with a woman, one commits an offense immediately upon that single night. Day.
This pertains to the preceding precept. Why is a three-night period permitted? Some cite the drinking of alcohol at improper times as an objection.

The ancient masters held that drinking alcohol at an improper time incurs both the offense of eating at an improper time and the offense of drinking alcohol; thus we know that staying overnight with a woman on the third night is permissible.

This also combines two offenses. The answer says: Since drinking alcohol was originally permitted at the proper time (*kāla*), why must one distinguish the offense based on the improper time (*akāla*)?

Whether it is the proper time or the improper time, it is not permitted; one simply needs to determine the offense based on the act of drinking itself. Regarding the "female constellation" (*nārī-nakṣatra*), there was originally no permission for two nights;

how could the offense be determined by exceeding three [nights]? The Noble Ones did not permit storing [alcohol]; all stored [alcohol] constitutes an offense. Since there was originally no prior permission, it cannot be [otherwise].
To clarify the transgressions by way of the offenses: regarding the prohibition of alcohol, the Holy One did not grant any exceptions; thus, all forms of alcohol constitute an offense.

Originally, there was never an allowance for consuming it at improper times, so one cannot claim an exception based on the time of day (this is the opinion of the ancient masters). Because this involves staying overnight with a man, the limit is set at three nights. The present *Chao* differs from this.
If one stays overnight with a woman, the nature of the offense is as previously described; if one exceeds that limit, both offenses are simultaneously incurred. Therefore, below this...
The text states: "If one has already stayed overnight with a śrāmaṇera for two nights, and then stays overnight with a woman on the third night, one incurs two *thullaccaya* offenses.
The *Shushu* (Commentary) says: "The ancients established the conditions as follows: first, it is a male who has not received full ordination;

second, it distinguishes the woman from those with whom one might stay without fault for up to three nights. The explanation says: "The Buddha prohibited staying overnight with a woman, even if they merely turn over to each other."

Regarding the establishment of the offense: since staying overnight was originally not permitted, how can there be the fault of "three nights"? Furthermore, you cite a passage from the *Gāthā* stating:
"If one stays with a woman continuously for more than three nights, there is only the offense of sharing a room, but no offense of exceeding three nights. This is a mistaken citation of the text.

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle two, states: "If one has already spent two nights with a man, and on the third night stays overnight with a woman, for every turn one makes while lying down, one commits two *thullaccaya* offenses.
The present explanation follows this treatise: staying overnight with a woman [constitutes such an offense].

Although it is prohibited by the rules, there is still the offense of exceeding three nights. If one sleeps with a woman and does not incur the offense of exceeding three nights, then my excessive non-designation would itself constitute an offense;
there should be no offense of obstruction or difficulty. Furthermore, the mere fact of having stayed overnight is itself an offense;
there should not be further offenses such as those for improper timing. If you say that multiple offenses are incurred because the conditions differ, [this is not so].
"Furthermore, I am also a woman and have not yet received full ordination; this too is a different condition. Why, then, are two offenses not established?

As for the remaining meanings, they are as explained elsewhere. Regarding this, the *Lì* (Establishment) states: "If one were to extensively analyze the characteristics of male and female, it would be as in the *Jièběn shū* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa).

Moreover, the *Shǒu shū* (Initial Commentary) and various other schools frequently cite explicit texts from the various Nikāyas. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: 'There was a lay follower who, for the sake of the Buddha...'"
He built a latrine. Although the Buddha had no need for it, he accepted it to conform to worldly custom. When Rāhula was sleeping out in the open, the night wind and rain blew.
He went to the World-Honored One’s latrine and lay down upon the wooden planks of the pit. That night there was a black snake; fearing the wind and rain as well, it wished to enter the latrine.
The Buddha constantly observes sentient beings; seeing that the snake wished to enter and would distress Rāhula, he immediately emitted a radiance and went to the latrine himself. With...
With his golden, smooth hands, he helped [Rāhula] up, brushed the dust from his body, and led him into his own room.
Pointing to a bed, he said, "Dwell here. The Tathāgata has established precepts for his disciples; therefore, practice these precepts accordingly.
Thus, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged until the end of the day. (From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: The monks expelled Rāhula from the latrine.)
At Zhongsu, fearing that a snake might bite him, the Buddha went to the latrine and rubbed Rāhula’s head with his hand, speaking this verse for him:
"It is not because of poverty, nor is it because you have lost wealth and honor; it is solely for the sake of seeking the Way that you have left the household life—you should endure this suffering."
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha took him by the arm and led him to his own room. Once he had reached the ground, the Buddha said, "O bhikṣus, this śrāmaṇera is to be pitied;
he has no father or mother. If we do not show him compassion, by what means shall he live? If he encounters a predatory beast, he will suffer great distress.
His kinsmen will surely resent it, saying: 'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are able to keep a śrāmaṇera, yet they cannot even provide for his basic needs.'"
[The Buddha] was able to guard [the Dharma]. Having rebuked them, he established the precepts. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:

"You foolish people! How can you drive away a wild fox to chase after a lion cub? In the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, he rebuked them, saying: "You foolish people, devoid of compassion, you do not protect my intention.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, after the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he said: "From this day forward, for the sake of two benefits, I permit [this practice]."
An unordained person may stay overnight with [a monk] for two nights. This refers to either a *śrāmaṇera* or a layperson (*avadātavasana*) who has entered the room.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, fascicle 15, states: "The reason one enters the Buddha’s latrine to sleep is because it is clean and pure;

many people offer incense and flowers there, and for that reason one enters. The commentary notes: "According to this, not leaving [the latrine] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is what [Master] Li means.

One should depart; if one does not depart at that time, because of the loss of the [proper] method, one first incurs a *duṣkṛta* (transgression). Looking toward the passing of two nights until the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*), one incurs the fundamental *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) for oneself.
Now, regarding the failure to depart before the appearance of the dawn light when one ought to have departed, one incurs the offense of *ayathā-vihita* (improper action).
Furthermore, according to the agreement between the diligent and the negligent: if one constantly maintains careful restraint, even if one happens not to depart, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. If...
Regarding the "lazy and arrogant": originally, there was no intention to depart, so this is the same as the case of *kuśaladṛṣṭi* (one who sees well) mentioned below.

It also refers to those who are diligent but suddenly fail to leave. According to the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa-sūtra), during the three nights, before the light of dawn has appeared, one should rise and move away.

The commentary states: "Regarding 'not committing a *thullaccaya* offense,' [the author] establishes this by citing the *Vinayavibhaṅga* to prove that, according to our own school, if one does not depart before the appearance of dawn, although one does not commit a *thullaccaya*, it is known that one commits a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, this proves that for the diligent person who does not depart, there is only a *dukkaṭa*.

The commentary further states: 'According to this, one must certainly separate from the place on the fourth night. For one who remains seated during the first watch of the night, the exemption is not established."
Jingyun says: "This refers to the four nights of staying together, during which one constantly guards against the appearance of dawn. Lili says:
"Having first completed two nights of staying together, on the third night, because there is no place to go, one should remain seated until the appearance of dawn; one must not lie down."
By the fourth night, one must necessarily go outside; it is not permissible to merely wait for the appearance of the dawn. The following passage from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Regarding the rule that one may remain awake throughout the entire night without lying down—this refers to sitting constantly without lying down from the first night until the fourth night, reaching dawn;
thus, one is permitted [to remain awake] for four nights. The essential meaning of this precept is that one must depart [from the dwelling] on the fourth night. If...

There is no offense in not remaining separated from the bedding that adheres to the side. The commentary states: "This does not mean that protecting the appearance of dawn (āloka-nimitta) applies to all four nights;

rather, it is an exception for not lying down throughout the night. This refers back to the preceding passage. It means that during the four nights, from the first watch until the appearance of dawn, one must remain constantly seated and not lie down.
If one were merely to protect the appearance of dawn, this would not be permitted; it must be observed during the fourth night.
"Separating from it. Regarding "the offense further increases": this means that once one has committed an offense, one ought to perform repentance (*pāpadeśanā*).

If one does not repent the offense, or if one continues to stay overnight with others without having repented, the offense increases further. *Shen* (深) says: "Once the offense has already been committed, yet one still has not repented it."
Even though many days have passed since one finished staying in a separate room, if one stays together again, the offense increases accordingly;
it constitutes an offense on the very first night. Therefore, it is said that there is no allowance for a second night. Once the repentance has been performed, one must stay in a separate room;

even if one obtains a second night thereafter, [the rule remains]. Jing says: "Though one repents their transgression, they may not stay together on that same day; following along and sleeping together results in a downfall. One must repent the offense."
It is finished. One must stay in a different place for one night; after that interval has passed, one may again stay together.
Regarding the three nights mentioned in the initial opening of the rule, as for the four cases in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:

"one person in one room" being different refers to staying in this room for two nights with the novice Zhang, and then going together to another room for the third night. "One room" being different refers to [staying] with Zhang... in two rooms.
The novice (śrāmaṇera) has completed two nights of staying. On the third night, he stays with the King’s novice. Regarding the case where three people share one room:
it is like staying in the same room as the novice for all three nights without moving. Regarding the case where four people have separate rooms:
it is like staying with the King’s novice in this room for two nights, and on the third night staying with Li’s novice in that other room.
"The conditions for the exemption are the same as above" means that the text regarding the exemptions in the previous precept on "staying overnight with a woman" applies here as well.

There is no offense if the nine types of rooms are not established, or if there are circumstances such as life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening difficulties. Zhiyi says: "If one avoids the appearance of the dawn-light (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*), there is no offense until the third [watch] has passed;
it becomes an offense on the fourth night. If one has committed the offense on the third night and has not yet repented, there is no second [offense]."
It is opened at night. It is bound according to each night’s stay. What was explained previously is the text of the *Mahīśāsaka* (祇).

Regarding the sixth point, the recitation of the precepts together with those who are not yet fully ordained: the *Mahīśāsaka* states that the Brahmins were dissatisfied and said, "But here [in this assembly], they are all so relaxed."
It is like children in a schoolhouse reciting aloud; they do not even know who is the teacher and who is the disciple.
When others see them, they do not give rise to faith. Therefore, the Buddha established the rule that it is not permitted to recite together.

Regarding the "two characters, phrases, and meanings": one character is called a name (*nāman*); four characters constitute a phrase (*pada*); and the underlying significance beneath the phrase is called the meaning (*artha*).

The opening commentary states: "The teaching that expresses [the truth] is called a 'phrase' (pada) because it provides a representation. The intended meaning expressed beneath the phrase is taken as the 'meaning' (artha).
These characters, phrases, and flavors take sound as their essence; they do not refer to ink on paper or written graphs. This is precisely the formal appearance of the teaching.
Because the time since the Sage has passed is distant and we do not behold the True Buddha, the verbal teachings must rely upon the world."
Ordinary paper and white silk are the media through which the Buddha’s teachings are transmitted; they are not the essence of the teaching itself. What, then, is the essence of the teaching?

It refers to the words spoken by the Buddha as taught by the Buddha. The nature of these words is sound, which constitutes their essence. This function of sound consists of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).

The essence of these names, phrases, and so forth is a conventional existence (*prajñapti-sat*), for they do not exist apart from sound. According to the newly translated sūtras and śāstras, one should speak of "names, phrases, and phonemes" (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*).

Regarding the terms "name" (*nāman*), "phrase" (*pada*), and "syllable" (*vyañjana*): the ancient translations were erroneous. As will be described below, names, phrases, and syllables are functional applications upon sound that are capable of expressing meaning;
it is by means of these names, phrases, and syllables [that expression occurs]. There are differences in the tenets of the two schools.

The Sarvāstivāda school maintains that names, phrases, and syllables possess their own distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and do not take sound as their essential substance. The Satyasiddhi school, however, maintains that this name...

Phrases and words have no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they are merely the winding turns of speech that serve to designate things, yet they possess no separate essence and take sound as their substance.
This is explained according to the principle of subsuming the provisional under the real: namely, that sound is real while names, phrases, and so forth are provisional.
They are called "provisional" because names, phrases, and the like lack an intrinsic nature. The Sarvāstivādins, however, treat the provisional and the real as distinct categories; therefore—
They maintain that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) possess their own distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and function as the substance of the teaching (*deśanā*).
Therefore, the Sarvāstivādins refute the Sautrāntikas (Saṃmitīyas), saying: "Speech is not different from the expressive [sounds], as is commonly understood by humans and devas" (and so forth).

Master Bin says: The Sanskrit term is *vyañjana*, which here means "phoneme" (*wen*). The ancient translation of it as "flavor" (*wei*) is erroneous. In the Western lands, one calls a phoneme *vyañjana*, *saṃjñā*, or *lavaṇa*.
The male and female faculties are both termed *piñjana*. This is because the word [itself] serves as the basis for manifesting names and phrases;

just as a fan manifests wind and salt manifests flavor, the two faculties of male and female manifest the distinction between their respective karmic retributions. Due to the confusion arising from the similarity of the terms, the translators rendered it as "flavor" (*wei*).
However, this is actually the meaning of "salt" (*yan*), and has no relation to the original word. Since the translation contains an error, the interpretation is likewise incorrect. Thus, Li said:
That which aids the spirit is called "name" (*nāman*) and "phrase" (*pada*). Now, upon careful examination, these do not at all accord with the principles of meaning.

According to the intent of the sūtras and śāstras, that which elucidates the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena is termed a "name. That which reveals the meaning in its full extent is termed a "phrase. For example, the term "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the essence of the conditioned;
further, the term "impermanence" (*anitya*) reveals that all conditioned phenomena are certainly not eternal. Since it thus excludes permanence, [it constitutes a phrase].
It clarifies the meaning of distinctions. Once the meaning is fully complete, it is termed a "phrase" (*pada*). Thus, the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature; phrases (*pada*) express distinctions. Syllables (*vyañjana*) are the letters (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for the two [names and phrases].
Jì (Jie-shen) says: "Letters are not the characters on paper; these are merely the phonemes (*jihvāmūlīya*). They are not the physical form of the characters, but must emerge from the voice."
It is called a "name" (zi). A name is simply a character (wen). Sometimes a single character constitutes a name, such as saying "water" or "fire.
Sometimes two characters constitute a name, such as saying "Great Enlightenment" (Dàjué). There are also names consisting of three, four, or five characters.
All of these are indeterminate. That which merely summons the substance of an object is called a "name" (*nāman*). As for "phrases" (*pada*), their length is also indeterminate.

For example, the statement "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" consists of four characters as a phrase; in a five-character verse or a seven-character verse, five characters constitute a phrase;
there are also cases where nine characters form a phrase, and at most eighteen characters are used to form a single phrase. Thus, Sa...
The Bāṣpa school generally takes these names, phrases, and syllables as the substance (*śarīra*) of the teaching to conclude its doctrinal classification.

Since these names, phrases, and so forth are the provisional functions of sound and do not exist apart from sound, they take sound as the substance of the teaching; this is because they subsume the provisional under the real.
This is what Master Nanshan meant when he stated that "sound is the teaching. Master Li quotes the *Ji*: "Nowadays, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) strikes for silence and says: 'One...'"
Recite all [verses]. If there is a śrāmaṇera in the hall who chants in unison with a bhikṣu, causing him to recite even a single verse, this constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

If one follows this principle, then at present, when prostrating before the Buddha, if one chants "Namo" for that Buddha in unison with those who have not yet received full ordination, it is entirely an offense.
Therefore, the *Cīvaravastu* (or *Jiǎo-shì jīng*, T.1435), fascicle 13, states: "When verses are being chanted and recited within the Saṃgha, one must not speak the same [verse] in unison."
Verse: One may simultaneously recite other verses individually. Regarding "oral transmission" (*mukhāgama*):

it refers to when a bhikṣu has not yet finished speaking, and the person in front immediately reads and recites along with his words; this is called oral transmission. Regarding "written transmission" (*lekhāgama*):

it refers to when a bhikṣu recites orally and a śrāmaṇera recites along with him, and subsequently writes it down; this also constitutes an offense. It also applies when a śrāmaṇera recites orally while a bhikṣu writes it down by hand.
[The Master] said: "Yes. The Guest said: "This means that because one simply writes down and transmits the text, one speaks of it as being 'clear' or 'unclear,' and so forth.

The commentary states: "To resolve the unclear passages in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü). Cizong says: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely states that [the teachings] were spoken by Śrāvakas, celestial beings, or seers;

it does not say they were authorized by the Buddha. This statement is general. Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Zhiji) says: 'That which must be authorized by the Buddha is called a Sūtra. Although..."
The teachings spoken by śrāvakas, celestial seers (*ṛṣi*), and others that are not authorized by the Buddha are not called "sūtras.
Regarding the seventh [point], the precept against speaking of the grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) of others: it is taught that one would rather destroy a stūpa than speak of another’s grave offense;

for by doing so, one destroys the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This clarifies that even if one commits a grave offense, one does not lose one's faith and may still cultivate other practices. However, if one... [text fragment ends]
Upon hearing others speak of my transgressions, you immediately joined in the chorus to commit evil, abruptly abandoning all other karmic duties; therefore, I did not permit you to speak.

Now, while the offense of destroying a stupa constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), it is slightly lighter than a *pārājika* (defeat). In terms of karmic retribution, they differ: destroying a stupa merely damages the physical form, whereas speaking coarsely destroys the *dharmakāya*.
To say that one destroys the *dharmakāya* by speaking of another's faults is because, by speaking of others' crimes, one ruins oneself and harms others, creating an obstacle.
It abandons right cultivation, causing that which ought to be attained not to be attained; thus, it destroys the Dharma-body. Second, regarding those who commit offenses of the first two categories:

Lì says that while the faults of the [remaining] three categories below are subtle, the first two are equally coarse and carry the sense of destroying the Saṃgha. Because their transgressions are grave, they are classified as *pārājika*.

As for shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—these two are *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses). Although their names are light, their karma is profound and heavy; to speak of them also constitutes destruction.

The assembly is the same as in the previous case regarding the offense of *pāyattika*. If this is so, why distinguish their characteristics? It is simply to manifest that they are defined by two factors, rather than listing two types of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses).

If one were to list their names, it would be confused with other *sthūlātyayas*. For this reason, it merely says "except for the *saṃgha-karman*," which already clarifies that the *karman* is not permitted.
By stating "shedding the blood of a Buddha," it clarifies that these are identical offenses, differing from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. This refers to—

If one sees another commit the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha or drawing blood—both of which constitute *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses)—one must not subsequently speak of it to an unqualified person.

This is as in the case of what Devadatta and others did; one must employ the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) and appoint a person to report it before one may speak of it oneself. To speak of it directly and arbitrarily constitutes an offense of *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) as well.

Question: Speaking of offenses belonging to the first two categories [of the Prātimokṣa] equally results in a *pāyattika*. However, there is a difference in gravity when slandering another regarding these first two categories.

Answer: Regarding the punishment for slander, there are degrees of severity depending on the extent of the damage; thus, there are graduated levels. To speak of another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) entails no formal disciplinary action (*karmavācanā*);

however, in terms of the point where it disrupts the community, it is uniformly classified as a *pāyattika* offense. The *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials) asks: "If one slanders another with malicious speech, does one receive that same malicious speech?

If the slanderer commits a grave offense, should the slanderer likewise commit a grave offense? Answer: When the slanderer commits a grave offense, there is further offense below that level, which is called "repetition" (*punar*).

Because he descended from his status, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. To slander others with malicious speech is the most base of offenses; since there is no name for an offense more base than this, he incurs the same penalty.

Regarding the four cases where the monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*) are waived: it is established that if one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), one should appoint a person by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

He went to inform the laypeople that this bhikṣu had committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), so that the worldly might distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox and not indiscriminately defile the pure ranks of the community.

Just as when Devadatta split the Saṃgha, the Buddha ordered the monks to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) and dispatched Śāriputra to inform the white-robed laity, saying:
"What Devadatta has done is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, contrary to the Buddha's teaching, and contrary to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha."
This is the matter. Regarding the phrase "if one asks about a person who has already been dealt with," Jing says: "This is not a person who has been formally dealt with by the *saṃgha*;
since he is still merely another bhikṣu, it is permissible to ask him. If one speaks of it immediately, one commits this offense. Li states:

"If there is a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), and the *saṃgha* has completed the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and the laypeople are fully aware of it—if someone then asks [the bhikṣu], the bhikṣu..."
Upon receiving this, he should answer by asking the donor, "Where did you hear this?
If the person says, "I heard it at such-and-such a place," the bhikṣu should then reply, "I too heard it at that same place.
Regarding the laywoman who spoke the verse, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, among the many well-known bhikṣus who were dining with householders in Śrāvastī, there was an elder bhikṣu who...
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) whose preceptor had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense was performing the *mānatva* penance and sat in the lowest seat.
When a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) donor saw him, she asked, "Why are you sitting here?
At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda said to her, "Your preceptor has not yet outgrown his childhood games. Upon hearing this, the upāsikā was displeased and thought to herself, "The preceptor..."
"Is it because you are a pear that you must act thus? Sit here in this lower seat. He then seized the food basket and the provisions, threw them on the ground, and departed.
He then entered his room, bolted the door, and spoke this verse: "I have long since gone forth And practiced the holy life (brahmacarya).
How can I accept the faithful offerings (śraddhā-deya) Of a youth who will not cease his play? Regarding the censure found in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, some say: [text continues].
"This is the woman's reproach. "The woman says that within the Buddha-dharma there are such deluded people as these" refers to the response given by a bhikṣu of our own school.

Regarding "one should answer concerning one's family and so forth": this refers to the words of reply used by Buddhist monks. First, "if one mentions their name" means stating their *zì* (surname) as such-and-such and their *míng* (given name) as such-and-such.
Second, "lineage" (*zhòngxìng*) refers to cases such as when a monk of noble lineage (*dàxìng*) among the assembly commits an offense.

"Offense. The rest are all minor clans; when speaking of them as major clans, one says they have committed such-and-such an offense, or refers to them as "the bhikṣu of the Zhang family," "the bhikṣu of the Wang family," and so forth.
Third, regarding clothing: this refers to wearing cotton garments, or garments of a brownish-yellow (kāṣāya) hue such as those from Gandhāra, and so on.

Fourth, regarding dwellings: this also refers to saying "the first or second room coming from the south," and so forth. Fifth, regarding physical appearance: this refers to the size of the body's stature.
This concerns length and brevity. Regarding "not forming a notion of coarseness or evil": this does not mean that one disregards the fact that another person has actually committed a transgression;

rather, it means that while one’s own mind forms a notion of goodness, one speaks in four ways as if no offense were committed. If a layperson, upon hearing these words, understands them for themselves, there is no offense.
Eight cases of actually attaining the Path and speaking of it to one who is not fully ordained. Question: This precept requires five conditions for its completion:

first, actually attaining the Path—excluding cases of overweening pride (adhimāna) as they are not transgressions due to being false; second, personally claiming to have realized it; third, speaking to one who is not fully ordained.
Fourth, the words must be clearly articulated. Fifth, the person before one must hear and understand the formulation. Huili asked:

"Regarding the precept against great falsehood, it is stated that both claiming to have attained [realization] and manifesting such through bodily signs constitute a grave offense. Yet, within this current precept, if one has actually attained the Noble Path but speaks of it verbally, it is immediately a *thullaccaya*."

When Piṇḍola manifested his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), why was it only deemed *kuśala* (wholesome)? The answer is: verbal speech involves ambiguity and overlap, and thus incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
manifesting supernatural powers lacks such ambiguity, and thus Piṇḍola is judged *kuśala*. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

manifesting supernatural powers is permitted for the sake of benefit, as it may inspire faith at times; thus, when it serves to benefit others, there is no fault. However, if it provides no benefit, one incurs an offense.

If Piṇḍola took up his bowl, it would likewise be useless; therefore, the Noble One established the precept. When speaking to laypeople, he said that the original rule had not yet been opened [for him], and thus he incurred a *pāyattika* offense.

It is said that the intention behind the prohibition was solely for the sake of ordinary people: if a noble one did not state that he had attained the fruit, ordinary people might claim, "I am a noble one.
If they were later seen to speak thus, they would know he was not a noble one, thereby protecting against the transgression of the great precept against false speech.
The Ninth Precept: Teaching the Dharma to a Woman Beyond the Limit. Excluding a man who possesses wisdom. Liang says:
"Even if one has not been invited, if there is a man present, one may exceed [the limit]. Question: The root precept merely states "excluding a man who possesses wisdom."

Why does it not say "excluding the invitation"? The answer is that an ancient interpretation states: if one were to say "excluding the invitation," there is a fear of confusing it with the requirement for a wise man, leading one to think that even at the time of the invitation, a man must still be present.
To clarify that the opening of the rule applies whenever any such condition exists, it does not repeat the exclusion of the invitation.

Now, examining this more closely, this is not the case. For example, regarding eating in a group apart from one's own community (*pṛthag-bhaktika*), there are likewise many conditions for its opening; thus, the *Prātimokṣa* [exhausts the matter].

[The] judgment: Why not fear over-extension [of the rule]? Thus we know that this "not excluding" is an abbreviation within the text of the request. Regarding the statement that "this precept does not permit [teaching] one who knows [the recipient] is a relative":
according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, because [a woman] was able to be released through five or six words, it was subsequently prohibited.
In that Vinaya, there was once a woman who was about to give birth; the bhikṣu did not preach the Dharma for her, and as a result, she gave birth and died. Consequently, he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "How many words of Dharma must you speak for one to attain understanding?
The bhikṣu replied, "Five or six words suffice for understanding. Thereupon the Buddha praised this bhikṣu and immediately established a rule based on this.

The commentary further explains that "five words" refers to preaching that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are impermanent, and "six words" refers to preaching that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are impermanent. Huiliang says: "As for 'five or six words'..."

This is the Dharma-gate of the fivefold enumeration. The Dharma-gate of the sixfold enumeration refers to this: not requesting permission to break the fast, but rather explaining it when invited; regardless of whether it is much or little.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states that "five phrases" means five kinds of statements:

"Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. The "six phrases" may be understood accordingly. The *Abhidharma-darśana-śāstra*, fascicle 15, states: "One sentence of the sūtra text has five meanings."
The commentary states that there are six phrases in total that do not constitute an offense. Jingyun says:

"If one were to analyze the five aggregates and six sense bases and explain their meaning in detail, it would still be acceptable provided it does not exceed the number six or five, nor does it clarify any other separate meanings.
The primary commentary states: "In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one has finished speaking the 'five or six phrases' to a woman, one says: 'Sister, the Dharma is correct.'"
In this regard, if one rises from one's seat and says, "I have other business and shall return later to explain it," there is no offense.
If one has finished speaking five or six words and then speaks further for another woman, and this continues in such a manner for an unlimited number of women, there is no offense.

If one is reciting a sutra oneself and a woman comes to listen and asks about its essential meaning, and one explains it for her, even if it exceeds the limit, there is no offense. May you quickly bring an end to suffering.

As for the term "one who stands" (*sthāpaka*): it means that once the exposition of the five aggregates and six sense bases is concluded, if one further says, "May you swiftly sever all fetters," or "Exhaust all suffering and eliminate [defilements]," such a person also falls [from the status of a witness], because they have exceeded the limit.

Regarding the claim that this must necessarily be a layperson and not one who has gone forth, because their circumstances are identical—Vasumitra clarifies that although they wear the dress of a layman, once they have gone forth, their disposition is equal to that of a bhikṣu; therefore, they do not fail to constitute a witness.

[The commentary] says: "Therefore, one must distinguish them from worldly people" (Jing’s reading is the same). The current translation of this interpretation is irrational, as it breaks the syntactic structure.
Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Duolun*) states: "If there is a wise man whose class or type is different [from the woman], he is not permitted in any case.
A man must be a layperson (*avadātavasana*); even any ordained person is not permitted, because the circumstances are identical. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (*Zhīlù*), fascicle 13, says: "If..."
Whether seven years old or over seven years old—even if over seven years old—if one does not understand the meaning of the words, they are also said to be "without wisdom. Furthermore, it is said:
if many women wish to hear the Dharma, each may be taught six phrases. One should say to the first woman: [insert the six phrases].
"I shall speak six phrases for you. Having spoken them, he again said to the second woman, "I shall speak six phrases for you.

In this manner, many were rendered free from fault. When the bhikṣu had departed, the women saw him out and took their leave. If he offered a blessing, saying, "May you reach the end of suffering," he incurred a *pācittiya*.
If he said, "May you be free from illness, at peace, and free from fault," he likewise incurred [an offense]. He then proceeded to another house.
When a bhikṣu sees a woman who has previously been his wife, he may say to her, "You may listen," yet although he sees her, he does not speak with her;

he simply speaks and teaches the Dharma for the sake of the woman. Although the former wife incurs no offense by listening, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*) states that one incurs an offense in relation to her.
If one does not know that a woman is inside, there is no offense. It is further stated that if one recites a sūtra [for her], it is likewise a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for each instance.
(Commentary: To recite a sūtra for a woman means to cause her to listen attentively; this is equivalent to preaching the Dharma. If the recitation is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing):
if one stops before the speech is finished, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if it is finished, it is a *thullaccaya*. The following clarifies the cases where there is no offense.
Regarding the bestowing of the five precepts and the Dharma: the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that "receiving the five precepts" refers to the essence of the three refuges;

it is for the purpose of explaining their characteristics. As for the method of the eightfold fast (*bāguānzhāi*), it is explained in the same manner. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The eightfold fast consists of the eight precepts."
One should close the gates of the sense faculties, just as the bolts of a worldly gate provide a defense. Alternatively, regarding the "eightfold fast" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*):
"fasting" (*upavāsa*) is fundamentally defined as not eating; it is so called because the remaining eight matters are employed to support that fasting.
The Ten Precepts on Digging the Earth: 1. **Not to disturb sentient beings.** This refers to the fact that there are many insects within the earth.
2. **To cease slander.** This has two meanings. First, outsiders consider plants and trees to possess life; thus, they claim that injuring them constitutes killing living beings.

This results in the loss of the path of compassion and invites slander, as people will ask: "Why does he not sit in meditation and diligently cultivate his religious practice, but instead damage the grass and dig the earth?
What kind of business is this? Regarding the three great protectors of the Buddha-dharma, the text states that they were intended to prevent kings and ministers from conscripting labor.
The commentary explains that those who falsely seek fortune—encountering blessings to which they are not entitled—are called "those who seek fortune by chance."

This clarifies that monks and nuns today commit offenses by relying on merit; specifically, they claim there is no fault in digging the earth for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha, and that they ought to obtain merit.
This is a false claim through which they incur offense. Regarding the phrase "having been rained upon for four months," Jing says: this refers to the four months of summer;
whenever rain falls during that period, if one digs, one commits an offense. This is because there is much rain during the summer, which can cause the earth [to become saturated].
"Shi" (勢) means "to produce. "Xi" (銇) is said to mean "victory. It is the opposite of "lu" (盧); it is a farming implement. Upon examining the Vinaya, this character "xi" does not exist;

there is only the character "zhuo" (斲), formed with the radical for "gold" (金) and the phonetic "yong" (甬). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "zhuo" means "to hew. Master Ying said: "The correct form of the character is 'zhuo';
the current form [with the radical for 'metal'] is not the standard form. "He" (扴) is pronounced "gongba" (公八); the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means "to scrape. If one does not instruct...
"Knowing this and seeing this as auspicious" refers to the auspiciousness of attaining the Dharma of gain and loss; according to the root text, one also incurs a *thullaccaya*.

Regarding the "Sichuan edition of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*," Jing said: "Previously, when the *Mahāvibhāṣā* was translated in Guanzhong, there were only eight fascicles, which did not fully explain the ninety [rules].
Later, the Sichuan edition of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* appeared in nine fascicles; this is what is meant by 'thus it says. Li stated that its *Mahāvibhāṣā*..."

It was translated in the region of Shu, which is why it is so called. Bin said: "Previously, the edition in the capital consisted of only eight fascicles, which did not fully explain the ninety rules of the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya*.
Master Shou cherished this treatise and constantly sought out its remaining portions.
He did not know whether the translator had failed to complete it or if it had been lost. Later, while conversing with a monk from Shu, he encountered [the text]."

"I have heard that in the land of Shu there exists a nine-fascicle version that fully explains the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. I shall wait for my return to send it to you, Ācārya, immediately upon my arrival.
Three years passed after that monk returned, yet [the text] had not been sent. He sent a letter requesting it, and only then was it dispatched.
Upon its arrival, I immediately transcribed several dozen copies and deposited them in the various repositories, so that they might circulate widely. It was because of this...
Each [version] constitutes a "Shu Edition" of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Within ancient scriptural collections, many of these fascicles were missing;

however, in the modern Tripitaka, they comprise nine fascicles. Regarding the fourth and eighth months, Jingyun states: this refers to regions with heavy rainfall, where rain falls during both the four months of spring and the four months of summer.
In regions with less rain, it occurs only during the four months of summer. This passage thus distinguishes between areas of greater and lesser precipitation.
However, in reality, one must follow the falling rain; one must not fail to do so regardless of whether it is spring, summer, or winter. Regarding the phrase "the base of the wall is uniformly damp":
this refers to the fact that in northern regions, earthen walls are commonly built such that the lower part is connected to the ground and remains damp, while the upper part is dry.
If one destroys a damp place, one incurs a *thullaccaya*; if it is a dry place, there is no offense. Regarding "if one damages a wall and completes the act of transgression":
this refers to a wall within a dwelling that has been constructed through labor; such a wall may not be damaged. If one destroys or strikes a wooden beam, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding "drawing lines on the ground that have not yet reached their limit," [Dao]li says: It is like when the sky has been clear for a long time and dust rises from the sun's glare; if one destroys it, there is no offense.
Regarding "if one destroys a wall and causes a *śuddhaka* (pure person) to remove the mud and so forth," [Daoying] says:

This refers to walls in an open space. Regarding "wells, ponds, ditches, pools, and water after new rain," [Daoying] says: This cites wells and such in exposed locations; if one draws water for the first time after rain, one should incur an offense.

This constitutes a *ti-zui* (offense of confession). Because rain can cause the earth to grow [living things], yet there is no textual authority in the Vinaya for this case, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

Regarding the term "shu" (pronounced with the initial *xú* and the final *lǚ*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to ladle out or take up a substance. As for the phrase "when defecating or urinating, using water or the hand to rub the ground," Jing says:

This refers entirely to open ground. Even under a roof, if rain washes over the ground outside and it becomes damp enough to grow grass and weeds, touching this ground also incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
Such instances are frequently seen nowadays; one must be especially careful to guard against them in order to avoid such transgressions.
If the ground contains sand that has been washed by water, it is considered [as follows]:
That ground originally had sand; later, when rainwater washed over it, it mixed with the soil.

If a wild fire approaches the temple, even to the point where one may clear away the grass and such, this is considered a prohibitive precept (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) that may be relaxed under specific circumstances. Thus, the *Ten Gates* states:
The meaning is that prohibitive precepts (*pratiṣedha-śīla*) are generally restrictive, yet they are opened when there is benefit.

If the three assemblies do not act for the benefit of the Triple Gem and so forth—nevertheless, because the three assemblies receive the precepts and observe the fast together with the great *saṃgha*, it is opened as non-offensive provided there are such conditions as the benefit of the Triple Gem.
As for the establishment of a *kaukṛtya* (an offense of wrong-doing) within the Vinaya, this is based on cases where such conditions are absent.
Regarding the rule that one may dig the ground oneself in a covered area within a *saṃghārāma*, Jing says: "This refers to a 'covered area' to clarify what is inside [the building].
If it were to refer to the exterior boundary, then digging under the eaves would constitute an offense, as it is not included within the category of a 'covered area.

However, one is permitted to dig oneself within the interior because the covered soil is incapable of producing grass or seeds. The commentary notes: "The text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is unclear on this point."

As for this, the established view is that the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely states that a place of birth (*jāti-sthāna*) cannot be destroyed, whereas a place of death (*maraṇa-sthāna*) can be destroyed;
it does not clarify the distinction between covered (*āvṛta*) and exposed (*vivṛta*) places. Consequently, the assertions of the ancient masters differ:

some say that earth which has been disturbed is "dead ground," while even that which is beneath a house is considered "living" provided it is connected to the earth. This statement is erroneous because the relevant section of the Vinaya is not explicit. Therefore, I shall now cite the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
To cover the ground is called "dead soil. Jingyun said: "The ancient masters used the example of earth from a collapsing bank to raise an objection.
According to the permissive text in the Vinaya, taking earth from a collapsing bank does not constitute an offense; however, one may take the earth but must not damage the ground.

I also hold that in the case of covered ground, one may only take the earth and must not damage the ground. This citation is not a valid precedent, because there is a difference between covered and exposed ground when it comes to rain. (From the *Shi*).

The preceding text is extremely clear. What follows clarifies the rules regarding non-offenses. Regarding the case where one turns over bricks or stones and it does not constitute an offense, Jing says:

"Because there is no damage to the ground. [However,] this land is entirely a covered area (a doubt arises: since it is already a covered area, why is it necessary to say that it is because of the absence of intention that it is initially not an offense?).

The eleventh precept on destroying living beings: Regarding the conditions, they are as stated above. As for the intent of this precept’s formulation, it shares the same basis as the previous precept on digging the earth.

*Lü* (the Vinaya commentary) states: "This precept does not have a distinct origin story (*nidāna*); rather, the account of cutting down trees within the origin story of the previous precept concerning dwellings is cited here as its origin.
The *Zhù* (Commentary) says: "Fearing that those who are ignorant might apply it indiscriminately. *Lì* (Establishment) states: "An ancient said: 'Trees... [text fragment].
Regarding "wood": it refers to that which serves as a dwelling for non-human beings (*amanuṣya*). Small grasses and seeds, however, do not serve as such dwellings.

What fault is there in destroying them? [The author] now distinguishes this case from those. Ancient masters established the name of this precept as either the "Precept Against Destroying Living Grass and Wood" or the "Village Precept," because they considered grass and wood to be "villages" (*grāma*) by virtue of being the dwellings of non-humans;
seeds were not included in this category. Now, this commentary establishes the name as the "Precept Against Destroying the Living."

Regarding the various types of precepts and the mention of butterflies and the like: the preceding section concurrently addresses the counter-argument. The Guest (the interlocutor) says: According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, [the term] "village" applies generally to ghosts and animals;

thus they are collectively termed a "village. Therefore, the tenth fascicle of that Vinaya states: "A ghost-village refers to growing grasses and trees upon which sentient beings depend for their dwelling.
'Sentient beings' refers to tree spirits, host-spirits, river spirits, house spirits, crossroads spirits, market spirits, and city [spirits]."
The "divine beings of the Path" (mārga-devas) include mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, butterflies that feed on hemp, scorpions, moths, and the like.
Sentient beings take grasses and trees as their dwellings, and they also regard these places as villages, hamlets, towns, and cities, relying upon them for habitation. The commentary states:

"In this way, one should understand that [the various accounts] are identical, like a clear mirror. This means that each school speaks of different things, such as the seeds of growing grasses and so forth.
This is not something upon which a person relies. To cite the explicit texts of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the matter is as clear as a bright mirror.
According to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If a bhikṣu cuts down a village of spirits or a village of seeds, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding the five kinds of villages mentioned in the Vinaya, Li states: although there are five meanings for "growing," they are combined into three categories: first, growth from roots; second, growth from branches.
There are three types of seed-growth. Regarding roots and stems, each is divided into two. First, those that grow from within a root without requiring a node are given the name "root-seed.
Second, those that grow from within a root by means of a node are designated as "covered-node" (*pallava*). Regarding branches, there are likewise two types.
First, those that grow from within a branch without requiring a node are given the name "branch-seed. Second, those that grow by means of a node are designated as "node-born."
Regarding the "seed from a node": within the category of seeds from nodes, a single entity is established from beginning to end, yet it differentiates and develops through separation;

thus, there are five parts. As for "root-seeds" (*mūla-bīja*): because the root itself serves as the seed, they are called root-seeds. These include such things as ginger, taro, and radish. As for "branch-seeds" (*kāṇḍa-bīja*):

because the branch itself serves as the seed, they are called branch-seeds. These include such things as willow, pomegranate, and *gouyi* (a type of willow). As for "node-seeds" (*parva-bīja*)... [text continues].
This means that they take joints as their seeds; thus it is said. Examples include *śāla* (a type of dockweed) and sugarcane.
Regarding the term "mixed species" (*pūrala*), the *Jieshu* states: "As for the term *pūrala*, it refers to those that grow from joints within the root, such as celery and bamboo."

"Upright growth" refers to those with roots and trunks, such as oranges, citrons, and the like. If a tree lacks roots while possessing branches, or possesses roots while lacking branches, it cannot grow.
Because it grows from what are merely provisional roots and joints, it is called "miscellaneous growth. As for "seed from seed," this refers to things such as mustard seeds.
Regarding the phrase "if one cuts, roasts, or drives a stake [into it], it follows": Li asked, "If one strikes a stake into a tree, does it follow? [The Master replied: "It does."
"How many times must one strike? Each instance constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Why does killing not constitute a *pāyattika* for every blow dealt?

Must it wait until life is severed? Answer: "Grasses and trees possess many signs of growth; therefore, at every point where they are damaged, the arising of that portion of growth is obstructed. For this reason, one incurs an offense according to the degree of damage.
As for the retribution of animals, life is a mere designation (*prajñapti*), and an offense is committed only when it is severed. Regarding teeth and eyes..."
When clouds are over the earth, they are called *ya*; when they emerge from the earth, they are called *mu*.

As for *luoqin*, its original name was *luole*; the Zhao ruler Shi Le changed it to *lanxiang*. Regarding the seventeen kinds of grain, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: first, rice; second, red unhusked rice;
third, wheat; fourth, barley; fifth, small beans; sixth, horse beans (*hudou*); seventh, large beans; eighth, peas; ninth, millet; tenth...
Eleventh, broomcorn millet; twelfth, hemp seeds; thirteenth, ginger; fourteenth, *jambu*; fifteenth, *pāṣāṇabhedaka*;
sixteenth, awns; seventeenth, *ciñcā*; eighteenth, *kūṭaśālmali*. The verse says:
Rice, red barley, wheat, small beans, peas, large beans, millet, broomcorn millet, hemp, ginger, *jambu*, *pāṣāṇabhedaka*, awns, and *ciñcā*—these are the seventeen kinds.
*Ḍasa*. The seventeen types mentioned above are all purified by removing the skin. The commentary states: "This refers to the two kinds of jujube—raw and cooked.
That which is not yet dried is called raw; what is currently dried is called cooked. Both must have sufficient moisture to allow them to fit into a bowl for eating.
Jing says: "In this text, the five types of raw produce are fully enumerated: namely, (1) roots, (2) branches, (3) joints, (4) *pavāra*, and (5) seeds."
This refers to the following: first, the five fruits. These are: (1) drupes, (2) pomes, (3) capsules, (4) tubers, and (5) berries.
One must examine the text closely to see this. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Provided they merely touch one another, it is sufficient," and so forth:
"Establishment" means that all dharmas must cause the fruit and the seed to be in contact; they may not be separated by a stem or trunk. If they are clean, purification is not achieved.
It is like sugarcane: it must have its husks removed. Only when combined and quickly purified is it accomplished.

If the husks are not removed, only that which is touched becomes pure, while the rest does not, because the husks act as an internal barrier. Furthermore, it is said: "Regarding the aforementioned grain and fruit, since it has already been stated that there is..."
"Seeds are pure. Now, if seeds are upon weeds and the like, and they are bound together and attached, they too should be considered pure;
this is merely an inference based on the principle. Regarding "moss growing upon stones," this refers to flowers growing upon stones.
Regarding "hairs growing upon cakes and the like," Jing says: "These are all deemed auspicious because they are signs of decay. As for "turning over and crossing the floating duckweed," [it means]...
Jingyun: This action does not depart from water; to depart from it is to obtain *ti*. The commentary states: "According to the previous case of 'temporary. Shen says:
The aforementioned tying of grass at the place where one walks and the pressing down with stones to obstruct bamboo in this context are both referred to as "temporary";
therefore, they must be removed. To cite the Vinaya rule regarding "one act destroying many types, resulting in a transgression according to the number of types": [this establishes...]

That is to say: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one type of the ten [kinds of food] is spoiled, one *pāyattika* is incurred; if all five types are spoiled, five *pāyattikas* are incurred. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* is not so;
rather, it imposes a penalty for each type spoiled according to their respective number, which differs from this *vinaya* (the *Daśabhāṇavāra*).

For example, if a bhikṣu takes a handful of beans and cooks them all at once, he incurs one *pāyattika* for each individual bean according to its number. This is the general rule in the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Regarding the single offense: "Whether on the ground or off the ground, destroying [a seed] results in a *pācittiya*. This refers to the aforementioned willow (*liǔ*) and pomegranate (*liú*).

The willow is the *yángliǔ* (poplar/willow), and the pomegranate is the *shíliú* (pomegranate). These two types of seeds continue to grow even when removed from the ground; therefore, destroying them constitutes a *pācittiya* both on and off the ground.

However, for species such as the *huái* (magnolia) or *kuài* (walnut), one commits an offense only by destroying them on the ground; once they have been removed from the ground, destroying them does not constitute an offense.

[This constitutes] an offense. If there is still the characteristic of being alive, one may only incur a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Regarding this precept, there are two levels of objective perception (*saṃjñā*).
To establish the distinction between the *huái* and the *kuài*: according to the *Erlǚpǐ*, the *huái* tree has large leaves and a black color, which is called *kuài* (pronounced *huài*).

[The commentary] states: the small is called *huái*; the large is called *kuài*. As for "leaving the ground and the color not yet changed" being a *duṣkṛta*, there are seven [cases] mentioned in the Vinaya.

Colors are: first, blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; fifth, black; sixth, *piǎo* (pǐ miǎo fǎn); and seventh, purple. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "*Piǎo* refers to a light blue color.
These are all colors of the "arising phase" (*shēngxiàng*). Even if the color has not yet changed or deteriorated after being separated from the earth, it may still be considered auspicious.

This [text] precisely clarifies the deterioration of the arising phase. Below, the rules for non-offenses are explained. If one excludes the case of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), [the following applies].
Regarding "earth and soil," Jingyun says: this refers to the dead earth upon the ground.
The twelve precepts on the ornamental precepts of body and speech follow Master Guang’s nine sections; the citation below is the second section.

Up to the precept against exceeding the size when covering a roof, there are nine precepts that clarify how to properly lead people's minds and protect the community's will without causing disturbance.
[The Buddha] said: "According to the origin stories (*nidāna*) of the Vinaya, these arise sequentially and should be divided into two precepts.

However, because although the two types of karma—bodily and verbal—are distinct, the point of violating the regulation is the same, they are combined into a single precept. Regarding 'frivolous speech' (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) as verbal karma, it is a name for speaking in a discordant manner;

regarding 'frivolous speech' as bodily karma, it is a designation for causing provocation and distress. As for the third case, where the *saṃgha* issues a formal motion (*jñapti*) to reprimand and stop [the offender], although [the act was committed] by the body..."

Second, frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): If the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal motion (*jñapti*), one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*; however, because one violates the rule after the procedure has been established, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding bodily conduct within the Saṃgha: if one should sit but does not sit, or should stand but does not stand, thereby disturbing the Saṃgha with bodily actions, a *saṃvāsana-kaṭhina-karman* (act of censuring for causing disturbance) must be administered.
If one enters the midst of the Saṃgha and disturbs it with verbal conduct—such as by assembling the monks at an improper time or asking "Where have you come from?"—[the same penalty applies].
Answer: "From the past. When asked by a monk, "Where are you going? he answers, "I am going to the future. Or, when conversing with a monk, he instead asks the monk, "To whom are you speaking?
What matter are you discussing? This is called *mukha-vipralāpa* (verbal wrangling) and is also called *anyavāda* (irrelevant speech).
The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*, fascicle 14, states: "If someone asks, 'Where have you come from? [and the response is evasive, the offender is subject to the *anyavāda-karman*].
He replies, "I come from the past. "Where are you going? He replies, "I am going to the future. "Where do you sleep?

"On eight pieces of wood" (a bed has four wooden legs; together with the four seasons, they make eight). "Where do you eat? He replies, "I eat with five fingers. One who answers in such an improper manner commits a *vinayātikrama* (an offense against the discipline).

This refers to the case where, after having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), one speaks evasively to avoid the point at issue. If one speaks thus after the motion has been made, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation), specifically a *tatsvabhāva-vāk* (an offense consisting of the specific words spoken).

If one has already spoken other words, one immediately commits this offense. Regarding "the rest is as in the rule on frivolous speech" (mukhavicāra-dharma): Ciyun explains that it is like the aforementioned frivolous speech;
before the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); after the announcement, the offense committed is a *pāyattika*.
"Because the words lack fundamental meaning and the logic is disordered" means that the speech uttered provides no benefit and does not accord with the Buddha’s teaching.

The Thirteenth Precept on Scolding or Reviling the *Karmadāna*. First, regarding the term "one appointed by *karma*": this distinguishes those appointed by a formal motion (*jñapti*) from those previously mentioned who were appointed by mere word of mouth;

it refers to one who is not appointed by a non-formal act. If one reviles someone who has not been appointed by *karma*, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the term "appointed," Master Li states that this Vinaya refers to appointment by a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü) allows for appointment by either the single-proclamation method (*jñapti-ekakarman*) or the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* method, depending on the circumstances. Regarding the term "the person being formally appointed," Master Li states that this refers to calling out to the individual who has been selected for the appointment. This is called "formal" (*zheng*).

He bows to the person. This person has the requisite conditions; he further requests another person to temporarily oversee the affairs of the Saṃgha. The person thus commissioned, due to other business, again commissions another person.

If [the original monk] subsequently reviles these three people, all are guilty of a *thullaccaya* offense. Jing says: "This refers to one who was appointed by the Saṃgha through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation)."

This is called "the person who performs the prostration" (*zhèngbài-rén*). It refers to performing a prostration similar to that of a secular official receiving his office. The guest says: "The term 'prostration' (*bǎi*) is used because it is designated as such in the ritual texts.

This is likely because the translators took the underlying meaning; thus, they referred to the person as "the one who prostrates," and even when assigning the five virtues (*wǔdé*), they likewise used the term "prostrate."
Regarding the "one who has accomplished the five dharmas" acting as the person performing the *pravāraṇā*: now, upon careful examination, this refers to the act of formal investiture (*bai-ce*).

It is like the current state’s investiture of the Crown Prince, the King, or the Prince Consort; all these are termed "investiture. It does not mean that when appointing those with the five virtues or assigning administrative duties, one must perform an investiture ceremony because they must possess the five virtues.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qiwen), it says: "If there is one being invested, one who is entrusted with the investiture, and one who is entrusted with the entrustment..."

"Person. The commentary below explains: "The person to whom one bows" refers to Ṭhapaka himself. "The person to whom one entrusts by bowing" refers to Ṭhapaka delegating another person to manage monastic affairs.
"The person to whom one entrusts by entrusting" refers to the person thus delegated further delegating another person to manage monastic affairs.
To harbor resentment toward these three types of persons constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. This was said in reference to the hundred great fish.

Regarding the "Head": according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is said that while the Buddha was traveling through the human realm among the people of Vṛji with a great assembly of bhikṣus, he came to the bank of an old river.
There he saw fishermen holding a large net, using stones as weights and gourds as floats, moving upstream against the current.
On each side were three hundred and fifty men, shouting and pulling the net toward the shore. At that time, the entire multitude fell further into the net.
There was a great fish with a hundred heads, each head being distinct from the others. When the World-Honored One saw it, he called out its name, and it immediately responded:
"World-Honored One! World-Honored One! The World-Honored One asked, "Where is your mother? It replied, "She is in the latrine, acting as a worm."
This great fish was, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a *tripiṭaka* bhikṣu. Because of his harsh speech, he received the retribution of having the heads of various animals.

His mother, because she had accepted his offerings, became a worm in a latrine. When the Buddha spoke of this causal connection, five hundred people immediately ceased their work with nets, left the household life to practice the Way, and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "As it is said in a sutra, there was one..."
This ghost has a head resembling a *zhé* (a type of horned animal). Extremely foul-smelling insects emerge from its mouth. Its body possesses a golden radiance.
In a previous life, this ghost was a bhikṣu who used harsh words and reviled visiting bhikṣus; however, because he maintained the precepts, his body now possesses this radiance.

Because there are evil words in the mouth, stinking insects emerge from it. Regarding "slandering and reviling": Li [Daoqian] says that to speak of the presence of attachment, aversion, and so forth in a place where one sees but does not hear is called "slandering" (miǎn);
to speak of it in a place where one hears the sound but does not see the person is called "reviling" (mà). These are indeed real occurrences.
This refers to the actual existence of craving, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding the fourteenth precept on bedding and requisites left in the open air:

the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that if one sees monastic bedding and requisites in the open air, even if they were not spread by oneself but were instructed to be spread, if one sees them and does not pick them up, it constitutes an offense according to that Vinaya code.

Regarding the case where a monk prostrates before an image placed upon a monastic bed but does not lift it up: Jing says that this constitutes an offense because one sees the image on an open space and fails to lift it.

Lì states that when monastic bedding is spread upon a bed and a Buddha image is placed thereon, once a monk has finished prostrating to the Buddha while standing upon it, he must lift the bedding as soon as his hands have touched it; this applies even if there are many people present.
One commits an offense if it belongs to the last [person].
"One should return quickly during the rain" means that there is no rain on the way back after having departed.

Regarding the rule that if two people share a bed, the one of lower rank should collect [the bedding], and if they do not, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing): Jing says this refers to the case where the person of lower rank ought to collect it, but does not.

Failing to gather [the bedding] constitutes an offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Therefore, it is auspicious [to do so]. The Vinaya states: "Because it is contrary to proper decorum (*anācāra*), one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

It is explained that if the senior monk (*sthavira*) and the junior monk (*navaka*) share the same bed, when rising, the senior monk instructs the junior monk to gather [the bedding]; if the junior monk does not gather it, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* for disobeying the senior monk’s instruction.

Furthermore, if he himself does not gather it, he also incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). If the senior monk sees that the bedding has not been gathered and the junior monk does not gather it..."

One should immediately withdraw together with the other. Since one does not withdraw oneself, one incurs only a *pācittiya* offense; hence it is said that for the senior monk (*sthavira*), it is a single *pācittiya*.
If neither withdraws and both incur offenses, Jing says: "In the former case, they were sitting together; because the junior monk withdrew, he incurred a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa*.
In the latter case, they sat separately; since each did not withdraw themselves, both incur *pācittiyas*. Therefore, in the Vinaya, if two persons are neither ahead nor behind [in withdrawing]..."

"Neither is collected; both are *pāyattika* offenses. Regarding "the outer and inner linings of bedding and mats," Jing says: these refer to the garments that cover one’s robes, such as blankets and felt rugs.
This precept is restricted to bedding and the like; if one spreads out mats or straw mats on the open ground, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

The Fifteenth Precept: Regarding the Concealment of Items Belonging to the Saṃgha. The intent of the regulation is the same as before. As for the distinction between "concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) and "exposed" (*appaṭicchanna*), there are two differences:
first, the timing of the offense differs; in the case of the exposed, it occurs upon leaving the door, whereas in the case of the concealed, it occurs upon crossing the boundary (*sīmā*).

The point at which the intention is finalized remains as previously described regarding crossing the boundary—whether temporary or permanent, the offense is committed after the night has passed. Second, the conditions for exemption differ; in the case of concealment, both parties may have varying degrees of urgency, according to the Vinaya.
It is said: If one departs immediately and returns immediately; if there is a violent wind or heavy rain and one returns quickly; if it rains moderately and one travels at a moderate pace;
or if it rains slightly and one travels slowly—in all these cases, it is permitted and does not constitute an offense. Regarding "in private," two nights are permitted.

As for "leaving the boundary" or "exceeding three nights," those who commit the offense do so with two underlying intentions: either departing without the intention to return, or leaving the gate [with no such intent].
One then incurs an offense. If one intends to return late and, due to obstacles, is unable to return immediately, two nights are permitted.
If one does not return by the third day, an offense is incurred when the dawn appears.

16. The Precept on Forceful Laying Out [the Seat]: If one has already spoken and another person is staying there who was previously granted permission, one must clarify that the other person’s speech has concluded;

if one hears this and yet continues, one commits an offense. Furthermore, if someone first granted permission for questioning and another arrives later, laying out the seat in such a case also does not constitute an offense.
As the ancients said: "When the mind harbors love or hatred, the space provided will be either broad or narrow. As it is said: [The text continues with the analogy].

It is said that one may lie upon the Long River and rest one's head upon the crossroads; there is no need to come to such a cramped place. If the sentiments were the same, one might say to lie at the bottom of a peck-measure and rest one's head upon a grain pellet;

you would simply come to such a spacious place. Now, the occasion for this precept concerns precisely the discordance of sentiments: because one forcibly spreads out [one's bedding] and thereby causes distress.

The Seventeenth Precept on Expelling Another from a Room: Regarding the first case: if one expels another from a room used during spring or winter after having entered a room designated for summer, the offense is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Master Bin says: "Spring and winter rooms are not [exclusively] allotted; since they have a common character, the fault of expelling someone is grave, and thus it is a *thullaccaya*.
However, during the summer, the room is allotted and belongs to oneself; when one expels another from such a room, the mental transgression is light, and one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*)."

In the *Lì míng* (Establishing the Clarification), regarding the division of summer quarters within the Vinaya: if the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) arrives after the quarters have already been divided, the Buddha stated that they should be moved; this makes it clear that [the quarters] belong to him.

Once they have been assigned to a specific person, even if one forcibly drags them away, there is no sense of separation [from the original occupant], as the offense is minor due to the lightness of the disturbance caused.

However, if the quarters are divided during spring or winter and the senior monk arrives, according to the current Vinaya rules, one must yield and move; this makes it clear that [the quarters] do not belong to oneself.

"Leading away" carries the sense of departing; since the place of affliction is deep, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, regarding the summer quarters, once their affiliation is fixed, taking them away is considered minor (*kṣudra-āpatti*) because the mind of the one who takes them is weak.
