In all these cases, eating in a separate group is permitted. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, eight conditions are generally permitted: first, during illness; second, during the [distribution of] robes;

third, during the time of receiving robes; fourth, during the making of robes; fifth, while traveling on a road; sixth, while traveling by boat; seventh, during a great assembly; and eighth, during a gathering of śramaṇas.
Regarding "the time of robes," this refers to the period of the *kaṭhina* robe, during which the five privileges and so forth are permitted. As for...

"Regarding the donor of robes": this refers to when a *dānapati* offers robes along with food at the time of giving alms; one may accept these robes, and it is permitted to do so even if it constitutes the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
"Regarding the time of making robes": this refers to when a bhikṣu intends to make a robe, but because he must go out for alms, the robe is not completed immediately.

[The monks] were hindered and neglected their practice of the Path. They then thought: "If the Buddha would allow us to accept food from a separate group while making robes, our robes would be completed quickly and we would not neglect our practice of the Path.
They informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "I allow you to accept food from a separate group while making robes."
The statement in the *Chao* that "the time for the five-part robe" (*pañcavargika-cīvara*) is mentioned is an error; it should have cited "the time for making the robe" (*cīvara-kāla*).
When it refers to the "time for the five-part robe," this actually corresponds to the time for making robes after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is a separate "time for making robes" that extends through all twelve months. It was precisely this phrase that the *Chao* intended to cite, and thus the character "making" (*zuo*) must be included.

If one were to speak directly of "the time for making robes," it would be identical to the rule in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding "the time for making robes. Since there is no distinction made, why would it be necessary to cite it?
Thus, it is clear that the character "to make" (作) is missing. Regarding the explanation of the intent behind the opening of this precept:

because a sick person suffers and is distressed, if this exception were not granted, they would have no means of survival. Furthermore, there is no sense of causing distress to the Sangha through other schemes; therefore, it is opened.
Agreed. Regarding "the time for robes": because making robes takes a long time, there is fear that it will interfere with one's primary practice;

therefore, the "time for giving robes" is established so that benefit may extend to both the monastic and the laity (if one does not accept them at the time of giving, they will be difficult to obtain later; this is how the path is benefited. Furthermore, it allows the donor to practice giving toward the "field of merit" that is the Sangha, thereby obtaining the karmic reward of retribution;

this is how the laity are benefited). If one were to speak simply of "the time for robes," such as one month or five months, these would merely be times for receiving benefits. As for traveling by land or by boat, these two involve many hardships.

Furthermore, because food is difficult to obtain [and there are many dangers from bandits, as explained in the *Nidāna*], it was permitted when a large assembly gathers, so that the many might be relieved.

Regarding the term "śramaṇa," it is for the sake of providing some small benefit to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Question: Since non-Buddhists and the like have no fixed [monastic rules], how can it be said that listening to the separate meal (*pṛthag-bhakta*) provides them with benefit?
Answer: The text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is not explicit on this point; it is as in the case of the five...
Among the Magadha kings, there was a younger brother named Kāla who served a certain type of non-Buddhist practitioner.
Every year, he would invite ninety-six kinds of śramaṇas for a great assembly.

Having heard that the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya do not accept food from a separate group, yet lacking the power to provide for such a vast multitude of monks, he was distressed at being deprived of the presence of the śramaṇas of the Buddha-way. Thus, he remained in sorrow.
Delighted, he thought to himself, "How can I bring about this for the śramaṇa, the son of the Śākyas? I must first entrust it to the King; only then can it be accomplished.
He then informed the King of his brother's intention. The King reported his brother's wish to the Buddha, and the Buddha consequently granted permission. It was then the time for the śramaṇas to eat.

Regarding the acceptance of separate invitations for communal meals, a guest asked: "Separate meals are fundamentally difficult to manage; yet out of compassion for laypeople, the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* provides further clarification.
Since this Vinaya allows seven exceptions, how can one avoid the two faults? The answer was: "Acting in accordance with the permitted rules makes it clear that these are not difficult to manage;
therefore, they do not contradict the principle. As for the case of the householder Siṃha inviting five hundred arhats separately, according to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, it says: [text follows].
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a householder named Siṃha who went to Śāriputra, paid his respects, and said: "I pray that you will accept my invitation.
He then went to Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Kātyāyana, Upāli, Subhūti, Rāhula, Cunda the novice, and others—inviting all five hundred [monks] in total.
The leader returned home and prepared an offering. The elder personally served various foods and drinks.
He bestowed a piece of white cotton cloth upon each person. When the meal was finished, Rāhula came to the Buddha’s presence and asked, "Was today's food fine or coarse?
The Buddha replied, "It was most excellent and also abundant. Furthermore, he bestowed white cotton cloths. The Buddha then asked, "How many people are in the assembly of monks? Who is the leader?"
He sat down. [The Buddha] replied, "My preceptor Śāriputra is the foremost among them, along with five hundred other beings of divine virtue.
The Buddha asked Rāhula, "Does that elder obtain much merit? He replied, "If giving to a single arhat brings immeasurable merit, how much more so for five hundred true persons?
What limit could there be to such merit? The Buddha said, "Now, five hundred arhats have been invited."
It would not be equal to inviting a single śramaṇa from among the multitude to provide for his offerings;
the merit obtained from this would exceed the former merit by thousands of myriads of koṭis, beyond all comparison. It is like a person who wishes to drink all the waters of every river and stream.

In the end, it cannot be accomplished. Because Jambudvīpa is vast and possesses four great rivers, each of which has five hundred channels—if one now wishes to drink them all dry, it would merely exhaust one’s efforts and could never be finished. It is better to drink the water of the ocean;
for all streams flow back into the sea, and by this means, the waters of all those streams are encompassed. Now, if one were to [drink] each one individually...
"Individual invitations are like various rivers; some may gain merit, while others may not. But the Saṃgha is like that great ocean.
This is because when river waters enter the sea, they lose their original names and are designated simply as 'the ocean.
Thus, those of the three vehicles and four fruits all arise from within the assembly and do not stand independently. When the Elder Siṃha heard these words spoken by the Buddha, at a later time...
He came and informed the Buddha: "From this day forward, I shall constantly make offerings to the Saṃgha. The Buddha said:
"I do not intend for you to offer sustenance only to the Saṃgha and not to others. Even by giving to animals, one still obtains merit; how much more so when giving to other persons?"

"But as for what I have taught, it concerns the amount of merit and the duration of years. The elder said, "From this day forward, I shall constantly provide offerings to the assembly without discriminating between individuals.
The Buddha said, "This is able to be impartial giving; one does not say, 'This person observes the precepts,' or 'This person violates the precepts.'"

Giving such impartial alms brings merit throughout the long night. Gao says: "When it is said that the merit of an Arhat is small, this refers to the number being restricted to five hundred people, and further restricted to Arhats alone;
for those in the three fruits and four stages of realization, as well as the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), are all excluded.

If one invites even a single person from within the Saṃgha, one obtains merit by reaching the field of both the ordinary and the holy. This is based on the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish).
Regarding the phrase "the *kambala* offered to the Buddha and others," the *Rong shu* (Commentary by Rong) states: Mahāprajāpatī is translated as "Great Love-Path" (*Dà àidào*).
She was the Buddha’s paternal aunt and fostered the Tathāgata with her own milk. After the Buddha had left the household life, Mahāprajāpatī remained behind in longing and remembrance;

she personally wove a *kambala* of gold-thread, awaiting the Buddha’s return to the palace, intending to offer it to him. Later, when the Buddha returned to his kingdom, Mahāprajāpatī was about to present it to him...

The Buddha said: "When the Buddha speaks of giving with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, it does not constitute great merit; do not make offerings to me. You should instead make offerings to the Sangha.
To make offerings to the Sangha is to make offerings to the Three Refuges. If you follow my words, you are making an offering to the distinct characteristic of the Buddha.

For the sake of liberation, you are making an offering to the distinct characteristic of the Dharma. As for the requisites used by the assembly of monks, you are making an offering to the distinct characteristic of the Sangha."

He was a monk. According to the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, at the time when the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, had already seen the Buddha renounce the world, she personally spun and wove a single bolt of golden cloth. With her mind focused on this intention, she hoped only to see the Buddha so that she might offer it to him.
Later, when the Buddha returned to the palace, she took the cloth and presented it to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Take this cloth and go present it to the Saṃgha."

Vāseṭṭhī addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Since the time the Buddha went forth from home, I have constantly thought of him. Therefore, I have spun and woven this cloth with my own hands, intending to offer it to the Buddha.
I only pray that you will take pity on me and accept it. The Buddha told her: "I know that your mother is single-mindedly desiring to offer this to me;
however, because it is an act born of affectionate attachment, its merit will not be vast or extensive. If you were to give it to the Saṃgha, the reward would be far greater. I know this."
For this reason, I urge you by way of these matters. The Buddha further said:
"If there is a donor who makes specific invitations to sixteen individuals—though they may obtain a reward of merit—it is not yet considered much. What are the sixteen?

They are the eight classes of bhikṣus and the eight classes of bhikṣuṇīs (consisting of the four fruits and four stages of practice). This is not as good as making a general invitation to four members within the Saṃgha; the merit and blessings obtained from the latter exceed those of the former."

It does not even approach one-sixteenth part [of the merit]. In the future final age, when the Dharma is about to perish, even if there are bhikṣus who keep wives and harbor children, and groups of four or more who are merely "monks in name," they should be respected and looked upon as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the like.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī’s mind was finally opened and understood; she first offered her finest robes to the Saṃgha. Within the Saṃgha—
Next, regarding the one who practices without desire for gain: upon reaching the presence of Maitreya, he immediately accepted [the robe].

Maitreya was properly wearing a golden *kambala* (woolen blanket), the inner and outer surfaces of which were harmonious; his majestic deportment was dignified and orderly as he entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for alms.

People beheld his physical form, and those who looked at him never grew weary [and so forth]. The Vinaya clarifies that when a monk accepts [an offering] according to the sequence of the community, this single type of meritorious benefit benefits both himself and others.

This means that one does not commit an offense oneself, and furthermore, one can cause others to avoid the faults of receiving individual invitations or meals for a separate assembly; thus it is said that the merit and benefit extend to both self and others.

Moreover, when an invitation is received according to the sequence of the Sangha, it enables the donor to generate great merit; this is also called the meaning of benefiting others. The commentary states:

"Regarding 'benefiting oneself' as the allowance and 'benefiting others' as the offense of receiving an individual meal,' this refers to a case where there were originally three people who were entitled to receive food through the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. By [the arrival of another],...
The last person is one who makes robes for those practicing the path (yogācāra) or those who are ill; together with the previous three, they form four.
If one has the personal conditions to make robes for a practitioner of the path, this is permitted without fault. Adding this person to the previous three completes the number of four.

Because of this one person, the previous three are made to incur offenses. Question: It was previously stated that if a sick person completes the number of four, it does not constitute a limit of offense. Why is this?
Regarding this present sick person, as for the question of whether he commits an offense [by performing the *sthāpanīya-karman*], the answer is that the circumstances of the illness differ.

In the previous case, it was designated as "illness" because of insanity and delusion; since his nature did not constitute membership in the Saṃgha, it was so classified. This present sick person, however, suffers from a minor ailment.
Therefore, the text below states: "down to the splitting of the heels. Thus, it differs from the previous illness. The term "splitting" (*pi*) refers to being suppressed and broken. Now...

In the winter months, there was a person whose foot was broken and covered in sores (the character for "sores" is pronounced *pi* [bǐ]). Regarding the various precepts that permit exceptions for illness, illnesses differ from one another. This precept extends downward to cases where the foot is split open;

bathing is permitted for those with illness, even down to cases where the body is foul-smelling and filthy. Exposing oneself to fire is permitted for those with illness, even down to cases where one must defecate while standing.

Accepting invitations from behind is permitted for those with illness, even down to cases where one is unable to eat a single sitting meal. Eating more than one meal is permitted for those with illness.
If one is free from those causes for agitation, although the names of the illnesses may be the same, each should be understood according to its specific characteristics as described in the text.

Regarding the rule in the Vinaya that if there are none of the aforementioned conditions, one must announce [one's departure], the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "To go out directly without cause;

the reason one must announce is to protect the donor. As for the subsequent passage where one must announce even when entering directly due to having a cause, it is for the purpose of protecting the announcement by analogy.
For this reason, I have entered with a specific purpose and according to the prescribed ritual; thus, I shall explain [the rules] in their proper sequence to resolve any doubts.

If one enters without having announced their arrival, they are considered a member of the monastic community who has entered without a valid reason following me. Therefore, such a person is excluded by means of a formal announcement (*śrāvaṇa*). One who has no valid reason must announce their departure.
The same applies to doubt. If there is a reason for eating separately from the community and one wishes to enter [the assembly], one must announce it. This is because one stands to dispel doubt;
if one does not personally state, "I have such-and-such a reason," others who do not have such a reason might see one entering and follow suit.
Furthermore, it serves to demonstrate that one is not violating this precept; therefore, one must announce, "I have such-and-such a reason, and thus it is appropriate for me to eat separately."

The third-fourth precept: Taking food for a group, for a bride returning home, or for merchants. This precept has two bases for its origin; however, because the meaning of "taking food" is the same, they are combined into a single precept.
Both monks and nuns incur a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding the first [of the two bases], there are two conditions: [The text continues with the specific conditions of the rule.]
The woman returning from her husband’s home is one instance; the merchant is another. Thus, they are said to be two. Regarding the third case, which involves no offense:

it is permitted during times of illness. Regarding the fourth, taking more than three bowls: this is established on the grounds that taking in excess fosters greed and causes others to suffer depletion;

whereas taking less would fail to alleviate hunger and thirst, thereby diminishing the merit of the donor. By limiting oneself to exactly three bowls, one does not harm the donor and yet obtains sufficient sustenance.
Lì said: "If one takes from the superior bowl, taking one is without offense; taking two is an offense. If one takes from the middle bowl, taking two is without offense;

taking three is an offense. If one takes from the inferior bowl, taking three is not an offense; taking four is an offense. When it is now said that 'exceeding three,' this is stated with reference to the inferior bowl.
If one person takes more than three bowls, the preceding person is without offense, while the subsequent person commits an offense."

It was previously stated that three bowls had already been brought; you must not bring [another], for the fault lies with those who follow. Therefore, it is said that four persons each take one bowl. Regarding the transgression of exceeding [the limit]:

if one intends to reduce [the amount] but exceeds three, one incurs the offense immediately; if one does not intend for the food to enter one's own possession but exceeds three, one also incurs the offense immediately.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, both accepting food in excess and failing to distribute it among the monks constitute a *pāyattika* offense. However, according to this Vinaya (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*), [it is different].
Not so. Regarding the thirty-fifth precept on "Sufficient Food": ancient masters have established different names for this precept; it is also called the "Precept Against Eating Again and Again.
For a nun, [violating it] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. As for the establishment of two sets of five conditions in the current text, the commentary explains that the former is from the *Chao*.

The household establishes five conditions to lead to the manifestation of an offense. Regarding the latter five conditions, these are the five points enumerated in the Vinaya that explain the meaning of "having finished eating" (*paryāpta-bhojana*).
According to the Vinaya text: first, knowing it is rice, parched flour, dry rice, or the like; second, knowing it has been brought;
third, knowing there is a prohibition; fourth, knowing the deportment; and fifth, knowing the abandonment of deportment. These, within the Vinaya texts, are termed the "five."
Regarding the term "place" (*sthāna*): it is explained that the "place" referred to is fundamentally the knowledge that these five things, such as rice, are the locus where one’s meal is completed;
thus they are called "places. This refers to the passage in the Vinaya where Upāli asked the Buddha: "How many places are there where a bhikṣu should consider his meal to be finished?"

The Buddha said: "There are five instances where one has fulfilled the requirement of having eaten enough (*paryāpta-bhojana*). What are these five? They are those listed above. The commentary states:

'Regarding long benches, boats, vehicles, and so forth,' this clarifies that if one was previously sitting and eating upon such [an object], and then suddenly moves the bench so that one's body parts from the seat, or if the bow of a boat strikes the shore and one subsequently separates from the boat, this is called 'breaking the deportment' (*īryāpatha-bheda*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is termed "long" (*dīrgha*).
"Bed and seat" (*śayanāsana*). The sub-commentary explains it as follows: A small bed for sitting alone is called a "seat-bed. Regarding the phrase "the four do not again receive benefit":

this refers to when one is established in the state where the object of food is sufficient to satisfy hunger; yet, one does not accept [the food], thinking, "I have not yet formed the resolve to renounce eating;

I intend to eat later. The note states: "Eating with no expectation of satiety, determined by the object, constitutes an offense. This means that after finishing a meal, when hunger returns after a short time, one goes back [to eat].

If one wishes to eat, with what shall one establish the limit for satiety? For this reason, it is not permitted. Regarding *bì* (pronounced *bei*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "dried rice.
Lì says: "The *Shisong* school calls the dried rice of the *Sifen* school *bì*; they are one and the same entity.
As for the other items being the same as those in the *Sifen*, the *Shisong* designates the dried rice of the *Sifen* as *bì*, while the remaining four types are identical.

The four items—rice, parched grain flour, fish, and meat—are named the same as the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra*. Regarding "mí" (糜), it is read with the pinyin *mí* (with the *pí* rhyme); see the *Cāngjié piān* (Cangjie Pian), which states [as follows].

The statement that "there is someone who says [it is pronounced] with the *li* (力) and *wai* (外) finals" is a reckless and ignorant remark. Master Ying stated: "In Guansi it is called *mian* (穈); in Jizhou it is called *ji* (穄), the character being written as *mian* (穈, with the phonetic *mi* and *pi*).

Tuoba changed it by removing the 'forest' (*lin*) radical and retaining the 'grain' (*he*), so it is not recorded in the dictionaries. From the Song to the Chen dynasties, there was never anyone who recognized it, which led to the claim of the *li* and *wai* finals.

As for "the seeds of *you* grass": [Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary commentary on the pronunciation and etymology of the grain name *mian* (穈/穄), contrasting regional dialects and historical orthographic changes, while noting the lack of scholarly consensus on its phonology.]
In the present day, it is simply *kodo* grass. Regarding "Kōmaku-kashi": some maintain that "Kōmaku" is the local dialect and "Kashi" is the Sanskrit term;
since both the Sanskrit and the vernacular are cited here, it is so called. Northerners call it "swallow millet," while southerners call it "sparrow millet.
Furthermore, according to another interpretation, it has been traditionally handed down since ancient times to refer to "barley" (*yavaka*).
*Kaśi* refers to small wheat (*kaṇika*). According to the Master of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan Shili), *caomaī* (mistake-wheat) and *kaśi* are one and the same term.

As previously explained, the reading "mistake" (*cuò*) found in the transmitted text of the *Jiāocháo* is an error. Upon examining the text of the *Shísòng lǜ*, it is clear that it is indeed *caomaī* (pronounced *shǎo*).
The five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods) refer to roots, stalks, and so forth; "fire-taken juice" refers to [juice extracted by heating].

Regarding the statement that the five *bhojana* (soft foods) in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are the same as these, it means that the names and essential natures of the five *bhojana* in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are identical to the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

As for the "five miscellaneous *bhojana*," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls non-*bhojana* food the "five miscellaneous *bhojana*. Regarding "fine powder ground," the commentary states this refers to flour.
These are equivalent. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Grinding rice and large barley. Regarding "large and small groats," these refer to green sprouts or large barley.

As for "eating in various places until satisfied" and so forth: since this is not considered "proper food" (*bhojana*), eating it in various places does not constitute a violation of the rule against being "satisfied" (*pūrṇa-bhakta*).
Although one eats in various places, one does not incur the offense of "separate assemblies" (*gaṇa-bhojana*). This applies even if there is a small amount of rice mixed with much water.

Regarding the term "and so forth": when the Vinaya Master [explains] the five types of formal meals (*pañca bhojanāni*), by combining them with one another, a total of three hundred and twenty phrases are obtained;
for each of these, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense. This means that taking rice as the primary item, there are sixteen phrases. Eating rice alone constitutes one phrase.

By mixing rice with each of the other four types of food—such as parched flour (*saktu*) and so on—one obtains four phrases (namely: rice mixed with parched flour, rice mixed with dry rice, and so forth).

By mixing rice with fish, meat, and so forth, there are four permutations. Furthermore, by adding the remaining four items two by two to the rice, there are six permutations (taking rice as the primary element and adding parched grain, small quantities of various substances, and so on, one obtains six permutations).
Adding them three by three results in three permutations. Additionally, by adding all four remaining items together to the rice, one obtains one permutation.
Furthermore, by adding *khajja* (hard foods) to the rice, one obtains one permutation. In total, this amounts to sixteen permutations.
Taking the remaining four items, such as parched flour (*maṇḍa*), as the heads, each obtains sixteen [phrases], totaling eighty phrases.
Since there are eighty phrases for each of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), multiplying eight by four yields thirty-two; thus, there are three hundred and twenty phrases in total.

If one makes porridge by mixing vegetables with what is permissible and what is impermissible, and if one mentions the name of the permissible [ingredient], it constitutes a valid prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Observance), if one makes a soup by mixing vegetables with fish or meat, if one says, "I accept vegetable soup," the prohibition is not established; if one says, "I accept meat soup," the prohibition is established.
If permissible and impermissible [ingredients] are mixed to make porridge, and if one mentions the name of the permissible [ingredient], it constitutes a valid prohibition. Thus it is said.

[The text] states: "Improper [speech] is called 'non-establishment' (不成) and 'prohibition' (遮). [Wén] Zhèngqí says: "If one calls it 'rice gruel,' it constitutes a prohibition; however, if one refers to it as 'vegetable porridge,' it does not constitute a prohibition.
Lì says: "Because one sees that this porridge is thick like rice, if one first says, 'This porridge is sufficient for satiety,' having made this statement, it becomes a prohibition.
If, however, one says, 'This porridge is thin and sparse, and is not sufficient for satiety,'..."
The explanation is finished. Although one may eat, it does not preclude [the observance of] subsequent rules.

At that time, there were bhikṣus who saw an elder approaching and so forth; they remained standing, meaning that if a junior sees an elder coming and does not rise, he commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
Therefore, one must state the reason for this. Regarding "a bhikṣuṇī not showing respect to the Saṃgha" within the precepts, this refers to the eight [gurudharma] rules observed by bhikṣuṇīs.
Reverence! When a nun of a hundred years’ seniority sees a monk who has newly received the precepts, she must rise to meet him, welcome him, and inquire after his well-being.

However, in the present circumstance where they are sitting together to eat, although she does not rise upon seeing him, she must simply say: "I have not performed the *kṛtāvadāna* (the ritual for leftover food). Having made this announcement, there is no offense of violating the teaching.
Based on this, it can be seen that nuns also possess the *śeṣabhaktavidhi* (the rule regarding leftover food). How much more so, then, regarding the eight prohibitions in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*?

According to the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, there are eight types of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) that constitute obstruction: first, sufficiency through self-indulgence; second, sufficiency through few desires;

third, sufficiency through impurity; fourth, sufficiency through mixture; fifth, sufficiency through inconvenience; sixth, sufficiency through deceit and crookedness; seventh, sufficiency through lingering; and eighth, sufficiency through self-satisfaction.

Regarding "sufficiency through self-indulgence," this refers to when a donor offers self-indulgent food, such as the five kinds of formal meals including parched grain and rice, and encourages one to eat until satisfied.
The bhikṣu says, "I am already satisfied. If he rises from his seat and eats without performing the *kṛtākṛta* (the ritual for leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.

Second, regarding those who are "satisfied with little desire": even if one gives food at will—meaning a person offers the five kinds of formal food—and the bhikṣu makes a gesture with his hand to manifest the sign of having few desires, yet rises from his seat and eats further, it is a *pāyattika*.
Third, regarding those who are "satisfied by being defiled": when the food is being served, the attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) himself... [text continues]
1. Regarding "having sores and various impurities": when a bhikṣu sees [food] that is defiled and foul, he says, "I do not need it," and rises from his seat;

this constitutes a *thullaccaya*. 2. Regarding "the fourth case involving a mixture": a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) holds a vessel of milk or curd that has been contaminated by parched rice flour (*maṇḍa*).

When the bhikṣu sees this, he likewise says, "It is foul; I do not need it. 3. Regarding "the fifth case involving inconvenience": while a lay attendant is serving food, the bhikṣu asks, "Is this... [and so forth].
"What is the food? He replied, "Roasted flour. The bhikṣu said, "This will aggravate my wind-disease; it is not suitable for me.
Having spoken thus, he left his seat and took further food. If, when rice is being served, a bhikṣu asks, "Is it hard or soft?
and the other replies, "It is hard," the bhikṣu says, "This non-glutinous rice is difficult to digest; it is not suitable for me. If he says, "It is soft," [the bhikṣu says], "This..."
"It is rotten and difficult to eat; I will not pass by. If meat is being distributed and a bhikṣu asks, 'What kind of meat is this?
and it is answered, 'It is beef,' the bhikṣu says, 'Beef is warm; I will not pass by. If it is said to be bison meat..."
The bhikṣu said, "Its nature is cold and difficult to digest; it has passed, and it is not suitable for me. If he says, "It is venison," the bhikṣu says, "This is of a windy nature;

it is not suitable for me; it has passed. Having thus left his seat, he eats the food; this constitutes an offense of expiation (pāyattika). Regarding the six types of those who are deceitful: [text follows].
When a layperson offers the five kinds of formal food (*bhojana*) or the five kinds of mixed formal food, a bhikṣu who fears verbal expressions regarding food should manifest a physical gesture.
Whether by shaking the head or by withdrawing the bowl to signal "no need," he avoids the offense of eating again after having finished. Regarding the seven ways of remaining satisfied:

when a layperson offers the five kinds of formal food, the bhikṣu must not be the first to take rice; fearing that people might be startled, he should first set down vegetables and cold water as he pleases.

This refers to rising from one's seat and taking further food, which constitutes an *adhiṣṭhāna* (transgression). If one acts as the *karmadāna* (steward) or the month-steward (*māsa-vārika*), and merely points toward or indicates [the food] without [properly] manifesting it, it is not called "sufficient.
Regarding "being sufficient for oneself": when a bhikṣu goes on alms-round and arrives at a house, he sets his flour-bag (*piṇḍapāta-kośa*) on the ground and asks the host for water to drink.
The donor (*dānapati*) thinks, "This bhikṣu must surely need flour," and immediately asks, "Do you need it? [If he accepts, it is considered sufficient.]
[The donor said,] "Rice flour? The bhikṣu thought to himself, "This donor surely wishes to take rice flour from his own home and give it to me.

He replied, "I need some. At that time, the donor immediately took the bhikṣu’s bag of rice flour and handed it to him. Because the bhikṣu was attached to his own rice flour, he feared the donor would touch his bowl;
he then said, "Put it down! Put it down! Having spoken thus, he rose from his seat and went elsewhere to eat. It was deemed an offense of *thullaccaya*.

According to the intent of the Vinaya texts, regarding these eight types [of food], if one has already left one's seat and has not performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food), it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all cases.
Some say that these eight all pertain to when one has not yet left one's seat; this is because once these eight acts have been completed, there is a fear that one may already have had enough.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to eat any food at all. Although one has not yet left one's seat, due to these eight circumstances, one must not eat further.

Only if the *kṛtya-karaṇīya* (the formal procedure for leftover food) is performed again will eating be permitted. This is because the person who offered the food says, "The bhikṣu did not use [it], so he will not eat further.
It is stated that the "eight prohibitions" (*aṣṭau vāraṇāni*) are simply the aforementioned acts of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

The two types of beds—long and short—and the boat-vehicle constitute eight [items] (this is likely incorrect). "One who is a bhikṣu" excludes the three lower assemblies, as they do not possess the *anaśiṣṭa-bhakṣaṇa* (the practice of eating leftover food).
Although the bhikṣuṇīs have this practice, it is according to the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*; the *Caturvargika-vinaya* does not clarify that there is a rule for leftover food.
"The three bodies being healthy and harmonious" excludes times of illness, when taking several meals is directly permitted; how could one discuss the rule for leftovers in such cases?

1. During times of abundance, one excludes those who are practicing austerity (*dhūta*). This means that among the eight items [of the *atireka-āhāra*], the rule regarding not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-pratiniḥsarga* (the ritual of declaring the meal finished) is waived.
2. The person addressed must be a *bhikṣu*. This distinguishes it from addressing other, lower classes of the community. 3. The person must not have already finished eating (*pūrva-bhukta*).

This excludes those who have already completed their meal; they may not face each other because the latter cannot eat again, and thus one may not perform the *ucchista-kalpa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining) for them.
This is the Dharma. Regarding "timely food" and "pure [food]," these distinguish it from "untimely food," for which no ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is required.
"Pure" means distinguishing it from food that has the eight defects; such food does not fulfill the requirements for the ritual procedure.

"New and pure, not the leavings of one who is ill" distinguishes it from "leavings," as leavings do not require the ritual procedure and may be consumed directly. "Not concealed" indicates that it was brought while being hidden. Lì says:

It is not that others conceal it; because it is solid, one fears others, and because it is solemn, there is concealment. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*’s statement concerning "holding a bowl or the like," the *Lì* (立) commentary states:

if one follows the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, one must necessarily eat from it; even if one eats only from the bowl and not from the *wǎn* (a shallow vessel), eating from the *wǎn* does not constitute "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*).
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is not necessary to eat from it; it is sufficient for the person who sent [the food] to inform [the recipient].
If it is my leavings, then it constitutes *vighasa* (remnants).

Furthermore, according to the text of the *Ji*, if one performs the ritual while holding a bowl or a dish and eats from within that bowl, it means that even within a dish, it also constitutes *vighasa*.

If one holds two dishes side-by-side and performs the ritual, placing a flat cake across the two bowls—if the cake is at the center, then both bowls together constitute the ritual of *vighasa*. Below, the meaning and interpretation are clarified.
Regarding those who do not violate the Vinaya by eating what they perceive as non-food, or by eating without having received the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa* (the ritual for leftover food):

Lü states that "perceiving food as non-food" means, for example, if one eats thick gruel at the morning meal but perceives it as thin, and then eats at the midday meal without having received the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa*, there is no offense.
There is another interpretation: it is like eating thick gruel at the morning meal while firmly resolving that it is thin gruel as it leaves the pot.

It may be that by midday one becomes unable to endure hunger because of the insufficiency of what was previously received; thus, it is said that "one does not receive," which clarifies that one resolutely refuses to accept.
It is said that "the person has merely come and has not yet received food. Regarding "that which is not food for which the *śeṣa-kalpa* (procedure for leftovers) need not be performed":
since these are not the five types of formal meals (*bhojana*), why would it be necessary to perform the ritual for leftovers? They are simply called "non-food" because they are not the formal meals.
Yeli said: "Those who do not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) rite" refers to those who have previously consumed only thin gruel.
"Those who have already performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite" refers to those who have previously performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite. (The above is Yeli’s interpretation.)
Precept Thirty-Six: Exhorting [a Monk] to Eat When Satiated. Nuns commit only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding "knowing":

if one knows that [the monk] has already eaten his fill and yet exhorts him to eat, it is a *pāyattika*. If he has actually eaten his fill, but one exerts him while harboring doubt as to whether he is full, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If he has not yet eaten his fill, yet one acts with the perception or doubt that he is full and exhorts him, in both cases it is a *duṣkṛta*. Baoliang says: This precept and the preceding one are identical in that they both concern eating when satiated.

Because there is a distinction between oneself and others, two types of precepts are established. Zhiyi says: "This precept differs from the preceding precept in four ways. First, there is a difference in action (*karman*).

The preceding precept on 'sufficient food' (*paryāpta-bhakta*) consists of verbal restraint while being physically involved in the offense. [Commentary: Verbal restraint means not performing the *kṛtānna-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food);
furthermore, it relies on physical action, namely swallowing mouthful by mouthful. This [present] precept on encouraging sufficient food consists of verbal restraint while performing the action."

The other person commits the offense. As for "stopping" (*niṣṭhāpana*), it means to cease by means of speech, saying "enough" (*sthāpana*) without performing the ritual of "remaining food" (*atiriktapiṇḍapāta*). To speak words exhorting another is called verbal action (*vākkarman*).

Only when the other person swallows does one first incur the offense; therefore, it is said that it relies upon the body of another. Second, there are differences regarding the opening of the conditions (*pratyaya*).

The allowance for "sufficient food" applies to those who are ill; there is no allowance for one who encourages another to eat until full. These two cases differ in their origin: eating until full is an offense committed through a mind of greed, whereas encouraging another to eat until full is an offense committed through a mind of anger.
This is explained according to the specific circumstances of their arising; however, if one encourages another with a virtuous intention, it likewise constitutes an offense.

There are four distinctions regarding eating and not eating: the distinction between being satisfied and the necessity of swallowing oneself; the offense incurred when one encourages another to eat until satisfied while one does not eat oneself;
and the offense incurred when another swallows after having been so encouraged. Because there are these four distinctions, they are separated into two precepts.
The Precept Against Eating at Improper Times, Number Thirty-Seven. This precept is a shared offense for both monks and nuns.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one perceives it as improper time when it is actually improper time, or if there is doubt regarding the time, both constitute a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding what is called "improper time," Master Hui states: "At dawn, the preparation of food has just begun and is not yet distinct from the evening;
at sunset, the meal is finished and the day ends. Therefore, the period between the morning and noon is the moment of initial completion; thus, from noon onwards [is improper time]."

Thus it is called "non-time. Lü [Daoxuan] said: "In order to explain 'non-time,' one first explains 'time' in reverse. If dharmas have no time, how can one permit eating at the proper time (*kālabhojana*) while prohibiting eating at improper times?

According to the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in explaining the meaning of "Thus have I heard at one time," the characteristic of time is dismantled and found to be unobtainable;
that is, seeing the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) is merely provisional.

This is called "time," referring to such designations as unity and difference, long and short, and so forth. These arise from the minds of ordinary people (for within the true nature, names and marks exist neither as being nor non-being;

the path of language is cut off, and they cannot be found throughout the three periods of time—how, then, could one discuss "time" therein?). He then asked: "If there is no time, how can you permit eating at the proper time and prohibit eating at improper times as a precept?
He replied: "I have already explained that these are merely worldly conventional designations. There is 'time' and 'non-time' [only in this sense]."

This is a real dharma; you should not raise objections against it. It is also a method for establishing precepts within the Vinaya, and it is real within this world, though not the mark of the ultimate real dharma.
This is because the mark of a self and its dharmas cannot be found as real, and also because of the anger and reproaches of the multitude.

Furthermore, it is intended to protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure for a long time and to establish the ritual protocols for disciples. Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have established [this rule].

Regarding all precepts, one should not seek therein what reality exists, what names and so forth exist, what is appropriate, what is inappropriate, what is the Dharma with such characteristics, or what is the Dharma without such characteristics.
For this reason, these matters should not be questioned. The intent of the question is: since principle is fundamentally timeless, why rely upon time?

The precepts were established prohibiting untimely eating. The answer states: The formulation of the precepts relies upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because sentient beings conceive of time as being real, the Sages follow worldly conventions and, relying on provisional designations, establish the prohibition against untimely eating.
Regarding those who criticize [this]: if this precept had not been established to restrain untimely eating, it would have invited the censure of non-Buddhists.
This was the fault of being reviled by worldly people. It was just as in the following incident: Kāḷodāyin, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
It happened to be a dark, overcast day, and he arrived at the house of a pregnant woman to beg.

As the woman came out of her door carrying food, she encountered a flash of lightning and caught a fleeting glimpse of his face. At that moment, the woman was struck with terror and cried out, "A ghost! A ghost! Immediately—
He fell to the ground. Kāliya replied, "Sister, I am not a ghost; I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya. The woman spoke in anger, "Śramaṇa, son of the Śākya!
It would be better for you to tear open your own belly than to beg for alms at night. When Kāliya heard this, he returned and reported it to the Buddha.
Therefore, [the rule] was established to put an end to such public reproach. Regarding the phrase "one should not seek what corresponds to having a name," etc.: [it refers to seeking fame].

In the past, the Sages established the precepts to restrain and prohibit conditions that are contrary to the Way. They established teachings according to the capacities of beings, matching the medicine to the illness.

Originally, these were merely coarse manifestations; the True Doctrine was not yet revealed. Even when profound meanings were explained through subtle interpretations, how could they have shown the reality within the robes?

Therefore, all that was established was a regulation tailored to worldly conventions. How can one, from within this, analogize it to the Way of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and claim that the dharma of the precepts and...
Is this consistent with principle or inconsistent? Speaking from the ultimate standpoint, there is nothing that does not reach the extreme limit;

yet, when viewed through the lens of conventional phenomena, precepts are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). If this is so, why do you speak only of "provisional names" and "time"? The intent of this question is as follows:

Since you claim that within the true reality (*tattva*) there is neither time nor non-time, why not refrain from discussing time altogether and instead insist on establishing it? This is because [the teaching] must be universally applicable.
Regarding the phrase "for the most part" (*prāyeṇa*): [Seng]liang states that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) conceptualize provisional names (*prajñapti*) as being either "time" or "non-time.
Within True Suchness (*tathatā*), however, there is neither time nor non-time. Worldly people do not understand this, and those who do are few. For now, I shall set it aside and not discuss it;
rather, since most worldly people conceptualize time and non-time, I shall discourse according to what is prevalent for the time being. Thus, within the context of "time," I establish this rule.
This precept was established for this reason. Furthermore, it is because the multitude ought to hear it; if one were to speak of the truth at the wrong time, sentient beings would not awaken to it.
As for the scripture stating that "at dawn, the various devas eat," according to the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, upper fascicle, it says:

"At dawn, it is the food of the sons of the devas; at midday, it is the food of the Buddha; in the afternoon, it is the food of the various animals; and at night, it is the food of ghosts and spirits. Only...
Eating at midday and at the morning meal brings merit; eating two meals in the afternoon and at night causes one to fall ill.
Regarding the division of day and night into nine periods each, some say this is according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which likewise divides [the day] into thirty *muhūrtas* (須臾).

When the sun descends near the earth, the heat gradually diminishes and becomes extremely cold; this refers to the winter solstice when the sun falls toward the south. Because it is close to the earth, the days are short and the nights are long. One must...

There is no increase or decrease. As for the twenty-four *qi* (vital energies), this refers to the period from the midpoint of the day until the appearance of light (*prabhāta*), which is reckoned as one *qi* every fifteen days;
this corresponds to the twenty-four half-months in the Buddhist system. When the day is at its longest, the daytime consists of eighteen *muhūrta* and the night twelve;
for a single day comprises thirty *muhūrta*, and when the day is long, it is eighteen [and the night twelve].

There are twelve [units of time]; when the days are short, there are twelve [units] and the nights are eighteen. According to the *Cīvaravastu*, twenty *kṣaṇas* (moments) are called one *tatkṣaṇa* (instant);
twenty *tatkṣaṇas* are called one finger-snap (*acchaṭā*); twenty finger-snaps are called one *lava*; and twenty *lavas* are called one *muhūrta*.
That it is the same for the four continents means that in all four continents, the period before noon is [reckoned in this manner].
Regarding the calendar: today, the sun and moon complete one circuit of the four continents in one day and night.

For example, when it is noon in the south, the sun rises in the western continent, sets in the eastern continent, and it is midnight in the northern continent. Such shifts can be understood by comparison.

Now, there are those with supernormal powers who, having finished their meal here in this region, may go to the western continent to eat without violating the precepts; this does not refer to the aforementioned [case of the same moment]. It is as follows:

Within a single day, one may eat four times without committing an offense because it is before noon. Regarding "eating at the time" (*kāla-bhojana*) and "eating at the improper time" (*vikāla-bhojana*):

when one eats at the time of midday, it is called "time"; otherwise, it is "improper time. As for the statement that eating at such a time brings auspiciousness, Jingyun says: it is named "time and improper time" because it lies between the two.

Regarding "drinking non-time liquids (*vikāla-pāna*) after the dawn light has appeared, which results in a downfall": Lì states that this refers to having first performed the ritual of adding [spices] to the mouth.
The formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is completed. When the dawn light appears, it becomes an "improper time" (*akāla*). There is an apology for this; the method of acceptance has already been lost.

If one drinks [liquids], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for consuming food not formally accepted. If one receives rice from a lay attendant (*upāsaka*), it is likewise auspicious. The *Liyi* (礪意) states: Food taken after midday is called "improper time.
When the improper time passes until the dawn light, it is called "the improper time of the improper time. Taking medicine seven days after its permitted period is also termed [improper].
It is not "out-of-season" (akāla). Since life-long medicines (*yāvajjīvika*) have no time limit for their use, there is no such thing as "out-of-season" regarding them;

one cannot be censured for missing the [prescribed] time. However, for those who take them when they are not ill, the formal act of taking them (*samādāna*) is not appropriate. The commentary states that there are degrees of lightness and heaviness in the offense. This means: if a seven-day medicine (*saptāhika*) is taken after its period has expired, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense;
for a life-long medicine, taking it when not ill is permissible. One should understand other cases by this analogy. The commentary further notes: "If one does not add the oral [formula...]"

Regarding the statement in the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao* that "the Dharma does not permit taking the four medicines at improper times, as all would constitute a downfall," and thus excludes water and tooth-sticks from the root precepts (*jiben*):

the tradition of the Great Master [Daoxuan] maintains that it is inappropriate to cite this exclusion of water and tooth-sticks here; rather, this pertains to the section on the precept against eating food not formally received (*bushi shi jie*).
To cite it here is an error. Some say that the author of this *Chao* (the *Shanfan buque xingshi chao*) followed the *Liaoyi shu* by Paramārtha in making this interpretation.

[The Master] said: "Because his practice of restraint was too strict, Daoli (礪) remarked: 'An ancient master had this interpretation: if oil, honey, and so forth undergo the ritual of oral transformation (*mukha-dharma*), they may be consumed for seven days;
if they do not undergo the ritual of oral transformation, they may only be consumed at the proper time. Daoli further stated:
'If oil, honey, fresh butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth are mixed with food that is permissible at the proper time, one should perform the ritual of *kṛtānna* (the treatment of leftover food).'"
Regarding those who eat alone: since this is not a medicine to be taken at improper times, there is no fault in eating it whenever one wishes. How is this known?

For instance, during the Seventh Council, it was asked: "After having finished a meal and relinquished the formal posture, [one may consume] ghee, oil, honey, fresh butter, and rock sugar mixed with curd."
"Is it permissible to receive food in one location? Līṭavata replied, "It is not permissible. He asked, "Where was this established? He replied, "In Śrāvastī;

it was established within the rules concerning the *kṛtāvadhi-śeṣa* (the practice of declaring surplus food). This refers directly to the text of the precept on "sufficient food" (*paryāpta-bhojana*).

Therefore, it is known that when butter, oil, and other such items are mixed with food eaten at improper times, one must perform the *kṛtāvadhi-śeṣa* rite; if they are not mixed with food eaten at improper times, the *kṛtāvadhi-śeṣa* rite is not required. This makes it clear.

It is known that one may consume ghee or oil at improper times. Regarding the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Section Vinaya) statement that one may taste food but not swallow it, the commentary by Daoyi citing the *Śāriputra-abhidharma* says:
"Tasting food is permitted, yet one must not swallow it. The origin story (*nidāna*) is as follows: Various bhikṣus hired laborers to cook for them.
When the food was prepared, they complained that it was either too bland or too salty, saying, "We cannot cook for bhikṣus. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.

When the Buddha permitted the boiling [of food], he tasted it but was unable to swallow it. If this is food for offerings to the Sangha, such as at a formal assembly, the *Hujing jing* (Sutra on Protecting Purity) stipulates that tasting it is in all cases forbidden.
To taste it constitutes "leftover" (śeṣa); to offer such leftovers to the Buddhas and the Sangha brings no merit but incurs sin, resulting only in the exhaustion of labor and suffering.
Now, the present commentary cites the text to clarify that one must know that even during improper times (*akāla*), one must not taste the food; otherwise, one commits an offense in both instances.
Regarding "falling" (*pātayantikā*): it refers to causing a bhikṣu to perform such superior acts, whereby both the instructor and the instructed commit the offense together.

Regarding the statement in the *Five Hundred Questions* that "none of all material things with form may enter the mouth," [the commentator] Li states: this means they may be received [into the mouth].
This is likewise explained in the *Mahāgaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*. Bin states: however, as for the precept against eating at improper times, though one searches throughout the various...
[This] section has never had an explicit textual opening [for this rule]. It is only because the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) provides an opening for the medicinal use of honey.
That Vinaya, at fascicle sixty, states: A disciple of Nanda was ill and took a purgative; after midday, he felt a sense of suffocation. The Buddha said, "Give him boiled rice-pollen juice.

After it was given, the suffocation still did not cease. The Buddha said, "Give him bamboo shoot juice. When that did not cure him, the Buddha said, "Boil rice in a bag and strain the juice of the gruel."

[The text] says: "Do not give [it]. Do not give. The Buddha said: "Administer rice gruel in a secluded place. (Shu’s commentary states: This refers to rice juice, bamboo shoot juice, or rice juice contained in a bag.

If administered in succession while the patient is gasping for breath, the principle is that it will not be opened. Only after the patient has reached the height of distress at the point of death should the gruel be opened. Nowadays there are foolish people [who act otherwise].

He did not take the purgative medicine, nor was he extremely distressed. Relying falsely upon the sacred teachings, he proceeded directly to consume thick gruel; with every swallow, his throat became constricted.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning is honey," the phrasing "opening the gruel" actually means it is not opened, because the rice-juice and other ingredients remain sufficient until dawn.

In the eighth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, concerning the taking of emetic and purgative medicines: when one has not eaten before the meal and feels oppressed within the belly, the Buddha said:

He anointed his body with ghee, yet it was not cured. He anointed his body with parched grain flour, yet it was not cured. He anointed his body with a mixture of ghee and parched grain flour, yet it was not cured.
He bathed himself with warm water, yet it was not cured. He was given warm water to drink, yet it was not cured.
He sat inside a vessel filled with meat broth; by such means as these, he remained until dawn. Under no circumstances may one eat at an improper time.

One must clearly understand the intent behind the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding rice-water and similar substances: they serve to gradually lead one toward clarity, rather than being a direct permission [to consume them]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 17, also states:
"If a bhikṣu has taken emetic or purgative medicine and the physician says he should be given clear congee (*prasannā*), but it cannot be obtained and he will die, what should be done?
At that time, one should place the sick bhikṣu in a trough filled with the rinsing water of rice (*tā-mi*; the character is pronounced *fan*, meaning *gān*)."

If the patient is unable [to eat], one should take unbroken grains of rice, millet, or wheat, wash them seven times until clean, place them in a clean bag, tie the top, and boil them in a thoroughly cleaned vessel.
The tips of the rice grains must not break; if they do break, it must not be given to the sick bhikṣu.

The thirty-eighth precept: Regarding the consumption of leftover food from the previous day. As for the nuns, the determination of the offense regarding the transgression of time limits for the four types of medicine is as explained previously.

Regarding the term "precept" (*śīla*), Zhen Di states that it refers back to the section on the precept against eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*). It says: "Once one has accepted the timely medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*), if one passes the midday limit by even a hair’s breadth, the acceptance is lost.

This refers to the passages concerning non-timely liquids (*akālapāna*) and the seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*) falling into violation after the seventh day, and so forth. Thus it is established.

It says: This is a general reference to the four types of medicine; "exceeding the time" carries the meaning of "storing overnight. If a *kālabhojana* (timely medicine) is taken after noon, it loses its status as received food (*paribhoga*), and eating it incurs an offense.

For a *akālabhojana* (non-timely medicine), once the two methods of mouth and hand have been performed, if it is brought out at the appearance of dawn, it constitutes eating at the improper time (*vikālabhojana*).

This constitutes an offense. Regarding seven-day medicines: once the seven days have passed, they are termed "out-of-season" (*akāla*). Regarding lifetime medicines: once the illness has been cured, they are termed "out-of-season. All of these carry the meaning of exceeding the limit.
One who consumes them all commits the offense of *śeṣa-saṃstuta* (eating what has been stored overnight). Therefore, this is now explained comprehensively. To answer in four propositions:
first, that which is *śeṣa* but not *saṃstuta* is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Lü [Yuan] says: there is also the offense of improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśana*). Third, likewise...

Regarding "the remainder is also *sukhita*": Lì says that obtaining one *dukkaṭa* is also one *sukhita* for internal storage (*antovuttha*), along with one *dukkaṭa* for the spontaneous loss of the formal act of receiving (*paṭiggaha*) and for improper contact (*duṭṭhullā-saṃsagga*).
From this point downward, the categories of "remainder" (*sesaka*) and "internal storage" (*antovuttha*) also have fourfold logical permutations (*catukka*).
As for the second case, "internal but not remainder," Lì says it is a *dukkaṭa*. Some say that in a pure area (*parisuddha-bhūmi*), there is no internal storage; this clarifies the ancient [view].

The Master holds this view: once the *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground) has been demarcated, even if the sun rises while monks are still within it, there is no offense of "storing overnight" (*antarvasati*).
If, however, the demarcation were completed [before sunrise], one could not avoid the offense of storing overnight; therefore, what is the use of performing the demarcation? I say this is not so.

According to the Vinaya, with the exception of the bhikṣus themselves, one must recognize that the presence of bhikṣus constitutes "storing overnight. Your objection—that once the demarcation is finished, one cannot avoid the offense of storing overnight—is incorrect.
Regarding the offense: what is the purpose of establishing this boundary? Previously, had it not been established, one would have committed an offense throughout the entire monastery (*ārāma*).

Now that it has been established, one commits an offense only for staying overnight on non-pure ground; within the great boundary (*mahāsīma*), there is no offense. Why, then, would it be useless? However, externally, the entire monastery is generally established as pure ground;

this is also understood to mean that while the monastic cells themselves are not individually demarcated, the courtyard below them is collectively established as such. As the text says, "The bhikṣus were removed," from which we know [the distinction exists].

This is the intention of the commentator (*caojia*). It means that pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) does not permit the presence of bhikṣus; since the Vinaya text commands their removal, it says "remove the bhikṣus.
If they are not removed, one incurs the offense of "storing overnight within" (*antaruparata-doṣa*); therefore, we know they must exist [on such ground].
The former [commentator] eliminates this. He removes the word "bhikṣu" because his perspective differs.
Some say that the removal of the word "bhikṣu" refers to Upāli’s summary of the preceding words, stating: "As previously established, I have already mastered it. [The question asks:
"Apart from the bhikṣu's quarters, if there are further nuns' quarters, may they be used for purification? The Buddha said: "They may be used. Therefore, he says "removes," which is not [the case].
This means that one is not permitted to stay overnight together; this is what is meant by "removal. Regarding the case of the *yogācāra* (meditation) bhikṣu as the origin of the rule:
in the Vinaya, the bhikṣu Kāla said, "Because I have few desires and little business, I now beg for food only once, which suffices for many days.

Is this not a saving of effort? This was a transgression of the precepts committed with a virtuous intention. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Although your mind is characterized by few desires and contentment, later..."

To act on behalf of a bhikṣu by performing his duties is improper. One who reveres the precepts and increases their practice of the Way does so because, through the precepts, they give rise to wisdom, destroy afflictions, and ultimately obtain the benefits of the Path; thus, the merit returns to the precepts.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a bowl has been used to hold impure substances such as oil or ghee, or if it receives roasted flour (*maṇḍaka*) and so forth, it is said that even if washed, the odor of the oil or ghee will not leave.
If one now stores *piṣṭa* (flour) and eats only from the center of the bowl, there is no offense regarding "leftover overnight food" (*śeṣabhakta*).

Regarding the "eating of impure leftover overnight salt," Jing says: "This refers to salt that has been consecrated with a ritual formula (*adhivāsita*). Because it is consumed by one who is not ill, it is merely 'permissible' (*kṣema*).
Alternatively, it was permitted during times of scarcity. Apart from these two conditions, it is in all cases improper to eat. Shen says: "That salt is for life-long use (*yāvajjīvikam*)."

Regarding medicine: if one first performed the ritual of adding [the consecration] to the mouth, and now the illness has been cured and one takes it, it is appropriate that one obtains a favorable result.

If one previously ate food with salt without having performed the ritual of addition, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. In the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, it says that if grease does not come off, it is "not because of the grease of food.

This clarifies two or three instances where it does not come off even after washing with soap powder (*kaṣāya*); this refers to newly acquired [external] impurities. As for other types of grease that do come off, it is not because of the grease of food.
The commentary states: "The meaning is to be understood by analogy with the case of giving leftover food to laypeople and others.

This means that if, after passing the bowl to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) or a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) to have more food added, there is still food remaining in the bowl, one passes it to them with the intention not yet severed—that is, intending to take it back later.
If that attendant then takes this food and subsequently touches the pure food belonging to the Saṃgha, [the following occurs].
This is called "defiled contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*). It causes all the monks to incur the offense of impure food.

If such a situation arises now, one must sever one's intention and relinquish it to a pure person (*pariśuddha-pudgala*). Another interpretation states: by not severing one's intention, one passes [the food] to a pure person and thus incurs the offense of defiled contact oneself;
once it subsequently enters one's hand, the offense is formally established. A bhikṣu transmits the food to a śramaṇera.

Regarding "Mī" and so forth: it is established that when a bhikṣu and a śrāmaṇera pass a bowl back and forth while eating together, if the śrāmaṇera passes food to the bhikṣu, he must wash his hands before receiving it;
if he passes it to the śrāmaṇera, he must sever the mental connection [of ownership] before giving it; and if he receives it from him again, the same applies.
As when washing hands previously, there is no offense of improper contact. The commentary states: "As in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, 'good' means as stated in the *Sudarsana-śāstra*:
many bhikṣus were traveling with one śrāmaṇera; each bhikṣu carried his own food, yet they exchanged it with the śrāmaṇera.
Regarding the Buddha’s statement that "one should not have a śrāmaṇera carry the bowl except in cases of urgency," this means:
When a śrāmaṇera has finished eating, he takes the bowl containing the leftovers (aśuci-pātra) to give to his teacher;

therefore, [the teacher] does not permit it. If, however, one receives [food] from him every morning, there is no fault. The text clarifies that this refers to the point of not receiving [it]. Regarding the character *tì* (扟): according to the *Shīshī* (師), it is pronounced *sōu lín* (所隣反).
The *Shuowén* says it means to scoop up from above. The *Tōngsúwén* says it means to take by diminishing what is above. The *Qièyùn* says it means to select from above.

"Taking up objects. Regarding the statement that "the causal conditions of the Five Hundred Questions are the same as above," Master Li states that this treatise clarifies the causal conditions for taking food upon a stone in the wilderness;

these are the same as the two passages from the *Cīvaravastu* (The Section on Robes). Regarding the phrase "as is the custom in Uttarakuru," Master Li states that in that country, there is no sense of "mine" (*mamakāra*) regarding any object.
Now, citing this principle, it is clarified that there is no [sense of ownership] regarding food already present upon a stone.

Regarding the "mind of ownership": when the donor relinquishes [the food] and the bhikṣu, in turn, relinquishes it to a bird, and the bird does not come to take it, this food has no owner to whom it belongs.

As for the statement in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that one need not inquire whether it is the proper time (*kāla*) or the improper time (*akāla*), this means that regardless of whether one receives food during the proper time or the improper time, if even a single hair’s breadth of the meal passes midday, it constitutes eating at the improper time (*vikālabhojana*) and incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if one places food on the ground for even a brief moment (*kṣaṇa*), one incurs a *pācittiya* offense for "storing food" (*āhāra-sannidhi*) after having received it.

If one stores it for longer than a brief moment and then eats it, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense for eating stored food. According to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is explained directly in terms of "timely food" (*kālika-bhojana*). The text states:

"If it concerns the five types of formal meals (*pañca-bhojanāni*), if one receives them during the proper time and eats them during the proper time, there is no offense. If one receives them during the proper time but eats them after the proper time has passed—even for the duration of a hair's blink—one incurs an offense."

To explain further: if one leaves food aside for more than a brief moment (kṣaṇa) before eating, one incurs another *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense—namely, the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*) as well as the offense of eating food that has been set aside (*sthāpanīya*).

If one eats during an improper time, one incurs one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one leaves it aside for more than a brief moment, one further incurs the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for setting aside food, as clarified above.
This is because within the *Prātimokṣa*, there are both the precept against eating at an improper time and the precept against eating food that has been set aside.

Regarding the combined regulation for the precept on eating, one should know that the intention cited by the author of the *Xūzhīchāo* (Notes on Essential Knowledge) refers directly to eating at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), exactly as in the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
It does not refer to non-proper-time liquids (*vikāla-pāna*); this is to be understood. The commentary states: "If it passes the two times, it is called 'non-proper time' (*vikāla*).

This means that if food is received during the proper time, even if it passes into the non-proper time by as little as a blink of an eye or the growth of a hair, it is still considered "one time" (*eka-kāla*). Furthermore, if one enters the non-proper time...
At that time, after a brief moment has passed, it is again "another time"; thus, these are called the two times. This refers to receiving food before midday;

[This concludes the explanation of the intent behind the prohibition. Those who are able to receive [offerings] from such a bhikṣu are distinguished from the lower assemblies and other realms of existence. This is for the sake of...

"Abiding in one's own nature" means that "seeking and obtaining" refers to this location. To establish what is meant by "seeking and obtaining": it refers to the food being sought.
As for "this location," it refers to a single bhikṣu who, having received [the food], passes it on to other bhikṣus;
this person who receives it is designated as "this location. All the other bhikṣus may take [the food] from this bhikṣu and all obtain it together.

[The bhikṣu] had a long bag made of clean cloth to hold various provisions, measured out the daily portions of food, tied them together into a single bundle, and fastened it onto the ox. Upon arriving...

At the time of eating, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take [the food]. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one person should pull the drawstring while another receives it, saying aloud, "I receive, I receive.

According to that Vinaya, when there was a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) frying beans and a bhikṣu desired some, he asked the attendant for it.

It is not proper decorum (*airyāpatha*). Furthermore, when a monkey is eating fruit in a tree and a bhikṣu desires that fruit, he says to the monkey, "Give me some fruit.
The monkey shakes the tree so that the fruit falls; if the bhikṣu receives it in a vessel as it falls into the vessel, this is called "receiving," yet it is still not proper decorum.

"Marsh. Thus it is said. This refers to a place where there are no people; one merely opens a span's width [of the robe] to receive food, and it must not exceed that.

This refers to the common practice in the West of using food tables. Grass is placed upon the table, and when a pure person serves food that falls onto the grass, if it remains there for even a short time, it constitutes formal acceptance (*pratigraha*).

Jing says: "This citation provides a specific exception; merely placing [the food] on the table constitutes acceptance, whereas receiving it directly with the hand and letting it fall onto the grass does not."
The note states: "Regarding 'sitting in a squatting posture on clean cloth': in the Western regions, during mealtime, everyone sits in this squatting posture.

The commentary explains: Why are they called "delicious foods"? Because they are expensive; because they are difficult to obtain; and because they cure illnesses. There are four permutations:

however, one still must not solicit from the aforementioned eight types of households. If one obtains [food] by begging from them...

Precept 41: Regarding the Prohibition Against Giving Food to Non-Buddhists. The offenses for monks and nuns are identical; the differences in their circumstances can be understood accordingly.

At the time this precept was established, there was no formal censure (as detailed in the commentary). As for "one who is a non-Buddhist," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: this refers to those who have left the household life to follow non-Buddhist paths.
Because those who live at home distinguish between the secular and the monastic, no confusion arises; they merely commit minor offenses.

However, because those who have left the home life share a common name, it is difficult to distinguish the true from the false, which gives rise to delusion and inversion in people. This is why [the offense] is considered grave. Gao asked: "There are ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).
Does the Buddha-way fall outside this number or within it? The answer is that various Vinayas and treatises differ on this point. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*...

"In trading with any of the ninety-six types of renunciants, there is no offense. Since it makes no distinction, the Buddha’s Dharma is clearly contained therein.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, regarding the pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), it says: "Among all ninety-six types [of schools], none possess the method of the pure gift; only the Buddha’s Dharma does."
There is. Furthermore, it is said that these names for the three robes are not found among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders, because they are secret and superior.

These then belong to separate categories. Attachment to them is difficult to abandon; because they are rare, [the offenses] are light. Regarding the fifth point, that one commits an offense upon receiving [an object] with the hand:

"Finished. "Other families" refers to the houses of laypeople (*avadātavasana*). A guest said: "In the Vinaya texts, the terms 'before eating' and 'after eating' are inverted from the Sanskrit.
It should be stated as 'before the meal' and 'after the meal'; the translator did not adjust the phrasing. (The Commentary states: This means "before the midday meal" and "after the midday meal.

Regarding the four instances of visiting other families without cause: if it is during the month of Kārttika, or if one has already performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then departs, these are all [permissible].

It is said: "The conditions. Regarding the two *pārājika* offenses incurred by going to another's house: one is a *thullaccaya* for violating the prior prohibition against accepting invitations [for meals];
