If two bhikṣus each accept regular invitations and interact with one another, it is likewise; according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are two bhikṣus who each separately accept [invitations].

When invited by a single family, if the first bhikṣu says to the second bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, come with me today to my donor's house for a meal," the second bhikṣu should inform [the donor] before departing.
If he departs without informing [the donor], it is a *thullaccaya*.
If the second bhikṣu invites the first bhikṣu, it is also the same (according to the meaning of the text, it seems one should inform the donor). This also applies to standing [invitations].

It is said: The families of Zhang and Wang each invited one person. The bhikṣu from the Zhang family wished to go to the Wang family, while the bhikṣu from the Wang family wished to go to the Zhang family;

each was [invited by] their own respective patron (*dānapati*). Regarding the period "from the time of eating until midday," the intent of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*) is that, according to the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, this corresponds precisely to the *yuzhong* (approx.
9–10 a.m. period; therefore, it is the "time of eating. The commentary states: "According to this, it accords with the 'time of eating' in the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*."

Regarding "the same": this refers to the fact that this sutra explains eating while measuring one's shadow, which is identical to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), because both define the limit as noon.

The text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi wen) is not so; according to it, even if one finishes early, it is already called "improper time" (*vikāla*). Regarding "the storehouse area and the peripheral rooms," some say:

These are all remote areas within the monastery grounds. If one goes to such places, the previous authorization (*anujñā*) is lost. If one goes to another monastic temple (*saṃghārāma*), there is likewise no loss of the formal procedure (*vidhi*).
However, if one goes to other storehouses or similar locations, it is lost. *Lì* (Lì Daosheng) says:

"This means that once the authorization has been completed, if one goes to other storehouses, nunneries, and so forth, the previous procedure is entirely lost; one must authorize them again. The subsequent text provides the opening for this exception.
It is said: "If there are no bhikṣus, one does not incur an offense by going to other storehouses, nunnery temples, and so forth without having made an entrustment.
This refers to a situation where there is no one to whom an entrustment can be made; because no entrustment is possible, entry into such places is permitted even without an entrustment.

Regarding cases where many sitting mats and other items are spread out at various households, Jing says: "This refers to a single village where many families collectively provide a single offering, yet each household [provides its own]."
Each [monk] appoints attendant bhikṣus. Wherever they go, it is all a place of invitation; therefore, there is no offense. This is because the original invitation was general.
The details are as explained in the lower fascicle, specifically within the section on the method of formal invitation (*nimantraṇa*). Jing asked:
"In the case of a large village with many households, when first entering the village gate, how is the limit of an offense determined? He replied: "At first..."

Upon entering the village gate, one incurs one *pācittiya* offense; subsequently, as one passes beyond the boundary of the house and reaches the collective boundary (*saṃgha-sīma*), many offenses are incurred.
It is not necessary to actually enter the house for the offense to be committed. Bin says: "The meaning of the words of entrustment. Li says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], having previously accepted an invitation from [Name], now have a certain business matter and wish to enter a certain village and go to a certain house."
"Venerable Sir, please take note. Now, it is sufficient to specifically entrust this matter to one person so that they may remember it well;
it is not necessary to say 'Venerable Sir, please attend closely,' and so forth. Even if one were to announce it from afar, such a procedure is likewise permitted."
The Forty-third Precept: Forcibly Sitting in a Family’s Dining Room. This precept constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for both monks and nuns alike.

Regarding the phrase "from among the four types of food, up to the point of touching the food," there are four kinds of food: *kabaḷīkāra-āhāra* (morsel food), *sparśa-āhāra* (contact food), *manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra* (volitional food), and *vijñāna-āhāra* (consciousness food).

As for *kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*, the old translation is "lump food" (*tuánshí*), also called "segmented food" (*duànshí*). The term "segmented food" encompasses a broad range of meanings. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: [text follows].

The four nutriments (*āhāra*) are: first, the nutriment of mouthfuls (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*); third, the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*);

and fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Regarding the nutriment of mouthfuls, its characteristic is transformation. Why is this? Because when this mouthful undergoes transformation, it can perform the function of benefiting the body;

thus it is called the nutriment of mouthfuls. Regarding the nutriment of contact, its characteristic is dependence upon objects. By taking form and other sense objects as conditions, it can perform the function of benefiting the body.

This is called the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). As for the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*), its characteristic is the act of hoping. This hope, when fulfilled, is able to perform beneficial functions.

It is like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who reaches a place where food and drink are available; by hoping to obtain food and drink, their life and body do not perish. This is called the nutriment of volition.
The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) has the characteristic of sustaining. Because of this consciousness, the body is able to be maintained; thus it remains in the world without perishing.

If there were no sustaining by consciousness, one would be like a dead person, and the body would immediately rot and decay. This is called the nutriment of consciousness. Among these four nutriments, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) belongs to the six consciousnesses.

The nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) belongs to the mind (*manas*). With respect to obtaining edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it belongs to form (*rūpa*) and does not concern the mind. As for the nutriment of consciousness, regarding the three [realms]...
Regarding the meaning [of this]: to which meaning does it belong? If you do not assert the existence of the *ālayavijñāna*, on what basis is this consciousness explained as "nutriment"?

Furthermore, when a person is asleep without dreaming, or when the mind is fainting, or has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six consciousnesses have already ceased.
Moreover, since the three nutriments of physical food, mental volition, and contact are absent, what dharma sustains this body so that it does not perish? If there were no [ālayavijñāna]...
If the ālayavijñāna were to cease to sustain this body, it would perish; therefore, one knows that it must necessarily take the ālayavijñāna as its nutriment.

As for the statement that "this is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*)," according to the interpretation in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, everything obtained by the six consciousnesses belongs to the nutriment of contact. Thus it is established.

When a man and a woman gaze at one another, their minds become stained by mutual passion; this principle is like that of food. Because they face one another with their eyes, it is called "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*).

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The man takes the woman as his food; the woman takes the man as her food. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, parched grain, rice, fish, and meat are called "food.
Furthermore, there is another kind of food: when the eye-consciousness sees a form and gives rise to affectionate thoughts, producing desire and attachment, and so forth.

The nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this; all are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*). Furthermore, there are nutriments such as: the cauldron has its lid as its nutriment; the mortar has its pestle as its nutriment; the bushel has its pint-measure as its nutriment. Again, there are nutriments such as: the man is the nutriment for the woman, and the woman is the nutriment for the man. All the above are termed "nutriments. Bin says: Master Nanshan states that among the four nutriments—*Commentary on the Abhidharma-kośa*, fascicle 19: "The four nutriments are: first, the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), which refers to the coarse and subtle foods of the desire realm; second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*), which refers to the six types of contact of the three realms; third, the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*), which refers to the volitions of the three realms;
It is an error to say that this refers to the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). This intention actually explains craving (*rāga*); it does not intend to distinguish the nutriments.
Now, regarding the phrase "a family with treasure," this is a designation based on a metaphor. Because they consume the flavor of desire, it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*);

because they cherish one another, it is called "treasure" (*ratna*). As for the first point, "a family with nutriment," Lì (Lì Daoyuan) says: "When a man and a woman regard each other with amorous feelings, it is called a 'family with nutriment'. If...

A household that has abandoned sexual misconduct and the like is not designated as a "household that eats" (a *bhojana-kula*). Regarding the mutual undertaking of the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), this was established as a regulation because of the potential for obstructing the arising of the practice;
however, when husband and wife mutually observe the one-day precepts today, since there is no sexual misconduct to obstruct it, it is permitted and does not constitute an offense.
Bin says: "This refers to receiving the eight precepts. As for the absence of a fourth person among the four [parties], these are the husband, the wife, and the bhikṣu.
Third is intentional transgression. Furthermore, there are other people who constitute the fourth [category]. This is because obstructing matters does not pertain solely to oneself;

thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that those who wear jeweled robes and so forth do so because it is established that their households possess the significance of jewels—meaning, for instance, that the women wear jeweled robes.
The light and clarity illuminate the interior of the body, while externally manifesting the arousal of desire; therefore, it is said that "there is a treasure.
According to the *Cīvaravastu*, even if both male and female are present, there is no offense, because it is not a household where food is being consumed.
The forty-fourth precept on sitting with a woman in a secluded place: "If a nun sits together [with a man] in a secluded place, it is a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding "whether it be a male or female attendant," the commentary states: "It refers to those aged eighty or ninety who are senile and ignorant of worldly affairs, or those under seven years of age who do not yet understand worldly matters.
The note states: "As for what was previously explained in detail, the meaning of 'secluded place' (*paṭicchanna-ṭhāna*) has already been extensively analyzed within the two *aniyata* rules."
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Ten, Part One;
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Ten, Part Two. Precept 45:
Sitting Alone with a Woman. *Ni-ti*. (The note states: A pure attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) sees or hears [the act] in a secluded place.

As clarified in the section on the two *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses: if one sees or hears [the act] from either party, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); only when both seeing and hearing are absent is it a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession).
This means that if one is constantly speaking but not being heard, it is termed "hearing in private"; if one is in clouds, mist, or darkness, it is termed "seeing in private.

Regarding the phrase "not committing an offense while eating at a house," this establishes a re-explanation of the precept concerning sitting forcefully at a house during a meal. That is to say, the aforementioned...

The conditions for the transgression and the intended meaning of these three precepts are identical; therefore, the preceding precept is now explained again. Furthermore, within the previous precept regarding sitting by force, the text concerning the exceptions was not clarified.

That is to say, in the context of the previous precept on sitting by force, if one mutually receives the one-day precept (*upavāsa*) and does not commit an offense, it means one does not commit a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), but it is not the case that one does not commit a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). Thus, the current text states: "If one mutually receives one..."

"One-day precepts" (*ekarātra-śīla*) refers to the aforementioned precepts. If one sits alone with a woman, or sits in a secluded place with her—regarding these two precepts, even if one has mutually received the one-day precepts, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense, as the intent is to provoke public censure.

When it is said that "one receives the one-day precepts," this refers entirely to the eight precepts, by which one is designated a "pure-practice *upāsaka*" (*pariśuddha-caryopāsaka*). If husband and wife mutually receive the five precepts...

Furthermore, for a bhikṣu to sit down forcibly [in such a place] is also a *pāyattika*. This is because one’s own wife does not constitute a violation. Another interpretation states that the previous explanation was incorrect. Furthermore, another interpretation says:
"Regarding the statement that there is no offense when sitting in a family before a meal, this refers to the precept concerning sitting in a family before a meal.

If husband and wife have both received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), then the bhikṣu commits no offense by sitting there, because the husband and wife are present together. Now, in this context...

Monk, if one sits with a woman in an exposed place, even if the woman has received the one-day precepts (upavāsa), it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is because it gives rise to public censure when seen by others.

If we discuss the matter of the exposed place, it would normally incur a *pāyattika* offense due to the provocation of censure; however, because the woman has already received the precepts, the transgression is light and is therefore only a *duṣkṛta*.
Expulsion from the Assembly: Forty-sixth Rule. A bhikṣuṇī incurs a *pāyattika* offense. There are three circumstances where there is no obstruction:

first, if one stands because of life-threatening dangers, such as those involving non-Brahmins; second, if that person has abandoned right view or proper deportment; third, if one is being formally censured within the assembly.

If one is expelled due to being censured (*pravāsanīya*) or other such reasons, there is no offense in driving them out. Regarding this precept, the *Jiechao* (Commentary on the Precepts) establishes four conditions, while the *Jieshu* (Exegesis on the Precepts) establishes five:
first, a *bhikṣu*; second, having previously consented to his meal; third, not giving him food; fourth, expelling him with a malicious mind; and fifth, departing from his sight and hearing.
If the grindstone is too coarse, there are six conditions, such as the absence of causal conditions.

Regarding the transgression of the four-month medicinal precept, [the *Lì*] says: "In terms of the three types of medicine—those for a limited time, those for seven days, and those for life—one commits an offense.
This refers to the fact that various schools maintain this principle. If it is a single type of medicine taken at an improper time, it is because its substance is base."
Therefore, since the purpose of treating illness is subtle and the purpose of receiving [offerings] beyond the limit is rare, one incurs a minor offense.

As for the statement "four months," it is established that this refers to the four-month period according to the *nidāna*. Now, we do not inquire whether it is four months, one month, half a month, spring, summer, or the like;

rather, as long as one exceeds the donor’s limit, the offense is incurred. Regarding the five circumstances under which there is no offense: these refer to having the circumstance of illness, whereby one may receive [offerings] beyond the limit.
Regarding the statement that "one commits an offense throughout spring, summer, autumn, and winter": this means that each of these three seasons consists of four months.

Because the donor has restricted the period to four months, one incurs an offense upon exceeding that limit. As for the four exceptions mentioned in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, they are: first, a permanent invitation where no time limit is set;
second, a renewed invitation, meaning that although a four-month limit was previously established, the donor subsequently continues the invitation; third, a partial invitation...

"Those who hold medicinal substances" refers to those who carry medicinal drugs to the monastery and divide them; having divided them, they distribute them to the bhikṣus. Regarding "invitations for as long as life lasts":
this means the donor constantly provides medicine for the duration of one lifetime. When these four conditions exist, there is no fault or offense.

Regarding "falling into an offense for exceeding the limit of medicine or staying overnight," it is established that the donor merely provides a single dose of medicine without limiting the number of days or nights.

If a bhikṣu accepts [medicines] after this limit for medicines has passed, he commits a *pāyattika*. If the donor originally invited him for one month or half a month without limiting the duration of the medicines, then staying overnight beyond that constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One should formulate four permutations: first, exceeding the limit for medicines but not the limit for nights—a *pāyattika*;
second, exceeding the limit for nights but not the limit for medicines—a *duṣkṛta*; third, exceeding both the limit for medicines and the limit for nights—a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.
If all four [conditions] are not exceeded, there is no offense.
The Precept on Surveying Military Arrays (Sūtra 48). According to Master Kuang’s nine sections, this section—extending down to the three precepts concerning dyed robes—comprises thirteen rules;
it constitutes the fifth section, which clarifies fixing the mind upon its object, remaining free from negligence, cultivating the path, and being without attachment.

[The Buddha] said: "To march. *Li* says: A gathering of chariots and tents is called an army; when ranks face one another, it is called an array (from here on, the three cases involving a nun also constitute a *thullaccaya*).
Regarding the 'three absences of conditions': this refers to the absence of the condition of being invited. In the Vinaya, there were at times high ministers who were within the army."

If one wishes to see a bhikṣu, the Buddha permits one to go. Regarding the phrase "if an army is ahead, one reaches [the destination] through skillful means, otherwise one falls into [transgression]," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four types:
namely, the elephant force is the greatest; four men following it constitute one elephant division (*hastibala*).
The horse force is next weakest; eight men following it constitute one cavalry division (*aśvabala*). The chariot force is next weakest; sixteen men follow... [it constitutes one chariot division].
This forms one chariot unit (*ratha*). As for the infantry unit, there are thirty-two men including reserves, which constitutes one infantry unit.
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the distinctions are slightly different: regarding the elephant force, one person rides the elephant and eight persons follow him;
for the cavalry, one person mounts a horse and two persons accompany him; for the chariot force, four persons serve as the footmen; and the infantry likewise consists of four persons.
Forty-ninth Precept: Regarding Excessive Travel within an Army. First, concerning those with a "cause" (*sahetuka*): One who has been previously invited is said to have a "cause.
To permit such a person to go is for the sake of attaining the fruits of the śramaṇa. This means that if a powerful minister issues an invitation and one does not go, it may cause harm or loss.
Therefore, permission is granted to go so that one remains free from affliction and injury, stabilizes the mind to practice the Way, and long-term cultivates the fruits of the śramaṇa.
The Fifty Precepts on the Prohibition Against Viewing Armies in Battle: These four constitute offenses upon mere sight, as they violate the Buddha’s regulations.
The Fifty-first Precept on the Prohibition Against Eating Alcohol: For a *bhikṣuṇī* to drink it is likewise a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the ten faults of alcohol, the *Vinaya* states: first, the complexion becomes ugly; second, physical strength diminishes; third, vision becomes unclear; fourth, one manifests signs of anger and resentment; fifth...
1. It destroys one's fields, livelihood, and means of subsistence. 2. It increases the onset of illness. 3. It aggravates strife and litigation.
4. One lacks reputation; an evil name spreads abroad. 5. Wisdom diminishes. 6. When the body breaks up at the end of life, one falls into the three evil realms.
Regarding the "five divisions" concerning the subduing of the dragon and others: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha [departed] from the country of Kauśāmbī.

He traveled to the village of Bhadrayāṇī. At that time, there was a venomous dragon dwelling in the residence of a matted-hair brahmin who constantly rained down great hailstones, destroying the crops.
When the local householders heard that the Buddha, together with twelve hundred and fifty disciples, had arrived at this village, they all came out to welcome him.
Having paid their respects, they said to the Buddha, "In this village there is always an evil dragon."
"He destroys the crops in the fields; I have always wished for a person of great majesty and power to subdue him.

At that time, the bhikṣu Śākyamuni was fanning the Buddha from behind. The Buddha immediately commanded him to go and subdue the dragon. Having heard the Buddha’s command, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
He went to the place where the dragon was, entered its dwelling, and sat to one side. Then the dragon’s body...
Smoke issued forth; smoke also issued from the body of Śaṅkhadhara. The dragon’s entire body burst into flames, and Śaṅkhadhara’s entire body also burst into flames.
The dragon’s fire emitted five colors, and Śaṅkhadhara’s fire also emitted five colors.
Thereupon, he transformed his dragon body to be as small as a chopstick and placed it inside his almsbowl. Carrying it to the Buddha’s presence, he said: "This evil, venomous dragon..."
"Once it has been subdued, where should it be placed? The Buddha instructed that it be placed in the midst of the world-system.
Śākyata received the instruction and, in the time it takes to bend and stretch one's arm, he carried it to the center of the world-system and returned in an instant.

When the lay devotees heard that the evil dragon had been subdued, they were all greatly rejoiced; they all paid homage and said, "We pray that you will accept our invitation. He accepted their request by remaining silent.
This bhikṣu was by nature fond of wine and meat. He went to his home, drank wine to his heart's content, and then returned to Kauśāmbī.

Outside the monastery, he lay down drunk, vomiting and sprawled out; his robes and bowl were strewn about in disorder. The Buddha, seeing this from afar with his divine eye, went with Ānanda to look at him outside the monastery.
The Buddha and Ānanda lifted him up and placed him by a well; the Buddha drew water himself and had Ānanda...

It was difficult to wash [the stain]. He put on his robes and lay down upon a rope bed, with his head directed toward the Buddha. After a short while, he turned over and stretched out his feet, treading upon the Buddha.
Because of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Did Śāketa formerly revere the Buddha? Can he do so now? They replied, "He cannot. The Buddha asked again: "Was that man formerly able to subdue a venomous dragon? Can he subdue a frog now?"
He replied, "I cannot. Because of this, the precept against alcohol was established, extending even to smelling the contents of a vessel that once held wine.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, at that time the bhikṣu Śākyaṭa, having been forbidden from drinking again due to the Buddha’s establishment of the precepts, felt as though his life-breath were ceasing and he was on the verge of death because of his former habituation;
his food and drink did not digest, and he did not know what to do. He reported this to the Buddha, who ordered him to smell the odor of wine. He smelled the wine.
The illness did not improve. The Buddha said, "Add wine to his cakes, his soup, and his porridge. Still it did not improve. The Buddha then permitted that he be given wine.
Having received it, he recovered. The Buddha said, "I have already prescribed that you gradually cease [using] it, until you no longer find it offensive even to smell the vessel that held the wine.
He need not wait to smell it again.

Regarding the statement that "this precept is extremely grave," Falin says: Among all prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*), this one is the most serious, as it can lead to the commission of the four *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses—excluding only the schism of the Saṃgha.
To cause a schism in the Saṃgha, one must possess a pure status;

if one’s status is impure, who would believe them when they claim to be a Buddha? Furthermore, for example, among the five precepts, regarding insentient things, only [the prohibition against] killing is restricted.
First, regarding the precept against alcohol, the underlying intent can be understood.

As for the phrase "that which lacks the color, fragrance, and flavor of alcohol," according to the Vinaya texts, it states: "If this alcohol possesses color, fragrance, and flavor, one should not drink it.

However, provided it is alcohol, regardless of its specific attributes, it must not be drunk. Furthermore, even if it is not alcohol, should it possess the color, fragrance, and [flavor] of alcohol...

"The flavor should be drunk. Thus, one should construct the phrases by alternating them, beginning with "non-liquor," which all should be drunk. *Lishi* (Commentary on the Vinaya): This is condensed into two sections:
first, "should not be drunk," because it is liquor; second, "should be drunk," because it is non-liquor. Gao says:

"These latter four phrases do not constitute an offense because they concern the substance [of the drink]. However, in light of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, these four phrases carry the sense of an offense, as the schools differ."

(Note: The above differs from the text cited in the *Śarīra*; one should further examine the Vinaya text itself. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If this liquor possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor;

drinking them all constitutes a *pāyattika*). There are also things that are not liquor but possess the color, fragrance, and [taste] of liquor..."

Taste: Drinking it causes intoxication; if one drinks it, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. There are substances that are not wine but possess color, fragrance, and flavor, yet do not cause intoxication;
those who wish to drink them are permitted to do so in a secluded place. "Dregs" (*jiaozui*) refers to the sediment at the bottom of wine. Lì says: [text follows].

According to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If one eats yeast that can intoxicate a person, for every swallow it is a *pāyattika*.

If one eats wine dregs, for every swallow it is a *pāyattika*. If one drinks wine sediment, for every swallow it is a *pāyattika*. If it is other types of yeast that do not cause intoxication, there is no offense. As [the Master] Hui-lü stated: "It is like..."

This is the yeast commonly used nowadays. Regarding the aforementioned statement that "the yeast for mixing wine is dried," this refers to first mixing the yeast with wine and then drying it in the sun;

eating it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. As for the commentary stating, "Is it not the case that one commits an offense by taking the object? this means that ancient masters have said that the formulated precepts do not have a fixed characteristic.
Some are formulated such that the mind follows the object, while others are formulated such that the object follows the mind. This precept...

In those cases, the mind is constrained by the object. However, regarding the precept against killing, the object is constrained by the mind; that is to say, if the object is actually a human being, but one perceives it as a non-human, a log, or has doubt about it, one does not incur a grave offense (*pārājika*).
This precept is not like that: provided it is indeed alcohol, even if one perceives it as non-alcohol or has doubt about it, it is still a *thullaccaya* (offense of wrong-doing).

The commentary states: "This refers to one who previously employed the preparatory means. This clearly establishes that one originally intended to drink the alcohol, yet upon reaching [the point of consumption]...

Regarding the limits of the object: it does not matter whether one perceives it as alcohol, suspects it to be so, perceives it as something other than alcohol, or suspects it to be so; provided the actual object before one is indeed alcohol, the offense is incurred.
If there was no prior intentionality regarding the object, even if one obtains it and drinks it while perceiving it as something other than alcohol, there is no offense.

This is because, due to an original lack of intent and being deluded, no offense is committed. The *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precept Text) states: "Of the three propositions concerning the perception of the object, all are grave. All [offenses]...

Regarding the Master’s [opinion] that one is restrained by the mind following from the object, my view differs. There is a specific reason for the Sage’s regulation; the scriptural text does not omit anything.
How could there be a wise person who has never drunk wine or spirits from the outset, yet who—having mistakenly drunk them—is to be charged with a *thullaccaya* offense? This refers to a grave case:

where one first employs the means of intending to drink this wine, and as it is brought to the mouth, one then gives rise to a thought or doubt that it is not wine. This is determined by the subsequent state of mind.

It is merely a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) regarding the limits; since it constitutes a preliminary effort (*pūrvaprayoga*), it is not grave. How then can there be such a strict formulation in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*?

It is as listed in the text [of that work]. This explanation is largely identical to the established interpretation. If one perceives through observation that it is not [an offense], yet it is opened up as above, [then it is permissible].

This means that although it was actually alcohol, the bhikṣu, having examined it, claimed it was not alcohol; furthermore, because there was originally no intentional contrivance (*upāya*), this constitutes an original delusion and thus there is no offense.

As for the phrase "as stated above," this refers to the words of Zhuzi (Zhu Daosheng). It means that because there was originally an intentional contrivance, one who lacks such a contrivance is not subject to formal disciplinary action (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Regarding the passage on illness where other medicines fail to cure it and so forth, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It does not mean that [the condition] exists..."
In the event of illness, one may consume it; however, it must first be treated with other medicines until the condition fails to improve, only then may one begin to take it.
Regarding "moldy drink mixed with food" (*ti*), this refers to the mold used for brewing wine as described in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*).
Since one is now eating it mixed with rice, it constitutes an offense. If it is not mixed with wine, there is no fault even if one eats it. As for "eating malt," this refers to using barley sprouts.
This refers to the one who commits the offense.
Regarding the fifty-second precept on playing in water: *Niti*. The former patriarch Guangtong explained the intent behind the regulation:

since the nature of water is shifting and unstable, it cannot always be kept shallow. To play and laugh within it invites derision and reproach; therefore, it is forbidden. Furthermore, the upper current may suddenly rise.

First, it endangers one’s body and life. Second, it obstructs and causes the abandonment of right practice: the original aspiration of a bhikṣu is to remain tranquil in conditions and advance toward the Path;

yet by entering the water to wander about, he violates his dignified deportment, and thus it obstructs right practice. Fourth, it causes the loss of right mindfulness: [the mind] becomes distracted, drifting and sinking.
This is a violation of the ultimate truth. To enter the water and frolic therein is to lose right mindfulness. The opening commentary cites the *Mahāmegha-dharmagarbha-sūtra*, which states:
"The king and his consort were watching from atop a tower when they saw [the monks] playing in the mud and water. The king spoke a verse to the consort, saying:
'I have heard that the bhikṣus are supposed to have minds free from worldly entanglements; yet here they play recklessly in the mud and water. How can they act as teachers of men? At that time...
When the seventeen groups of youths had finished their play, one among them put on his robes and stepped onto the bank.

Entering meditative concentration, he discerned the king’s thoughts and immediately performed eighteen miraculous transformations to dispel the king’s doubts. Then, by means of his supernormal powers, he departed in the formation of a flight of geese.
When the queen saw this, she spoke a verse to the king, saying: "The bhikṣus of my family have long since been free from the bonds of dust and worldly entanglement. Sa...
"If even Maitreya is like this, how much more so is the Teacher Śākyamuni? Thus the King conceived faith within himself. As stated in the other three Vinayas:
"The group of seventeen [monks], having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), were still rebuked for playing in the water; how much more so for inferior ordinary beings?

Therefore, by citing the superior sages, the inferior ordinary beings are restrained. Upon examining the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*, there is no such text. The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* (vol. 19) states: "A child..."
The youth Kāśyapa reached the age of eight and left the household life, attaining arhatship. Together with the group of sixteen, he entered the water to play and float.
King Prasenajit, looking down from his palace, saw them. As the king had not yet placed faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, seeing this, his lack of faith redoubled.
He immediately said to Queen Mallikā, "Look at the field of merit you serve! There, in the midst of the water, is the youth Kāśyapa."
He entered the fourth dhyāna at the summit of existence and heard with his divine ear. He said to his companions, "The King is doubly distrustful, and Queen Mallikā’s heart is likewise displeased.
Kāśyapa said, "Now we must cause them to give rise to a heart of joy. They all replied, "Excellent!"
Each carrying a water pitcher filled to the brim with water, they placed them before them and sat in the full lotus posture.
Arranged in successive rows, they ascended into the clouds and departed, passing through the air above the king’s palace. When the queen saw this, her heart was filled with great joy.
He then addressed the king, saying, "Behold my field of merit; such is its divine power. The king was greatly delighted.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, after the group of seventeen bhikṣus had finished playing in the water, they stood upon the water to put on their robes.

The queen said to the king, "Behold the field of merit to which I devote myself. Having finished putting on her robes, she filled a jar with water and threw it into the air; she then flew after it. From...
The King passed by on the upper terrace like a king of geese. The Queen again said to the King, "Let me further behold my field of merit. The King also gave rise to a mind of faith.

Other circumstances are the same as in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. Bin says: In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it is mentioned within the water [precepts]; however, according to the origin story (*nidāna*), even playing with water in a bowl constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This is also stated in the subsequent commentary (*vibhaṅga*).
The fifty-third precept on pinching and poking: *Niti*. Regarding the rule that pointing at a bhikṣu with one’s finger also constitutes a *pāyattika* offense:

Jing says, "This refers to pointing from a distance and incurring a *pāyattika*; it does not mean that the offense is committed only when touching [the person]. Examining the nineteenth chapter on the characteristics of offenses in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it appears to differ slightly from this *vinaya*.
In the origin story (*nidāna*) of that *vinaya*, the sixteen groups of monks saw a nun sitting improperly and pointed her out.
[The Buddha] smiled. For this reason, he established the rule. It says: "One finger, two fingers, and so on up to five fingers—it is the same for all fingers.
To point with fingers made of bamboo or wood constitutes a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya). This applies even to pointing at a meeting place;
because it is pointing from a distance, one commits an offense. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if it is the turn of the month or if it concerns an official duty, [one may assign tasks].
Next, regarding eating: if one points with a finger and says, "So-and-so, go away," it is a *pāyattika*. According to the text, this appears to refer to pointing from a distance;
however, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the offense is committed only when [the finger] actually touches [the person].

54. The Precept on Not Accepting Admonition (*Anādāna-śikṣāpada*). *Niḥsargika-pāyattika* 13: Violating the admonition of the Saṃgha constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This [present case] is a *pāyattika* because it violates the admonition of an individual.
That is to say, at the time of such admonition, one who does not accept it commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

When others are about to commit an evil act, they must abandon it upon being admonished; therefore, by violating this and refusing to comply, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Subsequently, if one performs any of the six classes of offenses, one universally incurs a *pāyattika*. Since one has already refused [the initial admonition], [the subsequent offense is established].

Regarding the admonition: whatever offense was previously committed, one incurs the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for refusing the admonition. This is because the prior announcement [of the offense] serves as the cause, which results in the final effect.

If one performs the aforementioned act, one incurs the fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*) among the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍvarga*), namely *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *prāyaścittika*.

Therefore, it should be understood that the *thullaccaya* offense of refusing the admonition is established only when the preceding offense from among the six classes has been completed; it is precisely upon the completion of that offense that the *thullaccaya* of refusing the admonition is formally incurred. — *Lì* (Polished/Refined).

Following this explanation, Li asked: "In the case of violating the Sangha's admonition, one commits an offense once the admonition is finished, without waiting for the act to be carried out. In this present case, the admonition has not yet been finished and no offense has occurred;
it is only upon the performance of the act that an offense arises. What, then, is the nature of the offense for violating the admonition? The answer was:

"In the previous passage concerning the Sangha’s admonition, there were matters such as the life of a monk or the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) which could be violated; because the gravity of the transgression was so great, an offense was committed once the admonition was finished, without waiting [for the act]."

Regarding the performance of the task (*kṛtya*): herein it is stated that this is an admonition by a single person. There is no communal decree (*saṃghājñā*) that can be transgressed; therefore, at the conclusion of the admonition, there is as yet no offense.
It is only upon the actual performance of the task that the meaning of "transgressing the admonition" is established. For this reason, it is not analogous [to other cases].

If that is so, then in the case of the precept against rejecting exhortation to study (*śikṣāsamādāna-pratyākhyāna-śikṣāpada*), this too is an admonition by a single person, and there is likewise no communal decree to be transgressed. Why, then, does an offense occur at the conclusion of the admonition in that instance? [Why is it] different?

Is this not a contradiction? Answer: That [case] concerns the cessation of an offense. One who previously did not train in the cessation of offenses speaks to reject the admonition, saying, "I have already ceased training.
This constitutes the completion of the contradiction; therefore, it is an offense. This [present case] concerns the commission of an offense.

Although one speaks to reject the admonition, saying, "I am the one who acts," they have not yet actually acted. The contradiction has not yet been established; it must await the actual performance [of the act].
Regarding the matter of violating advice, the principle is established that this is not of a single category. For example, as in the opening of the final rules concerning the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses:

it is required that one who exhorts another to advise in accordance with the Dharma must accept it; however, if one advises in a manner contrary to the Dharma, there is no offense in violating such advice.
Fifty-fifth: Causing Fear in Bhikṣus. Regarding the third point, "by means of the six objects such as form and sound":
as for causing fear through forms, it refers to wearing animal skins or assuming the shapes of birds or ghosts—terrifying appearances intended to induce fear in those who encounter them.
This is the demonstration of fear (*bhaya-nidarśana*). The speaker may understand it. Regarding the sound of fear: one produces the sounds of tigers, leopards, spirits, ghosts, and the like;
this is the demonstration of fear, which the speaker can recognize (the following example contains both demonstration and speech). Regarding the smell of fear:
one produces extraordinary odors, whether foul or fragrant, claiming they are the breath of tigers, wolves, or lions. Regarding taste: one produces bitter or sour tastes, causing [fear].

He tastes it and says, "This is a medicine for killing people. As for "touching": he causes cold, hot, rough, or slippery sensations to arise, or uses poisonous insects, snakes, and scorpions to cause another's hand to touch them, thereby inducing fear in the nun. As for "the Dharma":

he tells her various evil things, saying, "In a dream last night, I saw that your preceptor, father, and mother have fallen ill, or have died, or have abandoned the path," and so forth. (The above is...)
Regarding the phrase "individually demonstrating and explaining": "establishing" (*sthāpana*) means to manifest and explain, which refers to verbal expression.

This clarifies that among the aforementioned six types of matters, there is both "demonstrating fear" (*darśana-bhaya*) and "explaining fear" (*kathana-bhaya*). If one causes another to fear by performing an act with one's own body, it is called "demonstrating fear.
If one causes another to fear by speaking of these six matters, it is called "explaining fear. For example: "I heard this sound," or "I saw this form," and so forth.

Furthermore, within each of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), there are the characteristics of both "indicating" (*darśana*) and "explaining" (*bhāṣaṇa*); therefore, it is said that each one indicates and explains. Fourth, regarding the manifestation of two characteristics:
there are the two characteristics of indicating and explaining. This is also called the two characteristics of body and speech.

This clarifies that the aforementioned six sense objects that terrify others do not go beyond the two types of karma of body and speech; the body is "indicating," and speech is "explaining. Thus, it is still "indicating."
It is said: Formerly, it was traditionally held that there were only the terrors of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and no terror of verbal instruction; however, this is not the case.

It possesses both the terrors of demonstration and verbal instruction, as is clearly evident in the Vinaya texts. How could one fail to discuss them? The *Śāstra* (Commentary) likewise establishes these two terrors: demonstration and verbal instruction.

Regarding the variant reading in some transcribed texts that says "each individual characteristic appears," this means that among the six sense objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*), whichever single characteristic appears.

Regarding the *vinaya* rule stating it is a *duṣkṛta* offense when the person does not clearly perceive it, this refers to cases where one produces a terrifying appearance and the other person has not yet clearly seen it.
As for the phrase "or seeing it in a dream" and so forth, this is a textual provision that extends the application of the rule to include instances of fear arising from such phenomena.
Precept 56: Bathing More Than Once Every Half-Month. *Niti* (Commentary): Gao says that this does not mean one must wait until half a month has passed before bathing;
rather, it refers to bathing more frequently than once within the half-month period, hence the term "exceeding" (*guò*). This refers to the excess of bathing, not the passing of days.
The phrase "forty-five days after spring" refers to the first day of the third lunar month until the middle of the fourth month.
The first month of summer refers to the period from the middle of the fourth month to the middle of the fifth month. This interval comprises seventy-five days;

this is the "hot season" (referring here to the hot season in India). Therefore, the text below states: "In India, the heat comes early, from the beginning of the third month until the middle of the fifth month.
Jing says: "This is because the heat arrives early in China. However, one must not rely on this [Chinese perspective] now; rather, one should simply...
It depends on the region and the season as to when it becomes hot; however, it must not exceed seventy-five days.

Regarding "the time of work," even down to sweeping the ground—according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, even five or six sweeps with a broom constitutes the "time of work. As for "the time of traveling":
If one travels as far as one *krośa*, whether coming or going, this is called bathing while traveling, and there is no offense.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it states that if one intends to travel and bathes after having finished traveling, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense; it is only while actually on the road that bathing is permitted. That Vinaya (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*), chapter sixteen, says: "If one came yesterday and bathes today, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If one is to travel tomorrow and bathes today, it is a *thullaccaya*. If one travels and bathes on the very same day, [it is permitted]."
There is no offense. According to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*), once the formal practice is completed, bathing is permitted for all.

Regarding "if one repents upon returning and it is auspicious": this refers to when one reaches the bathing area and immediately regrets not having bathed. Regarding "if there is a reason and one bathes without informing others, it is auspicious":

this means that one must inform others to clear away their suspicions. The commentary states, "as is good according to the treatise," which follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya*). It is not shared with other schools.
It is appropriate for laypeople (avadātavasana) to bathe together. As for the *kṣepa*, it is the same as the *saṃkakṣikā*. Regarding "giving rise to desire in others":
because one does not wear the *kṣepa*, the body is exposed; when people see this, they give rise to lustful thoughts. Regarding "losing the male organ":
the gender shifts to female, but upon subsequent regret, the original male organ is restored. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Duo lun), fascicle nine: "Whenever a bhikṣu bathes, if..."

Regarding the "exposed upper body": one must not cause distress to laypeople, and when covering the upper body, one must wear the *saṃkakṣikā*. (The commentary states: This refers to exposing the upper body with the *saṃkakṣikā*.
First, it is because of a sense of shame; second, it is because it gives rise to lustful thoughts in others.
For instance, there was an Arhat bhikṣu who was bathing. Another bhikṣu saw his body—fresh, pure, delicate, and soft—and immediately conceived a lustful mind.
Not long after he was born, his male organ fell away and a female organ appeared; he then abandoned the monastic life to become a layman and father children.

Later, he encountered [the monk] again and immediately recognized him. Knowing the origin of his condition, he returned with sincere devotion and, following the Arhat’s instruction to repent, applied himself with such purity that his male organ was restored.
Therefore, one should not expose one's form. Furthermore, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct:
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states that for both great bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras, the offense is equal to destroying a stupa made of the seven precious jewels;

encouraging others to leave the household life and practice with diligence brings merit equal to that of building a stupa (the above is from the treatise). Regarding "striking wood to make a sound" and so forth, Daoli (Daolilü) says:

"In the present day, when bathing the Sangha, since the permanent property (*saṃghika-vastu*) is being used, one must necessarily make a signal. Jing asked: "May one use the property of the Sangha for a bath every half-month? He replied: "It is permissible. This is from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The Vinaya contains explicit instructions: "If one is to bathe, first prepare the water and fire, then strike a wooden block to make a sound, so that all the monks may enter in succession.
If one were not permitted to use the property of the Saṃgha, why would it be necessary to signal them to enter in succession?
Furthermore, according to various Vinayas, bathing is a regular practice for the Saṃgha. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states there are five benefits to bathing: first, the removal of impurities.
Second, the purification of the two bodies; third, the removal of cold from within the body through bathing; fourth, the removal of wind disorders; and fifth, the attainment of peace and stability.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Jentākasūtra*, by bestowing seven items, one eliminates seven ailments and gains seven merits. The ritual procedures are detailed extensively in the *Jentākasūtra-ṭīkā*.

[This concludes] the section on "Waiting for the Explanation" (and so forth). However, the merit of bathing the Sangha is difficult to describe in full, as clarified in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (*Chidu lun*).
For instance, when the bhikṣu Nanda bathed the Sangha, he made a vow, saying: "May I be handsome and pure in every lifetime.
Furthermore, in another life, he encountered a Pratyekabuddha stūpa; he adorned it with colorful paintings and embellished the image of the Pratyekabuddha, and then made [a vow].
He made this vow: "May my physical form adorn my body in every lifetime.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he obtained an upright and handsome physique in every life, until today he was able to leave the household life and attain the Way.

When the assembly of monks saw him from afar, they took him for the Buddha and all rose to welcome him. The Pratyekabuddha Liangyan, having also bathed the monks, extensively made vows, thereby obtaining this karmic fruit.
Regarding the method for making earthenware, the established view is that one washes from the bottom upward in successive order.

This text from the *Ji* (Mahīśāsaka) is somewhat broad and differs from the *Sifen* (Dharmaguptaka). As for the statement "the rest is as explained in the lower fascicle," this refers to the detailed exposition found within the *Zazaoxing* (Essential Practices of Various Matters).
The Fifty-seventh Precept on Lighting a Fire: *Niti*. Regarding the two cases where there is no [valid] reason:
it is established that these refer to instances such as when one is ill, or when cooking food for the sake of a sick person.

As for "if another has already lit a fire and one subsequently performs any action," this means that after another person has finished lighting a fire in an open space, a bhikṣu subsequently approaches the fire, fans the flames, stirs the heap of embers, or adds fuel, and so forth.

For each individual act performed, a *pāyattika* offense is incurred accordingly. Regarding "one who requires fire for the sake of the body": this refers to one who, due to illness, relies upon fire to benefit the body;
thus it is said. If it is charcoal that is half-burnt, or if one does not say "I know" regarding such things, it is auspicious (*kṣema*) because it burns without flames.
Furthermore, if one causes another to light it, it is also auspicious if one does not utter the words "I know it is pure."

Regarding "whirling fire to form a wheel," Jingyun says: this refers to creating a circle of fire; even if it does not touch the ground, one commits an offense because one has willfully caused the fire to fall to the earth.
This simply means taking embers and whirling them through the air. Alternatively, if there is grass or wood within the fire and one gathers it together, one commits an offense.
Lili says: having seen another finish lighting a fire, one orders them to advance the flame, or one gathers and piles up sufficient fuel and so forth.

"Also. *Bō* (pronounced *bǔdá*) means "to reason" or "to apply logic. The *Guǎngpǐ* states that *bō* means "to remove. It is also said to mean "to reason," and furthermore, one obtains one *tí* [offense]. This establishes the clarification:
first, there is one *tí* for burning fire upon living grass, thereby destroying what is living; second, there is another *tí* for violating this precept on open ground;
and since there is yet another *tí* for damaging the earth beneath living grass, one thus incurs [these offenses]. Therefore, one obtains [the respective penalties].
Three *ti*. The precept on concealing another's robes and bowl (No. 58). In this text, three conditions complete the offense; for the [precept on] sharpening [tools], four conditions are required.
Adding one: "if there is no cause or condition. If there is a cause or condition, there is no offense. This applies if it concerns a robe of the five primary colors that is impure.
"An *āpatti of wrong-doing* (*dukkaṭa*) [is incurred] because these are not items that the Buddha has always permitted.

'If one keeps them after performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), one falls into [an offense]' means that if a bhikṣu merely declares a robe or bowl as purified, yet hides it, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The note says: 'According to current regulations, private ordinations are not permitted;

furthermore, this clarifies that based on the aforementioned [rules], even if one hides another's robe due to the two difficulties of life or the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), one incurs no offense.'"
"Since I have not committed an offense, and as I was privately ordained, I fear that if my master sees my robe he might hide it away and I would not wear it;
how then could this constitute a violation of the rules of decorum? Shen said, "Since the authorities do not permit private ordination, you must not wear [the robes].
Hide them elsewhere and stay outside for the night; you will not incur the offense of being separated from your robes overnight."
59. Truly Pure Precepts (*bhūta-śīla*). The Commentary states: "To renounce completely and without falsehood is called 'truly' (*bhūta*);
to forever sever defiled thoughts is termed 'pure giving' (*śuddha-dāna*); hence the name. This refers to personally presenting an object and performing a pure act of giving to another person.
Later, one might simply take [the item] without informing the owner; this is why it constitutes an offense.

Regarding the listing of the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*) in the root precepts (*śīla-mūla*), the *Lì* (Lì Míng) clarifies that a non-monk may perform "true purification" (*yathābhūta-pariśuddhi*) in the presence of the four lower assemblies, provided that it is performed face-to-face within the assembly itself.
Lì states: "According to the *Sudarśana-vinaya*, if there is a succession of donors, they may act as mutual donors for one another, because they do not face [the original recipient]."

Because the donor has performed the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), and furthermore, because the object is not handed over to that person, no fault of censure arises. This is for the sake of the Great Saṃgha obtaining [the item];
thus, the three lower assemblies and the nuns take the two assemblies of the Saṃgha as their respective successive donors. This is the true method of purification (*bhūta-śuddhi-dharma*).

The monks and nuns must act before the assembled community; two or three individuals may not perform these acts for one another. Although they wear the same black robes, men and women are distinct from one another.
How could it be appropriate for a *bhikṣu* to take an object and perform a ritual for a nun? Furthermore, this would allow for the arising of defiled attachments and invite external censure.

Regarding the listing [of the five groups] in the text: since these are the common precepts for both monks and nuns, the five groups are mentioned collectively because the text speaks of both monks and nuns.

As for the statement that this clarifies the meaning of transgression and non-transgression, Master Li states: the reason the five groups are listed in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is to clarify that all five groups possess the characteristics of transgression.
For example, if a bhikṣu has performed the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) with respect to another bhikṣu, it is a transgression not to inform him when returning; however, if he does inform him...
If one has already returned [the object] before taking it, there is no offense. This applies even down to the case of a śrāmaṇerikā;

if one has performed the *śuddhi-dāna* (purification-gift) in the presence of a śrāmaṇerikā, there is no offense in taking it provided one informs the owner at the time of taking it. To take it without informing them constitutes an offense; thus it is said. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"This is to clarify that all five assemblies possess the characteristics of offenses. Although they differ in gravity, the principle of *śuddhi-dāna* is the same; therefore, their names are listed collectively. As for the *śuddhi-dharma* itself..."
Regarding "distinguishing the characteristics according to the Vinaya for one who possesses full understanding": this refers to the explanations provided within the Vinaya itself.

As for "obtaining [the merit] whether the formal inquiry is made or not through successive pure gifts (*pariśuddha-dāna*)," this is because when performing the ritual act, one acts in relation to another person;
subsequently, when using the object, it is unnecessary to inquire of the original donor.

The Sixtieth Precept on Wearing New Clothes: To wear [new clothes] without cause. However, if one encounters circumstances such as being robbed, plundered, burned, or swept away by water, it is permitted to wear the five great primary colors.
If one first obtains them from another person, although they are called "new" by name, they are not considered such because their color is not yet according to the Dharma.
Regarding the rule that one must apply the three types of discoloration to the cloth before wearing it, this refers specifically to not applying the color blue.

"Black wood is dyed [with lacquer]. Bin says: 'In the Mahāsāṃghika and Daśabhāṇavāra Vinayas, for white-clad laypeople, it is merely an offense of transgression (duṣkṛta) and not a formal offense (pātayantika).

This is exactly the opposite of what is stated in this Vinaya. Regarding the fact that heavy and light robes may be kept without being formally purified (pariśuddhi) yet only result in an offense of transgression, Falin says:"

"Heavy" refers to items such as rugs, mats, and bedding; "light" refers to items such as cloth, silk, garments, and blankets. If one does not dye them, one incurs a *thullaccaya*; if one does not mark them, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*. Jing says:

"Heavy clothing refers to items such as woolen carpets and long-pile rugs; light clothing is understood by analogy. Regarding heavy clothing, failing to perform the ritual of purification (*visuddhi*) incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
The *Jieshu Chengfan* (The Commentary on the Precepts: Establishing Offenses) states: "In the first case, because one did not dye it with the three colors, one falls into a [grave offense]."
This clarifies that it refers specifically to the three robes (*tricīvara*). If heavy or light garments are not dyed with the [prescribed] colors and marked with dots, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Bin says: "Heavy garments" are winter clothes; "light garments" are summer clothes. Since these are not the three robes, they are subject to this rule.
All other minor or fine items must likewise be marked with dots for purification; this does not refer to leather shoes, which are further processed by dyeing them with the three colors.
This is a startling and most laughable view. Jingyun says that while the three robes and other garments must all be purified through dyeing, those made of silk need only be purified by marking them.
If it were not for robes, bowls, bags, leather sandals, and various towels, it would not be permissible to remain unpurified.
Lì says this refers to purification by marking; however, if one has not yet dyed one's robes and is staying with a layperson, Lì maintains that if [the robes] have not yet been...
One dyes it with a ruined color (kāsāya), fearing that white-clad laypeople might use it. The commentary states that "pure" refers to clothing that has been made into a colored garment.
My own interpretation is that once the ruined color has been achieved, it must still be further purified by marking (*parimārjana*).

The commentary says, "or by patching it with other materials," which clearly establishes that even if one patches the garment with other old materials to create a purification, it likewise constitutes purification; this refers to the purification by marking. Indeed...

When robes are obtained, regardless of whether they are new or old, all must undergo the three kinds of purification (*tri-vidha-pariśuddhi*). Since those first received from others are treated the same as new ones, the commentary states:
"This does not mean that only the three robes (*tricīvara*) must be dyed while the others need only be purified.

While it is true that the three robes must be dyed, all other garments must likewise be dyed to change their color (*rañjana-kāṣāya*) and furthermore must be marked with the *pariśuddhi* seal; it is not merely a matter of marking them directly.

This is all there is to it; that is, not staining it. Lüyì says: "According to the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya*, if one does not mark a pure-colored robe for purification, it is an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*);

if one does not stain a white robe that has become soiled, it is a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). This is the opposite of the present case: here, failing to stain it constitutes a transgression, while failing to mark it is merely a minor offense."
Regarding the reason why the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is pure: it differs from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and is distinct from the laity;

furthermore, because it possesses three kinds of purity, when a transgression occurs, it is easy to investigate. According to the *Pañcavargika*, there were certain bhikṣus who encountered bandits and had their robes completely stripped away.

When they returned, the local guards asked them, "Where did you encounter the bandits? They replied, "At such-and-such a place. Thereupon, the guards captured the bandits and brought them before [the bhikṣus].
The robes of the Bhikṣus, the robes of laypeople, and the robes of non-Buddhists were all placed in one location.

The guards ordered the Bhikṣus to take whichever they recognized as their own. However, the Bhikṣus did not recognize their own robes; consequently, the non-Buddhists first selected and took away the best ones.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "From now on, if you obtain new robes, you should [perform the *tri-kaṭhina* ceremony] three times..."

One should mark it with three colors: blue, black, or madder. If one does not mark it with these three colors, there is a *pāyattika* offense. If one does not mark it at all, for every instance of wearing it, there is a *pāyattika*;

for every night one sleeps while wearing it, there is a *pāyattika*. Regarding the "three marks," Master Li says they are blue, black, and madder; Master Jing says they refer to the "purification by marking" (*piṇḍa-śuddhi*).
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, the five great primary colors do not constitute a valid acceptance [of the robe], as they include blue, yellow, red, and so forth.

The white and black [colors] below describe their respective characteristics. Regarding "dyed with *loha-śā* (red ochre)": according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, fascicle eight, there are five primary colors, namely:
yellow, red, blue, black, and white. Yellow is dyed from the root of turmeric (*uragasāra*) or from indigo;
red is dyed from *eḍagaja* grass or *loha-śā*; blue is said by some to be indigo or antimony (*añjana*), while the origins of the others are not yet identified. These five—
"Great color. If one dyes it oneself, it is auspicious; however, if one makes a robe from it, it cannot be accepted [as a formal gift].

It is further stated: "Luo-sha dye" is a foreign method of dyeing that kills many insects; therefore, it is not permitted. Now, the dyeing methods of the land of Qin also kill many insects and thus fall within the category of the five major types of dyeing prohibited by the Great Precepts.
Li states: "Luo-sha dye" refers to dyeing with the blood of peacocks or parrots. It is also stated: [that it is so named because]...
This refers to the "growing hair" [robe] (the meaning is not fully established). If one dyes it oneself and it is auspicious, this refers to dyeing the five great superior colors oneself.

Regarding the statement that "acceptance is not accomplished," it means that if one takes these aforementioned five great colors and uses them to dye a robe for the three robes (*tricīvara*), the acceptance of possession is not accomplished;
the addition of the ritual formula (*vidhi*) is likewise not accomplished. As for "measured" and "unmeasured," this refers to [robes of] three *hasta* or five *hasta*.
Those below this [measurement] are also called "improper measure. If they exceed three or five cubits (*hasta*), they are called "proper measure.

This refers to the fact that one must not wear these five major primary colors. Regarding the statement, "If one wears them with spots, it is a *duṣkṛta* (this Vinaya prescribes a *pāyattika*)," Sengshen says:

"Regarding these five major colors, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, wearing them without spots constitutes a *pāyattika*; wearing them after having applied spots constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, even if one applies spots..."

That which has already been worn falls [into the category of] "returning to the ground" (pratyāpatti) because it is a large-colored garment. Regarding the three types that mutually constitute purification:
this means that blue, black, and madder-brown, when used in combination, constitute purification; if they are not pure, it constitutes a downfall (pāyattika).

Taking the five great superior colors and making them into "spot-purification" (tilaka-pariśuddhi) brings auspiciousness. As for "first purifying with water": Jing says that one first washes the newly obtained robe with water, and afterwards...
Purification is not required. Furthermore, having first performed the purification by marking (*tilaka*), one subsequently washes it with water;
once removed, there is no further need for marking. *Kauśeya* refers to that which first emerges from the mouth of the silkworm. *Kambala* is translated here as "fine woolen garment.

It is clarified that since the substance of these two types of garments is fine and soft, the Buddha permitted their use without dyeing or purification, fearing they might be damaged. However, one must simply...
"Cutting and marking are the two purifications. Jing said: "The items above are fine, soft garments; as the dye is coarse, there is fear that it might damage these clothes.
The Buddha therefore permitted the provisional use of the two purifications, such as cutting threads and marking. Once three or five threads have been cut away, it is called 'purified.
Later, when the dye is obtained, one must re-dye it; one does not simply remain unpurified after the two purifications are completed. According to the case:
The *Zhi* [Vinaya] says: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. There was a bhikṣu in the wilderness who had obtained a *kauśeya* garment and wished to dye it with a decoction.
The World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, stayed suspended in mid-air and asked the bhikṣu, "What are you about to do?
The bhikṣu replied, "I am dyeing a *kauśeya* garment. The Buddha said, "The *kauśeya* is soft and delicate, while the dye is coarse and harsh; it will damage this garment. From...
From this day forward, this *kauśeya* [silk] shall be prepared in two ways: purification by cutting the threads and purification by blue dyeing.
Furthermore, there was a monk from Vaiśālī who obtained soft *kṣaumapāla* (linen) and, wishing to dye it, boiled a dye solution.

The Buddha, again using his supernormal power, went to that place and instructed him as before (*etc.*). Regarding the phrase "covering copper vessels with fermented vinegar," etc., the following clarifies this.
There are three types of colors according to the Dharma. The first clarifies that saffron, turmeric, and so forth are non-Dharmic colors.
Copper vessels are blue-green. Fruit juices, clay, and the like are black. *Molana* (madder) constitutes the red color.

Regarding the phrase "using the aforementioned fruit to rub it on superior iron" and so forth, this refers to a garment dyed with *molana*. As for what substance is used to mark it as pure, it refers to the aforementioned fruit.
The juice serves as the purifier. Regarding "fruit juice," it refers to using *harītakī* fruit; it is also said that one may use *āmalaka* fruit.
It should be ground upon an iron surface. The commentary states: "This is the same as the *mūlana* bark mentioned in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Shen [Daoxuan] explains:

"The color of the paste resembles that of the *mūlana* tree found in the Shu region. Since the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was translated in the northern regions, this specifically clarifies the *mūlana* of the Shu region."

This is for the sake of the proper mūlana (dyeing/patching) color. Regarding cases where many small scraps of cloth are joined together in one place to form a patch, the established rule is as follows:
For example, when patching a garment, if two holes are separate from one another, each must be individually marked with the *jñapti* (purification rite).
If they are patched together in the same location, even if there are many fragments, it is sufficient to mark that single spot. If many scraps are joined to form a single garment, however—
Mark one point: there is attainment.
Regarding the precept against taking the lives of animals, number sixty-one—according to Master Guang’s nine sections, this corresponds to the sixth section.
It extends up to "traveling together with thieves," which comprises seven precepts clarifying the constant practice of distancing oneself from evil and cultivating compassion for all beings.
[He] acted. This refers to Kāḷudāyin shooting crows until they formed a heap; therefore, this precept was established. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Kāḷudāyin detested crows, saying:
"They have ten kinds of faults: first, stinginess; second, greed for food; third, brazenness; fourth, endurance of humiliation;
fifth, being infested with maggots; sixth, lack of compassion; seventh, covetousness; eighth, lack of satiety; ninth, hoarding; tenth, delighting in [evil]."

[Omitted]. Because these ten factors are present, [the offense] may be considered a killing. Regarding "having the four immeasurables as one's intention": these are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding "the five conditions being the same as those for the major precept on killing": first, it is an animal; second, the perception that it is an animal; third, the presence of the intent to kill; fourth, the application of the means;
and fifth, the severance of life, which constitutes the transgression.

Precept 62: Regarding the Prohibition Against Drinking Water Containing Insects. Regarding the phrase "the limits and divisions of the preceding precept," this refers to the preceding precept concerning the taking of animal life.

One commits that preceding precept only when the life of an insect is actually destroyed. This present precept provides a deeper safeguard; one incurs the offense simply by drinking water containing insects, without waiting for their lives to be severed.

Therefore, the Commentary states that this differs from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), which says that for every insect that dies, there is a separate *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

This refers to the offense incurred when insects are actually harmed. In this Vinaya, regarding water containing insects, the offense is established immediately upon drinking, without waiting for the insects to be harmed;
this belongs to the preceding precept on killing animals. First, regarding "water with insects" and second, "the perception of it as having insects":

according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the objective condition follows the mind, and thus the offense is light. If one consults the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong), however, the mind follows the objective condition; therefore, in that system, there are five permutations of objective conditions and perceptions.
The verses state: 1. Using water with insects that one perceives as having insects: a *thullaccaya*. 2. Using water with insects that one perceives as being without insects:
a *thullaccaya*. 3. Using water with insects while suspecting it has insects: a *thullaccaya*. 4. Using water without insects while perceiving it as having insects: a *dukkaṭa*.
It is auspicious to have doubts regarding water that is free of insects. If it is indeed water free of insects and one uses it with the perception that it is so, there is no offense.
Regarding the case of a person who died of thirst and was reborn in heaven to see the Buddha: according to the *Naiyāyika-vinaya* (鼻奈耶律), fascicle eight, it says: "The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus dwelling in the mountains deep within the realm of Kośala; they had never before seen the Buddha."
Constantly harboring a longing, they desired to see the Buddha. The two of them consulted together and set out on their journey to behold the World-Honored One.
It was during the month following spring; they encountered a vast wilderness where there was absolutely no water.

Their bodies were parched with thirst, so the two monks searched for water everywhere until they came upon a pool of clear water. However, the water was scant and teeming with insects. One bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣu, "Drink..."

This water contains worms. Having crossed this vast marsh, they were able to see the World-Honored One. One companion replied, "Having received the precepts of the World-Honored One, how could we ever violate them?
At that time, one person drank [the water] and the other did not. The one who did not drink passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Wearing a crown of a hundred jewels, he came to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and stood to one side. The Buddha—
He preached the Dharma to them, and they had already attained the vision of the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*). Those who had been drinking water arrived later;

the Buddha saw them coming from afar, removed his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and revealed his golden body, saying: "You are foolish people! Why do you gaze upon this body composed of the four great elements (*cāturmahābhūtika*)?
It is merely a mass of putrid matter. He who sees the Dharma sees my body. As for those who used tree leaves to wipe themselves, he said: "These are called 'dead leaves. If...
This refers to the offense of destroying living beings. Regarding the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*), which states that Śāriputra saw insects in the air:
according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Śāriputra, using his pure divine eye, saw insects in the air as numerous as the sands along a riverbank or the grains in a vessel—boundless and immeasurable.
Having seen this, he ceased eating for two or three days. The Buddha then commanded him to eat again; thus, there is a general prohibition established.
