Regarding "insect-water": this refers to what is visible to the naked eye and what is caught by a water-strainer; it does not refer to what is seen with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
As for the phrase "one must not be weary of inspecting," Jì explains that this is a colloquial expression of the northern people, where "roughly" is called *yànkè* (厭課).
Regarding "a large elephant making one circuit with a bamboo cart": according to the *Ji* (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*), one should observe this with a sincere mind;
it must not be too fast, nor should it be too long. It should be for the duration of a large elephant making one circuit, or for the duration of a bamboo cart making one circuit.
If there are no insects, one may use [the water]; if there are insects, one should strain it before using it. Jing says: "This refers to the time taken for one complete turn. One must not speak."
Regarding the instruction "do not kill or harm insects and the like": this is out of fear that the person might hold wrong views or have a natural disposition toward killing;

if they were told to refrain from killing, they would willfully disobey and continue to kill and harm based on their hateful nature. As for the phrase "not digested after seven days," the Upādhyāya said:
"Insects undergo a transformation every seven days; therefore, one should have them sent to a place where they do not digest for seven days, so as to avoid the fault of taking life."
Regarding the method for straining water, it is as described in the *Shizong ji* (Record of the Essential Precepts) concerning the ninety precepts;
the text is most worthy of study. One must not shout out, "There are insects in this [water]," as Sengshen explains: "The previous user formed the perception that there were no insects.

Because you shouted that they exist, you cause others to harbor doubt, thereby incurring the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave fault) or *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Therefore, I urge you to examine it yourself. The *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Essentials) cites the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), stating: [as follows].
There were several generals who, having been converted through the teachings of a nun, were dispatched by the king to lead an expedition. At the head of their bows, they all carried water-strainers;
if they encountered water containing insects, they would strain it before drinking. When the king heard of this, he was greatly incensed and said, "You have deceived me!

If you will not even drink water because of tiny insects, how can you possibly slay the enemy? The generals replied, "If an insect commits an offense, we shall deal with it accordingly; however, it does not [harm] the kingdom."
[It causes] harm. Therefore, one must strain it. The King was greatly delighted. At that time, when the generals reached the battlefield, some attained the *maitrī-samādhi*;
by entering into the power of loving-kindness, they broke the enemy's ranks. Sometimes they subdued them. (Commentary:

Based on this, straining water not only serves to protect life and prevent transgressions in the immediate term, but can also remotely give rise to the mind of loving-kindness and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Precept on Causing Distress through Doubt, Number Sixty-Three. First, regarding the intention behind the prohibition of causing distress through doubt:

The goal of those who have left the household life is to set their minds upon a distant objective, to devote themselves to the path until the end of their lives and the exhaustion of their existence. Now, by means of the six factors such as one's age and so forth, to cause others distress and harbor doubts, thereby obstructing their correct practice, constitutes an excessive offense of harm and affliction;
this is why it was prohibited. Regarding the fifth point, "the person before whom [the words] are heard": an offender is established when the person hears and understands them.

Lì asked: "If it is said that when a previous person hears and knows [the offense], they incur a transgression regardless of whether they are distressed or not, and that merely hearing it constitutes an offense, why does the text say 'for a short time they are unhappy'?
Answer: It is not that one must wait for unhappiness before the offense is committed; this is stated from the perspective of the one who causes the distress.
Even down to the intention of wishing to cause unhappiness, it does not mean that one must wait for the previous person to actually become unhappy for a short time.

Only then does the offense become established. This is certainly not the case when it first occurs at the time of hearing and knowing. Regarding the "six matters that cause affliction": first, the time of birth; second, the year;

third, receiving the precepts; fourth, the *karmavācanā*; fifth, committing the six groups of offenses; and sixth, committing offenses against the noble Dharma. Thus it is said. If one refers to the time of birth, the Vinaya text asks:
"What is meant by the time of birth? To which the doubter replies: "You were not such a person at that time."

Regarding "birth" and "years": the Vinaya text states, "When questioning about years, if one has doubts, it means saying, 'You are not that many years old,' or saying, 'You have not yet completed so many *vassa*s (rainy-season retreats). Regarding the receiving of the precepts, the Vinaya says:"

Regarding the question concerning those who harbor doubts about the arising of the precepts: it is said, "Since your age was not yet full at the time you received the precepts, and furthermore, the assembly within the boundary was divided, the receiving of the precepts was invalid.
If this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it means one should inform them: "At the time you received the precepts, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) was not successfully performed."
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is not accomplished. If one has committed an offense belonging to the six classes of transgressions, one says:

"You have committed a *pārājika*, or even a *duṣkṛta*. If one has violated the noble Dharma, one falsely says: "You have committed a superhuman state (*uttarimanuṣyadharma*). This matter originated from the group of seventeen questioning the group of six:
"What is called the first dhyāna? ... up to: what is the fourth dhyāna? What are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?"
[The questioner asks: "What is a *srotāpanna*? ... up to: what is an *arhat*? The group of six replied:

"What you have said constitutes a transgression of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); therefore, we say that you have violated the noble Dharma. Regarding these six matters, for each word one obtains one offense, and for all six words together one obtains six offenses of *thullaccaya*.
Because this causes others to fall into doubt and distress, leading them to be unhappy, it was established as a formal rule (*prajñapti*). It states: "If anyone uses..."
Regarding "speech permitted as in the Vinaya": this refers to cases where, upon hearing the words, the other person develops faith and does not give rise to doubt or distress;

such speech is permitted and constitutes no offense. Furthermore, for those who are by nature coarse and lack understanding of the nuances of language, or where the other person’s disposition is negligent and they fail to recognize the gravity of their words—fearing that their speech might lead them to transgress the human dharma—one may say to them: "What you have said constitutes an offense."
The intention behind this noble Dharma is to bring about reform; it is not intended to cause distress.
This concludes the sixty-fourth precept regarding concealing the gross offenses of others. As for why the preceding text does not permit one to hear of another’s gross offense: [it is because...]

This external protection was established out of fear that [the public] might develop a lack of faith and thereby bring harm and dishonor to the Buddha-dharma. Now, this internal protection is instituted to prohibit concealment, purifying the minds of the assembly and preventing transgressions from arising.
"First, 'a great bhikṣu'" distinguishes him from the other four assemblies. If a bhikṣuṇī conceals [an offense] among her own peers, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

if a bhikṣu conceals [an offense] for a bhikṣuṇī, it is also a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If he conceals [an offense] for the three lower assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the three lower assemblies conceal [offenses] among themselves...

This is also auspicious. Regarding the statement that "a hundred thousand [people] together cover one person," some say this means they cover him by passing the concealment from one to another; in such a case, the monk incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
However, if he does not have the intention to conceal it, once he has finished speaking to one person, he stops, and there is no further need to speak to others. This is the profound explanation.

When hundreds or thousands of people simultaneously and collectively conceal [an offense], each incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), for this is not a case of successive concealment (*pārampariya-paticchādana*). Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "If one confesses to another person, there is no offense.

From this, we know that successive concealment does not constitute [the full offense of] concealment (this point remains unclarified). Regarding the phrase "at that time, corresponding with a protective mind" (*cittena rakkhati*), the established view is as follows:

that which resides in the mind is called "protection" (*rakkhā*); that which resides in body and speech is called "precept" (*sīla*). When one encounters another's transgression, it is in relation to the precept...
When one confesses a transgression without concealing it, it is called being "in accord with the mind of protection" (*ārakṣa-citta*).

Now, for such a person who is fierce and evil, if one were to speak [of their faults], there would arise threats to life or obstacles to the holy life (*brahma-vihāra*). Since speaking now would not be in accord with the mind of protection, it is said that at this time one is "in accord with the mind of protection.
Whether one speaks or does not speak, it is simply because one knows the proper time that it is called being "in accord with the mind of protection."

Jingyun said: "One should preserve one's own root and not involve oneself in other matters. If one suspects that a matter is unresolved or unnecessary, even if the preceding person has committed an offense, if my own mind remains hesitant, I shall not declare it as a transgression.
Regarding the removal of coarse concealment and remaining offenses: this refers to the [offenses of] the lower three categories, for which one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). Lì asked:

"If one conceals another’s offenses of the upper two categories, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), whereas for the lower three categories, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For what reason is it so for oneself?"

Regarding the concealment of the seven groups [of offenses], as for why it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) when limited to a single grade: the answer is that concealing another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) causes harm to both oneself and the other;
therefore, it is serious. Concealing one’s own grave offense involves only self-harm. Since there is no harm to others in this case, it is treated as a *duṣkṛta*, the same as the lower category.
Regarding the two sections on concealing [offenses] from others, both are *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṃghāti). Why is it that accusing another based on these two sections involves degrees of gravity? Answer:

To falsely accuse someone of a grave matter results in severe punishment and causes permanent harm; because the distress inflicted is particularly deep, the first section is grave. To accuse another with a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (Nissaggiya Pācittiya) offense is a transgression that can be expiated;

since it does not result in permanent exclusion and the harm is slight, it is minor. As for citing the middle section regarding concealing from others, this is because [the concealment] was not disclosed to the community.

Regarding the principle of disciplinary punishment: since these are equally gross offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) that disrupt the harmony of the Saṃgha, they are equally classified as *pāyattika* (offenses requiring confession).

As for "concealing one's own offense," this refers to concealing any of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaṭ-naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, etc. that one has committed; the concealment itself constitutes one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Therefore, the Great Commentary (*Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states:

"Committing seven [offenses] results in seven [punishments], but concealing seven results in only one. Regarding the exclusion of the case where a nun conceals the offense of another: Master Li establishes that concealing the offense of a nun constitutes a *pāyattika*, whereas concealing the offenses of those in lower categories constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
65. Regarding those under age who receive full ordination: Although the prohibitions and obstacles are not limited to one, none are permitted to receive it.

As for the category of "obstacles," there is no sense in which the precepts can be obtained. The other various prohibitions differ in their nature and precedent, such as the requirements for robes and alms bowls.

To accomplish the Dharma, it is as follows: regarding the ten precepts, one may obtain the precepts or incur offenses; however, this is not the case with age. Being under the required age is a prohibitive obstacle;

once the age is reached, one obtains them. This principle allows for consideration: what urgent matter is there to treat the Dharma with such a frivolous mind and negligence? Therefore, it is irrational.
It causes others to receive [the precepts] in vain, and having already incurred a heavy offense of *pārājika*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: The Buddha asked the King, "The Prince’s age..."
Several times he was not permitted to enter the palace. The King said, "He has reached the age of twenty. The Buddha said, "I have likewise established a precept for my disciples:

when one has reached the age of twenty, one is granted the full ordination (*upasampadā*). This is explained in detail in the two volumes [of the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*] above and below, as well as in the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra*, the *Śrāmaṇera-prakīrṇaka*, and the *Vinaya-śāstra*.
Regarding the statement in the *Vinaya-śāstra* that there are two circumstances where both [the *śikṣamāṇā* and the *bhikṣuṇī*] are permitted, the former [the *śikṣamāṇā*] is more frequent.
The *Śāstra* states that those over sixty years of age may not be ordained; the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* (Sengqi) prohibits it for those over seventy.

Since these two texts appear contradictory, they are referred to as "the shield" (*mǒudùn*). Now, if one seeks to harmonize them—given that both are sacred teachings—one may employ either at will. However, one must observe the recipient:

even if they are over sixty, if they are still capable of performing the duties [of the Saṃgha], then despite contradicting the *Śāstra*, one should grant ordination in accordance with the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*. If...
"One who has passed sixty cannot perform the duties. According to the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, such a person cannot be ordained. Jì (Jie) says:

"The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* refers specifically to those above seventy based on their inability to perform duties, whereas the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* refers to those above sixty based on their lack of capability.

Now, when observing the candidate for ordination, one must determine whether they are capable or incapable. If they have indeed passed sixty yet remain capable, one may grant the ordination according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. If not..."
It is capable [of being applied]. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is not permitted; therefore, it is said that "the two sentiments both apply. Below, the non-offense rules are clarified.

Regarding the sixteen phrases concerning the opening for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the falling into an offense (*pātayantika*): Lì (Lìzǐ) says that based on whether the preceptor and the community of monks know or do not know, there are sixteen mental states with distinctions in the resulting offenses.
The Vinaya text fully contains these; as for the mention of "sixteen," it is provisionally based on the preceptor.
Above, there are four states of mind: first, knowledge; second, assumption; third, doubt; and fourth, ignorance. These four states of mind are auspicious.

Because the Upādhyāya clearly knows that the candidate has reached the required age, it is called "knowledge. When one has not yet reached the age but perceives only the outward signs and forms the intention that one must have reached it, this is termed "assumption.
To be hesitant and undecided is called "doubt. To have no understanding whatsoever is termed "ignorance."

The other members of the Saṃgha perceive that same object; the four mental states [of the Saṃgha] are likewise. Taking the four mental states of the Saṃgha in relation to the preceptor’s knowledge, there are four permutations:
first, the preceptor knows while the Saṃgha does not; second, the preceptor knows while the Saṃgha doubts; third, the preceptor knows while the Saṃgha is uncertain;
fourth, the preceptor knows while the Saṃgha is ignorant. These are the four permutations regarding the preceptor’s four [mental states].
*Tī*. There are two types of *dukkaṭa* (offenses of wrong-doing) for the Saṃgha: that is, the first and third phrases constitute a *dukkaṭa*, while the second and fourth involve no offense.

Next, taking the four mental states of the Saṃgha and correlating them with the preceptor’s mind, there are likewise four phrases: first, the preceptor says it, and the Saṃgha knows; second, the preceptor says it, and the Saṃgha says it;
third, the preceptor says it, and the Saṃgha suspects it; fourth, the preceptor says it, and the Saṃgha does not know it.

The preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is entirely without offense. The community of monks (*saṃgha*) is the same as in the preceding section. Next, one should apply the four mental states of the community of monks to the preceptor’s state of doubt;

these too can be understood through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The preceptor incurs four *thullaccaya* offenses, while the community of monks remains the same as before. Next, one should apply the four mental states of the community of monks...

Regarding the ignorance of the preceptor’s mind, there are likewise four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) to be understood. In the first permutation, the preceptor is entirely without offense; for the Saṃgha, it is as before.
Among these forty-six permutations, in the first and third sets of four permutations, the preceptor commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense);

in the second and fourth, the preceptor is without offense. Within the sixteen permutations concerning the Saṃgha, in each case, the first and third involve a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), while the second and fourth do not.
There is no offense. Question: Since the preceptor harbors a doubtful mind, the offense should be minor. Why, then, is it classified as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense)? Answer:

Previously, when receiving the precepts, the candidate had a physical body that could be examined; why did [the preceptor] not carefully examine them to ascertain the truth before conferring the precepts?

Now, harboring doubt while being arrogant regarding the Dharma, one confers full ordination (*upasampadā*), causing the candidate to fail to obtain the precepts and deeply distressing others. Therefore, the rule establishes that the offense is equal to that of the one who knows [the truth]. This should be verified against other calendars.
"Master" (*shù*) refers to one who examines names and exceeds others in their proficiency with calendrical arts; it is the Way (*dào*) and the Method (*fǎ*).

Just as in the current calendar, where months have varying lengths and intercalary months may precede or follow, the encroachment of yin and yang upon the seasonal signs is in truth difficult to discern—this is what is called "arts.

"Calendar" (*lì*) refers to the calendar days themselves. To display these to people constitutes the principle of the calendarist (*lìjiā*); thus it is termed "arts. To not display them to people [is not so].
Furthermore, I once questioned Du Sheng of South City, who also said that regarding the other [text], there were previously two interpretations.

As for what is called "calendrical technique" (*lìshù*), Du Sheng said: "Technique" (*shù*) refers to calculation (*huàn*). It is a system of calculation used to reckon the numbers of days and months.
For instance, the twenty-four solar terms correspond to the seasonal nodes of the four seasons; yet those who enter [this field] are all ignorant of them. This is why...

However, it is thus called a "method" (*shu*). Furthermore, another interpretation is that "examining others" refers simply to examining and comparing the calendrical systems of other masters (this constitutes two interpretations).
Regarding the phrase "Although I understand it thoroughly," Jì says: This is the master’s intention as expressed in the *Chao* [the *Xingshi chao*]. He states:

"Although I possess a complete knowledge of the Vinaya and the calendar, if I were now to provide a detailed exposition, how could later generations fully comprehend it? Therefore, I shall not trouble myself to describe it exhaustively; I will briefly cite a single phrase."

Regarding those who have erroneously interpreted this since ancient times: The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Ancient interpreters said that when receiving the precepts, if both the secular age and the days and months were few, the fetal period and intercalary months were not included;
only when the secular age was full but the days and months were not, would the fetal period and intercalary months be included. Our current interpretation is not so:

one simply counts the fetal period and intercalary months until the twenty years are complete; even if the secular age is not yet full, there is no offense in including them. Polished [by Zhili] as well.

This is not accepted. Furthermore, it is said that this country uses a calendar in which an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) occurs every three years, formed by subtracting days from small months (meaning that the occurrence of "large" and "small" months results from accumulating one day from each small month to form an intercalary period).
This is not the correct theory and does not accord with common practice; it has been examined against other calendrical systems and found to be incorrect.

Regarding the distinction between the solar day (*jīrì*) and the intercalary month (*rùnyuè*), Lì says: "If the intercalary month exists because of small months, then even three years would still be insufficient.
He explains that because the sun completes its circuit through the heavens, these twelve months leave a remainder of eleven days; thus, there is an intercalary month.

(This means that within one year, the sun traverses three degrees beyond the full circuit of the heavens, which constitutes one year. There are twelve months, yet they remain eleven days long. These surplus days are accumulated to form the intercalary month; therefore, within three years, thirty or more days have been accumulated.)

This constitutes one intercalary month (occurring because the sun moves slowly while the moon moves swiftly). It is further said: "One must certainly harbor doubt regarding the subsequent [calculation] before the allowance (*anujñā*) is opened.

Previously, it was asked because [the candidate] was young; now, it is likewise not the same. This opening permits the attainment of the precepts; it does not mean that this essential karmic substance is obtained only after the calculation has been performed.
Rather, it arises at the time of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* on the ordination platform. The present opening of the calculation is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.

Regarding whether one attains [the precepts], it is not by means of calculation alone. Therefore, we know that when the years are completed through the accumulation of lunar months and intercalary days, this is logically the fulfillment of the required age; thus, it is said that one attains the precepts. Now, first let us calculate:

if one is born on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month and receives the precepts on the first day of the first month upon reaching twenty years of age according to the calendar, their actual age is as follows: [Note: The original text appears to be a fragment from a Vinaya commentary (e.g., the *Shishi yaolan* or similar), discussing the determination of the age for ordination (*upasampadā*).

It argues that the attainment of the precepts depends on the completion of the full term of years, including intercalary months, rather than a mere count of solar or lunar months. The final sentence indicates a calculation of the actual age based on a specific birth date and ordination date.]
Eighteen years and two days. Master Li says: "The day prior to birth is counted as one year; the day one receives the precepts is counted as one year.

These are both cases of "empty years" (nominal years). Now, first calculating from the time in the womb: however, it is discussed that the duration of receiving the vital breath is generally indefinite.
For example, Rāhula was in the womb for six years, while the Bhikṣu Śrīgarbha was in the womb for sixty years; there are also other such cases.
In the fifth month, there are cases where a child is born after being in the womb for only one year; however, these cannot be taken as the standard rule.

Following the majority of accounts, both secular and monastic texts establish nine months as the fixed duration of gestation. How is this known? As stated in the *Pañcarājāsūtra* (Five Kings Sutra): [text follows].

In seven weeks, the human form is completed. It is said that at each seven-day interval, the embryo undergoes a transformation: in the first week, it is like thin curd; in the second week, like thick curd;
in the third week, like solidified butter; in the fourth week, like a mass of flesh; and in the fifth week, the five fetal membranes are fully formed.
After six or seven days have passed, the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) unfold. Thus, while in the womb, there are a total of thirty-eight rotations, with each rotation lasting seven days;

this amounts to two hundred and sixty days. Now, calculating by way of nine months—assuming one month consists of thirty days—the nine sets of thirty days constitute three nines, which makes twenty-seven, totaling two [hundred and seventy days].
One hundred and seventy days; however, because there are four "small" months within the nine months, one obtains only two hundred and sixty days.
It is clear, therefore, that this is identical to the thirty-eight rotations, and that the actual time spent in the womb is nine months.
From within the nine months, the fetus shares the same vital breath as its mother; that is, its exhalation and inhalation are identical to those of the mother.

Approaching the time of birth, four days beyond the nine months, the fetus' breath becomes distinct from the mother's (meaning that at the point of imminent delivery, when the mother exhales, the child inhales, and when the mother inhales, the child exhales;

this causes the mother’s abdomen to ache). When these four days have ended, it is born. Thus, it receives an additional four days, remaining in the womb for nine months and four days. This concludes the preceding section.
The second day of the eighteenth year totals the sixth day of the ninth month of the eighteenth year. Regarding the calculation of intercalary months, even these are not fixed;
for example, King Bimbisāra added an intercalary month every six years, whereas nowadays one is added every three years.
However, we do not actually require three years [for each intercalary month] now; rather, by using thirty-three months alternately, one obtains one intercalary month.

For the time being, let us calculate based on the number of nineteen years, which yields seven intercalary months. This refers to having one intercalary month every three years, three intercalary months every nine years, two intercalary months every five years, and four intercalary months every ten years;
thus, there are seven intercalary months. That is to say, it stops at one intercalary month every three years and three intercalary months every nine years.

In five years there are two intercalary months; in ten years there are four. Thus, there are seven reasons [for this calculation], which means that the cycle is limited to nineteen years and divided into two segments.
The first nine years constitute one segment, which contains three intercalary months. The subsequent ten years are further divided into two segments, each consisting of five years.
Within each five-year period, there are two intercalary months, thus resulting in four intercalary months [in the second decade].

Combined with the preceding first section, this totals seven intercalary months. However, based on what has come before, after a full nineteen years, there are only eighteen years, nine months, and six days;
yet we have provisionally treated it as nineteen years. Thus, by subtraction, two months and twenty-four days are lacking.
Now, having subtracted three days from within the intercalary month, only six intercalary months and twenty-seven days remain. This concludes the point.
The闰家 (Rúnjiā) [calendar] places it on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month; when combined with the aforementioned items, it totals the third day of the fourth month of the nineteenth year.

Regarding the inclusion of an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) within this nineteen-year cycle, there is no textual authority in the various Vinayas; however, the local calendar does include such a nineteen-year cycle.
This totals fourteen days, referring to the fourth month of the nineteenth year above. When expanded, these altogether constitute two hundred thirty-two months.
These are divided into four large sections, with forty-nine months allocated to each section.
Thus, the four sections together comprise one hundred ninety-six months, leaving thirty-six months remaining. Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned four...
Within the section consisting of nineteen months, it is further divided into two parts: taking thirty months as one section and the nineteen months as another section.
From within the nineteen-month section, one *bimba* (orb) of the Great Sun is extracted; furthermore, within the thirty-month section...
Furthermore, within the two segments, there are fifteen months each.
From one of these fifteen-month periods, one extracts one *pinda* (a large day), and together with the one day from the preceding nineteen-month segment, a total of three days is obtained.
Since three days are obtained from one of the four great forty-nine-month segments, the same applies to the remaining three great segments; thus, a total of ten [days] is obtained.
Two days. Furthermore, there remain thirty-six months from the previous period;

among these, another *bhinna-dvika* (double-large) day is extracted, which, together with the previous twelve days, totals fourteen days (a month being termed *bhinna*—or "double"—whether it consists of two or three large [thirty-day] months).
This brings the total to nineteen years, four months, and seventeen days. Next, regarding the calculation of the fourteen-day *poṣadha*, there are ten [days] prior...
In the fourth month of the ninth year, one extracts [the days].

Since a year consists of twelve months—six being large and six being small—one extracts six days from each small month and two sets of six days (twelve days) from each large month; thus, three times six makes eighteen days.
Having obtained eighteen days in one year, one obtains one hundred and eighty days in ten years.
Nine years plus ninety days: eight times nine is seventy-two. This totals one hundred and sixty-two days.
Together with the previous period, this amounts to three hundred and forty-two days. There remain four months, consisting of two large and two small months, which yield another six days.
Adding these to the previous total, they combine to form three hundred and forty-eight days. Twenty-eight days are used to constitute one [unit].
The moon completes three hundred and sixty days as twelve months, forming one year; there remain twelve days.
Adding these to the previous seventeen odd days results in one month and one day.

Continuing this addition for twenty years, there still remains five months and one day. These remaining days contain what is called the "empty" or "intercalary" month; thus, there are still five [months] remaining.
Regarding the "first day of the month": among these five months, there is an intercalary *poṣadha* day that is added as an empty increment, resulting in several extra days.
This means that within the five months, the *poṣadha* intercalary day is included; this is an empty day. Now, by including this empty day, it is increased to become the first day of the fifth month.
Therefore, when one reaches nineteen years of age, one may receive the precepts on the thirtieth day of the seventh month. This is why [it is so].
Regarding those who receive the precepts on the ninth day of the eighth month: this is because the fifth month begins on the first day.
Since both [the months] take twenty-eight days as their duration, this "five-month" school allows it to be said:

"Since you are nineteen years old and received the precepts on the thirtieth day of the seventh month, you have not yet completed a cycle through my 'first day of the fifth month. How can you claim [to have fulfilled the requirement]? Thus, they exclude my five [days].
The first day of the month is a *poṣadha* day. If you have not yet completed five months and you nevertheless count [the days] as such, you should still receive the precepts;
once they are finished, one should ask, "Do you have the summer retreat (*varṣā*)? For this reason, nine more days are returned to him.
Consequently, it is only on the tenth day of the eighth month that he finally receives the precepts. These five days are then returned to him as *poṣadha* days.

Furthermore, another four months are spent returning to the *rūṇa* (intercalary) family. According to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), one returns to the *trayodaśī* (thirteenth day) on the thirteenth day;
on the eighth day, one returns to the *poṣadha* family; and on the fifth day, one returns to the *rūṇa* family. Thus, by the fourteenth day of the eighth month, one merely obtains the precepts.
As for the statement that "this [calculation] contains empty additions and the like," it means that this first day of the fifth month is reckoned as an empty acquisition, because it is empty.
Because of these calculations, the inclusion of intercalary months and the frequent occurrence of the fourteenth-day *poṣadha* (full moon) cannot be accommodated; therefore, it is now reduced.
Previously, on the first day of the fifth month, [the calculation] was thirteen days [ahead], leaving only the eighteenth day of the fourth month remaining.

According to this, for one born toward the end of the year who has reached nineteen years of age, they should receive [ordination] in advance on the twelfth day of the eighth month. If the frequent occurrence of the full moon (*pinda-mahā*) is entirely removed...
Four days later, he received [the precepts] on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month.

As for the current *Chao* (Excerpts) stating that he received them on the ninth day of the eighth month, this remains unclear. Regarding the statement that, according to actual calculation, his age was nineteen until the eighth day of the eighth month:
if one adds five months and one day to this, his age would reach twenty. Lì states that thirty days constitute one month.
This refers to the actual moon; therefore, it is said to be "according to reality. It must still return to the ninth day, hence it is called "retrogression" (*apacaya*).
Regarding the seven days added within the eighth month, Jing says: "The first day of the fifth month fulfills the 'empty month. Why is it called an empty month?
Because all *poṣadha* ceremonies are held on the fourteenth day. Now, if [the month] were nineteen days long, it would be the eighth month."
The recipient is indeed the true moon. Regarding those in various schools who obtain the precepts despite being underage:

according to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), specifically in the section concerning the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one is under twenty years of age but does not personally know it, or forgets and is unaware of it, and the Sangha asks whether they are of age and they answer that they are, they obtain the precepts;
if they answer that they are not, they do not obtain them. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one is under twenty, for the most part it is said that there is no offense.
"Half" refers to one who is not yet full [of years]; this is called "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*). "Both" refers to one who is not yet full; this is not called "receiving ordination.
This may be sought in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), etc. (so forth).

The Sixty-sixth [Section] on the Precepts Concerning the Arising of Disputes. First, regarding the four matters of dispute (*adhikaraṇa*): there are four types of disputes. First, dispute by speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*).

Second, dispute by investigation (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*). Third, dispute by offense (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*). Fourth, dispute by legal procedure (*kicca-adhikaraṇa*). Commentary on the names of these four disputes:

First, as for "dispute by speech," since principles do not manifest themselves spontaneously, they must rely on speech to be revealed. By carefully evaluating right and wrong and determining what is correct and what is erroneous, the disputing words of both parties ultimately result in discord.
Anger is called "dispute" (*adhikaraṇa*). Since dispute arises from speech, it is termed "verbal dispute. The Vinaya states that there are eighteen legal matters (*dharmas*) concerning disputes:

whether it is a *dharma* or a non-*dharma*, whether it is *vinaya* or a non-*vinaya*, and so on, up to whether it is a legitimate statement or an illegitimate statement. To dispute in this manner, with both parties contending against one another, constitutes a verbal dispute.
Second, regarding the "dispute for investigation" (*anveṣaṇādhikaraṇa*): internally, there are three roots by which one investigates prior offenses and, based upon them, brings a formal charge.
They went before the Saṃgha, and thus a dispute arose. Because the dispute originated from seeking [faults], it is called a *paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*.

In the Vinaya, when one seeks out the offenses of a bhikṣu by means of the three types of formal accusations—namely, regarding violations of the precepts (*śīla*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and conduct (*ācāra*), based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected—it is a dispute over seeking out offenses;

hence it is called a *paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*. Third, as for the dispute over transgressions (*āpatti-vivāda*): when the conditions are complete and an offense is committed, it is termed a "transgression. A dispute arises from the evaluation of that transgression.
Therefore, it is called a dispute concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*). The Vinaya says: "What is a dispute concerning offenses?

Committing the seven types of transgressions, from *pārājika* down to *duṣkṛta*, constitutes a dispute concerning offenses. Regarding the fourth type, the dispute concerning matters (*vastu-adhikaraṇa*):

when one hundred and thirty-five types of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) have already been initiated, and because the specific details of the matter are evaluated and lead to resentment, it is called a dispute concerning matters. The Vinaya says: "What is a dispute concerning matters?"

Matters arising from disputes over speech (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*), matters arising from disputes over accusations (*adhikaraṇa-anuvāda*), and matters arising from disputes over offenses (*adhikaraṇa-āpatti*) constitute "disputes concerning matters" (*vastv-adhikaraṇa*).

This is because disputes arise regarding the formal procedures (*karmavastu*) within these three types of dispute. The terms "dispute over speech" and "dispute over accusation" receive their names based on their respective causes.
This means that this dispute arises from seeking [a resolution]. Regarding the dispute over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), the name is established based on the object;

that is, this dispute arises from deliberating over an offense. Now, to briefly explain the names of the four types of disputes once more: they are called "disputes" (*vivāda*) because they involve words concerning principles.
That which consists of verbal dispute is *vāda-vivāda*. That which consists of seeking out the faults of others and thereby giving rise to anger and contention is *anveṣaṇa-vivāda*.

That which consists of committing an offense and thereby causing anger is *āpatti-vivāda*. That which consists of the matter of one hundred and forty-five types of *karmans* being contested as to whether they have already arisen or not is *adhikaraṇa-vivāda*.
Because these disputes arise, the Saṃgha employs seven medicines to pacify them harmoniously; yet the group of six bhikṣus subsequently incited them once again.

It is said that because [the monks] previously failed to observe correctly when [a conflict] was about to cease and failed to extinguish it properly, there arose disputes where none had existed before, and existing disputes were not eliminated.
For this reason, the Buddha established the precepts.
Precept 67: Agreeing to Travel with a Thief. Regarding "exceeding the limit": if one travels through even a single village boundary, there is the offense of exceeding the limit;

if one has not yet passed through a single village, it is not termed "exceeding the limit. As for "agreeing to travel with a debtor," failing to repay a debt is indeed part of the thief's sphere of influence;
therefore, agreeing to travel with such a person incurs the minor offense of *kṣudra-āpatti*. Master Yuàn states: [text continues].
If one agrees to travel with a female thief, two *thullaccaya* offenses are incurred: first, for agreeing to travel with the woman; second, for agreeing to travel with the thief.
According to the *Cīvaravastu*, it is likewise.

Precept Sixty-Eight: Refraining from Adherence to Evil Views Despite Being Admonished. Based on Master Guāng’s nine sections, this begins with the seventh section, extending up to "not lending an ear.
There are six precepts here that clarify the practice of profound faith, understanding, and respectful compliance with the teachings.

Regarding the definition of the name: that which opposes principle and extinguishes goodness is called "evil" (*akuśala*); that which penetrates through with perverse views is termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); and that which is stubbornly clung to...
To reject the Sangha is called "defying admonition. This meaning is clear.
Regarding the seventy-first precept on rejecting exhortations to train in the precepts, Master Li says: Former commentators explain that there are two types of "private admonition.

The former refers to not accepting admonition regarding an offense already committed; this is the person who violates through action. This present precept on rejecting exhortations refers to the person who violates through cessation [of practice]; for its sake...

The admonitions do not exceed the two modes of action: abstaining and acting; thus, two precepts are established in total. However, the current interpretation is not so. To speak according to the principle:

refusing what is improper and violating an admonition—furthermore, if one says, "I will not train in this precept now," it does not necessarily mean that one has ceased from the dharma or committed an offense.
Therefore, the text states: "I shall question other bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya. For this reason, I shall now provide another explanation regarding the private admonition.
This is a single offense, encompassing seven categories; its meaning extends to both prohibitions and prescriptions (referring to the previous precept on disobeying another’s admonition).

This present precept concerns one who treats others with contempt and refuses instruction; therefore, it is established as a *pāyattika* offense. Thus, the text states: "I will not now train in this precept."
When he questioned other holders of the Vinaya, and when the bhikṣus of the Pañcavargika group alone admonished him, saying, "You repeatedly violate the precepts;
do not engage in such conduct, for you betray the faithful offerings of others," the group of six replied, "We do not study this as being the precept.

We shall first question those who uphold the Dharma and Vinaya whose wisdom surpasses yours. It was on account of this that the Buddha established the precept. According to the intent of this passage, however—
To repeatedly violate the precepts is also something that must be studied; this principle applies to both prohibitions (*saṃvara*) and prescriptions (*vidhi*).

If one simply refrains from studying these precepts with the intent to focus exclusively on prohibitions, this should be termed the "precept against treating others lightly and refusing their instruction.

Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* statement that the four matters lead to each respective *pārājika* offense, Sengli (Saṅgharakṣa) asserts that these are precisely the four grave offenses (*pārājika*). As for why he says, "I do not study [them]," it is because...
Regarding the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: there are five types of persons to whom one should not explain the *vinaya*. As checked in the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they are:

first, those who inquire merely for the sake of testing; second, those who inquire without doubt; third, those who do not inquire out of remorse for their transgressions; fourth, those who inquire with verbal reproach; and fifth, those who inquire while refusing to accept the words [of instruction].
The opposite of these five types may be explained as follows: namely, not inquiring through testing; having a question regarding doubt; inquiring out of remorse for what has been committed;

and not inquiring through interrogation. I now cite this passage merely to provide a general and broad overview; it does not specifically pertain to the subject and object within this particular precept.

Seventy-two cases of violating the *vinaya* precepts: If it is said that one falls [into an offense] for everything that follows the Sūtras and Vinayas, this refers to violating the Vinaya that follows the Sūtras, such as the *Śālistamba-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and others.

Regarding the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* establishes that the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts is contained within the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (the Preface to the Precepts).
Therefore, if one reviles or disparages the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra*, one also falls [into an offense]. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra*.

It is said: "If one recites the *Śikṣāpada-uddāna* (the Prologue to the Precepts) and disparages it as 'trifling,' this is also a *pāyattika* offense. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* asks: "The *Śikṣāpada-uddāna* is not itself a precept;

why does disparaging it also incur an offense? The answer is: "The *Śikṣāpada-uddāna* explains the meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts. If one disparages the *Śikṣāpada-uddāna*, [one incurs an offense]."

This is equivalent to reviling all precepts, and for this reason one incurs an offense. Lì asked: "If reviling the *vinaya* constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), while reviling other sūtras results only in a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), why is this so?
The answer, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, is that there are four reasons why it is grave:

first, the precepts are the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues arise; second, all disciples of the Buddha abide in reliance upon the precepts; third, they are the path leading to *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the initial gateway: if one lacks the precepts, there is no means by which one can enter the city of Nirvana.

These four precepts are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma; they adorn the Buddha-dharma. Because possessing these four meanings constitutes a power superior to that [other practice], the offense of their destruction is grave.
Since the sūtras do not contain this specific meaning, the offense is therefore light. As for other sūtras, the traditional interpretation states that they refer to the sūtras of the Hīnayāna.
Sūtra: If one slanders the Mahāyāna, the transgression is extremely grave. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The *sūtras* speak from the perspective of the Hīnayāna;
the gravity of the offense in the Mahāyāna cannot be determined by mere comparison. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "When such a person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell for a full kalpa.
When that kalpa ends, they are reborn again; thus revolving through countless kalpas, [they remain] from hell..."
[If one] departs [from this], one shall fall among the animals (and so forth). Regarding the term "Sūtra" (*kīya-āgama*): "Kīya" means "to accord with" (pronounced with the departing tone).
This refers to the Buddha’s teaching of this Dharma; because it accords with principle and accords with the capacities [of sentient beings], it is called a Sūtra.

As for those who first study the *Abhidharma* and so forth, Master Li states that if one does not harbor the intention to destroy the Dharma, even if one recites the Sūtras first and the Vinaya later, there is no offense. However, once the illness has been cured, one should recite the Vinaya and so forth.

As for this, the established view is that if one has completed receiving the precepts but encounters illness such that one cannot recite the Vinaya, and only recites it once the illness has subsided, one does not violate this precept.
This was stated previously; the seventy-third precept concerns the fear of being accused. Furthermore, Master Yuàn of the [Vinaya] School named this the "Precept on Pretended Reverence" (詐敬張戒).
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) and the *Lishu* (Commentary on the Whetstone) designate this as the "precept against not listening attentively to the Dharma. They state:

"If one is not listening attentively, why would one say, 'I have only now come to know [this]'? Furthermore, since lack of attention resides within the internal mind, how could a bhikṣu verify that another had previously heard it?
If one were not listening attentively, one should be permitted to listen again; however, according to various Vinayas and treatises, they mostly address this in terms of [not listening].

Regarding the summary of the offenses: since it is stated in both the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and the *nidāna* that one should speak out of fear of being accused, and because in the *nidāna* it is said that one who knows of their own offense and fears its exposure first goes to the water's edge to listen, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "I have only now come to know."
I reckon that my previous actions may have involved some transgression. Therefore, within the text, one examines the matter according to the Dharma.

As for the present statement, "fearing that [the offense] will be raised," this means that since a transgression exists, one fears that others will accuse and bring it forth; thus, there is no voluntary confession. Hence, it is called "fearing that [the offense] will be raised.
This refers to first claiming, "I have such a fault," whereas previously one claimed to be without guilt, and only now does one admit the transgression, and so forth. Thus it is established.

It is said: "This person, having already committed an offense, later hears the recitation of the precepts and immediately says, 'Previously I did not know that by doing such-and-such a thing, I had committed such-and-such an offense.
Fearing that the Sangha will not censure or discipline him, he says, 'I only now realize this; this dharma comes from within the Sūtra of Precepts,' and so forth.

Therefore, the author of the *Chao* (the Vinaya Commentary), based on the intent of this precept, establishes the offense of ignorance resulting from a failure to study, stating: [The text continues with the formal conclusion of the rule.]
This refers to *ti* (negligence). Furthermore, there are those who do not accept the position held by Nanshan; the reasoning behind this is difficult to examine in detail.

If one follows the *Lì shū* (Commentary by Senglì), it states that when this precept mentions "further increasing the *pāyattika*," it refers to negligence (*ti*) due to failing to pay attention, rather than implying that one incurs a *pāyattika* through ignorance.
Although Master Gao’s statement—that Nanshan’s claim that one incurs a *pāyattika* through ignorance also possesses its own logic—is correct, the current text of the Vinaya precept...

The *Benzhong* (Original Section) states: "Because of ignorance, it is a *pāyattika*. In the subsequent detailed explanation (*guangjie*), it further states: "Because of ignorance, [the offense] is again a *pāyattika*.

According to these texts, it appears that a *pāyattika* is incurred due to ignorance. Since it says "again" (*chong yu*), it is clear that this is a *pāyattika* for ignorance, which is not subsumed under the "not listening" category;
there is a separate *pāyattika*. The intention of the commentators (*shujia*) differs from that of Nanshan.

This is the explanation. Regarding the phrase "the four, three, or two assemblies are as in the first sentence," this means that if one can recite five sections (*pañcavargika*), or according to one's ability, four sections, three sections, down to the *Nidāna* (Introductory Section), it is "as in the first sentence. As the commentary above states, this refers to the five sections;
however, in the present case, it refers to four sections, three sections, two sections, and so forth. One must not engage in seated meditation or idle talk while doing so.

Establishing the Clarification. When the formal recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) takes place, one must listen with single-minded attention; one must not practice seated meditation (*dhyāna*) or other such activities therein.
This concludes the seventy-fourth rule concerning regretting the precepts after participating in a *karmavācanā*. According to Master Kuang’s nine sections, this is the eighth section.
From here until the rule against groundless accusations of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, there are seven rules that clarify dwelling together in peace, happiness, and harmony.
Do not follow these two views. Regarding the first condition, that the object must be a gift obtained by the *saṃgha*:
Lì (Lìzuò) says it must be a gift obtained by the *saṃgha*, not referring to property belonging to the permanent *saṃgha* (*zhǒngcháng sēngwù*).

If one uses the clothing, furs, grain, silk, fields, or groves belonging to the permanent *saṃgha* to reward those who manage affairs, both the giver and the receiver incur an offense. Zhǐ (Zhìshì) says this refers to items that may be divided among the assembly of monks. (10)
"Reciting" refers to the statement that the property belonging to the Saṃgha should be divided and given as a reward to those who have served as administrators.

"Not giving consent regarding the precept" (75): when there is business and one goes after having given consent, it means that once the matter has been discussed and the consent (*chanda*) has been declared, one may then depart.
Regarding "not giving consent for what requires three *karmavācanās*": this refers to cases where, although one has a personal reason [to leave], one must nevertheless [remain].

Regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*): if one leaves without having granted consent and exits the door, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense. If one returns and exits again, one commits another *thullaccaya*. If on open ground one leaves more than one *vyāma* (fathom) away from the Sangha, it is a *thullaccaya*.
Having already left, if one returns and then leaves again by more than one *vyāma*, one commits another *thullaccaya*; therefore it is said that for every exit there is a separate *thullaccaya*.

As for the "three *karmas*," these refer to the single motion (*ñattī*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*). This applies within the building as well.

Regarding "going out," Jingyun says: This refers to stepping outside the boundary of the enclosure, which constitutes an offense; it does not mean going beyond the eaves. This is because the area under the eaves is not included within the definition of a "room.
Regarding "leaving the ground by one *zhang* (approx. 10 feet) incurs a *thullaccaya*," Lì says: A monk with supernormal powers who leaves the ground by four finger-widths incurs a *thullaccaya*.
According to current regulations, this fault is exempted. Regarding "listening to others recite the scriptures or receiving the scriptures," Lì states: The assembly...

When in a gathering of people, one may leave while listening to the sutras without informing others; this is deemed auspicious (*kṣema*). Regarding the phrase "in the midst [of the assembly], one stops and engages in other talk," Jing says:
"If one engages in other talk during a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), there is no offense.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu listens to many bhikṣus preaching the Dharma, expounding the *vinaya*, or reciting the sutras, he should inform them when he departs; otherwise, he must rise. If they are reciting, he should stop; if they are performing [a ritual], he should cease.

There is no offense for speaking otherwise. Furthermore, if one listens to another bhikṣu receiving instruction in the sūtras, or listens to another bhikṣu reciting the sūtras, one should inform [the presiding monk].
To depart without informing him constitutes a *vyatikrama* (transgression). Regarding "a śrāmaṇera being among them" and so forth:

according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if the Saṃgha is not performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to settle a matter, or if a private room is settling a matter, a śrāmaṇera may be present therein. If he rises and departs, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
"Luó (meaning that one incurs an offense against a *bhikṣu*, not an offense against a *śrāmaṇera*). Lì states: 'Since no *karmavācanā* was performed, there was a *śrāmaṇera* present in the assembly;

if the *śrāmaṇera* left abruptly, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, upon examining the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, this is not the case; it merely refers to a *duṣkṛta* offense against the *saṃgha* of great monks (*mahā-bhikṣu*)."
76. The Precept on Regretting After Granting Consent (*yuyu yi huijie*). The commentary states: "If the matter is indeed true," according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun), fascicle 8:

"If the entire monastic community performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that is contrary to the Dharma, and at that time one lacks the power to change or alter it, yet remains silent and does not protest, there is no offense in subsequently saying it was improper."
The seventy-seventh precept on eavesdropping during the settlement of the four types of disputes:

Regarding "the former person deliberating in private," this refers to a situation where one intends to settle a dispute in a secluded place, yet before the bhikṣu has heard it, one intends to report it to others so as to provoke the dispute. Even if one has not yet spoken, if one intentionally listens and hears it, an offense is incurred.
[Lì] asked: "If an offense is incurred upon hearing the words, why does the root text of the precept say 'to listen to these words and report them to others'?"

Regarding the statement, "He speaks to Devadatta," this refers to one who listens in secret. The intention is fundamentally to listen in secret with the desire to report these words to another, intending to cause strife and discord.
One incurs the offense at the moment of listening; it does not depend upon reporting it to that other person.

If one were to incur the offense only upon reporting it to that person, it would fall under the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*) and would not be included here. Question: Why is it that for this precept, the offense is incurred at the very moment of listening, whereas for the preceding [precepts], it is not?

Regarding the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*): What constitutes an offense for one who waits to transmit [words] from one side to another? Answer: In the case of the preceding precept (lying), there was previously no dispute;

when one merely went to listen, a dispute did not necessarily arise. It is only upon speaking that one commits this offense. However, if there is already a matter of dispute and one goes to listen, the dispute will certainly be provoked, and the transgression is deep and grave.
Therefore, one incurs guilt at the very moment of listening. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Jìzhǐ*), fascicle 20, states: "If two parties... [text fragment].

When the Venerable Kāśyapa was in the hall engaged in private conversation, a bhikṣu wished to enter. He should snap his fingers or move his foot to make a sound. If the person inside remains silent, he should withdraw.

If the person inside continues speaking without ceasing, he may enter without fault. (If two people are conversing privately outside and one person inside the hall repeats their words, this should be noted;

if [the speaker] remains silent, the person inside the hall should come out). If bhikṣus are quarreling and harboring resentment, cursing one another and saying, "I must kill him," [one should not enter].
Having heard this, he says to that person: "Venerable one, take good care of your own preparations; I have heard an evil report.
If a steward hears a visiting bhikṣu say, "I shall steal such-and-such items from the storehouse or the stūpa," and having heard it, he should return in silence.
Having returned, he should announce among the community of monks: "Venerable sirs, such-and-such items should be guarded against; I [have heard this]."

If one hears an unpleasant report that a bhikṣu has many disciples who, at dusk, wander through the various rooms to see whether they are practicing according to the Dharma, and if one hears them engaging in worldly talk—discussing kings, thieves, and the like—one must not immediately enter and rebuke them.
Instead, one should wait until they come of their own accord, and only then instruct and reprimand them, saying:
"You have left the home life out of faith and eat the alms-food given by the faithful; you ought to be practicing meditation and reciting the scriptures."
[Sūtra]: What is it that the treatises say regarding matters that are not the Dharma? This is not for a renunciant to follow in accordance with wholesome dharmas.

If one hears a treatise or the exposition of the meaning of a sūtra, and engages in questioning and answering, one must not immediately enter into praise or desire. One should wait until [the interlocutor] comes forward of their own accord, and only then offer commendation.
You all should be able to discuss sūtras and expound their meanings, discourse upon the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, as the World-Honored One said: "The bhikṣus have assembled."
At that time, two practices should be observed: first, the noble silence; second, the discussion of the meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding the seventy-eighth precept on striking or beating a bhikṣu: if one strikes a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense (a *pārājika*), it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

This means that because the person previously received the precepts, even though they have committed a grave offense, striking them still constitutes a *pācittiya*. If, however, the person is one of the "thirteen difficulties" (*trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharmāḥ*) and was originally ineligible to receive the precepts, then striking them [does not constitute a *pācittiya*].

It is merely a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The meaning is the same as striking a layperson; it also constitutes only a *duṣkṛta*. According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, however, the karma is grave.

Regardless of whether one possesses the precepts or not, if the saṃghāṭī robe is worn upon the body, all such acts are equivalent to shedding the blood of a Buddha. Gao asked: "In this case, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense)."

Regarding the question of why the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* treats [the offense] as grave and immediate: the answer is that the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts takes into account the rarity or frequency of the occurrence; thus, it does not consider the retribution in future lives.

As for the establishment of the *pāyattika* (defeat) offense, it is considered light because it pertains to rare instances of commission. However, according to the principles of karma, it is equivalent to shedding blood.

Furthermore, it is said that shedding blood is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) based on the formal teaching (*śāsana*), yet the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the *sthūlātyaya* and the *pāyattika* is somewhat similar. According to these sūtras and vinayas, there is likewise no [distinction].
Regarding the gravity [of the offense]: another interpretation holds that according to the Vinaya, it is light because it involves members of the same monastic community striking one another;

whereas according to the Sūtras, it is grave because a layperson strikes the Saṅgha, thereby insulting those who are venerable. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425), vol. 18, it states: "If one strikes a nun, or even a layperson, it constitutes a *pācittiya*.

If various kinds of vicious beasts such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, dogs, and so forth should come, one must not strike them; to do so incurs a *pācittiya*. [The same applies to] using a staff, wood, or stones."

One may manifest a terrifying appearance. If someone enters a monastery and offends an image, or damages flowers, fruits, or trees, one may likewise use a staff, tiles, stones, or the like to strike the ground in a threatening manner to make them leave. One may take sand or beans and scatter them;

the number of *thullaccaya* offenses incurred corresponds to the number of beans that stick to the monks, not to the number of people they adhere to. The *Samantapāsādikā* (Jian lun), fascicle 16, states: "If one is angry..."

If one strikes with the intent [to kill], even resulting in death, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; even if it results only in the head being split or the hands and feet being broken, one still incurs a *pārājika*.

If one strikes someone who has not yet received full ordination, down to the level of an animal, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one strikes with the desire [to strike] but seeks only to release [the victim], there is no offense.

It is established that this statement clearly proves that the aforementioned striking of the Saṃgha was formulated as a prohibition based on the specific circumstances of the case, rather than by observing the relative gravity of the transgression in future lives.
Although the offense may be minor, the karmic retribution is grave. The precepts established by the Buddha were formulated based on their frequency of occurrence;
since offenses such as striking, fighting, and killing are rare for bhikṣus, they were designated with light names. Yet, in terms of actual karma, they are indeed heavy.

Conversely, regarding precepts such as those concerning praising, matchmaking, or building houses, because these actions occur frequently, they were designated with heavy names. However, in terms of their karmic retribution, these are actually light and not heavy.

The Seventy-ninth Bhikṣu Precept on Throwing: Regarding the phrase "this precept deeply guards against [the offense]" and so forth, it does not require that one actually puts on the garment before an offense is committed.

Merely raising the hand constitutes an offense; once the garment is put on, one automatically commits the preceding precept. To say that "making a gesture" constitutes an offense is clearly established.

If one raises a hand to threaten another bhikṣu, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (saṃghādisesa). The *Jieshu* states: "If the original intent was to strike rather than to seize, the act of seizing is merely a preparatory stage (*pācittiya*) for striking.

If the original intent was to seize rather than to strike, the movement of the mind is the preparatory stage for seizing; raising the hand constitutes a *thullaccaya*. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Zhi) 18 states:
"The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) used their palms as blades, threatening the group of sixteen (Ṣoḍaśavargika), saying: 'I shall strike you down with my palm-blade.'"
Because of that fear, your face [was distorted] and you cried out loudly. The Buddha asked the group of six: "For what reason are you acting like this?
They replied, "It was for the sake of amusement. The Buddha said, "Foolish men! Do not treat him with contempt; if he enters meditative absorption, he can exercise supernatural powers."
"Cast you away to another world. (Commentary: Regarding "holding the hand sideways like a blade," this refers to raising the hand with the palm turned sideways;

its shape resembles a blade. In this very Vinaya, raising the hand with the palm sideways is termed a *pāṭa* (a blow). Question: In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are seventeen groups; for what reason does the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* list only sixteen? Answer:
It is explained that while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* records seventeen based on the original source, it was because the first person among them was... [text ends].
He struck and killed them; therefore, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* cites only sixteen people. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"If one raises a hand or a blade toward many bhikṣus, each and every one of them incurs the offense."
The Eighty-first Precept on Entering the Royal Palace: Jì (濟) says, "According to the bhikṣus of foreign lands, they may enter and leave royal palaces because those kings maintain few defenses.
However, as for the kings here, they are guarded by weapons and the prohibitions at the gates are extremely strict;
one must have a formal introduction to enter or exit. How could one possibly enter by force? Even if one were to enter, it would not be permitted; thus, there is no offense [in refraining]."
This is the meaning of the precepts (*śīla*). According to Master Daoguang’s nine sections, this shall now be the ninth section. Regarding the exposition of this chapter:

there are ten precepts that clarify the external deportment and the proper measurements of clothing, as well as the practice of careful restraint and freedom from negligence. The first concerns a *kṣatriya* king.
According to the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, "Kṣatriya" is a term of Brahma-voice; here it is translated as "Field-Lord" (田主).

This refers to the time at the beginning of the kalpa when the system of dividing fields was established, and they were appointed as lords of these fields. This tradition has been passed down to the present day as kingship.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, in a past age, at the time when this world’s kalpa was ending, all sentient beings were born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. When the world was once again formed, the beings of the Ābhāsvara [Heaven...]
When the devas descend to this world, the devas and humans—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—take the joy of dhyāna as their food.

At that time, there is no distinction between day and night; the sun, moon, years, and seasons have forever departed. The essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) arises everywhere, like the nectar of the devas.
People then began to eat this essence of the earth. Their bodies became coarse and heavy; they lost their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and their radiance was completely extinguished.
In the world, there then appeared the sun and moon, the alternation of darkness and light, years, and the seasons. At that time, sentient beings were neither male nor female.
Due to eating the essence of the earth, their physical forms and complexions all became diverse: those who ate much had coarse and ugly complexions, while those who ate little had upright bodies.

It was so. Those who were upright and handsome, relying on their own excellence and looking down upon others, gave rise to arrogance. Because of this, the *rasa* (earth-essence) immediately vanished, and the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-crust) appeared;
its taste was like pure honey. At that time, all the sentient beings were struck with alarm and said, "How is it that the *rasa* has suddenly vanished?
They then all ate the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*. Later, arrogance arose once more, and the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* also vanished, whereupon the *pṛthivī-meda* (earth-fat) appeared; its taste—

It was like stone honey (*śarkarā*); when sentient beings ate it, they became increasingly arrogant, and the earth-fat (*pṛthivīrasa*) vanished. Next, there appeared natural non-glutinous rice (*śāli*).
After eating this rice for a long time, natural male and female forms emerged, and they became mutually attached to one another.
Their lust grew ever more intense, and they eventually formed couples. At that time, some sentient beings gathered the rice together to take for both today and tomorrow’s meals, and so it continued.
Having acquired [grain] for ten days, twenty days, one month, or two months, because they stored it with a greedy mind, the non-glutinous rice turned into husks and chaff;
what was harvested in the morning would not grow back by evening. At that time, sentient beings established regulations, dividing the fields and setting up boundaries.
They then partitioned them, saying, "This portion belongs to me; that one belongs to you. Thereupon—

Sentient beings gradually practiced theft, seizing the portions of others' fields (and so forth). The owners of those fields inherited and succeeded to their positions, and up to the present day they have become kings;

thus, [entering] for the sake of profit is permissible. Regarding "the king": according to the *Jì* (Commentary), there may be one who is a king but not a Kṣatriya—entering [his domain] in such a case incurs no offense.

Or there may be one who is a Kṣatriya but not an anointed king (*abhiṣikta*)—entering in such a case also incurs no offense. Or there may be one who is both a king and a Kṣatriya... [is... *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Vinaya commentary discussing the conditions under which entering a royal domain does not constitute an offense.*

Regarding consecration (*abhiṣeka*): there is no offense for one who has not entered [the palace]. This refers to a king, a *kṣatriya*, or one who has been consecrated; if there is a restricted territory within the palace that one may not enter, entering it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding the phrase "the king has not yet emerged and the treasures have not yet been stored," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: this means the king has not yet come forth and the women have not yet returned to their original quarters.

As for "the treasures have not yet been stored," the *Apidamo Dapiposha Lun* (Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) says: when the king approaches the ladies-in-waiting, he causes them to wear garments adorned with precious jewels.
This is because his inner body manifests externally, giving rise to a desire for lightness and clarity; it is for this reason that this bhikṣu has now suddenly arrived at this place.

According to the meaning of the *nidāna*, when Kāḷodāyin saw Queen Mallikā’s form exposed, he returned to the saṃghārāma and said, "I have seen the one whom the King holds most dear," calculating her to be a "woman-jewel" (*strī-ratna*), as the King values her like a treasure.

Therefore it is said. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Da lùn), there are two interpretations. Thus, the ninth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states: "The 'gate' refers to the exterior of the royal palace;
the 'threshold' (*kǔn*) refers to the wooden crossbar at the front of the palace gate. To pass beyond this wood constitutes an offense for one who has not yet hidden the treasure."

The King has already gone outside, but the Queen has not yet risen. When he approaches her for union, the precious robe she wears is so light and translucent that it shines through, revealing her body within;
this arouses his desire. Because she has not yet removed this garment, it is called "the unhidden treasure" (*asaṃvṛtamaṇi*). Furthermore, a woman is a "treasure" for a man;

when the Queen has not yet covered her body with another garment, she is likewise called "the unhidden treasure. As for the term "one whose head is sprinkled with water" (*abhiṣikta*): [it refers to one who has received royal consecration].
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "Take the waters of the four great oceans; take the horns of a white ox;

collect all types of seeds and fill [a vessel] with them, then place it upon a golden palanquin. Have the various minor kings carry the palanquin, while the King and his first consort sit together upon it.
A great Brahmin then pours water over the King’s crown, thereby establishing him as king; this is called a Kṣatriya."
Because they establish the king in this manner, he receives that name. Whether one is a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra—these five types are also called Kṣatriya kings.
One of the "water-sprinkled" lineage is called an Anointed King (*abhiṣeka-rāja*). Gao says:
"The above, based on what is distinguished in the Vinaya texts, is the method for establishing a king in foreign lands. Because the seeds are moistened by water, there is [the quality of] sprouting."
The meaning of "birth" (jìng) signifies that the King nurtures all living beings as his own children. The white ox with stone horns symbolizes not practicing heterodox paths;
for all auspicious matters, one must circumambulate and proceed toward the right. Lì states:
regarding the fifth of the five conditions, the causal condition, it refers to cases where one is summoned or invited, and thus does not commit an offense due to various such circumstances.

The Eighty-second Precept on Handling Valuables: Regarding the explicit text of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Exposition) concerning this precept on handling valuables, the eighth fascicle of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"As for 'valuables,' these include gold, silver, musaragalva, agate, lapis lazuli, and pearls; as well as gold leaf, golden images, and all such precious vessels.
