To handle any of these constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, it says: 'If one handles them oneself or causes another to handle them after they have been declared pure (*pariśuddha*),' [it is likewise an offense]."
*Pātayantika*. Now, this passage is cited in order to refute the former interpretation. "Not using the old terminology" means not following the explanations of past masters.
Former teachers established the name of this precept as the "precept against picking up lost treasures," because the occasion for its formulation was the act of picking up what had been left behind.

Therefore, to pick up something lost constitutes a *pātayantika*; to pick up anything that is not lost constitutes a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). As it says in the *Sūtra*: ... [text continues] ... as in the case of the *Sūtra*.
Because Tiṇa committed sexual misconduct, the precept against sexual misconduct was established. Because Dhanika committed theft, the precept against theft was established.

Since this case involves the picking up of what has been left behind, it must likewise establish a rule that one may not pick up fallen items; the *Lishi* (Commentary on the Vinaya) is also thus. Now, we do not agree with that view.
As clarified in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and other schools, merely picking it up constitutes an offense; why then discuss "picking up what has been left behind"?

Therefore, in the initial recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, it is stated that grasping precious objects constitutes an offense, with only two exceptions. Below, the permission to collect items belonging to a stūpa is granted, yet there is no separate provision for other cases.
How can it then be claimed that grasping precious objects incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) while leaving them behind constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense)? The *Karmavācanā* states:

The ancient masters took up the "dropped jewels" [incident] as the *nidāna* (causal origin). Therefore, they maintain that seizing any remaining jewels now constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Xuán says this is not so.

For within the Vinaya, the rules are generally established based on the *nidāna*, yet once the law is enacted, its application regarding transgressions does not necessarily conform to the original circumstances.

The precept against sexual misconduct was originally established based on the two [types of] persons; subsequently, the offense of *naihārika* (the specific category of violation) was incurred. Why, then, inquire whether the case is new or old? Master Bǐn cites...

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duo lun), fascicle five, regarding the precept on possessing precious objects (*ratna-parigraha-śīla*), states: "This is the essence of the precept (*śīla-tattva*). It is precisely because of the prohibition against possessing precious objects that this rule was established;

even if one does not intend to possess them, if one takes hold of another's treasure, or if one takes hold of one's own 'purified' (*viśuddha*) treasure, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense (*pāyattika*) merely by taking hold of it.

As for all coins—whether copper coins, or even wooden tokens—whether belonging to oneself or another, merely taking hold of them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense (*dūṣkṛta*). This is not the essence of this precept."

The ninety matters concerning the handling of valuables (the above is from the *Śāstra*; the commentary states): Since this section specifically addresses the precept against handling valuables, it should not be stated exclusively as "dropped items";

rather, it should simply be named the "Precept Against Handling Valuables. Regarding the three types of non-residences and so forth: this clarifies the circumstances under which handling valuables is permitted according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Regarding the fourth point, "having no intent to steal and intending to return them to the owner": Master Li [Lì] asserts that merely handling such items constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

If one has the intent to steal, it is subsumed under the first category of offenses. As for the statement "even including those who know the affairs of the Buddha and the Sangha," this is likely said out of forgetfulness or a sense of recklessness;

it suggests that because they act on behalf of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they should be permitted to seize [the property]. Now, this is clarified: even though they are administrators (*karmadāna*), seizing is not permitted.

If, however, someone has already seized [an object] and it cannot be released, [the Vinaya] establishes the precedent: "A lay attendant (*upāsaka*) was holding a golden image. This is compared [to the case at hand].
Regarding Kyo-shojo: having first seized it and then released it, and then lifting it again—this would constitute two *pāyattika* offenses. However, I personally suspect this is not the case;
I have merely cited the circumstances of the preceding and succeeding moments, and it is not necessarily that a single seizure results in two offenses.

When acting as an assistant, one must wrap one's hands and must not touch the gold. As for the instruction to "recognize the characteristics of the bag and examine it," this is because, in the *Nidāna*, a bhikṣu...
A bhikṣu picked up another man’s gold purse. Later, when the owner came to claim it, the bhikṣu returned it, saying, "My own purse originally contained more gold than this.

The bhikṣu replied, "It contains only this much. They continued to dispute without end until they reached the magistrate's office. The magistrate relied on their words and took a hundred thousand taels of gold;
because he had seized the purse, he could not dismiss them. Upon investigation, it was proven that the owner was lying, and the magistrate then spoke to him:
"This is not your bag. At that time, having verified and dispatched [the messenger], he took the object to the authorities. He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha commanded:
"From now on, you must ask about the characteristics of the bag and how much gold it contains. If the answer corresponds [to what was reported], return it to him.
If the answer does not correspond, you may say: 'I did not see this object. If one picks up a lost or fallen object elsewhere,"
This refers to places that are neither monasteries nor lodgings; all locations other than these two are called "other places.

If the Buddha had not established the precept against looking with the eyes at what should not be seen, then by virtue of observing the precepts, he would now have returned this object to you. Had there been no precepts at that time, [he would not have done so].
"I have picked up your belongings; even if you see them with your own eyes, I will not return them to you. The precepts were established by the Buddha;

you should revere the Buddha so as to give rise to faith and hold the three realities in high esteem. As for the statement, "If the owner of the robe comes to take it back, there is no offense," this means that since it is one's own property, there is no transgression even if one has left it behind and the owner comes to retrieve it.
Regarding the instruction that "one must not trust a *karmadāna* (attendant) and should inform the King," this was established out of fear that—
This is a case of improper use. It is like a treasure storehouse where even those with iron-bound contracts and their names recorded may use the goods directly.

As it is said: "If someone asks for them, one must still say they have been claimed. If they have already been used for meritorious deeds such as constructing a stūpa, and the owner comes to reclaim them...

"If there is something in the stupa, take it back; if there is nothing, ask for it to be returned. Regarding the phrase "advancing or retreating as above," this refers to the precept concerning theft (*adattādāna*).
Furthermore, it says "referring to the preceding text," which refers to the passage: "If one digs into the earth and finds a treasure trove, the attendants do not believe [it]," and so forth.
As for the statement "the noble Anāthapiṇḍika also took [it]," this refers to the elder Sudatta approaching Prince Jeta.

When he was purchasing the garden to build a vihāra for the Buddha, the gold he had spread out did not cover it entirely. He thought to himself, "Which treasury should I take so that the gold will suffice?
and thus he took the hidden treasure (*nidhi*). Yet, since even Sudatta, who was an *ārya* of the third fruit, still took this object, we know it does not belong to the king.
Regarding the phrase "trampling with his foot to break [the seal]" and so forth: on a desolate road he encountered a garment, and upon it there were jewels tied; he took them.

He was returning the robe when he stepped on and broke the jewel. Had he not been aware that the robe contained a jewel at the time of his return, and had he only discovered it upon arriving back at the monastery, there would have been no offense;

he should have had a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take charge of it. Regarding the "Five Hundred Questions" concerning the entrusting of clothing and other items: this refers to the robes of visiting monks.

It was entrusted to a lay white-robed householder, who did not take it because the appointed time had passed. The householder subsequently brought it to offer to the Sangha; thus, there is this matter of its acceptance or rejection.
The 83rd Precept: Entering a Village at an Improper Time. 1. Regarding "an improper time": this refers to entering [a village] after the conclusion of the fast-day (Uposatha).

This is not a fixed period of time. Regarding the "five entry points" (pañca-dvāra): Jing says that one commits an offense upon first entering the village gate, and again upon entering each individual house.
As for "entering a monastery within a settlement," this refers to a case where the boundaries of a settlement enclose a monastery within them;
if one wishes to enter such a monastery from outside the settlement, it is not necessary to announce one's arrival. Entering one’s own original residence does not constitute an offense.

"Zhe" (者) means "established"; it refers to a dwelling place being a monastic residence (*saṃghārāma*). Even if one is within a village, if one returns from outside, there is no offense even if one passes through the village.
Shen (深) says: "This clarifies that when staying at a layperson's house, if one later goes out briefly and returns, one does not need to announce [one's departure].
Regarding "non-time and so forth" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*): in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this refers to the period after midday.

It is called "the improper time" (*akāla*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi) does not define it by reference to time, but only discusses it in relation to after the meal; thus, even though one has already finished eating, it is immediately termed "the improper time.
Regarding the statement, "Venerable ones, we [shall enter the village]," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi) Twenty, it says:

"Venerable ones, I shall enter the village at the improper time"; the person before him says, "So be it" (the above is from the *Qishi*). Now, examining this closely, the method of entrustment (*anujñā*) is intended to inform other people.

This immediately serves as a protection against transgressions. It differs from other *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) methods where, if the phrasing is deficient, the ritual act is not accomplished.

Therefore, phrases such as "May the Venerable One attend to me with a single mind" are not yet required; rather, the phrasing must be complete and sufficient. Thus, the third fascicle of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one is on the ground and makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to someone in the air, is the announcement accomplished? The answer is: it is accomplished. Now, examining this closely, it should specifically belong to me alone.

"Go to the house of so-and-so," and so forth; one should properly remember these [instructions], for they constitute the *śukladharma* (white dharma). The *Śīla-viniścaya-ṭīkā* quotes the *Vinayavibhaṅga* as stating:
"I have such a reason that I must go to such-and-such a place; I inform the Venerable One. If the response is "It is granted," this is called *śukladharma*. This is for two reasons:
first, to indicate an obstacle to monastic affairs, fearing that a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) might be performed; second, because other circumstances necessarily require it.

They act together, yet do not know where they have gone; thus, they cause distress to the assembly. Second, it is because they would enter the homes of laypeople without being self-restrained. *Li* says:
"If there are no bhikṣus at the residence to whom one may entrust oneself, and there is a matter concerning the Three Jewels, one is permitted to enter without fault.

If one travels until nightfall and wishes to enter a village to stay overnight, according to the *Ji-lü*, one should pass the time by turning toward one another; there is no fault [in this]. To enter without having announced one's intention constitutes an offense."

According to this Vinaya, it may be permissible not to announce one's arrival and thus remain free of offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one travels through a village, or arrives at dusk to stay overnight, or if the eight calamities arise, there is no offense for entering the village at that time.
Regarding the rule that one falls into an offense (*pāyattika*) if one turns off the main road to the left or right, the *Lishi* (立) states:
if one passes by a temple and turns off the main road, one incurs a *thullaccaya*. One must proceed straight ahead to avoid the offense. If...

Regarding the statement, "Whether one makes a general announcement according to where one has gone, or it is also well to make a specific announcement," the term "general" (*sāmānya*) means that one must not simply say, "I have arrived at many villages;
I know there are many, but whose houses are they? This should be expressed using the formal terminology of the Dharma, saying "many.
One should speak all at once: "I have arrived at the house of Zhang Somesuch, Wang Somesuch, and Zhao Somesuch."
"Equal households. Thus it is said that each person makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*). Regarding the phrase "first examining this matter," the *Liaoshu* states:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to enter another's house, he must first examine the matter before he may enter. The commentary explains:
When one who has left the household life enters the houses of laypeople on his own initiative, various faults arise because of it; therefore, a regulation must be established to prevent them.
This prevents them from entering the homes of laypeople at will; if they do enter, they must first deliberate upon the matter thoroughly before they may do so.

Furthermore, a verse in the *Śāstra* says: "Observing the correct conduct of the same precepts and the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) within the Vinaya, such as tying the waist-string and fastening the knots of the *saṃghāṭī*.
The commentary explains: "Those of the same precepts" refers to those who possess the full set of precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) equally; they should be paired with one another.
"Kauṣṭhila said: 'I now have a matter of such causes and conditions that I must go to a certain place; I inform the Venerable One for his knowledge.

He replied, 'Listen, Elder,' and only then was he permitted to depart. Regarding the statement, 'observing the correct practice of the Vinaya and its dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*),' the commentary explains:
'Vinaya' is *samvara*; in this context, it is translated as 'correct practice' (*samyak-caryā*). This refers to the bhikṣu as elucidated within this Vinaya."
One must observe correct conduct and deportment. That is to say, within a village settlement, one must not allow one’s deportment to falter;
one should fasten a waistband so that the robe does not slip down, and secure the fastenings of the *saṃghāṭī* so that the garment stays close to the body and cannot be blown open by the wind.
If one’s deportment is impaired, one will be held in contempt and ridiculed by others, giving rise to unwholesome thoughts in the minds of laypeople. If one’s deportment is [proper]...
The Dharma causes others to show respect and gives rise to wholesome thoughts in laypeople; this is the "vow for entering a village" established by the Buddha.
One must examine all such matters thoroughly before entering. Therefore, it is said: "First, one should discern," and so forth. The following clarifies the rules regarding non-offenses.

Regarding the three occasions involving the Triple Gem that require entrustment as mentioned above, [Master] Li states: "Although these are occasions involving the Triple Gem when entering a village, one must still announce [one's arrival].
To claim arbitrarily that there is no need to announce is an error. He now refers to the aforementioned passages concerning the Sangha, stupas, temples, and so forth; therefore, he says "as above."
Precept 84: Regarding Bed Legs Exceeding the Prescribed Measure. Jingyun states: Whether for the Sangha or for private use, if the bed legs exceed the prescribed measure, it constitutes an offense.
This applies equally to the eight precepts of the laity. The present text enumerates five conditions for the commission of the offense;

these are established collectively based on various Vinaya schools, not solely according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Second, both beds belonging to the Sangha and one’s own bed constitute an offense [if the legs exceed the measure].
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qīwén) stating that there is no offense for a monastic bed, while the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Sēngqí) states they both constitute an offense:

the former clarifies that if one originally intends to cut [the wood], there is no offense at the time of completion; it is only when one does not cut it that an offense occurs. Conversely, if one did not originally intend to cut it, an offense is incurred immediately upon its completion.

Regarding "one finger is two inches" and so forth: this refers to the essential measurement of a Buddha's finger. As for "one foot three inches of the Tang *chi*," it means one foot three inches of the Tang *chi*;
even when converted to one foot six inches of the Zhou *chi*, it still does not exhaust the full length, which is why the word "slightly more" (*qiáng*) is used.

Regarding the rule in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that one may accept the gift of a high bed provided one first forms the thought of cutting it down, failing to do so constitutes an offense: Jing says this means that if one raises the thought [of cutting it], one does not commit an offense;
if one does not raise the thought and subsequently sits upon it, one commits an offense. This also clarifies that the offense is incurred at the very moment of initial acceptance.
As for the case where there is no offense regarding a high bed in a layperson's home: this refers to temporarily taking a high bed from a layperson’s home and giving it to a bhikṣu.
"Regarding 'sitting without violating the eight-finger measure using my finger-width': this means that [the seat] is measured at sixteen *cun* (one foot and six inches);

exceeding this constitutes a violation. The commentary states: 'The upper allowance for the wooden frame of the legs uses the human eight-finger measure. This refers to the aforementioned finger-width measurement."
If the bottom of the niche is low, it is permissible to use a piece of wood eight finger-widths long to support the leg. Regarding the third part entering the mortise hole and so forth, [Dao]li says:
"This is the interpretation of the commentators on the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Shisong-lü). Divide this leg into four parts, measured by human fingers."
Four *catur-bhāga* (fourths) consist of eight *aṅgula* (fingers), which is equivalent to eight *cun*. There are four such sets of eight *cun*: one set of eight *cun* enters the mortise hole;
one set of eight *cun* serves as the leg; one set of eight *cun* is cut off and used again to support the leg; and the final set of four [sets of] eight makes thirty-two [total *cun*].
It shall measure three chi and two cun. This clarifies that if one acts before this measurement is reached, it constitutes an offense; once the cutting is finished, there is no offense.

If one subsequently uses the portion that was cut off as a support for the legs, it again constitutes an offense. Some say that "cutting away" refers to cutting away eight finger-widths from above the hole of the crossbar.
It is not that the lower part [of the bed] was cut off. If one were to say the lower part was cut off, why would it be said that "the third part entered the mortise"?

Regarding the statement that it was divided into four equal parts, Jing said: "Eight finger-widths of a human enter the mortise; eight finger-widths of a human are the space between the supports for the feet.
Eight finger-widths of a Buddha constitute a foot, which is sixteen human finger-widths, equivalent to one chi and six cun. This applies even to long beds."

Regarding the statement that those who have been ordained for four years may sit together: Jingyun says that this indicates those with four years of seniority are permitted to sit together; however, one with five years of seniority already holds the rank of *ācārya*, and thus [sitting together] is not permitted.

This does not mean that the seat is too small to accommodate them. As for the current order of seating, it is based on the time of receiving the precepts as the moment of the arising of the *dharmakāya*;
this constitutes the sequence for seniority in seating. It is not determined by the number of summer retreats completed through the rainy season residence (*varṣā*).
This refers to the order of seating. Thus, the Bodhisattva Precepts state: "Those who have received the precepts earlier sit in front; those who have received them later sit behind.
This is precisely that meaning. If one is assigned a specific number of years since ordination (*kṣānti*), they act as a superior in harmony and receive formal reliance (*niśraya*).
This is because one knows that [the space] is free from reliance. If it cannot be reduced, this refers to the fact that the measurement for four people sitting on a bed cannot be reduced.
The following clarifies the rules regarding non-offenses.
Precept 85: Regarding the Prohibition on Using Cotton for Bedding and Mattresses. As for "cotton" (*tūla*):

because there are many minute insects within this flower that would lose their lives [if crushed], it was prohibited and one is not permitted to sit upon it. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a sacred tree near Rājagṛha to which the people paid homage;
when the festival arrived, they would attend for seven days. There were four types [of cushions] stuffed with cotton.
[The Buddha] discarded it and departed. Later, the bhikṣus collected it to use for corded beds, wooden beds, and as frames for mats.
Laypeople criticized them, saying: "These things are foul and filthy, breeding many insects; how can bhikṣus sit or lie upon them?
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and violate the dharma of a śramaṇa. For this reason, he established this precept. Regarding the "four kinds": [the text continues].
The flowers of the willow, the flowers of the *yang* tree, the flowers of the *púlí* (reed-lily), and the *shǎnpó* flower constitute the four. The commentary states:
"The *pútái* (reed-platform) is precisely the flower of the winter reed. Jì says: "Nowadays, many people use reed flowers as a 'mud-pounder' (*níjīn*), which kills countless insects."
"Be careful not to use it. "One must first discard it, lest one later regret it" means that one should first discard this mat; it is because one would otherwise later regret the transgression.

The eighty-sixth precept concerning needle cases made of bone, ivory, or horn. The five conditions are the same as those for the preceding precept; that is to say, they are identical to the previous rule. One should...
It is said: first, ivory or horn; second, making a needle case; third, for oneself; fourth, having another person make it; fifth, the offense is incurred upon completion.

Regarding "such small items" and so forth, this refers to how, among the thirty precepts, all are established as *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses requiring forfeiture) because they involve the accumulation of material goods.

This precept should likewise have been placed among the preceding conditions; however, because this object is small, it was not listed previously. Furthermore, regarding that which ought to be broken:
the established rule is that one must first break it and only afterwards repent for the offense.

If, on the contrary, one returns it to the owner and they do not accept it, the established rule clarifies that it may not be returned to the original owner, nor may it be given to another, as this would cause distress to the owner. If it is given to the Saṃgha, furthermore—

It may be accepted; it only needs to be broken. The following clarifies the rules regarding non-offenses. Regarding the term *biāozuǎn* (the first character pronounced *pǐ shāo*; the second character is *zuǎn*):

the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to the copper [sheath] of a sword. The *Shiming* states that the lower end of a spear is called a *zuǒn*; this is the name used in the region south of the Yangtze River, while in the Guanzhong region it is called a *zuàn* (pronounced *zǐ luàn*).
The Vinaya text uses the character *biāozuǎn*. It is not the actual object itself. As for the word "umbrella" (*sǎn*; pronounced *xiān bàn*): it means a canopy. See the *Dongguan Hanji*.
Commentary: According to the sources, a *gai* (蓋) is an implement used by people to ward off wind and sun; it is also called an *san* (繖). Regarding the term *jue-niu* (玦鈕):
Du Yu stated that a *jue* is like a ring, but with a gap so that the parts do not connect. The character below is sometimes written as *niu* (鈕) or *niu* (鈕), both of which are identical.
The *Guangzhu* says: "The knob of a seal is called its 'nose' (*bi*); the present image is like this. Furthermore, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to a silk thread.

"Yīguǎ" (pronounced huá) means "to obstruct horizontally. The origin of this character is not clearly known. According to the *Tōngsúwén*, that which is hard, stiff, and indigestible is called "mò" (reading as mòbā).
"Hú" (reading as húbā) is what is currently called "bone" in Shandong. As for "wǎnniǔ," it refers to the "mòfēnzi" (a type of knot or fastener);
it likely takes its name from this. Regarding "wǎnzhǐchǐ," if one reads it as "hài," it is so; if one reads it as "zhé" (dūcǎo), it means "to pluck. If one reads it as... [text breaks off].
"Pick" (摘) means to remove. It also means to pick out or to distinguish.

The precept regarding a *niṣīdana* mat exceeding the prescribed measure is number eighty-seven. This precept is largely identical to the preceding one; the only difference is that it concerns exceeding the measure.
If both dimensions are reduced or both exceed the limit, it constitutes an offense (*pācittiya*), following the nine clauses of the precept on building a hut. Thus, it is said to have "nine clauses."

[Regarding] those: exceeding the length within the long; exceeding the width within the long; as [the measure] within the width, exceeding the length within the long; decreasing the width within the width, as [the measure] within the length;

exceeding the width within the width, as [the measure] within the length; decreasing the length within the length, exceeding the width within the width; decreasing the length within the length, as [the measure] within the width;
decreasing the length within the length, decreasing the width within the width. If one makes it in two layers, there is no offense. "Standing" refers to that which was previously single-layered.

If it has already been made and exceeds the prescribed measure, because it was made as a single layer, there is no offense; now, however, having finished making it as two layers, if it does not exceed [the limit], there is no offense.

If, after finishing the assembly, it still exceeds the square [measure], the commentary states: "Now there are those who make it according to the general measurement, yet the various schools do not permit this.

The intent of the *Chao* (Commentary) is that one should follow the original measurement when making it; as for the allowance, one should provide an additional patch outside the main border. If, at the beginning...

If one acts according to the method for exceeding [the prescribed size], and the basket (or container) extends beyond what the maker is authorized to do, then it constitutes an offense; this refers to the custom of the Vajjians.

The commentary states: "This means that if the initial measurement is already outside [the limit] and not an addition, one must cut away the middle portion where the original excess occurred, rather than cutting away the outer edge where the addition was made.
Regarding "the remainder is to be purified": once the construction has been completed in excess of the limit, if one now cuts [it down].
Although what has been cut off is not an object of standard measurement, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it must still be formally dedicated (*paryavadāpana*).
If it is of standard measurement and more than eight finger-widths, it certainly must be dedicated. Regarding cases where ten days or more have already passed, [the author] states:

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if a robe does not conform to the prescribed measurements, one must relinquish it and perform a *pāyattika* confession; therefore, it is said that this follows the robe regulations of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
Regarding the eighty-eighth precept on oversized sores-covering robes: the cases of non-offense are largely the same as those for the preceding precept.

That is to say, as with the precept on sitting mats, if the robe is made according to measure or even smaller than the measure, there is no offense. As for the downfall incurred after ten days have passed since the formal binding [of the robe], [the details follow].
Because of the wound on his body, the Buddha permitted its use to protect the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*. There was no need to preach the Dharma for this purpose.
Now, after the wound has healed, one must perform the *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa* (declaration of purity) within ten days; if it is not performed after that period, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
The Ninety-ninth Precept on Excessive Rain-Cloths: The *Caturvargika-vinaya* account of the origin.

Vimalā (Vaiśākhamātṛ), having first provided the occasion for the invitation and offering, sent a messenger to the monastery to invite the monks. Upon arriving at the site, she saw them bathing naked and sent the messenger back with the report.

She requested the Buddha to grant her permission to give alms, making a total of eight vows; this is one such vow. When the Buddha beheld these eight vows of the woman, he immediately granted his consent and spoke this verse:

"Those disciples of the Buddha who maintain the precepts, Who joyfully bestow food and drink upon all people, And subdue their hearts of stinginess and envy, Relying on the pleasant to receive pleasant retribution, Shall forever attain peaceful and secure bliss, And reach the heavens."

Abiding in this place, one attains the untainted noble path; the mind delights in merit, its happiness beyond compare, and one is born in the heavens, long-lived and ever at peace. (These are three lines of verse.)
The Ninetieth Precept on Receiving Robes Equal in Measure to the Buddha’s. Regarding that which need not be described in detail but must be known:

the origin of this precept is stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Jìzhī), chapter eighteen, as follows: The bhikṣu Nanda was the Buddha’s own younger brother, born of Mahāprajāpatī. He possessed thirty of the marks of a Great Man;

he lacked two marks compared to the Buddha—namely, the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) and the protuberance on the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*). As for the protuberance, it was four inches shorter than the Buddha’s. When the monks saw him from afar...
Seeing him, they said, "This is the Buddha," and all rose to greet him, each feeling ashamed. This led to the monks' reproach:
"How can you have us, the elders, rise to greet you? Consequently, it was established as a rule that Nanda should wear black robes so that his appearance would differ from the Buddha's.

"O Bhikṣus, there were those whose robe colors were identical to the Buddha's. When the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) saw this, and since their robe colors were the same as the Buddha's, they thought that their dimensions should likewise be equal.
They consequently made robes the same size as the Buddha’s, and thus the precept was established.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Elder Nanda, the Buddha’s younger brother born of his mother, resembled the Buddha’s body and possessed thirty of the marks; he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha.
At that time, Nanda made robes for himself the same size as those of the Buddha. When it was mealtime, the bhikṣus saw Ānanda coming from afar while they were eating;
thinking he was the Buddha, they all rose to welcome him, saying, "Our Great Teacher is coming! The World-Honored One is coming!
Only when he drew near did they realize it was not so, and the elders were all ashamed. They thought to themselves: "This man is our junior; how could this be?"
He rose to greet him, and Nanda was also ashamed, saying, "You have caused the senior monks to rise and greet me. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From now on, robes should be made with reduced measurements. If one makes them equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe, or exceeds it, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
[The Buddha then] questioned [the rules regarding] oversized sitting mats, oversized wound-covering cloths, and robes equal in measure to the Buddha’s.
Regarding these three precepts, nuns commit only minor offenses. As for the precept concerning rain-cloths exceeding the proper measure, why is it that nuns are subject to the same measure?

The answer is: because a woman’s body is characterized by unattractive features, she displays outward signs of joy and pleasure; thus, if she makes a rain-cloth of excessive size, she commits the same offense as a monk. As for the remaining three [precepts], [the same applies].
It is for constant use. Nuns prefer small-sized [robes], as it is rare for them to exceed the prescribed measure; therefore, only the *kṣudraka* (minor offense) is established here.
Regarding the fourth *pratideśanīya*, all schools provide a detailed analysis in seven sections within this chapter; I shall now omit those and present only four sections. First:

The purpose of this section and the explanation of its title. Second, the reasons for establishing the four categories. Third, the similarities and differences between the two schools. Fourth, the rules for maintaining and violating the precepts. Regarding the first, the purpose of this section:

although one may have perfected the practice of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) as described above, if one does not distance oneself from what gives rise to suspicion, one may still incur reproach and transgression.
Thus, the mind harbors defiled attachment and cannot give rise to goodness; therefore, these four [precepts] were established. Regarding the explanation of their names:

as has been handed down from antiquity, one confesses toward another, as explained above. Now, as for the term "dharmas subject to censure" (*pācittiya*), this is also a name derived from its function as an antidote.
The *Mātṛkā* and *Vinayamātṛkā* state: "The essence of this precept carries no [inherent] offense; it is [resolved] before a single person through a single recitation."
Confess the transgression. If one contemplates this within one's own mind, all such faults can be extinguished. Regarding the second point, the four reasons for the prohibition:

generally, when criticisms regarding transgressions arise, they do not exceed the categories of internal and external relatives. First, concerning the internal, it does not exceed the two spheres of private and public. As for the first case, occurring in a secluded place:

since a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī share the same dharma-robes, yet their male and female positions are distinct, it is logically necessary that they remain free from defilement; this is the fundamental principle.
In a village, taking food with one's own hands may give rise to defilement and impurity; to avoid this fault, the first precept was established.

Furthermore, within a community, if one points out [food] to a specific individual, the conduct involves partiality and private favoritism; accepting it in silence is censurable as it is not manifest before the assembly. To avoid this fault, the second precept was established.
Regarding those who rely on the "external transcendence," they do not go beyond villages or forest hermitages (*araṇya*); in the village, [defilement] arises...
Regarding the first [precept]: because receiving food in excess from a family would cause them to be depleted and lead to public reproach, the third precept was established. Regarding the second:

because a bhikṣu, out of laziness, might sit at ease in a remote and dangerous place to receive food, thereby allowing bandits to harass him or causing women to be sent to provide food—due to these faults, the fourth precept was established.
These were thus instituted based on internal and external circumstances.
Fourth. Regarding the similarities and differences between the two sections of the third [category]: as for nuns, they all incur a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) because such instances are rare.

In the first two precepts, since the Saṃgha is honored and the nuns are of lower status, it is logically not something that should be granted; because it is rare, there is only a *duṣkṛta*. As for receiving food from a family under [monastic] protection, the offense for a nun is light.
Nuns are of lower standing; their feelings toward such [offenses] are thin, and they will certainly not exhaust themselves [in repentance].

This is why they are treated lightly. Regarding the fourth point, the rules for observing and violating the precepts: Li states that among these four precepts, the second and fourth possess two modes of both observance and violation. As for the "two observances":
if one sees [someone] pointing out [the food] and refrains from eating it, this is "observance through abstention" (zhi-chi). If, upon seeing the situation, one immediately accords with the Sage...

Instruction: Reprimand according to the ritual procedure: "Sister, cease for a moment. Regarding bodily action, eating does not give rise to an offense; this is called 'performing the maintenance' (*kṛta-dhāra*).

These two conditions—[the act of eating] and [the failure to reprimand]—are distinct both in their nature and their substance. As for the two offenses: if one observes a transgression and fails to reprimand, and the other then eats, one incurs an offense.

Because this offense arises from the act of ceasing [to reprimand], it is called a "cessation-offense" (*sthiti-āpatti*). Even if one ceases [from eating] but fails to reprimand, if the bodily action [of eating] does not occur, there is no offense.
There is no offense through mere omission (*virati*). Furthermore, because it arises from bodily action (*kāyakarman*) while eating food, it is called an "active offense" (*kṛtāpatti*).

In relation to the former, which is termed "omission," this is termed "action. The substance of these offenses is one, though their names differ. Moreover, there are two types of observances (*saṃvara*); these too are of one substance with different names.
Acting in accordance with the prescribed method of censure is called "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇī*). Because of this censure, although one eats, there is no fault;

this is the opposite of the previous case of committing an offense, and is it not indeed superior? Fourth, in the *araṇya* (wilderness), abstaining from eating is called "cessative observance" (*sthita-dhāraṇī*).

If one follows the words of the holy teaching by saying, "Donor, do not send food here," yet the donor, knowing [of this], sends it anyway, then although one eats, there is no transgression; this is called...

Regarding the two types of transgressions: not informing the donor is termed a transgression of abstention (*virati-āpatti*), whereas accepting and eating the food is a transgression of action (*kriyā-āpatti*).
For the remaining two precepts, abstention constitutes observance (*dhāraṇa*), while action constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the first precept, "taking food from a nun who is not a relative while residing in a layperson's house," etc.:

In the circumstances of this precept, the nun Utpalavarṇā, during a time of famine, obtained almsfood and gave it to the Saṅgha. After two or three days had passed, she herself had not eaten anything and collapsed on the ground, her head and face covered in mud.
A layperson witnessed this and gave rise to criticism. The Buddha then established the precept concerning those who are not relatives. Second, [the rule against] non-relatives.

Regarding this: it is similar to the precepts concerning sitting together with superiors and so forth; external appearances are not the basis for the rule, as both close and distant relatives are equally subject to the same prohibition, and the concern regarding censure is identical.

Therefore, when laypeople invite [a monk], if the relationship is sufficiently intimate such that no censure would arise, permission is granted to accept. As for the "three conditions where there is no basis" (for refusal), these are exceptions permitted in cases of illness.
Because a sick person suffers from affliction and the resulting censure and disgrace do not arise, permission is granted to accept [the invitation] in order to sustain the body and life.
Regarding the fourth point, "taking food with one's own hand": if the food is placed on the ground or sent by another person as a sign of respect, it is not bound by the formal rules [of receiving];
since there is no fault of reproach, this is also permitted. As for the two types of eating—by oneself and by others—these are applied according to the circumstances.

This refers to: if a *bhikṣuṇī* has already eaten, or if a *bhikṣuṇī* has obtained food from a donor; in both cases, it constitutes an offense. Regarding the offense incurred while in an alleyway according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, consult the *Pañca*.
The *Fen* [of the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*] states: At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who found almsfood easily; she gave it all away to the bhikṣus.
This continued until the third day, when everything she received was given away. Having failed to obtain food for three days, she encountered an elder traveling in a horse-drawn carriage.
Desiring to avoid him, she fell to the ground. The elder alighted from his carriage, helped her up, and asked: "What..."
Having thus fully answered the matter, he spoke with derision: "Although the nun’s giving may be inexhaustible, the recipient ought to know contentment.
For this reason, they reported the incident to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One must not receive food from within the streets; if one does so, the recipient commits an offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is inside a village while a bhikṣuṇī is outside the village, or if a bhikṣu receives food in an open space..."
Auspicious. The following clarifies non-transgression of the law.
The Second Precept on Receiving Food from the Homes of Laypeople: Regarding "the three cases where the assembly accepts in silence and does not reprove," the Commentary states:

"If the assembly witnesses a transgression and remains silent while accepting it without reproving, this indicates that the entire assembly consents to and tolerates the evil. Therefore, the rule is established to address the whole assembly, and none [are exempt]."
One may eat while listening. If one hears a reproach, one must stop immediately; it is not appropriate for the assembly to tolerate what is improper, and thus one eats while listening.

For this reason, eating is permitted, as it fulfills the merit of the donor. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if monks from two separate groups sit and eat separately, they must also inquire separately.

Regarding the phrase "instructing those who have not yet been instructed," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the characteristics of an offense herein are as follows: if a bhikṣu accepts instruction from a bhikṣuṇī...
Regarding eating: whenever one receives it, one incurs a *pāṭidesanīya* offense accordingly.
If two groups of the Saṃgha are sitting together, if even a single person within one group speaks to this bhikṣuṇī, the second group is also considered to have spoken.
If they enter separately, sit separately, and exit separately, then the bhikṣu who enters the donor’s gate should ask the bhikṣu who is exiting:
"Which bhikṣuṇī instructed the donor here to give food to the bhikṣus? He should say, "That bhikṣuṇī should be asked whether she has already given her instructions.
If he replies, "She has already finished giving her instructions," then that entering bhikṣu is also considered to have given his instructions. There are some bhikṣus...
When leaving the city gate, those bhikṣus who enter should ask those who are exiting. If the one exiting has not yet given instructions, the one entering should give instructions;
if the one exiting has already given instructions, the one entering should likewise each give their own instructions.
The phrase "those sitting behind do the same" clarifies that those sitting behind must also ask those sitting in front for instructions regarding the nuns and so forth. Below...
Regarding the clarification that there is no offense in waiting until the meal is finished: Lin says this means waiting for the announcement that the meal has been served to all.
As for the case where a nun acts as her own *dānapati* (donor), Lì states that if the nun herself serves as the host providing the food, it is not an offense because she is acting on her own behalf.

The Third Precept on Receiving Food from a Family. *Li* says: A husband and wife who are disciples of the realization of the Truth (*dṛṣṭiprāpta-śrāvaka*)—meaning those who have realized the three lower fruits—are called disciples of the realization of the Truth.
However, regarding the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for such a family, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is as follows: [text continues].
If a husband and wife are respectively ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*), the *karmavācanā* for a family under training (*śaikṣakula*) may not be performed for them.

However, if both are among those who have attained the three fruits of the path, or if one or the other is so, this method may be granted; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is likewise. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If the wealth and property of that household are completely exhausted, the Saṃgha should provide them with gardens and fields so that they may fulfill their regular obligations, and [the remainder] shall be used..."
Regarding the offering of white rice: if there is none, when the Sangha has finished its meal offerings, one should have the family prepare it so that they may send it.
If there is still nothing else, at the time of eating, one may go to their house to eat and give them what remains.

If this is not done, then sons and fathers shall establish bhikṣus in monasteries, wives shall provide for bhikṣuṇīs, and they shall provide rooms, bedding, and robes to be shared—all of these must be given.

However, these four sections merely establish monastic regulations; they simply prohibit one from going to such households. Regarding the five conditions in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts): first, the family of those who have seen the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya-kula*);

second, the establishment of monastic rules (*dharmavinaya*) by the Saṃgha; third, the absence of a valid cause or condition; fourth, taking it oneself; and fifth, setting it aside on the ground and having someone else remove it.
The fifth section on the offense of eating [inappropriately];
the fourth precept concerning receiving food in an araṇya. This refers to an araṇya that is a dangerous place, abounding with wicked bandits, lions, tigers, and wolves.
When a woman brings food, she may be terrified or even violated. Yet the bhikṣu sits down peacefully to receive the food without first...

[This is] a transgression committed through verbal knowledge and because of not going out to meet [the donor]. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: At that time, some bhikṣus were dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
When laypeople sent food for them, it was plundered by bandits. The Buddha said: "One should tell the food-deliverer to not come.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who did not know that outsiders were coming; he reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should always remain at a distance."
[The Buddha] looked out. Seeing someone approaching, he hurried to speak with them, saying, "There is food; go and fetch it. He sent them far away to return.

At that time, a person delivering food suddenly arrived and had already entered the monastery. The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow one person to receive it immediately.
He shall set aside one portion for himself and distribute the remainder to the assembly. From his own portion, he shall take [a share] from the assembly."
Among them, one person trades food and instructs [the others] to depart quickly. If they cannot depart, they should hide and escort the person carrying the food so that the bandits do not see them.
If that is still not possible, they should seize a shaven-headed man, clothe him in Dharma robes, and send him away, and so forth.

Regarding the second point, "not having previously informed the *dānapati* (donor)," Li says: "If one tells them 'do not come,' yet they come and are permitted to receive [the food], it is therefore called 'not having previously informed.'"

Although it was previously stated that one may receive food outside the monastery grounds (*ārāma*), it is therefore said: "One does not receive food outside the monastery, yet one receives food within the monastery.

Even when within the monastery, there is no offense due to the circumstance of illness; hence the phrase "when not ill. The rule regarding the appropriate ground (*yogya-bhūmi*) is likewise permitted;

thus it says, "receiving with one's own hand. According to this interpretation, although receiving food within the *araṇya* (wilderness) or within the monastery grounds constitutes an offense, other paths and monastery grounds are not.

[The Master] Wai said: "In no case is there an offense. Lü offered another interpretation, saying: "If one first says, 'Do not deliver it,' then there is no offense whether the recipient is at the monastery or on the road;

for an offense is committed only when one accepts [the robe] at both locations without having made such a restriction. That it is not mentioned here that there is an offense on the road is merely a matter of cross-referencing (qihù)."
The Fifth Section: The Precepts of Training for the Assembly.
These one hundred precepts, along with the seven methods for settling disputes, constitute the fifth section. Within this, I shall briefly cite and analyze them according to three categories.
First, the enumeration and explanation of the names; second, differences among the various schools; third, distinctions between monks and nuns. Regarding the first:

the reason this chapter does not enumerate the items is that the rules of decorum are so minute that their measure is like the sands of the Ganges; how could one establish fixed names for them by means of a numerical count?
Therefore, they are collectively designated as the "Chapter on the Many Trainings" (Saṃvara-skandha). Among the various schools, the number and names of these rules are likewise not uniform.
Furthermore, to summarize those instances where people are prone to transgressions, I have compiled them here in this volume as a framework for offenses.

Beyond these, there are miscellaneous categories of rules according to their specific characteristics within the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, numbering forty-two thousand, or eighty thousand types, or even extending throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Regarding the preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the fundamental acts (*maula*), and the subsequent movements of thought and objective spheres—wherever an object exists, it must be guarded by the precepts. This guarding occurs at three times: before, during, and after.
It is appropriate. There is nothing that is not *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Transforming evil into good constitutes the two types of restraint (*saṃvara*).

Since restraint must rely upon an object, they are called the "Training Rules" (*śaikṣa-dharma*). In the Sanskrit language, they are called *śikṣā-karaṇīya*. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: *Śikṣā* is translated as "training.
As for *karaṇīya*, it means "that which should be done. Because the word order is inverted, it is said "one should train. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: For what reason?
This chapter alone is titled "That Which Should Be Studied. Answer: Other precepts are easy to maintain but carry heavy offenses; thus, their confession upon transgression is difficult.

This precept is difficult to maintain but easy to violate; it must be constantly remembered and studied. Therefore, the names of specific offenses are not listed, but it is simply stated that one "should study."
Furthermore, it is said that if the name were established based on what is being prevented, one should speak of "various *duṣkṛta*s" (minor offenses).

However, here the object of prevention is concealed, and the name is established based on the conduct that effects the remedy; therefore, it is called "training" (*śikṣā*). Regarding what is studied, this actually applies to all four preceding categories and is not restricted to this chapter alone.

Nevertheless, human nature tends toward laxity: people are more diligent in observing heavy offenses while showing little respect for minor ones. If we discuss the actual accomplishment of practice, however—

Without diligent protection and maintenance, it can never be accomplished. Therefore, the Great Sage, observing the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, added exhortations and granted them the name of "training" (*śikṣā*).
Furthermore, when one is able to uphold these precepts completely and without deficiency, this is called the "accomplishment of training and practice.

Since the name is established at the conclusion [of the process], the meaning of the merit of training becomes manifest; thus, it is specifically regarding these precepts that the title of "receiving and training" is applied. Second, there are differences among the various schools.
There are only sixty-six precepts; eighteen of these are not found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. There are one hundred and seven precepts in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*;
forty-seven of these are not found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. There are one hundred precepts in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*; forty-four of these are not found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
There are ninety-six precepts in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*; fifty-three of these are not found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. [The precepts for] monks and nuns are not... [the same].
Regarding "the same": walking upon living grass is a grave offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* and a light offense for a *bhikṣu*. For all other cases, the offenses are identical.
Within this section, the rules regarding deportment are disordered and difficult to discern at first glance; therefore, they are grouped and divided into four sections.

First, from the beginning of the chapter until the rule "one must not stand while defecating or urinating," there are fifty-one precepts that clarify the conduct of revering the monastic deportment. Second, from [the rule] "one must not... [until the end of the first section].
He taught the Dharma to those with their robes draped over one shoulder. When he encountered those on horseback, there were eight precepts clarifying the majestic conduct of respectful behavior.

From the third [section] onward, it is not permitted to stay overnight beneath a Buddha-stūpa; when he arrived at the lower chambers where the Buddha resided, there were twenty-six precepts clarifying the majestic conduct of revering the Buddha.
From the fourth [section] onward, one must not teach the Dharma while standing to someone who is seated. Below, for...
The Fifteen Precepts. These produce those capable of reverence. Within the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), they clarify the practice of honoring and revering the Triple Gem.

Regarding why the initial section clarifies the reverent conduct of the monastic deportment (*vinaya-īryāpatha*): indeed, the formalities of attire, as well as walking, sitting, advancing, retreating, eating, drinking, and attending to nature’s calls, all constitute the dignified bearing of the Sangha.
If these are orderly, majestic, and their movements conform to the Dharma, they manifest [the virtue of the community].
Internally, they possess the practice of the Way; externally, they give rise to faith and reverence. They cause the Buddha-dharma to shine forth and benefit all sentient beings.
If the monastic community transgresses, their own mental conduct is ruined, and they foster evil in others. Consequently, their feelings toward this Jewel of the Sangha become thin and indifferent;

they do not avoid defiling it with contempt. Or, they may extend such disrespect to the Triple Gem as a whole, failing to honor it. Therefore, having previously explained that the Sangha constitutes the maintenance of the teachings, next [the text addresses] what is...

Regarding the clarification of reverence for the Dharma and its dignified deportment: the Dharma is indeed the excellent medicine that delivers one from birth and death, and it opens the eyes of the cognitive nature.
If one can certainly revere and practice it, one will transcend all burdens and ascend purely to the other shore.

However, if one treats it with arrogance and slights or destroys it, one will sink forever into birth and death and remain long submerged in the sea of suffering. Since the gravity of such calamity is profound, one must especially guard against it. Therefore—
Because the monks practice the Dharma, it is prescribed in this sequence. Third is the observance of reverent deportment toward the Buddha.

Now, the Dharma does not propagate itself; it is disseminated by means of the Teacher. Therefore, reverence for the Buddha is listed next. Furthermore, the Buddha is the King of Dharma, uniquely transcending the mundane world.

With great compassion, he takes pity on all beings, providing boundless instruction and transformation to benefit all conscious beings. His kindness is profound and vast; thus, one must respectfully honor him in order to seek [the Dharma].
Because it transcends the mundane world, one is enjoined to show reverence; because it seeks transcendence from the world, one is enjoined to honor stupas and sacred shrines.

To bring great benefit to humans and devas, those with a sincere heart should properly turn toward them, offering devotion day and night, maintaining purity and reverent aspiration; in principle, they ought to be solemn and respectful.

The "Table" expresses a longing for those who are as if present. Among those capable of reverence in the four modes of deportment, there are various explanations regarding the practice of honoring the Triple Gem.
Although the Triple Gem is generally listed above, the miscellaneous rules remain numerous; this clarifies the common monastics of the final age.

If one lacks the Way and Dharma within and treats the holy teachings with contempt, speaking at will according to circumstances, one not only fails to benefit others but also personally violates the precepts.

For this reason, many categories and sub-clauses have been established, so that there may be a standard by which to measure conduct, ensuring that no one slips through the net or transgresses to lose the great benefit.

As for why the Sangha is placed before the Buddha, it is because there are many forms of the Triple Gem and their respective positions differ. Regarding the "single-substance" Triple Gem, the Dharma is [the central element].

The Sangha must come first; this is the Teacher’s (the Buddha’s) own dharma. Speaking in terms of their distinct characteristics: when the Buddha first attained the Way, he next turned the Wheel of Dharma, and those who were ready for it realized and entered [the truth];

thus the Sangha was third. Now, however, we prioritize the Sangha as the preservers of the tradition. It is through the Sangha that the transformation of beings is carried out and the teaching is used to benefit others.
The Dharma is no ordinary task; its efficacy is revealed by the Sages. Therefore, the Buddha is placed last, so that one may rely upon the Dharma and pay reverence according to it. Only then...

Regarding the *Zhuchi* (The Abiding Master), which is contained within the various sections and is largely summarized therein: all the preceding and succeeding chapters clarify the practice of dignified demeanor (*vīrya*), thereby comprehensively collecting the minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
Now, I have extracted several dozen [points] to give rise to the intention of explaining their characteristics in the following section.
*Nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is also called *nirvāṇa-saṃgha*. In this land [China], it is translated as "inner garment. Regarding the "elephant trunk":
Jing said that one corner hanging over the left arm is called the "elephant trunk. Others say it is one corner hanging over the waist. This refers to the wearing of the inner garment;
in the Western Regions, this differs from the local practice. As for the mention of "hanging a corner," it means hanging down one [corner].

"Corner. Or, "two corners" refers to the bordering ground [of the garment]. The shape of the robe resembles a *śatapattra* (a type of leaf or food); it is used to cover the body and is bound with a cord.
Some say that "hanging" (*chui*) refers to the upper corners hanging down (Ji also says this). Other masters say it refers to the lower corners hanging down.
The translation was not definitive, leading to these divergent interpretations (and so forth).

Regarding the offense of violating non-dignified conduct (*avinaya*) through intentional action, which constitutes a *dukkaṭa*, one must confess it before another person. Seng-shen states: "This passage clarifies three points.

If the act was intentional, there is first the root offense itself, which is a *pācittiya*; furthermore, because it was improper, there is additionally the violation of non-dignified conduct, which is a *dukkaṭa*.
These two, together with the root offense, constitute three. If the act was committed unintentionally, there is no violation of non-dignified conduct; there is only the root offense."
This is fundamentally one offense. Ninety precepts are similar in this regard. If it is not done intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅), and one must repent by reproaching oneself.

For the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This refers to among the *śaikṣa* (衆學) precepts; this particular precept constitutes the same offense as for the *bhikṣuṇīs*, namely a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "draping over both shoulders" (*paryasya ubhayataḥ skandhau*), it means draping [the robe] over both shoulders from both sides.

Regarding the phrase "henceforth, approximately, up to 'not recorded as a number'": this refers to brevity. For instance, within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there may be two precepts concerning a single matter;
for example, regarding the "lifting of the robe," there is both "entering the house of a layperson" and "sitting in the house of a layperson"—these are the two.
Now, when it is said "brevity," it means that only the preceding act of "entering" is explained, while the subsequent act of "sitting" is not; therefore, it is called "abbreviated."
This commentary is extremely extensive, so I shall not record its count; its general direction can be understood.
That is to say, it does not mention a second, third, fourth, fifth, and so forth.
Regarding "wrapping the neck with a robe," Jing says: "The 'neck' does not refer to any other part of the robe. Whether it be for repentance or for receiving instruction and admonition.
In the Western lands, those who use sitting cloths do so solely to protect the monastic bedding and never to spread them upon the ground;
when performing repentance, they simply remain on the ground.

Regarding the term *kuāngzhǒu* (crossing the elbows): Master Ying states that the character for this in the Vinaya is written with the "moon" (*yue*) radical and the phonetic *kuāng* (pronounced *qūfàng*). It refers to extending the elbows horizontally.

The origin of this character is not yet clear; it appears to be merely a vernacular form. This corresponds to the passage in the *Liji* (Book of Rites) which says, "When sitting side by side, one does not cross the arms.
As for the two variant forms *qū* (軀) and [the other form] found in the Vinaya texts, both remain unexplained.
Regarding "turning the body to the left and right while hurrying" (*li-shen qù-xíng*): Master [Hui]lin says that *li* (pronounced *lì*) means to bend or curve.
The character is derived from a dog exiting a door and curving its body. *Qùxíng* (hurrying) is also written as *qǔxíng*; they are identical (pronounced *qū*).

The *Shìmíng* states: "A swift walk is called *qù*; a swift *qù* is called running. The *Lǐjì* states: "One does not hurry outside the *wéibù* (the outer boundary). Zheng Xuan says: [The text continues with his commentary].
To walk without spreading one's feet is called *tū*. One does not walk in this manner on the upper hall because it is too close [to the honored guests].
"If one requires only soup" or "if one requires only rice" means that one may desire only soup or only rice;
therefore, eating exclusively in this way does not constitute an offense.
"Not picking at the bowl" means eating from various places within the bowl rather than following a sequential order;
it refers to taking a single spoonful from one side or reaching down to pick up what is below.

Regarding looking at one’s neighbor: In the tenth chapter of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the initial rule was established as a direct prohibition that one should not look into the bowl of a neighboring seat-mate to see how much food remains.
Later, this occurred because five hundred bhikṣus were eating at a single household. After they had finished eating, they spoke among themselves, saying, "Rare indeed is this food.
A junior bhikṣu said, "The seniors have obtained good portions; we did not obtain any. The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "If..."
"The Buddha has permitted us to inspect the bowls of others so that we may know who has not received [a portion]. To those who have not received, we shall respectfully give.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I permit you to inspect the bowls of your neighbors, provided that you do not give rise to feelings of resentment."

Regarding the practice of maintaining mindfulness upon the alms bowl, the *Jìzhī* (祇) states in fascicle 22: "With a composed mind, one observes the bowl before oneself while conversing with one's neighbor.
If there is a necessary reason to speak to those on the left or right, one must first touch the rim of the bowl above.
When the person distributing food reaches the third person, one should first wash the bowl and wait in anticipation."
Regarding those who wait with their mouths open for food: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when the food reaches the mouth, the bhikṣus still did not dare to open it. The Buddha said:
"Neither too far nor too near, one should then open the mouth."
Regarding "speaking while containing food," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T.1425) states:

"If one is at a meal and the Upādhyāya, Ācārya, or an elder bhikṣu calls out, if one can respond without the sound of one's voice changing before the food has been swallowed, that is permissible. If one cannot do so, one must swallow first and then respond.
If the person who called is displeased, one should reply: 'There was food in my mouth; for that reason, I did not [respond immediately].'"
At that time, the bhikṣus of the *Pañcavargika* school were asked by laypeople who were adding more food whether they needed anything further;

they did not dare to answer and were consequently criticized for being arrogant and refusing to speak with people. The Buddha said: "When answering during a meal, you are permitted to speak; those who need something may say so."

Regarding "leaving behind food": the *Jìzhī* (祇) volume twenty-two states that the group of six bhikṣus bit off half of their food and returned the other half to their bowls, which was censured by the world.

It further states that one should eat in mouthfuls of a size suitable for the mouth; if a ball of roasted flour (*maṃsa*) is too large, it should be divided with the hands until it is a suitable size for the mouth.
If it is melon, sugarcane, or radish roots, there is no offense in biting them. If it is a cake, one should handle it with the hand [to break it into portions].
[He] divided [the food] so that it was edible. Zhi also said: The layman remarked, "I have taken away my wife and children's share to give as alms and cultivate merit.
Calculating this single grain, it was produced through a hundredfold labor; one ought to eat it entirely. Why, then, do you discard it on the ground?"
Regarding "not stuffing the cheeks," the *Ekottarika Āgama* (Sectarian Text) states: One must not turn food around in the mouth.
While holding a morsel of rice in the mouth, one must not move it from one cheek to the other; rather, one should chew on one side and swallow from that very side where one is chewing.
Regarding "not making noise while chewing food," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425), fascicle 22, states: "One must not eat making the sounds 'pu' or 'ji';
furthermore, one must not swallow food whole, making the sound 'huat-huat. However, if one makes such sounds due to a disease of the throat, there is no offense."

Regarding "sucking while eating" (the character *xi* is pronounced as *hù*): the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 23, states that if one has thin gruel, milk, curd, or soup, one must not suck them to make a sound;
rather, one should swallow them slowly. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 19, states that Mahānāma personally served rice and milk with his own hands.

"O monks, there were those who made a sound while inhaling. At that time, there was a monk who had previously been an actor; upon hearing this sound, he immediately began to dance. The other monks laughed loudly.
As they laughed, grains of rice came out from their mouths, and some even emerged from their nostrils.

The lay devotees (gṛhapati) rebuked them. After the meal, the Buddha asked: 'With what intention did you dance? They replied: 'We wished to express our joy. [The Buddha then addressed] the monks who had been inhaling..."

Regarding the offense of eating too much and the fault of eating while laughing or joking, the Buddha said: "One should train oneself not to slurp while eating. Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, one must not shrug the nose while eating.
Water used for washing the bowl, mixed with rice water, should be discarded inside the house of a layperson. According to the *Pañcavargika*, when various laypeople build new [dwellings...]
[They] would take water from a bhikṣu’s bowl and sprinkle it on the ground for good fortune.
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to use water from their bowls that was free of food to sprinkle on the ground. From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"One should train oneself not to sprinkle water containing rice from one's bowl inside the house of a layperson. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If one picks up rice grains to give to the assembly..."
If [the water] has become [stagnant], it is not an offense to discard it at the house of a layperson.

Regarding the prohibition against voiding excrement or urine upon living grass, consult the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Qizhi wen); it provides an exception for when one must remain in a place devoid of grass.
If, during the summer months, the grass is so lush that no empty space remains, one should instead go to a place where oxen or horses frequent. If, furthermore...
If there is none, one should place it upon bricks, tiles, or stones. If there is still none, one should place it upon something dry.
If there is still none, one should support it with a wooden branch so that it falls first onto the wood and only afterwards onto the ground; in this case, there is no offense.
"Spitting into water" means that one must not defecate, urinate, or spit mucus and saliva into water. Regarding the passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that provides an exception:
if it rains and the water suddenly overflows, one should do so upon a clod of earth;
if there is none, one should first drop it onto wood, stone, or the like, and only then let it fall into the water. If one digs a pit in the ground to serve as a latrine, the bottom of the latrine...
Regarding water sources: a bhikṣu must not be the first to use it for defecation or urination. He should first have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) use it, and only then may the bhikṣu use it himself.
If there is a constant flow of water at the bottom of the latrine, one must use a wooden board to receive the waste before allowing it to fall into the water.
When a bhikṣu enters the water to bathe, he must not spit into it. If he is far from the shore, he should spit into his hand. However...
If one subsequently discards the water, there is no offense. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "If it is water that people do not use, or seawater, there is no offense.
Even if water is suitable for use, if it is situated in a remote place where no one uses it, there is no offense."
Regarding "preaching the Dharma for those who show respect," the *Prātimokṣa* states: "One must not preach the Dharma to a person riding on a mount.
Checking the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says there are eight kinds of mounts: elephant mounts, horse mounts, ox carts, donkey carts, boat mounts, and carriage mounts.

"A carriage has eight [parts]. According to this principle, if one sees people traveling by boat today and, while still standing on the shore, seeks to preach the Dharma for their sake as an act of instruction, it constitutes an offense.
In the tenth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is recorded that various bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people wearing leather shoes and straw sandals.
The laypeople (gṛhapati) criticized them, saying: "This Dharma is noble and honorable; it is foremost and most subtle. Yet these..."
"Monks, one should also preach the Dharma to those wearing leather shoes or straw sandals;
yet they treat this Dharma with contempt, even to the point of tucking up their robes and so forth—all as described above. The *Jìzhù* (Commentary on the Vinaya), fascicle 22, states:

"If a monk is preaching the Dharma for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha to kings or local lords, and they say, 'Monk, preach the Dharma for me,' he must not rise [to greet them], out of fear that they might harbor suspicions. If it is at the border...
If there is someone who establishes [the stupa], and one intends to preach the Dharma for that person’s sake, the monk incurs no offense even if the king listens.
Regarding the precept on not concealing items within a stūpa for the sake of making it secure: tradition states that this is based on the precedent of opening up property belonging to the Buddha.
Now, upon detailed examination, if property belonging to the Dharma or the Saṃgha should suddenly encounter a crisis and must be secured as a safeguard, there would likewise be no fault in doing so.
Those who wear leather sandals give rise to many arrogant thoughts.
Regarding the prohibition against carrying a corpse past the base of a stupa, it is said that the guardian deity of the stupa becomes resentful because the corpse emits a foul odor.

"The three openings are likewise" means that there are four precepts concerning the large and small excretions; this text explains one of these precepts, while the conditions for the remaining three precepts are identical to this one.
Although at first it was permitted for those who were proficient in the Dharma, it was further permitted to recite the precepts in the presence of King Bimbisāra.

This was done because there was concern that the king might doubt what the bhikṣus were discussing; therefore, it was permitted for the king to hear them so that he might know they were proficient in the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the phrase "reaching the common people" (*qianli*): during the time of the First Emperor of Qin, the populace was called *qianshou*.
*Qian* means black; *shou* means head; and *li* means multitude. This clarifies that the King thoroughly understood the True Dharma and extended its benefits to the people.

Because they will surely remain reverent and respectful in the future, there is no need for the Dharma to be opened [to them]. At that time, because the King harbored doubts, it was opened so that he might hear it.
Now that his respectful faith has been established, he is no longer permitted to hear the Buddha’s precepts and other teachings.

Regarding those sections concerning deportment that are circulated separately within the *Deciding on the Correct Dharma* (*Weiyi jue zhengfa*), their reasons are fully explained in the "Protocol for Robes and Attire" (*Zhangfu yi*).
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, "Explanation of the Section on Characteristics."
End of Fascicle Ten;
Beginning of Fascicle Eleven of the *Śarīrārthagāthā* (Commentary on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*).
Compiled by the Monk Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Chapter Fifteen: The Methods for Observing and Violating the Precepts.

Although the preceding sections have clarified the various aspects of the precepts according to specific phenomena and categorized them by case, they have not yet provided a comprehensive exposition of the essential principles governing the mind and its objects.

Therefore, this chapter is now established to extensively elucidate the essence and characteristics of the mind and its objects, summarizing and encompassing all matters while comprehensively relating them to the teachings.

This text has been brought forward for that reason.
