If one follows the sequence established by various commentators, this section would stand before the "Explanation of Characteristics" (*xiexiang*), where it fully clarifies the essential nature of upholding and violating precepts, the interplay between mind and object regarding the meaning of offenses, and the establishment or rejection of points across three chapters and five sections.
Its textual meaning is vast and comprehensive. However, the intention of the present *Chao* (Commentary) is to serve those who are beginners.

First, I shall clarify the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For now, I will list the conditions for transgression (*āpatti-pratyaya*), distinguishing the characteristics and providing exemptions so that people may easily understand them.
Following this, I shall list the analysis of the characteristics in this chapter. This analysis of the characteristics of observance and transgression serves as a mirror for the mind and its objects.

What is meant here by "observance and transgression" and so forth? "Observance" refers to the two types of observance: prohibitive (*vāraṇa*) and active (*karaṇa*); "transgression" refers to the two types of transgression: prohibitive and active. Lì (Lì Wénji) says: "To rely on the teachings and maintain control is called..."

To "hold" (dharana) means to maintain; to contravene prohibitions and give rise to what is improper is therefore called "offense" (apatti). Furthermore, it is said: practicing in accordance with the teachings is called "holding," while violating the practice and giving rise to what is improper is called "offense.
"Method" (fang) refers to the Dharma; "rule" (gui) refers to the standard. This section thoroughly distinguishes the methods and rules for both types of holding and both types of offenses;
thus, it is so described. Moreover, regarding the terms "holding and offense": this generally elucidates the Vinaya Pitaka. It does not... [text ends]

It brings forth the two terms "observance" (*zhi*) and "violation" (*fan*). As in the preceding two sections of the *Prātimokṣa*, it explains "observance by abstention" (*zhichi*) in detail and "observance by action" (*zuochi*) in brief;

subsequently, the twenty *Khandakas* explain "observance by action" in detail and "observance by abstention" in brief. If one contravenes the preceding *Prātimokṣa*, it is termed "action-violation" (*zuofan*);
if one contravenes the subsequent *Khandakas*, it is termed "abstention-violation" (*zhifan*). It is called thus because these names are manifested from this point onward.

The note stating, "The preceding [section] distinguishes [the characteristics] according to phenomena," intends to introduce the following text; it first restates the meaning of the preceding section.

That is to say, within the "characteristics that follow" (anulakṣaṇas), there is a restriction based on phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to clarify what constitutes upholding and what constitutes violating [the precepts];

therefore, it says "distinguishing them according to phenomena. This concludes the previous chapter. The note beginning with "As for 'comprehensively clarifying,' etc. introduces what follows. Above...
Having already distinguished [the categories] according to phenomena, if one were to comprehensively clarify the relationship between mind and objects, this present section follows that intent:

to provide an extensive explanation of mind and objects so that they may be precisely understood, this separate gate is established; it is, in fact, a term for "discernment" (*vivecana*). As for the word "discernment," it means "clarification."

"Jian" (簡) means "to distinguish. This refers to distinguishing between the precepts (*śīla*) and transgressions (*āpatti*) as a single category. Regarding this character *zhēn* (甄), there is an account of a single event:
Formerly, Guo Pu was constantly reading books when a man would frequently come to discuss matters with him;

he was unlike ordinary people. Guo Pu asked him, "Where do you come from? What is your surname and given name? He replied, "My surname is Shu and my name is Zhēn Zhòng," and having spoken, he departed.

Park Si pondered this for a long time and then realized: "The character *shu* (舒) is composed of 'house' (*she*) on one side and 'I' (*yu*) on the other; 'I' means the self, so it refers to the person within my house.

The character *zhen* (甄) has 'west' (*xi*) below and 'earth' (*tu*) on the side, with a 'tile' (*wa*) added to it. The character *zhong* (仲) has 'person' (*ren*) on one side and 'middle' (*zhong*) on the other.
This must mean a person from within the earth beneath the tiles to the west of my house. He then grasped the ground and found a creature about five or six inches long.
"Chi" (尺) is the essence of the earthworm. After this, it never came again. The commentary states: "As for 'if one takes from the path' (*youtu*)," Master Li says:

if one takes from the "path" (*tu*) of the ancients—that is, their tracks—then logically it should have been placed before the section on "Explaining the Characteristics" (*shixiang*), where the observance and violation of the precepts are clarified.

However, because new students do not yet understand this, it is appropriate to place it here at the end. Furthermore, the original work was titled *Sichao* (斯鈔); it was not intended [to be called otherwise].
It refers to exposition.

Regarding the Vinaya school (*vinaya-piṭaka*), its essence lies solely in the observance and transgression of precepts; it is called "Vinaya" because it defines and evaluates the gravity of offenses. It is called a "school" (*piṭaka*) because it serves as the primary authority.

Since ancient times, masters have established this Vinaya school, yet various views have differed: some take the practice of the teachings as the school's core, while others take the cultivation of wholesome restraint as the core.

This is taken as the primary tenet (*śāstra*). Alternatively, the observance and violation [of precepts] may be taken as the tenet. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) takes the three wheels as its tenet;

however, judging by the intent of the present text, it correctly takes the observance and violation as its tenet. This is because, for example, when the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates eternal abiding (*nityatva*), it takes that eternal abiding as its tenet;

and when the *Lotus Sūtra* elucidates the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it takes that One Vehicle as its tenet. Since this Vinaya elucidates both observance and violation, how could it not take observance and violation as its tenet?

This constitutes the primary theme. That is to say, although this single Vinaya-piṭaka is vast and extensive in its textual expression, when its general purport is summarized, it does not go beyond "observance" (dhāraṇa) and "violation" (āpatti).

Specifically, the two *Prātimokṣa* texts represent "abstaining from transgression through observance" (*pratiṣedha-dhāraṇa*), while the twenty *Khandakas* represent "engaging in observance" (*anuṣṭhāna-dhāraṇa*) and "abstaining from transgression through non-engagement" (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*).

Since these two terms, "observance" and "violation," encompass the entire meaning of the treatise, how could they not be the primary theme? Not only is "observance and violation" the primary theme of this Vinaya; [it is so] throughout the five [parts].
The Vinaya-piṭaka of each school all elucidates the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts. The nature of these acts of upholding and violating is indeed profound;

this is because the teachings presented here are vast and their underlying principles are subtle and deep. Unless one has accumulated merit over a long period, how could one possibly understand and clarify them?

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One who thoroughly understands even a single character is called a Vinaya Master. This is said because the meaning of characters encompasses all things. This refers to—
The characteristics of the teachings that can express [the truth] are difficult to discern.

Unless one is a person who has accumulated learning and penetrated the subtle, such that they have studied for many years and investigated with rigorous scrutiny, one will not reach its profound and recondite principles. Master Ying said: "Profound" (you) is a description of being deep and far-reaching.

"Dong" (cave) means "to penetrate. "Yuanqiong" (far-reaching penetration) refers to the written word. This means that only those who have practiced and studied for a long time are able to transcend the written word and grasp its underlying principles.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "successive generations have followed this," it refers to the lineage of masters transmitted from the time of Zizhijue (Self-Awakened Wisdom) down to the present day.
In practicing the precepts, observing or violating them, and maintaining views, although there are slight differences, the general intent ultimately converges upon a single path.

Some say that from antiquity, the compiled teachings have been the same and their great meaning has not differed; thus it is said there is no "different art. "Art" (shu) refers to the Way (Dao), and is also called the Dharma (Fa). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"The road within a city is called 'art' (shu); 'art' means to penetrate. Although there are minor variations in the paths and scales, they are fundamentally one.

Regarding the phrase "pointing out those who do not err," Zhiyi states: Some masters take such acts as sexual misconduct or theft to be "untrainable" (asikṣya), whereas I maintain that it is the delusion and forgetfulness of the mental state that is untrainable;

the actual acts themselves are all trainable. Although this differs slightly from the views of the ancients, the general meaning is not lost, for it does not fall outside the characteristics of observance and violation (*dhāraṇa* and *āpatti*).
The term "徑" (*jìng*) refers to a minor path; it denotes the tradition of the ancient masters.
Regarding the term *wàng* (market/stall): although the established doctrines differ in their paths and routes, their general intent remains the same.
As for the phrase "when the time has passed at the school-stall (*xué-sì*), how could one know [the truth]?"—*sì* means to display or to arrange.

It refers to displaying goods in a market where people may choose between two options as they please; the "school-stall" is likewise so called because, during the time of listening to lectures, one is allowed to freely select and choose from among them. Therefore, it is said:
"Academy" (*xué sì*). This is just as it is said in common parlance that during the Han dynasty, Zhang Kai exhaled his breath as the five-star mist while residing north of Mount Hua.
As many people came there to receive instruction, it was popularly known as the "Market of Flower-Shade.

Thus, the *Shuowen* says: "The seven noble families filled the marketplaces; if one goes to the market of Huayin... Now, when we speak of an "academy-market" (*xué sì*), "market" (*sì*) is simply another name for a marketplace. That is to say:
Within a single summer, or even within a single lifetime, one has perhaps not passed through the marketplace of the Vinaya more than two or three times.

How could one who speaks of the Vinaya today recognize the beginning and end, the lightness and gravity, or the nature of upholding and violating the precepts? Therefore it is said: "The time has passed the school.

This phrase is directed at those who have accumulated learning and penetrated the subtle; only they can know the characteristics of the beginning and end of upholding and violating. It is further said: "The two types of upholding accord with what is received."
The essence is called the beginning; the two transgressions that violate the received essence are called the end.
However, the texts concerning observance and transgression run throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, clarifying only these two types of observance and two types of transgression.

The former, in the *Śīlaskandha*, is termed "observance through abstention" (*zhi-chi*); the latter, in the *Khandhaka*, is termed "observance through action" (*zuo-chi*). By reversing these, the two types of transgression can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "designating names based on the objects [of transgression]," if one were to clarify the names of the offenses in relation to the previously mentioned objects such as sexual misconduct and theft, this has already been fully discussed in the preceding section on the individual precepts (*śīla*).
Now, to attempt a general discussion by way of their underlying meaning, this serves as the formal introduction to the present text.
This means that by discussing the principles of the Vinaya, one comes to understand the underlying intent of the disciplinary framework regarding what constitutes an offense and its maintenance.

Just as lifting the collar at the beginning allows those who grasp the main cord from the tip of a hair to straighten their eyes, this present chapter may be called the "collar and main cord" of the five categories of offenses.

To clarify this by citing specific instances, the text below mentions sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying, or it cites matters such as monastic dwellings, measurements in cubits, and extra robes.

Whether large or small, all are termed "citing instances. This is also like the four or five propositions within the section on "perceptions regarding objects," where all cite killing and stealing to clarify the point.

First, "knowing the names of observance and violation" means understanding the terminology of the two types of observance and the two types of violation. Second, "understanding their essential natures and characteristics" refers to...
Regarding these two types of observance and transgression, what constitutes their essential nature? This will be explained in detail below: they take the mind as their essential nature.

Third, concerning the accomplishment [of practice]: this refers to the karma of the four modes of conduct regarding observance and transgression. Within what limits of the mind is this karma accomplished?

The sub-commentary explains: "The conclusion establishes that [the practice] is restricted to the mind of cultivation. Regarding the fourth point, "penetration and obstruction": there are two types of observance and transgression, totaling four modes of conduct.

If these are mutually inclusive or coexistent, they are said to be "penetrating"; if each of the four is individually absent, they are termed "obstructed. Regarding the fifth point, "gradual and sudden":
the practices of the two types of observance and transgression may be accomplished gradually, or they may be achieved instantaneously. Sixth, excellence...

"Inferior" refers generally to both the observance and transgression of the two types of precepts, each having its own degree of excellence or deficiency; hence they are called "superior and inferior.

First, regarding the clarification of the two kinds of observance and transgression, this explains the meaning of the terms for observance and transgression in the initial section. First, the two types of observance are explained: [The text continues with the definitions of the two types of observance.]

The reason why the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) are explained first, followed by the two types of transgression (*āpatti*), is that observance accords with the essence of the precepts and thus should be explained first;

transgression violates the essence of the precepts and is therefore described later. Furthermore, regarding the two types of observance, the observance of restraint (*saṃvara-dhāraṇa*) is explained first, followed by the observance of action (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*);

this is because one must first cease from evil and distance oneself from sexual misconduct and killing so that the practice of observance is established, thereby becoming capable of upholding and governing [the precepts]. Thus, it is explained first.
The preceding section clarified *zhichi* (abstaining from what is prohibited); this next section clarifies *zuochi* (performing what is prescribed).

The following section clarifies the rules for transgressions (*fan*), first explaining *zuofan* (transgressing through action) and subsequently distinguishing *zhifan* (transgressing through non-action), as these correspond to the two types of observance mentioned above. This is because violating *zhichi* is termed *zuofan*, while violating *zuochi* is termed *zhifan*.
"Complying with what was originally undertaken" means that at the time of undertaking [the precepts], one made a solemn vow and commitment to sever all evil;

therefore, not committing evil now is to comply with what was originally undertaken. Regarding "such as the first category," this is because the four precepts of the first category consist solely of *śīla* (restraint) and *dhāraṇa* (maintaining), whereas the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of the second category encompass both restraint and performance (*kriyā*). Thus, only the first category is mentioned here. The above explains restraint (*virati*).
The explanation of the meaning of *dhāraṇa* (retention) is complete.

Below, the meaning of *kṛta-dhāraṇa* (active retention) is clarified. Regarding "there is one who initiates protection for the sake of the wholesome": this refers to whatever wholesome dharmas arise, such as the ritual purification (*śuddhi*) of robes through *dhāraṇa*.

Because it necessarily involves the cultivation of the mind, it is termed "active" (*kṛta*). As for "retention is as explained previously," this briefly indicates that it is the same as the preceding text.
Therefore, while the preceding text spoke of "stopping without transgression," here one should speak of "acting without transgression.
When the essence of the precepts is radiant and pure, acting in accordance with what was originally received is called "upholding" (dhāraṇa).

Regarding the sequence of "before" and "after," this intends to explain the reasons for that sequence. First, let us examine the question ourselves: Why is it that "restraint through non-action" (*śīla-virati*) is explained first, followed by "performance of action" (*kriyā-vidhi*)?
Furthermore, why are the two types of observance (*dharana*) explained first, and the two types of transgression (*āpatti*) explained later?

The explanation is as follows: One must first distance oneself from evil; this is restraint through non-action. Subsequently, one cultivates virtuous conduct; this is performance of action. Since these observances depend upon the essence of the precepts received (*samādatta-śīla*), they are presented in this order.
The former clarifies the offense incurred by violating [the precepts], while the latter explains them. The *Śāstra* states, "The characteristics of the precepts are cessation (*śīla-lakṣaṇa-sthiti*).
This citation from the *Śata-śāstra* was indeed composed by the Bodhisattva Devanāga. Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the precepts are cessation": it refers to guarding against evil;

to cease and not transgress is called "cessation-maintenance" (*sthiti-śīla*). Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of practice are performance" (*caryā-lakṣaṇa-kriyā*): it refers to cultivating goodness; to perform [virtuous acts] is called "performance-maintenance" (*kriyā-śīla*). Therefore, it is said: "practice."
[The text] explains: The treatise itself asks why *śīla* as restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) is placed first, while *śīla* as performance (*kriyā-śīla*) follows later.

The answer in the treatise states that one must first possess the precepts (*śīla*), and only then initiate practice; since the precepts involve restraining conduct, they constitute "restraint," and thus restraint comes first and performance follows.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that *śīla* as restraint is superior because it abandons gross transgressions, and is therefore explained first, whereas *śīla* as performance abandons minor transgressions.

Because it is inferior, it is explained later. Gao says: "The *zhichi* (observance through abstention) is fundamental, so it is clarified first; the *zuochi* (observance through performance) is secondary, like a branch, so it is explained later. Li asks:

"Why is abstention mentioned first and performance second within the category of observance (*shou*), while within the category of transgression (*fan*), performance is mentioned first and abstention second?
He answers: "Throughout the course of spiritual practice, if one does not abandon faults, there is no way to perform wholesome deeds. Therefore, abstention comes first to abandon faults."

This constitutes the primary tenet. Next, the aspect of "action" (作) is clarified, as its meaning consists in the cultivation of goodness. The *Śata-śāstra* states: "The characteristic of precepts is cessation; the characteristic of practice is action.

Cessation comes first and action follows, according to the sequential order of their meanings. Alternatively, the observance of cessation (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) must be explained first regarding one's own conduct, while the observance of action (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) pertains to external actions and is therefore explained subsequently.
This is also like the Vinaya, where the *Khandhaka* follows after the main body of the precepts (*sūtra*).
Regarding the two types of transgressions, that which is first committed and later ceased is examined first and then maintained, as they are contrasted with one another.
Furthermore, since the commission of a transgression is coarse, it is logically appropriate to prohibit it first; whereas the cessation of a transgression is subtle, it should be explained later.

This is intended so that monks and nuns may abandon both the coarse and the subtle, thereby attaining a high level of realization on the Path. Moreover, the phrase "ceasing evil and practicing good" and so forth is also from the *Śata-śāstra* (Treatise in One Hundred Verses).

This is the "Pattern" (Wen). It means that only after first ceasing evil does one then practice virtuous conduct. The explanation of the meaning of the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*) is now complete.
Next, the two types of transgression will be explained. Regarding the phrase "I have inverted views in my breast," an ancient said: "I possess three things. The first is the Tathāgata..."
First is the "Self of Sovereignty," which refers to the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of *nirvāṇa*; this is called the true self of the Buddha.
Second is the "Self of Worldly Convention," which refers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats who speak in accordance with worldly usage;
as it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "The Buddhas, following worldly convention, also speak of a self. Third is the "Self of Deluded Inversion" held by ordinary beings. As [it says]:
The non-Buddhists and others calculate the self to be like a minute atom, or like a sesame seed or a grain of rice, or like a thumb, or as being all-pervasive;

what is now called the "perverted view of self" refers precisely to these meanings. Such are the calculations of the self by the non-Buddhists of the West; yet among the people of this world, it is likewise so.

In the Buddha-dharma, even in the future, there will still be those who cling to the existence of a "person" (pudgala) or a "divine self" (ātman). As stated in the *Zhijing* (Sūtra on Roasting): "On such-and-such a day, the person or divine self resides in the feet;

on another day, it resides in the head. This, too, is a false attachment to a self (*ātman*). It is also associated with the perversions (*viparyāsa*). There may be those who violate this [teaching regarding] the person or divine self, or who cause death because of it.
To speak of the Western Regions (India), there was the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, who subdued the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). These non-Buddhists constantly say:
"There is a self. In your Buddha-dharma, you say there is no self; this is a false teaching. He spoke this meaning to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
Dharmapāla said, "You say there is a self; what are the characteristics of this self? He replied, "I observe within my own body..."
"The mark of my self is yellowish. The Bodhisattva said, "It is certainly that there is a self; it is not only yellowish in color, but there are also hairs upon it.
He had the non-Buddhist practitioner observe this. When the non-Buddhist returned home and examined himself closely, he indeed saw hairs growing all over his body.
Later, he came back and said, "It is truly so; there are hairs. The Bodhisattva spoke again, saying, "There are not only hairs, but there is also a tail. Again...
He further observed the tail. Once his visualization was perfected, he likewise saw the tail. He came again and said, "There truly is a tail. He spoke further of the four legs;
he was made to observe them, and so on until he spoke of the head and horns, to all of which he replied that they existed.
The Bodhisattva said, "Since you now possess hair, a tail, four legs, and two horns, you may go to the manger to eat grass. Outside...

The ox went immediately to the manger to eat grass. After many days had passed, driven by delusion, it became extremely exhausted from eating grass and came to the Bodhisattva, saying, "How can I endure this suffering?
The Bodhisattva instructed him, saying, "Practice the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). First contemplate that the two horns are non-existent; gradually contemplate the head, tail, and so forth;
next contemplate that the entire body of the 'self' is entirely non-existent. Because of this, the ox awakened to the Way.

Thus, we know that false attachment is precisely the view of existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Regarding "stirring up body and speech to create objects contrary to principle," this means that within one possesses the afflictions of the three poisons, such as greed, which can incite and agitate the body and speech.

Because these stir up the body and speech to create objects such as sexual misconduct and theft while viewing them in opposition to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "action" (*karma*). This refers to those who take the commission of unwholesome dharmas as their primary tenet; this concludes the text.

This clarifies that committing evil is necessarily termed "transgression through action" (*kṛta-āpatti*). Therefore, the practice of unwholesome dharmas constitutes the primary category of transgression through action.

As for "conduct that violates what was originally received": at the time one originally received the precepts, one intended to train in the myriad practices; now, being indolent, one refuses to cultivate them.

This constitutes an action that violates one’s original undertaking (*pratijñā*). To "contravene that undertaking and vow" means that at the time of the initial undertaking, one vowed to study all dharmas;

now, since one does not study them, this is a contravention of the undertaking and vow. This refers to those who take the non-cultivation of wholesome dharmas as their primary principle—for example, ceasing to maintain the robes or to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), and ceasing to read and recite the scriptural teachings.
Such cessation constitutes a transgression; taking this non-cultivation as one's basis is precisely [the violation].

This concludes the explanation of the primary principles of the two types of observance and transgression. Lü states: "The two types of observance receive their names based on their functional efficacy; the two types of transgression receive their designations based on the faults involved.
Thus ends the exposition of the first meaning of observance and transgression.

Second, regarding the clarification of the essence and the manifestation: Sengli states that the two types of observance and transgression take the mind as their essence, while body and speech constitute their manifestation.
For example, in the case of the dispute concerning the holding of robes (*cīvara*), kneeling before the robe and speaking words with the mouth constitutes the manifestation.

Nevertheless, although one externally relies upon body and speech, when discussing the nature of the karmic act, it must refer to the internal mind. As stated in the Vinaya: "In all cases, one asks: 'With what intention do you wish to use [it]? "

"Taking the mind as the essence and discarding other meanings": some commentators explain this by saying that ancient masters considered [certain] matters to be unteachable, while Master Nanshan considered the delusion and forgetfulness of the mind and its objects to be unteachable;
it is for this reason that he discarded those ancient interpretations. Now, upon careful examination, this interpretation is incorrect.
Li: This section intends to clarify the essential nature (*tǐzhuàng*). Why is it necessary to speak of "that which can be learned" and "that which cannot be learned," and so forth?

However, "that which can be learned" and "that which cannot be learned" belong to the category of the distinction between upholding and violating [the precepts]. What relevance do they have to the matter of establishing the essential nature? Shen says:
"The essential nature was explained extensively as a phenomenon that is neither form nor mind; since it is not being clarified further now, he says it is 'set aside' (*fèi*). Li says: "No."

This is because it relies on the former interpretation. Therefore, it is said that other meanings are set aside. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As for what was said in the past" (this refers to the interpretation of emptiness as the precept).

To distance oneself from the three evils of the body, the four transgressions of speech, and not to commit the three unwholesome roots of the mental ground—this is called the essence of *zhichi* (maintaining through restraint).

As for bowing and prostrating, practicing giving (*dāna*), releasing living beings, praising the Three Jewels, and reciting the scriptures and teachings—these are the cultivation of the three virtues of the mind. In contrast to [the former],...

To remedy the three poisons by practicing various contemplations, up to and including the cultivation of detachment, pure conduct, great compassion, and the Four Great Vows, is termed the essence of active observance (*kṛta-śīla*).
To give rise to the ten unwholesome actions is termed the essence of active transgression (*kṛta-āpatti*).

To cease performing prostrations, giving, cultivating loving-kindness, and even [engaging in] contemplative practice is termed the cessation of transgression (*sthāpana-āpatti*). Someone asked: "If one ceases to practice giving, prostrations, and recitation, does this constitute a transgression?"
From which Vinaya does this passage originate? To which *skandha* (category) is it subsumed? As the Vinaya text states: "That which the Buddha did not prohibit, he did not prohibit.

How is this known? Regarding the fact that failing to give is not an offense: as stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there were two brothers who left the household life and committed [certain] actions;

each of them failed to practice giving and the precepts for many years. The younger brother became a white elephant because he did not uphold the precepts, while the elder brother attained the state of an Arhat.

In China, there are those who go begging for alms but receive nothing because no one practices giving. How can it be said that failing to give constitutes a transgression? Furthermore, within the Vinaya, the focus is solely upon body and speech;
regarding the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), no such preceptual instruction has been heard. How, then, can it be said that failing to cultivate the Four Great Vows constitutes a violation?
Moreover, as for transgressions—if one were to commit them—when has anyone ever been seen to repent of sins such as failing to practice giving? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
It says: "If one does not practice the twelve dhūtas and the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa), it is not called a violation of the precepts;

yet, because one is not adorned with the precepts, we know that what was established previously contradicts the Vinaya and the Śāstras. If one speaks of personal cultivation, it may only contradict principle; if one does not cultivate compassion..."

How can one accomplish the path? As long as the venomous snake has not been removed, the principle does not allow for peaceful sleep; one must act as if saving one's head from fire. Because such a person is called "one who possesses shame," it is said that [worldly affairs] are abandoned.
At present, we concern ourselves only with correct understanding; therefore, it is said that we shall discuss this directly, and so forth.

Although my younger brother practiced giving (*dāna*), he fell into the realm of animals. This clearly shows that practicing giving is not the same as upholding the precepts (*śīla*). My elder brother did not practice giving, yet he did not fail to beg for alms.
It is so. Since he had already realized arhatship, it is clear that not practicing giving was not a violation of the precepts.

How can the ancients judge that the failure to practice *dāna* constitutes a transgression of the essential nature (*tattva*) of the precept? Such an interpretation is logically flawed. Furthermore, they judge the practice of *dāna* and the recitation of sutras to be "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*).
If practicing *dāna* were indeed active observance, why did his younger brother fall as a white elephant? First, regarding those who maintain the precepts (*dhāraṇa-dhara*): it is said that...
It takes the practitioner’s capacity for observing precepts and the capacity for violating precepts as its essence.
Regarding the statement that "taking the mind as the essence and body and speech as the instruments": the essence of the karma of observance and violation must be driven by the mind;

body and speech are merely the instruments for performing good and evil. Even if body and speech exist, if they are not directed by the mind, karma cannot be accomplished. According to the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra]...

The *Panhui jing* (Discourse on the Manifestation of Wisdom) clarifies the meaning of the three types of karma (*trikarma*). It designates bodily and vocal karma as "appointed karma" (*qiyè*), because they are so named due to their prior initiation;
thus, they are called "mental karma. Bodily and vocal karma arise from mental karma. The commentators explain that because cause and effect correspond, there is a similarity to a formal agreement;
hence it is called "appointed karma. This means that the mental karma arises first and acts as an appointment for the bodily and vocal karma. Therefore, the body...
Vocal karma follows later; it should be preceded by mental karma. As for the phrase "the treatise says," it refers to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Regarding the three types of karma—body, speech, and mind—the body is the instrument for performing good and evil deeds. Karma does not arise spontaneously; it must depend upon the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), which serves as the basis that can bring about bodily and vocal actions.
"One should carefully examine the mind" is from the "Exhortation to Believe" (*Kṣānti-prastāvanā*) in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Verse: A brief citation of a single line. It says: "One who wishes to cultivate wholesome dharmas should be fully equipped with the three types of action and must carefully examine their intention. As stated in the Rāhula-sūtra:
A certain person of frivolous character (referring to a brahmin who treated him with contempt) gave rise to a malicious intent and took sand and dirt, placing it in Śāriputra’s alms bowl.
[He] struck Rāhula, causing his head to split open and blood to flow, staining his face. Śāriputra said to Rāhula, "You should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
As Rāhula washed the blood by the water, he spoke to himself, saying: "My pain is but momentary; how can it compare to that long-lasting suffering?"

As explained extensively therein, regarding the subsequent clarification: Vasubandhu states that although it was previously discussed that the mind is the root of karma, as in the "Gate of Superiority and Inferiority" (*śreyāṃsa-dvāra*) below, the lightness or gravity [of karma] is distinguished by the single mind across the three time periods, as in the *Śraddhākaravarman* and other texts. Thus, one knows that when karma arises, it takes the mind as its basis.
However, if one discusses the formation of karma by a Śrāvaka, it necessarily depends upon body and speech; the mental faculty alone does not constitute it. If it were single...
Regarding "accomplishment" (*siddhi*): this is restricted to the Mahāyāna. Since there is such a distinction in the text below, it says "as intended in the following.

This likely refers to the citation from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* below, which states that for an offense to constitute a completed karma, it must necessarily involve the mind; thus, one knows it must depend upon the mind. The above has explained the author's own interpretation of "the one who maintains" (*dhāraka*).

Second, regarding that which is upheld: this refers to clarifying the essence by means of the two teachings—prohibitions and permissions. The former is the mind capable of upholding; the following concerns the meaning of what is upheld.
That is to say, in relation to the aforementioned phenomena, the phenomena themselves are what is upheld. This shall now be discussed in terms of upholding and violating.
This is clarified within the two teachings of prohibition (*saṃvara*) and permission (*anujñā*).

Regarding the two types of prohibitive teachings, Xuán says: "As for the various natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), their essence contradicts the principle; even if the Buddha did not prohibit them, [they would still be transgressions]."

Secular society constantly imposes prohibitions; teachings arise from such regulations. Therefore, it is called "prescriptive teaching" (*zhìjiào*). This interpretation accords with the meaning of "restraint" (*zhì*) that follows; it does not mean that one should not act.

Regarding the statement that "acting [accordingly] incurs no fault, while non-compliance entails guilt," this refers to the *zì* (unrestricted) practices and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the three robes and one alms bowl, these were prescribed by the Buddha; non-compliance constitutes an offense.
As for the phrase "the two types of restraint and prohibition entail transgression when acted upon," this refers to [acts such as] sexual misconduct, theft, and lying.

It is so. The preceding exposition on the prohibitive teachings (*pratikṣepa-śāsana*) is now complete. Regarding the term "permissive teachings" (*anujñā-śāsana*), Xuanchun stated: "As with various prohibitory precepts (*pratiṣedha-śīla*), their substance is cumbersome and complex;

their practical application is disorderly and obstructs the Path; and logically, they are difficult to relax. Nevertheless, for those of inferior capacity, they must rely upon these [prohibitions] to establish themselves.

Therefore, while the prohibitions are established according to conditions and based on circumstances, they are universally permitted when one acts according to one's own inclination. Because they cannot be looked up to [as absolute], they are called 'permissive teachings. As for whether they are performed or not performed, all..."

Regarding "being without fault": the furnishings for the two types of dwellings, the one hundred and one items of surplus property, and the granting of permission (*anujñā*)—all these are permitted by the Noble Ones.

Therefore, they are called "allowed. While it is most excellent if those of superior capacity practice accordingly and do not store such items, for those of middling or inferior faculties, using them is likewise without fault and does not contravene the teaching;
thus, it is said that "everything is without fault. Accordingly, the *Bhūmivastu* states: "That which involves faulty conduct is prohibited; that which involves no faulty conduct..."

This means "it is permitted. This is a textual proof (*viniścaya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states: if it is an action involving transgression, such as sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth, the Buddha does not permit its performance.
If it is an action free from transgression, such as the allowance for keeping extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and so forth, the Buddha permits its practice.
Therefore, it is said that actions involving transgression are subject to prohibition, and so on.
Why must there be two? This explains the reason for establishing the two teachings; it arises as a hypothetical inquiry:

"If, according to what you have heard in the teachings, there is no offense whether one acts or does not act, what is the use of hearing the teachings? Therefore, the purpose of the two teachings—prescriptive and permissive—is to provide a complete framework for guiding sentient beings:

prescriptive teachings are intended for those of superior faculties, while permissive teachings open the way for those of middling and inferior faculties. Thus, there are these two teachings: the prescriptive and the permissive.
Encompassed by the three faculties, its meaning is exhaustive; thus it is called "Sufficient in Meaning" (*Arthaviniścaya*).

Now, regarding the division of the Dharma into two teachings according to their respective scopes: within the two teachings of Prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and Permission (*anujñā*), there are both phenomena (*vastu*) and principles (*dharma*).

In which teaching is there principle without phenomenon? Now, these two teachings will be contrasted with the four practices (*catur-caryā*); in which of them are both phenomenon and principle present? If [it is] only...

The current text and ancient interpretations distinguish between "abstention" (*saṃvara*) as upholding and "action" (*kriyā*) as transgression; these merely encompass matters such as the four grave offenses (*catur-uttara-pārājika*), wherein abstention constitutes upholding and action constitutes transgression, with no further dharmas to be included.
If, however, one takes "action" as upholding and "abstention" as transgression, then it encompasses both types of teaching.

This refers to dharmas and matters such as the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, where action constitutes upholding and abstention constitutes transgression; thus, it is said that for the *pravāraṇā* and other such rites, there are both dharmas and [matters].

[This refers to] "matters" (*vastu*). Therefore, "performing and maintaining" (*kṛta-ādhāra*) encompasses the dharmas and matters within both teachings. That this is the established doctrine of the ancient masters is known from the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), which says:

"As the ancients explained: 'The dharmas encompassed by the two teachings each have their respective limits. Stopping and maintaining, as well as performing and violating, apply only to the two teachings;

they clarify them through the characteristics of matters (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*), and so forth. Question: According to the established doctrine above, does "stopping and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*) refer only to matters? No.

Regarding those who understand the Dharma: such things as the five perversions and the seven non-principles are not the True Dharma; if one acts in violation of them, they must necessarily be restrained and curtailed according to their meaning.
Since these dharmas and these matters are no different from killing and stealing, for what reason are they not included within the scope of restraint?

As in the interpretations of the past, to claim that restraint is explained only in relation to specific matters is contrary to the true meaning. Now we do not follow that view; whether it be a matter or a dharma, it is the Sage’s prohibition that is paramount.

Regarding "action" (*karman*), it applies to both upholding and violating [the precepts], for their essence and characteristics are not distinct. Thus, one should know that within the four types of conduct, there are always objective matters (*vastu*).

Although this is not extensively refuted in the current text, it is clarified regarding matters within the first section, the "Gate of Distinguishing by Stages," among the various analytical summaries (*viniścaya*).
Following the statement "having completed the formal motion (*jñapti*)," it says: "It can be understood by analogy with the *Abhidharma*. This implies...

This clarifies that the categories of *zhichi* (maintaining through cessation) and *chafan* (violating) still possess their respective methods. Furthermore, the nine phrases in the subsequent section all concern these matters and methods of the *shangzuo* (senior monks).

As for explaining *zhichi* and *zuofan* (committing through action) solely in relation to the matters within the two types of teaching, this represents the ancient interpretation as previously detailed at length.
The "two teachings" refer to the two teachings of prohibition (*zhì*) and permission (*tīng*). For example, [the prohibitions against] sexual misconduct and theft are the teaching of prohibition.

The "house" refers to the acts of commission and omission regarding the observance of the precepts. To be free from defilement despite being pressed by resentment throughout the three periods [of time] constitutes the observance of the precepts through commission and omission while following the teachings.
To take pleasure [in transgression] constitutes commission and omission; to remain undefiled is the observance through non-commission.

Since this is permitted by the Buddha, it is called "following the teachings. Furthermore, constructing a dwelling is following the teachings; to refrain from exceeding the prescribed dimensions is the observance through non-commission. When a dwelling is completed that exceeds the dimensions, it is called...

"Committing an offense. This refers to the school that emphasizes following the teachings (*śāsana*). It concerns the matters of maintaining through abstention (*virati-dhāraṇa*) and committing through action (*kriyā-āpatti*). (The preceding [explanations] are my own reflections and are not yet fully detailed).

Regarding the two types of matters corresponding to the two schools of teaching—the school of following the teachings and the school of realizing the truth—these refer to "maintaining through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) and "offending through abstention" (*virati-āpatti*). In the school of following the teachings, these are "maintaining through action" and "offending through abstention."

There are also cases where there is both a dharma and a matter, such as the construction of a dwelling. In the system of prohibitive teachings (*pratikṣepa-śikṣā*), there are both the dharma of "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) and the matter of "abstaining from transgression" (*virati-vipatti*).
There are also cases where there is both a dharma and a matter, such as the three robes and one bowl; these can be understood by correlating them with their respective matters.

That is to say, within both the prohibitive and permissive teachings (*vidhi-śikṣā*), there are both dharmas and matters. As for why the preceding [section] did not encompass the dharmas, this is actually an explanation of that previous statement. Therefore, it was previously called "abstaining and maintaining" (*virati-dhāraṇa*).

The passage beginning with "Acting as such clarifies the matters corresponding to the two teachings" refers to the section on the "Prohibitions" (zhi-men). For example, the *varṣā* retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony are "dharmas," while the four [offenses] such as sexual misconduct and theft are "matters" (*vastu*).

Now, if one were to categorize these by means of "acting in accordance with the prohibitions" (*zhichi*) and "acting in violation of the prohibitions" (*zuofan*), one would only be subsuming the matters themselves, such as sexual misconduct and theft.

Conversely, if one were to categorize them by means of "acting in accordance with the observances" (*zochi*) and "ceasing from violations" (*zhifan*), one would instead obtain the "matters" and "dharmas" of the *varṣā* retreat and the *pravāraṇā*. This is what is meant by "expounding the *pravāraṇā*."

Within this, there are both dharmas and matters. Furthermore, within the teachings on listening, "keeping [an extra robe] beyond the limit" is the matter, while "purifying through declaration" (*śuddhika*) is the dharma.

All of the above are the established doctrines of the ancient masters. Regarding the phrase "matters such as those in the section on prohibitions within the two teachings corresponding to the preceding 'abstention and maintenance' (*zhi-chi*)," Shen (Shenxiu) says:
"One must grasp the character 'abstention' (*zhi*); do not become confused when reaching the following text. This means that we are now dealing with the matters within the section on prohibitions.
The above clarifies *zhichi* (stopping and maintaining).

Regarding the statement that sexual misconduct applies to the three objects: these are humans, non-humans, and animals, as well as the "right path" (the anus). Some say that engaging in sexual misconduct in three locations constitutes the three objects;
this is not the correct interpretation. Therefore, the *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) states: "That which can be learned through restraint" refers to sexual misconduct applying to the three [objects].

Regarding the realms of rebirth (*gati*) and so forth: however, by citing three realms, one encompasses all six paths. This is because the single realm of "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*) includes the four [paths] of devas, asuras, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and hell-beings (*naraka*).
The *Karmavibhaṅga-viniścaya* (Jie-mo-su) states: "When clarifying the realms according to the Vinaya, they are spoken of as only three—namely, humans, non-humans, and animals.

This is because the two realms of humans and animals are easily known through their manifest forms, whereas the realms of devas, asuras, hells, and *asura*-like beings are difficult to discern due to their hidden and subtle nature; therefore, devas and *asuras* are combined."
The four realms of the hungry ghosts constitute one destination (*gati*). They all possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and differ from the human race;

therefore, they are called "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*). I once questioned several lecturers on this point, and they replied to me: "It can be understood by not reading [the passage] concerning 'humans and non-humans' in the *Avalokiteśvara* [chapter].
What is called 'non-human' refers here to the 'doubtful deities' (*saṃdeha-deva*), which are the *kiṃnara*s among the eight classes of beings mentioned in the sutras. Their form..."
It is like a person who merely grows horns on his head. One who interprets it in this way understands the four categories of ownership:

first, the Three Jewels; second, the property of the master; third, non-human property; and fourth, animal property. Second, regarding the manufacture [of robes] according to the dimensions of the body, such as those for the *kaṣāya* (robe) and the *pātra* (bowl):
if the tree bark is coarse and the body of the robe does not equal the Buddha’s proportions, then the measurement is incorrect. This applies to stone, wood, copper, and so forth.

Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat): its substance must not exceed three *dōng* (斗) nor be less than one and a half *dōng*. If it is of such a measure, it is not a [proper] bowl; it merely borders on what is non-Dharma.

This is called "abiding in the observance" (*zhǐchí*). As for the passage appearing later in the text, it refers to the border of what is made according to the Dharma, because it constitutes "maintaining through fabrication" (*zuòchí*).

Thus, the two [passages] appear alternately in the text and differ from one another. Question: Since this has already clarified the gate of abiding in the observance, how does it clarify the process of fabrication, as in the case of robes?

[Question: Regarding items such as the alms bowl, are these not instances of "active observance" (*zochi*)? That is to say, since they necessarily involve active fabrication, they should be "observance through cessation" (*shichiji*).

Why, then, is it stated here within the section on "observance through cessation" that this constitutes the practice of "observance through cessation"? [Answer: Although these robes and bowls are indeed "active observances," in the present context we are taking up the aspect of "cessation" by ensuring they do not exceed the prescribed measure.
Thus, the act of fabrication itself results in "observance through cessation. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For example, regarding the three robes, the teaching..."

One prepares the requisites and does not dare to treat them with contempt; this is called "stopping and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*). Furthermore, it is said that if one acts beyond the prescribed measure, it constitutes an offense;

conversely, acting according to the rules is surely "stopping and maintaining. Moreover, it is said that if one does not act in accordance with the practice, it is an offense of commission (*zuo-fan*); now, by acting in accordance with the teachings, [one avoids such offenses].

This then constitutes "cessation-and-maintenance" (*zhi-chi*). The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "matters that cannot be studied," the ancients’ intention was to take "cessation-and-maintenance" as referring to cases of transgression, such as sexual misconduct or theft.
Because these matters are established phenomena (*sthita-dharma*), they are not things that ordained monks and nuns ought to study;
since they must be studied, the Sages did not prohibit their study, and thus they could not be recognized [as prohibited]. Therefore, it is said they "cannot be studied. Master Bin says:
The intention of the ancient masters is as follows: because acts such as sexual misconduct and theft are inherently improper, they are termed "untrainable" (*aśikṣya*).

Even if one were to harbor ignorance or doubt regarding them, how could it be permissible to commit them? An offense (*āpatti*) belongs to the category of transgression (*virati-āpatti*), which is the object counterposed to the practice of restraint (*saṃvara*).

These objects are all matters that are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). If one practices observance through performance (*kriyā-saṃvara*) and restraint through non-performance (*akriyā-virati*), then both the matter and the Dharma are "trainable," for through performance one maintains the observance.

[Included] within this. Because these matters accord with the Dharma—namely, the substance, dimensions, and so forth of the robes and bowl—monks and nuns who have left the household life must train in them.
The ancient masters did not categorically state that such matters are not to be learned; thus, we know there are things that can be learned and things that cannot be learned.
Li shared this interpretation. Bin summarizes Li’s intent as follows: "That which can be learned refers to such things as the construction of dwellings and robes, and the [training of the] body."

Measuring with the hand, as well as uttering verbal expressions such as the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) and formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*), these matters must all be performed through the training of body and speech;

they are termed "trainable" (*śikṣitavya*). As for what is termed "untrainable," this refers to not performing with the body acts such as sexual misconduct, theft, and killing, nor speaking with the mouth falsehoods, slander, frivolous chatter, and so forth;
these are all instances where one does not train the body and speech, and are thus called "untrainable. (The intention of the various masters is as follows:)

This is entirely different (it is precisely this that is the *chao*). Regarding the "gate of prohibitions" (*zhi-men*; i.e., the prohibitions against killing, etc.), there are two distinctions within the category of what can be learned: those that apply universally to both prohibitions and permissions (such as reciting the precepts, etc. and those that do not (such as building a dwelling, etc.).

Within the latter category of what cannot be learned, there is only the practice of restraint (*zhi-chi*; e.g., killing or stealing while perceiving the victim as a human or a non-human). Within the former category of what can be learned, there are naturally these two distinctions.

If this refers to the gate of prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), it concerns only that which is maintained through performance (*kriyā-dhāraṇī*)—such as the rules for recitation, the *karmavācanā* rituals, and the receiving of food.

Since violations are the opposite of such maintenance, they are all already explained above. By clearly memorizing these words, the meaning of the ancient masters regarding the following text will become self-evident; if one were to provide further elaborate explanations, it would only result in confusion.
Regarding the two matters communicated from within the gate: these refer to the two categories of what may be learned and what may not be learned.
As for "what may be learned," such as the measurements of rooms, the dimensions of long robes, and so forth—this is still "stopping" (*śīla*).

To act without exceeding the prescribed limits is called "stopping and maintaining" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*). If one constructs a room that exceeds the limit, is this not an offense of commission? Conversely, acting according to the teaching [within the limits] constitutes non-offense.

Thus it is performed; hence it is called "stopping and maintaining" (*zhǐchí*). This constitutes the dual sense of maintaining and violating precepts, though here it is explained by focusing on one side or the other.

Furthermore, within this category of "allowance" (*tīng*), there are cases identical to "prohibiting" (*zhì*) and "instituting" (*zhìzuò*). The Commentary (*Shū*) states: "If one necessarily possesses a dwelling and wealth, it is logically necessary to apply the ritual procedure (*fǎjiā*);

therefore, it is permitted to perform [the rite]. Conversely, "if there are obstacles or difficulties, it is improper to apply the ritual procedure to clothing or wealth that has been transgressed; therefore, it is permitted to stop [the rite]. This is so.

This refers to the maintenance of the prohibitions (*śīla*). It is explained in detail within the section on the "Regulations" (*vinaya*) as previously set forth; it is merely omitted here in this section on "Permissible Practices" (*anujñāta*). Regarding matters that cannot be learned, which are the same as those described above:

just as with the aforementioned confusion and forgetfulness, these are not things that can be learned. Therefore, the Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "That is to say, regarding the size of robes, confusion and forgetfulness arise alternately;
regarding the performance of rituals, delusion and obscurity arise in a jumble. Looking at these, they are termed 'not violating the teachings' [even though they are errors]."

Regarding the observance of the prohibitions (*śīla*): delusion is not something that can be learned [as a rule], therefore no offense is established for it. As for those whose perceptions shift before and after such that the formal determination (*niyata*) of the offense is uncertain:

suppose, for instance, that at the time one constructs a dwelling without having requested the formal authorization (*jñapti*), one’s mind is confused both before and after, leading one to believe that the authorization has already been granted.

In this case, the offense is never established from beginning to end. Even until the dwelling is completed, if the intervening thoughts and perceptions remain constantly deluded and do not shift, then there is no offense whatsoever. If...

If one changes one's perception, there is only the *pūrvakarmapatha* (prior preparatory offense) of *sthūlātyaya*; therefore, it is called "indeterminate. It is like one who intends to kill a human being, but upon reaching the victim, changes their perception to that of a non-human animal and kills them;
they incur only the *sthūlātyaya* of the prior intention, while regarding the non-human animal, they incur the *duṣkṛta* (misdeed) of the subsequent intention.

If one originally intended to kill a non-animal, but then shifted their perception to perceive it as a human and killed it, they incur the preparatory offense (*prayoga*) for a non-animal, which is a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed);
however, with respect to the subsequent human, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate."

Next is the section on the gate of maintaining through performance and prohibition (*kṛta-pratiṣedha*). Above, the meaning of maintaining through cessation (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*) has been fully explained. Below this, the accomplishment of practice through maintaining through performance (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) is clarified.

This involves both the teachings of prohibition and permission, which clarify the principles (*dharma*) and the practical matters (*vastu*). Within the text, these are further analyzed in terms of the substance and measure of the robe and the alms bowl. "Teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka;
it clarifies that the Vinaya teaching defines and measures what constitutes maintenance and violation, instructing people thereby, and for this reason it is called "teaching."
This teaching is that which is studied by those who maintain through performance (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). If one does not study it, this constitutes a transgression of omission (*virati-āpatti*).

Regarding "practice" as "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*): this refers to the time of performing maintenance; it means using the mind to give rise to antidotes to prevent wrongdoing, and giving rise to the intention to perform all wholesome deeds in reliance upon the teaching.

All of these are the essential characteristics of maintaining through performance. If one does not give rise to the remedial mind, this constitutes a transgression of omission. The above explains the prohibitions (*pratikṣepa*).
The exposition of the doctrine is concluded.

Regarding the gate of hearing, as for matters that can only be learned, this is also the interpretation of the ancient masters. That is to say, within the context of "active maintenance" (*dhāraṇā*), in terms of the matter itself, it is exclusively something that can be learned;
there is nothing that cannot be learned. This means that regarding the matter, since delusion is not permitted, it is said that "the matter can only be learned."
Regarding "learning": "matters" refers to the dimensions of rooms and dwellings; the length, width, and breadth of extra robes are also such matters. As for that which cannot be learned:
for instance, in constructing a room, one must first clearly visualize it in the mind before proceeding with the actual construction.

If the mind is confused or forgetful, how could one possibly build a room? Therefore, regarding the practice of making and maintaining [robes], the category of "that which cannot be learned" is not opened. Now, my interpretation is not so. Furthermore...

"Unlearnable" (*aśikṣaṇīya*) is also opened up [as a category]. Therefore, in the nine phrases concerning "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) below, it says: "the unlearnable dharma is delusion. There are likewise nine phrases;
thus we know that delusion is also opened up. Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As previously explained, within the gate of active observance..."

The Dharma matters clarify only what is learnable and what is unlearnable; this is not what is clarified here. Because these do not pertain to progressive cultivation, the Sages did not enjoin their study.

They differ from the "abiding in observance" (zhi-chi), which universally clarifies what is unlearnable, because [the latter] is understood only as the avoidance of transgressions. (This refers to the aforementioned "observance" section.)

Because of the prohibitions established by the Noble Ones, one may suddenly become deluded in mind and thus commit what is considered non-offensive; yet this constitutes a transgression of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). Now, regarding these acts of commission and maintenance—such as the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and so forth—advancing toward them constitutes "commission. Since there is no principle of "non-commission" once the state of mental delusion has ended, it follows that there is no such thing as a transgression of the training rules in this regard.
However, our current interpretation is not so. A delusion concerning the training rules cannot be fully understood through mere study;

even those who have attained the three fruits of the path still possess delusions regarding specific matters, let alone ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, regarding the phenomena of concrete actions, there is delusion concerning both the two methods of abstention and performance, regardless of whether they are prescribed or prohibited.
It is forgotten, yet it is not subsumed under an offense. How is this clarified? The *Vinaya* states that regarding surplus wealth, forgetting it does not constitute defilement;

likewise, regarding the assignment of a dwelling, it also permits [acting upon] a mistaken perception or doubt. Since these are not formally adjudicated as offenses, it is clear that there was confusion, and thus no violation is established. This is what is cited in the present *Chao*.
This is precisely the meaning of the previous argument; it cannot yet be accepted as a settled conclusion. Therefore, the subsequent text raises an objection, stating:

"Within the factors that serve as subsequent conditions, there are also instances where perception (*saṃjñā*) arises and so forth. This refers back to the same point. The response is that this was stated with reference to the nine categories of factors within the context of "active maintenance" (*kriyādhāra*).

Since it is specified that these were stated in reference to active maintenance, it is clear that active maintenance certainly encompasses all [categories] and is not restricted [to a specific subset].

In the section on "Holding after Learning" (*śaikṣa-dhāraṇa*), it is stated that there are likewise nine propositions regarding the delusion concerning dharmas that cannot be learned (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, one knows that this applies universally to what cannot be learned.
How can you now claim that the matter pertains solely to what can be learned?
Regarding the reason why [certain things] are not permitted and cannot be learned: this explains the meaning of why they are not opened up for study.

According to the interpretation of the masters of antiquity, that which is called "active maintenance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) necessarily involves directed effort and purposeful activity; it constitutes a prior undertaking. If the mind were confused or forgetful, how could one perform such tasks?
For example, when maintaining robes through the ritual of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification), one must certainly rely upon a clear and conscious mind. Therefore, these are not permitted.
"It cannot be learned. This is the intention of the ancient masters. Regarding the observance of prohibitions (*śīla*), both that which can be learned and that which cannot be learned are included;

however, regarding the observance of prescriptions (*vidhi*), it is exclusively that which can be learned and does not include that which cannot be learned. Therefore, he explains the reason for this, stating that the Dharma can only be known through diligent cultivation.

Matters involve merely distancing oneself from faults and maintaining self-restraint. Since this is called "progressive cultivation," deluded matters are not opened up; rather, it is precisely because one distances oneself from faults that delusion is permitted.

As for the phrase "as explained extensively below," this refers to what is stated in the section on the nine propositions of the *jiachi* (maintaining and practicing) gate in the subsequent classification of stages (*bitui*).

Furthermore, regarding the delusion concerning the dharmas that should not be learned (*aśikṣā-dharma*), there are likewise nine propositions; this present text points to these very passages to simultaneously refute the ancient interpretations.

All [of these] are termed "active transgressions" (*kṛta-āpatti*). As for the precepts of restraint (*virati-śīla*), one must logically adhere to and follow them; because one fails to revere the sacred words [of the Buddha], it is therefore called an active transgression.
"Laxity and lack of study" refers to not studying the *vinaya*. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the second section, the "Gate of Essential Characteristics.
Third, regarding the "Place of Accomplishment": this refers to the four modes of conduct—observance and transgression—which define the boundaries of the precepts;

it concerns within which state of mind these are accomplished. It is said that they are accomplished within the fourth mode of conduct. Therefore, one knows that the mind of conduct is the locus where observance and transgression are established.

This refers to the specific scope of the subject matter. Within this single section, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the practice of *śīla* (restraint) through the initial three mental states alone;
second, the explanation of the accomplishment of both *śīla*—restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—through the mental state of counteractive application;
and third, the explanation of the accomplishment of the four types of conduct (*caryā*) in relation to the three karmas. Although there are these three parts, they consist of only two [categories].

The first two [categories] are explained in terms of the mind, while the last one distinguishes both body and speech. Within the explanation in terms of the mind, *śamatha-dhāraṇa* (maintaining through cessation) has two distinctions, whereas *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (active maintenance) is of only one kind.
This is because when practicing the preceding three [types of] mental action, there is no sense of "unmanifest maintenance" (*avijñapti-dhāraṇa*). Regarding the two types of *śamatha-dhāraṇa*:
the first is the "clearly manifest *śamatha-dhāraṇa*" as an antidote; the second is that which is called "not being defiled by evil" when it does not arise.

Regarding "maintaining through cessation" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*): why is this "maintaining through cessation" attained within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state? It is because the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*) originally received remains in the mind;

since it is not defiled by the characteristics of evil, even though one enters the indeterminate state, one has not yet violated the essence of what was received. Because this name is not abandoned, it is called the practice of "maintaining through cessation.

It is also termed "maintaining through cessation while sitting with folded hands" (*dhyāna-sthita-śīla*). Lì asked: "How does one practice the three preceding minds? Since they are already indeterminate, how [can they be considered maintaining the precepts]?"
"Is it by means of accomplishing the karma? Answer: "In the three preceding moments of mind during the practice, there exists the original body of the precept which is pure and uncontradicted;

this is said to be 'upholding' (dhāraṇa), but it is not 'upholding through cultivation' (bhāvanā-dhāraṇa). The *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface) asks: "The reason why 'stopping-upholding' (saṃvara-dhāraṇa) can exist within the three preceding [moments] is clear.

However, as for 'stopping-transgressions' (saṃvara-aticāra) within those same three preceding [moments], why is it that these do not exist? The intent of the question is: "Since the name 'stopping' (saṃvara) is the same, why is it that only 'stopping-upholding' is absent [in those moments]?"

[The interlocutor] says: "It is cessation. [The Master] replies: "Precepts are that which one has received and thus belong to oneself. By means of these three mental states, one compares them to what was originally received;

since no evil comes to contravene it, this is called 'maintaining' (holding). Evil, however, was not originally received and does not belong to oneself; therefore, one cannot employ the aforementioned three mental states to compare them with what was originally received.
Since there is no good that comes to defile it, this is called 'transgressing. Gao says: This is intended to clarify the original basis of the reception [of the precepts]."

Regarding "intending to maintain" (*ni-chi*): once one has received [the precepts], they already belong to oneself; thus, the violation of the "cessation" (*shi*) aspect is not what is being clarified here. This is because [the precepts] do not belong to oneself beforehand. Jì (Jizang) says:
Since this section states that "no evil comes to defile," the second section below must be where evil comes to defile, yet it clarifies the maintenance [of the precepts].
Therefore, it is called "counteractive practice" (*dui-zhi-xing*), which clarifies both the maintenance through cessation (*zhi-chi*) and the maintenance through action (*zuo-chi*).

Regarding the practice of the three preceding minds, there is that which maintains cessation (*śamatha*). This refers to form, sensation, and perception. Because of the three types of form, there are three types of perception;

because of these three perceptions, there are three types of sensation. Specifically, upon seeing a beautiful form, one has the perception of pleasure; regarding an ugly form, one forms the perception of suffering;
and regarding a form that is neither beautiful nor ugly, one forms the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Due to these three perceptions, there are thus three [types of sensation].

Feeling (*vedanā*): The experiencing of the agreeable and the disagreeable is called feeling. That is to say, in relation to the perception of pleasure, there is pleasant feeling; in relation to the perception of suffering, there is painful feeling;
and in relation to the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, there is neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Because of these three feelings, there are the three poisons:

namely, pleasant feeling gives rise to greed (*rāga*), painful feeling gives rise to hatred (*dveṣa*), and neutral feeling gives rise to delusion (*moha*). By means of these three poisons, the three types of formative action (*saṃskāra*) are established.
Furthermore, it is said: if the mind is in any of the three types of neutral (avyākṛta) states, it is designated as "observance through abstention" (śīla-dhāraṇa).

This is because the essence of the non-informative (avijñapti) precept, which was produced by the original formal undertaking, remains constantly present. Although one has now entered a neutral state, because one does not commit evil, there is no violation of the original essence;
thus it is designated as "observance through abstention. Jì says: "Consciousness (vijñāna) takes 'discriminating' as its meaning; that is to say, when one suddenly perceives a form..."
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) has the function of discernment. Perception (*saṃjñā*) means to construct and grasp; it refers to the mind’s measurement. Feeling (*vedanā*) means to experience and receive;
it refers to the fact that once there is measurement, one experiences its pleasant or unpleasant nature. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) mean to perform and create;

it refers to the fact that once good or evil has been experienced, the mind immediately engages in activity to produce karma. Therefore, it is said that volitional formations are the "recording of the mind. The first three [aggregates] are without... [text ends].
This is a record. The commentary states: "That which flows into the *citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra* (the active mind) and becomes a distinct cause refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Among these, one is form and four are mind. Within the four types of mind, the first three belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); even if one performs good or evil therein, they do not constitute karma.
Upon entering the fourth, the *citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*, it becomes a distinct cause. A 'distinct cause' means a karmic cause. If one performs a good deed within this active mind, it is good."
If the cause of karma is an action where the mind is not evil, this is the cause of non-evil karma. Regarding what is called a "distinct cause," Vinītadeva says:
because actions such as greed and anger constitute the cause for transgression, while actions such as non-greed constitute the cause for observance, they are called distinct causes.

Alternatively, it may be said that because greed, anger, and delusion each act as individual causes for karma, they are termed distinct causes. As for the statement "therefore they are divided into two," this refers to the explanation.
This refers to the preceding passage. Remaining upright and motionless while practicing the first three minds constitutes the first [aspect], *śīla-dhāraṇa* (maintaining through cessation).

When the practice-mind is perfected and counteracts non-action, this is the second [aspect] within the practice-mind, clarifying *śīla-dhāraṇa*. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

Therefore, the four aggregates are divided into two parts; hence it is said that they are "divided into two. Regarding the statement that "the substance of the precept is held within the determinate (vyākṛta) and the three indeterminate (avyākṛta) minds":
this means that at the time of receiving [the precepts], one acquires this substance while within a determinate mind.
Since it is not possible for a person to always maintain a determinate mind, one is also able to uphold this substance of the precepts while within the three indeterminate minds. This passage also...

This is so. The Buddha questioned this because he feared that people might think: "The substance of what is received is *vijñapti* (definitive), whereas the three moments of mind prior to it are *avyākṛta* (neutral).
If one enters those three moments of mind, the precept should then be considered forfeited. Now it is clarified that this is not the case. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Even though the mind may dwell within the midst of evil or neutral states, the original precepts one has received are not called 'lost' (*asravita*)."

"Regarding the statement that 'the mind of application (pravṛtti-citta) necessarily accomplishes the three preceding [minds] and thus they cease': this means that the mind of application is capable of accomplishing both the observance and the violation [of precepts].

Once the mind of application is present, the three preceding neutral (avyākṛta) minds then pass away.
