This is because these three minds—reception (vedanā), etc.—cannot possess the two types of observance (saṃvara), namely the restraint of cessation (nivṛtti-saṃvara) and the restraint of action (kriyā-saṃvara).
As for the statement 'whenever it is of a wholesome nature, [the others] then exist': this was explained above in terms of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and the mind."

Now, based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), we clarify the observance and violation of precepts. The two types of restraint—restraint by abstention (*virati-dhāraṇa*) and restraint by action (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*)—are essentially wholesome;

they do not possess an evil nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*) nor an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*). Therefore, it is said that within these two natures of evil and indeterminacy, the two types of restraint as antidotes (*pratipakṣa-dhāraṇa*) cannot exist.

"Because they are restricted to a wholesome nature. *Lì* (礪) says: "The two observances (*dhāraṇa*) are wholesome; the other two are not offenses (*āpatti*). The unwholesome [nature] does not apply to the other two.
Regarding the first three, there is likewise no restriction to an unwholesome nature; this, conversely, refers to the two observances mentioned above to clarify the two offenses.
Thus, they lack the nature of goodness and the nature of the indeterminate, possessing only the nature of evil; hence it is said that they are restricted to the unwholesome.
This refers to the three minds beginning with consciousness, which cannot possess the remedial practices of both the prohibitive and the prescriptive disciplines.

If there is a distinction between preceding and succeeding moments of mind regarding upholding or violating [the precepts]—that is, in the case of wholesome or neutral mental states—and if these are viewed from the perspective of a single moment of mind, they do not constitute a point of completed transgression;

however, if they are considered in terms of their mutual formation across preceding and succeeding moments, then such a transgression does generally exist. This is just as in the case of the prohibition against confining a śrāmaṇera.
This refers to the fact that within a single [moment of] mind, all four types of mental activity are present. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:

since it was previously clarified that the three moments of mind prior to the actual performance of an action are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not constitute the cause for karma, they are termed "prior minds. The subsequent moment of mind that enters into the actual performance is termed the "subsequent mind.

Only through these can one achieve observance (*dhāraṇa*) or transgression (*āpatti*). Therefore, they are called "prior and subsequent minds" because there is a distinction between observance and transgression. Li (Lì) states: "The three moments of mind prior to the performance are termed 'general' (*tōng*)."

"Maintaining [the precepts] is accomplished within a mind of neutral (avyākṛta) nature. If it occurs within a mind of active engagement (pravṛtti), it is termed 'distinct maintenance' or 'violation. Furthermore, Li states:
'The above discussion restricts maintaining to wholesome (kuśala) nature and violating to unwholesome (akuśala) nature; this is explained from the perspective of a single moment of mind.

However, regarding successive moments of mind, as well as instructing others, violations such as 'active commission' can occur within the other two natures. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) reiterates this."
Regarding this meaning, it is said that although the designations differ: if one examines the sequence of events, the mind arises differently, and thus distinct transgressions can be identified.

As for the clarification of the accomplishment of the latter three karmas, this is the meaning of the third section; it distinguishes the fulfillment and maintenance [of precepts] in terms of the karma of body, speech, and mind.
This refers to the locus of transgression. Although the preceding section dealt with the mind, it did not yet discuss body and speech; therefore, the three karmas are now explained in detail.
This is the locus of upholding and violating.

Regarding "the two types of bodily upholding," Li says: "If one distinguishes the two types of bodily and vocal upholding and violating based on the established teachings, [one must consider] abstaining from killing..."
Sexual contact and the like constitute the restraint of the body through abstention (*kāya-virati*).

As for those things that should come according to the rules—such as gathering the requisites, lighting lamps at the time of the *poṣadha*, preparing the voting sticks (*śalākā*), not sitting down to eat, and the manner of receiving and eating food—these constitute the observance of the body through action (*kāya-karman*).

Regarding the four faults of speech, such as lying, abusive speech, slander, and frivolous talk, these are actions of the mouth; since all such things are completely ceased, this is the restraint of the mouth (*vāg-virati*).

Holding [the precepts]. This includes: receiving and holding robes and bowls; assigning [robes] and declaring them pure (*śuddhi*); being separated from one's robe for six years; carrying a staff and a bag; the two-year period for the six dharmas; making a declaration of purity (*jñapti-vākya*);

damaging the earth or destroying living plants; the two instances of entering a village; and practicing according to the instructions, and so forth. These constitute "holding through verbal action" (*vāg-kṛta-dhāraṇa*).

As for those involving both body and speech, they may be understood by analogy with what has been explained. Regarding offenses committed by both body and speech, they are explained as the reverse of the preceding cases. Those committed by the mind alone...

Regarding why there is no formal transgression or observance within [certain] karmas, the preceding commentary states: "In this teaching, the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) is not guarded; therefore it is so said.

This means that if one merely gives rise to a defiled thought at the initial moment, without intending to move the body to perform an action, this constitutes a violation according to the Mahāyāna, whereas for the Śrāvaka there is no offense.
Therefore, it is said that there is no formal transgression or observance. The precepts of the Śrāvaka require the intention to move the body or speech; as for the arising of the thought—
At that time, one incurs an offense. Therefore, in the Vinaya, it is said: "To give rise to the thought and form the mental intention" refers to this. Lì says:

Regarding the observance and violation of the mental karma (*manas-karman*), since this merely brings about [the completion of] bodily and vocal actions, it does not accord with the separate explanation [of mental action]. Inferring from this, we know that on the level of the mind-ground (*manobhūmi*), there are no two types of observance and violation.
If it refers to volition involving body and speech, this means that when one gives rise to the thought intending to perform the aforementioned act, this very volitional mind constitutes an offense;

the physical action is merely a remote preliminary (*pūrvaprayoga*), which differs from a case of mental karma alone. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Within the category of mental karma alone, the distinction between maintaining and violating the precepts is not clarified."

Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If it is merely in the mind, it is not called an offense. If this is so, and there is no offense, why does the Vinaya state that "arousing the intention" and "forming a mental resolve" are both called offenses?
The answer is: this refers to the arousal of the intention with the intent to move body or speech; although the physical manifestation has not yet occurred, it is already termed an offense.
This is stated in reference to those for whom the Śrāvaka precepts are prescribed. As for a solitary mental resolve (*cittotpāda*) that is sudden...

If one acts with the intention to initiate [the offense], it is not called a transgression. However, if one turns toward a heavy condition and, though capable of reflection and awareness, fails to exercise restraint, this constitutes a violation of the precepts.

Therefore, the text states: "To act through mental intention and so forth—this is its transgression. Between the two interpretations regarding the nature of the mind, the latter is taken as the correct meaning.
This is the position of the author of the *Shu-chao*, who adopts the latter interpretation as the primary text. Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, there are three...

There are three kinds of volition: first, the impelling; second, the intentional; and third, the determinative. This concludes the preceding explanation of the third section on the meaning of the locus of accomplishment.

Regarding the four clarifications of "penetration and obstruction": this refers to the two observances and two transgressions. When they are mutually present, it is called penetration; when they are mutually absent, it is called obstruction.
As for the Gate of Single-Mindedness explaining matters solely in terms of karmic action, this clarifies that within a single thought-moment, things do not arise sequentially.

This is called "single-mindedness" (*ekacitta*). This refers exclusively to the "obstructive" (*sai*) because it concerns the solitary mind; that is, setting aside the object to discuss the mind alone, it does not extend [to other categories].
When comparing the mind of upholding with the mind of transgression, their good and evil are mutually contradictory, just as when the mind arises and takes an object as its condition.
Having abandoned killing and stealing, one may no longer take other wholesome or unwholesome things as objects of focus.

That is to say, at the very moment the mind of "abstaining-and-maintaining" (*zhi-chi*) is present, there is no "acting-and-maintaining" (*zuo-chi*), nor even the mind of "abstaining-and-transgressing" (*zhi-fan*). This is because the mind does not simultaneously attend to multiple objects;

it merely blocks [unwholesome paths] so that they do not pass through. The Commentary states: "Since these are actions performed by a single mind, when comparing 'maintaining' to 'transgressing,' the wholesome and the unwholesome are mutually contradictory; thus, maintaining and transgressing..."
Each category has its own specific prohibitions and prescriptions; therefore, these four modes of conduct cannot be interchanged.

For example, when a person resolves to abstain from killing, stealing, and so forth, they may further cultivate wholesome deeds based on that resolve. Furthermore, this section on "permeability and obstruction" consists of four parts:
the first explains the four modes of conduct by examining the mind alone; the second clarifies the four modes of conduct by comparing the mind with its objects; and the final two [parts] address...
This clarifies the four practices regarding phenomena (*vastu*). They are so called because each has its own points of penetration and obstruction.

Furthermore, when it is said that they are explained solely in terms of the performance of action (*karma*), this refers to the first gate, which distinguishes [the mind] based on the mind alone. This is indeed a discourse on the mind that sets aside the object; however, in reality, one performs those preceding actions.

Moreover, because it is distinguished solely from the perspective of the mind, it is so stated. Essentially, regarding the four practices concerning the performance of action, they are now divided into two.

The purpose is to clarify the limits of the mind (*citta*). Regarding the phrase "merely blocked and not penetrating," Gao says: "The four practices are all blocked; therefore, it is said they are 'simultaneously blocked.

This means they are blocked because they are fixated upon the extremes of achieving cessation (*śamatha*) or achieving activity (*pravṛtti*). Because upholding and violating are diametrically opposed as good and evil, they are blocked and do not penetrate.
Within the respective categories of upholding and violating, there are each their own instances of cessation and activity; thus, they also do not penetrate. This is what is meant by 'upholding.'"
Although they are the same [in nature], because "stopping" (*zhi*) and "acting" (*zuo*) are distinct, it does not apply [to both].

The two types of transgressions are likewise so. Regarding the second point, "directing the mind toward the object": some say that when the mind is applied to an object, the object may be either accessible or obstructed;

thus it is said that directing the mind toward the object involves accessibility or obstruction. If one speaks directly of the mind alone, it is only obstructed and not accessible, which belongs to the preceding category. Lì says:

This refers to the gate of directing the single mind toward two objects; this is the meaning of maintaining both [the precepts] and violating them simultaneously. Now, we simply speak of directing the mind toward an object.

That is to say, regarding a single object, there are both the maintenance of cessation (*śamatha*) and the maintenance of action (*pravṛtti*). As the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "There are two ways of maintaining both [precepts] and violating them.

First, it concerns the application of the mind (which corresponds to the passage below: 'If one explains it according to practice,' etc.). Second, it concerns the teaching and its practice (which corresponds to the present meaning). It says:

Regarding the "functioning of the mind": this refers to the aspect of the mind’s movement and activity as it is designated. In relation to all the precepts, each possesses both types of observance (*dhāraṇa*).

For instance, in the case of the precept against sexual misconduct: to follow the teaching and exercise restraint is the meaning of "observance through cessation" (*virati-dhāraṇa*); prior to the arising of aversion through contemplation, the absence of thoughts of defilement constitutes the other.

Even if one comes into contact with the object, the absence of pleasure throughout the three periods [of past, present, and future] is termed "observance through restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*). Other cases may be understood by analogy.

If we rely on the teachings regarding practice and understanding, this gate encompasses the dual meaning of both observance and transgression. For instance, regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*): to not dare to disobey the teaching that they must be fully prepared constitutes "observance through restraint.

To cultivate according to the teaching and practice accordingly without transgressing constitutes "observance through action" (*kriyā-śīla*). Conversely, the opposite of the aforementioned observance through restraint is...

Regarding the commission of offenses (*āpatti*), the opposite of the aforementioned "observance" (*dhāraṇā*) constitutes the cessation of offense. Therefore, it is said that "the two offenses are likewise so. In Master Lì’s commentary, there are also two meanings.
First, regarding the two teachings of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and permission (*anujñā*), it clarifies the two observances and two offenses;

for example, the requirement to perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite in a designated place and the formal acceptance and maintenance of robes and bowls, and so forth. Second, regarding the progressive cultivation of practice, such as studying, reciting the precepts, and performing *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), and so forth.

This clarifies the two aspects of restraint and action regarding observance and violation (*dhāraṇa* and *atikrama*). (The subsequent passage in the text which states, "If one explains the aforementioned 'observance' and so forth in terms of practice,' shares the same intent as this latter section.

The Master’s [Zhi] commentary on the preceding section shares the same meaning as this former section. Lì says: Within action there is restraint; when restraint is gathered to accomplish action, this constitutes the separation from [afflictions] through antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), which is the cause for becoming a master of the Way.
When action is separated [from afflictions], it becomes the fruit of being a master of the Way. This is because, by means of these antidotes...
It is the pacification and cessation of the mind. It is able to accomplish the practice of its activity, which is the ultimate fruit. Within this cessation (*śamatha*), there is an agent;
this activity is the antidote and separation [from distraction], which is the cause of cessation. Cessation itself is the separation from activity, which is the fruit of cessation.
This means that by means of this active mind, the fruit of cessation is accomplished. Nevertheless, it refers to a single object.
There is a distinction in the underlying intent; therefore, it is said: "How could this be the same as the general [rules]?

According to the meaning of Master Lì’s commentary, the principles of "simultaneous observance" (*sāṃvara*) and "violation" (*asāṃvara*) herein must not be applied to cases such as killing or stealing. This is because killing, stealing, and so forth all pertain to the principle of "individual observance" (*ekasaṃvara*) or "single violation" (*ekāpatti*), as has been explained previously.

Regarding "the non-existence of mutual possession between observance and transgression": this means that observance does not extend into transgression; within observance there is no transgression, and within transgression there is no observance.

If one considers the two types of observance—restraint (*saṃvara*) and performance (*karaṇa*)—they possess the sense of mutual establishment; however, observance and transgression are contradictory and lack the sense of mutual establishment. Gao says:

"When observing observance in relation to transgression, they are blocked because good and evil are mutually exclusive. Regarding "the mutual possession of observance and transgression themselves": [this refers to their internal relationship].

This means that "maintaining" (śīla) is characterized by the mutual maintenance of its own characteristics, and "transgressing" (āpatti) is characterized by the mutual transgression of its own characteristics;

both refer to the fact that within "maintaining through cessation" (virati-śīla) there is "maintaining through action" (kriyā-śīla), and within "transgressing" there is "transgressing through cessation. For example, regarding how "maintaining through cessation" contains "maintaining through action," Śaṅghabhadra says:

"For instance, not exceeding the prescribed measure is 'maintaining through cessation. Because one relies on the teaching and does not overstep the proper limits, it is called 'maintaining through cessation. By examining the teaching and measuring accordingly, one knows [this].
The division is approximately as follows: that which is called "active observance" (作持) establishes cessation through the measurement of scriptural authority.
Therefore, within cessation (止), there is activity; this refers to subsuming activity into cessation. Lì says: "Within the observance of cessation (止持), there is active observance (作持).

For example, in the case of 'cessation' regarding not exceeding the prescribed measure for building a dwelling, the act of requesting formal permission (白二羯磨) is 'activity. The same applies to extra robes. It is the cessation of a mind of indolence."

This is *śīla-dhāraṇa* (observance through abstention). When one adds the ritual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and performs the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-uddeśana*), it is called *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (observance through action). Furthermore, it is said: "When making a *kāṣāya*, one should make it according to the prescribed measurements;

there is no offense for transgression if one does not exceed those measurements. This is termed *śīla-dhāraṇa*. When one adds the ritual empowerment and performs the declaration of purity, it is further termed *kriyā-dhāraṇa*.

Furthermore, when one acts in accordance with the teachings, this is also called "active observance" (*jiezhi*). Within active observance, there is "observance through cessation" (*zhizhi*). Ciyun says:

"For example, regarding the three robes and one bowl, the Sages ordained that these must be possessed; this is active observance. By training and practicing in accordance with the teachings, one remains compliant and does not commit offenses."

Is it not that "observance through performance" (作持) means not daring to transgress or show contempt? Because one restrains unrighteous conduct and measures its substance, hoping to avoid committing an offense, it is called "observance through restraint" (止持).
This observance through restraint is subsumed to constitute the objective sphere of performance; therefore, the subsequent text states: "It is likewise within performance.

Thus, restraint is based on non-transgression to constitute observance, while performance is based on compliance with the teachings to constitute observance. Lì says: "It is like building a house [and first] begging..."

The method of formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) is termed "active" (*kārya*). By requesting this rite and constructing a dwelling according to the instructions, one avoids the offense of constructing a dwelling;

this is termed "cessation through observance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*). Thus, while the substance is one, the names differ. Furthermore, the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-vidhāna*) is "observance through action" (*kārya-dhāraṇa*);
because of the declaration of purity, one avoids the offense of possessing robes through action, and conversely, [if one fails to do so,] it is termed an offense.

Regarding "cessation-maintenance" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*): as for the two types of offenses being likewise so, one should understand by analogy that the opposite of maintenance constitutes an offense; hence it is said they are "likewise.
For example, constructing a dwelling of excessive size that exceeds the boundaries prescribed by the prohibitions of the teaching is called an "active offense" (*kriyā-āpatti*);

because it does not comply with the teaching, it is also called a "cessation offense" (*virati-āpatti*). Within cessation offenses, there is also the element of action: failing to maintain the three robes is a cessation offense, yet the intentional contravention of the teaching constitutes an "active" aspect.

Lì says: "To build a house without seeking formal authorization constitutes an offense. What is called 'abstaining' (zhǐ) refers to the offense itself; the physical act of building the house is its actual execution.
Thus, while the substance is one, the names are distinct. Is this not an instance of 'action' (zuò) existing within 'abstinence' (zhǐ)?"

If one were to establish a distinction between them, it would involve counter-interrogating the previous statement: since you have already said that "possession" (dhāraṇa) possesses its own specific characteristic and "offense" (āpatti) possesses its own specific characteristic, how then can they be distinguished?

Answer: Regarding the statement that "cessation contains activity, and the completion of activity constitutes cessation," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "For example, in the case of keeping robes, failing to perform the ritual of 'purification' (*śuddhi*) is a transgression of cessation;

exceeding the prescribed time limit is a transgression of activity. Furthermore, in the case of constructing a dwelling, failing to request the formal authorization is likewise [a transgression of cessation]."
This refers to an offense of commission (*kṛta-āpatti*). This very act constitutes a violation of the teaching; it is an offense of abstention (*vārita-āpatti*).

Now, by including these matters of making robes and constructing dwellings, one establishes the offenses of abstention such as "not begging" and so forth; thus it is said. "The same applies within commission" means that this includes the abstention that results in the commission.

For example, when one wishes to make a robe, first abstaining from exceeding the prescribed measure is called "abstention"; once it has been made, one incorporates the prior mind of abstention [into the completed act].
This refers to the practice of maintaining the activity of making robes. Li asked: "In a state of single-mindedness, how can there be activity within stillness, or stillness within activity?
He replied: "Single-mindedness means achieving and attaining stillness; it may also be called 'activity' because it excludes [distractions].
If one considers the two gates of objects, taking the antidote as the point of reference: 'stillness within activity' means that this activity is the antidote for abandoning stillness."

This refers to the separation from the fruit of action. Within "action" (*zuo*), there is "cessation" (*zhi*); this cessation is the separation through antidotes. This constitutes the separation from the fruit of action. To clarify the essential tenet (*zong*) is as follows:
for instance, when it is said that within "cessation-and-maintenance" (*zhichi*) there is "action," cessation-and-maintenance itself is the tenet.

Although it contains "maintenance-through-action" (*zuochi*) within it, all of it serves to accomplish the practice of cessation-and-maintenance; therefore, it is called "clarifying the essential tenet. It is precisely by clarifying this essential tenet that [the meaning] is made manifest.

Although within stillness there is activity, and within activity there is stillness, how could this constitute a state of pervasive diffuseness? Therefore it is said: "How could this be such [a state]?

Regarding the distinction between the one who maintains stillness and the one who maintains activity: these following four lines precisely explain the aforementioned phrase, "The fundamental principle is clearly manifest.
It says: "This still mind and the object of stillness are each distinct; how could this be a state of pervasive diffuseness? Thus, he establishes the four lines to clarify this.
This is the reason for their distinction. One must necessarily explain this in relation to a single object; do not apply it to other objects, as then it would not correspond.
Since this section clarifies the meaning of both upholding and violating precepts, these are all based upon a single precept, and thus there is a "duality" therein.
Therefore, when now analyzing the fourfold categories of upholding and violating precepts, one may only apply them to a single object. Thus, [Master] Li [states].

It is said: "In this case, the substance is one while the names are distinct. How can one claim they form a pair based on their respective objects and characteristics? If one further discusses them as having different objects, how can it be called 'one substance'?

The various explanations of the past are truly not in accord with the intended meaning. As for the statement that "the mind of non-transgression (saṃvara) and the mind of formal undertaking (karmavācanā) are distinct," it is like the case of making the three robes:
the mind of non-transgression, which prevents exceeding the prescribed measurements, and the mind of formal undertaking, which follows the subsequent ritual procedure—how could these [be the same]?"

There is no distinction between them. Regarding the authorization for building a dwelling, it is permissible to simply stop after the initial construction. This refers to, for example, when one seeks authorization to build a dwelling with the intention that it not exceed the prescribed dimensions;

this is the mind of "maintaining through cessation" (*zhi-chi*). Subsequently, following the formal teaching, one proceeds with the actual construction according to the rules; this is the mind of "maintaining through action" (*zuo-chi*).

Since the two minds are distinct, the objects they refer to are likewise different; as the teaching says, "the essential points are clearly set forth," and so on. Regarding the distinction between the objects of the two—cessation (*śamatha*) and activity (*pravṛtti*):
for example, when one is making the three robes (*tricīvara*), at the moment of ceasing once they have reached the proper measure, the object of the robe is completed.

Later, when the time for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) arrives, the objects of the robes are distinct. Furthermore, it is said that there are two distinctions regarding the mind of restraint (*saṃvara-citta*): First, the distinction of the mind of restraint:
the mind that intends not to take coarse, loosely woven cloth to make the three robes is called the "mind of restraint" (*saṃvara-citta*).

This is contrasted with the mind that intends to take fine silk to make the three robes, which is called the "mind of undertaking" (*ārambha-citta*). Second, the distinction of the objects of restraint and undertaking: the object of restraint is coarse material, while the object of undertaking is fine silk.
[The first] is the object of wealth; [the second] is the distinctness of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, this is discussed in terms of constructing a dwelling.

That which is constructed constitutes the objective realm for "abstention and maintenance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*), because by constructing the dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, one does not incur the offense of non-action (*akriyā-āpatti*); conversely, to do otherwise would constitute an offense, and thus it is "abstention and maintenance. Viewed in relation to the dwelling, it is the objective realm for abstention and maintenance.

As for the objective realm for "active maintenance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*), it refers to the community of monks (*saṃgha*) and the teachings of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), which serve as the objective realm for active maintenance.
Regarding the third [type of restraint], "restraining the mind with respect to the object of activity":

this refers to the case where, for instance, one intends to make the three robes (tricīvara), yet restrains the mind so as not to exceed the prescribed measurements. One should fashion the robes according to the teachings;

since the robe is the object of the activity of making and maintaining, it is by means of my restraining the mind from exceeding the measurements that I apply this restrained mind toward the object of the robe. Some say that coarse silk is unfit for making [the robes].

Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*): for now, one restrains the mind and does not use them; this is "maintaining through cessation" (*zhi-chi*). However, fine silk is suitable for making them, and this is what is currently used;
it is called the "sphere of maintaining through action" (*zuo-chi-jing*). Therefore, it is said that "restraining the mind is in opposition to the sphere of action. Zhen Di says:

"Restraining the mind is in opposition to the sphere of action" means that one gathers cessation to accomplish action. As for the passage below stating "directing the mind toward the sphere of cessation," it means gathering action to accomplish cessation.
Jingyun said: "If one simply does not study any dharmas, that is the 'cessation of the mind' (*zhi-xin*). Because of this non-study, one universally violates all precepts;

therefore, it is said that [the violation] acts as an object (*jing*) in opposition [to the precept]. (This point remains unclear. Regarding the fourth, "the mind of action acting in opposition to the object of cessation" (*zuoxin dui zhijing*):

Jingyun said, "This means that because one has previously studied the teachings and clearly understands what constitutes upholding and violating the precepts, one does not commit an offense when encountering an object of violation; thus, it is 'acting in opposition to the object of cessation. Lili said, "[It refers to] acting in opposition to sexual misconduct."

Regarding "theft" and so forth: these are originally objects for the practice of restraint (śīla). Now, the mind that gives rise to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is an active mind (*kṛti-citta*), which stands in contrast to the aforementioned objects of restraint such as sexual misconduct.
(This interpretation is likely incorrect. It should rather be that the mind which applies the ritual procedure (*adhikāra*) to the robes is the active mind;

this stands in contrast to the aforementioned objects, namely robes that are compliant with the Dharma and not excessive in size. Someone has said: "With body and mind, one prepares fine silk to make the three robes. This is [the correct view].
One forms the intention to maintain [the precept]. When encountering coarse silk or fine cloth, one stops the mind and does not use them; this is the "object of cessation" (*nirodha-viṣaya*).
If one explains "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "maintenance" (*dhāraṇa*) in terms of their cultivation, this clarifies the aspect of the mind's application:

all precepts possess both maintenance and violation. That is to say, regarding acts such as sexual misconduct or theft, from the perspective of progressive cultivation, they can also possess the meaning of "double maintenance."

Furthermore, "advancing in practice" (jinxiu) refers specifically to cultivating compassion, few desires, and so forth. Therefore, it is said that "cultivating practice explains the cessation and maintenance" (jie zhichi).

This cultivation of a compassionate mind and few desires is distinct from what was discussed above regarding the "twofold maintenance" (shuangchi), which—concerning items such as robes and alms bowls—was merely an explicit teaching on conduct based on separation.
That previous section spoke from the perspective of advancing in practice; now, this subsequent section specifically addresses the cultivation of compassion.

Regarding the aspect of having few desires (*alpeccha*), although acts such as sexual misconduct and theft are singlefold observances and transgressions, when considered from the perspective of cultivating compassion and having few desires, they likewise possess both the two types of observance and transgression.
This applies to the precept against grinding [grains] as well; therefore, the Commentary states: "These four gates are all explained in reference to two types of teachings:
first, the teaching of progressive advancement, which encompasses the three trainings; second, the teaching of disciplinary regulation, which is restricted to the practice of the Vinaya."

The teaching penetrates the excellence of principle; therefore, it is called "cultivation. For example, regarding the cessation of killing and stealing, the prior cultivation of compassion, few desires, and so forth means that, for instance, in order to cease killing, one first cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Only by gathering this practice of cultivating loving-kindness does the meaning of ceasing killing become established.
Thus it is said. Compassion serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to killing, and having few desires serves as the antidote to stealing; hence, it is stated thus.

Furthermore, regarding the side of the mind that commits an offense, there is "commission through non-restraint" (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*), such as when a person performs evil deeds without having previously cultivated goodness.

This means that if one has not previously cultivated goodness, this constitutes commission through non-restraint; because of this non-restraint, one subsequently performs evil deeds, which is then termed "commission through action" (*kriyā-āpatti*).
Regarding the statement that "there is a transgression of commission within a mind of non-transgression, such as when a person keeps extra robes or constructs a dwelling," Jing says:

Keeping extra robes without declaring them pure (*asuddhika*) is called a transgression of omission (*śīla-āpatti*); because one previously kept the robes, this constitutes a transgression of commission (*kriyā-āpatti*). Alternatively, wearing them after ten days have passed is also called a transgression of commission;

therefore, it is said that "at the limit of the transgression of omission, there is a transgression. As for the person who commits the act, such as constructing a dwelling, they do not beg [for materials].

As for the act of disposal (*pratiniḥsarga*), it constitutes a cessation-offense (*virati-āpatti*). Because one previously violated the teaching by constructing a dwelling, that constitutes an action-offense (*kriyā-āpatti*).
[The author] states: "When originally making the robe, if one does not perform the ritual of dedication (*pariṣkāra-vyavahāra*), but merely thinks [of it], this is a cessation-offense.

Since at the time of the original action one intended not to dedicate it, and now ceases from dedicating it, it is called a cessation-offense. In comparison with the previous intention, it is called an action-offense. The case of the dwelling is likewise. It is not...

I request a formal decision. This refers only to the offense of abstention (*virati*). Since the original intention was not to seek the formal procedure (*dharma*), yet it was subsequently carried out, this constitutes an offense of commission (*kṛta-āpatti*).

If one considers the offense of abstention as being without the offense of non-commission (*akṛta-āpatti*), this means that from the perspective of one who does not study [the rules], it is an offense of abstention.

Among the types of abstention (*virati*), there is no such thing as an active transgression (*kṛta-āpatti*). How is this known? For example, if I abstain from study, this is merely an abstention-transgression;

since it does not involve the actual commission of a fault, how could there be an active transgression? What has been clarified above concerns the context of engaging in the cultivation of specific matters:

within that context, one can understand that where there is an abstention-transgression, there may also be an active transgression. This does not mean they are mutually constitutive, yet it is not the case that subsequent habituation is absent.

This means that if one merely ceases [practice] now and does not study any of the holy teachings, this is simply a transgression of cessation (*virati-āpatti*). Since one has not yet committed evil, there is no transgression of action (*kriyā-āpatti*).

Nevertheless, because one ceases and does not study due to the mind, one becomes confused regarding the characteristics of the teachings; subsequently, one will inevitably commit offenses according to the various categories of the *Skandhaka*.

Therefore, this is a subsequent habituation. This is still an explanation from the perspective of the mind of the aforementioned transgression of cessation, wherein the sense of a transgression of action exists.
Regarding the four permutations of "both performing it oneself and instructing others," these clarify that the four modes of conduct— observance and violation—
when involving both instructing others and acting for oneself, may be completed simultaneously; thus they receive the designation "comprehensive" (*tong*).
To have others strain water for one’s own use constitutes *zhichi* (abstaining from transgression).

Previously, had one been unwilling to strain the water and instead drunk water containing insects, that would constitute *zuofan* (committing a transgression). Now, by reversing that act of transgression, it is called *zhichi*.

If speaking in general terms, this might appear to be *zochi* (performing a virtuous act); however, this present commentary treats it as *zhichi*, though ancient masters also treated it as *zochi*. In reality, it is both.
Regarding the meaning of upholding and violating [the precepts]: the substance of these matters includes both "restraint-upholding" (*saṃvara-śīla*) and "performance-upholding" (*anuvartana-śīla*).

Here, I shall explain them by focusing primarily on one side. Because of using a water-strainer, one refrains from harming insects; thus, it is called "restraint-upholding. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that by restraining one's own mind, one causes others to act; when others act, my own restraint is fulfilled.

This is because, with respect to the objective of not damaging the environment, the restraint is thereby accomplished. Moreover, one does not request permission from others before sending someone else to perform the task.
"Room" (fang) refers to this method of non-seeking; it is the practice of ceasing transgressions.

"Having performed the four matters" means that after having performed the aforementioned four practices, if the karma is completed within each of the individual practices, the four types of karma are simultaneously bound.
"Free from all faults and transgressions" refers to entering the practice of cessation and maintenance (zhichí). As for "ceasing transgressions and so forth," there are two reasons why this is so.

Regarding the phrase "up to and including" (*zhì yǐ zhì*): the first instance of "up to and including" serves to conclude the preceding section, clarifying that within the practice of *zhǐchí* (restraint through non-transgression) there are four modes of conduct, beginning with the restraint of transgressions.
The latter instance of "up to and including" indicates what follows below;

that is to say, since the practice of *zhǐchí* already possesses these four modes of conduct, it follows that *zuòchí* (active observance) and *zuòfàn* (active transgression) likewise each possess four modes of conduct.
There is an omission in between; hence the expression "up to" (*yāvat*) is used.
Regarding "obstructed" (*sai*), it is easily understood as meaning that one cannot simultaneously accomplish all four modes of conduct; thus it is called "obstructed.

This is also like what was stated previously in the section on the Single Mind Gate (*ekacitta-mukha*), which says that when practicing *śīla* (observance), there is no transgression, and so forth. The statement here that it is "only obstructed" refers to it being exclusive.

This is clarified within the context of a single practice (*ekācāra*) of mind. Regarding the statement that "penetration requires skillful means" (*upāya*): this means that if one speaks of penetration, one must first perform various skillful means;
subsequently, by entering into the single practice, one's prior karma is spontaneously perfected and the four practices are simultaneously accomplished.

Thus, the meaning of "penetration" is established. Regarding the phrase "four times four makes sixteen": this refers to the four practices consisting of the two pairs of cessation and cultivation, as well as upholding and violating.
The former [set] already possesses these four; therefore, it is said that "four times four makes sixteen.

As for the statement that "the reliance on characteristics is slightly different," this means that the former is the gate of "acting oneself and teaching others," whereas this is the gate of "mutual establishment through preceding and succeeding [factors] within one's own characteristics"; hence, it is said to be slightly different.
"Providing one's own water-strainer" refers to *śīla-virati* (abstention). It is so named because it constitutes a transgression when performed in the opposite manner.

From the perspective of not killing insects, this is *śīla-virati*. This "providing one's own water-strainer" is merely the preparatory means (*upāya*), as the actual straining has not yet taken place.

"Confining the śrāmaṇera" refers to the practice of maintaining discipline through skillful means (*upāya*). Some say that just as one keeps a śrāmaṇera, one should establish two masters to instruct and admonish him;
if they do not admonish him, he incurs an offense of omission. Now, by confining him, one ensures that he does not give rise to evil, which constitutes the practice of maintaining discipline.
Furthermore, it is explained that one knows music will occur in the future; if one does not confine him, he will go to watch it and commit an offense.
Therefore, closing [the door] now constitutes the act of preparation (*prayoga*). To set out the instruments of killing is itself the act of transgression;

this is the preliminary means (*upāya*) for the act of killing, not yet the actual killing itself. It awaits the subsequent karma to complete it spontaneously. As for closing the door and manifesting signs while not granting consent (*chanda*): [this refers to the aforementioned].
This constitutes a transgression of the precept of cessation. It means that because one is currently not present in the room, one closes the door and does not grant consent to the Saṃgha.

After having performed the four aforementioned actions, one returns to the room; whatever state of mind one enters upon entering, if the four prior acts have been completed in their entirety, [the offense is established].
This refers to attaining the four modes of conduct (*caryā*).
These latter two gates both clarify the cessation and transgression (*śamatha-āpatti*) in relation to the cultivation and construction of phenomena.

That is to say, within the third and fourth modes of conduct, sixteen modes of conduct are established; these all concern the cessation and transgression within each individual phenomenon when it is being constructed. Therefore, this treatise discusses this cessation and transgression.
This constitutes the sixteenth [offense]. Now, let us examine it briefly. As explained in the latter two sections above, each clarifies four types of conduct.

Among these, regarding the construction of a dwelling, there are two matters—failing to request permission for the site and refusing to close the door—which constitute a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense because one is unwilling to comply with these two requirements.

That is to say, regarding the matter of constructing a dwelling, failing to request the formal procedure (*dharma*) before the Saṃgha constitutes an offense. Regarding the matters to be performed before the Saṃgha...
The "consent to desire" (yù-yù) constitutes a transgression of cessation (zhǐ-fàn), which differs from the transgressions of cessation resulting from a lack of study.

If it were a transgression of cessation due to a lack of study, there would be no corresponding matter of active construction (xiū-zào) to counterbalance it. One cannot apply this transgression of cessation to encompass all four types of conduct;

thus, there would not be sixteen. The aforementioned "sixteen types of conduct" are established as sixteen by taking the transgressions of cessation regarding the side of active construction into account. Therefore, they constitute sixteen.

Therefore, one cultivates the practice in response to specific matters to clarify the prevention of transgressions. While all previous commentaries have been sharp and incisive, this interpretation is superior;

yet it still has slight limitations. Looking back at the section on "Accomplishing the Site" (*sthāna-sampad*), there are two types of observance (*samvara*): the first is observance through remaining composed and inactive (*pratyupasthāna*).
The second refers to the "cessation and maintenance" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) regarding specific matters. This present section on cessation and maintenance likewise concerns specific matters;

therefore, it is not singled out [from the general category]. Why? Because there are two kinds of transgressions of cessation: this [present case] is a transgression of cessation regarding specific matters, whereas the other is a transgression of cessation consisting of failing to learn [the precepts] while remaining idle.
The preceding sections have been diverse; this concludes the general explanation of the four chapters.
The section on the meaning of the gates of penetration and obstruction is concluded.

Fifth, regarding the gradual and sudden [approaches]: this section is divided into three parts. First, concerning the four practices according to the intent of the treatise, all possess both gradual and sudden aspects.

Second, distinguishing them in relation to practice, they are exclusively gradual and not sudden. Third, clarifying the gradual [process] solely in terms of cessation and transgression. This is followed by four sub-sections.

This can be understood through careful investigation. Regarding the terms "gradual" (*jiàn*) and "sudden" (*dùn*): that which is formed through accumulation and progressive increase is called gradual; that which is performed all at once is called sudden. Lì says:

"If one interprets the meaning based on these two modes of operation, it is only gradual and not sudden; however, if one considers the two types of cessation (*śamatha*), they encompass both the gradual and the sudden."

If one discusses the gradual nature of the mind by analogy with its categories, it is as follows: for instance, when the mind ceases from killing but does not cease from falsehood and so forth, this is the gradual development of the mind in terms of the observance of cessation (*śīla-virati*).

If one merely observes the summer retreat (*varṣā*) but does not observe the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), this is the gradual development of the mind in terms of the observance of performance (*kriyā-virati*).

If one wishes to practice both aspects of transgression, the two types of observance (*dharma-vinaya*) accord with the essence of what is received, whereas the two types of transgression contradict the essence of what is received; for at the time of receiving the precepts, one intends to sever all evils.
If one now completely cuts them off, this accords with the essence of observance (*āśraya*). If one forms a mind to simultaneously commit various evils, then one violates the essence of observance.

This also serves as a summary of the preceding text: that which accords with the essence of observance is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), and that which violates the essence of observance is called "transgression" (*āpatti*).

Since violating and acceding are different, upholding and transgressing likewise diverge; hence it is said they are "divided into two. As for the previous statement that "in terms of the mind, they encompass both gradual and sudden," this means:
Regarding the clarification of the mind, there are both gradual and sudden approaches. However, regarding practice in relation to its objects, it is only gradual and not sudden.
For example, when one is correctly cultivating the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one cannot simultaneously cultivate other remedies;

the mind of loving-kindness can only remedy killing, while the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) remedies lust, and having few desires remedies stealing—each has its specific object of application. It is not otherwise.
This is because they occur at one time.
Furthermore, regarding the seven mental states that commit killing while in a male body, this refers to the three poisons arising either individually or in combination:

three single instances and three pairs, making seven mental states in total. Now, if one commits killing while a single instance of greed arises, one only violates the one precept against killing; the remaining six [precepts] are not violated.
The precept against killing remains entirely intact and undamaged; its essence is perpetually pure. Regarding the forty-nine precepts:
based on the aforementioned transgressions within the male body, with the single branch of killing excluded, there remain six branches; adding one more—the wound-opening—makes seven.
Since the seven poisons pass through these seven branches, it is said that none of the forty-nine precepts have been violated. Thus, they are called "the fifty [unviolated precepts]."
Regarding the "six precepts," Jing says: Among the bodies of other men, there are no violations whatsoever of the precepts previously undertaken.

For a man, there are eight members (*aṅga*) and seven poisons (*viṣa*) pervading them, which amounts to fifty-six (7 × 8). For a woman, there are three orifices (*vraṇamukha*), and she gains one additional member, totaling sixty-three precepts (63).
These are clearly untainted. As for the statement that it is "also as previously explained," it is as [explained] in the *Śāstra*.
This was already distinguished within the preceding section on the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*).
Regarding the third point—dividing the cessation of transgressions into four propositions through detailed analysis—I privately remark: this belongs to the gate of gradual and sudden [attainment].
This is the final third section. The preceding two sections have completed the explanation of the three types of conduct (*tri-carita*).

From here on, we treat the offense of cessation (*nivṛtti*) alone, divided into four parts, to clarify the meaning of the gradual and sudden nature of the offenses of non-learning and ignorance. That is to say, "non-learning" and so forth are all offenses of cessation.

Therefore, it is clarified here: why is it that one does not study? This constitutes a transgression of the precepts. Master Li states: "The text of the formal exhortation for receiving the precepts says: 'You should engage in study, inquiry, and the recitation of the sūtras.
Furthermore, in the subsequent section on the *karmavācanā* for writing out and reciting the precepts, it is stated that those who do not recite them shall be subject to discipline.

Because of this, the rule of five years of seniority (*pañca-varṣa*) was established. If one does not recite the precepts or the *karmavācanā*, they shall be dealt with according to the law; that is, they shall be dealt with according to the law of a *duṣkṛta* offense."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "to be ignorant," what is meant by "ceasing to commit an offense"? Thus, the lower section of the Vinaya states: "That which was previously recited has now been entirely forgotten; one must wait for the formal instruction of the Dharma.
It also says that it is an offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) not to listen to the Dharma with a single-minded ear.

Because of such ignorance, when questioned at the time of receiving the precepts, one is commanded to engage in study; failing to do so constitutes ceasing to commit an offense. At the time of receiving them, one claims to have attained the fruit, yet now that fruit has not been attained.

[Question: This must be an offense. [Answer: Regarding "not training," it is based on one's own level [of practice]. Therefore, it is said that there is a cessation of the offense. Because the power of having attained the fruit is not yet capable [of preventing it], it is similar to ignorance;
thus, it is not called a cessation of the offense. [Question: Furthermore, it is asked: "Not training in the two cessations is a *duṣkṛta*. *Duṣkṛta* is translated here as "evil doing" (*èzuò*).
Since it is already called a "cessation of the offense," and originally there was no offense, why is it named "evil doing"? [Answer: If it were truly non-existent...
Regarding the mind: it cannot be called an "offense" [in the formal sense]. However, if one gives rise to the thought of not training or not understanding, this is termed "acting.
What is now called "ceasing an offense" refers to the cessation [of the act] with respect to the object.

I say: The first section above concluded the general explanation of the two offenses of "not learning" (*aśikṣita*) and "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

The previous explanation of "not learning" was sudden (*tun*), yet its meaning was not yet complete. Now, I shall further provide a separate and specific explanation of the offense of "not learning," which includes both gradual (*jian*) and sudden aspects.
Shen says: The preceding section clarified "not learning" in contrast to "ignorance," but it dealt only with the gradual and not the sudden; now, it is explained separately.
Regarding "not learning": there are gradual and sudden [approaches].

If one intends that while the mind can learn, the objects of perception—such as the cessation of action—are not to be learned, yet knows that sexual misconduct applies to three types of objects and theft is divided according to four kinds of owners, all of which are matters that ought to be learned, then to now cease from learning them is to suddenly incur many offenses. Jing said: "The teachings of the Tripiṭaka..."
All of these are matters that ought to be studied; yet now one ceases to study them. For each and every object, one incurs many transgressions.

If we discuss the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as being strictly gradual, it is established that when one encounters a phenomenal object (*vastu-dharma*), if one fails to recognize it upon its arrival, or if one harbors doubt, only then does the offense of ignorance accrue.
This is because the mind cannot entertain two thoughts simultaneously, even though objects and events may appear all at once. This is due to...

Because one forms the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*) only when the object and the matter are not understood, it is gradual rather than instantaneous. Question: What are these two offenses of non-learning and ignorance?
In order to explain the offense of non-learning and ignorance, I shall first pose a preliminary question and then proceed to the explanation.
Answer: Some say they are *duṣkṛta* (transgressions). This is how the various masters of antiquity explained non-learning and ignorance.
"Jiye" (It is a *ji* offense). Li [the commentator] interprets this in the same way as the present *Chao*, yet they differ here.

If one does not study the ancient explanations, there are two kinds of "ignorance. If one does not recognize it at all, then it is a *ji* offense; this will be explained in the following nine phrases.
Thus, citing the Vinaya text, it says that ignorance constitutes a *thullaccaya* (*ti*) offense. As Li explains: "Regarding the *thullaccaya* offenses established in the Vinaya text, this is..."
The offense of not listening to the Dharma with attentive ears is not a formal charge (saṃghāvaśeṣa) levied against one who lacks knowledge.
This is just as the rule regarding receiving food in more than three bowls: it is a formal charge only for exceeding three bowls, and not a formal charge for not giving food to other bhikṣus.
Now, let us leave this matter open to interpretation according to one's own judgment. If one follows the explanation of Vimalamitra, there is no *pātayantika* at all within the latter nine clauses.
Regarding the offense:

it should be understood that the term "not training" constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). In the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, within the *Śīla-skandhaka*, the exhortatory passage states: "You should study, inquire, and recite the sūtras.

Furthermore, the subsequent *karmavācanā* for dispatching [a monk] to recite the precepts states that each [monk] says they do not recite them; consequently, the rule was established that those with less than five years of seniority (*pañca-varṣa*) must recite the precepts.
If one does not [recognize it], one is punished according to the law. If there is doubt, one incurs a minor offense, a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅); this is the meaning of the Nanshan [Vinaya Commentary]. It says:

although "recognition" (*vijñāna*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) are both forms of ignorance, the offenses incurred differ in severity because doubt arises from two objects—namely, by taking both the true and the false as its conditions.
Doubt belongs to the category of those who seek resolution and must be decisively settled; because it possesses a nature of discernment (*jñāna*), it is considered light.
Furthermore, I do not know why you have persistently given rise to delusion; it is because of this ignorance and mental darkness that [the offense] is grave.
Regarding the "demarcation of the three periods": this refers to citing a specific passage to conclude the two offenses of "not learning" and "unknowing.

As for the demarcation of time, there are three distinct divisions: first, the demarcation of the offense as established within the Vinaya teachings, which refers specifically to those who have completed five years of summer retreat (*varṣa*).
Second, the delimitation is explained in terms of practice: specifically, that from the age of ten, one follows [a teacher] for five years.

Third, the delimitation is explained in terms of the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings: those with sharp faculties incur two offenses, while those with dull faculties incur one offense. Regarding "learning" (*śikṣā*) based on the beginning and end:

"beginning" refers to the completion of the initial reception of the precepts; "end" refers to the perfection of the *dharmakāya* through the fivefold division of the Dharma. This concludes the middle section.

To fail to study at any time is to contravene the Sage. However, since the current monastic regulations require that one study for as long as one lives, if one does not study now, one incurs the offense of non-study (*aśikṣamāṇa*).

This is the demarcation established according to the teachings. From the perspective of those who aspire to the level of the Sages and Worthies—that is, regarding the clarification of practice—one must still study throughout one's entire life with diligence.
Even if one has only five years of seniority (*pañca-varṣa*), one must study for the rest of one's life; otherwise, the offense of non-study is incurred. This is why such a rule was established.
Regarding those who instruct: it is said that some, possessing only a slight understanding, claim their merit is equal to that of the worthy sages (ārya).

Therefore, it is stated that if five years have not yet been completed, one must rely upon a teacher of ten years' standing. As for "the inferior relying upon the superior": since there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority in both practice and understanding, the inferior must rely upon the superior;

however, only one who excels oneself is considered truly superior. Thus, the following citation from the Vinaya text states: "For five years, one receives dependence from a teacher of ten years' standing."
Stop. Ten years is superior; five years is inferior. Regarding the statement that one only leaves behind dependence once the fivefold Dharma-body is established:

the fivefold refers to precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Guarding against what is improper and ceasing evil is called precept (*śīla*). Calming the mind through meditative absorption is called concentration (*samādhi*).

Contemplating emptiness is called wisdom (*prajñā*). The total exhaustion of accumulated afflictions is called liberation (*vimukti*). The knowledge and vision regarding this liberation is called the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*).
That which clearly illuminates and fully understands the state of liberation for oneself and others is called "knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).

These five are the standards of conduct and are thus termed *dharma*. They are the causes for the formation of the [noble] body and are termed "factors" (*aṅga*). In the newer sūtras and śāstras, they are called the "five untainted aggregates" (*anāsrava-skandha*).
This concludes the explanation according to the teachings.

The following clarifies the explanation of the number of offenses based on one's faculties (*indriya*) and other factors. If one of sharp faculties easily realizes [the precepts], there are two offenses from beginning to end.

This means that if a person of sharp faculties understands [the training] upon being taught, yet now stops and does not train—remaining ignorant of the matter—they incur the two offenses of non-training and ignorance (*aśikṣita-ajñāna*).
These are not to be deferred until after five years of residence (*pañca-varṣa*). Thus, the moment one ceases to train is the "beginning."

From the time one fails to learn and understand until the conclusion, two offenses are incurred; hence it is said that "from beginning to end, there are two offenses. The *Shengyun* (Commentary) states: "Receiving [the precepts] later is called the 'beginning';
the exhaustion of the physical form at the end of a single lifetime is called the 'end. If one takes a more distant perspective, the attainment of the fivefold Dharma-body is the 'end.

If one fails to learn until the end, the offense is incurred. Regarding the incurrence of the offense for one who possesses understanding: the offense of failing to learn is incurred immediately at the time [of the transgression]; this is not due to ignorance.
The offense must be incurred after five years of residence; thus, the five years mark the beginning, and the exhaustion of one's life marks the end.
If one is of dull faculties and difficult to awaken, there is no offense of ignorance regarding the beginning and the end. This statement is somewhat obscure;

it means that since such a person is dull-witted, if they do not study, they incur only the offense of failing to study from beginning to end, but they do not incur the offense of ignorance, because this is beyond their capacity.
This is not something acquired all at once. Thus far, we have discussed the dullness of faculties; the explanation regarding the meaning of the quantity of offenses incurred is now complete.
Although there are differences between those with sharp and dull faculties, by the very nature of committing an offense, it logically necessitates confession.

From this point onward, the text correctly clarifies the principle that certain offenses are subject to confession and repentance. Regarding the four types of offenses that can be confessed because they are not equal [to the grave], Zhi Liang states:
"This is presented in contrast to the views of the ancients. The ancient masters explained that the offense of failing to study [the precepts] is subject to confession.

Because one trains by generating the resolve [for awakening], this is the severing of the continuity of the mind; therefore, it is subject to repentance. If one commits an offense without awareness, then it cannot be repented.

This is because although one generates the intention to focus on the object, the object is still not fully understood; thus, there is no sense of severing the continuity, and so it cannot be repented.
It is like facing a subsequent matter that arises again and yet remains uncomprehended—how could there ever be a time of severance? Now, the intent of this *Chao* (Commentary) is not...
Nevertheless, it is said that both may be confessed. Thus, the opening commentary asks: "Regarding those who do not learn and are ignorant, can their offenses be confessed?

The answer is that there are two types of understanding. First, some understand that the offense of not learning can be confessed, while the offense of ignorance cannot be confessed. The reason for this is as follows:
The offense of non-learning carries the meaning of severing continuity. If one resolves to return to learning, then there is no longer the offense of non-learning;
because continuity is severed, it can be expiated. As for the offense of ignorance, although one may intentionally desire to know, one fails to comprehend due to conditions;
because this ignorance does not involve the severance of continuity, it cannot be expiated. However, if one later comprehends through conditions, then it is [otherwise].
When ignorance (*moha*) and delusion (*moha*) cancel each other out, there is no further need for repentance (*pratideśanā*). Someone has refuted this interpretation of the ancient masters, stating:

"Perhaps 'delusion' refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of ignorance, while 'sin' refers to karma (*karman*). Since karma that has already arisen must be removed through repentance, and since karma is fundamentally not the same as delusion, how can you say they are mutually exclusive?
Furthermore, if one says 'delusion' refers only to the five [hindrances], then it would not be mutually exclusive with karma. If that were so, then upon generating the resolve [for awakening]...
If you wish to know: if one does not personally understand [the nature of the offense], and because the continuity [of ignorance] is not severed, one cannot perform repentance;

then, when I mount the vehicle with the intention to study, but because I have not yet attained that study, the continuity of non-study persists—would it follow that I should likewise be unable to perform repentance? Answer: The term "study" refers to the initial cultivation and progressive advancement.
"Knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the ultimate realization of the object. Since the beginning and the end are not the same, how can they be treated as analogous? Furthermore...

The interpretations of the two masters are identical with the intent of their respective commentaries (*caoshu*). Because they did not study [the texts] from the beginning, they remained ignorant of the circumstances;

thus, the Sage imposed the offense of ignorance upon them. Now, if they have already studied, even though they may still not fully comprehend the objects of their contemplation, the Sage does not impose the offense of ignorance.

Therefore, we know that if one has studied, there is no offense of ignorance; since there is no offense of ignorance, it cannot be said that the offense continues. This is because there is no offense of ignorance.

It can be restored. How can you further claim that it cannot be expiated? Daolì refutes ancient attachments and likewise judges that it can be expiated; therefore, I shall now provide a further explanation.

When one commits an offense with a conscious mind, the continuity of the [precept] is severed; thus, repentance is possible. When one resolves to train [in the precepts], yet due to external conditions fails to fully comprehend them, the Sage does not establish an offense for this;
therefore, this constitutes the meaning of "severance. One should know that such cases are expiable. This principle is clear. Above.
The fifth section, explaining the gradual and sudden meanings of upholding and violating [the precepts], is now concluded.

Sixth, clarifying the relative superiority and inferiority of upholding and violating: this is further divided into two parts. First, regarding the two types of upholding, there is superiority and inferiority in upholding;

second, regarding the two types of violating, there is superiority and inferiority in violating. As for why there is a sequence [of priority] between them: upholding accords with the essence of what has been received.
It should first be made clear that violating [the precepts] contradicts the essence of what has been received; therefore, it is discussed later.
Regarding the "precept of dignified demeanor" (*airyāpathika-śīla*), it is established that this refers to the external ordinary monks (*bāhya-prthagjana-bhikṣu*).

In the previous analysis of the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*), it was stated that the first three are "precepts" (*śīla*) and the latter four are "dignified demeanor. However, the judgment presented here differs from that previous classification; the first three and the latter four are [treated as] common.

The first is called the *īryāpatha* (dignified deportment). This refers to those who receive the full ordination (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) at the present time; all such individuals are said to possess the *īryāpatha-śīla*.

Second is the *indriya-saṃvara-śīla* (restraint of the sense faculties). This is established as follows: internally guarding the gates of the six sense faculties so that they do not become defiled by the external six objects is called the *indriya-saṃvara-śīla*.

As stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*: "One should guard and collect the sense faculties and cultivate right mindfulness. Regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, [one should not grasp at] forms..."

Not giving rise to negligence regarding odors, tastes, and tangibles is called the precept of guarding the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*). Bin said: "This is *indriya-saṃvara*. In newly translated sūtras and śāstras, it is termed *indriya-saṃvara*;
in the terminology of the vehicle, it is termed "guarding" (*saṃvara*). In older translations of sūtras and śāstras, there is only the name "guarding.

As for what is called the "faculties," they refer to the six faculties, beginning with the eye. As for "restraint" (*saṃvara*), it has the meaning of protection; that is to say, mindfulness and wisdom protect [the senses].
Guarding the six sense faculties is called "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*). Regarding the term "guarding" (*saṃvara*) used in older translations, Paramārtha’s commentary states:

it is so called because it can obstruct evil matters and gather wholesome matters; because it can guard the gates of the six faculties, preventing afflictions and karma from entering; and because it can protect the practitioner.

It is called "protection" (*rakṣā*) for many reasons: because it prevents one from falling into the four miserable destinies; and because it can guard the practitioner, enabling them to transcend the stage of an ordinary person and enter the stage of a noble one.

From the stage of initial practice—maintaining the precepts and guarding the sense faculties—until the realization of the fruit of no-more-learning, whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, and whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), at all times it ensures that the gates of the senses do not [admit defilements].
The outflows (*āsrava*) and all evils are entirely established as the restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).

In the twenty-first and twenty-third [sections] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the restraint of the faculties regarding the śrāvaka precepts is explained in detail; it is the provision (*sambhāra*) for both the mundane and supramundane paths.

Therefore, it should be known that this is precisely the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*) on the path (the commentary’s statement that it refers to the two middle stages of the inner ordinary persons [*antara-pudgala*] is an incomplete explanation). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 40) asks: "What is meant by 'protecting the perfection'?"

[The interlocutor] asks: "What is the perfection [of restraint]? [The respondent] answers: "It is the restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*). One should know that herein, the faculties are what is to be guarded.

By the power of mindfulness and wisdom, one guards the faculties such as the eye, not allowing them to give rise to various faults regarding their objects, just as a hook restrains an elephant so it does not bolt away.

Therefore, for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), being possessed of right mindfulness and right situational awareness is called the perfection of guarding. The guest says: "As for this restraint of the faculties, it begins from the stage of a beginner."

It is only upon reaching the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) that it becomes fully perfected. (The present *Jiaochao* judges this to be the stage of the Inner Worldling (*antarapṛthagjana*), omitting mention of the Outer Worldling and the Noble stages; thus, its explanation is incomplete in principle.

As for what constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of these precepts for guarding the sense faculties, according to the Saṃmitīya school, their essence consists of the three dharmas of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), right awareness (*samyak-saṃprajanya*), and right equanimity (*samyak-upekṣā*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) has the nature of clear recollection with respect to an object; that is, it is able to remember and maintain what was previously experienced and so forth.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of virtues and faults. Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the state of the mind being impartial, having distanced itself from the two categories of greed and sorrow.

As the *Vyākhyāyukti* verse states: "Those who possess the Vinaya and Abhidharma as expressed in their texts, and who are endowed with the precepts and protection"—this is the intended meaning of that verse.

It is said: In truth, the *vinaya* contains many meanings. To speak briefly, the precepts of good conduct regarding body and speech, as well as the meaning of guarding the sense faculties, are all *vinaya*.
However, within the *Vinayapiṭaka*, only the precepts (*śīla*) are clarified while the guarding [of the senses] is not.

Therefore, the present *Abhidharma* fully reveals both types—precepts and guarding—so that it accords with the *Vinayapiṭaka*. Since its principles are thus complete and sufficient, it is called the "Vinaya-Abhidharma Text."

This is what is revealed. Regarding "the person who is endowed with morality (*śīla*) and restraint (*saṃvara*"): morality refers to the restraint of the body (*kāya-saṃvara*), while restraint refers to the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).
Because the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) are endowed with these, they are called "endowed persons.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, this is termed "restraint of the mind" (*manasaḥ saṃvaraḥ*), yet it is designated as "restraint of the faculties" based on its function; the general meaning is the same. For a detailed explanation, one should consult the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol. 197) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (vol. 23) discuss this at length; as the text is voluminous, it is not recounted here. Bin states:

"According to principle, this faculty-restraint (*indriya-saṃvara*) applies to both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). One who is simply able to guard the six faculties may be termed 'possessed of faculty-restraint.

To now judge it exclusively as belonging only to the internal ordinary person (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*) contradicts the meaning of the characteristics of the Great Boundary (*mahādhātu*). [This concludes] the third section on the commonality of meditative concentration.

Regarding "precept" (*śīla*): it is established that this refers to the practice of the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) by those on the level of the inner ordinary person (*prthagjana*).

At the time of entering meditative absorption, the essence of this precept is radiant and pure; once one has emerged from absorption, it is no longer present. Because this precept co-exists with meditative concentration, it is called "precept co-existent with concentration" (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*).

In the new sūtras and śāstras, it is termed "precept co-existent with dhyāna" (*dhyāna-sahagata-śīla*), and is also known as the "restraint of meditative absorption" (*dhyāna-saṃvara*). The four paths...

Regarding the "precepts conjoined with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*): it is established that from the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, one realizes the fruit of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and attains cessation.

Because the precepts of the Path arise simultaneously with the Path itself, they are called the "precepts conjoined with the Path. In the new sutras and śāstras, these are termed the "precepts co-arising with the Path.
