From the initial consciousness until the final consciousness, it is clearly designated as "person. There are many in the world who claim that the fetus is not yet a person. Regarding the term "consciousness-offense" (*vijñapti-āpatti*):
if one is conscious of killing a human, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense; if one kills a non-human animal, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the principle of theft:
if one is conscious of stealing, it constitutes five *pārājikas* and four *sthūlātyayas*. The term "offense" (*āpatti*) refers simply to the transgression itself. [End of] Preface.

The nine phrases in the *Śāstra* are termed "recognizing the matter" and "recognizing the offense"; the remaining meanings are identical, differing only in the character used here. The *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"Matter" refers to killing, stealing, the three robes, and the one alms bowl; "offense" refers to the formal adjudication of the transgression, such as *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *duṣkṛta*.
If one can clearly understand these matters and the Dharma without doubt and practice them accordingly, one may be called a practitioner of the superior grade of the Vinaya.
The middle grade consists of four phrases. Regarding "knowing the matter but doubting the offense": "knowing the matter" is explained as before.

As for "doubting the offense," this refers to doubting whether killing constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or doubting whether stealing five [units] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; this corresponds to the passage in the subsequent explanation which says, "doubting lightness or gravity.
Second, regarding "knowing the matter but not knowing the offense": "knowing the matter" is explained as before; it means one does not know that killing results in a *pārājika* (defeat).

It is said that one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense), yet it is not known that stealing five [units] constitutes a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion). One considers this to be a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). The explanation in the following text states:
"To mistake what is light for what is heavy" refers precisely to this passage. Thus, one cannot say that an offense is incurred when it is actually not incurred.

Since it is stated that "one recognizes the matter," this means one knows the Buddha’s prohibition against killing. How, then, can one further claim there is no offense and assert that one did not recognize the offense? It is simply...
This refers to being deluded regarding what is light, taking it to be heavy, and being deluded regarding what is heavy, taking it to be light.

It is further said that although one knows the Buddha’s prohibition against killing, one does not know the distinctions between the *pārājika*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *duṣkṛta* offenses; hence it is said, "one recognizes the act but does not recognize the offense. Third is "recognizing the offense while doubting the act."
One also knows that killing a human being incurs *pārājika*. However, regarding this matter, doubt arises.

Doubt as to whether it is because of the knife that one incurs *pārājika*, or because of causing an abortion, or because the life has been severed, or because of the wound from the knife—this state of indecision is called "doubt. Furthermore, regarding "doubt":

does one incur *pārājika* for killing a male, or is it the same for a female? Does one incur it only when committing the act with the intent of sexual pleasure, or is it incurred the moment one enters [the womb]? These are such doubts.

As for the statement, "doubting whether the object before one is a human or a non-human," this refers to a deluded mind and belongs to the category of that which cannot be learned [through formal precept].
How could it come here to be explained? Regarding the fourth case of transgression through ignorance of the matter: the explanation of the transgression is the same as before.

As for the phrase "ignorance of the matter," it simply means that killing with a blade constitutes a *pārājika* offense, whereas one might claim that inducing abortion or administering poison and so forth does not constitute an offense. Within the category of theft...

It is said that stealing within a village constitutes an offense, whereas stealing from an *araṇya* (wilderness hermitage) does not. Furthermore, regarding the burning, burying, or discoloring [of items], it is considered an offense when one is unaware of it;
thus, the subsequent passage explains this by stating: "to mistake what is light for what is heavy" refers precisely to this text.
One must simply not say that this phrase [refers to] an offense. Jue says: "Not recognizing the matter" means not recognizing that sexual misconduct applies to all three types of objects.
This refers to matters such as the four types of owners regarding theft (this interpretation is excellent).
Next, the explanation clarifies the aforementioned nine phrases. Regarding the statement "to claim one has not committed an offense when one has":

for example, if one commits sexual misconduct under duress by an enemy, the prohibition of the teaching holds that one is only called "non-offending" if there was no pleasure during the three stages [of the act]. Now, this person lacks such awareness and teaches others, saying: "I have committed [it]."

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): it may be appropriate for an offense to be established. Now, if one is coerced by an enemy and teaches [the precept] that there is no pleasure during the three periods [of the act], only then is it called "no offense.
Now, this ignorant person says: "I created the object; it may be appropriate for an offense to be established. But now I am being coerced by another; it was not my original intention.
Although I experience pleasure, how could an offense be established? This is a case of what constitutes an offense being called "no offense. It is also like the precept against killing.

The Vinaya clarifies that from the initial consciousness until the final consciousness, all who kill commit a *pārājika* offense. Those who do not study today claim that once the human form is fully formed, one may incur a *pārājika* offense by destroying it.
Yet, if it is like fresh butter or curd, where the human characteristics have not yet been perfected, how can there be such a grave offense?

Furthermore, if one steals the original object and gains wealth to benefit oneself, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; however, if one burns or buries it to destroy its color and appearance, they claim there is no offense—this is incorrect.

This is all due to not understanding their teachings; it is entirely the sin of ignorance. To mistake what is light for what is grave is precisely this failure to understand the teachings, resulting solely from a lack of study.
It is said that killing animals and stealing are called by the same name [as the gravest offenses]. Bin (Binyou) stated:
"This is mistaking what is light for what is grave."

"Because the middle grade involves consciousness, one gives rise to doubt regarding the object; there are eight offenses for not recognizing [the transgression]. This clarifies that within the four phrases of the middle grade, where there is both consciousness and doubt, there are eight offenses in total.

There are two doubts and six instances of non-transgression (*kṣema*). Regarding "not recognizing": one is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession) and one is a non-transgression due to not having studied.
Because of ignorance, not recognizing it constitutes a *pāyattika*. Within the category of doubt, there are two instances of non-transgression, namely, those arising from not having studied.

"Returning auspiciously" means that because one lacks knowledge, doubt constitutes an offense of *jì* (auspicious). Within these four phrases, there are two instances of *tí* (reproach) and six instances of *jì*.
That is to say, within the text, two cases of doubt result in four *jì*, and two cases of not recognizing [the offense] result in two *tí* and two *jì*;

thus, there are eight offenses. Regarding the sixteen offenses in the four phrases of the lower grade: this indicates that this category consists entirely of cases of not recognizing and doubting; therefore, it is designated as the lower grade.

Four *thullaccaya* and twelve *dukkaṭa*; now there are sixteen. Among these, there are twenty-four offenses, meaning that the sixteen minor (*mudu*) offenses are combined with the eight intermediate (*majjhima*) offenses, thus totaling twenty-four.
The commentary states: "Those who incur a grave offense through ignorance commit a *pācittiya*;
the rest are all *dukkaṭa* offenses. These are all formulated as offenses for one who is capable of training but is deluded regarding the precepts.

Regarding "not committing the root offense and so forth": this means that although the present discussion concerns killing and stealing, it clarifies the offense of ignorance due to not having studied the precepts.
Since this is established in relation to the *śīla* of restraint (*saṃvara*), it must now be explained.

When one has not yet committed the actual acts of killing or stealing, but merely encounters the objective conditions of those acts and fails to recognize them, one incurs the offense of ignorance due to not having studied.

It is simply that one knows when to stop, which constitutes a transgression. As for the statement that this is called "stopping and maintaining" (*zhichí*), the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks:

"Since it is called 'teaching for the ignorant,' it belongs to the category of transgressions; what meaning does it have to be termed 'stopping and maintaining'? The answer is: "Because one does not commit a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*), it is termed 'stopping and maintaining.'"

Regarding the confusion over specific matters, both are equally categorized as "foolish teachings" and are subsumed under "cessation-offenses" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). When establishing the fundamental tenets to judge the meaning, how can one hastily determine what constitutes observance or violation?

That is to say, according to the fundamental tenet, this is an instance of "cessation-observance" (*virati-śīla*); yet, based on a lack of training and ignorance, it constitutes a "cessation-violation. The Guest says:

"This school clarifies nine propositions regarding 'cessation-observance' that can be learned. For what reason does the school [also] bring forth twenty-four offenses of 'cessation-violation' arising from a lack of training and ignorance?"

This is a clarification. The commentary explains: Although the root treatise concerns *śīla-vāraṇa-dhāraṇa* (the observance of restraint), we do not here speak of this offense in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Rather, it refers to the offense of ignorance regarding the instruction (*ajñāna-śikṣāpatti*) arising from a lack of discernment at the time of the causal condition (*pratyaya*). It may be that the causal condition is present.

In the case of *vāraṇa-dhāraṇa*, if one’s own mind lacks discernment and fails to recognize or suspects another matter, no offense is incurred; this is a transgression of non-knowing (*ajñāna-virati-āpatti*). If...

Regarding the "offense of ignorance due to non-learning" within the context of formal observance (*dhāraṇī*), this refers to the formal conclusion of a matter based on one's own conditions when the task at hand was not fully understood.
"All [cases] cease with the act" means that in the case of the precept against killing, nine permutations (*navapada*) are obtained because it is an intentional act;

if applied to all precepts such as those concerning sexual misconduct and so forth, each likewise obtains these nine permutations. The explanation of the meaning of the nine permutations regarding what can be learned is now complete.

Regarding the clarification of the nine propositions by means of matters that cannot be learned: here, the mere citation of matters serves only to accord with the preceding "Gate of Essential Characteristics" (*tǐzhuàngmén*).
This is just as the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) again cites both matters and dharmas. These subsequent nine propositions are entirely different from the previous nine;

the former belong to the teaching for the ignorant (*yújìào*), which is why they were not recognized, whereas these latter ones all belong to the teaching of realization (*liǎojiào*). One might suddenly become confused regarding them.

Because one forgets, the conditions are not clearly perceived; thus, one becomes deluded regarding the matter and fails to recognize that there is absolutely no fundamental offense, nor is there an offense of ignorance due to a lack of training.
However, if one harbors doubt or lacks recognition regarding a transgression, then the offense of "lack of training and ignorance" is incurred.
This, too, is not the correct interpretation. It is as in the later case where it is difficult to know whether an understanding has arisen.

However, regarding these nine phrases, if one treats them as "not recognizing the object," then such a person would be entertaining the doubt that a tree is a human, or the doubt that a human is a non-human, and so forth; the application of the offense should be understood by analogy.
This is simply because the mind is deluded, resulting in doubts such as "not recognizing" and so on. As for the offenses based on the object, each is divided into three mental states.

This refers to the presence of three states of mind regarding both the object and the offense: namely, certainty, doubt, and lack of recognition. All of these pertain to the object; that is, regarding the commission of an offense, there are these three mental states.

According to the *Lishi* commentary, the formulation of the phrases is based on the objective perception (*saṃjñā*) of the object. Among the five phrases, the first three constitute the three mental states.
For example, regarding the precept against killing, there are five phrases concerning the perception of the object, which constitute the three mental states. First, the person...

To perceive [the first person] as a human is called "recognizing the object. To have doubt regarding the second person is called "doubting the object. To perceive the third person as a non-human is called "not recognizing the object.
These are merely provisional pairings; the intended meaning of establishing these categories does not necessarily require them to be so strictly.
The text divides each into three types of mind and so forth, while the nine subsequent phrases are divided into three grades, with three distinct intentions within each grade.

Regarding "offenses committed with one consciousness": this is explained by way of the precept against stealing. It refers to being conscious of the distinctions among objects in the three realms, such as burning, burying, or altering their color;

being conscious of stealing human property constitutes five *pārājika* offenses and five *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, while stealing four [coins] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding "offenses committed with two consciousnesses and doubt about the matter": the consciousness of the matter is the same as before;
"doubt about the offense" refers to stealing five coins and doubting whether it is a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The rest may be understood by analogy. This is the [unmanifest]...
One may study the nine propositions, but this applies only to matters; regarding what is not permitted to be studied, it does not apply to transgressions.

This was also how the ancient masters established the nine propositions, failing to open up [the possibility of study] regarding transgressions. Now, this commentary synthesizes and reconciles them: regardless of whether it concerns a matter or a transgression, [the principle remains the same].
All of these are "untrainable" (aśikṣamāṇa) and thus cannot be learned. According to the New Commentary school, they do not establish these nine categories of the untrainable at all.
Now, since categories are established for the purpose of defining offenses, why would one need to list that which is offenseless?
One might ask: "If it is not listed, how can we know it is offenseless? For this reason, it must be listed. These are the three sets of three categories.

Regarding the statement that "the two lines at the end of each [section] are doubtful and the distinct categories of offenses are not recognized, such that there are two offenses per category totaling twelve offenses":

because these involve matters that cannot be learned [as formal training], no offense is formally incurred regarding the matter itself. There are offenses only based on the six lines, which collectively comprise three *pārājika* (defeats).
Nine [offenses] plus [three] makes twelve; all of these are defined as offenses based upon the transgression, rather than the matter itself possessing this offense. That is to say:
Within the three grades, one takes the final two phrases from each respective grade; thus it is said that "each has the latter two phrases.

Regarding the phrase "because thoughts and doubts arise falsely": this means that at times, with respect to an object that is actually a human being, one falsely gives rise to the thought that it is a non-human being, an animal, or a tree stump, or one entertains doubt [regarding its identity].
Since these do not constitute an offense against the actual object, it says "arise falsely," and so forth.

Question: Regarding cases such as killing or stealing, where one perceives a human as a non-human, or perceives what is ownerless as having an owner, and so forth up to the point of committing an offense—what is the intent of this question?
From among the nine subsequent phrases mentioned above, the three middle and lower phrases concern not recognizing the object (*vastu*) and doubting the object;

in these cases, no offense is incurred. Furthermore, at the conclusion [of the rule], it says: "The object is something that can be learned; because perception and doubt arise falsely, the Noble One [is not guilty]. How is this to be understood?
This question arises from the preceding statement regarding non-restraint, offenses, and so forth. However, to provide a direct explanation: this question arises from the words spoken above.

Since it was stated above that "one is declared free of offense when [an action] arises through perception, doubt, or delusion," one might ask: "But what of those cases where there is still an offense?
The intent of the question is as follows: in the case of the precept against stealing, if one acts with the perception or doubt that the object belongs to no owner, then—

Regarding the thoughts of doubt and delusion: why does the Vinaya state that one who commits the precept against killing while perceiving a human as a non-human—such as in the case of Dharmānanda—is not guilty?
This is because you claim that when the mind is confused and forgetful, failing to recognize the object or harboring doubt constitutes a fundamental delusion.

All of these are without offense; they merely incur an offense regarding the transgression itself. Why is it that, when one does not recognize or suspects the object of an action, no offense is incurred?
For instance, in the two precepts concerning theft and killing, the wording is not different: if one kills a human being while perceiving them as a non-human being, [an offense is incurred].

Or is it that one is fundamentally deluded regarding the object itself? For what reason, then, would the precept against stealing—wherein there is the perception of no owner—also be fundamentally deluded such that there would be no offense?
Killing, however, is fundamentally deluded and yet still carries an offense. Furthermore, the intent of this objection is that people might not understand and might say:

"If one is fundamentally deluded when acting toward a tree stump and thus incurs no offense, then being fundamentally deluded constitutes an offense; by that logic, animals should also incur no offense. It is for this reason that this [objection] arises.

This is a question. There is a slight incongruity in this question; it is quite extensive. Since this text already clarifies the "stopping and maintaining" (of precepts), why do questions regarding killing and stealing arise?
For killing and stealing pertain to the meaning of "active transgression," which is not analogous [to the preceding].
The preceding questions have been concluded. From here on, Qing answers the reasons for them.

Regarding the answer that "if one forms a mental offense by taking a non-human being as the object of the transgression," the intent of this reply is as follows: if one gives rise to the perception of a non-human or an animal, there is an offense.
Because it is a transgressive object, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in relation to the non-human, since killing a non-human being is not permitted. Therefore, it is said:
Thus, because there is the formation of the mental intention (*cetanā*) and the commission of the act, the Vinaya establishes the offense. This refers to the conditions that give rise to the offense.
If, at the time of killing, one perceives a non-sentient object such as a wooden stump, or if, in the case of theft, one perceives it as ownerless, then there is no offense.

Since these are not conditions for the arising of an offense, the Vinaya does not establish an offense. However, the reason no formal offense is established for those whose minds are deluded is based on the [nature of the] faculty (*indriya*).

Regarding the offenses concerning the actual object (*vastu*): because of this deluded mind, no offense is established. That is to say, in cases of such conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), delusion, or forgetfulness, none of these establish the fundamental *pārājika* offense.
Now, within the aforementioned section on "that which cannot be learned," for what reason is delusion permitted regarding the actual object, yet delusion is not permitted regarding the offense?

The intention of the ancient masters is to clarify this by means of the Vinaya texts; the Vinaya clarifies the objective basis (*viṣaya*) with respect to the actual object and the conceptualization thereof. Thus it is said.

There are texts that clarify delusion; however, they do not explain the distinctions regarding the object and perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) in relation to the commission of an offense. Therefore, regarding the commission of an offense, there is no mutual delusion; these are invariably offenses of restraint (*pratiṣedha-śīla*).

When have we ever heard of such things as committing a *pārājika* while perceiving it as something other than a *pārājika*, or entertaining doubts about it, or committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* while perceiving it as something other than a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or entertaining doubts about it?
All of these cases are understood through consensus. Is it not the case that whether an offense exists or not differs depending on the specific conditions (*pratyaya*) of the transgression? This...

Based on different objects and categorized by the offenses committed, there are differences in the nature of the transgressions. This refers to intention (*saṃjñā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*). When one takes a non-animal as the object, this constitutes a transgression regarding the objective basis of the offense;

thus, there is an offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*). However, when one takes a stump or ownerless property as the object through intention or doubt, this does not constitute a transgression regarding the objective basis of the offense;

thus, there is no offense of preliminary effort. Nevertheless, these offenses are considered in relation to the original deluded mind. If the perception were to change, then [the offense would not be established].
The same applies here. This will be explained more extensively below in the section on "perception regarding objects.

Furthermore, it differs from the preceding section where both the object and the phenomenon were identified as consciousness; this refers to the further delineation of the differences among these nine propositions.

Among the nine propositions, the preceding ones refer to what is "trainable," meaning they point to the objects that are subject to training. Within these nine propositions, regarding the phenomena among the objects, one is inherently deluded.

If one does not recognize [the rule] because it is not taught, rather than through delusion or forgetfulness, then it is something that can be learned; therefore, in all such cases, an offense is incurred.
However, in this case, because it cannot be learned, no offense is incurred. Jì also says: "Furthermore, this is not the same as the preceding section.

'Both the dharma and the matter are recognized' refers to the nine phrases concerning matters that can be learned; since both the matter and the dharma are learnable, they are called 'dharma and matter.'"

"Both recognized" means that both can be recognized. However, because one has not studied [the rules], one does not recognize them; due to this intentional doubt, a transgression is incurred in all cases.
Regarding the term "dharma," it simply refers to an offense. Lì (Lìyán) says: "The statement here—that 'both the dharma and the matter are recognized'—is different from the preceding section.
This text contradicts the *Tǐzhuàng mén* (Section on Essential Characteristics). One should know that the former represents the interpretation of the ancient masters. As stated previously:

The maintenance of cessation (*śīla*) and the commission of transgressions were previously explained solely in relation to the matters within the two teachings. Now, however, it is stated that one "recognizes both the Dharma and the matter.

Is this not in contradiction with what preceded? If one follows the previous meaning, according to reason, it should have been stated that it is "not the same as the preceding section because one recognizes both the Dharma and the matter.

How could it simply say "the Dharma"? Since it says "both the Dharma and the matter," we know for certain that the maintenance of cessation and the commission of transgressions apply universally to both the matter and the [Dharma].

It is the *dharma*. One interpretation states: "To recognize both the *dharma* and the matter" refers here to the transgression of the *dharma*. Since the *dharma* itself constitutes the offense, it is a transgression (*āpatti*).

Now, regarding "recognizing both the matter and the [transgression]," as previously stated, one recognizes the matter and recognizes the transgression; the transgression is also termed *dharma*. What is referred to here by the word "*dharma*" is this very term "transgression.
It does not concern the essential nature of the thing itself, nor does it imply that while the *dharma* is pervasive, the transgression is not (this is my own view).
This is the explanation. (The superior [view] is also the same as this latter interpretation).
If that is so, since there are also perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) within the subsequent objects of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*), Jing says:

"The intent of this objection is that while the category of 'having perceptions' and 'doubt' is opened up as being 'not to be learned' (*aśikṣya*), how can it be that within the *dharmas* there are also perceptions and doubts, yet one claims that regarding *dharmas* there are none?"
"It can be studied. As for the statement "there are those who say," this is the meaning of the objection:

it asserts that while the preceding section clarified the ancient masters' views on cessation-and-maintenance (*saṃvara*) and commission-and-transgression (*āpatti*) as applying only to concrete matters (*vastu*) and not extending to principles (*dharma*), the present section clarifies that cessation-and-maintenance and commission-and-transgression also apply to principles; thus, it is based upon these principles.
There are also things that may be learned and things that may not be learned. I have now clarified this regarding the matters of *śīla* (observance) in the preceding section;

hereafter, within the context of *samādāna-śīla* (formal undertaking), I shall further clarify that within the Dharma itself there are likewise things that may be learned and things that may not be learned (one has not yet reflected upon this). Some say:

"Just as in the section on *samādāna-śīla*, because it forms a phrase based on the Dharma, it is called 'within the subsequent Dharma'. Others say: "The intent of this repeated objection follows from the [final] nine [points]."
[This is] a phrase. Regarding the aforementioned doubt and lack of recognition, it concludes with the offense of ignorance due to not having studied.

Furthermore, within the preceding section on "essential characteristics" (*tǐzhuàng*), regarding the categories of "maintaining" (*chí*) and "ceasing" (*zhǐ*) versus "offenses" (*fàn*), these apply universally to both types of teachings—those concerning *dharmas* (principles) and *vastus* (matters)—but they apply only to what can be learned, not to what cannot be learned.
Now, I shall here translate this meaning. As for the underlying intention, the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Regarding the matter..."
There is confusion; therefore, it is permitted and not established as an offense. Regarding the violation of the rules, there is likewise confusion and forgetfulness.

As cited above from the Vinaya, if one has the perception or doubt that a house exceeds the prescribed dimensions, these are all permitted. Why, then, in this case, is "lack of training and ignorance" established as an offense?

However, the objection that one cannot commit an offense without lack of training and ignorance is itself a difficult point; furthermore, even now, there is no such thing as "lack of training and ignorance. This is for the following reason:

The ancient masters committed offenses because they were not entirely incapable of learning; that is to say, when one acts with doubt regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense and not a heavy *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Therefore, it is the same as when one returns to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense through a mistaken perception (*vikalpa*)—within the rules permitting such acts, there is no confusion—and in all such cases, one is charged with the offense of ignorance due to a lack of training.
Such is the intent of the objection. [The respondent] establishes that while confusion is permitted regarding the matter (*vastu*), you [the opponent] judge it regarding the rule (*dharma*).

It would also follow that there could be delusion regarding the nature of dharmas—such as perceiving what is not a formal act of adjudication (*adhikarana*) as being one—and yet the Vinaya does not prescribe a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for this; thus, it appears to permit such delusion.
Why then do you now also impose the [offense of] "lack of training due to ignorance" (*aśikṣitājñāna*) upon those who have committed an offense? [The respondent’s] own intention is as follows:

To say "if that were so" is to raise a further objection based on the preceding answer. The intent of the objection is: since you have already answered that "it may be conditioned by what is not an offense,"...
Regarding the object: because it is an ownerless thing. As for why, subsequently, a deluded mind does not incur a formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*):

why is it that in the section on "making" (*kṛta*) within the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, such as when one builds a house without asking for permission, yet has the perception that permission has been granted—this too is an instance of taking a non-offensive object as a condition, where originally no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is incurred.
Why, then, is delusion not explicitly excluded there, while a rule against the offense of ignorance due to lack of training (*aśikṣitājñāna*) is established? Śaṅguo (Sheng) also says: "In vain..."

However, that deluded mind does not incur a formal offense (*samyak-pāpa*). There is something that cannot be learned; do not raise this objection. What constitutes a "prohibitory offense" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
Jingsheng says: Since one does not incur an offense when there is doubt based on a mistaken perception, it is clear that the root [offense] is not incurred.
How can you fail to allow for what cannot be learned, yet establish for me the offense of ignorance for not learning?
Answer: This is stated for the time being based on the *zhichi* (abstention and maintenance) section, speaking in terms of specific matters (*shi*).

Sheng says: "This follows the ancient interpretation; it is not the same as the *zhichi* that is universally 'not to be learned' (*bù kě xué*). Because the matter here merely involves avoiding transgressions, it can be clearly defined.

Therefore, it is said to be 'speaking in terms of specific matters. Li says: The meaning of the answer is that, as you have objected, there are also things within the *Abhidharma* that are "not to be learned. I...

For now, within the section on "abiding in observance" (*zhi-chi*), I shall clarify this by way of concrete matters. Even regarding the principles of the Dharma (*fa-shang*), there may still be confusion;

this will be clarified later in the section on "maintaining observance" (*xià zuò-chí*). That is to say, since even thoughts of doubt regarding concrete matters are declared unlearnable (*bù kě xué zhě*), how much more so would actual transgressions be?

Within the Dharma there are likewise perceptions and doubts; how can one claim that, regarding the Dharma, there is nothing that cannot be studied? The intent of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) is also thus.

The meaning of this current response is likewise to provide a comprehensive interpretation of the text. Some say that the intent of this objection is not yet exhausted, asserting that this response answers from the standpoint of the Dharma.
However, although it answers from the standpoint of the Dharma, it is actually an answer concerning transgressions (*āpatti*). If [the offense] were to exist within the Dharma...

"Delusion. This also opens up the possibility of delusion regarding transgressions. Therefore, the purpose of these questions and answers here is to clarify that according to the interpretation of the ancient masters, one would incur an offense based on the violation itself and the rule (*dharma*).
However, in this present response, both the rule and the violation may involve delusion.

I shall now, within the context of "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*), formulate nine propositions based on the specific facts; it is not yet a matter of discussing delusion regarding the rule. This will be addressed later.

Regarding "holding the middle," it is said that these are dharmas that cannot be learned. There are also nine phrases concerning delusion. If one follows the present meaning, among the nine phrases of what cannot be learned, there is in total no offense of neither learning nor knowing.
Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "When calculated according to principle, this establishes the precedent;

this is what should not cause confusion," and so forth. Question: Since this current *Chao* (Digest) has already refuted the former interpretation, why is it still necessary to list the nine phrases? Answer: These are listed here for the time being...
I shall set forth the interpretations of the ancient masters and subsequently refute them. If these were not listed, one would not know where the refutation applies.

According to the present interpretation, within each of the four lines there are many sets of nine phrases; that is to say, regarding the "object" (*vastu*), there are nine phrases concerning what is learnable and what is unlearnable, and the same applies to the "dharma.
Thus, the four lines collectively constitute sixteen sets of nine phrases, along with the section on the cessation of offenses.

The eighteen points must necessarily be as cited. "Establishing" refers to the fact that your refutation follows the instructions [of the master]; this is the intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts), which differs from the ancient interpretation.
One must rely on the *Vinaya* text regarding the categories of objects and perceptions (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), for these cannot be learned through mere imitation.

In this context, it is revealed that within the preceding section on "essential characteristics" (*tǐzhuàng mén*), the act of maintaining [the precepts] also applies to what cannot be learned through imitation. Therefore, the Preface states: "From beginning to end, they mutually illuminate one another. This is...

As for its meaning (this refers to the eminent master; having finished explaining the meaning of "cessation and maintenance" above), next, regarding the matters that can be learned within the context of "commissioned offenses," the nine phrases are as at the beginning.

This is the same as the nine phrases of what can be learned listed first in the section on "cessation and maintenance" above. As for the phrase "matters of the dharma that can be learned," those dharmas are in fact the meaning of "offenses. It is called...
The transgression is for the sake of the Dharma. The preceding case, in which the fundamental offense has not yet been committed, is called "abstaining from what is prohibited" (zhichi).

This present case involves committing the fundamental offense; as it is the opposite of the aforementioned abstention, it is called "committing a transgression" (zuofan). It likewise consists of two parts and nine phrases, differing only in that it involves committing a fundamental sin.

Why was "abstaining from what is prohibited" explained above, while "engaging in what is prescribed" (zuochi) was not explained in sequence? The explanation is as follows: indeed, it should have been explained in sequence.

"Maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*). This now reverses the previous "maintaining by cessation" (*niḥśrita-dhāraṇa*) and constitutes "committing an offense through action" (*kṛta-āpatti*). This is established for the sake of convenience in the formulation of the principles.

Next, the explanation of "offenses" (*āpatti*) follows after "maintaining by cessation. Regarding the phrase "one must not train as in the latter nine phrases," this refers to the "phrases on what must not be trained in" listed at the end of the preceding section on "maintaining by cessation.
As for the distinction that "only the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) constitutes a transgression," since it is called "committing an offense through action," how could one not be in violation?
This refers to the fundamental [offenses] of killing, stealing, and so forth.

Among these, regarding the fundamental lack of awareness of the matter—specifically, cases where there is no offense because one was ultimately without intent, such as accidentally killing a person—this is a case of "distinguishing what cannot be learned" (an object of study that must be avoided).
Within the nine phrases concerning the commission of an offense, these constitute the three phrases of the lower grade (*mṛdu*) of the fundamental [offense].

The meaning of "offense" does not clarify the fault of ignorance due to a lack of learning; rather, it refers to cases such as killing, where the fundamental act is committed while mistaking the victim for a tree stump.

Because there was no intention during the three periods [of preparation, execution, and completion], and because of this lack of intention, there is no wrongdoing from beginning to end. Thus, one incurs no guilt.

This citation of the fundamental delusion serves as a preliminary analysis of the performance of an offense, leading from here to the point where the prior act is not actually committed. Hereafter follows the detailed examination.
The last three phrases of the nine-phrase section concern the failure to recognize the nature of an act.

Some say that within this, from the fundamental failure to recognize the matter down to the point of not having previously committed such an act, this passage is intended to analyze the meaning of whether there is a fundamental offense or no offense among the nine phrases regarding "not learning" (ignorance) as a cause for transgression;
it does not clarify the offense of ignorance itself. This excludes the precepts concerning sexual misconduct and alcohol.

As for this, it is established that the Buddha’s regulations concern either the mind following the object or the object following the mind. Regarding the two precepts against sexual misconduct and intoxicants, the mind is regulated according to the object. These apply to all three realms of existence;

if one engages in the actual path, it constitutes a transgression regardless of whether there was a mistaken perception or doubt. Thus, the ultimate offense is incurred in all such cases. Therefore, the text states:

"Even if one perceives the path as not being the path, it is still a *pārājika*. Master Li says: "Of the five propositions regarding the perception of the object in this precept against sexual misconduct, the first three..."

The first phrase constitutes a grave offense at its completion, because it involves the primary object (*mūla-viṣaya*). The latter two phrases constitute the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) of preparatory effort, because they involve a different object that has intervened.

The Upādhyāya said: "Regarding these two precepts, one refers only to the primary object; whether there is a shift in the object or a confusion regarding the primary object, both constitute a fundamental grave offense.
For all other precepts, confusion does not constitute an offense. However, these two precepts also depend on the original state of existence."

If the preparatory effort (*upāya*) is not initiated, then even if doubt were fundamentally non-existent, it likewise should not constitute a formal offense. This has already been explained at length in the preceding discussion on the precept against intoxicants.

If, during the intermediate stage, one’s perception shifts and one doubts the object—failing to recognize the facts because of a mental error—and this is considered a preparatory effort, it refers to cases where a preparatory effort was originally present, such as in the case of killing a human being.
If, during the process, one’s perception shifts and one kills what is perceived to be a non-human, an animal, or a wooden stump, this is [an instance of a shifted intention].

This concerns the object of consciousness. One may doubt whether it is a human, a non-human, an animal, or a wooden stump; this is the matter of doubt. Although one commits the act of killing, one does not incur the root offense (mūlāpatti).
There is only the preparatory offense (prayoga) of the *sthūlātyaya* regarding a human being, because of the shift in perception;

this is termed a "deviation of mind" (*cittaviparyāsa*). If there were no such deviation and the root offense were incurred, it would mean that one clearly and fully knows the object to be a human and yet intentionally [acts].

He kills them. Throughout this process, there is no shifting of thought nor any doubt. Because the mind and the object correspond, it constitutes the fundamental meaning of the formal offense (*mūla-āpatti*).
Alternatively, regarding one who does not commit the act: it is established that he originally intended to kill a human being. Upon reaching the location of the object, he knows it is indeed a human;

or, upon reaching the location, he knows it may be either a human or a non-human; or, upon reaching the location, he knows that a human or a non-human has come to take his place, and he knows it to be so.
It is not a non-human being. However, because one merely gave rise to the thought [of killing] but did not actually kill, there is no offense. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"This clarifies that when the mind clearly perceives the object, one does not commit the aforementioned act.

Conversely, regarding cases where one suspects but does not recognize [the object], or where one commits an act that was not intended to be committed—such as when a virtuous mind arises and one desists from acting, or when the object is powerful and circumstances change, etc.—because one does not commit the act, there is no offense. Furthermore, [Master] Li says: "Because of the original intention..."

Regarding killing: when one approaches the object of the act, if one says it is not a human being and mistakes it for an animal or a wooden stump, one stops and does not kill (this point is not fully detailed).
The nine subsequent phrases concerning the recognition of the object in three grades refer to matters that cannot be learned [in advance] and constitute an offense through action.

The three phrases of the superior grade of recognizing the object consist in clearly perceiving the object and knowing it is a human; therefore, the killing is completed. The three phrases of the middle grade of doubting the object...

Doubt arises regarding the object; whether it be a person, an animal, or a tree stump, because one does not clearly discern the object, the conditions are deficient and one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
Therefore, it is called "medium grade. The three phrases concerning the "inferior grade" of not recognizing the object constitute the absence of conditions (*anālambana*).

This means that because of fundamental delusion, there is no root grave offense; thus, it is classified as inferior grade. Lì says: "The three phrases of the superior grade, where one recognizes the object, involve a correspondence between mind and object."

When one attains the ultimate gravity [of the offense], it constitutes the upper grade (uttama-pakṣa). The next grade, and the subsequent middle and lower grades, are all established as prohibitions because they involve preparatory means (upāya).

However, regarding the very lowest grade, this is based on a shift in perception (*vikalpa*). If one is fundamentally deluded and lacks recognition [of the object], then there is no commission of an offense even at the lower level.

If one asks, "How then are the intermediate and lower grades—such as the *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*—distinguished and ranked? the intent of this question is to inquire about the middle and lower grades.
Both cases involve the same object and perception; since both the second and third instances are committed with the same intention (*laṅ*), why are they divided into medium and inferior grades?
Answer: Because the mind that takes the object as its condition has varying degrees of duration, there is a difference in lightness and gravity. The meaning of this answer is as follows:
regarding the medium grade, it concerns the object and perception in the second case, where the person harbors doubt from beginning to end—doubting whether it is a human or a non-human. This...

This refers to "long. Regarding the third phrase of the lower grade, which concerns the object and perception (*saṃjñā*): perceiving a human as a non-human is called a "transferred perception" (*parivartita-saṃjñā*).
After this transferred perception occurs, there is no further mental engagement with the person; this is termed "short. Master Bin says:

when doubt repeatedly divides its engagement upon the original object, it is termed "long"; this is judged to be grave. Because the perception and mind exclusively abandon the original thought for another, it is so described.

It is called "short"; this is judged to be a light offense. Question: Since one intends here to clarify the offense of ignorance due to a lack of training, why is it necessary to discuss the root offense?
Answer: Because this root offense serves as the basis for the offense of ignorance due to a lack of training.
It is like seeking lice within a garment: one first distinguishes the garment, and only then finds the lice.
The lice are a metaphor for the offense of ignorance due to non-training; the garment is a metaphor for the root offense.

Regarding the statement "or there is no offense," this means that since it is a matter that cannot be learned [in advance], these three phrases concerning the inferior grade—the phrase regarding not recognizing the object—constitute no offense of ignorance due to non-training; therefore, they are specifically treated as such.
In one place, the text says: "As for the previous statement that there is no offense, this means there is no matter of failing to train or being ignorant;

it does not mean there is no root offense. This refers to the present passage (the specific source remains to be determined). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "no offense" (*anāpatti*) is an indefinite term.
It refers to the three propositions regarding the minor grade of ignorance of the matter; because this is a fundamental delusion, there is no root [offense].

Regarding the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*): there is an offense only in the six preceding phrases. However, as for these three subsequent phrases of the lower grade, if one has a mistaken perception (*vikalpa*), there is the preparatory offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: all cases are based on fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), yet there is also uncertainty as to whether an offense exists.

If one acts out of fundamental delusion thinking [the object] is not an animal, then there is an offense. If one acts out of fundamental delusion taking [an object] while perceiving it as a stump or as belonging to no owner, then there is no offense.

Regarding the statement "it is said 'or' because there is no offense": this refers to the discussion within the section on "not recognizing" (*asañjāna*) concerning the fundamental act (*mūla-karma*).

That is to say, among the three grades of the three phrases, since one has already committed an error of perception (*saṃjñā-vibhrama*) and thus does not incur the fundamental offense, the determination of whether an offense is incurred based on the subsequent thought (*paścāt-citta*) is not fixed.
For example, if one mistakes [an animal] for a non-animal (a human), and subsequently incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) through that subsequent thought, it is so designated.

If one acts out of delusion, thinking it to be a wooden post, there is no offense at all; hence it is said, "or there is no offense. Regarding the phrase "it can be understood by knowing the categories of the Abhidharma":

the preceding section clarified the nine cases of committing an offense based solely on the object (*vastu*), explaining the offense of not training or ignorance in terms of specific matters such as sexual misconduct or theft.

If, however, this is explained in terms of the *dharma* (the category), then there should likewise be nine cases concerning the commission of an offense through ignorance of the *dharma* and so forth.
[This is] a phrase. It means that within the Dharma there is still that which is neither learned nor known. Herein, the meaning of the "foremost" (the primary precepts) is implicitly refuted.

Therefore, within the section on their essential characteristics, the maintenance through restraint (*śīla*) and the commission of offenses are explained solely in relation to the matters found within the two teachings [of the Pratimokṣa].

Now, when it is said that one knows by analogy from the Dharma, is this not because the maintenance through restraint and the commission of offenses certainly apply universally to all dharmas? If one now wishes to perform [an action], it does not go beyond the matters mentioned above.

The phrasing is the same, with the only difference being that "matter" (*vastu*) is changed to "dharma. Therefore, it is said that it can be understood by analogy. Śaṅghabhadra says: "There are two interpretations here.

The first interpretation is the same as the previous one [which] was deemed inappropriate. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: the preceding phrase 'or there is no offense' distinguishes this based on the matter itself.
This phrase 'in contrast to the dharma' refers to the formal rule (*dharma*) regarding the offense; it establishes the status of 'not having studied' and 'ignorance,' just as previously maintained."

Therefore, it can be understood through analogy. Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "As with the latter nine phrases, the number of offenses incurred and their relative gravity are all the same;
however, regarding the commission of the root offense (*mūlāpatti*), that which can be distinguished is taken as the reason."
Regarding the one phrase of the highest grade among the nine preceding phrases, which states that "because both the matter and the dharma are fully understood, the offense cannot yet be discussed":

this refers to the first phrase within the section on "Training in Matters" (*śikṣāpada*) concerning matters of the highest grade in the context of "Transgressions through Action" (*kṛta-āpatti*). It corresponds to the first phrase in the section on "Maintaining Training" (*sthiti-śīla*) concerning matters of the highest grade.
Because one recognizes both the matter and the transgression, there is no offense of non-training or ignorance; therefore, it is said that "the offense cannot yet be discussed. However...

There is a root offense. As for the subsequent nine phrases, each being divided into three grades, this refers to the nine phrases concerning the "untrainable" state following the commission of an offense.
This is also a detailed analysis of two sets of nine phrases. The meaning is that among the preceding nine phrases, the highest grade consists of a single phrase:
merely acknowledging the offense (*vijñāta-āpatti*). Even if one possesses such a mind regarding a single matter, there is no offense. As for my subsequent nine [phrases]...

Regarding the statement that "each category generally consists of three phrases": this means that with respect to a single object, there are three mental states—namely, recognition, doubt, and non-recognition.
These are treated separately because it is easier to determine the resulting offense based upon them.

As for the phrase "not all arise from a single object, as they may involve combinations and so forth," Sheng says that both sets of nine phrases arise from the objects themselves. Li states that "may" (rong) implies indeterminacy.
This is a commentary on the phrases such as "that which can be learned" and "that which cannot be learned," all of which refer to matters that may be either doubted, recognized, or unrecognized.

Fearing that others might suspect there is an inconsistency in establishing two sets of nine stages (*navāṅga*), I shall now explain according to the intent of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts):

regarding the first nine [stages] concerning matters that can be learned, because there is an offense when one doubts or fails to recognize the matter, the "superior grade" (*adhimātra*) constitutes one stage, while the "middling" and "inferior" grades each constitute four stages.
Regarding the "phrases": because one perceives the object with doubt and fails to recognize it, they are interwoven and clarified to reveal the characteristics of the offense.

Nine phrases concern the actual object; in each case, the offense is finalized upon completion. Furthermore, if one perceives the object but does not understand it, one is also charged with the offense of ignorance due to failing to study the teachings.
This offense of ignorance is likewise finalized. If there is recognition accompanied by doubt, it is not subsumed under an offense. As for the latter nine phrases, they are grouped in sets of three.
Regarding "classification": because it cannot be learned, there is no offense regarding the objective matter (*vastu*) due to ignorance or doubt;

since it is not something that can be learned, there is no fault in the matter itself, though it does not preclude the commission of an offense. This is what is meant by "it can be learned. To enumerate their characteristics:

while the objective matters are general, the offenses are distinct (for example, in the cases of killing and stealing, although the objective matter is one and the same—hence "the matter is general"—the offenses differ according to the specific conditions of the object, such as whether there was knowledge or doubt, or lack of knowledge or learning; thus they are called "distinct offenses"). [The] private commentary says: the preceding...

The nine items are matters that can be learned. If one is doubtful of or does not recognize these matters, one incurs an offense in every case. Therefore, the single phrase "recognizing the matter and recognizing the offense" is entirely free of offense;
thus, it constitutes the highest grade (upariṣṭha). As for the four phrases each for the middle and lower grades, this is because they all involve offenses.
One cannot apply the same textual formulation regarding "no offense" as in the previous case; therefore, the middle and lower grades each have four distinct categories within their own positions.

As for the final nine phrases: the matter is not something that can be learned [by rote]. Regarding doubt and lack of knowledge, both constitute a lack of awareness; in neither case is there an offense. This applies only in relation to the transgression itself.
If there is doubt and one does not recognize [the offense], this is a retribution for sin. Now, discussing this transgression alone, it is categorized and arranged according to its stages;

thus, each of the three [categories] is divided into three parts. In this way, the principles become easy to understand; hence it is said, "to make the determination of the offense easy to understand," and so forth. As for the statement, "Is it not all due to a single matter?
and so on, these all refer to a single matter—whether it be the matter of killing or the matter of stealing. Although the matter is one, it is distinguished in relation to that matter.
Regarding the offenses based on conditions (*pratyaya*), there are three types of mental states—namely, consciousness, doubt, and lack of consciousness—which result in different degrees of offense.
Therefore, it is said that they do not all arise from a single matter. Thus, the Commentary states: "The matter is general, while the offenses are distinct.

Now, it is also appropriate to apply this to nine persons, or it may be applied to the preceding and succeeding moments of mind of a single person. Jing says: "It is permissible that they do not all arise from a single matter."

Regarding the phrase "doubting both," this refers to the nine permutations within the commission of an offense: six permutations constitute an offense, while three do not, as the agent was aware [of the object].
However, in this context, the primary training rule is cited; because one becomes confused or forgetful upon reaching the actual object, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (light offense).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "arising from a single matter," this refers to the nine permutations based on the matter itself. Taking the matter as the primary factor and traversing through the various factors (*dharma*), the nine permutations are thus established.

Although these nine phrases are established through the enumeration of phenomena, they pertain solely to the level of conventional reality (*vastu*). Within each of these nine phrases, there exists that which is neither learned nor ignorant.

The *Xinshu* (Heart Commentary) asks: "For what reason are they divided into nine phrases? The answer is: "It is intended to make the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts easy to distinguish.
Some say: "How can one learn the matter of the 'superior grade' single phrase? It is for the sake of instructing people so that their minds are free from delusion and forgetfulness."
There is no further meaning of delusion or lack of understanding. Should there be any confusion or forgetfulness, it belongs to the subsequent section on the "unlearnable phrases.
Therefore, the teaching of understanding alone is designated as the superior grade (*uttama-pada*). One cannot take a state characterized by doubt or ignorance and designate it as a grade;

thus, there is only this single phrase. As for the unlearnable phrases, since they pertain to a mind of confusion and forgetfulness, they are categorized according to the object and perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) and established [as such].
It must be divided into three groups of three. This is done by applying it to the upper three phrases of the "object" (*viṣaya*) and "perception" (*saṃjñā*).

As for the preceding nine phrases, since they do not involve delusion or forgetfulness and are truly instances of progress toward realization, how could they be divided according to the three grades of the objective fact? One case involves a mind that is deluded despite having understood the teaching;
the other involves a mind that is deluded while the teaching itself is ignorant. Therefore, they are not analogous.

Regarding the discussion of the twelve offenses—comprising the two lower minds of doubt and ignorance (*ajñāna*) concerning the offenses of the *pārājika* category—if one proceeds from this point onward, both ignorance and doubt are considered ultimate [factors], and all are subject to heavy scrutiny.
The final nine phrases refer to the twelve offenses of ignorance regarding the non-training rules (*aśikṣamāṇa*).
This is also established according to the tenets of the ancient masters; thus one incurs these offenses. If, however, one relies on...
The Commentator states: "There is no such offense at all. This 'auspicious' [offense] is simply the fruit-offense of cessation; therefore, it is called 'ultimate.

Regarding the nine phrases concerning matters that cannot be learned, there are twelve offenses in total consisting of non-learning and ignorance. Although there are nine phrases, they are reduced to six;

regarding the commission [of the offense], there are three doubts and three instances of not recognizing [the rule], resulting in three *thullaccaya* and nine *dukkaṭa*, which together constitute ten."
Second. Regarding the phrase "the two subsequent minds," I privately explain that these refer to the mind of doubting an offense and the mind of not recognizing an offense.

Regarding the statement "all constitute ultimate offenses," this means that the aforementioned twelve offenses, being of the nature of ignorance due to a lack of training, are ultimate resultant offenses;
they are so called because they do not serve as causes for others. Since these offenses are things that ought to be learned, one fails to recognize them precisely because of a lack of such training.
This refers to those who foolishly instruct others, failing to recognize the relative gravity of the characteristics of offenses.

They claim that [offenses such as] *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are all equally "trainable" (*śikṣamāṇā*), asserting they differ from cases where the mind is deluded and the Sage has opened an exemption from offense. Now, because they do not train, they lack this recognition; therefore, no exemption is granted.
Regarding ignorance and doubt being ultimate: because of ignorance, one does not recognize the matter nor recognize the offense;

and because it is not for the sake of another’s means, this constitutes an ultimate [offense]. As for doubt regarding the matter and doubt regarding the offense, because it is not for the sake of another’s means, this is an ultimate [offense].
Since there is no separate fruit toward which one can proceed, it is its own fruit; therefore, it is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*).
If one does not doubt and recognizes that there is exclusively no fault and no fruit toward which to proceed, this is the meaning of "ultimate" as it refers back to the preceding text.

Fearing that people might think that, just as in the case of an action, doubt constitutes the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) while recognition constitutes the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā*), consider, for example, the act of killing.

If one suspects that it was a non-human being who killed, one incurs the offense of preparatory action (*prayoga*). If one recognizes it as a human being who killed, one commits the offense of completion (*niṣṭhāpana*).
Thus, we know that doubt serves as the cause for recognition. Now, this doubt arising from ignorance and lack of learning is not analogous to such a case;

for while there is an offense at the time of doubting, if one subsequently ceases to doubt, there is no offense. Whereas there is an offense at the time of not recognizing [the object], once it is recognized...
Sin is itself non-sin; therefore, one cannot take "non-doubt" and "cognition" as its fruit. Hence it is said that there is no fruit toward which one can proceed.

Setting aside this lack of cognition and doubt, one should realize that these themselves constitute the fruit. Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is no fruit toward which one can proceed:

since one both cognizes the object and doubts it, there is no further sin that can be designated as a fruit. Again, the question was asked: "In the cases of killing and stealing, one cognizes the object."
Only when one has just formed the fundamental [intention] is there a fruit toward which one may proceed.

As for the previous statement regarding "the absence of offense" and so forth, this refers back to the preceding text, stating that because both the objective act and the mental factor have already been completed, it is not yet possible to discuss an offense; this refers specifically to a person who has committed an act of the highest degree.
There is only the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). Li states that the preceding text points directly to this, saying:

"If one does not doubt and recognizes [the nature of the act], there is invariably no fault, as there is no fruit toward which one can proceed. This text means that within the section on the commission of offenses, this clarifies the principle:

this is the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) that when one commits an offense, there is only the fundamental offense. That is to say, since one recognizes [the rule] and has no doubt, it is distinct from the fault of being unlearned or ignorant.
These are the nine phrases regarding what may be practiced; they pertain to those of superior capacity. Therefore, the *Shoushu* states: "These are the persons who practice learning;
they are invariably without fault. Here, the phrase "not doing" refers back to the preceding section on "abstaining and maintaining," referring simply to the nine phrases of what may be practiced.
Regarding the question: "If the three phrases concerning 'fundamentally not knowing the matter' are without offense, then they constitute six phrases, etc."—the intent of this question is as follows:
Among the nine phrases of "not being able to train," the three lowest-grade phrases concerning "not knowing the matter" involve a delusion that lacks the fundamental offense of commission;
furthermore, regarding the matter itself, there is no offense of "not training" or "ignorance. Thus, at present, it should logically follow that...

There are six phrases. For what reason, then, does one speak of nine phrases? This is intended to include the three phrases concerning the difficulty of removing [faults], the inferior grade, and the lack of awareness of the matter.
The response, "If one proceeds from the perspective of the root, there are only six phrases," etc., means that this answer refers to the basis of the actual commission of the root offense.

However, there are currently six phrases. Yet, within these three phrases of the lower grade, because one may fail to recognize or may have doubts regarding an offense, and because there is also the case of not having studied or being ignorant, nine phrases are formed.
This means that among these nine, there are cases where one has doubt regarding an offense and fails to recognize an offense.
There are cases where one incurs no offense due to ignorance because of not having studied; thus, nine permutations arise.

This means that although there is no offense regarding the matter itself, one may have doubts or lack recognition regarding the transgression. These constitute the eighth and ninth permutations, namely: "doubting a transgression" and "not recognizing a transgression."

These are the latter two phrases. Although the seventh phrase is entirely without fault, it is necessary to cite this single phrase—“not recognizing the matter but recognizing the offense”—in order to invoke the following two phrases.
As for the “three preceding phrases,” this refers to the three phrases in the third category mentioned above;
namely, the eighth and ninth [phrases], which involve fault regarding the offense. This is what is meant by the statement “if one proceeds according to” [the preceding].

Regarding "the root offenses" and so forth: this refers to the fundamental transgressions of sexual misconduct and killing. When considered in terms of the offense itself, there are those who are neither trained nor ignorant;

however, there are only six permutations. That is to say, there must first be a manifest transgression regarding a fundamental matter, and upon that transgression, there is the offense of being neither trained nor ignorant.

"If that is so, then these subsequent items, such as 'doubt' and so forth, are precisely the same as 'not having trained' and so forth. This objection means that it follows from the previous answer. The intent of the objection is as follows:
since one has given rise to confusion regarding the matter, one does not recognize it as being without fault;

rather, one incurs the offense of "not having trained" and "lack of knowledge" regarding what was above. Thus, these are consolidated into nine. However, this offense regarding what was above arises because of a lack of training and a consequent lack of knowledge.
This "lack of learning and ignorance" should properly be categorized as a *sthāpanīya-āpatti* (an offense of suspension).

How can it be brought here into the enumeration of offenses, making nine categories? This means that although one has performed the aforementioned act, because of delusion, there is no fundamental offense such as killing;
rather, one incurs only the offense of "lack of learning and ignorance" as previously defined. It should properly be called a *sthāpanīya-āpatti*. The following says:
Regarding "doubt and so forth," this includes the phrase "lack of recognition" by way of the term "and so forth. As for the answer, "it receives its name from the root":

this means it is named after the fundamental acts of killing or stealing. Although these are acts of a deluded mind, because one has performed the preceding fundamental act, even if one does not incur a *pārājika* offense, one still incurs the offense of "lack of training and ignorance" regarding that [root] act; thus, this offense likewise derives from the act you committed.
[The offense] arises from the superior [intention]. Therefore, this offense of ignorance due to lack of training is subsumed under the category of "committed through action.

Furthermore, the phrase "necessarily by performing the preceding act, etc. still addresses the meaning of the previous objection. Its intent is as follows: although one who is deluded might mistake [a person] for a tree stump, there is no offense at the time of killing;

yet because I myself have performed the act—just as the deluded person mistook [the victim] for a stump—how could I not have moved the blade? Therefore, it is said that "one performs the preceding act."

It is because of this lack of understanding that one further incurs the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna-ajñāna*). This offense of ignorance arises from having previously committed the aforementioned act;

it is generally subsumed under the category of offenses arising from commission. The *Shu* (Commentary) asks: "If one fundamentally does not recognize the matter, this is delusion and constitutes no offense."
This means that one has not committed a root offense; how, then, can it be said that an "act-offense" (kṛta-āpatti) has been committed? Answer:

If one fells a tree stump, although there is actually no [intentional] transgression regarding the object of the sin, because one was deluded as to whether it was a human or a non-human animal, the matter can still be clarified.

Therefore, it must be judged as an act-offense. Master Bin’s commentary on the meaning of the sub-commentary states: "If one fundamentally does not recognize the object, then the three lower categories of offenses do not exist. This refers to a person who is fundamentally deluded.

One may kill while perceiving the victim as a wooden stump, or one may perceive what is excessive as non-excessive; because of this fundamental delusion, the lower grade [of killing] lacks the three factors of recognizing the object.

To discuss this more precisely: if a person who is confused perceives a human being as a non-human spirit (amanuṣya) and so forth, there is still the auspiciousness of the subsequent thought, which likewise constitutes nine cases.
Even if one takes a being of the same realm (*nikāya-sabhāga*) as a different object, although this is a failure to recognize the object, it remains a case of killing.
This is because the meaning is the same as [the case of] "not recognizing the matter" (*avijñāta-vastu*), as there is no gap in the conceptualization of the person.

If it is argued that "if one does not recognize the matter but recognizes the offense, this is likewise without fault," this constitutes a further, weightier objection. This objection removes the seventh category.

Since this category already establishes that there is no fault when the matter itself is not recognized—as the rule was originally opened for such cases—and yet one recognizes the offense, the fault remains even upon that recognition.
There is no offense for not learning or for ignorance. Therefore, we know that the seventh phrase—“not recognizing the matter” and “recognizing the offense”—is entirely without fault.
There should properly be eight [phrases]; how can nine be asserted? One interpretation states:

If there were nine based on the offenses of not learning and ignorance, then since the matter itself is inherently unlearnable, it was fundamentally opened as being without offense. Now, regarding this one phrase, "not... [it continues].
"Recognizing the matter and recognizing the offense"—this phrase is entirely without fault. It is not appropriate for this phrase to exist;
there should only be eight [phrases]. How can it be said there are nine? Answer: As previously explained regarding the method of the phrases following one another:

since it was already established that there should only be six and that nine are not permitted, the response is: "However, within these three phrases, with respect to the latter two phrases, they do not constitute an offense against the former."

Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) also constitute offenses, it is necessary to include the seventh [category], "attainment of life" (*jīvitendriya-prāpti*), to provide the basis for the latter two phrases. Thus, nine [categories] can be spoken of.
Furthermore, the intent of this response is as follows: although there is no offense, it is only by means of this one phrase that the latter two phrases can be summoned;
therefore, they follow one another according to the nature of things (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that "if one gives rise to delusions concerning the objects of training (*śaikṣa*) upon those very objects of training," this section below constitutes a second, distinct approach intended to provide a comprehensive explanation for the differences among the six, eight, and nine propositions mentioned previously.

In its essential meaning, this is not something I have personally conceived; rather, it is the interpretation of an ancient master. Therefore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) addresses this as follows:
It is said that some commentators explain [this] as follows: "Why must it be so? (This is a refutation of the various preceding interpretations. Now, I shall provide a general analysis.

If one generates delusion regarding the phenomena of what is to be learned (*śikṣitavya*), there are invariably nine categories [of persons], etc. (As stated in the *Shu-chao*, this is no different). Therefore, we know that these are entirely the interpretations of the ancient masters.
What is now stated—that if one generates delusion regarding the phenomena of what is to be learned, there are invariably nine categories—refers to this:
To be indolent and fail to learn, yet to teach others—indeed, all matters are capable of being learned; it is only because they cannot be learned that one becomes deluded.
Though one may harbor doubts and remain ignorant, these constitute the root of bondage as well as ignorance resulting from a failure to learn. Thus, the text says:
"One cannot attain liberation through ignorance. This results in nine possible cases, for since one has committed a fundamental transgression, there is none who does not violate the root precepts.
Lin says: This also serves as an explanation for both delusion and awakening. It contains the general interpretation of the preceding two sets of nine phrases;
thus it says, "Regarding that which can be learned, one may learn delusion," and so forth. "Mo" means "none. This refers to these three phrases of yours:

they may be cases where it is possible to learn, yet if one falls into delusion, one commits a root offense and must therefore come [to confession]. If it is not possible to learn, then delusion constitutes an offense of only six [categories]. Or...
This is the "transformation of thought" (*pariṇāma-vikalpa*). There is also the "prior mind" (*pūrvacitta*), which likewise must be obtained.

If one can study the delusion regarding superior matters, yet cannot study the delusion that is merely sixfold—this is the fundamental phrase for delusion. As the subsequent text states: "The transformation of thought and so forth" refers to the delusion of the transformation of thought.
Now, this refers to one who diligently teaches others but suddenly becomes deluded regarding the matter, just as with thought, doubt, and so on; therefore, [it is so designated].
This excludes the three phrases of the lower grade, namely the three phrases concerning "not recognizing the matter. Therefore, it is said that there are only six phrases involving an offense.

If one shifts their perception (*saṃjñā-vivarta*) based on the preceding mind and so forth—since the previous section clarified that when a matter is learnable (*śikṣitavya*), giving rise to confusion regarding the unlearnable (*aśikṣitavya*) constitutes a fundamental delusion, and thus there were only six phrases—now, clarifying the shifting of perception, there are nine phrases. As in the original text.
