If one intends to kill a human being, but in the interim changes their intention—thinking instead of a non-human, an animal, or a wooden stump—they likewise incur nine cases.
This is because there is still the *pārājika* offense of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for killing; thus, it is said that these are all preparatory offenses.

Since an offense is committed by virtue of this [intentional] action, the characteristics of "not having studied" and "ignorance" arise accordingly; hence, there are nine cases. If, however, one is deluded regarding the object and acts upon the final thought, only six cases apply.
This refers to the delusion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). Looking toward the subsequent mind, one may obtain either nine or six cases.
That is to say, if one mistakenly perceives [an object] as a tree stump or as property belonging to no owner, there is no offense from beginning to end; thus, there are only six cases.

For example, if one takes property belonging to an owner while perceiving it as belonging to no owner, there is no transgression, because it is not an offense regarding the objective condition (*ālambana*). Since this is not an offense...

Fundamentally, there is no case where the absence of learning and the absence of knowledge follow one another. As for the nine cases where one perceives a human as a non-human and the final mind is auspicious (*kṣema*):

this refers to a deluded perception (*saṃjñā-vibhrama*). Because it is directed toward a sentient object (*sattva-viṣaya*), there are nine such cases. This differs from the previous instance of shifting perception (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*) regarding a non-sentient object.
In the present case, it refers to one who originally intended to kill a human, but shifted their perception to that of a non-human or an animal; this is considered in relation to the subsequent mind.

Auspicious. This means that it is improper to kill a non-human being, and because it constitutes a condition for the arising of an offense. In this case, there are again nine permutations (*navapada*).
Regarding the previous statement about perceiving what has an owner as ownerless, this does not constitute a condition for the arising of an offense; therefore, there are only six permutations.

If one includes the cases where the prohibition is violated, there are eight permutations, as in the aforementioned nine permutations of committing an offense. However, when discussing the fundamental matter itself, there are only...
There are six phrases. Because the three phrases concerning the lower grade of non-recognition of the object lack a fundamental basis, they consist only of the cessation of the offense;
when these are combined with the latter two of the three phrases for the lower grade, they are termed "cessation-offenses. These aforementioned six phrases thus constitute eight phrases.

Furthermore, if one discusses the method of the phrases according to their mutual correspondence, by taking the seventh phrase, nine phrases are formed; therefore, it is said that this is also permissible.

It is said that there are nine. Regarding the statement that "the commission of an act may also be said to be ninefold," this means that when one commits an offense through active engagement (*kṛta*), it necessarily involves the prior fundamental act (*maula-karman*). Therefore, it is called "commissioning an act. This refers to the seventh category;

although there is no offense of ignorance or lack of learning (*aśikṣita-ajñāna*), because this arises from the performance of the fundamental act, it is also said to constitute nine. Thus says [Master] Li.
Since the three lower phrases constitute non-learning delusions and there is no fundamental commission of an offense, the upper six phrases are the phrases concerning the commission of offenses.
I shall now exclude the seventh phrase on non-offense and take these six phrases concerning the commission of offenses.

Furthermore, when the two phrases of "cessation" (*śamatha*) and "transgression" (*āpatti*) are combined, they form eight phrases; hence it is said that there are eight [cases] including both cessation and transgression.
As for the seventh phrase, although there is no offense therein, because one has already completed the preceding action and it follows from that sequence, a ninth case may also be established.

Regarding why the first two lines are called "cessation of transgressions" (zhifàn), Jing said: "If one proceeds from the perspective of the gate of progressive cultivation (jìnxiū mén), these lines would not exist;
it is because we are now proceeding from the perspective of the cessation of transgressions that these lines are present."
Regarding the statement that "one does not know that the mirror is not equal," [the Master] established that "mirror" means "to reflect. The purport of the *Chao* (Commentary) states:
"In this section on the observance and violation of precepts, I have analyzed it for you with extreme detail; yet, you do not realize that your reflection is not something to be considered well."

From this point onward, the nine phrases concerning "performance and maintenance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) are explained in sequence. If one were to distinguish them based on the two categories of "concrete objects" (*vastu*) and "dharmas," there would indeed be two sets of nine phrases.
Seng-sheng says: As stated in the preceding section on "essential characteristics," performance and maintenance apply to both concrete objects and dharmas;

therefore, two sets of nine phrases are established here by way of concrete objects and dharmas respectively. That is to say, when taking concrete objects as the basis for the offenses... [text continues].

There are nine phrases. Applying the *dharma* to the offense (*āpatti*), there are likewise nine phrases. What is now called "matter" (*vastu*) refers to the dimensions of the dwelling, which must be known.

What is now called "dharma" refers to the formal procedure of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, which must also be known. What is called "offense" refers to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *duṣkṛta*, and so forth, which must be known.
However, because the sequence and gradation of these phrases and procedures do not differ, they are now explained together by correlating the *dharma* with the matter.

This consists merely of nine sets of nine phrases. All refer to the presence of both formal rules (*dharma*) and specific matters (*vastu*) within the commission of an offense. For example, regarding the matter of constructing a dwelling:

the dwelling itself is the "matter," while the formal authorization for that dwelling is the "rule. As in the previous case of the fourfold gravity of offenses based on the perception of the object, there are differences depending on whether one refers to the matter or the rule.
Now, in relation to this specific matter and these specific rules, there are nine phrases for each; here, they are simply combined and explained together.

Furthermore, regarding the nine propositions concerning the training rules (*dharma*), the actual matters (*vastu*) are omitted for brevity. Moreover, within this section, only the propositions of the rules are clarified while the propositions of the matters are not;

this is because the meaning of the propositions of the matters is identical to that which was already concluded in the previous section on "Restraint through Observance" (*śīla-saṃvara*) regarding the application of the matters.
Next, since the propositions were formulated solely in terms of the rules, fearing that others might not yet understand them, the many instances of formal offenses (*āpatti*) are now set forth.

[Briefly] stated, it can be understood from the preceding examples. As for the distinction made specifically regarding those that are "trainable" (*śaikṣa*), this is likely the statement of an ancient master;

however, Xuánzàng does not hold this view. Rather, [the categories] apply to both the trainable and the non-trainable (*aśaikṣa*), each having nine phrases. Therefore, he states here that for the non-trainable dharmas, confusion (*moha*) likewise consists of nine phrases, identical in wording.
Thus, we know that it applies to both the trainable and the non-trainable. [The author] privately notes: This was the previous section on the "Gate of Essential Characteristics."

In the middle [section], the "active observance" (*jiezhi*) is clarified; it is also called "affairs" (*shi*). It is only that which can be learned, and its loss is identical to the present. Both are ancient interpretations. Some say:
"This must be an interpretation from the past, and we do not agree with it now. If one were to say they are the same, why does the text below state that 'delusion cannot be learned'?
There are also nine phrases there, therefore it is not the same as this. Thus, as mentioned above, the 'stopping observance' (*zhizhi*) consists of affairs that can be learned."

As for the "intermediate" [category], it refers to present observance (*dhāraṇa*). It is identical to the first nine phrases among the matters to be learned within the aforementioned observance by abstention (*saṃvara-dhāraṇa*).

This merely involves performing actions in accordance with the teachings; each is considered, as in the aforementioned observance by abstention, to be the recognition of the matter and the recognition of the transgression, such that one does not commit evil.

This is called "abstaining and maintaining" (*śīla*). This single phrase constitutes the highest grade of maintaining the precepts. Now, I am likewise so; that is to say, by recognizing the Dharma and recognizing transgressions.

To engage in an action is called "performance. This single verse constitutes the highest grade. Therefore, it is said that this is performed merely in accordance with the teaching, which differs from the former.
The former was solely the abstention from evil, termed "maintaining"; this, however, is the performance of good, termed "maintaining. Thus it is said.
This is a distinction.

The commentary states: "Regarding the requirement to request the *śuklā* (white) [announcement] twice": this means that if one does not understand the Dharma, they might say that constructing a dwelling does not require formal authorization, or they might think it refers to a single *śuklā* announcement.

Furthermore, regarding those who do not recognize the offense, they might say that even if one does not request permission, one does not commit the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension). Therefore...
Knowing these nine points, one comes from the teachings of the foolish who are still in training; therefore, failing to recognize them is not called a deluded mind, yet it constitutes a root offense.

Regarding the four phrases of the lower grade, "doubting the Dharma" and "doubting the offense": doubting the Dharma means doubting whether the construction of a dwelling requires a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, or a *jñapti-mātra-karman*.
Doubting the offense means doubting whether, if one does not request the formal authorization (*dharmaprārthanā*), it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This applies to the *laṇḍī* and the *tiki*. Other cases may be understood by analogy. Regarding the phrase "not knowing the Dharma," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"If it is a simple *jñapti* (motion), a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation) is not required. Even if one knows the *jñapti-dvitīya*, if one does not understand its application and restrictions, this too constitutes 'not knowing.'"

Regarding the statement, "The nine phrases concerning delusion regarding the *aśikṣamāṇadharma* (untrainable rules) are also as in the preceding section," this refers to the current text’s clarification of the nine phrases for the *karmavācanā* (formal act) of the *aśikṣamāṇadharma*.
These are no different from the nine phrases for the *pratiṣedha-saṃvara* (restraint through prohibition) in the preceding section; they are likewise divided into three groups of three.
The current text does not repeat the formulation, but merely changes "matter" (*vastu*) to "rule" (*dharma*). This text precisely refutes the former interpretation. Formerly...

It is said: "Regarding the performance of ritual acts, one may only learn what is permissible; that which is impermissible is not to be learned. Now it is clarified that this is not so, for there are instances of confusion and forgetfulness in all cases.

Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Although the Dharma may be learned, delusion and inversion may suddenly arise; the Buddha has opened the way for non-offenses in such cases, which differs from the interpretations of former [masters]."

Therefore, within the Vinaya, if one does not intend to perform an act that requires formal authorization, or if one has such an intention but harbors doubt, neither constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Furthermore, as stated in the previous response:

"One must proceed according to what was cited; this will be further analyzed under the section on 'formal authorization' (*karmavācanā*). This precisely refers to the present passage. The explanation of the meaning of "formal authorization" is hereby concluded.

Next, regarding the discussion of *saṃvara-āpatti* (cessation-offenses), whether there be nine or eight [categories], my own view is as follows: If one considers how *saṃvara-āpatti* arises based on the aforementioned preparatory acts, then there are nine cases.
For example, constructing a dwelling without requesting the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), or possessing an extra robe without declaring it pure (*viśuddhi-uddeśana*)—these are *saṃvara-āpatti*.

This is because, at times, one may fully understand the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), yet simply fail to request the formal authorization; this is termed *saṃvara-āpatti*. It is exclusively a *śeṣa* (remainder) offense.
Regarding offenses: there is no offense of ignorance for one who has not studied. This arises from having committed the preceding acts;

it is based on the fundamental existence of an offense that there is the phrase "one who possesses consciousness and recognizes the transgression," which should constitute nine categories. This is discussed from the perspective of a person who has not studied or inquired.
Regarding the "cessation through non-transgression" (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*), there is no such phrase because it does not involve the construction of something in response to a specific object;

rather, it is simply remaining stationary, as there is no distinct fundamental matter to respond to. Therefore, the phrase "knowing the dharma and knowing the transgression" is not counted among the categories of cessation through non-transgression.

Consequently, since this [category] is without offense, it cannot be placed within the discussion of cessation through non-transgression regarding those who have not yet entered the householdless life. Thus, only...
There are eight phrases. These entries all constitute the offenses of non-learning and ignorance (*aśikṣita-ajñāna*). Within this section on cessation (*sthiti*), no further phrases are listed;

rather, they are simply the reversal of the preceding [section] to form the nine [phrases] of observance (*dhāraṇī*). First, the nine phrases are clarified. As for the eight phrases, they will be explained below in their own right.
Although no phrases are listed here, they all pertain to the path of conduct (*mārga-lābha*); it is simply that the quantity of the offenses of non-learning and ignorance varies.

The four phrases of the superior grade comprise sixteen offenses; those of the middling grade comprise eight offenses; and the single phrase of the inferior grade involves only the commission of the root offense.
The nine phrases elucidated here are identical to the nine phrases for training in the "abstention and maintenance" (*śīla*) mentioned previously.

The sixteen offenses of the highest grade (*uttama*) mentioned here refer to the sixteen offenses consisting of four sets of four phrases within the previously discussed "restraint through cessation" (*pratiṣedha-śīla*).
Since these are now explained in terms of their transgression (*āpatti*), many offenses are grouped together to constitute the highest grade.

Regarding the statement "sixteen offenses," there are four instances of doubt, four instances of lack of recognition, four *thullaccaya* (grave) offenses, and four *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offenses. Within the category of doubt, there are eight *dukkaṭas*; thus, the twelve *dukkaṭas* and the four *thullaccayas* together constitute ten offenses.

Sixth: Regarding the eight offenses of the middle grade, there are two cases of not recognizing [the offense] and two cases of doubt; these comprise two *pāyattikas* and six *dukkaṭas*, totaling eight.

Regarding the single offense of the lowest grade, which consists solely of a violation of the root rule: this means that once one recognizes the Dharma and recognizes the transgression, there is no offense of "lack of training" or "ignorance.
For example, if one constructs a dwelling without requesting formal authorization, one directly commits the single root offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Therefore, it is said:
This constitutes the root formulation.
The reason why the preceding sentence is inverted and differs [from the current one] is that this clarifies what is about to be explained; first, it raises its own inquiry:

"Why was it previously stated within the section on 'Retaining' (*dhāraṇa*) that knowing the rule and knowing the offense constitute the upper grade, while being accompanied by such knowledge or by doubt constitutes the middle grade?"
In this chapter, regarding the classification of offenses as lower-grade when one is ignorant or doubtful, it follows that what is actually non-offensive would be classified as upper-grade.

Now, since we are currently addressing only the commission of middle-grade offenses, for what reason is a great offense treated as upper-grade while a non-offense is treated as lower-grade? The answer is:

The previous explanation was based on the principle of maintaining the precepts (*dhāraṇa*), where the application of knowledge—specifically knowing the Dharma and knowing the offense—is considered upper-grade even when there is no offense. This current explanation, however, is interpreted from the perspective of committing an offense; therefore, the meaning is presented in reverse.
Regarding this: to recognize an offense as being without fault is classified as the lower grade. Question:

Since it has already been stated that an offense with many interpretations is of the upper grade, why is this not applied to the nine phrases concerning offenses previously established? Answer: These cases all concern the mutual relationship between observance and violation;

they do not need to be exhaustive. It is necessary to establish the upper grade based on the abundance of offenses. Since the principles established at one time differ, how can there be any room for confusion regarding violations?
Regarding the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, each is augmented by the faults of "not training" and "ignorance. As for the phrase "up to 'not many'":
this indicates the underlying intent, clarifying that the meaning of establishing these offenses as being of the "superior grade" (*uttama*) is simply that they constitute a multitude of faults.

This means that within the four sentences of the superior grade, since there are already the respective faults of not training and ignorance, and furthermore, within each of those four sentences, there are separately the faults of not requesting formal authorization and building a hut.
Is this not a case of many offenses? Therefore it is asked: "What is meant by 'not many'?

Regarding the four phrases of the superior grade, since there are already two phrases where one is ignorant of the facts, both should logically constitute two fundamental *śeṣa* (residual) offenses, which would be *sthūlātyaya*.

Now, regarding the statement that the four *mūla-pārājika* offenses constitute a *thullaccaya*, what is its meaning? The explanation is as follows: These are cases where one is capable of training (*sikkhā-sakka*) but commits an offense through negligence.

Because of delusion regarding the teachings, both doubt and ignorance constitute the commission of a *mūla-pārājika* offense. If these were instead matters beyond the capacity for training (*asikkhā-sakka*), then such delusion would be the fault of the Tathāgata.
The Great Commentary (*Taishō Daizōkyō*, Vol. 40, No. 1805) also refutes these four *thullaccayas* in accordance with the intent of the preceding inquiry. However...
This summarizes the correct meaning of the refutation, as intended by the response.

Regarding the statement that "the eight phrases contrast with the teaching and practice, while the single phrase 'not learning through illumination' clarifies the absence of the dharma of consciousness and so forth, which is of inferior grade": [this means that] the eight phrases correspond to the teaching and practice, whereas the single phrase "not learning through illumination" elucidates the lower grade of the absence of the dharma of consciousness and so forth.
This explains the preceding passage. Whether it be nine, eight, or nine, as clarified previously, this is the formal explanation of the "eight.

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with teaching and practice": "teaching" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka; by not studying the meaning of this Vinaya, one is said to "cease from transgression. "Practice" refers to the practice of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*);
because one must give rise to a mind of counteraction toward what is non-virtuous, this mind is called "practice. Not giving rise to this mind is called...

This refers to the offense of cessation (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*). As for the statement that there are eight cases (*aṣṭau padāni*), it is established as follows: such a person is one who does not study and does not teach others.

Since they have neither studied nor inquired, how could they possibly recognize the Dharma or recognize an offense? Therefore, it is known that this refers to the offense of cessation. In relation to those who do not study the Dharma, there are only these eight cases.
Because they have not studied the sacred teachings since birth, how could they be able to recognize the Dharma or recognize an offense? Consequently, this [other] case does not exist.

This is also the interpretation of the ancients. The *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary) states: "Regarding the statement that there are eight propositions, this refers to the single proposition of 'unintentional transgression' (*wushi fan*).

This is translated as 'advancing toward cultivation and study. Once 'cessation of transgression' (*zhifan*) has been clarified—meaning that by reversing cultivation and study, one is no longer practicing;

because one does not practice, there is the single proposition of 'unintentional transgression'—there are thus eight propositions. Since it speaks of "cessation of transgression," how could there be intentional knowledge of the dharma or intentional knowledge of the transgression for one who does not practice? Therefore...

However, the eight [categories] above (the preceding section was composed by an ancient individual; this is merely an explanation) state at the beginning: "Now, regarding the explanation of translating to clarify *śamatha* (cessation):

there are only eight [categories], not nine" (this means that translating the explanation is itself a lack of understanding. Because of this lack of understanding, there is no separate category for "knowing the dharma" and "knowing the offense"; there are only eight).

If one translates "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) to clarify *śamatha*, then there are nine categories (translating "cultivation" as "non-cultivation" refers to the performance of rituals within practice. This refers to the characteristics of the teachings of this consciousness; however, if one does not rely on them, there are nine categories—namely, including the category of "knowing the dharma" and "knowing the offense").

For example, if one understands the rules but fails to perform them—such as not receiving the three robes (*tricīvara*) or not performing the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification)—how could it be that there is no offense of "cognizing the dharma" (*dharmajñāna*)?

In relation to the fundamental non-performance of the rite, this is termed a "cessation-offense" (*virati-āpatti*); in terms of its classification, it is called "ignorance" (*moha*) and is categorized as a minor offense (*mṛdu*).

Each of the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) incurs one offense. In the case of the four permutations of the major offenses (*adhimātra*), each incurs two offenses; for when explaining the meaning through the gateway of offenses, those with many offenses are classified as major.
The first phrase of the preceding "Holding Without Fault" (翻前持中無罪) may be understood as the primary meaning of the commentary by referring back to what has been stated above.
If one analyzes the cessation of offenses (*śikṣāpada*) from the perspective of practice and understanding, there are nine phrases;

however, if analyzed from the perspective of non-learning and understanding, there are only eight phrases, because for those who do not study, it is logically impossible to possess knowledge of the Dharma or knowledge of offenses. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Some explain it as follows..."

Within the category of offenses arising from cessation (*niḥsaraṇa*), there are only eight permutations regarding non-learning with respect to the teaching, excluding the permutation where both the legal act and the object are recognized.
Regarding non-learning with respect to the object, nine permutations are possible. This refers to cases such as constructing a dwelling, or [receiving] robes and bowls;

even if one understands the characteristics and is fully aware of them, what prevents one from failing to request formal authorization, or failing to accept and purify [the items], thereby incurring offenses such as *sthūlātyaya*? (The preceding mention of "with respect to the object" refers to the construction of a dwelling.)

[This concerns] matters regarding the robe and alms bowl). If explained in relation to specific matters, there are likewise two sets of nine phrases. This arising [of the categories] is based on the matter itself;
it also contains the sense of the nine phrases concerning what is learnable and what is unlearnable. Sheng says: "Since it was previously stated that the stages and gradations do not differ..."
These form a total of nineteen phrases. Why are they further distinguished here?

Because the previous section dealt only with the Dharma (dharma), whereas within the section on the "Gate of Upholding through Practice" (kriyā-dhāraṇī-mukha), nine phrases regarding that which is "untrainable" (*aśikṣya*) were presented without explicit clarification. Therefore, these are restated here to show that within the matters of practice (*kriyā-karma*), there are likewise phrases concerning the untrainable.
If they were not included, one might fear that people would doubt whether there are no conditions for the untrainable within practical affairs. Thus, [the ancient masters]...
"O teachers who have come here: one must not fail to follow [the precepts] when serving one's superior; therefore, we now precisely distinguish this from the ancients. Someone says:

"Regarding the two practices of 'maintaining through action' (*zuo-chi*) and 'ceasing transgressions' (*zhi-fan*), the nine phrases concerning the methods already explained for what may be learned are concluded."
Now, regarding the matters at hand, there are likewise two sets of nine points, which will not be set forth again; they may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Within the previously established *zhichi* (abstention through maintenance), there are also two sets of nine points, comprising both those concerning the rules (*yuefa*) and those concerning the matters (*yuoshi*). Within *zuochi* (active maintenance) there are also two sets of nine points.

For *zuofan* (active transgression) and *zhifan* (abstention through transgression), there are likewise two sets of nine points each, consisting of both those concerning the rules and those concerning the matters.
There are sixteen sets of nine phrases and one set of eight phrases; these refer to those who are capable of learning yet are deluded, as well as those who are incapable of learning yet are deluded.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the two sets of nine phrases. Regarding the phrase "those who are capable of learning yet are deluded," this refers to the aforementioned nine phrases concerning those capable of learning.
These individuals are deluded regarding the teachings because they have failed to study them; that is, they are deluded regarding matters that ought to be learned.

This refers to delusion that can be learned; thus it is said so. As for "delusion that cannot be learned," this refers to the following section, where there should be nine phrases concerning "delusion that cannot be learned.
They are simply omitted here for brevity. Because the delusive confusion of mind and object cannot be understood through mere study, the Sages did not establish offenses for them;
these are termed "delusions that cannot be learned. When an offense is seen [in such cases], it is because...
"Not initiating" refers to that which is learnable (*śikṣaṇīya*). Some say: "Not learning" clarifies the rules regarding what is learnable and what is not learnable, as explained previously.

Now, herein it is clarified that one should perform the preceding action to avoid an offense of omission (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*), such as failing to perform the *śuddhi-viśuddhi* (purification) by the end of the day.
If one is unwilling to change one's mind and perform the purification, this is termed the ninefold category of the learnable; it is a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) in every respect.
Root. If one forgets, it constitutes delusion and is not a transgression. These training clauses (śikṣāpada) should comprise nine items;
because they involve a transgression of the root, they do not compare with the previous "non-training" [clause], as clarity excludes that first item.
To master this is to achieve a universal penetration of the Dharma-realm. It is established that by taking any single precept as a point of reference, one makes this kind of analysis;

once the underlying intent is fully understood, one can apply it to all precepts and attain a comprehensive understanding. The four preceding sections have collectively explained the first topic, "Ignorance of What Has Not Been Studied.
This concludes the section on the meaning of the "Analysis According to Stages."
Second, regarding "approaching the fruit through skillful means": this clarifies that there is a skillful means for the resolution of committed transgressions.
Furthermore, because there is both the cause and the skillful means, one proceeds toward its fruit; that is to say, the fundamental offense is termed the "fruit."

Regarding the necessity of there being three periods: Lì (Lìzǔ) states that these are the beginning, middle, and end. Dēn (Dēnhuì) says they are the preparatory stage (*upāya*), the fundamental stage, and the subsequent mind.

Regarding the statement that "the Great Sage established them according to the occasion": this means that both fundamental and preparatory offenses were established by the Great Sage in accordance with individual capacities.
Regarding the phrase "briefly as listed above": Lì states that this refers to how the characteristics of the preparatory stages are explained within the *Piānjù* (Varga/Chapter-Cluster).
However, regarding cases where the mind gives rise to body and speech but there is only the root offense (*maulāpatti*) without the preparatory offense (*prayoga*):
this means that there is only the root *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and no further preparatory offense. Jing says: "This refers to the moment when one intends to initiate action through body and speech;
although the mind has arisen, the body and speech have not yet moved. It is so called because the mind alone forms the intention to act."
If there are distant and proximate preparatory acts (*upāya*) involving both body and speech, they are as follows: first, climbing a tree with the resolve to ascend is the distant preparatory act;

when one has reached the base of the tree and grasps it with the hand in order to climb, this is the proximate preparatory act. If one successfully climbs, this constitutes the fundamental offense (*maula-āpatti*).
In the Vinaya, it is only clarified that if the act is completed, it is a *pārājika*, and if not completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Ji says: "And..."
The Vinaya Master Bu-wan maintains this text, asserting that there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) [that constitutes a formal offense]; it is merely termed "seven non-completions.

For example, if one intends to kill a person, as long as the preparatory effort has not yet resulted in a formal name for the offense—because the intention has not yet ceased—how could the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) be established?

It can only increase one's unwholesome state. Only when one reaches the object of the act, but the conditions fail and the intention ceases so that the fundamental offense (*maula-āpatti*) is not committed, is the *steya* (theft) offense then established.

"Because it is 'unaccomplished,' it is called *laṇ* (a minor offense). As explained at length in the beginning of this fascicle, this meaning has already been fully established within the section on the names of the *Piñjū* (the clusters of offenses) in the *Bào* (Retribution).

If one asks, 'In that case, how does this differ from a mere thought (*citta*)?', the intent of the objection is as follows: [it differs] from the mind you have produced, which constitutes a formal act of will."
If one commits [an offense] through mere thought, how does this differ from the offenses of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva committed through a single thought? Answer:

Regarding the Vinaya regulations on the movement of body, speech, and the intention of the mind—the answer implies that according to the Vinaya, an offense is committed only when there is movement of body, speech, and mental intention.

This "intention of the mind" is not the same as the "single thought" of the Mahāyāna. In the Mahāyāna, even if one does not intend to move body or speech, if such a thought arises, it constitutes an offense. It is simply the arising [of that thought].
The mind incurs an offense at the very first thought. This is because those of the Two Vehicles must intend to move body or speech before the thought arises;
if one merely moves the mind without intending to move body or speech, there is no offense. Regarding the term "karmic action of a fixed commitment" (*niyama-karman*), the Commentary states:

"Because cause and effect correspond, there is a mutual agreement or doubt; hence it is called 'karmic action of a fixed commitment'. Some say it refers to the intentional resolve of the mind to commit acts such as killing or stealing.

It is said: "The period of the undertaking. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "This refers to the arousal of the mind. Although one has not yet manifested the signs through body or speech, it is already termed a transgression.

It further states: "In establishing the Śrāvaka precepts, this is spoken with respect to those things that can be regulated. A solitary mental thought that suddenly arises and encounters an improper object is not termed a transgression.
However, if a heavy object turns toward the mind and one is capable of reflection and awareness, yet fails to exercise restraint, then it constitutes a transgression. Thus it is.

This constitutes an offense against the regulations. Therefore, regarding the scriptural texts (*vinaya*), one may take either the mental intention or the physical and verbal action as the basis, according to one's judgment. Jingyun states: "When the mind gives rise to the expectation [of acting], it joins with the actions of body and speech;
therefore, it is called 'expected action' (*ākṣepa-karman*). As for ordinary people who constantly dwell upon objects of desire, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*Shanjian lun*) says:

The minds of ordinary people are constantly conditioned by desire and have never abandoned it. If a sage were to restrain them through body and speech alone, no one would be able to escape the accumulation of offenses.
Therefore, when a sage establishes precepts, he requires that they transform both body and mind.

Thus, in the Vinaya, it is said that there is no offense when one gives rise to the thought but does not move body or speech; this is called being without offense. However, if one gives rise to the intent to steal, one must physically act upon it.
Reproach. [The mind] returns to its original wholesome state.
Regarding the three conditions that lead toward the stage of fruition: first is called "the three skillful means," second is "auspiciousness," and third is "conditions approaching the fruit.
If those seven pervasive conditions intervene and obstruct them, one cannot reach the fruit; therefore, the former three are designated as [the preliminary stages].
This refers to the offense of preparatory action (*upāya*). The commentary states: "The meaning of the seven conditions will be explained below.
This refers to the seven gates within the third section, "Completion of the Offense through Conditions," which are termed the "common conditions" (*sāmānya-pratyaya*).

"All enter into the fundamental fruit" means that if there are no intervening obstacles from these seven conditions, the fundamental fruit of the offense is established; therefore, it is called the "fundamental fruit."
Regarding the statement, "Unlike other schools, once the fruit has been produced from the cause, there is no longer the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and so forth," the Upādhyāya says:

"In the *Pañcavargika*, even after one has committed a root offense (*mūlāpatti*), the preparatory offense (*prayogāpatti*) still remains. Thus concludes the explanation of the second section, the gate of the preparatory stage leading toward the fruit.
Third, regarding the fulfillment of the conditions for an offense: this section below establishes the conditions for violating the precepts, which apply universally to all rules.

As for the statement that "the offenses, based on causes and conditions, reside within the six categories of transgressions," this means that the commission of any violation necessarily relies upon both a cause and a condition.

This is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). However, regarding the statement that "offenses reside within the six categories of transgressions," this refers to the fact that both the offenses of these expedient means and those of the resulting fruits reside within the six categories;

therefore, their methods of repentance differ. As for the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teachings), they discuss only the formation of karmic fruits and do not clarify matters such as expedient means, nor do they address the absence of offense or the absence of offenses for violating the teachings.
This differs from the *Hua-jiao*, which discusses only the formation of karma and its binding results.

Regarding "transgressions," this clarifies the transformative teaching (*śāsana*) by directly discussing the formation of karma and concluding with the offenses of the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*);

there are no further offenses of contravening the teaching through expedient means (*upāya*). The meaning of the preceding passage clarifies these expedient means, which reside within the six groups and five categories [of precepts];
therefore, they must be clearly identified so that one may perform repentance according to the specific articles and categories, rather than treating them all indiscriminately as one.
This is the transformative teaching (*nirmāṇa-śāsana*).

Now, regarding the two types of conditions—the general and the specific—of the various precepts: these seven [precepts] constitute the general conditions, while those within the "following the characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*) section are the specific ones.

These two types of conditions, general and specific, each have their own deficiencies; one must rely on both texts to fully understand the characteristics [of the offenses], as is the case with the precept against killing.
Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): it merely states "one person" and "the perception of two persons," etc., but does not say "a bhikṣu. Thus, one does not know who is the actual killer.
Furthermore, since it does not state that the Buddha established the detailed teachings (*vyūha-śāsana*) later on, one does not know when an offense occurs.

Other meanings are left to the discretion of the speaker at the time of explanation. Some people establish five conditions universally to explain all the precepts, asserting that they are combined with the *Vinayavibhaṅga*.

I wish for this to be the Vinaya Master’s [view]. What are these five? First, there is the bhikṣu who is the actual offender. Second, there is that which is confronted, namely the object of the offense.

Third, there is the mind. Fourth, there is the correspondence between the mind and the object. Fifth, the completion of the act. With the sole exception of sexual misconduct and intoxicants, there is no lack of correspondence [in these cases].
Now, the present *Chao* (Excerpts) states that it is not the case that this principle does not apply; however, this is far too broad and inclusive, and therefore I do not retain it here.

There are five conditions. Based on the *Liaoyi shu* (Commentary on the Meaning), three conditions are established to explain the various precepts: first, that a person has already received the full bhikṣu precepts;
second, that the Tathāgata has already promulgated the extensive teachings; and third, that the person has not reached a state of delusion. Bin says:
Based on these three conditions, all bhikṣus at present should, in principle, be considered offenders;

that is to say, the monks and nuns of today have already received the full ordination (*mahā-upasampadā*) subsequent to the promulgation of the extensive teachings, and they are not subject to the state of being "unconscious" (*amūḍha-dharma*). Now, one further condition should be added:

the fourth is the offense committed according to the specific act. Thus, it should be said that there are four general conditions: first, being a *mahā-bhikṣu*; second, [the rule] being established by the Tathāgata; [and so forth].

Following the *Guangjiao* (Extensive Teaching), there are three points: first, if a person does not fall into the state of delusion; second, the offense is established according to what was actually done; third, by establishing this, the full scope of the meaning is exhausted.

Alternatively, regarding those who belong to the five assemblies (*pañca-varga*) but have initiated an act toward an object that has not yet been completed, it is established that although they belong to the five assemblies, they intended to perform the aforementioned action.
Without having attained the ultimate goal, he passes away; there is only the offense of the preparatory act (*prayoga*). Or, as for one who is killed by another:

for example, if one originally intends to kill a person, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense at every step; yet, upon reaching the object of the intent, one is instead harmed by another; in this case, there is only the offense of the preparatory act.

Regarding the phrase "or abandoning the fundamental precepts, holding wrong views, or the arising of both sexual organs, etc.": it is established that because one holds wrong views, one immediately loses the wholesome precepts;

therefore, even if one commits an offense, there is no precept to violate. As for "both sexual organs" (*ubhayavyañjana*): if they arise before one has received the precepts, one cannot obtain them even upon receiving the precepts.
If the precept-body suddenly ceases upon receiving [the precepts] later, it is not because the volitional thought (*cetanā*) of the fivefold assembly has been fully expressed.

This refers to those mentioned above with differing physical forms and so forth, who are not called members of the fivefold assembly; although they commit the aforementioned transgressions, their original intention is resolved, precisely because they lack the precepts.
This is not termed a violation of the regulations.
There may be cases where there is confusion regarding the object or an error in the act. It is established that "confusion" pertains to the state of mind.

As for "error," it is like intending to kill Zhang but mistakenly killing Wang; although the objects are distinct, from the perspective of the person [killed], both are equally grave. Furthermore, it is said that as for "error":
To take two objects as a dual condition is like the simultaneous presence of Zhang and Wang, where an arrow is released and hits Wang instead of Zhang.
"Error" (*wu*) is like killing a human being when a non-human has come to substitute for them; thinking it is a human, one kills them—this is called error.

The *Śāstra* states: "Error" refers to a discrepancy based on the object; "error" refers to a delusion based on the mind. When two objects intersect, it is termed "error. To perceive this while intending that, is called... [error].
This is an error. As for those who record other conditions as neutral (*avyākṛta*), such as supporting wood or stones, these are recorded as neutral.

Regarding the attainment of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) and a grave offense (*guru-āpatti*): one attains an immediate transgression because it violates the debt of gratitude and nourishment;

one commits a grave offense because one kills while perceiving the victim as a human being. Concerning the neutral offenses committed against an Arhat, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Does an Arhat commit an offense with a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral (avyākṛta) mind? The Buddha said:
"Whatever offenses an Arhat commits are all neutral. What is meant by a 'neutral mind'? The Buddha said:

"If an Arhat does not recall having extra robes, eating at improper times, eating in a group apart from the community, entering a village without announcing his presence, or failing to wear the saṃghāṭī."
Entering a village; or while sleeping, being placed by another upon a high and wide bed; or while sleeping, being placed by another upon a grove of women;

or while not yet asleep, entering a dwelling for a senior monastic without having received permission; or while sleeping, a person who has not yet received full ordination (upasampadā) entering the room.
Upon waking and seeing this, one immediately confesses the transgression. These are called the offenses of an Arhat, and they are all of an indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature of mind.
Regarding the statement that Arhats do not dream while sleeping, but only rest briefly for the sake of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 90, states:
"Sleep is of two kinds: first, sleep with dreaming; second, sleep without dreaming.

An Arhat does not sleep for the sake of seeking security or attachment to pleasure; rather, because they possess a body composed of the four great elements, they must naturally partake of food and rest."
Sleeping and waking: therefore, a brief period of rest is called a dream.
Regarding the examples such as the grass binding the wooden board at sea and so forth, they are as explained in the *Yuan* (Commentary) [and so on].
The intent of this passage cited in the *Chao* (Excerpts) is that once the power of the Path has been established, one is also able to maintain even those prohibitive precepts (*śīla*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "The five [cases] where there is no offense regarding the difficulty of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

it clarifies that once one has obtained this life-force and encountered the conditions of the difficulty of the holy life, one is permitted to perform the aforementioned acts. Because these conditions of life-force and the holy life exist, no offense is incurred. Therefore, this is cited here;

that is to say, it establishes the principle of having complete conditions versus incomplete conditions (this may be understood through reflection). As for the term "hidden treasure" (*nidhi*), the established view is that it is so called because it is concealed.

Regarding the term "treasury" (*zàng*): that which has an owner belongs to the owner; that which has no owner belongs to the king. This is because if a bhikṣu were present nearby, he might harbor a greedy mind and thus commit theft or damage.
When the Buddha said, "one should depart immediately for this reason," and so forth, this refers to the Buddha’s regulation concerning the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

If one does not comply with it, one incurs an offense; this is called a prohibitive precept (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*). Now, because there are superior circumstances of difficulty, the Buddha has permitted going directly.
This passage is cited here to clarify that although it is a prohibitive precept, it may be waived when there is benefit.
Regarding the fact that the three lower sections consist of rules of decorum (*vinaya*) and do not open up natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): this is established as clear.

For instance, [acts such as] striking, wrestling, drinking, or taking the lives of two types of insects and so forth must certainly not be opened up, because these are grave natural precepts. Alternatively, there are those that prohibit evil;

for example, grasping jewels, injuring the earth, or destroying living beings—these are prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Even in cases such as a wild fire burning, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to kill [the creatures therein].

Cutting grass, digging the earth, and extinguishing fire—these are permitted as they are beneficial; thus, exceptions are made for acts such as saving [life]. Alternatively, these may be minor matters;

for example, regarding the precepts on not listening attentively, entering a village at an improper time, or bathing more than once every half-month, exceptions are granted when there is a beneficial reason. Or, it may be that a light matter serves to exclude a heavy one;

as the established rule states, for instance, if a forest-dweller seizes another's [belongings] and does not meet with the owner until dawn, the exception of "mental relinquishment" (*dūrībhāva-citta*) is granted.

[The Buddha] relinquished [the prohibition], thereby preventing the commission of a *pārājika* offense while limiting the transgression to a *duṣkṛta*. Thus, it is said that "the light is used to block the heavy.

If one does not grant such an exception, the opposite of the above should be understood; that is to say, it is not a case of blocking unwholesome discipline (*dauḥśīlya*), and matters such as those involving grave consequences would all remain unpermitted.
Regarding the "single condition" (*eka-pratyaya*): according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, there are generally three kinds of offenses. First is the condition for the initial commission of an offense.
For example, when Sūdanaputra engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus on account of this;

this is called the "condition. Second is the "prohibition" (*prajñapti*). The treatise states: "Second, regarding the prohibition due to an offense: if a bhikṣu practices unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*), it is a *pārājika* offense."
"A *pārājika* offense means one may not dwell together; this is the formal rule (*sikkhāpada*). Regarding the 'triple restriction,' the *Śāstra* states:

it refers specifically to engaging in sexual desire within a forest with animals, even down to a dead horse and the like. Regarding 'one lenient and one strict,' the *Śāstra* states: this is in reference to the aforementioned grave offenses."
There are two kinds of causes and conditions: the first is lenient, and the second is urgent. Regarding the lenient:

if a bhikṣu wishes to renounce the precepts, return home, and engage in sexual conduct, the Buddha immediately permits it. If, at a later time, he desires to remain in the Path, he is permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination;
this is the lenient case. Furthermore, as in the case of the bhikṣu Nandika, who committed sexual misconduct but had no intention of concealment, the Buddha permitted [his rehabilitation].

"To grant *śikṣādattaka* (probation for training) is also lax. As for what is called "urgent," it refers even to cases where animals and humans commit the same offense; this is what is meant by urgent.

Regarding the statement that "the three points of adjudication pertain to the Vinaya masters (*vinayadhara*) and others," the treatise says: first, laxity; second, formal regulation (*prajñapti*); and third, repeated regulation (*punar-prajñapti*).
These are termed the three points of adjudication concerning the matters of offenses committed. Furthermore, there are three points of adjudication concerning non-offenses.

First, the occasion (*nidāna*); second, the enactment (*prajñapti*); third, the re-enactment (*anuprajñapti*). Regarding "the occasion": when the Buddha had not yet laid down the precept, the initial transgression constitutes the occasion. Regarding "the enactment":
the laying down of the rule for the sake of the initial transgressor so that they do not commit the offense is called the enactment. Regarding "the re-enactment": if a bhikṣu...
If one is coerced by force and engages in sexual misconduct and the like, yet does not experience pleasure, this constitutes no offense. This is called the "heavy regulation.

These three cases definitively determine that there is no offense (and all other precepts are likewise). Jing says: The three stages of definitive judgment cited above from the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* are intended to clarify how a Vinaya master adjudicates offenses.
Regarding all precepts, for one who acts as a judge for others, one should examine the prior commission of the offense.

Regarding those who observe the precepts: if they have committed offenses repeatedly, they should be judged according to the more serious penalty. If their nature is generally cautious and they have committed an offense only by accident, they should be subject to a light ruling.
This means that while protection [of the precepts] should be applied with urgency, the adjudication of the offense should be lenient. This is the principle.
"Seventh, advancing toward the ultimate fruit": this refers to committing the fundamental root offense, which is termed the "ultimate fruit. "If one abides, it constitutes the preparatory stage":
this means that one has not yet committed the fundamental offense but remains [in the state of preparation]. "The characteristics consist of four parts":

my private opinion is that within this process of advancement, they are divided into four conditions. What are these four? First, separation by dharma; second, cessation through indolence; third, preference...

The mind ceases. It ceases because of four kinds of doubt regarding the mind. Due to these four conditions, what was previously wholesome becomes [unwholesome] again. There are four distinct sections concerning abiding in the preparatory stage (*upāya*).
This is now the first. First, "due to being separated by a formal act (*dharma*), it constitutes the preparatory stage for all admonitions and precepts," as in the thirteen cases below;
that is, when the Saṃgha issues an admonition, yet [the offender] does not relinquish [the offense] once the formal act has been completed.

First is the "single instance" (*eka-lava*). Therefore, it is called a "separation by dharma. If one reaches the completion of the third dharma, the offense of the fruit is fully established. If one has not yet reached the third, one abandons [the intent];

this is the stage of abiding in the preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Regarding "the conditions being destroyed or obstructed": "conditions" refers to such things as the implements for killing; for example, suddenly losing them or the blade breaking.
It is also like the disappearance of the object in the case of sexual misconduct. Alternatively, it may be that the victim is too powerful and cannot be assailed.

Regarding the term "to assault" (*ling*) and so forth, Master Li Ming explains: Suppose one intends to kill a person; when arriving at the victim's location, if the person is strong and robust, it is not possible [to kill them].

The word "strong and robust" pertains to the precept against killing. If the word is "to assault," it pertains to the precept against sexual misconduct. This means that although one originally intended to commit an act of lust, the object of lust does not consent;
therefore, it is said that "one cannot assault. Regarding "the three wholesome minds cease," this is also called "wholesome minds cease."
Furthermore, the opening commentary asks: "Since this is the arising of a wholesome mind, why do you say it is 'cessation'? The answer is: "It is indeed the arising of a wholesome mind;
this mind is that which can cease, while the unwholesome mind is that which is ceased. Here, the name is designated from the perspective of that which is ceased; therefore, it is so called."

Regarding "the four types of mental doubt cause the cessation of the act to be different from the intended thought": this refers to a case where the original intention of the mind was to kill a human being, but the perception shifted so that one killed what was actually a non-human animal;

thus, the offense is classified as indeterminate (*aniyata*). Now, when the doubting mind remains unresolved and the action is immediately halted, one incurs the offense of preparatory effort (*prayoga-dukkaṭa*).
Regarding "arousing the thought that it might be a human while doubting whether it is a non-human": this means that the object before one is actually a human, but...
If one gives rise to a doubt as to whether it is a non-human being, and because there is no intention to kill a non-human being, one immediately stops;
one incurs only the *pāyattika* offense of "convenience" (*upakkama*) regarding the original person.

The "various general conditions" listed above are precisely the seven conditions mentioned previously. Regarding the dual clarification of the two types of offenses and the knowledge of the gravity of cause and effect, as well as the characteristics of offense and non-offense:

this means that by correlating these general conditions with the specific conditions within the "particular characteristics," one determines the two types of offenses—cessation and performance—and only then can one know whether they constitute the cause for abiding or the arrival at the fruit.
Thus, one incurs a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). Therefore, it is said that one must know the lightness or gravity of cause and effect;

this means that one must possess both these general and specific conditions (*pratyaya*) for the two types of offenses—cessation (*virati*) and commission (*karaṇa*)—to be established. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that regarding the "two offenses," by comparing the general and specific conditions:
where the conditions are complete, a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is established; where the conditions are incomplete, a *duṣkṛta* offense is established. Hence, they are called the "two offenses."
The above seven sections conclude the general explanation of the third gate: the fulfillment of conditions for an offense (*pārājika*).

Regarding the fourth gate, the fivefold distinctions in the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), this corresponds to the fourth section within the miscellaneous analysis (*saṃkīrṇa-viniścaya*).

It provides a comprehensive clarification of the meaning of the perception of the object within the five categories of offenses (*pañca-varga*). First, as for the necessity of establishing the intention: this refers to establishing the intention regarding the perception of the object, so that—
This concerns the characteristics that constitute an offense and the meaning of its gravity. Second, regarding the general clarification of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*):

since the text has already clarified the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) in relation to the precept against killing, it would have been appropriate to clarify only the objective spheres for offenses under the precept against killing. However, because it now discusses all five categories of offenses (*pañca-varga*) in passing, it is termed "general.

It is established that, among the five categories of precepts, what constitutes the objective sphere of an offense? It refers to the objective sphere of the offense in terms of the counterpart against whom one acts.

The objective sphere (*viṣaya*) extends to both the internal and external, namely sentient and insentient things. Since there are many distinctions and differences therein, it is necessary to clarify them.

Regarding the third point, "existence or non-existence," this refers to how, within the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), there may be an objective sphere and a perception thereof, or there may be no objective sphere and no perception thereof; thus, it is necessary to clarify the reasons for such non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "the commission of crimes is *yōuman* (浟漫)," it is explained as follows: *yō* (浟) means *yōyō* (浟浟), and *man* (漫) means *màn màn* (漫漫).
The *Erlǐ* (爾疋) states: "Yōu (悠) means distant; it refers to the distance of one's conduct, and also implies length.

This means that if one does not regulate the perception of boundaries and distinguish between light and heavy offenses, then even if one commits numerous transgressions, one will remain ignorant of whether those offenses are light or heavy, or whether they constitute an offense at all. Thus, one’s conduct becomes vast and unbounded, lacking any standard.

Regarding those who do not distinguish between the light and the heavy, it is established that, for example, if one intends to kill a human being but mistakenly perceives the object as a non-human animal and kills it, one incurs only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If, however, one perceives a human as a human, such that the mental state and the objective reality correspond, only then does one incur a *pārājika* (defeat). Thus, based on perception (*saññā*), there are always degrees of gravity.

If we do not now establish the four or five propositions (*catuṣkoṭi/pañcakoṭi*) to delimit the relationship between the object and the perception, how could one recognize these differences in gravity?

Furthermore, there are cases where neither "existence" nor "non-existence" is manifest. For instance, regarding the offense of killing: if one intends to kill a non-human or an animal, and subsequently performs the act, it is considered "existent," and thus termed "existence.
However, if one acts with doubt or suspicion toward a non-sentient object—such as a wooden stump—with the thought that it has no owner, then there is no offense; hence, it is called "non-existent.
Therefore, when the Buddha provides detailed explanations at the conclusion of each precept, it refers to the two hundred and fifty rules within the Vinaya-mūla. If...

Regarding those points that ought to be present, they are all clearly explained within the "Discrimination of Characteristics" (Bianxiang) section of the following text, including the fourfold and fivefold categories of objective reality and perception;
these were all spoken by the golden mouth of the Buddha. Even if there are omissions in the text, these are merely abridgments, as indicated by the reference to the Vinaya text itself.
Alternatively, there may be those who have a deficiency in their precepts but lack the perception of the object; this should be considered an omission. Question:

Within the four or five propositions regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), there is always a state of doubt; this is precisely doubt regarding the object (*ālambana-vicikitsā*). Why, then, do you speak only of the "perception of the object" and not establish a category for "doubt regarding the object"?
The answer cannot be fully set forth here; for now, we shall speak of the objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Second, regarding the five distinct stages of the objects of transgression: whenever a precept is violated, the act of transgression is only established in relation to a specific object (*viṣaya*).
Thus, there are five different types. First, the "internal retribution" refers to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-vastu*): humans, devas, and non-animals.

1. Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): this refers to sentient beings as the object of transgression. 2. Regarding external matters: this refers to insentient things, such as grass, trees, earth, water, robes, bowls, food, drink, and so forth, as the objects of transgression.
3. Regarding the Dharma: this refers to the Abhidharma (the analytical teachings) as the object of transgression.

4. Regarding time: this refers to the specific occasion as the object of transgression. 5. Regarding the conditions for offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*): this refers to the specific offense itself as the object.

Regarding the objects of transgression: if one commits the offense against all four objects simultaneously—as in the case of the first precept—the "four objects" refer to those listed above: humans, devas, non-humans, and animals;

all of these constitute a transgression. The "first precept" refers to the precept against sexual misconduct, for by committing sexual misconduct against any of these four objects, one simultaneously incurs the offense. Alternatively, [one may commit it] against any single object.

"Each has its own ascending and descending [grades], as in the cases of killing, stealing, and so forth" means: for killing, it is *pārājika* (defeat) for a human; *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for a non-human; and *pācittiya* (expiation) for an animal.

For stealing, it is *pārājika* for property belonging to a human; *thullaccaya* for property belonging to a non-human; and *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for property belonging to an animal. Regarding great falsehood, the grades are the same as for stealing; therefore, they are said to have "ascending and descending.
"Descending" refers to going down; "ascending" refers to rising high.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the ordained and the laity among human beings: since there are both those who follow the Way (the ordained) and those who are laypeople among humans, one may take an ordained person as the object of an offense, or one may take a layperson as the object of an offense.
Regarding "laypeople," such as those who run food stalls or possess jewels and so forth:

according to the precept on buying and selling, there is no offense in trading with the five groups of monastics; however, if one engages in buying and selling with two laypeople, it constitutes an offense.
An offense of falling (pāyattika). Regarding the precept on sitting forcefully in a family home (*kuladūṣaka*), this defines the sphere of transgression in relation to laypeople.

As for the path, it is as explained in the context of slandering, concealing, striking, and hiding while harboring doubt. By using such [unfounded] charges to slander another renunciant, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; by using a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* charge to slander another renunciant, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Therefore, the latter part of the ninety [minor rules] states: "If one slanders [another] with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma, it is a *pāyattika*."

*Pāyattika* (逸提) is its meaning. "Concealing" (*chādana*) refers to concealing another's grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). "Speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*) refers to speaking of a grave offense to one who is not a *pariśuddha* (one who is not fully qualified).
"Beating" (*tāḍana*) refers to striking or punching a *bhikṣu* with a mind of anger. "Doubt" (*vicikitsā*) refers to causing agitation regarding the precepts.
"Concealing" refers to concealing the robes and bowl of another bhikṣu. All of the above are defined according to the monastic community as the object of an offense.

Regarding those that apply to both monastics and laypeople, this means that both the monastic and lay communities may be designated as the object of an offense. As for the phrase "like two nights, sexual contact, and the two coarse words":
"two nights" refers to sleeping together with a woman and sleeping together with one who has not received full ordination; these two—

Regarding the precepts, both monastics and laypeople commit offenses equally. For example, staying overnight with a laywoman constitutes a *pāyattika*; staying overnight with a *bhikṣuṇī* likewise constitutes a *pāyattika*.

Staying more than two nights with a layperson, as well as staying more than two nights with a *śrāmaṇera*, both constitute *pāyattikas*. As for sexual misconduct, both laywomen and *bhikṣuṇīs* are objects of the offense.
Regarding physical contact, touching a laywoman or a *bhikṣuṇī* constitutes an equal offense. There are two types of coarse speech: one is coarse language, and the other is...
These two precepts—reproaching the body and seeking sensual desires—are equally violated by both nuns and laywomen;

therefore, they are said to "apply to both monastics and laity. Regarding the phrase "internal and external within the path": this refers to further distinguishing between internal and external aspects within that same path.

"Internal" refers to the inner mind and the parts of the body; "external" refers to what is outside the body, such as food and clothing. As for the restriction of the external to food and clothing, it is like [the case of] anger.
Taking another’s robe by force; likewise, eating while praising the food of a *bhikṣuṇī*;

and as in the *Triṃśaka*, taking a *bhikṣuṇī*’s robe, washing robes, praising food, and directing the serving of food—all these constitute the objects of offense with respect to external things. Master Bin explains it in this way. Some, however, say:
Regarding the division of the Path into internal and external: this refers to the Buddha’s Path and the paths of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

"The external is restricted to food and clothing" means that if a monk gives food with his own hand to a non-Buddhist, he commits a *thullaccaya* offense; if a nun gives either food or clothing with her own hand to a non-Buddhist, she commits a *thullaccaya* offense.

This is based on the non-Buddhist as the object of the offense. Examining the meaning of the subsequent text, which states that "within the internal, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are included," it is clear that [the discussion] pertains to those within [the Buddhist fold].

"Dao explains 'non-Buddhists' as 'clearly [distinguished]'; this interpretation is excellent. Bin also says: "The old masters interpret this passage as referring to robes, bowls, food, drink, and so forth.

That would result in a confusion of the topical headings (*chapters*). It simply takes non-Buddhists as the object of transgression, just as when giving robes to non-Buddhists."

It is food. "Internal" refers to the two types of destruction. "Destruction" means reviling; "two" refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*). This is defined as the object of offense according to the Inner Way (Buddhism).

That is to say: if one falsely accuses a *mahābhikṣu* of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense or robs a *mahābhikṣu* of his robe, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one falsely accuses or robs a member of a lower order, one commits only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). These two precepts take the major precepts as their objective for transgression. "Minor" refers to those under age;

Regarding the object of the offense: a śrāmaṇera belongs to the lower assembly and is termed "small" in comparison to the great saṃgha.

These four precepts take nuns as the objects of the offense. As for the offenses of slandering and concealing, their meaning applies to both assemblies:
that is, when a monk slanders a monk or a nun, and when a nun slanders a nun or a monk, both incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. When a minor [offender] slanders a major one, both likewise incur a *pāyattika*.

Thus, it is known that both major and minor slander result equally in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or *pāyattika*. According to Bin, concealing the gross offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) of either a monk or a nun both incurs a *pāyattika*. Bin states: "For nuns, there are eight."

Thus, we know that if a nun conceals four or eight grave offenses, she incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) in each case; whereas if a monk conceals four or eight grave offenses, he commits only a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, regarding the concealment of minor offenses (*pācittiya*) by a nun, the rule is listed directly in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Therefore, we know that for offenses from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downwards, concealing them results in the same [consequences].
If one speaks of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense or a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to a person who is not fully ordained, it is equally a *pāyattika*.
