The front chamber has four types of boundary-delimitation perceptions (*sīmā-saṃjñā*): namely, the one-layered boundary perception for that which is not formally demarcated, the one-layered boundary perception for that which exceeds the measure, the one-layered boundary perception for that which causes obstruction, and the one-layered boundary perception for that which causes difficulty.
The rear chamber has three types of boundary-delimitation perceptions. Therefore, it is said that the two chambers contain seven [perceptions], including the one-layered boundary perception.

Each of these has five further permutations. The Vinaya states: first, if the Saṃgha has not made a formal assignment (anujñā), and one perceives it as not having been assigned, this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;

second, if it has not been assigned and one suspects it has not been assigned, this is a *sthūlātyaya*; third, if it has not been assigned but one perceives it as having been assigned, this is a *sthūlātyaya*; fourth, if it has been assigned but one perceives it as not having been assigned, this is a *sthūlātyaya*;
fifth, if it has been assigned but one suspects it has not been assigned, this is a *sthūlātyaya*. [The same applies to] exceeding the prescribed dimensions.
The five phrases for this case are likewise; they may be understood by analogy. Regarding the obstacles (*vighāta*), there are also five phrases:

first, when there is an obstacle and one perceives it as such, it is auspicious; second, when there is an obstacle and one has doubt regarding it, it is auspicious; third, when there is an obstacle and one perceives it as no obstacle, it is auspicious; fourth, when there is no obstacle and one perceives it as an obstacle, it is auspicious;

fifth, when there is no obstacle and one has doubt regarding it, it is auspicious. The five phrases for the hindrances (*antarāya*) may be understood by analogy. The three [cases] for the subsequent room are as follows:

Regarding the perception of heavy objects, there are five phrases for each, identical to those previously mentioned and without difference. As for "stealing, acting as a matchmaker, coarse [destruction], and harming living beings each having two heavy [offenses]," etc.:
the former refers to stealing five or more than five; these constitute the category of heavy offenses, treated as a single perception of the object.

Next, referring to stealing four or fewer, which constitutes the category of light offenses, they are likewise treated as a single perception of the object, each having four phrases. The Vinaya states that the former refers to exceeding five.
[The offenses] are committed with money. First, if one steals five *kārsāpaṇas* or more from that which has an owner, while perceiving it as having an owner, it is a *pārājika*.

Second, if one steals five or more [coins] from that which has an owner, while suspecting it as having an owner, it is a *thullaccaya*. Third, if one steals five or more [coins] from that which has no owner, while perceiving it as having an owner, it is a *thullaccaya*.

Fourth, regarding the doubt that what lacks an owner has an owner: if one steals it, there are five cases; if it exceeds five *laṅkas*, there is an offense. Next, taking the reduction of five coins as one category, there are likewise four permutations.

First, when there is an owner and one perceives it as having an owner, stealing less than five *laṅkas* constitutes an offense. Second, when there is an owner and one doubts whether there is an owner, stealing less than five constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
Third, when there is no owner and one perceives there is an owner, stealing less than five constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. Fourth, when there is no owner and one [perceives there is an owner]...

Regarding "doubtful theft is reduced by five, [resulting in] a *pāyattika*": as for the statement that "mediating marriage constitutes two *dva-guṇa* offenses," first, taking the perception of mediating a marriage as one category of objective perception (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), and taking the perception of a human female as another category of objective perception, there are five propositions for each.
The Vinaya states: (1) Mediating a marriage with the perception that one is mediating a marriage: a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

(2) Mediating a marriage with doubt regarding whether one is mediating a marriage: a *sthūlātyaya*; (3) Mediating a marriage with the perception that one is not mediating a marriage: a *sthūlātyaya*; (4) Not [mediating a marriage]... [text fragment].

Regarding the five cases of acting as a matchmaker while perceiving [the woman] as a human female: first, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a human female as a human female constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); second, acting as a matchmaker while doubting whether she is a human female constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);

third, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a human female as a non-human female constitutes a *dukkaṭa*; fourth, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a non-human female as a human female constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. Next, regarding the five propositions concerning the perception of a human female: first, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a human female as a human female is a *saṅghādisesa*;

second, acting as a matchmaker while doubting whether she is a human female is a *dukkaṭa*; third, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a human female as a non-human female is a *dukkaṭa*; fourth, acting as a matchmaker while perceiving a non-human female as a human female is a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding the five cases of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) involving non-human women, human women, or doubt concerning mediation in marriage: as for what is called "harsh speech," first there are four permutations based on harsh speech and the perception of harsh speech;

next, there are five permutations based on a human woman and the perception of a human woman. As for the first four permutations: (1) harsh speech with the perception of harsh speech is a *saṃghādisesa*;

(2) harsh speech with doubt regarding harsh speech is a *thullaccaya*; (3) non-harsh speech with the perception of harsh speech is a *thullaccaya*; (4) [non-harsh speech with doubt regarding harsh speech is a *dukkaṭa*].

Harsh speech and the suspicion that it is harsh speech constitute a *sthūlātyaya*. Next, regarding the five cases concerning a human female: (1) a human female, perceiving her as such, is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

(2) a human female, suspecting her to be so, is a *sthūlātyaya*; (3) a human female, perceiving her to be a non-human female, is a *sthūlātyaya*; (4) a non-human female, perceiving her to be a human female, is a *sthūlātyaya*;
(5) a non-human female, suspecting her to be so, is a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the term "defiling" (*bhañjana*), there are two [types] for each.

Regarding the "heavy" offenses: first, concerning non-living seeds—such as willow, pomegranate, and various leaves—if one destroys them while they are on the ground or off the ground, it is considered a single heavy offense based on the perception of the object.
Next, concerning living seeds—such as the examples of cypress, bamboo, and rattan—if one destroys them while they are on the ground, it is an offense of *pācittiya*;

if one destroys them while they are off the ground, there is no offense. These are each considered a single heavy offense based on the perception of the object. For each of these, there are five permutations (*pañca-vākya*).

Fifth, regarding the five cases: (1) if one perceives what is living as living, it is a *pārājika* offense; (2) if one perceives what is living with doubt, it is a *thullaccaya*; (3) if one perceives what is not living as living, it is a *thullaccaya*;
(4) if one perceives what is not living as not living, it is a *dukkaṭa*; (5) if one perceives what is not living with doubt, it is a *dukkaṭa*. Next, to clarify the latter five cases:
they differ only in that they are based on destroying what is already dead; the resulting offenses are otherwise the same as above.
It is not that these [rules] do not exist among the nuns; rather, they have been omitted for brevity. Sengliu states:

Among the five categories of precepts for nuns, those that are identical to the monks' precepts—excluding ten precepts from the twenty-six precepts held by the monks—are as follows. The verse says: Sexual misconduct, physical contact, two types of rooms, and coarse speech.
The ten offenses of praising and encouraging [another] to eat: first, sexual intercourse; second, physical contact; third, an unoccupied dwelling; fourth, an occupied dwelling; fifth, harsh speech;
sixth, praising one's own body; seventh, praising food; eighth, instructing at sunset; ninth, eating after having finished a meal; tenth, encouraging another to finish their meal.
The Bhikṣuṇīs do not have these various precepts; the remaining sixteen precepts are the same as those of the Mahāsaṃgha (Bhikṣus). These are:

killing, stealing, lying, acting as a matchmaker, slandering, digging the earth, destroying vegetation, eating what is not left over, consuming food received twice, [killing] insects, drinking alcohol, concealing [faults], harsh speech, and inciting disputes—namely, killing, stealing, and lying, which constitute the three [grave offenses].

4. Acting as a matchmaker; 5. Returning an object; 6. Speaking of a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); 7. Digging the earth; 8. Destroying living plants; 9. Eating at an improper time; 10. Consuming food kept overnight; 11.
Eating food not formally offered; 12. Drinking alcohol; 13–14. Drinking or using water containing insects;

15. Concealing another’s grave offense; 16. Inciting a dispute. These are the offenses that require the consent of the Saṃgha. Regarding the perception of the object, it is as follows: [the same as above].

Regarding the points where these differ: only two precepts involve the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). These are the precept against sexual contact and the precept against accepting food or clothing from a man with a defiled mind.
Regarding the five clauses on sexual contact: (1) a human male, with the perception of a human male; (2) a human male, with doubt regarding a human male—both incur a *sthūlātyaya*;

(3) a human male, with the perception of a non-human male—incur a *sthūlātyaya*; (4) a non-human male, with the perception of a human male—incur a *sthūlātyaya*; (5) [a non-human male, with the perception of a non-human male].

Regarding the *thullaccaya* for doubting whether the person is male: there are four permutations concerning robes and food with a defiled mind. First, a defiled mind, perceiving a defiled mind, constitutes a *pārājika*.

Second, a defiled mind, suspecting a defiled mind, constitutes a *thullaccaya*. Third, a defiled mind, perceiving a defiled mind, constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. Fourth, a non-defiled mind, suspecting a defiled mind, constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
By applying these two sets of differing precepts to the preceding set of identical precepts, there are sixteen permutations, which form ten [categories].

Regarding the eight precepts, there is the perception of an object. In relation to them, there are twenty-one cases: namely, theft, acting as a matchmaker, and destroying life, each having two grades;

and for the [remaining] three, there are three grades and not three. These, when combined, total eighteen; with the aforementioned three added, they become twenty-one. Since the present *Chao* (Excerpts) does not clarify these, it is said that they have been omitted.
Regarding the statement "as previously mentioned," this refers to what was stated above concerning the fundamental basis of the *Saṃgha-vinaya*.

That is to say, for now, it is explained by way of the *bhikṣu-śīla* (monastic precepts). It is established that, as in the intent of the previous regulations, even if there are missing passages, they are generally merely omissions.

The preceding explanation of the meaning of "perception of the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) is complete. Next, regarding the term "absence" (*abhāva*), it generally refers back to the five [categories] mentioned above.

That is to say, within the three categories of precepts in the *Vinayamātṛkā*, the reason why there is no "perception of the object" is either because it is non-existent in principle—that is, the principle itself renders it non-existent—or for some other reason.
Now, I shall further explain that reason.

Regarding the statement that it "generally corresponds to the preceding five," this means that within the second section above—the general exposition on the gate of objects (*viṣaya*)—there are five categories.

Now, in clarifying the meaning of the perception of non-existent objects (*anālambana-saṃjñā*), we again explain it by means of these five categories; since there is no separate treatment for the absence of objects and so forth, it is said to generally correspond to the preceding five.
First, regarding "the absence of internal retribution": this refers to the sentient being as the internal retribution, which is the same as explained previously.

Alternatively, it may mean "absence in principle," such as when there is a lapse due to contact with conditions; thus, one commits an offense by losing seminal purity. This applies to all sentient and non-sentient objects;
for while earth, water, wind, and form can all serve as objects, how could there be a distinction in the gravity of the offense based on differences in the object?

[This is] grave. Or, is there an opening where one does not incur an offense? Therefore, it is unnecessary to clarify the perception (*saṃjñā*) regarding the object. This is because [the offense] is non-existent in principle.

As for the statement "by means of which one ascends to the stage of an offense," this means that as soon as one touches the object through emission, one immediately ascends to that stage of an offense.

Alternatively, the phrase "or perhaps lacking" and so forth further explains the aforementioned precept against emission; it may also mean that there is currently a perception regarding the object, such as when one regards the three lower realms as the right path, or acts wrongly toward them.

Regarding the doubt concerning the perception of a path (*mārga-saṃjñā-vicikitsā*), it constitutes a loss of the outflows (*āsrava-vaipulya*) and a loss of the limit (*anta-vaipulya*). It merely results in the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya-vikalatā*).
One should know that there is currently the perception of an object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). For this reason, I now cite the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to clarify its existence.

This term "perhaps" (*vā*) means "it may be so"; it is an indefinite particle. That is to say, what prevents there being the perception of an object? If one has the perception of a path or is in doubt, [the offense] is established.
That is to say: although it was stated above that [the offense] does not exist according to principle, we now say this is not so; it is likewise an omission.

For example, regarding "leakage" (a seminal emission), if one acts upon what is not the path while perceiving it as the path, or if one doubts, one incurs only the *duṣkṛta* (offense of deficient conditions). Thus, we know that for eating, if there is the perception of the object, [the offense is incurred]. Furthermore, the passage below cites the Dharmaguptaka school:

if one acts upon what is not the path while perceiving it as not the path, and there is no doubt, one incurs only the *śeṣaka* (residual offense). It is certain that this is an omission based on the Dharmaguptaka school.
Since these words exist within the text, it is possible that there was an intention regarding the object; thus it is said, "or perhaps [the object] is absent.
Regarding the previous statement, "if one perceives what is not the Path as the Path, or if one doubts," this refers to doubting whether something is the true Path while perceiving it as such;

failing in this regard is called "the mind not corresponding to the object," and thus one incurs the offense of *pāyattika* (deficiency of conditions). Only if it is not the Path and one perceives it as not the Path, without doubt, is it permissible.

The remainder [of the offense] consists in the correspondence between the mind and the object. If one forms the perception that it is the Path (*mārga*), since it is not the actual object of the "remainder" offense, it constitutes the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) of "deficient conditions.
Yaśomitra states: The Dharmaguptaka school says that there is a *duṣkṛta* for perceiving what is not matter as matter, and a *duṣkṛta* for doubting whether it is the Path when it is not the Path.

Although these involve perception and doubt, they are all formulated with respect to the primary object; there is no formulation regarding a different object. In the two fixed offenses (*niyata-āpatti*), such as slandering or seizing property, the details are omitted.

"Existing now" (*idānīṃ-sat*) refers to that which exists according to principle; "not existing" (*asat*) is an abbreviation for what is not found in the Vinaya. "Slander" (*abhyākhyāna*) refers to slandering the precepts;

it is restricted to slandering a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī* regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Regarding the slander of the three lower assemblies, one should understand that there is the intention (*saṃjñā*) toward an object (*viṣaya*) that exists according to principle, while "not existing now" is an abbreviation.

As for "depriving," it means that depriving a *mahā-bhikṣuṇī* of her robe constitutes a *pāyattika*; depriving the three lower assemblies merely results in the removal [of the robe]. This is the principle concerning an object that exists now.

[The term] "perception" (saññā) is not abbreviated in the text. Regarding "double-tongued speech, disparagement, resentment, and abuse," this means that if one addresses the four lower assemblies [of the Saṅgha], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);

however, if one addresses the Great Saṅgha alone, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Therefore, it is now clarified that there is the perception of the object. As for "resentment and abuse," this refers to abusing an administrative official (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*).

If the person is an administrative official and one perceives them as such, one incurs a *thullaccaya*. If the person is an administrative official but one perceives them as not being so, or if there is doubt, [the penalty is different].

Now, regarding the minor offense, there ought to be the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). That this is not mentioned in the text is an abbreviation. Regarding the statement that "there ought to be the perception of the object for an offense restricted to this specific object," and that its omission in the text is an abbreviation and so forth:
this means that the objects restricted here are those of the bhikṣu who is the subject of slander, theft, defamation, and the like.

If these distinctions were omissions of necessary conditions, then since there are now both light and heavy [degrees of] offenses, the perception of the object must necessarily be required; yet it is not mentioned in the text for this reason.
Briefly stated:
regarding the two external matters, there is no mention of the distinction between those spread in an open space and those spread in a screened place. This refers to non-sentient external objects;

namely, monastic bedding spread in the open and monastic bedding spread in a screened location. These two currently involve the perception of an object, yet this is omitted from the text. Thus it is abbreviated.

It is just like perceiving an open space as an open space, or perceiving a covered place as a covered place; likewise, perceiving what belongs to the Saṃgha as not belonging to the Saṃgha, or perceiving a secluded place as secluded—or being in doubt about it—and so forth.
It is also like spreading out a mat while perceiving it as not spread out, or being in doubt about it. Regarding "exposed": this refers to the precept concerning lighting a fire in an open space.
That is to say, lighting a fire in an open space while perceiving it as such, or being in doubt about it; lighting a fire while perceiving it as such, or being in doubt about it.

...and so forth. Alternatively, it may be considered that there is no offense if one perceives the place as being open. Regarding "hiding clothes and so forth," this refers to hiding another person's clothing.

It would be appropriate to say that if one hides [the item] while perceiving it as not hidden, then within the category of non-offenses, such a case is logically impossible; for there is no corresponding factor (dharma) to which it relates.

This means that, for example, in the precepts against killing or stealing, there is no separate corresponding factor; how then could one distinguish the perception of the object based on the factor? As in...
The tortoise’s body appears to be hairless; how can one ask about the length or shortness of a tortoise’s hair?

Theft, as a fundamental dharma, lacks [a distinct] mental object (*ālambana*); how can one clarify the mental object by means of the dharma? This merely refers to the matter at hand, clarifying the mental object in relation to the objective field (*viṣaya*). Some say that regarding the dharmas of killing and stealing, there is no mental object;
this too is a concealment of the aspect of the dharma, for it focuses exclusively on the matter itself to clarify the mental object. For instance, consider instructing another to kill.

Regarding theft: one uses false words to manifest it through speech. Based on these verbal expressions, how could they not constitute the *dharma*? This refers to cases such as acting according to instructions while having the perception that one is not being instructed, or harboring doubt, and so forth.

When we say "there is no [offense]" in the present context, it simply means that one conceals the act of instructing another by claiming it was done by oneself; or perhaps it means that, as a matter of principle, there is no offense.
Nevertheless, even when instructing another, the act performed by the person being instructed prior to the instruction likewise lacks a corresponding *dharma* to counteract it. Jing also [said this].

It is said: This citation speaks of the non-existence of the object (*dharma*) from a general perspective. For instance, when one commits murder while lamenting [the victim's death], is this not also a case where the object is non-existent?
Regarding the statement that "there is no mention of the two types of false speech, great and small," some say this clarifies the "great falsehood.

However, in the present *Abhidharma* (the *Prakaraṇapāda*), there is an explanation regarding the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). In the current Vinaya texts, it merely clarifies the perception of the object in relation to the person being deceived. Based on this, [the present text]...

There is a dharma: by means of the perception of an object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). "Object" refers to the noble Dharma (*āryadharma*), as in the phrases regarding the perception of or doubt concerning the noble Dharma.

Regarding minor falsehood, there is no offense in the case of one's own speech; however, for it to constitute deception, one must now consider the dharma of one's own speech, wherein there must be the perception of an object.

The absence of wording here is an abbreviation; it merely conceals the peripheral details of the dharma to directly clarify the person being deceived, thereby elucidating the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*).

This includes the intention [of the offender] as well as the admonisher, meaning the admonition regarding the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), all of which are completed through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed by the Saṃgha. Therefore, they are explained within this section.

That is to say, regarding the method of performing an admonition toward such a person, there are now phrases such as "perceiving the object," "admonishing while perceiving it as an admonition," and "doubting [whether it is an admonition]," and so forth. The text [proceeds as follows].

"Non-existent" (*abhāva*) is an abbreviation. Regarding "following the citation," etc.: it refers to when a bhikṣu develops wrong views, and the Saṃgha performs a disciplinary act (*sāmīcī-karman*) against him in accordance with those wrong views.
There must be the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), meaning that one perceives this person who has been subjected to the disciplinary act as one who has attained the [proper] dharma.

The phrases such as "raising [a formal act] while perceiving it as being raised" or "suspecting it," etc., are abbreviated in the text; this is because, as in the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya], two [factors] are reduced. It is thus because there is the perception of an object.

Regarding those who comply with a monk who has been formally charged and those who comply with a śramaṇa who has been formally charged, since this results in a *thullaccaya* offense due to the legal procedures of the Saṃgha, one must rely on the Dharma.
There must be the perception of an object within the context of the Dharma; that which is not present in this Vinaya is abbreviated.

Indeed, the *Jī* (Cīvara-vastu) contains the details regarding the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). According to the *Jī*, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning the perception of the object when following a monk who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhittaka*).

First, if one follows one who has been suspended while perceiving them as not suspended, there is no offense. Second, if one follows one who has not been suspended while perceiving them as suspended, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Third, if one follows one who has been suspended while suspecting they have been suspended, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Fourth, if one follows one who has not been suspended while perceiving them as not suspended, there is no offense. This also applies to following a *śrāmaṇera* who has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*).

There are four propositions: first, if one drives [the animals] while having no thought of driving them, there is no offense; second, if one does not drive them but has the thought of driving them, it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor fault); third, if one drives them while suspecting whether one is driving them or not, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;

fourth, if one does not drive them and has no thought of driving them, there is no offense. (The citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* serves as proof that this exists in the present case. Regarding the "mediator" (*dūtī*) and "coarse speech" (*pāruṣya*), etc., the opposite of this applies where there is the perception of a formal rule (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
Gao says: this means that in the present case, the principle is the reverse of the above and thus non-existent; furthermore, although the text contains the reverse of the above, it is omitted here.

Therefore it is said: "The opposite of this. Regarding the absence of principle (*yul med*), such as killing, stealing, and so forth—because there is no phenomenon (*dharma*) that can serve as an object for them—it is termed "absence of principle" within this context of the Dharma-gate (*dharmaparyāya*).
As for attachment, whether it be the two types of delusion (great or small), or the admonitions, the *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*, and so on.

All of these are based on the formal rule (*dharma*). Now, regarding the perception of a boundary (*sīmā-saṃjñā*), its absence in the text is due to abbreviation. Here, the "coarse" act of matchmaking is based on the formal rule where there is a perception of a boundary;

this differs from the previous cases of "absence of principle" (*li-wú*) and "abbreviated absence" (*lèi-wú*). Therefore, it is said that "this is the reverse," referring to coarse matchmaking and the like.

There are dharmas that can serve as objects of perception (*ālambana-saṃjñā*). Therefore, this is the opposite of the principle found in the texts concerning theft, matchmaking, and so forth, which state that such [perceptions] do not exist.

Just as with matchmaking and coarse speech, there are two levels of object-perception: first, in terms of the concrete thing (*vastu*), and second, in terms of the dharma. The clarification of object-perception is as described in the previous analysis of the number [of offenses].
Some interpret "giving" (*dāna*) as being the same as "understanding" (*parijñāna*); however, here it is clarified that "matchmaking" and "coarse speech" are the opposites of this.

Regarding "the perception of a dharma" (*dharmasaṃjñā*): this refers to its coarse medium; that is, it takes the dharma as its objective referent for the perception. Therefore, one should know that "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is an abbreviation.

As stated in the first five phrases of the section on intermediaries: "intermediating marriage while perceiving it as intermediating marriage, or being in doubt," these are instances of taking the dharma as the referent.

Regarding the four propositions concerning harsh speech (*pāruṣya*): "Harsh speech with the perception of harsh speech, or with doubt," etc., these take the actual phenomenon (*dharma*) as both the object (*viṣaya*) and the perception (*saṃjñā*).

This interpretation is correct, being identical to the previous explanation by Liang. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one may also contemplate it as a contemplative perception," this refers to the formulation of the precepts for the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).

The Vinaya’s mention of "object and perception" is made specifically in reference to the matters of dispute; however, it may also be understood as referring to the phenomena themselves. One should state: [the text continues].

One should form the perception of "contemplation" when contemplating, and the perception of "cessation" when ceasing; one must not harbor doubts regarding these. This refers to clarifying the perceptions of the objects based on the Dharma, though such details are omitted in the text.

Regarding the phrase "forming the perception of 'admonition' when admonishing, yet doubting whether it is non-Dharma," this refers to the precept of admonition, which is entirely a Dharma enacted by the Saṃgha.
Now, based on this Dharma, there should appropriately be the perception of the object, as well as the perception of "admonition" and doubts thereof. As for the phrase "non-Dharma and so forth":

This refers to the eighteen dharmas and so forth. Since there is currently the notion of an object [of cognition], one should say "dharma-dharma-notion" or "dharma-dharma-doubt," and so on, up to categories such as light or heavy offenses, transgressions, and non-transgressions.
That there is no mention of these in the current text is due to abbreviation.
"Time" is like one who is bathing; it refers to cases where there is actually time, yet one has the perception that it is not time, or doubts and so forth regarding what is not time.

There is no such omission in the Vinaya. Regarding "entering a village": this refers to entering a village before or after a meal without informing one's fellow practitioners (*sahāya*), or entering a village at an improper time (*akāla*).
Now, in defining the object through the perception of time, one should say: "at an improper time, with the perception that it is time," or "doubts and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "the offenses are briefly omitted": as in the case of the *ni-pācittiya* on concealment and so forth, this clarifies that within the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts, there is a rule concerning a *bhikṣuṇī* concealing another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

Now, in clarifying the perception regarding the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), one should state "grave offense with the perception of a grave offense," "doubt," and so forth; it is not that these are absent from the text, but rather they have been omitted.

This is known from the ninety rules in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "If one conceals another’s concealment of an offense, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation)," which fully includes the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*).
Since this is so for a *bhikṣu*, how could it not exist for a *bhikṣuṇī* who conceals another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*)? Question: Why is the *bhikṣuṇī*’s rule cited here? Answer:

It is explained that regarding the Sangha’s perception of another’s concealment of an offense, the text explicitly contains the perception of the object; therefore, one cannot claim that the Sangha’s rule is merely deficient in this regard. For other rules, there is no such principle [of deficiency].

Regarding those offenses that can be confronted: it is established that, apart from the two precepts concerning concealment (*paticchādana*), for all other categories of precepts, what offense could there be that is capable of being confronted?
Therefore, one cannot take the offense itself as the objective field (*visaya*) to clarify the perception of the object (*vatthu-saññā*).
The explanation of the third point—the presence or absence of the perception of the object—is hereby concluded.

Regarding the fourth point, "more or less": as for the dharmas of objective perception (viṣaya-saṃjñā), whether they be four or five, this refers to the meaning of the fourth section within the major chapter on visualization (saṃjñā).
This clarifies that the phrases concerning objective perception may be four or five, differing in their number.
Five phrases are termed "many," while four phrases are termed "few. First, the phrases shall be listed according to the Vinaya; below, these phrases will be analyzed.

To what extent? Therefore, with respect to the precept against killing, this establishes the categories of light and heavy; with respect to the precept against stealing, it establishes the categories of transgression and non-transgression.
Among these five phrases, the first is the result, while the latter four are the causes.

Regarding the two cases of "doubt concerning whether the person is human or non-human": this refers to one who originally intends to kill a human being. Upon reaching that person's side, they suddenly doubt whether it is a non-human (*amanuṣya*) or a human.

However, because the objective condition (*ālambana*) is in fact a human, and the mind remains in hesitation, it is called "doubt. Because the object is actually a human, it is termed "certainty of the object" (*viṣaya-niścaya*);

because of the false suspicion that it is a non-human, it is termed "distortion of the mind" (*citta-vibhrama*). One incurs the *duṣkṛta* offense of "deficiency of conditions" (*pratyaya-vaikalya*). This constitutes three types of [non-intentional] offenses.

Regarding "the perception of a human being," this is the same as the preceding phrase; the only difference is that the mind perceives it as such. Regarding "the fourth case: a non-human with the perception of a human being":
one originally intends to kill a human being, but a non-human comes to take his place. The mind takes the non-human as its object, yet says, "This is a human being," and proceeds to kill him.

Because the intent to kill remains fixed on the idea of a human being, it is called "fixed intention" (*cetanā-niyata*). Since, however, a non-human has come to take the place [of the intended victim], it is called "error of the object" (*viṣaya-viparyāsa*).

One may also lack the conditions for *ālambana* (the object) and *pratyaya* (the causal basis). Regarding the case where there is doubt concerning a non-human (*amanuṣya*) and the mental state shifts due to a discrepancy in the object—where both conditions are lacking—it refers to one who originally intends to kill a human, but a non-human takes his place;
having reached the presence of that non-human, he immediately gives rise to doubt as to whether it is a human or a non-human.
The object also differs, and the mind also shifts; therefore, it is said that both conditions are lacking. To give rise to doubt regarding what is not a human being is a shift of the mind;

since a non-human being has replaced the original object, this is called a "difference in the object. As for the phrase "doubt regarding a non-human being" in the present text: [This refers to the case where one mistakes a non-human being for a human being.]

This should be stated as: "it is not a non-human" and "there is doubt regarding it being a non-human. These five preceding phrases consist of three that constitute the primary object (*mūla-viṣaya*) and two that constitute the secondary object (*anya-viṣaya*).

(One must distinguish between the primary and the secondary; these will be indicated further below. Among these five phrases, whether an offense is incurred is certain in the first two and the last two;

only in the third phrase is the incurrence of an offense uncertain. Thus, there may be this phrase; if one’s perception shifts, it becomes five. If there is fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), then...
It forms four [categories]. Because the offense incurred by this single phrase is not fixed, the subsequent explanation states: "it may be four, five, and so forth.
If one understands this intent, the conceptualization of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) can be understood. As for these five phrases, they refer to the distinct textual passages of Dharmottara.
Regarding why there are more or fewer, before proceeding with the explanation, he first raises the question to bring out the underlying reason. The interlocutor says: "I wish to..."
To understand this section, one must know two points: first, to clearly comprehend the threefold relative distinctions; second, to discuss in advance the underlying intent of this section.
Regarding the threefold relative distinctions alone: there is the relative distinction between the two objects of heavy and light offenses.

For example, taking a human being as the object and comparing it to a non-human being—when these two objects are contrasted, killing either incurs sin; this is called the "Section on Heavy and Light."
Furthermore, it should be understood that the same applies when facing animals. Second, regarding the relative distinction between the two objects of transgression and non-transgression:

for instance, taking what is not given from an object belonging to another while the owner is absent is termed the "gate of transgression and non-transgression. It should be understood that this also applies to cases such as failing to designate [the property] and so forth.
Third, regarding the relative distinction between the two objects based on their original difference: herein there are two parts. First, with respect to the precept...

Explaining "original" (*mūla*) and "different" (*anya*). For example, regarding the precept against killing: a human being is the original object (*ālambana*). Even if, from beginning to end, one mistakes the human for an animal, this deviates from the original expectation;
since the animal is the original object, yet one now observes the precept with respect to the human, the human becomes the "original" [object of the transgression].

This is contrary to the former case and is termed a "different object. Second, explaining "original" and "different" in terms of the original intended mind: for example, if the original intention of the mind was to kill a human being.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): when one now initiates the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for killing against a person, that [person] is designated as the "original" (*mūla*).

After the preparatory effort has begun, if a different object appears, it is only then termed a "different object. Therefore, one should understand that there are two kinds of original objects regarding the restraint of the precepts.

Second, concerning the general discussion of the intent of this section: the ancient masters unanimously determined that killing, sexual misconduct, physical contact, harsh speech, and so forth constitute grave offenses.

The section on light offenses (*laghu-dvāra*). Regarding the section on whether concealment and speaking [of another's offense] constitute an offense or not: within the context of concealment and speaking, the term "coarse perception" (*sthūla-saṃjñā*) does not exclusively mean that it renders [the act] non-offensive.
Therefore, one should know that this is also a section concerning offenses. Now, the Master refutes their error in making a definitive judgment.

Furthermore, take for example the taking of life: when it is directed toward humans as opposed to animals and the like, there is a distinction between grave and light; if it is directed toward that which is not a sentient being, then there is the question of whether an offense is committed or not.

Thus, one knows that [the gravity of the act] is not fixed. Regarding theft: when directed toward ownerless property, there is the question of whether an offense is committed or not; when directed toward non-animal objects, there is a distinction between grave and light.
This is also indeterminate. There are cases where there is only the distinction between transgression and non-transgression, such as in the case of assigning tasks at an improper time and so forth.

Furthermore, one should understand that according to the explicit text of the Vinaya regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), it refers solely to the original intention; the determination of the offense based on a different original intention likewise applies only to the original object.

As for what is distinguished in the *Shu-chao* (Commentary) regarding the views of the ancients and the moderns: it is intended to encompass multiple meanings, namely, that which is based on the original intention and...

The two types of transgressions regarding the precepts differ fundamentally. Having clarified the primary offense, one must also concurrently understand the secondary deviations; this should be known according to the circumstances.
(The preceding preliminary discussion is concluded. Next, the text of the *Chao* shall be explained.)
If there were necessarily a third category when heavy and light offenses are contrasted, such that they would then constitute five categories, as some people of old have said:

"When discussing the contrast between the heavy and the light, there are necessarily five propositions. For example, within the precept against sexual misconduct, regarding the third proposition concerning the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), it states:

'Even if one perceives it as a non-path, it is still a *pārājika* offense. However, in cases such as killing or lying, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense. It is on the basis of this contrast between the heavy and the light that they argue this.
Therefore, there are five propositions. Regarding the case where one commits a *pārājika* offense through a shift in perception or through original delusion:

for example, if one originally intends to engage in sexual intercourse, but shifts the perception of the path to perceive it as a non-path, yet merely comes into contact with the object, it is still a *pārājika*. This is a determination based on the objective condition (*ālambana*).

This means that because one does not entertain the perception or suspicion [that it is] sexual intercourse or alcohol, it is called a *thullaccaya* (offense of grave wrongdoing). "Thullaccaya" refers to the offense committed when one forms the perception that it is a non-path [of sexual conduct], yet the actual leakage occurs;

this is the *thullaccaya* due to the deficiency of the objective condition. Because one formed the perception of a non-path, it was intended as a leakage [of semen]; had it been combined with the full offense, it would have been a *saṅghādisesa*.

However, because the objective condition is deficient on the side of the *saṅghādisesa*, one incurs only a *thullaccaya*. That is to say, although it was actually the right path, one now formed the perception that it was a non-path.

For example, if one engages in sexual intercourse with a woman who is partially defiled, yet claims she is one who is mostly defiled—where partial defilement constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat) and majority defilement constitutes the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense)—if one commits an emission therein, this constitutes a deficiency in the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The same applies to fundamental delusion:

when one is deluded regarding the right path and perceives it as a wrong path, entering it results in *pārājika*; this too is determined by the objective condition. [The offenses of] *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta* follow accordingly.
This is also tied to the deluded mind; that is to say, one is fundamentally deluded regarding the Path and forms the perception of it as a non-path, thereby committing a transgression.

Because the object was mistaken, there is only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) and no *pārājika* (defeat). Regarding alcohol, sexual misconduct, and killing: if one’s perception shifts from what was originally deluded, then for the offenses of killing and sexual misconduct, if the perception changes, it is a *pārājika*.

This means that according to the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*), if there is such a perception or doubt, it constitutes a *pārājika* through doubt. Since the precept against sexual misconduct does not allow for perception or doubt [to invalidate the offense], one incurs a *pārājika*.

Regarding the term "lán" (discrepancy): it refers to the discrepancy in the object (*ālambana*) among the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). One must understand the fundamental meaning: if the object is fixed while the mind is discrepant, it is called "doubtful perception" (*saṃjñā-vicikitsā*);
if the object is discrepant while the mind is fixed, it is called "discrepancy in the object. The latter specifically refers to a discrepancy in the mind.

Therefore, it is said that there is a "difference in the object" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*). The preceding phrase refers to a "difference in the mind" (*citta-viśeṣa*). Regarding the object, these are termed "misconception" (*saṃjñā*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*);

they are collectively designated as "deficiency of conditions" (*ālambana-vaikalya*). Thus, the subsequent passage states: "In cases such as killing, lying, or sexual contact, where one acts based on a mistaken perception, the offense is *sthūlātyaya*. This is based on the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprāyogika*):

*sthūla* refers to the *sthūlātyaya* arising from misconception and doubt, while *tyaya* (or *atya*) refers to the *pāyantika* arising from the difference in the object. In relation to the subsequent categories of non-humans or animals, one incurs a *pāyantika*; this constitutes the "difference in the object."

There is a discrepancy in the object (*viṣaya-viparyāsa*). The object is actually a human being, yet due to a shift in perception and delusion, one claims it is not an animal; when viewed from the perspective of a non-human, is this not a discrepancy in the object?

This is simply called a discrepancy in the object when the subsequent thought pertains to a different object. If, however, one discusses the attainment of a *sthūlātyaya* offense with respect to the original object, these are all termed "perceptual doubt" (*saṃjñā-vicikitsā*).

If, from the perspective of the original object, there is a *sthūlātyaya*, this is a discrepancy in the mind regarding that object. If, however, one views it from the perspective of a different object...

"Regarding this 'light offense' (dukkaṭa): it refers to cases where one's perception regarding the object differs from one's intention. If, for instance, in the case of killing, false speech, sexual misconduct, or the two types of harsh speech, one's perception shifts and results in a light offense (thullaccaya), let us explain this first by way of killing.

Suppose one intends to kill a human being; when arriving at the location of the victim, if one's perception shifts and one perceives the victim as a non-human being, one incurs the light offense (dukkaṭa) of the preliminary effort (pubba-pacittiya).
This is a light offense arising from a shift in perception or doubt. In terms of the act of taking a human life, one further incurs a light offense."

This "auspicious" [result] occurs when the object is not a human; it is the auspiciousness resulting from a deficiency in conditions or a discrepancy in the objective field. This constitutes the offense of the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of killing a non-human.
The same applies to lying: that is, one originally intends to deceive a human, but upon reaching the presence of the object, one instead perceives them as a non-human and deceives them.

This refers to the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) regarding the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) based on the perception (*saṃjñā*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*) that the person is human. It concerns deceiving a non-human being.
Furthermore, one incurs the *duṣkṛta* of a "difference in the object" (*viṣayāntara*) regarding the preparatory effort when the intended object changes. As for "touching":

if one originally intends to touch a human female, but upon reaching the location, touches a non-human female instead, one incurs the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) based on the original perception or doubt regarding the human female, while incurring the *duṣkṛta* of a "difference in the object" regarding the non-human female. Regarding the two "coarse" [offenses], the original...

One praises a human woman, speaking coarse words of praise regarding her body. Upon reaching the vicinity of the object, one transforms this into the perception that she is a non-human woman and continues to speak words of praise.

One incurs only the *pāyattika* offense of the preparatory stage (*upakrama*) regarding a human woman; however, with respect to the non-human woman, it is a *duṣkṛta*. These five precepts all concern the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyaya*).
Because they concern non-humans and animals, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense based on the original object of the initial mind, while the subsequent mind constitutes a different object.

Regarding the establishment of the offense: if one considers the distinctions such as shifting the perception (*saṃjñā*) or regarding an object that lacks an owner, then [the offense] would only apply to the previous state of mind where the original object was present;
there would be no offense regarding the subsequent state of mind involving a different object. This constitutes the principle of the "gate of transgression and non-transgression.

Therefore, it is necessary to confront the shift in perception from what is not an animal to an animal. As for "the original delusion also being an offense," this is because it was originally intended...
The original object [of the act] is not different; however, with respect to a different object, there is merit (śubha).

Since it is stated here that even being originally deluded is meritorious, one knows that the absence of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) regarding the object constitutes the merit of the difference from the "non-animal" object.

This means that although the person was originally deluded as to whether it was a human or a non-animal, from the perspective of severing the life of a non-animal, one merely obtains the merit of the preparatory effort for the deficient object, because there was no intention to kill a human. A human...

Because [the victim] was dead, there is no offense. Since the expectation was directed toward a non-human being, this constitutes a deficient object (*viṣaya-vaiṣamya*). Because it is incomplete, it is precisely a case of a deficient object;
therefore, it is merely *śuddhaka* (a minor offense). Thus, the third category is required to complete the five stages.

This means that when explaining the meaning in relation to the aforementioned various precepts, although they differ in gravity, there is no case that does not involve an offense; consequently, there exists a third category. It is because of this category that...
Thus, five propositions are established.
Regarding the statement, "If there is an offense or no offense when two objects are contrasted, such as stealing without formal authorization," the two objects are explained below:
one concerns non-authorization and one concerns the precept against stealing; hence they are called "two objects. In this context, it thus constitutes either...

Four or five. This means that when one is about to commit an offense, it does not necessarily involve the mutual confrontation of factors; thus, four or five conditions may be fulfilled. For example, in the precept against stealing, there is no third phrase.
If a third phrase were established, it would have to state: "there is an owner, but one perceives them as having no owner," which would result in a total absence of guilt.

Therefore, a third phrase is not established. This is based on fundamental delusion, and thus there are only four phrases. As for the case of "not obtaining permission," this is based on a shift [in perception].

Regarding the perception (*saṃjñā*), there are five propositions. That is to say, the third proposition states that if one does not occupy [a place] while perceiving it as occupied, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
thus, five propositions are formed. As for the precept against stealing, there are four [propositions] based on the perception of whether an object has an owner or is ownerless.

According to this commentary, all [cases] fall under the third proposition. Since there is no offense associated with this specific proposition, it is set aside and placed within the section on exemptions (*anujñā*).
Therefore, the precept against stealing consists of only four permutations. The case of "not having obtained authorization" (不分) possesses five permutations;
this refers to the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyaya*), which concludes the previous section on the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. This will be explained below.

The reason for clarifying both the object of stealing and the object of authorization is that, within the Vinaya texts, the precept against stealing—concerning fundamental delusion—contains only four permutations, whereas the case of "not having obtained authorization," being a matter of transformed perception, contains five permutations.

This is now set forth according to the Vinaya text. If discussed from the perspective of principle, it would suffice to take a single object and apply the transformation of perception (*parivṛtti-saṃjñā*);
even so, the original delusion would be established. However, because we now wish to harmonize with the Vinaya text, it is necessary to cite two objects.

Regarding the fifth point—that the transformation of perception entails the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) due to the preceding thought—it refers to the status of "not having been assigned" mentioned above. This means that such non-assignment consists of five phrases.
This refers to the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). This clarifies why five phrases are provided:

because there is the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) regarding the original preparatory act (*prayoga*), it is clarified that although one did not originally intend to seek formal authorization (*anujñā*), one subsequently transformed it into the perception of seeking authorization;

thus, while one does not incur the root offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one still incurs the prior mental offense of *duṣkṛta*. "The fourth [phrase] concerns the original delusion," etc., refers to the four phrases concerning the aforementioned theft.
Because of fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), there is no offense due to lack of skillful means. Therefore, regarding the perception of the object, there is no third alternative.

To say that both objects are entirely without fault is merely a summary of what precedes. Regarding theft, there are four alternatives; this refers to fundamental delusion. "Both objects" refers to two fundamentally different objects.
If there is an owner, but one is fundamentally deluded and perceives it as ownerless, one does not commit an offense; this is called the "fundamental object. If it is actually...
If one perceives it as having no owner, there is no offense; this is called a "different object. Therefore, it is said that in both cases of the object, there is entirely no fault.
As for the statement "by this principle there are five," this merely reiterates the previous point regarding the failure to assign [the robe] being a case of a changed perception;
for this reason, the full five propositions are established. Some say: "Not so. The 'five' mentioned above refers to the changed perception, and by this, the conclusion is finalized."

Why is it necessary to re-establish [the boundary]? It must be as previously explained. As it says below: "If there are four or five cases of transgression or non-transgression, where would one re-establish [the boundary]?
For what reason? Because according to this principle, it is exclusively a case of re-establishing [the boundary], not a case of formal distribution (*avakāśana*).

If there are cases of transgression and non-transgression, then the establishment of the boundary for theft applies generally to both those who have committed the offense and those who have not. Since the establishment of the boundary for theft already covers both those who have committed the offense and those who have not, it likewise applies to the present case.

The phrases "not being subject to formal disciplinary action" (*adhyāpattika*) and so forth are absent in the ancient masters' texts; therefore, those who attempted to explain them [based on those texts] were incorrect.
Thus, I shall now provide the correct explanation. This concludes the general clarification of the two gates. These two phrases are brought forward to conclude this section of meaning.

Fifth, they further conclude the preceding gate of lightness and heaviness (*laghu-guru*), meaning that these two gates clarify the sense of the fivefold determination of lightness and heaviness mentioned previously.
Regarding whether there is an offense or no offense—whether four or five cases—this refers to the section on subsequent offenses and non-offenses after the initial binding.
Whether there are four or five is indeterminate: fundamentally, there are four; when conceptualization shifts, there are five.
Furthermore, regarding the three types within the intermediate degree of gravity and lightness: this refers to the meaning explained by the ancients as "breaking the upper [category] from below.
Now, concerning the gravity and lightness of the upper category of killing, there are inherently three types—namely, five definite [factors], or four, or five—which constitute the three types.
This means that although the Vinaya text establishes the gates of gravity and lightness based on the precept against killing, it applies the same framework to the precept against stealing.
Regarding the "Gate of Transgressions and Non-transgressions," this is merely a mutual citation found in the Vinaya texts. Examined from the perspective of principle, each has three positions.
Although previously the gravity of the offense was fixed as fivefold, the transgressions and non-transgressions may be either fourfold or fivefold.

From the section beginning with "Furthermore, [it] explains" below, there is an attempt to harmonize these two textual traditions so that both may possess all three positions. Gao says: "The intention of this master is to refute the previous [view]. That is to say, I..."
Within a single gate, there are three positions: namely, the gate of light and heavy [offenses], and the gate of transgression and non-transgression.

Each of these possesses five delusions regarding the transformation of perception—either four or five—thus constituting the three. This differs from the ancient masters who, within two gates, established a third position based on the gate of light and heavy offenses.

In the present system, the three positions are established across all [the gates]. The ancient masters of the past determined that a third [position] existed specifically in relation to the gate of light and heavy offenses.

Thus, five [offenses] are established. If categorized by the gate of "whether an offense was committed or not," there may be four or five; therefore, these two gates together constitute three positions.

As for the statement that "the five are established through the transformation of perception" (*saṃjñā-parāvṛtti*), this explains the preceding text. It means that because the perception is transformed, it connects to the previous state of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

thus, five are established. For example, in the case of killing a human being, one incurs *sthūlātyaya* at every step taken toward the victim. Later, upon reaching the destination, if one perceives the victim as a non-human being (*amanuṣya*), [the offense changes]. If...
If one refrains from killing, there is the preliminary offense of *duṣkṛta*; if one kills, there is likewise the preliminary offense of *duṣkṛta*. Therefore, there are definitely five [offenses].
As for the confusion regarding four or five, this refers to the external basis: if one is confused, there are two cases, namely, when one perceives a non-human being as an animal.
If one is deluded regarding a different object, there is still a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); thus, it is "either five. If one faces an insentient object, such as a stump or a log, there is no offense;
this constitutes only four. Therefore, it is said to be "either four. As for the phrase "why either four or five," what is the meaning of "either four or five"?
What are its characteristics? Thus, it says "why" (*kathaṃ*). This is intended to explain the meaning of the delusion regarding "either four or five. If one faces that which is not... [text ends].

One gives rise to delusion regarding livestock; subsequently, there is a favorable outcome, which again constitutes five propositions. There is no offense when one gives rise to delusion regarding an insentient object (a stump).

Therefore, there are only four [offenses]. As for those who give rise to delusion regarding two realms of existence—namely, non-humans and animals, which are called the "two realms"—if one kills these two realms...

One also incurs an offense; therefore, it is called "transgressing the object. As for the notion that there is no offense at all when facing insentient objects—meaning that if one kills while deludedly perceiving them as inanimate stumps—there is no offense.
Thus, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the phrase "as with the previous case of 'concealing' (*praticchādana*), so it is here as well":

this section below refutes the ancient masters' position that the category of "concealing" consists solely of offenses and non-offenses. Now, we shall distinguish the cases of "concealing" in relation to the [lower] three categories of offenses.
This concludes the section on the classification of light and heavy offenses. This passage refutes the errors of the ancient judgments.

It means that these two precepts regarding concealment are explained as being similar to the preceding section on light and heavy offenses concerning the precept against killing. Since the meaning and principle are analogous—specifically, that they may each consist of five propositions—it is said to be "categorized as before.

For example, regarding "concealing a coarse offense with a coarse [confession]": if one says it is not an offense at all, there is no transgression; however, if one commits an offense belonging to the three lower categories, [the case is different].
Regarding the phrase "if one speaks while harboring doubt," it would likewise result in a favorable outcome and should consist of five clauses.

Since this current instance of speaking while harboring doubt consists of only four clauses, it follows the previous statement regarding the perception of an inanimate object; in all such cases, there is no offense. Therefore, it contains only four [clauses]. This statement is analogous to the preceding one.
Therefore it is said that the preceding cases are likewise so. In the Vinaya, it is stated that when one commits a non-offense and conceals it, there are only four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

If one speaks according to the lower three categories of offenses (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *pāyattika*), logically there are now five permutations as in the original text, including those involving delusion or the fourth and fifth cases.

The mind is erroneously taken as the object. Why is this so? When presently perceiving two objects, their distinct characteristics are clearly manifest; yet when it comes to the process of mental engagement, errors may occur.
Thus, the mutual interference of various objects is termed "error" (*cakra*). As for what constitutes "mistake" (*bhrānti*), the mind spans both the preceding and succeeding moments.
One cannot take both as objects simultaneously. Just as the preceding mind refers to "this" and the succeeding mind refers to "that," such mental conceptions are erroneous;

therefore, they are called mistakes. Having thus distinguished the two aspects, we shall next correlate them with the four precepts. First, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct: regardless of whether it is an error or a mistake, the affliction arises from within the mind.

If, due to this circumstance, one refers to another and is mistaken, one still commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). Even if the objects are exchanged, being mistaken still constitutes a grave offense.

Section Sixteen: The Method for Repenting the Six Classes of Offenses.

Regarding the intent behind the inclusion of this section: following the explanation of the characteristics of the offenses according to their principles, it would have been appropriate to clarify the methods for repentance immediately thereafter.

However, because the essential nature and characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts are difficult to discern, this section is not placed before the explanation of those characteristics; rather, it follows them, thereby delaying its presentation.

Regarding the methods of repentance, they are now finally being revealed. Having already identified the characteristics of offenses above, the principles of maintaining and violating the precepts have been manifested (the term "manifested" means made apparent).
Nevertheless, once one has received the precepts, if one initiates a sincere and earnest resolve and strives to honor them, one would rather die than commit a transgression.

Therefore, the preceding two chapters have fully elucidated the characteristics of upholding [the precepts]. Although they discuss transgressions and cite instances of violating the Dharma, these serve to establish the practice of non-transgression for those who are single-mindedly diligent.
However, as the turbid winds of the five corruptions gradually spread and stir up the realm of dust, people have long been steeped in emotional indolence and arrogance.

If one violates the precepts according to circumstances and does not purify them, how can such a person be called wise? Therefore, this chapter extensively clarifies the methods for repentance (*sānti*).
Regarding the term "repentance" (*chàn*), the *Jīemó sū* (Karmavācanā-viniścaya) states: "Sāntimā is the Tang-language term for 'regretting the past,' and it is also called 'humility and reverence.'"

Two dialectal interpretations currently exist. Therefore, it is called *chàn-huǐ* (repentance). The character for "repentance" (*chàn*) exists as a later addition and is not part of this original text;

however, its meaning is adopted here. This means "not creating anew. Thus, "repentance" (*chàn*) refers to the cessation and severance of future faults, while "regret" (*huǐ*) refers to a sense of shame regarding past transgressions.

Because of this goodness, that which has already arisen lacks conditions, and that which is yet to arise lacks continuity. When both conditions are obstructed and continuity is severed, this is described as "practice" (*xing*).

[The term] *chū* (removal) is used. Furthermore, because this goodness brings about a pleasant retribution that eliminates the conditions for suffering, it is called "removal by retribution" (*pāochú*).

If one wishes to perform repentance (*chàn*), one should briefly understand this meaning. According to the interpretation of the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of Nanshan: "Repentance" (*chàn*) is a Sanskrit term, while "regret" (*huì*) is a Chinese term.
To cause already committed offenses to be removed is called "regret" (*huì*); to ensure that uncommitted offenses do not arise is called "repentance" (*chàn*). There is...
It is said that the Sanskrit term *kṣamā* is translated here as "patience" (*ren*). This means to tolerate, forgive, and accept one's transgressions.

If one can be single-mindedly diligent and not commit [transgressions], this is the first pure dharma (*śukladharma*); if, having committed them, one immediately repents, this is the second pure dharma.

The Sūtras state that there are two types of wise persons; this refers precisely to that meaning. The present text extensively clarifies the faults already arisen within the five categories and seven groups of offenses, providing their remedies.
Because the ritual procedures are gathered in one place, it is called the "Chapter on the Ritual for Confessing the Six Classes of Offenses.
Master Jing (Tang Yongtong) stated: In Sanskrit, this is called *āpatti-pratideśanā*. *Āpatti* means "offense" (*zui guo*) in Chinese;
*pratideśanā* means "to confess before another" (*dui ta shuo*). It refers to declaring one's own offenses with the hope that they may be purified. The older translation was "confession" (*chan*).

Repentance (*huǐ*) is not related to the confession of offenses (*shuōzuì*). Why? *Sānmó* (懺摩) is a Western [Indic] term; it corresponds to the meaning of "patience" (*kṣamā*). "Repentance" (*huǐ*) is an Eastern [Chinese] word;
its name derives from "regret. Repentance and patience are entirely unrelated. If following the Sanskrit texts, when removing an offense, one should say: "Confess the offense with a sincere mind.
In the Western lands, if there is a physical error resulting in mutual contact, for a major offense, the senior [monk] extends his hand to stroke [the junior].
With the body slightly bowed in reverent devotion and hands joined, the mouth says "kṣamā," while the mind requests forgiveness, wishing that one will not be rebuked with anger.
Therefore, when expressing thanks to another in the Vinaya, one utters the word *kṣamā*. However, if one is confessing one's own transgression, one says *deśanā*.
Although these customs have long been established through practice, matters must ultimately rely upon the Sanskrit originals.
Regarding the principle that the seeds of committed offenses must be expiated through repentance: I privately observe that when a person commits evil, there are always seeds of evil.

These are stored within the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), maintained without interruption, and by their very nature cannot be extinguished. Only upon realizing the untainted (*anāsrava*) state can they be eradicated.
What is now called "expiation through repentance" has a broad and inclusive meaning; for repentance merely suppresses karma, it cannot yet incinerate it.
It is extinguished; it is merely suppressed so that it does not arise, and for this reason it is said to be "removed. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the seeds of transgression:

these are the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*), which serve as the primary cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If this cause is severed, the subsequent fruit will not arise. Once the causal habituation has been overturned, the fruit of suffering is then lost.

Regarding the principle that one whose physical form is pure and whose mind is clean should accord with the Dharma of the Saṃgha: if one harbors internal transgressions while externally manifesting a state of complete purity, they are like a tree harboring a scorpion, which will inevitably be broken and destroyed;
such a person is not called a monk. Therefore, one must repent and eliminate these faults to accord with the true meaning of being a monk.
Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There is no one among the Saṃgha who is not pure; one who is impure is not called a monk. Seeing this now, one should immediately repent.

It thus becomes usable by the Saṃgha; therefore it is said that one should follow the same rules as the Saṃgha. Had one not previously repented, one would not have been counted among the members of the Saṃgha, which is called "not conforming to the Saṃgha's rules.
There is no dharma more swift than the mind. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Duolun), fascicle 2, it says:
"The Sūtra states that there is no dharma more swift than the mind. The mind of an ordinary person is light and fickle, whether toward the good or the evil, and cannot [be restrained]."
Because one might abandon [the mind] forever due to a momentary evil. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:

The Buddha said, "I do not see a single dharma that changes as rapidly as the mind. This is difficult to understand through analogies. Question: As other sūtras state, the monkey is used as an analogy;
why then is it said here that it is difficult to know through analogy? Answer: This statement means it is difficult to find an adequate analogy.
"Know. This does not mean knowing through analogy; it means that one can attain knowledge without requiring great effort. Zhi Liang says:

"The arising of good and evil in the mind, and its ascent or descent, occurs in an instant. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a śrāmaṇera who gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind immediately enters the stage of a bodhisattva, whereas as soon as he conceives a thought of regression, he returns to being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
According to the seventy-eighth fascicle of the *Śāstra*: "There was one..."
The Arhat, together with the śrāmaṇera, had him carry his robes and bowl as they traveled along the road. The śrāmaṇera reflected, "By what vehicle shall I enter nirvāṇa?
He then resolved, "The Buddha is the World-Honored One, the most supreme and most wondrous; I shall enter nirvāṇa by means of the Buddha-vehicle.
The teacher, knowing his mind, immediately took back the robes and bowl to carry them himself and pushed the boy from behind.

As they walked, the śrāmaṇera reflected again: "The path of the Buddha is extremely difficult. To remain long in saṃsāra and undergo immeasurable suffering—let me instead enter nirvāṇa early through the Hīnayāna.
His teacher then returned the robe and bowl to the śrāmaṇera, ordering him to carry them and follow behind.
This was repeated three times. The śrāmaṇera said to his teacher, "You are old and senile; your behavior is like that of a child at play."
"First you ordered me to walk in front, and now you have made me walk behind. Why was this change so sudden?
The Master replied, "Śrāmaṇera, when you first conceived the thought of enlightenment to become a Buddha, that mind was most precious; thus, you abide within the path of my teachers.
A person such as this should be honored even by Pratyekabuddhas, let alone by Arhats. For this reason, I pushed you to the front. You..."
His mind turned back in regret, wishing to take up the Hīnayāna, yet he had not yet attained it. "You were far from me; therefore, I have placed you behind.
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera was startled into realization: "My teacher truly knows my mind! My single resolve has already surpassed that of an arhat;

how much more so once it is fully accomplished! He immediately became firm in his resolve to enter the Mahāyāna. This statement regarding "surpassing" does not necessarily refer to a single [instance].
In all matters, one is superior; however, it is only because of the resolve to become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings that this matter is considered superior.
Since various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth have not yet been attained, how can one claim superiority?
Ji said: "There is not a single dharma more swift than the mind. According to the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, it asks: "What is heavier than the earth? What is higher than..."
"Space. What is more abundant than grass? What is swifter than wind? He replied: "The observance of precepts is weightier than the earth; the conceit of self is higher than space;
deluded thoughts are more abundant than grass; and mental volitions are swifter than wind. This is precisely their meaning.
Nevertheless, as for the fact that the masters of antiquity all administered the methods of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*), this was because they abided [by the precepts].

That is to say, since the Buddha-dharma was transmitted to the East and has reached the present day, there have been no few who established methods of confession (*sāntika*), yet many schools have adhered to divergent views.

Thus it is said that while the methods of repentance were universally applied, there were variations in their expansion, contraction, concealment, and manifestation. Sengsheng stated: "The masters of antiquity, such as when taking a nun’s robe or other goods for sale, once the wealth entered their hands..."

Furthermore, to commit a transgression of greater duration is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*). For example, regarding the first category of precepts on sexual misconduct, repentance through training is permitted, whereas for theft and other offenses it is not;

this is called "decrease" (*hrāsa*). The Buddha said that if one has committed an offense and is unable to repent, nor can perform a formal confession according to the Dharma, then one who has already committed it should disclose it to others, saying, "I repent," while looking toward those who have not yet committed it, vowing with single-minded diligence not to do so, thereby severing the continuity of the offense.
The mind: that which causes what is not [yet] arisen to arise is called *chàn* (repentance).
*Gé* means correctness and measure. As for the term "mirror," it means illumination. Regarding the clarification of gain and loss through the capacity and the object, this is established as follows:
The person who is able to repent and the presiding master (*śāstr*) who receives the repentance both attain this as "observance" (*dhāraṇa*) and lose it through "transgression" (*āpatti*).

It is clear that the person who repents and the object of repentance must recognize what constitutes observance and transgression. My own view is that this may also be understood as clarifying both the repentance of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
"Able" refers to one's own mind; "object" refers to deluded karma. When the sins that are the objects of repentance are extinguished, it is called [attainment].
