Regarding the practice of concealment (*parivāsa*): it is called "provisional" (*jia*) because it can be practiced only when there is a preceding community of monks (*saṃgha*), and cannot be practiced where no such community exists.

This refers to the practice of *parivāsa* and so forth; as for the time, it is determined by how many people are present within the boundary (*sīmā*), for it is performed based on the specific number of persons present.
The phrase "at least one person" means that while actually performing the *parivāsa*, one must announce (*śrāvayati*) what is being done.
Regarding the Sangha: at the time of the *poṣadha*, one must inform the Sangha that a guest has arrived; this is accomplished simply by having one pure monk within the boundary (*sīmā*).
When it comes to the *poṣadha* itself, one enters the midst of the Sangha and declares, "I am practicing concealment (*parivāsa*)," and so forth;
it is not necessary to make this declaration every day. However, when practicing the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*), one must declare it daily. Next, regarding the single person facing the Sangha...

Regarding the *ṣaḍrātra-dharma* (the six-night rite): it must be performed in the presence of at least four persons before it can be attained. This is because the six nights must be spent staying within the *saṃgha*, and one must announce [one's status] to the *saṃgha* every day.
As for the single-session rite for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna-ekāsana-dharma*), this refers to performing the ritual procedure all at once with a group of twenty.

Since the procedure is completed in a single session, the assembly disperses immediately; why labor over it again at a later time? It is essential that one must still announce [one's intention] to the people.
This is because they have already been purified.

Regarding the fourth section, the treatise states: "Observing the training rules associated with karma. Master Li says: This refers to the three grades—great, medium, and small—according to the magnitude of the matter;

thus, there are *jñapti-karman* (motions consisting of a single motion), *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motions consisting of one motion and one proclamation), *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motions consisting of one motion and three proclamations), and so forth. Now, the Saṃgha observes the preceding acts of repentance.

Regarding "large and small": whichever *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is employed, it must correspond appropriately to the matter at hand; thus, it is said that one should "observe the correspondence with the action. The training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is explained as before.

As for this *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (residual offense) procedure being categorized in the "superior grade" (*uttama-pakṣa*), this means that although the matters are immeasurable, they are divided into three grades of dharma.

Three types of *karmavācanā* correspond to these three grades: namely, the *jñapti* (motion) corresponds to the inferior grade, and the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation) corresponds to the [middle] grade.

The middle grade [of the *jñapti-caturtha*] should be the superior grade. This treatment for residual offenses (*śeṣa-āpatti*) is a superior *karmavācanā*, and thus it must strictly employ the *jñapti-caturtha* procedure.
Therefore, regarding the application of the middle-grade method, the positions [of the stages] are at most four. Lì says: "This is spoken of merely in terms of the stages;

if one considers the actual matter and the timing according to the *Pudgala-vastu* of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, there are seven periods for repentance through the upper and lower practices. First, the period of requesting and obtaining..."

1. At the time of concealing the offense; 2. at the time of practicing concealment; 3. at the time of attaining the original date; 4. at the time of practicing the original date; 5. at the time of six nights; 6.

at the time of practicing for six nights; 7. at the time of expiation (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). Regarding "punishment on the original date" (*mūlāpakarṣa*): it means returning to the original date to undergo punishment;
hence it is called "punishment on the original date. I do not know what the Indic characters for this term are. This refers to one who has personally violated the rules of practice, and...

If one violates the Sangha’s command, they shall be punished and ordered to return to their original status. As for those who have newly committed an offense, they must be disciplined regardless of whether the previous offense was concealed or not.

Regarding what is called "punishment according to the original date" (*bon-nichi-tai*): suppose a person previously committed an offense and concealed it for ninety days, completing the required period of probation (*parivāsa*).

If they subsequently commit a new offense, the prior legal process is nullified; they must once again begin the *parivāsa* from the first day. Therefore, it is termed "punishment according to the original date."

Regarding the establishment of the *pūrvavastu-mānatta* (probation for past offenses) and so forth on grounds such as "with concealment" (*sāvaraṇa*) or "without concealment" (*anāvaraṇa*), Lì (Dali) says:
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) is a term for a location. This means that if there is concealment, one undergoes the *pūrvavastu*; *pūrvavastu* refers to dwelling separately (*pṛthag-vāsa*).

One must necessarily undergo the method of dwelling separately for the duration of a night; therefore, it is called *pūrvavastu*. In the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, this is termed *parivāsa*. If there is no concealment..."

One proceeds directly to the *mānatta* (probation); four parts of this are termed *mānatta*. Regarding the statement "there are three dharmas for one who has concealed [the offense] while practicing," these refer to the *parivāsa* (seclusion), the six-night *mānatta*, and the rehabilitation (*ābṛti*).
As for the statement "there are two dharmas for one who has not concealed [the offense]," this excludes the *parivāsa*.

In the *Lìwèn* (Questions of Lì), it is asked: "Among the five categories of offenses, why is the first category [pārājika] and the last three categories [saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, and śaikṣa-dharmas] not subject to treatment for concealment? Only the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*..."

Regarding the offenses: why are they treated individually? The commentary explains: the transgressions of the first section are so grave that they cannot be remedied through repentance; what need is there, then, to punish those secondary or derivative offenses?
As for the three sections below, since their fundamental nature is light, they do not require communal repentance; one simply performs a confession for the concealment of the offense.
One does not deal with the branches; this article is the most serious among those involving repentance.

To feign being a monk and thereby bring about extinction [of the Dharma] is an offense of concealment for which a severe punishment should be imposed, so that body and mind may be humbled and the practice of the path thereby brought to fulfillment.

From this point onward, the ritual for performing the *pratideśanīya* (confession) is correctly explained. Regarding the statement in the Vinaya, "One name has many kinds because the bases (*āśraya*) differ," [Daoshi] states:
"The ancient commentators explain that 'the bases differ' means that the preparatory offenses (*prayoga*) of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class are distinct from the actual *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses themselves."
This interpretation is not correct. The commentary on the *Śīla* (Lìshū) explains: "As for 'one name,' it is because they share the same name, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

As for 'many kinds,' it refers to the distinctions among the thirteen [offenses]. As for 'abiding in distinct differences,' it means that within the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, there are four categories."

Because their constituent elements (*dhātu*) differ, it is said that their "abidings" (*sthiti*) are distinct. This is intended to clarify that because the categories of their natures (*svabhāva*) are different, they are called distinct abidings.
Furthermore, it is said that the thirteen residual offenses (*śeṣa-āpatti*) are so called because they belong to the same category as the four grave prohibitions (*catur-uttara-pārājika*).
This commentary (*chao*) cites the Vinaya text in brief. The Vinaya states: "There is a bhikṣu who commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;

he knows the number of days [of concealment], whether he concealed it or did not conceal it, whether his concealment was equal or unequal, whether his concealment was of one kind or many kinds, and whether it was of a nature that is intrinsic or non-intrinsic, as well as its various distinctions.

The *Li shu* (Commentary by Daoshi) explains: "Concealment (*paticchādana*) means that after committing the offense, one does not confess it. Non-concealment means that after the circumstances have changed, one returns [to confession]."
It constitutes a concealment; therefore, it is called "equal concealment" because the duration of the day varies. Regarding "one name for many types," this has already been explained previously.
As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): among the thirteen *śeṣa* (residual) offenses, ten are intrinsic precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), which are termed "intrinsic nature.

There are three precepts—namely, the two [types of] building a hut and matchmaking—which are prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*); these three are termed "non-intrinsic nature. Regarding "abiding in distinctness":

This has already been explained above. The purpose of citing this passage in the present *Chao* (Excerpts) is to provide scriptural proof for the necessity of knowing the characteristics of the various categories (*nāma-jāti*).
One must not simply state, "I have requested [the confession of] purity," on the grounds that one thereby knows the full extent [of the period].

This clarifies that one must know the length of time—whether days, months, or years—since the attainment of purity. If one merely says "from the time of purity" without specifying the days, months, or years, it is insufficient.
Regarding the counting [of days] while practicing *parivāsa*: one who practices it in this manner does not know the point of completion, nor do they know by which month and year it will be fulfilled.

As for one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense after being formally admonished three times within the assembly, it is said that this refers to having completed the offense by violating the Sangha’s three admonitions.

Even if many people know that the offense is complete, one must still confess it again; otherwise, it constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*). Therefore, one knows that although many may know the offense has reached its end...
Regarding the requirement to confess (*āviṣkaraṇa*): it is established that even if many people are fully aware [of the offense], one must ultimately confess it to oneself.

As stated above, if one does not proclaim it despite being exhorted against it, then the transgression constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*). Is this not indeed called "concealment" even when many people already know of it?
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the established ritual for repentance (*kṣamā-vidhi*). From this point forward, the general and specific methods of repentance are clarified;
the textual characteristics therein will become somewhat more evident. As for the eight matters beginning with the formal announcement (*jñapti*), they shall be explained in their own context below.
Regarding the case where a guest arrives and is sent away: [the commentary] states that even when sending a guest away, one must say, "Venerable sir, please go out;
I am a person practicing *parivāsa* (probation), and two people may not dwell together.

Regarding the rule that two persons undergoing *parivāsa* may not sit on the same bed: [the commentary] states this refers to two individuals practicing *parivāsa*. This Vinaya merely prohibits [this].
Regarding dwelling in the same room: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not permit ordinary co-seating, as it states that the respective schools differ in their positions.

As for the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-saṃgraha* that one may obtain twenty-five nights by informing the Saṃgha to suspend the practice—even up to the six-night rite—it means that while one is undergoing the formal parivāsa (probation) and the six-night period, one may inform the Saṃgha to suspend the practice for twenty-five nights.
It merely requires that the preceding conditions be such as to produce good and extinguish evil. [My] private opinion is this: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not limit the number of days.

Even after the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, if one has not yet formally announced the practice (*śuklavidhi*), there is no fault regarding staying overnight, nor has one forfeited the thirty-five matters.
If the formal announcement of the practice has already been made, the opposite of the above should be understood.

Regarding "going to another monastery without informing [the resident monks]," etc.: according to the Vinaya, there are eight matters for which a person undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation) must not fail to inform others;

for each failure, one loses one night [of the probation] and incurs one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). As for "going to another monastery without informing," this means that when traveling from this monastery to another, upon seeing other bhikṣus, one must inform them.
Failing to inform results in losing one night and incurring one *duṣkṛta*. Second, there is the case of a visiting bhikṣu...

Regarding "entering the boundary without informing [the assembly] and so forth": one loses the protection of the night and incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one informs a guest, there is no need to convene the assembly again;
this is because the host has already made the disclosure through that notification. Third, regarding "leaving the boundary for a reason without informing [the assembly]": [one incurs an offense].
This refers to monks on a road between two non-white (i.e., secular) realms; thus the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one must announce [one's presence] upon seeing a bhikṣu on the road.

Regarding the fourth point—that there is no offense for walking slowly within a monastery without announcing—this means that if one is traveling quickly on a road or within a monastery and does not announce it, there is no fault, provided the person ahead is moving so fast that one cannot catch up. This refers to a visiting bhikṣu (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*).
Upon entering the boundary, one must announce it. If a guest travels in haste and cannot catch up, there is no offense.

If one travels slowly and could have caught up, yet fails to announce it, one loses one night and incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense. The mention of "within the monastery" excludes those outside the monastery;
the mention of "traveling slowly" excludes traveling in haste. This refers to cases where someone passes through this boundary from afar while traveling quickly. [The five types of illness.]

Regarding "not sending a messenger to inform": According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a person undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation) should enter the midst of the Saṃgha during the *poṣadha* ceremony and three times personally confess their offense.
If they are ill, they should send a messenger to the Saṃgha and announce: "The person undergoing *parivāsa* is ill and cannot come; may the Saṃgha take note.
The remaining cases of six, seven, or eight [offenses] may be understood accordingly. (The above is the explanation by Li). Question: If one commits eight matters simultaneously on a single day...
Does this mean that eight nights are forfeited simultaneously, or is it only one night? Answer: Violating one matter at the outset results in the forfeiture of one night;

if one commits further violations subsequently, there are no further nights to forfeit, though one incurs offenses. Even if many matters are violated, one cannot be deprived of eight nights all at once, because they occurred on the same day.
If one violates eight rules on the eighth day, one forfeits one night for that [eighth] day. (The commentary notes: "Already obtained.")

Regarding "not losing what has not yet been attained" and "not establishing [what has been attained]": it is established that if one has previously attained [a state], even if a subsequent loss occurs and intervenes, the prior attainment is not lost.
However, if it has not yet been attained, it does not constitute a prior count.
Regarding the statement, "On another day, it differs from that for the monks": Zhi Li states that this means the preceding eight matters all employ this same formal announcement (*jñapti*).

In the current text, however, the announcement is restricted solely to addressing the visiting bhikṣu; the other cases—sending a messenger to announce and walking slowly within the monastery to announce—are excluded.
All of these employ this same formula; hence it says, "the remaining various *śuddhaka* [announcements]," etc.

The announcement made at the time of the *poṣadha* also employs this same formula, differing only in that the term "monks" (*bhikṣu*) is changed to "days" (*divasa*). As for practicing the *parivāsa* (probation), one need only know how to provide offerings to pure (*viśuddha*) bhikṣus.

Regarding the performance of the first eight matters: for those [matters] that do not require daily announcement (*ārocana*), one may practice them for six nights; however, for those that must be announced daily, one must announce them every morning.
If I am now going to the place where the preceding bhikṣu is, and if I go there and then depart, I shall stand and say:

"If I reach the aforementioned place, I must announce my practice so as not to lose the night's residence. If, however, I suddenly fail to reach the aforementioned place and there is no bhikṣu on the road, then [if I stay] overnight...

The night is lost. Furthermore, one who commits an offense must intentionally reflect; otherwise, having abandoned the practice of the *dharmas*, it is clear that upon seeing a bhikṣu, there is no need for a formal announcement (*jñapti*).

If one were to make such an announcement while on the road as described above, it would mean that one had already abandoned the practice of the *dharmas* while previously within the boundary (*sīmā*).
Since one has already completed the abandonment of the practice of the *dharmas* within the boundary, there is no need for an announcement when subsequently seeing people. However—
Upon arriving at another monastery, one should again seek out those monks who practice the observance; this is the same as the previous day within one's own original boundary. Ryō states:

when performing the rite of relinquishing the observance (*śikṣāpada*), if the place of practice is not restricted to either [the original or the new location], one may relinquish it here and resume practicing here, or practice elsewhere.

Whether one relinquishes it in one place and practices it in another, or practices it in this very place, there is no hindrance; it is sufficient that the calculation of the days continues until completion.
Regarding the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* stating that a *dharmabhikṣu* may perform the *parivāsa* (probation) as described above in the fifth section:
my own view is that this must refer to what was stated in the preceding passage concerning "speaking by way of a provisional object (*prajñapti*) while practicing. The former...

"From one person down to a single individual" refers to the text itself. Regarding "discarding the small and adopting the great," [the Master] establishes that this refers to the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) scriptures based on the names of the Buddhas, which are termed "great.

Regarding "the paths of karma are left to your own quiet reflection," [the Master] establishes that while for karmic offenses you may perform repentance based on names, contemplation, and intellectual understanding, for offenses that violate the formal precepts (*śikṣāpada*), you must rely on... [the formal ritual].
Regarding the Vinaya confession: one must not harbor shame or deceit; for a deluded mind that clings to its own logic, there is ultimately no method for extinction [of offenses].

As for the various masters who establish their principles and mutually add points of agreement or difference, Master Sheng says: "Some masters do not perform the *parivāsa* (probation), but instead perform only the six-night purification of the offense (*ṣaḍrātra-pāpadeśanā*).

Some masters do not even perform the six nights, but proceed directly to the purification of the offense. If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the separate residence (*parivāsa*) and so forth are not required.
Lì says: "However, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong) does indeed contain the relevant textual passage. Even if it is not put into practice here, it is still permissible;
one may still incur the offense of 'not doing what is proper' (*na karaṇīya*), and so forth. If you take that text to challenge this principle and insist that they must correspond, Lì argues:

you are taking the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to challenge the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen). Since that text permits one to receive absolution (*pārivāsika*) even without practicing the formal period of *parivāsa*, this Vinaya requires that it be practiced."
As for this, how should one now choose between what to adopt and what to discard? It is said that when the present monastic community examines past conditions, both [approaches] may be applicable.

Within the texts of the various *karmavācanas*, it is necessary to refer to the specific matter at hand. Fearing that the matter might not correspond to the formal rule (*dharma*), one might alter the traditional practice; however, such concerns are unfounded.

This means that if one has already been practicing *parivāsa* (probation) but the allotted days are not yet complete, or if one has not practiced it at all, then to recite the formal declaration according to the text, saying "I have completed the *parivāsa*," is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*).
One should instead say, "I have completed [the practice for] so many days; now the Sangha grants me [the remainder of] so many days," and so forth.
If the days of practice are complete and one recites according to the rule, this is called "established practice" (*sthita-parivāsa*). Thus, one knows that it is indeed a practice.

Regarding the removal of the offense through the six-night probation for one whose period has not yet expired: one must state the specific number of days and so forth; one may not merely recite the old formula.

If the Upādhyāya says, "Because this person’s days of concealment were many, they were unable to complete the practice," and if—relying on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations)—one still permits them to be released from the remainder of the days even though the practice was not completed, then one may only record it within the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) as follows:
Once the days of the *parivāsa* (concealment) have been completed, one may not say that they "have been finished. This applies to all subsequent *karmas*. Therefore, it is said:
"the days of the *parivāsa* have already been performed.
The explanation of the ritual for confession is hereby concluded. From this point forward, the second section clarifies the method for bestowing the *mānatva*. If...
Regarding the two cases where both offenses are grave and both require *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning):

Sengli states that according to the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahīśāsaka*, and *Sarvāstivāda* Vinayas, if one commits a grave offense while already under discipline for a previous one, both are treated with *mūlāpakarṣa*. However, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika* Vinaya, they are not combined;

rather, one simply fulfills the remaining days of the original period. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika* text says: "A person practicing *parivāsa* says to a bhikṣu, 'I have committed an offense. [The bhikṣu] asks: 'What was the original offense?'"
[Question: Regarding the intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), what is the answer? [Answer: It is an intermediate offense. [Question: When was it committed? [Answer:

It was committed during the period of *parivāsa*. [Question: Was it concealed or not? [Answer: It was concealed. [He says: "Venerable sir, having previously undergone *parivāsa* in accordance with the Dharma, I have fallen short by one night.

Now that I have concealed it, I must again request *parivāsa* and undergo it together [with the original period]. This is called requesting *pārivāsika-parivāsa* (supplementary *parivāsa*). [This is] the joint performance of *parivāsa*.

*Vibhāṣā*: They undergo the *ṣaḍrātra-parivāsa* (six-night probation) together, and they emerge from the offense together. Next, suppose one person, during the course of the six nights, commits another offense and conceals it.
He says, "Venerable sir, I have already completed the *parivāsa* and have duly performed the six nights;

however, regarding this one night of the six nights that I have now concealed, I should again request *parivāsa*. Having performed it, I shall again request the six nights. This [period] should be combined.

[He] practices. This is called "separately begging for separate residence" (*pārivāsika*). He practices separate residence; he separately begs for six nights; he undergoes the six nights together; and they undergo the purification from the offense (*ābhisamācaraṇa*) together.
Next, there is one person who, having practiced until the completion of the purification from the offense, says: "I have committed an offense. [The others] ask: "When was it committed? He answers:

"It was committed during the period of separate residence. They ask: "Was it concealed or not? He answers: "It was concealed. [The others] should say to him: "Since you have already completed the separate residence, practice according to the Dharma; however—"

One night was missing; the six-night parivāsa (probation) for the removal of the offense was not accomplished. Now, he requests a further *parivāsa* for this offense. This is called "requesting separately and practicing separately.

[The rule is that] one should request the *parivāsa* collectively and practice it collectively for six nights to accomplish the removal of the offense. Next, there was one person who, while undergoing the probation, stated that he had committed an offense before the removal of the offense was complete.
When asked, "Where did you commit the offense? he replied, "I committed an offense during the interval of the six nights and concealed it," and so on, until he spoke thus: "The removal..."

The offense is not established. According to this procedure for performing *pārivāsika*, it must necessarily reach the full number of days before it is completed; thus, it differs from the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Examining this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* along with other schools, there are two types of *mūlāpakarṣa* (punishment by returning to the beginning): the first refers to when one commits an offense while performing the *parivāsa* (probation).
One must perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (penance of returning to the beginning). Second, if one commits an offense while performing the six-night penance, it is called the "six-night *mūlāpakarṣa*.

For other details, refer to separate expositions. According to the commentary (*śāstra*), there are great differences between this and methods such as *praticchādana* (concealment); for the time being, there are four categories.

There are four cases regarding the acquisition of legal procedures (*dharma*) for offenses: first, one offense and the acquisition of one procedure; second, many offenses and the acquisition of one procedure;

third, many offenses and the acquisition of many procedures; fourth, one offense and the acquisition of many procedures. Regarding "one offense and the acquisition of one procedure": this refers to, for example, having committed one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and knowing it was concealed until its completion;

one then grants him the single procedure of concealment (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), followed by the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra-carita*), and finally the rehabilitation from the offense (*ābṛhaṇa*). Regarding "many offenses and the acquisition of one procedure": this refers to having committed a multitude [of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses].

"Many *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. This refers to the practice of three dharmas. For example, if one previously commits one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it for one, two, or three days, and subsequently commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, that too may be concealed for another two or three days, continuing even until ten *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses have been committed.
Later, when requesting the formal rite (*yācanā*), one is granted [the probation] according to the length of the days of concealment.

Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If on the first day of the month one commits one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and recognizes it as such while forming the intention to conceal it, [and so on] until..."

If one confesses [the offense] to another on the second day after having committed it, and subsequently commits one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and so on up to confessing on the tenth day after having committed ten such offenses, and each has been concealed for one night, one must undergo ten separate periods of *parivāsa* (probation), etc.

Alternatively, three such legal acts (*dharmas*) may also be treated as a single period of *parivāsa*, etc. If one grants these three legal acts as a single *parivāsa*, etc., this constitutes the second section above.
"Many offenses, one attainment of the dharma" refers to cases such as performing the ten types of *parivāsa* (probation) and other threefold dharmas; this is the aforementioned third gate:
"many offenses, many attainments of the dharma. Regarding the fourth case, "one offense, many attainments of the dharma," this is determined based on whether the offense was remembered or not.

For example, if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it for many days, later confessing it while remembering only half of it, and the Saṃgha grants the *praticchādana-dharma* (the rite of concealment) for that portion;

if one subsequently remembers more and requests again, the Saṃgha may grant the *praticchādana-dharma* once more. In this manner, as each further portion is remembered, the rite may be granted repeatedly.

Is it not the case that for one who has committed many offenses, there is a method for concealment? However, at the time of prior concealment, one may receive the rite of concealment either individually or perform it separately;

or one may receive it individually and perform it collectively. If, however, one is to undergo the six-night penance for purification of the offense, it is mandatory that the begging, the granting, and the performance must all be done collectively.

It is determined that all cases are common. If one has completed two *dharmas* (formal procedures) for the removal of guilt (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) over six nights, and only then remembers what was previously forgotten, this six-night removal of guilt is not established;
one must necessarily perform the six-night removal of guilt again, because the concealment performed for the first offense was insufficient.
Therefore, the offense does not emerge. This differs from the previous *Mahīśāsaka* text, where multiple offenses are combined and, by performing the rite together, the act is accomplished.

However, in the *Dharmaguptaka*, even when there are many offenses, a single dharma is still accomplished; it is not only the case with the *Mahīśāsaka*. Thus, when this school performs the *parivāsa* (probation), if one recalls a second offense while in the process, the Buddha said:

One who has obtained *parivāsa* (concealment) shall undergo *parivāsa* together with others; they shall all receive the six-night penance together, perform the six-night penance together, and together emerge from the offense.

This is the rule. Next, there should be one who has completed the *parivāsa*; if he also remembers [the offense] during that time, he should likewise be granted the *parivāsa*. This refers to obtaining *parivāsa* separately and performing the *parivāsa* separately.

The three heads mentioned above each have three types of persons beneath them; since there are three grades for each person, there are nine grades under one head.
With three heads, there are a total of twenty-seven persons. Thus, for each offense and each attainment of the Dharma, there are twenty-seven phrases.
There are twenty-seven phrases concerning many offenses and obtaining the Dharma once; likewise twenty-seven phrases concerning many offenses and obtaining the Dharma many times;
and twenty-seven phrases concerning one offense and obtaining the Dharma many times. Combining these four sets of twenty-seven results in one hundred and eight phrases.
Next, regarding the four stages, it is explained that during the period of formal practice for concealment (*paryuṣaṇā*), there are one hundred and eight phrases. [The period of] practice...
The concealment [of the offense] concludes with one hundred and eight phrases; the period of practicing the six-night penance also consists of one hundred and eight phrases;
and the conclusion of the six-night penance likewise consists of one hundred and eight phrases. Altogether, these comprise four hundred and thirty-two phrases. Li asked, saying:
Regarding a single offense, it may be said that the number of days is known, or it may be said that the number is unknown; these two cases are plausible.
Since it is stated to be "one offense," how could there be a case where both knowing and not knowing are combined into a single phrase? Answer: It is possible.

For example, one might commit a single offense and conceal it for one year, yet clearly remember the specific dates from within the last hundred days, while being unable to recall the number of days prior to those hundred days.
It cannot be definitively determined; this is precisely the meaning. If one intends to administer punishment, then the longest period must be taken into account.
Regarding the terms "concealed" and "unconcealed," this phrase refers to concealment as measured by days.

For example, if one commits one, two, or three offenses and conceals them for one hundred days, but now confesses only fifty of those days, this constitutes concealing half and revealing half. Therefore, it is called "concealed and unconcealed."

Furthermore, once a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has been committed, if one subsequently remembers it, concealment (*praticchādana*) is established; if one does not remember it, concealment is not established. If one recognizes the offense and has no doubt, concealment is established;

if one does not recognize it or has doubt, concealment is not established. If one conceals it in such a manner, concealment is established; if one does not conceal it in such a manner, there is no concealment.

Moreover, if, after committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one conceals an offense belonging to another category [of offenses], one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. In this case, *parivāsa* (probation) need not be granted; rather, having performed confession, one should be granted the six-night *mānāpya* directly.
This refers to the expiation of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the procedure for practicing *mānatva*. From here on, the actual method for the expiation of offenses is clarified.

Regarding the phrase "like the *aśoka* flower," I privately identify this as the *utpala* (or *udumbara*) flower. Regarding the phrase "returning to being a pigeon," Fazhi states that it refers to one who has much lust.
Such a person dies and enters hell; even after emerging from there, because their karma of sexual misconduct is not yet exhausted, they are reborn as this creature.
The preceding explanation of the method for expiating the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is now complete.

The Third Method for Confessing *Thullaccaya*: If a light offense arises from the first category (*āpatti*) and a heavy offense arises from the second category, it is established that the light offense refers to the *thullaccaya* of the preliminary stage (*upakkama*) of the first category, while the heavy offense is equivalent to the *thullaccaya* of the proximate preliminary stage (*āsanna-upakkama*) of the second category.

If one wishes to repent, it may be done outside the boundary (*sīmā*) with four persons. Taking four coins constitutes a heavy *thullaccaya*; this is a primary offense (*mūlāpatti*). If the original...

Regarding "one who intends to steal five but obtains only four": this constitutes a grave *pārājika* offense. Because it involves the preparatory effort (*upakrama*) of a heavy case, this is termed a "causal *thullaccaya*" (*hetu-thullaccaya*).

If one originally intended to steal four but obtains four, this is termed a "resultant *thullaccaya*" (*phala-thullaccaya*); this offense is somewhat lighter. As for "breaking the *saṃgha* through formal procedure" (*karmabhedaka-saṃgha*):

it requires that they be within the same boundary (*sīmā*), that two groups perform the ritual, and that each gives rise to a divergent view; furthermore, it is not [necessarily] a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Jingyun says: Gayāśīrṣa Mountain is three hundred *li* from Rājagṛha City; it constitutes a single boundary (*sīmā*).

As for "one who practices nakedness," this refers to seeing the Buddha while naked. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* rule that one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for tearing one's three robes out of anger or destroying a stupa, and that this may be expiated by a single person—Jingyun says: "This stupa is a stupa of a human being, not a stupa or temple of the Buddha."
This is also a case of another person [acting]. Regarding the fact that in the first two sections, teaching others to commit offenses of *thullaccaya* (grave offenses) is all considered consummated:

this means that when one instructs another to commit sexual misconduct or theft, or instructs another to commit a *saṅghādisesa* (offense requiring suspension), if the instructed person carries it out, the instructor incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
These are all resultant offenses; therefore, they are termed "ultimate. If one instructs another to commit theft, it is a grave *duṣkṛta*;
if one instructs another to commit a *sthūlātyaya*, it is a light *duṣkṛta*. Therefore, it is said that their gravity or lightness is as described above.

Regarding the rules for the great assembly, the small assembly, and the single individual: it is established that they depend on ten categories. Specifically, eight people constitute a great assembly;
four people constitute a small assembly. Furthermore, four or five people constitute a great assembly, while two or three people constitute a small assembly.
One person refers to the *pratimokṣa* (face-to-face) rule.

Regarding the "single announcement" (*śuddha-śrāvaṇa*) followed by the "confession before another" (*pratideśanā*): this clarifies that although a formal assembly of the *saṃgha* is required for the *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *sthūlātyaya* offenses, one may instead personally invite another individual to perform the confession before them.
The three types of confession mentioned above constitute the methods for repenting the three categories of offenses: *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *sthūlātyaya*.

"Ensuring that there is no concealment between the two parties" means: the person receiving the confession is able to examine the actual facts, and the person performing the confession fully reveals what they have transgressed;
this constitutes having no concealment between the two. Regarding "confessing all three types of retribution together," Zhiyi says:
it is to confess the past, future, and present together. My own opinion is: first, fixed retribution; second, unfixed retribution; third, [unfixed retribution].

Regarding the fixed and unfixed retributions, it is further said that these are the retributions of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

The retribution of the present life is easily understood, referring to such things as physical illness and suffering. The retribution of the next life refers to entering hell. The retribution of subsequent lives refers to emerging from hell and becoming an animal or other forms of existence.

Furthermore, it is said that the three types of retribution correspond to the obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The above explains the repentance for *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
The section on prohibitions is concluded.
The fourth [section] concerns the confession of *pāyattika* offenses.

Now, since one must maintain and uphold all received precepts, the reason for requiring confession after an offense has been committed is that having incurred such a transgression can cause a practitioner to fall into the Avīci Hell for a certain number of years.
Because the Buddha possesses great compassion, he teaches and commands that one must perform repentance (*pratideśanā*), for this can extinguish such karma and restore one to purity.

As for the statement that "one need not face an external object," this means that one simply destroys [the offense] within oneself, without having to relinquish it before the two objects of the monastic community (*saṃgha*) and the laity.

Regarding the two types of "precious precepts" (*ratna-śīla*): the first refers to the two precepts concerning the possession and trade of precious objects; these require one to renounce the precepts and return to lay life.

The single precept concerning begging for a bowl requires that it be done at one's original residence and in the midst of the Saṃgha. This means that at the time of relinquishing and repenting, one must not go to another territory or a *sīmā-kṣetra*;
it must be at the very place where the offense was committed, and the relinquishment must be made before the assembly of monks, not before an individual.

This is the method for manifesting that within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there is one pure person to whom [the bowl] is entrusted; it is because a fine bowl is to be entrusted to the Sangha as a whole.

Regarding the twenty-six remaining locations that apply to both parties, it is clearly established: if one commits an offense within this boundary, one may perform the confession by going to another boundary.
Furthermore, it is permissible both inside and outside the boundary; therefore, they are said to "apply to both. Each has its own...
Regarding the phrase "the intention is as follows," it is like cutting and destroying silk floss so that it no longer requires an external object; the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"Silk clothing is contrary to the Dharma, for its substance involves the destruction of life. If it is not cut and destroyed, how can this craving be exhausted? As for why the two treasures [gold and silver] are confronted with the laity:

their substance is precious and increases craving, which is utterly unsuitable for the possessions and use of those who have left the household life. Therefore, they are to be relinquished to the laity to manifest what is not the Way.
Regarding the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), one may fully understand their general and specific applications in relation to the Saṃgha.

As for the meaning of "requesting robes" and "receiving robes," it applies both to cases where there is an offense and where there is no offense. This is clearly established by the fact that these two precepts involve both offenses and non-offenses.

Specifically, requesting robes from one who is not a relative constitutes an offense, whereas requesting them from a relative does not. Furthermore, regarding the loss or theft of the three robes: at the time of requesting, one loses the three; at the time of receiving, one [receives] the three.
Then there is an offense. Receiving two [robes] is not an offense. Losing two and receiving two is an offense. Receiving one is not an offense. Jing (Jingxiu) says:
"Are there also offenses regarding extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and being separated from robes (*nissīva-cīvara*)? The present text merely cites one or two examples.

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics of long-term [retention] do not exceed five types," Ji says: first, a long-term bowl; second, long-term medicine; third, the thirty-day robe; fourth, the one-month robe;
and fifth, the urgent gift robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*). These must necessarily be formally accepted and maintained.

Regarding the point that "if one has a robe-bag, a pouch, or a cloth, it need not be purified (*asuddhika*)," Li states: the bags for the three robes and the pouch for the bowl do not require purification. The text says: "containing robes."
"Storage vessels" refers to the name for the bags for the three robes; these are the storage vessels that contain the robes, bowl, and so forth.
Regarding the sixteen items that a *bhikṣuṇī* must undergo the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) for: there are two cauldrons, two jars, four basins, four lids, and four ladles.

The reason for this is clarified within the section on the "Lowering of the Alms Bowl" (*pātra*). Regarding the fourth case, "entering [the category of] other *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses involving impure wealth," the established view is as follows:
This refers to clothing that has already been subject to a prior offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, such as taking a nun’s robe or robes obtained through trade and the like;

once these have entered one's possession, the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* has already been incurred, and there is no further transgression regarding exceeding the limit of storage. If an ancient master were to judge that there is still a further limit to be exceeded, [that would be incorrect].
Regarding the offense of *atireka* (excess): we do not treat it in the same way here. As for why wealth cannot be relinquished twice and why offenses are not doubly incurred, Jing asked:

"If one takes a nun’s robe and exceeds the limit without declaring it, there is no offense of *atireka* because there is no repeated offense. For what reason, then, does one incur three *pāyattikas* for having a nun wash, dye, and beat it?
Answer: This refers to the simultaneous performance of the preliminary preparations; because one dispatched [the nun] to wash, dye, and beat [the robe] at the same time, one incurs all three.

Regarding the offense: if one has already sent [the garment] for washing, a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is incurred; if one subsequently sends it for dyeing or beating, only a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) is incurred.

As for "a single offense with separate forfeiture that differs from other schools," this refers to cases such as taking a nun’s robe: if ten days have passed since it entered one's possession, when one now proceeds to perform the forfeiture and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*), one incurs only the offense of taking a nun’s robe and no further offense of exceeding the time limit.
Therefore, it is called a "single offense. One simply performs the forfeiture by treating it as a nun’s robe.
It is unnecessary to say that it constitutes an offense of "excess" (*atireka*) requiring forfeiture; therefore, it is called a "separate forfeiture. *Li* says:

"Just as with merchandise for sale, it is not subject to the rite of *śuddhi* (purification), nor is it tainted by the status of 'excess. However, the ancient masters said: 'Excess robes can indirectly taint merchandise for sale.

This means that if one previously possessed an excess robe that had not yet been forfeited, and subsequently obtained merchandise for sale, that merchandise would not be tainted by the prior excess robe. Now...

These cases are not the same. There are certainly no robes that have been stained by improper means or obtained through trade; once they have entered one's possession, there is no further increase in their length.

How, then, could they be considered "stained by excess"? Since the robe cannot be relinquished twice, the offense is not doubly incurred. If one were to follow the former judgment, at the time of relinquishing and confessing [the offense]...

One should perform the relinquishment twice. First, one should sell this single robe; after the relinquishment has been made and the payment returned, one then performs the formal act of relinquishment.
Since there is no such principle [in the Vinaya], there is no secondary defilement (*pārājika-anuśaṃsa*). (This is my own interpretation.)
Regarding the passage on mutual contamination already explained above, it is as clarified at the beginning of the thirty articles in the *Śīla-varga*.

"It does not apply to the three robes" means that if one stays overnight separated from a robe, one commits an offense requiring forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) regarding whichever specific robe was left behind; one must now formally state its name when entering the forfeiture procedure.
One may not say generically, "the three robes. Although the text lists "three robes," this is merely the terminology used by the masters of the Dharma; it is not [a formal requirement].
One must completely relinquish these three. It is necessary to say, "The *ānanda* assembly, etc. (and so forth).
Although it is not a violation of the rule against keeping an excess (*atireka*), it is nonetheless a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense because it involves buying and exchanging.

This refers to the aforementioned case where a bhikṣu buys paper, pens, and so on for himself and haggles over the price with a layperson; while obtaining the goods does not constitute a violation of the rule against keeping an excess, it is nevertheless the bhikṣu’s own act.
If one purchases this article and does not employ the formal language of purification (*viśuddha-vākya*), all such monks commit an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Regarding the offense of "excessive attachment" (*dīrgha-saṃrakta*) where other factors are abandoned and the conditions for completion are met, it is established that, for example, if a monk exceeds ten days with an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), he commits an offense.
Furthermore, regarding the taking of a nun’s robe or the selling of robes, if at the time of later confession one forgets to relinquish them entirely, there are two cases:
if what was forgotten is a nun’s robe or a robe for sale, then the previous relinquishment remains valid;

however, if what was forgotten is an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), then the previous relinquishment is invalidated due to mutual defilement, and it is necessary to relinquish them all completely. Sengshen says: "This does not yet concern the case of forgetting the actual value."

This treatise discusses whether the relinquishment is complete or incomplete. If one has committed an offense regarding an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), it must be relinquished in its entirety; if any portion remains, there is mutual defilement (*saṃsarga*) and the relinquishment is not accomplished.

However, in the case of a nun’s robe or a robe purchased for sale, there is no mutual defilement. If one relinquishes what is to be relinquished, the relinquishment is accomplished; if one does not relinquish it, it is not accomplished.
Because there is no principle of non-accomplishment due to mutual defilement in these cases, it is said that "the relinquishment of the remainder is universally accomplished."
Furthermore,

regarding the statement that both methods of relinquishment (*nihsargika*) and purification (*viśuddhi*) are accomplished simultaneously: this means that when one has many robes acquired through transgression,

if at the time of relinquishing them one forgets some— whether one, two, or three— and after performing the ritual act of relinquishing those which were not forgotten, the original items are subsequently returned.

The explanation of *śuddhi* (purification) is concluded. Regarding those things forgotten: the previous relinquishment (*pratyāga*) is still valid, and upon obtaining the robe again, the *śuddhi* is likewise valid;

thus it is said that "two dharmas are both established. However, for what was forgotten, one must perform a separate act of relinquishment and confession. Lì asked: "At the time of relinquishing the robe-material, it is said that if there is no realization [of the transgression], the relinquishment is not accomplished.

Yet, if a bhikṣu acts without the thought [of performing the ritual], should it not be accomplished? (The intent of this question is: at the time of relinquishing the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, if one forgets and does not complete the relinquishment, regarding what has been relinquished...")"

[Question: If one returns [the object] and completes the *śuddhi* (purification), yet it is not free from the stain of forgetfulness—since there was already forgetfulness at the time of the previous relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*), this would constitute a "volitional act without intention" (*sābhisaṃskāra-nirvikalpa*).

How, then, can it be established? [Answer: Because the object is insentient, it cannot obstruct the relinquishment. Furthermore, once the *śuddhi* has been completed, it is therefore established [as valid]. (This means that although the cloth was returned and the *śuddhi* completed, because one sees that the original object was forgotten, it is permitted to be established.

Since persons are both sentient beings, they can potentially obstruct one another; therefore, the two cases are not analogous. If one returns the wealth but has not yet performed the *śuddhi*, and then sees that the object was forgotten...

"Et cetera" means: if one has obtained a robe that was returned but has not yet mentioned it, and then sees an object that was forgotten, although the original relinquishment was already accomplished, because it was defiled by the state of being forgotten, if one now further relinquishes the forgotten item, then the previous relinquishment made at the time of acquisition must also be relinquished once again.

Furthermore, although these items were originally robes belonging to a *bhikṣuṇī* and so forth, because they have now been relinquished and purified, their status from the time they were acquired is equivalent to newly obtained items;
thus, they follow the precedent of "long robes" (*atireka-cīvara*). Therefore, those that have been forgotten by others are subject to the rules of dyeing.

Even if the previous property was obtained through begging for robes or through trade and exchange, and was subsequently relinquished and returned—thus being equivalent to a new acquisition—it cannot be said [that the rule does not apply], because it is merely characterized as a long-forgotten item subject to the rules of dyeing.
Regarding those who practice the "long-term relinquishment" (*dīrgha-pratyāgama*), the established view is as follows: that which was forgotten is the very robe that was relinquished.

Although it may be a robe obtained through trade or begging, once it is later recovered from the Saṃgha, its status is equivalent to newly acquired property; it is not termed "trading" (*vaṇijya*). Because it has been stained by the fault of being a long-kept extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) that was forgotten, one must relinquish it entirely along with its associated faults.
As the preceding text states, "the remaining relinquishments are generally effective," this refers to cases where the fundamental substance [of the robe] does not conflict [with the rules].
Dyeing. Now, this person who traded [the cloth] has instead turned it back into a long robe (*dīrghacīvara*). Therefore, this constitutes dyeing a long robe that was originally forgotten.
The reason for this is that because a long robe is kept as an excess, it is prescribed that one must relinquish it; whereas requesting or trading for such a robe constitutes an offense of acceptance.

If one relinquishes it, the transgression is extinguished once the penalty is paid. Since the robe has already been obtained and is now reverted to the category of a long robe, [this rule applies] when it is subsequently seen.
Regarding surplus items: the previous case of requesting robes for gambling and so forth is identical to newly acquired items; thus, they are subject to the same rules of defilement (*saṃsarga*).

If one first designates [the item] as belonging to oneself and only later fears it will become defiled and discards it—meaning that upon seeing it, one realizes it was forgotten clothing—one then says the gift is not established.
Because of the prior intention to claim it as one's own, it caused fear of defilement; only then can it be called "given to another."

Therefore, this is incorrect. The text states: "If one discards [the object] and only afterwards sends it away," this means that if one later discovers a forgotten item and then forms the intention to give it to another, it does not constitute a valid gift.
However, if one has previously made a formal resolve, saying, "Should there be anything forgotten, I shall give it all to others," [then giving it later is valid].

If one later forgets [the object] but gives it to another, the act of giving is still accomplished. This means that although the original intention was to relinquish it, one now sends it to another person;
hence it is said, "only then does one send it.
As for the forgotten object, if it is a commodity for sale or other items that are not subject to defilement—referring to the forgotten object itself.
If it is an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), one is able to defile the robes that others have relinquished and returned;

however, if what was forgotten pertains to trade or similar activities, then one cannot defile the items that have been relinquished and returned. Therefore, it is said that "there is no mutual defilement.

Regarding the "ten-day robe" and so forth, up to the "emergency gift," this refers to the standard practice of keeping an extra robe for more than ten days. As for the term "one month," it refers to...
The *māsa-cīvara* (month-long robe) refers to the expectation of receiving a robe after one month has passed; if this period exceeds one month, one incurs an offense.

Regarding the statement that the three subsequent precepts concerning "urgent gifts" (*akālacīvara*) share a common characteristic of defilement, this has already been clarified above according to their specific characteristics. These three types of robes mentioned above share a common characteristic of defilement because they are all considered "extra" (*atireka*).
Therefore, there is the principle that offenses extend to the full length [of the garment]. This causes mutual defilement; all such cases are said to be "forgotten" (i.e., overlooked).
If it concerns garments such as these, then they do indeed defile one another. Master Li says:

"If it concerns bowls or medicines, then each defiles only its own kind—meaning bowls defile bowls, medicines defile medicines, and garments defile garments. A bowl does not defile a garment or medicine, nor does a medicine defile them."
"Robe and bowl" refers to robes that have not been dyed, bowls, medicinal decoctions, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because this matter involves such toil," Saṃghabhadra states: if one does not relinquish them completely, they must be relinquished again later, thereby causing hardship for both oneself and others.

He refers to the Sangha. One should anticipate this and deliberate beforehand; if there is anyone who might forget, one should intend to relinquish the item to the Three Jewels or to another individual so that it is not lost or forgotten.
Regarding those who do not enter into this precept and must be made aware of it: if one does not give [the item] later, one commits the grave offense of theft (*steya*);
furthermore, if ten days pass without confessing it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding "tying the bundle at three places": This is established for clarity, requiring that it be tied at three locations. Why?

Because one must return to the owner on the same day after being separated from the robe and receive it back for formal possession (*dhāraṇa*); otherwise, there is a fear of forgetting its characteristics or it becoming defiled. Therefore, it must be tied at three places.

Furthermore, in cases such as trading or bartering, one must necessarily stay overnight before returning; that is why this is so. Regarding "the three miscellaneous relinquishments": These refer to taking the robes of a *bhikṣuṇī* or engaging in trading and bartering.

This concerns the begging for robes and the like. If the materials for a robe consist of many pieces and must each be relinquished individually, this is clearly established by the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

However, according to the *Vinayavibhaṅga-śāstra*, it is permitted to relinquish them collectively as a bundle. Regarding the statement that "if there are long robes, those that are stained or mixed are relinquished universally," this is clearly established because there are three distinct bundles.
If, at the time of the initial relinquishment, something was forgotten, and what was forgotten happens to be a long robe that is subsequently stained and returned, [the following applies].

Therefore, it is said that they do not defile what is "excessive" (*dīrgha*). If the forgotten item is a "miscellaneous relinquishment" (*miśra-pratyāśraya*), it cannot defile the separation from robes or excessive robes;

for as soon as the miscellaneous relinquished robe enters one's possession, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. This is based solely on the offense incurred at the time of receiving [the robe], and not on the offense incurred by storing it.
For this reason, its substance is not capable of defiling; thus, even within its own category, there is no sense of defilement. Therefore, it is said: "Then..."

[The text] connects [the following]. If one forgets what was intended, this constitutes being separated from one's robe (*cīvara-vipravāsa*). Furthermore, it cannot defile a discarded robe (*pratyākhyāta-cīvara*) or an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*);
therefore, it is said that "even by defiling, one does not obtain [the offense]. This being separated from one's robe also does not defile another’s, nor is it defiled by another;

that is to say, an extra robe also does not defile the three robes (*tricīvara*). This is the definitive interpretation. Shen (Shen Xiu) says: Since there are these three types of offenses involving the discarding of robes, each...
Having made the three robes, one discards them; subsequently, one receives them from the Saṃgha. Upon returning, one sees that the original items have been forgotten.

If what was forgotten consists of the five *dīrgha* (long) materials, then one may dye the long materials as well as the mixed materials and discard them. If what was forgotten consists of the mixed materials, then one cannot dye the five *dīrgha* materials.
Because even their substance is free from the defilement of attachment. When it is said that "the five types of long-cloth" are included, these refer to:

the ten-day robe, the one-month robe, the extra alms-bowl, the extra medicine, and the cloth given as an urgent offering that has passed its deadline. As for the statement that "one type of robe separated from the body" is also not permitted due to defilement, [it refers to this same principle].

This refers to the offense of forfeiture for being separated from one's robe. Once the robe has been forfeited and the confession performed, and the robe has been returned but the formal ritual (*adhikāra*) has not yet been conferred, if one sees an object previously forgotten, there can be no mutual defilement.
That is to say, both the subject and the object are non-defiled; it does not defile others, nor is it defiled by others. It is resolved immediately upon its forfeiture.

Regarding the statement in the Vinaya that "this *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, and one must not relinquish it to a separate group (*bhedasaṃgha*) and so forth," Shen [Daoan] remarked:
"Based on this single passage, it is clearly understood that when distributing the belongings of a deceased person, one must first harmonize with the Saṃgha;

only then may the robe be relinquished. To relinquish it before achieving such harmony is equivalent to relinquishing it to a separate group. This is because the robe is being relinquished to the Saṃgha, and since this [act] is prohibited..."
When coming to seek [the forfeiture], one may not do so separately from the assembly. It is clearly understood that those rules also require initial harmony before the forfeiture is made.

A guest asked: "This refers to clothing and wealth, which must be forfeited in the presence of the *saṃgha*. As for the three precepts concerning gems and so forth, they apply exclusively to individuals. Question:

Since these apply only to individuals, can one perform a confession as a separate group (*bhedasaṃgha*)? Answer: Regarding these thirty precepts, it is permissible to perform confession as a separate group. Some say: 'Within the boundary...'"
If there is no *saṃgha*, one may confess before another person. If there is a *saṃgha*, one must first nominate the *saṃgha* and then perform the confession.

If it were not so, what would be the purpose of the formal motion (*jñapti*) for receiving the confession? Now, examining this in detail: if one wishes to seek confession within the *saṃgha*, one must formally announce the reception of the confession. If one does not wish to confess within the *saṃgha*, it is also permissible to do so separately from the assembly.

There is no textual authority regarding whether one may confess before another person when apart from the assembly; thus, it is called "confession before another" (*pratimukha-kṣānti*). When apart from the assembly, [it is not called such].
It is established. In the ritual practices of the Western Regions, it is likewise permitted to perform individual confession before another person (*pratyekapratideśanā*).

Furthermore, observing this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, in the section on the *Poṣadha* (*Śīla-kaṇḍa*), it is stated that if the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense and does not recognize its name or characteristics, and a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is capable of providing instruction, [the resident bhikṣus] shall take him to a secluded place and have the other bhikṣus stand where they are within sight but beyond hearing, and instruct him to act according to the Dharma.
Having completed the confession, he returned to where that bhikṣu was and spoke these words: "The offense committed by this bhikṣu has now been confessed. (Commentary:
Since it is stated that [the confession] is established in a place where one can see with the eyes but not hear with the ears, it seems to be a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).

Regarding the phrase "having already relinquished [the offense], yet still possessing it with a greedy mind, the knot remains tied, even to the point of being unlike other miscellaneous categories of offenses," Jing says:

If one commits the offense of possessing surplus goods, although one may relinquish the goods and repent for the transgression, if the mind does not relinquish them and one commits the offense again, it constitutes a violation.

However, if other miscellaneous items are relinquished, even if the mind does not relinquish them, they are nonetheless considered relinquished. This is because the offense incurred through formal acceptance differs from that of mere possession.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* school is Mahāyāna, vast and unconditioned. The reason it must be clarified as Mahāyāna is that one wishes to demonstrate that Mahāyāna transcends all objects of the mind.
If one were to abandon [the precepts] now, making a resolve of permanent renunciation, one would leave one's heart empty and should not hope for their return.
(This meaning is somewhat difficult; it has been explained in the preceding text. If one follows other schools, once the abandonment has occurred, there is no possibility of seeking restoration.
I say: the "other school" (*itara-nikāya*) refers specifically to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations). Furthermore, when it says "other school," it generally indicates all schools;
the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the *Pañcavargika*, and the *Daśabhāṇavāra* all possess this meaning. This [term] is used as a general designation here. From the character "or" (*vā*) onwards...

This is to cite the intention of other schools. Alternatively, regarding those who require [the items]: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, at the time of the formal renunciation (*pratikṣepa*) of the two types of treasures, if they are few, they are renounced permanently;

if there are many, they are renounced and entrusted to a lay attendant (*upāsaka*), and the lay attendant renounces them as four parts for the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha, while the offense is confessed within the Saṃgha.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, five types of bedding and furniture enter into the common property of the monastery (*sthavira-saṃgha*); only the original owner [retains the remainder].

One must not sit or lie down [upon them]. If one relinquishes the medicine for confession (*pratideśanīya*), it shall also be relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall then give it to a layperson or a *śrāmaṇera*.
It may be used for anointing the feet or lighting lamps, but the original owner may not use it themselves, nor may any *bhikṣu* consume it. Regarding the *Saṃghāṭi* robe:

if one possesses or trades the two types of precious items (*ratna*), they must be relinquished and placed into the Saṃgha’s inexhaustible wealth (*akṣaya-nidhi*). If it concerns the five kinds of bedding and furniture, they must be relinquished for the use of the Saṃgha. If one diverts these items to the Saṃgha...
As for the items, the Saṃgha may use them as it sees fit. If they are made of pure black *kauśeya* silk, the Saṃgha must not wear or use them;
however, they may be used as floor coverings. If they have not been folded [or repaired] for six years, they may not be used as floor coverings, though the Saṃgha may wear or use them.

According to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, after having relinquished long robes, monthly robes, rainy-season robes, emergency gift robes, or bowls that have exceeded their limit to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha asks:

If it is needed, it should be returned for use. If one has no need for it oneself, it should be permanently relinquished to the Saṃgha. If one takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī, it should be returned to that original bhikṣuṇī;

if there is no original bhikṣuṇī, it should be relinquished to the community of bhikṣuṇīs to have her wash the robe. If one diverts property belonging to the Saṃgha, it must be permanently relinquished to the Saṃgha.

If a householder who is not a relative asks for a robe, or if one is urged to increase the amount of thread for a robe, it should be relinquished and returned to them. If they are not present, [the robe should be kept].
If one does not take [the robe], it should be relinquished to the Saṃgha. If the robe was seized out of a mind of anger, it must be relinquished back to the bhikṣu who was the object of that anger.

If it is discarded in the mountains or by a river, one should perform the formal act of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika*) before the fivefold assembly or the two groups of jewels, and relinquish it to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha shall appoint a person to permanently discard it.

If the Saṃgha does not discard it, a lay attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) shall trade it for food and clothing on behalf of the Saṃgha; these may be used by the Saṃgha for consumption, but the original owner may not use them under any circumstances, for fear [of transgression].

Because it accords with his original intention. Regarding gold and silver belonging to the Saṃgha: if there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one may instruct [the monk] to discard them.
After the Saṃgha has performed the *kamma*, it shall appoint one bhikkhu who possesses the five qualities; once that person has received the *kamma*, he should discard the items.

He should discard these objects with his eyes closed, throwing them into a pit, into fire, into flowing water, or into the wilderness. He must not mark the location. Having cut and destroyed them, they are entered [into the earth].
Regarding the "kitchen" (kūṭi): it refers to the rule that when wool is sought for bedding, it must be cut into small pieces and mixed with clay to form a plastered floor.
Regarding the phrase "entering the kitchen": this refers to seeking many extra bowls; one inferior bowl is set aside while the remaining fine ones are distributed among the Saṃgha.

He followed them into the monastic kitchen. Regarding the statement that "medicines are given to the monks or to the laity," my private opinion is this: medicines for a period of seven days are given to the monks;
medicines exceeding seven days are given to the laity and the gardeners. Alternatively, they may be given to the monks alone, as clarified in the various sections mentioned above.

If the mind does not abandon the two aspects of weariness and agitation—namely, weariness regarding the Sangha and weariness regarding oneself—one must not follow even a single hair’s breadth [of them].
Regarding this, a private commentary states: The sutra says that there was a man who kept three wives; one he loved most dearly, the next was merely tolerable, and the last was most frivolous.
As that man approached his death, he said to the one he loved, "I have always loved you, and now I wish for you to accompany me. She replied:
"Indeed, words cannot follow one after death. After you have passed away, there will be many who require me.
He then asked the one he favored, "Can you go? He answered as before. Next, he asked the one he treated with disdain, "Can you go? Thereupon, that person gave rise to this thought:
"In life, one was always treated with contempt and disdain; now, suddenly, no one has forgotten me. Why would you not agree? He immediately replied, "I can go.
That which he loved most is likened to gold, silver, and wealth; that which he cherished is likened to servants, slaves, fields, and houses;
and that which he loathed and despised is likened to all the merits he had cultivated. Thus we know that during his lifetime, he held all merit in low esteem, yet at death, it is only...
Regarding the phrase, "Following these signs yet not contemplating the Great Matter," Siji (Private) says: "The fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi is the Great Matter;
[these people] merely know how to follow worldly custom to see out the end of a single lifetime. Lili (Established) says: "The Great Matter is precisely the exhaustion of life;
it means they do not contemplate that death has arrived. Therefore, the Great Master Tiantai said: "Though the monastics of the present day possess overflowing knowledge and understanding..."
Chest. Or, one may exert diligence to extinguish the fires [of passion] yet fail to realize impermanence; thus, the common saying goes: "Pitiable is the lack of the five charms;
diligent is the lack of the Way-mind. This is precisely its meaning.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The robes have already been relinquished and the offense has already been confessed," and so forth. This treatise contains six phrases;

although there are currently three distinct phrases here, the intent of the passage takes up the third phrase, which means that one must first sever the intention to possess [the robe] before one can receive it back.

Regarding the statement, "On that very day, one obtains both the original property and unexpected property," this establishes that for one who has committed an offense and performed the relinquishment and confession, each of these is termed "original property" (*mūla-dravya*), as they are distinct from one another.

"Obtaining a gift" refers to external wealth beyond one's expectations. Regarding the phrase "the remaining clauses are as in the *Śū* (Commentary)," this refers to the *Jièxīn shū* (Commentary on the Precepts and Mind), or it may refer to the *Dàshū* (Great Commentary).

According to the *Lìshū*, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* contains six clauses: 1. The robe has already been relinquished and the offense already confessed, yet the intention to possess it has not been severed;

if one receives another robe on that same day, it becomes a defilement regarding the previous robe, resulting in the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). 2. The second clause concerns the robe... [text continues].

The robe has already been relinquished and the offense already confessed. However, if the intention to seek clothing persists for up to one month, then whatever robes one obtains, as well as any unexpected acquisitions of clothing, constitute a transgression involving forfeiture;
by retaining them through an improper mental state that has not ceased, one incurs this offense.

This is because, while the first four mental states have ceased, the [forfeiture] offense has not been incurred (this refers to the third phrase cited in the *Chao*). In the third phrase, the robe has already been relinquished and the offense already confessed.
The first case: the intention to keep [the robe] has been severed. If one obtains a robe on that very day, there is no offense (this is the first sentence cited in the *Shuochao*). The fourth case:

the robe has already been relinquished, the offense has already been confessed, and the intention to keep it has been severed. If one subsequently seeks and obtains another robe, there is likewise no offense of relinquishment;

because the intermediate period was spent with the intention to keep it severed through non-dharmic means, there is no fault. The fifth case: at the time the ground is cleared, the robe is relinquished, the offense is confessed, and the intention to keep it has been severed.

If one seeks to obtain clothing again toward evening, one commits a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding the sixth case: the clothing has already been relinquished and the offense has not yet been confessed, yet the intention to possess it has ceased.

Even if one obtains clothing many days later, one incurs a minor offense (this is precisely the second case cited in the *Śāstra*). The six cases cited in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) are likewise the same.
The commentary states: "If one exceeds the limit, then one speaks of it; as for the rest that does not exceed the limit, one merely recites the preceding words.
This means that if the fundamental possession [of the robe] exceeds ten days, it is termed "exceeding the limit.
