If it has not yet reached ten days, but is merely something that has been defiled by another, then one cannot say it "exceeds the limit. Therefore, the phrase "the rest does not exceed the limit" refers to the robes that have been defiled.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case, it is difficult to open [the confession] to him" and ending with "even when both are opened," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

there was a sick bhikṣu who committed an offense and said to another bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, I have committed an offense. The other replied, "I too have committed an offense. No [confession was performed].

He died before he had been able to confess his transgression. The bhikṣus thought to themselves, "If the Buddha would allow one to confess their faults before a bhikṣu who has committed an offense, this bhikṣu would not have died without having confessed.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to confess your faults before a bhikṣu who has committed an offense;
however, you must not confess before one who has committed the same offense. Furthermore, there was another sick bhikṣu...
A bhikṣu committed an offense. He said to another bhikṣu, "I have committed this offense. The other replied, "I too have committed this offense.

[The first bhikṣu] died without being able to confess his transgression. The bhikṣus thought to themselves, "If the Buddha would permit one to confess toward a bhikṣu who has committed the same offense, this bhikṣu would not die without having confessed.
... [They reported this to the Buddha], and the Buddha said, "Now, I permit [confession] toward one who has committed the same offense."

Different offenses can all be confessed before others. [The author] privately comments: I fear this was an opening by the Buddha for those who might pass away while still bearing their transgressions.
Ancient masters have applied this method indiscriminately; however, it is not correct to simply allow confession before another provided they are not of the same category as the one being opened.
"Appearing in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, how could these be the words of an ordinary person? According to the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dazhidu lun* (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), it says:
"If a person who has broken the precepts wears the Dharma robes, they are like wrapping their body in sheets of glowing red-hot iron.
If they hold an alms bowl, it is like a vessel filled with molten copper. If they eat what they consume, it is like swallowing burning iron balls and drinking hot molten copper. If they receive...
If one receives offerings and provisions from others, one is being guarded by the wardens of hell. If one enters a vihāra, it is as if entering hell.
If one sits upon the beds and couches of the Saṃgha, it is as if sitting upon beds of glowing iron, and so forth.

I privately remark that when one dons the Dharma robes, this is precisely the cause for donning iron armor. Because of violating the precepts regarding food and clothing, one enters among the animals.

Regarding the phrase "sentient beings such as hairless worms and birds that eat excrement who receive separate retribution": "receiving separate retribution" means receiving distinct karmic results after emerging from hell.
Regarding the phrase "the robe of broken precepts": this refers to the transgression of selling or trading [forbidden goods], which is termed the "robe of broken precepts.

While the primary retribution (*vipāka*) was hell, upon emerging from it, one receives the separate retribution of hairless worms and birds; these are specifically of the class of earthworms and the like. Thus it is said.

Regarding "food that violates the precepts": this refers to food that is leftover from a previous night, defiled by improper contact, consumed at the wrong time, or not received through formal acceptance; such is called food that violates the precepts.
Its retribution in the present life is birth as a worm in a latrine or as a *pūtanā* spirit that devours excrement.

According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, those with excessive lust are born among sparrows, pigeons, mandarin ducks, and the like; those with excessive anger are born among vipers, snakes, and venomous scorpions; and those with excessive ignorance...
Those in whom greed is predominant are born among pigs and sheep; those in whom arrogance and self-indulgence are predominant are born among lions, tigers, wolves, and the like;
those in whom restlessness and playfulness are predominant are born among monkeys; and those in whom stinginess and envy are predominant are born among dogs and similar creatures.

Because of the predominance of such various other afflictions, they are born among the various kinds of animals. However, if there is one who possesses a small portion of fewness of desire and practices partial giving, even though they are born among animals, within that state—
They experience pleasure, like the garuḍa, dragons, elephants, horses, and so forth. Even if they should obtain human birth, killing leads to a short lifespan;
stealing leads to poverty; sexual misconduct leads to an unfaithful wife; lying leads to being slandered; divisive speech leads to discord among one's kin;
harsh speech leads to constantly hearing unpleasant sounds; frivolous speech leads to others not believing or accepting one’s words; and greed and lust—
Excessive desire leads to much anger; anger leads to a malicious nature; wrong views lead to much delusion;
arrogance leads to birth in a lowly station; self-exaltation leads to being short of stature; jealousy leads to a lack of majestic virtue; stinginess leads to poverty; and anger leads to ugliness.
Harassing others leads to much illness; engaging in sexual misconduct with those who are not one's path leads to the form of a eunuch.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names of the offenses, there are three types, which are likened to putting on or taking off clothing:

one first puts them on from the inside, and when wishing to remove them, one first removes them from the outside. The method of repentance is likewise: a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is the first to be committed, and it is the last to be repented.
Thus it is said. Second, regarding the three types of *kṣānti* (merit/virtue) that follow from the root of arising: Master Li states that the first is the *kṣānti* of concealing the root;
the second is the *kṣānti* of attachment and use; and the third is the *kṣānti* of silent falsehood regarding the precepts as taught in the Sūtras.

These should be confessed prior to the preceding [root offenses]; hence it is said they are "confessed before the roots. Third, regarding the six categories of concealment (*tirobhāva*) that arise therefrom.
Regarding the statement that "the *duṣkṛta* is foremost in the confession," this is established as clear: these six categories of *duṣkṛta* arise from the three preceding categories of *duṣkṛta*.
This means that once one has committed the aforementioned three categories, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* for each after a single night has passed.

From the second night onward, by concealing those previous *duṣkṛtas*, they are termed "successive concealment according to the nights," and one further incurs *duṣkṛtas*. Therefore, it is said thus. First.
Regarding the term "the root concealment is a *duṣkṛta*": this means that by concealing the root *pārājika* offense, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Having passed the first night, one incurs another *duṣkṛta* for concealing this [secondary offense]. On the second night, it is called "successively increasing concealment" (*anuvartana-paticchādana*);

furthermore, beneath each category of *duṣkṛta*, there are two types of offenses—concealment and subsequent concealment—each involving silence and falsehood. Excluding the root *duṣkṛta*, these thus constitute [the full set].
Six categories. If one speaks of these six categories: it means that once a robe has been committed as an offense requiring forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), one must immediately confess it.

Because one does not confess it immediately, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* for concealment (1). Furthermore, if one does not confess this *duṣkṛta*, another *duṣkṛta* is incurred for each night it passes (2).

Furthermore, as one proceeds through the watches of the night, they become innumerable; this constitutes another category (the third). Next, regarding the attainment of auspiciousness through application:

the initial auspiciousness is auspicious, and the subsequent covering of that auspiciousness is also auspicious; proceeding through the watches of the night, it remains auspicious, thus forming three. Regarding silent falsehood:

the first instance of falsehood is auspicious, the subsequent covering of that is also auspicious, and proceeding through the watches of the night, it remains auspicious, thus forming three. Combined with the preceding, these constitute nine categories. This is established.

[The opponent] says: "It is like the offense of *thullaccaya*. On the first night, one incurs one *dukkaṭa* for concealing the *thullaccaya*; on the second night, one incurs further *dukkaṭas* corresponding to each subsequent day.
There is no separate *dukkaṭa* for concealing the original *thullaccaya* itself; concealing the original *thullaccaya* results in only one *dukkaṭa*. Now, I fear this is not so.
If you say there is only one *dukkaṭa*, why is it that by concealing a remainder for a hundred nights, one incurs a hundred *dukkaṭas*? [Cai] says:

It is said: Regarding the statement that "the merit (*puṇya*) increases with each successive night of concealment," this does not mean that the merit of the first night arises from the concealment of the second night.
Rather, it arises from the underlying *pārājika* offense itself; for every single night, one merit is produced.
Thus, after a hundred nights, one obtains a hundred merits, all of which arise from the fundamental *pārājika*. This is what is called "increasing" (*vistara*).

"Transformation" does not mean that it arises from the second night during the third night. It is like the case where the auspicious signs (*kṣema*) produced by the application of *mauna* (silence) arise;
all hundreds of thousands of auspicious signs arise solely from such application.

Some say that within the *karmavācanā*, there are only eight categories of auspicious signs, and that the nine categories mentioned in the *Shuochao* are incorrect in meaning. However, Li’s commentary also favors eight categories, excluding this *chufu* (covering/obscuring).

The "Auspiciousness" (Ji) below refers to the "Overturning" (Fu) being auspicious. It means that simply by overturning the root, one attains auspiciousness; furthermore, it is auspicious to proceed through the stages of the night. These are the two types of auspiciousness.
The application of the term "Hei" (Darkness/Secret) has the same meaning. Moreover, because there are two categories, the Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) states: "Its positions are fourfold."

First, one should repent of the four *duṣkṛta* offenses of wearing [robes] while being silent and concealing [the offense], as well as subsequent concealment. Second, one should repent of the two *duṣkṛta* offenses of wearing [robes] while being silent.

Third, one should repent of the two *duṣkṛta* offenses of concealing and subsequent concealment for the *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offenses. These three stages of repentance all involve self-reproach (*cittapratideśana*).

Only at the fourth stage does one then repent of the *sthūlātyaya*. According to Nanshan, there are only these three stages: first, repenting of the *sthūlātyaya*, as well as the *duṣkṛta* of wearing [robes] while being silent and the concealments.

There are six grades of *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) for concealing [a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense]; next, one confesses two grades of *duṣkṛta* for "adhering" (*dhāraṇa*) and "remaining silent" (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*);
only thereafter does one confess the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* itself; thus, three stages are distinguished. Master Bin says: "By calculation according to principle, there are only eight grades of *duṣkṛta*.

Nanshan, however, maintains nine grades of *duṣkṛta*, because the *duṣkṛta* of concealing that arises directly from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is identical in meaning to 'adhering' and 'remaining silent,' and since it arises directly from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, he maintains this direct [derivation]."

Concealment (*mrakṣa*) and attachment (*gardha*) serve as the roots. Within these, there are respectively concealment and secondary concealment (*anuvr̥tti*), thus forming nine categories (and so forth).
Fearing that those who recite this might wonder what to do when they encounter such states again and again, [Master] Ji said:
"For now, let us simply console you for having encountered them once."

Regarding the "three questions at nine locations," my private opinion is that various interpretations differ. As Li [Liyun] states: in the initial preface, one question is posed; if it is not answered, one *jī* (minor offense) is incurred.

When reaching the specific offenses listed below, a question is posed for each section; if it is not answered, another *jī* is incurred for each. If one has committed two or three offenses, one incurs one *jī* for each individual offense.
This differs from the interpretation of the Master of the *Shō* (the *Zengyi Ahan Jing Shu*), according to whom the three questions at the nine locations all [apply simultaneously].
This constitutes a transgression. This is a general principle for simplifying purification; how could it be restricted to the specific offenses of each chapter?
Furthermore, one question and one offense across nine locations total twenty-seven, which are identical in being twenty-seven offenses of concealment.

Thus, these six categories of *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) are those whose numbers one does not recall; this text precisely refers to first repenting these six categories of *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture). Text.

Although the middle section clarifies the auspiciousness of *chiding* (reproaching) and the auspiciousness of *mo-wang* (silent falsehood) when employed, this is merely a restatement of the reasons for the transgressions committed;
it is not the actual repentance for these auspicious acts. This means that by citing these three grades, one is thereby enjoining the six lower grades.

The repentance for the three grades shall follow later, as may be sought. As for the phrase "it may be so," it means that one should respond to the higher positions, as discussed above in the treatise.
"Text" refers to the passage in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning the six cases of robes already relinquished and offenses already confessed, and so forth.
Regarding "entrusting them to the Saṃgha in a secluded place for the performance of a *karmavācanā* by successive transmission":

this clarifies that once the monk who has performed the relinquishment and confession has already surrendered the robe and intends to travel far the following day, it is impossible to assemble the Saṃgha to return the robe. Now, since he may directly entrust it [to others], [the procedure is established] right then and there.

While seated in the assembly, one should perform the *karmavācanā* of successive transmission. This robe should be entrusted to a friend of the person who has performed the confession (*pratideśanā*).

Once that friend has received it, they shall take it to the original owner in a private place. Regarding this, some say that both conditions—being on a long journey and the impossibility of assembling the Saṃgha—must be present for this rite to be performed;
others say that it may be performed even if only one condition is met. Addendum: [The procedure is as follows:]... [Addendum].
The term "yún" (cloud) refers to the direct bestowal of the Dharma; it is, for instance, like the method for distributing the light belongings of a deceased person.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "as found in the various sections on ritual procedures in the latter volume," this is fully explained in the final thirtieth chapter.

Answer: "As it is not different from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. My private opinion is this: since the Vinaya text states that for the confession of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the prior concealment is a *duṣkṛta* offense, one knows that the same applies to the repentance of all offenses.
If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the confession is combined with the root offense; this too is a matter of brevity and ease.

If four persons perform the rite of *pratideśanīya* (confession) face-to-face as described in the preceding fascicle—that is, as explained in the section on the boundaries of the *saṃgha*—it is as clarified in the separate chapter.
Here, we clarify only matters such as the possession of extra robes and the separation from them;

other matters, such as the possession and trading of the two types of precious objects, washing, dyeing, carrying, and spreading out [robes], shall be clarified under their respective precepts within the *Prātimokṣa*.
[The Buddha] spoke.

The above concludes the explanation of the *pāyattika* offense regarding the ritual for monks (*saṃgha-karmavācanā*). From here below, the procedure for a group of many persons (*bahujana*) is correctly explained.

Regarding the two groups returning robes, it must first be a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed by oneself or others; as for those who are members of the Saṃgha, this refers to the preceding section.
The monastic legal procedures for a community of five or more persons, as well as those for a group of four who perform the formal acts of a larger assembly, are termed the "two groups.

When performing the confession and renunciation of these two types of offenses, if a community of five persons receives the confession, they may achieve harmony with the assembly through a single formal motion (*jñapti*). If it is a community of four persons...

A simple announcement (*jñapti*) alone may not be used; rather, one must employ verbal reconciliation. This is because the person receiving the confession is measured by the Saṃgha, yet does not count as a member of the Saṃgha.

The formal request (*yācanā*) requires both five and four [members]. Now, when returning robes to a group of five monks, it is permissible to use a "motion and second" (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) procedure to return them.
As for the statement that a formal act (*karman*) is required beforehand, this refers to cases of five or more persons, where they are authorized to perform the *karman* to return the items.
When there are three or fewer people present, one may only return the robe orally. Regarding the statement "the self and others constitute the *saṃgha*":

this means that at the time of the previous acceptance of the confession (*pratideśanā*), because the presiding confessor (*karmavācaka*) was formally appointed and integrated into the legal procedure, he was evaluated by the *saṃgha* and did not count toward the required number for the *saṃgha*. Now, at the time of returning the robe, the presiding confessor, together with the other three people, completes the quorum of the *saṃgha*.
Therefore, it is said that "the self and others constitute the *saṃgha*," and one is permitted to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to return the robe. — *Li* (Commentary)
It is said: At the time of relinquishing the robe, there must be no confusion. That is to say, if one relinquishes it before the Saṃgha, one must return it before the Saṃgha;

if one relinquishes it to an individual, one must return it to that individual. It is not necessary for the person who originally performed the formal act to be the one to return it. As for why some matters are not described because they are easy to understand, it is because their textual meaning and categories are already evident;
therefore, it is said they are "easy to understand and thus not described."
The explanation of the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules is hereby concluded. Below, the confession rituals for the ninety *pāyattika* rules are clarified.
Regarding the phrase "or nine grades," I privately note that within the ninety rules, there are also those possessing nine grades of *duṣkṛta*.

This is, for instance, like the three white robes (*tricīvara*) or the oversized sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), which may still be worn and used; thus, they are said to have "nine grades. As for the "new-colored three robes":
This refers to a white *kāṣāya*, which has not been dyed blue, black, or madder-brown.

Regarding the instruction that one should perform repentance at the place of *nirvāṇa*, according to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), the Dharma Master says: "If a person reviles a noble one, or if a great *bhikṣu* speaks thus:
'Venerable One, I now repent before you; may you, Venerable One, accept it. If this is not done..."
If he has gone to another region or arrived at another monastery, he should come to where the bhikṣu is and say: "Venerable sir, this was my transgression;
I now repent. May the Venerable One accept it. If [the bhikṣu] has entered parinirvāṇa, one should perform the confession at the place of his parinirvāṇa.
In this way, the gates to the heavenly realms and the door to nirvāṇa are not closed. Furthermore, it is said:

"If a person commits grave karma, because of that grave karma, the gates to heaven are closed and the gates to hell are opened. I privately reflect that when the one being reviled dies, the one who reviled them fears that the karmic path of their own offenses will obstruct their access to heaven;
therefore, they should repent at the place where the reviled person died, begging for their joy and forgiveness. That...
All of these attain joy; therefore, it is said that the gates to the heavenly realms are not closed. The explanation of the fourth category (*pācittiya*) is hereby completed.
Regarding the fifth category, the *pratideśanīya*, those points identical to the *pācittiya* are, according to my private opinion, mentioned only because they appear in the Vinaya text.
The text for the *pratideśanā* (confession) does not appear elsewhere; consequently, ancient masters have employed this method of confession from the point of the *pratideśanā* onwards.

Now, I shall differ from them. Regarding the phrase "not adopting human speech," Sheng says that it simply refers to the previously mentioned *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession), which is not different from the "one recitation" (*ekavācikā*), though distinguished by its specific name;
thus, it is merely human speech. As for "wearing it upon the crown of the head," this expresses the sense of holding it with uplifted reverence.
From this point forward, the method for repenting the *pāyantika* (吉羅) class of offenses is explained. Regarding the method for repenting the *pāyantika* class:

although these offenses are minor, if one commits them and does not repent, they can cause the practitioner to fall into hell. As the Sūtra says: "Do not treat small evils lightly, thinking they will bring no calamity.
Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. In a single kṣaṇa, one may commit an offense whose calamity leads to a fall into the Avīci Hell. One.

"Once one loses the human body, ten thousand kalpas may pass before it is regained"—this is precisely the meaning [of those words]. Furthermore, the Preface to the Vinaya states: "Though a wildfire may be small, do not underestimate it as trivial;
whatever grasses and trees it encounters, it burns them all away until nothing remains. So too, though the evil one commits may be slight, do not dismiss it as insignificant;
it is like breaking a leaf of the *elāpattra* tree, which results in one's constant rebirth among the nagas. Bin said: "Kāśyapa."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who thought to himself: "If the leaves of the sandalwood tree cause the destruction of one's beauty, what harm can the leaves of the *elāpattra* do?
Yet, due to this karmic retribution, he has been born among the nāgas; atop his head grows an *elāpattra* tree whose roots enter the nāga’s head.
When it is buffeted by the wind, thick blood gushes forth from all sides, causing him great suffering and distress. [He will remain thus] until the time of Maitreya.

He emerged; it was only then that he was freed from his dragon body. This is none other than the Nāga King Elāpattra mentioned later in the Vinaya. Question: Since destroying life constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, it should not be used as a metaphor for a *duṣkṛta*.

Answer: For now, this is based on the fact that [the offender] acted with a light mind and did not follow the Buddha’s teachings; it is not necessarily the case that the gravity of the offense must correspond exactly to the gravity of the metaphor.
Furthermore, regarding the *duṣkṛta* offense of violating non-dignified conduct (*a-vinaya*), Jì (Jie) says: "Master Vinayadhara, this should be called the *duṣkṛta* of slighting the Buddha’s words.
This means that among the offenses of the five categories (*pañca-āpatti-nikāya*), each precept involves the binding of this *duṣkṛta* of non-dignified conduct;

that is, it is bound from the perspective of slighting the Buddha’s words. Furthermore, as for not distinguishing between the two methods of repentance, according to the Vinaya there are only intentional and unintentional [offenses], but no confession before another person (*pratideśanā*).
The first part concerns the two methods of mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Regarding the phrase "relying on the text, one carefully recites [the precepts] while equally reproaching the mind":

*lì* (礪) is likewise used here to mean "to reproach the mind. As for the fact that this text is not yet fully explained: it merely states that minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) are not confessed before another person;

furthermore, because the distinctions have not yet been made, the characteristics of light and heavy offenses are erroneously conflated. Thus, the methods of confession (*pratideśanā*) are divided into two types. When it is said, "It is easy to destroy [the precepts], but difficult to violate the sacred treatises," this clarifies—
The aforementioned ancient masters unanimously criticize the practice of performing a single session of mental repentance (*citta-vipaśyanā*) for all offenses; this must be rejected.

Since the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) and the *Prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Vinaya-saṃgraha*) require that both types of repentance—verbal and mental—be performed, it is difficult to contradict these two treatises. Therefore, it is best to rely on these two texts and perform separate repentances for each category.

Regarding the hundred minor rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), from those arising after the various sections down to those committed through either intentional or unintentional transgression, they should likewise be repented according to the two methods mentioned above.
"Zhè" (者) refers to what is established [in the text], namely the *duishǒu* (confession before another) and *zéxīn* (self-reproach) mentioned in the preceding treatise.

Regarding the question as to why the preparatory acts (*fangbiàn*) for the first category [of offenses] are grave while those for the subsequent categories are light, etc., [the author] Liù (Lì) clarifies that the intent of this question is as follows:

although the very first preparatory acts for both the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories are equally termed *dukkaṭa* (transgression), there are nonetheless differences in their gravity; why, then, are they treated identically here?
"Is it that one must be made to reproach the mind and repent? The answer intends to say: Because they share the same name, they are equally subject to reproaching the mind and repenting.
As for what is called "light or heavy," it refers merely to the gradations within karma. Now, if one reproaches the mind, one must apply remedies according to whether the offense is light or heavy.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the offenses encompassed by the six groups (ṣaḍ-varga) have names that apply to both superior and inferior [levels]," this means that *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) serves as the cause for all six groups.

Moreover, based on the nature of *duṣkṛta*, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness; since the term *duṣkṛta* alone now encompasses these degrees, it is said that "the name applies to both superior and inferior.
As for the phrase "when the mind dwells in intensity or mildness, the karma must be heavy or light," this refers to actions performed with an intense state of mind.

If one performs an action with a heavy mind, that karma is grave; if one performs it with a detached mind, that karma is light. This is as previously cited from the *Śrāmaṇerakārikā* within the section on upholding and violating precepts, concerning the eight grades of karmic actions.
It is not permissible to perform a combined confession with the root offense simply because the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) shares the same name. This is clearly established:

whenever one commits a *duṣkṛta* and fails to repent after the night has passed, there is an offense of concealment (*praticchādana*), and furthermore, a secondary *duṣkṛta* arises from that [concealment]. This [secondary] *duṣkṛta* is light.
One must first repent. If one were to repent it together with the original primary offense as being equally grave, that would be contrary to the Dharma.

This is because although they share the same name of "grave," there is a difference between the root offense and its derivative; they cannot be suppressed. "Suppression" (yō) means to cease; it is also called "karma" (gyō).
Regarding the slight differences: Sheng says that within the *pratideśanīya* (提) there are texts such as "confession leads to peace and happiness," which are numerous;
these are absent from the *duṣkṛta* (吉), hence it is said to be "few. As for "the *duṣkṛta* is most minor and cannot be recited extensively like the rules on *pāyattika* (墮法)":
this means that when confessing a *duṣkṛta*, there is no textual basis in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (四分). Now, one should rely on both the *pratideśanīya* and the *pāyattika*.

The textual accounts regarding offenses also differ to some degree. This must now be briefly clarified: because the offenses are minor, one cannot rely on the extensive recitation rules for *pāyattika* (falling) offenses;

hence it is said they are "not the same as the *Mahāsāṃghika*," etc., which will be explained below. Regarding the statement, "Not being the same as the *Mahāsāṃghika*, because there [in that school] the *pāyattika* offense is combined with it":
this establishes that the *Mahāsāṃghika* text prescribes the confession of both the root *thullaccaya* (grave offense) and the derivative *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). They are identical.
"Repentance at that time. Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*," I privately say it refers to the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*. Others say it must be the *Prajñā-śāstra*.
As for "the rest as described in the *Caryā-dharma*," Zhen-sheng says it refers to the *Caryā-dharma* for ordinary and holy beings;
that is, the six dharmas of Master Zhengchan and so forth.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), regarding those who perform repentance before an elder (*sthavira*), one possessing five qualities may do so; for a junior, four qualities are required, excluding prostration at the feet.
As recorded in the "Supplementary Text on the Five Matters" (*Wenzhong wufa wen*) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:

Upāli asked the Buddha, "How many qualities must a junior bhikṣu possess when performing repentance before an elder bhikṣu? The Buddha replied, "There are five qualities: baring the right shoulder, removing leather sandals, and prostrating..."

"Place the feet together. Kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms—this is the fifth [method]. Furthermore, it was asked: 'Elder, when one performs repentance before a junior bhikṣu, how many dharmas are there?
The Buddha said: 'There are four dharmas. With the exception of prostrating at the feet, the rest is as explained above.

As for the instruction to 'carefully examine from top to bottom,' it is because I feared that in the course of practice, one might be negligent or forgetful. I have sent this so that you may investigate with single-minded scrutiny and thus achieve full understanding; hence, the phrase 'from top to bottom.'"
A Detailed Commentary. The above concludes the explanation of the six categories of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga-dharma*) within the sixteenth [section].
*Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (Sifen lü chao pi), Volume 12, Part 1;
*Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Volume 12, Part 2.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Section XVII: On the General and Specific Aspects of the Robes (Part One).
Since one who has committed an offense is able to repent, their body and mind become pure and they are capable of cultivating the path. However, the Way does not achieve itself; it relies upon...

Regarding the physical vessel: the vessel relies upon necessary provisions to remain and advance in its practice. Although these provisions are numerous, they do not fall outside the categories of external and internal.
Externally, there are clothing; internally, there are medicine and food. Now, the external provisions are explained first; therefore, this passage follows. Furthermore, the Commentary states:
All forms that depend on external conditions must rely on nourishment. As for the essentials of the person, they do not exceed clothing and food.

The reason clothing is mentioned before food is that clothing covers the body and is required at all times; it is intended to ensure the body is prepared for ritual decorum while the mind maintains right contemplation.
Therefore, clothing is explained first. Food, however, is consumed only at specific times, and thus is listed subsequently. Xuán said: "Stop."

This clarifies the ritual for the method of repentance (*pratideśanā*). When the vessel of the body is pure, the provisions for practice are opened and unimpeded; thus, the principle achieves its purpose.

To save the age and assist the Path, these supporting conditions are essential. Just as outer clothing and inner medicine have distinct requirements for the physical form, it is for this reason that this text has come forth.

Regarding the "two types of robes," this refers to both that which is prohibited and that which is permitted. "Prohibited" refers to the three robes and the six requisites; "permitted" refers to the one hundred and one items and various surplus articles.

Because there are these two distinctions, they are called the "two types of robes. Regarding "general and specific": within the prohibited category there are general and specific elements, and within the permitted category there are likewise general and specific elements.
As for the general and specific within the prohibited: stating directly "the three robes and six requisites" constitutes the general; within those...

Regarding the names such as *antarvāsa* (inner robe) and so forth, these constitute the specific [distinctions]. As for what is permitted among the general and the specific: the "one hundred and one" various extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) are the general name;
the lower garment (*nivasana*), requisites, rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), robes offered by donors (*dānapati-deya-cīvara*), and so forth are called the specific.

Discussing it in this manner, they possess both the general and the specific. Some explain that regarding the term "general and specific": the general regulation of the three robes is called "general," while the one hundred and one...

Master Changbie said that they are distinct; therefore, he spoke of the two robes as being both general and specific. Furthermore, some others say that "two robes" is an error, and that one should refer to them collectively as the three robes, both general and specific.
Now it is clarified that this is merely the speech of the blind; having failed to examine the holy teachings, such a statement was made.

One must understand that these refer to the two types of robes—those prescribed by prohibition and those permitted by allowance. How could they possibly be called the three robes of superior, middling, and inferior?
Based on this naming, there is a vast difference between their breadth and narrowness (and so forth).
Now, as for "the form dwelling amidst worldly burdens," this establishes that the burden refers to the human person dwelling in the world, which is indeed a heavy encumbrance.
Thus, Laozi said: "Of all great calamities, none is greater than having a body. If I had no body, what calamity would I have?
Therefore, the sage extinguishes the body to return to non-existence. As for "obstructing and defiling by means of the dusts," the dusts refer to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
"Stain" (*rañjana*) refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). It is also said that "dust" (*rajas*) means defilement.

Regarding "if there is a proper method for using [the robes]," this means that for extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), one must perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification) within ten days; once the three robes (*tricīvara*) have been formally dedicated (*adhivāsita*), one is not permitted to be separated from them overnight.

This constitutes having a proper method of use. As for the word "fault" (*guo*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "calamity. In the *Shangshu*, it appears as the character *gao* (臬皋), meaning a boundary marker or a mound.
Kong Anguo said: "Jiù (咎) means evil. The *Mao Shi* says: "Sorrowful and fearful of jiù. The commentary states: "Jiù is synonymous with guò (transgression).
Regarding the term "lì (戾)," the *Erlie* says it means "crime. If one accepts what is contrary to the proper standard, one immediately falls into deep transgression.
This means that if the clothing itself was obtained through wrong livelihood, such as trading or gambling, then at the very moment of accepting it, one has already committed an offense.

Furthermore, if the subsequent ritual addition (*adhivāsanā*) is not performed, it is likewise invalid. This extends to cases such as not performing the purification (*pariśuddhi*) for extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), keeping the three robes apart overnight, or keeping the one hundred and one items apart overnight after they have already been ritually added;
all such instances constitute a violation of the proper form. "To fall" (*kṣipta*) means to sink; "transgression" (*āpatti*) refers to a fault or offense.

Regarding "permission granted according to [one's] retribution": this means that there are six different types of retribution, beginning with those such as Māṇava and including those such as the divine Subhūti (and so forth).
Regarding "no fault in either following or opposing": this means that for the one hundred and one types of long robes and so on, not keeping them constitutes "opposition."
To keep [the robes] and perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) is compliant with the Dharma; in both cases, there is no fault.

Regarding the phrase "because one wishes to manifest a previously non-existent phenomenon": these names and characteristics of the three robes appeared only through the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Prior to this, throughout kalpas of vast antiquity, these names did not exist; therefore, they are called "previously non-existent phenomena. All ninety-six [heretical schools]... [text ends].

Regarding the various types of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the disciples of the six teachers of the non-Buddhists—each teacher having fifteen kinds of teachings to bestow upon his disciples—developed divergent views because their respective doctrines differed.
Thus, each teacher produced fifteen kinds of divergent views; the teacher possessed distinct doctrines that were not shared by his disciples. Teacher and disciple...
My son, these collectively constitute sixteen types. Thus, these six masters have ninety-six other masters who employ their respective methods;
as they approach their end, they transmit them to their disciples. In this manner, from master to master, there are always six fundamental teachers.
Beneath each of these fundamental teachers, fifteen kinds of divergent views arise, which are like branches and twigs—just as in the Buddhist tradition, where the Dharma was divided into ten schools.
The eight schools all originated from the fundamental Mahāsāṃghika. Regarding the three robes, it is said that they were worn even in winter because they were heavy.

According to the fourth fascicle of the *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), there was a bhikṣu named Bumī who maintained the three robes, never parting from them even for eating or resting.
Some say that the "maker of the three robes" is so called because of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma; others say... [text fragment ends].
It is said that they are for the three periods of time; alternatively, it is said they are for the three seasons. Therefore, the three robes were established:
one wears heavy robes in winter, light ones in summer, and medium ones in spring and autumn. It is for these three seasons that one possesses the three robes.

The heavy ones consist of five strips (*pañcaka*), the medium ones of seven strips (*saptaka*), and the thin ones of fifteen types (*pañcadaśaka*). When it is extremely cold, one wears the three robes layered together.
This can be used to illustrate it. Some say that the three robes were also established for the sake of mosquitoes, gadflies, and moths;

for this reason, one should always maintain them without forgetting. Regarding "also for the sake of various insects": if one wears only a single robe, one will be bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the noble disciples of the Buddha wear the three robes because they abide in the Middle Way. (End of excerpt from the *Jizhi*).
The sixty-eighth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "The practitioner has few desires and is content; his robes merely suffice to cover the body, being neither too many nor too few.
Therefore, he undertakes the practice of the three robes (*tricīvara*). Laypeople, because they delight in worldly pleasures, accumulate various kinds of clothing;

some non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), because of their ascetic practices, go naked without shame. For this reason, the disciples of the Buddha abandon these two extremes and abide in the Middle Way, whether walking or staying."
The three robes are for constant use while staying in a monastery. Regarding this, I privately remark: in secular life, people are excessively extravagant;
among the non-Buddhists, they are excessively frugal. Each clings to one extreme. The present regulation of the three robes avoids these two extremes, manifesting the practice of the Middle Way.
Regarding the statement that "one who harbors the four [faults] within their breast and is possessed by the fetters (saṃyojana) should not don the kāṣāya," it is recorded in the Kauśāmbī-khandhaka:
"The bhikṣus of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī were engaged in strife, mutually slandering and reviling one another, causing the Saṃgha to be split and remain discordant.
The Buddha, employing the metaphor of a mirror, spoke a verse to reconcile and extinguish the conflict. Within that verse, there is this statement: 'Even though...'"
One who wears the *kāṣāya* robe yet harbors the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and cannot eliminate the bonds of enmity is not worthy of that robe.
One whose fetters have already been extinguished, who is adorned by the observance of precepts, and who has subdued their enemies—that person is truly worthy of the *kāṣāya*. The commentary explains:

This clarifies that the robe serves as the outward sign of the Path. It distinguishes between the two types of persons—the ignorant and the wise—by whether they are worthy or unworthy of it. Though the robe is honorable, [it is only the latter who truly embody its significance].

One's virtue is base; one feels personal shame that one's virtue does not match one's robes. It is for this reason that one dons the armor of patience when leaving the household life to practice the Way.
For a person free from desire to harbor anger is utterly improper. It is like lightning striking and fire erupting from within clear, cool clouds;
it is simply not what should be.
Regarding the statement that "a single robe cannot ward off the cold," Huiliang said: "If one wears only a single robe, the body becomes soiled and filthy, which gives rise to much shame.
As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* stating that "the three robes are the insignia of the noble śramaṇas," according to that same text: there was once a non-Buddhist practitioner who...
Her parents had both gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma. When the non-Buddhists were cold and lacked clothing, her mother took off her *uttarāsaṅga* and gave it to him.
Having received it, he put it on and entered a tavern. People despised him, saying, "This donkey with wrong views who eats dregs of wine wears the insignia of a holy man.
A bhikṣuṇī reported this transgression to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Śramaṇa..."
The robe is the insignia of the noble ones (ārya). If one gives it further to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), one commits a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding the reason why the various schools of our own tradition generally prescribe three robes because of the cold, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha traveled gradually from Vaiśālī..."
He arrived at the Cāpāla Stūpa. At that time, it was the great cold of winter; he put on a single garment and stayed overnight in the open air.

When the first watch of the night had passed, he felt cold and put on another garment. When the middle watch of the night had passed, he again felt cold and put on another garment. Then he was no longer afflicted by the suffering of the cold.
He then had this thought: "If future bhikṣus cannot endure the cold, these three robes will be sufficient for them to ward it off.
The next morning, he assembled the bhikṣus and fully explained his intention from the previous night regarding the establishment of the precept, enjoining the keeping of the three robes.

Having finished explaining the intent behind the regulation above, he now clarifies the definition of the names below. The commentary states: "As for this *kāṣāya* robe being named after its color, it is according to Master Ying."
It is said: According to foreign [traditions], it is generally called *kāṣāya*. This is translated here as "improper color.
Among various plants, whatever is neither bark, leaf, nor flower—that which cannot form the five flavors and is difficult to use as food—is termed *kāṣāya*.
Because this substance dyes clothing with a turbid red color, the term *kāṣāya* is also used for the "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) among the five turbidities in the Sanskrit original. In India...
The Master [Kāśyapa] frequently used this color. Some say that when it was first translated, its hue appeared turbid, and thus it was named accordingly.

In the *Yùnjí* (Rhyme Collection), the character for "kāṣāya" is pronounced with the phonetic "jiā" and originally written with the radical "hair" (毛). It was only after Gé Hóng composed the *Zìyuàn* (Garden of Characters) that he changed the radical to "clothing" (衣).
The *Jiémósū* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "Among the six flavors, there is the flavor of the kāṣāya," meaning that the kāṣāya is a bland, light color.
It is a flavor. According to this, "kāṣāya" is a name for color. Tripitaka Master Jing said:
"Kāṣāya" signifies the meaning of red, such as that produced by dyeing with the heartwood of the *dhātaki* tree."
Regarding the statement that the *saṃghāṭī* is called the "garment for the assembly": this refers to entering royal palaces or villages, which is termed "the assembly.

(This point remains unexplained). Regarding the statement that it is called the "nine-seven-fold" (*saptanavaka*) garment: according to the Vinaya, the number of strips (*koṭi*) is distinct [for each type of robe], and it does not refer to the *antarvāsaka* or other such garments.
It does not state that the five-striped robe is the *antaravāsaka*; this person refers to it as the "seven-five-striped" [robe] and so forth.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty says: *saṃghāṭī* (or *saṃghaṭi*) is translated as "joined" or "layered," meaning it is made by cutting and joining pieces together, or it is double-layered.
*Uttarāsaṅga* is translated as "upper garment," meaning it is the one worn most prominently among those garments normally used.
This is because it is worn above those [other garments]. *Antarvāsa*, or *antaravāsaka*, is translated as "inner-layered garment" (*zhōngsù yī*) or "undergarment" (*lǐyī*).
As for its division into three types according to usage, this refers to the plain cloth (*mànyī*) which can serve the function of both the upper and middle garments.
Therefore, it is said that this is based on practical application. It is not that the fundamental essence of the primary school of thought is absent;

rather, the established position is that the *maṇḍala* (unsewn) robe is the proper attire for the two groups of *śrāmaṇeras*. They ought not to wear robes with strips or leaves (*sāṇḍa-sapatta*), but should possess only two *maṇḍala* robes.

One [robe] corresponds to the *uttarāsaṅga*, and one corresponds to the *antarvāsaka*. Now, for the sake of the Great Saṃgha, [the robe] is made by cutting; yet the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is insufficient, so it is permitted to be made as a seven-strip robe.
Still, that is insufficient, even down to making it as a seamless robe (*sāṇḍasaṃghāṭī*). Therefore, it is said: "according to what can be accomplished by one's own ability.

Because the Great Saṃgha is able to use it, it is said: "it is not that the essential substance of the great category is absent. My own intention is that [the classification] is divided according to its use.
"Third, it is not that the essential substance of the categories is absent. This is a general conclusion summarizing the names of the three robes explained above.
That is to say, these three names—*kāṣāya*, *antarvāsaka*, and so forth—have no direct translations in the various schools.
Regarding the various texts listed above that explain the names of these robes, they all apply the names based on their functional use; therefore, it is said they are "divided according to use."
Third: This explains the three [robes] by way of their function; it does not contradict the general path of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Therefore, it is said:

"It is not that the fundamental substance of the Great Vehicle is absent" (this interpretation is excellent). Jì says: These words conclude the preceding discussion on how the *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī* robe universally applies to the meaning of the three robes.

Although the *maṇḍala* robe universally applies to all three locations, according to the fundamental treatise on their substance, they remain ultimately distinct from one another. For that which is made for the function of the *saṃghāṭī* robe, its dimensions...
It is long and wide. If it is used for the purpose of an undergarment (*antarvāsaka*), its dimensions are likewise short and narrow.

Although the name "plain cloth" (*maṇḍala*) is a general term, according to its specific application and essential nature, each is distinct. Therefore, it is said that they are not without their respective major categories and essential natures.
(The explanation of the definitions and meanings above is concluded; from here on, its functional utility is clarified.)
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Provided that one's nature is that of a śramaṇa, even if one defiles the practices of a śramaṇa.

This means that because one possesses the nature of the precept-substance (*śīla-dhātu*), it is said that "one's nature is that of a śramaṇa. According to the third fascicle of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there shall be bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who, within my Dharma, shall attain [liberation]."
Having left their homes, they walked hand-in-hand with their children from one tavern to another, engaging in unchaste conduct within my Dharma.
Although they acted thus for the sake of wine, all of them shall attain nirvāṇa during this Bhadrakalpa.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas shall appear in the world; I am the fourth, followed by others.
"Maitreya shall succeed me in my place, continuing in this sequence until the final Tathāgata, Ruci;

you should know this, Ānanda. Within my Dharma, there will be those who are śramaṇas only by nature, who defile the conduct of a śramaṇa, who claim for themselves to be śramaṇas, and who are śramaṇas merely in appearance—even those who wear the kāṣāya robe. This shall occur beginning with Maitreya during this Bhadrakalpa."
Up until the time of Tathāgata Luṣi, those śramaṇas, in the presence of such Buddhas, will successively enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder, leaving nothing behind. Why is this?
Because among all these śramaṇas, even for one who utters the name of a Buddha or gives rise to a single thought of faith, the merit they have performed shall never be in vain. I...
This is because the Buddha’s wisdom perceives and knows the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s vow for the *kaṣāya* to possess five merits under the Buddha Ratnagarbha, it is as stated in the *Excerpts from the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (and so forth).
As for the passage concerning "holding even a small portion of this robe while in the midst of battle," this is explained here by way of a proximate application.
Regarding the distant transmission of the teachings: During the early Tang dynasty, there was a Vinaya Master named Quan, a native of Goguryeo.

When the Great Tang army swept across the world to campaign against Goguryeo, Quan was then serving as a soldier in those forces. Having previously heard the Dharma and witnessed the power of the *kāṣāya*, he had obtained several pieces of it and sewn them into his clothing.
At that time, as the Tang troops advanced for battle and the two armies engaged, Quan feared he would perish on the battlefield; he then [copied...]
Laoquan cast off his armor and advanced on foot to surrender. Seeing Quan from a distance, the tens of thousands of Tang soldiers perceived him as if he were a host of a million;
all were clad in radiant armor and advanced with a formidable presence. The Tang troops were struck with great fear and likewise laid down their weapons to offer their submission.

When they reached Quan’s side, there was no longer any remaining multitude. Astonished by this divine marvel, they immediately dispatched a report to inform the throne. Quan was taken to the capital, where an imperial edict was issued.

He was granted an official post. Since Sengquan had long possessed faith and his resolve was set upon seeking the essential Way, he requested permission to leave the household life and resided in Chang’an.
That monastery was renowned for its divine wonders; light emanated from his shoulders, and when he traveled at night, people saw torches held upright upon his shoulders (and so forth).
As for the phrase "to deceive the Buddhas of the ten directions," "deceive" (qī) means to betray, to mislead, or to insult. It refers to if I—
If the *kāṣāya* lacks these five benefits, it is a betrayal of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If monks or nuns possess the virtue of the precepts, and a layperson requests their *kāṣāya* to ward off calamities and the like," according to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, if there is a monk of virtuous precepts and someone requests a piece of his *kāṣāya* desiring to use it to ward off calamities, he should cause it to be purified (*pariśuddha*).
When giving to others, one must not give large pieces; one should give small ones (this is the direct meaning of the text). The *Zishu* states: "To 'rang' means to remove or to reject.

(The three preceding sections—concerning the intent of the regulation, the explanation of the name, and the functional utility—are now complete. From here on, the second section clarifies the method for making robes).
Regarding the fact that one who has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) may not make use of the cloth: this is because its substance is not [proper].

As for *hu* (縠), Master Li says it resembles light gauze (*qingsha*) and is commonly seen in the northern regions; Master Ji says it is simply thin and light gauze, such as that used by women’s families to make upper covers or petticoats.
As for *xiao* (綃, pronounced xiao), Master Li says: "Xiao" refers to coarse gauze; that which is half-raw and half-cooked is called *xiao*. This applies generally.
A secular text states that raw silk fabric is called *xiāo*. Regarding the account of a dragon wearing a *kāṣāya* to escape the danger of the *garuḍa*:
according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, in a past age by the shore of the great ocean there was a *śāla* tree, upon which lived a *garuḍa*.
This bird’s body was immense, its two wings spanning one hundred and fifty *yojanas*. It habitually took dragons as its food; whenever it desired to eat a dragon, [it would...]
At that time, he first struck the ocean water with his two wings to part it, whereupon the dragon appeared; he then seized and ate it.
It is the constant custom of the dragons to fear the garuḍa and to constantly seek out a *kāṣāya* robe to place upon the palace gate.

When the bird sees the *kāṣāya*, a spirit of reverence arises within him, and he no longer proceeds to eat those dragons. At that time, this bird struck the sea with his wings and saw the dragon about to [emerge].
The dragon was greatly terrified by this. He immediately took the *kāṣāya* and placed it upon his head, then fled along the bank.
The bird was unable to harm him (and so forth).
It must not be the case that those who are powerless to follow the teachings are excluded.

It is established that what was explained above—namely, that the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe) can generate meritorious power, ward off calamities, and provide immunity from misfortune—is only effective when its substance is authentic and not produced from wealth obtained through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

[The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of the substance of the material. Below, the meaning of the color being in accordance with the Dharma is clarified. Regarding the term for "dyeing" (*rañjana*), there is a direct equivalent, namely *kāṣāya*.
*Śāṭaka*. In the Qin language, it is correctly translated as "dye. Regarding the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*’s phrase "the three colors: blue, mud, and *zhàn*": *zhàn* refers to *mùlán* (magnolia).

This is seen in the *Suixiang* (Corresponding Characteristics) section on the ninety offenses. The commentary explains: "Do not use *gàn* (pale blue; *gǎn* is pronounced *gǎn* in the ancient reading); this refers to the colors blue and red."

The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "Gan" means "to contain. This refers to a blue color that contains red. The *Shuowen* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states: "Silk dyed blue with a slight trace of red.
If red, white, or yellow are not pure primary colors (*mahāvarṇa*), it is clearly established that these are called "half-colors" (*ardhavarṇa*).
This means they are not entirely primary colors; however, even if they are only half-primary colors, they may still be used. For example, as in the case of [tying]...
Regarding "love and so forth" (*rāga-ādi*) being called "the defiled one" (*rakta*): the Master [Seng]liang says that taking the meaning of "defilement" (*rañjana*) is what makes them equivalent.

Regarding "yellow": the Master says it refers to the yellow dye of the *utpala* flower. As for the note stating "by way of comparison" (*upamāna*): the Master says "comparison" (*bi*) means "near" (*vi*) or "together.
He explains that this Vinaya was translated in the land of Wu; because there were no *mūlana* trees in the north, and since they could not be seen, it was translated as *jia*.
Yan-shen said: "The 'northern region' refers to all directions. It is said that in the north there is the *mūlāna* tree;
its bark was used for the *Cīvara-vinaya*, which was translated in the Wu region. I did not recognize this wood, but nowadays the juice of various fruits is used as the *mūlāna* dyeing method.
As for what is stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, according to that treatise, the saffron robes (*kāṣāya*) of the *svāgata* bhikṣus were as bright and clear as..."
The red lotus flower. Eight items were carried with him: namely, the three robes, an alms bowl, a needle, thread, a small axe, and a water-strainer.
Now, this passage is cited to clarify that when [the Buddha] said "Welcome," he was wearing red garments, thereby proving that the color of Mūlan’s meditative absorption was indeed red.
As for the *Yijiao falü jing* (Sutra on the Bequeathed Teachings and Vinaya Rules) up to this point, it is a spurious scripture; it is not included in the catalogs. This sutra...
It is permitted to wear robes of the five primary colors. Regarding the phrase "as in the *Śaikṣa-dharmas*," etc.:

if one obtains a new robe from among the ninety [rules] and accepts it without applying the three types of dyeing to ruin its original color, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. (The above concludes the explanation of the third point, the meaning of "color according to the Dharma.
Below follows the fourth point, which correctly clarifies the matter of measurement.)
Therefore, regarding the establishment of three grades for each of the ten *krośas*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: The Buddha said, "I allow you to possess three kinds of robes, namely:
superior, middling, and inferior. A superior robe is five cubits (*hasta*) in length and two cubits in width;

one that is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width—these two being between the extremes—is called a middling robe. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, within a single robe there are three [grades].
Regarding the measurement: the text states that the *saṃghāṭī* has three grades—superior, middling, and inferior. The superior is five cubits in length and three cubits in width.
The middling is five cubits in length minus one extended hand-span and three cubits in width minus one extended hand-span.
The inferior is four and a half cubits in length and three cubits in width minus one extended hand-span. The *uttarāsaṅga* also has three grades; the superior is five [cubits in length]...
The elbow-width is three elbows. The medium [robe] is five elbows in length minus one span of the hand, and three elbows in width minus one span of the hand.
The inferior [robe] is four and a half elbows in length and five elbows in width minus one span of the hand. The antaravāsaka (inner robe) also has three grades:
the superior is five elbows in length and two elbows in width; the medium is five elbows in length minus one span of the hand and two elbows in width minus one [span].
"Not extending the hand" means that the lower garment is four and a half cubits in length and two cubits in width, excluding the "not extending the hand" portion. The commentary states:

"The declaration (*sūtra*) should occur after the acceptance. This clarifies that if the three robes exceed the prescribed measure and have not been cut down, the portion exceeding that measure must still be formally declared pure (*śuddha*).
If one were to first perform the formal declaration of purity and subsequently apply the ritual addition (*adhikāra*), the rite of purity would then be lost. This is essential.
This refers to first performing the ritual of formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) and subsequently declaring it as pure (*śuddhi*).
Regarding the statement that one need not necessarily rely on the *hasta* (cubit) measurement: this is because robes are nowadays generally made according to the proportions of the body.

Therefore, one cannot simply take the fixed measurements of five or three *hasta*. Thus, the text says: "Eat according to the capacity of the belly; measure [the robe] according to the dimensions of the body."

Regarding its meaning (the preceding section concludes the explanation of the principles of evaluating right and wrong; hereafter begins the fifth [section], which correctly clarifies the number of categories):

The reason it is singular is that, as in the *I Ching*, the pair belongs to Yin, while the single belongs to Yang; Yin belongs to generation, while Yang presides over destruction, because Yang is able to give birth to the myriad things.
Taking the śramaṇa as an analogy, [the practice] has compassion and benevolence as its fundamental basis for action. Because it is a manifestation of worldly yang, the number is not even.
It is like saying that when the yang energy descends, the myriad things are brought forth; this signifies that those who now wear [the robes] are able to produce all manner of goodness.

Regarding the erroneous inclusion of the character "not" (不), Master Li states that within the Vinaya texts, the character "also" (亦) was mistakenly written as "not"; it should properly read "also" (亦應).
"Chù" (to store/possess) is an error in the Vinaya. Regarding the current mention of "thirty-three strips" and so forth, Master Lì says:
it is likely an error; what should be "thirteen strips" has been mistakenly increased by thirty-three. This is because the language of the Western Regions is inverted;

it is feared that there was originally a case where "three" was mentioned first and "ten" later, thus resulting in "thirty. In the language of this region [China], "ten" is mentioned first and "three" later, which would then result in "thirteen."

Third, therefore, we know that the claim that there are thirty-three [patches] is incorrect, as there is no authoritative scripture (āgama) to support it. Consequently, the subsequent citation from the *Śrīlaṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata wore a robe of thirteen strips," which serves as proof for the aforementioned thirteen; this is the correct interpretation.
Regarding the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that this is a coarse cloth *saṃghāṭī*, according to the first fascicle of the *Śāstra*: "At midnight, the Bodhisattva crossed..."
Leaving the city, he traveled twelve *yojanas* to the forest grove where the seer Bhārgava resided.
There, he shaved his hair with a blade and exchanged his exquisite garments for a coarse cotton *saṃghāṭī* robe by the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
He then practiced austerities for six years. (The fifth section, explaining the meaning of the numerical counts, is hereby concluded.)
Regarding the "six *dīna* measures," Ji says that a dammed water reservoir is called a *dī*.

As for the "incompleteness of the text in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*," I privately note that this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely clarifies the number of items and the fixed dimensions of the five and seven robes, but does not clarify the *saṃghāṭī*.
Now, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, it is clarified that there are three grades of *saṃghāṭī*, each with its own specified measurements.

Regarding "four long and one short," Xuān says: The reason for displaying these lengths is that because the rice fields of the world vary in height from place to place, the robes of the śramaṇas manifest these variations in length as well;
this is so that the dharma-robes may serve as a field of merit and benefit all sentient beings.
The noble increase while the ordinary decrease; this is like a field where the long plots are many and the short ones few. Therefore, it is called in the world the "Robe of Merit.

By means of the characteristics of its furrows and ridges, just as worldly fields use furrows to hold water so as to nourish fine seedlings for the sake of physical life, the field of the Dharma-robe uses the water of the four benefits and increases the mind of the three virtues to nourish the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body. This is why—
Regarding the limit of twenty-five items: some say this is because one wishes to serve as a field of merit for the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

As for the case where one sews new cloth into layers, if it exceeds the limit at the time of completion, Master Li states: "It is precisely because the act was performed in violation of the Dharma that it was not accomplished.

Now, to indiscriminately include such items in the count of the three robes (*tricīvara*) and fail to perform the ritual of 'purification' (*viśuddhi*) for ten days constitutes the offense of possessing an extra robe."

Because the Buddha permitted one layer and two layers to be made of new material, the three-layered robe made entirely of new material would be longer [in length]. One layer is not a restrictive limit.

Regarding the fact that a *duṣkṛta* offense is committed at the time of making it, while a *sthūlātyaya* offense is committed on the day of wearing it: the statement that the *duṣkṛta* is removed through repentance in the interim means that there is still the possibility of remediation (*pratīkāra*).

Regarding the term "one who does not sleep apart from their robes": I privately explain that although one may leave behind one or two layers, because the substance of the robe remains with the body, the fault of sleeping apart from the robes is not incurred.
As for the previous statement regarding "within the original boundary" in the case of death:
this means that if a bhikṣu has his robes inside the boundary and takes the substance of the robes out, and dies on the road while having an attendant, [the following applies].
Regarding the three robes obtained [from the deceased], some say that since they were set aside within the boundary (*sīmā*), they belong to those within the boundary;
others say they belong to those within the boundary; and others say they belong to the caregiver (*glānopasthāyaka*). The Vinaya Master says: this refers to the author of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*).

He states that because the caregiver possesses virtuous qualities (*guṇa*), they must be granted a reward. If they do not possess such qualities, then [the robes] shall be divided among the monks within that boundary. Above.
The explanation of the seventh section concerning the meaning of the number of robes is concluded.

As for the phrase "fearing that it might not be completed in one day," this likely refers to those who do not keep extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*)—namely, those who possess only the three-month robes—and thus fear exceeding the time limit.
It was the World-Honored One himself who cut the three robes for Aniruddha, while eighty thousand bhikṣus did the same.
Regarding the "Confederates" (the *saṃghāṭas*), it is as recorded in the *Madhyama-āgama* excerpt (*yathā madhyamāgame uddhṛtam*, etc.).
As for Ānanda following the instructions to make robes for the bhikṣus, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

"The Buddha, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people, was traveling through the south. Descending from a mountain, he saw a rice field with excellent Buddhist ridges and furrows, and he thought..."
He said, "Bhikṣus, you should make robes using this material as the source. He then asked Ānanda, "Do you see this field? He replied, "I have seen it.
Again he told Ānanda, "It would be fitting for the bhikṣus to wear robes made like this. Are you able to make them? He replied, "I am able to make them.
Thereupon, following these instructions, he made them himself and also taught the bhikṣus how to make them—some being one long and one short, or two [long and one short].

One strip is long and one is short; or three are long and one is short. The strips on the left slant toward the left, the strips on the right slant toward the right, and the central strips slant in both directions.
Once finished, when worn, it is most appropriate for the body. The Buddha saw this and addressed the bhikṣus: "Ānanda possesses great wisdom;
having heard my brief instruction, he has fashioned it exactly according to the Dharma. This is called the 'cut-and-sewn' robe, which is not shared [with other schools]."
[The] Robe. It is different from those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and cannot be seized by enemies or thieves. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* asks:

"If it was only at this time that the monastic robes were prescribed, what was worn on the body prior to that? Moreover, as soon as [the Buddha] uttered 'Welcome' (*svāgata*), the three robes were complete upon his person.
Since Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to be ordained into the Dharma-robes, how can one reconcile these earlier and later accounts? Answer: At the very beginning of the Dharma...

In the Immortal Garden (Āśramapada), the five companions were first ordained and donned the three robes (*tricīvara*). However, because the Dharma-garments were established by the Sage’s regulations long ago, they have been produced according to circumstances over time, resulting in variations in their design and color.
Since the net of the Teaching was first spread, most followed the practical requirements of the monastic life; as for the formal vestments, [they followed these established precedents].

This was certainly not his original intention. Consequently, various instances of laxity appeared according to the times, as he perceived the underlying conditions; thus, the establishment of the rules of discipline was naturally appropriate. Lì asked:

"When Ānanda and others received the full precepts through *karmavācanā*, how could they have lacked the three robes (*tricīvara*)? Why, then, do the teachings instruct them to follow worldly customs in making their robes? The answer is:
Because the robes from previous lives were transformed by the power of the Sages, it would have been difficult for them to follow [worldly] practices at that time. Now, one follows worldly customs.
This is because the field serves as a demonstration of ease of accomplishment.

Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule that one must not paint [the pattern] and sew it with the edges facing each other, "standing" refers simply to having finished sewing with the edges facing each other.
To draw lines and leaf-patterns [on the robe] is contrary to the Dharma. Regarding "extremely narrow like *yavekṣu*": the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *qǐ* refers to millet (*sù*).
Today, the green-stalked large barley is called *yavekṣu*. Regarding "horse-tooth seams" (*mǎchǐfèng*):
Jì says that when making the scale-like borders of a *kāṣāya*, one bends the scales inward and secures them with thread; each of these constitutes a horse-tooth seam.

Regarding the instruction to place the leather strap (*kṣaumaka*) four finger-widths from the front: Jì (Jie) says that the "strap" (*kṣaumaka*) refers to the long strip, while the "knot" (*nīvi*) refers to the short piece currently placed at the front.
Because people nowadays have reversed this, they place the knot at the back and the strap at the front, thereby losing the original regulation.
Regarding the phrase "departing from conditions," this refers to departing from external conditions such as the kaṣāya; it does not mean that internal conditions are being discussed.
Since the scope of these conditions is indeterminate, how could one refer to internal ones?
Regarding items that should be extracted and given to the Saṃgha: if such an item is sewn onto [the robe], it is no longer included within the category of the *kāṣāya*.
Even until death, one may not keep this patch as a personal possession; it must be extracted and distributed among the members of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the folding of the shoulder area where it is soiled or greasy: I have privately remarked that this was intended for those who wear only the three robes (*tricīvara*), which is why they were instructed to fold it.

At present, since one wears a separate inner garment (*antaravāsaka*), it is not strictly necessary to fold it. Nevertheless, it may also be appropriate for people today to fold the shoulder area as well.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding the case where a bhikṣu wearing refuse-rags (pāṃsukūla) heard that the Buddha had established the precept prohibiting entry into a village without wearing cut-and-sewn robes (khaṇḍa-cīvara), he then patched and added borders to his rags.
The Buddha said: "One must indeed cut [the cloth] into pieces and so forth. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
there was a certain bhikṣu who possessed refuse-rags; having heard that the Buddha had formulated the rule that one should not enter a village wearing uncut clothing, [he acted accordingly].
[The monk] fell [into reflection]: "I have a rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*) that is torn; I should mend it by adding patches and applying a border with a hook-pattern.
He then took his needle and thread and, near the gate of the Jetavana, mended the robe and applied the border as intended for a cut-and-sewn garment (*khaṇḍa-sīvana*).

The Buddha, while walking for exercise (*caṅkrama*), saw him and went to his side to ask: "What are you doing? He answered in full detail. The Buddha said: "Excellent! You should mend rag-robes in this manner."
It is for use as a robe to be cut and pieced together. Some say that the four borders are called *laṅ* (fringe) and the patches applied in the middle are called *gū* (hook).
Now, examining this closely, it remains unsettled; since it is stated that one makes hooks and applies fringes, it is clear that the *laṅ* and the borders (*yuan*) are distinct.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* provides a clear text permitting the wearing [of such a robe] when entering [a village], which refers to entering a village while wearing a robe patched with the aforementioned appliqués.
The preceding eight sections have collectively explained the second topic, the method for making robes. From here on, the third section correctly clarifies the formal undertaking of wearing them.
Regarding the seventy-two types of robes: the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) properly consists of eighteen varieties, beginning from nine strips up to twenty-five strips.
This means that since there are nine varieties of the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa-sīvana*) style, there are likewise [nine] varieties of the folded-leaf (*pattāvali*) style.
Nine. Two nines make eighteen. Regarding the "derived" (*anugata*) categories, there are six types. Specifically, for the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*), there are exactly two types:

the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa*) and the folded-leaf (*pāṭaka*). Together with the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*), which has exactly four types—namely, the cut-and-sewn, the folded-leaf, the pleated (*saṃvartita*), and the seamless (*maṇḍala*)—these four, combined with the previous two, constitute the six derived types of the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*). This completes the preceding [count].
Eighteen [is the same as] twenty-four. The seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) properly consists of two categories; from among these there are twenty-two.
