Furthermore, taking the eighteen categories of the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and the four categories of the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*), they form the sub-categories of the seven-strip robe family, totaling twenty-four when combined.

The five types [of robes] actually comprise four categories. As previously stated, there are twenty [varieties]: namely, eighteen for the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe), plus two for the seven-strip robe, thus making twenty.
Including the combined discussion, there are also twenty-four. In total, there are three sets of twenty-four, which amounts to seventy-two.
As for why the present *Chao* (Commentary) speaks of "seventy kinds," it means that the *maṇḍala-cīvara* (patchwork robe) applies only to the lower robe (*antarvāsaka*), and not otherwise.
This is because it encompasses both the medium and superior grades. If one includes the *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī* among the three robes, the total becomes seventy-two.
Regarding the *antarvāsaka* being listed first, I personally say that ancient masters would first receive the *saṃghāṭī* when performing rituals;

however, the intent of this commentary is to proceed from the subtle to the manifest, and thus it begins with the smallest. This is because, at the time of wearing them, one first wears the small inner garment.
The commentary states: "Regarding 'if both sides are sewn together': nowadays, when folding the leaves of a robe, one sews and closes both sides;
this is contrary to the Dharma, as it effectively constitutes sewing the robe shut. Recently, bhikṣus in the Western Regions entered a royal palace along with non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
While the bhikṣu was receiving offerings, a non-Buddhist thrust a sword into the folds of his *kaṣāya*. He then informed the king, saying: 'This bhikṣu intends to rebel. At that time...
All the bhikṣus were subsequently massacred. Yaśas then provisionally decreed that both sides be sewn together;
this was done to prevent such slander.
Regarding those who receive this saṃghāṭī with a certain number of strips, one asks why, when receiving the two lower robes, the number of strips is directly specified. Why?
When receiving the *saṃghāṭī*, one immediately says "so-and-so many. The response "it is not the time for receiving" refers to saying "so-and-so many.

This is from the terminology of the Dharma masters (*dharmavādins*). Because the number of strips for the two lower robes is fixed when they are received as formal robes, there are no variations in their categories.

Now, coming from the Dharma masters, they simply state the number of strips. Although all *saṃghāṭīs* are indeed formal robes, the category of "formal" encompasses many varieties; therefore, the Dharma masters [specify] this.
Because one wishes the expression to be inclusive, it is said "several" (*yāvat*).
Regarding "receiving at one time and relinquishing at one time, which transgresses the Vinaya," this refers to receiving and relinquishing the three robes (*tricīvara*) all at once.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives the other two garments, they are the saṃkakṣikā and the uttarāsaṅga. [My] private opinion is that these robes were prescribed for her to wear because they might arouse lustful thoughts in laypeople;
as for the monks, the matter was restricted to Ānanda, whom the Buddha ordered to wear them because his physical appearance was so handsome that many who saw him would give rise to desire.
Thus, the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing) says: "In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman who, taking her child..."
As she was at the well, wishing to draw water, a handsome young bhikṣu passed by the side of the well.
Upon seeing him, the woman conceived a lustful attachment; her eyes did not blink for a moment as she gazed at the man, while her hands continued to hold the rope fastened to the jar.
Because his lustful mind was so intense, he acted in error; he momentarily tied the child’s neck and pulled him out, only to find the child already dead.
His lustful mind and breath ceased, and through mindfulness he attained awakening. Therefore, he spoke this verse:
"The arising of all phenomena / Is entirely due to two things: / Internal causes of vitarka and vicāra, / And external conditions of the five desires.
This is the sublime verse spoken by the Buddhas of the past. The Buddha commanded Ānanda to receive and uphold it (and so forth).
Tradition says that this woman conceived a lustful mind upon seeing Ānanda; however, since no such account has appeared in the sūtras, it may have been due to some other circumstance.

As for the term *kūlāra*, it is simply a different transliteration of the Sanskrit *saṃkakṣikā*. Regarding the note which states, "If one does not specify the measurement of the elbow, it would fail to be complete," I privately remark:
because people of the present day make robes such as the *kaṭhina* (shoulder-covering garment) without adhering to the original measurements, this [specification] is now recited.

The text states that when receiving [the robe], one does not specify the number of cubits, but simply says that it should be made according to the Dharma. If one were to specify the measurement in *chi*, this would constitute false speech.

The commentary notes: "According to this school, there are differences. I [the commentator] say: For example, in the *Dharmaguptaka* school, there is only the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering garment).
Now, in the *Mahāsāṃghika* school, there is no *saṃkakṣikā*; rather, the bathing robe (*snāna-śāṭī*) is counted as one of the five robes. This is the position of this school.
They are distinct and not the same. Although they are not included in the count of five at present, they must nevertheless be worn.
As for the other two that are the same, these are the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka*.

The explanation of the method for receiving and maintaining robes is hereby concluded. From this point forward, the fourth section, the "Extensive Gate of Miscellaneous Analysis," is properly elucidated.
Regarding the phrase "broad by eight finger-widths and long by one span": the horizontal width is called "broad" (*pṛthu*), and the vertical dimension is called "long" (*dīrgha*).

The commentary states, "This differs from the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vinaya*)," which clarifies that although the three robes are not [explicitly] mentioned in the text of that treatise...

Furthermore, according to the *Karmavibhaṅga*, one incurs a *pāyattika* for staying overnight [with an extra robe]; however, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* does not hold this view. It maintains that there are only two offenses: the deficiency of clothing and the impairment of dignified deportment, as may be sought in the passages above.

Regarding the two kinds of purification methods (*viśuddhi-dharma*), the established position refers to the "declaration of purity" (*śuddhikaraṇa*) and the "marking of purity" (*tilaka-viśuddhi*). This means that when one intends to store an extra robe, one should [perform these purifications].
Because it is pierced by something pure or impure, it is called "purity through conjunction" (*saṃsṛṣṭa-śauca*). There is no need to further discuss the [case of] "spotting" (*bindu*);
therefore, it is said that [the rule] applies universally. The commentary states: "According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā*, it is lost when the conditions are severed;

according to the two treatises based on personal opinion, it is lost when one returns to rely on the *Sudarsana-sūtra* [which states] that it is lost as soon as there is a hole, and furthermore, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā*, it is lost only when the conditions are severed. Thus, we know that these two texts...
It is clear that both must rely on practical application; thus, it is said that "two treatises" [are required].
Regarding the statement that one must not take a large hole and patch it with a small object to make it shrink:

this means that once a hole is large, if one attempts to patch it with a small object, one must pull the four edges toward the object, thereby causing the four edges to contract. Hence, it is said that it "shrinks. This should be understood accordingly.
Regarding "a hole as large as two fingers' breadth that must be mended": this means that when a robe is torn, if the hole is exactly the size of two fingers, it must be immediately mended.

The statement that "this applies to both [types of] *maṇḍala* (patches) and there is no loss [of the vow]" refers to the circumstances described in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, where even if a seam is severed, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is not lost;

however, this text is too broad regarding the *maṇḍala*. Now, one must follow the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya*, which states that if a hole is as large as a fingernail, the acceptance is lost. This must be so...

Regarding "the seam breaks before it has been sewn," this also constitutes a loss of the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; therefore, it is said that there is no impairment in either case.

As for "spreading out bedding and sitting mats," this refers to the time when one is engaged in service; it means that while wearing the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one must not spread out bedding or sitting mats.
"One must not tread upon them with the feet" means that one must not step on the great robe and so forth with one's feet.
Furthermore, one must not sit upon the great robe (saṃghāṭī); hence it says "spreading it as a seat. One must also not lie down upon the great robe; hence it says "lying upon it.
One must not fold it inside [the garment] and wear it; hence it says "wearing it against the body.

As for the passage concerning sweeping the stūpa and clearing away refuse for eight hundred days, and so forth, it is as explained in the *Chao* (Excerpts) of the *Zhanchanbing jing* (Sutra on Treating the Illnesses of Meditation) [etc.]. Regarding entering the stūpa to contemplate the image, it is as follows:
The *Excerpts from the Sūtra on Healing the Ailments of Dhyāna* and likewise the *Excerpts from the Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* (and so forth).

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* that "having received the *kaṭhina*, one is permitted to separate from the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), while the remaining two are worn together in layers, and the lower garment (*antarvāsaka*) pressed against the body is called 'wearing'": this refers to the seventh [category].
The strips are sewn together and called *pī* (a patched robe). Regarding the application of the *gūlán* (border), Jì says that the four surrounding edges are called *gūlán*.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is likewise permitted to borrow a *saṃghāṭī* to enter among the laity;

this means that even if one does not possess a *saṃghāṭī* oneself, one may borrow one from another to wear when entering a layperson’s house. The commentary states: "This refers to the *saṃghāṭī*. Lì says: "This..."
This is the robe for entering a village; it is not the robe for being within a garden. Why is it called a "garden robe"?
Because in the Western lands (India), many people would donate their gardens to establish *saṃghārāmas*, such as Anāthapiṇḍada and Āmrapālī. It is named after its original source;
thus we know that a "garden" (*ārāma*) is simply a monastery (*vihāra*). As for the "ewe-ear" [robe], it refers to the manner of wearing robes seen on the image of King Aśoka today.
It is because he grasped it with his hand.
In several passages of the *Madhyama Āgama*, it is stated that one lies down using the *saṃghāṭī* as a pillow and the *saptaka* (seven-strip robe). According to the *Madhyama Āgama*:
"At times, the World-Honored One would fold his *uttarāsaṅga* into four layers and spread it upon the mat, then arrange his *saṃghāṭī* to serve as a pillow, and lie on his right side."

He lies down with his feet stacked one upon the other, establishing a mind of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). He constantly maintains the thought of awakening, meaning that while sleeping, he remains mindful of waking up quickly.

The various *bhikṣus* also practice this; judging by the text and its intent regarding using the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) as a pillow and the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) as a cushion, it clearly means that when putting on the seven-strip robe, one wears it as an undergarment. If anyone nowadays performs this practice, [it is correct].

This is truly strange. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states: "The World-Honored One folded his *uttarāsaṅga* four times, spread his *saṃghāṭī* beneath him, and lay down with his head as a pillow.
Jì remarked: "In an entire country, it is only within the city of Cháng'ān that monks and nuns carry their three robes in a bag (*bǔ*).
This accords with the Dharma and gives rise to wholesome merit; for they carry the robe-bag upon their arm and place the *kāṣāya* [upon it]."

Outside the *saṃghāṭī*, one should properly hold the water jar with one hand and proceed along the road. According to the natural law (*dharmatā*) of those who have left the household life, one must carry the three robes, the water jar, and the alms bowl;
it is just as a secular official must carry his staff and pouch—it is a legal requirement.
Only in remote border regions do people often place the three robes inside a cloth bag within the *kāṣāya*. When bystanders see this, they find it utterly improper.
Excellent. It appears as though a thief is returning with stolen goods.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* which first instructs one to bared the right shoulder out of respect for those attending to affairs, and later instructs one to cover both shoulders to manifest oneself as a field of merit, and so forth:
according to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Śāriputra asked the Buddha:

How is it that within the precepts one instructs disciples to bared the right shoulder? Furthermore, in the *Nagara-upama-sūtra* (City Simile Sūtra) preached to the people of Kāśyapa Village, it says:
"My disciples should properly don the kāṣāya, covering both shoulders, and must not expose their flesh."

He caused [the robes] to be even and level above and below, manifesting the appearance of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). His gait was composed and orderly. Furthermore, he said, "Do not expose the chest.
Regarding each of these, how should they be observed? The Buddha said: "When practicing offerings, one must bared the right shoulder so as to facilitate the performance of tasks."
When acting as a field of merit, one should cover both shoulders to manifest the sign of the field. How should one practice making offerings as if seeing the Buddha?
When greeting teachers and monks, one should act according to the specific circumstances: whether it be at the Buddha’s seat, while sweeping the ground, or while folding robes.
Whether it be the offering of mats during the Zhou calendar’s first month, or drawing patterns on the ground with mud, how does one cultivate the field of merit?

This refers to when a king invites one for a meal, entering a village to beg for food, sitting in meditation or reciting the sutras, or walking beneath the trees; people see one’s dignified and majestic bearing.
There is something worthy of observation.

Regarding those who resolve and determine the Vinaya and Śāstras of the two divisions (monks and nuns), it is established that this treatise is so called because it explains the Vinayas of both the monastic and nun communities.
The commentary states: "When you encounter a teacher, a senior monk (*sthavira*), or an individual, you should express your intention, saying: 'I am wearing...'"

Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*: one must not perform prostrations [in this manner], nor should one reproach someone for it. The commentary states: "That which is called 'elephant trunk' refers to the upper edge hanging down;
this means that when donning it, the left side is left exposed, which is termed 'elephant trunk'."

Regarding "the inner robe not being close to the body, being clean, and so forth": this refers to wearing the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) without having previously used it as a lining against the body.
Because it is clean, one may wear it when entering the assembly to prostrate, attend lectures, listen to the Dharma, and so on; otherwise, one may not.

Regarding "borrowing someone else's robe, one must not go beyond the boundary": this means that if one takes another's robe to go outside, or fears that it might remain overnight, one risks committing the offense of being separated from one's robe (*cīvaravippavāsa*).
This is why leaving the boundary and so forth are not permitted. Regarding the offense for eating without wearing the *kāṣāya*:
according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says that if one eats food without wearing the *kāṣāya*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Regarding the passage in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* stating that one obtains merit by having a virtuous person temporarily wear a new robe:
Master Ji said, "During the lifetime of the Nanshan Ācārya, whenever he obtained a new robe, shoes, or socks, he would first place them before the Buddha and offer incense in worship.

Next, he would place them before the Holy Sangha, perform offerings and recite prayers, and only then give them to his preceptors and teachers to wear. He also used this practice for his own personal use."

This Dharma not only brings merit, but also ensures that one’s own person is always abundantly provided with clothing. If one obtains fruits, food, or the like, one should likewise first offer them to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

Regarding the passage in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* where the Buddha had Ānanda take his *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) and give it to the woman Vāsīṭhī to wear, it is as recorded in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* Excerpts (*Yàohán chāo*) [and so forth].
In the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, it is said that the lion honored those who wore the *kāṣāya*.

Regarding those who thus attain Buddhahood: according to the thirteenth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, in ancient times there was a king of this Jambudvīpa named Tivi, who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms. At that time, the Buddha-dharma did not exist in the world, though there were pratyekabuddhas.
While he was dwelling among the mountains, sitting in meditation within the forest, all the wild beasts came to associate with him.
There was a lion named Caṅkīla (in the Jin language, Jiānshì), whose body was golden in color. At that time, there was a hunter who had shaved his head and donned the kāṣāya robe.
Wearing spears and arrows at his waist, he was traveling through a marsh when he saw this lion. Thinking he wished to kill it, the hunter happened upon the lion while it was asleep;
he then shot it with a poisoned arrow. The lion woke up in alarm and immediately sought to charge and harm him.
Seeing him wearing the *kāṣāya*, he thought to himself: "A person such as this will not remain long in this world; his mind has attained liberation. Why is this?
This dyed robe is the distinguishing mark of the sages of the three periods of time.
If I were to harm him, it would be as if I had given rise to an evil mind toward the worthy sages of the three periods. Having reflected thus, his intent to harm subsided, and he spoke.
The verse says:
*Yalālava śaśavaha*. When these words were spoken, heaven and earth shook violently;
rain fell from a cloudless sky, and the devas were struck with awe and alarm.
Immediately, with his divine eye, he looked down upon the world;
seeing the hunter killing the Bodhisattva lion, he rained down celestial flowers from the midst of the sky as an offering to the corpse.
At that time, the hunter flayed the lion’s skin and presented it to the king, thinking to himself:
"The scriptures state that if there is a beast with a golden-colored body, it must be a bodhisattva. He asked the hunter: "When the lion died, what auspicious signs were there?
The hunter replied: "It was as described above in those eight characters. Thereupon, he summoned his ministers and wise men, and ordered them—
When they attempted to explain this meaning, none among the multitude were able to do so. In an empty forest thicket, there was a rishi who explained the meaning as follows:
"Yarala" means that one who has shaved their head and dons dyed robes shall swiftly attain liberation from birth and death.
"Vaśaśa" means that those who have shaved their heads and don dyed robes all possess the marks of a worthy sage (*ārya*). They are near [to liberation]."
He attained *nirvāṇa*. Pāha said, "One who has shaved his head and donned dyed robes shall be revered and honored by all gods and people of the world.
Having heard this explanation, the king summoned eighty-four thousand minor kings and assembled them all in one place.
He constructed a high carriage made of the seven treasures, covered it with a lion skin, displayed it for all to see, scattered flowers as an offering, and fashioned a coffin out of gold.
They took the lion’s skin and used it to erect a stūpa.

At that time, because the lion had given rise to a virtuous mind toward the one clad in dyed robes, for ten billion kalpas he served as a Wheel-Turning Sage King and later attained Buddhahood—he is the present Śākyamuni.
The king was Maitreya; the seer was Śāriputra; and the hunter was Devadatta.
Second, regarding the clarification of the ritual procedure for establishing the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-holding boundary): the *Lishi* explains the name as follows.

It is called the "robe-holding boundary" (*cīvara-sīmā*) because once the ritual formula has been added and the boundary established, even if one travels far away, the robe still remains the property of the person; hence it is named the robe-holding boundary.

Alternatively, it is called the "boundary for not losing the robe" (*a-cīvara-vipravāsa-sīmā*), because when this boundary is established, the person commits no offense of being separated from their robe; therefore, it is termed the ritual method for not losing the robe.

Regarding the fact that there are three types of all great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*): namely, the boundary being large while the *kaṭhina* [enclosure] is small; the boundary being small while the *kaṭhina* is large;

and the *kaṭhina* and the boundary being equal in size. The *Karmavibhaṅga-vyākhyā* states: "If the boundary and the *kaṭhina* are equal in size, or if the boundary is small while the *kaṭhina* is large, it is unnecessary to perform the formal ritual of demarcation (*sīmā-bandhana*)."

Since the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) naturally arises from the confines of the monastery courtyard (*ārāma-maṇḍala*), it extends as far as its perimeter, yet still leaves open its sphere of influence (*prabhāva*).

Now, regarding the two aforementioned types [of boundaries], if the robe-boundary has not yet been formally established, the robes are contained within the courtyard; if the ritual for establishing the boundary is completed only after one has already entered the courtyard, then there is no need to establish it.
Alternatively, if the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is already within the sphere of influence, it is likewise unnecessary. One should reflect further on these various exceptions.

Various schools differ in their establishment of the rules. Some establish the rule for "binding without a village" (*amūla-bandha*). The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The ancients said that where there is a village, it must be excluded;
where there is no village, it need not be. How can one indiscriminately claim that both must be excluded?

Just as in the Vinaya texts, there are cases where the formal act exists but the underlying matter does not, such that the act is not valid; the same principle applies here when 'no village' is added. Furthermore, some others...

Regarding the statement, "there is the formal delimitation of a village (*grāma-sīmā-bandha*)," this means that while currently there is no such delimitation, if one were to establish it, later when the village moves out, it would not be appropriate to retain the robe.

Regarding "there is no formal delimitation of a village," this means that while currently there is a delimitation, if it is subsequently removed, even if the village comes back, the robe is not retained; if the village departs, the delimitation is restored. The author of the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) holds that there is no formal delimitation of a village here.

This refers to the interpretation of the later masters. Regarding the phrase "by tying [the boundary], one removes obstacles and difficulties," Jì states: "A village (*grāma*) is the dwelling place of men and women.
Men are an obstacle for *bhikṣuṇīs*, and women are an obstacle for *bhikṣus*; therefore, they must be removed. Thus, Śaṅguò quotes the *Karmasūtra* (Jiémósù):

"Since one establishes the boundary based on the territory and universally designates the interior as having the same 'holding of robes' (*cīvaradhāraṇa*), the robe does not depend on the village for its arrival."
The boundary is then dissolved. It is not because the village exists within the robe-boundary that the boundary is not all-pervasive;

rather, it is because a village is a dwelling place for men and women, where many instances of lustful attachment and slander arise, and whose nature is such that it brings reproach upon the conduct of bhikṣus. Therefore, the rule was established to exclude it.

Thus, in the Vinaya, when first establishing a robe-boundary, if there is a village, it is not said to exclude the village; only later, when placing robes within the village creates obstacles and hindrances, does one then exclude it.

In this context, the village is excluded [from the boundary], but the substance of the village itself is not excluded. How is this known? The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* offers two interpretations. According to the former interpretation, if a village exists, it must be excluded;

if no village exists, it need not be excluded. The latter interpretation, however, states: "This is the inherent nature of the *karmavācanā* ritual; one need not inquire whether a village exists or not."

In all cases, these must be removed; it is not permissible for the village to remain. When the village has departed, one should gather up the robes. Question: Since there was originally no village, why do you speak of "removing" it?

Is this not like applying a remedy when there is no illness—how can such a ritual action (*karmavācanā*) be valid? Answer: This boundary for gathering up the robes exists within the area of common residence.
As for what is called "excluding," it excludes the obstruction of the robe but does not exclude the village itself; therefore, there are no men or women [within the boundary].
Since one dwells with the intention of wearing the robe, how could it be that the monastery was originally non-existent? If one does not exclude it, doubts will arise:
namely, that once the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) has been established, even if a village subsequently enters it, the robe would not be lost. Therefore, the prior boundary is excluded.

As previously stated regarding the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*), both [the village and the robe] are listed together; this may be explained as follows: it must be mentioned in the text that the prior establishment of the boundary does not prevent the subsequent establishment of the commonality (*sāmānya*).
The same applies to the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). To explain the subsequent removal (*uddhāra*), one may understand it by analogy. Question:

Once a village has been established within a boundary, one is unable to assemble the robes. Why is it necessary to perform the removal (*uddhāra*) when there was originally no village? If there was neither a village nor a boundary, how could a village subsequently arise to act as an obstruction?
The robe is identical to the fetter of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*). Why must it be worn and then removed? The intent of the question is difficult to understand. The meaning is this:

if there is no village within the boundary (*sīmā*), yet the village comes and obstructs [the space], how does the robe differ from the fetter of existence such that one says it must be worn and then removed? If there is no village, why must it be worn and then removed?

A village also obstructs clothing. If there is a village, it is removed when one puts on [clothing]. A village exists and also obstructs; when clothing is put on, both are removed, yet they both obstruct the clothing.
Why must one put on [clothing] and remove [the obstruction]? If both presence and absence were equally obstructions, then presence and absence might equally be put on and removed.

Since there is that which obstructs and that which does not obstruct, how could there be simultaneous obstruction by both presence and absence? Answer: It is for the purpose of resolving doubts that this is so.

If the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) has not yet been demarcated, the boundaries of trees, vehicles, and the like—which are naturally present as clusters—will be extinguished by the current ritual act of binding the robe-boundary.
Fearing that this might lead to confusion with village boundaries, these [natural] boundaries likewise cease to arise.

To resolve this doubt, the term "excluding" (*varjayitvā*) is applied to both. The phrase "excluding what is currently suspended" establishes that there was previously a village, and one is now excluding the obstacles within that village.

Regarding the area below a suspended village: it is intended that one may subsequently go to another village and still maintain the protection of one's robes. As for "presently suspending and excluding," this means that because there was originally no village, the current location is taken as the boundary;
therefore, it is called "presently suspending. If a village were to exist later, one would not be able to maintain the protection of one's robes.

It is called "Hanging Knot. Regarding the statement that "if a village is removed or added, or if one comes from or goes to a village, it causes the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) to increase or decrease," Jì (Jie Daoshi) says:

"The substance of the robe-boundary is pervasive; however, when a village arrives and there are men and women obstructing the path, even if the robe is placed [there], it does not mean the boundary ceases to exist.
Based on the substance of the boundary itself, there is no increase or decrease. Therefore, Master Yuàn used the analogy of an ox-hide: the hide is supple...
When it is pulled back and forth, whether long or short, does the hide itself increase or decrease? The boundary of the robe is likewise:
although the boundary contracts when the village approaches and extends when the village departs, it is still not called increasing or decreasing.

Regarding the explicit texts of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and other codes: the *Pañcavargika* states that if there was originally no village and one establishes a "non-lost-clothing" boundary (*akalpiya-sīmā*) such that the village is subsequently included within it, there is no need to re-establish the boundary, because it has already been established previously. However, if there was originally a village and one has already established the clothing boundary...
"Later, the village was moved out; immediately in this empty space, the 'boundary for not losing one's robe' (*acīvara-sīmā*) arose. This interpretation is certainly incorrect.

Some cite a passage from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* as proof, stating that when sentient beings of the upper realm are separated by the four obstructions (*catur-āvaraṇa*) within a defiled realm, they lose their robes;

this is not because the substance of the boundary itself increases or decreases. According to the *Pañcavargika*, the bhikṣus performed a *karmavācanā* to establish the boundary for not losing one's robes. At...
One cannot freely come and go within it; this is called "losing one's robe. Regarding the first case, where the robe-boundary of a village (*grāma*) is indefinite while the boundary itself is fixed:
this refers to a village, which is the same as a settlement (*sanniveśa*). Within it, men and women come and go without restriction;

when they arrive, there is no robe-boundary, but when they depart, it becomes a robe-boundary. Therefore it is said: if one discusses the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the robe-boundary, there is no coming or going. Thus it is said.
This is for the sake of establishing discipline. Regarding "to remove slander and the like": it refers to a bhikṣu who leaves his robes within a village and goes to retrieve them at night;
because he passes by women, his tracks may give rise to scandal and suspicion. Regarding "to prevent quarrels and disputes":

it is because entering a village to retrieve robes may lead to the occurrence of quarrels and disputes. Regarding "to protect the holy life (brahmacarya) and so forth": there are women in the village, and one must enter [the village].

"Village" (*grāma*) refers to that which can cause the destruction of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are five meanings for "village," though only four are enumerated in the text;

the term "and so forth" includes those cases involving suspicion (*śaṅkā*). Together with suspicion, these constitute the five. Because villages are inhabited by both men and women, these five conditions are fully present therein.

It is difficult for a *bhikṣu* staying within such a place to protect his robes; therefore, it was prescribed that they must be kept on one's person. Subsequently, due to the arising of certain circumstances, [the following] was said:
Regarding its exclusion: it is said that a bhikṣu went to a village to fetch robes and saw a woman whose garment had come loose, leaving her body exposed;
feeling ashamed, he reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered that a rule be established.

Regarding the phrase "excluding the village and the area outside the village," the *Shūsō* (Initial Commentary) explains: "Excluding the village" means excluding the physical substance of the village itself.

"The area outside the village" refers to excluding the ground of the village's peripheral influence (*seshibun*). Therefore, it says: "Excluding the area outside the village" means [the distance] up to where a person throws a stone from within.
My personal opinion is that this implies the village is situated within the boundary (*kai*), and one may not [enter] even from within the sphere of influence of the village households.

This refers to the setting aside of robes. Regarding the ritual for releasing the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), Master Li states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lacks the text concerning the release of the robe-boundary;

here, we provide both the formal establishment and the release. Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* contains both the formal establishment and the release through two *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (procedures consisting of a motion and one announcement). Thus, there are many such differences above.
This concludes the general explanation of the first point: the meaning of the three robes."

Second, regarding the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*): the Sanskrit term is *niṣīdana*. "One must not treat it with disdain or perform it perfunctorily" means that one should not handle this small object haphazardly or merely according to the occasion.
To act without a joyful intention is called "disdain" (*yàn*);

to act as if compelled by others is called "perfunctory performance" (*kè*)—this is the correct interpretation. If it is a single layer of *kambala*, it refers to a wool garment. (This is the explanation of *Lì*).
It is said: *Kambala* refers to a woolen garment (*cīvara*). If one uses wool for a single layer and cotton for two layers, it is translated as "tree-flower" (*śākapuṣpa*).
Those who uphold the Vinaya call it "grass-flower. According to the *Śabdavidyā* (Grammar), the Indic term *śākapuṣpa* is translated as "tree-flower garment";
this is what is meant by "white cotton cloth" (*pata*) today. Regarding the prohibition against measuring by bending the head: this means...
If one measures an object using a *lan* (cubit) scale, it will appear longer than it actually is. Regarding "contracting measurement" and "measuring by sprinkling water":
this refers to the functional property that [materials] contract when wet and expand when dry.
As for "using old borders to mottle the color of a new *niṣīdana*," this means that one should take a new material and use an old material as its border, thereby applying it to the four edges.

"Dividing the house" refers to folding [the cloth] as was done previously. If the maker is to install it on a tiered platform, this clarifies that at the present time, when making a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one must necessarily provide a border (*saṃstara*) around all four sides.
Regarding the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* that "the four corners must be folded," this refers to those who construct a platform with four corners.

As for the phrase "if not folded, then leave it as is," this means that at the time of construction, one should fold it according to the previous method; if there is no such precedent, one may follow others.

One searches; having searched and not found [the required measurement], with what could one fold it? One simply stops and does not fold it; therefore it is said, "it is finished. "Finished" means it has ceased.

Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) statement that "if one makes it by reducing the measure, or if one folds it double-layered, both are permissible": this refers to cases where the original measure was exceeded.

This constitutes an offense for exceeding the measure, but not for reducing it. As for "folding it double-layered," it means that although it was originally made as a single layer, because it still exceeded the measure, one must fold it in half.

Once the two layers have been finished, if they do not exceed the prescribed measure, there is no offense; therefore, it is said that folding them into two layers is also permissible. The note states:
"This means that taking two layers as the base is done for fear of exceeding the measure; thus, one who folds [the cloth] does so. This refers to the preceding passage.
It means that while originally two layers were intended as the base, since it is now made single-layered and yet remains wide and large, one must fold it into two layers to avoid an offense.

Regarding the second and third layers, which are sewn directly opposite one another: it is said that once the initial measurements have been established, any subsequent additions may be made according to the circumstances.
One should take the added material and attach it to both sides, ensuring that both edges are level before sewing them together.
One must not sew directly [through both layers]. Therefore, it is said that one should "sew back-to-front" (*pratimukha*) and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "According to the characteristics of the *upāyāsa* (excessive thread), if one does not cut it, there is no offense;

even so, there should be no fault," this sentence is the word of an ancient master. It expresses the intent of extracting the meaning of the *vyañjana* (phonetic/grammatical form). That [master] devised this calculation. The following note is as follows:

The commentary states: This refers to the matter of the *vaṃsaka* (bamboo). It means that according to the rule among the thirty [Naiḥsargika-pāyattikas] concerning the exhortation to increase the threads for a weaver, although one commits an offense when the [excess] comes into one's hand, once the forfeiture has been performed and the confession completed, there is no fault in using it again;

furthermore, it is not necessary to cut off the additional threads. If I now make a sitting mat of excessive size and do not cut away [the excess], it would be equivalent to that case of adding extra threads.
"The characteristic of not cutting [the cloth] should likewise be without fault. This is the erroneous calculation of Bhaṭṭa. Jì says:

"Regarding the phrase 'according to the characteristics of adding threads,' it means that Bhaṭṭa saw the Buddha permit the increase of the sitting mat (niṣīdana), further increasing its width and length by half a span (vitasti) each."
Regarding the subsequent additions: those called "added threads" (*yishou*) are things that, once joined together, do not require cutting.
Since this is not an offense, if I now exceed the increased limit and add more length without cutting it, it likewise conforms to being non-offensive;
therefore, it is said that there should be no fault. It simply means that although the initial addition already exceeded the original measure, not cutting it is not [an offense].
"An offense? But I have now exceeded this limit; since I have not cut it down, what further offense could there be? This was all that Vajjī calculated.

Bhaddāli said: "If, according to the characteristics of adding thread, one commits no offense by not cutting [the border], then keeping a sitting mat that exceeds the measure without cutting it should likewise be without fault.
This means that because the addition of thread is permitted without cutting, [the same logic applies].
"It would not constitute an offense. If I were now to obtain an oversized sitting mat and keep it without cutting it down, there likewise should be no fault.
As stated in the Vinaya text above, when the group of six monks made their *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) wide and long, the Buddha immediately established the prescribed measurements.
Later, because Kālodāyin pulled at his sitting mat with his hand, the Buddha then granted an exception, saying: "From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to increase the width further."
Each is half a *vitasti* in length. Since it is stated that they are "further added," we know that the threads are removed and these are added in their place.
Now, the *Bajia* (跋闍) relies upon this text. Nanshan says: "To cut them off and separately add [new ones] is logically impossible. The commentary states:

"This *bajia-dan* (跋闍檀) refers to ten matters" (*dan* is pronounced *shi-zhan-fan*). The *Guangpi* (廣疋) states: "*Dan* arises from *zhuan* (專)," meaning to be single-mindedly devoted to one's own actions. Furthermore...
Regarding the term *dāna*, it means "to do for oneself. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) made with unsewn borders is pure.

This is interpreted to mean that if one makes it according to the original dimensions without adding extra threads—since no offense is committed by not increasing the size—it is therefore called "pure" (*śuddha*).

[This point is not fully clear and awaits further investigation. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, making a mat without joining the ends results in a *pāyattika* offense. Based on the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, this explains the context of the Seventh Council (*Saptama-saṃgīti*).
The text states: Among the ten matters of the *vañjapāda* practice, there is the purity regarding the *niṣīdana* with threads. The commentary below explains:

"Regarding the purity of the *niṣīdana* with threads: if the edge of the *niṣīdana* is not joined with threads, the Buddha said that for one who does not join the threads, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
This offense was established due to the case of Kāḷudāyin (Jì’s commentary). Lì states: "If the intent of the text is to increase [the measurement], one must add to the exterior of the boundary;
one may not take the increase by extending it inward from the boundary. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states:
'To take the increase by extending it throughout the measurement constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*. Jì says: 'Citing this is a biased adherence of Nanshan. At the end of his life, Nanshan..."
At that time, he also did not stubbornly cling to this matter. Liang said: "The *bhaṣaja* (or *bhañja*) merely prohibits the possession of oversized sitting mats;
it does not prohibit the failure to cut them down. Now, since you are taking one that exceeds the limit, how can you claim this is the custom of the *bhaṣaja*?"

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that while the Buddha was alive, monks were not permitted to lie down; at most, they were allowed to increase the length of their sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) by one span (*vitasti*) so that they might recline.

This establishes the rule for the bedding of the Saṃgha. Regarding the statement in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* that one should further increase it by one span each time, this does not refer to the current sitting mat (*kaṭhina*).
Rather, it refers to the separate preparation of an additional bedding layer placed beneath the *niṣīdana* to protect the Saṃgha’s sleeping mats.
Because it is complete. If one *vitasti* (a span) is added to the small [measurement], it should be eight feet long and four feet wide.

This is according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya); that which is currently used in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four Part Vinaya) is an error. The commentary states: "At that time, there was one who possessed only a single leaf of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
I say: In the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is mention of such a robe for protecting the bedding of the Saṃgha, which should be joined at one end;
its length is increased accordingly. At present, it measures six small cubits in length and three in width, which does not fail to meet the dimensions of a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).

Now, as for the statement in the *Dharmaguptaka-prātimokṣa-sūtra* that says "one [cubit] hand-span," this is an error. If one possesses such a robe, one may provisionally perform the ritual of *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa* (declaring it pure).

This is because it is received and maintained within [the Sangha]. Regarding the fourth point, the differences in the rules for sitting mats (*niṣīdana*) are as follows: the standing posture refers to joining together [the mat] with an additional half-*prādeśa*.

The commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'must be used accordingly' and 'must also be kept,' this means that if one possesses the aforementioned ten types of bedding and sitting mats protected by the *kaṭhina* (the robe-pledge), their use is permitted;
however, they must still be subject to the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (the ritual of purification). One simply may not apply the formal rite of *dhāraṇa* (receiving and maintaining)."

When one arrives at the place where one is to sit, one should spread out the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and sit; or, having placed it in its original position, one should fold it in half across the middle, carry it on the shoulder, and upon arrival, unfold it slowly and sit.
According to the *Śāriputra-vinaya*, one must not select or examine the *niṣīdana* inside the room. One should always fold it in half, place it over the shoulder, and depart.
Having arrived, one should fold it in half across the middle, spread it out, and sit. When returning, one should likewise fold it in half and place it on the shoulder.
Having returned from the upper [floor], if one wishes to place it in the center and cover oneself while returning, one should slowly unfold it and sit within the meditation hall;

the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) should be used in this manner. As for placing the *niṣīdana* on the right shoulder when entering the assembly to subdue those of heterodox paths, it is as described in the *Excerpts from the Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xianyu jing chao*), etc.
Regarding the method for the water-strainer bag (*parisrāvaṇa*): in Sanskrit it is called *paryasūtrodana* (with the final syllable in the departing tone).

In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is described as a water-strainer made in the shape of a *ku* (a ladle). According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the character used is "shao" (杓); the current use of the character "shao" (勺) is an error.
If one makes it in the shape of a large chest (*hongguo*), I personally say this refers to the square frame outside the water-strainer bag. Master Ying says it should be... [text ends].
*Héngguǒ* (橫槨). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it refers to a horizontal railing. The Vinaya text reads *hóngdà* (宏大), with the phonetic component *gù* (故) as the radical.

It means the depth or orientation of a house; "hóng" (宏) does not carry this meaning here. *Guòhuī* (郭恢) refers to a "walled enclosure" (*guòluò*); it is a term for that which is situated outside the perimeter wall.

If it is made into a strainer-jar (*lùpíng*), it is the same as the *yīnyángpíng* (陰陽瓶). Regarding the permission to place it inside a sand-bag: this was established to clarify that because insects are minute and difficult to filter out...
Take fine sand and place it inside a strainer; the insects will settle upon the sand. Afterwards, pour this sand back into the well.
The reason for using sand is that because the sand is fine, it allows water to pass through while preventing the insects from escaping.
This matter is understood by analogy with the method of filtering alkaline ash-water.
Regarding the phrase "the remaining modes of conduct, such as seeing life, are constantly submerged therein," this means that killing insects is a natural precept (*prakṛti-śīla*).
If one cannot maintain and uphold even this, how can one avoid matters concerning improper conduct, wrong views, and wrong livelihood?

Since these precepts, views, conduct, and livelihoods are what those who have left the household life must cultivate, and one is currently unable to follow them, it is said that one is "constantly submerged therein. [This refers to] the hindrance of fleas.
Regarding "clothing": those in the north call it *pīpa* (bedbugs), while those in the south call it *mùshī* (woodlice) or *gūshī*.
This clothing is called a *pālikāra-cīvara*. My private interpretation is that this translates as "miscellaneous fragments" (*zásuì yī*);
it is also called a "body-assisting garment" (*zhùshēn yī*). If one wishes to receive and maintain [this robe], one must first formally designate its name; thus, up to the *pālikāra*...

Regarding "the *lāva* robe and so forth," these refer precisely to the one hundred and one items. Regarding "miscellaneous robes according to their quantity," I privately say these are minor miscellaneous items for mending robes.
As for the reason why the confession of a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) is distinct [from others], it is because a *śrāmaṇera* has not yet received full ordination;
therefore, it differs from the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Regarding the phrase "because it is completed in one day": Master Li states that this refers to the offense incurred because [the garment] was not declared [as surplus] on the eleventh day (this is not the correct interpretation).
The present explanation is that because the robe was obtained on the first day and not declared, by accumulating [the period] until the eleventh day, one incurs the offense;

this is because the first day is referred to as "one day. Regarding the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning entering a village with the chest exposed, etc., Master Li clarifies that from here below, it explains...

The matter regarding the *bhikṣuṇīs* is thus. The commentary states: "There were masters who modified the rule by cutting and sewing [the robes]. Zhi says: "The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clearly explains the measurements in cubits;
the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* simply states that the robe is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.

During the Later Wei dynasty, there was a master who did not follow the four-cubit and two-cubit measurements of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, but instead followed the *Dharmaguptaka* method of making the robe narrow at the top and wide at the bottom. Nevertheless, this was also permissible.
Receive and uphold [this teaching]. When upholding it, one should state the name; simply say, "I act in accordance with the Dharma. One must not state the specific measurements in cubits.
Regarding the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*—here translated as "inner garment"—it is established that this refers to the skirt worn nowadays. In Central India, it is made in a different shape:
like a mantle, it is used to wrap around the waist, and the waistband is made of leather to bind and secure it around the waist.
Regarding the account of the Buddha of the *Saṃghāṭa* [Vinaya] personally wearing an inner robe before the Saṃgha and instructing the bhikṣus, thereby establishing the precepts:

according to the *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya*, the group of six bhikṣus wore their inner robes either too high or too low; some made them like the tail of a fish, others like the trunk of an elephant, and others like the leaf of a *tāla* tree.
They were reviled by worldly people who said, "They are just like courtesans. These transgressions were reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha...
He assembled the bhikṣus and, in the presence of the Saṃgha, put on his inner robe himself and addressed the bhikṣus: "You should know this:
such a manner of wearing robes has led me to establish a precept for the bhikṣus. The upper part should reach as high as the knees, and the lower part should reach as far as the ankles."
The "fish-tail" [style] has two corners hanging down, resembling a fish's tail. The "elephant-tail" [style] has one corner hanging down to one side.
The "tāla-leaf" [style] has the tāla-leaf pattern embossed in relief.

Regarding "if it is very cold, one may tie it around the feet": this refers to tearing the back of the lower garment (*nivasana*) and tying it to the sides, similar to the method of wearing square skirts (*catur-asra-patta*) by people today;
however, even that does not yet reach the sides. If one uses two, three, or four strips sewn together in a disordered manner, this is called wearing the *nirvana-saṃghāṭī* belt.
If one makes a new one, its width should be three finger-breadths; those already in use today are small.
Therefore, three or four may join together to form it. Regarding the "jue-niu" (loop-fastener):

according to Dugu Pi’s commentary on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, a "jue" is like a ring but not connected [in a circle]. As for "passing through the bifurcation from behind," this means passing from the back.
Regarding "those who wear the *kushura*": I privately note that it is also called *kesura*; it resembles a skirt.

It was sewn together and worn over the head. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it was worn as a skirt after being torn open; however, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* prohibited its use due to criticism.
Regarding "square skirts" (*fangqun*) and other types of skirts:
I have heard that these were in use in recent times. This was because Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty saw that the various great virtuous ones (*bhadanta*) were cold.

As for these, they were made accordingly, though their craftsmanship differed from that of the common world. Regarding the "arm-clothing" (*bāhu-vastra*), [Dao]lin personally stated: "This refers to the arm-hooks used today.

However, none of the aforementioned garments exist in the Western Regions; they were created by the ancient virtuous ones of this land. Regarding the "double-layered clothing" (*pūrvaka-vastra*), [Dao]lin stated:
"This refers to double-stuffed clothing; it is the same as the padded cotton clothing worn at present. Regarding "all hooded garments," [Dao]lin stated: "These are the skirts of women."

This is so; it is called such because it is worn by passing the head through the neck-opening. As for "a garment with two sleeves," this refers to the *zhuobu* (shoulder-covering robe) worn by laypeople.
One must not wear a *aoxie* (the character is pronounced *xi*, or alternatively *zhi*), which refers to a garment with large sleeves.
Regarding the *xingteng* (the character is pronounced *tu leng fan*): the commentary on the *Liji* states that the *fubing* (seam-width) is the *xingteng*; it is also referred to as...
Regarding the "entanglement" (纏) of conduct: the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) states that it refers to wrapping the feet with cloth so that one may leap and bound with ease and agility.

One must not wear any of the garments of laypeople or non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka-tīrthika*); if one does wear them, they shall be dealt with according to the law. This statement applies generally to both light and heavy offenses:

if one wears the clothing of a layperson, one may be punished according to the "auspicious law" (*jifǎ*); if one wears the clothing of a non-Buddhist, one shall be punished according to the "fragrant law" (*lánfǎ*).
Therefore, King Bimbisāra sent the expensive garment he was wearing, privately remarking, "This is the lord of the kingdom of Magadha;
he is the father of King Śreṇya. Upon learning that the Tathāgata had permitted the bhikṣus to accept robes from donors, the king immediately brought that expensive garment.

[The text] states: "Give it to the Sangha. The Buddha permitted its storage after declaring it *śuddhi* (pure). The masters of antiquity, following this passage, determined that this refers to expensive lay clothing;

since the Buddha required it to be declared *śuddhi*, it must be categorized as light property. Thus, all garments of white-clad [laypeople] are analogically included within the category of light property.
During the Qianfeng era, the author of the *Chao* (Commentary), Xiangtian, pointed out that there was an error in the determination of what constitutes light or heavy property.
This is the text. It is an error of translation, not the fault of the Vinaya scholar. Therefore, it was revised with care.

Regarding the "costly garments for kings and nobles," these are actually the three robes (tricīvara); they are so designated only because their price is high. If one were to take them as ordinary secular clothing, [it would be a mistake].
To take this as a precedent for dividing all secular clothing is a great error. As for the "five-part robe," this is merely another name for the three robes (*tricīvara*).
How could there be secular clothing that would be subject to division?

If it is said that expensive clothing cannot be worn when it lies upon the ground, I privately surmise this refers to when Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal; the robes covered both the ground and the air.
Expensive silks were spread out from within the palace hall, extending in rows to the entrance of the monastery. The Buddha and the Sangha were invited to tread upon them as they passed.

When the Buddha reached the edge of the cloth, he looked toward Ānanda and ordered it to be removed. Because future disciples would have meager merit and find it difficult to bear such weight, he established this as a precedent for later generations.

Regarding the *dhyāna-bandhana* (meditation belt): I have heard it said that because one becomes weary from sitting in meditation for a long time, one uses this to wrap around the body while sitting on a rope bed (*śayyāsana*).
Another account says it is simply used to encircle the two knees, passing behind the back. It may be made of hemp or of colored silk, and should be three or four finger-widths wide.
Regarding the waistband (*kaṭibandha*): I have heard it said that this is what is known today as a waist-cord. *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 15.
Regarding the matter of borrowing the clothes of a layperson and not returning them:

according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there were five precept-observing upāsakas who, having been stripped of their clothing by bandits, came to the bhikṣus to borrow garments. The bhikṣus did not dare to give them any, and they therefore questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to borrow [the precepts]. If they are returned, they should be taken up; if they are not returned, then it is finished. "Finished" (*yi*) means to cease.
The commentary states that the three-year period for the assembly refers to the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, who resided in the western country of Aparāntaka.

He was a disciple of Kātyāyana. Because there were few monks in this frontier region, he sought out a community for three years before finally being able to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). This refers to receiving the precepts.

Thereafter, he went to see the World-Honored One. His preceptor submitted a petition to the Buddha requesting that five matters be permitted. The commentary notes: "Because that region lacks other bedding materials.
My private opinion is that in the country of Aparāntaka, people wear only skins as clothing; therefore, [skins] were permitted to be used as bedding.
However, where cloth or silk is available, they must not be used. The commentary further notes: "According to the *Liang Shi Gong Fu Tu* (The Tribute Map of the Liang Dynasty), it means..."
During the Liang dynasty, people from the country of Pārasīka came here, offering a gift of a fine red horse and claiming it had come from the west.
Based on this single statement, it is certain that Pārasīka belongs to the eastern border of this region. Thus, it is said that this [country] lies to the east of that.
"Lì" means that in the Central Kingdom, white wooden strips are called "east"; since white wooden strips are called "east" in Qi, this is a frontier region.
Here, Emperor Wǔ calls wooden strips "west," which clearly shows that this is a borderland.
Regarding the phrase "if one uses the skin of a *jū*": *Jū* is the name of a beast. It resembles a wolf with a red head and is like a *tā* (pronounced either *tā-hè* or *tā-hé*).
The *Shuowen* states that its shape is small like a dog; it is this creature that dwells in water and eats fish. In the Vinaya text, it is written as *jū* (pronounced *dīng-hè*).
The *Zilin* states that *gē-jū* is the name of a beast; it resembles a wolf with a red head. *Jū* is not the correct orthography. If the door pivot does not turn...
"Et cetera" (*ādi*): This means that when door pivots become stiff and do not turn, one should wrap leather around the head of the pivot to make it turn easily.
"One should maintain a 'good assistant,' namely the meditation belt" (*dhyānabandhana*): According to the *Tri-sahasra-vidhi* (*Sanqian weiyi*), one should maintain a good assistant;
a good assistant refers to the meditation belt. There are five requirements for a meditation belt: first, its width should be one chi; second, its length should be... [text continues].
1. It should be eight chi in length. 2. Third, there should be a hook at the head. 3. Fourth, it should have three layers. 5. One must not use fresh grass, nor may one use a golden hook.

It is said that because practitioners of seated meditation fear falling asleep and collapsing, they take a band of mature hemp, about three or four inches wide, which they wrap around from behind over the knees and fasten so that it does not move; therefore, it is called "a good aid."
Regarding "partial exposure [of the shoulder] being abandoned," Sheng says it refers to cases such as abandoning the practice of begging for food after midday.

Regarding "not being permitted to possess shoes made of the four kinds of precious materials," the *Pi-p'o-chieh Kien-tu* (Kāṣāya-vastu) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that these four kinds are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and jewels;
however, "jewel" (*ratna*) is a general term.
Second, the explanation of the ritual for performing *viśuddha-dāna* (pure giving) has six sections. First, regarding the intent behind the regulation and its exposition:

Lì states that the original purpose of the *viśuddha-dāna* method was primarily to prevent attachment to long-term possession, in accordance with the practice of Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) who remain free from clinging. Although one may not yet have fully attained this state, whatever one receives and keeps must all be brought to fulfillment [through this method].

Thus, through the skillful means (*upāya*) of great compassion, the teaching establishes the ritual of pure giving, so that one always maintains the mental attitude of regarding the object as belonging to another; once this is done, [the fault of attachment] no longer exists.
Regarding the faults of hoarding, it benefits other bhikṣus, brings merit to the donor, avoids external criticism, and thus the "Dharma-purity" (dharmaviśuddhi) was established.
Among the more than ninety types [of acquisitions] in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there is no substitute for this; it is because this method differs from those of outsiders that it is so.

As for the distinction between two or three donors: my private opinion is that the Saṃgha itself acts as the intermediary, while the true [donor] and the layperson together constitute the three donors.

Regarding the account of how, at one time in the past, he opened a chamber of the seven precious jewels: according to the *Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), Deva Subhūti was of royal lineage.

He was named "Deva" because for five hundred lifetimes he had always been born among the devas, and having descended from the heavens to be born into a royal family, his enjoyment of merit was spontaneous.
Later, he followed the Buddha and left the household life; upon hearing the Buddha’s instruction...

The bhikṣus said, "One who practices the Way should restrain the body and maintain its integrity, wearing coarse clothing, eating poor food, sitting on grass mats, and taking excrement and urine as medicine.
Upon hearing this teaching of the Buddha, they could not endure it; their thoughts remained fixed on the fine and exquisite food and clothing within the palace, and they wished to return home.
Ānanda said to them, "Stay for one night. I shall now prepare the necessary offerings," and he immediately went [to do so].
At the king’s residence, he sought various precious canopies, fully equipped with all manner of ornaments. There the bhikṣu stayed overnight and attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Contemplating the Four Noble Truths, by the time of the final watch of the night, he realized arhatship. He then flew through the air. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Regarding clothing and food, there are two kinds:
those that may be approached and those that may not be approached. Which ones may be approached? If one wears..."

Fine clothing can at times increase one's resolve for the Way; such things may be approached. However, when wearing fine clothing causes one's resolve for the Way to diminish, it must not be approached.

Therefore, Ānanda, whether one attains the Way through fine clothing or attains the Way through the five rags, the reason for this awakening lies in the mind and is not constrained by outward form or dress.

If one is negligent and fails to confess [the offense] until ten days have passed, thereby committing a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, it is because of that negligence that the offense is incurred as soon as the item enters one's possession;
it does not wait for the ten days to elapse. If one is careful and protective [of the precepts], even if one forgets and more than ten days pass, there is no offense.
Therefore, one should know that the meaning of "negligence" (*pramāda*) does not include mere forgetfulness.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s method of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*):

according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, all the requisites and articles for giving possessed by a bodhisattva are relinquished as pure gifts with a pure mind to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.
For example, suppose a bhikṣu takes his own robes and clothing and offers them as a pure gift (śuddha-dāna) to his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya).

Because he has thus established the conditions for such a pure gift, he is permitted to possess various and immeasurable wealth and goods; therefore, this is called "dwelling in the noble lineages" (āryavaṃsa).
In the same way, a bodhisattva also attains immeasurable merit. At all times, he constantly recollects such merit. Always...
Whatever items have been accumulated through pure giving (śuddhadāna) as they increase, one should regard them as being entrusted to and guarded by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

When seeing someone come to request them, one should examine that person; if they possess the signs of accomplishment, then regarding the previously relinquished items that were made objects of pure giving:
He takes it and gives it to them. Regarding all sentient beings, there is nothing that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will not relinquish;

knowing this, he fulfills the wishes of those who seek. He observes that person and, seeing no other way to bring them to fulfillment, he uses the pure gift to provide liberation and consolation, addressing them as "Virtuous One":
"This object was previously given away and thus already belongs to another. Speaking with gentle words, he dismisses them so as not to cause distress.

This leads to resentment. If one were to provide double or triple the amount with other items as a skillful means, it would cause [the recipient] to understand that the Bodhisattva does not act out of stinginess, but rather because of a lack of autonomy. The same applies to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
although it permits the acceptance and keeping [of robes], they must necessarily be offered through a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) by donors of firm faith, and so forth. (etc.)
Regarding the "three types of donors mentioned above," I privately interpret these as the three: robes, medicine, and alms bowls.

Therefore, the passage below concerning the "precious donor" refers to the subsequent category of lay donors. Master Li states that these are the three: the real [donor], the indirect [donor], and the money/precious object [donor].
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* explains that "indirect" means that among the five groups of monastics, one may designate any individual as the donor; this is the "real" [donor].

Regarding "going to a certain bhikṣu": the *Lìshìmíng* (Explanation of Names) states that because these individuals transmit and bestow [the object] upon one another, each acting successively as the owner, it is called the "successive method" (*zhǎnzhuǎn fǎzuò*).
Because the entrustment to the other is not in vain, it is termed "true. Since both involve severing greed and giving to others, they are called "pure gifts" (*jìngshī*).
These two types are both formal methods; the object does not truly belong to the recipient. If this is so, how can it be called "true"?
"True. The answer is: one must directly hand over the object to the other party; only after they have asked may it be used. Therefore, it is called "true.
This means that as for objects received through intermediaries, they do not belong to that [other] person; thus it is so named.
It does not say "not before a śrāmaṇera," because the true purifier (viśuddha-dātṛ) must specifically act within the assembly; hence it says "not before a śrāmaṇera."
"The five types of persons consisting of five individuals who should not perform [the role of a steward]" clarifies the true pure steward (*śuddha-sthāpaka*).

Since these five types of persons do not know one another and are not familiar with each other—meaning they do not associate closely or follow one another's conduct—it is feared that they will ultimately not return the entrusted items;
therefore, it is said that one "should not act" as such. Regarding the "five types of improper times," it refers to those who have perhaps not yet received full ordination, or...
There is a vast difference between the old and the young; thus it is said. Regarding the "three who should perform the purification for the fivefold assembly":
this refers to the successive purifiers, whose primary requirement is that they belong to the fivefold assembly. One must not designate two or three individuals as the purifiers;

the donor may only be a single person. If there were three or five donors, because the procedure would have been completed and the robes would become confused, the purification rite (*śuddhi-dharma*) would suddenly fail if one person were to die.

It is lost according to the circumstances. One must know which garment it is. However, if the donor dies and another person is invited to take charge, all the clothing and goods are taken and declared as "pure" (śuddha) for storage;
for this reason, only one person may possess them.

A śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts is one who undergoes training and repentance (*śikṣādattaka*). Regarding those such as the "six-night" and "five-fold" persons, it is established that there are five stages:

the concealment, the completion of concealment, the six nights, the completion of the six nights, and the formal removal of the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). Alternatively, the removal of the offense may be counted as the fifth.

Regarding the one-night penance (*ekarātrika-dharma*): apart from this expiation of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*), these five types of persons—including those subject to the *mūlāpakarṣa* (penance involving returning to the beginning)—are not permitted to act as a pure donor (*śuddha-dānapati*).

The note states: "This appears to be an instruction for the time [of the rule's promulgation]," meaning that according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is not necessary to request [the status] beforehand.

When it comes to the time of actually addressing others and speaking, one may simply point and give to a single person; thus it is said that this is like pointing out [the recipient] at that very moment.

Regarding the note stating that there is no text in this specific section [of the Vinaya] and that one should follow the practice of both divisions: this means that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) lacks a formal text concerning the invitation of a donor.

Regarding face-to-face invitations and remote invitations: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü), if a person of such high reputation and virtue that they cannot be approached for a face-to-face invitation, one may perform a remote invitation (*dūre-āvāhana*) according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
However, if it is possible to summon them, one must follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Duolun) and perform a face-to-face invitation for it to be valid.
Thus it is said that "one follows the usage of both schools. Now, we invite the Bhikṣuṇīs to act as the intermediaries (*saṃkramaṇa*).
Regarding the donor: this was permitted only because there were no monks at that time.

As for the "mental declaration of purity" (*cittavijñapti*) and so forth mentioned in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmasūtra) states: "Since it is an individual, the intention to relinquish [the object] is difficult to bring to completion."
Furthermore, this allows for the conversion [of the robe] so that the time limit may be extended; however, it must ultimately be finalized through formal recitation (*pratideśanā*).

This is not like receiving a robe merely to wear it, but rather involves adding the noble dharma (*āryadharma*) to what one already uses. Therefore, the mental reception (*manasikāra-parigraha*) is identical to the formal recitation before another person (*sammukhībhūta-pratideśanā*).

Regarding the mental application of the Dharma, the text is divided into three parts. First, because one bestows [the robe] upon the recipient from afar, exceeding the prescribed limit, it is said to be "eleven days.

Later, because one returns and adds [the period] without transgressing the standard allowance, it is simply "ten days," for fear that by the appearance of dawn one would incur an offense against the teaching.
Furthermore, it is stated that giving to him is as previously permitted to exceed [the limit]; thus, the text says to discard the old and receive the new, changing every ten days.

Furthermore, there is a distinction between two types: first, the "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*), and second, that which is "held in possession" (*parigṛhīta*). One must alternate between receiving the purification (*śuddhi*) and holding it in possession, and must not exceed the limit.

Regarding the calculation of what is held in possession, one does not fear violating the rule against extra robes; however, as for the purification, since it is subject to the limit, one must ensure it is transferred within ten days.

This aforementioned method of mental purification (*manasikāra-śuddhi-dharma*) is also called an "exceptional allowance" (*anujñā-pratyaya*). Even if no person is present throughout the entire boundary (*sīmā*), [the rule still applies].

There are those who are obstructed by ignorance, or perhaps these are not [proper] enumerations; though one seeks fulfillment, it is difficult to obtain. One may only rely on the previous ten-day period to apply the additional usage.

If one suddenly departs for another place and returns during the night, one has not yet obtained [the status] to rely upon this. According to the Vinaya, because the old [period] is relinquished and the new is received, one should change [the period] every ten days;
this should be understood as not being "unclean" (asuddha). I privately say: regarding the above from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are two meanings, namely, that this person...
Originally, although he had not performed the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), he still possessed one extra *kāṣāya*.

Upon reaching the tenth day, fearing he might commit the offense of keeping an extra robe, he immediately relinquished the one he had previously been wearing and accepted the one that was extra. When the next tenth day arrived, he did so again. Therefore, it is said that "he changed them once every ten days."
If one were to speak in terms of changing [the robes] every ten days, those who serve as the "mindfulness-purifier" (*cetanā-viśuddhi-pudgala*) would not be numerous;

there would simply need to be someone to change the three robes once a year. This method of mindfulness must be performed only when ten days have passed and before the dawn light has appeared, provided that no one else has arrived within the boundary.
The commentary states: "Alternatively, because it may be necessary to perform the *viśuddhi* (purification), one may cause it to be transmitted in succession. Now, based on this...
Regarding these words, although the commentator (*chaojia*) offers two interpretations, it is difficult to rely upon them for understanding.

As for "transferring face-to-face," the *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Ritual) states: "The text is divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that the owner of the property, fearing the offense of 'excess' (*changguo*), relinquishes the object to another person as a 'transferred purification' (*zhuanzhuan jing*).
If one did not mention 'transference,' it would be taken as a literal [gift]. Second, the acceptance..."

Regarding the "requester": this refers to the fact that the previous acceptance of the property was communicated through a series of intermediaries and was not exclusively dedicated to oneself (meaning it was not specifically intended for me).

It was further intended to be given to another person, yet that other person did not grant sole permission (meaning one must not arbitrarily give it to others; rather, the wealth must be given to the original patron’s household, as they were originally invited to act as the donors).
