According to the Vinaya, one must obtain their consent; therefore, one asks the original owner, "To whom do you give this?
Once these three points are settled, the *jìngzhǔ* (the one who purifies the gift) must necessarily provide a remote entrustment (*yuǎozhū*) and further fold [the cloth] over it.
This is the original context: it clarifies that [the object] was previously accepted. Furthermore, it reiterates the previous instruction to entrust it to a steward (*śuddhikara*), stating:

"For now, I return it to you; you shall act as the steward and guard it well. Regarding the phrase "to wear and use," words are added or subtracted according to the occasion. As for this process of transmission:

when the original owner first entrusts it to the steward, this is the first stage of purification. When the steward, in turn, makes a remote request to another person, this is the second stage of purification. Purification.

If the owner does not know [the recipient] and returns the property, it is established as a pure object belonging to the owner; these are the three ways of purifying through transformation (*parivartana-śuddhi*).
All serve to purify the mind of attachment. Regarding the "three external Vinayas," they are the *Pañcavargika*, the *Mahāsāṃghika*, and the *Daśabhāṇavāra*—these constitute the three.

As for "arising disputes by performing purification in the presence [of the donor]," this refers to when one performs purification in the presence of a specific donor, and that donor immediately says: "Since you have already given..."

"This belongs to me; it must belong to me. Because of this dispute over the object, the Buddha said: "Even though one has invited him to be the donor, one must not perform the *viśuddhi* (purification) rite in his presence.

Furthermore, do not let the donor know [of the transgression], for fear that this person might commit the offense of *atireka* (excess). Moreover, if the donor later finds out, he too might commit the offense of *atireka*.
The Buddha said: 'One should not speak so as to let him know. As for the instruction to explain it in another place, this is according to the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*."
This refers to the section clarifying the successive purification through gifting (*pariṣkāra-pariśuddhi*). The text states:

"After the bhikṣu who received the gift and performed the purification has spoken of this matter to a bhikṣu whose name is invoked, [the latter] fears incurring the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and does not dare to accept it, not knowing what to do."
They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should not speak of the bhikṣu by name.

It is permissible to use [the property] when it has been properly entrusted for protection, but one must not use it when it has not been so authorized. This clarifies that a true *śuddhika-puruṣa* (pure person) or a donor may not use another's property.

The note stating that "the two types of purity are transcribed according to the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*" refers to the "successive true purity" (*krama-śuddha-tattva*), which is found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

This is from the Vinaya text. Regarding the instruction to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") perform the act of purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*), this means that one must indeed perform the purification.

It is necessary to have a layperson know that these are [purified] objects; thus, it is said that although the Buddha permitted the practice of declaring things pure (*sāmaṃ-kappiya*), he still required them to be appraised by a layperson.
If, after the declaration is complete, one keeps the items for oneself, this also constitutes an offense.
The above concludes the explanation of the fourth point, the meaning of the ritual for purifying the body (*śauca*).

From here below is the fifth point, which correctly clarifies the meaning of whether one’s status as living or deceased can be determined, and whether one may proceed or not. Regarding "exactly three *yojanas*": this means that within this distance, one's status as living or deceased can be known;
beyond this, life and death cannot be distinguished. Because the road is so distant, it is not permitted [to cremate] if it is unknown whether one has died within ten days.
Since the *yāvad-bhūta-viśuddhi* (as-much-as-is-pure) dharma has already been completed, the new rules are entirely lost; one must again request a donor (*dānapati*) to perform the *viśuddhi*.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states that it is lost immediately upon reaching a foreign land or a different region. The text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it is lost beyond three *yojanas*; this interpretation is somewhat stricter. Lì says: [the text continues].

Silks, brocades, embroideries, furs, tree bark, and items such as those involving human hair, horsehair, or animal skins that constitute offenses of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (舍墮) cannot be made *viśuddha* (pure).

If the donor dies or renounces the path after the items have already been formally purified (*viśuddha-datta*), one must declare the purity (*viśuddhi*) before another person when the items are exhausted;
otherwise, one commits the offense of *atireka* (excess). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one must ascertain whether [the donor] was in the world or on the path; if they have died...
If one's name is no longer known in the world, or if having returned to lay life one's name is no longer in the Path, both cases constitute a failure [to fulfill the requirement].
If one must rely on the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is necessary that only those whose virtue is far-reaching may be invited.

If it is difficult to know whether they are alive or dead, one may rely on the three *yojanas* mentioned in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. If it is easy to know whether they are alive or dead, [the rule] applies.

According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, one loses [the status of] a renunciant by leaving the country. If, in a general sense, merely being in the same monastery as ordinary people constituted a loss of the Dharma, Jie says:
"Since such a person has no name, even if they were to die suddenly within the monastery, no one would know; thus they would lose the pure Dharma, for it is possible that they remain unknown.
If one who has received full ordination claims to have no years of seniority and then dies, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi), the *upāsaka*...

Upāli asked the Buddha: "To whom should a monk make a formal declaration of purification (*śuddhi*) regarding an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*)? The Buddha said: "One should make the declaration of purification before the fivefold assembly (*pañca-varga*).

Upāli asked again: "At what distance apart may one receive such a declaration of purification? The Buddha said: "Within a range of three *yojanas*. Once it is known that [the recipient] has died," Upāli asked again:
"If an extra robe is declared pure with respect to a *śrāmaṇera*, and that *śrāmaṇera* subsequently receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), how should it be addressed?"

"What? The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu who has not yet completed his year [of ordination] is designated as 'pure' (kappiyakāraka). Again he asked, "What if a bhikṣu who has not yet completed his year dies?
The Buddha said, "He may be kept for ten days; one may designate another knowledgeable person as pure. [The Master] privately remarked: "First, one invites a śrāmaṇera to act as the donor;
later, once he has received full ordination, he becomes a bhikṣu. If one designates him as pure before others, one asks him: 'Are you the donor?'"

"To whom [is it given]? He replies, "It is bestowed upon the bhikṣu named So-and-so, who has no fixed residence (avarṣika), and so forth. The commentary states: Some say that if the actual recipient dies, the gift is lost;

however, in the case of a succession [of recipients], it is not lost. This master’s intention is that [the gift is valid] when made directly to the actual recipient; once they die, there is no one present to face them, and thus it is lost. In the case of a succession, it is not done face-to-face;
since one merely points to [the successor] from afar, why bother to request [permission] again? Therefore, it is not [lost].

This is an error. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the two treasures refer to the lay donor," some say that because gold and silver constitute one [category] and coins constitute the other, they are called the "two treasures.
As for the phrase "being rebuked by the teacher so as not to perform the purification (pariśuddhi)," this means that if the donor is a disciple and has been rebuked by the teacher.
That teacher may no longer perform the *viśuddhi* (purification) rite for his disciple; he must instead seek another person.
Regarding the death of a donor whose property does not enter the Sangha—this refers to "true purification" (*bhūta-viśuddhi*).

If that person received an object from another as purified property and has not yet returned it, and now dies with the object still by his side, the Sangha is not permitted to divide it; it must be returned to the original owner. The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "according to this, successive [transfers] do not require [the donor's] consent": this means that the statement by the ancient masters in the preceding text—that there is no loss through successive transfers—is incorrect.
Since [the gift] is already lost to the donor after death or when the preceptor rebukes the recipient, how can it be said that there is no loss upon death?
Furthermore, another interpretation of "according to this" is that, based on the text stating that the object does not enter the Saṃgha, these are all merely nominal gifts.

How can you claim that the previous statement was true? This property has a formal owner who may be invited [to receive it] after death; however, the successive owners do not permit such an invitation.
If it were truly [theirs], then since the formal owner has passed away, why would this object not enter the Saṃgha? Since it does not enter the Saṃgha, all such offerings are merely provisional;
how then can one not invite [the recipient]? The commentary states: "Furthermore, as mentioned above, when one person acts as the owner, it is not permitted [to transfer it]."

Regarding the mention of "two or three," this refers to the aforementioned ten recitations. As for the note stating that this contradicts the general rule in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, [Dao]li clarifies that the *Pañcavargika* does not require prior invitation;
rather, at the time of addressing others, one may designate any single person as required, thereby successfully completing the ritual.
Subsequently, one should constantly remember that this object belongs to a certain donor, as the donor is not fixed.

Therefore, as for the discrepancies between the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and this *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it refers to the fact that the *Daśabhāṇavāra* states one must not invite two or three people, but should instead invite only one;
thus, because the texts of the *Daśabhāṇavāra* and the *Pañcavargika* differ on these two points, they are said to be contradictory. The commentary notes:
Alternatively, regarding the establishment of rules to include the five groups (*pañcavarga*) and yet, when performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*),
always designating a single individual— this commentator reconciles these two texts. He states that while the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* provides a general indication for the five groups as a whole,
when the ritual is actually performed, it must specifically designate one person.

Regarding the passage in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concerning the forgetting of many robes, up to the point where one says, "I shall relinquish this," and states, "I have given these robes as a pure gift (*śuddhaka-dāna*) to so-and-so;

I now relinquish them," and that one should speak further [of the new ones]—this refers to cases where the robe-material has been either spoken of or not yet spoken of, such that it is disordered and difficult to distinguish.
Now, gathering them in one place, one relinquishes them all to another person; this is the prior method of purification (*śuddhi*).

Regarding the phrase "purify for [the sake of] so-and-so," this refers to stating the name of the original donor of the pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*). It is said that one must not state it twice; therefore, having relinquished it, one speaks of purifying it again.

As for the discussion on opening up the period of ten days after forgetting, this refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Manyu-lun). The commentary states: "This refers to those things which can be distinguished."
This means that because one has definitely known that the forgotten object was not previously mentioned, one may obtain an extension of ten days. This is explained in contrast to the preceding text.
In the preceding text, to speak again after having already relinquished [the object] would constitute a confusion between what has been spoken and what has not been spoken.
Regarding "accepting the two purities": this refers to designating a single [act of] speaking as two names.

Regarding the statement that the five primary colors and the superior colors of brocade, though combined, do not constitute *saṃsṛṣṭa-śuddhi* (purification through mixing): "superior colors" refers to true crimson and genuine purple.
This means that even if one mixes these five major superior colors with brocade according to the rules for dyeing them into *kaṣāya* (discolored) hues, it does not achieve *saṃsṛṣṭa-śuddhi*.

This is because the five major superior colors themselves are mixed with one another; therefore, they do not constitute *saṃsṛṣṭa-śuddhi*. The preceding sections have presented various differing views.
The general explanation of the one hundred and first section on the various meanings of "long" is concluded.

Second, regarding the intention behind the regulation for wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*): Dali states that these are items discarded by worldly people, and their meaning is the same as that of "rubbish."
Therefore it is so called. It may also be named according to its place of origin; that is to say, it was picked up from a place where refuse is discarded, hence the name.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, ten distinct types of *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) are explained: first, a cow-chewed robe; second, a rat-chewed robe.
1. Robes burned by fire; 2. Robes from the fourth month of the rainy season (also known as robes for women to manifest their integrity); 3. Robes from a woman who has recently given birth; 4.
Robes from within a shrine that have been carried off by birds or blown away by the wind; 5. Robes from among graves; 6. Robes obtained through a vow; 7.
Robes received upon assuming office; 8. Robes used for traveling back and forth.

Regarding the case where a garment is carried off by a bird or blown away by the wind from its original location and can be recovered: one should know that it is not the case that a bird carried it off or the wind blew it away.
As long as it has not left its original place, it certainly still belongs to a non-human being; therefore, it may not be taken. Regarding those who seek garments through prayer:

the established rule states that if one takes a garment to a shrine of spirits or ghosts, makes a request, and subsequently discards it upon a tree, it may be taken because it has been abandoned by a human, and thus no longer belongs [to the spirits].

Regarding "clothes left behind by non-humans": Bing says that in the West, when conducting a funeral, they take folded cloth to make banners, which are then discarded at the tomb and not collected again;
since these have no owner, a bhikṣu may take them. Lin says this refers to the clothes used for summoning the soul at a layperson's grave site.
Li states that it refers to the clothes used to wrap the deceased, which are brought back and offered to a bhikṣu, who may then take them. Furthermore—

Regarding the taking of the clothing of one who has died but not yet decayed: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was once a bhikṣu traveling on a road who, upon seeing the clothing of a person who had died but not yet decayed at a distance from a cemetery, went and took it away.

The deceased person then rose up and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, do not take my clothes. The bhikṣu replied, "Since you are dead, where would you have clothes? That is precisely why I am taking them."
The corpse did not stop moving. At that time, the dead man pursued the bhikṣu until he reached the gate of the Jeta Grove, where he fell to the ground on his knees.
Other bhikṣus saw this and questioned him; the bhikṣu answered them fully regarding what had happened. The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not take the robes of a corpse that has not yet decomposed. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "This was a *utthāpaka-yakṣa* (a reanimating spirit) that had entered the body of the deceased person."
When the bhikṣu Śiśuka arrived at the gate of the saṃghārāma, he was struck down because a benevolent deity would not allow him to enter.
Regarding "soiled clothes" (tuyī), which refers to those from the streets and lanes: it is said that they are called "soiled clothes" because they are defiled by earth.
This refers to Queen Mallikā, who, out of faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, saw the bhikṣus in the lanes while she was atop a high tower.
She gathered discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*). She then had someone take new garments and go to offer them to Mahākāśyapa;
however, Mahākāśyapa, who always wore discarded rags, would not accept them because of his fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).

Thereupon, the lady took various materials—some one foot, three inches, or five feet long—and cut them into pieces, which she then had people discard among the mud, filth, and discarded rags, intending this as a skillful means for the bhikṣus.

[One] may relinquish [the robe] and take it to be made into a garment. Regarding the three types of robes given by lay donors (*dānapati*), the second refers to those given at the proper time or improper time.

Li states: "The first is for the sake of fulfilling the request of the donor; the second is because the practice of contentment with *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) has a superior benefit, whereas the meaning of benefiting others is slight.
If one discusses the benefit of robes given as gifts, it encompasses both self and others; therefore, the World-Honored One permitted the acceptance of such gifts."

Regarding the statement "giving at the proper time" (*kāla-dāna*): this refers to the period after the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has ended, during the month of Kārttika, when there is cloth available for five months.

This is what the Buddha intended for the benefit of the bhikṣus. [The commentary] states: although it is within this period, if the gift is not given specifically for the sake of the *anvāraka* (the post-retreat period), it is called "improper-time giving" (*akāla-dāna*).
Even if it is for the sake of the *anvāraka*, if it enters into a period that is not the designated time, it is also called "improper-time" and is not [considered] [proper-time].
"Timely giving" (*kāladāna*). Li says: "Timely giving refers to that which is obtained during the period of one month or five months;

this is called timely giving. It applies equally to what is obtained by the *saṃgha* present at that time. Because it must be for the sake of the rainy season retreat (*varṣāvāsa*), a gift that possesses both of these conditions is called timely giving.
If it is not for the sake of the summer labor [of the retreat], it is called untimely giving (*akāladāna*). Question: For what reason is it called 'timely'?"

It is a "timely gift" (*kālika-dāna*). This refers to the month of Kārttika; if there is a robe [offered] during the five months [of the rainy season], the Buddha permitted monks to receive these five benefits within this period, which is termed "timely.
Regarding the statement that the time for rewarding labor with these five benefits is called "timely giving," Master Li (Lì) says:

"To clarify these five benefits, although they are restricted to those who have completed the prior retreat (*pūrvavarṣika*), at the time of distributing the goods, they also apply to those who have completed the subsequent retreat (*paścimavarṣika*)."

Furthermore, regarding the "fixed at one time" due to the four types of fixed times: this excludes untimely giving (*akāla-dāna*). That is to say, receiving [offerings] prior to the fifteenth day of the seventh month is termed untimely giving.
Among the masters of antiquity, there were also those who accepted [offerings] after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day was concluded.
When the robes are being made, the donor’s gift is exclusively "out-of-season" (*akāla*), because the summer retreat has not yet concluded;

it is only when sixteen days remain until the appearance of the morning light that it is designated as a "seasonal" (*kāla*) gift. Regarding the two fixed locations, these apply specifically to those who have entered the prior summer retreat within this boundary.

This excludes those from other realms (*dhātu*). As for the phrase "the three persons are definitely not those outside the realm who are present and dwelling together," this distinguishes those outside the realm;

they are not what is meant by "present. Regarding the fourth rule—"all legal acts (*dharma*) must directly count the number of people, with them consulting one another, casting voting sticks (*śalākā*), and distributing [the items]"—Deshan (Shen) says:
"In antiquity, there were masters who established a division of *karmavācanā*. Now, the main intent of this *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo chao*) is that since there is a distinction..."
Regarding the fourfold determination (*caturvidha-viniścaya*), why is it necessary to perform a formal ritual?
As for the division into two factions to distribute the number of people among them, this is distinguished according to the false and the correct.

That is to say, when a donor gives with a universal mind to the monks who are in retreat, one must divide [the community] into two parts: one part is given to the faction of Devadatta, while the other follows...
He divided it among himself because the donor’s intention was to give universally; thus, he distributed it.

In the Vinaya, regarding the distinction between what is obtained after first breaking [the robe] and what is obtained after later breaking it, each has its own differences, which will be explained further below (etc.).

Furthermore, as for the statement "giving the three robes to the Buddha and others," this refers to the Brahmin Vairaṇya in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, who invited the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus...
The Buddha had intended to provide offerings during the summer retreat, but later, as Māra entered his mind, he forgot the Buddha for that entire summer and subsisted only on horse fodder.
Once the retreat was concluded, the Buddha instructed Ānanda to inform the brāhmaṇa, saying, "The Buddha’s summer retreat is finished;
He now wishes to travel. The brāhmaṇa immediately came to the Buddha’s presence, sought mercy and repented, and promptly prepared offerings.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him. He immediately offered three robes to the Buddha, while the other bhikṣus each received two pieces of woolen cloth (*kambala*).

The bhikṣus did not dare to accept them. The Buddha said, "I permit you to take them. This was because they were given for the purpose of the summer retreat (*varṣā*); thus, this passage is cited here to clarify that it refers to what is manifest during that season.
As for the previous offering, no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) was performed. Regarding the division of food intended for the summer retreat, Master Li states: "This..."

It is clear that the donor also invited the monks for the *vassa* (rainy season retreat) and provided them with food. When the summer retreat had concluded, there was a surplus of food remaining, and the bhikṣus wished to divide it.
The donor did not permit this. The Buddha said, "One must follow the donor's intention; it should not be divided.
Now, citing this as proof, all items related to the *vassa* depend upon the donor's intention; therefore, it is unnecessary to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). This is another interpretation.

The reason for citing the two preceding passages is as follows: the former clarifies that when objects are present at the time [of distribution], the Sangha shall divide them equally among themselves.
The present case, however, concerns instances where a donor brings items to be given to the Sangha but still designates unequal portions;
this follows the donor’s own intent and cannot be treated like the previous requirement that they must necessarily be distributed evenly, depending on the specific circumstances.
To distinguish [the cases], it is therefore clarified. The preceding explanation of the meaning of "manifest at the time" is complete.
Regarding the second point, "attained by the Saṃgha at that time," Dali states: according to the Vinaya, there are three types. First, the method of inclusion within two divisions;
second, mutual inclusion between two divisions; third, distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox. Within the first, the method of inclusion within two divisions, some say it must...
Regarding the ritual procedure (*vidhi*): some say that no procedure is required; this has been a point of dispute since ancient times. Now, Li [Lì] says:

because the time and labor are fixed, it is divided among several people. There is also an interpretation stating that when the Saṃgha receives [the offering], because the intention of the donor is universal, the legal procedure must also be performed (meaning the *karmavācanā* is required).
Therefore, the text below states: "There was a bhikṣu who was in retreat during the summer rains and obtained a great amount [of offerings]."
Regarding robes for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), the Buddha said that the bhikṣu should mentally reflect and speak aloud: "I accept [them].

Since there is already mental reflection in this acceptance, it is clear that if one must perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) before another person, the proper procedure (*dharma*) is likewise required. Lì then asked:

"If it is said that one must divide them through a formal ritual, why is it permissible to take them by means of an entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇā*)? Is there any case where a formal ritual is strictly required, yet the ritual itself is not fulfilled?"
Regarding those who receive the entrustment: for what purpose would one employ this method? It is certainly not so.

Although the mind is universally directed, the donor obtains the merit of the "field of the Saṃgha" (meaning that if the donor’s intention is universal, it is intended that they obtain great merit). This is to prevent greed;

therefore, receiving robes from another location is not permitted (meaning that according to the Vinaya texts, it is not permitted to receive robes from elsewhere while observing the rains retreat within this boundary; this is my own interpretation). Because the Buddha has definitively determined that the place of receipt is restricted, there is no need for [further deliberation].

Regarding the ritual procedure (*vidhi*): it must simply be for the purpose of consuming [the *kaṭhina* robe]. As for the text concerning "receiving through mental intention" (*cittānujñā*) by a single bhikṣu, this is not the method of mental intention (*cittānujñā-dharma*).

Rather, it should be understood that the arising of the thought belongs to oneself (However, since the two previous judgments [of the Li and Shi commentators] are incorrect, how can one accept the text on mental intention which says "the arising of the thought belongs to oneself"? The Vinaya text clearly requires both mental intention and verbal expression, making it evident that this is a formal ritual act.

How can one skillfully reconcile this? The intent of the present *Chao* is that one must certainly add the ritual formula). An ancient master judged: "One does not permit entering the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) in a different boundary (*sīmā*) and taking [the robe] in a different boundary."

Regarding "robes": this refers to those that are present at the time. If the Saṃgha acquires them at that time, they may be obtained by a person coming from outside the boundary (*sīmā*), and the legal procedure (*dharma*) is likewise obtained.

Thus, one knows that the legal procedure is required. As for the objection that the *Śarīra-vibhāṣā* does not permit this, saying that if taking them were not allowed, then since these robes are present at the time and their ownership has already been determined, how could such a matter require a judgment by the Buddha?
Therefore, one knows that this is not the case. Second, regarding the mutual inclusion of the two divisions:

Lì said: "As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, this is incorrect. When a gift is offered to the community of bhikṣus during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), it should be divided among both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

When not during the rainy season retreat, if a gift is offered to the bhikṣuṇīs, it should be divided among both bhikṣuṇīs and bhikṣus. Furthermore, it is said that when gifts are received during the rainy season retreat, all cases are likewise [treated].

Once the mutual affiliation has been fixed, they shall divide the portion accordingly. Whether the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed or not, the matter is not settled until the person understands."
As previously stated, the third [category] is distinguished by what is improper and what is proper. *Li* says:

"If one obtains a summer robe that is torn, or if after it is torn one obtains the material, or if after obtaining it it becomes torn—these three cases are all counted as the share of the person. This is because, regarding the time and the specific location, the recipient is fixed.
If one interprets the meaning based on the act itself, it is no different from the case of 'what is obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time. This is merely a provisional [explanation]."

To speak of the improper method: if two groups are present, there are likewise three ways [to distribute]. Either by one group, or by two groups, or by counting the number of people to divide [the portion].
If distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, one should invite both the heterodox and orthodox groups and ask them as they face one another to receive the offering.
The donor should accept [the distribution] according to what is said; if they say "I do not know" or "Give to both," then it is divided by counting the number of people.
The Vinaya states: "If one obtains summer robes and departs before they have been divided, or even if one does not leave them for the sake of those who travel...

Regarding this passage, Master Li maintains that no formal ritual (karmavācanā) is required; since it is permitted to take the robes after entrusting them to others, what is the use of performing a ritual? My current explanation differs: I maintain that a ritual must necessarily be performed.

As for the phrase "allowing those who travel to share [the robes]," this refers to those who were present during the rains retreat (varṣā) and who have rendered service through their practice of the summer sitting. Therefore...
This refers to the distribution [of robes]. It is also like providing clothing and medicinal herbs for a patient while attending to their illness.

Since the [specific] time was not present, and because one would incur an offense regarding one's share if the Sangha distributed the robes later, there is no fault even now in taking [the robe] by request, provided one has performed the summer retreat (varṣā) and possesses the requisite merit.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "a single bhikṣu who obtains a robe during the rainy season retreat must even mentally reflect and speak it aloud," according to the intent of this text, it is essential that...
Regarding the ritual procedure: if one follows the judgment of the *Nai-li*, how should this text be understood?

If, during the [rainy season] retreat, the distribution is not divided and flows into the eighteenth day of the eighth month, which is outside the proper time (*akāla*), and one instead performs the ritual for "non-timely gifts obtained by the Saṃgha," then it is clearly established that when there are both resident and visiting monks in joint residence and they receive gifts during the proper time, if the visiting monks wish to depart at the conclusion of the summer retreat, they must cause the residents to perform the distribution.
Regarding the robes: the host was unwilling to share them, intending to have the guest leave; later, he wished to appropriate them for himself.

Once the guest had departed, after the sixteenth day of the eighth month, the Buddha established the practice of "non-seasonal gifts obtained by the Saṃgha" (*akāla-saṃghalābha*) as a penalty for this host-monk.
Thus, he did not allow [the robes] to belong to him alone; rather, they had to be assembled from all quarters and distributed collectively. This was intended to clarify that since it was already...

If an item is obtained during the [proper] season, it must be distributed during that same season. Since it was not divided during the eight months of the summer retreat, it enters the category of "non-seasonal" (akālika) acquisitions;
thus, it is to be divided according to the shares for non-seasonal gifts received by the Saṃgha.

As for one who has moved to another region before the end of the rains retreat and does not receive a share of the robes, this establishes clearly that he is a guest-monk (atithi-bhikṣu). For this reason, the host is unwilling to divide [the robes] with him. Guest—
They immediately moved to another location, yet they did not receive their share of the robes there.

Regarding "taking [robes] at the place where one has stayed for more days": this refers to the postponement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) due to difficult circumstances; if one has stayed at a certain place for more days, one takes the robes from that place.

If the number of days stayed at two places is equal, it means that each [share] is designated for the monks within the respective boundary of the distribution. Third, regarding "identical *karmavācanā*," it is as follows:
The Sangha has completed the *poṣadha* ceremony last night. Fourth, when the Sangha obtains these aforementioned items, they are all termed "obtained by the Sangha" (*saṃghalābha*).

In the first three locations, the application of the rule is restricted and is fixed as following the three types [of procedures]. Only the fourth case, that which is obtained by the Sangha, must be determined by means of the formal procedure (*dharma*).

There are three levels of formal procedure: namely, the mental reflection (*cittavijñapti*), the face-to-face (*sammukhībhūta*), and the *karmavācanā*. The above concerns only one category: the distribution to the assembly of the Sangha.
If one gives to both the community of monks and nuns, there are likewise four types. First, giving to the permanent property (*sthavira*) of the two communities;

because it is restricted to a specific location, it is divided into two portions according to the two communities of monks. Second, obtaining [the property] through the boundary (*sīmā*). Third, common *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action).

Because the location and the legal status are fixed, one simply counts the number of persons and divides accordingly. Furthermore, since they are already designated as two groups, it is also not improper to divide them into two portions based on the principle of being two groups.
Regarding the fourth category, property acquired by the Saṃgha, one must use the two groups' separate ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) to likewise divide it into two portions.
This refers to the distribution of the two assemblies (bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī) in their presence; therefore, it is divided into two portions.
If one assembly is absent from the other, they are subsumed under that remaining group, as it is impossible to calculate [the quorum] when both assemblies have not gathered in full.

Furthermore, since there is no common ritual procedure for monks and nuns to divide the community together, they are provisionally divided into two portions, each being governed by the specific rules of its own section, just as in the case of a single assembly previously mentioned. Moreover, regarding mutual...

They are included within the two groups (*dvaya-nikāya*). As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When giving to the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) at a time other than the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), if there are no monks, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it.
When giving to the community of bhikṣuṇīs at a time other than the rainy season retreat, if there are no bhikṣuṇīs, the monks should divide it.

Although this specific passage does not appear in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, the principle should likewise apply. Since the mutual inclusion of these cases has been established above, as for the respective legal procedures (*dharma*):
Yes, it is obtained. Furthermore, there may be a confusion between the heterodox and the orthodox, as was the case with the faction of Devadatta and others.

If the Saṃgha is divided only after the donated object has been received, it should be divided into two equal portions. However, if the Saṃgha has already been divided into the two factions of the heterodox and the orthodox before the object was received, [the distribution is determined by that prior division].

This must be asked of the donor to be known. Regarding the instruction to divide [the property] into two parts: since this is the property of the *saṃgha*, both the heterodox and the orthodox have a share in it;
it is not restricted to those currently present. How, then, could one calculate and divide it among the people currently here?

Since the orthodox and heterodox from the four directions do not all assemble together, one must apply a formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) to determine who is orthodox and who is heterodox. Furthermore, there is no scriptural principle for a joint procedure. Therefore, it is divided into two parts for the sake of "this" and "that."

Each shall divide it according to their respective procedures. The above concerns the case where the legitimate assembly (*samyag-saṃgha*) receives the property; the same applies when the illegitimate assembly (*mithyā-saṃgha*) receives it.

Regarding the statement, "When the property is used for distribution, one must perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) to resolve the matter," Li states: This refers to gifts obtained by the Saṃgha at an improper time (*akāla*).

The reason a *karmavācanā* procedure is required is that [the recipients] are not fixed; thus, a formal addition (*adhikāra*) is necessary to establish certainty. As for what is meant by "not being fixed," first:
First, the time is indefinite; this excludes giving at a fixed time. Second, the place is indefinite, because one may receive offerings from different realms.

Third, the persons are indefinite, as this excludes the two types of "presence" (sammukhībhāva), since it pertains specifically to those present before one. Fourth, the dharma is indefinite, because the giving occurs through various or identical formal acts (karmavācanā);

that is to say, it refers to receiving the gift of objects after the recitation of the Prātimokṣa has concluded. There are cases where people offer objects after the recitation of the Prātimokṣa is finished.
This applies exclusively to the Saṃgha; there is no need to perform the formal act of dividing the property again. Now, regarding this donor:

at the time the goods are sent, although the number of people within the boundary may be small, if others arrive later, they shall take half of the share of the robe. First, concerning those who appear out of season:

this refers to cases similar to the present time when one receives items from a lay household where a vegetarian feast (*śrāddha*) has been prepared, and so on, up to a hundred people for a hundred [shares].
Regarding the mingling of good and evil aspects: within these two types of manifest states, there are four propositions for analytical discernment.
First, both giving and dividing; second, giving but not dividing; third, dividing but not giving; fourth, neither.
Among the four cases, the first two obtain [the portion] because they involve the act of giving as a fixed rule; the latter two do not obtain it because they do not reach the point of giving.

Regarding the two kinds of *saṃgha*-attainment, there are likewise four propositions, which shall be explained later. As for the statement that "if a garment of great value cannot be divided, one is permitted to cut it," this means:
if a piece of cloth is so precious that it is worth its weight in money, it is called a "garment of great value. Now, since it is not...
It may be given to one person in its entirety; therefore, it is ordered that it be cut and divided into portions.
If the *dānapati* (donor) does not divide it into four parts or the like, it is established that the donor delivers the object to the bhikṣu.
Regarding the division of portions for oneself: it is not that one shares equally with a śrāmaṇera; rather, three śrāmaṇeras should share the portion of one *bhikṣu*.
As for one *bhikṣu*’s portion being shared with three śrāmaṇeras, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The śrāmaṇeras occupy the same rank [as the *bhikṣu*]."
The Sangha lends to one another because they share the same status; however, it is because [the recipient] is of low rank and deficient in conduct that there is a reduction [in the offering].

Furthermore, as for the reason why [offerings] are given equally, it is because [all recipients] are alike fields of merit and equally worthy of offerings. The commentary states: "Regarding 'giving equally when two types are present,' this is established by Ming."

Regarding the two types of property that appear before [the assembly]: in accordance with the donor's intention, it may be distributed equally to the śrāmaṇeras. Regarding the two types of property obtained by the Saṃgha:

it is established that they follow the harmony of the Saṃgha. As for the aforementioned two types of property that appear before [the assembly], in accordance with the donor's intention, they are made to be obtained by one type of Saṃgha.
Regarding the fact that at that time the Sangha may receive either the full portion or half a portion, this is because the donor bestowed the goods with the Sangha in mind;
therefore, it depends upon the Sangha. As for the statement that even down to the *kappiya-kāraka* (the pure attendant) they all receive their share, the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (*Jie-mo-su*) states:
The temple attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) who maintain the monastery should be given an equal share; even those to whom only one-fifth of a share is given are not true fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

This is because they provide labor for the Saṃgha and look toward the Saṃgha for their livelihood; therefore, they are included. The Vinaya states: "If they are not given [a share], they should not be divided [among themselves]," because the regulation resides with the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha must provide for all.
Now, if one only succeeds those of high status and does not extend [the distribution] to those below, one fails in the duty toward the Saṃgha.
To be in harmony and without obstruction is not the meaning of the Saṃgha. Although they may be divided, they do not join together; furthermore, this constitutes an act of theft.

It is established that these words refer to many matters: if a nun or a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) is present at a monastery, she is not entitled to receive a share, because it is improper to maintain her [as a member of the community].
The nuns' monastery is the reverse of this. Furthermore, although they may be male attendants (*upadhivārika*), those who have labored in service to the Saṃgha may receive [the robes];

those who are young or old do not qualify. Moreover, at the time of distributing the robes, those within the boundary (*sīmā*) may receive them; those who have gone outside the boundary may not. The preceding explanation of the *asamaya-pratyutpanna* (distribution for non-seasonal purposes) is hereby concluded.
Next, regarding the "non-timely alms received by the Saṃgha," this refers to when a donor directs their intention to encompass all three seasons—namely, spring, summer, and winter.
That is to say, the donor’s intention is vast and expansive, such that the time extends through all twelve months, and they offer gifts to the community of monks and to a single individual.
According to the Vinaya texts, these non-timely alms received by the Saṃgha have four distinct types: first, constant giving (*nitya-dāna*).
Abiding. Because the two realms (dhātu) can equally possess the *sabhāga* (homogeneous), it is necessary to apply the *dharma* [analysis] to distinguish them;

this is why they are not the same. Now, because there are four types of indeterminate cases, the method is established to define them. As for the remaining two, since they are present before one, they are fixed as pertaining to persons. Lì says: "This is property donated to the Saṃgha."
Since it is determined by the rule of the dharma, one must analyze it through four propositions: (1) both the gift and the dharma are reached; (2) the gift is reached but the dharma is not;
(3) the dharma is reached but the gift is not; (4) neither is reached. Among these four, the first three constitute a "reaching" (*prāpti*).

If there is a partial reaching and a partial non-reaching, because two dharmas are involved, it is appropriate to call it "reaching. To say that it merely reaches a portion and does not reach the difference is, in meaning, also to reach the dharma.
Furthermore, it must be understood that both conditions are required; the two sets of four phrases cannot be separated, for they do not meet the requirements of the dharma.

As for a novice (śrāmaṇera) who employs another person, although they do not perform the ritual together, if that person is within the boundary at the time the ritual is performed, they shall indeed fall within the limits of the dharma.
There were visiting bhikṣus who came repeatedly to receive their share of robes until they became utterly exhausted.

It was established that when the Saṃgha receives an offering at an improper time, such as the property of a deceased person, if the distribution of the items is not yet finished and another visiting bhikṣu arrives, the distribution must be performed again.

Because they came so frequently in this manner, causing the Saṃgha weariness and distress, the Buddha commanded that from now on, a formal ritual (karmavācanā) must be performed to bring them into the presence of the assembly.
Regarding those who do not meet the criteria for the Dharma, they are not permitted to receive a share. As for the "four types of mutual correction between the two assemblies," Shen says:
this refers to the two types of *saṃmukhībhūta* (those present before one) and the two types of offerings received by the Saṃgha; hence there are four. Li says:

as for the four types, since the donor’s original intention was to give universally to the monastic community of both monks and nuns, if at present there are only monks and no nuns, or only *śikṣamāṇās*...
First, śrāmaṇerikās also comprise one major portion; this is the first. Second, if there are only bhikṣuṇīs and no bhikṣus, but there are śrāmaṇeras, they likewise comprise one major portion.
Third, if there are only bhikṣus and no bhikṣuṇīs or the other two groups [of female novices], the bhikṣus themselves comprise [the full assembly].

Fourth, if there are only bhikṣuṇīs and no bhikṣus or the other two groups [of male novices], the bhikṣuṇīs may comprise [the full assembly] for themselves. Hence it is said there are four types. Furthermore, there is a version of the text where these are presented as "mutually" [inclusive].

"Correcting the Characters" (Zhèngzì): This refers to the two assemblies acting as mutual primary authorities. When there are no nuns but there are monks, the monks are the primary authority for receiving [the offering].
When there are no monks but there are nuns, the nuns are the primary authority for receiving it. It is further said: "If both assemblies are present, each takes its own portion as the correct one.
If only one assembly is present, that assembly immediately takes exclusive possession; this is called 'mutuality' (hù). Nowadays, if a single [offering] is bestowed...
Regarding the two assemblies: if at any time one gives to the assembly of monks, it may be accepted even from a single *śrāmaṇera*;
if at any time one gives to the assembly of nuns, it may be accepted even from a single *śrāmaṇerī*.

If the gift is intended for both assemblies, whether they come to the monasteries of the monks and nuns or the donor remains in their own home, the bell should be struck to assemble them; then this property should be divided into two portions, with one portion given to the monks.
One portion is given to the *bhikṣuṇīs*. If there are no *bhikṣuṇīs* present, even down to a single *śrāmaṇerī*, she may also receive one large portion.

It is the same for the *saṃgha*; although each group receives their share, they must return it to the original monastery. There, the bell must be struck again to assemble the community, and the distribution must be performed through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
This applies even if, at the time of the original offering, it was intended for both divisions; if there are only monks and no nuns, the monks may take possession of it themselves.

Even a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) may be included in the gathering. If there are only nuns and no monks, even down to a single novice, they may still be gathered because both are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Nevertheless, although one has obtained one's own property, it must be entered into their collective assets and ultimately deposited into the permanent endowment (*sthavira-saṃgha*).

In the present time, the practice of the monastic community has been obtained. If nuns were to divide [the offerings] immediately after the *karmavācanā* of the monks is concluded, this would be entirely contrary to the Dharma.

However, within this there is again a distinction between the deviant and the correct, as has already been analyzed above. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states: "Regarding the offerings received by the two assemblies of monks:
because the original gift was made universally, even when there are no nuns or the three other groups, it belongs entirely to the monks; and when there are no monks..."
The assembly also collectively belongs to the *bhikṣuṇīs*. Therefore, the number of individuals is not calculated; rather, they are divided into two groups based on their respective orders.

This division according to group is because the positions of the *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* are distinct, yet the original donor’s intent applies universally. Since the gift is made with respect to the *saṃgha*, it is thus categorized by group. Regarding the fact that the two assemblies may mutually receive [offerings] from one another:

this is based on the universal nature of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), wherein the meaning of "monastic community" (*saṃgha*) does not differ. If they were not to receive from one another, there would be fear of losing the conditions for merit.
Therefore, the principle of mutual inclusion is established. Since the mind penetrates the single transformation, all who enter the ocean of the Saṃgha are equally moistened by its reception.

If one does not apply the Dharma according to the present Saṃgha, there would be no basis for distribution. At the commencement of the ritual procedure, it is further treated like the light rules concerning deceased property.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "There are those who donate items to the Sangha, yet it is said that even if the *gandī* (wooden gong) has been struck, they may not receive them.

According to that treatise: Question: Suppose someone entrusts property to be donated to the Sangha of a particular location. When the property arrives, other bhikṣus have already arrived and are seated at the time of distribution.

Should they receive a share? Answer: If the *gandī* was struck, they should receive it; if it was not struck, they do not receive it. (The text concludes here. This has been handed down through tradition.
The commentary explains: When a donor gives property to the Saṃgha, the *gandī* (wooden gong) must be struck at the time of distribution.

If a guest arrives after this, they shall receive a share if they arrive before the next *gandī* is struck; if they do not arrive before the next *gandī*, they shall not receive a share (this point remains unclear).

Regarding the passage, "If there are remaining *dakṣiṇā* (donations), after the original monks have departed, the subsequent [monks] should inquire," according to that treatise it says: Question: [Regarding] the robes...
If there are remaining items of alms-food, and the original recipient has departed and they are given to a subsequent person, may the subsequent person take them?
One should answer by asking the owner: "Will the original recipient come back? If the answer is, "He will never come," then one may take them after reciting a prayer of blessing.

If it is said, "He might still come," they must not be taken. To take them while he is alive constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); to take them knowing he is dead constitutes an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*). This is because these are the property of the Saṃgha. (The text is straightforward; this is the explanation. Master Li says:

Regarding the "recitation of vows" (*pranidhāna*): one should first recite, "May such-and-such a person be safe, peaceful, and auspicious on their journey," and so forth, and only then take [the object].
As for what is called "abandonment through transgression": this is because it involves diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha. If [the recipient] dies, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense;

that is to say, since they have died, the property now belongs to the permanent endowment of the Saṃgha, yet one has taken it for oneself—therefore, it is a *pārājika*. However, the specific characteristics [of these cases] are difficult to discern and should be [carefully] excluded. The above explains the third *dāna* (giving).
The explanation regarding the transgression of giving robes is concluded.
Fourth, concerning those who misappropriate the property of the five groups of monastics: Zhiyi states that the principle is the same as that of "non-timely" acquisitions by the Saṃgha.

However, while alive and practicing the Way, one relies on clothing and requisites to sustain the body; now, when the retribution is exhausted and the allotted span has ended, impermanence confronts them. For this reason, the Sage... [text continues].
People cultivate the fruit of longevity, yet they do not nourish this body which is like a banana trunk or foam on water. Once dead, there is a prescribed method for its disposal;
therefore, within the rules for robes, it is explained how the property of the five groups of monastics belonging to the deceased is to be handled (and so forth).
Wealth is that which benefits petty men, not that which is cherished by Great Beings (mahāsattva). A "Great Being" refers here to a Bodhisattva.

It is said that Great Beings value things through the Way (dharma), while petty men prize them for their wealth. Thus, there is a common saying: "The gentleman delights in the Way; the petty man receives wealth.

How much more so for those who have left the household life—exalted monks—who would bring themselves into the dust of worldly entanglements for the sake of food and clothing? Those who have left the household life to seek the far-reaching goal intend to save [sentient beings].
To pull those from the three evil paths and the six realms of existence, enabling them to leave suffering behind and attain liberation, is called "rescuing from afar.

To undergo toil and subsequently experience joy refers to those who have left the household life; they are able to uphold the precepts, practice the ascetic discipline of eating once a day, and cultivate the myriad virtues through training that spans three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
This is because such toil and hardship serve as the cause; hence it is called "undergoing toil," after which one realizes the fivefold Dharma.

The body attracts the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said to "participate in bliss. Regarding "not aspiring to worldly renown": this means that the fame, profit, and pleasure found within the mundane world are not what one should delight in or aspire to.
What is meant by "renown"? It refers to speaking of one's virtues beyond their actual measure; this is called "renown" (*yù*).
The Chan Master Jiangcun Cishan of the Western Capital used six characters as a single phrase, saying: "The *Jiuyuan jing* [Sutra on Saving the Distant] for those who have left the household life."

"Labor" constitutes one phrase. "Engaging in worldly pleasures and fame rather than aspiring [to the Dharma]" constitutes another phrase; this means that the pleasures of the five worldly desires and such renown are laborious and not objects of aspiration.
As for the two types of persons mentioned above who both participate in the stream of the Dharma:

the first refers to those listed above whose high integrity makes them transcend the mundane world; the second refers to those whose dispositions have not yet been harmonized and who were originally not pure.

Jie: Since these capacities and natures differ, the Buddha established two distinct regulations for what is permitted and what is prohibited. For those of superior capacity, he mandated the possession of the three robes;

for those of inferior grade, he allowed the possession of various extra garments. Although these form two paths, both follow the Buddha’s intention; they are none other than practices of the single path of ultimate reality (*ekayāna*).

Regarding the establishment of laws by the supreme ones to save those who are suitable vessels: "establishment" refers to relying on the laws of frugality according to the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*). By means of...
The body is a vessel. Regarding those who receive the Dharma at the lower level and act according to their inclinations, the *Lì* (Establishment) states:

"To comply with the acceptance of the teachings on keeping extra robes and so forth, one provides them for their use in accordance with what they hold in mind. It further clarifies that both must conform to the Buddha-dharma.
Although these two types of persons mentioned above differ from one another, both accord with the mind of the Noble Ones and do not contradict the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, it is said that their practice leads universally to the single path of pure conduct.

Regarding the so-called "south-pointing chariot" (*zhinan*): it refers to the fact that since ancient times, various commentators have each claimed their own interpretation to be the correct one. Jie said:
"It is like the people of the Han dynasty, all of whom made south-pointing chariots, yet none captured its true essence;

some even pointed toward the west. Only Zhang Shouzi’s chariot truly points south. According to historical records, the south-pointing chariot originated with Emperor Huangdi, when he was at war with Chiyou.

They fought on the plain of Zuòlù. Chīyóu raised a great mist, causing the soldiers to lose their way in the four directions. The Emperor used a south-pointing chariot to show them the cardinal points.
It is also said that the Earl of Ěr presented a white pheasant; fearing it might be lost on the return journey, the Duke of Wǒgōng fashioned a south-pointing chariot to escort it back.
Today, among the North Gate of the Imperial Workshop (Shàngfāng Jiān), there is a south-pointing chariot. Upon the chariot is...
The Immortal held the banner of faith; as the carriage traveled east and west, people constantly pointed toward the south. It is also said to have been constructed by Guan Zhong.
Those who present both [traditions] as ultimate teachings maintain that while the various masters' adjudications follow different paths, both capture its wondrous essence.
They say, "That which I have adjudicated is the ultimate destination and the definitive direction. As clarified in the Preface, there are six such examples, as detailed in the preceding fascicle.
Within the ten gates, the differing views held by the six masters regarding the observance of the Vinaya are enumerated.
Regarding the statement that the value of Kātyāyanīputra’s (Cundapanthaka) deceased belongings was five *kārsāpaṇas*:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, whenever Kātyāyanīputra went into a village to beg for food at the proper time, after receiving his meal, he would return to the homes of cowherds in the wilderness. At that time, there was a cowherd’s wife named...
Śivālī, with a heart of faith and joy, provided him with milk and curds. Having eaten, he returned to his dwelling place and thought to himself:
"What use is this vessel of suffering for remaining long in the world?

Loathing this body, he placed his robes and bowl in one spot, leaned his head upon the elephant-hide mat beneath the trees, lay on his right side, and with a single-minded focus free from distraction, entered into *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, the cowherd waited for him to arrive at the appointed hour; he spread out his bedding and swept the ground. When the time had passed and he did not come, he thought to himself, "Is he perhaps ill?
Or has he been harmed by a venomous insect? He went to look for him and saw him lying beneath a tree.
Thinking he was merely asleep, he stood by his side and listened, but heard no sound of breathing. He felt the man's chest with his hand and found his body already cold. Then he said:
"How marvelous! they exclaimed, and immediately made offerings to the relics. The husband and wife took an axe and cut firewood, whereupon they performed the cremation.
They collected his robes and bowl and sent them to the king. The king then weighed these robes; they were worth five coins. The court officials declared, "This śramaṇa has passed away."
The robes and bowl were returned to the bhikṣus. The Buddha said they belonged to the Saṃgha. Regarding the forty thousand pieces of gold worth of goods belonging to the deceased Upananda:
according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the Śākya son Upananda died, his robes and bowl were worth forty thousand pieces of gold.
King Prasenajit of Kosala said, "Since this man has no son, these goods should belong to me.
The Buddha sent a messenger to say to the king, "When you bestowed cities, towns, and villages upon people as their sustenance, did you give them little or much? Did you give a share to Upananda?
The king replied, "I gave him none. The Buddha said, "By whose power does he obtain his livelihood? That [livelihood] should be shared; it is the power of the Saṃgha."
"Therefore, you should take it. Upon hearing these instructions, the king desisted.
The kṣatriyas said, "This bhikṣu is of the same lineage, the same birth, and the same kṣatriya caste as we; these garments and belongings should belong to us.

The Buddha sent a messenger to tell the kṣatriyas, "When you were attending to matters of state, great affairs, or official business, did you ever consult Upāli (Bhadanta)? They replied, "We did not consult him."
"When Baddhālī was away, you performed official business; did you wait for him? He replied, "I did not.
The Buddha said, "When Baddhālī performs *karmavācanā* together with the Saṃgha, if he is absent, the Saṃgha does not perform the *karmavācanā*. This property should belong to the Saṃgha.
Upon hearing this teaching from the Buddha, the Kṣatriya immediately desisted. Furthermore, among his various kinsmen—relatives by blood, by marriage, and those both near and distant—they all said:
"Bandhula is my relative in such and such a way; this property belongs to me.

The Buddha sent a messenger to say, "When you marry off a daughter or take a wife, or when you gather together and distribute wealth, will you perhaps wait for Bandhula to give him his share? He replied, "No."
The Buddha said, "Those who shared food and clothing with Baddhālinda shall receive these garments and articles.
Because the Saṃgha gave the food to Baddhālinda, these garments and articles should belong to the Saṃgha. Upon hearing this, his kinsmen desisted.

Regarding the distinctions among the ten types of forfeiture: the first nine do not require a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); they are taken directly. The final one is taken through a monastic ritual (this is stated as a general rule).
For example, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is said that when a person was killed and swept away by water within the boundary, the robes were recovered by whoever saw them.

According to the twenty-first fascicle of the *Pañcavargika*, at that time there was a bhikṣu who was killed and swept away by water, and his robes and bowl remained hanging on a tree within the boundary.

The branches were seen by the bhikṣus; thinking they had entered within the boundary of the saṃgha and thus belonged to the saṃgha, they did not dare to take them. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I allow you to take them with the thought that they are *pāṃśukūla* (cast-off rags)."
Regarding the second point, "those present at the time who see before them," [the commentator] states that this refers to those currently present at the time.

Regarding the passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) undergoing penance dying, up to a monk observing the precepts dying, and the rule that they may take [the property] by mutual succession:
according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, the Buddha said to the monks, "In a certain residence, there was one monk observing the precepts and one..."
If a suspended bhikṣu lives together with one who maintains the precepts, then upon the death of the precept-maintaining bhikṣu, his robes and requisites belong to the suspended bhikṣu;
if the suspended bhikṣu dies, his robes and requisites belong to the precept-maintaining bhikṣu. If the suspended bhikṣu comes [to claim them], they should not be given to him.

In this manner, one who maintains the precepts and two who have been expelled cohabiting is likewise [the first case]. One who maintains the precepts and three who have been expelled is also the same as above.

Two who maintain the precepts and one who has been expelled; two who maintain the precepts and two who have been expelled; two who maintain the precepts and three who have been expelled—four such cases are likewise [treated].
Three who maintain the precepts and one who has been expelled; three who maintain the precepts and two who have been expelled; three who have been expelled and four... [and so forth].

The same applies to those who have been expelled (*pravāsanīya*). Four [cases] involve those who maintain the precepts, and one involves those who have been expelled; this pattern continues up to four cases involving those who have been expelled.

Furthermore, the same logic applies when taking one who has been expelled as the head [of the group]. In the text, only two types of persons are clarified, and the *śikṣādattaka* (one undergoing penance for training) is not mentioned; this should be verified by examining the preceding and following contexts.
This meaning is not seen [in the texts], and the intent of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā*) remains unclear. Lì says: "Observing the precepts" refers to pure bhikṣus;

however, because three people live together and do not suffice for one another, they cannot perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). This is precisely what is meant by "taking directly in the presence" (*pratyakṣa*).
These three people lived together. When one of them died, the value of his robes and belongings belonged to the other two.

If he had been integrated into another faction, the property of one who has undergone *parivāsa* (probation) and *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement after probation) upon death would go to his lay relatives, because during his lifetime he did not share in the community's benefits.

However, since there are currently no lay relatives, it belongs to those present at that time. Furthermore, if a person observing the precepts dies, those undergoing training (*śikṣādattaka*) and those undergoing *parivāsa* and *mūlāpakarṣa* share [the inheritance] equally.
As for "those who see": each takes half for themselves. This is the standard procedure for those undergoing *śikṣādattaka* (probation) and so forth when they die.

Regarding the third case, "entering the same community as those with differing views," such as the two factions of the heterodox and orthodox: it is established that Devadatta was the heterodox faction, while the orthodox faction is understood by implication.
If someone dies, they are divided according to their respective faction—heterodox or orthodox—and do not follow the rules of the unified Saṃgha. This is cited from the *Lìshū* (Commentary on the Li).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If one turns away from the correct toward the deviant, the object enters the category of the deviant.

Examining its original intent, the paths of the deviant and the correct diverge; therefore, the robes and bowl may be kept wherever they happen to go. If one turns from the deviant toward the correct, the object enters the category of the correct.

This phrase does not appear in the Vinaya text; it is merely an abbreviation. Furthermore, regarding the robes worn on the body, they are judged as previously stated; this applies to those [robes] outside [of what is normally worn].
Regarding the property [of the deceased], it may be indeterminate. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If a monk who upholds the Dharma dies within a community that does not uphold the Dharma, his robes and bowl are to be summoned back to a monk who upholds the Dharma.

If he does not come to take them, they shall be made into bedding and seating for the Saṃgha of the four directions within that community which does not uphold the Dharma. If a monk who does not uphold the Dharma dies within a community that upholds the Dharma..."
The opposite case can be understood (the recipient of the teaching refers merely to one who accepts the five false dharmas). To establish this clearly:

if those of the false faction turn toward the correct, or those of the correct faction head toward the false, and they die on the road before reaching the midpoint, they belong to the destination toward which their minds were directed. Because the mind has made its decision, if they reach that faction, [they are reborn there].

The same applies to the case where it is unnecessary to debate; one enters exclusively into that [new group]. If a person belonging to a heterodox sect turns their back on the heterodox toward the orthodox, even though their clothing and belongings still remain with the heterodox sect, those objects belong to the orthodox.
The same principle applies when one turns from the orthodox toward the heterodox.
Regarding the passage, "The four groups of monks who share functions, up to those who share the same *karmavācanā* (formal act) as the suspended monk," the Master Li says:

"If this person who has been suspended dies, the Buddha stated that the monks who shared the same *karmavācanā* for the suspension should be given [the property]. The various masters' interpretations of these words differ.

One explanation states they are those who were treated identically. The reason for this is that after the formal act of suspension and treatment, [there is no longer] commonality in either material goods or the Dharma."
The same. For what reason does one die? Who [is responsible]? Another interpretation states: those who enter the *śramana-karmika* (monks of labor) are also called *guṇa-karmika* (monks of merit).

Liang asked: "This person under suspension has received no benefit from himself; how can he look to the Saṃgha for it? Since these monks of labor have already disciplined another," [how can they be considered benefactors?]
This would result in harming others; how, then, could it be called "rewarding labor"? The explanation says: This refers to labor performed within the Saṃgha itself;

it does not mean that one expects a reward for the specific treatment administered. Because the merit lies in the lawful disciplinary action of the Saṃgha, one is entitled to a share of the goods simply by participating in the formal motion (*karmavācanā*) at that time.
Therefore, it is said: "According to the formal motion to which one has consented, the Saṃgha should grant [the share]."
The *Mahāsāṃghika* is not like this. Thus, its twenty-sixth [section] states: "If that monk who has been censured falls ill, one should not allow him to be looked after.
One should tell his relatives to look after him. If he dies, the Saṃgha should not divide his robes and bowl; they should not be given away.
One should cremate the body and take the bed upon which he lay, place the corpse upon it, tie the robes and bowl around his neck, drag the bed out, and proclaim this:"
He said: "The matter of the Saṃgha is settled; the matter of the Saṃgha is settled. [This robe] has been cast away in the wild fields.
One should not give rise to an evil mind toward this person. Why? Because one should not give rise to an evil thought even toward a charred wick.
One should form this thought: 'May future people not practice such wrong views. If it is a cowherd, a woodcutter, or someone who brings this robe to offer it, one should treat them as such."
If a donor has passed away, there is no offense in accepting their property.

Regarding the "five groups entering the two divisions of the Saṃgha": this establishes that the Great Bhikṣu-saṃgha together with the Śrāmaṇeras constitute one division, while the three groups within the Bhikṣuṇī community constitute another division.

This refers to the passage in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) which states: "Those belonging to the five groups who have come forward may receive [the offerings]. This is precisely what is meant. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Regarding the phrase "dying in the home of a layperson who has no fixed residence," Lì says:

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu dies in a place where there is no fixed residence, and there is a faithful upāsaka or a park-keeper there, they should be entrusted with the responsibility of recording [the death]. If it concerns members of the five groups of renunciants, [the same applies].
Those who arrive first shall receive [the property]. Since the items are located in a secular place, there is concern that they might be used and thus result in transgression;

therefore, those among the five groups of monastics who arrive first shall obtain them, regardless of whether the items are heavy or light. For one who arrives first, light items may be taken into personal possession, but heavy items do not belong to an individual person and must be disposed of according to the first arrival, returning to the common property (*sādhāraṇa*) of the Saṃgha, because at the time of their initial acquisition, they were entrusted to the two divisions of the Saṃgha.

Because the donated items have been received, after the donor’s death, they shall be returned to the two assemblies (bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī). If none of those previously mentioned are present, they shall be sent to the two assemblies in the nearest location;
one should simply take them to the nearest place without distinguishing between monks and nuns. A guest asked:

"The masters of both ancient and modern times all say that light items go to those who first see them, whereas heavy items follow the disposition of those who first see them, being returned to the permanent property (saṃgha) of the monastery. Now, let us examine this in detail.
Not so. The text states that those who arrive first among the five groups obtain [the property]. Where does it say they must be assigned to the permanent endowment (*saṃghika*)?

Rather, provided that both light and heavy items are entirely taken into one's own possession, there is no fault in principle. This applies similarly to cases where someone dies on the road, dies while living alone, or dies at a private estate. The judgment is as follows.
If the items are located in both the monastic and nunneries, it is not the same as this case. Therefore, regarding the ten points concerning items deposited elsewhere when one dies:

if a bhikṣu dies while staying at a certain place, and his robes and requisites have been deposited in a nunnery, the Buddha said that they should be divided among the bhikṣu-saṃgha and sent back to the deceased’s original monastery.
If the location is unknown, they should be given to the Mahāsaṃgha of the nearest region. Not so.
One may enter a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery for personal use. The same applies when a lower-ranking *bhikṣuṇī* entrusts property to a *bhikṣu*.
Furthermore, if a *bhikṣuṇī* dies while staying in a residence where her belongings were previously entrusted to a *saṃgha* vihāra, the Buddha declared that the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha should divide them.

This is because both communities are equally versed in the Dharma; unlike secular dwellings, there is no fear that laypeople (*avadātavasana*) might misappropriate or damage the monastic property. Thus, the five groups [of renunciants] share with one another.
It is obtained. Now, because these two groups know that their legal status (*dharma*) differs, they must return to the place of death and divide [the property] according to their respective classes.
Furthermore, it is distinct because there was a bhikṣu at the place of death. Regarding one who dies while living alone, someone asks:

"Did the five groups come beforehand to take possession of the robes and perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*)? Someone says: "There is no need for a formal act. If a formal act were required, [it would require] one person...

When one has previously arrived but has not yet performed the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), and a moment later another person arrives and likewise receives their share, how can the former be called the "one who came first"?
Therefore, we know that there is no such rule. Some explain it thus: performing the ritual procedure is virtuous; the text simply ordains that [the share] be given to the one who arrived first.
It should be granted to one who follows the prior ritual procedure. If that is so, since you have already mentioned the five groups [of practitioners], do the lower three groups possess this ritual?
