Answer: For a *śrāmaṇera* who possesses the precepts, it is logically appropriate for there to be a ritual procedure; for one without the precepts, logically there is no such ritual.
According to the intent of the *Chao*, the ritual need not be performed; however, it may also be necessary to perform the ritual.

Regarding the "monastic community toward which one is heading" within the context of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): it is established that there was a bhikṣu who, taking his robes and bowl, set out for a certain monastery.
Before he had arrived there, he died midway between the two boundaries. The Buddha said: "The monastic community toward which he was heading shall obtain [the property].

Although he has not yet reached that place, because he has resolved to go there, he is considered to have obtained a share of this item within the boundary of the monastic community toward which he was headed. Furthermore...
One interpretation holds that it refers to observing the direction facing east or west when the face of the deceased is turned at the time of death. This interpretation is likely incorrect;
for if one dies suddenly with the face turned upward, the meaning [of the ritual] would be defeated.

Regarding the rule that when a *śrāmaṇera* dies within the *jñapti-caturtha* [saṃgha], his requisites belong to the *upādhyāya*: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there was a *śrāmaṇera* who died in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, "To whom should these requisites belong? The Buddha said, "They should belong to the *upādhyāya*.

The text concludes its account here. The commentary in the *Chao* explains: "As for the statement that it causes the *upādhyāya* to distinguish the nature of the property and so forth—this is not [the case]."
The *Jiwen* (Text on the *Mahāsāṃghika*) is merely a later commentary on its meaning. The opening section of the commentary cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, stating:

"Regarding the phrase 'entrusting to the upādhyāya,' it means to have the upādhyāya distinguish between the teacher’s property and that which enters his own possession. As for the property of a śrāmaṇera, it should be handled according to the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) for the Saṃgha;

it need not necessarily all enter the teacher's possession. Bin refutes this interpretation, saying: "In the text, it is judged that the upādhyāya is immediately [instructed] to give [it] to the Saṃgha; this should also be [governed by] the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*."

One should take [the robes] with the perception that they are refuse-rags (pāṃśukūla), and they should not be entered into by oneself. Now, examining in detail the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* which ordains that they belong to the preceptor (upādhyāya): this is likely because the disciple’s training has ceased.
If that were so, when a bhikṣu passes away, his teacher should likewise be permitted to take them, as they equally share in the cessation of training.

Answer: In principle, it should also be permitted. However, for the time being, based on the absence of explicit instruction (avijñapti), it is judged that they are not to be given. The commentary states that the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Daśabhāṇaka) makes such a judgment.
Regarding the question of a *bhikṣu*: it is established that when a *śrāmaṇera* dies, his robes and requisites belong to the Saṃgha for distribution.

This is the same as the procedure for the death of a full monk (*mahāsaṃghika*). It does not matter whether he possessed the precepts or not; since his physical form and his dharma are the same [as those of the monks], all must follow the Saṃgha’s rules.

This is because he shares the same benefits and offerings as the monks. Lì (Lìzuǒ) says: "As for the death of a *śrāmaṇera*, there is no textual authority for this in this Vinaya; according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they go to the *upādhyāya*."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* follow the same rules as those for monks. In current practice, many matters are handled by assembling the great saṃgha;

since these follow the procedures of the great saṃgha, there is no harm in dividing [the property] accordingly. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a śrāmaṇera died in the kingdom of Kośala, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.

The Buddha said: "The inner and outer robes he was wearing should be given to the caregiver by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. As for his other light articles, the saṃgha should [distribute them]."

[The property] should be divided. Heavy items (valuable objects) should not be divided. By this principle, the same applies to the three lower classes of the community. However, as for the performance of rituals and the place of residence, they follow one particular school.

Regarding the note stating that "the *Pañcavargika* is also like this," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a śrāmaṇera dies, if he had already given [his belongings] to someone while alive, they should be given to that person;
if he did not give them away, they should be divided among the *saṃgha* present."

Regarding the entrustment of the robes and bowl of a bhikṣu who has been expelled (niḥsāraṇa) and has died to those with whom he had prior connections, Lì states: "This refers to the death of one who has committed a grave offense (pārājika).

There are three distinctions: first, if he has not yet been expelled, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Duolun*) says he is judged according to the standard rules. Bǐn says this is the same as the death of a pure monk.

Second, if he has already undergone the formal act of expulsion and has entered into close association with laypeople (as listed here in this *Chao*), Bǐn cites the tradition of the Three Kingdoms..."
The *Zang* (Commentary) says: "In the Western Regions [India] even to this day, the practice of formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) still persists.

If there is a single person within a monastery who has committed a grave offense while outside, they are not permitted to re-enter the monastery; instead, another person is instructed to return their bedding and bowl to them and escort them out the gate.
If, however, they commit an offense within the monastery and are formally accused before the community of monks, and the investigation confirms the facts, [the procedure continues as follows...]"

Permission was granted for him to return to his quarters. Immediately, another person was sent to the room to retrieve his belongings and return them to him, and he was driven out through the temple gate.

The entire assembly ascended to the upper stories of the gate-towers to watch him, wishing to serve as an encouragement for those who would follow. However, Westerners (Indians) place great weight upon their adherence to views.
Once all the monastics and laypeople knew that this monk had been expelled, they all ceased speaking with him and stopped associating with him.

Even his brothers, parents, and relatives could no longer bear to see him. He could not obtain almsfood even when begging. Even if he were to return to secular life and take a wife, the men and women of the world would not allow them to marry;
they would not give their daughters to him in marriage. However, as for those who had been expelled, the people would personally cultivate fields and lands for them.

[The text continues] with the search for livelihood (and so forth). Third, regarding repentance at the point of death: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this refers to the *saṃgha* present at the time of death.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In cases of censure (*tarjanīya*), banishment (*pravāsanīya*), dependence (*niśraya*), prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*apratisaṃkhyāniṣedha*), the four types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*), and the rules for separate residence (*parivāsa*), these are judged in the same manner as the death of a pure person (*pariśuddha*)."

Regarding the phrase "the person who can receive the entrustment and the place where it is entrusted," Zhiyi states: To clarify the original residence of the deceased bhikṣu, he is called "the person who can receive the entrustment.
The term "that which is entrusted" refers to Ānanda’s location. The term "the place where the object is entrusted" refers to the location to which Ānanda sent the entrustment.
As for the Buddha’s statement, "it belongs to the Saṃgha at Ānanda’s location," according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is...
A certain bhikṣu died. These robes and personal effects had originally been entrusted to Ānanda. That deceased bhikṣu died in one location, while Ānanda resided in another location;
furthermore, the place where the items were entrusted was yet another location.

The place of death, the place where Ānanda resided, and the place where the entrusted items were kept all claimed that the property belonged to their respective monasteries. The Buddha said to Ānanda: [that it belongs to...]
Regarding the distribution of items within the boundaries of the monastery, it is established as follows:
Suppose a bhikṣu entrusted his robes to Ānanda, who then went away on a journey and sent these robes to another bhikṣu in a different location. Later, the original owner of the robes passed away.
Three parties disputed over [the property]: namely, the deceased’s original residence, Ānanda’s own dwelling place, and the place where Ānanda had deposited it.
The Buddha ruled that it belonged to the Saṃgha residing at Ānanda’s own dwelling place, because of the person to whom it had been entrusted at that time.
If the object is deposited in a place but not with a specific person, the Sangha may take possession of it.
Regarding the aforementioned nine types of items that are divided directly, Shen says: "The methods for dividing these ten types differ;

for the first nine, there is no need for a formal ritual (karmavācanā), as they may be taken directly. He then raises an objection: "This would be like entering two groups of like views or depositing clothing [with them]."

In such a location, there are many monks; logically, there must be the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) procedures. How could one simply enter this place and separately perform the division of the *karmavācanā*?
Regarding the eleventh point, "the death of a harmonious and pure assembly," Lì says: this refers to the death of a person who belongs to a single harmonious and pure community (*nikāya*).
He states that the term "a single community" serves to distinguish this from the five groups of practitioners mentioned previously.
This is the formal procedure (*vinyāsa*). The term "harmonious" (*sāmagrī*) excludes those who belong to either the heterodox or the orthodox factions.
The term "pure" (*pariśuddha*) excludes those previously subject to expulsion, censure, or suspension.

Regarding the three types of co-residents and shared property, there are two meanings. As for "co-resident" (*sahavāsin*), it means that one does not distinguish between one's own and another's quantity;
rather, one regards the other's goods as one's own, just as one would think of one's own child.

As for "shared property" (*sādhāraṇa-dravya*), this refers to mutual contribution and mutual use while merely residing together in one place; however, after death, each shall divide the property equally. It is established and clarified that if they are co-residents...
Regarding the living and the dead: the clothing worn by the deceased shall certainly belong to the Saṃgha. As for other belongings remaining, they shall be divided among the people present;

these shall be brought forth and shared with the Saṃgha. If it concerns communal property—that is, where there is no formal agreement with the teacher—then even if such items exist, [they are not to be treated as personal inheritance].
Whether one dies or leaves the monastic order, the property shall be divided equally. Now, if they die while living together, the personal clothing and belongings naturally belong to the Sangha;

however, all accumulated wealth must be divided equally between them. This is certainly not a case of someone falsely claiming to be a co-resident when they are not actually a partner in shared property, yet falsely pretends to be so. Thus it is clearly established.
Regarding those who have returned to secular life or reverted from the Path: this refers to those who have engaged in secular livelihoods or have abandoned the monastic life.
According to secular regulations, one should clarify that for those who have already donned monastic robes or used monastic utensils, the same principles apply as in secular law.
If the person was a co-owner of property, then in the event of their death, the clothing and personal utensils they possessed belong to the Sangha, while the remaining property is divided equally.
Regarding the offense of falsely claiming a share where both the agent and the object are transgressed: it is established and clarified as follows.

For instance, when a deceased master, while at the point of death, confides with a disciple, saying, "After I have passed away, you may claim that we lived together, so that you may obtain a large portion of my possessions.

Having made this scheme, the disciple acts accordingly. Now, if they obtain the property, both master and disciple commit an offense. If they obtain property of great value, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). If they obtain [property of lesser value], it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Regarding light objects and incense: while the Preceptor was still alive, it was improper to settle matters concerning his death after he had passed away. Since the deceased’s property had already been definitively assigned to the Sangha, pre-emptive adjudication would not be valid;
thus, both teacher and disciple would incur an offense. Therefore, it is said "agent and object," where the teacher is the agent and the disciple is the object.

It is also clearly established in the *Śrī-saṃbhava-sūtra* that there are two types of adjudication, both based on light objects. That sūtra also states: [The text continues with the citation from the *Śrī-saṃbhava-sūtra*. Thus, it is clear that even in that sūtra, [the same principle applies].

One incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*. However, this is determined based on light objects. If the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been completed and the items have been brought into the presence [of the assembly], then with respect to the Sangha, if five members are present, one incurs a heavy offense (*pārājika*).
If the ritual has not yet been completed and the number of Sangha members does not reach five, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the entrustment (*śāsana*) of what is right and wrong, Li says: "There is good and bad in entrusting, and there is also good and bad in not entrusting;

thus there are four propositions. "Vulgar disposition" (*sùtài*) refers to one's intent. Alternatively, it is explained that to maintain a constant will without changing it is called "disposition" (*tài*).
Regarding the matter of the bhikṣu’s attachment to a copper bowl among the Five Hundred Questions (*Pañcaśata-praśna*), an examination of that treatise states:

Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who was greedily attached to a single copper gong. After he died, he became a hungry ghost (*preta*). When the community of monks had finished distributing their belongings, he appeared;
his body was immense and pitch black, like a mass of pure black clouds. The bhikṣus were startled and wondered, "What is this thing? Among the assembly, there was one who...
The Way [teaches]: "This bhikṣu, because he was greedily attached to this gong, fell among the hungry ghosts (preta).

Now, out of greedy attachment, he desires to come and reclaim it. The bhikṣus immediately returned the gong. Having received it, he grasped it and licked it with his tongue before setting it on the ground and departing.
The bhikṣus took it back again, but it was so foul-smelling that they could not approach it. They then had it recast into another vessel; yet it remained foul-smelling and unusable.
By inferring from this, one knows that greed is a great affliction. Regarding the matter of stinginess with robes, according to that treatise:
Once there was a bhikṣu who delighted in making fine robes and was obsessed with them day and night. He fell gravely ill and, knowing he was about to die, raised his head to look at his robes;
a poisonous thought arose within him, and he said, "After my death, who would dare to wear these robes?"
Before long, he passed away and was reborn as a nāga born by transformation, who returned to coil around his robes.

When the community of monks had carried the corpse out for burial, they sent someone to retrieve the clothing; however, seeing the snake coiled around the robes, extending its neck and spitting venom, they did not dare approach it.
They immediately returned and informed the assembly, describing exactly what they had seen. The bhikṣus then went together to look at it, yet none dared to draw near. There was one...

The bhikṣu had attained the Path and entered the four immeasurable contemplations (*catur-apramāṇa*), so that he could not be harmed by poison. He immediately approached it and said, "This was originally your robe;
now it no longer belongs to you. Why do you protect it? The snake immediately abandoned it and departed.
Not far away, it entered a clump of grass where its venom emerged and ignited the grass, which in turn burned its own body until its life ended. It then entered hell, where it was scorched by fire.
Within a single day, he was burned three times, all due to his greed and harmful intent. Regarding the note which says, "as in the case of woolen rugs, cloth, and so forth," Shen (Shenxing) explains:
this refers to being inside a container where it cannot be physically handed over; however, if one receives an entrustment (*śāsana*), its meaning is equivalent to receiving the object itself.
Therefore, it is said that "this entrustment is the same as the gift. As for the mutual appearance of the three types of persons, Liuming states: "Sometimes the person is present..."
The sick person is on one side while the object is in another place; or at times the person is in another location while the object is by the side of the sick person;

or both are not present—these constitute a formal entrustment (*anuśāsanā*) rather than a formal bestowal (*arpaṇā*). This refers to a case where the person to whom the entrustment is made is in another location and the object is likewise not present before them.
"However, it is permissible to entrust [the bowl]. This refers to a case where neither the person nor the object is present.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when entrusting it to many people, the last person receives it and may then bestow it upon the first person among the group.
Some say that, although reasoning suggests the last person should receive it, this is because it would otherwise violate the agreement made for the sake of the sick person."
Regarding the determination of offenses based on this precedent: it refers to a case where a deceased person first entrusted something to a certain individual, but that person did not accept it;

subsequently, the deceased entrusted it to another, thereby committing a grave offense (*guru-apatti*). The same applies to the act of bestowing. Once the item has been bestowed upon the former person, to then take it back constitutes a grave offense.

As for the previous mention of "frivolous speech," [the author] interprets it deeply as follows: if one says that [the entrustment] is not established after death, the situation is identical to the passage in the preceding text concerning "giving to me."
After death, it is not permissible to produce scriptures, images, and so forth.
Regarding the three robes and six articles which must not be disposed of by oneself: this means that while one is still alive, one may not be separated from the three robes.

If one intends to give clothing to another but fails to provide it, one incurs two offenses: the offense of obstructing the gift of clothing and the offense of violating dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).

If one says, "I will give this to you before I die," and then dies, one still commits these two offenses. If one says, "I will give it to you after I am dead," this likewise does not constitute a valid gift, because after death the property belongs to the attendant.

If the attendant lacks virtue, the property then belongs to the Sangha of the four quarters. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if the wealth has not yet been transferred, or if [the recipient] obtains it...
If one has not performed the formal act of purification (*pāriśuddhi*) and returns the items to the side of the sick person, they are both invalid. The *Lishi* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states:

"The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* contains three points. First, the entrustment has not yet been made: this refers to when a sick person says to a bhikṣu, 'Look after me; I shall give my robes and bowl to the Elder.
After death, when the Sangha assembles to divide the robes, the caregiver says, 'When this person was alive, he said he would give his robes and bowl to me,' and reports this to the Buddha."

The Buddha said: "It should not be given. Regarding the next phrase, "having already given it but not yet performed the *śuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity)," he returned it to the side of the sick person;

the Buddha said: "It should not be given. Regarding the next phrase, "giving it and immediately performing the *śuddhi*," the Buddha said: "It should be given. Regarding the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* passage stating, "If at the time of birth it has already been given...

up to 'it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal motion with one proclamation),' " Li says: "In the *Pañcavargika*, if it has already been given at the time of birth, but has not yet been held..."

Regarding one who is departing, the Saṃgha should grant it to them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). This Vinaya does not distinguish between whether the recipient has been consulted or not, nor whether the gift is pure or impure;
if it is granted unconditionally, it differs from the Mahāsāṃghika, which merely constitutes a direct handover, and is also distinct from the Pañcavargika.

Regarding "establishing" (the formal act): as for the requirement that the Saṃgha perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) for the two [parties], it is because the deceased’s property has already been designated for the person previously mentioned;
however, as it remains by the side of the deceased and has not yet been taken away, there is now a concern that people might harbor doubts regarding its transfer.

Therefore, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed to bestow it. Furthermore, all such prior entrustments mentioned above must likewise be bestowed through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, so as to conform to the practice of the contemporary Saṃgha.
The reason for this harmony is unclear.

Regarding those who do not share in the common property of the Saṃgha: this refers to cases where the permanent endowment (sthavira-vastu) previously owed heavy items to a deceased person, but now intends to repay them with light items.
These items must be returned to the permanent endowment and may not be distributed among the present members of the Saṃgha. If the permanent endowment owes [the debt]...
The deceased person possessed light items; now we shall return the heavy items and instead take light items to divide among ourselves.
Since the previous sentence differs from this one, it is said that they do not conform to the rules for sharing with the Saṃgha. If nothing at all can be obtained, then one simply stops.
That is to say, if one is already impoverished and constantly destitute, and although they have borrowed the property of the deceased, there is no one to repay it and no place to seek it,
then ceasing to return it constitutes no offense.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated: "If a bhikṣu dies while in debt for property belonging to the Triple Gem, that debt should be repaid.

This applies even to loans from the Triple Gem to a bhikṣu, or to those owed to the present and visiting bhikṣus from the four quarters. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, there was a bhikṣu who borrowed and used property belonging to a stūpa.
When this bhikṣu died, the other bhikṣus did not know what to do. The Buddha said: "His robes and bowl [should be used to repay the debt]."

When an object is returned, its value shall be calculated and offered to the stūpa; the remainder shall be divided among the resident monks. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu whose robes and bowl were used for the stūpa.

This bhikṣu [died], and even though the Buddha had stated that property belonging to the Saṃgha should be calculated by value and returned to the portion of the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present community), [the matter remained].
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who borrowed property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions for private use. When this bhikṣu died, the various bhikṣus did not...
"How should this be understood? The Buddha said: "The goods and wealth shall be returned by calculating their value and offered to the Sangha of the four directions.

The remainder shall be divided among the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the resident monks present). Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who lent his robes and bowl to the Sangha of the four directions for use. When this bhikṣu died, [the matter arose]. Even unto the Buddha’s words:

'One should take the property of the Sangha of the four directions, calculate its value, and return it; the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* should then divide [the remainder]. [This applies to] visiting bhikṣus as well."
The same applies to an *upāli* (former monk). The text states this directly;

the commentary explains "to judge according to the original" as meaning that at the time of the original loan, one must determine whether it was a heavy or light object, and now that it has been recovered, it is judged according to its original status as heavy.
Regarding the case of wine purchased on credit and so forth, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There was once a bhikṣu who had purchased wine on credit but had not yet repaid it.
He then died. The wine merchant demanded payment from the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus replied, "Why did you not demand it while this bhikṣu was still alive?
The wine merchant said, "If you do not pay the price of the wine, I shall spread a bad reputation for you, saying:
'The Śākya śramaṇas drink wine and yet refuse to pay for it. The bhikṣus did not know what to do. The Buddha said, "This bhikṣu..."
If there are robes or bowl items [belonging to the debtor], they should be used for repayment. If there are no such items, one should take property from the Saṃgha to provide repayment.

Why? For fear that it might bring ill repute upon the bhikṣus. Bin says: Although the Vinaya text states this, it does not distinguish between the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) and the current property (*pratyutpanna*).
Now, seeking the meaning through reasoning, it is superior to take property from the current Saṃgha and return it. Furthermore, regarding interest on debts...
Regarding the five points concerning different locations: this refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* account of Bāṇaṃda’s lending of goods at interest, which comprises five points.
First, when robes and bowls are deposited in one place while the person is in another: this means a bhikṣu deposits his robes in the Eastern Monastery but dies in the Western Monastery;
both monasteries dispute [the ownership], and the Buddha rules that the monks of the location where the items were kept shall receive them. Second, the location of the debt.

Regarding "the place of death, the place of debt, and that which the Saṃgha obtains": suppose there is a person who owes goods to another; now that he has died, the place of death and the place of debt dispute over them.

The Buddha ruled that the Saṃgha obtains them at the place of debt. Regarding "the place of death, the place of interest, the place of surety, and that which the Saṃgha obtains at the place of surety":
this refers to when a bhikṣu lends money to another, and that other person [receives it from] the bhikṣu.
Money. The place where this money was obtained is called the "place of interest. Furthermore, there is a guarantor. Now, after a bhikṣu has died, these three parties dispute over it.
The Buddha ruled that it belongs to the community of monks at the place of guarantee; it does not belong to the place where the money was taken, nor does it belong to the place of death.
This is because if the interest is not repaid at the present time, the guarantor must pay on his behalf; thus, even after death, it still belongs [to the guarantor].
Regarding "the portion of the monastic community belonging to the guarantor": some say this refers to property lent to laypeople. How could a monk residing elsewhere act as a guarantor?
It is simply that the property belongs to the monastic community of the residence of the monk who acts as the guarantor.

Regarding "places where one has died" and "places where property was pledged," these refer to what was pledged by a deceased person during their lifetime; the place where it was pledged during life is called a "pledge."
Regarding the location of the object: when a person brings an object to pledge it in exchange for money, that place is called the "place where the money was taken.

Now, if a bhikṣu dies in another location, there is a dispute among three parties. The Buddha ruled that the object belongs to the monastery where the original pledge was kept, and that the monks there shall receive it. There is an interpretation which says:

This refers to the case where a deceased bhikṣu possesses property that has been pledged as collateral with a bhikṣu residing in a separate location; the Saṃgha should divide [the proceeds] at the place where the pledge was held by that bhikṣu.

However, if the money was taken from a place where there is doubt as to whether it belonged to a layperson, and if it is indeed from a place belonging to the Saṃgha, then those [residents] should rightfully receive it.

Regarding the phrase "at the five places of death and the place where money was taken," this sentence is identical to the third sentence mentioned previously; it should be understood according to the guarantee.

Regarding the location: it refers to the place where the contract (券) is held and written. The preceding section pertained to the guarantor (保任); this section pertains to the holding and writing of the contract.
As for the character for "contract" (券), its lower portion is formed as "part" (分). It is called "half-part" (半分; *bàn fèn*). Within these five phrases, the meaning is not yet fully resolved;

therefore, the author of the *Chao* (Commentary) himself provides an analysis (*yùn yùn*). Li also says: "If one investigates through reasoning, it may differ from that [previous case], such as in the case of a layperson's household."
Regarding items lent out that have not yet been recovered from the borrower: one may follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) or rely on promissory notes and the like to collect the debt.
If the items were located within the monastery grounds, after the monk has passed away, they should be acquired by the Sangha of the specific location where they were found.

However, fearing they might not be recoverable, one may rely on promissory notes and the like to mutually secure these items, as both parties involved are members of the Sangha; thus, it is permissible to take them.
Regarding this property of the Saṃgha, it belongs to those [who claim it] as determined by the first case;
that is to say, the Saṃgha acquires possession of the object according to its location, and it cannot belong to the place where the deed is recorded (and so forth).
As for the five cases of determination in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it means that if many people come to dispute and a decision cannot be reached, one may rely on the preceding five [cases].
"Decide the case by severing the dispute. Regarding "or, as in the previous instance of entrustment, there are two types of 'entrusted'":

this refers to cases such as the passage concerning Ānanda’s receipt of an entrustment, where either the place of entrustment is specified but not the person, or the person is specified but not the place. In all such instances, the matter is decided according to what was entrusted.

This applies whenever many people come forward disputing a decision that cannot be reached; one should rely on this method of adjudication (and so forth). As for "one who does not provide trustworthy evidence should not be granted [the claim]," it means... [as previously explained].
This means that since it is neither trustworthy nor supported by witnesses who can be relied upon, it cannot be granted. The following establishes the principle of determining degrees of gravity.

Regarding those cases where the various schools have not reached a consensus and which are difficult to believe based on mere sentiment, [the author] clarifies them using examples such as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, in which all types of vessels are classified as heavy, while the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) clarifies the distinction between light and heavy based on measures of capacity (*dou*). Such instances are termed [the basis for this determination].
This has not yet been fully integrated. Now, regarding the determination of which Vinaya school a deceased person followed when receiving the precepts:

if one judges according to the school to which they belonged, then for those who performed their affairs according to a specific school—meaning those who were not well-versed in other traditions—it should be determined by whichever school they received the precepts from.
That is to say, one should follow the school currently used for such regular practices and determine the gravity of the offense according to that school. This constitutes an offense due to greed.

It is not the case that something is a transgression merely because it is so taught. This is established and clarified: although within the teachings there are distinctions between light and heavy offenses, here we must rely on the essential substance (*tattva*) of the precepts according to our own school.

If one were to perversely follow other sects to adjudicate matters of knowledge, then those close to the permanent residence would cite light offenses to follow the heavy, while private individuals would seek their own benefit by citing heavy offenses to follow the light; this would only bring about punishment for oneself and is not [the correct path].
This constitutes an error and a loss regarding the teachings within this school.

As for the six different ways of upholding the Vinaya listed in the preface, it refers to the fact that since ancient times there have been six masters of the Vinaya, each adhering to their own tradition.
Now, these six are condensed into three stages. The first consists solely of those who employ the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. As for those...

Based on this: first, if [the Vinaya] did not exist, there would be no clarity. Second, one should first employ the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) Vinaya, as its categories of meaning clarify matters concurrently with other schools.
Third, one should generally utilize the *Vinayapiṭaka* to establish or discard the formal texts. For instance, the former Master Sengzong mostly relied on the first approach;

likewise, when Master Daoli adjudicated matters of light and heavy offenses, he held that all jars and bottles were distinct, whereas the *Sarvāstivāda* (*Shisong*) limited them by measurement, regardless of their size.
All [these items] are categorized as grave offenses; each section differs from the others, yet it is not because this particular section fails to understand them.

Regarding the "thirteen chapters on gateways," these are fully recorded according to the Vinaya within the *Qingzhong yi* (The Ritual of Light and Heavy Offenses); they are not set forth here [as indicated by "and so forth"].
As for the *kūnyara* vessel, this refers to small bowls, ladles, and the like.
This school’s correct severance (*prahāṇa*) is also without a second; this is clearly established.

This master relies on the severance of a single category, yet it also universally penetrates without the two distinctions of existence or non-existence. One cannot say it is "that" [the other], nor can one say it is "not that.

Regarding "it cannot be suppressed or seized," this means one must not judge it as something else, nor suppress its principle or seize its principle. [The author] privately comments: This person relies upon...

Regarding what is listed in the Vinaya: minor offenses are resolved by severing the sūtra, while the remaining grave offenses are not so listed. From the outset, there was no intention to employ external doctrines for reconciliation;

thus, "not employing external doctrines" is termed "having no counterpart. Since this is already settled according to the Vinaya, there is likewise no basis for suppressing or overturning its principle.
As for the division into seven types, it should refer to the summary of the seven gates in the subsequent text. [The text here] unfolds and spreads out gradually.
Regarding "carrying" and so forth: *pi* (pronounced *bi-mai*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "to split. To split means to tear apart. According to the *Guangyi*, it means "to divide.
Alternatively, it may be read as *bi* (pronounced *bi-chi*), which the *Shuowen* defines as "the seam of a garment" (*qiu-ruan*). The *Guangyi* defines it as "to fold.

In the *Vinayamātṛkā*, both [meanings] are taken to refer to the case where one places clothing and requisites before the Saṃgha and dispatches one person to determine what may be divided and what may not be divided.
Regarding the phrase "even down to the specific characteristics as explained therein," according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* (Mo-lun): "Why is it called a 'heavy robe' (*guruka-cīvara*)?
There are two kinds of 'heaviness': first, heaviness in value; second, its capacity to ward off cold. Therefore, it is called 'heavy.

Furthermore, it says that Piṅgala was held in high esteem by the people of the country; they would give him gifts such as nets, elephants, horses, chariots, and even the construction of small temples."
The Buddha permitted its acceptance. Such items as these belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions. Why, then, are they called "heavy objects" (dhāraṇīya-vastu)?

Previously, when explaining heavy objects, the name was derived from the robes; now, when explaining heavy objects, the designation is derived from the objects themselves. Since there are seven categories [of heavy objects], this is the first.
Regarding sitting mats and bedding that fall under the category of "heavy": this is clearly established. It does not matter whether they are large or small;
provided that both edges are made of cloth or silk and the interior is filled with felt, wool, or similar materials, they are included in the category of heavy items.
Regarding the statement that "a woolen rug five cubits long enters the light category," this establishes the principle: it must be of a pure, single color;
because it can serve as one of the three robes (tricīvara), it is classified as light. If it has variegated colors, regardless of its size, it enters the heavy category.

If it is not variegated and is suitable to be made into a *kāṣāya*, even if it has not yet been fashioned into a robe, it still enters the light category. This applies equally to items made of leather; therefore, the use of leather is permitted.

Regarding bedding and requisites: it is established that these are worn because they are in frontier regions where cotton cloth and silk are unavailable. After death, they enter the category of light items.

However, if this were the case in this land [of China], the three robes made of skin would instead have to be included among the heavy items. Therefore, the *Qingzhong yi* (Ritual of Light and Heavy Items) states:
"If one arrives in a region where cotton cloth is available, the wearing of such [skins] is no longer permitted," and so forth.
Regarding "lighter fabrics such as *ruì-luó* (gauze/silk)": I privately say that Master Lì once categorized *luó* (gauze) as heavy, but that is no longer the case.

The subsequent text instructs one to wear expensive, coarse garments (*sū-yī*), and further specifies wearing garments with the "goose-pattern" (*é-wén-yī*). Thus, we know that *luó*-garments are classified as light.
As for the passage in the text that is not clear, some say that the *Tiānrén* (Heavenly Humans) precisely clarify this meaning when they speak of "expensive garments," which refers to the *kāṣāya*.
The *sāṭa* is merely expensive; it is not a garment for laypeople.
Regarding the two kinds of waistbands, it is established that one is the meditation belt (*dhyānabandhana*), which is what was described above as "good assistance" (*śubhasahāya*).

The other is the ordinary waistband. As for the term "hair-cloth" (*māṇava*), the character should have hair attached to its side (the *bàng* radical with the *mǎo* radical); this refers to hair cloth (*maobù*). This is the character.

Lin Yun states: "The square-patterned variety of *karpāsa* is called *bimao qū*. The two forms are identical; the *Ziyuan* dictionary writes it as *qū sǒu* (the second character pronounced *qiáng zhū*)."
Regarding the character *xià* (pronounced with the "shuāng zhū" rhyme): the *Shēnglèi* states that it refers to the shearing of fur. The *Shìmíng* writes it as *qiú bèi* (furs and coverlets).
The *Tōngsùwén* states that woven-fur mats are called *máo shū*. Those of fine quality are termed *tǎmó*. The *Guǎngyǐ* states that *tǎmó* refers to fur with decorative patterns.
The *Shìmíng* states that these are spread upon small couches placed in front of large beds; they are so named because they serve as the means for ascending onto the bed.

If it is argued that true crimson and the like are determined to fall under the category of heavy [colors], while yellow and white should not fall under the category of light and so forth, this is established as a refutation of the ancient masters' interpretation.
The ancients judged that only crimson and purple fell under the category of heavy; now, by citing yellow and white and the like, they raise an objection (and so forth).

If it is asked, "In the case of woolen carpets (*kūlū*), the Buddha’s regulations place them in the category of light, yet he did not mention color and so forth," [the response] is established as follows: this is for the purpose of...

The ancient masters intended this as a challenge: "Since you do not permit true crimson and other such colors to be considered 'heavy' [in terms of forfeiture], yet the Vinaya regarding woolen rugs (*kūṭā*) specifies only their dimensions and not their color—why then do you treat patterned silk as heavy while pure-colored silk is light?
Thus we know that it is the patterned variety that is heavy. Now, how could my crimson and purple not be heavy? Therefore, we know that it is simply a matter of acquisition."
Wearing [a garment] that enters the category of light [offenses] is not permitted; wearing one that falls under the heavy [offenses] is likewise forbidden. Therefore, it must not be of a purple hue.
As for the single type of variegated woolen rug (*kūrpa*), neither may be worn. How can one distinguish between one being light and the other heavy? This is the position held by the ancient masters.
Regarding "containing straw" (*hán-gǎi*): Master Li says that "straw" (*gǎi*) refers to the stalks of hemp or ramie used as a girth-band.

Master Ying says that "straw" (*gǎi*, with the second tone *gōng-bā-fǎn*) may be written with the "grain" radical and the character *jí*, or with the "grass" radical and the character *mù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Straw (*gǎi*) is the stalk of grain from which the husk has been removed;
it is used for ritual offerings and as fodder. Regarding "connected bags": I [the author] say this refers to the kind of bag used on the backs of donkeys in the northern regions. Two.
The one with a seam at the crown and a hole opened in the center is this [type of garment]. The long bag is for containing grain-dust.

All secular garments such as skirts and jackets that have been dyed a faded color (ruined color) and torn are included among the light [weight items]; that is to say, although these are secular clothes, [they are permitted].

Since it was already torn beforehand, and because it has been dyed according to the Dharma, it falls into the category of light offenses. This means it was already torn previously; it is not something torn for the first time now.

It should be understood that regarding embroidered silk alms-bowl bags, one frequently sees many such items among the venerable ones (bhadanta), which are made entirely of embroidery and cost five or six strings of cash;
these all fall under the category of heavy offenses.
Regarding the statement, "It refers to the tools of creation and so forth, not to the created objects themselves," this clarifies that these words refute the interpretations held by former scholars.
They claimed that all instruments of action as well as the products of such action fall under the category of "heavy" (guru). Now, we do not agree with this.
To say they "fall under the heavy" means that the instruments which perform the action are what is heavy; however, the objects produced may be either light or heavy.
Regarding the character *hùfěi* (戶扉): it is formed by combining the radical for wood with the character *fěi* (蒲皆反). This refers to a wooden door-panel or shutter. Regarding the *kuāng* (筐):
this is the common domestic spinning basket used by women today. Regarding the *jǔ* (筥): it is also written as [竺-二+旋] (同力與反), or as 紀 (紀與反).
The *Zìlín* (字林) states that a *jǔ* is a basket; it is a vessel for rice with a capacity of five *dǒu*.
Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* being categorized as a "shearing" text for those who carry four-inch knives, it is established that there is Mount Laṅkā in the Western Regions and the South Seas;
this sutra is named after that mountain. The Buddha entered this Mount Laṅkā and preached this sutra.
Within the text, the use of a knife is permitted, its blade being like a crescent moon. As for the rosary being included in the "light" category and so forth, this...
Objects that accompany the person are beneficial for aiding the path; they keep the mind focused during recitation and thus are permitted as minor items.
If there are no such items, and the monastic community takes them and adds them to the common property (*sāṃghika*), this is established as improper.

It is said that while the deceased was alive, if he had relied upon the communal quarters, these rooms would have been divided among the assembly three times a day; therefore, it is not right to adjudicate otherwise. Since he maintained separate rooms while alive, [the community may take them].
It applies to all three periods and is called "non-existence" (wúfǎ). After death, the monastic community picks it up. Regarding "ochre soil" (zhětǔ):
the character *zhě* (赭) is composed of the radical for "red" (*chì*) on the left and "earth" (*tǔ*) on the right; it refers to red earth. In the *Sāncāng*, it is stated that "ochre is red earth.
The interpretation that the character is formed with "earth" on the left is not the correct meaning.

Regarding "leather boxes and leather cases": raw hide is called *ge* (leather), while processed hide is called *wei* (soft leather); this refers to processed deer hide. "Lower-grade processed *wei*" refers to various types of processed hides.
Regarding "flat boots and slanted boots": the established interpretation states these are the boots of laypeople; they all fall under the category of heavy items.
Even if flat boots have a level front, if their shafts are very deep, they also fall under the category of heavy items. Regarding "paper, pens, and ink": [these are light items].
Regarding the classification of "standing" offenses: if one originally intended to attach oneself to the Path and record the sutras and treatises, the offense is light;
if one originally engaged in secular affairs, or accumulated [goods] for trade and profit, it is invariably a grave offense.

Regarding "only those that are utensils for use": I privately say, if they are light enough to be carried on one's person, they may be included in the allotted portion; if they are heavy, they should be returned to the permanent property of the monastery.
As for items used specifically within a particular room, there should be no further alteration or transfer. Regarding items not required by humans or animals:
since vessels and implements were originally intended for personal use, if they are no longer needed by people, what is the point of laboriously hoarding them?
Regarding the term "monastery attendants" (*saṃghārāmika*): it is established that this refers to those such as Piṅgala who have their own separate small temples.
If a bhikṣu dies, these attendants enter into his heavy property; as for all private belongings, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, they are all taken into their own private possession.
It is established that this means they enter into the private possession of the slaves. If a slave belonging to the Saṃgha dies, this section below provides a general explanation.

"Monastic slaves" refers to those whose property belongs to the community [of monks]. "Clothing and goods given to their relatives" means they enter the possession of the relatives of the deceased slave.
"If there are none" refers to the deceased slave himself; that is, if the deceased slave has no relatives, the property reverts to the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) of the monastery.
As for the death of a private slave: the above clarifies the permanent endowment slaves of the monastic community; now, below, it clarifies this permanent endowment [itself].
Regarding the "slave": one who has private property is a "slave-slave.

If they share food, clothing, and necessities, even down to the distribution of their assigned duties, it means that while the master provided for the slave's livelihood during his life, once he has died, all his clothing and belongings may be taken at the discretion of the master-slave.
If they did not live together and the master simply took possession of them, this refers to a "superior-grade slave."
She is a female slave. If such a male slave dies, his property belongs to his wife and children.

As for the statement that "the master directly takes possession," this refers to permanent slaves who, although raised separately, are merely made to perform labor; these are slaves whose produce is delivered as tax.
"If there are none" means they are like unowned property within the monastery; that is to say, if this slave has no wife or children, it is the same as property without an owner. This property...

It should be brought into the permanent property (*sāṃghika*) of the monastery. This case is the same as the belongings of a visiting monk; it is termed "ownerless property" (*anadhiṣṭhita-vastu*) and ought to enter the permanent property.

The commentary states: "If it was provided by the Sangha, it is not the same. This means that if the permanent property of the Sangha had previously provided this slave, he is termed "provided by the Sangha.
In such a case, one may not take the object into one's personal possession; it must be entered into the Sangha.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If there are slaves or servants who should be released, this refers to a slave whom a bhikṣu supported during his lifetime;
as long as the bhikṣu is alive, they must be released. If they are not released, they become 'pure persons' (*kappiya-kāraka*) for the Saṃgha.

This means that if they were not previously released, upon the bhikṣu’s death they may enter the permanent property of the monastery and are thus termed "pure persons" for the Saṃgha. According to the commentary, "releasing them" refers to this.

Regarding the phrase "granting surnames and admitting them as commoners" (*shìxìng rùliáng*): this refers to the interpretation of the passage stating that they should be released and allowed to depart.

As for the note stating "later, upon death, they shall follow the Vinaya," I privately interpret this to mean: if their surnames are granted and they are admitted as commoners, then they are released;

if not, then after the bhikṣu’s death, they shall follow the latter section of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, whereby they are assigned to the permanent property (*sthavira*) and made into a *saṃghika* pure man (*śuddha-puruṣa*). Therefore, it says "later."
This refers to the preceding text and the subsequent statement.
Regarding the rule for the distribution of robes when one has passed away after having requested food: this food re-enters the category of "heavy" (valuable) items;
it is simply that the deceased's clothing and belongings are brought into the midst of the Sangha, where the heavy and light items are then distinguished.

Third, regarding those who employ the *Vinaya-piṭaka* universally: this is precisely the practice of the Third Master. As for the extensive coverage of its text and meaning, it is as described in a separate fascicle;
it is established and clarified in the *Chóngqǐng yí* (The Ritual of the Double Light). Now, according to the Second Master:

this is established and clarified based on the second of the three masters mentioned above. It correctly adopts the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* while concurrently employing other schools. Based on this one...
The Master’s feet are now fit for action. Above, seven sections were established in length; this is the second Master’s interpretation.
Thus, these seven distinct segments complete the general explanation of the sixth section, the "Section on the Lightness and Heaviness of Clothing and Utensils.

From here below, we shall properly clarify the seventh meaning: the distribution of rewards according to merit. Regarding the "six items" of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: the three robes and the container for robes.

Regarding the "receptacle, cloth bundle, and so forth," Fazhi states: "There are differing interpretations among various masters concerning these six items. If one follows the Master of the [Dharmaguptaka] Vinaya School, the three robes are combined into one;

the cloth bundle for storing robes is the second; the alms bowl is the third; the bag is the fourth; the sitting mat is the fifth; and the needle case is the sixth. However, the Nanshan school does not hold this view;
it maintains that the cloth for storing robes and the container for utensils belong respectively to the three robes and the alms bowl. Do not [hold otherwise].
Regarding the enumeration: simply by opening the three robes into three separate items, and adding the bowl, sitting mat, and needle case, there are six.
If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the water bag replaces the needle case; thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Sutra 28) states: "The six articles are: the three robes, the bowl..."

The water-strainer, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and the whetstone—Lì says that these six items above are specified for monks; a nun should have eight articles. There is also an interpretation which states:
the five robes are combined into one; the container for the robes and the storage vessel are counted as two;

together with the bowl, the sitting mat, and the needle-case, these constitute six, which is the same number as for a monk. If the five robes are separated into five, and the container for the robes and the storage vessel... [text continues].

Regarding the combined discussion on the utensils that accompany the robes and bowl: these include the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and the needle case (*sūcigāla*). For monks, there are six items; for nuns, there are eight. One may take either set as desired.

Regarding the four permutations concerning the possession or lack of both virtuous qualities (*guṇa*) and material objects (*dravya*): first, one who possesses both virtuous qualities and material objects is to be rewarded; second, one who possesses virtuous qualities but lacks material objects.

If all three virtues and the requisite objects are lacking, these two lines are to be interpreted according to one’s discretion. If four virtues are lacking while the initial [virtue] is present, it is improper to grant the reward.
One should take the presence or absence of virtues as the basis for determining the quantity of the object and the conduct (the "conduct" is pronounced *xíng* with a departing tone).

This means that one must measure the virtue and conduct of the caregiver—whether they are complete or incomplete—and the Sangha shall collectively deliberate and determine the appropriate amount to bestow. Regarding the phrase "one who is thorough and quick-witted": "quick-witted" (*mǐn*) arises from being perceptive (*dá*). This is intended to clarify...
Tending to the sick involves great labor; although the caregiver may not possess full virtue, if they are not generously compensated with even a small reward, then later no one will tend to the sick.
When affairs become congested, no one will go to do so. Now, since they are generously cared for and rewarded, both matters are resolved;

hence it is called "thorough and skillful" (*tōngmǐn*). Furthermore, another interpretation is that although virtue may not be complete, the one who bestows harmony and [rewards] ensures that affairs proceed smoothly.
One attains supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). There is no virtue that is not harmonized when it is bestowed; otherwise, the emotional and situational conditions would not be communicated.

Regarding the three among the *bhikṣuṇīs* who receive [the precepts] while the other four are not permitted: this refers to when a *bhikṣuṇī* is ill and is attended by members of the seven assemblies.
Only the *bhikṣuṇī*, the *śikṣamāṇā*, and the *śrāmaṇerī*—these three—are permitted. The *bhikṣu*, the *śrāmaṇera*, and the two assemblies among the laity—these four are not permitted.
This refers to the fact that there is no fatigue from [physical] labor. Monks and śrāmaṇeras do not have the labor of massaging and so forth; laypeople do not have the labor of preaching the Dharma.

Regarding the rule "one should give it to a single person to divide in a secluded place": this means that when many people are tending to a patient, they all equally contribute their efforts, yet it is not known who should be rewarded.
Now, the rule specifies giving it to one person, who is then to divide it among themselves in a secluded place. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*...

The text states: "One shall also reward their labor with robes and alms bowls, as well as provide them with the remaining medicine they received. Those who came from outside the boundary to look after the patient must also be rewarded.
Although these individuals were in retreat outside the boundary, since they came here to nurse the sick, it would be an act of extreme callousness not to reward them for their labor.
That person possesses virtue; it is logically appropriate to grant [the portion] to him.
The explanation of the principle of rewarding labor is hereby concluded. Below is the eighth section, which correctly clarifies the timing for the distribution.

Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* account of the bhikṣus dividing the robes by the corpse, where the corpse rose up to protect the robes: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, this occurred in the kingdom of Kośala.

There was a certain residence where a bhikṣu died. While the Saṃgha was dividing the robes and bowl in front of the corpse of the deceased bhikṣu, that bhikṣu stirred and rose up, saying to the bhikṣus, "Venerable elders and seniors, do not divide my robes and bowl.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Do not divide [the belongings] right in front of the corpse. If the corpse..."

[The deceased] has already departed. If the Saṃgha is in a different location, it should be divided. Regarding "assembling the Saṃgha and dividing [the property] according to the Dharma as mentioned above," this refers to the method for assembling the Saṃgha in the preceding fascicle.
Jì remarked: "This *karmavācanā* text for the distribution of a deceased person's belongings is somewhat prolix.

This is because in the fourth clause, the circumstances are restated and the original matter is restated again. Compared to other *karmavācanās*, the fourth clause here follows the pattern of a single restatement."
In the original [text], the formal motion (*jñapti*) is not repeated; however, in the *karmavācanā* for deceased persons and property, it says:

"Which elders (*sthavira*), venerable ones, consent? The monk so-and-so has passed away," and so forth. According to the underlying principle, one should say: "Which elders consent? The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles..."
"Together with bhikṣu [Name] and others"—reflecting on this, it should be understood. This is likely due to the omission of the preceding portion by the translator.
If five persons may perform the two dharmas of distributing rewards and dividing robes, Lì says: "If there are five or more..."

It employs three formal procedures (*karmavācanā*). These are: the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for rewarding labor; the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for appointing a person to distribute the robes; and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for entrusting the robes and collecting the items.
Although the Vinaya text contains only two instances of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the appointment of a person to distribute the robes is absent;

however, according to the underlying principle, it ought to exist, just as there is a formal procedure (*karman*) for appointing a person to distribute gruel and so forth. If there are four monks, one proceeds directly with a single [procedure].
Regarding the Dharma: for three persons or fewer, it should be understood that this is performed through face-to-face address or mental recollection (*manasikāra*).

Furthermore, if there are four persons or fewer, once the three dharmas have been completed according to the procedure of face-to-face address and mental recollection, one rewards their labor with a robe; there is no separate ritual for this, as the robe is simply handed over directly.
Furthermore, regarding the distribution of the personal effects of one who has passed away, this depends on the number of people involved;

that is to say, between a large assembly of monks and a single individual. Within the assembly of monks, there are again two distinctions: namely, the procedures for four or five persons, which follow accordingly. If there are four persons, they may properly divide the property equally according to the rule.
[My private opinion: It is not permitted to appoint a person to distribute the robes; this is excluded from the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure).
"Take these robes and give them to such-and-such persons. However, one may only perform a direct distribution among three people as a reward for their labor.

If one performs it according to the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha, even though the procedure has been performed, if the robes have not yet left their original location and another person arrives, the procedure must still be revised.
If one has already made a mental resolve (*manasikāra*) alone, no further person may arrive.

Regarding the instruction that after the prior collection of wealth, one should subsequently strike the bell to summon [the assembly], this refers to the distribution of the deceased’s property and the *karmavācanā* for obtaining offerings from the Saṃgha at an improper time;

these differ from other procedures. If one establishes a boundary (*sīmā*) and does not perform the formal gesture (*cihna*) when reciting the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), it merely avoids the fault of losing the legal efficacy [of the boundary];

however, provided the boundary is not divided by a separate assembly, the ritual act will be accomplished. If, however, one is to consume food belonging to the Saṃgha, it is absolutely necessary to perform the formal gesture.

Even if the boundary (*sīmā*) is not assembled, there is no fault. However, regarding this single dharma, its meaning requires two conditions: it is necessary to strike the bell, and it is also necessary for everyone to assemble.

This is not the same as the case of the permanent residence (*nitya-vihāra*). The commentary states: "The Vinaya clarifies the six requisites; according to the Śāstra, it is not strictly necessary for them to assemble."

"Established" refers to this *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*). The text itself provides the explanation below. *Śaṅ* states: "According to the *Vinaya*, the text for relinquishing [the robes] lists the names of the three robes and six articles as what is to be relinquished.
If one follows the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, regarding the three robes and six articles that are in another location, one requests them to be brought here so they may be rewarded."
If these virtues are not fully possessed, one follows accordingly according to those respective portions; therefore it is said that, based on the treatise, they need not necessarily be assembled.
Since there are cases where they are assembled and cases where they are not, it is said that they are "not necessary."

Regarding the aforementioned instructions: if [the items] exist, they shall be returned accordingly; if they do not exist, they shall be returned by way of mutual forfeiture. This refers to one who "claims credit for their own achievements.
According to the commentary on the *Shangshu*, "to claim credit for one's own achievements is called *fa* (伐), and to boast of one's own worth is called *jin* (矜).

Another source states: "To exalt oneself and be self-important is termed 'claiming credit' (*fa*) regarding virtue. As for the phrase "whether the bonds are formed or not, it is according to one's will," this means that the Saṃgha possesses autonomy.
"To grant the robe" constitutes speech; "not granting the robe" constitutes non-binding. These words appear in the *Poṣadha-khandhaka* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

When the initial rule for binding the *poṣadha-hall* was established, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the great assembly of monks gathered at a certain residence, but the *poṣadha-hall* was too small to accommodate them all.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "The World-Honored One has prescribed the precepts, yet he did not establish a binding [hall]."
Regarding the Poṣadha hall: if the Poṣadha cannot be recited there, what should be done now? The Buddha said, "The Saṃgha has autonomy;

whether it is formally designated or not, they may recite the Poṣadha as they see fit. Now, taking that text as evidence: whether [an item] is granted or not depends upon the Saṃgha. The commentary states:
"One should take one item from among those normally used for service and offer it as a reward. This refers to the deceased person’s usual clothing. (3)
"Regarding the robes and the alms-bowl bag: these are given as a reward. The commentary states:
"If one is permitted to give them when the three robes are contained within three bags, this means that each robe has its own bag; now, all three bags are being given."

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the meaning of rewarding labor. The following clarifies the distribution of light items. Regarding the practice where, at the time of distribution, one uses oral instructions instead of formal *karmavācanā* (procedural motion), which some claim does not violate the Dharma:
I personally maintain that various masters do not permit this interpretation. It is necessary to formally designate persons to distribute the robes and so forth;

therefore, in the *Vinaya*’s section on the Rules for Quarters (*Śayanāsana-vastu*), after designating persons to distribute the quarters, it subsequently states that persons are designated to distribute the robes and other items.

It is the same in this case; therefore, one must know that a formal appointment is required. The *Lishi* (Commentary on the Vinaya) also states that one must perform the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), and so forth.

When it is now said that violating the rule results in the attainment [of the offense], if one seeks the intent of the Vinaya text, one must perform the *karmavācanā* to appoint a person to distribute the robes. If, at the time of the occasion, one were to appoint someone merely by word of mouth, [it would be invalid].

This does not constitute a formal *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure); it merely violates the regulations (*dharma*). However, in principle, it can still be accomplished. Therefore, it is so stated. Master Bin says:

"Nanshan states that there is no need for a formal procedure to appoint a person to distribute robes; even by calculation of principle, it would be accomplished. Although the present chapter does not permit this, it represents one specific interpretation.

By calculation of principle, both [approaches] are valid. There is no fault in appointing someone, nor is there failure in not appointing anyone. Throughout the *karmavācanās* of antiquity, only this has been set forth."

Regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the distribution of robes, the *Daishu* (Great Commentary) does not permit it, stating that one must first perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint a person to distribute the robes.
As for the phrase "the rules for śrāmaṇeras, etc.," Lì Míng explains that since such a person lacks virtue, it is improper to appoint them through a formal ritual (*karman*); rather—
One may appoint [a person] based on the oral instructions of a śrāmaṇera to distribute the robes. This means that when appointing a śrāmaṇera, one must not perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
The commentary states: "Therefore, it is necessary to employ those who are broadly learned and harmonious among those present. "Broad" (bo) refers to exchange or substitution.
Since the deceased’s three robes and six requisites are already in another location, and the current caregiver lacks the requisite virtue, there is no need to pursue those items back from that place.
Rather, the community should take the items currently available and use them as a reward for the caregiver;
that is, one should employ these present items to exchange for the location where those six requisites reside. Jì further explains this as a general exchange.
This means that one must observe the timing and circumstances regarding whether to advance or retreat, weigh the merits, and determine whether a reward is merited or not;
one must investigate the underlying facts and be well-versed in what is open or obstructed, possessing broad knowledge of current affairs (the previous interpretation is incorrect).

Regarding the inner and outer robes belonging to a deceased śrāmaṇera according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is established that there are two types of upper and lower garments: one corresponds to the *uttarāsaṅga* and one corresponds to the *antarvāsaka*.
Therefore, it is said that there are two types of robes: upper and lower. Regarding the note stating that "the text in the Vinaya is brief and incomplete," I privately remark:

the Vinaya does not set forth this specific *karmavācanā* for the distribution of the deceased's property; however, beneath the *karmavācanā* for the distribution of dwellings, there is a note stating "the distribution of the light belongings of the deceased," to which one adds:
"The Saṃgha now takes these articles of clothing and gives them to the bhikṣu [Name]; [Name] shall..."
It is returned to the community of monks. Therefore, we now follow the text concerning "non-timely gifts received by the Sangha.
According to this commentary, one simply has the administrative officer (karmadāna) kneel before the monks in turn and act as the distributor of the robes.
The phrase "the wisdom of ordinary people does not surpass the mind of the sage" means that how could the deliberations of ordinary beings ever excel the mind of a sage?
If one’s private management of Buddhist affairs is improper, one should go out to beg for medicine, mostly for the sake of the sick, and provide service to the Sangha.

Regarding these matters concerning the assembly: although one’s person is within [the community], it is logically appropriate to give [possessions] to others; to manage them privately is clearly improper.
Next, to clarify the distribution of the four parts to śrāmaṇeras and *karmadānas*, and the cases from "if the Saṃgha is in harmony" down to "giving one part out of four":
Lì says that if the Saṃgha is in harmony, it should be understood that they should be given equally, or perhaps half should be given—meaning to the bhikṣus.

"To receive the full amount" means that a *śrāmaṇera* receives half of the full amount. Regarding the expression "giving one part out of three," it means that while a *bhikṣu* receives three parts, a *śrāmaṇera* receives one of those three.
Bin says: "A *śrāmaṇera* receiving half of the full amount" means that if the *mahāsāṃghika* monks receive twenty [units], the *śrāmaṇera* receives ten.
This continues up to "giving one out of four," which refers to approximately forty units; for the *śrāmaṇera*, it would be ten.

The *śrāmaṇera* receives ten; the *bhikṣu* receives thirty. Some have become confused by this statement and claim that it should be applied only to the case of thirty [units of currency], such that the *bhikṣu* receives twenty and the *śrāmaṇera* receives ten.
But how does this differ from the previous rule that he receives half? Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"One *bhikṣu* with three *śrāmaṇeras* is also the same as this. Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned non-seasonal offerings (*akāla-dakṣiṇā*)...
The middle section states: "Divide it into four parts. Three parts are given to the bhikṣus; the fourth part is given to the three lower assemblies.
This means that one bhikṣu gives [his share] to three śrāmaṇeras.

Regarding the provision of one share out of five for the *kappiya-kāraka* (the "pure person"): Sengli states that although a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*) is not a monk, they must still be given a share because they labor for the Saṃgha;

furthermore, because they differ from laypeople and are distinct from śrāmaṇeras, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) provides for one share out of four, or in some cases none at all, in which case the property should not be divided.
This four-part textual passage clearly establishes the rule, stating: "If the *kappiya-kāraka* is not given [a share], the property should not be divided."

Regarding whether or not to give [a portion] to a female attendant (*kappiya-kārī*), the interpretations differ. Some say that it is improper for a monastery to keep a female attendant; therefore, one should not give [to her].
Others say that since she is of the same class as those who labor for the Sangha’s offerings, why should she not be given [a share]?

It should be decided according to the time and in harmony with the Sangha. The ancient masters all said: when the Sangha receives an offering, the female attendant is entitled to a share; this refers to the time of distribution.
Those who remain within the boundary receive [the share]; it is not appropriate to give a portion to those who have gone outside the boundary. A guest says: "That is not so.

It was with the original intention that they were to provide for the labor of the Saṃgha that the Buddha ordered them to be given. Now, because they are acting as messengers for the Saṃgha and have undergone labor by going outside the boundary, the judgment is that they do not receive it."
To sit within the boundary and then have the portions distributed to one by inversion is logically improper;
therefore, it is now correctly determined that regardless of whether one is inside or outside the boundary, anyone who has performed labor shall receive a share.
"When the time comes, Yi laughs; how can his face be so thick-skinned? This describes the appearance of one who endures shame. "Not contemplating from beginning to end" means, as Li says:

not reflecting upon the Buddha’s original intention is called "not contemplating the beginning"; not awakening to the fact that one's own body will inevitably become impermanent in the future is called "not contemplating the end.
The commentary states: "There are those for whom non-conceptualization is not achieved," meaning there are people...
They are summoned within their respective boundaries and assemble together. Once the assembly has gathered in the hall, how could the ritual proceedings be accomplished?
The above concludes the explanation of the rules for the Saṃgha regarding the distribution of robes. Below, the method of face-to-face (pratimukha) practice is correctly elucidated.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "The first is the method of correspondence (*ekasaṃvāsa-dharma*). [My] private commentary says: this refers simply to the method of mental reflection (*cittamanasikāra-dharma*). There is no hindrance to either party being present.
Regarding "inclusion": it is established that the term "non-garment" (*a-cīvara*) is not explicitly defined within the Vinaya. Masters of both ancient and modern times have each held different views;
some say it refers to banners or canopies, others say it refers to leather sandals, bags for bowls, and so forth, while still others say it refers to pieces of cloth-material.

Now, we shall provide a comprehensive synthesis: it should be understood as being inclusive of all such items. Since they are not garments, they are included among "acquired objects. Thus, the term "non-garment" applies to all these things.

Because it encompasses things from both sides, it is called "this" and "that. Therefore, in the Vinaya, a bhikṣu incurs a *pāyattika* offense for taking a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, yet taking a bhikṣuṇī’s non-robe (*a-cīvara*) is permitted;
that which is outside of the *kāṣāya* (monastic robes) is termed a "non-robe. Furthermore, a later passage in the Vinaya states:
"When a bhikṣu has obtained many robes and does not know what kind of robe to give to a bhikṣuṇī, the Buddha said: 'I permit you to give a non-robe, such as a bowl (*pātra*), to a bhikṣuṇī.'"

[This refers to] the bag. Furthermore, regarding the white three robes (*tricīvara*), the section on the precepts states: "If one does not perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) for items that are not robes—such as leather sandals, alms-bowl bags, hats, socks, and so forth—it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"Nor may they receive a portion from the community of nuns" means that since these are the goods of a monastery or estate, they belong to the share of the monks of that specific monastery.
