This is not like being in a place without a permanent residence, where the first among the five groups of practitioners to arrive receives them. Because this is a secular location, there is concern that laypeople might damage the monastic property;

therefore, it belongs to whichever of the five groups first possesses [the right to it]. The note states: "The monastery lacks the monastic rules" means that there is no communal food or *kaṭhina* cloth.
Regarding the three periods for the distribution of rooms and other items (and so forth):

as for those among the five groups of monastics who arrive first, [the Buddha] permitted them to take what they see first, fearing that laypeople or non-Buddhists might otherwise squander or waste the property of the Sangha, thereby causing the original donors to lose their merit.
Since all five groups are fields of merit, the Buddha opened this allowance so that the merit of the original owners would not be diminished.

If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī share the same master and the items are to be divided among their respective communities, those who arrive first—even if they belong to the five assemblies—shall receive them.
However, if both the saṃgha of monks and the saṃgha of nuns arrive together, one may not rely on the previous rule. If the deceased was a monk, the property belongs to the saṃgha;

if the deceased was a nun, it belongs to the nuns. Regarding "distance based on sentiment," this means that according to the feelings of those present, the items are sent to a permanent residence (sthiti) far or near.
Furthermore, regarding the case where one takes the robe separately and does not give it to a bhikṣu within the same boundary:

this establishes that there was a bhikṣu who carried a robe for another while traveling on the road, and the owner of the robe passed away. Although there was a saṃgha within the *araṇya* boundary, he did not share [the property] with them, but instead brought it into his own possession;
this constitutes an offense of *vyatikrama*. Such is the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this would constitute the offense of theft (*steya*).

The sub-commentary states: "It is not established that there is a *bhikṣu* who is without the *saṃjñā* (perception/consent). This means that when there are *bhikṣus* within the same boundary (*sīmā*), they must perform the ritual act of partitioning;
now, by entering it oneself, the ritual act is not established. Regarding the phrase "not sharing with those within the same boundary":

this refers to the presence of monks within the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) where the ritual act is performed, yet one does not share [the space] with them. Furthermore, another interpretation holds: "There is a *bhikṣu* who lacks the *dharma*" means that since [the boundary] is already within the enclosure...

There is a bhikṣu who does not summon others to perform legal acts (*dharmakarma*) together, but rather performs them alone. Because he does not perform legal acts with others, it is said that there is "no dharma.

If, after a *karmavācanā* has been performed, one measures the shadow [of the sun], or even if a guest arrives, and it is known whether [the arrival] was before or after the *karmavācanā*, then according to the *Lishi* (Commentary on the Vinaya), the deceased’s property is divided at this point.
Alternatively, if they die together, or if they encounter the performance of the *karmavācanā*, there are four possible cases.

Regarding the analysis: herein, one encounters the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act). Or, one may encounter both and thus be entitled to receive [the portion]. In the remaining two cases, one does not obtain a share of the goods.
If someone is sent to fetch it on one's behalf and a share should be given, Shenxiu says: "In this case, four parts are permitted to be received; other schools do not permit it.

Thus we know that one must go in person to take it for the procedure to be complete. Therefore, the note below cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stating: "As for those who go to fetch it, they should be the same [as those who receive it]."
It is alive. Regarding the fact that various schools state that committing an offense does not constitute [the completion of] the act, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* cited by the Master says:
"If one takes property obtained by the Saṃgha and goes outside the boundary, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); it should be shared with other bhikṣus. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says:

"Regarding cloth obtained by the Saṃgha that is divisible, if a single bhikṣu takes it to the boundary of the *sīmā* and performs the *karmavācanā* to receive it, the Buddha said this is improper; one commits a *duṣkṛta*. It appears...
The previous monks should divide [the property]. If one follows the third fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* regarding the precept on stealing, it says:

"If a bhikṣu takes the robes of a deceased person out of the boundary and thinks [of taking them] for himself, or takes them by means of three verbal requests, the Buddha said this constitutes a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline). The commentary notes: "Receiving the robes according to the Dharma, or from those who are in agreement.
Master Li states that he cites the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika* to resolve the text of the aforementioned *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. If one sends someone to come [to claim the property], one should...
"Those who give" refers to co-residents and others who, being unable to come in person, send someone to collect their share of the robes;
it does not mean taking light items and dividing them in order. Alternatively, they may have already been within the boundary and thus entitled to a share of the robes.

Now, as for moving [the object] to another location, one should dispatch someone to fetch what ought to be obtained. Regarding the statement that various schools establish offenses without saying they can be accomplished:
this means that while dispatching a messenger to fetch it does not accomplish the act itself, it does not invalidate the monastic law, which is self-evident.
Regarding the question of when an object belonging to a deceased person is brought within the boundary and a monk does not know it, yet subsequently carries it out of the boundary:
this refers to a case where, for example, a layperson brings the property of a deceased monk who has no fixed residence and delivers it to within the boundary of the Saṃgha.
A certain monk sees it and asks, "What is this? and is told, "It is the property of a deceased monk. Once the monk has recognized it, he is called the "one who saw it first" (*pūrvadṛṣṭa*).
One should immediately lead them out of the boundary so that those within the boundary do not know.

Upon reaching the interior araṇya site or along the way, one may assemble the Saṃgha according to the Dharma and divide [the property], and it will be valid. This is because those within the boundary were unaware, and they have now gone to the araṇya site.

It is accomplished because they have assembled together in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the time of distribution, those who share the same Dharma establish that one should go to that location within the boundary and distribute it by assembling the Saṃgha according to the Dharma; thus, it is accomplished.
Commentary on the *Sifenlü Chao*, Fascicle 12b and Fascicle 13a,
composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
△ Section 18: The Rules for Receiving and Purifying the Four Medicines (Part One).
Although clothing is sufficient to cover the body, it only provides external support; furthermore, one must rely on food to fill the mouth, thereby providing internal sustenance.

When both internal and external conditions are complete, one is then able to advance in their practice. Therefore, immediately following the section on robes, the rules for medicine are clarified. There are four distinct types of medicine, namely:

those taken at specific times, those not restricted by time, and the two types of "all-allowing" (sapta-jīvitaparyanta). Thus they are called the "four. Although these four types differ, they all serve to alleviate hunger and treat illness; therefore, they are collectively termed "medicine.

Because they are acquired through formal ritual (*vidhi*) and worn after being accepted, this is called "receiving and purifying" (*pariśuddha*). Within the text, the two methods of receiving—by hand and by mouth—are explained in detail. This is the summary.
This is the track for receiving [robes]; thus, they are called "dharmas. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "A conditioned form requires external support to be established.

If there were no clothing to shield the body, the four great elements would mutually impair one another; how then could one cultivate the Way? For this reason, it was previously explained that the two types of robes are used to shield the suffering of the physical form.
Although the external form is supported by these, if there is internal hunger and emptiness, there is no means by which one can advance in one's practice. Therefore, with respect to the internal..."
These are provided to clarify the four medicines. Thus, Liu Zi said: "Food is sufficient to fill the void and sustain the vital breath;

clothing is sufficient to cover the body and ward off the cold. These words are correct. Li said: "In the preceding section, clothing was treated as an external provision; here, we distinguish the medicines as internal sustenance.

Although the things that sustain the physical frame are numerous, when summarized according to their nature and their timing, they do not exceed four. Therefore, they are called 'the four. It is these four medicines that can..."

Because it cures the disease of hunger, it is designated as "medicine. To acquire and maintain [these requisites] through the performance of ritual procedures is called "receiving. If one maintains them according to the Dharma, they become aids to the Path;
however, if one maintains them in a manner that defiles the holy teaching, many transgressions will arise. As these impurities entangle the practitioner, such possession is therefore termed "impure."

Therefore, the Buddha permitted people to perform ritual acts in accordance with the Dharma; when these acts accord with proper decorum, they do not give rise to karmic offenses. Being free from the aforementioned defilements of sin, such acts are designated as "pure" (*śuddha*).
There is a prescribed procedure for performing purification, and thus it is called "Dharma. Hence, it is said: "The Dharma of receiving the four medicines through purification.
Regarding "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*), this refers to the period from dawn until midday, provided that the actions accord with the facts and conform to the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "not giving rise to offenses," the *Lì Jīemó Shū* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*) refutes this interpretation. It states: "As the former interpretation held:

'When a matter accords with the Dharma and does not give rise to the burden of offense, it is called "timely" (*kāla*). This meaning applies universally; provided that there is no offense and it accords with the Dharma, it is all termed "timely.
According to this explanation, all four medicines are termed "timely," as they all accord with the Dharma. This is similar to... [the example].

There is no fault during the [proper] time; after midday, there is transgression, which is termed "improper time" (*akāla*). Taking [medicines] beyond the seven-day limit, or taking them for as long as one lives provided one remains free from illness—categories such as these are called "improper time.
This can be understood by reversing the explanation. Thus, we know that the four types of medicine all possess the dual meanings of "proper time" and "improper time.

To provide the correct explanation now, they are distinguished according to the twelve periods of the day: the period before midday is called "time," while what follows is "improper time," as is the case with...
This is an exposition on the precept regarding improper times. That is to say, the period before noon is designated as "time," while that which passes it is "improper time.

In the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, the Buddha spoke for the sake of the Bodhisattva Prajñā-dharma: "There are four kinds of eating times: the morning is the time of celestial food; midday is the time of dharma-food."
The evening meal is the time for domestic animals to eat; the night meal is the time for ghosts to eat. These latter two meals mostly give rise to illness.
Therefore, a renunciant should partake of the former two: the meal of the devas and the meal of the Dharma. Hence, these are called "timely meals" (*kālabhojana*).

After noon has passed, it is no longer the time for those two meals; hence, it is called "untimely" (*akāla*). Regarding the classification of medicines, there are only two types: first, timely medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*); second, untimely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*).
The "timely medicine" (kālabhaiṣajya) is established based on its substance. The latter three medicines are all collectively termed "non-timely.

What is here called the "fourth" refers to the addition of "non-timely gruel" (akālikapāna) within the category of non-timely [medicines]. It is named "non-timely" because it is permitted for consumption in contrast to the "non-timely" [restrictions] of those who observe the proper time.
The remaining two medicines originate from the "timely" (kāla) family; they are defined by the "untimely" (akāla).

Therefore, based on the duration of the period from the day one receives the precepts, there are long and short limits (seven days being short, and for as long as one lives being long). Thus, two [categories] must be established. Following this distinction, four types of medicine are obtained. However, these four names—
"Time" and "non-time" are relative designations; the latter two types are termed according to the dharma-reception, as they possess varying durations.

Regarding the statement that "if the matter accords with the dharma, no offense shall arise," this means that if the medicinal substances are prepared according to the dharma, there will be no faults such as boiling or storing overnight.

When an action does not contradict the teaching, it is called "conformity with the action" (*kriyā-anuloma*). When an action accords with the Dharma, it is called "accordance with the Dharma" (*dharma-anuloma*).
Regarding "seven-day medicine," this refers to that which, by its capacity, conforms to the Dharma and exhausts its allotted duration;

that is to say, this medicine possesses the efficacy of seven days. Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states: "If one takes it for seven days, chronic illnesses will be eliminated. It is on account of this efficacy that the designation "seven-day [medicine]" is established.

This is the dharma of purification; therefore, it is said that one proceeds from the capacity to the dharma. Since the seventh day is the limit of the medicinal substance's functional efficacy, it is said that one exhausts its full measure.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle four, states: "From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of meat, even to the extent that one should regard it as the flesh of one's own child.
The commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "In the past, there was a husband and wife who were traveling through a vast wilderness with their only son.

During a time of famine, their provisions were exhausted. The parents thought to themselves: 'If we do not kill our son, our lives will not be sustained; yet if we kill and eat our son, our hearts will be filled with love.'"

It is difficult to endure. Because their own lives are so precious, they kill their children and eat them while shedding tears; they find no flavor in the food. A bhikṣu who accepts food should likewise be so [sensitive].
Now, as for those who eat meat and sever the seeds of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*):

the commentary states that great compassion is the cause of Buddhahood, and thus even a small measure of compassion is called the "seed" of the great. Furthermore, it says that killing and wounding [beings] injures great compassion, while eating [their flesh] injures small compassion. This is because [of this causal relationship].

From a small amount, one obtains a great result; therefore, the small is called the "great seed" (*mahā-bhūta*). Furthermore, it is said that the fruit is great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), while the cause is minor compassion.

If the cause perishes, the fruit is severed; thus, the cause is designated as the "seed. Because [eating meat] can sever the Buddha-seed, the consumption of the three kinds of pure meat is not permitted.

To be free from seeing, hearing, or suspecting [the meat being for one's sake] constitutes the threefold purity. How much more so, then, should one not intentionally consume that which lacks these three purities?

That which is said to be "not the flesh of the four modes of birth" refers to flesh that is not produced through the womb, egg, moisture, or transformation. Indeed, all flesh is encompassed within these four modes of birth.

There is no meat other than that of the four modes of birth. Since the eating of the flesh of these four births is not permitted, one should know that this is precisely the meaning of the present prohibition against meat-eating.
Furthermore, meat does not arise spontaneously; it is obtained entirely through the taking of life. If a person does not abstain from meat, they are truly a thief who robs others of their lives.
Regarding the statement that there are immeasurable causes and conditions in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* for which one should not eat meat, and that ten types have been briefly explained:
according to the eighth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, in the chapter titled "Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat," the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmati: "I observe sentient beings..."
Transmigrating through the six realms of existence, we have repeatedly been each other’s parents, brothers, sisters, and various kinsmen and relatives.

When I observe sentient beings devouring one another’s flesh, there is not one who has not been my kin; yet, driven by a craving for the taste of meat, they devour one another and constantly give rise to harmful intentions.
"Suffering and bitterness increase; one wanders through birth and death, unable to attain liberation.
When the Buddha spoke these words, there were certain evil rākṣasas who, having heard them in the presence of the Buddha, all abandoned their malevolent intentions and ceased eating meat.

Looking at one another, they gave rise to hearts of compassion and, weeping with flowing tears, addressed the Buddha, saying: "From this day forward, we shall renounce the eating of meat. O younger brother of the Tathāgata..."
"Son, for those who do not eat meat, I shall personally approach and protect them day and night.

But for those who eat meat, I shall bring them great harm. The Buddha told Mahāmati: 'Even rākṣasas and evil spirits who constantly eat meat, upon hearing what I have said, will give rise to a mind of compassion and abandon the eating of meat;
how much more so should my disciples who practice the wholesome Dharma refrain from eating it?'"
Meat. If there are those who eat it, you should know that they are great enemies of sentient beings.
If any of my disciples, having heard what I have taught, still eat meat, you should know that they are of the *caṇḍāla* caste; they are not my disciples, and I am not their teacher.
Regarding "that which grows from the three impure odors," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, one should contemplate as follows: first..."
All flesh is produced from the impurity of the parents' thick blood—the union of the red and the white—resulting in an unclean body.
One should contemplate the impurity of meat and not eat it. Furthermore, one should contemplate that all meats are like human corpses, which the eyes do not wish to behold.
One should not even smell the odor, much less eat it by placing it in the mouth. It is the same for all kinds of meat.
How could one then distinguish between what is edible and what is inedible? Regarding the point that "all sentient beings feel fear upon smelling the odor," that sutra states:
Furthermore, when sentient beings smell the odor of a person who eats meat, they all become terrified and flee far away.
A doubt arose in him: "Am I dead now, or am I alive? Such an evil person does not cultivate a heart of loving-kindness;
he is like a jackal or a wolf, wandering through the world constantly seeking meat to eat. Like an ox chewing grass or a dung beetle pursuing excrement, he knows no satiety.
My body is the cause; it is precisely his food. He should not see me from afar and then flee in haste, abandoning me. Having left, [he thought:]...
They depart far away; therefore, they are called the great enemies of sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having cultivated immeasurable causes and conditions in the past, possess subtle roots of goodness and thus hear my Dharma. With faith, they leave the household life.

Yet, within the state of being a householder, they were once born as members of the rākṣasa clan, or among tigers, wolves, lions, cats, and wildcats. Although they are now within my Dharma, they [continue to] eat...
They have the residual habit of meat-eating; upon seeing those who eat meat, they rejoice and draw near to them.
Entering cities and towns, they drink alcohol and eat meat just like rākṣasas, no different from those who scramble over and devour corpses.

Although they wear the kāṣāya robe and have shaved their hair and beards, living beings who see them feel terror in their hearts, as if fearing a rākṣasa. Therefore, if you take me as your teacher, [you must not do such things]. One.
One must not eat meat. It is that which is foul, filthy, and impure, practiced by the six classes of ordinary, deluded beings. That sūtra says:
"Furthermore, for one who eats meat, the greedy mind is difficult to satisfy; they do not know moderation in eating, and it is not properly digested, yet it increases the four great elements."
The breath is fishy and rancid; within the abdomen there are many immeasurable evil worms; there are many sores, scabs, and malignant leprosy, as well as various kinds of impurities.
People do not delight in seeing such a person, let alone seeking a future body free from disease, fragrant, and pure—such characteristics are entirely absent.
All things such as onions, leeks, garlic, and shallots are foul-smelling and impure; these obstruct the Noble Path and likewise obstruct worldly people.
In the pure realms of the devas, how much more so in the pure lands of the Buddhas, which are the fruit of their karmic retribution?

Seventh, regarding the point that incantations and arts will not succeed: that sutra states, "Furthermore, if the teachers of worldly, heterodox incantations and arts do not succeed in their arts when they eat meat—since they do not even eat meat for the sake of accomplishing such heterodox arts—how much less so my disciples, who seek the unsurpassed noble path?"
"Supramundane liberation consists in cultivating great compassion and diligent ascetic practice; one fears that even with such effort, liberation might not be attained.
How could such liberation ever be achieved by those deluded people who eat meat? As for the phrase 'by eating meat, consciousness arises upon seeing the physical form' and so forth, I say:
if one eats meat, the mere sight of sentient beings gives rise to the intent to kill, and one becomes attached to the flavor of their flesh."
If one encounters flying birds or running beasts and thinks of roasting them in a kitchen, this refers to the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "abandoned by the various devas and characterized by many evil dreams," that sutra states: Furthermore, those who eat meat are shunned by the devas, let alone by the sages.
Those who eat meat constantly experience evil dreams; they are struck with terror and their hair stands on end; their minds are perpetually restless, and they lack a heart of compassion.
Therefore, this is called "exerting wholesome power. If one dwells alone in a secluded place, non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) will watch for an opportunity;

tigers, wolves, and lions will seek to devour one's flesh. Regarding the statement that "tigers and wolves smell the scent," I privately explain: when tigers and wolves smell the scent of blood and flesh from a person who eats meat, they come to harm them.
This is as explained in the *Pāṇḍubhūti-rāja-sūtra*; it is summarized here in the *Laṅkāvatāra* text.

Regarding the account of King Citrāṅgada eating meat, it is not yet fully detailed here. Because the author of the *Chao* (Excerpts) cites this statement, he specifically points to the meaning of a separate sutra so that people may observe it separately.
The full details of this account are as found in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Xiányújīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish).
(And so forth.)

Therefore, one should know that those who eat meat are the same as those who engage in the occupation of the butcher. This means that for the eater, the butcher is the instrument; since the act of butchering constitutes a karma, it is difficult to seek a different result [for the eater].

Regarding the statement that "one shares in the portion of killing," the ancients said: "For a person who eats meat, the taking of life throughout the ten directions all has a share in their portion. Why is this?
It is like when one commits adultery with a single woman, one's mind universally conditions all objects of form; or like when one steals from a single household.
Wealth. A greedy mind pervades the Dharma-realm; it devours the bodies of a single sentient being and exhausts the lives of all conscious beings.
Those who take wine and meat as their practice and understanding claim, "I am a great practitioner who makes no distinctions regarding objects.

They hold that eating wine and meat is the practice of the Mahāyāna, and those who form such an understanding consider themselves to have attained the essential meaning. Therefore, it is said: "Wine and meat constitute one's practice."
Those who understand this but do not realize they are consuming [forbidden things] are, in fact, followers of the Hīnayāna. To abstain from wine and meat is the practice of the Mahāyāna.

Nowadays, most people consume these things because they follow their afflictions, yet they insist on claiming there is no greed; this is a contradiction between mind and mouth, which brings calamity upon themselves.
An ancient said: "The mouth is the tomb-door of a thousand families; the belly is the ancient grave of ten thousand families.
The generals and officials of Yama—referring to the ox-headed attendants and others—are none other than the jailers.
Because they constantly boil and roast sinners within hell, how does a bhikṣu differ from them when he boils and roasts himself? Furthermore, his evil karma is already vast.

It is said thus because, having died, one becomes a jailer in the realm of Yama. This is because while alive one acts as a thief of the Buddha, and upon death one becomes the cause for becoming a ghost.
Regarding "meat from places of great sacrifice," this refers to what is called a "great sacrifice," such as the state's ritual worship at the Southern Suburb (Nanjiao).

Regarding alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, garlic, and their like: according to the *Cīvaravastu*, if a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says that he will recover only if he takes [these medicines], and that there is no other remedy if he does not, then taking them is permitted.
Having taken them, he must observe the "conformity rules" (*anuvartana-dharma*) for seven days:
he should stay in a small, remote corner of a dwelling, he must not lie upon the beds or bedding belonging to the Saṃgha, and he must not ascend to the Saṃgha’s latrines or urinals.
One must not enter the monks' sauna, lecture hall, or dining hall. One must not accept an invitation to a communal meal assigned by the monastic order.

One must not enter among the monks for a meal, nor enter the meditation quarters, nor join the assembly of monks for preaching the Dharma or the *poṣadha* ceremony. One must not go to any place where the entire monastic community has gathered.
One should not circumambulate a stupa; however, if the stupa is situated in the open air, one may perform a prostration from afar while remaining downwind.
When seven days have passed and the eighth day arrives, one bathes and washes one’s clothes; having done so, one may enter among the assembly.
To eat while not ill constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding "non-timely liquids," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: in the original context, it says that if they do not cause intoxication, drinking them at non-timely hours is permitted.

Thus we know that that which causes intoxication is, at that moment, the "medicine" [of alcohol]. Nowadays, there are those who use various grasses and trees, blending them to ferment into a liquor that possesses color, fragrance, and flavor no different from [actual] wine;
yet it does not intoxicate. The Buddha permitted this to be drunk in a secluded place.

It must not be the case that it lacks the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine, for if one drinks it and becomes intoxicated, they shall be punished according to the law. Regarding the fourteen kinds of fruit juices, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the first is as follows: [text continues].
1. Āmalaka juice; 2. Koli juice; 3. Anjīra juice; 4. Tinduka juice; 5. Pūga juice;
6. Bālūṣa juice; 7. Karkandhu juice; 8. Plantain fruit juice; 9. This is the Kāśika [juice].
10. *Pāraṅga* juice; 11. *Bāluka* juice; 12. Sugarcane juice (also called *śarkarā* juice); 13. *Harītakī* juice; 14.
*Khāraparika* juice (*from fascicle three and fascicle twenty-nine*). These fourteen kinds, when clear and pure, are all permitted to be drunk.

However, if they change into the color, fragrance, or flavor of alcohol, none of them are permitted to be drunk. If water remaining at the bottom of a vessel is washed by rain, it is also considered pure.

Regarding this, the *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "This water-drop purification is for the sake of purifying the flavor. Although the text mentions it in the context of fermented liquors (*pāna*), its meaning applies to all four medicinal substances (*catvāri bhaiṣajyāni*).

Just as clothing must be folded and marked with dots to destroy its original color, and just as food must have a drop of water added to it to destroy its original flavor, and just as footwear must be worn by a person to destroy its 'newness,' in all such cases, there is nothing that does not involve the destruction [of the original state]. I.
This is a skillful means (*upāya*). Otherwise, if one were to forcibly consume [the fruit] as if it were robust and use it exclusively for oneself, how could one forget [the need for moderation]?
Regarding "two cups of wine already prepared": the aforementioned "bitter wine" refers to vinegar.
According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, at one time the bhikṣus obtained many kinds of fruits; however, as there were few people and many fruits, they could not finish eating them, and the remainder—
[The monk] did not know for what purpose [this was intended]. The Buddha said: "I permit you to press the *nāḍika* fruit to extract its juice; it may be drunk until the first watch of the night.
If it does not reach the first watch, the flavor of the juice changes and becomes bitter and sour; it must not be drunk. Why? Because this has already become two-fold as alcohol. (The text ends here.
My private opinion is that "two-fold" refers to the completion of both the flavor of alcohol and the aroma of alcohol. Furthermore, it is also said to mean possessing the color of alcohol.
Regarding the phrase "the two are accomplished" (*liǎng chéng*) due to the flavor of wine, [Ji] says: In the common parlance of that time, people called "flavor" (*wèi*) "two" (*liǎng*).

For instance, upon smelling the aroma of wine, one would say, "There is the 'two' of wine. Likewise, seeing someone who has finished drinking and has the scent of wine on them, one would say, "It seems you have the 'two' of wine."
Regarding the eight kinds of juices from the four categories, which were consumed by the sages of old who were free from desire, they are not fully set forth here in this excerpt.
According to the Vinaya, these are: first, pear juice; second, jambu fruit juice; third, sour jujube juice; fourth, sugarcane juice;
fifth, *mṛdvīkā* (grape) juice; sixth, *śāluka* juice; seventh, *pālusa* juice; and eighth, pomegranate juice. All of these are derived from trees.
Fruit. Therefore, it may be used as non-time (vikāla) gruel. This refers to the *lūṣa* fruit given by a Brāhmaṇa to be offered to the bhikṣus;
the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said: "If it does not intoxicate a person, it should be drunk; if it intoxicates a person, it should not be drunk.

As for the sour jujube (*āmlavetasa*) mentioned above, it is common in the northern regions. The tree is five or six feet high; its seeds are small and red, and their taste is sour. It is not the [jujube] found today.

At that time, it was dried jujube. Regarding the term *piṇḍaphala* (pronounced with the *ruo shui* rhyme), Guo Pu stated: "It is a small shrub growing in clusters with thorns; its fruit is purple-red and edible.
Regarding the term *śālukapāna*, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "This refers to the roots of flowers such as the *utpala* and *kuvalaya*;
when pounded to extract the juice and refined until clear, it is called *śālukapāna*. The preceding text cited the *Vibhāṣā*.
"Jie" (解) means "the root of the lotus," which is its intended meaning. Regarding the term "bālūshī," Lì states that it resembles the āmalaka fruit.
Regarding what people of the world recognize as "proper food" and "proper medicine": it is like eating dry rice, ensuring that it does not appear coarse. Lü [Xinzhong] says:
Medicine possesses the efficacy of curing illness, hence it is called "proper medicine. Furthermore, it has the function of sustaining the body, thus it is named "proper food.

Because it incurs no fault of eating at improper times and does not invite reproach or disgrace, it is said that "it does not allow for coarseness to manifest. It is also said that one does not violate the proper time.
Regarding the fault of eating [at improper times]: thus it is said, "one must not let it appear coarse. The Upādhyāya says: this refers to the aforementioned five types.
Worldly people all recognize these as non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*) and know that bhikṣus may consume them outside of the proper time.

However, these seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), like rice and dried foods, can serve both as food and as medicine. As for the phrase "not letting it appear coarse": if worldly people were to... [the text continues].

"Consciousness" is censured by the world as being coarse and manifest. Now, since worldly people know that this is non-time medicine (vikāla-bhaiṣajya) which a bhikṣu may consume, it is not considered coarse.
Regarding the term "coarse," there are two interpretations. The first interpretation is the same as above.
The second interpretation is that this non-time medicine is similar to dry rice; if a bhikṣu were to consume it now, he should do so in a concealed place and not let [others see].

Regarding "worldly views": fearing the censure of others, it is said that one should not let [the substance] appear coarse. This applies even until its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been discarded.
The *Gāthā* treatise states: Question: May sugarcane syrup be accepted for seven days? Answer: It may be drunk. For how long may it be drunk? Until its intrinsic nature has been discarded.

As for the addition of "lard" (*vasā*) as a single item in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, these are ghee (*sarpis*), oil (*taila*), honey (*madhu*), lard (*vasā*), and fresh butter (*navanīta*).
Clarified butter (*sarpis*): these various medicines are pure and free from the odor of food consumed at improper times; they are taken all at once and may be consumed for seven days.

Therefore, they are called "seven-day medicines" (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*). Regarding the fact that the present commentary first cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and subsequently cites the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is done so to resolve doubts.

An ancient saying held that "fat is a timely medicine (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) because fat is produced from meat. It is for this reason that the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited here to demonstrate [the correct view].
Regarding fats among the seven-day medicines: when a physician instructs one to take the five kinds of fats, the Vinaya Master Ce (Cai) says:

"The Vinaya Master Xuanzang explains that if the 'oral consecration' (*karmavācanā*) is not performed, they may not be taken outside of the proper time; only after performing the oral consecration may they be taken for seven days. This applies to oils as well:
only after performing the oral consecration may they be taken for seven days. If the ritual is not performed, they are categorized as 'timely food' (*kālabhojana'). Now..."

The various masters do not accept this interpretation. They state that there are scriptural passages in all the schools which say: "Even if the formal rite (*vidhi*) is not performed, it may be consumed at improper times.
Regarding the "four hundred and four diseases": each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) has one hundred and one diseases; thus, there are four hundred and four diseases in total.

This is as explained in detail in the *Pañcarājāsūtra*. Regarding the use of the aforementioned three medicines for miscellaneous illnesses, some say that "miscellaneous" refers to a combined illness of water, fire, and wind elements, with no mention of illnesses of the earth element.

As for the passage in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* stating, "At that time, the bhikṣu Revata ate rock honey at an improper time," and so forth, even down to the instruction that the method of preparation should be thus:
according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it says: "At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Revata who ate rock honey at an improper time."
Regarding honey: Ānanda said, "It must not be eaten at improper times. I saw when they were making stone-honey that they pounded rice and put it inside.
He immediately became doubtful and informed the Buddha. The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and questioned Ānanda:

"Did you see when they were making stone-honey that they pounded rice and put it inside? Why was it done so? He replied, "The method of preparation requires it to be so. The Buddha said, "From now on, this is permitted."
This refers to taking food at an improper time.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, honey-candied sugar (śarkarā) must not be eaten indiscriminately, except by five types of persons.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states that when various lay devotees (gṛhapati) in the kingdom of Kośala encountered places along the road where there was no water, they offered water and also offered honey-candied sugar. Regarding this, the group of six bhikṣus...
While traveling, they arrived at this place; they ate only rock honey and did not drink water. A householder asked, "Why do you not drink water but eat only rock honey?
The group of six replied, "We are fond of rock honey and do not like drinking water. The householder censured them with disdain.
The bhikṣus heard this and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, I permit the consumption of stone honey (phāṇita) during five occasions.
What are these five? First, when traveling a long distance; second, when ill; third, when eating little; fourth, when unable to obtain food; fifth, when receiving an offering in a small place."
These were the five occasions on which the consumption of rock honey was permitted. From now on, if one does not drink water, the consumption of rock honey is not permitted;

if one consumes it [without drinking water], it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, during the two times of hunger and thirst, one may drink by mixing it with water.
If one follows the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, eating is permitted during the time of hunger, and drinking by mixing it with water is permitted during the time of thirst.
Regarding the rule that if one obtains curd while eating and does not finish it, one may churn it to make butter (*navanīta*):
Jì (Ji) says that if there is a vessel to hold it, one may churn it to make the butter; if there is no vessel, one must use a leather bag to hold it and shake it to make the butter.
"Shaking" is synonymous with "churning. Alternatively, even merely churning it may be termed "churning. The commentary notes: "This is verified as the method for making butter-oil."
