If there is someone sleeping, one must not disturb them abruptly; this is the same [rule]. One must not strike the ribs.

One should hold the staff against the front with both hands together and strike three times. If they still do not wake, if on the left side, one should press against the right knee; if on the right...
The edge [of the cushion] should support the left knee. Once one has awakened, one should take up the staff and walk away. This is the method for calling oneself to wakefulness.
Regarding the *dhyāna-guḍa* (meditation ball): it is pronounced "qiú jù" (求掬) with a reversed final; it is made of hair into a ball, extremely light and soft like a worldly hair-ball.

When sitting, if one fears falling asleep, it is placed upon the crown of the head; once one awakens, it immediately falls onto the knees, preventing pain. Regarding the *dhyāna-śilā* (meditation weight): it is made of bone.
As for the "Cornered" [image]: it may be about one inch square, and its application is the same as before. If there is someone who falls asleep, place it upon the crown of their head;
if the head remains upright, it will not fall. If the head moves while sleeping, it will fall onto the knees. As for the "Skeleton": [the application is the same].

"Standing" (li) refers to drawing a human skeleton and contemplating it while seated, according to the method of the "White Bone Contemplation" (śvetāsthi-smṛtyupasthāna); the contemplation of the body is likewise performed, whereby the White Bone Contemplation is perfected.
"Sūtras on Dhyāna" (chan jing) refers to the instructions for the practice of sitting meditation, utilizing the words of the sūtras;

these include such works as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Dhyānarahasya-sūtra*. "Virtuous Masters" (hao shi) refers to the teachers and craftsmen who instruct in the practice of sitting meditation.

Regarding "good mirrors," Zhiyi states that by having a good teacher, one is able to be taught so as to attain understanding and contemplative insight, thereby knowing the true characteristics of phenomena as they are;
if one holds divergent views, one is a non-Buddhist. Regarding "clothing," Zhiyi states that these are the garments and requisites necessary for seated meditation to sustain the body;
if the clothing is torn, there will be many fleas and lice, and one will be unable to sit in peace.
Regarding the Buddha personally taking up woodworking tools to repair the temple gate:
according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the Buddha was in the country of Āravī, the lintel of the temple gate had broken. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Why is the lintel of this temple gate broken?
He replied, "The carpenter was in a hurry and could not finish the work. The Buddha immediately ordered that wood and tools be brought. After Ānanda had fetched them, the Buddha—
He repaired the lintel of the gate of the Ātavi-stūpa. Having finished the repairs, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From now on, I permit you to keep all kinds of wooden tools;
whichever bhikṣu is able to perform repairs should do so. As for Mahākāśyapa’s frequent treading of mud to plaster the monks' quarters:
when the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra went to visit the Bamboo Grove to observe it. The king asked the Elder Mahākāśyapa: "Now..."
"Where is he? The bhikṣu replied, "He is currently on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa treading mud. The king went at once to see him and asked, "Venerable sir, why do you do this yourself?
He replied, "Great King, who would do it for me? The king said, "I shall provide you with laborers.
Having spoken, the king returned. At a later time, the king went again to the Bamboo Grove to observe as before and inquired after him.
Mahākāśyapa, the bhikṣus replied, “He is on Vulture Peak Mountain treading mud. The king went to see him and engaged in the same exchange as before.
The king said, “I shall provide you with laborers. Kāśyapa replied, “Great King, you have said this many times already.”
But he was not granted [the boon]. The king then felt ashamed and asked his ministers, "Did I previously say such a thing?

They replied, "Your Majesty did indeed say so. He asked, "When was that? They replied, "On such a day and month. Calculating from the time of that previous statement, exactly five hundred days had passed.
At that time, the people captured five hundred bands of thieves and brought them to the king to be executed. The king questioned the thieves, saying:
"Are you able to provide for these good people? He replied, "I am able. The King wished to have these five hundred men provide for the bhikṣus;
fearing they might steal or seize the monks' property, he granted them many fields, houses, and subjects, and provided double their rations.

Not far from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), he established a village of *kappiyakārakas* (pure-men) to constantly supply the Saṃgha. The *Siyi* (Private Record) states in its third fascicle: [text follows].
The five hundred *śrāmaṇeras* who guarded Zhuyuan Temple harbored doubts regarding this passage; some said it referred to them.
If there is a layperson capable of repairing a dilapidated room and offers it [to the Sangha], it is established that the Sangha performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

"To entrust this dilapidated room to a layperson for repair. [The author] privately notes: "In the Vinaya, there are two types of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and one announcement).

One is to entrust the Sangha with the repair of a room; the other is to entrust a layperson with the repair. It is essential that the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* be performed in harmony with the Sangha before it may be granted. If there is no such harmony, it cannot be granted.
As for the practice of inscribing 'the room of donor So-and-so,' this refers to a layperson acting on behalf of the Sangha within the monastery."
Since there are many who build houses, the name of the donor is inscribed so that they may know where [the house] is located.
One who repairs a ruined house may reside there for six years, while one who builds a new house may reside there for twelve years.

This is according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya); however, it differs slightly from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it states: "Dhaniya built [a hut] upon the ground belonging to the Saṃgha."
A dwelling was constructed, and not long after it was finished, many senior monks (*sthavira*) arrived. They were granted residence there according to their seniority.

In this way, as more dwellings were gradually built, they were all eventually divided among the Saṃgha. Consequently, complaints arose: "I labored hard to build this dwelling, braving both cold and heat;
before the building was even complete, the seniors have already seized it. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From this day forward..."
When a *karmadāna* bhikṣu constructs a dwelling, he should be granted a five-year residency. He must come before the Saṃgha, kneel with palms joined, and request the formal procedure (*dharma*).

The Saṃgha then performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) to grant him the five-year residency. Regarding those who should be granted a "one-time" residency:
this refers to the fact that one year consists of three seasons, each season comprising four months; since he is now granted a stay of four months, it is called "one time. Thus far.
The commentary on the nineteen chapters is hereby completed.
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (Sifen lü chao pi), Fascicle Thirteen, Part One;
*Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Thirteen, Part Two.
Chapter Twenty: On the Method for Cultivating [Meditation] in Response to Alms.

First, to clarify the intent of this section: the preceding chapter explained the alms bowl, which is fundamentally for receiving food. When partaking of food in response to such offerings, it is necessary that one’s conduct accords with the proper ritual.
If one does not establish contemplative observation, this becomes the root of suffering; therefore, this text follows. Regarding the term "in response to alms" (*daishi*): now...
Plowing fields and cultivating crops are not the proper observances for those on the Path. Food and material provisions are all offered through the power of faith.

Since one faces such substantial benefits, it is only right that one should maintain a spiritual mind and practice frugality, severing all greedy attachments. These are intended solely to sustain the Path, not to nourish resentment.
One must examine one’s own conduct to see if it accords with this Dharma; if one truly lacks the Path, then even a single cup of rice and a single robe would be more than enough.
It is difficult to digest. It can eliminate the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*). One may receive a million [offerings] daily, and all the sages permit it.
Therefore, one must establish the gate of remediation (*pratipakṣa*) in relation to giving. Thus it is said. "In relation to" (*prati*) refers to the person who receives;

"giving" (*dāna*) refers to the object offered; "establishing" (*utthāpana*) means to initiate; "remediation" (*pratipakṣa*) arises from principle. Because one establishes the contemplation of remediation in relation to what is received, it is so called. Ji says: "In relation to giving."

The two characters "object" (所) refer to that which is to be remedied, while the two characters "remedy" (能) refer to the means of remediation; that is to say, one gives rise to the remedy in response to the object to be remedied.
Because both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is so called.

Now, as for "merit arising from a pure field," this is clearly established: one who has donned the saffron robes and maintains the banner of the monastic marks, observing the precepts with purity, is called a "pure field.
Such a person is worthy of receiving the four types of offerings from gods and humans, and can cause the donor to receive the merit of protection and its subsequent recompense;

therefore, it is said that "merit arises from a pure field. The meaning is like that of an Arhat, who is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat). Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One leaves the household life for the sake of liberation."
[One who is thus] may receive their turn in the monastic succession. Therefore, we know that if one now leaves the household life for the sake of the Way, only then is one called a *saṃgha*.

Those who seek fame and profit are not fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Xuān said: "In these times, practitioners merely accept the resources of a field of merit, yet for the most part lack the thought of liberation.
This is a blemish upon the Buddha’s intent; it does nothing but weary and obstruct the spiritual consciousness. Jì said: "The Buddha-field is the most pure. Ló... [text fragment].
The Han dynasty [view] ranks purity next. This is because the merit of giving to a Buddha is greater than that of an Arhat, and so on, down to ordinary monks whose merit gradually diminishes.
Because the Buddha has exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*), he is designated as a "field of purity" (*śukla-kṣetra*). Regarding the statement that the Way gives rise to few desires, Master Li says:
it is said because those with few desires are without artificiality or worldly affairs, and thus accord with the Way. As the sutra says regarding those with few desires—
For a person, this is precisely what constitutes *nirvāṇa*. One should cultivate even a mere lack of desire (*alpecchatā*);
how much more so when a lack of desire can give rise to all manner of meritorious qualities (*guṇa*). The *Shoushu* states: "What is called 'having few desires'? As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
not giving rise to greed for wealth not yet obtained is called having few desires; not giving rise to greed for wealth already obtained is called contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*). Therefore...
Contentment pertains to the present; fewness of desires pertains to the future. These constitute the essence of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

That is to say, contentment arises in relation to the present state, while fewness of desires arises in relation to the future state. It is difficult not to take even a single coin in the present, yet it is easy to renounce the status of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) in the future.
Regarding "the family of merit" and so forth: this refers to the person capable of giving; such a person is a family of merit. Since...
Because one seeks merit, one must simply practice extensive and generous giving. Now, when a steward provides offerings for the great assembly, they must simply exert their utmost sincerity.
Yet, [the donor] instead says, "How could your parents in a secular home have such cakes and food? As for the monks within the hall—
At first, one must think: "My parents have supported me for ten thousand days; how could there be such food [as this]? One must give rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
The administrative monk (*karmadāna*) must certainly not speak such words.

As for the recipient who accepts the offering with moderation and restraint, it means that the person receiving the gift, bearing the offerings of another's faith, knows that the gift is difficult to digest; therefore, they must exercise self-restraint and measure their intake. They must not...
One accumulates much karma that results in the long-term bondage of craving. Thus, the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
"The hand that is able to extend and give is called 'Exalted Adornment' (*vyūha-viśeṣa*). But if the recipient is able to withdraw their hand, the 'Exalted Adornment' surpasses that even further.

If a person says, 'I shall give,' the value of these words is difficult to measure; yet if the recipient says, 'I have enough,' that which is difficult to measure surpasses even that. It further states: "Freedom from illness is the foremost."
"Profit. Contentment is the supreme wealth; a virtuous friend is the supreme relative; Nirvana is the supreme bliss.

Regarding the phrase "one who gives much without weariness," this clarifies the person capable of giving. Regarding "receiving little in limited measure," this refers to the person who receives the gift.

"The form participates in the sacred robes; the form that awaits is established by relying on material sustenance. This clarifies that although the physical form and robes are sublime, they merely represent the outward observance of learning from the Sages.
However, because the physical body and its life-force remain coarse, one must rely on food to sustain and maintain it.

Regarding "skillfully responding to the Dharma such that there is no flaw between subject and object," the *Zilin* (Lexicon Forest) states that "responding" (*ying*) means "to be appropriate. It refers to the assembly where the faculties (*indriya*) and the phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are in mutual correspondence. Thus, [the term] is established.
[The Master] Ming said: "If one thus guards and upholds the prohibitive precepts without defiling the received essence, this is called being 'well-attuned to the Dharma.
Consequently, both the giver and the recipient will not fall into the error of [clinging to] giving. Therefore it is said that 'giver and recipient are without flaw.

The several phrases below present both aversion and aspiration side by side, and manifest both gain and loss together. As for the statement, 'One must not take worldly affairs as a standard; otherwise, where would the guiding rule find its reliance?'—it is because there is no other way."

There is none. "Gauge" (*gui*) means circularity. If one cannot maintain the precepts and practice meditative concentration when responding to and guiding acts of giving, there will be transgressions and failures;

therefore, it is said that one must not rely on such matters. This causes both the path of merit and the path of wisdom to have no place to rest. Regarding "compassion" (*ci*), there are two interpretations.
First, "gauge" (*gui*) means circularity, while "square" (*ju*) arises from rectitude; this refers to the principles of squareness and roundness. If one receives [offerings] contrary to the Dharma...
Giving is the function of the compass and square; it has no place to which it may be attached. Furthermore, another interpretation is that "gui" (compass) means "to seek.
When a donor (*dānapati*) gives food, they originally intend to seek the cultivation of merit (*puṇyakarman*). Now, if a bhikṣu acts contrary to the Dharma, he causes the donor to seek merit for him;
thus, the meaning [of the gift] has no basis. Regarding "having power but no task," Lü says: "By being able to be skillful, one neither exceeds nor falls short; there is none..."

It refers to increasing and decreasing. Because one uses it to sustain one's own body, it is called "having power. To say "without affairs" means there are no matters of increasing or decreasing suffering.
[The author] privately comments: For one who aspires to the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*), the conditions for the Path possess power.

Furthermore, it is said that being able to sustain the physical form is called "having power," while contemplating in stillness without greedy seeking is called "being without affairs. [Master] Li says this refers to the highest grade (*uttama*).

By relying on the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), even those of middle or inferior capacity can obtain the one hundred and one types of long robes and other requisites; thus they are fully provided for and free from suffering and distress—hence it is so called.
Regarding the establishment of the meaning of "conditions for the Path" (*mārga-pratyaya*): this means that clothing and food are the conditions for practicing the Path. "Practice arises from these":

because these material conditions are complete, the practice of the precepts (*śīla*) arises therefrom. Furthermore, the practices of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) [arise] only...
It can give rise [to delusion].

As for the statement that "if one indulges the mind, it is not the flavor that gives rise to delusion," this means: if one gives free rein to a greedy mind, even though it is not actually a delicious flavor, it nevertheless gives rise to confusion and dissipation.
For example, wine is a drug of madness; once drunk, it exhausts one's household wealth and leads to wild delusion.
Lust and debauchery—these are not wholesome flavors. That people greedily drink them is entirely due to the unrestrained mind.

Just as the *chāngbǔ* (a type of fermented plant) is extremely foul-smelling, yet King Wen of Zhou made it into a soup; or as scabs and crusted sores are utterly filthy, yet Liu Yong delighted in them.

The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "King Wen of Zhou was fond of *chāngbǔ* pickles. The *Songshu* by Shen Yue states: "Liu Yong was by nature addicted to eating scabs and crusts. The officials of Nan-kang...

There were about two hundred people; regardless of whether they were guilty or innocent, they were given lashes one after another. The scabs from these lash wounds were constantly provided as food for Yong.
Regarding the phrase "Yue-zhi," "yue" means to limit, and "zhi" means the mind.

If one can limit and cut off the mind, then even if one were faced with the celestial kitchen, one would not give rise to impure thoughts. Furthermore, take milk, for example: it is a delicious dish. However, if...
If one forms the perception of pus and blood, then a sense of revulsion arises. When good and evil emerge from within the breast, it refers to the arising of attachment or revulsion toward food;
both are driven by the mind. As for the term "within the breast," the human mind resides in the center; thus, the breast is centered within the mind.
Therefore, it is called "harbored within. The phrase "rising and sinking are entrusted to the *fāngcùn*" (the square-inch) serves to explain the preceding sentence. *Fāngcùn* is also the heart;
the human heart dwells within the abdomen, residing solely within that space of one square inch. Its color is intensely red; thus, it is as when Jie and Zhou cut out the hearts of the worthy.
If one can cultivate the prohibitions and precepts and develop revulsion toward food, this is good, and one will ascend.

For humans and devas, when reaching the path to Nirvāṇa, if one damages one’s practice and extensively commits various transgressions, being greedy for food is an evil that causes one to sink into the paths of the three miserable realms.
These preceding phrases clearly elucidate gain and loss and fully manifest right and wrong.

Regarding "not contemplating the conditions of time": cherishing and nourishing this body results in its ultimate end, death; this is called the "condition of time. To neglect or overlook it is a transgression.

Regarding the "deep net" (*gahana*): it is established as meaning the "net of the teachings. Since the monastic community lacks frugality and thus violates the Buddha’s net of teachings, this is termed a "leak" (*āsrava*).
Because they do not abide within the net of the Dharma, it is called a "leak."
"How can one allow such defiled traces within the context of formal matters? Here, "matters" refers to the four types of material offerings; "traces" refers to the traces of the mind.

This means that in relation to matters such as food and clothing, one allows for the acceptance of such defilements. Master Jianyi stated: "This refers to disturbances and commotion during the major and minor meals.
The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) explains: "It arises from not revering the Dharma, such that the mind has no aspiration [for purity]."
The Way involves letting go of body and speech, manifesting through the pretext of eating. Even worldly scholars say: "Do not speak while eating; do not speak while reclining."
"Stately as if in thought; composed in speech. Arrogance must not be fostered; desire must not be indulged; ambition must not be overfilled.
The Way stands high above the mundane world—how could one act contrary to this? However, the phrase 'the nine schools are worldly' uses the mundane to illustrate the Way.

It may also be said that it uses what is below to illustrate what is above. As for the nine schools: first, the School of the Way (Dao); second, the School of Confucianism (Ru); third, the School of Yin and Yang."

The streams: 1) the stream of the Dharma; 2) the stream of names; 3) the stream of words; 4) the stream of the four dharmas; 5) the stream of names; 6) the stream of ink; 7) the stream of the vertical and horizontal; 8) the stream of agriculture; 9) the stream of the miscellaneous.
The explanations are as found in the *Chongqing yi ji* (Record of the Ritual for Weight and Lightness), etc. Regarding "the various secularists":

this refers to the various masters of the hundred schools, such as Master Hui, Laozi, Master Liu, Confucius, and other such worldly persons. Laozi said: "The five flavors cause the mouth to lose its sense of taste; the five notes [cause the ear to lose its sense of hearing]."
"It deafens the ears; the five colors blind the eyes," and so forth. "In eating, one must yield; in labor, one must take it upon oneself. Furthermore, a book says:
"One who eats the five grains should remember the exhaustion of the plowman; one who wears a single piece of silk should reflect on the toil of the weaver.
For one who is delayed at the starting point, clarity arises immediately: if one wishes to travel far, one must rely on feet capable of traveling far. If...
If one lags at the start of the journey, how can there be any destination reached? Now, when a bhikṣu guards the precepts, the precepts are likened to the feet for proceeding toward Bodhi.
Since he has now broken the precepts, this is to lag at the start of his journey. Otherwise, by setting out, he would sever delusions and ultimately obtain the benefits of the Way.
Therefore, the text says: "For example, it is like a person whose feet are injured; they are unable to go anywhere and will surely fall into the mire.
This means that once the feet of the precepts are broken, one will inevitably incur retribution in the three miserable realms; hence these words.
There are four ways in which a bhikṣu may utilize donated goods. First, "using like a thief" and so forth. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), these are:
first, using like a thief; second, using as a debtor; third, using as a kinsman or friend; and fourth, using as an owner. What is meant by "using like a thief"?
It refers to a bhikṣu who, lacking precepts, receives food and drink according to the order of the saṃgha. Regarding "debtor," it refers to a bhikṣu who accepts...
When a person consumes food, drink, or clothing, they should first form the thought: "This is the use of what is owed.
If a bhikṣu of sharp faculties, at the time of receiving food, forms this thought for every morsel; or if one of dull faculties, before eating, first forms it once;
or when receiving clothing, the one of sharp faculties forms the thought day after day—the same applies to dwellings and bedding. If one of dull faculties, he should first form it [once].

A single thought. "Not so" refers to the function of being accountable. Regarding the "function of a kinsman and friend": the seven types of trainees (śaikṣa) enjoy the gifts they receive just as a son enjoys his father's property;
thus, it is called the "function of a kinsman and friend. Regarding the "function of a master": this refers to the Arhats.

They are those who enjoy the gifts offered. As for the "seven learners" (*śaikṣa*), they consist of the three fruits and the four candidates (*pratipannaka*). The three fruits are well known. The four candidates refer to the stages prior to the four fruits;

because they have not yet entered the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they are called "candidates. These seven individuals have not yet completely exhausted their fetters and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
They are not true *arhats*. Only when one has attained the stage of an *arhat* and exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms is one truly worthy of offerings.

Therefore, [the gift] is regarded as one's own property. Thus, the treatise clarifies that while the giving is pure, the recipient is impure. Regarding these four propositions, according to the treatise, it says:
"When the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was being preached, the Buddhas of the other directions each commanded their bodhisattvas to send flowers to present as offerings. This is the explanation.
Kāśyapa Buddha, Śākyamuni accepted these thousand-petaled golden lotuses and further scattered them upon the Buddhas in other Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because of the Buddhas—and because the Buddhas of the ten directions are the foremost field of merit—this offering brings manifold merit.
Why is this? It is because many Buddhas are personally honored. Within the Buddha-dharma, there are four kinds [of fields of merit].
Regarding giving: first, the giver is pure while the recipient is impure; second, the giver is impure while the recipient is pure;
third, both the giver and the recipient are pure; fourth, both the giver and the recipient are impure.
Now, when the Buddha gives medicine, it is a case where both are pure; this merit is the greatest.

Regarding the statement, "This person immediately attains the Dharma as it truly is," some say this means that by contemplating the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as empty of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*), one attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Their intention is that even an Arhat still possesses attachment to dharmas (*dharma-abhiniveśa*). Bin (Bian) counters this, saying: "As for the emptiness of persons, that is what is attained by Śrāvakas;

the gate of contemplation on the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) belongs to the stage of Bodhisattvas. Bin refutes this, not permitting it, and states that Śrāvakas likewise do not [possess such attachment].
One attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the passage from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and so forth: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (20) and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (166–167), this meaning is explained in detail within the exposition of the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*).
Specifically, the statement that one generates revulsion toward food and so forth, and perceives the world as undesirable, is intended to reveal the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
This is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the textual exposition. Furthermore, regarding the perception of repulsiveness in food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*):

it means that when a practitioner gives rise to revulsion toward food, they contemplate the food in their hand as having originated from grains and the like; those grains, in turn, from seeds in the field; and those seeds, from soil, mud, and filth.
Since it has thus arisen through a succession of impurities, what wise person would feel attachment to it? Moreover—
When begging for food, at the time of morning ablutions and chewing the *śīrṣa* twig, one should regard the water as urine and the *śīrṣa* twig as a dry bone.
When putting on robes and entering a village, one should regard the robe as moist human skin, the waistband as human intestines, the alms bowl as a skull, and the mendicant’s staff as a shin bone.
Upon seeing pebbles and stones on the path, one should regard them as skeletal remains. Having arrived...
When seeing a village, one should avoid it by forming the perception of it being a cemetery. When seeing men and women, one should form the perception of them as skeletons.

When obtaining a cake while begging for alms, one should perceive it as a human stomach. If one obtains parched flour, one should perceive it as bone-dust. If one obtains coarse salt (*khaṇḍa-lavaṇa*), one should perceive it as human teeth (referring here to granular salt).
When obtaining rice, one should conceive of it as maggots; when obtaining vegetables, as human hair; when obtaining soup or broth, as filthy dregs;
when obtaining milk, as human brain; when obtaining ghee or honey, as human fat; and when obtaining fish or meat, as human flesh.
When drinking [liquor], one should conceive of it as human blood. When receiving *hlādana-guḍa* (joy-pills), one should conceive of them as dry excrement.

If eating among the Saṃgha, one should conceive of the pure grass as the hair of a dead person, and the seat as a heap of bones. Regarding the food and drink received, it is as explained extensively above.
Question: Why is it necessary to cultivate the perception of impurity regarding food, drink, and so forth? Answer: One reflects extensively on this:

throughout beginningless birth and death, one has transmigrated through the five destinies because of taking the impure to be pure; now, wishing to oppose that [delusion] and proceed toward the bliss of nirvāṇa, one must do so.
If one conceives pure thoughts regarding food and the like, it increases craving and obstructs the Noble Path; therefore, one must cultivate revulsion.
Once revulsion has been produced, having brought body and mind under control and refinement, why would one find joy in the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of birth and death?
(This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Shijia zongji*; one should consult it at the appropriate time.)
Regarding the passage, "It would be better to take red-hot iron as one's garment," etc., the sixtieth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala. While traveling among the people with the bhikṣus, he saw a great mass of fire along the way.
He asked the bhikṣus, "Are you able to throw yourselves into this fire? The bhikṣus all replied that they could not. The Buddha said, "It would be better to throw oneself into this fire."
Their skin and flesh will be burned away, and their tendons and bones will be consumed until nothing remains.

This is the transgression of concealing a breach of the precepts: by touching the women of other kṣatriyas or brāhmaṇas, one commits a sin that is rotten and decayed within, yet appears whole and pure without.

Consuming the faithful offerings of others, because one cannot digest them, one falls into the three evil realms and suffers for a long night. It would be better to have one’s feet pierced with a hot trident than [to commit such an act].
One may accept the prostrations and offerings of faithful men and women;
one would rather wear garments of hot iron that burn the body to its very marrow than accept various fine robes from men and women.
One would rather swallow a hot iron hook that burns through the five viscera and exits from below than accept food or drink from faithful men and women. One would rather sit upon a bed of hot iron...
An iron house. One does not accept beds, seats, bedding, or dwellings from those with faith. Why is this?

Because one who accepts hot iron hooks, iron beds, or iron houses will not, by reason of this, fall into the three evil realms. Such a person is not a śramaṇa though claiming to be one, nor is their conduct that of a brahmacārin, and so forth.
The rest is as explained in the *Śāstra*. When the Buddha spoke these words, the blood of sixty bhikṣus boiled up from their faces.
When Kong [Zong] emerged, the guest said: "Because there were indeed transgressions in the past, sixty bhikṣus attained the fruit of untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).

Because the sages advance upon the Path, sixty bhikṣus became free from dust and defilement (*viraja-vigata-mala*), thereby entering the state of sainthood (*ārya*) from the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Regarding those who committed offenses in secret while their insides were empty and rotting, this is extensively cited from the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* (Fo zang jing); it is left for the speaker to elaborate."

(As stated above). The preceding section concludes the explanation of the second meaning: the skillful means of cultivation through aversion. Below is the third section, which correctly elucidates the teaching on the contemplation of existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the Vinayamātṛkā: a bhikṣu of sharp faculties, while eating, forms a mental note with every morsel; when putting on his robes, he forms a mental note with every act of dressing.

Regarding this, an examination of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* reveals that these words are not found therein; rather, the matter originates from the *Sammohavinodanī* (the *Kṣudrakavastu-bhāṣya*), as previously cited.
The *Buddhapiṭaka* states: "Having begged for food within the village, he departs from the village and proceeds to the water's edge," and so forth.
As stated in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra-śāstra* (and so forth):
Although there are those who occasionally give rise to longing for gains and the like, it is established that one must always practice contemplation regarding all gains and such.
However, clothing is rare [in its occurrence], whereas food must be taken into the mouth daily and thus constitutes a frequent occurrence. For this reason, we shall now proceed based on...
Regarding the establishment of this contemplation: that which does not arise within a solid rock—according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, in the chapter on "Clarifying Causes," it states:
"All bodily karmas and sensations arise from afflictions (*kleśa*); furthermore, one who has severed the afflictions no longer undergoes rebirth.
Thus, we know that the existence of a body is entirely due to afflictions. Question: Do all sentient beings not already lack afflictions?
[Objection: They arise only after birth; for example, a person has no teeth at the time of birth, but they grow later. [Response: This is not so.

For those possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*), whatever characteristics exist—such as weeping—are present at the very moment of birth. Therefore, all [characteristics] arise simultaneously with the afflictions.
Furthermore, it is observed that sentient beings are mostly born in places such as latrines, and not upon things such as solid rocks. It should be understood accordingly.
Because one knows that through attachment to odors, tastes, and so forth, one is born therein; therefore, it is known that birth arises from afflictions (*kleśa*). Question:
One should not be born in places such as the hells, because there is no mental craving for the pleasure of the hells and so forth. Answer:
Due to the power of ignorance (*moha*), sentient beings give rise to perverted thoughts. At the time of death, they see the hells from afar and mistake them for lotus ponds.
Because of attachment, one is born therein. As it is said in the sūtras: those who die of heat and thirst are born in the Cold Ice Hell;
those who die of cold are born in the Hot Hell; and those who die of thirst are born among the water-insects.
If one is greedy for food and drink, one will be reborn as a worm within a corpse; all of this is due to food.

Since [giving] is performed for the sake of seeking merit, how can one discard it? According to the *Śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada* regarding the precept against dropping food and drink, laypeople reproached him, saying:
"Venerable sir, do you think this greed is something produced by interest-free money? I shall seize the share belonging to my wife and children!"
"One gives out of merit; even a single grain requires a hundred labors to produce. Why, then, do you cast it upon the ground?
This is a ruined person; what path or Dharma does he possess?"
"Not reckoning others" means, as Jì explains: when one's body and mind are robust, one becomes arrogant and conceited, failing to reckon with others or counting them among the ranks of people.
Regarding "giving rise to anger upon receiving inferior food and giving rise to delusion during midday meals," this is because three perceptions arise based on three objects;

because three perceptions [arise]—namely, the perception of suffering, the perception of pleasure, and the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—three feelings arise based on those three perceptions.
The three types of conduct (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate) lead, by means of these three conducts as causes, to rebirth in the three realms—the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Master Bin says: "Based on the three kinds of food (manifesting the first consciousness-mind), the three perceptions arise (manifesting the second perception-mind).
Because of the three perceptions, the three feelings arise (manifesting the third feeling-mind). Because of the three feelings, the three conducts are produced (intended to manifest...)"
This is the fourth stage of mental activity). According to the Satyasiddhi school, the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise in succession;

they do not arise simultaneously. Furthermore, there are no separate mental factors apart from the mind itself. Most other schools do not hold this view, as they maintain that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the mental factors each have their own distinct measure [of duration].
Now, in the Satyasiddhi school, there are no mental factors apart from the mind. The mental faculty (*manas*) arises immediately after consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Perception (*saṃjñā*). Following perception, feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] arise in succession (and so forth). The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states: "However, there are three kinds of food: namely, the excellent, the inferior, and the mediocre.
Due to these three types of objects, three perceptions arise; next, three feelings arise; and subsequently, three formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, thereby accumulating suffering.
For example, with delicious food, a pleasant feeling arises first, followed by the formation of greed; with poor food, a painful feeling arises."

Afterwards, one gives rise to conduct born of hatred. During the meal, one gives rise to equanimity, and afterwards, one gives rise to conduct born of delusion. These conducts lead toward the three paths: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Alternatively, it may be explained as follows: in response to delicious food, the mind gives rise to a favorable perception; after this favorable perception arises...
Immediately a pleasant sensation arises. Following the pleasant sensation, the mind gives rise to greed. Regarding unpleasant sensations, the mind gives rise to unwholesome perceptions.

Following these unwholesome perceptions, the mind gives rise to painful sensations. Following the painful sensations, the mind gives rise to aversion. This occurs in relation to food that is to be consumed in moderation.

One should contemplate while arising from the middle state. After contemplating the middle state, the mind gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*). After equanimity, the mind gives rise to delusion (*moha*). It is essential that contemplation arises first;
then the three unwholesome states will not arise, and one’s karma will not deceive them, for one experiences the fruits of good and evil by oneself.

Thus, the popular proverb says: "Calamities and blessings have no gate; they are summoned only by people themselves. This indeed has its basis. Regarding the phrase "the midday meal is not divided": [it refers to the fact that] one does not distinguish between [the various flavors].

Regarding the "mind’s eye" (*cittanetra*): Ciyun says that this refers to eating food that is neither good nor bad, giving rise to a mind of the Middle Way (*madhyama*), and being unable to give rise to greed or anger due to ignorance;

this is called the "undiscriminating mind’s eye. As for the latter two [phrases] being "knowable": Ciyun says that by being free from anger one is born among humans, and by being free from ignorance one is born among the *asuras*.
This is because, within the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*), three are considered wholesome paths.
Regarding the second section, the "Contemplation on the Four Right Practices as Good Medicine," the *Śāstra-vṛtti* states:

First, to eliminate old illnesses; second, to prevent new illnesses from arising. Hunger is an old illness; if one suffers from hunger or thirst, it hinders spiritual cultivation. To eliminate this illness, one must eat.
As for "new illnesses," if one does not know the proper measure and consumes food in excess, it will inevitably lead to disease; therefore, one must be mindful of moderation.
Contentment. Thus, one does not give rise to new ailments. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of removing old ailments," the commentary states that hunger and thirst are considered old ailments.
"Not giving rise to new ailments" means that once food has been obtained, the suffering of the four great elements—namely hunger and thirst—does not arise.
Furthermore, regarding the two similes used, according to the *Lun-shu* (Commentary on the Treatise), it says: "The first is like oiling a cart. The *Lun-shu* further states: "It is like a person..."

When riding in a carriage, one applies oil to the hubs and axles not out of attachment to them, but because one fears that these hubs and axles might burn or become so stiff as to be difficult to turn, thereby obstructing the journey;
therefore, they must be oiled. Raising this body is likewise: one does not give rise to attachment toward it.
Second, it is like a person wishing to cross a perilous difficulty who, though his son has already died, manages to cross over despite hunger and poverty.
One should reflect: "If my son were already dead, I would not eat his flesh; my life would not be preserved, and I could not cross over this perilous difficulty.
Thus, one eats the flesh of one's son. At the time of eating, there must be no attachment. My receiving food now is also like this.
If one eats only after completing such contemplation, then one incurs no debt toward the donor and further increases merit. Otherwise, it is not so.
*Duṣkṛta*. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the continuity of life," the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "If one does not consume [food], life will be severed.

Because it is necessary to increase and sustain the life-force so that it continues, one must accept food. *Lokadhātusthiti-sūtra* says: "If one does not eliminate the inversion of self, this is external..."
The Way does not permit one to accept even a single cup of water from another. The Buddha-treasury is likewise.

According to the *Lokadhātu-parivarta Sūtra* (Holding the World Sūtra), the Buddha expounded the Dharma of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) for the Bodhisattva Lokadhātu. This is to extinguish the reality and unreality [of the aggregates] and cause those within the five aggregates to cultivate supramundane dharmas.
If a person is greedily attached to the five aggregates, they are not my disciple; I am not their teacher; they do not follow me forth.
"Householder, such a person has merely entered a deviant path. I would not even permit such a person to leave the household life, let alone accept their offerings.
Why is this? Such a person belongs to the faction of external paths;

when the Dharma is about to perish in the future, they will leave the household life within my Dharma, yet they will be deeply attached to the five aggregates and enter into false and deviant views, thereby gaining [a semblance of] attainment within my Dharma."
Having left the household life, they wrap their necks in saffron robes, yet constantly delight in frequenting the homes of laypeople.
Know that such persons are no different from non-Buddhists; nevertheless, because they claim to follow my Dharma, they receive much respect and offerings from others.
For such people, I do not permit even a single cup of water. The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Śāriputra, "If there are those who say of me..."

To speak of "persons" or to speak of "sentient beings" is merely the use of provisional designations. Even those who conceive of attaining even the slightest dharma oppose the Buddha and contend with him;
they have all entered onto a false path and are not my disciples. One who views things in this way—clinging to self and person—is not permitted to leave the household life or receive the precepts.
Nor is such a person permitted to receive even a single drink of water for their own sustenance in future lives.
There may be a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma to laypeople, delighting in eloquent speech and being well-versed in the various sūtras.

Relying on mere words, he delights in literary embellishment; he seeks only to please people's minds and prizes fame and profit. Skilled in worldly affairs, he delivers impure teachings and relies solely on clever rhetoric.
Lacking true majesty and virtue, he destroys the causes for nirvāṇa and takes no pleasure in meditative concentration, constantly [engaged in such pursuits] day and night.

They delight in talk and litigation; they lie upon thick quilts and mattresses, yet lack even a single thought of compliance with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), let alone being able to attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
They take pleasure in shallow and mundane speech, and are unable to diligently study the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Such evil persons, for the sake of gain and offerings, praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they seek only to sustain their lives for the sake of wealth and profit.
[Śāriputra] replied, "I did. I also received much offerings of clothing and food.

Within the Abhidharma and Sūtras, I engaged in debates of my own, sometimes speaking of annihilationism or eternalism, sometimes of action (*saṃskāra*), or of non-action (*asaṃskāra*). At that time, there were many non-Buddhist teachings;
they caused the right view of sentient beings to be destroyed, and my pure Dharma gradually declined and vanished, Śāriputra."
"No. I have long dwelt in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction. The *bodhi* I have realized has been destroyed by these wicked people.
Thus ends the explanation of the fourth method of contemplation. Below follows the clarification of the fifth [method], the dharma of various characteristics for treating [afflictions] accordingly.
The tradition states that one must not exceed three spoonfuls of food when eating in order to sever all evils and so forth.
These subsequent phrases constitute the essence of bodhi, for they represent the three clusters of pure precepts (tri-śīla-skandha).

Furthermore, it is said: "Because one knows moderation in eating, old suffering is extinguished and new suffering does not arise; one possesses strength and has no [excessive] business. According to the Vinaya text, it should be stated:
"Old suffering is extinguished, new suffering does not arise, there is neither increase nor decrease, one possesses strength and has no [excessive] business, and the body is made peaceful and happy.
The *Lì shū* commentary explains: According to the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, if a person is able to [endure] hunger and thirst...
The arising of painful sensations in body and mind is called "old sensation. If one eats to excess, painful sensations in body and mind arise;
this is called "new sensation. If one eats with moderation, one avoids the old hunger, which is termed "the cessation of old sensation," and there is no excessive suffering.
This is called not giving rise to new sensations (*vedanā*). In the current Vinaya text, the phrase "old suffering and new suffering" should have the same meaning as "old sensation and new sensation.
Since it is neither more nor less, it is said that there is no increase or decrease. "Having power" refers to using one's own limbs and body.
"Having no business" means having no matter of suffering—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither more nor less. It means to cause the body to be at ease.

"Joy" means that the body does not become impaired or scattered, because one is able to cultivate pure *brahmacarya*. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karma-vibhāṣā) states: "The bowl must always be held at chest level.
When pouring the food and observing it with focused attention, if the mind becomes stifled and surges with agitation, know that you cannot endure it.

Close your eyes for a short while and wait until it is settled before proceeding. Examine each spoonful in advance before placing it in the mouth. For what reason? Because internally one recognizes greed."
One who craves it will vomit it up in an instant; one’s eyes do not wish to see it, let alone endure its flowing, oozing stench and filth.
This is not worth coveting. Yet, out of delusion, one does not realize this. If one obtains foul food, one should first allow the mind of anger to subside, and only then consume it.

If one does not practice contemplation, the rākṣasas will snatch it away. Only after one has eaten one's fill will one remember the previous contemplation; by then, the karma is already established, and regret is in vain.
It is of no benefit; one must be aware beforehand. What is it that causes such delusion? It is only when one is at the point of eating that one realizes the proper measure.
This is the state of a true man (*mahāpuruṣa*): he cannot commit a great transgression and enter hell. How could he be submerged by the sake of a single mouthful of food?
Suffering is the result, yet what one does is extremely weak. I privately say that those who commit great transgressions [are not like this].
This refers to Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha and his vying with the Buddha for converts. His name has been preserved through the ages.
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit’s body was so stout that sweat flowed from his entire frame.
He came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sighed deeply. The Buddha asked the king, "Great King, your body is exceedingly robust."
The King said, "It is so. Troubled by his own corpulence, he was constantly ashamed of it and spoke this verse:

"One should bind one's own thoughts; In every meal, know the proper measure. Thus, all sensations will be slight, And one may digest with ease while preserving life. As for what is meant by "digesting with ease":
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter Sixty-six. Explaining the meaning of the four nutriments (*catur-āhāra*). Regarding the edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it says:

"If it is properly digested and transformed, it can provide nourishment; if it is not properly digested and transformed, it results in depletion. It further says: "If, after being consumed, it is digested and transformed with ease and stability..."

It increases joy and bliss; at the time of digestion and transformation, it is called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). This indicates that during the process of digestion, the internal faculties and the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are nourished;
it is precisely because of this digestion that a desire for food arises. Upon smelling odors or touching tangibles, one immediately desires to eat (and so forth).
When the King heard this verse, he offered a reward of one hundred thousand gold coins to anyone who would recite it for him whenever mealtime arrived. At that time...
There was a youth named Uttara who was destined for this royal command. Every time the mealtime arrived, he would constantly recite this verse.

Gradually, as time passed, the king’s body became slender and his appearance became upright and handsome; every day from the palace tower, he joined his palms in reverence toward the World-Honored One and three times uttered:
"Namo! I pay homage to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Regarding the account of a king who tested the food—both fine and coarse—of the *bāhyaka* (non-Buddhist) monks:

according to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a king named Ajātaśatru. Because he practiced cruelty and his false views were rampant, the Buddha dispatched Kātyāyana to convert him.
Since Kātyāyana was of the Brahmin caste within the kingdom of King Ajātaśatru, the Buddha ordered him to return.
He converted the king of that country and, together with him, converted the people. However, the king harbored a particular hatred for those who shaved their heads;
upon seeing Kātyāyana, he immediately sought to harm him. Kātyāyana said to the king, "What fault have I committed that you wish to harm me?
The king replied, "You are a shaven-headed man; to see you brings ill fortune, and for this reason you must be killed. Kātyāyana [remained silent].
He said to the king, "That which is now inauspicious falls upon me, not upon you. Why is this?
Although you have seen me, you have suffered no harm; yet as for me seeing you, you desire to kill me. Judging by this, that which is called inauspicious truly rests with me.
The king was wise and immediately understood, whereupon he released Kātyāyana and sent him away in secret.
The two men followed after him to observe where he stayed and what food he ate. They saw Kātyāyana sitting beneath a tree;
having received alms-food, he ate it, and when there was a small remainder, he poured it into the river.
The two men sent someone to report the matter in full. Later, the king invited Kātyāyana and offered him coarse [food].
[The King] provided food and drink. He sent a messenger to inquire, saying, "Is this food now to your liking? The Venerable One replied, "The power of this meal has already sufficed.
Later, he provided him with superior flavors and fine foods, and again sent a messenger to inquire, saying, "Is it to your satisfaction?
He replied, "The effect of the previous meal has already rendered it sufficient. Later, the King himself questioned the Venerable One, saying, "As for what I have..."

When food was offered, regardless of whether it was coarse or fine, [the recipients] all said they were fully satisfied. What does this mean? The Venerable One replied: "The body and speech are like a hearth;
it burns sandalwood and it also burns filth. The body and speech are likewise:
whether the food is coarse or fine, the limit is simply being satiated. He then spoke this verse: "This body is like a carriage, Making no distinction between good and bad."
"Scented oil and foul fat are equivalent to seasoned delicacies. When the king heard these words, he conceived deep faith and recognized him as a great virtuous one (*bhadanta*).
He then offered both coarse and refined food to the brāhmaṇa. When the brāhmaṇa first received the coarse food, he was filled with indignation and, with a wrathful countenance, reviled [the king].
Later, when he received the refined food, he rejoiced and praised it. Having witnessed this, the king...
Kātyāyana conceived deep faith and reverence, while looking down upon the various Brahmins of the non-Buddhist paths.
Regarding the phrase "that son of noble family for the sake of the Dharma": he belongs to the same Śākya clan, and is thus called a "son of noble family.
According to the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, it says: When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus.

In the course of life, one goes to the very lowest limit, namely, practicing alms-gathering. This is what the world greatly disparages, calling it "shouting for food" (śrotriya) as one walks with bowl in hand.
That son of noble family accepts this for the sake of the ultimate goal. Why is that?
Because he is weary of birth, old age, sickness, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and despair. You, however, have not left the household life to study the Path with such a mind.
"Yes. At that time, the bhikṣus replied, "We truly have no such thought. The Buddha said, "You are foolish!

Having left the household life to study the Path, you instead harbor a craving for desire that is exceedingly heavy; your observance of the precepts is extremely lax, you are indolent and lack mindfulness, and you do not cultivate the conduct of a śramaṇa.
It is like using ink to wash away ink, using blood to remove blood, using filth to remove filth, or using thirst [to quench thirst]."
It does not quench thirst; it only increases its filth. It leads from darkness into darkness, from gloom into gloom.
Your observance of the precepts is likewise so lax that you do not cultivate the conduct of a śramaṇa. As for what I privately call "receiving for the sake of the goal":
it is because one seeks to weary oneself of the suffering of birth, old age, and death, and thus cultivates the supramundane path that this is called "receiving for the sake of the goal."
Chapter Twenty-one (Part One): On the Rituals of Dhūta Practice.

Having clarified the provisions of clothing and food, as well as internal and external requisites, such that the conditions for the Path are fully prepared, it is only right to reduce attachments and exert oneself in diligent cultivation.
Among all forms of practice, none surpasses *dhūta*. Therefore, this chapter extensively clarifies its ritual procedures. *Dhūta* is a term from the heavenly language (Sanskrit);
in this land [of China], it is translated as "shaking off" (*dǒu shuǎo*). The new translation states that the Sanskrit term *dhuta* is translated here as "shaking" (*yáo dòng*).
It is also called "washing away" (*xi-dǎng*), which means to shake off and cleanse the afflictions (*kleśa*). This is not different from the meaning of "shaking out" (*dǒu-suǒ*).

However, there has been a corruption in the transmission of the Sanskrit term. According to the *Yīyào lùyí yìnyì* (Phonology and Meaning of the Vinaya-yāna-uttara), it is translated as "removing filth.
"Shaking out" is a metaphorical rendering, whereas "removing dust" is the literal translation. Master Ying stated: "The old term was *dhūta*; now it is called..."

*Duṭo* (dhuta) is a term in the Sanskrit language that varies in its phonetic weight. It is translated here as "cultivation" (*xiūzhì*), also as "purification" (*tāotài*), and further as "shaking off" (*dòusǒu*);
these are all synonymous. Although there are twelve different types according to their specific practices, they are categorized into only four kinds based on their ritual forms.
Since this section extensively explains the methods for these practices, it is titled "Practices and Rituals" (*xíngyí*).
Regarding the phrase "the power of retribution increases, etc.," it means that the power of retribution is firm and strong, enabling one to practice;
because this application can adorn the categories of precepts, it is called "pure. Regarding the phrase "transcending all burdens," Ji (Jizang) says:

"The reason all people cannot practice this Dharma is precisely because the burden of their afflictions (*kleśa*) is heavy. Since the afflictions and burdens of the multitude are many, they are called 'all burdens. Now, there is a person..."
If one is able to practice it, one transcends the common crowd. Regarding the phrase "towering and excelling beyond the masses," "towering" (竦) means rising high.
Just as a tall tree that rises above the surface of other trees is called "excelling" (拔萃), this is what is meant by "towering and excelling.
Now, if among hundreds or thousands of people there is suddenly one who can practice this Dharma, they rise above the common crowd; is this not indeed to be "towering and high"?
This is the meaning. Regarding the statement, "All that has been prescribed is for the sake of those with excessive greed and so forth," I privately remark:

Within the text of the two hundred and fifty precepts generally prescribed by the Vinaya, there are rebukes such as, "What you have done is wrong; it is not the way of a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya; it is not conduct in accordance with the Dharma; it is something one ought not to do.
Among these, there are those who possess few desires and are content, who practice the dhūta austerities, and who delight in training in the precepts—all of whom [participate] together.

They rebuked him for his transgressions and reported the matter to the Buddha, requesting the establishment of precepts and regulations; therefore, it is said that most of what was established was for the sake of those with excessive greed.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that among the precepts concerning food and clothing in the Vinaya, most were established because of the Śākya son Upananda;

regarding the various types of precepts concerning sexual misconduct, most were established because of Kāḷudāyin; and regarding matters of improper conduct, most were established because of the group of six monks. All of these were for the sake of...

Because of greed for wealth and sensual forms, the Sages established the precepts. Regarding the statement, "In all the teachings that open the way, one first extols these practices," I privately say:
if one wishes to instruct the bhikṣus, one should praise the twelve dhūtas, such as having few desires and knowing contentment.

This is intended to encourage those who are weary and indolent; thus it says, "In all the teachings that open the way, one first extols [these]. Furthermore, it says: "As stated in the Vinaya texts..."
In all instances where [the practice] is introduced, it is stated that "this is the dignified dharma of dhūta. Therefore, it is said that "first one proclaims this dharma.

This is intended to encourage those travelers who are weary and indolent; these two subsequent lines describe how, within the aforementioned general introduction of the teaching, one first proclaims this practice.
Alternatively, they may be explained as a general exposition on the intent behind instituting the dhūta observances. As for the term "traveler," it refers to the śramaṇa.

These are the honored guests of the triple world; thus they are called "guests" (*ātithya*), meaning that such persons do not dwell long in the triple world, for they shall swiftly attain liberation from birth and death.
Regarding "those who proceed toward the city of meditative concentration": if one can practice the *dhūta* ascetic virtues, one will then accumulate and give rise to *samādhi*;
this is what is meant. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Precepts, concentration, and wisdom serve as the walls and moats. This is intended to convey that meaning.
"The man stained by dust ascends the steps of *śīla*, etc. These two subsequent lines clarify that all which has been prescribed above is for the sake of those with excessive greed.
As for the phrase "ascending the steps of *śīla*," why is *śīla* taken as the stairway?
According to the Preface to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "It is like the hall of Śakra, adorned and fashioned from various jewels; the seven treasures serve as..."
The steps are that which is traversed by devas and humans; likewise, this Hall of the True Dharma is adorned with the seven factors of enlightenment. The prohibitive precepts serve as its steps;
this is precisely the meaning of "that which is traversed by the worthy and the sages."
Regarding the Buddha’s intention that his disciples follow the Path and renounce worldly pleasures and the like, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 68, states:
"These twelve dhūtas are what the Buddha intended for his disciples to follow the Path and renounce worldly pleasures; therefore, he praised the twelve dhūtas. This is the Buddha’s intention:
one should take the dhūtas as the foundation. Only when there are compelling circumstances and no other choice should one depart from them."

He listened to other matters as well. At the time of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma, after the five bhikṣus had attained the Path, they said to the Buddha, "What kind of robes should we wear?
The Buddha replied, "You should wear robes made of discarded rags (pāṃśukūla).

Furthermore, within the rules for receiving the precepts, it was ordained that one should wear robes of discarded rags, beg for food, sit under trees, and take discarded medicine for as long as life lasts. Among the four ancient noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), these constitute the dhūta practices.
These are the three matters. The Buddha-dharma takes wisdom alone as its foundation; it does not prioritize suffering. These teachings all assist the Path and follow the Path;
therefore, the Buddhas always praise them (the text ends here). [The author] privately comments:

"When there are causes and conditions that leave no choice" refers to the fact that for those who have left the household life, *dhūta* practices are originally the fundamental conduct. However, if physical illness becomes severe...
Only when conditions such as the heat of summer or the cold of winter prevail may one engage in other activities.
Regarding the individual analysis of each of the three realms and six sense bases: each possesses its own specific antidote for the afflictions of the respective realm.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "To extinguish the three poisons and emerge from the triple world"—this is precisely its meaning.
Furthermore, it can be understood that this also serves as the antidote to the afflictions of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding "neither grasping nor abandoning," I [the author] say:

this refers to the Middle Way contemplation, which is neither cultivated nor clung to. Master Bin says: the lower fascicle of the *Śrī-mahādevī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (or *Ārya-bhadrā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*) states: "Shake off greed, anger, and delusion."

Scraping away [the scabs]. To shake off and sift through the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) both within and without the three realms—of such a person I say they can speak of *dhūta*. To shake off in this manner:
neither grasping nor abandoning, neither practicing nor not practicing, neither clinging nor not clinging—of such a person I say they can speak of *dhūta*.
(Commentary: This means that by means of shaking off [defilements], one is able to realize the principle (*tattva*). Having realized the principle, one is able to rely [upon it].
Because he proclaims to others what he has realized for himself, it is said: "I say that such a person can preach *dhūta*;

because they have committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), they are not one whom I have extinguished. According to the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, at that time the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"Having violated the prohibitions and lost the *dhūta* [practices], because they have committed an act of immediate retribution..."
When I have passed into parinirvāṇa, as taught by the Buddhas of the past: those who have violated the pure precepts shall not enter the assembly.

All matters pertaining to śramaṇas shall be abandoned by them, like scorched wicks. They shall not be permitted to take even the slightest portion of the livelihoods and requisites belonging to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
If one commits the four grave root offenses, they shall be cast out by the assembly like a corpse. Why is this?
This sutra teaches patience. It calls for the arousal of compassion toward evil bhikṣus and the restraint of all accusations against them;
furthermore, it enjoins that one should provide offerings to such evil bhikṣus. To understand the intent of this passage, one must refer to the preceding sutra. That preceding sutra states:
"A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts shall not participate in the distribution of any monastic affairs or offerings, nor shall he be permitted by kings or ministers to bring accusations."
Reproach. Why is it thus? It is because of the aforementioned statement that "it is due to creating an offense against the Dharma (ānantarya) that this occurs;

it is not I who extinguish [the practice]. Rather, it is the breaking of the precepts that is called an 'offense' (ānantarya). Because of breaking the precepts, one extinguishes the dhūta practices oneself; it is not I who cause the dhūta practitioner to lose them. Therefore, it is said, 'It is not I who extinguish them.
As for the *Huashou jing* (Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra) stating that "because Kāśyapa practiced the dhūtas, the Buddha shared his seat with him," it is as follows:
The *Huashou jing chao* (Excerpts from the Puṣpamālā-sūtra) states [as follows].

Regarding the passage in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* where the Buddha personally offered half of his seat and handed over his saṃghāṭī robe to Kāśyapa, it is as recorded in the *Za ahan jing chao* (Excerpts from the Saṃyukta Āgama) [as follows].

As for the phrase "except for one person who made offerings," according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there were many bhikṣuṇīs and upāsakas residing at his dwelling place."
Upāsikās, kings, ministers, non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I wish to sit in quiet meditation and contemplation for three months; do not allow outsiders to enter, except for one person who provides offerings.
The bhikṣus then established a regulation among themselves: "If anyone enters, it shall be an offense of pāyattika. At that time, the Elder Sāriputra...

Previously, Upasena, together with sixty bhikṣus from the country of Bārāṇasī—all of whom were practitioners of the twelve *dhūta* ascetic practices—went to the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī and asked the bhikṣus, "Where is the Tathāgata? I wish to go and see him.

They replied, "The World-Honored One has been sitting in silent meditation for three months, except for one person who provides offerings. If anyone enters, they commit a *dukkaṭa* offense. Upasena...
He asked, "World-Honored One, do you have such words? He replied, "We, the bhikṣus, have established this regulation ourselves.
Huìxiān said, "I do not require your regulation. Why? Because the Buddha has spoken thus: 'What the Buddha has not prohibited should not be prohibited;
what he has already prohibited should not be violated. We are all forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), even to the point of wearing only the three robes."
The man, having been permitted to inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being at his own discretion, went to where the Buddha was. After offering his greetings, he asked:
"Did you not hear what the other bhikṣus said? He replied: "I heard what the other bhikṣus said; I [was with] sixty bhikṣus from the country of Bāla."
Both were forest-dwellers (*araṇyaka*). Because they carried the three robes (*tricīvara*), they came to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
You are truly practitioners of the forest (*āraṇyaka*) who, by carrying the three robes, are permitted to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health as you wish.
Should there be others like you, they too shall be permitted to inquire as they wish. The *Sudarsana* states: For what reason did the World-Honored One [remain] for three months?
He sat in meditation. The World-Honored One surveyed all sentient beings and saw that during these three months, none had attained the Way; therefore, he remained in meditation.

The bhikṣus, failing to understand his intention, established improper regulations and so forth. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Because the Buddha was preaching the esoteric Dharma for the sake of the devas.
The Great Master [Vasubandhu] says: "It was because he did not wish to allow non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to slander him. For...
I have often seen the Buddha traveling through various countries, appearing as if he were merely wandering aimlessly and lacking any internal realization; therefore, I sit in meditation.
Furthermore, it is because I wish to establish a model for future disciples, and because in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) it was intended to restrict the accumulation of extra robes;

thus, I sit in meditation. This is also what the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) states: "Because of sitting in meditation, [the Buddha] praised those bhikṣus who practice the dhūta ascetic virtues. This is the causal basis for my practice.

This refers to the practice of setting aside robes to form a heap. A separate ritual manual states: "When Kāśyapa went on almsround, the Buddha commanded him to share his bed. Andhaka first practiced moderation in eating;
this is called true offering."
Regarding the allowance for entering stūpas, monasteries, and so forth when there are specific causes and conditions, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states:

"Although a bhikṣu has taken up residence in the forest (araṇya), if there is a matter involving a cause and condition, he may enter a stūpa or monastery. The Buddha-dharma has both open and restricted aspects;
it is not like the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). What are these causes and conditions? The answer is: first, to provide for the sick; second, on behalf of the sick..."
1. Seeking medicinal requisites; 2. Seeking a caregiver for the sick; 3. Seeking a caregiver for the sick; 4. Preaching the Dharma for the sick; 5.
Preaching the Dharma for other bhikṣus; 6. Listening to the Dharma and transforming others through teaching; 7. Making offerings to and revering those of great virtue;
8. Providing for the noble Saṃgha; 9. Reciting and chanting profound sūtras; 10. Teaching others to recite and chant profound sūtras. If there are...

Regarding these various causes that lead to [the prohibition of] stupas and the like, I privately remark: the Buddha-dharma adapts to the capacities of beings, and its manifestation or concealment depends on the times;

thus there are periods of openness and obstruction. If it were the Dharma of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), once closed it would never open again. This differs from the non-Buddhists who remain in empty places for the duration of their lives;

as for those practicing asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*) among the *araṇya* (hermitages), they are not permitted to do so for the rest of their lives. Ji said: "The non-Buddhists have a single regulation with no exceptions. Among the *araṇya*, if one practices asceticism, it is not permitted for the rest of one's life."
Upon entering the city, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) would expel anyone who did so.

Therefore, before Master Xuanzang first departed for the Western Regions on his return journey, King Śīlāditya, wishing to manifest the Master’s virtue, said to him: "I wish to establish a great hall of debate to test you, O Master.
Only after you have composed a treatise shall I permit you to return to the Eastern Land. Consequently, within the city, the drum of debate was struck with great solemnity.
He assembled the seven classes of disciples as well as the non-Buddhists by the banks of the Ganges River and had Xuanzang ascend the seat of debate.
The fourfold assembly raised objections for seven days, yet Xuanzang remained undefeated.

Initially, from within the city, Xuanzang traveled with King Śīlāditya and the master Śīlabhadra in a single boat toward the site of the debate. On the way, they encountered a non-Buddhist standing atop a tall banner; the banner...
He placed a wooden tray upon his head and stood atop it, joining his palms toward the sun from dawn until dusk, gazing at the sun without ceasing.
He did not descend until nightfall, continuing in this manner for the rest of his life. Śīlabhadra wished to convert him and advised him not to go, but he could not be dissuaded.

Paramārtha previously used increased inducements and parables to lead [the man] into the Buddha-dharma and cause him to leave the household life. The non-Buddhist replied, "I also know that the Buddha-dharma is superior to my own dharma;
however, this occupation has been inherited from my ancestors, and I shall never change it. Having failed to convert him despite his efforts, he departed.

Regarding the statement that "the dhūta practices are common to both villages and wildernesses": this means that among the twelve dhūtas, there are two methods—dwelling in the forest (araṇya) and dwelling among tombs (śmāśānika)—which necessarily require going outside of cities and towns;
the remaining ten are common to both the wilderness and the village. However, the Vinaya Master alone does not permit this interpretation.

He maintains that among the five types of locations, the forest (araṇya) is the only one that constitutes a distinct category, while the other four—dwelling among tombs, under trees, and so forth—are subsumed within it.
This is the distinction. If one is in a village, even though one may sit exposed in a cemetery and so forth, it is not called *dhūta*.
Among the four types of eating, the single method of begging for food (*piṇḍapātika*) constitutes the category; however, taking only a single morsel at a single sitting is the specific detail.

Because one has obtained food by begging, one is restricted to a single morsel and a single sitting, and does not prepare leftover food; this is what is called *dhūta*. If one eats the food of the Sangha, even if one sits only once—
Those who merely collect [rags] and so forth are not called *dhūta*. However, there is no such text in the Vinaya; I only wish that the Vinaya Master would provide his own explanation.

The above concludes the explanation of the general meaning of the name *dhūta*. Below, the enumeration and the essential nature of the practices (*dharma*) are clarified. Regarding "rag-robes" (*pāṃśukūla*):
Some say that the Sanskrit term *pāṃśukūla* means "a bag of dung" or "a sack of refuse. This refers to the rag-robe (*pāṃśukūla-cīvara*).
