Because one who wears the Dharma-robes is easily seen to have faults, Master Ci said: "If evil thoughts arise, you should contemplate this robe:

'Now that I am wearing these robes, how could I possibly commit evil? Therefore, the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* says: "Seeing yourself in this way, if arrogance should arise, you must extinguish it immediately."
Regarding the śrāmaṇera Cunda and others: according to the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, in the chapter on "Bhikṣus Wearing Rag-robes," the Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"If there is a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes, who is free from attachment, and who is able to abandon arrogance because he is content, then devas, nāgas, and yakṣas will always delight in wishing to see this bhikṣu.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings will join their palms [in homage]."
"If even he who causes such disorder [is thus honored], how much more so the other minor devas. He further addressed Kāśyapa:
"Do you see the śrāmaṇera Cunda picking up impure, foul-smelling, and filthy discarded items while begging for food?

When he reached Lake Anavatapta wishing to wash and cleanse them, the resident devas all came from afar to welcome him, bowing their heads to his feet in salutation. Those devas all delight in purity and cleanliness."
He took the impure rag-robes belonging to the novice Cunda and washed them until they were free of filth.
He then took the wash-water and used it to bathe his own body. The devas, knowing that Cunda was able to maintain the precepts and enter into the various meditative absorptions, [rejoiced].
He possesses great majesty and power; therefore, we have come to welcome him, paying him respect and prostrating before him.
Kāśyapa, you saw the brahmin Subhadra, dressed in clean garments after begging for alms, intending to go to Lake Anavatapta.

At that time, the resident devas surrounding the lake—each side extending five *li*—obstructed the brahmin from afar, not allowing him to approach the lake, fearing that he might defile it with impure food and [impurities].
With leftover food, they defile this great pond. Kāśyapa, who has heard of such a thing? Within the Noble Dharma, one does not diligently practice and study.
*Sudarśana* states that the noble ones of the Three Vehicles all beg for their food. *Lì* says: "The Buddha himself begged for his food; let us discuss what exists."

There are four intentions: first, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for the Buddhas of the three periods of time to beg for food; second, it is to provide the sustenance for the body so that one may practice the Way oneself and benefit others;
third, it is to bring benefit and merit to the donors and to repay their kindness; fourth, it is to serve as a model for the śrāvaka disciples to emulate.
Third, regarding "the color and mind being unsettled due to observing the intentions of others," Ciyun says:
If one serves as the *zhisui* (steward) or the *weina* (rector), one constantly observes the conduct of the administrators and the assembly, fearing that they may not act according to the Dharma.

Consequently, one's facial expression remains perpetually rigid, or it shifts and fluctuates because the mind is also trembling with fear. As for "lacking supplementary flavors," this refers to calling a great abundance of vegetables "supplementary flavors."
Alternatively, one may add ordinary flavors to the food; hence it is called "conjoined flavors" (*jān-mei*).
Regarding those who walk along the roadside begging for alms in succession and so forth, the text of the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (寶梁經) is extremely essential.

When the time comes, these points will be extracted as in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* excerpt (*yún-yún*). Having received the food, one should form this thought: "This is the food of a thief; this is my own [food]."
Regarding "food and so forth," this passage cites the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 34, which states:
The Buddha said, "If there is a bhikṣu who resolves to beg for food and premeditates, thinking: 'I shall go begging; I hope to obtain what is good, and may I not receive anything that is bad.'"
"May I certainly obtain much; do not let it be meager. May I obtain it quickly; do not let it be delayed.
A bhikṣu who thinks thus is said not to have conceived the perception of revulsion toward food. His cultivated wholesome dharmas will decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will increase.
It shall gradually increase. If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to go for alms, he should first make this aspiration:
"May all those who beg obtain full satisfaction; may those who give food attain immeasurable merit. If I receive food, it shall be only to heal this poisonous body."

One cultivates wholesome dharmas and benefits the donor. While dwelling in this aspiration, the wholesome dharmas one has cultivated increase day and night, and unwholesome dharmas will gradually be extinguished.
If there is a bhikṣu who can cultivate in this manner, it should be known that such a person—
He does not consume in vain the faithful offerings made within the kingdom.

Regarding the seventh root of goodness, the Unseen Crown: as previously explained regarding the cause for the inexhaustibility of alms-seeking, so too is the retribution of the Unseen Crown described.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha took the Śākyas fifty *li* away from the city of Kapilavastu," Zhi [Daoxuan] says: "The Western language is inverted;
it should be fifteen *li*. This is an error of the translators. How could there be alms-seeking at a distance of fifty *li*?
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, after the Buddha attained enlightenment, King Śuddhodana ordered the Śākyas to leave the household life and become disciples of the Buddha.

The Buddha then took the sons of Śākya to Śrāvastī. The reason for doing so was that, as they had not yet abandoned desire, he feared they might break their precepts if they remained near their own kinsmen;
therefore, he brought them to Śrāvastī and had Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others instruct and transform them.

Throughout the first and last watches of the night, they applied themselves with single-minded diligence and did not sleep, practicing with such fervent exertion that they all attained the fruits of the Path. Thus they attained the Way.
The fruition was thus completed. The Buddha, intending to return to his native land, stayed in the forest of the ṛṣis at Kapilavastu.
This forest was fifty *li* from the city of Kapilavastu; it was a park where the Śākyas had previously gone for recreation.

When the Śākyas were in Śrāvastī, they remained diligent and did not sleep during the first and last watches of the night, so that the night seemed long to them. Now, moreover, [they were] from the forest...
He came from within and entered the city to beg for alms. Perceiving that the road was long and distant, the Buddha knew his thoughts.
At that time, a lion came and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, standing to one side. Due to these three preceding causes and conditions, the Buddha intended to speak a verse.
"To those who do not sleep, the night is long; to those who are weary, the road is long; to the foolish, the cycle of birth and death is long, for they do not know the True Dharma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Before you left the household life, your minds were dissolute and you slept much; therefore, you did not perceive the length of the night.

Now, during the first and last watches of the night, you apply yourselves with diligence to seeking the Way and diminish your sleep; therefore, you perceive the night as long. Furthermore, this [Kāśyapa]..."

Rāvaṇa Forest. Formerly, when you were riding in a carriage for pleasure, you did not realize how far it was; now, wearing robes and carrying a bowl, you walk until you are utterly exhausted, and thus you perceive the road as long.
Furthermore, this lion was a brahmin during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.

When the lion saw the Buddha preaching the Dharma, he came to where the Buddha was. At that time, because the great assembly was listening to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, there was no one [to accompany him].
As for speech: when one gives rise to evil thoughts in the mind and utters abusive words, saying, "How do these shaven-headed ones differ from beasts?

They cannot distinguish the good, nor do they know how to speak," then because of such karma of harsh speech, this person shall fall among the animals for ninety-one kalpas, from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until the present day.
At that time, this person’s mind should have been capable of attaining the Way, yet due to their folly...
Because of delusion, one creates for oneself a long cycle of birth and death; now, because your mind is pure toward me, you shall attain liberation.

As for the account of Mahāmaudgalyāyana being surrounded and beaten by brahmins while begging for alms, until his flesh and bones were mangled, this is as recorded in the *Ekottarika Āgama* (and so forth).
Regarding Śāriputra entering parinirvāṇa first due to the gravity of his illness: this refers to the circumstances of Śāriputra’s passing.

As will be clarified later, the reason those who passed into parinirvāṇa first were that the foremost disciples of the Buddhas of the three periods all entered nirvana before their respective Buddhas, because they could not bear to witness the extinction of a Buddha.
Furthermore, it is like when a king in a secular land intends to go on a tour.

The Great Minister (Mahāmaṇḍalika) must always go first. Therefore, in this context, the fact that Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa before Maudgalyāyana indicates that, regarding his initial awakening and entry into the Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra was foremost; now, in his parinirvāṇa as well, he is foremost.
Because Śāriputra suffered from chronic wind-disorders throughout his life, compounded by headaches, it is said that his afflictions were heavy. Thus, the devas of the three realms fell [into tears].

Regarding the statement "tears falling like rain": if it is said that [this refers to] the three realms, then since the Formless Heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) fundamentally lack form, how can it be said that they shed tears?
Furthermore, there are sutras stating that the gods of the Formless Realm stand by the side of the Buddha. Answer:

Traditional exegesis has held that although the gods of the Formless Realm lack coarse form (*audārika-rūpa*), they possess subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*); therefore, it is said that they shed tears. My current interpretation, however, is not so.
However, although there may be distinctions between coarse and subtle, they are all nonetheless form (*rūpa*). Why, then, are they called the Formless Heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty explained: "In truth, the realm of retribution for the Formless Heavens has no form at all; it is simply because those born there [are so designated]."
All of these are associated with a concentrated mind. Therefore, by the power of entering meditative absorption, their consciousness is transformed into a physical body (rūpakāya).
Consequently, they are able to stand beside the Buddha, or even shed tears, and so forth.
Regarding the loss of half a day’s merit due to seeking morning food (*pūrvāhṇa-bhakta*), midday food (*madhyāhna-bhakta*), or post-midday food (*paścād-bhakta*):

it is established that "morning food" refers to the *prātar-āśa*, "midday food" refers to the *upavāsa* (fasting meal), and if one performs the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa* (the rite for leftover food), it is termed "post-midday food."
Regarding "one lump of food" (*ekapiṇḍapāta*): I privately explain that this refers to eating from a single bowl.

As for "moderation in food" (*mātṛkābhojana*) in the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra*, according to the second fascicle, the *Dhūta-paṭala*, which clarifies the thirteen *dhūtas*, it adds "constant moderation in food. The text asks:
"What is moderation in food? If one consumes food and drink without measure, it increases physical lethargy and heaviness, and constantly gives rise to craving and attachment."
The belly knows no satiety. Having recognized this fault, one perceives the merit of moderation in eating.

From this day forward, I shall renounce greed and indulgence, practicing moderation in food—meaning, weighing what is consumed without yielding to the belly’s demands, thereby eliminating greed, curing illness, and severing all forms of indolence.

Regarding the phrase "the practice of virtuous persons" and "extensive remedies," according to the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra*: "What is meant by receiving rag-robes? It means abandoning gifts from householders.
What is meant by receiving the three robes? It means abandoning the excess of extra robes. What is meant by begging for food? It means abandoning invitations from others."
What is "begging in sequence"? It means abandoning skipping houses. What is "moderation in food"? It means abandoning greedy indulgence. What is "sitting at the foot of a tree"?
It means abandoning dwelling in a house. What is "dwelling among tombs"? It means abandoning other superior locations. What is "always sitting without lying down"?
It means being free from sleeping (and so forth). Below, each [practice] is explained individually. Regarding the acceptance of offerings from householders: [text follows].
There is such-and-such a fault in receiving an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*). There is such-and-such a fault in accepting an invitation.
There is such-and-such a fault [in each case], up to and including eating greedily and at will, and dwelling under a roof; each has its respective fault (and so forth).
Regarding the "seven araṇyas," the *Yāoyào lǜyí yīnyì* states: the Western [Sanskrit] term is *araṇyaka*, which means a "place of tranquility.
The *Zhìlùn* (Treatise on Wisdom) calls it a "place of seclusion," ranging from a minimum distance of three *li* to places where various activities occur, as found in the sixty-eighth fascicle.
This is as stated in the *Zhìlùn chāo* (*...*). Regarding the tiger’s roar around the Jetavana, this text is cited.

The "Aranyaka Monastery" (Āraṇyaka-vihāra) refers to a monastery located outside the city walls. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there were tigers and wolves that would kill deer;
having eaten their fill, they would leave the remains behind. When the bhikṣus saw these leftover meats, they would take them back with them.

At that time, a hungry tiger rose up to search for the remains of the deer and circled the Jetavana grove, letting out a roar. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "For what reason is the tiger roaring? Ānanda answered him in full detail.
The Buddha said: "From now on, one must not take the remains left by a tiger; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Why? Because the tiger’s expectation has not been severed.
If one takes the remains left by a lion, there is no offense. Why? Because the lion’s expectation has been severed."

If there are two kinds of *araṇya* (wilderness) regarding monastic robes as clarified previously—namely, the *araṇya* boundary of the Saṃgha as clarified within the discussion of the assembly’s general and specific [procedures]—and the *araṇya* boundary of the robe as clarified within the precept on protecting robes according to their characteristics;

this clarifies the establishment of the *dhūta* (ascetic) *araṇya* and those who rely upon the four supports (*niśraya*), such as wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) and sitting at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūla*). Now that one is already able...
Sitting beneath a tree, one should know that this accords with the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

As for the statement "the bones have six hundred and sixty pores and ninety thousand [hair-follicles], even unto what is called the Dharma of Ultimate Emptiness," according to the *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits), regarding the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*), one contemplates the thirty-six impure substances and foul secretions; thus, the mind attains *nirvāṇa*. Why is this?
He knew this because of the following: Once there was a bhikṣu practicing the path in an araṇya. While begging for food, he ate by the side of a river.
Having finished eating and washed his bowl, he noticed on the bank upstream, amidst some brushwood, the severed head of a dead woman. A gust of wind blew her hair, which suddenly fell into his bowl.
The bhikṣu grasped the hair with his hand, examined it closely, and rebuked it, speaking to himself: "If this were a horse's tail..."
"This is still too fine. If it were a man's hair, it would be too soft and delicate; it must be a woman's hair. He then conceived lustful thoughts.
"Such is this hair; the person must be exquisite. Her face is like a peach blossom, her eyes like pearls, and her nose like a cut tube."

Her mouth was as if containing vermilion; her eyebrows were like centipedes. Having formed this thought, he immediately gave rise to a lustful mind and followed the current to search for her, imagining he would see her features.
Searching without ceasing, he saw a woman whose body had been half-devoured by a fox and a wolf;
the flesh was putrid and rotting, yet her hair still remained. Comparing it with [his own], the length was similar. At that moment, his previous lustful thoughts were suddenly dispelled.
He understood it for himself and observed it again. "When this person was born, his form was handsome and fine; now it is decayed and ruined, visible to all.
The thoughts I previously gave rise to were merely born of desire for the body and craving for sensual pleasure.
That body is like this—what am I any different? Truly considering my own body, it is a composite of the four great elements; when merit is exhausted, conditions depart, and it naturally [perishes]."
The assembly dispersed. Witnessing this transformation, his mind attained awakening, and he immediately realized the stage of the Path (srotāpatti).
Regarding the seventh point—that one is not pierced by the thorns of sound—there are five aspects: first, sitting beneath a tree;
second, many birds on the tree making noise, which disturbs the bhikṣu; third, the tree also having thorns that prick people; fourth, now being in the open air.
There is no such fault. Regarding "not causing others to rise," this means that one sits wherever one finds a place, without requiring others to yield their space.
Regarding "the fifth, not following the body's desires," this refers to one who is lying down; whether wishing to stretch out, or to contract, or to lean while lying, these are called [the faults].
This is according to one's personal preference. Since one now practices constant sitting (*prahāṇa*), one is free from this fault. Seventh, regarding those who change while reciting the scriptures:
since they sit and do not lie down, they may simply change their position whenever they wish to continue the recitation.
Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Kṣāntivāda-sūtra*, the *Jyotiṣa-sūtra*, and so forth: the fifty-sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"An araṇya bhikṣu should know the good paths; he should know the days well, know the nights well, know the divisions of the night well, and know the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) well.
He should recite the *Jyotiṣa-sūtra*, know the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma well, and know the first dhyāna well."

The second, third, and fourth dhyānas; the thorough knowledge of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], etc.; the account of the bhikṣu of the village of Yana is explained at length in the same manner.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a forest-dwelling (*araṇya*) bhikṣu did not distinguish the constellations. Some bandits stayed overnight and said to the bhikṣu, "We shall sleep; tell us when it is about to dawn.
After the bandits had slept for a short while, they asked the bhikṣu, "Is it early or late? The bhikṣu replied, "It is still..."
"It is early. Thus he asked three times. When night had already turned to dawn, he still said it was early. The pursuers of the thief arrived and seized him to take him away. He then spoke in anger:
"If this bhikṣu had told me the time, I would not have slept until dawn; now I am being seized because of this bhikṣu.
Because of this matter, [the matter] was reported to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "An araṇya-bhikṣu must know the directions, the signs, and the stars."
Regarding the characteristics of the timing of seasons, such as early or late, as well as the records of the days, months, and years (and so forth):
as for the opening of the fire-jewel, it is because this jewel can produce fire. When the sun rises, if one holds this jewel toward the sun, fire is obtained.
If it is a water-jewel, it produces water when held toward the moon. This is the nature of dependent origination.
Section Twenty-two, Part One: Paying Homage to the Monastic Image.

The regulations concerning robes, alms bowls, and other requisites are the essentials for supporting the Path; next, the rules for *dhūta* practices are revealed as the framework for superior conduct.
It is necessary to revere the Dharma and honor the person, so that the Ultimate Way may be brought to glory. This is the intended purpose of this section.

The meaning is as follows. Furthermore, it is said: from the initial establishment of the fundamental tenets to the conclusion of the dhūta practices, all clarify the methods for both the collective and the individual.
These methods do not establish themselves; there must necessarily be a master who can expound them, and there must also be those who propagate them.

Since the Dharma must rely on people for its propagation, it is only logical to accord special reverence to these people. This is why this chapter has come into being. A question is raised: "The Sangha is..."

"Is able to revere. "The image" is that which is revered. "To bring about" (*chi*) means to arrive at; "reverence" (*jing*) means respect. Now, the term "Saṃgha" (*seng*) generally encompasses both the agent and the object.
In this text, it clarifies that the members of the Saṃgha mutually show respect; therefore, we know it applies to both agent and object.

Here, when the word "Saṃgha" is used, it refers to the Saṃgha as a conventional designation for the real dharmas of the five aggregates. When "the image" is used, it refers to the Buddha-image that sustains the Dharma. That is to say:

Having shaved their hair and donned dyed robes, they receive the precepts through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Their status encompasses both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*); this clarifies what is meant by "Sangha. As for "images" (*bimba*), it means "resemblance.

This refers to clay shrines, plain paintings, and the sacred icons that maintain the presence of the spirit. Within the text, the rules for reverence and deference are extensively elucidated; therefore, it is stated as such. Question:
Regarding the titles and ranks of teachers and disciples, logic dictates that images should come first, followed by the Sangha. Why, then, in the present title, is [the Sangha] placed first?
The image of the Sangha follows. The commentary explains: Regarding the sequence of the Three Jewels, the Jewel of the Buddha comes first, with the Dharma and Sangha following.

This means that after the Buddha had fulfilled his practices over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and perfected the merit of myriads of virtues, he renounced the golden wheel-turning kingship to leave the household life and sat beneath the King of Trees (*pārijātaka*) to attain enlightenment.

This is called the Jewel of the Buddha. Next, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and even the twelve divisions of the scriptures to the five men, including Kauṇḍinya;
this is the Jewel of the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, they attained realization and their spirits were nourished.
The Holy One commanded, "Welcome! Upon this, they attained the fruits [of the path] and received the precepts; their hair and beards fell away naturally, and dharma robes appeared upon their bodies.

This is what is called the Jewel of the Sangha, and such is the sequential order of the transformative rites for a single period. Now, regarding the transmission of the teachings to the Eastern Land, the Sangha comes first.
This is because the two masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, arrived in Luoyang; thus, the Sangha was the beginning. It was then that the White Horse arrived, carrying the sūtras.
This refers to the sequence of the Dharma. Those who arrive later shall then depict the *dharmakāya*; this represents the Buddha’s final stage.
Because it illustrates this meaning, the Saṃgha is placed first. Furthermore, what has been described above—the golden countenance and the *dharmakāya*—constitutes the Buddha Jewel;

the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma constitutes the Dharma Jewel; and the severing of fetters and detachment from defilement constitute the Saṃgha Jewel. This is still an explanation of the Three Jewels based on conventional phenomena (*nāma*).

This refers to the Three Jewels as distinct entities (*biphasa*). If one discusses the Three Jewels from the perspective of principle (*li*), they are again distinct; within a single essence, three are complete. That is to say: ultimate awakening is called the Buddha;

ultimate principle is called the Dharma; and ultimate harmony is called the Sangha. In the *Jie xin shu* (Commentary on the Precepts and Mind), the meaning of the Three Jewels is analyzed through four distinctions.
First, the Three Jewels as the essence of principle: for example, the fivefold dharma-body is the Buddha Jewel; [the cessation of suffering is the Dharma Jewel...]

The principle of unconditioned reality (*asamskrta-dharma*) is the Jewel of the Dharma. The merits of the Śrāvakas, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the three Jewels as manifested through transformation (*nirmāṇa*): for example, when Śākyamuni attained the Way and ruled over the trichiliocosm, he was the Jewel of the Buddha; his proclamation and dissemination of the teachings of the Truths was the Jewel of the Dharma;

and Kauṇḍinya and the other four were the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Regarding the three Jewels as maintained through sustenance (*pratipālana*): physical images, stupas, and temples are the Jewel of the Buddha; [the written scriptures on] paper...
That which has been transmitted from of old is the Dharma Jewel; the precepts, the Dharma, and the ritual forms constitute the Sangha Jewel. Bin said:
Regarding what is called the "embodied Three Jewels," first, to clarify the Buddha Jewel: the ancients all stated that Buddha stupas, images, and śarīra relics are termed the "embodied Buddha.

Thus, according to the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) and other texts, when the Buddha was in the world, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to dwell in retreat and preach the Dharma. At that time...

King Udayana, longing for the World-Honored One, carved an image upon an altar. When the Buddha descended from heaven, the sandalwood image rose to meet him and prostrated before the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One prophesied, saying: "In a future age, you shall extensively perform the work of a Buddha; your name shall be Sustaining Buddha (Dhṛtarāṣṭra).
New masters of the sūtras and śāstras rely on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which states: "Your emanation-body is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata."

Therefore, the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is taken as the Buddha who sustains the teachings (*zhuchi*). Now, upon detailed examination, both of the two aforementioned meanings are subsumed under "sustaining the teachings.

Next, regarding the Jewel of the Dharma: it has been consistently stated since antiquity that the Tripitaka, as recorded in paper and ink, is called the "Dharma that sustains the teachings" (*zhuchi fa*).
Next, concerning the Sangha: according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, there are five kinds of Sangha: first, the sheep-like Sangha; second, the shameless Sangha; third...

There are five types of Saṃgha: first, the Saṃgha of ordinary monks; second, the Saṃgha of those who have attained the fruits of the path; third, the Saṃgha of those who have entered the path; fourth, the Saṃgha of the pure; and fifth, the Saṃgha of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-saṃgha*). Among these, the ultimate Saṃgha is the true Saṃgha.

The remaining four types are subsumed under the Saṃgha of maintenance (*saṃdhāraṇa-saṃgha*). According to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, the shameless and immodest monks [are included] within my True Dharma.
Although they may be like corpses, they are still superior to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for they can show people and devas the place of wholesome dharmas.

I shall never permit them to be insulted, beaten, or reviled. These renunciants are protected and remembered with compassion by the Buddhas of the three periods of time; according to this sutra, such is the case.

Even a monk devoid of shame may be said, in one respect, to be a member of the Sangha who maintains the teachings. Regarding the "Three Jewels as a single essence," this refers solely to the essence of the mind, which is conceptually divided into three aspects;
in ultimate reality, there are no three. These are distinguished according to their characteristics for the sake of transforming beings in various ways.

Thus, from the perspective of illuminating principle, it constitutes the meaning of *Buddha* (Awakening); from the perspective of the essence being free from names and words, it constitutes the meaning of *Dharma*; and because the ultimate truth is unimpeded and harmonious, it constitutes the meaning of *Sangha*.

This is the meaning of the "harmonious Sangha. The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated: All sentient beings possess the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which is precisely the ninth *amala-vijñāna*.
Through the cultivation of skillful means, this original enlightenment—which was originally hidden—is now made manifest, thereby constituting the Buddha Jewel.
Furthermore, the sense of being a standard for emulation within original enlightenment constitutes the Dharma Jewel, and the sense of being free from conflict constitutes the Sangha Jewel.
Tripitaka Master said: "The nature of the Three Jewels does not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*). Since True Suchness is the actual nature of awakening, it is established as the Buddha Jewel.
Furthermore, the nature of the guiding rules and the nature of non-contention are both inseparable from Suchness; these constitute the Dharma and Sangha Jewels. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
'If one considers the Three Jewels to be eternally abiding, this is indeed the ultimate truth. This is the supreme [teaching] of all Buddhas."
In the aforementioned vows, it is further stated: "The Buddha is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha is eternal; the eternal is space; space is the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu);
and the Buddha-nature is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). (Commentary: This is precisely the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā).
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are suchness; all dharmas are also suchness;
and all noble sages are also suchness. To clarify the sequence of these stages: first is the Dharma-body (li-ti) Three Jewels, following the order previously established.

Their sequence is established as follows: if one examines their fundamental basis, the realization of the principle (*tattva*) is fully accomplished. The Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*) is primary; however, since the principle does not manifest of itself, it relies upon practice (*caryā*) to become evident.

Therefore, the fivefold [classification] is presented first. Alternatively, the Jewel of the Buddha (*buddharatna*) is placed at the beginning because the principle is manifested by the person, and the Path (*mārga*) is accomplished through provisional practice.

It was only after the World-Honored One Śākyamuni appeared in the world that the Three Jewels were heard of; thus, following the conventional signs of his transformation (*nirmāṇa*), the principle is not [independently prior].

[This is distinct from the "dual regulation" which speaks of the principle-reality (*li-ti*) Three Jewels; it follows the same sequence as the manifested-form (*hua-xiang*) Three Jewels. Second, to clarify the manifested-form [Three Jewels]: Buddha first, Dharma second, and Sangha last.
This is because when Śākyamuni first attained realization, he was the Buddha alone who was supreme. Since nothing that is not supreme can occupy the first position, the Buddha is placed at the head.
Although the Great Sage appears, he can only move one's ears and eyes; as for the afflictions and delusions, they must rely upon the Dharma for their removal.

Next is the unfolding of the verbal teachings (*śabdadharmadeśanā*) to cleanse the afflictions of the mind; thus, the Dharma comes next. As for the reach of these teachings, practice is their ultimate destination.

Although one may preach without realization, it is no different from not preaching at all. Therefore, when Kauṇḍinya attained realization, the Sangha Jewel first appeared, followed by the Dharma and then the Buddha.

This sequence of the transformative ritual (*nirmāṇavidhi*) must not be contravened. Third, regarding the Three Jewels as maintained in the world: the Sangha comes first, the Dharma second, and the Buddha last. This is because—
The Way relies on individuals for its propagation; this is the natural course of the world. Thus, when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, they manifested the monastic deportment.

They expounded the Five Vehicles as the causes of goodness and clarified the Three Paths as the results of evil; this was the manifestation of the ritual of the Dharma. This Dharma is profound and vast, not something that can be opened up by ordinary or inferior beings.
Therefore, they depicted images upon the cool terrace to represent what they had taught; this was the manifestation of the ritual of the Buddha. (41)
Regarding the essence of the Three Jewels, the Dharma comes first, the Saṃgha second, and the Buddha last. This is because their essence is the nature of the mind, which is fundamentally undefiled.

Because it is obscured by delusion and inverted views, the categories of the heterodox and the orthodox arise. Now, having realized the fundamental nature of phenomena, one understands that in principle there are truly no three;

yet, according to their phenomenal functions, they are divided into three so as to guide beings in various directions. Thus, to illuminate the aspect of principle is the meaning of *bodhi* (awakening); for its essence to transcend names and words is the meaning of *dharma*; and to—
The absence of obstruction in principle is the meaning of the *saṃgha* as a harmonious assembly. Because they do not know what is non-Dharma, the Dharma is placed first.

Because there are those who do not understand it even without the Buddha, the Buddha is mentioned last. As for the *saṃgha* being placed in the middle, its essence is not yet purely pure; like milk mixed with blood, it still has portions that must be eliminated, so how could it be compared to clarified butter (*sarpis*)?
Therefore, it is not the same as the Buddha. To clarify their respective functions, these are spoken of as the "Four Jewels," among which the Jewel of Principle is supreme.
Because it is eternally abiding, it is that to which the world turns for refuge; the other three [natures] are established accordingly, yet their essence is a conditioned phenomenon (*dharmasat*).

Question: The mind is fundamentally pure and is not defiled by the world; its single substance is eternally abiding. Why is it not considered supreme? Answer: Speaking from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), it is indeed as you have asked.

However, when discussing conventional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), impurities and defilements are not manifest. How, then, could they be identical to the source of the mind realized by the Buddha? Therefore, [it is called] *nirvāṇa*.

Baoyun said: "There are those who possess the Buddha-nature, and there are two types of people who lack it. This clearly shows that while practice and its fruit differ, both exist. As for the maintenance of the Triple Gem, in the final age it is considered superior.

Its principle lies in profound, unobstructed penetration; it is simply a matter of profound virtue (*xuan-de*). In the world, things exist only through marks (*lakṣaṇa*); one relies on provisional marks to open the way to understanding.

Those in the turbid age have dull faculties; they cannot be moved unless by means of marks. To accommodate the capacities of beings and engage with the mundane world, it is therefore said to be superior. (Continues below)
In the context of guiding the laity to receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, one must cite this meaning to provide a brief demonstration.
*Jing* (景) is glossed in the *Erbai* as "great. *Yang* (仰) is defined as "to look up with reverence"; it is also called "to honor and look up to. To gaze upward is called "looking up" (*yang*);
to look down from above is called "bending down" (*fu*). The *Mao Shi* says: "The high mountain is looked up to; the great path is trodden. This clarifies—
If the era holds this Buddha-dharma in great veneration, then the Buddha-dharma will be established and not fall into ruin. "Compassionate Cloud" (Ji-yun):
"Jing" means shadow or reflection. If one wishes for the image of the Tathāgata to pervade the age, one must regard it with reverence; therefore, it is said that [the teaching] is thus established.
In the "Chapter on the Mandate of Worldly Rites," it is stated: "Even within the secular world, there still exist rites and ceremonies through which one shows mutual respect and honor.

This method of paying such homage was originally established at the beginning of secular classics. For example, in the first fascicle of the *Liji* (Book of Rites), the *Qu li* (Ceremonial Usages) says:

There is nothing that does not involve reverence; ritual (*li*) is simply reverence. Reverence is the root of ritual. Because one yields out of reverence, one expresses inner feeling and exhausts outward propriety;
thus it is called "ritual" (*li*). Furthermore, ritual means "principle" (*li*); because it accords perfectly with the correct principle, it is called "ritual.
As for the *Liji*, the *Qu li*, the *Zhou li*, and the *Yili*, they all fully elucidate humility, deference, and the art of bowing.

The method of yielding is contained within the chapters on ritual (*lǐzhāng*). Since the chapters on ritual clarify the protocols for extensive reverence, they are called the "Chapters on Ritual Commands" (*súlǐ mìngzhāng*).
"Command" (*mìng*) means to summon; it is also called "to inform" and "to enact.
This refers to the method of humility and respect enacted as formal chapters and sections within secular ritual. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To cause the mouth to speak is called..."
Regarding "life" (ming): thus, the character for "life" is composed of "mouth" (kou) and "to command" (ling). As for "humility, diligence, and maintaining decorum," this establishes clarity:

being humble, respectful, and diligent in governing one's deportment is the fundamental source of the Way; therefore, it is called the "beginning. The *Zilin* states: "Humble" (sun) means "cautious" (shen) and "modest" (qian);
some say it means "yielding" (rang). Regarding "diligent" (ke), the *Zilin* states: "Respectful" (gong), "reverent" (jing), and also "restrained" (le)—meaning to be reverent.

Furthermore, "qín" (勤) means "kè" (恪, reverent diligence). As for the word "yuán" (爰), it signifies "yú" (於, at/in) and "jí" (及, reaching/to). Now, regarding the mention of "beginning" (*shǐ*) and so forth:

while the aforementioned humility and respect are what is clarified by worldly etiquette, the present regulation of deportment marks the beginning of the Way's tradition. For instance, the *Vinaya-śāstra* preface states:
"I bow my head in worship to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus. Moreover, in all the various treatises, they invariably provide a preliminary introduction first.
These are words for revering the Triple Gem; hence it is said that "the Way's lineage begins here. Regarding the term *jùmàn* (倨慢): the first character, *jù*, is pronounced *yù* (豫) in reverse.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To be *jù* is to be insolent; to be *màn* is to be arrogant," meaning to lack reverence.
Regarding the two dharmas of *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (modesty): to manifest disgrace externally is called *hrī*; to feel shame within internally is called *apatrāpya*.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "Shame toward oneself is named *hrī*; shame toward others is named *apatrāpya*. It further states, "Shame toward the heavens is named *hrī*;
shame toward people is named *apatrāpya*. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are two sublime dharmas that protect the world; namely—"

This is the mind of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*). If these two qualities did not exist, the world would not recognize the existence of parents, siblings, wives, children, friends, elders, or those of higher and lower status;
it would be no different from the category of domestic animals such as pigs, chickens, dogs, oxen, and sheep.
Yet they are all of one and the same kind. Because there are two factors in the world, one distinguishes between parents, elders, men, and so forth.
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way. Having heard this, the bhikṣus rejoiced, believed with gladness, and respectfully upheld it.
Therefore, the *Sutra of Bequeathed Teaching* says: "Those who lack a sense of shame and dread are no different from birds and beasts."
Regarding the phrases "the times have shifted" and "affections have grown thin": "the times have shifted" refers to the passage of time into the Age of Semblance (xiàngmò).

"Affections have grown thin" means that people gradually become washed out and superficial, no longer possessing the flavor of propriety and righteousness (*lǐyì*). As for the expression "propriety and righteousness have perished": to respect one another is called propriety (*lǐ*);

to yield to one another is called righteousness (*yì*). Furthermore, *yì* can mean ritual form (*yí*); when one's conduct accords with ritual propriety, it is therefore termed "propriety and righteousness."
At present, such a thing does not exist; therefore, it is said that he has "passed away. As for "eyebrows" (*méi*), it refers to the height of the Cloud of Compassion (*Cíyún*).

Just as a person's eyebrows are situated at the highest point, those born into a state of loftiness are called "eyebrows" (*méi*). The *Mao Shī* says, "How far is it until one attains long life with eyebrows?

The commentary states that "long life with eyebrows" means having prominent eyebrows, and further explains them as "fine hairs" (*háo méi*), meaning that among the eyebrows of an elder, fine hairs emerge prominently.

Furthermore, it says "eternal eyebrows" (*yǒngméi*) and "luxuriant eyebrows" (*háoméi*); this refers to the eyebrows being old. Thus, one calls them "old eyebrows" (*méilǎo*), meaning "longevity of the eyebrows" (*méishòu*). I [the author] say:

the phrase "The Commentary states" (*chuán yuē*) refers to the *Fǎnzhōu Shīchuán* (Commentary on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry). This means that the notes on the *Máoshī* refer to the *Chuán*. Furthermore, regarding the word "longevity" (*shòu*):
one who reaches the age of one hundred and twenty is called "long-lived. It is clear that such beautiful eyebrows and high longevity are mentioned in the subsequent lines.

Those with wrinkled backs and white eyebrows are the physical characteristics of old age. As for the phrase "those with patterns on their fingers are called *yingyan* (talented elites)": one who possesses talent equal to ten people is called a *hao* (hero);

one who equals a hundred is called an *ying* (talent); one who equals a thousand is called a *jun* (distinguished); one who equals ten thousand is called a *jie* (prodigy); and one who exceeds ten thousand is called a *sheng* (sage).

One whose talent and virtue are both excellent is designated as a *yan*. This is intended to clarify that even a minor monk of the present day can study and read secular texts, and is capable of composing them.

To consider oneself a distinguished scholar merely because one composes five-character verse, yet fails to understand even a single point of the Three Piṭaka scriptures of the Holy Teachings—this means that the Dharma will soon perish.
Such a person is "mào" (pronounced *máo* with the tone of *dào*), meaning to cover over or conceal; as seen in the *Mao Shi*, it also carries the sense of greed.
Consulting the *Zuǒchuán* (Spring and Autumn Annals), the division within it into two parts as distinguished by the title refers to the duality of the Sangha and the Image.

Regarding the passage in the *Zhìlùn* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) concerning the Buddha descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and so forth: according to the *Zhìlùn*, Subhūti was fond of practicing the samādhi of emptiness.

When the Buddha, having completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*) while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, returned to Jambudvīpa, at that time Subhūti— [The text continues: ...was [staying] in... (the remainder of the passage follows).
Within the stone chamber, he dwelt in solitary reflection: "The Buddha is descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

should I go to where the Buddha is, or should I not? He further thought: "The Buddha has often said that if a person observes the Buddha’s Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom, they see the most excellent among Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha was descending from heaven and remained in the midst of Jambudvīpa. (4)
The assembly gathered; the devas saw humans, and humans likewise saw the devas. Such a gathering of the celestial hosts was unprecedented.
Subhūti thought to himself: "Although this great assembly is truly extraordinary, its power will not endure for long; it is subject to the law of decay."
"All things return to impermanence. By contemplating impermanence in this way, he came to know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty; they are empty and lack any substantial reality.

While performing this contemplation, he immediately attained the realization of the Path. At that time, the multitude all desired to see the Buddha first in order to pay him homage and make offerings.

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Huase (Yashodharā) who, by means of her supernatural power, transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rājā*) together with the seven treasures and a thousand sons. When the multitude saw this—

They all rose from their seats and departed. Once the Transformation King had reached the Buddha’s presence, he resumed his original form as a bhikṣuṇī and was the very first to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed the nun, saying: "It was not you who first paid homage to the Buddha; Subhūti was the first to pay homage to me. Why is this?
Because Subhūti contemplates the emptiness of all dharmas; this constitutes seeing the Dharma-body of the Buddha and attaining true offering."
Nurturing. This is the supreme among all forms of making offerings; it is not that one makes an offering merely by performing prostrations to produce a physical body. [The Master] privately remarked:

"By citing this passage as proof, he causes people to perform salutations without becoming attached to external appearances. Regarding the Bhikṣuṇī Huase, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Dolun), fascicle five, states:
This woman’s countenance was upright and beautiful, with the hue of an *utpala* lotus. In a past life, many eons ago, she was the daughter of a brahmin.
When her parents and family members went out to sea to gather treasures, she remained behind;

unable to support herself, she lived together with various courtesans in one place, selling her beauty to provide for her needs. Her appearance was not particularly abundant, and no one [desired her].
As she came and went, she constantly reproached herself, wondering, "Why am I alone like this? At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha whom everyone revered with deep respect.
Someone said to her, "If you can make offerings to the Pratyekabuddha, whatever your heart desires, you shall have it according to your wishes in every lifetime.
Thereupon, the woman followed these words; she prepared exquisite food and drink, covered them with *utpala* flowers, and presented them to the Pratyekabuddha.

The *Madhyama Āgama* clarifies that Madhyāntika shared a room with his mother (and so forth). The fourth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: "Utpalavarṇā was startled by the pair of mandarin ducks.
In the past she shared a husband with her mother; now she shares a husband with her daughter. Such is the confusion of birth and death, reaching even this point.
If one does not sever craving and leave the household life to study the Path, how can such inverted delusions ever be stilled? She then abandoned him and departed, going straight to the Jetavana.
The realization of the truths and the exhaustion of outflows are as explained at length there. According to the *Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Meritorious Qualities):
While the Buddha was teaching the Dharma and transforming beings in the kingdom of King Udayana, he had been preaching the Dharma for ninety days to his mother, Māyā, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the nun Padmā wished to go ahead alone to see the Buddha, while the various kings had not yet seen him for nine [days].
On the tenth day, everyone was filled with longing and came together in great numbers like clouds.

Thinking, "As a bhikṣuṇī, it is not appropriate for me to remain amidst such a noisy crowd," she immediately transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), accompanied by a retinue according to the manner of a noble king.
When the various minor kings saw the noble king, they each fled and dispersed. The bhikṣuṇī then restored her original form and, seeing the Buddha, paid him homage.
They paid their respects and inquired after his well-being. The various kings each came to see the Buddha, but not seeing the Holy King, they realized he had been transformed by the nun.
They said to the nun, "Was we deceived in such a manner just now? At that time, the nun thought to herself, "I saw the Buddha first. Then the Buddha addressed the nun, saying:
"You yourself claim that you dared to see the Buddha first, yet there were others who saw him before you.
It was Subhūti, who was mending his robes in the mountains east of the city of Rājagṛha. A deva said to him, 'The Buddha has already descended.
Subhūti replied, 'According to the dharma for a disciple, I ought to go and pay my respects. He then reflected further: 'Where might the Buddha be? Perhaps he is golden-colored...'"
"Is this the Buddha? "What limit could there be to gold? The Buddha said, "All dharmas are empty and non-existent.
If one understands that the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination is neither created nor made, that is to see me. At that very moment, he sat down to mend his robes.
Viewed in this light, Subhūti was the first to see the Buddha. The Buddha told him that by mastering the emptiness of all dharmas, one becomes the master of all dharmas. Thus it is.

This is the reflection on the Dharma. Regarding the passage concerning the bhikṣus’ ignorance of seniority, up to the mention of the three birds, the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, in the *Vihāra-khaṇḍa*, states:
“The Buddha, departing from Rājagṛha with the bhikṣus, proceeded to Vaiśālī.

At that time, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks went ahead of the Buddha to a certain residence and took possession of the best rooms for their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), co-preceptors (*sārdhamvihārin*), and instructors (*ācārya*).”
Because his preceptor was a close friend, he obtained a fine room. Since Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra could not obtain rooms, they stayed overnight on the outer terrace.
The following day, the Buddha asked Śāriputra, “Was your sleep last night peaceful? Śāriputra answered in detail regarding the aforementioned matters.
The Buddha then assembled the bhikṣus and asked, “Who do you think should receive the foremost seat? The second [question].

"First water; first meal. The bhikṣus each gave different answers—some said "noble lineage," some "great learning," some "begging for alms," some "wearing rag-robes," and others "upholding the Vinaya" or "practicing meditation.
The Buddha said, "Listen well, all of you. In the past, there were three close friends."
Once, a monkey and a *kalaviṅka* bird (also read as *dúhuá* or *dútán*) were dwelling together in a single *nyagrodha* tree. They thought to themselves:
"We are living together; it is not right that we should not show one another respect. We should now determine our relative status based on the order of our seniority."
They showed mutual respect. The monkey and the francolin bird together asked the elephant, "How far back do you remember events?
The elephant replied, "I remember when this *nyagrodha* tree was at my navel as I walked past it during my youth.
Next, the elephant and the francolin bird asked the monkey, "How far back do you remember events? The monkey answered, "I remember when this tree was as high as my head during my youth."

The elephant reached its trunk to the monkey’s head. The elephant said to the monkey, "You have lived longer than I. Then the elephant and the monkey together asked the partridge, "How far back do you remember events?
He replied, "I remember that on the right side of the King of Snow Mountains, there was a great nyagrodha tree."
I ate those fruits and came here, whereupon I was immediately born from this tree. He thought to himself, "The partridge has lived for more years than I.
Then the elephant placed the monkey upon its head, and the monkey placed the partridge upon its shoulder.
The monkey thought privately, "It is fortunate that the bird is large and the elephant is small; thus the noble one is high and the humble one is low. How could I possibly bear them both? Together—
He wandered among humans, going from village to village and city to city, preaching these words: "Those who revere their elders are able to protect the Dharma;
you all [should do likewise]," and so forth. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the connection between past and present is as follows:
at that time, the bird was the Buddha; the monkey was Śāriputra; and the elephant was Maudgalyāyana.
The reason I cite this matter now is to use the lower to illustrate the superior.

If in these times there were no mutual respect and no distinction between the honorable and the humble, according to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, it would be the law of heretics, soldiers, and slaves. The Master [Daoxuan] says:

The *Eryi* (Explanations of Names) states that the *tiao* (zhua, first tone) is a "crowned pheasant. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "It is as large as a pigeon; it resembles a *ci-bird* pheasant. It is like a mouse.
It has no hind toes; its forked tail resembles that of a bird. It is fierce and flies in flocks.
It originates from the desert lands of the north and is commonly known as the *Tujue* (Turks). It thrives amidst the *caulis* and wild greens.
Regarding the phrase "teaching and transforming the people," this refers to these three birds and beasts preaching the Dharma and wandering about to transform human beings.
As for the fact that no humans or animals in the mountains and forests failed to bow down upon seeing the Buddha: this is because they practiced respectful conduct in past lives;

thus, even insentient things now respond with reverence. Question: Mountains and forests are insentient; why do they manifest such respect? Answer: It is due to the [virtue of] rivers and mountains... [and so forth].
The great earth is the retributive support (*niśraya-vipāka*) for sentient beings. If one’s karma is wholesome, it invites a pure land; if one’s karma is evil, it invites a defiled realm.

For this reason, the sentient elicits the non-sentient. This is like the phenomenon of the earth quaking at the time of a Buddha’s birth or parinirvāṇa, which is the sentient eliciting the non-sentient.
It is also like the auspicious river with its surging waves and the jewel-tree with its freely extending branches.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states that those who lack reverence for the Buddha are reborn among dragons and snakes.

According to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, when the Buddha was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude as he preached the Dharma, there was an elder bhikṣu in the assembly who stretched out his legs toward the Buddha and fell asleep. There was also a novice named Māyā...
At eight years of age, not far from the Buddha, he sat cross-legged with his mindfulness fixed before him. When the World-Honored One saw him, he immediately spoke this verse:
"One who is called an elder Is not necessarily one whose hair and beard are shorn; Though one may be advanced in years..."
One who cannot avoid the practice of afflictions—of this I now speak, O Elder:
happiness must first come from leaving the household life to cultivate the roots of one’s own wholesome karma.
One who discriminates in right practice—even if they are young and their faculties are not yet free of outflows—is what is called an “Elder” who discriminates in the practice of the True Dharma.
He asked again, "Have you seen anyone sleeping with their legs stretched out? This bhikṣu has constantly been in the form of a nāga for five hundred lifetimes.
If he were to die now, he would surely be reborn among the nāgas. The reason for this is that he lacks a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If there are sentient beings who lack a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, their bodies..."
When their lives end, they are all reborn among the *nāgas*.

Regarding the statement in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* that "because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) follow a different dharma, they come to the Buddha’s presence and sit down of their own accord," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:
"In the Buddha-dharma, when various non-Buddhist renunciants as well as all lay followers (*avadātavasana*) come to the Buddha’s presence..."
They sit because the teachings of other outsiders are inferior. Laypeople sit like guests. All members of the fivefold assembly stand because their bodies and minds belong to the Buddha.
As for those Arhats who have attained the Way, such as Śāriputra, Subhūti, Maudgalyāyana, and others, they are permitted to sit because they have already accomplished what was to be done.
Others, though they may have attained the three lower stages of the Path, are not permitted to sit. This is a matter of great importance.
Not yet accomplished; the bandits have not been defeated. For example, it is because kings and ministers possess great meritorious achievements that they are permitted to sit.
To say that those below the three paths are not allowed to sit refers to those at the stage of the three fruits, as their virtues are not yet perfected.

Regarding the absence of a separate community of Bodhisattvas, this does not mean that there are no Bodhisattvas whatsoever within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha; rather, it means that those Bodhisattvas have all undergone tonsure and donned the dyed robes.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas, he conceals his bodhisattva deportment and assumes the appearance of a śrāvaka. As the sūtra says:
"Internally he keeps secret the practice of a bodhisattva; externally he manifests as a śrāvaka," and so forth.
The above explains the meaning of "respectful demeanor. Below, the second section correctly clarifies right and wrong in relation to external conditions.
Regarding the passage "even on this great earth there is no place for spittle or snot," the Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not a śramaṇa yet claims, 'I am a śramaṇa,' or who does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet claims, 'I possess the holy life,' then upon this great earth, there will be no place even for his spittle or snot."
It is so even at the place where one spits, let alone when lifting or placing the feet, or when going, coming, bending, or stretching. Why is this?
In the past, great kings took this great earth and gave it as a gift to those who maintained the precepts and possessed virtue, so that they might practice the Path upon it.
Kāśyapa, such a precept-breaking bhikṣu must surely repay the faithful offerings given to him, yet it would be like a single hair-tip, or like one part of a hair divided into a hundred parts.
"A precept-breaking bhikṣu cannot properly digest even one portion of an offering, let alone [offerings for] a monastery, a *caitya*, or a walking path for the Saṃgha.
At that time, there were two hundred bhikṣus of pure conduct among the assembly who, having heard this, wiped away their tears and said:
"World-Honored One, we shall now die; we do not wish to live without attaining the fruits of a śramaṇa."
Regarding the acceptance of others’ offerings of faith, even as little as a single meal, the Buddha said, "Excellent!
Such shame and remorse, and such fear of future worlds, are like a diamond. If one practices with such diligence, one shall also attain liberation.

One who firmly upholds the precepts and accepts the offerings of faith equal in volume to Mount Sumeru likewise repays the merit of those offerings; it would still be less than all the great oceans within a thousandfold world-system."
While [the material resources] may be exhausted, the merit of this donor cannot be exhausted. Furthermore, according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra:

"If a son or daughter of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet then gives rise to the thought of violating these sacred precepts, they shall not receive the offerings of any donors.
They shall not walk upon the ground of a king, nor shall they drink the water of a king. (Five thousand...)
A great ghost constantly blocks his path ahead. The ghost cries out, "Great thief! Furthermore, whenever he enters a room, a city, or a house, the ghost constantly sweeps away his footprints.
This is precisely what is meant by all people of the world reviling him as a thief within the Buddha-dharma;
that all sentient beings do not wish to see him with their eyes; and that a person who breaks the precepts is no different from a beast or a block of wood. Such is the meaning.

Regarding the initial statement that "one should not pay respects when there is no convergence of conditions," the established view is that one must mutually respect one another provided there is no cause for illness and no circumstance involving the ten types of improper conduct (*a-vinaya*).
As for the instruction that "one should not bow while defecating or urinating," Zhen says:

this does not mean that someone might come to pay respects while one is actually in the process of relieving oneself—how could such a thing ever happen? It refers rather to the period after one has finished defecating or urinating but before one has washed.
When purified, one must not receive the prostrations of others, nor may one prostrate to the Buddha. One should say, "I have not yet washed myself" (the details are unclear).
This is also analogous to the rule regarding failing to rinse the mouth after eating. [The author] says privately that there is no explicit text in the Vinaya for this;
however, it would be logically unobjectionable as a matter of principle during the actual time of defecating or urinating.

Regarding the chewing of *śalākā* (tooth-sticks) and so forth, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* mentions three matters that must be performed in a secluded place: defecating or urinating, and chewing tooth-sticks.

Since these are activities for secluded places, it is improper to perform prostrations [during them]. The *Lishi* commentary cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, stating: "If one prostrates before a Buddha stūpa, a bhikṣu commits a *pāyattika* offense;
when wearing only a single robe, one should not prostrate. Regarding this, Cien says: "The five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭi*) constitutes 'one' [robe]."
It refers to the robe (*cīvara*). Some say: "What prevents one from wearing the five-strip robe as the inner undergarment? The commentary states:
"I am among the Saṃgha" means that one is among the *saṃgha* of those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
First, regarding "handsome appearance" and so forth: by prostrating to the Buddha and seeing the Buddha’s physical form, one gives rise to a heart of joy;
through these causes and conditions, one obtains a handsome appearance. Second, regarding "fine complexion" and so forth:

by seeing the Buddha’s physical form and three times orally professing the name, "Namo Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," one obtains a beautiful voice through these causes and conditions. Third, "much... [text continues].

Regarding "wealth and so forth": because one beholds the Tathāgata and performs great acts of giving—such as scattering incense, lighting lamps, and offering other gifts—one obtains vast treasures through these causes and conditions.
Regarding "being born into the families of the four classes of elders and so forth":

having seen the form of the Tathāgata, with a mind free from defilement or attachment, one places the right knee on the ground, kneels with palms joined, and pays homage to the Buddha with a sincere heart. Through this...
Regarding these causes and conditions for being born into the family of a householder, or for dying and being reborn in the heavens:

it is the constant law of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that any sentient beings who pay homage to the Tathāgata through five kinds of causes and conditions shall be reborn in a favorable place, in the heavens above.
Therefore, monks, if any man or woman wishes to pay homage to the Buddha, they should skillfully accomplish these five merits;
they should train themselves in this way. Furthermore, although the merits of paying homage to the Buddha are many, to speak of them in brief, one obtains two kinds of benefit.

The first is personal practice; the second is adornment. From personal practice, one internally increases merit; from the adornment of the assembly, one externally engenders goodness in sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the Buddha’s grace. One should contemplate the Buddha’s compassion: how he manifests in the forms of the six realms to guide and transform sentient beings;

how he undergoes ascetic practices throughout kalpas, sacrificing his body, head, and eyes, seeking only Bodhi; and how he teaches us without ever growing weary. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter eighteen, states:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva practiced with such single-minded intensity for seven days and nights that he forgot to set down a single foot. By means of this wondrous...
He praised Tiṣya Buddha with a verse called "The Perfection of Diligence," saying:

"In heaven, on earth, in this world, or in the abode of the learned (Mañjuśrī), In the palaces of the departed or in the celestial realms throughout the ten directions— Nowhere in the mountains or forests across the earth can an equal be found To this Great Śramaṇa, the Bull-King among men.
Because of this praise, Śākyamuni bypassed nine kalpas of Maitreya. (Commentary: "In heaven, on earth, in this world" refers to...
This refers generally to the heavens above and the lands below; it is this Sahā world. "Viśvāmitra" (Vaiśravaṇa) translates as "Much-Hearing.
Among the Four Heavenly Kings, he is the sovereign of the north. The name "Hall of Much-Hearing" is derived from the location of that king, which is the first heaven of the Desire Realm.

The "Abode of the Departed" (*śivamandira*) refers to the palace of Brahmā, the first heaven of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). "Departed" (*śiva*) carries the meaning of death. Non-Buddhists falsely reckon that Brahmā is eternal;
thus, they call that place the "Abode of the Departed. As for the "Celestial Abodes," these do not exist in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon this to be nirvana; however, what is now stated is that it is merely a place where sentient beings dwell.

What has been explained above clarifies that such a thing does not exist within this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds. Not only does it not exist here, but throughout the ten directions, across all three thousandfold worlds, it likewise does not exist.

Therefore, it is said that it does not exist in the ten directions. This is done to extol the virtues of the Buddha as a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), the virtues of a Bull King (vṛṣabha-rāja), and the virtues of a Śramaṇa.

One seeks the peerless virtues of the stages [of the bodhisattva path]. Regarding the mindfulness of the Buddha, the sutras, and the precepts: by practicing in accordance with the teachings of the sutras and precepts, one discerns the correct from the deviant;
from the subtle to the manifest, and from the mundane to the sacred, all proceed in this manner. Furthermore, regarding the mindfulness of the kindness of teachers, monks, and parents:
teachers and monks give birth to one’s dharma-body, while parents nurture one’s physical body; therefore, one must be mindful of them. Thus it is said:
Regarding the kindness of fellow students: this refers to how fellow students encourage one another to advance in wholesome deeds.

Thus, the worldly saying, "Without friends for study, one is narrow-minded and hears little," is indeed true. Yet, friends serve as the primary means for mutual accomplishment, providing the benefit of mutual critique and refinement.
Furthermore, it is said: "Parents give us life; friends bring us to fulfillment. In light of this, one must...
Regarding the citation from the *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra* concerning the story of a bhikṣu who became a butcher (and so forth),

and Śāriputra’s prostration before the Buddha and his circumambulation of the Buddha one hundred times on his knees (and so forth), these are as recorded in the excerpt from the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
Second, the explicit explanation of the characteristics: The above was a citation of scriptural evidence to demonstrate that one must certainly exercise reverence;

from here below is the explicit explanation of the ritual for reverence. "Reverence means viewing the Ultimate Truth with equanimity" means that when one reveres a clay or painted image of the Honored One, it is no different from revering the Buddha of Ultimate Truth himself;
therefore, it is said they are viewed with equanimity. Regarding "rolling up the sleeves": "ruang" (攘) means to push back or roll up. As for...

"To push back" (*kyaku*) refers to moving the arm backward. Alternatively, it may mean taking the garment on one's arm and moving it toward the back, as in the expression "to push away calamity" (*nyōsai*), which likewise means to ward off disaster.
"To point out the sacred ritual implements in their entirety" refers to pointing at the images [of the Buddhas] and saying things such as, "This artisan was clumsy;
they are too long or too short," and so forth.
If one who respects others is still subject to reprimand, consider for a moment: when bowing to an official while on a bed, would one not be reprimanded?

How much more so, then, regarding the worship of the Buddha? Nowadays, this occurs occasionally in small temples in the capital; people perform their prostrations to the Buddha entirely upon their beds.
I have heard of a young traveling monk who went into the refectory and ascended the platform to prostrate before an elderly senior monk. The elderly monk immediately—
[The teacher] rebuked him, saying, "From where have you come? You have suddenly become deficient in the application of the Dharma. How can you prostrate to me upon my bed?
He replied, "Is the Ācārya greater than the Buddha? The Ācārya is a disciple of the Buddha; even he prostrates to the Buddha while remaining on his bed.
I am on the bed, prostrating to the Ācārya—what is wrong with that, that you should rebuke me? At that time, the teacher was rendered speechless and could not utter a word.

Regarding the statement, "One may perform prostrations on behalf of the Upādhyāya": it is as when a disciple wishes to travel abroad and says, "If you see the Venerable One [Name], please pay homage for me.
The Upādhyāya then performs the prostration on the disciple's behalf, saying, "I transmit my salutations to him."

The disciple receives the honors due to a teacher because he has received [the teacher's] entrustment; thus, upon reaching that person, he performs prostrations. Nowadays, many secular families have this custom.
Both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Lokadhātu-sūtra* state that for the sake of sentient beings, one may shatter one’s body like hemp seeds, rice grains, or even mustard seeds.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 59:

"If a man or woman makes offerings to the relics themselves, or if there is another person who divides the relics into portions as small as a mustard seed and gives them to others to make offerings, the merit thereof is exceedingly great.
World-Honored One, seeing this benefit for sentient beings, [the Buddha] entered the Vajra-samādhi and spontaneously shattered his own vajra-body into fragments."

Śāriputra, why is this? If there are those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics—even as small as a single mustard seed—their meritorious reward will be boundless, continuing until the end of suffering. Furthermore, according to the *Lokadhātuvyūha-sūtra*, it says:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni practiced with diligent vigor; therefore, today he has attained unsurpassed Bodhi, a Bodhi that is difficult to attain. It was through vigor..."
Cease. Even at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, he still exerts diligent effort, breaking his own body and bones into pieces as small as mustard seeds and dismembering his limbs and joints.

Why is this? Out of compassion for all sentient beings of the future, he gives rise to great pity (*mahākaruṇā*) and distributes the *śarīra* relics, down to those as small as mustard seeds, all imbued with supernatural power.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the *śarīra*, their hearts—

[He] attained purity. It is traditionally said that when the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he entered the *vajra-samādhi* and spontaneously shattered his own body, bones, and flesh, so that the skin-bag [remained] upon them like sand within a pouch.
No such textual evidence can be found in the *sūtras* or *śāstras*. Regarding this, the *Sectarian Tenets Commentary* (or *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*) states:
"Furthermore, even regarding the date of the Buddha’s birth, the accounts in the *sūtras* and *śāstras* differ. Now, we shall adopt one definitive judgment based on the second month."
The eighth day of the month is established as the date of birth. This is determined by calculating the ten months spent in the womb;
since he entered the womb on the eighth day of the fourth month, it is clear that he was born on the eighth day of the second month, as this accounts for exactly ten months.

Furthermore, prior to his descent from Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva—being a *ekajātipratibaddha* (one who is bound to only one more birth) among the Buddhas of the three times—had frequently been born therein. From that celestial realm, for the sake of the devas...
The Son preached the Dharma and dispatched the various devas to descend and be born among humans, intending for them to receive transformation later.
When the Bodhisattva was about to descend and be born, he first contemplated five matters: first, he observed whether the karmic conditions of the sentient beings to be transformed had ripened;
second, he observed which country’s lineage and ancestors were such that his parents would be authentic; third, he observed which country within this Jambudvīpa was the most central.
Fourth, he observed his past lives to see who had been his parents through the conditions of karma. Fifth, he observed at what time he would enter the womb;

thus, on the eighth day of the fourth month, riding upon the King of Elephants, he descended into the womb of his mother, Māyā. While in the womb, the Bodhisattva preached the Dharma three times each day:
at dawn, he preached the Dharma for the devas of the Form Realm; at midday, he preached it for the devas of the Desire Realm.
The Dharma. In the evening, he preached the Dharma to the spirits and deities. When the ten months were complete, at the time of sunrise, his mother entered a garden to play.
Seeing that the flowers on a tree were lovely, she raised her right hand to grasp one. The Bodhisattva was born from her armpit. Beneath the earth were seven stalks of lotus flowers;
they supported the Bodhisattva’s feet as he took seven steps in each of the four directions. Pointing with his fingers to heaven and earth, he said:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored. Nine dragons spewed forth water to bathe the Bodhisattva’s body.
The reason the Bodhisattva in his final birth was born at the time of sunrise was to manifest himself as the eyes for all sentient beings and to bring forth the Great Illumination.
After he was born, the seers examined his marks and wept with compassion, saying, "No, it shall not be so. When the King, his father, asked them, "What of my son? they replied:
"Is this not an ill omen? The immortal replied, "It is auspicious; there shall be nothing that is not beneficial. It is where the Way and Virtue converge, and the world shall receive its benefit.
I grieve only because I shall not live to witness the arising of the Buddha.

When he reached the age of nineteen, on the eighth day of the second month, at the moment the morning star appeared, a deity spoke from within a window with palms joined, saying, "The time has come for you to depart. He immediately commanded Chandaka to prepare the horse and let him go slowly.
He saddled the horse. Chandaka asked in alarm, "It is now the middle of the night; there are no enemies here. Why do you saddle the horse?
The Bodhisattva replied, "There is a great enemy: the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death. After he had requested the horse two or three times, he finally obtained it.
The devas supported the horse’s hooves as he leaped over the city walls and passed through; therefore, it is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*).

Regarding the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* concerning the twelve billion households in Rājagṛha and so forth: according to the ninth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, there were nine billion households in Śrāvastī.
