Of these, three billion households saw the Buddha with their eyes, while another three billion households heard that the Buddha existed. However...
The eye does not see them; three hundred million households neither see nor hear [them].

Although the Buddha resided in Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, these sentient beings neither heard nor saw him, let alone those who were far away (the text ends here). Furthermore, the third fascicle states:

"In the city of Śrāvastī there are nine hundred million households, and in the city of Rājagṛha there are twelve hundred million households" (the text simply states this). [Regarding] the city of Śrāvastī...
This refers to Śrāvastī; it is merely a corruption of the name.
The tradition states that when the Buddha saw monks standing, [the monk] Li said: "This is a teaching transmitted among women. There is no separate record or transmission (details unknown).
Regarding the statement that showing respect to the Saṃgha is not the way for a disciple: this refers to a teacher who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and requests twenty [monks].

Regarding those who have emerged from offenses (*pāpadeśanā*) and who were formerly one's disciples: it is permissible to pay them homage because they are members of the Saṃgha; it is on this basis that they receive homage.

As for the corpse prior to burial, according to the principle of the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), although the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) permits paying homage to the corpse, when analyzed according to the underlying logic, the Prātimokṣa precepts follow only the physical form.
Once the form has perished, the precepts are lost; therefore, it is not appropriate to pay homage [at that stage]. Now...

Regarding the allowance for prostration: it applies only to one’s deceased teacher; as for other deceased bhikṣus, because they did not possess the virtue of being one's benefactors, prostration is certainly not permitted.
This interpretation is flawed, for the explicit text of the *Catuḥpariṣat-sūtra* states: "The stūpas of the five assemblies must be venerated;
the great stūpa [of the Buddha] is likewise to be venerated" (and so forth).

Regarding the statement in the *Madhyama Āgama* that one should first take a seat when visiting the home of a layperson and only afterwards pay respects, as explained at length in the *Gaurava Sūtra*, it should be noted that the *Gaurava Sūtra* exists within the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. This sūtra clarifies only the matters concerning the duties of respect that a bhikṣu must observe.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should practice respect, and you should carefully observe and honor your fellow practitioners of the holy life" (and so forth).
As for Maudgalyāyana personally taking artisans to the heavens and so on, this refers to when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for the three-month summer retreat.
When his mother preached the Dharma, those in Jambudvīpa yearned for the Tathāgata with great thirst, yet they were unable to discern how they might behold him.

They then requested Maudgalyāyana to go to heaven and fashion a likeness of the World-Honored One’s form and shadow, so that it might be brought down to the human realm to make offerings to the Tathāgata. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he returned to the human realm;
this image circumambulated the Buddha amidst the three jeweled stairways. Śākyamuni touched the crown of the image’s head and made a prophetic record, saying:
"In a future age, you shall extensively perform the work of a Buddha" (and so forth).

According to the *Buddhabhūmi-samādhi-sūtra*, when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, King Udayana, longing for the World-Honored One, cast a golden image. Hearing that the Buddha was about to descend, he brought the golden image on a carriage to welcome the World-Honored One.
At that time, the golden image descended from the elephant as if it were a living Buddha, walking with its feet.
From the void, rain flowers fell and light was emitted, coming to welcome the World-Honored One. That image joined its palms and pressed its hands together, prostrating before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One likewise knelt for a long time with palms joined toward the image. Then, within the void...
A hundred thousand transformed Buddhas likewise joined their palms and knelt long before the image. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the image, saying:
"In future ages, you shall perform great Buddha-work. After my parinirvāṇa, I entrust all my disciples to you."
The transformation Buddhas in the air spoke with one voice, all saying these words.

[The] annotation states: "Regarding the auspicious image at Changgan and even the inscription on the pedestal," I [the author] privately remark that this refers to the statement made concerning the pedestal inscription.
It is currently located at Xingshan Temple in the capital. This was entirely fashioned by the daughter of King Aśoka; there are now two [of these images].

This person came from overseas to the region of Wu; he is still living there today. A detailed account is found in the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Auspiciousness), excerpted as follows (*et cetera*).
Regarding the ritual of the "Jealous Wife" (*Dufu*): it is said that a husband went to the road of Shu to engage in trade and bring back a wife.
When the former wife saw him, she died immediately.

The sutras and images instruct the world and serve as the foremost objects of faith for all believers; yet those who instead treat them with self-deprecating contempt—where then is their majestic spirit?
It is said that the sutras, Buddha-images, and golden statues give rise to faith, and are thus called the "foremost of faith. Now, in this final age, the time since the Sage departed has long passed.

While the Sage’s countenance can no longer be seen, there remain only these ritual images to represent him in the world, showing what is to be revered. Relying upon these, one leaves the household life; yet [some] turn against them...
If one does not know how to show respect oneself, how can one cause worldly people to give rise to faith? Furthermore, if a layperson is unfilial, they will inevitably be despised by others;
now, if a bhikṣu does not revere the sacred images, it is equivalent to being unfilial, and thus the layperson will treat them with contempt.
This is because such a person violates both mundane and supramundane laws. Ciyun said: "Sūtras and images are the objects upon which the supramundane relies."
"If one now violates and destroys it, this would contravene the laws of worldly veneration; thus it is said. The commentary states:
"It has recently been observed that there were thieves who plundered auspicious images and the like. This refers to the Xingshan Temple in the capital.
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong Xiaohé, it was renamed Fengguo Temple. Previously, there was a standing bronze statue within its main hall.
The temple monks, loathing its ugliness, moved it to the north side of the shrine. That night, the image traveled back to its original location.

When the monks saw it there the next morning, they assumed it had been moved by humans; they questioned the assembly in astonishment, but no one had moved it. They then sent it back to the north side of the shrine once more.
When morning came, it was seen again in its original place; thus, its spiritual wonder was realized.

Later, there were thieves who entered at night intending to steal this bronze statue, but they suddenly became dazed and confused, not knowing how to exit. At dawn, the monks saw them and asked where they had come from.
He answered fully regarding his intention. Suddenly, the rear of the hall was set on fire; at that time, people saw the image ascend into the air and depart.
Regarding the Buddha’s right canine tooth, which is kept by Śakra, it is as described in the *Dantakathā* (Account of the Tooth) [etcetera]. Zhi Li says that the Buddha has four canines.
One was in the abode of Śakra; one was in a dragon palace; one was in the country of Uddiyāna in Northern India; and one was in a country in Southern India (and so forth).
It is further stated that the one currently at Dong Chan-ding Temple in Sīhaladvīpa is the very same as the one from Northern India.
At that time, the monk Shi Faxian of Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhongshan in the Song dynasty traveled to the Western Regions.
It was obtained and is currently in Jiangning. During the later Sui dynasty, when the capital was in the South, it was moved to Chanding Monastery in the imperial capital during the Renshou era.
Regarding the "deficient clavicle" (*quepen gu*), Ji stated that this refers to the two large bones flanking the neck below the throat and above the chest.
If these bones do not protrude, one possesses this mark; nowadays, in most people, these bones all rise high. According to the record:
The *Sudarsana* states: Two hundred and thirty-six years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma spread to the kingdom of Siṃhala.
The king was devoted and faithful, and wishing to erect a stūpa, he found that no śarīra remained.
There was a novice monk named Sumana who, soaring through the air, went to the abode of Śakra and obtained śarīra. In that abode of Śakra, there were two...

Śāriputra’s relics consisted of two items: first, his right canine tooth; second, his clavicle bone. A śrāmaṇera went to seek the clavicle bone, while the right canine tooth remained at the place of Śakra for veneration.
When Śakra saw the śrāmaṇera approaching, he asked, "For what reason have you come here?
He replied, "It is the Buddha’s right clavicle bone; I have come to offer it veneration. Śakra then took the door-key, opened the seven-jeweled stūpa, and retrieved it.
The Śrāmaṇera was entrusted with the task. The King of Siṃhala leveled the roads and prepared all necessary provisions.
The King himself mounted an elephant and held a white parasol over the śarīra, making various offerings. At that time, the earth shook violently and all the people gathered together.
The śarīra ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, manifesting various miraculous powers.

It transformed, appearing in the five colors—black and yellow—and at times emitted water, and at times emitted fire, no different from the supernatural powers [displayed] when the Buddha was in the world.
It descended from the sky, visible to the entire assembly, and alighted upon the crown of the king’s head, where it remained stationary.
Upon seeing this, the king experienced a joy beyond the ordinary and enshrined it within a stupa. At that moment, the great earth shook violently. Now, the king had a younger brother named Wu...

Bhīṣmottara. Together with a thousand people, he went forth from the household life. Five hundred youths in the kingdom likewise all went forth, until as many as thirty thousand people had gone forth.

The king’s consort, together with five hundred young maidens and five hundred palace attendants, also went forth from the household life (the details are not fully recorded here due to their complexity).
Regarding King Udayana’s creation of the sandalwood image and so forth, according to the *Avadānaśataka*...
The *Yujing* (Sutra on the Foolish) states: King Udayana was the sovereign of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, and King Prasenajit was the sovereign of the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Regarding this kingdom of Śrāvastī, it is sometimes called Śāvatthī; both are corruptions and abbreviations.
The correct Sanskrit pronunciation is Śrāvastī, which means "the land of things heard. King Bimbisāra is also named King Piṇbāsāro.
The King of Rājagṛha is King Ajātaśatru; his intention was that [the image] would be his son. King Brahmadatta was the King of Vārāṇasī; his intention was that it would be his [son].
King Śuddhodana—here translated as King Śuddhodana—was the sovereign of Kapilavastu; his intention was that it would be his [son].
Regarding the matter of King Udayana’s creation of the image, it is as recorded in the *Ekottarika Āgama* (copied...), yet it does not compare to this.
In our Tang Dynasty, at Da Cien Monastery, Emperor Gaozong commissioned a life-sized golden image and a life-sized silver image for Empress Wen-de.
Furthermore, there was a life-sized silver image of Emperor Gaozong at Hongfu Monastery.

Additionally, at Fuxian Monastery, Empress Wu Zetian commissioned a silver image of Maitreya from Puzhou measuring sixteen feet in height. Among the emperors and kings of this world, their reverence for these [images] has reached its ultimate degree. Compassion.
Regarding the gilded image: the steward (zhísuì) stole the copper to cast it [into something else]. At the time, he was not noticed; though it is known now, it is not known who replaced it.
Furthermore, there were many other small gilded images; when they were weighed on the scale at the end of the day, the large ones did not produce good results.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "That which contains relics is called a *stūpa*; that which lacks them is called a *caitya*. According to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is also stated thus.
That which is termed a *caitya* refers to places where the Buddha preached the Dharma during his lifetime—whether in the mountains or beneath trees.
Whether it be the house of a layperson or any place where the Dharma was once preached, all such sites are called *caityas*. Regarding the annotation that "a temple (*miao*) refers to appearance":
this means that an image representing the physical likeness of a predecessor is established and placed within it; therefore, it is called a temple.
Regarding the measure of *brahma-puṇya* obtained from first constructing a *stūpa* or restoring an old temple, it is as recorded in the *Ekottarika Āgama* (and so forth).

Furthermore, as for the statement that the merit of one Brahmā King is equal to that of the six heavens of the desire realm and the first *dhyāna*, this refers to the fact that merit becomes increasingly superior as one ascends through the higher realms.
For example, even if one were to take all the precious jewels, as well as the populations and settlements, and the kings throughout Jambudvīpa...
"His merit is not worth even the price of a single sandal for Śakra...
(and so forth). The commentary states: 'The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi. [My] private opinion: this is the form of the Tathāgata Lokeśvara currently at the gatehouse."
Because he grasped the vajra, people later called him Vajra-ear (*Vajra-karṇa*). Regarding those who used vessels made of gold, jewels, and the like, I privately say:
all ordinary monks and holy monks alike may not grasp precious objects while alive, but after death, they may all receive offerings in precious vessels.
Why is this? Because after Śāriputra had entered parinirvāṇa in his native village, the villagers [prepared] various...
He made offerings and addressed the Buddha, asking, "What kind of vessel should be used to hold these? The Buddha said, "It is permitted to use precious vessels to hold them;
this is because one has already died and must repent for violations of the precepts.

Regarding the making of hand-wheel images from fragrant clay, it is explained that one applies fragrant clay to the ground to form a *maṇḍala*, or fashions the shape of a Buddha’s hand, or the shape of a wheel, or even the hands and feet of the Tathāgata.
This is the image of the central wheel. Offer flowers and incense upon it.
The commentary states that the gates of monasteries in the Middle Kingdom all face east. This region values the south, whereas that region prizes the east.
The commentary further states that this is because the northeast wind is prevalent in that country; this explains the location of the kitchen and latrines in the Middle Kingdom.

Place it in the southwest. This is because there is much wind from the northeast, which would cause smoke and dust, as well as the foul odors from the latrine, to blow out toward the west so that they do not pollute the monastic quarters or the Buddha hall.
The commentary states: "In the Divine Land (Shenzhou), the south is still considered the direction of true Yang.

This refers to the country of Zhendan (China) being generally called the Divine Land; its center is intended to be Luoyang, which is the "Red County" (Chixian) of the Divine Land. Therefore, [it was located in] Luozhou.
Within the city walls of the Duke of Zhou, there is a gnomon platform for measuring shadows and a soil-dipper for measurement. Furthermore, among the Five Peaks, Song is the Central Peak.
In this land, the south is used as the primary direction of Yang; since the positive aspect of Yin is Yang, it presides over generation. Therefore, the south is esteemed as superior.
Regarding the matter of seeing birds or beasts trampling and destroying [a sacred site], which one must necessarily repair, sweep, and clean:
the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states that once there was a bhikṣu whose time of death was approaching.

At that time, an outside practitioner, a brāhmaṇa, observed his physical signs and knew that this bhikṣu would certainly pass away seven days hence. Then, as this bhikṣu entered a monastery, he saw a wall...
There was a hole, so he took some clay, kneaded it into a ball, and patched it over. By virtue of this merit, his lifespan increased, allowing him to survive for more than seven days.
When the brahmin saw this and marveled at the reason for it, he asked him, "What merit have you cultivated?
The bhikṣu answered in detail (as described).
Regarding the "Edict on the Founding of a Temple by Dharma Master Shengde," it is said that this refers to Dharma Master Lingyu.

As for the statement that "later there was nothing that could destroy it," some say that if a temple is established away from difficult locations such as the vicinity of markets or government offices, the temple will remain stable and endure without destruction.

Regarding the statement that "there are no markers such as ritual tablets outside the boundary," Ciyun says: For example, in places where a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is demarcated, there are no steles or monuments to indicate it.
However, according to the *Jiwen tu jing* (Sūtra on the Diagrams of Jetavana), every object established within a monastery has a symbolic significance.

For instance, if there is a pond outside the monastery, it symbolizes the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); if there is a wall surrounding the edge of the pond, it symbolizes the disciples who maintain the precepts (*śīla*). Thus, each element [has its meaning].
This indicates that beyond these limits there are no further ritual forms or symbolic signs to inform people.
In the *Jiwen tu* (Diagram of Jetavana), all the wooden structures, stone monuments, and earthen buildings have their respective symbolic representations;
these were obtained by the Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang from the Western Regions, based on the plans for the construction of the monastery provided by Prince Jeta and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Come! Within it there are many formal regulations. Inside the monastery, there are thirty-six courtyards, each distinguished by its own name;

all were constructed by the artisans of the Brahma Heaven. Within the monastic complex, there are separate courtyards for the Buddha, the stūpa, and the monks, each with a erected banner-pole (*yaṣṭi*) or an inscribed stone tablet indicating that it belongs to such-and-such a courtyard.
All of these are constructed of wood, stone, and other materials to serve as markers, signifying what they represent.
"Manifest" (*zhāng*) means to cause others to have no further need for cognitive discrimination. Furthermore, "to manifest" (*biǎo*) refers to what has already been explained above.
Regarding the phrase "shadows and coverings [ward off] heterodox arts, and birds and beasts fear its majesty," according to Faxian’s *Record of Travels in Foreign Lands* (*Foguo ji*), it says:
"Where the Buddha formerly debated with ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist heretics, a vihāra was erected. The building is six *zhang* high, and within it sits a Buddha."
To the east of the road is a non-Buddhist temple named Yingfu (Shadow-Overshadowing). It stands facing the Buddhist vihāra across the street and is also six *zhang* high.
As for why it is named "Shadow-Overshadowing": when the sun is in the west, the shadow of the Buddha’s vihāra falls upon the non-Buddhist temple;
however, when the sun is in the east, the shadow of the non-Buddhist temple falls northward and can never fall upon the Buddha’s vihāra.
[This occurred at] Śrāvastī. There was a brahmin who constantly sent people to guard a temple of the gods (*devāyatana*), offering incense and lighting lamps as an act of worship.
When morning came, the lamps would invariably shift to the Buddha’s vihāra. The brahmins spoke with resentment, saying, "The śramaṇas have taken our lamps to worship the Buddha themselves.
Later, on another occasion, the brahmin waited in ambush during the night and saw what happened there.
He served the celestial deities and, holding a lamp, circumambulated the Buddha’s vihāra three times. Having made this offering to the Buddha, he suddenly vanished.
The brāhmaṇa then realized that the Buddha’s spiritual power was great, whereupon he abandoned his home and entered the Buddha’s Way. If one asks whether it is as previously explained:

"Beasts and birds fear its majesty; how can this be dispelled? The commentary explains: "This sentence is a general reference to all ordinary monasteries where there is a place of accordance with the Dharma;
even birds and sparrows do not dare to trespass upon them."
The note states, "Regarding 'placing [the body] in a tomb and bathing': this refers to ignorant officials who frequently come to bathe inside the monks' bathhouse.
The note states, "Regarding 'Wenhou revering Ganmu': during the late Zhou period, among the six kingdoms, there was a king of Wei known as Wenhou. At that time...
In the state there was a man of virtue named Duan Ganmu. He lived in seclusion and did not serve in office. Lord Wen went to visit him;
when he knelt at the foot of the hall, his legs became stiff and he did not dare to stretch them. The King said, "I am wealthy in riches, while Ganmu is wealthy in righteousness.
I am noble in rank, while Ganmu is noble in virtue. He does not accept my wealth, nor does he seek honor in my position. The King [continued]: "I..."
A person’s legs become numb and they dare not extend them. At that time, the state of Qin intended to invade Wei;
however, upon hearing of the existence of Duan Ganmu, it did not dare to direct its military against Wei, for it was held that because the King possessed virtue, he could not be attacked.
Thus, the *Shu* records: "While Duanmu was in Wei, the people of Qin withdrew their troops. Furthermore, Zuo Taizhong’s poem on history in the *Wenxuan* states: "I emulate Duan Ganmu."
"Resting at ease, he was a lord among the vassals of Wei; I admire him as I do Zhonglian of Lu. With a mere laugh and a few words, he repelled the Qin army.

Thus it is said that in ancient times, when a state possessed a man of worth, foreign powers would not launch an invasion. Furthermore, according to the *Tongxian ji* (Record of Equal Worthies), Ganmu was a man of Jin during the era of the Six States.
His surname was Duan and his courtesy name was Ganmu. He was poor and lowly in his youth, making his living by hoeing and reaping. Later, he traveled to the West River.
He served Zi Xia as his teacher; he cultivated his virtue in silence, and his mind was thoroughly versed in the Six Arts.
King Wenhou of Wei, respecting his talent and virtue and desiring to appoint him to office, prepared his carriage and went to his home. When Gan Mu heard of this, he climbed over the wall to escape.

King Wenhou halted his carriage before Gan Mu’s cottage in respectful homage, and only then did he return. My servant said: "Gan Mu is but a scholar in plain clothes; why does Your Majesty halt your carriage for him?"
"Is this not excessive, Master Lu? Wenhou said, "Gan Mu does not hasten after worldly profit but dwells in the Great Way;

he lives in seclusion within a humble alley, yet his reputation spreads ten thousand *li*. His conduct relies upon virtue, and there has never been anyone who would willingly exchange it for my own brilliance in the world."
Gan Mu excels in virtue; I, the Ruler, am rich in wealth. Gan Mu is rich in righteousness. I have heard that the world is not as valuable as virtue, and wealth is not as valuable as righteousness.
How could I dare not honor the worthy and revere the Way? After a short while, Lord Wen summoned Gan Mu and said, "If you desire office, you may hold the position of Chancellor;
if you desire emolument, you may receive ten thousand *zhong*. You can assist me in governing the state. Gan—
Muzi said, "Since you have appointed me to office, you also demand that I observe the proper rites. To humble oneself to receive others—is this not difficult?

One who wishes to govern a state should ensure that administration is based on trust and that conduct is sincere; then the state will govern itself. What need is there for me? King Wenhou respectfully accepted his words.
They no longer interacted with one another. A song on the road went: "Our lord loves good governance; Gan Mu’s respect [for him] is profound. Our lord loves loyalty; Gan Mu’s honor [of him] is lofty.
Later, when the people of Qin raised an army intending to attack Wei, Sima Kang remonstrated, saying:
"Duan Ganmu is a man of great virtue whom the King of Wei honors. This is known throughout the world. One cannot attack a state that possesses such courtesy."
He mobilized his troops, but the Marquis of Qin then desisted, and Wei attained peace and stability. The commentary states: "This seems to refer to Liu Shi’s high regard for Kongming.

Liu Shi refers to Liu Bei; the intent is that this concerns the period of the Three Kingdoms. It means that the Wei ruler Cao Pi made Ye his capital—present-day Xiangzhou, which was formerly called the Capital of Wei.
The Wu ruler Sun Quan made Jiangning his capital—formerly called the Capital of Wu. Liu Bei made Shu his capital—formerly called... [the text here is incomplete].

The capital of Shu was known in the world as one of the Three Capitals, which governed the realm like the three legs of a tripod. In Shu there was a wise general surnamed Zhuge, named Gao and styled Kongming;
he was highly esteemed by the King. Liu Bei often said, "I have obtained Kongming, like a fish finding water."
Later, when Liu Bei launched a campaign against Wei, Zhuge Liang led his troops into Wei territory. The state of Wei engaged in battle with Shu;
at that time, Zhuge Liang was serving as Grand General and was skilled in strategic planning. The House of Wei feared only Zhuge Liang and did not dare advance.
Zhuge Liang fell ill and was on the verge of death. He said to his subordinates, "The ruler is weak while the generals are strong; thus we are beset by difficulties from them.
If they learn of my death, they will surely establish themselves as rivals to me. After I am dead, you may take a sack of earth and place it beneath my feet."
"Take a mirror and look at my face. Having said this, he drew his breath and passed away. Later, following this plan, Zhuge Liang was placed within the camp and surrounded by curtains.
During the night, the Liu family led their troops back and withdrew to Shu.
A skilled diviner in the state of Wei then remarked, "This man is not yet dead. How do we know? By treading on the earth and looking into a mirror, we can know."

He was not yet dead; consequently, [Zhongda] did not dare to engage in battle. Liu Bei withdrew his troops and returned to Shu. It was only after more than a month that the Wei people learned of this;
when they went to investigate, they saw only corpses and found that the soldiers had all dispersed. That those who were spared from disaster were able to do so was due to Zhuge Liang’s strategy.
People of the time said: "The deceased Zhuge Liang terrified the living Zhongda. Zhongda was a man of the Wei house.
He was a general named Sīmā Zhòngdá. It is also said that "the deceased Zhégě makes the living Zhòngdá flee.
Kǒngmíng possessed great ambition and capacity; his contemporaries called him Wòlóng (The Sleeping Dragon). He enjoyed the profound respect of the Liu clan. The commentary notes:
"Only those who can sit in dignity and stabilize [the realm] through the Way are like the case of Piṇḍola seeing a king and not rising, as recorded in the Vinaya."
The fifty-fascicle [version] presents these circumstances (as detailed above). Based on this, the Great and Small *Khandakas* were composed; such is the meaning of this text.
The explanation of the twenty-second chapter, "On Paying Homage to the Saṃgha and the Buddha Image," is hereby complete.
Chapter Twenty-Three: On the Procedures for Invitations and Announcements.

The preceding chapter sought to rectify the methods of the age; therefore, it was necessary to revere the Dharma and honor persons, resulting in the establishment of ritual protocols for venerating the Three Jewels.

This was enacted so that the fivefold assembly might cultivate and uphold the excellence of the Path. To the laity, these are truly called "fields of purity. Since the laity offer invitations for blessings and seek the prolongation of life, it is logically necessary to issue announcements.
[The preceding section] concluded. To avoid falling short of the prescribed measures or inviting censure by admitting the unseemly, this present chapter fully elucidates the ritual protocols.

When one arrives specifically for an invitation, it is termed a "funeral-invitation" (*fùqǐng*); when established according to the occasion, it is designated as "provisional rules" (*shèzé*). Thus it is said.

It is further stated that the two characters "funeral" (*fù*) and "invitation" (*qǐng*) encompass both the monastic and the secular: that is, the laity come to extend an invitation, while the monastics intend to go and notify [of the funeral]. Since going to notify has been permitted, it must...
There is a prescribed method; hence it is called "establishing the ritual.

Now, regarding the statement that "the worldly are preoccupied with many affairs and wisdom-observation is difficult to cultivate," this means that the delusions of worldly people burn fiercely, and they do not clearly understand the contemplation of the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Therefore, they are called "worldly. Furthermore, their activities of managing livelihoods are manifold and complex.

Furthermore, one must not allow them to cultivate the understanding of meditative concentration and wisdom through contemplative observation; hence it is said that "the cultivation of wisdom-observation is difficult.

As for the instruction to "restrain [them] and cause them to cultivate meritorious deeds," this means that since the illumination of wisdom is beyond their capacity, they should instead cultivate meritorious karma so as to obtain rebirth among humans or devas as a reward.
Furthermore, one may escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms; thus it is said that [the practice] is employed to receive [benefits] equally. As stated in the following passage:

"Because one is bound by the secular net, quietistic practice is difficult to sustain; whereas within the gate of the Way, being free from entanglements, one can devote oneself to superior conduct. Therefore, the two paths are distinguished—this is precisely their meaning.

As for the statement that "giving (*dāna*) is manifold and complex, involving the frequent provision of food and so forth," this establishes that giving encompasses the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), or alternatively, [it refers to the four types of giving].
One must practice the giving of robes, bedding, necessities of life, fields, gardens, utensils, and so forth.
However, among these many items, none exceed the offering of food. The purpose of this section is precisely to clarify the formal protocol for invitations made specifically regarding meals.
As for the statement that "if one violates the teachings during such invitations, one may even invite suffering realms as a result," this is intended to clarify the present situation.

When Master Qiu was giving alms, his deportment violated the proper rules. If it were not so, how could he have generated wholesome roots in sentient beings, let alone dispel calamities and extract them from suffering?
This was specifically because his movements and halts were contrary to the correct method, and his sitting and standing lacked a standard, thereby inviting the contempt and mockery of the laity.

Furthermore, had he instead given rise to a profound heart of reverence toward the realm of the Triple Gem, [the consequences would have been different]. Because of this contemptuous behavior, they all fell into hell; therefore, it is said that [such conduct] conversely brings about suffering.
Regarding the appointment of a *karmadāna* (Venerable Administrator): the *Chuyao lüyi yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of the Vinaya Essentials) states that the old translation is *vihārapāla*.
*Vihāra* means "monastery" (*sa*) and *pāla* means "protector" (*hu*); thus, it refers to one who protects the monastery. Bin says: the Sanskrit name is *ka...* [text truncated].
*Kṣāṇa*. *Karma* refers to the matter; *kṣāṇa* refers to the entrustment—meaning the entrustment of this matter. There is a reversal in the phrasing [of the original term].
If the text were rearranged, it should say "the one who entrusts matters," meaning one who assigns others to various tasks.
The old term *weina* (維那) means "to maintain the regulations. *Na* is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit sound. By combining the Sanskrit and Chinese explanations, it is called *weina*.

It is also called *yuezhong* (Pleaser of the Assembly). Regarding the original sound *póluò* (polo) and so forth, it is said that *yuezhong* is the meaning; this is the phonetic and semantic equivalent of the term for the one who maintains the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*).

It is stated that the name *weina* (upādhyāya) means "Pleaser of the Assembly. According to the *Shenglun* (Treatise on Phonology), this is an original foreign sound that should be pronounced as *póluò*.
This is translated as "succession" (*cìdì*). "Succession" refers to the further knowledge of the affairs of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the Buddha’s instruction to reject [the offerings] for the sake of future bhikṣus, this means:

since future bhikṣus will not be able to fully cultivate the prohibitive precepts, how could they possibly digest such offerings? The Buddha, knowing that the virtue of the monastic community today is meager, established this method in advance to serve as a guide for those who would come after.

Regarding the *Gṛhadevatā-bali-mantra* (The Incantation for the Offering to the Mother of Ghosts) for those who take [food]: according to that treatise, it asks itself: "May the food of the Mother of Ghosts be eaten? The answer is:
"It may be eaten after one has performed the incantation and made the aspiration. Having completed this, it is difficult for ordinary people to understand.

Regarding those who, according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, accept special invitations for offerings and take them for themselves: this refers to those who steal the property of the Sangha of the four directions. According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
"If a son of the Buddha, he must not under any circumstances accept special invitations for offerings and take them into his own possession.

Such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions; to accept a special invitation is to steal the property of the Sangha of the ten directions and take it for oneself. It further states: "If one accepts a special invitation..."
This is the teaching of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). None of the seven Buddhas ever practiced the method of separate invitations.

If an ordained bodhisattva who wishes to serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) should instead practice separate invitations, they commit a minor offense (*āpatti*). The *Ratnarāja-sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) likewise censures the fault of separate invitations.
According to the lower fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-ratnarāja-sūtra*, the Buddha said to King Prasenajit: "After my parinirvāṇa, in this defiled age..."
The fourfold assembly of disciples, including bhikṣuṇīs, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as kings and ministers, relying on their own nobility, shall destroy my Dharma.
They will openly establish restrictive laws to constrain my disciples, forbidding them from practicing the Way. They will establish registers for the community to record the monks;
they will force bhikṣus to stand upon the ground while laypeople occupy high seats; they will allow soldiers and slaves to become bhikṣus and receive invitations for separate meals. Know this!

"Know this, O Bhikṣu: it is not right for you to join with others in a single mind to hold a feast for the sake of seeking merit for a bhikṣu who is merely a personal friend, as is the custom of the non-Buddhists;
such is entirely contrary to my Dharma. At that time, the True Dharma will not long remain before it perishes. Furthermore, tell the Great King:
after my parinirvāṇa, in future ages, the fourfold assembly of disciples and the various minor kings shall be those who sustain and protect the Triple Gem."
Such a person further destroys the Three Jewels even more thoroughly, like a worm within a lion’s body devouring the lion itself; they are not outsiders.

Regarding the *Śāriputrābhidharma* and the *Upāsakajanālaṃkāra* which mention that five hundred arhats were separately invited, according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it was actually Mṛgāramātṛ who separately invited the five hundred arhats.
All of them possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); some entered through the windows, while others...
Regarding those who came from the air, some emerged directly from within their seats. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "It is not as good as inviting a single bhikṣu within the Saṃgha;

its merit surpasses that [of the former] (and so forth). As for the mention of "Śāṇakavāsin and others" in the present *Yao* (Excerpts), Śāṇakavāsin is not found in the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*;
there is only Mṛgāramātṛ. Furthermore, the *Śāṇakavāsin-sūtra* itself contains a separate account.

Regarding the condition: when one who has been well-nurtured by the Buddha’s teachings makes an offering, they believe with deep conviction that there are many meritorious qualities within the Saṅgha;
by making offerings impartially, they obtain immeasurable merit. Therefore, in my *Mṛgāramātṛ-sūtra*, I said to Mṛgāramātṛ:
Although one may later separately invite five hundred arhats, it still cannot be called "inviting the Sangha as a field of merit.

If this were so, then by giving even to a single person within the Sangha who resembles a most wicked bhikṣu, one would still obtain immeasurable fruits of merit and reward; it is like drinking from the great ocean, which is to drink all its rivers.
The only exception is the person of evil precepts, meaning monks and nuns who have committed the four pārājika or eight *gurudharma* offenses, who are termed "wicked."

"Jie" (戒) refers to a person of integrity. The term "yanyu" (諺語)—the "yan" being pronounced as "yian" (宜箭反)—is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "transmitted speech," meaning the common sayings handed down through generations.
According to the *Yaolan*, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, Yang Hu (字: Shuzi), a native of Taishan, served as the Grand Preceptor of the Jin.
It is said: Magnanimity is the foremost of virtues; caution is the foundation of conduct. Do not transmit unfounded talk; do not listen to words of slander or praise.
Whenever one wishes to form a friendship, nothing is better than virtue and righteousness. If you borrow with the thought that you will repay later, you must repay early.

Although this may seem a minor matter, it is the very root of integrity and shame (though these matters may be trivial, they must not be neglected). "To repay a loan when the time comes" refers to borrowing from others.
Regarding objects, one wishes to return them early. If one were to see someone demanding them back, it would be deeply shameful. Although the matter is small, the resulting humiliation is profound.
Now, the meaning of these characters is likewise: although the matter is small, if one does not understand them, it will greatly damage one's reputation and standing.
Regarding the rule for one traveling on the road among the *saṃgha* who thinks, "I shall eat at such-and-such a monastery," yet eats elsewhere and fails to repent:
this refers to a bhikṣu who intends to go to a certain monastery and mentally resolves that he will eat there, but then unexpectedly eats at another location;

this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), which is why it is called "repenting. This means repenting for the fault of the *duṣkṛta*. If he encounters a group of monks accepting an invitation, he may follow them.
Regarding "being without fault": this means that although one was thinking at the time of departure to go to a certain temple for a meal, someone invited the monks for a meal along the way;
having arrived there, if one follows the order of the monks of that temple and departs, there is no fault. Another interpretation states: it refers to passing through another temple on the way.
When it comes to the sequence of receiving invitations, one may follow along without a fixed path;
according to reason, both methods are permissible. Second, regarding the method for announcing the departure: among these, it is said that the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) should go at the front.

In the present time, the *karmadāna* (steward) must report the number of people assigned. The *upādhyāya* says: "In such-and-such a room, so-and-so and others, numbering so many, are those who are departing. As for the rest...
Once you know they have taken their seats, call them as you depart. Assemble at the entrance of the gate and proceed in a single file like a flight of geese;
do not go one ahead of the other, for the donor will be displeased and no merit will arise. Be aware of this; it cannot be recorded in full detail.
As for the method of inviting Piṇḍola, it is as described in the *Piṇḍolabhāradvāja-āmantraṇa-sūtra* (copied below, etc.).
Regarding the prohibition against sitting on a cramped or crowded floor and so forth: this clarifies that because the seating materials are insufficient, such faults arise.
Now, for poor laypeople who, despite having invited the assembly of monks, provide seats and mats that are base and inferior, no merit whatsoever will be produced.

Not only does one disparage the Triple Gem, but one’s merit and virtue also diminish. This is not as good as making offerings at a monastery, which also ensures that the assembly of monks remains free from disturbance.
Thus, in the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, there was an elder who prepared an offering and thought to himself:
"The Buddha said that the blessings of an offering are received according to their cause. If I invite the assembly of monks to my house for an offering, it will hinder [their practice]."
Abandoning the practice of the Path, one undergoes the hardships of coming and going through cold and heat;

yet when the time comes to receive the retribution, one must still exert oneself in pursuit and seeking before it can be obtained. If, however, one goes to provide offerings, then when the reward of merit is received later, it is simply received naturally while sitting at ease.
Regarding the bhikṣu on the left and the upāsaka on the right, [the commentator] states that this passage is cited to prove the preceding point:
that a bhikṣuṇī may not eat in the same place as the saṃgha. For instance, even ordinary women do not venture outside their gardens, courtyards, or rooms.

To sit upright and eat in the presence of those of long-standing virtue—even though one has shaved one's head and become a *bhikṣuṇī*, one still occupies the status of a woman—how could one so abruptly act without discernment and disregard shame?
Furthermore, to engage in conversation with the *saṃgha* is not even worth discussing.
Upon examining various sūtras and śāstras, there is no instance of *bhikṣuṇīs* sitting together with the great *saṃgha* of monks to eat. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle... [text continues]
The second account says: The Buddha was at the Veṇuvana Monastery when he traveled to the city of Pāṭaliputra. Upon arriving, he sat beneath a *pāṭali* tree.

At that time, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, hearing that the Buddha and his great assembly had come from afar to this place, went to pay his respects and requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately received the five precepts. He then invited the Buddha to a meal and personally announced that the time had arrived. The Buddha—
Together with the great assembly, he went to that lecture hall. Having washed his feet, he sat in the center.
At that time, the bhikṣus sat on the left side, and the lay devotees (upāsakas) sat on the right side.

Furthermore, according to the Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra, if a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for a meal from a donor, she should act in accordance with the Dharma and eat in accordance with the Dharma. There are three [points].
There are three matters: first, one must not sit and eat together with the great monks; second, one must not sit and eat together with upāsakas;
third, one must not greedily take food for oneself and feed it to young upāsakas.
A bhikṣuṇī, if she sees a great bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera on the road, should look upon them with equanimity, pay her respects straightforwardly, and depart.
She must not exchange glances with them; for if she gazes at their countenance, her mind will become impure.
One must not inquire after their well-being or ask where they intend to go; for if one does so inquire, there will inevitably arise feelings of attachment.
Regarding the phrase "the mahallaka sits improperly," according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when a mahallaka sits improperly, one should...

Tell her to sit upright. If she does not notice, you should tell her to straighten her robe. If she still does not notice, you should tell her to cover her body with her *mahāla* (outer garment), and so forth.
Regarding the instruction for the eight senior nuns: this refers to the regulations established within the *pācittiya* section for nuns;
the Sangha must follow this precedent. This is explained in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, from the "Snake and Gold" section up to the story of Pūrṇaka.
Regarding these two conditions, each is as explained in the *Xianyu jing chao* (Excerpts from the Sutra on the Wise and the Foolish), and so forth.
As for the term "bhāṇaka" (chanting monk) frequently found in the sūtras and vinayas, the *Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the *Chuyao lüyi* (Vinaya of Essential Discipline) states:

"Bhāṇaka means 'one who chants' according to those who uphold the Vinaya; it should also be called 'one who praises with verses. Now, I say this is a word from the country of Uḍḍiyāna; 'bhā' is translated as..."

*Zhi* (止) is translated as "cessation" (*nirodha*). Furthermore, it is said that *bai* (唄) is translated as *zhi* (止), and *ni* (匿) is translated as *xi* (息). *Bai* (唄) is translated as *zhi* (止), meaning to cease all evils;
*ni* (匿) is translated as *duan* (斷), meaning to be able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). It is also said that *xi* (息) means to rest from all labors and duties.
Regarding the passage in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning how the hearts of the devas rejoice upon hearing the *bai* (chanting), according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: there was one...
There was a bhikṣu named Bāḍhi, who was foremost among those capable of chanting. This bhikṣu’s voice was excellent, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will permit me to perform chanting with vocal melody. The Buddha immediately granted him permission. The Buddha said: "There are five benefits to chanting: first, the body does not become fatigued;
second, one does not forget what has been memorized; third, the mind does not grow weary; fourth, the quality of the voice is not impaired; and fifth, speech becomes easy."

Explanation: Furthermore, there are five benefits: first, the body does not become exhausted; second, one does not forget what has been remembered; third, the mind does not grow weary; fourth, the voice does not deteriorate;
and fifth, when the devas hear the sound of the chanting, their minds and hearts are filled with joy.
Regarding the phrase "those who generally extol the noble": "generally" (fan) refers to ordinary people; "竖" (shu) refers to young male slaves.

For instance, terms such as *cāngtóu* (blue-headed) and *shùzǐ* (young slave) are all common designations for minor servants. As for the phrase "the poor and lowly surpassing the consumption of food from tripods," it means to stand up [and praise them].
The state’s Chancellor struck the bell and presented the food from the tripods; hence it is called "tripod-food" (*ding-shi*).

For example, in the Xia dynasty, there were tripods before the Emperor’s hall, each containing nine *li* (cauldrons) to symbolize the nine continents. Food was placed within each, and on the day of the Great Year (*da-sui*), they were heated with fire.
If one [cauldron] cooked first, it signified that this continent would have a bountiful harvest that year; if they all boiled simultaneously, [it signified a universal abundance].
It is intended that there be peace throughout the world. If there is anyone who stirs up trouble beforehand, it is because someone in that province has committed rebellion.

As for this food, it is only those of the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers, the Nine Ministers, or the Great Officers and above who may obtain it. This clearly shows that the current praise is for the lowly; it says that people may merely offer prayers according to the occasion.
How could it be the same as the sounding of bells and the eating from tripods, which are the aspirations of those of noble lineage? "Yu" means "to exceed" or "to go beyond."
This statement is an exaggeration. The *Tattvasiddhi* states that even if it is a scriptural teaching, speaking at an inappropriate time is called frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "If one speaks the truth, yet the meaning is not correct, it is called frivolous speech.

Furthermore, even if it is truthful speech, because it is at an improper time, it is also called frivolous speech. Moreover, even if it is true and timely, if it accords with decline and affliction..."

Because it is without benefit, it is also called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). Furthermore, even if one speaks the truth at the proper time and it is beneficial, if the words lack coherence from beginning to end and the principles are disordered, it is called frivolous speech;
for such speech arises from a distracted mind due to afflictions such as delusion (*moha*).
This is called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Regarding new houses being completed, merchants wishing to depart, or taking a wife, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one enters a new house and provides an offering, it is said: [and so forth].
By providing shelter and shade, one obtains whatever one desires according to one's wishes;
amidst a multitude of auspicious, noble, and virtuous people, one enjoys [the fruits] therein.

In this world, those who are wise know that by maintaining pure conduct and the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in such a place, and by cultivating merit through the offering of food, the Sangha pronounces blessings with their own mouths.
The deity of the house is ever joyful, and with a virtuous mind, provides protection.
Dwelling within it through the long night, whether one enters a village or stays in a wilderness, whether by day or by night, the celestial deities always follow and protect.
If a merchant wishes to travel, one who has performed meritorious deeds should say:
May all directions be peaceful; may the gods grant auspiciousness. Having heard this, may the heart rejoice and all desires be fulfilled.
May bipeds be at peace; may quadrupeds be at peace.
May there be peace when departing, and peace when returning; may there be peace by night and peace by day.
The devas shall always protect and assist you; all your companions shall be virtuous and good.
May everything be peaceful, secure, healthy, and excellent. May your hands and feet be free from ailment, and may no part of your entire body suffer from disease or pain.
Whatever you may desire, you shall go forth having attained your heart's wish.
And regarding those who take a wife, it should be said in the context of giving and assemblies:
If a woman has faith and maintains the precepts, and her husband does likewise, Because of this faith, they are able to practice the cultivation of giving;
both persons maintain the precepts, Cultivate right view, and act together in the pursuit of merit.
The devas always rejoice in the retribution of this karma. Just as one travels without provisions, so it is for those who have gone forth.
If one holds a gathering and offers prayers, they should say:

"Whether encountering anger or meeting joy while begging from house to house with alms bowl in hand, one should always act to protect their minds; for it is difficult for those who have gone forth to practice giving."
Regarding the Buddha’s blessing of the merchants in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*:

according to the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment, there were five hundred merchants among whom were two leaders, one named Revata and the other named Bhāradvāja, who offered the Buddha parched grain flour and honey.
The Four Heavenly Kings presented the Buddha with stone alms bowls. The Buddha accepted the four bowls and pressed them together so that they merged into a single bowl.

Having accepted the flour and honey from the merchant, he then offered a blessing and departed. This is exactly as cited in the *Shao* (the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*). The blessing in the *Hetuphala-sūtra* says:
"By this act of giving, may those who eat obtain sufficient strength; may those who give obtain beauty, power, and renunciation."
One shall attain joy, peace, well-being, and freedom from illness, preserving one's lifespan until the end. All benevolent spirits and deities will constantly follow and protect one.
By giving food in alms, one cuts off the roots of the three poisons; in the future, one shall obtain the retribution of the three firm things (body, life, and wealth).

One will possess intelligence and wisdom, have sincere faith in the Buddha-dharma, and in every place of rebirth, one’s right view shall remain unclouded. In this present life, [one shall bring benefit] to parents and wife...
Their children, relatives, and kinsmen shall all flourish and prosper, free from all calamities, portents, and inauspicious events.
Should any among their family or clan pass away and fall into the evil realms, may they, through the merit of this present offering, be reborn among humans or devas;
may they not give rise to false views, but instead increase their virtues and always be able to attend upon and draw near to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, hearing the sublime [Dharma].
He spoke thus: "May you see the truths and attain realization; may all your aspirations be fulfilled.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished reciting this prayer of blessing, he accepted the food (according to the *Xītà*, it is said that based on the text of this sutra, one first finishes the prayer of blessing, and then places down the two bowls for the Buddha and the Sangha).
Regarding "Mahāla": The *Jiewen su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states that this is a foreign term;
here it is translated as "killer," for one who can damage the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom of sentient beings. Some say that "Mahāla" is translated here as "Gadū" (伽斗).

One who leaves home in old age is called "Gati" (伽底), and one who is stingy and deluded is called "Dū" (斗)—the latter is not clearly explained. Bin says: "Mahāla" is translated here as "ignorant. Alternatively...
This refers to being elderly. Regarding "being struck by seven blows," etc., it is as stated in the *Za baozang jing chao* (Excerpts from the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*), and so forth.
As for "sitting on clean clothes" and so on, up to "thus being able to guard the various precepts":

this means that since one is not sitting on a bed or seat, one avoids the fault of sitting together with a bhikṣu who is four years or older [in seniority], and also avoids the fault of overeating; therefore, it is said that one is "able to guard the various precepts."
Regarding the precepts: "The nine instances of sitting with the thighs pressed together constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense" refers to the nine methods of squatting, each of which incurs one *duṣkṛta*.
The phrase "monasteries and shrines of spirits in Western countries" refers to what has been transmitted through various nations;

it is a record of travels, such as the *Record of the Travels of the Monk Fǎmǐng to Foreign Lands* from the Jin dynasty. As for "shrines of spirits," this refers to the shrine of Hārītī. This is like traveling through various kingdoms.
[The text] was transcribed [as follows]. It is handed down that a certain monk from the northern region used to eat his evening meal while having a novice boy serve the food.
When the boy was about to set out portions for others, the master replied, "It is not the proper time. Where are there any sentient beings coming to eat? There is no need to set them out.
The boy said, "There may be shameless animals who still eat in the evening. Because of this, the master changed his practice.

The *Zhì* [Biographies] states that one should not eat at night for the rest of one’s life. Regarding the temples of the *ārāma-devatās*, these refer to the benevolent deities who protect the Dharma and guard the *saṃghārāmas*.
As for the statement that "the other bhikṣus do not go out," this means that when the monks take their daily meal, food is sent to these three places;
once the meal is finished, the various bhikṣus do not further go out to seek food for sentient beings. My private opinion is that recently...
The Ghost-Seeing One said, "The monks report that whenever the monks eat, immeasurable hungry ghosts are all gathered before the steps.
If there is a monk who upholds the precepts or a virtuous one of great reputation within the hall, the ghosts immediately show him respect and do not dare enter the hall.
If such a monk is absent, the ghosts intend to ascend the steps to the platform and snatch away the food and drink of the five groups. If the rice has already been served..."
The ghosts no longer return; thus we know that at present, it is necessary to set them forth.
When the ghosts are below the steps and hear the sound of the monks in the hall touching the vessels, they all flee in terror, falling prostrate and remaining unconscious for immeasurable time.

Therefore, the Buddha established the precept that one must not touch the vessels; this is the underlying intent. "To cause [the food] to emerge like a fingernail" means to cause the rice to emerge [from the vessel] like a fingernail.
It is even as large as a fingernail. According to the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 32:

"When a ghost or spirit receives a single mouthful of food from a human, it emerges [as nourishment] ten million-fold. (Commentary: If one is reborn now, one immediately obtains boundless and immeasurable fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

Regarding the phrase "providing food for the deceased," this refers to when laypeople provide offerings for the King of Ghosts; if [the deceased] is born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), they receive it.
Regarding sacrificial food: if one is reborn in another realm, one cannot receive it; rather, each receives the food appropriate to that particular realm, as their conditions differ.
Nevertheless, by merely forming the intention to give, one shall obtain merit and goodness.
This matter is explained in detail within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Regarding the passage "If one is not born among one's kinsmen in the intermediate state," etc., according to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. At that time, a certain brahmin came and asked the Buddha:
"I have a kinsman whom I hold very dear who has suddenly passed away. For his sake, I am making offerings with faith;
will he be able to receive them? The Buddha said, "Not invariably so.

If your kinsman has been reborn in hell, he may obtain the food of those hell-beings to sustain his life, but he cannot obtain the food you have offered. If he has been reborn among animals or as a hungry ghost..."
Regarding those among the hungry ghosts (preta) who are in the human realm: they obtain food and drink from among humans, but they do not receive what you offer.
However, within the realm of hungry ghosts, there is a particular place called the "Entrance-Place" (āpāyika) hungry ghosts.
If your kinsmen are born among those entrance-place hungry ghosts, they will obtain the food you offer. The Brahmin asked: "If my kinsmen are not born among the entrance-place hungry ghosts..."
Regarding those among the hungry ghosts: "To whom should the food I have offered be given? The Buddha said:
"If there are other acquaintances who have been born into this realm, they shall receive it. The Brahmin asked again:
"If I have no other acquaintances born into this realm, to whom should it be given? The Buddha said: "If there are no kinsmen or acquaintances born into this realm, then one who has faith..."
"The giver obtains his own merit. The brahmin asked again, "How does he obtain his own merit?
The Buddha said, "It means that after you die, you will be born among elephants, horses, and so forth; because of what they previously gave, they too shall receive this karmic reward.

If one is born into the realms of humans or devas, it is due to having practiced giving in the past that one sits and receives its retribution. This is called the giver practicing giving. Thus ends the section on the giver's giving.
The retribution received by such a person is never lost. Having heard this, the brahmin rejoiced and practiced accordingly. Jì (Jizang) said:

"As for the term 'entering the abode of hungry ghosts' (*preta-āyatana*), it refers to being born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is called the 'abode. If one born into the intermediate state is a hungry ghost, they obtain an abode.

If one's parents or six types of relatives are born into the realm of hungry ghosts, they are merely born into the abode of hungry ghosts, as opposed to those who have reached the place of full retribution."

The hungry ghosts all obtain sacrificial offerings. Those born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, humans, or devas do not obtain sacrificial offerings, because those places of retribution have their own inherent food.
All those born within the six destinies possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

If one is born into the intermediate state of hell, the head is inverted and facing downward, as stated in the newly translated *Abhidharmakośakārikā*: "The gods face upward; the three [other] realms are horizontal."
"Those in hell shall return to the lower realms," and so forth (as detailed). Even regarding the statement that "the donor may be reborn within the six destinies":
this clarifies the aforementioned question posed by the brahmin to the Buddha: "If one has no relatives or acquaintances and is reborn among the hungry ghosts, who should eat [the offering]?
The Buddha replied: "At a later time, you yourself, following your rebirth within the six destinies, shall receive its merit. Thus, it is known that if there is meritorious karma...
One follows birth in the six realms of existence, never losing [the karmic consequences] therein; thus, even now, one must perform meritorious deeds.
Regarding the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* account of King Aśoka offering half a mango fruit (*āmalaka*) to the Saṃgha:

Master Ying says that "āmalaka" is the name of a tree in foreign lands, which has not yet been translated into this land [of China]. Kumārajīva says its fruit resembles a peach. The old translations call it "sour."

Regarding the "fruit of taste": one merely obtains its flavor, not the name of the tree itself. I have personally heard it said that in the central region of the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), people have also obtained its fruit;
having eaten it, it was found to resemble a pear, being pointed at both ends and broad in the middle, with a delicious flavor.
As for the story of King Aśoka offering half a fruit to the monks, I have also examined whether it was actually half a fruit or not, as described in the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a nun has not yet had the 'invitation to eat at will' (*svairakalpika*) proclaimed at the place where she is requested to eat, for every mouthful [eaten], it is a *pāyattika* offense.

This means that the "proclamation of the food to be eaten at will" is merely another name for the "invitation to eat" (*saṃvibhāga*). This clarifies that when a nun arrives at a layperson's home, the invitation to eat has not yet been proclaimed at the dining place.
[Regarding] this: for every swallow, one incurs a *pācittiya*. When Śāriputra was eating fine food, Rāhula informed the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered that the meal be proclaimed as "equal offerings.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there was once a householder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who invited the Saṃgha to a meal.

The householder personally served water to the *sthavira* (senior) and *madhyama* (middle-ranking) monks, while providing them with many delicious foods; however, to the junior monks and śrāmaṇeras, he gave sixty-day-old rice.
[The Buddha] ate rice mixed with sesame dregs, boiling them together with vegetables and then consuming them. Having finished eating, he departed. At that time, Rāhula was serving as a śrāmaṇera.
Later, he went to where the Buddha was and stood to one side. It is the constant custom of all Buddhas, after a bhikṣu has eaten, to inquire with such courtesy:
"Was your meal sufficient? Rāhula replied, "If I obtained [food], I was satisfied; if I did not obtain it, I was not. The Buddha asked:
Having spoken these words, Rāhula recounted the preceding events in full. At that time, Rāhula’s physical strength and complexion had diminished.

The Buddha, knowing this, asked him: "Why have you lost your vigor? Rāhula spoke in verse: "By eating sesame oil one gains great strength; Those who eat clarified butter (sarpis) obtain a pure complexion.
Sesame dregs and vegetables lack both color and vigor. The Buddha, the God among Gods, shall surely rise [from his seat] himself."
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Rāhula spoke a verse in response to the Buddha, saying: "Those who eat ghee possess a fine complexion; those who eat oil possess strength.
But those who eat dregs and dried soup have neither complexion nor strength. The Buddha, knowing this, asked Rāhula: "Who is the senior elder (*sthavira*) among this community?
He replied: "My preceptor, Śāriputra. The Buddha said: "Does the bhikṣu Śāriputra eat [such things]?"

"Pure food. When Śāriputra heard the Buddha’s reproach that he was eating impure food, he immediately spat out his meal and, for the rest of his life, renounced all invitations to eat, constantly subsisting on alms.
After the Buddha had rebuked Śāriputra, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From now on, you should follow the rules for the senior elder (upādhyāya).
What are the rules for the senior elder? Upon hearing the sound of the ghaṇṭā or the announcement that the time has come..."

Go quickly to the place where food is served. If a donor offers you food, you should not eat before everyone else; wait until you have heard the signal that the offerings have been distributed to all, and only then eat.
The details regarding the story of Śrīgupta are explained extensively in the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Great Ornament Treatise), which are not recorded here in full;
it is better to follow what is clarified therein.
Regarding the passage in the *Ekottarika Āgama* concerning kings providing offerings and personally serving the food, etc., according to that text:

it describes how King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his palace and prepared a meal of a hundred flavors. Having personally served the food with his own hands, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the king.

The king was greatly delighted by what was taught, namely: the discourse on giving (*dānakathā*), the discourse on morality (*śīlakathā*), and the discourse on rebirth in heaven (*svargakathā*). At that time, those present in the assembly listened.
All have attained the stage of the Path (srotāpanna).

Regarding the term *saṃbhūta*, which refers to the fact that the meal provided by the Saṃgha is entirely equal, the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) of the *Chuyao lüyi* (Vinaya of the Essential Deliverance) states:
"The Vinaya-holders say this means 'equal offerings' (*samabhoga*). Alternatively, some say that *saṃbhūta* is one distinct category of dharma, while 'equal offerings' is another."

Regarding the single category of dharma: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) refers to it as "equal offering" (*sāmīcī-dāna*); the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) refers to it as "equal receiving" (*sāmīcī-lābha*);

and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that one must necessarily receive equally before being permitted to eat. Furthermore, it says that when the Saṃgha is large and the *sthavira* does not rise [to distribute food], if they receive food equally, the Buddha said:

"One should loudly proclaim 'Saṃghabhadra'. Based on such evidence, one should refer to it as "equal offering. However, this is merely seeking the literal meaning of the texts; the intended sense should be understood accordingly.
They are not the same. Now it is said that this must be the "equal offering" (*samasatkāra*). According to Śrīgupta, this was a test of the Buddha's deeds performed by Saṃgharakṣita;
his words were intended to cause the donor to offer with an equal mind—an impartial mind that approaches the signless (*animitta*).
That [donor] offered with an impartiality, and this [Buddha] received with an impartiality; he received their minds as being equal. For this reason...
It is able to eliminate poisonous harm. Therefore, the Tathāgata offers this blessing: "Lust, anger, and delusion are the poisons of this world.
The Buddha possesses the True Dharma, which removes all poisons. Is not the True Dharma precisely the mind of signlessness?
By making offerings with an impartial mind and conforming to that impartial mind, one may then eat. When both self and other are pure, there is no poison. Thus say the Buddhas.
Regarding the acceptance of offerings: one should always cause the donor’s mind to remain impartial. This is illustrated by King Bimbisāra’s gift of the Bamboo Grove to the Buddha;
at that time, the Buddha did not accept it immediately, but instead caused the king to form the intention to offer it to both the Buddha and the Saṃgha, after which the Buddha accepted it.

Inferring from this principle, it should be understood that this constitutes "equal offering" (*sama-dāna*), not "equal acquisition" (*sama-lābha*). As for those of other schools who consider it "equal acquisition," it should be [understood] as follows:
This is merely the intention of the Vinaya-holders. Furthermore, it says: "The *saṃghava* is equal offering. This must surely refer to the foreign monks who constitute the full assembly;
*va* means "great," and *saṃgha* means "assembly. These are all terms signifying equality. Now, regarding the statement that the *saṃghava* is equal offering:
when, at a layperson's home, water is first provided and food is subsequently served, this [preceding] part is the *bhadanta*.

The *Yujing* (Scripture on the Wise) says this. If one consults the text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding all rules for the place of offering and almsgiving, it states that water is used after the meal is finished;
there is no mention of using water before the meal (and so forth). Nowadays, there are those who do not permit the use of water after the meal, which is a delusion.
As for the rule that one must first wash the bowl and then preach the Dharma to laypeople, it is established that in the Middle Kingdom, whenever [the occasion arises]...
Regarding meals: first, one should receive the food with water; only after the meal is finished should one preach the Dharma.

This protocol was established by the Dharma Master Dao’an in this region, who ordered that the preaching of the Dharma, the recitation of sutras, and the offering of prayers be performed before the meal. He considered this essential and convenient for the purpose of generating wholesome roots.
The above concludes the explanation of the eighth section on the method of collecting [the robes]. From here below begins properly the ninth section, the method for the *dakṣiṇā* (offering).
Giving robes is called *dakṣiṇā* (pronounced with the initial as *cha-guan-fan*). In the sūtras, it is sometimes written as *dàqīn* (大[打-丁+親]), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit term.

According to the *Saṃghabhedavastu-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Zūnpóxùmìlùn), it is also rendered as *dānakṣīṇa*. This is translated here as "giving of wealth" (*cái shī*). The commentary explains: the dharma of giving in return is called *dakṣiṇā*;
that which leads one toward the ground of merit is also called *dakṣiṇā*. Furthermore, the *Xiyùjì* states: the correct pronunciation is *dakṣiṇā*, or *dakṣiṇī*.
It is named after the hand used to receive; receiving what is bestowed by others for the sake of generating merit for them.
Therefore, the name is established based on this.

As for the phrase "even down to a single verse" (the text of which is as in the *Śikṣāpada* on the method of receiving food), it refers to the aforementioned passage from the Vinaya which says: "If one gives for the sake of profit..."
This benefit shall certainly be obtained. If one gives for the sake of happiness, one will certainly obtain peace and happiness later on.

Regarding the instruction in the Vinaya to recite the *Sūtras*: because the *sūtras* accord with principle (*dharma*) and accord with the capacities of beings (*sattva*), they are called *sūtras* (契經).
This means they accord with and realize the principle of the Middle Way; thus, this Dharma may be explained to laypeople. The above explains the twenty-third [section].
The section on the rules for funeral invitations concludes.
End of Volume Thirteen of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (Sifen lü chao pi);
beginning of Volume Fourteen of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Jiangdong.
Chapter Twenty-Four, Part One: Guiding the Laity and Transforming the World.

Regarding the protocols for inviting [the Sangha] and the rules for providing offerings, and the established etiquette for the communal meal: since one has already been sustained by material provisions, it is necessary to repay them through the Dharma.

Medicine. Therefore, he stoops to uplift those who have lost their way and leads those bewildered by direction toward awakening. By enabling them to obtain benefits for their spirits, and through this mutual necessity, the principle is established;
thus both parties are equally benefited, and there is no failure of purpose. Such is the intent of this treatise and its underlying meaning. As for the term "guidance" (*dǎo*), it means to lead.
It refers to the methods for transforming and guiding worldly people; hence the word is used. Some editions read the character "Way" (*dào*) instead, which signifies—
Because the monastic and the secular require one another, it is called "the Way" (*dào*). This refers to the monastic person and the mundane laws of ordinary people. Ji said:

"The Guide" (*dǎo*) is that which transforms, and the "secular" (*sú*) is that which is transformed; since both the agent and the object are raised together, it is titled "Chapter on Guiding the Secular and Transforming the World.
As for the mutual dependence of the monastic and the secular, this means that laypeople seek merit and thus provide offerings through the four requisites. This is...
The giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) transforms people through the Way, leading them to observe the precepts and give rise to faith and joy;

this is the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Regarding the phrase "surpassing shadows and echoes": "surpassing" (*yú*) means to exceed or go beyond. The relationship between the monastic and the secular is more profound than that of shadows and echoes.

A shadow depends upon a form; an echo depends upon a sound. A shadow must correspond to a form; an echo must correspond to a sound. The Way must rely upon the secular; the secular must depend upon the Way.
They mutually support and complete one another; their meaning does not stand in isolation. As for the Way, it relies on the mundane for sustenance of the body;
as for the mundane, it relies on the Dharma of the Way to refine the spirit. Since the Sangha is not a household that stores provisions, how could they sustain their lives without the mundane?
When the mundane yearns for the Three Refuges and Five Precepts to create the causes for rebirth as humans or devas, this cannot be accomplished without the Way. Thus it is said: although the form...
Regarding the distinction between form (*rūpa*) and dharma: the worldly form consists of boots, shirts, caps, and sashes; the monastic form consists of tonsured hair and dyed robes.

Worldly dharmas consist of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity, or the five and eight precepts and so forth; monastic dharmas consist of the categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is said that form and dharma are distinct. "Two" (*liang*) refers to form and dharma being two separate entities, while "distinct" (*bie*) means they are not the same.
As for the statement that "the destination is the same," *you* (攸) means "that which" (*suǒ*).

This clarifies that although the physical appearances and deportment of the monastic and the lay differ, if one can practice diligently without ceasing, then regarding their ultimate attainment—the final goal—they both reach the eternal bliss of Nirvana; therefore, it is said that their destination is the same.
"Going toward" (*qù*) means "to arrive at. As it says in Sengzhao’s *Treatise on Emptiness*: "Though their outward forms differ, their wondrous goal is non-dual.
