"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "one who has stilled the mind" (*xīxīn*); it is also called "one whose will is tranquil" (*jìzhì*). Regarding the phrase "the conditions for the Way must be established":

this clarifies that since a bhikṣu dwells in the world yet wishes to cultivate the Way, he must necessarily possess the requisite conditions and resources (*pratyaya*) before he can advance along the Path; therefore, it is said that "the conditions for the Way must be established."

Furthermore, if one does not rely upon that external protection—the mind of those who do not cling to the Dharma—it means that laypeople are able to provide the four requisites to the Sangha, and it is by depending on this that one is able to advance on the Path;
this is the meaning of "relying" (*pratiśaraṇa*). If clothing and medicinal decoctions were lacking, one would be unable to cultivate the Path;
therefore, it is said that there would be no mind that clings to the Dharma.
Generally speaking, those whose transformative influence stops at the throat and heart are intended to clarify that monks of the final age are unacquainted with the net of the teachings.

Although they may personally commit offenses against the objects of their discipline, their minds remain dark regarding the monastic rules (*vinaya*); they speak from the depths of their own chests, never having any scriptural authority.

Hence it is said that [their teaching] "exits the throat and heart. This is merely a transmission from the belly (spoken with a departing tone). Ji said: "It is like Master Luohua, and others of ancient times who were so called..."
Foolish monks receive the five and eight precepts for others, yet fundamentally do not understand how to administer the three refuges for converting the heterodox.

Or they fail to explain the characteristics of the five and eight precepts. To claim that the timing for receiving the precepts is such that all acts of conversion must pass through the throat and heart is utterly absurd.
All of these are instances where events arise that are not in accordance with the Dharma, resulting in false and corrupt discourse. As for the phrase "there is nothing at all to be explained":

"explanation" (quan) refers to the teaching. Since you have cited scriptural authorities, yet lack the teaching that serves as the means of explanation, and since the teaching that explains is absent, from what source could the practice being explained arise?
"Admonition for those who have not yet heard [the Dharma]. "Admonition" (zhēn) arises from "warning" (jiè); it is also a form of "governance" (zhì).

Just as physicians of the world use admonitions to treat the illnesses of people, I now establish this teaching as a metaphor for such admonition, to treat the illness of ignorance. "Instruction" (huì) means "to show.
This refers to the fact that since ancient times, others have received the five or eight precepts without understanding whether they were properly fulfilled; this is the illness of the monastic.
Regarding the term "great *dānapati*": *dānapati* is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "donor" (*shizhu*).

According to the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, *tadāpatti*—wherein *tadā* is translated as "donor"—refers to one who gives. As for the "intoxicated *caṇḍāla*": a *caṇḍāla* is already called a "killer" even in ordinary usage;
when further compounded with "intoxication," the meaning requires no elaboration. According to the *Jingyin* (Phonetics of the Scriptures), *caṇḍa*...
*Caṇḍāla*. Some call them *caṇḍāla*; this is translated as "Fierce and Blazing. They refer to those who slaughter animals; it is a name for their caste.

One account says they are the wardens of the prison for those who kill humans. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), when such a person travels, they shake a bell to mark themselves, or carry a bamboo staff with a split head.
If they do not do so, the king will inflict punishment upon them.
Regarding the "five parts" of the twelvefold chain of dependent origination, I privately say they refer to the five-part Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*):
precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. These are profound teachings. As for the "sounds of men and women," this refers to local prohibitions;
it means avoiding words that refer to the sexes or speak of hidden evils. However, when speaking to laypeople, one must know the relative gravity of what is said, as was the case in the Jin dynasty.
There was a monk who, accompanied by a śrāmaṇera, went to the home of Zheng Xuan to beg for food. They knocked on the gate and called out to Zheng Xuan.
From afar, he asked, "Who is this? They replied, "It is the Master. Zheng Xuan said, "You call yourself 'Master'; who is the master of you?
He then came out to look and saw it was actually his *ācārya*. He asked, "And who is that little monk behind the *ācārya*? He answered, "He is..."
"My disciple. Zheng Xuan said: "Is he your younger brother's son? Tulu Molaoyi resembles his elder brother very much.

Furthermore, regarding the instruction that one should preach to the assembly on the dharma of weariness with suffering and the dharma of detachment—contemplating the body as suffering, empty, impermanent, and impure—and so forth:
according to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, it clarifies that when a Dharma master preaches the Dharma, they should follow the proper sequence.

Furthermore, one should preach the Dharma in accordance with the truth—teaching the Dharma of weariness and the Dharma of renunciation—to cause the minds of those before them to give rise to joy, seek liberation, and swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*.

If the bhikṣu preaching the Dharma should do so, he must also constantly maintain mindfulness and contemplate the body as suffering, empty, impermanent, non-self, and impure, ensuring that this practice never ceases. (My private note: "Weariness" refers to the cycle of *saṃsāra*.)
The five [aggregates] are subject to the eight sufferings, such as birth, old age, sickness, death, and separation from those one loves.
Furthermore, one feels weary of and afflicted by this body, which consists of thirty-six impure and foul substances, and is difficult to discipline and difficult to sustain.

Regarding the term "dharma of detachment," it refers to distancing oneself from the objects of craving and sensory clamor, as well as from unwholesome thoughts (*vitarka*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, unwholesome...

The Chapter on Awakening (*Bodhipakṣa*) states: What is called the "thought of sensual desire" (*kāma-vitarka*)? It refers to the arising of thoughts based on sensual desire; perceiving benefit and pleasure within the five objects of desire is termed the thought of sensual desire.
Regarding the "thought of kin" (*jñāti-vitarka*): it is the arising of various recollections concerning one's relatives, desiring that they obtain peace and happiness;
if one recalls their decline or suffering, sorrow and anxiety arise; or if one recalls performing activities together with one's kin.

This is called the thought of relatives. A practitioner should not dwell upon such thoughts. Since one has already abandoned relatives at the time of initial renunciation, to rely on these thoughts now is inappropriate.
If one thinks of relatives, then the abandonment of the household was in vain, and the family remains empty and unfulfilled.
Furthermore, by being reconciled with relatives, one cannot increase wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). One should instead contemplate all [beings].
In the cycle of birth and death of sentient beings, there is no one who has not been a relative. Why, then, do you remain so attached?

Furthermore, within this cycle of birth and death, because of attachment to relatives, the tears shed through grief, sorrow, and wailing would form a great ocean. If you continue to crave and cling now as well, suffering will be without end.
One who lacks the realization of death thinks thus: "I shall practice the Way leisurely; first, I must read and recite the Sūtras and the Vinaya..."

The *Abhidharma-miśraka-piṭaka* states: One who extensively recites non-Buddhist texts, keeps many disciples, attracts virtuous people, makes offerings to the four stupas, exhorts and transforms sentient beings to practice great giving, and thinks, "In the future, I shall cultivate the Way;

this is called the 'Awakening of Immortality,'" should not give rise to such thoughts. This is because the time of death is uncertain and cannot be known in advance. If one is occupied with other matters...
Then, when one's life is exhausted and one cannot practice the Way, at the time of impending death, the mind will be filled with regret, sorrow, and affliction; what else can be done then?
Furthermore, both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) must be abandoned.
"One who well understands a single word" refers precisely to the word "vinaya" (discipline). This single word encompasses all practices completely;

it means being able to evaluate the characteristics of gravity and lightness, what is permitted and what is prohibited, and what is correct and what is incorrect. Therefore, it is called "well understanding.
If, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, one must go to places that are contrary to the Dharma—actions which a śrāvaka ought not to perform—this refers to a Mahāyāna bodhisattva. Internally...

They are free from defilement and turbidity, yet they practice contrary transformations, appearing identical to sentient beings by fully performing the ten non-virtuous actions. These are things that even Śrāvakas cannot endure through their power;

thus, they are not within the scope of what such practitioners can perform. For example, just as a lotus in water cannot be soiled by the water, it is likewise difficult for paper thrown into water to be stained by it.
According to the *Ruyi Samādhi Sūtra*, there are three types of people who are able to engage in such extraordinary conduct.
Regarding sexual desire: this refers to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats.
Because those of these three vehicles are not defiled by the world, it is as when the Buddha entered the mother’s palace of King Prasenajit to engage in sexual desire. Why was this so?

Because the Buddha perceived that this mother had a karmic affinity with him, and furthermore, because the king himself had invited the Buddha to transform his mother who possessed great lust; thus, the king sought out various men for her.
Mother. The King feared that his mother might fall into hell; therefore, he demonstrated through the Buddha that his inner mind was free from defilement, unlike ordinary people and others.
Other bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) may not do this either; they must remain detached from the object and not draw near to it, let alone ordinary people.
As in the sutras, an analogy is given for ordinary people: their bodies and speech are like gold, yet their karma [is otherwise].
Thought is like water; the objective realm is like firewood. Within, there is the fire of afflictions; when it encounters the firewood of the objective realm, it cannot help but boil.
This is precisely what was the case with Sūdena. Nowadays, people engage in sexual desire while claiming they are free from defilement;
they drink wine and eat meat while claiming they have no greedy mind. How can this be so utterly delusional?
Regarding those who ask whether inquiring about the end of life is merely a futile labor: according to the third fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
"At that time, Ānanda was reflecting in a secluded place: 'In this village of Nāḍika, there were twelve lay devotees who have now passed away; where have they been reborn?'"
Furthermore, fifty people passed away, and another five hundred people passed away. "Where were they reborn?
Having had this thought, he went to ask the World-Honored One, "I only pray that you will explain this. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Those twelve householders had severed the five lower fetters;
at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the heavens and attained *parinirvāṇa* right there, never to return to this world again. As for those fifty..."

"Of those who have passed away, some have severed the three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion; they have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) and will return to this world once more to bring an end to the root of suffering.
Among those five hundred who have passed away, some have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer);
they shall not fall into the evil realms, but are certain to achieve the Way after seven more births and deaths, reaching the limit of suffering. He then addressed Ānanda: "As for birth..."
"There is death; it is the constant nature of the world. Why should this be considered strange? If every single person who dies were to ask me about it, would that not be a source of disturbance?
Ānanda replied, "It is indeed so, World-Honored One; it truly would be a disturbance."
Regarding the passage on entering another’s room, such as "knocking with a finger-snap outside," the *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Decorum) states:

There are five matters for which one should enter another’s room: first, to inquire after one’s health; second, to visit and look after one who is ill or emaciated; third, to inquire about the scriptures; fourth, when there is something to borrow;
and fifth, when sent by the assembly to summon someone. When going, there are five matters to observe: first, one should snap one’s fingers outside. Second... [text continues].

1. Upon entering, one must remove one's hat. 2. One must perform three prostrations. 3. One must stand upright; only when instructed by another to sit may one sit. 4. One must not enter while improperly holding a scripture.
There are five matters regarding the inquiry of a scripture: 5. One must descend from the platform in accordance with the Dharma to inquire.

6. One must not sit together [with the teacher]. 7. If one does not understand, one should simply ask. 8. One must not harbor thoughts of external conditions. 9. Even if one understands, one should...

Placing his head upon the ground, he prostrated himself and then turned back to leave the room (the preceding statement regarding the inquiry into the sūtra constitutes a single paragraph; the opening may not be joined directly).

As for those who hear and expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), these are called the "Twelvefold Teachings" in newly translated sūtras and śāstras. First is the *sūtra* (*sūtra*).
2. Geya (Verses); 3. Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies); 4. Gāthā (Recitations); 5. Udāna (Spontaneous Utterances); 6. Nidāna (also called Pratītyasamutpāda, Causes and Conditions); 7. Avadāna (Parables).
8. Itivṛttaka (Past Deeds); 9. Jātaka (Birth Stories); 10. Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings); 11. Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Phenomena); 12. Upadeśa (Exegesis).

Regarding the establishment of these chapter headings and their detailed explanation, as stated in the third fascicle of the *Binchō* (Commentary by Bin): 1. Sūtra: This is called the *Kyeong* (Sūtra). 2. Geya:

This refers to the *Chung-song-gyeong* (Repetitive Verse Sūtras), wherein there is prose (*dīrghapada*) preceding it, followed again by verses. 3. Vyākaraṇa: This is named *Suryu-gi* (Prophecy/Record of Prediction).
4. Gāthā: These are called the *Gekishige* (Isolated Verses). 5. Udāna: This is translated as "Unprompted Self-Exposition.
It refers to those sūtras of the Vinaya’s names and phrases that the Tathāgata spoke spontaneously without being requested. 6. Nidāna: This is called the *Inen-kyō* (Sūtra of Causes and Conditions).
7. Avadāna: This is termed the *Hiyu-kyō* (Sūtra of Parables). 8. Itivṛttaka: This is translated as "Past Events" (*Honji*).

*Sūtra* refers to discourses that recount past events, such as the statement: "The Dharma of Krakucchanda Buddha was called the 'Ambrosial Drum,' and so forth. *Vinaya* is termed the *Sūtra of the Good Path*.

As for the "Ambrosial Drum," it nourishes people through the teaching of the Dharma; in meaning it is like ambrosia (*amṛta*), and because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings, it is said to be "like a drum.
Ninth is *Jātaka*, which is translated here as "Birth Stories" (*pūrvajanma-sūtra*). This refers to accounts in which [the Buddha] himself recounts his own past lives. Tenth...
Vaipluṣya (毗佛略) means "Vaipulya" (方廣), which is the Mahāyāna. Eleventh is Adbhutadharma (阿浮陀達磨), meaning "Marvels.
Twelfth is Upadeśa (憂波提舍), meaning "Expository Treatises" (論議經). However, because the Great and Small Vehicles are either implicit or explicit, twelve categories are taught.
That is to say, the Vaipulya division constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, while the remaining eleven divisions constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. If...

The Great and Small Vehicles manifest each other through both existence and non-existence, each having nine divisions. That is to say, within the Mahāyāna, the *hetu-vidyā* (causal), *aupamya* (analogical), and *arthavāda* (explanatory) categories are excluded;
in the Hīnayāna, the *vaipulya* (extensive), *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), and *avyākṛta-svayambhūta* (unasked self-explanations) are excluded.

Thus, each has nine divisions. However, when the Mahāyāna is fully equipped with all categories, it possesses twelve divisions. Why, then, is the Mahāyāna sometimes said to have nine? It is because of [the capacities of] the faculties...
For the sake of benefit. Why is it that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) sometimes speaks of nine? Because its teaching is shallow.

"Not speaking at an improper time" means it is not the occasion for a combined exposition. According to the sixth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, regarding "not speaking at an improper time," the commentary (*śū*) states:
"When the time for awakening has not yet arrived, it is called 'speaking at an improper time. Once, in the past, the Buddha..."

A worldly person who is extremely learned, widely informed, and possesses clear discernment of characteristics says, "I have already explained the Dharma for you regarding the four foundations of mindfulness;
there is no need to recount it further. He then explains the four right efforts, to which he likewise replies, "I have already understood this.

He then explains the six perfections, to which he again says, "I have already understood this. In this manner, whenever one wishes to explain any dharma, they all say, "I have already [understood] this before."
[The Buddha] understood. The Buddha stopped and did not speak further. The man addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha to my home for a meal.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus went to accept the invitation. However, that man also possessed faith; he personally served the food with his own hands.

When the cakes were first being served, the Buddha said, "I have always received this kind of food; I do not need it now. Next, when the fruits, rice, and other foods were being served, [the same occurred].
All said, "I have always obtained this food; now I have no need for it. The man then replied, "Although you obtain this food constantly, you should not grow weary of it.
Why should I devise a plan to seek out different flavors? What is now being provided is the common food of the world;
the Buddha and the great assembly should eat it every day. He then reported back, saying, "If you say that one must not grow weary of food and that it is necessary to eat every day..."
The Dharma is also like this: one should not give rise to weariness. I have just now taught the Dharma; why do you not employ it?

How could one cease desiring to hear it simply because one has already understood it? One should hear it repeatedly, reflect upon it, and realize it for oneself (and so forth). Is it not said that the country [of the listener] is the speaker?

The Commentary states: "To preach in an unsuitable place is called preaching in a non-place (*asthāna*). 'There is no one who does not request the teaching' means that the transmission of the Dharma requires a person;

there is no one who does not request the teaching. These three await the right time, the right Dharma, and the right person before being preached. Do not preach with a frivolous mind, nor preach indiscriminately in every place.
A frivolous mind causes the speaker themselves to give rise to arrogance, while preaching everywhere fails to inspire devotion in others. Do not preach out of self-aggrandizement."
Do not disparage the teachings of others. Do not lament for yourself while claiming your own views as superior; do not hold other people in contempt.

Do not speak of extinguishing the Buddha-dharma or of causing worldly dharmas to flourish. To mutually revile and destroy one another is called speaking to extinguish the Buddha-dharma. When the Buddha-dharma is extinguished, worldly dharmas flourish.
The above is based on the interpretation of the sutras and commentaries; the author of the *Chao* (Excerpts) did not cite the full text (*et cetera*).
Regarding the seventh type of giving, "giving without depleting wealth," such as the "giving of eyes":

according to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, the first is called "giving of eyes," which means constantly looking upon one’s parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas with kind eyes, and never with malicious eyes. This is named...

Giving for the sake of the eyes: by relinquishing this body and receiving another, one obtains pure eyes; in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one obtains the divine eye and the Buddha-eye—this is called the first fruit of retribution.
Second, giving with a pleasant countenance and a cheerful expression: toward parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, one does not frown or show an unkind expression;
by relinquishing this body and receiving another, one obtains a handsome appearance; in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, [one obtains the same].
One attains a true golden complexion; this is called the second retribution. Third is the gift of speech:

toward parents, teachers, elders, and others, one utters gentle words rather than harsh or evil speech. Through the relinquishing of this body and the receiving of another, one attains clarity and eloquence in speech;

whatever one says is accepted with faith by others, and in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Fourth is the gift of the person: toward one's father...
To rise to welcome and prostrate before one’s mother, teachers, elders, and others is called the giving of the body (*kāyadāna*).

By relinquishing this body and receiving another, one attains a handsome body, a tall and majestic body, a body respected by all people, and, upon attaining Buddhahood in the future, a body like the *nyagrodha* tree whose crown cannot be seen.
Fifth is the giving of the mind (*cittadāna*). Even if one makes offerings with the aforementioned things, if the mind is not harmonious and virtuous, it does not constitute giving.

If one’s mind is harmonious and virtuous, and one generates a profound sense of veneration, this is called the gift of the mind. Through the relinquishing of the present body and the taking up of a future body, one attains a clear and lucid mind free from delusion or madness;
in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one will attain the mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). The sixth is the gift of seats and couches:

if one sees one's parents, teachers, elders, or others, one provides them with seats and couches so that they may sit. Through the relinquishing of the present body and the taking up of a future body, one will always attain a position of honor and nobility.
A bed and seat made of the seven treasures; in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the Lion Dharma-seat. Seventh is the gift of a dwelling:
when one causes one's parents, teachers, elders, and others to have the use of coming, going, sitting, and lying within a house, this is called the gift of a dwelling.

By relinquishing the present body and receiving a new one, one obtains natural palaces and residences; in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the dwellings of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). As it is said:
These seven kinds of giving, though they do not involve the depletion of material wealth, yield great rewards.

Regarding the phrase "raising one's hand toward the empty space of the four directions without attachment," this is a metaphor for an ordinary person raising their hand toward the sky without encountering any obstruction.
According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When entering a village, you must not be negligent or distracted."
In times of turmoil, one should always restrain the mind. It is like a person whose feet tread upon a high mountain peak—a precipitous, perilous, and narrow place;
in every thought-moment they give rise to fear and have no other thoughts, not grasping at the obscurities of the six sense-objects, just as one picking flowers on a mountain peak.
The Buddha then moved his hand in the air and addressed the bhikṣus: "This hand now revolves in mid-air without obstruction or bondage.
When you enter a village, your mind should likewise be without obstruction or bondage."

Regarding the Buddha’s acceptance of the old woman’s foul dregs: as recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (in extenso). Regarding the Buddha’s acceptance of the leftover soup from the ears [of a newborn]:
according to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, that child was born with golden earrings on his ears. His appearance was upright and handsome.
A physiognomist divined of him, saying, "This child truly possesses merit and virtue. As for the value of those ear-rings, various people...

Its value was equivalent to one hundred million *niṣkas* of pure gold; for this reason, he was named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. According to the accounts in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, he is simply referred to as the śramaṇa Koṭīviṃśa.
He offered excellent soup to the Buddha and gave the leftovers to King Bimbisāra. The current citation—that the Buddha accepted the leftover soup from Koṭīviṃśa—is an error;
it should simply state that the Buddha’s leftovers were given to the king. In other schools, he is also known by two names.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. A quarter of a *koṭī* is called a *śroṇa*. In a past life, he spread a single layer of cloth upon the ground and had the Saṃgha walk over it.
From that time until ninety-one *kalpas* ago, his feet have never touched the earth. Since being born in this life, hair has grown on the soles of his feet, several inches long.
Having entered the monastic order under the Buddha, his ascetic practices were peerless; wherever he walked, blood flowed from his feet.
In the *Dì* (Earth) [Sūtra], the Buddha permitted leather shoes. However, because a certain person’s asceticism was excessive, he did not realize the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The Buddha then spoke the parable of the lute, after which that person finally attained the Way (and so forth).
Regarding "seeing those who perform meritorious deeds and praising their generosity, precepts, and so forth," Ji says:
When one sees a person performing meritorious deeds, one must praise the blessings of their giving and maintaining the precepts, so as to cause their mind to rejoice and not regress or fail.

Regarding "always born into two families," this establishes that Kāśyapa Buddha and our own teacher Śākyamuni were born into the Kṣatriya family, while the future Maitreya Buddha will be born into a great Brāhmaṇa family;
these are called the "two families. Regarding "the two wheels of the Dharma and power" (*dharmabala-cakra*), I privately explain:

when a king possesses majestic authority, this constitutes the "wheel of power" (*balacakra*); when the Way-gate possesses many regulations and protocols, it is named the "wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*).
It serves as the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). If the Wheel of Power (*balacakra*) does not provide protection, there would be no means by which the Wheel of Dharma could turn;

this is the manner of praising a king. Regarding "praising according to actual facts": this refers to seeing a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) and praising him at the appropriate time, saying, "You are able to renounce the bonds of brotherhood, parents, and the affection of kin.
To speak of virtues that exceed [one's actual state] is called "glorification" (*praśaṃsā*).

Second, the explanation of the method for receiving the precepts is divided into three parts. [The author] privately states: these are the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Eight Precepts, which constitute the three.
According to the *Biànzhèng lùn* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct), it says: "The Three Refuges were taught because of Śrī; the Five Precepts were taught because of Mārga;
the Ten Precepts of Goodness were taught for the sake of the King; and the Six Fasting Days and the Three Refuges were taught for the sake of the Elder, in order to exhort him."

Abandoning the five heterodox precepts prevents one from committing evil deeds; the ten wholesome actions cause one to attract nobility; and the six fast days (ṣaḍ-upavāsa) enable one to attain joy. The commentary states:
"To take refuge (*pratiśaraṇa*) means to turn toward [the Three Jewels]. Precepts (*śīla*) arise from restraint. Wholesome (*kuśala*) means auspicious. *Qi* (fasting) means solemnity.

This teaches one to turn toward the Triple Gem, to restrain the five desires, to fully extend the auspiciousness of later times (this phrase is not clearly explained), and to maintain a solemn and respectful demeanor.

Regarding those who take the Three Refuges and so forth because all sentient beings fear birth and death and the four māras, this is explained in reference to the matters of the spirit Vajrapāṇi (Sanzhi), as found in the *Foshuo guanfo sanmei jing chao* (Excerpts from the Sutra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) [and so forth]. As for "the name being one while the meaning differs," Master Li states:
For example, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "The Buddha is permanent, the Dharma is permanent, and the Saṃgha is permanent"; this is "the name being one. Furthermore, it says, "The Buddha is named..."

Awakening (*bodhi*) is called "non-awakening" (*abodhi*) in terms of its name; the Sangha is called "harmony" (*saṃghāta*). These are differences in meaning. Furthermore, it is said: reaching awakening is called the Buddha;
reaching the norms is called the Dharma; reaching harmony is called the Sangha. These are differences in meaning. Jì says: speaking directly of taking refuge is what constitutes the "one."
This is because the name "refuge" (śaraṇa) is one and the same. However, while refuge extends to all three jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—their meanings differ.

Sometimes it is taught that the three are one; this refers to the claim that the "three jewels of the single essence" (ekakāya-triratna) and the "distinct three jewels" (pṛthak-triratna) share the same name but have different meanings.
If the three types [of jewels] flow forth from within the single essence, then this is "one within."
This refers to the teaching of the three. If one unifies these three into a single essence, it is the teaching that the three are one.
For example, to say that the Buddha is named "Awakening," the Dharma is named "Non-awakening," and the Sangha is named "Harmony" is to teach that the one is the three.
To say that the Buddha is eternal, the Dharma is eternal, and the Sangha is eternal is to teach that the three are one. Jì said: "To teach the three as one is 'one'."
Regarding the essence of the Three Jewels, explaining one as three refers to the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the statement that the three are explained as one, ancient masters interpreted this by saying: "The Buddha is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha. Master Xuanzang did not approve of this explanation.
He held that if one speaks of the names of the Three Jewels, they all arise from True Suchness (*tathatā*); since True Suchness is one, it is spoken of as one.
Third: because the three rely upon one to arise, it is said that the three are taught as one. How could one say that the Buddha is the Dharma, or that the Dharma is the Sangha?
It is like building a house or a stupa based on the earth; how could one say that the house is the stupa, or that the stupa is the house?
However, while the basis (*āśraya*) is one, that which depends upon it (*āśrita*) cannot be identical.
Regarding the two methods of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*): it is established and clarified that "repentance" (*chan*, *deśanā*) means causing what has already been committed to cease;

"regret" (*hui*, *kaukṛtya*) means severing the continuity of the mind so as not to act again. As for "reaching the place where there is no reaching," this refers to the ninth [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states: "From birth..."

"At the moment of death, all the evils one has committed shall be fully confessed until reaching the place where there is no reaching. The commentary asks: "What is this 'place where there is no reaching'?
It answers: "Nirvana is without location; it is called the place where there is no reaching. Another interpretation states: "'No reaching' means beginningless.
Since beginningless time, everything has been fully confessed; therefore, it is called the place where there is no reaching. Next, the conclusion.

Regarding the term "yun" (cloud/saying): I privately maintain that the threefold reception [of the precepts] mentioned above already constitutes the attainment of the dharma of ordination; the subsequent threefold formal act (*karmavācanā*) is merely for the purpose of demonstrating and exhorting its observance. The same applies to the sections below.

The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty stated that this is similar to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), which performs only a single formal act;

the fact that the present text contains three formal acts is merely a case of ancient masters translating while being confused by the teachings. When the Ācārya Nanshan performed the ritual procedures, he would sometimes perform it once.

[The section on] the fetters (*saṃyojana*). At times there are three fetters. Second, regarding the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy) states: "They correspond to the teachings of the 'Five Constants' found in external [non-Buddhist] texts, namely:

benevolence (*ren*), righteousness (*yi*), propriety (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), and trustworthiness (*xin*). To feel compassion and refrain from killing is called benevolence; to prevent harm and refrain from sexual misconduct is called righteousness;
to restrain the mind from alcohol is called propriety; to be clear-sighted and refrain from theft is called wisdom; and to speak nothing that is contrary to the Dharma is called trustworthiness."

These are the five virtues. They must not be treated with levity, nor may they be neglected for even a moment. Kings tread upon them to govern their states; gentlemen uphold them to establish their persons.
Their application never ceases for an instant; therefore, they are called the Five Constant Virtues (*pañca-dharmāḥ*). In the heavens, they are the Five Bindings (*pañca-bandhanāni*);
on earth, they are the Five Peaks (*pañca-śailāḥ*); in the regions, they are the Five Directions (*pañca-disaḥ*); in humans, they are the Five Viscera (*pañca-koshthāni*); and in things...

These constitute the five elements; upholding them constitutes the five precepts. Furthermore, according to the *Sūtra on the Original Arising of Heaven and Earth*, at the beginning of the kalpa, humans consumed "earth-fat.
There was a sentient being who took enough for five days' worth of food, and because of this, the precept against stealing was established.

Because they consumed earth-fat, desire for food arose, and because of this, the precept against sexual misconduct was established. Because of sexual desire, they began to deceive and rob one another, and because of this, [the precept against killing was established].

Regarding the precept against killing: because there was no yet existing desire [to harm], it was established as the precept against false speech and deceitful crookedness. Regarding the drinking of alcohol:

because it causes confusion and leads to the commission of improper acts, it was established as the precept against intoxicants. Thus, the origin and development of the Five Precepts have long been investigated;
they sprouted at the beginning of heaven and earth and took form prior to all things.
Regarding the question, "What is the fault in having worldly precepts? [the author] establishes the following clarification:

For those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), such as defiling a *bhikṣuṇī*, one may not grant them ordination, nor can they generate the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) essence of the precepts. If they wish to receive the five precepts, they should obtain the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*);
this is merely a worldly virtuous practice. They cannot obtain the unmanifest essence of the monastic precepts. Lì asks: "The five and the eight..."
Regarding the time at which the "equal undertaking" (samādāna) arises, various explanations differ. Some say it arises at the conclusion of the three refuges;

others say it arises at the conclusion of the explanation of the characteristics [of the precepts]. Now, let us definitively judge this: the vow of the precepts arises at the conclusion of the three refuges. As the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* states:
When one wishes to receive the five precepts, one first receives the three refuges. Once the three refuges are completed, at that moment one has already obtained the five precepts.
The reason for stating the names of the five precepts is to ensure that the person before one recognizes the names of these five precepts;

this is analogous to how, after the *jñapti-caturtha* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) for full ordination is concluded, the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) and so forth are explained. Do not underestimate the five precepts; they possess great efficacy. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Three..."
Regarding the arising of calamities: within the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), there are three minor calamities—first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.
At the time when the initial kalpa of weapons is about to arise, it means that the lifespan of sentient beings gradually decreases until it reaches ten years.

Their bodies are reduced to the size of a single span or a single fist; yet, due to the overwhelming power of the poison of unrighteous anger, as soon as they see one another, they give rise to a fierce and harmful intent.
They are like hunters who, upon seeing wild birds or beasts, immediately brandish whatever they hold as blades and staves.
Each person, driven by perverse wickedness and madness, slaughters one another. For seven days and seven nights, death nearly exhausts the population.

Within Jambudvīpa, barely ten thousand people remain; they each give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, and their lifespans gradually increase. At that time, it is called the *kalpa* of weapons (*śastra-kalpa*).
Next is the kalpa of pestilence. When the human lifespan is ten years, unrighteousness prevails;
non-humans vomit forth poison, and pestilence spreads so that those who encounter it perish immediately, being difficult to treat. There is not even the name of medicine or physician.

This period of pestilence lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days and nights. As the pestilence spreads, death nearly exhausts the population, leaving barely ten thousand remaining within Jambudvīpa.
Each person gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and their lifespans gradually increase. That period is called the intermediate kalpa of pestilence (*maraka-antarakalpa*).

During the intermediate kalpa of famine (*durbhikṣa-antarakalpa*), when the human lifespan reaches its minimum of ten years, unrighteousness (*adharma*) prevails; the devas and nāgas, indignant and reprimanding [the people], do not send down sweet rain.

Consequently, the world suffers from famine for a long time. In some families, they pass around a tally (*śalākā*) to determine who may eat; on the day the tally reaches them, they obtain a small amount of coarse food. Or...
They cleared out old threshing floors and obtained a few grains of rice; they would boil these in a large amount of water and drink them together.

Alternatively, they would take white bones and drink the broth boiled from them. Yet, for the benefit of future generations, those people of that time would set aside what they were eating, placing it in small baskets as seed.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one encounters even a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or barnyard grass, one stores it away in a chest or basket."
And they protect one another. Thus, for seven years, seven days, and seven nights, the famine persists. Pressed by the famine, death nearly exhausts the population;
within Jambudvīpa, only ten thousand people remain. Each gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and their lifespans gradually increase.
This period is called the *antara-kalpa* of famine. If one wishes to remedy these three calamities, if one can [practice] for even a single day and night—
By observing the precept against killing, one will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the kalpa of weapons in future lives.

If there is anyone who, with a heart of profound purity, can offer even a single harītakī fruit to the Sangha, they will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the kalpa of pestilence in future lives.
If there is anyone who, with a heart of profound purity, can offer even a single morsel of food...
Monks, in future ages, you will certainly not encounter the arising of an era of famine. Regarding the aforementioned "earnest and pure mind," this refers to a diligent and pure intention;
furthermore, one must use pure objects. Indeed, as for practicing giving, if one were to give impure food or clothing, [it would not be proper].

The resulting retribution obtained later will be entirely impure. Regarding the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if one has previously violated the five precepts, the eight precepts, and so forth, this is clearly established.
The first two lines of the preceding passage cite the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng lun), yet there is a contradiction between the texts.

In the aforementioned *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is stated that those who "dwell as thieves" (*caura-vāsin*) or who have defiled nuns may receive the five precepts; however, this current passage from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duolun) appears to disallow it (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "the sixth day of the third month": some say that the first, fifth, and ninth months—these three months—are the times when the Karma Mirror illuminates the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa).
For example, in the first month it illuminates the South; in the second month, the West; in the third month, the North (Uttarakuru);
in the fourth month, the East; and in the fifth month, it returns to illuminate the South. Thus, in one year, it completes three circuits.
As for the six monthly dates: according to the Vinaya, it only mentions the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. This is based on the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*);
by extension, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*) likewise has twenty-third days. That is to say, the twenty-third day corresponds to the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
the fourteenth and fifteenth days correspond to the twenty-ninth and thirtieth days [of the dark fortnight]. As the verse says:
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moons, it is likewise so.

Furthermore, the *Dapiposha jing* (Sutra of Parables) states that Śakra commands the Four Heavenly Kings to tour the world on these six fast days to observe and seek out the good and evil deeds performed by people;
therefore, one should restrain the body and observe the fast on these days.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the six fast days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) are days on which evil spirits seize human life.

Regarding the statement that in the beginning of the kalpa, a sage taught those who did not eat on one day [to observe the fast], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra-śāstrīya* (Excerpts from the Treatise) says [as follows]. Furthermore, concerning the phrase "sages at the beginning of the kalpa" and so forth, I privately note:
during the time of the kalpa’s beginning, there were many deaths and illnesses on these six fast days. At that time, there was a wise man who ordered that on these days...
If one does not eat afterwards, the ghosts will find an opportunity; if one eats, the ghosts are at a loss for what to do.

When the Buddha appeared in the world later, he commanded that on this day one should observe the fast and further add the eight precepts. Furthermore, regarding all those who are currently afflicted by violent illnesses:
One must simply abstain from food. Thus, when a disciple of Maudgalyāyana fell ill, Maudgalyāyana ascended to heaven and asked Jīvaka how he should be treated.
Jīvaka instructed him, saying that fasting is the primary method. This is recorded in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Kṣāranirdeśa-sūtra*. Regarding the illnesses of people in the present age:

Not understanding this teaching, they insistently urged him to eat; consequently, his illness was difficult to cure. Previously, when he met the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman, [the Master] said that if one were ill, one would not eat even a grain of rice.
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied, "This is simply the law of my country: I shall eat only when I have recovered."
The thirtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Sūtra on the Householder Sudatta*, clarifies the practice of the Dharma by laypeople and the ritual worship of the six directions (ṣaḍ-diś).
As recorded in the *Madhyama Āgama* excerpt (*yùn yùn*). Furthermore, according to the *Sūtra on Sudatta*: there was a son of a householder named Sudatta who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The six non-Buddhist teachers constantly preach the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, saying that if one can, at dawn..."
If one pays respectful homage to the six directions in the morning, one will increase in both lifespan and wealth.
Why is this? The eastern region belongs to Śakra; those who make offerings there will be protected and assisted by Śakra.
The southern region belongs to Yama; the western region belongs to Varuṇa; the northern region belongs to Kubera; and the lower region belongs to Agni.
"O Deva, in the direction above belongs the realm of the Wind Devas; those who make offerings there will all receive their protection and assistance.
Does the World-Honored One also have such six directions? The Buddha said, "Within my Dharma, there are likewise six directions, namely the six pāramitās."

The eastern direction is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Why is this? Because the sun, when it first rises, does so for the sake of providing the causal conditions for the radiance of wisdom.
That eastern direction belongs to the minds of sentient beings;

if there are sentient beings who can make offerings to that perfection of giving, their lifespan and wealth will increase. The southern direction is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
The south is the pāramitā of giving (dāna-pāramitā); the west is the pāramitā of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā); the north is the pāramitā of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
the nadir is the pāramitā of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā); and the zenith is the pāramitā of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā). There are those who make offerings to these six directions in this manner.
All shall obtain an increase in both life-span and wealth. These six directions pertain to the minds of sentient beings;
they are not as described by the six non-Buddhist teachers. Regarding these six directions, who is able to make offerings? Only a Bodhisattva is able to do so.
It is often said that among the five precepts, the precept against intoxicants is the most serious. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Intoxicants are unwholesome. All...

The root of evil. If one can sever it, one will remain far removed from all transgressions. Furthermore, regarding the commission of the four *ānantarya* (heinous) offenses and so forth, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*), it is asked:

"Among the five precepts, how many are *dharmatā-śīla* (natural precepts) and how many are *prajñapti-śīla* (prohibitory precepts)? The answer is: "Four are *dharmatā-śīla*, and one is *prajñapti-śīla*.
The reason they are collectively bound together as precepts is that alcohol is the basis of negligence; it is capable of causing one to violate the other four precepts. As [it is said]:...
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, because he drank alcohol, committed adultery with another’s wife, stole a chicken, and killed another person.

When questioned, he replied that he had not done so; yet, due to the influence of the alcohol, he had simultaneously violated four precepts. Furthermore, he was capable of committing four of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), though he alone could not cause a schism in the Sangha.
He also received the retribution of insanity and lost all his wholesome karma. Because of these many conditions, it is [classified] as a natural precept (*prakṛti-śīla*).
The offenses are the same. Regarding the three types of precept-holders: one who is able to fully observe the first five precepts is called a *pūrṇa-upāsaka* (an upāsaka of full measure).
Here, among the eight precepts, those specifically termed *brahmacāry-upāsaka* (upāsakas of pure conduct) are so named because these eight precepts involve following the Buddha’s renunciation;
since they do not violate even their own wives, they receive the name "pure conduct. The five precepts, however, only prohibit sexual misconduct. As for oneself—

When his wife performs [the ritual], there is no offense; therefore, he cannot be given the name "One of Pure Conduct" (*brahmacārin*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The eight precepts for an *upāsaka*—this is the Sanskrit term.
If translated directly from the original sound, it is *upāsakaga*, which in the Chinese (Tang) language is translated as 'Virtuous Abiding' (*shàn xiù*).

This is because such a person, through a virtuous mind, remains free from breaking the precepts; hence it is so called. The ancient records refer to him as a "Pure Faith Layman" (*qīngxìn shì*); "pure" (*qīng*) signifies being free from transgressions.
This is its name. Faith is the foundation for entering the Path. "Shi" (士) is a general term for a man. There is a master’s interpretation which says:
*Upāsaka* means "one who dwells near," so called because by observing the five, eight, and other precepts, one gradually draws near to the dwelling of the Noble Ones (*ārya-vihāra*).
To study and follow the various Buddha-dharmas is called *poṣadha*. [The master] Li establishes that *poṣadha* means "pure dwelling. The Five Precepts...
If one does not abstain from sexual intercourse with one's own wife, it is not called *poṣadha*. Because of the eight precepts of pure conduct, it is termed "Pure Abiding" (*viśuddhavāsa*).
Regarding the phrase "attaining *sarvajñatā*": Si says that "attaining" (*dai*) means "to reach. "*Sarvajñatā*" is a foreign (Sanskrit) term;
it is also called *sarvākārajñatā*, which is translated as "All-Knowledge" (*sarvajña*). Ji says it is translated as "Knowledge for Reaching the Other Shore. (*Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*)
The commentary on the meaning of "Buddha" states: "Buddha" is one who possesses all-knowledge (the fundamental wisdom) and all-aspect knowledge (the subsequently attained wisdom).
He is able to awaken all sentient beings by himself, like waking from a dream (a metaphor for fundamental wisdom), or like the blooming of a lotus flower (a metaphor for subsequently attained wisdom;

from this flow forth the fragrances of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, which perfume the noses of those whose minds respond to his influence). As described in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he extensively made great vows regarding the eightfold fasting observance (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).

Regarding the thirty-eight fascicles, it is as stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama* excerpt (and so forth). As for the term "eightfold precept observance" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:
"To prohibit and restrain non-restraint is to bring the body and mind to stillness and concentration."

"Extensively as in the *Uposatha Sūtra*" refers to the Āgama sūtras; each section should be understood as a distinct sūtra. Among them, there is a specific *Uposatha Sūtra* which constitutes one such sūtra.
Regarding the statement by Śīlāṅka that "one who receives the eight precepts extinguishes all other sins except for the five heinous crimes," according to the *Śīlāṅka-sūtra*, it says:
"Excluding the five heinous crimes, all other sins are extinguished. This may refer to a prior teaching.

Later, when he was observing the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts, he killed [the animal] while in the state of formal observance. Because of the power of the precepts, although he incurred no offense of killing, according to this principle, it constitutes a grave transgression (*mahāsāvadya*).
This is because his vow of mind for that entire period was pure, and his conduct was equivalent to that of one who is unattached (*asaṅga*).

Therefore, one is able to sever and eliminate karmic offenses. Regarding the statement that "one's merit is equal to that of those who have attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*)," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it says:
"The heavenly kings' rewards of merit cannot even compare to those of a person who observes the eight precepts. This is as when Śakra spoke a verse, and the Buddha rebuked him, saying: [as follows].

If it were one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*) who should speak this verse, the verse says: "On the six fast days of the month of the gods, one who observes the eight precepts obtains blessings and merit equal to ours;
by receiving the dharma of fasting, one shall attain the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, it is one whose outflows are exhausted who should speak this verse. I say: Śakra’s outflows are not yet exhausted, and he has not yet transcended the triple world. As for those who receive the eight precepts—
It is not the karma of the three realms; therefore, it is not equal to them. If one is an untainted person (*anāsrava*), one should say that they are equal to us.

Regarding the phrase "except for former adornments and so forth," the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface) states: "To be free from adornment means to be free from what was not formerly an adornment. Why is this?"
If one uses habitual ornaments that do not give rise to extreme intoxication or lustful attachment, the meaning of this is as follows:

if one has previously applied dark powder (kajjala) as an ornament and receives [the gift] without washing it off, there is no offense; however, if one applies it after receiving it, it is an offense.

This is because, in the case of prior adornment, there is no mind of extreme intoxication or sexual desire. Regarding the "attainment of male characteristics," the established view is that this refers to those who are neither eunuchs nor hermaphrodites. For...
This is because they possess great resolve and integrity.

As for the statement that "if a bhikṣu fails to provide his parents with offerings to the best of his ability, he incurs a grave offense," this means that such an offense is a heavy karmic transgression, comparable to a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
In the present day, monks and nuns deeply serve their parents with sincere hearts, following the dharma of a disciple attending to a teacher.
"Enlightening one's parents": "enlightening" (*qi*) means "to open" (*kai*). This refers to guiding and teaching the Dharma to benefit one's two parents.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Ānanda requested that Mahāprajāpatī be granted the precepts," etc., it clarifies that when the maternal aunt sought ordination from the Buddha and the Tathāgata did not grant it, she wept and shed tears outside the gate of the Jetavana.
Ānanda petitioned on her behalf, and the Buddha said, "Ordain her," thereby [establishing] the precedent.
"Regarding 'nurturing through kindness': when the Buddha was seven days old, his mother passed away, and his maternal aunt nursed him.

Now he may deliver her in order to repay that kindness. The Buddha said, "I have already repaid her kindness. Had I not appeared in the world, she would not even have heard the names of the Triple Gem.
Because I have appeared in the world, she now recognizes the Triple Gem and has attained the first fruit [of the path]. This is the great repayment of kindness. Thus it is said.
How much more so for those who have attained pure faith; these are the *srotāpanna* who have attained pure faith.

Regarding the Elder’s Daughter Maitrāyaṇī, it is as stated in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* (Cloud of Jewels Sutra) [and so forth]. Regarding the Parrot that made offerings to its parents, it is as stated in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vyūha-sūtra* [and so forth].
Regarding the merits of one destined for Buddhahood in their next life (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), Ji says: "It encompasses all those in the human and heavenly realms..."
He shall be born and attain Buddhahood, succeeding to the position of a former Buddha, just like Maitreya. Having lived out the full span of this human life, he will be reborn in the heavens;
when his lifespan in the heavens ends, he will be reborn among humans and immediately become a Buddha.

Counting from the time he receives his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), his birth among humans and his birth in Tuṣita together constitute a single lifetime. This Bodhisattva in his final birth before succession (*ekajātipratibaddha*) is, in his last body—

Regarding the Bodhisattva, if one wishes to distinguish [the stages], it is explained as follows: "Greatly distinguished" refers to Maitreya, who is currently correctly designated as a *caryā-pratipanna* (or *ekajātipratibaddha*) Bodhisattva;
only when he descends in the future to be born into the family of a great Brahmin will he be called a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*paścima-bhavika*). Reflect upon this.
Regarding the teaching that there are two persons whom one cannot repay for their kindness when they perform wholesome deeds:

according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "There are two persons whom one cannot repay for their kindness when they teach others to perform wholesome deeds. What are these two?"

This refers to one's father and mother. Suppose there were another person who placed their father upon the right shoulder and their mother upon the left shoulder, and for ten million years provided them with the four requisites of clothing, bedding, food, and drink, yet even while they were on their shoulders, they discharged excrement and urine upon them.
Even so, one cannot repay their kindness. Monks, you should know that the debt of gratitude owed to one’s parents is profound.

They embrace and nourish you, protecting you at all times and never missing the proper seasons for your care, so that you may see the sun and the moon. By these means, you should realize that this kindness is difficult to repay.
You, monks, should provide for your parents and always be filial and obedient, never missing the proper seasons. You should train yourselves in this way.

I said: "It is simply said that even if one carries [the burden] upon one's shoulders, the repayment of gratitude remains insufficient. If one were to instruct them to perform wholesome deeds, that would be called repaying their kindness;
yet such a repayment is difficult to achieve, which is why it is said to be 'unattainable.'"

Regarding the prohibition against calling [monastics] by their secular names: this is because in the southern regions of Wu, people generally lack faith and respect, and thus everyone calls them by their secular names.

Among the people of the north, once men and women have left the household life, regardless of whether they possess spiritual practice or not, their parents, brothers, and others never address them by name;
they always refer to them as "Upādhyāya" or "Ācārya," or as "Teacher-Uncle," "Teacher-Younger-Brother," "Teacher-Elder-Brother," or "Teacher-Uncle," and so forth.
Regarding those who share the name Śākya: Formerly, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a king named Ummāda.
His principal queen bore him only one son, named Jīvaka, who was stubborn, vulgar, and ugly, and was despised by all people.
The second queen had four sons: the first was named Ālokabandhu, the second Cakṣurbandhu, the third Damanakuñjara, and the fourth...
Nīlu was intelligent and martial, possessing great majesty and virtue. The first queen thought to herself, "Although my son is the eldest, his talent does not equal that of others;
yet those four sons all possess majesty and virtue. By what means can I secure my son's foundation and ensure his future?
She then addressed the king: "The king’s four sons all possess majesty and virtue; although my son is the eldest, his talent does not equal theirs."
"Regarding these possessions, they will surely be seized and usurped by others once our great enterprise is inherited. If Your Majesty expels us, my mind shall find peace.
The King immediately summoned his sons and commanded them to leave the country. At that time, the four sons' mother, as well as their uterine sisters, all departed together with them.
Many of the common people were also very eager to follow; the King granted them all permission. The four sons, having received their orders, departed and reached the Snowy Mountains.
To the north, he established a city and town. Within several years, his parents and king missed him and asked where their son was.
He replied, "I am in the north of the Snowy Mountains, near the Śākya forest, where I have built a city and established a town; the population is flourishing and the soil is fertile."
Their clothing and food were never lacking. When the king heard this, he sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses capability.

From this time on, he was consequently called the Śākya clan (Śākya being translated here as "capable"). Alternatively, it is said that his family name was Gautama; according to Western tradition, he belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.

Long ago, his father was usurped from the throne by a resentful king, and the son fled abroad. There, a rishi took him in and raised him until he grew up, and then had him succeed to the Kṣatriya lineage.
The lineage continued without interruption. A diviner informed the hostile Kṣatriya king that the constellation of the Kṣatriyas had appeared.

The king ordered his men to capture and bring the child before him, whereupon he was impaled upon the tip of a stake. The rishi arrived and exhorted the boy, seeking to arouse desire within him so that the progeny of the Kṣatriyas would not be cut off.
Although the boy suffered great pain, his desire did not arise; thus the rishi acted for him...
Dense clouds obscured the sky, and a fine rain moistened the earth, causing his suffering to cease for a moment. He then transformed himself into a woman and united with the young boy;
the semen was discharged onto the ground. The rishi then wrapped the semen in cow dung and took it back home, placing it within a sugarcane grove.
A sun-dried ball of dung gave birth to a son whose physical appearance was upright and handsome. Later, when he grew up, he succeeded to the royal throne.
Consequently, it was passed down that those who praised him were called the "Sun-Dried" (Āditya-bandhu) clan, while those who disparaged him were called the "Cow Dung" (Gomaya-bandhu) clan.
Therefore, when the various non-Buddhists addressed the Buddha as Gautama, they did so out of disparagement; "Gautama" is translated here as "Cow Dung."
The "Yi-zhi" clan is an ancestral lineage of former generations; the term "Śākya" refers to a lineage of later generations. Regarding the prohibition against following secular surnames and so forth:
the monks and nuns of this land have traditionally followed secular surnames, or in some cases those of their teachers.
Master Dao’an considered this to be improper, yet people did not yet submit to his view. Later, when the *Āgama* scriptures arrived, it was indeed confirmed [as he had said].

It is said that when the four rivers flow into the sea, they no longer retain their original names; likewise, when those of the four castes leave the household life, they are all equally called Śākyas.

The four castes are: Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Knowing that Dao’an was no ordinary person, the *Xiguo ji* (Record of the Western Regions) states that he was the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta.
When Kumārajīva was in Kucha, he paid homage to Dao’an from afar even before Dao’an had arrived there. As for Dao’an...
She had already entered parinirvāṇa. Kumārajīva remarked on this with deep lamentation; the details are clearly set forth in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Regarding the account in the *Ekottarika Āgama* concerning Mahāprajāpatī’s death, where the Buddha himself, together with Rāhula, supported one corner of her couch—this is as recorded in the *Excerpts from the Ekottarika Āgama* (and so forth).
Mahāprajāpatī means "Great Love-Way" in the language of Tang; she is also called Gautamī.

"Mī" refers to his maternal aunt. Regarding the passage "King Śuddhodana entered *nirvāṇa*, and the Buddha himself carried him [to the funeral pyre]," the Sanskrit term is *Ratnada* (or *Śuddhodana*), which translates here as "Pure Rice" (*Jìngfàn*).
He was the Buddha’s paternal uncle-king. Upon examining the *Ekottarika Āgama*, this specific incident is not recorded there;
it appears in the *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*. One should consult and transcribe that text when the time comes. (And so forth.)

The above concludes the explanation of the second point, the meaning of offering reverence as a condition for birth. From here below is the third section, which correctly clarifies the method for men and women entering a temple.

Regarding the phrase "those trodden upon by outflows and pride," this means that laymen and laywomen, by their very nature, are defiled by outflows (*āsrava*) and are largely possessed of pride (*māna*).
Bearing such stained desires and an outflowing mind, they furthermore lack respect and do nothing but engage in contempt.
[The interlocutor] says with pride, "Why must one enter a temple?

[The respondent] replies, "Regarding the former custom of Jetavana concerning those from among the Chinese gentry and commoners who leave their homes: it is privately said that in the *Jetavana-tu* (Diagram of Jetavana), there is a ritual for those from the Chinese gentry and commoners entering the temple.
The commentary states: 'The outward appearance is similar to that of a secular official’s absence, yet the underlying intent is distinct. [The respondent] further says, 'The monks see this.'"
When a layperson sits upright and motionless, refusing to rise to greet them, it may appear on the surface that they have failed in worldly etiquette.
However, if one examines this carefully through principle, the intention lies in the protection of the Dharma; thus, while their outward restraint differs from the norm, it is for a higher purpose.

As for the statement that "the matter appears to lack worldly propriety," this clarifies that when a layperson arrives at a monastery and sees monks debating the principles of the Dharma, it may resemble the quarreling of worldly people. Nevertheless...
In fact, the *Yìběnlùn* (Treatise on the Original Meaning) regards this in terms of the Way; therefore, it says, "they differ. Cíyún said:

"If one observes the faults of those who have left the household life and examines them with worldly sentiments, they may appear to have some slight deficiencies. However, when one examines their inner minds, they harbor the Way;

thus it is said that 'examining the intent, they differ. This is because among them there are those whose outward forms deviate while they inwardly preserve the Way, as well as those whose outward forms..."

Although one may maintain outward order, it does not preclude the mind from being occupied with mundane affairs; thus, one cannot verify [the state of the mind] by means of external conduct, for the internal intention is quite different.

Regarding "turning one's back on the Sangha and seeking what is divergent": privately, it is said that to be uncompliant with the teachings of the Sangha is called "turning one's back on the Sangha," while to investigate their faults and evils is called "seeking what is divergent.
This refers to those who, instead of showing respect, seek out the faults of others. However, the Triple Gem should only be treated with reverence and provided with offerings.
One must not harbor thoughts of malice toward others. According to the *Danyi Changrezizi Jing* (Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Danyi), in one fascicle, it is said:
The Elder Danyi invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home to provide offerings. The great assembly sat solemnly, and before the serving of food was finished, there appeared a beggar.

Previously, as he went from seat to seat begging, no one dared to give anything to him while the Buddha had not yet offered his blessing. Having gone everywhere without obtaining anything, he conceived an evil thought:
"The elder is confused; he thinks that by feeding me there is no intention of compassion. When I am a king, I shall [punish him] with an iron-rimmed chariot."
He crushed his head and cut it off. Having said this, he departed. After the Buddha had finished giving the *dakṣiṇā*, a beggar came in to beg for alms.
Everyone in the assembly gave him some; he obtained a great deal of food and drink, whereupon a wholesome thought arose in him: "How excellent, O Elder!"
"One who is thus able to serve such great beings as these will obtain immeasurable merit.

When I was a king, I should have made offerings to the Buddha and his disciples for as long as seven days. Having said this, he departed. After the Buddha had finished eating, he returned to the vihāra. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From now on, after the distribution of alms has been completed, let food be served; make this a constant practice. Xita (Xi-ta) spoke thus every time.
According to this scriptural passage, once the preliminary incantations and prayers were completed, the two plates for the Buddha and the Sangha were then set down.
At that time, the two beggars had traveled by stages to another country and were lying amidst the thick grass by the roadside. The king of that land passed away without an heir.

An interpreter of omens recorded in a prophecy that a person of low birth was destined to become king. Consequently, the ministers and officials went on inspection tours of the realm and, upon looking about, beheld them.

Upon the grass was a cloud-canopy. The ministers prostrated themselves in audience, each addressing him as their sovereign. Having bathed in fragrant water and donned the royal robes, his radiant marks were majestic.
With attendants leading and following before and behind, he returned to serve [his people] upon entering the kingdom.

At that time, one who harbored evil thoughts was lying asleep in deep grass; the chariot ran over him, severing his head. When the King arrived in the country, the people were peaceful and happy. He then dispatched—
The messenger went to invite the World-Honored One. When the meal was finished, the Buddha said to the king:

"As for that person of evil intent, once you have ascended to the throne, he will turn his chariot back toward the kingdom; it will run over and crush his head, and upon death he will enter hell, to be crushed by the fire-chariots."
Only after billions of kalpas does one emerge. One should know that because the mind has different qualities of good and evil, the retributions received are likewise unequal.
Regarding "lowering the head to look at the ground": according to the commentary, this internally corresponds to observing one's own body; it is called "observing the ground. It means:
"This body of mine is the ground of the Buddha," signifying that in the future there is the principle of attaining Buddhahood. Regarding "not spitting on the ground of the Sangha": this...
The sub-commentary (*zhù*) also states that this is an internal application (*nèitiè*). It is clearly established:

even though a child reciting the scriptures at present has not yet undergone tonsure, because they intend to leave the household life, they are already designated as belonging to the monastic community (*saṃghabhūmi*). If one were now to disparage such a child, it would be equivalent to spitting upon the monastic community.
To revile the Saṃgha constitutes an act of rebellion. The commentary states: "It creates the conditions for affection, respect, joy, and reverence."
This refers to expressing love and respect through songs of praise and the like; it is the reverse of wishing for [others] to be honored and respected. The commentary states:

"As for 'the Dharma is thus, and the Saṃgha is pure and faultless,' this establishes that since the Saṃgha is able to rely on the teachings to maintain their observance of the precepts, they are pure and faultless" (this point remains unexplained).
I say: When laypeople enter a monastery, they must not observe the faults of the monks; they should refrain from the practice of censuring or disparaging them.
They should always revere the monks and not perceive their transgressions or evils. Therefore, it is called "cleansing through non-observation."
Furthermore, regarding those who engage in jesting, laughter, and speak of unrighteous matters: this clarifies that worldly people today are ignorant and often delight in mockery.
They speak defiled words to *bhikṣuṇīs*, while laywomen (*upāsikā*) take pleasure in mocking *bhikṣus*.

According to the scriptural teachings, the karmic offense of directing a mind of lustful attachment toward one who has left the household life is extremely grave; it cannot be fully described here. This is as stated in the sutras.

Regarding "sitting half-naked on the same bed as a monk": the *Ratnamudrā-hasta Sūtra* states that those who sit on the same bed as a monk will suffer from the disease of half-body atrophy (*ardha-kāya-śoṣa*).
Furthermore, the *Karmavipāka Sūtra* says they will die as earthworms, and the *Mañjuśrī Sūtra* says they will die sitting upon an iron bed;
this is precisely the meaning [of the former statement]. As for "many instances of social visits and unlawful gatherings," etc., it refers to...
It would be even better to demonstrate this at length by citing the "Chapter on Saving the Dragons" (*Nāga-parivarta*) from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* (and so forth).
Regarding such things as painting one's eyebrows or using artificial ornaments: these are like indulging in a cesspool or being attached to a painted vase.

Since entering a temple is an act of taking refuge, one ought to reform such habits. If one sees a bhikṣu, one must not engage them with words of lustful attachment; rather, one should restrain oneself.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Maudgalyāyana was begging for alms when he encountered on the road a being of immense size whose entire body was溃烂 (ulcerated and putrefied) with pus.
It was foul, impure, and filthy, traveling upon a cloud while birds and beasts followed it, seeking to devour it. The creature wailed and shrieked in a manner beyond description.
Upon seeing this, Maudgalyāyana recalled that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a woman had, with an impure and defiled mind, invited a bhikṣu...
The Buddha set out a meal. The bhikṣu’s mind was upright and not compliant; the woman, however, felt anger and sprinkled water over the bhikṣu’s body.
Due to this cause, she entered hell and underwent immeasurable suffering. As her remaining karma was not yet exhausted, she has now obtained this body.
That which is accomplished through another means refers to the fact that all women lack independent power and are entirely subject to others; whatever they do [is thus dependent].

Matters must be carried out only after obtaining permission from others; therefore, it is said that "they are accomplished by others. This principle can likewise be understood regarding the stages of life:
while one is at home, one depends on one's parents; once married, one depends on the husband; and in old age, or after the husband’s death, one belongs to one's son.
If one sees a *śrāmaṇera* performing prostrations as if he were a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*), one should not fail to show him respect because his rank is low. Regarding this:
This cites the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* regarding a wealthy elder who invited monks but did not accept śrāmaṇeras; the details are as in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* excerpt (*yúnyún*).

It also cites the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* regarding the incident of a śrāmaṇera who took his own life while observing the precepts; the details are as in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* excerpt (*yúnyún*).

The commentary states that "down to sweeping away filth" refers to the following recent case: The court official Cui Zhití served as Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng), a rank of the third degree.
His elder brother served as Grand Secretary (Zhōngshū Lìng). Their father and brothers all revered and placed their faith in the Triple Gem.

Whenever Zhití entered a monastery to prostrate, upon his departure, he would invariably sweep the ground for the monastic community and fetch water to wash the latrines; on each occasion, he would remove his purple robes.
He sewed his own shirt with his own hands. If those of noble status and high rank act thus personally, how much more so should ordinary men? Yet they lack any sense of reverence.
Even if one has a wife and children, or even if one does not give rise to faults and errors, at such a time as this, in a world of clarity, there is only this field of merit.
This is because the karma of sentient beings today is solely characterized by its abundance of evil; it is only these monks who constitute the field of merit. (According to the text)
The *Mahāsannipāta-mañjuśrīparivarta-candragarbha-parivarta* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Candragarbha:

"If I were to remain in the world, the assembly of śrāvakas would be fully endowed with ethical discipline, fully endowed with wisdom, fully endowed with meditative concentration, fully endowed with liberation, and fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation."
