Up until my True Dharma is fully blazing in the world, and during the five hundred years following my parinirvāṇa, the community of bhikṣus will remain firm in liberation within my Dharma.
During the subsequent five hundred years, my True Dharma will remain firm in meditative concentration and samādhi.
During the next five hundred years, it will remain firm in the stability of recitation, study, and extensive learning. During the final five hundred years...
During the first five hundred years, many will build temples and stupas within my Dharma, and it shall remain firm and stable.
During the latter five hundred years, within my Dharma, there will be strife, contention, and litigation; the pure Dharma will be obscured, and its stability will decline.

Even those who understand this well and possess superior faith—from that time onward—though they shave their hair and beards and wear the saffron robes within my Dharma, they will violate the prohibitions.

Regarding those who break the precepts and act contrary to the Dharma, yet are merely called "bhikṣus"—even such bhikṣus who have violated the precepts, if there is a donor who makes offerings to them and protects them, I say that this person still obtains an immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) mass of great merit. Why is this?
Because they are still able to benefit many sentient beings. It is, for example, like genuine gold, which is a priceless treasure.
If there were no genuine gold, then gold and silver would be priceless treasures; even if there were no copper or iron, then lead and tin would be priceless treasures.
In this same way, the Buddha-jewel is priceless within all the worlds. If there were no Buddha-jewel, then the Pratyekabuddhas would be priceless;
even if there were no noble assembly of Arhats, the pure precepts of ordinary beings would be unsurpassed. If there were no pure precepts, then impurity...
The precepts are the unsurpassed treasure; compared to the ninety-five other heterodox paths, they are the most supreme.
They should receive the offerings of the world and serve as a field of merit.

There must certainly be a time for ultimate deliverance. For instance, when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he will first deliver those disciples who remain from the period of the Final Dharma (mofa) of Śākyamuni;
therefore, it is said that this can be expected. Regarding those of like dharma, Master Ying says: Wang Yi states—
Two people form a pair; four people form a cohort (*chou*). A "cohort" is also a category. "Transmitting and announcing" refers to proclaiming the intent to worldly people.
The preceding explanation of the twenty-four chapters is now complete.
Chapter Twenty-five: The Mutual Dependence of Host and Guest.
Since the preceding chapter was occasioned by offerings of merit, it provided instructions for bhikṣus; now, as the Dharma and food are mutually required, they benefit one another in turn.

It is necessary to ensure that the proper protocols do not fall into ruin for a thousand years. One cannot simply settle one's mind within a narrow, localized perspective; rather, one must observe the customs of foreign lands.

Between those who have long resided there and those newly arrived, there is no lack of distinction between host and guest; matters require mutual waiting, reception, and the respectful inspection of robes.

Yet, although the Śākya school is vast and open in principle and free from obstruction, this is largely due to people harboring worldly views and frequently failing to maintain the prescribed models. Therefore—

This chapter fully elucidates the formal standards, ensuring that those who have long resided there and those newly arrived are treated with propriety, so that no feelings of timidity or weakness arise.

Regarding the terms "host" (*zhǔ*) and "guest" (*kè*): the long-term resident and the newly arrived visitor are designated as host and guest; because they provide for one another in succession, it is called "mutual reception.

The commentary states that the four modes of deportment (*sìyí*) are appended here. As for the term "Sāṃgha companions" (*shāmén shìlǚ*), the *Jiémó sū* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "The old translation was..."
"Sengmen" (桑門) is a corruption of the sound. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "Śramaṇa" is the original term;

it is sometimes called "the way of exhaustion" (乏道) or "the way of poverty" (貧道), both of which are expressions of humble self-restraint. Now, translating it as "one who ceases evil" (息惡) captures its essential meaning.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated it as "diligent labor" (勤勞). Yong stated: "Śramaṇa here means 'one whose will is tranquil' (寂志). It is also...
"Śramaṇa" is a term of humble respect; it is also a designation for humility and emptiness. As the sutras clarify, "lacking the Way" (mò dào) is its meaning. The sutra says:
"Śramaṇa" means that "śramaṇa" signifies "lack" (mò), and "na" signifies the "Way" (dào); thus, it is called "lacking the Way.
The worldly expression "poor Way" (pīn dào) carries this same meaning. Furthermore, it is said: because one quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source, one is thus titled [Śramaṇa].
A śramaṇa is a guest of the triple world.
To establish this point, "guest" (bin) refers to a noble visitor; it means that the Saṃgha is a noble guest of the triple world.

Since those who have left the household life intend to transcend the three realms of existence (trai-dhātuka), they do not dwell long within them. They reside therein only temporarily, their situation being like that of a guest.
They are like guests. Thus, the Vinaya says: "to destroy the nests and lairs. The commentary explains: the human and celestial realms, pure and ethereal, are above, likened to a nest;
the three miserable realms, stagnant and submerged, are below, likened to a lair. Now, the five groups of the ordained cultivate renunciation equally;

above they must reach for the human and celestial realms, and below they must eliminate the three evil paths. Therefore, it is said: "to destroy the nests and lairs. This is an analogy for a traveler's inn.
There are some traces of this preserved here. The *Zuozhuan* states: "He stayed at an *inilu* (inn). Du Yu comments: "An *inilu* is a guest house;
it is so called because it receives travelers passing through. It is intended for a stay of one or two nights, not a place for long-term residence."
This clarifies that the current followers of the Śākya lineage maintain a disposition toward transcendence. Although they dwell within the three realms, they are like travelers in an inn;
furthermore, the body itself is the inn. Since the body is not permanent or stable, the mind dwells there only temporarily.
When the breath ceases and the soul departs, it is abandoned in the empty wilderness; thus, the body is an inn. As King Chu-zhi’s poem says: "The body is a guest."
The guest-house: the spirit is a lodging guest; when the guest departs, the guest-house is empty. Who knows whose dwelling it is? Jie said:
"When National Teacher Nanshan was alive, he often recited a verse: 'Like a bird in a bottle, with fine gauze covering its mouth.'"
The net is pierced and the bird flies away; what remains in the empty bottle? The commentary explains: the "bird" is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the "bottle" is the body; and the "net" is life-force (*jīva*). Once human life is severed and the spiritual consciousness has departed, what can the body possibly do?
Regarding the rule that one must not sleep with a person one does not know: this is clearly established. Since they are strangers, there is a fear that they may be thieves masquerading as bhikṣus;
therefore, one must not sleep with them, for one might suffer robbery or harm. If one is compelled to share a narrow bed, one must remain seated until dawn.

If a traveling companion has already departed and one cannot speak to inform them, "speaking" refers to speaking in order to protect the companion's feelings by asking them to stay for a while, so that they may later meet with others.
If one sees that the companion has already departed, one must report it immediately to inform them; otherwise, it would appear as if one wished to dismiss them.
Regarding the entrustment to the traveling companion: one should instruct the host, saying, "In such-and-such a direction, there will be a companion coming; you must take note of this."
(Not fully understood). "The four phrases concerning customs" refers to expressions regarding sexual desire that are taboo within the local secular conventions of various regions.
"The eight [phrases] stating that a certain thing may be eaten" means saying, for example, "First serve coarse food;

later serve fine food," or saying it to make one understand that future results depend upon present causes. Another interpretation holds that this refers to the donor's gift as a latent cause (*adṛṣṭa-hetu*).
To move the hearts of humans and devas is the manifestation of the fruit. How is this known? It is because one who has been born into a realm of goodness is worthy of receiving offerings;
that is to say, one gives rise to faith by observing proper decorum (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* cited below states:

"If one’s four modes of deportment are not in accordance with the Dharma, one does not serve as a great illumination for the world. This clearly shows that the thesis is established based on decorum. The word "relying upon" (*jie*)— [text continues]
"Standing as a model for the school" means that by observing one's physical demeanor (*ākāra*), one is able to recognize its underlying cause.
Regarding "Aśvajit Śāriputra," *Lì* says: "The four parts of Aśva are called Aśvabhī; the external tradition also calls him Aśvika Bhikṣu.

The oral tradition states this refers to the Bhikṣu Aśvika, whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) transformed sentient beings. Xuán says: "Majesty refers to a countenance worthy of being beheld; deportment..."

This refers to the standard for regulating things; it arises entirely from harboring the True Dharma within. Thus, his magnanimity transcends all others. When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he delivered the five bhikṣus;
this was one of those five. At that time, Aśvajit arrived at the hour, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
His countenance was harmonious and joyful, his faculties were tranquil and composed, his robes were neatly arranged, and his gait was dignified and measured.
Introduction. He did not look to the left or right, nor did he lose his dignified deportment. At that time, Śāriputra was the leader among the non-Buddhist brahmins;
being clever and of sharp intelligence, as soon as he observed Śreṇika’s such dignified deportment, he immediately went to question him:
"Who is your teacher? Whom do you serve? What dharma do you practice for awakening? He replied: "My teacher is the Great Śramaṇa; he is my..."

“Venerable One, I have awakened to that. Furthermore, in the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance), it is answered: “My Teacher is the God among Gods, the Supreme Honored One of the Three Realms.

His body, adorned with the marks and signs, is sixteen feet tall. With supernormal powers he travels through space; he transforms the deceptive and eliminates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). He uproots and severs the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Not craving the positions of gods or the world, his mind is pure as he opens the gates of the Dharma. [Commentary: “Eliminating the five aggregates” manifests the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
"Pan" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination having ignorance as their root; this reveals the wisdom that abandons the origin [of suffering].
He asked again: "What doctrine does your teacher teach? You may now explain it to me. Aśvajit replied: "I am young in years and my realization is but shallow;
how could I proclaim the vast and true meaning of the Tathāgata? Śāriputra said: "I do not ask whether it is extensive or brief."
"I only wish to hear what is essential. Aśvajit then spoke in verse: "All dharmas are fundamentally (Commentary:

the Truth of Origination) Empty of causes and conditions and without a master (Because they arise from conditions, they are empty and without self; this reveals the Truth of Suffering). The mind at rest (This refers to the wisdom of the Path) Reaches the original source (This is the wisdom of realizing Cessation).

Therefore, one is called a Śramaṇa. Upon hearing this verse, Śāriputra attained the Way immediately. (The preceding two verses are from the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*). He then asked where the Buddha was located.

Together with his former acquaintance, named Kauṇḍinya—now known as Maudgalyāyana—and their two hundred and fifty disciples, they simultaneously invited the Buddha to leave the household life and practice the Way.
The Buddha immediately prophesied, saying: "These two individuals shall be the foremost among my disciples;
their wisdom is immeasurable, and their supernormal powers are supreme. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Mahāmaudgalyāyana...
Even Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—these two men of comparable talent and wisdom—traveled together when on the move and stayed together when at rest.
Later, they became brahmins under a teacher named Sañjaya. One day, as their teacher lay ill, Śāriputra stood at his head and Maudgalyāyana stood at his feet.
When his life was about to end, he looked upon them with compassion and smiled; the two of them were of one mind.
Both asked about the meaning of the smile. The Master said, "In the mundane world, there are those who lack the eye of wisdom and are overcome by ignorance.
I saw that when the King of Suvarṇabhūmi died, his chief queen threw herself into a funeral pyre, seeking to be in the same place as him. The two men accepted these words, wishing to verify them.
Later, a merchant from Suvarṇabhūmi arrived from afar. The two men tested him, and it was indeed just as the Master had said. The two men [were thus convinced].
They sighed with emotion and said, "Are we not the right people [to receive the Dharma]? Or is it that our teacher is concealing it from us?
The two of them made a vow together, saying, "If one of us first attains the nectar of immortality, we must certainly share its flavor" (the remainder of the text is the same as in the Vinaya).
According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Śāriputra’s original name was Upatiṣya; upon meeting Aśvajit, he immediately conceived a sense of joy.
Citta asked, "What Dharma does your teacher teach? He replied, "Dharmas arise from conditions; the penetration of this is the cause.

Because causes and conditions cease, there is tranquility. The world is suffering; the cause of suffering is called 'origination. If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, the origination of the world ceases.
If there is neither suffering nor origination, my teacher declares that it is named Nirvana. My teacher teaches only this."
Having heard these teachings, Upatiṣya attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upon returning, he saw Kauṣṭhila and explained [the Dharma] to him in full;
he, too, immediately attained the first fruit [of the path], and so forth. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
In that town there was a brahmin named Śāriputra who had two hundred and fifty disciples under his tutelage.
Among these followers were two preeminent students: one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita.

At that time, Aśvajit, having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food; his countenance was serene and joyful, his faculties were tranquil and composed, and his garments were neatly arranged.

He walked while keeping his eyes fixed on the ground. At that time, Upatiṣya (who is now Śāriputra) was out for a stroll; seeing from afar the dignified and composed deportment of the bhikṣu Aśvajit, he marveled at such an unprecedented sight.
Waiting until he had approached, he sent someone to ask: "What kind of dharma do you follow? Your clothing is unconventional."
"Is there a teacher whom you follow? May we hear of him? Ājñātakauṇḍinya replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama is our great teacher;
he is the one we honor, from whom we have received awakening. He asked, "What kind of Dharma does your great teacher teach?
Ājñātakauṇḍinya answered, "I am young in years and my realization is but recently shallow; how could I proclaim the vast meaning of my teacher's teachings? Now, I shall—"
I shall briefly explain the essential point for you: that which my Teacher has taught is that all phenomena arise from conditions and likewise cease from conditions;
all dharmas are empty and without a master. Having heard this, Upatissa attained realization in his mind and heart, and he obtained the pure Dharma-eye.
He then went together with two hundred and fifty disciples to the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) seeking to leave the household life.
When the Buddha saw them approaching from afar, he addressed the bhikṣus: "These two individuals shall be the foremost among my disciples;

their wisdom shall be immeasurable, and they shall be the first in supernatural powers (ṛddhi). As for those two hundred and fifty followers—meaning those who were formerly his fellow students since his teacher had passed away—"
At that time, [the Buddha] instructed me. When I arrived before the Buddha, he preached for me the discourse on giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven;

he censured the impurity of sensual desire and praised renunciation. Thereupon, while still seated, my outflows were exhausted and my mind was liberated. I addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to go forth from the household life."
He purified his holy life (*brahmacarya*). The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! Within my Dharma, purify your holy life so that you may reach the end of suffering.

This is what is called going forth and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). The reason for citing this matter here is precisely to clarify how one guides sentient beings through proper deportment (*īryāpatha*);
the scripture explains this in detail, which is why it is said that the former scripture is fully listed. As for the phrase "the words are now [complete]," it refers to later people...
Biographies are taken as models for conduct. Furthermore, the term is fully explained in the *Fangbian* (Expedient Means):

it is said that since ancient times paper did not exist, square wooden tablets and bamboo were used for writing. What is currently called a "pen" (*bi*) refers to this. Writing on bamboo slips was called *fang* (tablet);
writing on wood was called *zhi* (board); writing on silk was called *su* (plain cloth). Thus, Emperor Wu of Liang convened the three teachings.
The poem says: "Filial piety and righteousness extend across the lands; benevolence and forbearance fill the annals. This refers to its righteousness.

As for the mention of "inscribed on tablets," this refers to the *Jiuhuan tu jing* (Sūtra of the Diagrams of Jetavana); it is also called the *Sengfa si gao* (Edict of the Sengfa Temple), though the latter is not clearly understood. Master Ying says:

"The bamboo slips and the tally-commands (*fuming*) are the same," as seen in the *Zuo zhuan*, which records the tally-commands from the *Zhushu*. This is found in the *Guoshi ji* (Records of National History).

Regarding matters of great importance, one likewise records them on bamboo slips or wooden tablets. Furthermore, the *Rites of Zhou* states: "In all cases concerning the various feudal lords, one then issues the royal mandate" (the commentary by Zhuanxu says:
this refers to recording the King’s commands upon bamboo or wooden slips).
Regarding those who rely on the laws of the hunting king, some say it is like the lion, the king of beasts, who lies down at dawn, goes out to seek food, and returns to his den after eating.
Jì (Jizang) says: "When a lion lies down, he must lie on his right side; furthermore, he seeks food at the break of day."
As the *Jiwen* states, "one must not sit in the camel posture," this refers to the small-sitting posture common among people today.
One should sit in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka*), or if sitting in a cross-legged posture for a long time, one should extend one leg alternately; one must not extend both legs simultaneously.
[The author] privately comments: "Sitting in a cross-legged posture" (*ji zuo*) refers to the half-lotus position (*ardhaparyaṅka*). "Extreme" (*ji*) means exhaustion. As for the full lotus position:
In the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are many successive explanations; I shall now briefly summarize them. Therein it asks:

"Among the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), one can cultivate wholesome states (*kuśala*). Why, then, is only the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*) mentioned? One interpretation states: "Because this mode of deportment..."
Because it gives rise to a mind of reverence and faith among humans, devas, and others.

That is to say, other modes of deportment cannot inspire a mind of reverence and faith in humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth, in the way that the mode of deportment of the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka) can. Therefore, one should maintain this deportment.

Even if it gives rise to unwholesome discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*), one should still abide in it for the sake of generating goodness in others; how much more so when it naturally gives rise to superior categories of wholesome qualities? (That is to say, if...)

When walking or standing, the body remains far removed from fatigue; whereas if one doubles the time spent lying down, it causes an increase in drowsiness. Only by sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*) is there no such fault; this is called "conforming to the wholesome" (*kuśalānukūla*). Furthermore, by abiding in this posture:
Because it terrifies the armies of Māra. That is to say, in the past, beneath the Bodhi tree, the Buddha sat in the full lotus posture and defeated two armies of Māra:

namely, Māra the Lord (Īśvara) and all the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, when the hosts of Māra now see this majestic deportment, they are immediately struck with alarm and fear, and for the most part retreat and scatter.
Furthermore, because this is a teaching not shared with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). That is to say, as for other modes of deportment, the non-Buddhists...

There is also [a specific type]: namely, those who sit only in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). This is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not [practice it]. Question: What is the meaning of "sitting in the full lotus posture"? Answer:

It means sitting with the body perfectly circular and symmetrical. The etymologists (*śabdavādin*) say: "By crossing the two feet so that the two ankles are joined like the coiled knot of a dragon, one sits upright in contemplation;
therefore, it is called 'sitting in the full lotus posture' (*paryaṅka-bandha*). The Venerable Pārśva said: "It is [so called because]... [The text continues with the term *punar* (again/repeated)].
Placing the two feet one upon the other with the toes interlaced on both sides and facing the object of meditation is called *paryaṅka-bandha* (the full lotus posture).

In the latter part of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, specifically in the *Mahā-śīla-kṣudra-śīla-khandhaka*, it is also referred to as *paryaṅka-paryañka* (the full cross-legged sitting). One should straighten the body, rectify the intention, and bind the mindfulness before oneself.

Furthermore, regarding the term "reaching the limit" (*ji-jí*): this refers to the cramping of the sinews after sitting for a long time, which is colloquially known in the capital today as "reaching the limit."
If one stands for a long time, it is superior to being utterly exhausted; all say this refers to "resting from exhaustion. Furthermore, this is not known through numbness of the feet.

The commentary states, "each has its own established [posture]," which means that for nuns, only the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyanka) is permitted, while the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) is not. For monks, both postures are permitted. Moreover, nuns may not sit with legs crossed (interlocking them);
they may only sit in the long-kneeling posture (utkuṭukāsana). This is because, within the *nidāna* (the account of the origin), the form of sitting with legs crossed was [prohibited].

[The nun] exposed her shame; therefore, the Buddha did not permit it. Monks must kneel alternately [with one knee on the ground], whereas nuns do not. Thus it is said that each has its own established rule. Another interpretation states:

kneeling with both knees on the ground (jang-kwi) corresponds to the formal act of reporting to the Buddha, while kneeling alternately (hu-kwi) is for the acts of requesting the Dharma and receiving the Dharma.

Therefore it is said that each has its own established posture. Jì says: "If listening to the Dharma, one must kneel with both knees on the ground; if performing repentance and the like, one must remain in a long-kneeling position (prāṇāmaka).
Thus it is said that each has its own established posture."
If the preceptor (upādhyāya) or instructor (ācārya), out of respect, rises from their seat, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This means that because the preceptor and others rise for a separate matter and manifest respect, the disciple must remain seated; if the disciple follows them by rising, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
"Those who do not lie down in a pack like dogs": Jì explains that this refers to bending one's hands and head together in one place, as dogs do when they lie down.

"One should reproach oneself for the original arising": Jì explains that this means reproaching the mind for the source from which delusions arise; since [delusions] originally arise from nowhere, it is called "original arising."
Regarding "one whose hair is dry": this refers to the practice of rising to bathe while still asleep. If one falls back asleep again, one should form the mental resolve:
"When my hair becomes dry, I shall rise. Regarding "observing the stars, moonlight, and shadows as a boundary":

this refers to the practice of looking toward the stars and moon when wishing to sleep while drowsy, and mentally noting, "If the moon reaches such-and-such a place, I shall rise," and so forth. This is the "receiving of others' offerings."
Regarding the statement that "one should not be indolent in giving," this is explained by means of the story of Bakula.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Madhyama Āgama*, the Bhikṣu Bakula said: "I have gone forth within the True Dharma and Vinaya; eighty years have passed."
I have never once given rise to thoughts of desire. Furthermore, for eighty years I have worn robes made of discarded rags, and I do not recall ever having accepted an invitation from a layperson.

Moreover, during my eighty years of begging for alms, I do not recall ever entering a bhikṣuṇī monastery, nor do I recall ever exchanging greetings with a bhikṣuṇī; I did not even speak with them on the road. Furthermore, for eighty [years]...
For ten years, I do not recall ever having asked a bhikṣuṇī whether she was keeping a śrāmaṇera.
Furthermore, for eighty years, I have never been ill—not even for as long as the snap of a finger—nor do I recall ever taking medicine, down to something as small as a harītakī fruit.
Moreover, for eighty years, I have sat in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) without ever leaning against a wall or a tree, even when approaching [death].
At the time of his passing, he entered final nirvana while sitting in the full lotus posture. This is called the extraordinary quality of Bakula.
The explanation of the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Mutual Relation of Host and Guest," is hereby concluded.
Chapter Twenty-Six, Part One: Visiting the Sick and Attending Funerals.
The protocols for monastics and laity have already been established, and the rites between guest and host have further been clarified. However, as for those of impure substance and ordinary form—

Resembling bubbles and illusions, one is bound and fettered by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Because of the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is conventionally designated as a "body.
If its protection is improper, the four elements fall into conflict; when even one of the solid, mobile, warm, or moist elements loses its place, various sufferings invade.
One must rely on others for strength, barely managing to prolong life from day to morning. Yet for the renunciant, relatives become strangers, and the monastic robes—*
Those of this kind should all lead their companions; it is only right that they provide for and sustain them so that both body and spirit may be sustained.

Should their karma be exhausted and their conditions depart, their worn-out remains must be buried. If fellow practitioners do not manage these affairs, it will immediately corrupt the Dharma and wound social custom. Therefore, this one chapter [is written].

To provide guidance and instruction for future generations, one attends to those in distress; thus it is called "attending to the sick. After death, when the body is moved to the grave, it is called "seeing out the end.

Since both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is termed "attending to the sick and seeing out the end. This is why it is said so. Ji says: "Attending" (zhan) refers to the one who attends.

"Sickness" refers to that which is attended; "sending off" refers to that which can be sent off; and "the end" refers to that which is sent off. Since both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is called "attending to the sick and seeing them off at their end.
Regarding those with many entanglements: "entanglement" (*ying*) means being bound and fettered, while "burden" (*lei*) means a heavy load. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "O virtuous one..."
This body is impermanent and powerless; it is suffering and affliction, a confluence of manifold diseases, like a mass of foam—this is precisely its meaning.
Regarding the formation of disease in the six *fu* (organs): the *Baitong* states, "A person has six *fu*: first, the large intestine; second, the small intestine;
third, the bladder; fourth, the stomach; fifth, the three *zhao*; and sixth, the gallbladder. It further says, "Among the six *fu*, there are three *zhao*."

It is the palace of the kidneys. That which is from the heart upward is called the upper *triple-burner* (*shàng jiào*). That which is from the navel downward to the heart is called the middle *triple-burner*.

That which is from the waist downward is the lower *triple-burner*. To clarify this: if the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are not in harmony, they cause the six palaces to fall into illness.
"Difficult to unify from beginning to end" means that ordinary sentiments are thin and indifferent, and one's preferences are inconsistent; when one is vigorous, one takes [what is right] as...
"Close friends abandon one another like rubble when ill; therefore, it is said they are 'difficult to be of one mind. I privately say: youth is the beginning, and illness is the end.
Since it is difficult to maintain a single kind of heart from beginning to end, it is said they are 'difficult to be of one mind.

Only the sage, indeed, can have both a beginning and an end. Now, there is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end. This is especially true for those who are close and intimate."

The character *ni* (written as 匿) is pronounced with the *li* rhyme (female *li* rhyme). The *Erlü* states: "Ni means 'to draw near' (*qīnjìn*). Furthermore, ni means 'to assist' (*chéng*). Assistance arises from frequency.
To be 'intimately close' (*qīnni*) means to be frequently near one another. Regarding "vulgar and worldly sentiments," the common saying is: "If one has money, one goes to court immediately;
if one has no money, one certainly will not go to court. Jì says: "When monastics look after one another, they must maintain [this practice], especially when someone is ill."
Thus one knows the depth or shallowness of the heart. Yet human life is of the utmost importance; that at such a time one would abandon it allows the heart to be known as well.

As for why life is said to be so precious: this land east of the Snow Mountains in the kingdom of China (Zhendan) is the domain of the lords of men, where humans are held in high esteem and not easily exchanged for anything else.
West of the Snow Mountains is the domain of the lords of gold, where gold and jewels are highly valued. The Snow...
To the south of the mountains lies the land of the masters of elephants, such as K’un-lun and others; they are highly skilled in training elephants because they hold them in great esteem.

To the north of the Snow Mountains lies the land of the masters of horses, such as the Turks and others; they value only horses. Since these are esteemed by humans, [the former] is called the "land of elephants" and [the latter] the "land of horses."
When one is ill, one must certainly attend to them. Regarding the phrase "knowing that good is not honored while evil is surely followed," Master Ciyun said:
"Good" refers to the virtuous practice of attending to the sick, yet this is not honored or esteemed. "Evil" refers to the failure to attend to the sick, yet people follow this evil practice.
Therefore, it is said: seeing good, they do not raise it up for study; seeing evil, they immediately learn from it. One ought to see...
One should regard goodness as something one cannot attain quickly enough, and view evil as if touching boiling water. How could one act contrary to this? Furthermore, "veneration" implies height.

This clarifies that if people in the world do not yet possess a high degree of goodness, they will take pleasure in following evil ways; it is said that because they lack the mind of the Way, they frequently fail to attend to the sick.
As for the statement that "evil must be followed," Jì says: if one calls others "evil" while oneself drinking alcohol and eating at improper times, [then one is indeed following evil].
"Et cetera" (*ādi*) refers to those who act together; therefore it is said that "evil must necessarily follow one another. Regarding the term "you all" (*rǔcáo*), Master Ying explains:
"Cáo" means a group or a cohort; it is also said to mean a multitude.
Regarding "descending personally to receive [them]," this is an instance of citing the superior to illustrate the inferior; it refers to stirring the assembly at that time.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is the constant practice of all Buddhas to inspect the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days for the sake of five benefits:
first, whether my śrāvaka disciples are attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); second, whether they are attached to worldly frivolous discourse (*prapañca*); third... [text continues].
1. Is it one who is not attached to sleep and does not hinder the practice of the Path? 2. Is it for the sake of a monk who is tending to the sick? 3.

A sick bhikṣu lay amidst excrement and filth, unable to rise by himself. The Buddha asked him, "Are you ill? Have you received food today? He replied, "No.
The Buddha asked again, "Did you receive it yesterday? He replied, "No," and so on, until he answered, "It has already been seven days since I have received any food.
The Buddha asked, "Do you have an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or fellow students? He replied, "No. The Buddha asked again.
"Is there a monk in the adjacent room? "There is. [The Buddha thought,] "Because of my foul odor, he has moved from the adjacent room to another place.
After the Buddha and Ānanda had washed [the monk], the Buddha washed his clothes again while Ānanda did the washing; the Buddha himself poured the water.
Even after having removed the filth and impurities, he rubbed the monk’s forehead with his golden, soft hand. All his sufferings were entirely eliminated, and he attained harmony.
He then preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Long ago, there was a king who established five hundred officials to manage state revenues.
Whenever anyone in the kingdom committed a crime, those who could pay a large sum of money were released, while those with no money were punished according to the law.
At that time, there was a virtuous man who observed the five precepts. Having committed a minor offense, he was brought before the five hundred elders to be judged according to the Vinaya;
he was sentenced to forty lashes. When the one administering the rod saw that he was a keeper of the five precepts, he immediately struck the ground to make a sound, saying:
"Because of my past habit of beating people, I now receive this painful retribution. Out of gratitude for his kindness, I shall stroke his head with my hand," and so he did.
This was the purification of the Dharma-eye. At that time, the virtuous one who observed the five precepts was none other than myself.
At that time, the one who wielded the staff was this sick bhikṣu. For this reason, you should know that one must attend to the sick. The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"If fellow practitioners of the holy life fall ill and do not look after one another, who then shall look after them? You all..."

Though they were each of different surnames, having faith that the home life is not the true home, they abandoned their homes to go forth; all became of one single surname: the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas.
Just as the many rivers returning to the sea all become of one taste, [the Buddha] therefore established the rules for attending to the sick.

...Indeed, it is only because of his illness and the current suffering of that disease that no one is looking after him. The Buddha praised him, saying: "You have been able to utter these words of truth.

Just as the five hundred *vajra*-beings of the *Pañcavargika* always follow and guard the Buddha, if you do not answer according to reality when I ask three times, then [the consequences will follow]."
He struck his head with a pestle until it was broken into seven pieces; because he was terrified, he answered truthfully.
Furthermore, the treatise says, "In accordance with my words," etc., as in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (*Chengshi lun*) below.
Because the Buddha’s maternal aunt had personally woven cloth to make a golden-threaded *kāṣāya*, she thought of the Buddha returning to the palace and offered it to him. The Buddha said:

this is called making an offering to the Buddha. Because it leads to liberation, it is called making an offering to the Dharma. Because the Sangha receives and uses these offerings, it is called making an offering to the Sangha.
Thus, among the eight fields of merit, that which regards the Three Jewels as the three and the Teacher as the fourth is the foremost. As for the Sangha, they are the fourth.
5. The father; 6. The mother; 7. The sick person; 8. The attendant. Regarding two people acting as companions to visit the Buddha while one companion passes by the sick person and leaves:

you may come after you have recovered. The sick man replied, "Venerable sir, wait for me. He answered:
"Because it has been a long time since I last saw the World-Honored One, my longing for him was like that of one who thirsts;

"Look! Who is it that shall look? You must go back and look after the sick bhikṣu. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425), fascicle 28, states:
"When traveling through the wilderness, one must look after one's companion bhikṣu and not abandon him; one should take him along and carry his robes and bowl for him.

Upon arriving at a village, one must not circumambulate a stupa to pay respects to one's upādhyāya or ācārya. Instead, one should say to the bhikṣus in the village:
"There is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness; let us go together to meet him and bring him back. If they ask, "Where is he? [one should inform them].

He replied by giving the location. If it was said that there were many tigers and wolves in that place, and that one feared they would devour them all so that not even one in ten thousand would remain, he must still go to see for himself despite hearing these words;
he must not return upon merely seeing crows and birds from afar, but must reach the spot itself.

He arrived. He spoke to the senior bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, this is a sick person from such-and-such a place.
Having provided for him in the wilderness, I have now come to the village. Venerable sir, please look after this sick person from such-and-such a place;

If there are no bhikṣus present, one should tell the upāsaka: "There is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness; lend me a vehicle to go and fetch him.
Upon arriving at the donor's house, one should settle him in a separate screened area and together encourage the donor to provide robes, medicine, food, and so forth.

Those who come to one, those who have traveled far, the sick, and those who tend to the sick—by bestowing gifts upon such persons, one obtains immeasurable merit.

The above concludes the explanation of the intent behind the prohibition against tending to the sick. Below follows the clarification of the criteria for selecting individuals and the rules for providing offerings.

[He] reflects (as detailed above).

this means that the setting of the sun is a sign of impermanence, and for this reason, [the items] are placed therein.
"Returning to one or two [stages]" means that one has attained a slight degree of progress. Nowadays, most people lack any portion of the Path and do not suddenly contemplate impermanence.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, when the Buddha was explaining the meaning of the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*) to the bhikṣus, a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am able to cultivate the perception of death. The Buddha asked him, "How [do you do it]?"
"What is your practice? He replied, "I do not expect to live beyond seven years. The Buddha said, "You are being negligent.
Again, another bhikṣu said, "I do not expect to live beyond seven months. Another said, "Seven days.

"Among those who have left the household life today, some possess overflowing knowledge and understanding, while others extinguish the fires of their passions through diligent effort, yet they fail to awaken to impermanence. As a common proverb says:"

having observed the sun repeatedly setting, and seeing that although many come, only one or two return—observing these facts and seeking within oneself, one asks: "Where lies my own path to life? It is for this reason.

Within this text, it is further divided into six sections; as there are six distinct gates, this is now the first.
Regarding parrots that hear the Four Noble Truths: the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that the parrot is a bird.

(3) Mārga (these four, in the Jin language, are called Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path). In front of his house was a tree. Two birds, having heard the Dharma, recited it with joy;

"Ānanda, tomorrow when the time comes, put on your robes, take up your bowl, and enter the city to beg for food. You will hear that two parrots have been killed by a wildcat.

Once it has passed through the ear, one will not fall into the evil realms after death at the end of one's life.
As for those who were his companions—namely, the individuals listed below such as Dabba and others—they were all sages;
thus it is said. Regarding Kāśyapa treading mud to construct five vihāras, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle four, it says: "Kāśyapa, in total, spent..."
He constructed five great monasteries: the first was the Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata Monastery; the second was the Veṇuvana Monastery;
and there were three other monasteries (the names of which are not recorded in the treatise). At times he would personally manage and maintain them.

Kāśyapa himself oversaw the construction of the monks' quarters, personally applying mud to the walls and personally leveling the ground. He questioned this great arhat: "Your outflows are already exhausted."
"Having already accomplished what was to be done, for what reason do you now again wander about, engaging in various activities and performing meritorious deeds?
The answer is that there are many reasons: first, to repay the Buddha's kindness; second, to nurture and foster the Buddha-dharma;
third, to eliminate the self-conceit of ordinary and inferior beings who perform minor meritorious acts and become arrogant; and fourth, to humble the pride of future disciples.

Because of the mind. Fifth, it is for the sake of initiating the meritorious karma of future sentient beings. Yet, as for that meritorious karma, even the Buddha cultivated it; it was not only the Arhats.
The reason this is known is, for example, in the case of Aniruddha, who was of the Śākya clan. When he first left the household life, he listened to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddha.
Due to the Dharma, his eyes momentarily grew drowsy. The Buddha spoke a verse, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? Like a clam..."
Such as the snail (a type of choking insect) and the scorpion (a type of wooden insect), they shall pass through eighty thousand kalpas without ever hearing the name of the Buddha.

It is said that these insects are by nature prone to excessive sleep; once they fall into this realm, they remain there for eighty thousand kalpas. Now you are so drowsy that I fear you too will fall into that state in the future.
Upon hearing these verses from the Buddha, Nanda vowed that for the remainder of his life, he would never again sleep, regardless of whether it was day or night.
He applied himself with diligence to the practice of the Path, until he eventually lost his sight. Thereafter, he cultivated the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). At the age of five...

Among his hundred disciples, he was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Later, when seeking a physician to treat his physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), the Buddha said, "This eye can certainly not be treated further.
However, the eye feeds on sleep; since you do not sleep, you are starving this eye to death."
Therefore, he could not be healed. Later, at another time, while he was praising himself for mending his robes, he lost his sight and could no longer pass a needle through a hole.
Although he possessed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it was present for him as a *śrāvaka* only when he was in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and absent when he had emerged from it.
Since he could not pass the needle, he thought: "Who would delight in merit? Let them come and help me thread this needle. The Buddha, knowing his intention, suddenly appeared before him.
Previously, he said, "I delight in merit; I shall help you thread your needle. Based on this scriptural evidence, it is clear that even the Buddha practiced meritorious deeds.
Therefore, even during one's leisure time, one must set aside a portion of the mind to practice meritorious karma, for such merit is also the sprout of liberation.
As for the *geya* regarding the woodcutter, the circumstances are as described at the end of the *Sengwang* (Monastic Net) chapter.
In the *Jì* (Record/Commentary), it cites the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*; one should consult it when the time comes.

Regarding the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Zhìlùn*) and the sūtras which states that those who perform good deeds while alive may harbor evil thoughts at the moment of death, etc., the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Zhìlùn* explains:

"As stated in the *Vibhaṅga-karma-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: 'A person who has committed evil deeds may be born in a good realm... [The text continues with the description of how such a person, despite their past conduct, may attain a favorable rebirth].
"A virtuous person is born in an evil place. Ānanda asked, "How is this so?

The Buddha said, "If a wicked person’s sinful karma of the present life has not yet ripened, but their wholesome karma from past lives has already ripened, then by these causes and conditions, although they commit evil now, they are born in a good place."
Or, at the time of death, wholesome mental states and their associated factors arise; by reason of these conditions, one is likewise born in a good realm.
As for those who practice virtue yet are born in an evil realm, it is because their wholesome karma of the present life has not yet matured, while their past unwholesome karma has already matured.
By reason of this, although they perform wholesome deeds now, they are born in an evil realm. Or, at the time of death, unwholesome mental states and their associated factors [arise].
Because of these causes and conditions, one is also born in an evil realm. Question: It may be so regarding the meaning of "ripened" versus "unripened.

But how can the mind for a brief moment at the time of death overcome the power of conduct performed throughout one's entire life? Answer: Although this mind lasts for only a short duration, it is [powerful].
The power of the mind is fierce and sharp, like fire or poison; though small, it can accomplish great deeds.

Because the mind is resolute and courageous at the moment of death, it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice. This final mind is called the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*), for the matter of relinquishing the body and the sense faculties is urgent.
It is like a person entering battle who does not spare his own body or life; he is called "valiant. Truly, of itself—

Regarding "empty and non-existent": I say that while it appears to exist from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is empty and lacks reality when viewed from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Although there is a single pure consciousness-mind, there are no external objects; these are all merely false perceptions. One should explain the Dharma in this way:
if the mind reaches the state of ultimate truth, it does not grasp at conventional truth; therefore, it is said that where the mirage reaches, there is no water.
This is a sign. Jì said: "In the midst of wild marshes, when viewed from afar, there is a mirage that resembles the water of a pond;
yet if one goes to its edge and looks closely, no water is seen."

Regarding the statement that "only consciousness exists and there is no external object; it is merely a false perception of the mind," this establishes that the myriad objects of the world and the bodies of sentient beings are all falsely existent;
in reality, they are empty. It is only because sentient beings are inverted that they falsely cling to them as being existent.

There is, however, only a single consciousness that persists through birth and death without being destroyed, continuing until the attainment of Buddhahood. Since it is said that there are no external objects, now, in this [Mahāyāna]...
What is the world of earth? The explanation says that it is also a manifestation produced by the consciousness-mind of sentient beings, appearing in response to their perceptions.
In its essence, it is purely delusory. If one were to claim that the objective realm is real, it would be like the case of water:
why is it that humans see it as water, hungry ghosts see it as fire, devas see it as a single path of lapis lazuli, and fish see it as their dwelling place? Therefore...
While the object of cognition is one, the perceptions of it differ. It is clearly known that the object is nothing but emptiness;
yet, according to their deluded attachments, people falsely claim that objects such as water or fire exist. Therefore, the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-siddhi* states:

"Regarding the beautiful body of a single courtesan, the ordained monk, the lustful man, and the starving tiger each have three distinct types of conceptualization: [the monk perceives] a foul corpse, [the lustful man] a seductive beauty, and [the tiger] delicious food."

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there is an illustration: it is like a vicious dog that comes to a well and barks at its own reflection. There is no dog in the water; there is only its appearance.
Yet, giving rise to a malicious mind, it throws itself into the well and dies. Sentient beings are likewise: they are but a combination of the four great elements.
It is called the "body" because it is a composite arising from causes and conditions that gives rise to consciousness. It performs various verbal expressions.

Within this, ordinary people falsely give rise to the notion of a "person," producing attachment and aversion, and committing various evil karmas, thereby falling into the three evil realms; therefore, it is said that these are merely deluded perceptions of the mind.
As for Bhikṣu Mianwang, it is clearly established that in the past he gave a single white woolen cloth to the Saṃgha, and as a result, throughout five hundred lifetimes...
He always wore white cotton cloth. When he emerged from the womb, his present body was born with clothing already upon it. Later, he went forth as a monk under the Buddha;
when the Holy One commanded him, "Come, well-come," his garment transformed into a Dharma robe, that is, a *kāṣāya*.
Throughout his successive births, there was the character for "king" (*rāja*) on his forehead, and for this reason he was named Māṇava (Face-King) and so forth.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "In the past, a king was deceived by a treasure," the specific wording is not found in the Sūtra itself;
the account appears in the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Adornment), and so forth.

"Acting according to the length of one's life" means that one guides the patient through the duration of their remaining time, whether long or short, before death occurs; hence it is said, "one acts. "Striking the gong of impermanence" refers to...
"Establishing" refers to striking [the bell] before the moment of death, intending to cause the patient to arouse mindfulness upon hearing the sound.
It is an error to strike the bell only after death has already occurred.

Regarding "elaborate burial" (*hòuzàng*): "burial" (*zàng*) derives from the meaning of "concealing" (*cáng*). To inter the corpse in the earth for a year is called "burial. "Elaborate" (*hòu*) refers to being grand and profuse.

As in the cases of the Venerable Chenghe and the Tripitaka Master Wanhui of the Tang dynasty, although their funeral processions were elaborate, this was merely because they were state-ordered ceremonial displays.
Wanhui’s provisions were supplied by the Princess; he is not the subject under discussion here. [This practice] does not involve wailing for the deceased.
Therefore, one must know the regulations:
if fire is used for cremation, it must not be placed upon living grass, as this is done out of fear of harming living things.

As for the customs of the Western Regions (India), they do not distinguish between the laity and the clergy; all practice cremation. Only within five days do they observe mourning, and even then, they do not change their clothing.

Furthermore, one does not install a spirit seat (*lingzuo*). These methods regarding the changing of attire and so forth in this region were likely established as ritual protocols by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius.
As for *jatu* (cremation), the *Yao lüyi yinyi shenglun* states that it is the correct foreign pronunciation;

it should be called *a-tu-wei-tuo*, which translates as "burning. Regarding the account of the belly bursting and money coming out: it is recorded that there was once a bhikṣu who was miserly and greedy.
Having accumulated [wealth], he possessed gold coins. Fearing that the monks would divide them after his death, and out of attachment and stinginess, he swallowed them.
After he had died, his corpse was abandoned in a wilderness śītavana (cemetery). A bird pecked at its belly until it burst open, and the coins came out.
There was a bhikṣu who entered parinirvāṇa in a forest village; the devas scattered flowers from the sky as an offering to his corpse.
At that time, there were also many bhikṣus who likewise scattered various kinds of flowers upon her corpse (and so forth).
As for the passage stating that the Tathāgata himself carried his mother’s bier and so on, this matter has already been cited previously from the *Ekottarika Āgama*;
as it has already been clearly explained, there is no need to cite it here.
Section Twenty-Seven: On Various Essential Practices.

Although the preceding sections have categorized matters according to specific events, established protocols based on robes and medicine, or opened up methods regarding the Sangha as a whole or individual monks, it was feared that the *paryāya* (details) were not yet exhaustive.
Therefore, a separate section has been established here to comprehensively clarify various miscellaneous affairs and duties.
However, as conditions for supporting the Path, these causes are immeasurable and cannot be individually specified; they are collectively termed "miscellaneous" (*miśra*).
Just as there is the *Miśraka-khaṇḍa* within the Vinaya and the *Saṃyukta-āgama* within the Sūtras, this present text is established according to that same principle.

Regarding the phrase "the myriad phenomena standing in dense array," Li Ming explains that when one receives the precepts and gives rise to the unmanifest (avijñapti) precept-substance, this occurs across all sentient and non-sentient conditions throughout the Dharma-realm;
the vast array of all phenomena is the field upon which the precepts are generated.
Now, one must maintain and protect them individually within each and every phenomenon. If one omits or fails to rely upon them, one will encounter profound calamity. Suddenly—*yan*.
"‘Is’ (shi) means ‘suddenly. ‘Obscure’ (you) means ‘profound. This refers to being suddenly met with that profound censure.

As for the phrase ‘if one follows the path of mutual inclusion,’ etc., [Master] Li establishes that from the initial statement of the thesis down to the examination of the illness, there are twenty-six chapters;

these merely clarify the origins, the paths traversed, and the methods of application of the Great Master. The distinct categories are collectively gathered and included in the following three [sections]."

Regarding "sections" (*bu*): I personally interpret this as referring to the matters concerning the three lower assemblies and their various similarities and differences, as clarified in the following three chapters.

Regarding "establishment" (*li*): speaking in general terms, it refers to the three subsequent chapters—namely, the *Śrāmaṇera-varga*, the *Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha-prakīrṇaka-varga*, and the *Prakīrṇaka-varga for Various Sections*.
These three chapters constitute distinct categories. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the "three sections" are: first, [the section on the three lower assemblies].
The first is a śrāmaṇera; the second is a śrāmaṇerī; the third is a śikṣamāṇā. Regarding the term *suǒ* (瑣): small fragments of jade are called *suǒ*.
When jade is broken into fragments, it is no longer fit to be made into vessels; thus it is named *suǒ*. Today, when we speak of a "trifling person" (*suǒ rén*), we likewise mean a petty person.

Regarding the "three times during the day and three times during the night" for a bodhisattva: this cites the noble ones to exhort ordinary people. The three times of day refer to morning, midday, and late afternoon;

the three times of night refer to the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night. As for the "summer *la* (vassa) meal," this refers to the offering on the sixteenth day of the seventh month.
This is because at the conclusion of the summer retreat, the Buddha and the bhikṣus together receive the *saṃgha-kṣamaṇā* (confession of faults), thereby attaining their summer *la*.
On that day, if there is someone who makes an offering of food to the Buddha, it is called "the Buddha’s meal on his birthday" (*buddhāṣṭamī-bhakta*).

Even if a bhikṣu has previously taken hold of it without the intention to consume it himself, once he has received it, he may take it to offer to the *saṃgha*. Furthermore, even if he takes this food and places it in exchange for something else so that the *saṃgha* may obtain food, there is no fault of improper contact (*duṣṭasparśa*).
Regarding the instruction that the same applies to instructing a śrāmaṇera or employing another person, this means: ordering them to manage the quarters.
"Abandoning" means to treat them as equals in one's thoughts.
Within the category of evil and rebellious sentient beings, those who treat them with the highest grade of discipline are said to be subject to the discipline of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the case where one person gains merit by destroying a Buddhist stūpa because it is poorly made, while another incurs sin due to an evil intention:
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 63, it says: "Suppose a Buddha image is painted;
one person destroys it because the image is not well-made, while another breaks it out of an evil intention. Because their intentions differ, one person gains merit and the other incurs sin."
Regarding the offense: it is like Devadatta shedding the Buddha’s blood and Jīvaka also shedding the Buddha’s blood.

Although they are identical in being called "shedding blood," because their intentions differ, one person incurs the sin of entering Avīci for one kalpa, while the other person gains merit and is reborn in heaven for one kalpa.

Regarding the case where one plants fruit and performs a single "cut" (*jiǎn*), [the commentator] establishes that it is permissible because it is based on the fact that the most [fruit] will grow once the cutting is finished;

however, if no growth occurs after the cutting is finished, then it is not permissible. I privately remark that this likely refers to calling a single handful "one cut. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ji lü), fascicle 33, states:
"There was a bhikṣu who planted mango trees in the land belonging to the Saṃgha. Once they had grown into mature trees, he took [the fruit] for himself and did not allow [others to do so]."
He took them. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "This planting has been productive; I allow you to give [the fruit] for one year.

If the trees are large and you do not wish to take everything at once after one year, those who take them are permitted to take one branch each year. When all the branches have been taken, they shall stop."
If one plants a grove of trees, it should be given [to the owner] year by year; even if one takes a single tree each year, this is permitted.

If one plants turnips, or other such vegetables, one should give [the produce] once it has been harvested; for melons and gourds, one should give [the produce] once a season has passed. (The Commentary states: This refers to those that regrow after being cut.
One may take a single portion. As for that which does not grow back, if one were to open [the field] for a single portion, how could the community of monks ever have a day to receive it?

Regarding the rule that "one must not sell communal property of the four-part Saṃgha and appropriate it for oneself," the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression) is incurred because it temporarily obstructs the use of the property by the Saṃgha.
If, however, one permanently divides or sells it, a heavier offense is incurred.

The commentary states: "The Sangha encompasses both the ordinary and the sagely, and its conduct ranges from coarse to subtle. This is a statement made by way of comparison. Subtle conduct belongs to the sages; coarse conduct belongs to the ordinary.
The Sangha wishes to clarify that within the assembly when it gathers, there may be sages who must not be treated with contempt.

Even among ordinary monks, conduct likewise has degrees of coarseness and subtlety. These five dharmas for entering the assembly are explained in the *Vinaya-vibhanga* (the supplementary sections of the Vinaya).
Regarding "first, with a mind of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-citta*): Jì (礪) says this means one must take pity on sentient beings and bestow happiness upon them;

thus it is so called. This interpretation differs from that in the *Jiě* (解). Xuān (宣) says it means one should revere the Dharma and honor others, as can be understood. Regarding "like a dust-wiping cloth":

Jì says that although the substance of a dust-wiping cloth gathers filth back onto itself, it makes the object clean; likewise, those who enter the assembly also secretly take upon themselves the transgressions [of others].

This refers to oneself. It is said thus because one attributes rectitude to others; the opening commentary likewise explains it in this way. Regarding the statement, "If one sees a senior (*upādhyāya* or *sthavira*), one should not remain seated," Li says:
this means to abandon arrogance. Regarding the statement, "If one sees a junior (*navaka*), one should not rise," [the meaning is as follows].
This is to be free from flattery and crookedness. Regarding Upāli ascending the high seat and so forth:
according to the *Samantapāsādikā*, at the time of the compilation of the Tripiṭaka, Kāśyapa made a formal motion (*jñapti*) and questioned Upāli.

After Upāli had likewise made a single formal motion to harmonize with the Saṃgha, he prostrated his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, ascended the high seat, took up a fan adorned with ivory, and one by one questioned [the members] regarding the Vinaya; Upāli likewise [answered] one by one.
Answer: After the compilation was finished, he set aside his fan and descended from the high seat. He prostrated toward the assembly of monks;
having completed the prostrations, he returned to his original seat. Next, the Elder Ānanda ascended to compile the *Sūtrapiṭaka*.

Having likewise performed the prostrations as before, he took an ivory-inlaid fan in his hand and engaged in a question-and-answer session with Kāśyapa regarding each of the various sūtras (and so forth). [The author] privately remarks: "I now cite this passage."
This clarifies that even a bhikṣu today must likewise observe such propriety. As for the one who holds the fly-whisk (*cāmara*), he was once a "Bull-King" (*go-rāja*) bhikṣu in a past kalpa.
Having walked along the edge of another's field and damaged a single stalk of rice, he was reborn as an ox for five hundred lifetimes to repay his debt to the other.
Although he has passed away in this life, his feet remain those of an ox; after every meal, he constantly ruminates like an ox.

This is because he has come from among oxen for five hundred lifetimes, and such is the result of residual habit. That man was skilled at preaching the Dharma, yet he feared that if people saw him chewing food in his mouth, they would not conceive wholesome roots of merit.

Therefore, the Buddha permitted him to use a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) to cover his mouth when preaching the Dharma. In the *Kauṇḍinya-sūtra*, it is said: ... [text continues] ... Kauṇḍinya... [text continues] ... *sūtra*.
Pāṭi was that very person.
Regarding the statement that the *gandī* bell should not produce a double resonance (*dvirghoṣa*): some say that a double resonance causes the assembly to become discordant.
As for the fourfold sequence of the *śāstra*, according to the third fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, Kātyāyanīputra said: "Now, as for shaving the hair..."
The Dharma-elder should shave first. Furthermore, there is another teaching that those with the longest hair should shave first.

There is yet another principle that those who have washed their heads first should shave first. Again, there is another principle: those who have business or causes requiring travel should shave first.
This is called shaving the hair in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the renunciant who abandons the five types of stinginess, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the five stinginesses are:

stinginess regarding dwelling places, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gifts, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dharma. As for "stinginess regarding dwelling places," it refers to thinking, "I alone shall dwell here; others shall not."
Second is stinginess regarding one's home (*gehamacchariya*): thinking, "I alone shall enter and exit this place;
no other person shall do so," or "If there are others, I must be superior among them. Third is stinginess regarding gifts (*āvakārāmacchariya*): thinking, "I alone shall receive offerings here;
let not others have any," or "If there are others, let none surpass me. Fourth is stinginess regarding praise (*vaṇṇāmacchariya*): thinking, "Praise me alone; do not praise others."

Even when praising others, do not allow them to surpass you. Regarding the five types of stinginess: [the first is] being stingy with one's knowledge, thinking, "I alone know the meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
furthermore, I know their profound meanings and keep them secret, refusing to speak of them. Question: What are the faults of these five types of stinginess? Answer:

These are the primary dwelling places and so forth, which are shared by many people. Since this person has already abandoned his own home, he now gives rise to further stinginess and attachment regarding what is held in common. This is...

Due to these base afflictions, one dies and falls among the hungry ghosts (preta), taking birth in various evil realms. If one is stingy regarding the Dharma, one will receive the retribution of blindness in future lives and remain perpetually deluded;
virtuous people will shun such a person, and they will further cause the extinction of the Buddha’s Dharma and Path.

If one is stingy regarding their home, they will obstruct laypeople from performing meritorious acts and prevent recipients from receiving offerings; because of this, in a future life, they will be born as a fly in a latrine within that very house.

Regarding ghosts: if one gives to a stingy person, they will always lack the necessities of life. If one praises a stingy person, when hearing praise for others, their mind will always be disturbed and turbid;
for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they will never have a pure mind and will constantly suffer ill repute.

Regarding those who may not practice divination or recite incantations: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a nun practices divination herself or facilitates divination for others, she commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the incident of the Arhat’s failed archery: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, at one time Maudgalyāyana entered a village to beg for food.
There was a householder’s wife who was pregnant, and she asked Maudgalyāyana whether it would be a boy or a girl. Maudgalyāyana replied, "A boy. Furthermore, there was a brahmin...
They came and entered his house. The householder questioned him as before, and he replied, "It is a girl. Later, a girl was indeed born.

The bhikṣus said that Maudgalyāyana had falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) and should be expelled. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Maudgalyāyana saw the beginning but did not see the end.
At the time, the child was actually a boy who later changed into a girl; Maudgalyāyana spoke according to what he perceived at that moment."
It is said that there is no offense. Furthermore, at one time, there was a great drought.

Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and saw that seven days hence the heavens would send heavy rain, filling the pits and overflowing the cities and towns. Hearing this, the people were filled with joy;

they abandoned their various affairs, covered and stored away their goods, and each counted the days on their fingers using tally-sticks. When the seventh day arrived, there was still not even a scent of rain. Why?

How much more so during the great rains! The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana, "You have committed a transgression against the superhuman state (uttaramanuṣyadharma) and have thus spoken a deliberate falsehood;
you should be expelled and sent away. Even unto this point, the Buddha said: "Maudgalyāyana saw what was before him but not what was behind him.

During those seven days, there truly were great rains, which the Asura King caught with his hand and cast into the great ocean. Maudgalyāyana acted according to his perception of the situation and did not commit an offense."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who asked Maudgalyāyana, "From where does the water of the Mahābodhi River come?
He replied, "It comes from Lake Anavatapta. The bhikṣu asked, "The water of Lake Anavatapta is sweet and possesses the eight meritorious qualities;
yet this water is boiling hot, salty, and bitter. How can such a thing be? You have spoken falsely! The Buddha said:
Maudgalyāyana did not speak falsely. Because Lake Anavatapta is extremely distant from here, this water originally possessed the eight meritorious qualities.
As it flowed through fifty minor hells, it became salty and hot; thus, he spoke according to what he had experienced.
When Empress Wu was contemplating the divine dragon, the Heavenly Emperor asked the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang whether [the dragon] was male or female. He also asked the Daoist whether it was male.

"Is it a girl? He first answered based on divination, saying, "The hexagram indicates a girl. However, she was actually a girl who could not study as a *sanzang* (Tripitaka master) or a Daoist priest.
When he replied that she was a girl, she instead answered back that she was a boy. Although the *sanzang* gave this answer, he knew it was incorrect.
Nevertheless, thinking that the power of the Triple Gem is great and that merit could still be cultivated for her, he went outside and gathered the monks and nuns of the capital city.
He ordered them to perform recitations so that the Empress would give birth to a son. Xuanzang remarked, "If these words do not come true, it will surely mean that the Buddha-dharma lacks power.
After the monks and nuns of the capital performed the recitations, the fetus was indeed turned into a male.

Consequently, although Prince Ying’s speech still sounded like a girl's voice, after he ascended the throne, the Tripiṭaka Master Jnanaprabha was subsequently commanded by imperial decree to establish the Three-Year [Retreat] at Ci'en Monastery.
His posthumous title was Dàbiànjué Fǎshī (Great Universal Enlightenment Dharma Master).
Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* passage stating that one should even draw marks on the ground while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:
"As for the method of walking in meditation, a bhikṣu should walk straight, neither too slowly nor too quickly. If he cannot walk straight, he should draw lines on the ground."
Walking straight along with the [proper] characteristics is called the method of *caṅkrama* (walking meditation).

Regarding the statement that there are also "halls for walking meditation," this clarifies that in the Western Regions (India), there are halls where one habitually practices *caṅkrama*. As for the statement that the Buddha has neither light nor darkness, and that there are no limits set by verbal or mental recitation, this means that the Buddha is without light or darkness;
even during the period of the *apakarṣa-kalpa* (the aeon of decrease), the Buddha is not dark. It is simply... [contrary to... (text fragmentary).

Regarding the "donor's mind": this clarifies that when a layperson offers a lamp, since no limit is specified for when it should be bright or dark—whether by day or night—it must remain constantly lit;
if the lamp is extinguished, one incurs an offense. According to the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), it asks:
"If someone continues the Buddha’s light, may it be extinguished during the day? The answer is: "It may not. If it is extinguished, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling). Although...
It is said that the Buddha stated, "The donor gains merit; therefore, one merely extinguishes what is sinful. (Commentary:

Based on this point regarding the incurrence of sin, the interpretations of the various masters hold that this refers to a long-lasting lamp, and thus they do not permit its extinction. This is based on the subsequent passage concerning Maudgalyāyana’s knowledge of the day's turn for service and so forth.
Regarding those who appear to extinguish the Buddha’s lamp, it is precisely because they continue the bright lamp that they are able to "extinguish" it.
As for Maudgalyāyana’s subsequent direct extinguishing of the lamp, according to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*:
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a woman in the country named Nanda. She was poor, destitute, and alone, sustaining herself by begging. She saw the various people...
He intended to make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, but reflecting on his own poverty and low status, he thought, "Though I have encountered a field of merit, I have no seed-grain.

Filled with grief and self-reproach, he went out to beg for alms in the hope of providing a meager offering; he did not rest until the end of the day, yet obtained only a single coin. Carrying it, he went to an oil merchant's house.
He bought oil to make a lamp, carried it to the vihāra, and offered it to the World-Honored One, placing it before the Buddha.
He then made this vow: "I am now poor; using this small lamp, I make an offering to the Buddha.
By this merit, may I obtain the lamp of wisdom in future lives and eliminate the defiled darkness of all sentient beings. Having made this vow, he prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
This continued until the end of the night, when all the other lamps had gone out and only this one remained burning. At that time, Maudgalyāyana was on duty for the day.

Observing that it was already dawn, he gathered up the lamps; seeing that this single lamp alone remained burning with a fine, bright light, its wick high and its oil undiminished as if it were a lamp newly lit, a thought arose in his mind.
He said, "There is no benefit in keeping this lamp burning; it should be extinguished now."
He did so, but immediately Maudgalyāyana raised his hand and fanned out the flames as before; he then fanned it with his robe, yet still they were not extinguished.
Seeing that Maudgalyāyana wished to extinguish this lamp, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "This lamp cannot be moved or extinguished by you, a śrāvaka.
Even if you were to go and pour upon it the waters of the four great oceans, or if the Vairambha winds were to blow over it," [it would remain unextinguished].
Even this could not extinguish it. Why was this so? Because these were the gifts bestowed by one who had set forth the great resolve for universal salvation.
After the Buddha had spoken these words, the woman Nanda came again to the Buddha’s presence and prostrated herself with her head at his feet.
The Buddha then conferred upon her the prediction: "In a future age, after two asaṃkhyeya kalpas and a hundred kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be..."
The Lamp. [Endowed with the Ten Epithets] (etc.). According to the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Ajātaśatru-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, King Ajātaśatru asked Jīvaka:
