Since these five hindrances already include greed, and even with greed one cannot attain birth in the heavens, how much less could a Bodhisattva be permitted to give rise to greed? Bin said.

The five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*) are: first, greed (one should say "greed for sensual desire" [*kāmacchanda*]; this is because "greed" applies to all three realms, and thus "sensual desire" is used to distinguish it); second, ill-will (*vyāpāda*); third, sloth and torpor (one should say "sloth-torpor" [*styāna-middha*]);

fourth, restlessness and regret (one should name them "restlessness and remorse" [*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*]. "Restlessness" is agitation; "regret" is remorse); and fifth, doubt (*vicikitsā*). Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 48, states:
"Craving and seeking after various sensual desires is the characteristic of greed for sensual desire; harboring hatred toward sentient beings is ill-will; the sinking of body and mind..."

Lack of clarity is the characteristic of *styāna* (sloth). Agitation of body and mind is the characteristic of *auddhatya* (restlessness). Causing the mind to become dull and withdrawn is the characteristic of *middha* (torpor).
Causing the mind to experience regret is the characteristic of *kaukṛtya* (remorse). Causing the mind’s mode of activity to be hesitant and indecisive is the characteristic of *vicikitsā* (doubt).

(Commentary: Among these, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are restricted to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—though if one speaks of "desire" in general, it extends through all three realms. Sloth (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) each extend through all three realms.
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) resides in the desire realm, while doubt (*vicikitsā*) extends through all three realms. These five are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they cover and obstruct;

as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states, they are obstacles to the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the first four hindrances are able to obstruct the [first] four of the five aggregates.

It obstructs three aggregates. As stated previously in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is further because of doubt that it can obstruct the two aggregates of liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), preventing them from arising (the private note states that these five aggregates are the fivefold body of the Dharma).
"Regarding the statement that 'the Bodhisattva attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), wherein all objects (*dharma*) do not appear,' the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:
'As for the attainment of non-conceptual wisdom, its characteristic is that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) attains non-conceptual wisdom. Regarding this, Jì says:
Wisdom is discernment; it is not non-discernment. Because its object is non-discernment, it is called "non-discernment.
Since the first stage realizes the principle of *tathatā*, and since *tathatā* is the object realized by wisdom, the essence of *tathatā* is itself non-discernment.
Because wisdom is able to realize this principle, it is termed "non-discernment" from the perspective of its object.
However, wisdom (*jñāna*) is non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*). Regarding the statement that "all objects (*viṣaya*) do not manifest," Ji says: "Objects" refers to the external environment.

This means that when a Bodhisattva attains non-conceptual wisdom, they no longer falsely cling to external objects; rather, [they realize] there is only the transformation and function of consciousness alone.
Since one is thus free from the false attachment to external objects, it is said that "all objects do not appear. [This state] is naturally devoid [of such appearances].

Regarding "defilements and turbid faults": this refers to a bodhisattva who, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, manifests the practice of the ten non-virtuous actions—such as killing, sexual misconduct, and stealing—yet has no defilement in his inner mind;
therefore, it is said that he is "without defilement or turbidity. Regarding "even if there is benefit, one does not act if there is a fault":
this means that although there may be external benefit, if there is internal defilement, one does not act. This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, internally...

1. One who is free from internal defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and for whom external benefit (*anugraha*) should be pursued; this one should act. 2. One who has internal defilement and for whom there is no external benefit; this one should not act. 3. One who has both [internal defilement and lack of external benefit];
this one should not act. 4. One who has neither [internal defilement nor external benefit]; this one also should not act.

According to the *Yiqieyixing Ruyi Sanmei Jing* (Sarvārthasiddhi-samādhi-sūtra), there are three types of persons who equally engage in unconventional conduct (*viloma-caryā*) to transform others: namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats. This is because these individuals of the Three Vehicles are undefiled by the mundane world (*loka*).
All other Bodhisattvas prior to the [Bhūmi] stages, up to and including those in the three fruits [of the Śrāvaka], are unable to practice it.
Regarding the "Immovable Stage" (Acalā-bhūmi), Ji said: Because the eighth stage attains effortlessness (*anābhoga*), it is called the Immovable Stage.

From the seventh stage and below, there must be intentional application and progressive cultivation, which is termed "with effort" (*sābhoga*); from the eighth stage onward, one advances spontaneously and effortlessly.
It does not rely on effortful practice, nor is there any further application of effort; therefore, it is called the "Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*). It is like a sail:

when first unfurled and set, the adjustments and preparations required are termed "effortful activity" (*prayoga*). Once the sail is fully hoisted, one simply lets the wind carry it forward, no longer requiring human labor;
thus, it is called "effortless" (*anābhoga*). The meaning of the stages from the eighth ground upward is the same as this. Alternatively, it may be understood as the purification of the mind.
Regarding the "stages" (*bhūmi*): the *Ciyun* [commentary] states that the first stage of a bodhisattva is called the "Stage of the Pure Mind.

As for the discussion of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this refers to the fact that the preceding section has completed the exposition on Mahayana precepts; from here below, the two trainings of Mahayana concentration and wisdom are clarified.

As for the statement regarding the "small-scale contemplation of the emptiness of characteristics," this refers to the small-bodhisattvas who contemplate the arising and ceasing of phenomena and realize the absence of self (*anātman*).
Regarding the characteristics of human good and evil, etc., one attains the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—which means realizing that form (*rūpa*) is empty.
This is as the sutras state: "Form is itself emptiness," and so forth. Śrāvakas extinguish form to realize emptiness; therefore, they differ from this [Mahayana approach].

Those who deeply contemplate *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) are the great Bodhisattvas. They practice the contemplation of consciousness-only, observing that all things are merely the conceptual discrimination of mind, thought, and speech. However...
Practice the contemplation of the single consciousness-mind. Thoroughly understand that all sensory objects and forms are fundamentally non-existent and no longer take them as objects of perception.
Know only that these are the conceptual constructions and fabrications of my own single consciousness-mind. When dull insight perceives emptiness, it does not differentiate forms.

This concludes the preceding minor contemplation. This is the bodhisattva for whom appearances are empty (*lakṣaṇa-śūnya*). Although this bodhisattva contemplates that the arising and ceasing of form is empty, their wisdom and practice remain dull;
they merely perceive that external appearances are themselves empty, yet they do not yet know the illumination of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Therefore, it is said that they do not conceptually differentiate form and so forth. Such a person realizes that form is empty and no longer relies on conceptual differentiation.

Regarding their form, if they were śrāvakas, they would discriminate that form; however, those with sharp wisdom who do not discriminate emptiness because they know it is mere consciousness—this concludes the section on the profound contemplation of mere consciousness by the great bodhisattvas. That is to say, these bodhisattvas practice the contemplation of mere consciousness.

This means that from the first bhūmi upward, the practice of wisdom becomes sharp and clear; one performs only the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), knowing that all appearances are merely mental verbal discriminations.
Because one realizes that these external objects fundamentally do not exist, one no longer discriminates this "form.
Since one no longer takes these external objects as cognitive domains (*ālambana*), it is said that one does not discriminate emptiness.
Regarding "merely similar paths" and "merely similar goodness," these are established as "clarity. However, the two natures of the false and the correct are difficult to clarify.

Scholars of the present day mostly fall into false views; hearing it said that there is attachment and permanence, or hearing it said that there is non-attachment and annihilation, they find it difficult to leave behind the mind of the two extremes.

Because they merely contemplate the words and believe they have understood, this is called "similar goodness. In principle, one must cultivate and study [the true path] before being capable of correct contemplation.

One does not take the mere recitation of words as the path of practice. Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it extensively elucidates the practices of bodhisattvas from the first through the fourteenth fascicle;
however, it specifically clarifies the methods for bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to cultivate their bodies and minds.
To speak in broad terms, it means that one should always delight in hearing the Dharma that is heard. Upon hearing—

Having already been able to practice as taught, relying on the Dharma, relying on the meaning, and relying on practice according to the teaching, they follow the intended purpose without being confused by mere words;

they do not lose their precepts or meditative concentration, maintain a pure livelihood, shatter the mind of arrogance, seek out merit, distance themselves from evil associates, and draw near to virtuous friends.
If a lay bodhisattva should thus distance themselves from flattery and crookedness, they will be like a tree standing in a dense forest.

It is difficult to escape. In this way, although a disciple of the Buddha has entered the Buddha-dharma, they are unable to emerge from the deep forest of afflictions within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Furthermore, by means of three matters, one can verify the three paths; thus, it is established that what follows will demonstrate the matters of acting for oneself and for others, thereby providing verification.
As for these practitioners, they represent the respective limits of the Three Vehicles. Regarding the phrase "the mind differs while the object is the same," Master Xiang says:

This means that as for the external objects that serve as the focal point (ālambana) for these three types of persons, there is nothing different among them. They both contemplate all four great elements (mahābhūta), the five aggregates (skandha), the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
therefore, it is said that the object is the same. That is, the objective realm is identical, yet the minds are distinct. This refers to those of the Two Vehicles.

To form an understanding of emptiness is the ultimate [for some]. Lesser bodhisattvas know that all things are falsely existent; yet they do not form an understanding of emptiness, nor have they realized *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
As for great bodhisattvas, they simply cultivate the contemplation of *vijñaptimātra*. Therefore, it is said that "the mind being discordant" refers to knowing them as distinct.
Regarding the bhikṣu who commits a *vyatikrama* (transgression): it is established and clear that if he expels [a fellow monk], he incurs the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*. Old.
Regarding the mother’s request for her son to leave the household life under the Buddha and so forth, it is as recorded in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* (excerpted, etc.).

Regarding the case where one wishing to burn down a monastery is permitted even if they have not informed their parents, according to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the Buddha established the rule that if one's parents do not permit it, one may not be granted ordination.
If there is someone who seeks to leave the household life, the bhikṣu asks: "As for you..."
"Mother, will you permit it? She replied, "I do not permit it. The bhikṣu was unwilling to ordain him. The man then said, "If you do not ordain me, I shall set fire to the monastery.
If there is such a difficult situation and one ordains and lets them go forth, there is no offense.

Regarding those who ordain by theft and commit a grave offense (pārājika), it is said that if one causes another person to intentionally evade royal taxes, it is a grave offense; if there is no such [intention], it is not.

[The text says: "The mind. One may obtain [the text] by merely crossing over [the boundary], provided one does not encourage others to avoid the recitation. As for those who obtain it according to the treatise (*śāstra*), I privately say that this refers mostly to the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*.

Regarding why the Master of the Sūtra (*sūtra-svāmī*) does not obtain it, the Master [of the Treatise] states: if the Master of the Sūtra has already paid money to purchase it, he does not obtain it because he has expended the money of others;
however, if one has merely transcribed it and has never been the Master of the Sūtra, then since no money was used, one obtains the crossing over. There is no [such] sūtra.
Regarding the "canonical text" (zhengwen): the proponent asserts that this is a passage from the treatise (*śāstra*), claiming there is no such canonical text within the *sūtras*.

Examining the *Pravrajyāguṇa-sūtra*, it merely states that by releasing slaves and servants, one attains vast merit upon leaving the household life; however, it does not explicitly permit the ordination (*pravrajyā*) of bhikṣus.
Therefore, it is said that there is no canonical text. Furthermore, there is no such text in the Vinaya either.
Regarding the statement in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that those who wish to newly enter the monastic order are first told of the hardships:

the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Jie-mo-su) states, "The reason for speaking of the hardships is that the world is ensnared by suffering and bitterness; many grow weary of it and seek happiness. Although they may initially be granted permission out of compassion, in the end they may fall away.

Therefore, in the sūtras and śāstras, those who experience suffering in the present life but attain happiness in the future are the renunciants. Day and night they whip their hearts, constantly gathering [their resolve]."

Maintain right mindfulness. If you do not perceive delusive conditions, immediately repent and reproach yourself. The *Sānqiān* (Three Thousand) states: "One must certainly practice the three [methods], such as sitting meditation;

otherwise, one's life will be spent in vain and one will die in vain. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching) says: "In the middle of the night, recite the sutras to examine yourself.
At other times, you must rely on the Vinaya texts to always maintain single-minded mindfulness and eliminate the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)."
Regarding "eating once": within the Buddha’s teachings, eating once is the fundamental principle. While two modes may be established based on specific conditions, these are not the standard practice.

Regarding "dwelling alone": one remains seated in the full lotus posture for an entire period before rising; were it not for a profound distaste for worldly flavors, how could such a state be achieved? Regarding "sleeping once":
during the middle watch of the night, one briefly reclines, then rises again at the change of the stars and moon to cultivate mindfulness. One who studies much [should practice thus].
This means that the mind of wisdom should be constantly active; it does not permit floating or scattering. Regarding the name "Crows-Driving Śrāmaṇera":

according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who took his son with him when he went forth from home. When they entered a village to beg for food, if they reached a marketplace and saw cakes or rice, he would immediately stretch out his hand and say, "Give me cakes and rice!
People all mocked and disparaged him, saying, "How can one who has gone forth still father a child? And so on.
He intended to take him along and informed the Buddha of this. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, you must not ordain anyone who is less than twelve years of age.
At that time, there was a donor's family whose home had been burned by non-human beings; everyone had died except for a single small child.
As they were approaching the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha asked, "What child is this? Ānanda explained the situation in detail.

The Buddha said, "Why did you not ordain him and let him leave the household life? He replied, "World-Honored One, there was a prior instruction that those under twelve years of age are not to be ordained; therefore, I did not ordain him."
He further questioned the boy: "Are you able to drive away the crows when it is time to eat? If you can do so, I will permit you to go forth.
Ānanda replied, "I am able to drive away the crows," and he immediately ordained him. Because of this, he was named the Cāṭapūta Śrāmaṇera (the Crow-Driving Śrāmaṇera).

From fourteen to nineteen years of age, they are called "Sāmaṇeras in accordance with the Dharma. This refers to those whose age is not yet sufficient to receive the full ordination (upasampadā) and thus properly qualify as [fully ordained] monks; they are designated as Sāmaṇeras because their age corresponds to the requirements of the Sāmaṇera dharma. As for "nominal Sāmaṇeras": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The following is a continuation based on standard monastic terminology to complete the logical structure of the classification.)* As for "nominal Sāmaṇeras," this refers to those who have received the precepts through a formal ritual but do not yet possess the requisite age or physical maturity to be considered true Sāmaṇeras according to the Vinaya rules.

They are so called because they bear the name "Sāmaṇera" despite not fulfilling all the conditions for the status. Thus, there are three types of Sāmaṇeras: those in accordance with the Dharma, those by age, and those by name. Among these, only the first two are considered authentic Sāmaṇeras within the monastic community. The third category consists of those who merely assume the title without meeting the formal criteria. Regarding the distinction between the "Sāmaṇera in accordance with the Dharma" and the "nominal Sāmaṇera": while both may undergo the same ritual of receiving the ten precepts, the former is recognized as a legitimate member of the Saṅgha due to his age and capacity, whereas the latter is a designation applied to one who has undergone the ceremony but lacks the necessary qualifications. This classification ensures that the integrity of the monastic order is maintained by distinguishing between those who are fit to uphold the discipline and those who are not. In summary, the term "Sāmaṇera" is applied based on a combination of age, capability, and formal authorization. Those from fourteen to nineteen are "Sāmaṇeras in accordance with the Dharma"; those below fourteen are "nominal Sāmaṇeras" until they reach the age of eligibility. This system reflects the careful balance between the spiritual potential of the youth and the structural requirements of the monastic tradition.

Since he has now reached adulthood, it is logically appropriate that he receive full ordination; he is no longer at the stage of a *śrāmaṇera*, yet he is merely designated by the name "śrāmaṇera," which is why it is called a "name.
Regarding the phrase "the original treasure-store and the original debt-interest are likewise," according to that treatise: Question: When a *bhikṣu* was formerly a layperson...
If one loses one's parents and siblings, and after having hidden one's possessions and gone forth as a monk, all the family members die;

if the bhikṣu returns to take those things for himself, he commits the offense of abandonment (pārājika). If there are laypeople who were close to him, he may speak to them and have them take the items to perform meritorious acts on his behalf; half of the property should be given to the authorities.
In such a case, this object has no owner and should belong to the state; it must not be taken in its entirety.

Regarding "the son of a master craftsman who was ordained," the Vinaya text states that a son of a master craftsman came to the monastery to observe, and the bhikṣus hastily ordained him without the community knowing.
Later, his parents came to the monastery and questioned the monks, but they all said they had not seen him. Afterward, he returned.
[The offense] was incurred within a monastery. [The accused] then said, "The bhikṣu spoke a deliberate lie. Because of this, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From now on, if you wish to ordain a person, you should inform the Saṃgha through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) so that the assembly may all know. If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, you may notify each dwelling (*vihāra*) until harmony is reached."
Regarding the phrase "having finished bidding farewell to his parents, he spoke these verses": Sthiramati says this refers to the one who has gone forth from home speaking these verses himself.

Regarding the phrase "he should explain [the nature of] hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and skin": Sthiramati says this is because he fears that this śrāmaṇera may have previously contemplated these things.
This matter is brought forward here because if one hears this teaching now, one may attain awakening and understanding; thus, the following passage cites the case of Rāhula as a proof.
For example, it is said that Rāhula attained arhatship before his tonsure was even complete. According to the *Samantapāsādikā* (Shanjian lun), when he was being ordained as a śrāmaṇera:
The preceptor should explain five things to him: first, hair; second, body hair; third, nails; fourth, teeth; and fifth, skin.

The reason for explaining these is that there are those who, in a previous life, had already contemplated these five things. Now, as their hair is being shaved and falls to the ground, they immediately activate their prior karma and attain arhatship.
For this reason, he first teaches these five things, and only then proceeds with the shaving of the hair, as was done in the case of Rāhula.
Before his hair had even fallen out, he immediately became an Arhat. It was like a boil that must be lanced by someone before it can be burst open;
or like a lotus flower that must wait for the sun to rise before it can bloom. This person who wished to leave the household life was just like this:
through the discourse on the five aggregates, he immediately attained enlightenment. The commentary states: "Rāhula was at the beginning of his stage as a śrāmaṇera, being nine years of age."
Regarding the renunciation [of the śrāmaṇera]: whenever the Western śrāmaṇeras reach the end of the summer retreat, they frequently offer incense and flowers into the air to scatter over Rāhula.
As for those who praise him by pouring scented water over his head, it is established that this verse was spoken by the barber. Thus it is said.
Regarding the verse that says, "I take refuge in the Great World-Honored One," Sthiramati states that this verse was spoken by the one who has left the household life himself.
As for the line, "One who alters their appearance and maintains their vows and integrity," this verse was spoken by a bystander.
Regarding *cūḍā*, Sthiramati states that it refers to the top-knot which must be left behind for the *upādhyāya* to shave off. "How great is the robe of liberation, the signless field of merit!"
Regarding the term "robes" (*cīvara*): *Lì* (Lì Wén) states that this verse was spoken by the *upādhyāya*.
As for the two people receiving ordination as *śrāmaṇeras*, one being deemed "inappropriate," *Lì* states that one must have both an *upādhyāya* and an *ācārya*; they cannot exist alone.

The *karmavācanā* master still silently cites the name of the *upādhyāya* for the sake of the single person. Regarding "grasping the corner of the teacher’s robe and emerging out of human feeling," it refers to the *upādhyāya*.
It is said: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Maudgalyāyana took a person to observe their past karma by soaring through the air, having that person grasp the corner of his *kāṣāya*.
Nowadays, when the masters of the *Daśabhāṇavāra* confer the precepts upon others, they have them grasp the robe; this is a false practice.

Regarding the instruction that "one should inquire about the obstacles and impediments according to the same rules as for the Saṃgha," this means: one should follow the procedure for bestowing the śrāmaṇera precepts when inquiring about the obstacles and impediments;

however, among the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), it is not necessary to inquire specifically about the crime of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, whereas all other [obstacles] must be inquired about.
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; I now follow the Buddha to leave the household life, with [Name] acting as my preceptor (*upādhyāya*)," and so forth.

This threefold refuge for the five and eight precepts is distinct from the threefold refuge used when overturning heterodox views, which simply states "I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha" without the inclusion of a formal vow.
In the case of the threefold refuge for the five precepts, there is a formal vow of commitment, lasting until... [end of fragment].

I, [Name], have become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) observing the five precepts. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. Had I been establishing the eight precepts, I would have said:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha," thereby becoming a lay follower of pure conduct (*śīlavat upāsaka*). Now, as I establish the ten precepts, I declare:
"I now follow the Buddha into the homeless life. So-and-so is my preceptor (*upādhyāya*); the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is [my witness]."
"This is my World-Honored One. Thus, one should know that they are distinct and not the same. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Under the words of the Three Refuges, if there is something added, one obtains the precepts; if there is nothing added under the words of the Three Refuges, one has the refuges but no precepts. Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
There are five kinds of taking refuge in the Triple Gem: first, the threefold refuge for those who have turned away from heterodoxy; second, the threefold refuge for the five precepts;

third, the threefold refuge for the eight precepts; fourth, the threefold refuge for the ten precepts; and fifth, the threefold refuge for the full set of precepts. This first [type] was already abolished during the Buddha’s lifetime (and so forth).
The verse on the ten precepts says: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants; perfumes, dancing, high beds, and money.

Regarding the "high, wide, and large bed" (*ucca-mahā-śayana*): according to the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Head), "high" refers to six *chi* or more; "wide" refers to three *zhou* square. One must not possess both [the high and the wide];
even a single high bed is prohibited. The *Ji* (Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya) states that there are two kinds of "high":

first, "high" by virtue of its great size, which excludes those lower than six *chi*, thereby permitting the use of such [beds]; second, "high" by virtue of being exquisite. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "There are [two kinds of] large beds..."
8. Fourth, greatness is spoken of in terms of the substance of the jewels: first, gold; second, silver; third, ivory; and fourth, horn.

Because these are cherished as treasures by human sentiment, they are considered great regardless of their physical size. Furthermore, greatness is spoken of in terms of the persons from whom the four types [of beds] are derived: first, the bed of a Buddha; second, the bed of an Arhat;
third, the bed of a Pratyekabuddha; and fourth, the bed of an Upādhyāya or Ācārya. These four types of persons are great regardless of their seniority or juniority.
One may sit upon these eight kinds of couches.

Regarding the dual presentation in both Hu (foreign) and Han (Chinese) terms: it means that in the Hu language, gold is called "vivid color" (*shēngsè*) and silver is called "resembling color" (*sìsè*), which refers to their respective images.

Thus we know that "cast and image" (*shēngxiàng*) is a foreign (Hu) pronunciation, while "gold and silver" (*jīnyín*) is Chinese. Since both are listed together in the text, they are said to be "demonstrated as two.
The *Jiemo shū* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), citing an ancient master, states: "The items listed in the text as 'cast and image' refer to worldly implements;
those resembling the forms of humans or animals are not permitted to be grasped. This is comparable to the regulations in the Vinaya which prohibit holding musical instruments. Now [this is] not...
The same applies here. However, in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says "jātārūpa" for gold and "rūpya" for silver. "Rūpya" means "resembling"; it is simply another name for silver.
Some do not permit the simultaneous manifestation of both the foreign (Hū) and Chinese terms. If gold and silver are indeed translatable, one need only translate the foreign term into Chinese;
why must both be displayed? There is no such precedent within the sūtras and vinayas. If the Sanskrit pronunciation is not...

Regarding those terms that may be translated: examples include *nirvāṇa*, *buddha*, and *bhagavat*. Because these names encompass multiple meanings, they are translated according to their original source;

it is not possible to translate them based on specific individual nuances, and thus they are retained in their Sanskrit form. As for terms such as "water" and "fire," which can be translated, one simply relies on these Chinese words.
Where, then, is there an example of displaying both the Sanskrit and the Chinese together? Now, upon careful examination, there are indeed instances of such dual display, as follows:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In settled meditation, with palms joined. "Palms joined" (*hezhǎng*) is the Chinese term; "settled meditation" (*ānchán*) is the Sanskrit term (*dhyāna*).

This is called "raw image" (*shēngxiàng*), meaning that the raw material has not yet been formed into gold or silver, following the analogy of "unrefined metal. Master Ji said: "As for 'raw' (*shēng*), it means gold is produced from the earth; hence the name.
This is like the character for "gold" (*jīn*), where both the left and right phonetic components are the character for "earth" (*tǔ*). Lín Bīn said: [End of citation].
That which is "naturally produced" (*jāti*) should be called "produced color" (*jātarūpa*). There are two kinds of characters: first, naturally produced color; second, that which is dyeable.
For instance, gold cannot change its color; such is its natural state. Silver and similar substances can have their colors changed, and are thus termed "dyeable.
Since "image" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of "color," it is called "naturally produced image" (*jātirūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "having neither partiality nor aversion," some say that once one has abandoned kinship to leave the household life, the mind and conduct become impartial;
there is no longer any specific "near" relative, yet no "distant" stranger. Confucian scholars of the secular tradition say that "partiality and aversion" refer to degrees of intimacy and distance.
Examining the second chapter of the *Lunyu*, it says: "The gentleman, in relation to the world, has neither 'this' nor 'that. This is how the Confucian students interpret it.

The text says: "It is said that there is neither 'thick' nor 'thin. This means that a person of noble character possesses a mind of equanimity; when viewing the people of the world, they perceive no distinction between the 'thick' and the 'thin.
It further states that one should explain this by means of ten points. The commentary (*shu*) says: "There are three points that must be clarified: first, to censure heterodox followers; second..."
This clarifies the correct principle. Third, the examination of those who dwell as thieves (*caura-vāsin*). If one understands these three intentions, then it can be known.
Regarding the "ten counts," this refers to the ten types of progressive numerical dharma-gates; hence the term is used. The *Jìzhī* (only twenty-three fascicles) states:

"Because there were those dwelling as thieves, they tested whether they were right or wrong by means of the ten counts. What are the ten? First, sentient beings rely upon and look up to [the Buddha]."

"Eating" is for the purpose of refuting those non-Buddhist practitioners who practice self-starvation. The *Karmasūtra* states: "Some subsist by consuming wind or ingesting vital breath, or they preserve life by taking medicinal herbs;
these are heterodox paths. The Buddha-dharma is not so. The body relies on food as its sustenance:

there is the edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) of the desire realm, the contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) of the sense bases and objects, the volition-food (*manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*) predominant among egg-born beings, and the consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*) of the higher realms. There may also be combinations of these, as described elsewhere."
Food is taken to sustain the physical form; the Way is taken to sustain the spirit. Therefore, one relies on the physical form and the conditions of food to practice the cultivation of the Way.

When it comes to discussing the Way itself, its essential principle is that cultivation must take detachment from attachment as its foundation. To fail to recognize the source of the Way and instead regard fasting as the Way—what is this?

Regarding the second point, that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is used to refute the naturalistic non-Buddhists (*prakṛtivāda*), the *Jielu su* (Commentary on the Karma-vibhaṅga) states: "The non-Buddhists reckon that all things are non-existent."

As for its cause: the Buddha-dharma is not like that. Both internal retribution and external retribution have their fundamental causes. That all sentient beings exist is entirely due to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The mind cannot be seen; it can only be discussed through names. Because it is the initial stage of the consciousness-link (*vijñāna-aṅga*), it transforms into "name.

When the defiled consciousness is provisionally maintained, that very defilement becomes "form" (*rūpa*). Therefore, at the stage of the *kalala*, the impurity of the congealed fluid contains the mind within it; thus, it unfolds.
It continues to grow and develop through thirty-eight transformations; after nine months, it is born. Having been entrusted to that fetal womb, how could it be spontaneous? Some say:
"In the past, ignorance conditioned volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); because of these formations, one experienced karma in accordance with those formations, thereby obtaining this present body.
Furthermore, it depends upon the union of father and mother to produce this body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). How could it be spontaneous? Others say:

Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): that which takes the seeds of karmic consciousness as its cause is called "name" (*nāma*); that which takes the physical constituents of the parents' semen and blood as its condition is called "form" (*rūpa*).
Because these aspects rely upon one another, this body exists. How could it arise spontaneously? It is like a calf that, upon birth, seeks milk.
The wind is light and the earth is heavy; the crow is black and the thorn is sharp. These are also due to the mutual resonance of the karmic retributions of sentient beings.
Because their internal retributions differ in being good or evil, they evoke external phenomena that vary in purity and defilement.

Regarding the statement that "the three—pain, itch, and perception—serve to destroy the Brahma Heaven," the translations of former sages were not skillful; they called them "pain, itch, and perception. Today, they are termed the "three feelings" (*trivedanā*). Ji says:

When the ancients were translating the sutras, they had not yet fully understood the distinction between the Middle and the Extremes. They wished to translate *sukha-vedanā*, *duḥkha-vedanā*, and *upekṣā-vedanā*, but the Han people did not understand the meaning of the Tripiṭaka.

[The translator] struck the Han person on the back with his hand to cause pain, intending to manifest *duḥkha-vedanā* (painful sensation), yet the Han person did not grasp it, so it was translated as "pain.
Furthermore, he scratched himself with his hand to show the Han person, wishing to demonstrate *sukha-vedanā* (pleasant sensation).
They do not understand one another; conversely, "yáng" (痒) refers to [the sensation of] itching. As for the term "xiǎng" (想), it refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

They reckon that the anger of sentient beings arises from that Brahmā Heaven; Brahmā Heaven is the first heaven of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Jiemo shu* (Commentary on the Karma-vibhaṅga) states:

"The terms 'tòng-yáng-xiǎng' (pain, itching, and perception) are alternative names for feeling (*vedanā*). They are also called the three feelings: 'tòng' (pain) is the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*), and 'yáng' (itching) is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*)."
Regarding feeling: it is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). This refutes those who hold the Brahmā heaven to be the cause [of all things].
At the beginning of the kalpa, when the Brahmā heaven was first established, because there were no other people, objects, or sentient beings, they reckoned that deity to be their father and mother.
Furthermore, when the three calamities arise, the Brahmā teaches humans how to practice so as to be reborn in the higher realms; thus, the Brahmā is born there last. And so forth...
When the world is formed, [beings] descend from the Brahmā Heaven. From the fourth, third, and second dhyānas, they gradually descend until they are born among humans.
Because sentient beings have already departed [from those higher realms], when they depart [from the Brahmā realm], they see that the Brahmā Heaven still remains.

Even until this day, as they descend again, they see the Brahmā Heaven still present and claim it is eternal, calling him their father and mother (and so forth). This is as explained in the *Saṃgītiparyāya* regarding the sixty-two views.
This is explained in the *Madhyama Āgama*. This arising of anger and hatred still stems from that heaven. The Buddha-dharma is not like this, as will be explained in detail below.
Furthermore, there is another non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who reckons Maheśvara to be the father and mother; he is the pinnacle of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), also called Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Taking service to this heavenly king as the ultimate goal, many [shrines] for the god have been established in the Western Regions today.
In the temple, a celestial image is enshrined; it is that to which the common people turn for refuge, known as Maheśvara (Mahesvara). He is my father and mother.
In Sanskrit he is called Maheśvara, which translates here as "Great Sovereign" (Dazizai).

If pronounced with a masculine voice, one should say Mahāśvara (*mahā* meaning "great," *śvara* meaning "sovereign"). Because it is now pronounced with a feminine voice, it becomes *Mahe-he*. The two syllables differ slightly in their weight.
It is distinct. The two sounds for "male" and "female" share the same phonetic inflection (*vṛtti*).

The reason they are addressed with the feminine sound is that non-Buddhists and others reckon this deity as both father and mother; since the mother is female, and the female possesses the sense of being able to give birth, it is therefore addressed with the feminine sound.
Therefore, he is called Maheśvara. Thus, in the temples of the Western Regions, an image of this deity is enshrined. Its body is made of white silver;
it has three eyes on its face, the pupils of which turn inward while their radiance shines outward. Those who behold it lose their souls. There was once the Bodhisattva Deva.

[They claim that] because [the Buddha] was able to subdue the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), he climbed a ladder and gouged out the pupils of the eyes on the face of a statue [and so forth]. The Buddha-dharma is not like this.

That one gives rise to hatred and attachment is truly due to the fundamental aggregates (skandhas); what concern does it have with Heaven? The mind that conditions form at the very first moment is called consciousness (vijñāna).
That which clearly discerns defilement and purity is called perception (saṃjñā). That which experiences the agreeable and the disagreeable is called sensation (vedanā). Because...
Due to the three perceptions, the three feelings arise; due to the three feelings, the three formations arise. Thus, one is long submerged in the cycle of existence, with no liberation.
Fourth, the refutation of the causeless non-Buddhists by means of the Four Noble Truths:
They reckon that all things do not arise from causes, but—as with grasses and trees—arise and die of themselves. Humans are likewise so. The Buddha-dharma is not thus; there is [causality].
Because there is cause, there is effect. There is cause and effect regarding the supramundane, and there is also cause and effect regarding the mundane.

To take the Four Noble Truths as an illustration: the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is the cause of the mundane; the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is the mundane itself; the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is the cause of the supramundane;

and the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the fruit of the supramundane. Therefore, the opening commentary states: "Although the Truths consist of four positions, they are divided into two kinds: suffering and origination..."

The two truths of suffering and origin are the cause and effect of the mundane world; the two truths of cessation and the path are the cause and effect of the supramundane. The *Karmasūtra-vyākhyā* states:
"Because various sentient beings do not know that suffering is without truth and fail to contemplate it, they ultimately never feel weary of or seek to leave [samsara].

The various noble ones who have emerged [from the world] understand that suffering possesses truth," as explained at length in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. [My private note: Question: Regarding these non-Buddhists who deny cause and effect...

"What is the difference between this and the 'Natural' (svabhāva) non-Buddhist school? He replied, "The previous second view, which posits 'naturalness,' differs from this causeless (ahetu) non-Buddhist school.
The Natural non-Buddhists do not cling to the absence of a cause; rather, they take naturalness itself as the cause, and thus they differ."
This is the tenet of the Zhuangzi and Laozi of this land; they reckon that nature (*ziran*) does not arise from causes and conditions.
Some say that "prior nature" means reckoning all phenomena as not being created by things, but existing spontaneously of themselves.

To speak of "no cause" is simply to negate the meaning of cause and effect; there is a distinct difference in their characteristics. [The five aggregates: the five *skandhas* refute that [notion of] a self (*ātman*).
Regarding the term "zhǎizhǔ" (ruler/master): as for "yīn" (yin), ancient translators did not fully grasp its meaning and thus used the word "yīn. This also renders the meaning illogical.

If one takes it in the sense of "yin-yang," it must be pronounced with a level tone (píngshēng). If one takes it in the sense of "covering and protecting" (fùyìn), [it should be pronounced differently].
Furthermore, [the term] *skandha* originally required the addition of the character for "grass" (*cǎo*). Since that phonetic element has now been removed, its underlying rationale remains unclear.

Therefore, in this new translation, it is termed the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "accumulation" or "hoarding. Because five types of elements are accumulated to constitute a person, they are called "aggregates.

The former references to the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) and so forth are not the same as the current usage; rather, it speaks of the "intermediate existence," the "prior existence," and the "subsequent existence," and so on. *Karma*.

The Commentary states: They reckon that within the body there exists a separate sovereign master, which they call the *ātman* (self), like [the husk of] sesame or rice, which governs the mind and consciousness.
The Buddha-dharma is not so; there are simply the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The combination of name and form (*nāmarūpa*) is called the "body. The first aggregate is form (*rūpa*).

The four lower aggregates are merely names; they are all without self and have delusion as their basis. There is no separate, divine self (*ātman*). As it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Form is not the self;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Where does the self reside? Does it reside within form?"

If one considers that the self exists within consciousness, there are only the five aggregates (*skandha*). To conceive of a self in accordance with these aggregates results in five types of such views.

Thus, by examining them through their combinations and separations in succession, one finds no basis for a self; one then realizes that this was a false attachment and attains the principle of non-self (*anātman*). Consequently, one becomes a semblance-saint (*ārya-pratirūpaka*) who is free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the claim that there is a distinct *ātman* within the body, Ji states: "This is seeking the self apart from the aggregates (*skandha*).
It means that outside the five aggregates, there is a distinct *ātman* which universally takes the five aggregates as its dwelling place; this is the locus upon which the self relies.

Alternatively, there are non-Buddhists who seek the self within the aggregates themselves, asserting that they take form (*rūpa*) to be the self, while sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, vijñāna*) serve as its dwelling place. Or...

One takes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the self, and the remaining four aggregates as its dwelling place. One regards one's wife, children, servants, and so forth as being likewise [the self] in relation to these five aggregates, which thus act as equals for one another (and so forth).
Regarding the "Six Sense Bases Breaking One Consciousness" non-Buddhist (tīrthika) view, the *Jiewen su* states:

They reckon that a single consciousness pervades the six sense organs, just as a monkey peers through six openings; those without discernment claim there are six monkeys, yet in reality it is but one.
Humans are likewise: the gates of the senses are six, but a single consciousness functions through them all. The Buddha-dharma is not thus; consciousness follows the sense organ.

It arises. Internally there are the six consciousnesses; externally there are the six sense objects. Because consciousnesses correspond with their respective objects, there are the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

If it were a single consciousness, the ear should be able to see, and the eye should be able to hear sounds. [The Master] said privately: "Indeed, what these non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive is not much different from the Buddha-dharma.
However, in reality, the root of consciousness is fundamentally one; its essence does not possess six parts. Yet the non-Buddhists calculate that consciousness can penetrate through."

It enters the ears and nose; it is explained in terms of this coming and going, and thus the directions are determined. However, the consciousnesses of the Buddha-dharma can be known to pervade all places.
For instance, although a human body has six sense organs, consciousness pervades the interior of the body, such that the entire body is consciousness.

Yet, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have heavy ignorance and delusion, while the six organs inherently possess seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they are able to see only through the gateway of the eyes.
The same applies to form, hearing, and so forth. If the six [faculties] were all-pervasive, they would each be capable of functioning [simultaneously].

Now, since consciousness is pervasive throughout the body, consciousness exists at the locations of all six sense organs. However, if consciousness alone were to be obscured, it could not see by itself;

it must rely on the location of the eye faculty to facilitate its vision. Even so, if the body remains within an obstruction, one cannot see external objects. If, however, the obstruction is pierced...

Holes are made so that one may see outward; these are the locations of the sense organs of the eye and ear. "Clear and distinct" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Just as it is with the visual consciousness, the same applies by analogy to the other five.
Since consciousness pervades the entire body, it is only through its reliance on the sense organs that the six functions can be exercised.

If the substance of consciousness is fundamentally pervasive, how could there be coming and going? Therefore, the metaphor of the monkey [moving from branch to branch] is incorrect. Jì (Jizang) said: "Nevertheless, the substance of consciousness is sixfold."
Because their locations and functions differ, they are established as six. The non-Buddhists' reckoning that there is only a single consciousness is erroneous.
Some non-Buddhists reckon that the consciousness-element is as vast as space; others reckon it to be as large as the human body, meaning the consciousness pervades the interior of the body.
Others say it is like a finger, or like a sesame seed or a grain of rice, or like an atom (*paramāṇu*); yet [they claim] it can nevertheless pervade the entire body.

It is like a whirling firebrand that appears to be large; yet the consciousness within it is actually small. Because it moves back and forth among the six sense faculties, it is said to pervade the entire body.
This is merely a matter of outsiders holding their own differing views and refuting one another. Now, we rely on the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching.

Consciousness is actually six; it cannot be said to be one. When reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, the six consciousnesses function interchangeably; this belongs to the stage of the Buddha and is not related to ordinary beings.

Regarding the Seven Factors of Enlightenment which destroy those who do not practice [the Way] but follow external paths, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) says: "Because they have attained the five supernatural powers, they can go against or with [the flow]."
In their contemplation, they hold that beyond eighty thousand kalpas, all is dark and obscure; this very obscurity they take to be the abode of the "Dark Principle" (míngdì) and Nirvana.
They believe that by simply following the natural course until the ultimate limit is reached, the fruit will inevitably be attained—so why is there any need for cultivation?

They claim that all sentient beings, after passing through eighty thousand kalpas, will naturally achieve liberation, just as when a ball of thread is released from a mountain peak: once the thread is exhausted, the ball comes to rest. Thus [they are saved].

It is said: That contemplation perceives only events within eighty thousand kalpas; beyond that, it lacks clarity. Thus, they designate this state of profound obscurity as "Nirvana," which constitutes the "Principle of Obscurity" (tattva).
If this state were Nirvana by its own nature, one would naturally arrive at it—what need would there be to cultivate the Path?

The Buddha-dharma is not thus; one must necessarily apply skillful means and practice with increasing diligence to achieve the fruit of liberation, as in the case of the seven... [as in the seven stages].

Only by discerning the correct principle through the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) can one reach [the goal]. How could one enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) without practicing them? Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, the scriptural teachings state:

first, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); second, the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya*); third, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*);

fourth, the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti*); fifth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi*); sixth, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti*); and seventh, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā*). These eliminate evil.
Practicing virtue is called the awakening factor of discrimination; a mind free from indolence is called diligence; body and mind being free from evil is called tranquility;
rejoicing in the happiness attained by others is called joy; not being distracted regarding objects is termed concentration;
recording the mind so it does not scatter is termed mindfulness; and practicing giving without weariness is termed equanimity. Thus are these seven kinds of awakening factors clarified.

Because it serves as the cause, it is called a "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, because it can support that enlightenment, it is called an "enlightenment constituent" (*bodhipakṣa*).
As for the statement that one perceives events of eighty thousand eons through retrogressive and progressive contemplation, this refers to those of the sharpest faculties;
others of duller faculties may perceive sixty thousand eons or forty thousand eons.

The Eightfold Noble Path destroys those who rely on false causes and follow external paths (tīrthikas). They take the observance of precepts regarding chickens, crows, deer, dogs, and so forth as their path;
therefore, it is called a "false cause. This is because they are deluded regarding the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these externalists emaciate their bodies, go naked without shame, use skulls to hold excrement for food, and pierce their hair upward or hang themselves upside down.
Grieving, he humbled himself. In winter he entered the water; in summer he scorched himself with fire. The *Karmasūtra* states: "Those who attain this state see chickens, dogs, oxen, and deer.
Now that their retribution has ended, past karma is about to arise, and they will be reborn in the Form Realm heavens.

Failing to contemplate the distant cause, they claim that the present retribution itself is [the goal], and thus they imitate those animals, taking the eating of grass as their precept, even practicing the eight worldly dhyānas and using them as [a means to] Nirvāṇa."

[The same applies to] wrong effort and wrong wisdom; all such cases are like this. The Buddha-dharma is not so. The four [practices], such as begging for food, serve as conditions for the Noble Path and together sustain the physical body.
The eight [factors], such as right speech, serve as causes for the Noble Path and together sustain the mind and spirit.

By observing their functions and deliberating upon them, one deeply perceives inverted perceptions and is thereby able to attain liberation. I privately remark: even when animals eat grass, they may later be reborn in heaven. This is because—
This eating of excrement and grass is the cause for rebirth in heaven; it does not arise from the evil karma of this animal existence.

Having inherited the merit of past virtuous conduct, they have now attained birth in heaven. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) emulate them, and thus eat excrement and grass. Ji said: "The non-Buddhists realize the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Those of sharp faculties perceive events of eighty thousand kalpas through their contemplation; those of middling faculties perceive events of sixty thousand kalpas; and those of dull faculties [perceive]..."
He sees back forty thousand *kalpas*. Thus, he sees that when a jackal or a dog dies, it is reborn in heaven;
he then claims that eating grass was the cause of this, asserting that this animal possessed virtuous karma eighty thousand *kalpas* prior. Bin says:

This notion regarding the precepts of crows, chickens, oxen, dogs, and so forth, arises from two causes for such false conceptualization. First, by means of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he sees sentient beings [reborn] from among crows...

From among chickens, they were immediately reborn in the heavens. Second, this false calculation arose from irrational discursive thought (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 114, states:
"There were two non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*): one named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who observed the cow-vow (*go-vrata*), and another named Ajita Keśakambala, who observed the dog-vow (*śva-vrata*).
At different times, these two men both went to the place where the Buddha was, and in various ways..."
After [the Buddha] had comforted him with kind words, Puḷina first asked on behalf of others:
"Where will this Kṣaṇika, who has observed the dog-vow and completed his cultivation of the path, be reborn? The World-Honored One replied: "Desist; do not ask.

Although he requested it a second and a third time, the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, said: "Listen attentively. If one observes the dog-vow without deficiency or transgression, they shall be reborn..."
"If there were any transgressions among dogs, they would surely be reborn in hell. Having heard the Buddha’s words, he wept with such grief and choked sobs that he could not restrain himself.
The World-Honored One said to him, "I told you previously that you should stop and not ask; now, as expected, you harbor resentment.
Pūraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is not because that person will be reborn in the realm of dogs that I weep. Rather, throughout the long night..."

"Observing the cow-vow (go-vrata), I fear it will likewise be so. I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will explain this to me truthfully. The World-Honored One replied, "As previously stated, it should be understood [that such practices lead to suffering].
All of these arise from failing to understand the True Path. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "How does one observe the cow-vow or the dog-vow?"
It is called "without deficiency or transgression. The answer is: it is like the law of the ox; it is like the law of the dog;

this is called "without deficiency or transgression. Such false conceptualizations are not the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). The Buddha-dharma is not thus; it takes the Eightfold Noble Path as its cause.

As for the "Eightfold Path": first, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); second, right action (*samyakkarmānta*); third, right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); fourth, right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); fifth, right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); sixth, right [speech]...
[The eight factors are: Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration; Right Wisdom. Clarity regarding the principle is called Right View. The movement and activity of the body is called Action (karma).

Deliberation regarding objects is called Volition (cetanā). Exerting [the mind] so that it does not remain [distracted] is termed Life-force (jīvita). The non-dispersion of the mind toward its object is termed Mindfulness (smṛti). Abiding peacefully without movement is termed Concentration (samādhi).

Penetrating observation of the object is termed Wisdom (prajñā). Now, as for "Right" (samyak): *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "今言正" (Now, as for "Right"), which indicates the beginning of an explanation of the prefix *samyak*. The subsequent definitions of the eight factors are presented here in their standard order, though the source text appears to have omitted the specific definitions for Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood, or they were intended to follow the initial definition of Right View.*
That which is characterized by a nature free from partiality and deviation is called "Correct" (*zheng*); that which penetrates principle is called the "Way" (*dao*).
There are those who formulate four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) regarding cause and effect, suffering and pleasure: first, a pleasant cause with a painful result, such as the five desires in the world;

second, a painful cause with a pleasant result, such as when a person of inferior capacity observes the precepts; third, both cause and result are pleasant, referring to a person of superior capacity... [and so forth].
Those who maintain the precepts are [the first]. Those for whom both cause and effect are suffering are these non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*):

because their practice is erroneous, they bring about the fruit of suffering and will certainly enter hell. Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who reckon that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) are the causes of the body.
To briefly describe those who reckon in terms of atoms, such as the Lokāyata non-Buddhists, who reckon all matter, mind, and so forth...

All phenomena (dharma) take the subtle atoms (paramāṇu) of the four great elements (mahābhūta) as their cause. Among these four great elements, that which is most refined and vital is capable of objective cognition;
thus, it constitutes mental phenomena (citta-dharma). This is just as, although all lamps are composed of fire, only the lamp emits light while others do not.

Therefore, there is no logical error in asserting that among the four great elements, there is that which is capable of objective cognition. If one discusses material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), the four great elements serve as...

The meaning of this is fully established. Furthermore, it is like the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists who maintain that the receptacle world is formed by eternal, dispersed atoms (*paramāṇu*) acting as its cause.
This non-Buddhist appeared at the beginning of the *vivartakalpa* (the eon of formation), at a time when the human lifespan was immeasurable years.
His name in Sanskrit is *ulūka*, which translates here as "owl. Privately, he is said to be the *chīyè* bird. This person avoids [activity] during the day.
Regarding "sound and form" (śabda-rūpa): it is said that these marvelous desires agitate the human mind; therefore, he went among people to beg for food during the night hours.
Because of this, the people of the time called him *ulūka* (an owl), and he was also named *kaṇabhuj*, which means "eater of rice-grains.
This man’s appearance was ugly and his hair was disheveled; people were terrified upon seeing him. Thereafter, he ceased begging and instead spent his nights threshing and winnowing grain.
He lived among the chaff and winnowed the rice grains; what the people of Wu called "rice-grains" (mǐqī) was this very practice.
He sustained his life by eating them, and for this reason he was known as the Immortal Who Eats Rice Grains (Shí Mǐqī Xiānrén). He was also called the Proponent of the *Vaiśeṣika*.

In Sanskrit it is called *Vaiśeṣika*, which means "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*). His old name was Vaiśeṣika. He composed the *Ṣaṭpadārtha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Six Categories); this treatise is preeminent.

Because it is distinct [from others], the treatise composed [based upon it] receives its name; thus, it is called the *Tattvārtha-śāstra* (The Treatise on Reality). (Regarding the six categories of meaning, they are as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Zishong ji* [Record of Adorning the School], in the chapter on the Four Noble Truths within the *Pravrajyā-vastu* [Chapter on Receiving Ordination]).
As for those non-Buddhists, they maintain that the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and their atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal. That which is eternally abiding...
At the time when the kalpa is destroyed, they each dwell separately. When the kalpa is about to be formed, they pair off and unite, giving birth to a "subtle offspring" (sūkṣma).
Yet the dimensions of that offspring are equal to those of its parents. From two such subtle offspring, another subtle offspring—a grandson—is born; and so on, continuing in succession.
The coarse characteristics arise; they form the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth. Once the subtle [atoms] have passed away, they are impermanent.
The explanation of the meaning of *paramāṇu* (subtle atoms) is now complete. Next, regarding "world-nature" (*jagat-prakṛti*):

in the sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes called *pradhāna* (supreme nature), sometimes *parameśvara* (the most supreme), sometimes *avyakta* (the unmanifest), sometimes *tattva* (the ultimate principle), or sometimes *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature). These are all one and the same. This refers to the Sāṃkhya outsiders.
It is the Way (*dharma*). It is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) because it is produced from the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) and also gives rise to the mental factor of wisdom;
its Sanskrit name is *Kapila*, which translates as "yellowish-red. This person was so named because both his head and face were yellowish-red.

Within the treatises he composed, he extensively analyzed the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). However, that rishi, fearing that his dharma would perish upon the destruction of his body, then departed.
He requested from Maheśvara the method for prolonging life. That deity replied: "Beneath Mount Vindhya there is the *āmalaka* fruit. When first crushed, its taste is sour and bitter;
however, after eating it and drinking water, its flavor becomes as sweet as honey. Therefore, it is called the 'Sweet Fruit' (*āmalaka*).
[The Master] Kuang asked: 'What is this *āmalaka*? [The deity said: 'If you eat this fruit, you shall attain longevity. At that time, that rishi—"
The man immediately took it and ate it, yet his mind remained undecided; he requested further essential instructions.
Īśvara said, "Transform it into a stone, and you shall be able to dwell for a long time. He then transformed it accordingly, making it as large as a single bed.
It remains beneath Mount Piṇḍa in a grove of āmalaka trees. After a thousand years had passed, the Bodhisattva Dignāga appeared there.
In the world, he extensively composed various treatises to refute their school.

When the followers of that school were unable to provide a defense, they went together to a stone and inscribed the treatises they had composed upon it. Some were explained and mastered after a single night;
others were debated repeatedly until they could only be understood after seven days. Finally, when he wrote further [treatises], they were no longer able to do so.
It was understood that the stone broke of its own accord, sweating and emitting a thunderous roar (the twenty-five principles are as described in the Chapter on the Four Truths).
These twenty-five principles are also explained in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (The Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya). Formerly, within this school of non-Buddhists...

There was a leader of a community who went to the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi. Carrying a fire-bowl upon his head and with his belly bound by iron plates, he beat the drum of the *Śabarasvāmin-śāstra* and challenged the monks to a debate on doctrine.
A monk from East India engaged in this debate with the non-Buddhist. The latter established that the world is eternal; the monk countered:
"It must certainly undergo extinction now, because the world is destroyed at the end of a kalpa. Thus it was proven that [the world] is currently...
[The opponent] refuted him, saying: "That [self] must not be extinguished.

At that time, the King sided with those non-Buddhists and caused this monk to suffer humiliation by riding a donkey (according to the laws of that country, it was considered an ultimate disgrace to travel on a donkey; one who had suffered a defeat would ride out on a donkey, and others would follow behind, breaking his vessels).
The King, who held the non-Buddhists in high esteem, bestowed seventy pieces of pure gold upon him, and because of this, he composed the *Saptati-śāstra* (The Seventy Verses).
The treatise consists of seventy verses that extensively set forth their school’s tenets, which were highlighted in gold in hopes of extolling their virtues.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu appeared in the world, he composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (Seventy Verses on Ultimate Truth) to extensively refute that school and rescue the meaning of the former Saṃgha.
At that time, the king held Vasubandhu’s treatise in high regard and further commanded the people of the land to widely disparage the [opposing] treatise. Thereupon—
Vasubandhu raised the corpse of a Sāṃkhya heretic and, as a witness to the truth, lashed its bones with a whip. Therefore, a Dharma Master said: "Vasubandhu followed the old ways;
he manifested his virtue by lashing the bones with the five-fold whip. Dignāga was the first to codify the three-part syllogism;
'roaring at the stone' and 'eating the grain' were such-and-such deeds. Furthermore, there were non-Buddhists who reckoned Īśvara to be the cause. In the West, there was...
The naked ascetics (Nirgranthas), also known as the smeared ascetics (Ājīvikas), along with various Brahmins, collectively maintain this doctrine.
According to their school’s tenets, Maheśvara has two abodes: one in the north of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat) and the other on Mount Malaya in the southern ocean.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Magadha, there were brothers who also served Maheśvara and lived together in the Snowy Mountains.
The mountain. Seeking an audience with that deity, he reached the mountain and suddenly saw a *brāhmaṇa* who said, "I serve Mahādeva;
why do you not pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha of your kingdom? His brothers replied, "We have inherited our ancestral practice and serve only the heavenly deities.
At that time, the *brāhmaṇa* transformed into the form of a deity, with three eyes on his face and four arms manifesting, or else [he appeared as]...
The Eight-Armed One addressed his brothers, saying: "You may return to your kingdom. To the east of the Bodhi tree, construct an image of Śākyamuni subduing Māra;
to the south of the Bodhi tree, dig a pond again to provide relief for those suffering from thirst. Because of this, that sect established two places of residence based on these plans.
I consider this to be without error. Furthermore, there are three bodies (*trikāya*): first, the *dharmakāya*, whose essence is eternally pervasive and whose magnitude is equal to empty space;

it is able to give rise to all things. Second, the *saṃbhogakāya*, which resides above the heavens of form (*rūpadhātu*). Third, the *nirmāṇakāya*, which assumes forms according to the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*) to teach and transform sentient beings.
Moreover, it is reckoned that the Brahmā King is able to give rise to all things, as was the case with the Bodhisattva Deva.
The *Treatise on the Refutation of the Nirvāṇa of the Heretics and the Hīnayāna* states:
"From the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower arises. Upon this lotus flower, the progenitor Brahmā is born (Brahmā is the ancestral patriarch who loves all things).
That Brahmā creates all sentient and insentient beings. From the mouth of Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇas are born; from his two arms..."

Subhadra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Previously, I contemplated that desire is impermanent, without bliss, and impure. I observed consciousness to be permanent, blissful, and pure..."

This state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is, [you claim], omniscience, tranquility, purity, eternal, and unchanging. The Buddha then refuted him, saying:

One attains *nirvāṇa*. You were previously able to censure coarse perceptions; why is it that now you are attached to subtle perceptions and do not know how to censure them?
Because such a state is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," it is like an abscess, like a wound, like poison, and like an arrow.
Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra possessed sharp faculties and great intelligence, yet he was still unable to sever such [perceptions].
They perceive the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and receive an evil body; how much more so for those in other states?

The same applies to visualizations such as yellow or red. Regarding the question: "Why do those who have not eliminated the view of self still undergo birth and death? I privately say: [This is] a question.

When the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says "one does not sever the view of self," this "self" belongs to the true self (*bhūtātman*). Therefore, these two [statements] are distinct.

The text is not contradictory. Thus, Master Rong’s commentary states: "To sever only the grasping for [external] objects, yet not sever the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), is because within birth and death one has not attained mastery;

the ancient masters said that the fact that the Vinaya does not formally establish a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *śrāmaṇera* constitutes a "superfluous precept. This is because it is not a formal establishment of a *śrāmaṇera* offense;

if their scope and framework were not shown in detail, it would be difficult for them to understand the principles and practices.

This section clarifies the specific rules for *bhikṣuṇīs*. The *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "If one were to discuss their rank in the ordination sequence, they should properly be explained before the *śrāmaṇeras*.

furthermore, since nuns do not constitute a quorum for the assembly, why would it be necessary to establish a boundary? However, the present [position] does not agree with this interpretation. Now, as for the current practice...

Regarding the "receiving the boundary" (saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharmas), there is likewise no textual authority to rely upon; it was merely established as a rule by the compilers of the *Chao* (the Vinaya-mātṛkā).
As for the statement that "the original bhikṣuṇī may remain outside the natural boundary (prakṛti-sīmā) while the two lower assemblies dwell together without hindrance," this is clearly established:

when a bhikṣuṇī comes into the midst of the bhikṣu-saṃgha to perform the boundary-binding ceremony, the position of that original bhikṣuṇī is superior to the two lower assemblies—namely, the śikṣamāṇā and the śrāmaṇerī.
Mīni: Although the two groups below [the bhikṣuṇīs] are within the boundary, they do not constitute a separate assembly (nānāsaṃvāsaka); therefore, it is said there is no obstacle.

As for the *mūlabhikṣuṇī*, if she were to go outside the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*), one might fear that—just as with a regular bhikṣuṇī sitting together [with others]—she would be ineligible to hear the *karmavācanā*.

If she were instead placed in a separate location, this would again constitute a separate assembly; furthermore, because the *mūlabhikṣuṇī* is also called a "bhikṣuṇī," [she would still be subject to the same restrictions].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the boundaries for the two assemblies are established identically for both the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses by nuns and the reception of the precepts:

this means that when nuns confess a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, they establish the boundary within the precincts of the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). At the present time of receiving the precepts, one must likewise establish the boundary according to this precedent.

Since the confession of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is a matter pertaining to the practice of following [the rules], and the present recipient of the precepts is undertaking the matter of receiving them, it is said that "receiving and following are identical."

This passage is cited as evidence to clarify that this matter must certainly involve the formal demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*). Regarding the statement that "it is not something shared by or taken away from the noble ones (*ārya*)," it is established that nuns must demarcate their boundaries.

Although there is no explicit scriptural injunction (*āgama*) for this, according to the tradition of the transmission of the Dharma in the Western Land (India) since ancient times—such as the examples of Buddhajīva, Dharmakṣema, and Paramārtha—all of whom were noble ones—it is understood that they did not say boundaries need not be demarcated; rather, they all required them and ultimately never failed to do so.
The principle of "seizing" (*āharaṇa*) its fetters is not clearly explained as being for the purpose of making the fetters unlawful; therefore, it is said that they are not shared and are not seized.

Regarding the statement in the two chapters that "concealing a single dharma is entirely non-existent," this means that even if a nun commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and performs penance, she may still conceal it.
Even if concealed for a hundred days or a thousand nights, it is not concealed [in the sense of requiring a formal penance];

the *pārivāsika* (separate dwelling) rule applies only for half a month, and one performs the *mānatva* within the two assemblies (*saṃgha*). Regarding why there is no *pārivāsika* rule [for nuns], Yeli says: "Because a nun may not be alone;

if she were granted a separate dwelling, it would constitute a transgression. Regarding the change from the six-night limit to the half-month limit for the *saṃgha*, Yeli says: "This was for the sake of women."
This is because it is difficult for those with weak faculties to accomplish the practice.

Regarding a bhikṣuṇī entering a monastery for monks, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 39, states: "She should stay beneath the gatehouse and dispatch a female lay attendant (*kappiya-kārī*)."
He addressed them, saying: "I pay homage, O Bhikṣuṇīs. I announce my entry; please grant me leave. This is because a Bhikṣu must deliberate whether he may enter or not.
